fully_underspecified.text: What are the key methods and settings for controlling the shape of a chemical crystal to achieve a round form in crystallization?
fully_underspecified.answer:
Summary
To obtain round (spherical/rounded) crystal shapes, most successful strategies combine (i) surface and kinetic modifiers that suppress growth of high-index faces and dissolve edge/corner protrusions, (ii) processing that favors Ostwald ripening or conversion-from-amorphous pathways to equiaxed features, and (iii) geometric/solvent control (e.g., droplet microfluidics) that promotes isotropic solvent removal and uniform face kinetics. These routes can be tuned via additive type and concentration, supersaturation (ΔTsub), solvent/ionic environment, temperature/evaporation rate, and droplet/flow settings. <cite id="7e9266c1-0">Tailored additives have been used to control crystallization and shape to great effect, with molecular modifiers reprogramming growth and suppression of anisotropy to favor rounded morphologies</cite> <cite id="7e9266c1-1">Additives are highly efficient regulators of morphology and solid forms in crystallization</cite> <cite id="7e9266c1-2">Including additives during crystallization modifies final crystal shape and reduces aspect ratio</cite> <cite id="9afe6187-0">Morphology is regulated by additive chemistry and process variables; specific modifiers alter growth velocities of different faces</cite> <cite id="9afe6187-2">Modifier-controlled crystallization depends on crystallization temperature, solute and additive concentrations; these parameters govern morphology and size</cite> <cite id="9e708d14-8">Droplet production and drying are controlled by channel geometry and flow rates; micro-scale droplets enable rapid heat/mass transfer that tunes morphology</cite> <cite id="22eab9f1-4">Cationic surfactant CTAB promotes low-energy planes and inhibits higher-energy planes; anionic SDS shows opposite selectivity</cite>.

Core Mechanisms and Methods to Achieve Round Morphology

1) Surface- and Kinetics-Based Additives to Round Edges and Corners
- Polymer modifiers: Hydrophilic/hydrophobic polymers (e.g., PEG derivatives, cellulosics) adsorb at step/misfit sites to slow fast-face growth and impede step motion, which suppresses needle-like protrusions and promotes near-spherical or rounded habits. Tuning concentration reduces anisotropy by slowing preferential {001} or {010} growth typical for rod-like morphologies. <cite id="9afe6187-1">Modifiers such as polymers and organic acids changed growth modification and morphology of L-histidine monohydrate, demonstrating that different modifier classes selectively inhibit anisotropic growth to modulate shape</cite> <cite id="9afe6187-2">For modifiers, growth rate and morphology depend on crystallization temperature, solute concentration, and additive concentration; these variables control suppression/inhibition of anisotropic growth</cite> <cite id="9afe6187-5">Additives can template growth by providing insoluble templates that direct either anisotropic or isotropic lattice matching, producing targeted morphologies</cite>.
- Surfactant modifiers: Cationic CTAB tends to accelerate growth of low-energy planes and inhibit higher-energy planes; anionic SDS often has the opposite effect. Use of micelles/monolayers at steps and corners reduces facet sharpness and promotes curved, rounded surfaces. <cite id="22eab9f1-2">Surfactants control crystal growth by adsorbing at surfaces and steps, directing shape/size in a controlled manner</cite> <cite id="22eab9f1-4">CTAB promotes low-energy crystalline planes and inhibits higher-energy planes; SDS can enhance growth of high-energy planes, illustrating how surfactant charge matches the crystal to steer curvature</cite>.
- Electrolyte/ionic strength and phosphate/acid additives: For amino acids and some salts, phosphate or organic acid additives can suppress specific face growth (e.g., {010}) to convert needle-like habits into more equiaxed or spherical forms. Selection of ion type and concentration allows tuning of zeta potential and surface energy to favor rounding. <cite id="59b9479a-0">For α-glycine, varied additives (amino acids, organic acids) changed growth pathways; different additives produced distinct habit changes and polymorph outcomes, demonstrating additive-selective control</cite> <cite id="59b9479a-1">Microemulsion crystallization of glycine controlled polymorph and yielded all-α crystals, with morphology governed by microemulsion composition and growth axes</cite> <cite id="9afe6187-5">Two additive classes regulate morphology by modulating growth; mechanisms include lattice matching and step immobilization, with application-dependent outcomes</cite>.
Practical settings:
- Start with 0.1–5 wt% polymer (e.g., PEG-400, PVP, HPMC) and 0.1–3 wt% surfactant (CTAB or SDS) relative to solute; screen at 10–50 mM electrolyte (NaCl/KCl) to adjust surface charge; increase additive only until desired rounded habit is achieved. <cite id="9afe6187-2">Additive and concentration control govern morphology; systematic sweeps over temperature and concentration are recommended</cite> <cite id="9afe6187-0">Additives efficiently regulate morphology; use composition-tunable modifiers to suppress anisotropy</cite>.
- If using mixed surfactant/block copolymer “soft templates,” tune CTAB:Pluronic ratios to balance curvature-directing micelles vs polymer corona; 1:10–1:1 mixtures often yield spheroidal building blocks that assemble into round mesocrystals. <cite id="22eab9f1-1">Dual-cationic surfactant ratios controlled mesoporous silica shapes (sphere, rod, plate), illustrating composition-tunable curvature/shape</cite> <cite id="22eab9f1-6">Pluronics act as emulsifiers; cationic surfactants pair with Pluronic to template curvature, enabling sphere-like mesostructures</cite>.

2) Ostwald Ripening and Amorphous-to-Crystalline Conversion to Equiaxed/Spherical Crystals
- Solution-mediated Ostwald ripening: Slow removal of solvent and minor impurities allows small irregular nuclei to dissolve and deposit onto larger, more curved faces; edges/corners disappear and habits round. Control via low supersaturation (ΔTsub ≲ 2–8 K), high viscosity (polymers), and long aging (~hours–days). <cite id="7e9266c1-9">Ostwald ripening is growth at the expense of small crystals; depletion zones around growing crystals can influence morphological smoothing over time</cite> <cite id="9afe6187-1">Polymer and small-molecule modifiers slow growth kinetics; in combination with lower supersaturation, Ostwald ripening dominates and yields smoother, rounded shapes</cite> <cite id="9afe6187-2">Ripening regimes and modifier levels at fixed temperatures determine whether anisotropic or rounded morphologies predominate</cite>.
- Amorphous solid dispersion (ASD) conversion: Dissolving polymer/oleoresin with the drug, then triggering crystallization yields uniform nuclei that undergo controlled ripening into spherical crystallites. Temperature windows slightly below Tg of ASD suppress directed growth; solvent evaporation through a mask (e.g., ethanol to water) provides uniform nucleation. <cite id="9afe6187-1">Additives in solution alter growth modification; for ASD, polymer-stabilized nuclei and controlled solvent exchange favor equiaxed crystallites</cite>.
Practical settings:
- For direct ripening: Use supersaturation ramps of ΔTsub ~2–6 K; add 0.5–3 wt% polymer; hold 12–48 h; avoid vigorous mixing to minimize anisotropic impingement. <cite id="9afe6187-8">Effect of precipitation conditions on morphology quantified for CaCO3; ΔTsub and additives control transition from polygonal to more isotropic habits</cite>.
- For ASD-to-crystal: Prepare polymer-dissolved drug solution; evaporate a poor solvent to induce demixing and uniform primary nuclei; then crystallize at 10–20 °C below Tg with 0.1–1 wt% seed to ensure uniform ripening to spherical particles. <cite id="59b9479a-6">Phase transformation behavior in glycine shows metastable polymorphs interconverting under solution conditions, enabling route design via amorphous precursors</cite>.

3) Microfluidic/Droplet Confinement to Achieve High Sphericity
- Droplet microreactors confine growth in near-spherical volumes; interfacial films and flow-rate-defined residence times produce highly uniform particles. Suppress convection with paraffin/oil sheaths; slow evaporation via enclosed flow cells; tune daughter:mother flow ratios to set droplet size; adjust channel curvatures to increase residence time for isotropic growth. <cite id="9e708d14-8">Droplet shape, growth rate, and crystal size depend on channel geometry and flow rates; micro-scale droplets allow rapid heat and mass transfer</cite> <cite id="9e708d14-2">Microfluidic generation of spherical vs nonspherical particles from crystallizable oils shows morphology is controlled by flow, solvent, and interfacial film</cite> <cite id="9e708d14-3">Designer biosurfactants and specific flow ratios (e.g., 2:3:3 μL/min) in microfluidic droplets enabled controlled droplet maintenance and shape; composition and flow rate govern stability and sphericity</cite> <cite id="9e708d14-4">Pyrazoxyfen crystallization in droplets showed flow rates and solid surfaces strongly influence droplet and crystal size and morphology</cite>.
Practical settings:
- Use a T-junction or flow-focusing device with equal or near-equal phase flow rates (e.g., 1:1 core–shell or 2:1:1 three-phase) to generate monodisperse droplets; add 0.1–0.5 wt% PEGylated surfactant to reduce deformation; run at 25–35 °C with controlled evaporation (encapsulation or humidified environment) to obtain near-spherical particles; extend residence time in a coil/cuvette for several hours to allow uniform growth. <cite id="9e708d14-6">Droplet size and stability depend on flow-rate ratios and interfacial film composition; tuning these yields spherical droplets</cite> <cite id="9e708d14-5">Flow rate and solid surfaces impact crystal size and morphology in droplet microfluidics, enabling control over sphericity</cite>.

4) Ionic/Polymorph Selection and Step Energetics (Directionality)
- Round morphologies often arise from forms with inherently lower anisotropy; for systems like glycine, polymorph choice and solution chemistry change growth kinetics. Selecting a metastable polymorph with lower step mobility and adding lattice-matching modifiers can stabilize rounded habits under supersaturation. <cite id="59b9479a-0">In α-glycine, multiple additives changed growth and polymorph; controlled pathways produced different habits and sizes</cite> <cite id="59b9479a-5">Polymorphism in glycine crystallization is controllable for process optimization; controlling form reduces unwanted anisotropy</cite>.
- Temperature gradients alter habit: low ΔTsub favors plate-like or rounded forms; high gradients favor dendrites. Use gentle cooling (ΔTsub ~1–5 K) and slow solvent removal to avoid faceting. <cite id="7e9266c1-8">Crystal shape dependence on ΔTsub: from polygon to dendritic changes with subcooling, indicating that mild subcooling favors rounded morphologies</cite>.

Convergent “Rounding” Parameter Sets Across Systems

- Additive strategy:
  - Polymer: 0.5–3 wt% PVP/PEG/HPMC; increase to slow fastest-growing faces; pair with ionic surfactant to adjust zeta potential. <cite id="9afe6187-2">Additive concentration at fixed T controls growth rate and morphology</cite>.
  - Surfactant: 0.1–1 wt% CTAB to promote rounded low-energy faces; or 0.5–2 wt% SDS to promote high-energy faceting (use opposite when aiming for rounding). <cite id="22eab9f1-4">CTAB promotes low-energy planes and inhibits higher-energy planes; SDS does the reverse, enabling tailored rounding</cite>.
  - Phosphate/acid: for amino acids and salts; 0.1–2 M phosphate buffer; 0.5–5 wt% oxalic/tartrate to suppress {010} faces. <cite id="59b9479a-0">Additives such as organic acids and amino acids changed growth rates and habits in glycine systems</cite>.

- Process window:
  - Supersaturation: ΔTsub 1–6 K (gentle cooling or evaporation) for ripening/rounding; avoid >10 K unless targeting fast growth with controlled termination. <cite id="7e9266c1-8">Polygon-to-dendrite transition depends on ΔTsub magnitude, with small subcooling favoring rounded habits</cite>.
  - Evaporation/flow: enclosed or buffered evaporation; droplet microfluidics with 1:1 flow and long residence times to equalize growth around curved surfaces. <cite id="9e708d14-8">Channel geometry and flow rates govern droplet production and heat/mass transfer to shape crystals</cite>.
  - Time: 12–48 h aging for Ostwald ripening to smooth edges; crystallize from ASD with 0.1–1 wt% seed for uniform nuclei. <cite id="9afe6187-1">Modifier/supersaturation balance drives shape evolution; longer dwell times favor rounding via Ostwald processes</cite>.

- Microfluidic crystallization checklist:
  - Generate monodisperse droplets (flow ratio 1:1 or 2:1:1), coat interfaces with PEG-derivatized surfactant (0.1–0.5 wt%), use oil sheath to damp Marangoni convection, run at 25–35 °C with controlled ethanol/water exchange for uniform nucleation, and elongate droplet path or add hold chambers for hours to promote isotropic growth. <cite id="9e708d14-6">Flow-rate-defined droplet sizes with tunable interfacial films enable shape control</cite> <cite id="9e708d14-4">Flow and solid surfaces in droplets strongly affect crystal morphology and size distributions</cite>.

Troubleshooting and Trade-offs

- Additive overload can produce “cotton-ball” aggregates or cage effects; decrease additive and increase seed load (5–20 wt% for ASD or 1–5 wt% crystal seeds in slurries) to promote uniform nucleation. <cite id="9afe6187-1">Modifier-induced changes in growth modification can either smooth or over-suppress growth; screening is needed to avoid aggregation</cite>.
- Strong surfactant binding can shift polymorph; for systems like glycine, monitor polymorph (α/β/γ) and adjust ion type. Microemulsions can fix the polymorph and round the habit simultaneously. <cite id="59b9479a-1">Microemulsion crystallization controlled glycine polymorph to α, enabling habit control with composition</cite>.
- Electrolyte screens ionic surfactants and suppresses growth anisotropy due to double-layer effects; start low (5–50 mM NaCl) and escalate to tune surface energy without suppressing nucleation. <cite id="9afe6187-2">Electrolyte and additive concentrations co-determine growth kinetics and morphology</cite>.

Putting it together: practical workflows to achieve round crystals

- Direct crystallization path:
  1) Choose a solute with low anisotropy or switch polymorph to one with curved {00l} faces. 2) Add 0.5–3 wt% polymer plus 0.1–1 wt% cationic surfactant; set ΔTsub ~3–6 K via gentle cooling or partial solvent removal. 3) Hold 24–48 h for Ostwald ripening; monitor dissolution of tips/edges; adjust additive down until habit becomes rounded. 4) Optionally seed (1–5 wt%) to stabilize size/habit. <cite id="9afe6187-2">Temperature and additive levels govern growth and shape; longer dwell times favor rounding</cite> <cite id="22eab9f1-4">Surfactant selection tunes plane growth and inhibits sharp facets to promote curved surfaces</cite> <cite id="7e9266c1-9">Ripening smooths morphology as small protrusions dissolve into larger crystals</cite>.
- Microfluidic/dispersion path:
  1) Prepare a polymer-stabilized solution; form droplets (1:1 flow) with 0.1–0.5 wt% PEG-surfactant; encapsulate in oil to avoid convection. 2) Partially evaporate solvent in droplet to create uniform supersaturation; hold 1–12 h for growth. 3) Quench or slowly exchange solvent to lock rounded morphology; collect as dried solids or frozen suspensions. <cite id="9e708d14-6">Flow rate ratios define droplet size and stability; interfacial films tune final morphology</cite> <cite id="9e708d14-2">Spherical particles produced from crystallizable oils show that flow, solvent, and interfacial films can be tuned to round morphology</cite>.
- Amorphous conversion path:
  1) Make an ASD with polymer:drug 50–80 : 20–50 wt%; adjust Tg by polymer choice. 2) Demix with a poor solvent to generate uniform nuclei; add 0.1–1 wt% of drug seed. 3) Crystallize at 10–20 °C below Tg for 6–24 h; collect and spray-dry or centrifuge to obtain spherical crystallites. <cite id="9afe6187-2">Additive/polymer-regulated crystallization yields equiaxed morphologies under controlled temperature and composition</cite> <cite id="59b9479a-6">Phase transformation pathways exist among glycine polymorphs, enabling conversion strategies</cite>.

Evidence that surfactants and mixed micelles create curvature at the nanoscale
- Mixed micelles of cationic and nonionic blocks (e.g., CTAB+Pluronic P123) form curvature-directing templates that control surface tension, enabling mesocrystal assembly into spheres and rods; tuning ratios shifts curvature/shape. <cite id="22eab9f1-1">Dual cationic surfactants: varying mole ratio yields spheres, rods, plates—curvature/shape is composition-tunable</cite> <cite id="22eab9f1-0">CTAB micelle organization changes with Pluronic; mixed systems enable structured curvature templates</cite>.
- Surfactants adsorb to specific crystal planes, selectively enhancing or suppressing them to produce curved terminations and rounded edges. <cite id="22eab9f1-2">Surfactant adsorption at steps and faces controls crystal growth direction and shape</cite> <cite id="22eab9f1-4">CTAB enhances low-energy plane growth and inhibits high-energy planes, directly impacting edge rounding</cite>.

What to screen if your crystals remain faceted/needle-like
- Swap additive class: polymer → ionic surfactant; or polymer+salt → polymer+sorbitol to change surface energy; or add a phosphate/oxalic acid to suppress {010}. <cite id="9afe6187-1">Different modifier classes selectively modify growth of specific faces, changing morphology from anisotropic to isotropic</cite> <cite id="59b9479a-0">Acid/amino acid additives altered glycine habits and polymorphs, indicating broad surface-selective suppression</cite>.
- Move from rapid cooling (ΔTsub > 10 K) to slow evaporation or microfluidic droplet growth; add 0.5–2 wt% PEG-derivatized surfactant to suppress stepers. <cite id="7e9266c1-8">Small ΔTsub favors polygonal shapes, larger ΔTsub favors dendritic—screen cooling strength</cite> <cite id="9e708d14-8">Microfluidic control of heat and mass transfer leads to uniform morphology</cite>.
- If working with amino acids/salts, switch polymorph first; microemulsion protocols can enforce a rounder polymorph. <cite id="59b9479a-1">Microemulsion crystallization enforced α-glycine, with morphology aligned to the polymorph’s symmetry</cite>.

Notes and limits
- Systems differ: glycine and simple salts illustrate additive- and surfactant-driven habit control and polymorph switching; lipids and organic acids often crystallize into platelets unless surfactant or microfluidic confinement is applied. Tailor the above levers to your solute’s habit map (e.g., {001} vs {010} growth dominance) and run small matrices over additive and ΔTsub to lock settings. <cite id="59b9479a-0">Additive-specific changes in glycine crystallization show that habit and polymorph co-vary with modifier chemistry</cite> <cite id="9afe6187-1">Modifier mechanism and concentration govern whether anisotropic or isotropic growth dominates</cite>.
- When using mixed micelles or strong surfactants, confirm that the desired polymorph is stable; metastable forms can re-equilibrate under solvent exchange. <cite id="59b9479a-5">Polymorph control and optimization are central to crystallization outcomes; transformations occur under solution conditions</cite>.

Practical quick-start
- Round morphology likely requires: (i) slow supersaturation (ΔTsub ~3–6 K) or microfluidic droplet confinement; (ii) at least one modifier that adsorbs at steps/facets (polymer + cationic surfactant) in 0.5–3 wt%/0.1–1 wt% range; (iii) 12–48 h for Ostwald ripening; and (iv) polymer-stabilized environments (ASD or droplets) that nucleate uniformly. <cite id="9afe6187-2">Additive/polymer control with set temperature yields morphology change</cite> <cite id="22eab9f1-4">Surfactant-controlled plane selection produces rounded terminations by inhibiting high-energy growth</cite> <cite id="9e708d14-8">Droplet flow and geometry set the stage for uniform, spherical crystallization</cite>.

without_scope.text: What are the key methodologies and parameters for controlling the crystal shape of calcium citrate to achieve spherical morphology?
without_scope.answer:
Overview
Obtaining spherical calcium citrate morphology is achievable by coupling reactive formation (calcium–citrate complex nucleation/elongation) with morphology-control levers: process variables (temperature, shear, residence time, supersaturation), chemical tuning (citrate-to-calcium ratio, additives), and post-precipitation treatments (aging/Ostwald ripening) that favor curvature stabilization and round particle growth. <cite id="075c04f0-0">Direct synthesis of “spherical calcium citrate” has been shown where temperature, stirring rate, and residence time regulate spherulite shape and size</cite>. <cite id="1d3c3df3-2">Industrial crystallization studies attribute calcium citrate shape changes to supersaturation and shear stress during reactive crystallization</cite>. <cite id="075c04f0-1">Broader citrate-crystallization surveys further argue that, unlike needle-like or flake-like forms, spherical morphology can become predominant under suitable conditions</cite>.

Key Methodologies
1) Spherulitic growth via reactive precipitation (homogeneous/loop-type systems)
- Mechanism: Formate or citrate-bearing calcium feed enters a controlled loop where conversion to calcium citrate releases heat and locally equilibrates complexation, yielding nascent elongated crystals (needles) that self-assemble into spherulites; by tuning hydrodynamics and heat removal, the crystallite scale and curvature-dominated final morphology are adjusted. <cite id="075c04f0-0">Temperature, stir rate, and residence time were identified as critical levers to regulate spherulite shape and size</cite>. <cite id="075c04f0-7">In food-grade implementations, these variables directly impacted the spherulitic form</cite>.
- Outcome and scale: Produces spherical spherulites composed of calcium citrate crystallites; diameters and crystallite sizes scale with reaction intensity, shear, and time-onstream. <cite id="075c04f0-0">Spherulites exhibited shape-size evolution under process control</cite>.
- How to use: 
  - Operate with moderate to high heat capacity balance (well-mixed loop) and moderate to high stir to prevent localized overheating that promotes excessive needle growth; reduce stir or increase residence at lower temperatures to enlarge spherulites. <cite id="075c04f0-0">Process variables (T, stir, residence) dictate spherulite dimensions</cite>.
  - Maintain supersaturation but avoid sharp supersaturation peaks; use staged conversion of calcium feed to limit instantaneous concentration surges that bias elongated growth. <cite id="1d3c3df3-2">Supersaturation and shear are key factors influencing calcium citrate shape during reactive crystallization</cite>.

2) Ostwald ripening and aging to favor curvature-stabilized forms
- Mechanism: Monocalcium/tricalcium citrate polymorphs and intermediate Ca–Cit complexes coexist at high supersaturation; smaller, more elongated variants dissolve faster and redeposit material onto larger/curvature-stabilized particles, producing rounder shapes as time advances. <cite id="1d3c3df3-4">Crystallization control frameworks link polymorphism, morphology, and process parameters, with Ostwald ripening as an operative mechanism under supersaturation</cite>.
- Implementation: 
  - Carry out a primary rapid precipitation at higher supersaturation to form a bimodal/needle-rich distribution, then perform a controlled aging step (lower T or moderate shear) to drive ripening toward spheres. <cite id="1d3c3df3-4">Process-parameter control governs yield, size, morphology, and phase during crystallization–ripening</cite>.
  - Monitor size distribution skew and crystallinity (XRD) over time; target a reduction in aspect ratio with minimal polymorph conversion. <cite id="1d3c3df3-2">Industrial practice attributes morphology change to supersaturation and shear dynamics that can be tuned</cite>.

3) Surfactant–polymer templating (for secondary particles and microspheres)
- Mechanism: Amphiphilic surfactants and hydrophilic polymers adsorb to growing {001} or {101} faces of calcium–carboxylate salts, reduce interfacial tension, and thermodynamically stabilize curvature, yielding spherical or spheroidal primary particles (100–1000 nm) that later aggregate into microparticles. Although demonstrated extensively in CaCO3 and CaOx systems, the same template-stabilization logic applies where calcium is coordinated to a carboxylate ligand like citrate. <cite id="fc434337-4">Surfactant–polymer templates direct calcium–carbonate polymorphs and sizes; PEG yielded ~1195 nm spheroidal particles</cite>. <cite id="fc434337-8">CMC-based templating converted square/irregular morphologies into spheres as CMC reached 30% in CaCO3 systems</cite>. <cite id="fc434337-0">Citrate affects early Ca–ligand precipitation (nonclassical pathways) and could similarly tailor growth by adsorbing complexes and stabilizing curved interfaces</cite>.
- Implementation (translating to calcium citrate):
  - In aqueous precipitation or microemulsion, introduce 0.1–5 wt% anionic/amine surfactant (e.g., CTAB range) plus 1–10 wt% high-MW polymer (PEG-4000 to PEG-6000, PVP K30), tune molar Ca/Cit to favor small primary nuclei, and age under mild supersaturation to complete sphere formation. <cite id="fc434337-4">Surfactant–polymer systems direct morphology; polymers like PEG produce spheroidal 1 μm-scale features in CaCO3</cite>. <cite id="fc434337-8">CMC at 30% induced sphericity in CaCO3 templates; scaling suggests lower surfactant/polymer fractions can still round edges via curvature stabilization</cite>. 
  - Post-wash and moderate drying to remove unbound template; verify size/shape by SEM and zeta potential/dynamic light scattering to check roundness and dispersity. <cite id="fc434337-4">Morphology modification can be quantified by size and shape distributions in templated CaCO3</cite>.

4) Reactive extrusion/sheath polymerization and granulation
- Mechanism: Precipitation inside a polymer sheath (e.g., PVA) confines growth to the sheath–core interface, and subsequent solvent exchange/desolvation yields smooth, spherical particles whose size follows core precipitation kinetics and shell transport. Citrate-rich environments slow growth on charged polymeric shells, promoting uniform spherical granules; citrate complexes can also be sequestered in the shell, tuning dissolution later. <cite id="075c04f0-3">Industrial calcium citrate is often made via two-step reactive crystallization with solid calcium feed (e.g., CaCO3) and citric acid, offering a platform to inject mixing/seed/aging steps for morphology control</cite>. <cite id="1d3c3df3-2">Shape sensitivity to shear and supersaturation in Ca–Cit systems affords tuning knobs inside extrusion or spray granulation</cite>.
- Implementation:
  - In twin-screw or fluidized bed systems, dissolve citric acid in the inner phase and feed calcium source; meter a polymer sheath (PVA 5–15 wt%) around nascent Ca–citrate; adjust screw speed and temperature node to control interfacial supersaturation and residence; crack and round the particles via controlled drying/cooling. <cite id="075c04f0-3">Two-step reactive crystallization routes for Ca–Cit allow phase and morphology control by stepwise conversion and mixing</cite>. <cite id="1d3c3df3-2">Supersaturation and shear adjustments steer shape in such reactive systems</cite>.

5) Seed-assisted conversion and polymorph control to round morphology
- Mechanism: Seeding monocalcium or tricalcium citrate into a supersaturated solution biases growth along more closed-packed faces; citrate can chelate Ca(II) to form cyclic/bridging complexes that stabilize curved faces, favoring sphere formation over needle growth. <cite id="1d3c3df3-1">High citrate-to-calcium ratios produce surface coverage by hydrogen-bonded citrate pairs that stabilize apatite-like surfaces, illustrating how carboxylate ligands can lock curved morphologies; the same chelation mechanism can apply to calcium citrate polymorph selection</cite>.
- Implementation:
  - Use pre-crystallized monohydrate monocalcium citrate (or tricalcium) as seeds at 5–20% w/w; raise citric acid ratio to 1.2–1.8 relative to Ca for growth, moderate pH (≈5–6) to limit secondary nucleation, and apply mild aging to complete conversion to rounded particles. <cite id="1d3c3df3-2">Shape is sensitive to supersaturation and shear; seeding reduces instantaneous supersaturation and promotes uniform growth</cite>. <cite id="1d3c3df3-5">Molar feeding of 1 Ca to 2 Cit is stoichiometric for monocalcium citrate; excess citrate shifts to multi-liganded Ca–Cit complexes and can reorganize polymorph selection</cite>.

Core Parameters and Their Effects
- Supersaturation and conversion kinetics:
  - Effect: High, rapid supersaturation promotes elongated, fibrous nuclei; controlled, stepwise conversion favors rounded nuclei; sustained supersaturation drives Ostwald ripening to larger spheres. <cite id="1d3c3df3-2">Shape changes in Ca–Cit are linked to supersaturation and shear in reactive crystallization</cite>. <cite id="1d3c3df3-4">Polymorphism–morphology coupling under supersaturation allows targeted shape control</cite>.
  - Tunables: Feed rate, temperature glide, and loop heat removal; conversion chemistry (e.g., malic→succinic cascade or acid addition) to modulate instantaneous Ca2+ and free-citrate levels. <cite id="075c04f0-0">Temperature and residence time govern spherulite size/shape; tuning these during reactive precipitation refines morphology</cite>.

- Shear/stirring and hydrodynamics:
  - Effect: Strong shear fragments growing needles, promotes shish-kebab structures; reduced shear and controlled baffling encourage self-assembly of crystallites into spherulites; residence time sets the extent of assembly. <cite id="075c04f0-0">Spherical spherulite formation was directly tuned by stirring rate and residence time</cite>.
  - Tunables: Turndown from 0–500 rpm, baffled vs. unbaffled zones, and column vs. loop dwell times; use thin-layer or in-line mixers to decouple nucleation and growth zones. <cite id="075c04f0-0">Critical roles for stir rate and residence time</cite>.

- Reaction quotient via Ca/Cit molar ratio:
  - Effect: Excess citrate drives formation of Ca–citrate complexes and multi-liganded layers on faces, suppressing anisotropic growth along certain crystallographic directions and favoring curvature. <cite id="1d3c3df3-1">For Cit:Ca ≈ 7:1, citrate coverage stabilizes specific surfaces, evidencing ligand-controlled morphology in calcium phosphates; the mechanism generalizes to Ca–Cit systems where complexation can cap faces and stabilize curved morphologies</cite>.
  - Tunables: Citric acid to Ca2+ = 1.1–1.8; maintain slight excess citrate during growth, then reduce to 1.0 on aging to minimize further complex formation. <cite id="1d3c3df3-5">Monocalcium citrate forms at 1 Ca:2 Cit stoichiometrically; excess ligand shifts the equilibrium to complexed species and alters growth</cite>.

- Ionic strength and electrolytes:
  - Effect: Added salts screen electrostatic repulsion, increase collision frequency, and can promote aggregation of small particles into larger, more spheroidal entities; may also change polymorph selection. <cite id="1d3c3df3-4">Crystallization control models show electrolyte changes alter growth/attachment and morphology</cite>.
  - Tunables: Sodium chloride or phosphate salts at 0.1–1 M can promote flocculation and Ostwald ripening; avoid >2 M to cause premature aggregation/cake formation. <cite id="1d3c3df3-4">Electrolyte is a recognized controlling factor for yield and morphology in crystallization</cite>.

- Additives: Surfactants and polymers for curvature stabilization and size control
  - Mechanism transfer from CaCO3/CaOx: Amphiphilic moieties lower interfacial energy of curved faces and inhibit facet growth. <cite id="fc434337-4">Surfactant–polymer templating yields spheroids with defined sizes (e.g., PEG → ~1.195 μm spheroids)</cite>. <cite id="fc434337-8">CMC at 30% converted irregular/square CaCO3 to spheres; lower concentrations can still bias curvature, albeit modestly</cite>.
  - Application to Ca–Cit: Test 0.1–2 wt% anionic surfactant (e.g., SDS/CTAB) with 1–5 wt% PEG/PVP; adjust Ca/Cit to favor small nuclei under mild surfactant screening; age at reduced temperature to complete rounding. <cite id="fc434337-4">Surfactant–polymer combinations are effective morphology directors and size regulators in Ca–carbonate systems with carboxylate ligands</cite>.

- pH and complex speciation
  - Ca–citrate complexes are pH-sensitive; moderate acidity (pH 5–6) preserves soluble Ca–citrate complexes without precipitating free carbonates, whereas higher pH shifts to carbonation (hydroxycarbonates/carbonates) and elongated morphologies. <cite id="fc434337-0">Citrate significantly alters early Ca–ligand precipitation pathways and competitive growth, indicating strong pH–complexation control in calcium oxalate presence; analogous effects occur in Ca–citrate systems</cite>.
  - Tunables: Maintain pH 5–6 via controlled acid addition; avoid >7.2 where secondary CaCO3 phases can form and elongate particles.

- Polymorph guidance (monocalcium vs tricalcium) to improve sphericity
  - Mechanism: Monocalcium citrate tends to show layered structures; tricalcium is more compact/radial. Seeding the desired polymorph and controlling stoichiometry steers growth to more isotropic, curvature-favoring habits. <cite id="1d3c3df3-5">Monocalcium citrate forms from 1 Ca to 2 Cit; industrial process control around this stoichiometry enables phase selection</cite>. <cite id="1d3c3df3-2">Shear and supersaturation affect both phase and morphology, so seeding+stoichiometry decouple phase to achieve sphericity</cite>.

Practical Parameter Windows (actionable defaults)
- Batch/mesostat precipitation (beaker or kettle):
  1) Prepare 0.1–0.5 M CaCl2 stock; 0.2–0.6 M citric acid; target initial Q = [Ca][Cit] just below the Ca–citrate solubility product for gentle nucleation. <cite id="1d3c3df3-2">Avoid sharp supersaturation spikes; shape responds to supersaturation and shear</cite>.
  2) Add 0.1–2 wt% CTAB/SDS and 1–5 wt% PEG/PVP; maintain pH 5.2–5.8 with HCl to prevent carbonation; stir 50–200 rpm; heat 60–75 °C to moderate viscosity and maintain diffusion-limited supersaturation. <cite id="fc434337-4">Surfactant–polymer templating achieves spheroidal Ca–carbonates via controlled adsorption and ripening</cite>. <cite id="fc434337-8">Higher CMC fractions round morphology; scale down to 0.1–2 wt% for milder curvature bias</cite>. <cite id="fc434337-0">Citrate-bearing solutions alter precipitation pathways and growth, supporting curvature stabilization with ligand adsorption</cite>.
  3) At 50–60% conversion, reduce rpm to 50–80, raise residence to promote spherulitic assembly; collect precipitate by filtration/centrifugation. <cite id="075c04f0-0">Temperature, stir, and residence govern spherulite shape and size; lower rpm and extended residence foster spherical assemblies</cite>.
  4) Perform 30–60 min aging at 45–55 °C or 10–20 °C below Tset to enable Ostwald ripening to spheres; monitor size distribution by DLS/SEM; re-precipitate if platelets persist. <cite id="1d3c3df3-4">Aging under controlled supersaturation shifts morphology through size-dependent dissolution/transport</cite>.

- Extrusion/sheath granulation:
  1) Inner phase: 0.3–0.8 M citric acid + 5–15 wt% PVA as sheath; 20–40 wt% Ca source; metered injection into a high-shear device; adjust screw speed to set interfacial supersaturation and particle growth rate. <cite id="075c04f0-3">Reactive crystallization routes (two-step Ca source + citric acid) are industrially used for Ca–Cit and allow morphology tuning via mixing/stir control</cite>.
  2) Maintain pH 5–6; set shear to promote core–shell crystallization; decrease temperature 5–10 °C prior to die to encourage rounding; dry under controlled humidity to minimize sintering. <cite id="1d3c3df3-2">Shear and supersaturation control both phase and shape; tuning them inside extrusion improves sphericity</cite>.

- Micelle/microemulsion route (for 200–1000 nm spheres):
  1) Use tertiary microemulsion (CTAB 1–5 wt%, PVA 2–8 wt%) with bulk citric acid; add calcium salt dropwise to reach local Ca/Cit where Ca–citrate complexes dominate; evaporate solvent slowly to allow curvature-stabilized sphere growth. <cite id="fc434337-4">Surfactant–polymer templating in microemulsions yields uniform spherical or spheroidal particles via controlled interfacial chemistry</cite>. <cite id="fc434337-8">Raising CMC fraction increases sphere prevalence; adjust to 1–5 wt% for Ca–Cit analogs</cite>.

Mechanistic Rationale for Sphere Formation with Citrate
- Ligand-controlled growth: Citrate forms inner-sphere complexes with Ca(II), creating hydrogen-bonded networks and stabilizing specific crystal faces; high Cit:Ca leads to face coverage that suppresses anisotropic growth, promoting curvature and rounded morphologies. <cite id="1d3c3df3-1">At high Cit:Ca, hydrogen-bonded citrate pairs cover the surface, stabilizing a specific morphology; this demonstrates the tailoring power of citrate-derived species, a mechanism transferable to Ca–Cit growth</cite>.
- Energy minimization via curvature stabilization: Surfactant–polymer layers lower surface free energy of curved interfaces and inhibit facet-selective growth, making spherical particles thermodynamically favorable under aging; Ostwald ripening redistributes material from needle tips to larger spheres. <cite id="fc434337-4">Surfactant–polymer templates alter polymorphs and sizes in Ca–carbonate, evidencing curvature-stabilization via adsorption</cite>. <cite id="1d3c3df3-4">Ostwald ripening is a mechanistic pathway connecting supersaturation and morphology</cite>.
- Chelation and polymorph coupling: Citrate speciation affects polymorph selection; selecting a seed polymorph (mono or tri) and maintaining excess citrate suppresses elongated habit growth, favoring more isotropic sphere-like particles. <cite id="1d3c3df3-5">Monocalcium citrate forms stoichiometrically; excess citrate and seeding steer polymorph and habit</cite>.

Process Analytics and Quality Checks
- Shape/size: Use SEM and DLS; target circularity sphericity index >0.85 and narrow d10–90 PSD (<2.5x). <cite id="075c04f0-0">Spherulitic growth produces characteristic circular structures; tuning variables changes the sphericity</cite>.
- Crystallinity: XRD peak sharpness and relative area indicate conversion to desired polymorph and extent of Ostwald ripening; FTIR confirms Ca–O–Cit stretching shifts consistent with increased complexation. <cite id="1d3c3df3-4">Crystallinity, polymorph, and morphology evolve together under process variables, requiring coupled measurement</cite>.
- Solubility/density and food-grade properties: Spherical Ca–Cit shows higher apparent density and improved solubility/dispersion; tune temperature/stir post-precipitation to increase density by consolidating spherulites. <cite id="075c04f0-0">Spherulite size/shape control via process variables is linked to functional properties</cite>. <cite id="075c04f0-8">Industrial tricalcium citrate emphasizes solubility and density as quality attributes</cite>.

Caveats and Mitigations
- Elongated nuclei and aggregation: If plates persist, slightly increase electrolyte (0.1–0.5 M NaCl) to promote flocculation into larger spheres, then size-classify and re-disperse; reduce shear to <100 rpm during aging. <cite id="1d3c3df3-4">Electrolyte alters collision/attachment rates, which directly affect morphology</cite>.
- Polymorph mixtures: To avoid uncontrolled phase evolution, seed the target polymorph and keep pH/citrate ratio fixed; use antisolvent (EtOH) to quench nucleation if necessary. <cite id="1d3c3df3-5">Stoichiometric control around 1 Ca:2 Cit for monocalcium underpins polymorph guidance</cite>. <cite id="1d3c3df3-2">Supersaturation and shear must be matched to desired phase during reactive crystallization</cite>.
- Case-specific routes: If using solid CaCO3/ Ca(OH)2 intermediates, ensure complete conversion prior to final Ca–Cit crystallization to avoid secondary Ca–carbonate needle morphologies; two-step reactive crystallization provides a robust scaffold. <cite id="075c04f0-3">Two-step methods are standard for Ca–Cit and allow stepwise morphology and phase control</cite>.

Summary: What to do
- Start with reactive precipitation of Ca–Cit at moderate supersaturation; add 0.1–2 wt% CTAB with 1–5 wt% PEG/PVP, hold pH 5–6; increase residence and reduce shear to form spherulites; then age 30–60 min at 5–10 °C below set temperature to ripen into spheres. <cite id="075c04f0-0">Spherulitic growth under tunable T, stir, and residence yields spherical shapes</cite>. <cite id="1d3c3df3-2">Shape control through supersaturation and shear is documented for Ca–Cit</cite>. <cite id="fc434337-4">Surfactant–polymer templates are an effective pathway to spheroids in analogous systems</cite>.
- For nanospheres, use microemulsion with CTAB/PVA; add Ca2+ to exceed complexation threshold to stabilize curvature; slow solvent evaporation and post-wash to remove templates. <cite id="fc434337-4">Surfactant–polymer templated microemulsion routes reach 1 μm spheroids</cite>. <cite id="fc434337-8">Higher CMC fractions round particles; scaling gives practical surfactant windows</cite>.
- Use seed-assisted conversion at Ca/Cit ≈ 1.1–1.8 with 5–20% seed; decrease stir and extend hold to promote three-dimensional growth; keep a small citrate excess during aging. <cite id="1d3c3df3-2">Seeding and tuning supersaturation mitigate elongated nuclei</cite>. <cite id="1d3c3df3-1">High citrate coverage stabilizes specific surfaces, consistent with rounded morphologies</cite>.
- Validate with SEM/DLS/XRD; adjust temperature by 3–5 °C and surfactant/polymer weight percent by 0.5–1 wt% steps to fine-tune sphericity and density; re-run with 0.1–0.5 M NaCl if elongated aggregates dominate, followed by classification. <cite id="1d3c3df3-4">Coupled analytics (morphology, crystallinity, supersaturation) are essential for control</cite>.

without_term.text: What are the key methodologies and parameters for controlling the crystal shape of a calcium salt to achieve spherical morphology in industrial crystallization?
without_term.answer:
Summary
Industrial production of spherical calcium‑salt crystals relies on controlling nucleation–growth kinetics and pathways to steer polymorph selection and anisotropy toward isotropic, spherulitic, or encapsulated morphologies. Across calcium salts, consistent levers include supersaturation management, temperature programming, seeding and controlled additive/impurity environments, and often anti‑solvent or constrained/guided growth; organic molecules and interfacial engineering reduce anisotropy and promote rounded shapes. Below, we distill the key methodologies and operational parameters that have demonstrated success for spherical/rounded morphology, with emphasis on CaCO3 (the most studied system), plus insights from CaSO4 (gypsum) and calcium phosphates where morphology depends on the same thermodynamic–kinetic controls.

Key Methodologies

1) Thermodynamic pathway and supersaturation management
- Select supersaturation mode and magnitude. Calcium salt crystallization exhibits multiple metastable and stable polymorphs; morphology is set by the supersaturation pathway and rate (SSGR), which dictates the balance of primary nucleation, secondary nucleation, and growth. Temperature programming across the metastability gap (e.g., fast formation of vaterite/calcite intermediates) reduces anisotropic edge growth and promotes spherulitic nuclei coalescing into near‑spherical aggregates in CaCO3 systems. <cite id="8a449bcf-0">Temperature and supersaturation determine the phase and particle morphology in CaCO3 precipitation diagrams used for process design</cite> <cite id="8a449bcf-3">Operating parameters including temperature, pH, and supersaturation govern polymorphism, microstructure, and growth kinetics</cite>. 
- For CaSO4·2H2O (gypsum), the supersaturation pathway directly controls the nucleation–growth trade‑off and the formation of acicular or more equant platelets, evidencing that “spherical” morphology is a mobility/impurity‑limited outcome of isotropic growth fronts rather than strictly a thermodynamic phase. <cite id="4441a4bd-8">Gypsum crystallization is highly sensitive to the supersaturation pathway, with different nucleation–growth balances producing distinct morphologies</cite> <cite id="8a449bcf-0">Precipitation design diagrams for CaCO3 show temperature/supersaturation windows mapping to morphologies, a concept that generalizes to pathway‑dependent salts</cite>.

Practical parameters: 
- Maintain low SSGR during early supersaturation bursts (chemical dosing or antisolvent addition) to favor nuclei merging into larger isotropic embryos, then raise SSGR in a second stage to promote isotropic face growth; stage timing and dose rate are critical. <cite id="8a449bcf-7">Supersaturation formation rate can be controlled by additive protocols to select polymorphism</cite> <cite id="6dfcb41c-1">Calcite grows as monocrystalline cubical particles at 30 °C from metastable vaterite; temperature and supersaturation ratio govern growth mode</cite>.
- Use early supersaturation at subzero or near‑ambient temperatures to form vaterite/calcite spherulitic nuclei, then warm to enable isotropic calcite conversion and growth; a canonical case shows spherulites when 0.2 M Na2CO3 is injected into CaCl2·2H2O at 5 °C with moderate stirring. <cite id="6dfcb41c-0">Spherulitic calcite crystals formed by instantaneous 0.2 M Na2CO3 addition into 0.2 M CaCl2·2H2O at 5 °C with 300 rpm stirring</cite> <cite id="6dfcb41c-3">Besides supersaturation, temperature significantly affects the growth mode toward spherulitic vs. anisotropic forms</cite>.

2) Polymorph engineering (vaterite → calcite; calcite orientation)
- Spherical morphology often arises from vaterite or magnesium‑calcite intermediates that have lower anisotropy, followed by conversion to calcite. Process conditions are tuned so that vaterite is kinetically trapped and later transforms to calcite with isotropic spherulitic structures. <cite id="6dfcb41c-0">Spherulitic calcite forms under metastable, low‑temperature, high‑supersaturation conditions</cite> <cite id="6dfcb41c-8">Calcite is thermodynamically stable while vaterite is metastable/less stable, consistent with morphology shifts upon transformation</cite>.
- Mg2+ impurities and Sr2+ can stabilize spherical nanoparticles and alter growth symmetry; such foreign ions and chelation chemistry can be exploited as morphology‑directing agents in solution. <cite id="6dfcb41c-2">Mg2+ substitution stabilizes spherical nanoparticles in CaCO3 systems in molecular dynamics, indicating ion‑induced morphological isotropy</cite> <cite id="8a449bcf-6">Sr2+ addition alters polymorph selection and morphology, shifting supersaturation formation and phase outcomes</cite>.

Practical parameters:
- Control Ca2+/CO32−/HCO3− redox and complexation; maintain CO2 partial pressure to suppress aragonite and steer toward vaterite/calcite with slower anisotropic growth faces exposed last. <cite id="8a449bcf-0">CaCO3 precipitation diagrams tie pH/temperature/supersaturation to polymorph outcomes (calcite vs aragonite vs vaterite)</cite> <cite id="8a449bcf-3">pH and temperature windows can be selected to preferentially produce a polymorph that exhibits rounded morphology</cite>.
- Phase transformation engineering: use temperature “sweeps” across the aragonite–calcite gap, or aging, to convert elongated polymorphs into more isotropic structures prior to final growth. <cite id="6dfcb41c-1">Calcite growth from vaterite and its temperature dependence underpin strategies that combine early metastable nucleation with later growth</cite> <cite id="6dfcb41c-8">Thermodynamics of polymorph stability (calcite most stable, vaterite least) guide aging and temperature programming</cite>.

3) Anti‑solvent addition and continuous crystallization
- Anti‑solvent programming (e.g., ethanol) is a powerful industrial lever to instantaneously raise supersaturation, trigger nucleation on existing nuclei, and then control growth via residence time and cooling. In CaCO3, lecithin‑containing media under gas diffusion enable spherulitic vaterite; analogous strategies in continuous loop reactors with staged antisolvent injection yield narrow size distributions and increased isotropy by keeping shear and growth face exposure uniform. <cite id="8a449bcf-6">Lecithin media modulate CaCO3 crystallization pathways; differing lecithins shift growth to spherulitic vaterite morphologies</cite> <cite id="6dfcb41c-0">Spherulitic CaCO3 formation under rapid supersaturation and low temperature with controlled stirring</cite>.
- Continuous antisolvent crystallizers allow precise dosing and mixing profiles; process variables such as solvent ratio, feed rate, and temperature profile set the SSGR and polymorph selection, yielding near‑spherical particles when anisotropy is suppressed. <cite id="6dfcb41c-7">Continuous antisolvent addition processes and systems control crystallization by dosing organic antisolvent and managing residence and interphase exchange</cite> <cite id="4441a4bd-9">Rapid process design methods in agrochemical crystallization emphasize antisolvent and mixing profile design to obtain target morphologies</cite>.

Practical parameters:
- Start with a supersaturation “bang,” then dilute and cool to slow anisotropic face growth; shape becomes more spherical as growth rate becomes diffusion‑limited and shear causes uniform rounding. <cite id="8a449bcf-0">Design diagrams map temperature/supersaturation to morphology; higher supersaturation at low T favors early nuclei formation and later isotropic growth</cite> <cite id="6dfcb41c-0">Low‑T rapid addition yields spherulitic nuclei; controlled stirring conditions demonstrate reproducibility</cite>.
- Use a two‑stage antisolvent feed (burst then taper) with downstream temperature rise to promote coagulation/merging of spherulitic embryos before slower isotropic facets predominate. <cite id="6dfcb41c-1">Temperature and supersaturation ratio affect growth mode; combining temperature steps with supersaturation steps switches between spherulitic and anisotropic growth</cite>.

4) Seeding and distribution control
- Seeded crystallization narrows size distribution and stabilizes a target polymorph; industrial protocols use in‑line recycle to maintain uniform seed concentrations. Seeding can either suppress or promote certain faces, thus reducing spindly growth and favoring rounded spherulites in CaCO3. <cite id="4441a4bd-6">Seeding strategy design must consider process parameters (e.g., polymorph, kinetics, mixing, residence time) to control morphology and monodispersity</cite> <cite id="8a449bcf-3">Seeding within controlled pH and temperature regimes tunes polymorphism and morphology</cite>.
- Recycle‑type crystallizers allow operating windows where secondary nucleation is minimized while growth remains isotropic; CFD and population balance coupling identify safe shear/residence‑time zones. <cite id="8a449bcf-4">Simultaneous bulk/surface analysis in CaCO3 crystallization highlights the roles of flow rate, metal ion nature, and supersaturation in microstructure and polymorphism</cite> <cite id="8a449bcf-9">Crystallization kinetics relate to surface structure and morphological control in CaCO3</cite>.

Practical parameters:
- Seed in the metastable zone edge to select calcite or aragonite depending on temperature/ionic strength, while avoiding secondary nucleation bursts that fragment spherulites. <cite id="8a449bcf-0">Metastable zones for CaCO3 are bounded by temperature and supersaturation; seeding in the metastable window selects phase and shape outcomes</cite> <cite id="4441a4bd-8">Control of pathway and polymorph via supersaturation in CaSO4 suggests analogous seeding boundaries for morphology control</cite>.

5) Interfacial engineering: organic additives, surfactants, chelators, and templating
- Amphiphilic additives and phospholipids adsorb on {01-2} or {10-4} faces, reducing growth asymmetry and promoting spherulitic growth; for CaCO3, lecithin media robustly favor vaterite spherulites when CO2 dissolution is managed. <cite id="8a449bcf-6">Lecithin media differentially influence CaCO3 crystallization, enabling reproducible spherulitic vaterite morphologies under gas diffusion</cite>.
- Trace metal ions (Mg2+, Sr2+) act as heterogeneously nucleating species or lattice substituents that stabilize spherical nanocrystals and suppress elongated growth, offering low‑cost morphology control at ppm levels. <cite id="6dfcb41c-2">Mg2+ stabilizes spherical nanoparticles in CaCO3 dynamics, showing substituent‑induced morphological isotropy</cite> <cite id="8a449bcf-6">Sr2+ ions can reorganize polymorphism and morphology through supersaturation kinetics</cite>.
- Biomineralization‑inspired templating (e.g., biomimetic silica or organic matrices) can direct CaCO3 to aragonite/vaterite with rounded morphologies; these concepts translate to industrial seed designs and antisolvent‑assisted precipitation. <cite id="4441a4bd-0">Apatite morphologies on silica surfaces vary with solution conditions and interfacial interactions</cite> <cite id="4441a4bd-2">Organic template design controls hydroxyapatite crystal and aggregate morphology, illustrating interfacial programming</cite>.

Practical parameters:
- Use nonionic surfactants (e.g., SDS/CTAB/zwitterionic) at sub‑CMC to coat prismatic faces and slow {01-2} growth; optimize adsorption kinetics vs. desorption under flow. <cite id="8a449bcf-6">Organic media (lecithin) control CaCO3 polymorph selection and morphology; surfactant chemistry modulates interfacial kinetics</cite>.
- Maintain Mg2+/Sr2+ within controlled ranges to “glue” isotropic nanocrystals into spheres or to stabilize the spherulitic precursor; avoid excessive Fe/Ca that create different polymorphs and needle morphologies. <cite id="6dfcb41c-2">Mg2+ promotes spherical nanoparticles</cite> <cite id="8a449bcf-6">Sr2+ affects nucleation/growth pathways</cite>.

6) Reactor hydrodynamics, residence time, and CFD‑guided design
- Spherical crystals require isotropic exposure of crystal faces and uniform growth probability; CFD plus population balance models identify zones with shear low enough to avoid edge‑face fragmentation but sufficient to promote uniform diffusion and coalescence. Loop‑reactor antisolvent designs are tuned for short induction times, rapid growth, and recycle that smooths size distribution and shape. <cite id="8a449bcf-4">Flow rate and supersaturation influence polymorphism and microstructure; surface structure governs morphology</cite> <cite id="4441a4bd-9">Process design frameworks tailor mixing, temperature, and antisolvent profiles to achieve morphology targets</cite>.
- In CaCO3 spherulitic growth, moderate stirring promotes spherulite formation, whereas vigorous shear can shatter spherulites into irregular polygons; industrial practice thus targets a Dn/Df window where growth outpaces fragmentation. <cite id="6dfcb41c-0">Spherulites formed at 5 °C with 300 rpm stirring in CaCl2–Na2CO3 mixing</cite> <cite id="4441a4bd-6">Seeding parameter design must account for mixing regimes that minimize irregular secondary nucleation while sustaining growth</cite>.

7) Field‑assisted or “constrained growth” strategies
- Electric fields and ultrasound can alter interfacial energy and growth selectivity to suppress prismatic growth; for CaCO3, constrained environments (e.g., lecithin microcompartments) produce spherical nanocrystals that assemble into larger rounded aggregates. While many proofs are bench‑scale, the mechanisms (isotropic nucleation, constrained growth, and uniform antisolvent exchange) translate to industrial atomization/filming‑and‑growth or field‑assisted crystallizers. <cite id="8a449bcf-6">CaCO3 crystallization in tailored constrained environments (lecithin) yields vaterite spherulites with controlled growth</cite> <cite id="4441a4bd-2">Organic templating controls crystal/aggregate morphology for Ca phosphates, showing that constrained growth and templating can program shape</cite>.

Cross‑Salt Lessons (beyond CaCO3)

- Gypsum (CaSO4·2H2O). Morphology is governed by the same kinetics: supersaturation pathway and mineral chemistry. Industrial seeding in a loop reactor, temperature windows, and gypsum aging promote equant platelet growth; careful control reduces acicular morphologies. <cite id="4441a4bd-8">The supersaturation pathway in gypsum controls nucleation–growth balance, leading to different morphologies; tuning this pathway enables more equant forms</cite>.
- Calcium phosphates (hydroxyapatite, dicalcium phosphate). Morphology varies with Ca/P ratio, solution pH, supersaturation, and seed structure; nanocrystalline, rod‑like, or flake/hexagonal morphologies arise under different conditions. Supersaturation‑controlled synthesis and seeding design are key to obtain uniform or spherical/rounded aggregates. <cite id="4441a4bd-1">Supersaturation‑controlled synthesis yields hydroxyapatite and nanocrystalline calcium‑deficient apatite; pH and S control morphology</cite> <cite id="4441a4bd-0">Apatite morphology depends on solution interfaces and conditions</cite> <cite id="4441a4bd-5">Calcium orthophosphate crystallization and dissolution show that phase selection and morphology depend on ionic conditions and ratios</cite> <cite id="4441a4bd-6">Seeding design with crystalline structure of seed minerals enables targeted morphology</cite>.

Industrial Parameter Set for Spherical Calcium Salt Crystals

Core control variables (same across salts)
- Supersaturation: generate rapidly then regulate. Use staged antisolvent dosing or CO2 gas‑diffusion to spike S, then dilute/cool to slow anisotropic face growth; target SSGR windows that favor spherulitic nuclei merging and isotropic growth. <cite id="6dfcb41c-0">Rapid Na2CO3 addition at 5 °C produces spherulitic CaCO3; stirring and temperature set reproducibility</cite> <cite id="8a449bcf-7">Antisolvent addition systems and protocols control SSGR for polymorph selection</cite>.
- Temperature program: “cold‑seed‑warm‑grow.” Form nuclei at low T (vaterite/calcite spherulites), then warm to encourage isotropic conversion and growth; avoid high T that yields cubical/anisotropic calcite. <cite id="6dfcb41c-1">Calcite grows cubically at 30 °C; lower T favors spherulitic formation</cite> <cite id="6dfcb41c-3">Temperature itself, beyond S ratio, affects growth mode to spherulitic/aggregative forms</cite> <cite id="6dfcb41c-8">Thermodynamics (calcite stable, vaterite metastable) underpin cold nucleation/warm growth strategies</cite>.
- Polymorph: deliberately select and convert. Use Mg/Sr ions or surface additives to stabilize spherical vaterite or magnesium‑calcite; then convert to calcite via aging/anneal to close porosity and round aggregates. <cite id="6dfcb41c-2">Mg2+ stabilizes spherical nanoparticles in CaCO3</cite> <cite id="8a449bcf-6">Sr2+ and lecithin modulate polymorph selection and morphology</cite>.
- Seeding/reactor design: maintain uniform seed in recycle‑type crystallizers; avoid secondary nucleation hot spots; use population‑balance‑guided residence times. <cite id="4441a4bd-6">Seeding strategy design considers polymorph, kinetics, mixing, and residence time</cite> <cite id="8a449bcf-4">Flow rate and supersaturation alter microstructure and polymorphism; process parameters are tuned to control</cite>.
- Interfacial chemistry: include nonionic surfactants, phospholipids, or controlled levels of Mg2+/Sr2+ to suppress {01-2} face growth and promote isotropic spherulite growth; control impurities (Fe/CO3 depletion) to prevent elongated morphologies. <cite id="8a449bcf-6">Lecithin media produce spherulitic vaterite CaCO3; interfacial composition controls morphology</cite> <cite id="6dfcb41c-2">Mg2+ substitution promotes spherical nanoparticles</cite>.
- Hydrodynamics and residence time: CFD‑coupled PBM to locate antisolvent dosing zones away from shear hot spots; maintain moderate turbulence for diffusion and uniform growth without shattering spherulites. <cite id="6dfcb41c-0">300 rpm stirring conditions are compatible with spherulitic CaCO3 growth</cite> <cite id="4441a4bd-6">Mixing regimes in seeding must be designed against morphology risks</cite>.
- Pathway engineering: in CaSO4 and Ca phosphates, explicit control of supersaturation pathway (chemical vs. antisolvent), pH, and Ca/P redox avoids acicular forms; maintain pH and Ca/P near target to stabilize the desired equant polymorph. <cite id="4441a4bd-8">Gypsum morphology depends on supersaturation pathway</cite> <cite id="4441a4bd-5">Phase selection is tied to solution stoichiometry and supersaturation</cite> <cite id="4441a4bd-1">Supersaturation and pH control apatite nanocrystal formation</cite>.

Concrete operating windows and examples
- Bench‑to‑industrial scaling example (CaCO3): Inject 0.2–0.5 M carbonate into 0.2–0.5 M Ca salt solution at 5–10 °C in a stirred tank or loop reactor; use antisolvent (ethanol) burst then taper to moderate SSGR; maintain 100–500 rpm to promote merging without fragmentation; age at 25–35 °C to convert vaterite/calcite spherulites into dense spheres; lecithin or SDS at sub‑CMC improves sphericity. <cite id="6dfcb41c-0">Spherulitic calcite formed by instantaneous 0.2 M Na2CO3 addition into 0.2 M CaCl2·2H2O at 5 °C with 300 rpm</cite> <cite id="8a449bcf-6">Lecithin‑containing media enable spherulitic vaterite with controlled crystallization</cite> <cite id="6dfcb41c-1">Temperature shifts from 30 °C to lower T favor spherulitic growth</cite>.
- Calcium phosphate fertilizer (dicalcium phosphate dihydrate, Ca(H2PO4)2·H2O): maintain Ca/P near 1.6–1.7 with controlled CO2/acid titration, low SSGR, and seeding of DCPD to obtain equant granules; higher Ca/P shifts to more acidic, amorphous precipitates that autoaggregate into near‑spherical particles. <cite id="4441a4bd-5">Lower Ca/P increases acidity and solubility; controlling stoichiometry selects crystalline forms</cite> <cite id="4441a4bd-1">Supersaturation‑controlled synthesis yields nanocrystalline apatite under defined pH/S conditions</cite>.
- Gypsum fertilizer/chemicals: operate in the metastable “wet” belt with slow antisolvent addition, recycle to maintain seed, and temperature profiles that favor equant platelets; impurity control (e.g., Al/Si) reduces elongated forms. <cite id="4441a4bd-8">Supersaturation pathway engineering in gypsum adjusts nucleation–growth balance to achieve morphology targets</cite>.

Monitoring and feedback
- Maintain target S(r) across the reactor via inline conductivity/pH/optical sensors; adjust antisolvent split to hold SSGR steady; use seed holdup probes and PBM to manage residence time distribution. <cite id="8a449bcf-7">Continuous antisolvent addition processes and systems provide feedback/adjustment to control supersaturation</cite> <cite id="4441a4bd-6">Seeding strategy design includes monitoring and control of process parameters</cite>.
- Track polymorph and shape online (Raman/polarization microscopy, DLS/SEM inline vision) and adjust temperature and impurity setpoints accordingly. <cite id="8a449bcf-0">Precipitation design diagrams tie polymorph/morphology to temperature/supersaturation and guide corrective actions</cite>.

Limits, trade‑offs, and failure modes
- Overdosing antisolvent or high shear produce irregular polygonal fragments from spherulites; avoid nucleation “spikes.” <cite id="6dfcb41c-0">Moderate stirring yields spherulites; conditions must be tuned to avoid irregular forms</cite> <cite id="4441a4bd-6">Mixing regimes that induce irregular secondary nucleation can degrade morphology</cite>.
- High temperature skews growth toward cubical/anisotropic calcite even when supersaturation is high; cool‑form‑warm‑grow strategies are needed for spherical targets. <cite id="6dfcb41c-1">Calcite growth at 30 °C tends to cubical morphology; spherulites require lower T</cite>.
- Organic additives can clog interfacial exchange or alter zeta potential in complex industrial mixtures; screen grades and dosing to balance interfacial isotropy with filtration/drying performance. <cite id="8a449bcf-6">Lecithin media strongly modulate CaCO3 crystallization pathways; formulation is critical</cite>.

Practical Starting Protocol (generic calcium salt)
1) Define target polymorph/shape (e.g., vaterite/calcite spherulites for CaCO3; equant gypsum; equant apatite/DCPD for Ca phosphates). 
2) Set stoichiometry window (Ca/P or Ca/SO4) to favor the target polymorph; add acid/CO2 control pH for supersaturation. 
3) Seed loop reactor with recycle; tune antisolvent addition to create a fast S spike then taper, with temperature profile that drops early (5–15 °C) then rises for isotropic growth. 
4) Add a mild surfactant/phospholipid or controlled Mg2+/Sr2+ to suppress anisotropy; maintain moderate turbulence (100–500 rpm) and uniform residence time. 
5) Age/anneal to complete conversion and densify spheres; monitor S(r), polymorph, and size distribution; adjust antisolvent split and recycle ratio via inline analytics. <cite id="4441a4bd-8">Supersaturation pathway control in gypsum underpins such staged programs</cite> <cite id="6dfcb41c-0">Rapid low‑T addition and stirring create spherulitic cores</cite> <cite id="8a449bcf-7">Antisolvent continuous addition provides feedback loops to hold supersaturation</cite>.

Summary of Key Parameters to Tune
- Supersaturation profile and rate (SSGR), temperature program across metastability, and polymorph selection. <cite id="8a449bcf-0">Temperature/supersaturation design maps directly onto morphology/polymorph selection</cite> <cite id="6dfcb41c-3">Temperature significantly affects growth mode toward spherulitic/aggregative</cite>.
- Hydrodynamics: moderate stirring (≈100–500 rpm), short induction zones away from high‑shear, uniform residence time. <cite id="6dfcb41c-0">300 rpm yields spherulitic CaCO3; stirring level matters</cite> <cite id="4441a4bd-6">Mixing must be engineered to avoid irregular nucleation</cite>.
- Interfacial modifiers: surfactants/phospholipids and trace Mg/Sr as heteroatoms or templates to suppress anisotropy. <cite id="8a449bcf-6">Lecithin/lecithin media control polymorph and promote spherulitic morphology</cite> <cite id="6dfcb41c-2">Mg2+ stabilizes spherical nanoparticles</cite>.
- Seeding density and CFD/PBM‑guided recycle design to maintain monodisperse, isotropic growth. <cite id="4441a4bd-6">Seeding design spans polymorph, kinetics, and residence time control</cite> <cite id="8a449bcf-4">Flow and supersaturation alter microstructure; recycle design mitigates</cite>.
- Pathway choice (chemical vs. antisolvent; pH and ionic strength) to avoid elongated polymorphs in CaSO4 and Ca phosphates. <cite id="4441a4bd-8">Gypsum morphology varies with supersaturation pathway; choose pathway for equant shape</cite> <cite id="4441a4bd-5">Phase/morphology selection depends on stoichiometry and supersaturation</cite>.

Outlook
Field‑assisted and microfluidic strategies (ultrasound/electrics) are emerging to directly impose isotropy; leveraging what works industrially—lecithin/phospholipid templating and antisolvent‑staged dosing—can yield spherical calcium salts at scale. Translating bench‑scale lecithin‑constrained vaterite growth to spray‑drying or atomizing growth modes, with controlled antisolvent quenching, remains a practical route to spherical CaCO3; similar logic applies to apatite and gypsum via seed design and hydrodynamics. <cite id="8a449bcf-6">Lecithin‑constrained CaCO3 growth demonstrates scalable principles transferable to industrial reactors</cite> <cite id="4441a4bd-2">Organic template design demonstrates morphology programming that can be adapted to process environments</cite> <cite id="4441a4bd-8">Supersaturation‑pathway control in gypsum enables industrial‑scale shape engineering</cite>.
