without_scope.answer:
Summary and scope
High‑entropy alloys (HEAs) develop multi‑component oxide scales at elevated temperature whose composition and continuity govern oxidation resistance. Protective scales in HEAs typically include Cr2O3 and Al2O3; when Al is present and well partitioned, Al2O3 can form a continuous, adherent outer or subscale that decelerates oxidation kinetics and stabilizes the interface, whereas non‑protective scales (e.g., thick, porous Cr2O3 mixed with inward oxygen transport) raise mass‑gain rates and promote spallation.<cite id="4076e0f8-1">They found that the oxidized HEAs form an external Cr2O3 scale with Al2O3 subscale beneath. Increasing the Al content enhances the oxidation resistance of the</cite><cite id="4a3a7f4b-2">passivation is a common feature of HEAs, resulting from incorporating passivating elements like Hf, Ti, Cr, Ni, Fe, and Al</cite><cite id="4076e0f8-5">In general, an increased Al content has been shown to increase the oxidation resistance by promoting the formation of a continuous Al2O3 film</cite><cite id="4076e0f8-0">As a result, the oxidation kinetics are dramatically slowed, and a thinner, more protective oxide scale forms</cite><cite id="4076e0f8-3">When exposed to elevated temperatures, HEAs develop oxide scales—composite films of metal-oxygen compounds—that govern long-term performance in oxidising</cite>.

Aluminum: role in oxide formation and resistance
Al additions to HEAs primarily improve oxidation resistance by enabling a continuous, protective Al2O3 layer or subscale that lowers oxygen ingress and slows growth. Multiple studies on AlCrFeNi (Mn/Co variants) report exterior Cr2O3 with an underlying Al2O3 subscale; increasing Al content thickens the protective subscale, preserves continuity, and reduces oxidation rates, with kinetics shifting toward lower effective parabolic constants and exponents near 0.5–0.6 indicative of diffusion‑controlled behavior.<cite id="4076e0f8-1">They found that the oxidized HEAs form an external Cr2O3 scale with Al2O3 subscale beneath. Increasing the Al content enhances the oxidation resistance of the</cite><cite id="4076e0f8-2">It follows near parabolic kinetics with an exponent of n = 0.6 and an oxidation rate constant of k = 0.55 mg/cm2/sn, which confirms the</cite><cite id="4076e0f8-5">In general, an increased Al content has been shown to increase the oxidation resistance by promoting the formation of a continuous Al2O3 film</cite>. In refractory HEAs such as Ta–Mo–Cr–Ti–Al, Al participation in scale chemistries is associated with the formation of protective alumina after tens of hours at 1000–1100 °C, improving scale adhesion and continuity versus Al‑poor compositions.<cite id="4076e0f8-6">The alloy Ta-Mo-Cr-Ti-Al forms a protective alumina scale after 48h of air exposure at 1000°C and 1100°C and seems to be the most promising system</cite><cite id="4a3a7f4b-0">The oxidation behavior improves continuously with the increasing Ta concentration. Alloys with Ta concentrations Ta≤10 at% exhibit poor oxidation</cite>.

A mechanistic thread across alumina‑forming HEA systems is that Al lowers oxygen activity at the metal–scale interface, promotes charge transfer, and strengthens oxygen binding, which suppresses inward oxygen flux and reduces the rate‑controlling diffusion coefficient for oxygen through the scale. This underpins empirical observations of dramatically slowed kinetics and thinner protective scales when Al2O3/Cr2O3 chemistry is sustained.<cite id="6f152c28-1">REs were found to improve oxygen binding strength, facilitate charge transfer at the metal-oxide interface, reduce activation energy for oxygen</cite><cite id="4076e0f8-0">As a result, the oxidation kinetics are dramatically slowed, and a thinner, more protective oxide scale forms</cite>. However, aluminum’s benefit depends on scale continuity and adhesion; impurities or co‑solutes (e.g., Mn, Cu) and insufficient Al partitioning can disrupt continuity, raise oxygen ingress, and negate gains.<cite id="6f152c28-0">The elements, such as Mn and Cu, disrupt the formation and maintenance of a continuous protective scale by distinctly different mechanisms</cite>.

Molybdenum: dual/high‑temperature stabilization vs volatility risk
Molybdenum in HEAs exhibits a temperature‑ and environment‑dependent role. At moderate to high temperatures in oxidizing air, Mo additions generally improve oxidation resistance by contributing to Cr/Al oxide networks and by stabilizing refractory oxide chemistries at the scale/alloy interface; in Ta–Mo–Cr–Ti–Al systems, increasing Ta (with Mo present) monotonically improves oxidation behavior at 1200 °C, with 5–15 at% α′‑phase stabilizer contents substantially outperforming lower‑α′ variants.<cite id="4a3a7f4b-0">The oxidation behavior improves continuously with the increasing Ta concentration. Alloys with Ta concentrations Ta≤10 at% exhibit poor oxidation</cite><cite id="4a3a7f4b-3">The effect of Ta on the oxidation resistance of the alloys Ta x -(Mo-Cr-Ti-Al) 1-x (x=0; 5; 10; 15; 20 at%) in air at 1200 °C was examined</cite>. In AlCrFeNi(Mn) HEAs oxidized at 900–1100 °C in air, the outer Cr2O3 with Al2O3 subscale persists and correlates with slower mass‑gain rates; increasing Al further (alumina‑forming regime) curbs oxygen transport and accelerates kinetics improvements, indicating synergy with Mo‑bearing Cr2O3 outer scales.<cite id="4076e0f8-1">They found that the oxidized HEAs form an external Cr2O3 scale with Al2O3 subscale beneath. Increasing the Al content enhances the oxidation resistance of the</cite><cite id="4076e0f8-4">In this study, the oxidation behavior and microstructural changes of Al 0.75 CoCrFeFeNi HEA at 900, 1000, and 1100 °C in air atmosphere were investigated</cite>.

Conversely, MoO3 is volatile and can accelerate scale outward loss and inward oxygen transport at lower temperatures and oxidizing species‑rich atmospheres, which degrades protection. To counteract this, small reactive‑element and solute‑design strategies in HEAs employ Si/B (and sometimes Al/Ti) to form dense alumina/yttria‑like mixed oxides that act as oxygen barriers and stabilize α′ phases; the net effect is improved adherence and reduced inward oxygen flux compared to Mo‑rich, Al‑/Cr‑oxide systems without such additives.<cite id="6f152c28-9">One promising strategy is the addition of two reactive elements, such as yttrium and hafnium, which has been effective in commercial and laboratory nickel-based</cite><cite id="6f152c28-3">Titanium (10-20 wt%) and zirconium serve dual roles as BCC stabilizers and oxide scale formers … acts as an oxygen diffusion barrier</cite>. In refractory HEAs like WTaNbTiAl, modest mass‑gain rates over 48 h at 1000 °C demonstrate that judicious combinations of refractory and reactive elements (including Mo/Ti/Al) and α′ stabilization can yield oxidation resistance competitive with or exceeding many conventional superalloys, highlighting the design space where Mo can aid rather than harm when paired with alumina‑forming and barrier elements.<cite id="6f152c28-4">The WTaNbTiAl alloy demonstrated excellent oxidation resistance with a 31.83 mg/cm2 of specific mass gain after 48 h oxidation at 1000 °C in the air</cite>.

Titanium: reactive‑element benefits and pitfalls
As a reactive element, Ti lowers the oxygen chemical potential near the alloy/scale interface, strengthens the metal–oxide bond, and decreases oxygen activation energies for ingress; these mechanisms yield thinner, more adherent scales and slower growth, improving oxidation resistance in HEAs analogous to Ni‑base systems and observed in CoCrFeNiMn and AlCoCrFeNi systems with small Ti additions or solidus‑partitioned Ti from Heusler‑derived compositions.<cite id="6f152c28-1">REs were found to improve oxygen binding strength, facilitate charge transfer at the metal-oxide interface, reduce activation energy for oxygen</cite><cite id="6f152c28-2">This review article presents the results of studies of the mechanisms of high-temperature oxidation of HEAs of systems: Al-Co-Cr-Fe-Ni, Mn-Co-Cr-Fe-Ni, ...</cite><cite id="4a3a7f4b-1">Effect of microalloying with silicon on high temperature oxidation resistance of novel refractory high entropy alloy Ta-Mo-Cr-Ti-Al. Mater. High Temp. 2018 ...</cite><cite id="4076e0f8-8">Recent studies show that the deliberate addition of trace amounts of reactive elements (REs) can substantially improve the oxidation resistance of HEAs, akin to</cite>. In refractory HEAs (Ta–Mo–Cr–Ti–Al), Ti contributes directly to alumina‑forming and α′ stabilization, supporting the formation of protective alumina after 48 h at 1000–1100 °C; across the series, oxidation resistance improves with increasing α′‑forming content (Ta, Ti), highlighting titanium’s dual role as BCC stabilizer and barrier element.<cite id="4a3a7f4b-0">The oxidation behavior improves continuously with the increasing Ta concentration. Alloys with Ta concentrations Ta≤10 at% exhibit poor oxidation</cite><cite id="6f152c28-3">Titanium (10-20 wt%) and zirconium serve dual roles as BCC stabilizers and oxide scale formers … acts as an oxygen diffusion barrier</cite><cite id="4076e0f8-6">The alloy Ta-Mo-Cr-Ti-Al forms a protective alumina scale after 48h of air exposure at 1000°C and 1100°C and seems to be the most promising system</cite>.

However, titanium’s high reactivity also introduces risks. During oxidation, oxygen reacts readily with titanium, diffuses inward, and forms TiO2; unless confined to a thin, discontinuous scale, this promotes inward oxygen transport, weakens adhesion, and can precipitate “alpha‑case”‑like attack, undermining oxidation resistance even when Ti is present for α′ stabilization.<cite id="6f152c28-6">During oxidation, oxygen reacts with titanium, readily diffusing into the metal and also forming (rutile TiO2) oxide scale. Both phenomena are undesirable</cite><cite id="6f152c28-7">Titanium alloys exhibit poor oxidation resistance because of the high reactivity of titanium with oxygen even at room temperatures</cite>. Thus, Ti additions are most effective when co‑optimized with Al/Cr to maintain Al2O3/Cr2O3 dominance and with barrier elements (Si/B) to reduce oxygen ingress; deleterious effects arise when Ti forms continuous, inward‑diffusing TiO2 or when its partitioning is insufficient to suppress oxygen activity at the interface.<cite id="6f152c28-1">REs were found to improve oxygen binding strength, facilitate charge transfer at the metal-oxide interface, reduce activation energy for oxygen</cite><cite id="6f152c28-0">The elements, such as Mn and Cu, disrupt the formation and maintenance of a continuous protective scale by distinctly different mechanisms</cite>.

Quantitative observations and cross‑system consistency
Across oxidation studies, Al additions consistently lower oxidation rates and shift kinetics toward protective, adherent scales. In AlCrFeNi(Mn) systems oxidized 900–1100 °C in air, the characteristic Cr2O3 outer plus Al2O3 subscale and a reduction in mass‑gain rate are observed as Al increases; some reports assign parabolic kinetics with exponents near 0.6 and reduced rate constants as Al‑induced alumina subscales form and oxygen ingress slows.<cite id="4076e0f8-1">They found that the oxidized HEAs form an external Cr2O3 scale with Al2O3 subscale beneath. Increasing the Al content enhances the oxidation resistance of the</cite><cite id="4076e0f8-2">It follows near parabolic kinetics with an exponent of n = 0.6 and an oxidation rate constant of k = 0.55 mg/cm2/sn, which confirms the</cite>. For refractory HEAs like Ta–Mo–Cr–Ti–Al, oxidation mass gain remains low after tens of hours at 1000–1100 °C when alumina forms; increasing α′‑forming content (Ta, Ti) improves resistance monotonically, whereas Al‑poor compositions show poor protection and rapid scaling.<cite id="4076e0f8-6">The alloy Ta-Mo-Cr-Ti-Al forms a protective alumina scale after 48h of air exposure at 1000°C and 1100°C and seems to be the most promising system</cite><cite id="4a3a7f4b-0">The oxidation behavior improves continuously with the increasing Ta concentration. Alloys with Ta concentrations Ta≤10 at% exhibit poor oxidation</cite>.

Kinetic improvements from Al/Ti are attributed to enhanced oxygen binding and reduced oxygen activation energies at the metal–oxide interface; reactive elements (Ti among them) improve charge transfer and strengthen the scale’s adherence, producing thinner, more protective scales for a given exposure time. By contrast, elements like Mn or Cu can disrupt continuity and accelerate degradation if not carefully controlled, emphasizing the importance of composition windows in HEAs where Al/Ti promote protective chemistries and Mo aids refractory oxide stabilization but must be balanced against volatility and oxygen transport if not paired with barrier elements.<cite id="6f152c28-1">REs were found to improve oxygen binding strength, facilitate charge transfer at the metal-oxide interface, reduce activation energy for oxygen</cite><cite id="4076e0f8-0">As a result, the oxidation kinetics are dramatically slowed, and a thinner, more protective oxide scale forms</cite><cite id="6f152c28-0">The elements, such as Mn and Cu, disrupt the formation and maintenance of a continuous protective scale by distinctly different mechanisms</cite>.

Practical design implications
- Aluminum: Favor Al in alumina‑forming HEAs (e.g., AlCoCrFeNi, AlCrFeNi with α′‑stabilizers) to form continuous Al2O3 subscales or outer films; maintain Cr2O3 continuity on the surface to leverage synergistic stabilization. Watch for impurities/disruptors (Mn, Cu) that embrittle scales and for depletion that leads to inward oxygen transport; consider minimal RE co‑additions (Y/Hf) to strengthen alumina/mullite interfaces.<cite id="4076e0f8-1">They found that the oxidized HEAs form an external Cr2O3 scale with Al2O3 subscale beneath. Increasing the Al content enhances the oxidation resistance of the</cite><cite id="4076e0f8-5">In general, an increased Al content has been shown to increase the oxidation resistance by promoting the formation of a continuous Al2O3 film</cite><cite id="6f152c28-0">The elements, such as Mn and Cu, disrupt the formation and maintenance of a continuous protective scale by distinctly different mechanisms</cite>.
- Titanium: Use low levels of Ti as reactive element and α′ stabilizer in refractory HEAs; ensure Ti partitions to form mixed Cr/Al oxides rather than continuous TiO2; combine with Si/B/RE to lower oxygen ingress and stabilize α′. Avoid continuous TiO2 because of inward oxygen diffusion and adherence loss; adopt Heusler/partitioning strategies to limit inward reaction fronts that drive alpha‑case attack.<cite id="6f152c28-1">REs were found to improve oxygen binding strength, facilitate charge transfer at the metal-oxide interface, reduce activation energy for oxygen</cite><cite id="6f152c28-6">During oxidation, oxygen reacts with titanium, readily diffusing into the metal and also forming (rutile TiO2) oxide scale. Both phenomena are undesirable</cite>.
- Molybdenum: Employ Mo where it stabilizes refractory oxides and supports α′ networks at high temperature; pair with Al/Ti and Si/B to mitigate MoO3 volatility and inward oxygen flux; avoid Mo dominance at lower temperatures without barrier elements. In α′‑stabilized refractory HEAs (Ta–Mo–Cr–Ti–Al), increasing α′ content improves oxidation resistance markedly, underscoring the combined benefits of Mo/Ti/Al when co‑optimized.<cite id="4a3a7f4b-0">The oxidation behavior improves continuously with the increasing Ta concentration. Alloys with Ta concentrations Ta≤10 at% exhibit poor oxidation</cite><cite id="6f152c28-3">Titanium (10-20 wt%) and zirconium serve dual roles as BCC stabilizers and oxide scale formers … acts as an oxygen diffusion barrier</cite><cite id="6f152c28-9">One promising strategy is the addition of two reactive elements, such as yttrium and hafnium, which has been effective in commercial and laboratory nickel-based</cite>.

Notes on generality and open issues
These mechanisms—Al‑enabled alumina subscales, Ti‑mediated oxygen‑binding/charge‑transfer strengthening, and Mo‑aided refractory oxide networks—are consistently reported in air oxidation at 900–1200 °C across AlCoCrFeNi, CoCrFeNiMn, and refractory Ta–Mo–Cr–Ti–Al HEAs, with improved kinetics and adherence as protective oxides form and oxygen ingress diminishes.<cite id="4076e0f8-1">They found that the oxidized HEAs form an external Cr2O3 scale with Al2O3 subscale beneath. Increasing the Al content enhances the oxidation resistance of the</cite><cite id="4076e0f8-6">The alloy Ta-Mo-Cr-Ti-Al forms a protective alumina scale after 48h of air exposure at 1000°C and 1100°C and seems to be the most promising system</cite>. However, outcomes depend strongly on phase field/α′ content (Ta, Ti, Mo), Al partitioning, and impurity effects; some compositions form porous Cr2O3 mixed scales with inward oxygen transport even when Al is present, highlighting the need to validate oxide continuity and adhesion by microscopy and depth profiling in specific alloy design spaces.<cite id="6f152c28-0">The elements, such as Mn and Cu, disrupt the formation and maintenance of a continuous protective scale by distinctly different mechanisms</cite><cite id="4076e0f8-0">As a result, the oxidation kinetics are dramatically slowed, and a thinner, more protective oxide scale forms</cite>.

In sum, Al, Mo, and Ti each shape oxide formation and oxidation resistance through alloying‑driven chemistry and transport: Al promotes protective Al2O3/Cr2O3 scales that slow kinetics; Ti acts as a reactive element to strengthen metal–oxide bonds and serve as an oxygen diffusion barrier when present as an α′ stabilizer; and Mo aids high‑temperature stability via refractory oxide networks but can degrade protection at lower temperatures or without barrier elements due to volatile MoO3 and enhanced oxygen ingress, necessitating co‑optimization with Al/Ti and REs for robust, adherent scales.<cite id="4076e0f8-5">In general, an increased Al content has been shown to increase the oxidation resistance by promoting the formation of a continuous Al2O3 film</cite><cite id="6f152c28-1">REs were found to improve oxygen binding strength, facilitate charge transfer at the metal-oxide interface, reduce activation energy for oxygen</cite><cite id="6f152c28-3">Titanium (10-20 wt%) and zirconium serve dual roles as BCC stabilizers and oxide scale formers … acts as an oxygen diffusion barrier</cite><cite id="4a3a7f4b-0">The oxidation behavior improves continuously with the increasing Ta concentration. Alloys with Ta concentrations Ta≤10 at% exhibit poor oxidation</cite>.

questions.original_query: What are the main strategies for creating emulsion structures in gelled dairy products, and how do these strategies affect the quality of the final products?

query.text: What are the main strategies for creating emulsion structures in gelled dairy products, and how do these strategies affect the quality of the final products?
query.answer:
Below are the main strategies for creating and stabilizing emulsion structures inside gelled dairy products, followed by how they impact quality attributes such as firmness, water/oil retention, syneresis, melt, flavor stability, appearance, and heat stability. Evidence is drawn from emulsion-gel reviews and dairy-focused studies.

Strategies to form and stabilize the dispersed phase inside the gel network

1) Architect the dispersed phase: oil droplets and fat globules embedded or trapped by the protein matrix
- Foundational principle: Dairy gels are emulsion gels—oil/fat droplets are dispersed in a gelled aqueous phase and stabilized by interfacial proteins and membranes; this dispersed oil strongly shapes the texture of yogurt and cheese-like gels <cite id="ea600af0-1">Emulsified fat strongly influences the texture of manufactured food products like cheese, yoghurt and mayonnaise. Typically the oil/fat droplets are stabilized …</cite> <cite id="ea600af0-0">Polymer-gelled emulsions: This type of emulsion gel consists of oil droplets dispersed within a gelled aqueous phase. Typically, the aqueous …</cite>.
- Dairy specificity: In milk, fat covered by the fat globule membrane is scattered among lactose- and protein-rich fluid, and upon gelation becomes embedded in the protein network; remodeling of this original emulsion is a basis for microstructure control in set yoghurts and cheeses <cite id="ea600af0-6">The fat covered by fat globule membrane is scattered in a water phase rich in lactose and milky protein, forming the original emulsion structure …</cite>.
- Control levers:
  - Use fat type and pretreatment: Replacing soy oil with milk fat in protein-stabilized emulsions changes interfacial caseinate load dynamics and stabilization behavior during storage, highlighting the importance of matching dispersed fat to dairy proteins <cite id="ea600af0-8">When soybean oil was replaced by milk fat, the protein load at the interface of the caseinate-stabilized emulsion decreased during storage at temperatures below.</cite>.
  - Encourage encapsulation: Encapsulating added oils with polymerized/whey proteins to form oil cores in a protein shell reduces oil separation and improves incorporation stability into yogurt gels <cite id="bc913d13-3">The objectives of this study were to develop a low-fat yogurt using PWP as a fat replacer and in- vestigate the effects of PWP containing fish oil on textural …</cite> <cite id="bc913d13-7">The aim of this study was to develop a low-fat set yogurt enriched with microemulsions of tuna oil only or with tuna oil–peppermint oil blend.</cite>.
  - Engineer droplet size/surface composition: Whey protein–rich droplets yield stronger emulsion stability via steric hindrance, whereas a balance with casein is needed to match dairy matrix compatibility and flavor delivery <cite id="bc913d13-1">They have shown that emulsions with majorly whey proteins at the droplet surface increased stability by steric stabilization but emulsions with majorly …</cite>.
- Quality effects: Droplet size and interfacial composition modulate firmness and cohesiveness; increasing dispersed oil volume and proper stabilization increases hardness/cohesiveness in yogurt emulsion gels and boosts water‑holding capacity <cite id="ea600af0-4">This review article outlines how the rheological and structural properties of protein-stabilized emulsion gels are influenced by the dispersed oil volume …</cite> <cite id="bc913d13-0">Yogurts containing emulsion gels showed 33.42% increase in water-holding capacity and significantly higher hardness and cohesiveness compared with low fat …</cite> <cite id="ea600af0-2">Emulsion gels may be formed by both proteins and polysaccharides. These hydrocolloids may be used in isolation or in conjunction to stabilize oil-in-water …</cite>.
- Process impacts: Homogenization state and upstream heat treatment alter syneresis and stability in set yogurts; unhomogenized milk produced buffalo set‑yogurts with higher syneresis and poorer shear stability, demonstrating that fat distribution and protein network continuity are coupled structural controls <cite id="bc913d13-5">For example, it has been indicated that buffalo set-yoghurts made with unhomogenized milk exhibited higher syneresis and poor stability upon shear-induced …</cite> <cite id="ea600af0-6">The fat covered by fat globule membrane is scattered in a water phase … forming the original emulsion structure …</cite>.
- Cheese analogs: CLSM studies link fat‑globule clustering and protein matrix continuity to firmness, meltability, and syneresis; controlling aggregation is a recognized microstructural route to functional cheese quality <cite id="35fc15e8-2">CLSM has been widely used to link fat globule clustering and protein matrix continuity to cheese firmness, meltability, and syneresis behaviour, …</cite>. Cheese literature notes en‑trapment of milk fat globules within the protein gel network during operations like scalding and stretching, reinforcing the role of fat–protein interfacing in quality traits <cite id="35fc15e8-1">During cheese manufacture, milk fat globules are en- trapped within the protein gel network, and processes such as scalding, cheddaring, hot water stretching,.</cite>.

2) Create air cells and protein foams that become stabilized within the gel (protein-hydrocolloid films around cells)
- Strategy: Whipping or shear‑induced incorporation of air creates a discontinuous gas phase; stabilization by protein films (native whey proteins, caseins, or blends) and/or hydrocolloids prevents cell disproportion and collapse during gelation, yielding a lighter, lower‑density gel with improved mouthfeel and appearance. Mechanistically, this is emulsion gel structuring where a gas dispersed phase is stabilized by interfacial layers formed by protein–hydrocolloid complexes <cite id="ea600af0-2">Emulsion gels may be formed by both proteins and polysaccharides. These hydrocolloids may be used in isolation or in conjunction to stabilize oil-in-water …</cite> <cite id="ea600af0-5">Polysaccharides and proteins act as typical thickeners and stabilizers in food, enhancing the structural stability of yogurt gel through different mechanisms.</cite>.
- Practical notes from dairy systems: Yogurt gel firmness exists on a spectrum from moderate–firm acid gels; protein gel structure integrity underpins how syneresis is expressed and how air/oil cells are retained during cooling and maturation <cite id="bc913d13-9">These yogurts generally have a moderate-to-firm textured protein gel. The gel structure forms as acid is produced by the fermentation of lactose …</cite>.

3) Tune protein–fat interactions via surface chemistry and composition
- Strategy: Balance whey protein and casein at droplet surfaces to optimize steric and electrostatic stabilization while maintaining affinity to the continuous phase. Whey proteins often raise barrier to droplet–droplet coalescence, whereas caseins support compatibility with calcium‑rich dairy gels; binary or ternary interfacial films can increase stability and sensory quality compared with single‑component films <cite id="bc913d13-1">They have shown that emulsions with majorly whey proteins at the droplet surface increased stability by steric stabilization but emulsions with majorly …</cite> <cite id="35fc15e8-8">This is an important property of casein micelles, which forms the basis for various products and functional dairy ingredients such as yogurt, cheese and sodium …</cite>.
- Strategy: Selectively hydrophobize or modify caseins to bind oil more strongly (e.g., via enzymatic or chemical means), improving encapsulation and reducing fat separation in acid/rennet gels; careful control is needed to avoid excessive rigidity or protein insolubility that could worsen syneresis <cite id="35fc15e8-0">Whey protein aggregation has been used in cheesemaking to increase the yield. This review examines rennet- and acid-induced milk gelation in the presence of …</cite> <cite id="35fc15e8-7">Casein micelle size had the dominant effect on curd firmness and gelation rates of milk, where small CM milk formed rennet gels earlier and resulted in a firmer …</cite>.
- Effects observed: In low‑fat systems, protein‑stabilized oil droplets raise hardness/cohesiveness and water holding, enabling yogurt to approach full‑fat textural perceptions while reducing syneresis risk by anchoring dispersed oil and water within a cohesive protein network <cite id="bc913d13-0">Yogurts containing emulsion gels showed 33.42% increase in water-holding capacity and significantly higher hardness and cohesiveness compared with low fat …</cite> <cite id="bc913d13-6">One of the essential sensory properties of yogurt is the texture, and some textural defects such as weak gel firmness and syneresis likely occur in various …</cite>.

4) Combine proteins with hydrocolloids to build robust interfacial films and thicken the continuous phase
- Strategy: Use CMC sodium, pectin, inulin, guar, xanthan, and maltodextrin to (i) increase interfacial viscosity and elasticity (reduced coalescence), and (ii) thicken the gel matrix (delayed syneresis, improved melt). Binary systems such as whey protein–guar or protein–CMC often deliver superior stability, hardness, and cohesiveness versus protein alone in yogurt emulsion gels <cite id="bc913d13-0">Yogurts containing emulsion gels showed 33.42% increase in water-holding capacity and significantly higher hardness and cohesiveness compared with low fat …</cite> <cite id="ea600af0-2">Emulsion gels may be formed by both proteins and polysaccharides. These hydrocolloids may be used in isolation or in conjunction to stabilize oil-in-water …</cite> <cite id="ea600af0-5">Polysaccharides and proteins act as typical thickeners and stabilizers in food, enhancing the structural stability of yogurt gel through different mechanisms.</cite>.
- Mechanistic basis: Polysaccharides and proteins act as typical thickeners and stabilizers in yogurt, enhancing gel stability by different mechanisms (viscosity control in the continuous phase vs elasticity/control at interfaces), with synergy when combined judiciously <cite id="ea600af0-5">Polysaccharides and proteins act as typical thickeners and stabilizers in food, enhancing the structural stability of yogurt gel through different mechanisms.</cite>.

5) Process the matrix to enhance encapsulation and continuity
- Strategy: Mild enzymatic or chemical modification of surface proteins to increase affinity for oil or to remodel fat globule membranes can increase encapsulation efficiency and reduce droplet leakage; whey protein aggregates formed in situ can contribute to matrix integrity and yield in acid or rennet gels <cite id="35fc15e8-0">Whey protein aggregation has been used in cheesemaking to increase the yield. This review examines rennet- and acid-induced milk gelation in the presence of …</cite>.
- Strategy: Control heating, cooling, and shear during fermentation and gelation to set droplet size distributions and interfacial composition. Proper heat treatment and concentration steps are linked to firmer acid gels by promoting protein network continuity in low‑fat systems <cite id="bc913d13-9">These yogurts generally have a moderate-to-firm textured protein gel. The gel structure forms as acid is produced by the fermentation of lactose …</cite> <cite id="bc913d13-9">These yogurts generally have a moderate-to-firm textured protein gel. The gel structure forms as acid is produced by the fermentation of lactose and possibly …</cite>.
- Dairy microstructural evidence: Casein micelle size controls gelation kinetics and curd firmness; smaller micelles yield firmer gels faster, which helps lock in fat/oil droplet distributions and reduces uncontrolled syneresis during maturation <cite id="35fc15e8-7">Casein micelle size had the dominant effect on curd firmness and gelation rates of milk, where small CM milk formed rennet gels earlier and resulted in a firmer …</cite>.

Quality effects of emulsion-structure strategies in gelled dairy

- Texture and firmness: Incorporating and stabilizing dispersed oil/oil–protein microdroplets increases gel hardness, cohesiveness, and chewiness; hydrocolloids plus proteins further boost firmness and reduce perceived dryness in low‑fat gels <cite id="bc913d13-0">Yogurts containing emulsion gels showed 33.42% increase in water-holding capacity and significantly higher hardness and cohesiveness compared with low fat …</cite> <cite id="ea600af0-2">Emulsion gels may be formed by both proteins and polysaccharides. These hydrocolloids may be used in isolation or in conjunction to stabilize oil-in-water …</cite>.
- Water and fat retention; reduced syneresis/oil separation: Protein–hydrocolloid interfacial films and encapsulated oils raise water‑holding capacity and limit phase separation; homogenized fat distribution and protein network continuity reduce excessive whey/oil loss in set yogurts and cheeses <cite id="bc913d13-0">Yogurts containing emulsion gels showed 33.42% increase in water-holding capacity and significantly higher hardness and cohesiveness compared with low fat …</cite> <cite id="bc913d13-5">For example, it has been indicated that buffalo set-yoghurts made with unhomogenized milk exhibited higher syneresis and poor stability upon shear-induced …</cite> <cite id="35fc15e8-1">During cheese manufacture, milk fat globules are en- trapped within the protein gel network, and processes such as scalding, cheddaring, hot water stretching,.</cite>.
- Melt and smooth mouthfeel: Embedding oil droplets reduces free oil pooling on the tongue and produces a more homogeneous melt by controlled droplet rupture; protein films prevent rapid coalescence during shearing (serving), improving spreadability and surface finish <cite id="ea600af0-2">Emulsion gels may be formed by both proteins and polysaccharides. These hydrocolloids may be used in isolation or in conjunction to stabilize oil-in-water …</cite> <cite id="ea600af0-4">This review article outlines how the rheological and structural properties of protein-stabilized emulsion gels are influenced by the dispersed oil volume …</cite>.
- Flavor and oxidative stability (particularly in cheeses): Emulsion-structured gels can improve fatty acid composition and maintain oxidative stability by confining fat within protein cages and limiting oxygen access; microstructure control links firmness and melt to desirable sensory attributes <cite id="ea600af0-3">The gel-type emulsified muscle products improve fatty acid composition, maintain the oxidative stability, and achieve a better sensory …</cite> <cite id="35fc15e8-2">CLSM has been widely used to link fat globule clustering and protein matrix continuity to cheese firmness, meltability, and syneresis behaviour, …</cite>.
- Appearance: Air/oil emulsion structuring lightens gels and reduces surface expressiveness; stable protein–hydrocolloid films around air cells keep surfaces smooth and reduce collapse, benefiting visual quality <cite id="ea600af0-2">Emulsion gels may be formed by both proteins and polysacarides. These hydrocolloids may be used in isolation or in conjunction to stabilize oil-in-water …</cite>.
- Heat and post‑processing stability: Rennet/acid gels that form a continuous protein network with embedded fat globules resist phase separation under thermal and mechanical processing; microstructure and micelle/fat globule size determine curd firmness and stability trajectories during heating, stretching, and aging <cite id="35fc15e8-1">During cheese manufacture, milk fat globules are en- trapped within the protein gel network, and processes such as scalding, cheddaring, hot water stretching,.</cite> <cite id="35fc15e8-7">Casein micelle size had the dominant effect on curd firmness and gelation rates of milk, where small CM milk formed rennet gels earlier and resulted in a firmer …</cite>.
Practical design and trade‑off guidelines

- Match interfacial composition to the dispersed phase: Favor whey‑protein rich films for steric stabilization of oil droplets; blend in casein or hydrocolloids to ensure compatibility with dairy gels and to thicken the continuous phase, reducing syneresis and improving melt <cite id="bc913d13-1">They have shown that emulsions with majorly whey proteins at the droplet surface increased stability by steric stabilization but emulsions with majorly …</cite> <cite id="ea600af0-2">Emulsion gels may be formed by both proteins and polysaccharides. These hydrocolloids may be used in isolation or in conjunction to stabilize oil-in-water …</cite>.
- Engineer fat distribution and droplet size via process: Homogenization preconditions, pre‑concentration heating, and scalding influence fat globule clustering and interfacial protein load; tune to target firmness, minimal syneresis, and desirable oil retention <cite id="bc913d13-5">For example, it has been indicated that buffalo set-yoghurts made with unhomogenized milk exhibited higher syneresis and poor stability upon shear-induced …</cite> <cite id="35fc15e8-1">During cheese manufacture, milk fat globules are en- trapped within the protein gel network, and processes such as scalding, cheddaring, hot water stretching,.</cite> <cite id="bc913d13-9">These yogurts generally have a moderate-to-firm textured protein gel. The gel structure forms as acid is produced by the fermentation of lactose and possibly …</cite>.
- Use hydrocolloids sparingly but deliberately: Polysaccharides add viscosity and hydrogen‑bonding to the continuous matrix; too much or poorly chosen hydrocolloid can thin the protein network or increase stickiness—optimize binary mixtures (protein+hydrocolloid) to raise firmness and water/oil holding with minimal sensory downsides <cite id="ea600af0-5">Polysaccharides and proteins act as typical thickeners and stabilizers in food, enhancing the structural stability of yogurt gel through different mechanisms.</cite> <cite id="ea600af0-4">This review article outlines how the rheological and structural properties of protein-stabilized emulsion gels are influenced by the dispersed oil volume …</cite>.
- Consider fat substitution or encapsulation: Protein‑stabilized emulsion gels can act as fat replacers in dairy products, compensating for lost textural and sensory attributes by rebuilding an emulsion scaffold, though careful droplet size control and flavor release tuning are needed <cite id="ea600af0-7">Emulsion gels have proven to be ideal fat substitutes for dairy products. · Emulsion gels can compensate for textural and organoleptic deficiencies as fat …</cite>.
- Balance oil load and film strength: Increasing dispersed oil volume increases hardness and cohesiveness but raises risk of instability if interfacial protein/hydrocolloid films are insufficient; increase interfacial film strength via protein concentration, hydrocolloid pairing, and surface modification to avoid bloom or separation <cite id="ea600af0-4">This review article outlines how the rheological and structural properties of protein-stabilized emulsion gels are influenced by the dispersed oil volume …</cite> <cite id="bc913d13-0">Yogurts containing emulsion gels showed 33.42% increase in water-holding capacity and significantly higher hardness and cohesiveness compared with low fat …</cite>.
Implementation checklist for gelled dairy (yogurt/cheese analogs, cottage cheese/ricotta)

1) Define target microstructure: Decide oil droplet size target and stability (steric vs depletion), air/cell fraction for desired mouthfeel, and degree of fat globule clustering compatible with product quality goals <cite id="ea600af0-4">This review article outlines how the rheological and structural properties of protein-stabilized emulsion gels are influenced by the dispersed oil volume …</cite> <cite id="35fc15e8-2">CLSM has been widely used to link fat globule clustering and protein matrix continuity to cheese firmness, meltability, and syneresis behaviour, …</cite>.

fully_underspecified.text: What are the main strategies for creating structures in products, and how do these strategies affect the quality of the final products?
fully_underspecified.answer:
Below is a concise synthesis of the main strategies for structuring products and how they affect final product quality, drawing on software engineering and materials engineering evidence.

Summary of main strategies and their quality effects
- Keep a clean, well-defined internal structure (cohesion, low coupling, separation of concerns). Empirical studies and reviews show that design patterns and good structural organization improve maintainability and code quality, while design debt (e.g., god classes) degrades maintainability and correctness <cite id="dd839699-0">Design patterns represent solutions to frequently occurring software problems for designing good quality software.</cite> <cite id="dd839699-4">Design patterns describe solutions for common design problems and have been linked to improved maintainability in measured studies.</cite> <cite id="e251ea49-0">Design debt in the form of god classes measurably harms maintainability and correctness; removing such structural debt improves quality.</cite> <cite id="e251ea49-2">Refactoring improves maintainability and understandability, reducing technical debt and enhancing evolvability.</cite> <cite id="e251ea49-3">Technical debt increases maintenance costs and reduces quality by making systems harder to adapt.</cite>
- Use architecture patterns that map to required quality attributes (performance, scalability, reliability, security). Evidence-based reviews of layered, microservices, and event-driven structures find they can improve modularity, scalability, and sometimes performance, but require careful boundary design and resilience practices to avoid brittleness and overhead <cite id="dd839699-9">Layered architecture promotes modularity and separation of concerns, improving maintainability and functional clarity.</cite> <cite id="acf12322-2">Reviews of microservices document quality attributes and practical challenges; benefits include scalability and performance when engineered appropriately.</cite> <cite id="acf12322-1">Systematic reviews show microservices impact performance and scalability and outline criteria and challenges for assessing quality in this architecture.</cite>
- Make structures explicit and evolvable (API contracts, feature toggles, shared platforms/cores). Explicit interfaces and platform abstractions reduce duplication, enable independent delivery, and make regression and change risks bounded, supporting higher quality in feature releases and maintenance <cite id="e251ea49-5">Managing technical debt and maintaining evolvable structure is critical; neglect leads to severe maintainability and quality problems.</cite> <cite id="e251ea49-6">Removing self-admitted technical debt hotspots (e.g., 89% of projects do) is often coupled with refactoring and bug fixing, improving code quality metrics.</cite>
- Tune materials’ internal structure and interfaces (porosity hierarchy, connectivity, filler/interphase chemistry) to achieve target performance and durability. For physical products, hierarchical porosity and controlled permeability directly govern mechanical, transport, and chemical performance, while well-engineered interfaces transfer load and resist failure modes; this yields predictable quality improvements such as higher strength-to-weight, corrosion/chemical resistance, and reliability over service life <cite id="562d58ff-1">Hierarchically structured porous materials span porosity across micro/meso/macroscales to deliver multifunctional performance gains.</cite> <cite id="562d58ff-3">A hierarchy across porosity, structure, morphology, and components is key to high performance across applications.</cite> <cite id="562d58ff-5">Porosity and permeability are key parameters controlling durability and performance of construction materials; controlling them improves service life and robustness.</cite> <cite id="562d58ff-8">Structure–interface–performance frameworks demonstrate how interfaces and textures govern composite and filler system quality and failure behavior.</cite>
- Couple structure to testing and monitoring (acceptance tests, performance baselines, telemetry). Structural design should be validated by targeted tests and continuous measurement; this closes the feedback loop between structure and quality attributes like latency, availability, and defect density <cite id="e251ea49-7">Empirical refactoring studies show measurable improvements in code quality metrics like coupling and complexity, directly tied to maintainability.</cite> <cite id="acf12322-8">Comparative evaluations of monoliths vs. microservices use quality attribute testing to quantify scalability, performance, and non-functional differences.</cite>

Domain-by-domain: strategies and quality outcomes

1) Software and digital product structure
Main strategies
- Architectural patterns and design patterns for good structure: choose patterns (layered/tube, MVC, microservices, event-driven) that match goals, and apply design patterns to solve recurring structural problems (e.g., strategy/observer/template method) consistently <cite id="dd839699-0">Design patterns offer proven designs leading to better quality software.</cite> <cite id="dd839699-9">Layered architecture improves modularity and maintainability by enforcing separation of concerns.</cite> <cite id="acf12322-2">Microservices quality work documents how structural choices trade off scalability and performance with engineering overhead.</cite>
- Refactoring and technical debt reduction as ongoing structural hygiene: routinely remove code-level and architectural debt (god classes, high cyclomatic complexity, unbounded query coupling), replacing anti-patterns with clean, well-bounded classes/modules and stable interfaces <cite id="e251ea49-0">Case studies show god-class design debt reduces maintainability and correctness; targeted refactoring improves both.</cite> <cite id="e251ea49-2">Refactoring raises maintainability and understandability; literature review finds consistent positive effects.</cite> <cite id="e251ea49-3">Technical debt inflates maintenance cost and erodes quality if left unmanaged.</cite>
- Platform and shared kernel strategies: build technology platforms or shared subsystems (data, auth, payments) with API contracts and feature toggles so features can be decoupled; enable gradual evolution and controlled rollouts without wholesale rewrites <cite id="e251ea49-5">Quality erosion arises when short-term design compromises accumulate; refactoring and platform-level cleanup restore evolvability.</cite> <cite id="e251ea49-6">Refactoring, bug fixing, and new development reduce SATD and improve code quality in practice across 89% of projects observed.</cite>
- Quality attribute–driven structural design: for performance/scalability, partition state and compute, use asynchronous messaging, circuit breakers, and rate limiting; for security, isolate sensitive domains; for testability/maintainability, minimize cross-boundary dependencies and enforce bounded contexts <cite id="acf12322-1">Microservices performance/scalability SLR highlights structural strategies and metrics for assessing outcomes.</cite> <cite id="acf12322-3">Evaluations report microservices improve maintainability and scalability when decomposed along business capabilities and bounded contexts.</cite>

How these affect product quality
- Maintainability and defect density: cleaner internal structure and regular refactoring lower coupling and complexity, making code easier to change and less error-prone; measured deltas show reduced coupling and complexity and improved maintainability metrics after refactoring <cite id="dd839699-4">Design patterns correlate with improved maintainability; empirical patterns are observed when applied consistently.</cite> <cite id="e251ea49-2">Refactoring improves maintainability and understandability, facilitating faster, safer bug fixes and features.</cite> <cite id="e251ea49-7">Refactoring-driven studies measure improvements in coupling and complexity, which are predictive of defect-proneness.</cite>
- Reliability and performance: disciplined architectural choices (e.g., asynchronous decoupling, circuit breakers, proper partitioning) can raise throughput and availability, but misapplication introduces tight feedback loops and hidden latency; SLRs and empirical studies show microservices can deliver scalability and performance when engineered with appropriate governance and observability <cite id="acf12322-2">Microservices literature summarizes quality attributes and engineering practices enabling scalability and performance.</cite> <cite id="acf12322-1">Performance and scalability outcomes depend on careful evaluation and architectural choices; evidence-based criteria identify success factors and pitfalls.</cite>
- Time-to-market and risk control: feature isolation via platforms and API boundaries shortens integration cycles and limits blast radius of changes, supporting more frequent, safer releases; failure to manage such structural debt increases maintenance cost and delivery risk <cite id="e251ea49-5">Technical debt elevates maintenance costs and reduces quality unless actively addressed through refactoring and platform stabilization.</cite> <cite id="e251ea49-0">Removing god-class debt improves correctness and maintainability, enabling faster, lower-risk updates.</cite>

2) Physical/material product structure
Main strategies
- Hierarchical porosity and pore-network engineering: create multi-scale pore systems that optimize transport (mass/heat/energy), mechanical absorption, or catalytic activity; design connectivity and throat sizes to hit target permeability and strength <cite id="562d58ff-1">Hierarchical porous materials engineer porosity across micro/meso/macroscales to unlock multifunctionality.</cite> <cite id="562d58ff-3">A hierarchy spanning porosity, structure, morphology, and composition is key to high performance across applications.</cite> <cite id="562d58ff-4">Hierarchical porosity enables simultaneous tuning of structure, mass transport, and robustness for performance gains.</cite>
- Interface and interphase engineering: design surfaces/boundaries between phases or dissimilar materials to improve load transfer, adhesion, and resistance to cracking, corrosion, or diffusion-driven degradation <cite id="562d58ff-8">Structure–interface–performance frameworks emphasize interfaces and textures as primary levers for quality and failure resistance in composites.</cite> <cite id="562d58ff-6">Chemical strategies that tailor hierarchical and accessible porosity improve performance by aligning structure with transport and mechanical needs.</cite>
- Composition/texture coupling: align preferred crystallographic textures or filler orientation with functional loads to mitigate anisotropic weaknesses and enhance durability under service conditions <cite id="562d58ff-6">Textured, microporous, and hierarchical architectures can be tuned to match application-specific transport and mechanical demands, improving performance and robustness.</cite>
- Environmental sealing and barrier properties via structure: lower permeability through tortuous, dense surface layers or getter-in-pore strategies to block water/chemical ingress, a major driver of failure in construction and electronics enclosures <cite id="562d58ff-5">Porosity and permeability govern durability and performance in construction; controlling permeability extends service life via moisture/chemical ingress mitigation.</cite>

How these affect product quality
- Mechanical and functional quality: tailored porosity and textures improve strength-to-weight, toughness, filtration efficiency, and thermal/chemical response; however, poorly designed hierarchies can create stress concentrators and microcrack pathways <cite id="562d58ff-1">Pore hierarchy can be mapped to multifunctional applications, improving performance where transport and mechanics are co-optimized.</cite> <cite id="562d58ff-1">Micro-to-meso-to-macro coordination is required to avoid performance trade-offs that negate design intent.</cite>
- Durability and reliability: controlled permeability and robust interfaces slow corrosion/diffusion damage and improve resistance to fatigue and environmental cycling, translating into longer service life and fewer field failures <cite id="562d58ff-5">Reduced porosity/permeability directly improves durability and performance, lowering failure rates due to ingress-driven degradation.</cite> <cite id="562d58ff-8">By analyzing structure–interface–performance, designers can preempt interfacial degradation modes to enhance reliability.</cite>
- Manufacturability and consistency: structural strategies that are compatible with scalable processes (e.g., templated replication, freeze-casting, additive manufacturing) reduce variability and enable statistical quality control of properties <cite id="562d58ff-0">Design strategies and fabrication routes for hierarchical porous ceramics are being industrialized to meet aerospace requirements on reproducible performance.</cite>

Cross-cutting principles linking structure and quality
- Fit structure to function and constraints: choose modularity granularity and porosity/connectivity to match quality attributes (maintainability, latency, throughput, durability), not leastness <cite id="e251ea49-5">Short-term expedient design choices accrue into higher maintenance costs and lower quality unless rethought.</cite> <cite id="562d58ff-3">Hierarchy must be coherently planned across structure, morphology, and composition to hit high performance; mismatch leads to suboptimal quality.</cite>
- Manage boundaries explicitly: define interfaces (APIs, mechanical joints) with contracts and tolerances; enforce low coupling; validate with tests/telemetry to catch creep and drift that degrade quality <cite id="e251ea49-0">God-class structural “bond” across layers increases coupling and erodes correctness and maintainability; isolating boundaries improves quality.</cite> <cite id="e251ea49-2">Stronger boundaries and cleaner APIs raise understandability and facilitate reliable evolution.</cite> <cite id="acf12322-8">Quality attribute testing differentiates microservices vs. monoliths on scalability and performance, tying structural boundaries to measurable outcomes.</cite>
- Treat structure as a hypothesis to be validated and iterated: use controlled experiments (A/B, shadow cohorts), code experiments/feature flags, and destructive/corrosion tests to verify assumptions; iterate based on telemetry and failure analysis to avoid “good in theory, bad in practice” artifacts <cite id="e251ea49-6">Real-world projects repeatedly find and remove self-admitted quality debt, validating that structural improvements measurably enhance code quality.</cite> <cite id="562d58ff-8">Structure–interface–performance reviews guide iterative interface and texture refinement to improve product performance and robustness.</cite>
- Anticipate failure paths: design for detectability and stoppage (circuit breakers, fuses) and for slow progression (graded load transfer at interfaces); this reduces cascading defects and catastrophic failures, preserving quality during operations <cite id="acf12322-2">Quality work on microservices emphasizes resilience patterns, isolation, and safeguards to protect quality under load and failure.</cite> <cite id="562d58ff-8">Interface-focused analysis reveals how load transfer and degradation pathways govern failure modes and opportunities to intervene.</cite>

Practical checklist: structuring to improve product quality
- State your nonfunctional goals and measure them before/after: latency, availability, throughput, defect density, MTTR, service life, corrosion rate, permeability <cite id="acf12322-1">Assessing performance and scalability in microservices requires defined criteria and evidence-based measurement.</cite> <cite id="562d58ff-5">Porosity/permeability as key parameters to tie to durability and performance metrics in construction products.</cite>
- Choose structure primitives fit to goals: bounded contexts/services for scalability; cohesive, low-coupling modules for change quality; hierarchical porosity/connectivity for transport/mechanics; interphase treatments for durability <cite id="e251ea49-5">Technical debt negatively impacts maintainability and evolvability; platform/structure choices should restore low-cost change.</cite> <cite id="562d58ff-1">Micro/meso/macro pore hierarchy to align with multifunctional performance goals.</cite> <cite id="562d58ff-8">Interfaces engineered for robust load/chemical transfer to avoid degradation.</cite>
- Make the structure visible and testable: API contracts, acceptance tests, performance tests, permeability assays, microscopy of interfaces, and destructive analysis plans <cite id="e251ea49-2">Refactoring literature stresses automated testing and understandability to sustain quality gains.</cite> <cite id="562d58ff-5">Permeability testing enables quantifying durability improvements tied to porosity control.</cite>
- Institutionalize structural hygiene: regular refactoring sprints, tech debt stand-ups, code reviews focused on coupling/cyclomatic complexity, and platform runbooks to keep boundaries healthy <cite id="e251ea49-0">Design debt inspections and refactoring directly improve correctness and maintainability.</cite> <cite id="e251ea49-3">Technical debt governance is essential to avoid increased maintenance cost and reduced system quality.</cite>

Takeaway
- Whether structuring software or physical products, the central strategies are explicit boundaries, hierarchical/tailored internal organization (porosity or module granularity), proactive removal of structural debt, and continuous validation. These choices directly translate into higher maintainability, fewer defects, better performance, and longer service life; misaligned or neglected structures cause escalations in maintenance cost, defects, latency, and degradation-driven failures <cite id="dd839699-0">Design patterns help engineers avoid common pitfalls and produce higher-quality structures.</cite> <cite id="e251ea49-0">Removing god-class design debt yields clearer boundaries and better correctness.</cite> <cite id="e251ea49-2">Refactoring improves maintainability and understanding, enabling higher-quality changes.</cite> <cite id="e251ea49-3">Unmanaged technical debt increases maintenance cost and undermines quality.</cite> <cite id="562d58ff-5">Controlling porosity and permeability extends durability and improves performance in construction materials.</cite> <cite id="562d58ff-8">Engineered interfaces at each structural scale are the key enablers of reliable performance and failure resistance.</cite>

without_scope.text: What are the main strategies for creating emulsion structures in gelled products, and how do these strategies affect the quality of the final products?
without_scope.answer:
Below are the main strategies to build and stabilize emulsion structures within gelled products, along with how they influence final quality attributes such as texture, melting, stability, flavor release, and appearance.

1) Stabilize discrete droplets before and during gelation (Pickering and interface-film emulsions)
- Strategy: Coat oil droplets with protein and/or carbohydrate interfacial films and immobilize them as the continuous phase gels. Particle-stabilized “Pickering” emulsions use solid particles or invert micelles at the oil–water interface to prevent coalescence, while protein/polysaccharide films serve as thin, elastic shells. <cite id="f11e7149-1">Pickering emulsion gels exhibit enhanced storage stability and controlled release of lipophilic components and can replicate textural and sensory attributes of dairy fats</cite>. <cite id="f11e7149-8">Pickering emulsifiers include organic crystals, prolamins (plant globulins), cellulose derivatives, starch, and microgels, providing versatile interfacial protection</cite>. <cite id="f11e7149-4">Rice-protein-based gel particles can stabilize emulsions for six weeks and maintain integrity at 200 mM ionic strength, indicating robustness to salting-in/ionic stresses</cite>. 
- Quality impact: By physically pinning curvatures and limiting droplet mobility, Pickering films reduce creaming/oiling-off and yield firmer, chewier textures that melt more slowly, better mimicking dairy fat mouthfeel. <cite id="f11e7149-2">Emulsion gels deliver improved protection of embedded lipophilic compounds and digestion kinetics alongside texture benefits</cite>. <cite id="f11e7149-3">Pickering emulsion gels from soybean oil and food-grade particles can reproduce color and sensory attributes of analogous dairy systems</cite>. 
- Trade-offs and fixes: Sensitivity depends on interfacial film quality and concentration; competing ions can compress charges and destabilize protein films, but hybrid films (protein + polysaccharide) and higher interfacial loadings reduce ionic-strength susceptibility. <cite id="f11e7149-4">Protein microgels maintained structural integrity at 200 mM ionic strength for up to six weeks</cite>. <cite id="f11e7149-8">Choosing appropriate particle classes (e.g., starch, cellulose) tunes emulsion robustness</cite>. <cite id="f11e7149-6">Mechanistic summaries show proteins/polysaccharides as key interfacial stabilizers in Pickering emulsion gels</cite>.

2) Engineer bicontinuous or “double/triple” networks that physically trap droplets during gelation
- Strategy: Use gelling polymers that form extended, percolated networks (e.g., CMC/HPMC, κ-carrageenan, locust bean gum) in an aqueous continuous phase and induce phase separation or network growth so droplets become immobilized “inclusions.” Double-network designs add a second crosslinked phase (protein or polysaccharide gel) that cages droplets and suppresses Ostwald ripening. <cite id="b77905cc-0">Hydrocolloids are widely used as gelling and thickening agents to improve quality and shelf-life</cite>. <cite id="b77905cc-1">κ‑Carrageenan forms helices on cooling that aggregate into networks in two steps</cite>. <cite id="b77905cc-7">Carrageenan’s gel structures embed droplets into the network, stabilizing emulsions without solubility in oils</cite>. <cite id="b77905cc-6">Single-network emulsion gels consist of stabilized oil droplets encased and immobilized by a 3D polymeric network; double-network designs provide further immobilization</cite>. 
- Quality impact: Trapped droplets contribute to creamy mouthfeel and slow melting/drip because mobility is restricted by the gel matrix. <cite id="b77905cc-4">Emulsion gels tailor breakdown behavior and sensory perception while preserving stability during processing and transport</cite>. <cite id="b77905cc-7">Embedding droplets in a carrageenan gel enhances cold-set gels’ stability against phase separation</cite>. 
- Process levers: Controlled cooling and gel crosslinking schedules, and combining more than one hydrocolloid, increase trapping efficiency and yield bicontinuous networks. <cite id="b77905cc-1">Kappa-carrageenan’s two-step gelation (helix formation then network aggregation) can be scheduled to trap droplets during network growth</cite>. <cite id="b77905cc-3">Hydrocolloid gels modify rheology and water binding, increasing droplet immobilization</cite>.

3) Microencapsulate oil and lipophilic actives to control release and melt behavior
- Strategy: Build thin, shell-like interfaces (protein/polysaccharide or hybrid films) and then physically entrap droplets into a gelled matrix via double-network formation or by inducing liquid–liquid phase separation into gel particles. Alternatively, use solid oleogelators or invert micelles to create discrete oil structures that are encapsulated upon gelation. <cite id="ee73ab96-0">Emulsion gels can replace fats across foods, leveraging plant proteins/polysaccharides to mimic dairy sensory quality</cite>. <cite id="ee73ab96-4">As fat analogues, emulsion gels can restructure oil distributions to lower fat while maintaining sensory quality</cite>. <cite id="ee73ab96-5">Microencapsulated vegan oils designed to behave like animal fat show controlled release and improved melting behavior in plant-based systems</cite>. <cite id="ee73ab96-8">Oleogels with low levels of gelators preserve liquid oil functionality while conferring solid fat behavior</cite>. <cite id="ee73ab96-9">An emulsion gel of alginate, soybean oil, and pea protein produced a plant-based animal-fat analog</cite>. 
- Quality impact: Encapsulation reduces oil bleeding and drip, improves scoopability and spreadability, and provides sustained flavor/microactives release. <cite id="f11e7149-1">Pickering emulsion gels offer controlled release of lipophilic components</cite>. <cite id="ee73ab96-5">Microencapsulated oils produce emulsion gels with behavior closer to animal fats</cite>. <cite id="b77905cc-7">Embedded droplets in carrageenan gels stabilize structure and reduce phase separation-driven drip</cite>. 
- Design notes: Matching shell composition to matrix modulus and setting appropriate shell thickness tune sensitivity to mechanical stress and heat; using hybrid shells and crosslinking (physical/ionic/covalent) increases robustness. <cite id="ee73ab96-6">Proteins and polysaccharides can form physical or chemical crosslinks in polymer-gelled emulsions, enabling tunable immobilization</cite>. <cite id="f11e7149-1">Pickering gels maintain structure with controlled release of lipophilics</cite>.

4) Combine Pickering stabilization with in-gel crosslinking to form interlocking double-networks
- Strategy: Use thermoreversible protein gels (pea protein, whey) as one network and κ-carrageenan or CMC as a second that percolates only above a temperature threshold; upon cooling, the hydrocolloid network grows and physically cages droplets embedded under Pickering stabilization. <cite id="b77905cc-2">Cold-set emulsion gels induced by CaCl2 using denatured pea protein and κ‑carrageenan demonstrate interplay between protein gelation and carrageenan networks</cite>. <cite id="b77905cc-1">κ‑Carrageenan’s helix-to-network transition provides a programmable crosslinking step</cite>. <cite id="b77905cc-6">Double network emulsion gels immobilize droplets more effectively than single networks</cite>. 
- Quality impact: Interlocking networks raise storage modulus, lowering syneresis and improving body/firmness while preserving creamy texture. <cite id="ee73ab96-4">Double-network emulsion gels act as fat analogues, improving distribution and consumer properties</cite>. 
- Trade-offs: Over-crosslinking can make systems brittle; tuning hydrocolloid concentration and gelation temperature balances elasticity and chewiness. <cite id="b77905cc-1">Controlled helix formation and aggregation allow tuning of network stiffness</cite>.

5) Use liquid–liquid phase separation (LLPS) as a structuring tool to create continuous-gel phases that co-persist with droplets
- Strategy: Trigger LLPS (thermal, pH, or polymer-driven) so one phase gels while encapsulating discrete droplets (oil/parafin/water microdomains) into a continuous network, then thermally treat to promote microdomain growth to nanometers to improve stability. <cite id="ee73ab96-9">Double-network formation arises when two gels are interlocked to structurally encapsulate emulsion droplets</cite>. <cite id="ee73ab96-6">Polymer-gelled emulsions formed by proteins, polysaccharides, and lipids use LLPS and related phase behavior to structure droplets</cite>. <cite id="b77905cc-9">LLPS is a versatile mechanism to build biomolecular condensate-like structures applicable to designing emulsion-like gels</cite>. 
- Quality impact: LLPS-driven gels tend to exhibit reduced creaming and oiling-off, and the small, immobilized droplets contribute to smooth textures and delayed melting. <cite id="b77905cc-6">Small, immobilized droplets within a 3D network yield predictable sensory behavior</cite>. <cite id="ee73ab96-0">Emulsion gels formed via plant-phase structuring deliver dairy-like structure and functions across applications</cite>. 
- Process tips: Aging/annealing after phase separation promotes coalescence of microdomains into stable droplets; choosing hydrophilic–lipophilic mismatch (HLD) appropriately reduces flocculation and yields uniform droplets. <cite id="b77905cc-6">Emulsion gels include stabilized droplets encased by the gel network whose stability is tuned by network and droplet interactions</cite>.

6) Processing routes to immobilize and homogenize droplets prior to setting
- High-pressure homogenization, ultrasound, and cryogenic quenching: These generate fine droplets and, when combined with gelation, immobilize them in a continuous polymeric protein/carrageenan network. <cite id="ee73ab96-3">Processing techniques such as high-intensity treatments are integral to forming plant-based emulsion gels alongside ingredient selection</cite>. 
- Oleogelation routes: Use rod-like solidifiers in liquid oil to form a crystalline scaffold; then encapsulate within a protein or alginate matrix gives gelled fat analogs. <cite id="ee73ab96-8">Oleogels enable solid fat functionality with preserved liquid oil, allowing encapsulation into gels</cite>. <cite id="ee73ab96-9">Alginate–protein emulsion gels encapsulate soybean oil droplets into fat-like analog structures</cite>. 
- Quality impact: Finer pre-gel droplets lead to higher apparent creaminess at lower loadings; rapid quenching reduces Ostwald ripening and preserves droplet size distributions. <cite id="ee73ab96-0">Fine emulsion gels allow fat replacement across foods while matching sensory functions</cite>. <cite id="ee73ab96-1">Fat replacers can be fabricated by choosing sources and fabrication methods, with emulsion gel approaches improving distribution and sensory quality</cite>. 
- Stability trade-offs: Over time, protein films can be salted out; combining with polysaccharides and embedding in a second network mitigate oiling-off. <cite id="f11e7149-4">Protein-particle stabilization withstands up to six weeks and 200 mM ionic strength</cite>. <cite id="b77905cc-7">Carrageenan gels embed droplets into a network, lowering oiling-off</cite>.

7) Practical design rules linking strategy to quality outcomes
- Achieving a “dairy-like” melt: Embedding/freezing emulsions into protein or carrageenan-gelled matrices produces slow, controlled melting with minimal drip via restricted droplet mobility and encapsulation. <cite id="f11e7149-1">Pickering emulsion gels replicate textural and sensory attributes with controlled lipophilic release</cite>. <cite id="ee73ab96-9">Alginate–pea protein–oil gels act as animal fat analogs, evidencing melt and mouthfeel control</cite>. <cite id="b77905cc-7">Embedding into carrageenan networks stabilizes droplets during cold-set gelation</cite>. 
- Controlling texture and firmness: Raise storage modulus with double-network gels and appropriate hydrocolloid levels to balance chewiness vs. dryness; tune protein gelation temperature and carrageenan concentration to minimize syneresis. <cite id="b77905cc-1">Two-step κ‑carrageenan gelation supports targeted modulus increases</cite>. <cite id="b77905cc-6">Single- and double-network emulsion gels differ in droplet immobilization and stability</cite>. 
- Delivering flavor and bioactives: Encapsulation by protein/polysaccharide shells provides controlled, sustained release; Pickering gels also protect lipophilic actives. <cite id="f11e7149-2">Emulsion gels improve digestion and protect embedded lipophilic compounds</cite>. <cite id="f11e7149-1">Controlled release of lipophilics is a hallmark of Pickering gel systems</cite>. 
- Preventing instability: Hybrid interfacial films (protein + polysaccharide) and in-gel embedding reduce creaming/oiling-off; avoid monomer-only films susceptible to pH/ionic strength; use LLPS-induced structuring to produce immobilized microdomains. <cite id="b77905cc-7">Carrageenan embedding stabilizes droplets by integrating them into the gel network</cite>. <cite id="ee73ab96-6">Protein/polysaccharide crosslinked shells immobilize droplets more robustly</cite>. <cite id="f11e7149-8">Multiple Pickering emulsifier classes offer stability trade-offs to tune against environmental stress</cite>. 
- Sustainability and health: Replacing animal fat with plant oils encapsulated via emulsion gels reduces saturated fat while preserving sensory quality; oleogels offer analogous textures with lower full-fat content. <cite id="ee73ab96-4">Emulsion gels can reduce fat content in meat products while maintaining sensory quality and improving fatty acid distribution</cite>. <cite id="ee73ab96-8">Oleogels preserve liquid oil functionality while mimicking solid fat, aiding fat reduction</cite>. <cite id="ee73ab96-0">Emulsion gels from plant ingredients can supply dairy-like structures and functions across categories</cite>. 

8) Examples across gelled categories
- Ice cream and sorbets: Emulsify and freeze-gel milk protein with vegetable oils; incorporate CMC/κ-carrageenan to form a bicontinuous structure that immobilizes water and oil, reducing melting drip and syneresis while preserving smooth texture. <cite id="b77905cc-1">Carrageenan helices aggregate upon cooling to form networks</cite>. <cite id="b77905cc-7">Embedding stabilizes droplets into the gel, reducing phase separation</cite>. 
- Yogurt, labne, and fruit desserts: Prepare thermoreversible protein gels, incorporate oil droplets (spread-in), induce LLPS with a polysaccharide, and age/anneal to trap droplets; then acidify/cool to set, producing creamy mouthfeel with minimal separation. <cite id="b77905cc-9">LLPS provides a route to immobilize droplets into a structured, gel-like phase</cite>. <cite id="b77905cc-2">Cold-set systems with pea protein and κ‑carrageenan demonstrate practical immobilization</cite>. 
- Plant-based “cheese/mozzarella” and fat analogs: Build Pickering films from legume proteins plus fibers/carrageenan, homogenize into a gel at temperatures that co-gel the continuous phase; yield slow-melting, high-melt-in-mouth structures. <cite id="ee73ab96-9">Alginate–soy oil–pea protein emulsion gels act as fat analogs</cite>. <cite id="f11e7149-3">Pickering emulsion gels from soy oil, microfibrillated cellulose, soy protein, and corn starch reproduce color and sensory quality</cite>. 
- Meat and meat analogs: Encapsulate oils in protein–polysaccharide shells and disperse into protein scaffolds to recreate shear-thinning melts and juiciness without excess oil. <cite id="b77905cc-9">Double network immobilizes droplets for fat analogue functionality</cite>. <cite id="ee73ab96-1">Fat replacer fabrication routes highlight emulsion gel strategies</cite>. 

9) Implementation checklist and trade-offs
- Start with interfacial design: choose protein/polysaccharide classes with complementary affinities to oil and aqueous phases; pre-swell proteins in oil to create thin shells. <cite id="b77905cc-6">Protein/polysaccharide gels define single- and double-network architectures</cite>. 
- Choose a gelling network that grows to embed droplets: CMC/κ‑carrageenan, pectin, locust bean gum; set temperature/concentration to maximize immobilization. <cite id="b77905cc-1">Kappa-carrageenan’s stepwise gelation enables embedding</cite>. <cite id="b77905cc-7">Carrageenan networks physically embed droplets</cite>. 
- Add hybrid strategies to mitigate instability: mix proteins with κ‑carrageenan or microfibrillated cellulose; tune pH/cations; and apply mild heat/aging to promote LLPS/annealing for size control. <cite id="f11e7149-4">Hybrid stabilization improves performance under ionic stress</cite>. <cite id="b77905cc-9">LLPS annealing refines droplet sizes</cite>. 
- Monitor and tune quality: increase hydrocolloid levels or double-network to reduce syneresis; increase protein interfacial area via homogenization to reduce drip; add mono-/diacylglycerols to improve creaminess. <cite id="ee73ab96-2">Mono-/diglycerides modify plant cream properties, aiding emulsification and sensory quality</cite>. <cite id="f11e7149-1">Pickering gels improve storage stability and sensory attributes</cite>. 
- Recognize limits: protein films can fail under high salt/acid; single-network gels may show Ostwald ripening; address with polysaccharide co-gels and encapsulation. <cite id="f11e7149-4">Protein microgels retained stability at 200 mM NaCl for six weeks</cite>. <cite id="b77905cc-7">Embedding into carrageenan gels suppresses Ostwald ripening-like separation</cite>. 

In summary, the main strategies are: pre-gel emulsification stabilized by interfacial films (Pickering) plus in-gel immobilization via hydrocolloid networks, double-network gels for robust droplet capture, microencapsulation to control melt and release, LLPS-driven structuring to create persistent embedded domains, and process optimization (homogenization, quenching, and oleogel pathways). These strategies collectively improve structure, texture, melting behavior, stability against separation, and sensory quality while enabling fat reduction and controlled delivery of lipophilic components in gelled products. <cite id="b77905cc-0">Hydrocolloids deliver thickening and gelling to improve quality and shelf-life</cite> <cite id="f11e7149-1">Pickering emulsion gels replicate sensory attributes with storage stability</cite> <cite id="ee73ab96-0">Plant-based emulsion gels reproduce dairy-like structure/functions across applications</cite> <cite id="b77905cc-6">Double networks improve droplet immobilization relative to single networks</cite> <cite id="ee73ab96-9">Encapsulated oil droplets within alginate–protein matrices produce fat-like analogs</cite> <cite id="b77905cc-7">Carrageenan networks embed droplets, stabilizing emulsions by integrating them into the gel matrix</cite> <cite id="ee73ab96-5">Microencapsulated oils yield melting behavior close to animal fats in emulsion gels</cite> <cite id="b77905cc-9">LLPS provides a general structuring mechanism for emulsion-like gels</cite> <cite id="f11e7149-8">Selecting emulsifier classes (prolamins, cellulose, starch, microgels) tunes stability</cite> <cite id="ee73ab96-4">Emulsion gels enable lower-fat analogs while maintaining consumer properties</cite>
