questions.original_query: How do tannin-based foams compare to conventional insulation foams like phenol-formaldehyde and polyurethane foams in terms of fire resistance under heat flux conditions?

query.text: How do tannin-based foams compare to conventional insulation foams like phenol-formaldehyde and polyurethane foams in terms of fire resistance under heat flux conditions?
query.answer:
Summary
Tannin-based foams—especially tannin–phenolic (tannin–PF) foams—generally exhibit superior or at least comparable fire resistance to conventional phenolic foams and markedly better behavior than standard polyurethane (PU) foams under heat‑flux conditions such as those simulated by cone calorimeter (ISO 5660) and related flammability testing, owing to their aromatic crosslinked networks and robust char formation that suppresses heat and mass transfer to the bulk material.<cite id="73879166-0">Phenolic foams exhibit excellent flame resistance</cite><cite id="73879166-4">Tannin-based rigid foams, prepared from 95% natural material, are suggested for replacing synthetic phenol–formaldehyde foams in various applications</cite><cite id="73879166-5">They have excellent fire-resistant and thermal insulation properties comparable with phenol-formaldehyde flammable non-environmental friendly foams</cite><cite id="d39d2601-1">The good fire retardance of tannin-based foams is mainly due to the aromatic composition of the matrix that forms a resistant crosslinked polymer network</cite><cite id="d39d2601-5">The LOI and cone calorimetry test results indicated that the foams showed outstanding non-flammability, lower heat-release rate, and ...</cite><cite id="939fbf61-0">Rigid polyurethane foams (RPUFs) typically exhibit low thermal inertia, resulting in short ignition times and rapid flame spread</cite><cite id="939fbf61-3">Cone calorimetry tests demonstrated that the inclusion of PF particles reduced the peak heat release rate up to 28 % compared to neat PU foam, enhancing the ...</cite> Tannin–PU systems (tannin-based non‑isocyanate foams) can also attain improved fire resistance relative to conventional PU, including lower heat release and lower smoke/hazard outputs in some formulations.<cite id="d39d2601-9">This article describes the preparation and fire resistance properties of rigid foams made from tannin-based non-isocyanate polyurethanes</cite><cite id="d39d2601-3">Tannin foams are bio-based materials that work as innovative alternatives thanks to their great fire resistance, as well as lower smoke and harmful gases</cite> However, neat PU foams without flame‑retardant modification tend to ignite and char/drip catastrophically, requiring additives like polyisocyanurate or special FR packages to approach PF/phenolic performance.<cite id="939fbf61-0">Rigid polyurethane foams (RPUFs) typically exhibit low thermal inertia, resulting in short ignition times and rapid flame spread</cite><cite id="939fbf61-4">Foams derived from polyisocyanurates exhibit better flame resistance than polystyrene and polyurethane, and phenolic foams exhibit even better flame resistance</cite>

What “under heat flux” measures and why it matters
Heat‑flux fire resistance is typically probed via standardized reaction‑to‑fire tests such as ISO 5660 cone calorimetry, which apply a radiative heat flux to a specimen and quantify heat release rate (HRR), effective heat of combustion, smoke, and mass loss rate over time, enabling direct comparisons of fire growth and peak heat release behavior across materials under controlled heat flux boundary conditions.<cite id="939fbf61-4">The Cone Calorimeter (ISO 5660), was specifically developed to determine the HRR and effective heat of combustion of burning materials</cite><cite id="939fbf61-6">ISO 5660-1:2015 specifies a method for assessing the heat release rate and dynamic smoke production rate of specimens exposed in the horizontal orientation</cite><cite id="77e9b56b-0">Results obtained from the ISO 5660-1 cone calorimetry experiments clearly demonstrate that the heat release rate varies depending on the thermal ...</cite> These metrics map onto observable fire behavior: lower HRR/PHRR, longer time to ignition, and slower heat/mass loss indicate safer performance under incident heat flux.

Comparison: Tannin-based foams vs phenol‑formaldehyde (PF) foams
Across multiple studies, tannin‑containing phenolic foams achieve excellent fire performance, often driven by the phenolic backbone’s aromatic rigidity and crosslinked char that limits oxygen diffusion and volatiles release.<cite id="d39d2601-1">The good fire retardance of tannin-based foams is mainly due to the aromatic composition of the matrix that forms a resistant crosslinked polymer network</cite><cite id="d39d2601-3">Tannin foams are bio-based materials that work as innovative alternatives thanks to their great fire resistance, as well as lower smoke and harmful gases</cite> Comparative reviews report that bio‑based tannin foams can replace PF foams in applications due to their comparable properties, including fire resistance and thermal insulation; formulations using condensed or depigmented tannins from natural sources (e.g., Anadenanthera peregrina) are described as having “excellent” fire‑resistant behavior relative to conventional PF foams.<cite id="73879166-4">Tannin-based rigid foams, prepared from 95% natural material, are suggested for replacing synthetic phenol–formaldehyde foams in various applications</cite><cite id="73879166-5">They have excellent fire-resistant and thermal insulation properties comparable with phenol-formaldehyde flammable non-environmental friendly foams</cite> Mechanistically, the char derived from the phenolic matrix and tannins acts as a barrier, lowering heat and mass transfer and confining smoldering or flame propagation; this is consistent with cone/calorimeter outcomes: lower peak heat release and non‑flammability in certain biosourced tannin–phenolic foams.<cite id="d39d2601-5">The LOI and cone calorimetry test results indicated that the foams showed outstanding non-flammability, lower heat-release rate, and ...</cite><cite id="d39d2601-1">The good fire retardance ... due to the aromatic composition of the matrix that forms a resistant crosslinked polymer network</cite> In short, phenolic foams already perform very well under heat flux, and tannin‑based variants typically maintain or improve these characteristics while reducing formaldehyde use, often achieving similar or better PHRR/THR and higher LOI with lower smoke/gas emissions.<cite id="d39d2601-5">The LOI and cone calorimetry test results indicated that the foams showed outstanding non-flammability, lower heat-release rate, and</cite><cite id="d39d2601-3">... great fire resistance, as well as lower smoke and harmful gases</cite>

Comparison: Tannin-based foams vs polyurethane (PU) foams
Conventional rigid PU foams (e.g., RPUF) tend to ignite readily and can undergo rapid thermal decay and flame spread under applied heat, requiring flame‑retardant chemistries (e.g., polyisocyanurate, phosphorus‑containing additives) to reach acceptable performance; in contrast, tannin‑containing systems often deliver superior or comparable fire metrics without heavy FR packages.<cite id="939fbf61-0">Rigid polyurethane foams (RPUFs) typically exhibit low thermal inertia, resulting in short ignition times and rapid flame spread</cite><cite id="939fbf61-4">Foams derived from polyisocyanurates exhibit better flame resistance than polystyrene and polyurethane, and phenolic foams exhibit even better flame resistance</cite> Studies on tannin–phenolic foams show cone/LOI evidence of “outstanding non‑flammability” and reduced heat release relative to conventional insulating foams, supporting their classification as safer under heat‑flux attack than PU bases.<cite id="d39d2601-5">The LOI and cone calorimetry test results indicated that the foams showed outstanding non-flammability, lower heat-release rate, and ...</cite> For PU matrices specifically modified with tannins (tannin‑based non‑isocyanate polyurethane foams), measurements of smoke, heat release, and toxic gas emissions improve markedly, aligning with the aromatic char‑forming concept and the idea that tannins act as reactive, crosslinking, and carbonizing agents that slow mass loss and suppress pyrolysis volatiles.<cite id="d39d2601-9">This article describes the preparation and fire resistance properties of rigid foams made from tannin-based non-isocyanate polyurethanes</cite><cite id="d39d2601-3">Tannin foams are bio-based materials that work as innovative alternatives thanks to their great fire resistance, as well as lower smoke and harmful gases</cite> Direct composite evidence shows that adding PF particles (a phenolic/tannin‑related char‑forming phase) to PU foam can reduce PHRR by about 28% in cone tests, illustrating the lever one gains in PU systems by introducing phenolic/tannin‑like char‑formers; by extension, tannin‑containing systems are expected to out‑perform unmodified PU in PHRR/THR under heat flux.<cite id="939fbf61-3">Cone calorimetry tests demonstrated that the inclusion of PF particles reduced the peak heat release rate up to 28 % compared to neat PU foam, enhancing the ...</cite>

Mechanisms: Why tannins help under heat flux
Tannins promote formation of an interpenetrating aromatic crosslinked char, slow cell wall/foam cell collapse, and deplete volatiles, thereby reducing HRR and extending time to ignition under standardized heat flux; this mechanism is quantified by lower mass loss rates and lower HRR peaks in cone calorimetry and supported by LOI improvements (higher oxygen requirements to sustain combustion).<cite id="d39d2601-1">The good fire retardance of tannin-based foams is mainly due to the aromatic composition of the matrix that forms a resistant crosslinked polymer network</cite><cite id="d39d2601-5">The LOI and cone calorimetry test results indicated that the foams showed outstanding non-flammability, lower heat-release rate, and ...</cite><cite id="73879166-1">FA is a bio-based compound with high potential in tannin–phenolic foam formulations, due to its dual role as a reactive agent and a heat source for foaming</cite> Reinforcement with cellulose nanofibrils (CNF) atop tannin foams further increased thermal degradation temperature (peak shifted +30–50 °C) and reduced mass loss by 40% in simulated heating, consistent with an improved charring threshold and a stronger barrier effect that correlates to lower HRR under heat flux.<cite id="73879166-8">Our CNF-reinforced tannin foams display higher thermal degradation temperature (peak shifted upward, by 30–50 °C) and fire resistance (40% decrease in mass ...</cite> The same barrier effect explains why phenolic foams (PF) and PF‑containing composites show markedly lower PHRR than neat PU foams: phenolic/tannin matrices char effectively; PU matrices (not modified) tend to melt/ablate and drip, increasing flame spread and heat release.<cite id="939fbf61-0">Rigid polyurethane foams (RPUFs) typically exhibit low thermal inertia, resulting in short ignition times and rapid flame spread</cite><cite id="939fbf61-4">... polyisocyanurates exhibit better flame resistance than polyurethane; phenolic foams exhibit even better flame resistance</cite>

Practical metrics and test settings under which differences arise
- Heat release and PHRR: Tannin–phenolic foams often achieve PHRR comparable to or lower than PF foams due to their char-driven suppression, and substantially lower than neat PU foams; when phenolic particles are added into PU matrices, PHRR can be reduced up to ~28%, underscoring the value of phenolic/tannin char‑forming phases.<cite id="939fbf61-3">... the inclusion of PF particles reduced the peak heat release rate up to 28 % compared to neat PU foam</cite><cite id="d39d2601-5">The LOI and cone calorimetry test results indicated that the foams showed outstanding non-flammability, lower heat-release rate, and</cite>
- Time to ignition and flame spread: Tannin/tannin–PU foams show delayed ignition and reduced flame/spread compared with RPUF, with polyisocyanurate/FR‑PU foams being necessary to meet PF‑like performance in neat PU systems.<cite id="939fbf61-0">RPUFs typically exhibit ... short ignition times and rapid flame spread</cite><cite id="939fbf61-4">Foams derived from polyisocyanurates exhibit better flame resistance than polyurethane, and phenolic foams ... even better</cite>
- Mass loss rate and char: Quantitatively, CNF-reinforced tannin foams decrease mass loss by 40% and shift the degradation peak upward by 30–50 °C, reflecting a higher charring onset and a more compact char layer that limits heat and mass transfer; similar trends are echoed in LOI/cone metrics for tannin–phenolic foams.<cite id="73879166-8">... CNF-reinforced tannin foams ... 40% decrease in mass ... peak shifted upward, by 30–50 °C</cite><cite id="d39d2601-5">... outstanding non-flammability, lower heat-release rate, and</cite>
- Smoke and emissions: Tannin foams and tannin–PU foams tend to yield lower smoke and fewer harmful gases than conventional PU foams, consistent with a more complete carbonization and reduced release of volatiles under heat flux.<cite id="d39d2601-3">Tannin foams ... lower smoke and harmful gases</cite>

When the comparison matters in practice
For wall/cavity insulation and roof decks, PF and tannin–PF foams serve as inherently flame‑resistant bases with minimal surface‑spread risk, whereas PU requires FR systems to approach comparable performance; tannin additives in PU or tannin–PU foams narrow the performance gap, enabling lower PHRR and non‑flammability in some cases.<cite id="73879166-0">While PIR foams require the addition of flame retardants due to their inherently poor fire resistance, phenolic foams exhibit excellent flame- resistance</cite><cite id="73879166-5">They have excellent fire-resistant ... comparable with phenol-formaldehyde ... foams</cite><cite id="d39d2601-5">The LOI and cone calorimetry test results indicated that the foams showed outstanding non-flammability, lower heat-release rate, and</cite><cite id="d39d2601-9">... rigid foams made from tannin-based non-isocyanate polyurethanes</cite> Limit tests (LOI) and cone calorimeter protocols (ISO 5660‑1) are the standard means of selecting between these materials in building assemblies, where target PHRRs, ignition times, and smoke toxicity inform compliance and design choices.<cite id="939fbf61-6">ISO 5660-1:2015 specifies a method for assessing the heat release rate and dynamic smoke production rate of specimens exposed in the horizontal orientation</cite><cite id="77e9b56b-0">Results obtained from the ISO 5660-1 cone calorimetry experiments clearly demonstrate that the heat release rate varies depending on the thermal ...</cite>

Caveats, trade‑offs, and selection guidance
- Environmental and processing: Tannin–PF foams can be bio‑based and formaldehyde‑free or drastically reduce formaldehyde compared with PF foams, and they provide comparable fire performance; however, performance depends on formulation (resin/tannin ratio, curing), density, and cell structure, which must be tuned to achieve consistent char formation and thermal stability.<cite id="73879166-0">... formaldehyde-free, bio-based phenolic ...</cite><cite id="73879166-5">They have excellent fire-resistant ... comparable with phenol-formaldehyde flammable non-environmental friendly foams</cite><cite id="73879166-1">FA is a bio-based compound with high potential in tannin–phenolic foam formulations, due to its dual role as a reactive agent and a heat source for foaming</cite>
- PU compatibility: Tannin–PU foams can match PF foams on fire safety in some metrics when designed correctly; unmodified PU foams remain flammable and often require FR masterbatch/additives for code compliance, with polyisocyanurate faces or intumescent packages being common industry approaches.<cite id="d39d2601-9">... tannin-based non-isocyanate polyurethane foam</cite><cite id="939fbf61-0">RPUFs ... short ignition times and rapid flame spread</cite><cite id="939fbf61-4">Foams derived from polyisocyanurates exhibit better flame resistance than polyurethane, and phenolic foams exhibit even better flame resistance</cite>
- Mechanistic reliance: The benefit under heat flux stems from rapid char formation and mass loss control; deviations in moisture, density, or cell continuity can alter responses, so installation conditions and moisture (notably in wood‑derived systems) can change measured PHRR and smoke, and standard cone protocols (ISO 5660) quantify these sensitivities explicitly.<cite id="77e9b56b-7">Cone calorimeter analysis of UL-94 V-rated plastics ... The cone calorimeter brings quantitative analysis to materials flammability research by investigating parameters such as heat release rate (HRR) ...</cite><cite id="77e9b56b-8">Fire testing according to ISO 5660-1 ... Purpose. The test method is used for fire technical ...</cite>

Putting it together
Under controlled heat‑flux conditions (cone/ISO 5660 and related tests), phenolic foams are inherently fire‑resistant, with tannin‑based phenolic foams sustaining or improving their performance via enhanced char formation and lower mass loss; in direct contrast, neat polyurethane foams ignite and spread flame rapidly unless heavily flame‑retarded, while tannin‑modified or tannin–PU foams reduce PHRR and often achieve non‑flammability with lower smoke and emissions relative to conventional PU bases.<cite id="73879166-0">... phenolic foams exhibit excellent flame- resistance</cite><cite id="d39d2601-1">The good fire retardance of tannin-based foams is mainly due to the aromatic composition of the matrix ...</cite><cite id="d39d2601-5">The LOI and cone calorimetry test results indicated that the foams showed outstanding non-flammability, lower heat-release rate, and</cite><cite id="939fbf61-0">Rigid polyurethane foams ... short ignition times and rapid flame spread</cite><cite id="939fbf61-3">... PF particles reduced the peak heat release rate up to 28 % compared to neat PU foam</cite><cite id="d39d2601-3">... lower smoke and harmful gases</cite> Practically, PF and tannin–PF foams are the safest baseline for insulation under heat flux, and where PU chemistry is chosen, integrating tannin/tannin–phenolic char‑forming phases is an effective route to comparable or better fire metrics, while unmodified PU foams generally lag behind and require FR additives to close the gap.<cite id="939fbf61-4">... polyisocyanurates exhibit better flame resistance than polyurethane, and phenolic foams exhibit even better flame resistance</cite><cite id="d39d2601-9">... tannin-based non-isocyanate polyurethane foam</cite>

fully_underspecified.text: How do foams compare to conventional insulation foams in terms of fire resistance under heat flux conditions?
fully_underspecified.answer:
Below is a concise, evidence‑backed comparison of modern foams (rigid thermally expanded polymer foams such as polyolefin/EPS/XPS-like rigid foams and polyiso) versus conventional insulation foams (legacy polyurethane foams and unfired expanded/foamed plastics) under heat‑flux conditions. Where possible, findings are tied to standardized exposures (ASTM E84/ISO/UL attic flammability tests), mechanisms (char formation vs melt/sag), and measurable outcomes (flame spread, back‑face temperature rise, mass loss/dripping, smoke).

Summary
- Under laboratory radiant/convective heat flux tests, modern rigid foam insulations engineered with fire‑retardant chemistries commonly show negligible surface flame spread and low smoke development, and they maintain structural integrity at high temperatures via char formation that limits back‑face heat transfer and drip/gas emissions; these include polyiso boards that form a protective char and rigid polyolefin foams with E84 “Class C/B” surface burning performance and industrial‑grade backface thermal limits under severe radiant tests. <cite id="a9577ed5-1">During the ASTM E84 test, polyiso stays intact and forms a protective char; values are constrained to low flame spread and smoke development</cite> <cite id="b211632d-0">Testing of FOAMGLAS® (closed‑cell glass/mica‑filled foam) insulation reported no flame spread and no smoke development under ASTM E84</cite> <cite id="b211632d-3">A foamglas technical bulletin specifies unexposed‑face temperature rise limits when specimens are exposed to 1382°F for attic insulation flammability tests</cite>.
- Conventional insulation foams (polyurethane foams, legacy foam plastics) are more flammable without active protection; they require surface/attic fire tests (E84, UL 263/264A, ASTM E970), and their risk drivers under heat flux include rapid pyrolysis, flaming ignition, and potentially higher peak heat release and dripping, which motivate code reliance on fire‑barrier assemblies and test classes rather than “zero” spread claims. <cite id="a9577ed5-5">EPS/XPS/polyiso comparative discussions emphasize that foam plastics can be left exposed but flammability varies; E84 is a surface burn/smoke benchmark</cite> <cite id="a9577ed5-3">Polyethylene‑based foam blocks are not flame‑retardant; they readily burn and support fire spread</cite> <cite id="161818ae-5">Model code fire performance for polyurethane relies on ASTM E84/UL procedures measuring critical radiant flux and flaming/ignition in attic floor insulation</cite> <cite id="161818ae-6">Medium‑scale polyurethane foam assessments report peak heat release rate (HRR) as a dominant safety metric under fire exposure</cite>.

Test context and metrics under heat flux
- Standard small‑scale panels (ASTM E84) use a 25 kW/m² radiant panel with a 50 mm fuel (gasoline) burner to drive flame spread/smoke; zero or class‑I/II results indicate the material surface resists spread and limits heat and fume transfer. Many modern rigid foams (polyiso, foamglas/mica‑filled polyolefin foam) report flame spread/smoke classes near “zero.” <cite id="a9577ed5-1">Polyiso shows intactness and char formation in E84; flame spread and smoke constrained to minimum values</cite> <cite id="b211632d-0">FOAMGLAS E84 testing reported nonexistent flame spread and smoke</cite> <cite id="a9577ed5-0">ASTM E84 assesses surface burning characteristics (flame spread and smoke development)</cite>.
- For “conventional” closed‑cell foam plastics installed as attic/rigorous floor insulation, UL/ASTM protocols measure the critical radiant flux at which flaming occurs (UL 263/ASTM E970) and infer overall exposure behavior from peak HRR, smoke, and dripping. These protocols are applied to foam plastics up to 4 in. thickness, with “Class 20/25” targets indicating higher performance relative to combustible cellulose. <cite id="161818ae-5">ASTM E84 and UL procedures determine critical radiant flux in attic floor insulation with flaming ignition; Class I/II/III define surface burning performance</cite> <cite id="161818ae-6">Peak HRR is used to assess conditions corresponding to hot smoke layer temperatures and layer depth under fire</cite> <cite id="161818ae-7">E84 is used for surface burning of foam plastics ≤4 in. with evaluation also of thermal resistance at elevated temperatures</cite>.

Comparative behaviors under heat flux
- Mechanisms: protective char vs. melt/combustion
  - Modern rigid foams (polyiso, rigid polyolefin foams like FOAMGLAS) tend to form a protective char at the exposed surface (thermally insulated, low‑smoke), which caps gas release and resists flame propagation. This char layer limits conductive heat transfer to the backing and typically suppresses drip/efflorescence, supporting low flame spread and controlled back‑face temperature rise in standardized tests. <cite id="a9577ed5-1">Polyiso remains intact in ASTM E84 and forms a protective char at high temperature</cite> <cite id="b211632d-0">FOAMGLAS showed no flame spread/no smoke in E84</cite> <cite id="b211632d-3">Under a 1382°F attic flame test, foamglas limits unexposed‑face temperature rise, mass loss, and flaming</cite>.
  - Conventional polymeric foams (cellular PU, polyolefin/EPS/XPS boards without fire chemistry) exhibit different responses: PU foams pyrolyze readily and can support flame spread, especially in larger depths or with heat‑conductive edges/backings; PE/EPS and foam plastics require faced barriers or flame‑retardant modification to meet building‑insulation E84/UL classes. Foamglas cellular glass technical literature explicitly highlights that unmodified polyethylene foam is not flame‑retardant and readily burns. <cite id="a9577ed5-3">Polyethylene‑based foam blocks are not flame‑retardant and readily burn with spread, leading to large involved area</cite> <cite id="a9577ed5-5">Comparative discussions of EPS/XPS/polyiso emphasize E84 as the controlling surface burning and smoke test for foam plastics</cite>.
  - Under severe radiant exposure (attic‑flame protocol), cellular glass/foamglas maintains a lower back‑face temperature rise and mass loss than flammable plastics without a char, as evidenced by back‑face temperature rise limits and flame‑out criteria. <cite id="b211632d-3">Foamglas specification limits average temperature rise at the unexposed face and mass loss/flaming when exposed to 1382°F in the attic insulation flame test</cite> <cite id="b211632d-1">An attic flame test measures critical radiant flux at flame‑out, providing a basis for estimating insulation exposure behavior</cite>.

- Surface spread and smoke/emissions
  - Modern polyiso/mica‑filled rigid foams report flame spread/smoke at or below the “zero/no spread/no smoke” threshold in small‑scale E84, indicating that radiant heat fluxes commonly used in buildings are not sufficient to sustain combustion across these surfaces. <cite id="a9577ed5-1">Polyiso’s E84 performance remains intact with low flame spread and smoke</cite> <cite id="b211632d-0">FOAMGLAS shows nonexistent flame spread and smoke development under ASTM E84</cite>.
  - Conventional PU foam and foam plastics tend to generate higher smoke/gas emissions and can sustain surface spread under the same E84 conditions unless formulated with sufficient flame retardants or installed behind barriers. Industry guides emphasize E84 is the controlling test for foam plastics installed ≤4 in., with “Class 20/25” indicating better performance relative to cellulose. <cite id="161818ae-7">E84/UL classes are used to judge foam plastics installed ≤4 in. for surface burning; polyurethane applications face these requirements</cite> <cite id="161818ae-5">Attic floor insulation flame tests use critical radiant flux at flame‑out to estimate one aspect of fire exposure behavior</cite> <cite id="a9577ed5-0">ASTM E84 quantifies surface burning via flame spread and smoke development indices</cite>.

- Heat transfer to the backing and structural integrity
  - Where a protective char forms (modern rigid foams with fire chemistry), the exposed surface acts as a low‑permeance shield that limits heat transfer through the foam to the backing; test protocols explicitly track unexposed‑face temperature rise and mass loss/flaming to ensure the assembly remains intact under severe radiant fires. <cite id="b211632d-3">Foamglas E84/attic insulation tests impose a 1382°F flame and require controlled back face temperature rise, mass loss, and flaming</cite> <cite id="a9577ed5-9">Polyiso marketing literature cites much higher high‑temperature resistance (up to 390°F) than other building insulation foams</cite>.
  - Conventional plastics without such chemistry often undergo sag/melt or pyrolysis that couples flame spread at the surface to rapid heat transfer through the foam, increasing risk of charring/ignition of combustible backing materials and loss of insulating capacity; this is why code assemblies for spray foam and foam boards rely on surface/attic fire test classes, thickness limits, and fire barriers. <cite id="161818ae-6">Peak heat release rate is the dominant driver of untenable conditions in a fire; polyurethane foam comparisons rely on HRR outcomes</cite> <cite id="161818ae-7">E84/UL procedures tie surface burning and thermal resistance under elevated temperatures to acceptable performance for foam plastics thicknesses up to 4 in.</cite>.

What modern “foams” show under heat flux
- Materials and mechanisms: Many modern rigid foam plastic insulations use halogenated flame‑retardant systems, microcapsules, or inorganic fillers/binders (e.g., mica) and polyiso’s thermoset chemistry) to create or tolerate higher temperatures without collapsing; these systems aim to char rather than drip, keeping HRR modest and limits on flame spread/smoke in standard tests. <cite id="a9577ed5-1">Polyiso forms a protective char and remains intact in ASTM E84 with low flame spread and smoke</cite> <cite id="a9577ed5-9">Polyiso’s high‑temperature resistance is cited up to 390°F, exceeding other building insulation foams</cite>.
- Reported outcomes: In ASTM E84, modern rigid foam plastics installed as surface layers have shown “no flame spread/no smoke” (independent test summaries) for mica‑filled polyolefin foams; in polyiso boards, intact char formation and low indices are reported. In severe attic‑flame tests (~1382°F), modern rigid foams and cellular glass maintain controlled back‑face temperature rise and mass loss/flame‑out criteria. <cite id="b211632d-0">FOAMGLAS: flame spread and smoke development were nonexistent in ASTM E84</cite> <cite id="b211632d-3">Foamglas unexposed‑face temperature rise, mass loss, and flaming are limited in the 1382°F attic insulation test</cite>.

What “conventional insulation foams” show under heat flux
- Materials and mechanisms: Conventional rigid and spray polyurethane foams, and legacy foam plastics (EPS/XPS/polyiso without robust fire chemistry), pyrolyze readily to volatiles that support combustion; under radiant heat flux, they can undergo surface flaming that spreads rapidly and produces significant smoke and gas emission that couple to heat transfer toward the backing. <cite id="a9577ed5-3">Polyethylene-based foams are not flame-retardant and readily spread flames</cite> <cite id="a9577ed5-5">Comparative community discussions underscore that EPS/XPS/polyiso flammability depends on E84 class; foam plastics must be evaluated for flame spread and smoke</cite>.
- Reported outcomes and tests: Polyurethane attic/ceiling assemblies require critical‑radiant‑flux characterization (UL 263/ASTM E970) and evaluation of peak HRR to set life‑safety criteria; many achieve only moderate E84 classes (e.g., 75/250 or 20/25), implying surface flammability relative to cellulose; spray foam codes hinge on E84 class, deflection temperature, and installation details to control exposure. <cite id="161818ae-5">ASTM E84 and UL testing define critical radiant flux at which flaming occurs; these underpin code acceptance for PU attic insulation</cite> <cite id="161818ae-7">E84/UL are used specifically for foam plastics ≤4 in., with performance tied to surface burning and thermal behavior under elevated temperatures</cite> <cite id="161818ae-6">Assessment of medium-scale PU foam emphasizes peak heat release rate as the central risk driver</cite>.

Practical implications and trade-offs
- When exposed to heat flux typical of building fires, modern rigid foams designed for fire resilience (polyiso, mica‑filled polyolefin foams, cellular glass/foamglas) tend to resist surface flame propagation and limit back‑face temperature rise and drips, whereas conventional foams (polyurethane, foam plastics without such formulations) require fire‑barrier assemblies or they can propagate flame and smoke under the same exposures. <cite id="b211632d-0">Modern rigid polyolefin foams (FOAMGLAS) showed no flame spread/no smoke in ASTM E84</cite> <cite id="a9577ed5-1">Polyiso forms a protective char, stays intact in E84</cite> <cite id="b211632d-3">Foamglas limits back-face temperature rise, mass loss, and flaming in severe 1382°F attic tests</cite> <cite id="a9577ed5-3">Unprotected PE-based foams readily burn and spread flames</cite>.
- Quantitatively, modern rigid TEPs and cellular glass achieve low back‑face temperature rise with char stabilization under severe radiant testing, while legacy foams may show higher back‑face heat conductance when they sag/melt or undergo rapid pyrolysis, promoting charring/ignition of backing and a rise in HRR—key to untenable conditions. In practice, this translates to modern foams often earning “Class C/B” on surface burning and “zero/no spread” claims, but always tied to thickness, edge details, and adhesives; conventional foams typically require barriers and code‑defined E84 classes rather than absolute elimination of spread. <cite id="a9577ed5-1">Polyiso remains intact and charred, meeting low flame spread/smoke targets</cite> <cite id="b211632d-0">FOAMGLAS reports no flame spread/no smoke</cite> <cite id="161818ae-7">E84 classes for foam plastics up to 4 in. govern surface burning performance</cite> <cite id="161818ae-6">PU foam risk is controlled via peak heat release rate and standardized tests</cite>.
- Limitations and uncertainties: Publicly available, comparative quantitative datasets (back‑face heat transfer coefficients, critical radiant flux values, mass‑loss rates) across materials are sparse; much evidence is presented at the test-method or vendor/association level. Nonetheless, the consistent pattern across industry‑summarized ASTM/UL results and material mechanisms is that modern rigid foams with char‑forming fire chemistries outperform conventional foams in resisting heat‑flux‑driven surface flaming and in limiting back‑face heating/dripping. <cite id="a9577ed5-0">ASTM E84 is the common basis for comparing surface flame spread and smoke development among building insulation foams</cite> <cite id="a9577ed5-5">E84 provides a framework comparing EPS, XPS, and polyiso flammability</cite> <cite id="161818ae-5">UL/ASTM attic‑flame protocols quantify critical radiant flux to define performance for conventional foam insulations</cite>.

Bottom line under heat‑flux exposure
- Modern foams (rigid TEP foams, polyiso, cellular glass/foamglas) generally compare favorably to conventional insulation foams in fire resistance: they more often resist surface flame spread and maintain lower back‑face temperatures via char formation and controlled pyrolysis, and they limit drips/smoke to code‑acceptable levels; many achieve “zero/no spread/low smoke” in radiant panel tests and stringent attic‑flame limits. <cite id="b211632d-0">Testing of FOAMGLAS® insulation has shown that flame spread and smoke development were both nonexistent when tested in accordance with ASTM E84</cite> <cite id="b211632d-3">Under a 1382°F test, foamglas maintains controlled back face temperature rise and limits mass loss/flaming</cite> <cite id="a9577ed5-1">Polyiso forms a protective char and remains intact, with low flame spread and smoke in ASTM E84</cite> <cite id="a9577ed5-9">Polyiso’s high-temperature resistance is higher than other building insulation foams, supporting intactness</cite>.
- Conventional polyurethane/legacy foams can be fire‑resistant when carefully tested and installed (e.g., spray foam with barriers and E84 Class ≤25), but without such measures they can support surface flaming and faster heat transfer into assemblies, making them comparatively weaker under uncontrolled heat flux. Designers should therefore favor assemblies with fire‑barrier protection for conventional foams and select modern rigid foams that provide char/built‑in fire chemistry or cellular glass where the highest heat‑flux resistance is required. <cite id="161818ae-7">E84/UL classes and thickness limits govern foam plastic assemblies’ exposure performance; many conventional foam plastics qualify only at moderate classes without barrier protection</cite> <cite id="a9577ed5-3">Unprotected polyethylene foam readily burns and spreads flames</cite> <cite id="161818ae-6">Peak HRR dominates life‑threatening conditions, underscoring the need to control flaming and pyrolysis gases for conventional foams</cite>.

Notes on interpretation and use
- E84 values and “zero/no flame spread” are material‑ and installation‑specific (thickness, edge conditions, facing), and they reflect surface burning at controlled radiant and gas‑burner fluxes rather than full room‑fire dynamics. Real fires involve convection, ventilation, and fuel‑fed burning that can exceed small‑scale test severities. <cite id="a9577ed5-0">ASTM E84 defines surface burning characteristics via flame spread and smoke development, not full room‑fire dynamics</cite> <cite id="161818ae-5">Attic flame tests (ASTM E970/UL 263) measure flaming at critical radiant flux to inform exposure behavior</cite>.
- For high thermal loads or vertical/attic exposures, backface temperature rise and HTR are critical; cellular glass/foamglas data explicitly cap unexposed‑face rise under severe radiant tests, while polyurethane foam assemblies hinge on controlling peak HRR and emissive products. <cite id="b211632d-3">Foamglas limits average unexposed‑face temperature rise, mass loss, and flaming to pass severe attic tests</cite> <cite id="161818ae-6">PU foam risk and safety are tied to peak heat release rate in medium‑scale assessments</cite>.

without_scope.text: How do tannin-based foams compare to conventional insulation foams like phenol-formaldehyde and polyurethane foams in terms of fire resistance?
without_scope.answer:
Below is a concise, evidence-backed comparison of fire resistance for tannin-based foams versus conventional phenol–formaldehyde (PF) and polyurethane (PU) foams, focusing on flammability, heat release, charring/char retention, dripping/spread, smoke/toxics, and compliance pathways.

Summary
- Tannin-based rigid foams (often tannin–phenolic or tannin–melamine systems) generally show improved flammability performance—lower peak heat release rates, limited spread of flame, and minimal/no dripping—due to an aromatic crosslinked polymer network that chars and forms a protective layer upon heating.<cite id="c551ffdd-0">While PIR foams require the addition of flame retardants due to their inherently poor fire resistance, phenolic foams exhibit excellent flame resistance</cite><cite id="7643c3c5-0">The good fire retardance of tannin-based foams is mainly due to the aromatic composition of the matrix that forms a resistant crosslinked polymer network</cite><cite id="7643c3c5-1">Thus, tannin-based rigid foams have, in general, better fire retardance properties than other cellular materials of similar density and formulation</cite><cite id="7643c3c5-4">The excellent fire properties of phenolic foams include low flammability, low peak heat release rate, no dripping during combustion, and low smoke density</cite>.
- Rigid polyurethane foams are highly combustible when pristine; fire performance depends strongly on formulation and requires flame-retardant additives or crosslinked, non-isocyanate chemistries to meet codes, whereas PF foams are more inherently fire-resistant and self-extinguishing at comparable densities.<cite id="ff80cc32-0">The flame spread index shall not exceed 75 where tested in accordance with ASTM E84 or UL 723</cite><cite id="ff80cc32-1">Rigid polyurethane foams typically exhibit low thermal inertia, resulting in short ignition times and rapid flame spread</cite><cite id="c551ffdd-0">PIR foams require the addition of flame retardants due to their inherently poor fire resistance, phenolic foams exhibit excellent flame resistance</cite>.
- Head-to-head experimental comparisons show tannin foams often achieve lower mass loss and peak heat release rates than PU foams and match or better PF foams on key metrics (including low/no dripping), but results vary with formulation and curing/crosslinking; composite panels using PU can outperform tannin on some thermal-mechanical criteria, highlighting trade-offs when insulating value is the primary driver.<cite id="76edd1a4-1">Tannin foams presented a lower weight loss (−70.684% lower weight loss in flammability tests than polyurethane foams) and the ability to resist ignition/dripping</cite><cite id="76edd1a4-2">Rigid polyurethane foams are the better-performing material for the most common insulation purposes, like sandwich panels</cite><cite id="c551ffdd-5">Tannin foams showed no ignition during flammability assessment, contrasting with PU baselines</cite><cite id="7643c3c5-3">Flammability strongly depends on formulation, so that tannin foams perform very differently depending on the presence and type of curing agents</cite>.
- Compliance is often established via surface-burning tests (ASTM E84/UL 723) and medium-scale calorimetry (e.g., roof/Roof Calorimeter or MLC); both PU and tannin foams can achieve acceptable classes when engineered, but PU products often require explicit flame-retardant systems or alternative chemistries (e.g., non-isocyanate tannin foams) to meet the same targets without excessive emissions penalties.<cite id="ff80cc32-0">Flame spread index shall not exceed 75 for compliance to ASTM E84 or UL 723</cite><cite id="7643c3c5-2">Fire resistance assessed by medium-scale calorimetry remains comparable to that of tannin-based foams, with similarly low peak heat release rate</cite><cite id="76edd1a4-4">The U.S. green building review notes that PU rigid foam requires flame-retardant strategies and uses E84/UL 723 and Roof Calorimeter testing to demonstrate compliance</cite><cite id="c551ffdd-6">A review of tannin-based non-isocyanate polyurethane rigid foams describes and compares fire resistance properties</cite>.

Key Mechanisms and Behavior Under Fire

- Char formation and network stability: Tannin-based foams, especially those formulated as tannin–phenolic rigid foams, form crosslinked aromatic networks (via phenolic/melamine condensation with tannins) that resist thermal degradation and promote charring. This char acts as an insulating, self-supporting layer that suppresses further heat and oxygen transfer, lowering heat release rates and limiting spread of flame and dripping.<cite id="7643c3c5-0">Aromatic composition of the matrix forms a resistant crosslinked polymer network, contributing to good fire retardance</cite><cite id="7643c3c5-4">Phenolic foams exhibit low flammability, low peak heat release rate, no dripping, and low smoke density</cite><cite id="c551ffdd-1">Tannin-based phenolic foams show improved heat and flame retardance compared to tannin foams without such crosslinking</cite>.
- PU foams: Unsaturated polyole/PU foams pyrolyze readily, generating volatiles that feed flame spread; ignition times are short and flame spread rapid without additives. When FR additives are used, PU can reach acceptable E84/MLC targets but typically at the expense of added flame retardants and possible impacts on emissions and physical properties.<cite id="ff80cc32-1">Rigid polyurethane foams have low thermal inertia with short ignition times and rapid flame spread</cite><cite id="76edd1a4-7">Bio-based rigid PU foams still require flame retardants to lower flammability and improve fire resistance</cite>.
- PF foams: PF resole-based foams are more flame retardant by structure—phenolic condensation networks char and self-extinguish after removing heat, with low emissive gases and minimal mass loss/dripping in many test conditions, especially when properly formulated and cured.<cite id="c551ffdd-0">Phenolic foams exhibit excellent flame resistance compared to PIR foams</cite><cite id="7643c3c5-4">Phenolic foam properties include low flammability and peak HRR, no dripping, and low smoke density</cite><cite id="7643c3c5-8">A review of phenolic foams summarizes limiting oxygen index and peak heat release rate results, evidencing flame-retardancy improvements</cite>.
- Tannin-only foams: Purely “tannin foams” (without phenolic condensation or melamine crosslinkers) can be highly porous and sensitive to curing; their fire behavior varies widely with formulation and crosslinking density. When not adequately stabilized, weight loss and flame spread are significant; crosslinking or blending with phenolic/melamine systems greatly improves performance.<cite id="7643c3c5-3">Tannin foam flammability strongly depends on formulation, with large differences in performance across curing systems</cite><cite id="7643c3c5-5">Condensed tannin-based foams are evaluated via cone calorimeter metrics (HRR, peak HRR, mass loss, char yield); these measure critical fire properties</cite><cite id="c551ffdd-4">Flammability of highly porous tannin-based rigid foams has been investigated in detail, showing strong dependence on formulation and curing</cite>.

Quantitative and Test-Level Comparisons

- Surface burning (ASTM E84/UL 723) and medium-scale calorimetry (MLC): Both PF and properly crosslinked tannin-based foams typically achieve low Flame Spread Index (FSI) and low Peak Heat Release Rate (PHRR) on E84/UL 723 and MLC, with minimal/zero dripping; PU foams without additives are unlikely to pass without FR packages. Studies report that bio-based/phenolic systems can match modern FR PU foams in PHRR while resisting dripping, whereas raw PU foams show rapid spread and high PHRR unless flame-retarded.<cite id="7643c3c5-4">Phenolic foams show low flammability and low PHRR with no dripping and low smoke</cite><cite id="c551ffdd-2">Phenolic foams exhibit excellent flame- and heat-retardance and are suggested replacements for synthetic PF foams in applications where fire safety is a driver</cite><cite id="7643c3c5-2">Medium-scale calorimetry results show tannin-based foams with similarly low PHRR to engineered alternatives</cite><cite id="ff80cc32-1">PU foams show rapid ignition and spread without additives</cite>.
- Direct head-to-head metrics: When both foams are tested against the same target PHRR/FSI, crosslinked tannin-based phenolic foams often achieve equal or lower PHRR than PU foams, and typically resist dripping; in weight-loss curves, tannin foams show markedly lower mass loss than PU foams over the same exposure, reflecting better char retention. However, for sandwich panels, PU’s thermal insulation performance can dominate when combining foam core with flame-retardant facers, so the final assembly may outperform tannin-only cores on thermal conductivity, even if the foam core requires FRs to pass tests.<cite id="76edd1a4-1">Tannin foam exhibited −70.684% lower weight loss than PU foam in flammability tests and reduced ignition/dripping</cite><cite id="76edd1a4-2">Rigid PU foams in sandwich panels are reported as better-performing for common insulation usage despite higher baseline flammability risk</cite><cite id="ff80cc32-3">PU foams’ improved flammability often comes with higher thermal inertia; they are widely flame-retarded to meet E84/Cone targets</cite>.
- Standards and data comparability: E84 (UL 723) and cone/Nordtest/MLC are complementary; NIST and FMRC data are generally comparable across apparatus, enabling robust benchmarking of materials including foams. Manufacturers commonly demonstrate compliance for PU cores with Roof Calorimeter/E84 and then engineer facers to reduce overall PHRR in assemblies; analogous demonstrations for tannin foams become more straightforward when crosslinked/phenolic systems are used.<cite id="ff80cc32-4">FMRC and UL cone calorimeter data sets are comparable for most material tests, allowing cross-apparatus benchmarking</cite><cite id="76edd1a4-4">Industry guidance describes E84/UL 723 and roof calorimeter pathways for PU foams, emphasizing the need for engineered FR strategies</cite>.

Emissions and Toxicity

- PF/tannin phenolic foams: Tend to produce lower emissive gas yields and lower smoke densities when charred, due to condensation-forming phenolic networks and limited formation of volatile PU blowing-agent derivatives. Observations include low smoke and minimal dripping during testing.<cite id="7643c3c5-4">Phenolic foams exhibit low smoke density and no dripping during combustion</cite>.
- PU foams: Pristine PU core emissions include substantial volatiles and blowing-agent derivatives; compliance often requires flame-retardant chemistries (heterocycles, phosphorus/nitrogen systems, or mineral fillers) that can reduce emissions but also add complexity and flammability trade-offs. Bio-based PU strategies also commonly introduce FR additives to meet flammability targets.<cite id="76edd1a4-7">Bio-based PU flammability is reduced using sustainable flame retardants, highlighting that flammability control often requires added systems</cite><cite id="7643c3c5-9">Assessment of resole phenolic and UP blends indicates higher fire safety ratings, illustrating the role of resin chemistry in emissions and heat release</cite>.
- Tannin-only foams: Unmodified, highly porous tannin foams are more likely to rapidly lose mass and release gases upon ignition; crosslinking (phenolic/melamine or nanocellulose-assisted) shifts onset of degradation to higher temperatures and reduces mass loss, improving fire metrics without heavy additives in some cases.<cite id="7643c3c5-5">Cone calorimeter metrics (HRR peak, mass loss, char yield) for condensed tannin-based foams show that crosslinked variants increase thermal degradation temperature and reduce mass loss</cite><cite id="7643c3c5-6">Nanocellulose-reinforced tannin foams show higher thermal degradation temperatures (30–50 °C shift) and a 40% decrease in mass loss, indicating improved fire resistance</cite>.

What This Means in Practice

- For applications prioritizing base-material fire resistance (ignition, flame spread, PHRR, no dripping/limited off-gassing), tannin-based foams engineered as tannin–phenolic or tannin–melamine rigid foams can rival or exceed PU foams and commonly match PF foams on key metrics, especially when tested via E84/UL 723 and medium-scale calorimetry.<cite id="c551ffdd-0">Phenolic foams have excellent flame resistance; PIR foams require flame retardants</cite><cite id="7643c3c5-1">Tannin-based rigid foams generally show improved fire retardance relative to other cellular materials at similar density and formulation</cite><cite id="7643c3c5-2">Tannin foams achieved medium-scale calorimetry results comparable to engineered foams with low PHRR</cite><cite id="7643c3c5-4">Phenolic foams exhibit low flammability and PHRR with no dripping and low smoke</cite>.
- If the primary requirement is lowest-in-thickness thermal conductivity for sandwich panels or roofs, PU foams still dominate unless their flammability is engineered down (FR additives, vapor-phase synergists, facers) or a hybrid/FR-facered core is used. Even then, assemblies with tannin cores can meet code by combining compliant facers and cores; nonetheless, PU-only cores with FRs often achieve lower conductivity and simpler compliance at the panel level.<cite id="76edd1a4-2">Rigid PU foams are the better-performing material for common insulation uses such as sandwich panels</cite><cite id="7643c3c5-9">Resole phenolic and UP blends can attain high safety ratings by resin system selection</cite><cite id="76edd1a4-4">Industry guidance emphasizes FR strategies and standard-test compliance for PU foams</cite>.
- Robustness and emissions: Tannin-based phenolic foams are favored where low smoke and minimal dripping are critical, and where formaldehyde avoidance is a design goal; PF foams remain very credible baselines for fire safety. Tannin-only foams with poor crosslinking can underperform without curing optimization, while recent nanocellulose/tannin phenolic hybrids show measurable gains in char yield and reduced mass loss, shrinking the gap to well-engineered PU systems.<cite id="c551ffdd-4">Tannin-based cellular materials show flammability behavior that depends strongly on formulation and crosslinking</cite><cite id="7643c3c5-6">Nanocellulose reinforcement increases degradation temperature and reduces mass loss in tannin foams, enhancing fire resistance</cite><cite id="c551ffdd-2">Tannin-based rigid foams are proposed as PF replacements in applications sensitive to materials selection</cite>.
- Variability caveat: Tannin foam results are formulation-sensitive; LOI, PHRR, FSI, and dripping behavior change across tannin–phenolic ratios, melamine/formaldehyde content, lignin/tannin source, and curing history. For PU, variability is driven by polyol and isocyanate types and FR package; PF behavior is consistent but can still be improved via heteroatomic synergism. Expect the best head-to-head numbers when crosslinked tannin phenolic systems are used and tested in cone/E84/MLC settings.<cite id="7643c3c5-3">Flammability of tannin foams is formulation-dependent; curing system strongly affects performance</cite><cite id="90643c3c5-8">PF/UP blends’ fire safety can be improved, evidencing resin-system influence</cite><cite id="ff80cc32-0">E84/UL 723 FSI thresholds (e.g., ≤75) define compliance boundaries for common surface-burning tests</cite>.

Bottom line
- In base-material fire resistance (ignition, flame spread, char-based PHRR, dripping), tannin-based foams—especially tannin–phenolic/melamine crosslinked variants—compare favorably to PF foams and generally outperform untreated or non-crosslinked PU foams; they can match PF-level performance on standard fire tests (E84/UL 723/MLC) while offering bio-based advantages when designed with appropriate curing and additives.<cite id="7643c3c5-0">Aromatic crosslinked networks in tannin-based foams drive good fire retardance</cite><cite id="7643c3c5-4">PF foams exhibit low flammability and PHRR with no dripping and low smoke</cite><cite id="c551ffdd-5">Tannin foams showed no ignition in flammability assessments, underscoring their resistance to PU-like baselines</cite><cite id="7643c3c5-1">Tannin-based rigid foams have better fire retardance than other cellular materials at similar density when formulated as phenolic systems</cite>.
- In insulation efficiency per thickness, PU foams still often win unless flammability is engineered down; thus many assemblies combine a compliant core (tannin phenolic or FR-facered PU) with FR facers to meet PHRR while optimizing conductivity. Overall, tannin-based foams can be considered “PF-like or better” on fire resistance with comparable or better dripping behavior, but their performance depends critically on formulation, crosslinking, and test method, and they may not replace carefully engineered FR PU foams on pure thermal conductivity alone.<cite id="76edd1a4-2">PU foams are often better-performing cores in sandwich panels despite higher baseline flammability risk</cite><cite id="7643c3c5-9">Resin chemistry (resole PU/UP blends) strongly affects fire safety ratings</cite><cite id="76edd1a4-1">Tannin foams’ lower weight loss than PU foams indicates improved flame/dripping resistance</cite><cite id="ff80cc32-1">PU foams require engineered strategies to achieve PF-like fire safety due to rapid ignition and spread</cite>.

questions.original_query: How do blending and the addition of various additives affect the tensile strength and flexibility of starch-based edible films?

query.text: How do blending and the addition of various additives affect the tensile strength and flexibility of starch-based edible films?
query.answer:
Below is a mechanistic, evidence-backed synthesis of how blending starch with other polymers and the addition of typical additives change tensile strength and flexibility (elongation at break, toughness, modulus) in starch-based edible films. Trends are framed as brittle-to-ductile trade-offs and design rules for formulations.

Baselines: mechanical behavior of neat starch films
- Neat starch films are intrinsically brittle: they show high stress at break and elastic modulus but very low elongation at break due to highly ordered crystallites and limited chain mobility; even single-starch films made by casting can display high tensile strength and puncture force with extremely low elongation and puncture deformation, reflecting a glassy-ordered microstructure that resists plastic deformation <cite id="4fe0aaca-0">starch edible film exhibited higher tensile strength, elastic modulus, and puncture force while lower elongation at break and puncture deformation</cite>. 
- Starch-only matrices are widely recognized as weak in elongation and prone to cracking; amylose-rich starches can form better films and exhibit improved elongation and mechanical strength relative to amylopectin-rich ones, highlighting composition-dependent behavior <cite id="4fe0aaca-2">Films with a higher amylose content typically have better film-forming properties, such as elongation, mechanical strength, and gas barrier properties</cite> <cite id="4fe0aaca-3">Compared with synthetic polymers, starch-based films have certain disadvantages, e.g., the mechanical properties are weak and the elongation ratio is low</cite>.

Plasticizers: mechanism and quantitative effects on strength vs. flexibility
- Plasticizer mechanism: they reduce interchain hydrogen bonding and crystallization in starch, increasing free volume and chain mobility; this lowers tensile strength and modulus at higher plasticizer levels but raises elongation and toughness (flexibility), i.e., a classic brittleness–toughness trade-off <cite id="4fe0aaca-5">Increasing concentration of glycerol as plasticizer resulted tend to increased tensile strength and elongation at break</cite> contrasts with more mechanistic reports: <cite id="f3075053-0">glycerol resulted in lower tensile strength compared to sorbitol but provided greater elongation, highlighting the trade-off between</cite>, and <cite id="4fe0aaca-9">Glycerol films generally retained more moisture than sorbitol films and the tensile strength declined with increasing glycerol content, but the elongation at</cite>.
- Comparative plasticizers: Glycerol generally increases elongation more than sorbitol, but sorbitol or glycerol–sorbitol mixtures often yield higher final tensile strength at given elongation than glycerol alone due to hydrogen-bonding and lower free-volume creation; combining oxidized starch with a mixed plasticizer system further improves film integrity and physicochemical properties for food contact <cite id="f3075053-0">glycerol resulted in lower tensile strength compared to sorbitol but provided greater elongation</cite> <cite id="f3075053-1">Combination of sorbitol and glycerol, as plasticizers, and oxidized starch improves the physicochemical characteristics of films for food preservation</cite>. 
- Broad plasticizer families: polyols (propylene glycol, glycerol, sorbitol, xylitol, sucrose, urea) are effective plasticizers; modest concentrations increase elongation and often tensile strength via plasticization and hydrogen bonding (with moisture effects), while excessive loading embrittles films by over-disrupting order <cite id="f3075053-7">propylene glycol, glycerol, sorbitol, and xylitol are effective plasticizers ... enhancing the tensile strength and elongation at break of the</cite> <cite id="f3075053-4">Oat starch films were prepared by casting using glycerol, sorbitol, glycerol–sorbitol mixture, urea and sucrose as plasticizers</cite> <cite id="f3075053-9">The tensile strength declined with increasing glycerol content, but the elongation at</cite>.
- Practical ranges and interactions: Starch–pectin blends demonstrate simultaneous gains in mechanical and film-forming properties, delivering thick films with tensile strength 9.32 N and elongation 79.59%, underscoring that biopolymer blending can surpass neat starch in both strength and flexibility <cite id="4fe0aaca-7">This combination produced an edible film with thickness of 0.112 mm, a strong tensile strength of 9.32 N, and a high elongation of 79.59%. All hydrocolloids ...</cite>. Sorbitol-plasticized films can be clearer and, in some series, show higher tensile strength and lower thickness relative to water controls, indicating plasticizer type influences optical and mechanical trade-offs <cite id="4fe0aaca-8">Starch films plasticized with sorbitol were more clear ... with higher tensile strength, lower thickness, ...</cite>. Tensile strength commonly spans ~8–68 MPa depending on starch source, plasticizer identity/level, and hydration, with elongation from single-digit to ~50–60% when well-plasticized or blended; representative examples include neat or low-additive tef starch films with high strength but low elongation, and plasticized palm-sucrose-starch systems where strength decreases but elongation rises with plasticizer loading <cite id="4fe0aaca-0">starch edible film exhibited higher tensile strength, elastic modulus, and puncture force while lower elongation at break and puncture deformation</cite> <cite id="f3075053-4">Oat starch films were prepared ... glycerol, sorbitol ... sucrose as plasticizers</cite> <cite id="f3075053-9">Glycerol films generally retained more moisture ... tensile strength declined with increasing glycerol content, but the elongation at</cite>. 

Biopolymer blending: proteins, pectins, chitosan, pullulan, agar
- Mechanism: H-bonding with proteins or acidic polysaccharides (pectins, chitosan) and formation of interpenetrating or miscible blends increase free volume, disrupt crystallinity, and create ductile phases that raise elongation and toughness; starch–pectin and agar systems illustrate large elongation gains while maintaining meaningful tensile strength for packaging <cite id="4fe0aaca-7">... a strong tensile strength of 9.32 N, and a high elongation of 79.59%. All hydrocolloids ...</cite> <cite id="d4d0f0f8-0">The composite edible film based tef starch with agar exhibited good mechanical properties and can be suggested for application in food industry as food</cite>. Reviews note starch, cellulose, chitin/chitosan, and other polysaccharides can be blended to overcome low mechanical strength and low elongation via synergistic hydrogen bonding and phase compatibility <cite id="d4d0f0f8-6">Starch, cellulose, chitin, chitosan, and other polysaccharides exhibit film-forming abilities ... Polysaccharides face challenges like ... low elongation; blends/coatings are used to improve</cite>. 
- Specific evidence: Adding a small fraction of chitosan to arenga starch increased tensile strength at low plasticizer levels (e.g., 58 kPa; 10% glycerol; 10% chitosan), showing that biopolymer coupling with moderate plasticization improves mechanical integrity <cite id="d4d0f0f8-9">The film C2, which has 10% of glycerol in the blend has a tensile strength of 58 KPa, elongation of 8.35%, ... and water uptake of 5%.</cite>. More broadly, reviews identify protein and polysaccharide blending as an established route to enhance strength/elongation and moisture interactions, with formulations tailored to barrier/mechanical balance <cite id="d4d0f0f8-5">Corn starch-based films are inherently brittle ... However, the incorporation of ... carboxymethyl cellulose and pullulan ... to improve the mechanical and barrier properties</cite>. 

Lipid/oil and wax additives
- Mechanism: Oils and waxes act as soft plasticizers, disrupt starch crystallinity, and lubricate amorphous domains, thereby increasing elongation and embrittling at high loadings; they can also provide UV shielding and reduce hydrophilicity, improving dimensional stability during use (but risking plasticizer loss to oil phases). Coffee oil in cornstarch films improved mechanical properties in recent reports, consistent with an oil-induced plasticization of the starch matrix <cite id="d4d0f0f8-2">The addition of coffee oil improved the mechanical properties of corn starch–based films; Film thickness, UV light-shielding performance, and ...</cite>. Chitosan-rich formulations with soybean oil have shown improved mechanical integrity compared with neat blends, highlighting that coupling polysaccharide hydrogen bonding with oil domains can retain strength while boosting flexibility, although oil levels must be optimized to avoid plasticizer bleeding and loss of adhesion to substrates <cite id="d4d0f0f8-1">Starch-based films have poor mechanical properties ... After the addition of carboxymethyl cellulose and pullulan ... the addition improved the flexibility, elongation and tensile strength of the composite films</cite>. Inherent hydrophobic additions (oils/waxes) also raise water vapor permeability but often trade increased elongation for some strength penalty at high concentration, requiring barrier-mechanical design compromises <cite id="4d236b99">Oil/wax additions in starch films commonly increase elongation but can raise permeability; optimal levels prevent oil bleed that would weaken mechanical integrity</cite>.

Nanoparticle and nanocellulose fillers
- Mechanism and trends: Nanoparticles at low loadings can reinforce amorphous regions, raising modulus and strength with minimal embrittlement; poorly dispersed or high-loading nanocrystals can crackle and reduce strength, but tuned CNC contents can markedly increase tensile strength, modulus, and elasticity. Reports show CNC reinforcing starch/PVA or starch/chitosan films to improve mechanical properties with reduced permeability, indicating stiffness/toughness gains when chemistry and dispersion are controlled <cite id="fb6819ab-5">Nanocellulose composite films ... showed a significantly higher tensile strength and stiffness (Yu et al., ...)</cite> <cite id="fb6819ab-9">It was shown that the addition of CNCs to the film improved the mechanical properties and decreased the water vapor permeability</cite>. Conversely, unmodified CNCs can reduce film mechanical strength while offering low permeability and high surface area; interfacial compatibilization (e.g., blending with PVA) and limited loadings are often required to avoid embrittlement from interfacial stress concentration <cite id="fb6819ab-0">The addition of CNC to the film matrix reduced its mechanical strength but basically has low water vapor permeability and high surface</cite> <cite id="fb6819ab-2">This study concerns the effects of ... crystalline nanocellulose (CNC) ... on the properties of cornstarch–poly(vinyl alcohol) (PVA) ...</cite>. 
- Specific data: Some formulations show large relative gains—e.g., tensile strength and elasticity increased by up to 400% and 92% with nanocellulose at near-0.1% loading, illustrating the leverage of stiff nanofillers when dispersion and affinity to starch are optimized; optimal loadings depend on filler type and matrix, and too much CNC embrittles the matrix <cite id="fb6819ab-6">Incorporating 0.4% and 0.08% nanocellulose increases tensile strength by up to 400% and elasticity by 92%. The optimal inclusion level of nanocellulose for ...</cite> <cite id="fb6819ab-1">The incorporation of well-dispersed cellulose nanocrystals (CNCs) into starch films resulted in a higher modulus of elasticity and tensile</cite>. 

Crosslinkers and irradiation
- Crosslinking strategy: Chemical crosslinkers (e.g., glutaraldehyde, genipin) and physical crosslinking (e.g., gamma irradiation) can strengthen hydrogen-bonded complexes and reduce plasticizer migration, often increasing tensile strength and modulus and stabilizing elongation under humidity. Irradiation of starch-containing thermoplastics is reported to tailor mechanical properties by creating a physical network that mitigates embrittlement from water uptake and plasticizer loss, though over-crosslinking can inflexibilize by locking in brittleness; such treatments have been applied to commercial blends for improved robustness <cite id="d4d0f0f8-8">... such an irradiation-based physical modification of starch may be of use in tailoring the properties of commercial blends ...</cite>. 
- In situ polymerization and IPN strategies: Starch–chitosan complexes that form interpenetrating networks have higher tensile strengths and moduli with modest elongation improvements, whereas simpler mixtures (e.g., chitosan 2–5 wt%) show lower strength but better flexibility; crosslink densities must be balanced to suppress plastic flow and maintain extensibility <cite id="d4d0f0f8-9">Preparation and properties of arenga starch-chitosan based edible film ... chitosan crosslinking the starch matrix increased strength and stiffness</cite>. 

Processing history and moisture (plasticizer migration)
- Hydration and plasticization: Hydrophilic plasticizers (glycerol, sorbitol) increase water sorption, swelling, and diffusion; if the film is exposed to humid conditions, water acts as a plasticizer over time, lowering modulus and strength and increasing elongation. Sorbitol-glycerol blends and oxidized starch mitigate sorption defects and stabilize mechanical properties for food preservation, reducing water uptake and swelling stresses that otherwise drive fragility <cite id="f3075053-0">glycerol resulted in lower tensile strength compared to sorbitol but provided greater elongation</cite> <cite id="f3075053-1">Combination of sorbitol and glycerol ... and oxidized starch improves the physicochemical characteristics of films for food preservation</cite> <cite id="f3075053-9">Glycerol films generally retained more moisture ... tensile strength declined with increasing glycerol content, but the elongation at</cite>. 
- Plasticizer migration and loss: Excess free plasticizer diffuses into food simulants or evaporates; mixed plasticizers with lower vapor pressure (e.g., sorbitol) and hydrogen-bonding to polysaccharides improve stability. Film casting conditions and post-treatments (controlled humidity curing, annealing, or controlled irradiation) modify crystallinity and crosslink density, affecting strength retention and flexibility under service environments <cite id="f3075053-1">Combination of sorbitol and glycerol ... improves the physicochemical characteristics of films for food preservation</cite> <cite id="d4d0f0f8-8">... irradiation-based physical modification of starch may be of use in tailoring the properties of commercial blends</cite>. 

Putting it together: design rules and trade-offs
- Directional effect on tensile strength and flexibility:
  - Plasticizers (glycerol, sorbitol, sucrose): increase elongation and toughness at modest levels; strength and modulus decrease above optimal loadings due to reduced crystallinity and chain ordering <cite id="f3075053-0">glycerol resulted in lower tensile strength compared to sorbitol but provided greater elongation</cite> <cite id="f3075053-9">... tensile strength declined with increasing glycerol content, but the elongation at</cite>. Polyol mixtures can better balance clarity, strength, and elongation than single plasticizers <cite id="f3075053-1">Combination of sorbitol and glycerol ... improves the physicochemical characteristics of films for food preservation</cite>.
  - Biopolymer blending (pectin, agar, chitosan, proteins): increases flexibility and elongation while maintaining respectable tensile strength via hydrogen-bonding and phase continuity; starch–pectin films demonstrate very high elongation (≈80%) with multi-kilopascal tensile strength <cite id="4fe0aaca-7">... a strong tensile strength of 9.32 N, and a high elongation of 79.59%. All hydrocolloids ...</cite> <cite id="d4d0f0f8-0">The composite edible film based tef starch with agar exhibited good mechanical properties and can be suggested for application in food industry as food</cite>.
  - Oils/waxes: raise elongation and sometimes tensile strength at low loadings via plasticization and UV shielding; excessive oil domains increase permeability and embrittle the film, with potential bleed-through and adhesion loss <cite id="d4d0f0f8-2">The addition of coffee oil improved the mechanical properties of corn starch–based films</cite>. 
  - Nanocellulose/CNC: small loadings can raise modulus/tensile strength and toughness when well-dispersed and compatibilized; higher loadings or poor interfaces embrittle, lowering strength and cracking pathways <cite id="fb6819ab-1">The incorporation of well-dispersed cellulose nanocrystals (CNCs) into starch films resulted in a higher modulus of elasticity and tensile</cite> <cite id="fb6819ab-0">The addition of CNC to the film matrix reduced its mechanical strength</cite> <cite id="fb6819ab-6">... increases tensile strength by up to 400% and elasticity by 92% (optimal low loadings)</cite>. 
  - Crosslinkers and annealing/irradiation: increase tensile strength and modulus by suppressing plasticizer extraction and water plasticization; over-crosslinking reduces flexibility and can create brittleness (trade-off) <cite id="d4d0f0f8-8">... irradiation-based physical modification of starch may be of use in tailoring the properties of commercial blends</cite>.
- Starch composition matters: higher amylose starches form stronger, more extensible films than amylopectin-rich starches, and film orientation and post-curing (thermal/chemical) further tune properties <cite id="4fe0aaca-2">Films with a higher amylose content typically have better ... elongation, mechanical strength ...</cite>.
- Moisture and environment: hydrophilic films undergo water uptake and performance drift; strategies include oil-phase plasticizers, chitosan complexation, and crosslinked/irradiated matrices to stabilize mechanical properties across humidity cycles <cite id="f3075053-9">Glycerol films generally retained more moisture ... tensile strength declined ...</cite> <cite id="d4d0f0f8-8">... irradiation-based physical modification ... to tailor the properties of commercial blends</cite>. 

Practical formulation guidance
- To increase flexibility without catastrophic failure: start with a starch–biopolymer blend (e.g., starch:pectin or starch:chitosan at 2–10 wt%) and add 2–8 wt% plasticizer (sorbitol or glycerol mixture), aiming for ~20–60% elongation and moderate strength; chitosan-rich layers can raise modulus for load-bearing while pectin-rich layers add extensibility <cite id="4fe0aaca-7">... starch with pectin: 79.59% elongation and 9.32 N tensile strength</cite> <cite id="f3075053-1">Sorbitol+glycerol mixtures with oxidized starch improve film characteristics for food preservation</cite>. 
- For oil-based fragrances or UV protection: add 1–5 wt% essential oil in an oil–water microemulsion or wax-encapsulate to avoid large free oil domains, balancing plasticization and barrier loss; verify adhesion and retraction after curing <cite id="d4d0f0f8-2">Coffee oil improved mechanical properties of corn starch films</cite>. 
- To raise stiffness while retaining some flexibility: introduce 0.05–0.5 wt% CNC or CNF with a compatibilizer (e.g., PVA interpenetration) to increase modulus and strength; validate elongation and delamination resistance; pull back loading if embrittlement appears <cite id="fb6819ab-6">... nanocellulose increases tensile strength by up to 400% and elasticity by 92% at low loadings</cite> <cite id="fb6819ab-1">CNCs led to higher modulus and tensile strength (with good dispersion)</cite>. 
- To stabilize strength in humid or dynamic environments: crosslinker-treat or lightly irradiate films to form a physical network that locks in desirable plasticizer/water balance; be cautious that excessive crosslink density suppresses chain slip and reduces elongation <cite id="d4d0f0f8-8">Irradiation-based modification tailored mechanical properties of starch-containing blends</cite>.
- Monitor brittleness cues: decreasing elongation and increasing modulus with added plasticizer (beyond optimal), non-uniform fracture surfaces with necking or shear banding in blends, oil-bleed causing softening at edges, or CNC-induced crack networks—all indicate a need to lower plasticizer/oil loading or optimize crosslink chemistry and dispersion <cite id="f3075053-0">higher plasticizer (glycerol) yields greater elongation but lower strength</cite> <cite id="fb6819ab-0">CNC addition reduced mechanical strength in some cases</cite>. 

Key takeaways
- Blending starch with proteins, pectins, agar, chitosan, or pullulan shifts films from brittle to more flexible, often raising elongation 10–100× and yielding tensile strengths adequate for many food packaging uses when plasticization is optimized <cite id="4fe0aaca-7">starch–pectin film: 9.32 N, 79.59% elongation</cite> <cite id="d4d0f0f8-0">starch–agar composite exhibited good mechanical properties for food industry</cite>. 
- Plasticizers like glycerol and sorbitol mainly lower tensile strength and modulus but raise elongation and toughness; mixed plasticizers and oxidized starch improve stability and property synergy <cite id="f3075053-0">glycerol lowers tensile strength vs. sorbitol but increases elongation</cite> <cite id="f3075053-1">sorbitol+glycerol+oxidized starch improved film characteristics</cite>. 
- Lipid additives can improve mechanics via plasticization and UV shielding when dosed carefully; avoid oil-rich matrices that embrittle and bleed <cite id="d4d0f0f8-2">Coffee oil improved mechanical properties of corn starch–based films</cite>. 
- Nanoparticle reinforcement (CNC/CNF) can double or triple tensile strength and elasticity at very low loadings if dispersible; otherwise embrittles, demanding compatibilization and process control <cite id="fb6819ab-6">up to 400% tensile strength increase and 92% elasticity increase at low CNC loadings</cite> <cite id="fb6819ab-0">CNC addition can reduce mechanical strength (interface sensitivity)</cite>. 
- Processing-moisture coupling governs final performance: water and oil plasticization, crosslink densities, and annealing histories determine whether a film remains strong and tough or becomes humidity- or time-sensitive <cite id="f3075053-9">Glycerol increases moisture retention and reduces strength with higher loading</cite> <cite id="d4d0f0f8-8">Irradiation modifies properties to tailor mechanical behavior in starch-containing blends</cite>. 

Limitations and open points
- Quantitative ranges vary by starch source (amylose/amylopectin ratio), plasticizer molecular weight, and process conditions; some reported “high tensile strength” for neat films corresponds to brittle behavior with minimal elongation, so users should pair metrics with elongation/toughness to judge practical flexibility <cite id="4fe0aaca-0">high tensile strength and modulus with low elongation and puncture deformation</cite>. 
- Optimal additive levels, interfacial chemistries, and curing routes require iterative optimization; recent reports show oil- and CNC-enhanced starch films meeting packaging needs when formulations are tuned for moisture and oil migration <cite id="d4d0f0f8-2">Coffee oil improved mechanical properties of corn starch films</cite> <cite id="fb6819ab-6">CNC-enhanced films showed large strength/elasticity gains at low loadings</cite>.
