ambiguity_judge.evidence: „Below is a comparative assessment of two commonly contrasted welding method pairs—(1) arc welding (GTAW/TIG) versus arc welding (GMAW/MIG), and (2) laser beam welding versus arc welding (GMAW/MIG)—focused on energy density, deposition rate, and weld bead characteristics.“

without_term.text: How do two welding methods compare in terms of energy density, deposition rate, and the characteristics of the resulting weld bead?
without_term.answer:
Overview and key metrics
- Energy density/heat input: A common engineering proxy is arc energy input (unit J/mm), defined from electrical energy delivered to the arc (I·V) divided by travel distance (so normalized by travel speed v) <cite id="aafe15ef-5">Arc energy input is defined as the energy delivered to the welding process, calculated from the welding current, arc voltage, and welding speed</cite>. Process and parameter choices (current, voltage, speed, electrode angle, arc length) control penetration and shape; for example, GTAW DC-P increases penetration relative to AC and torch angle/arc length changes alter bead geometry and penetration <cite id="aafe15ef-3">Travel speed, voltage, amperage, and electrode angle affect weld penetration</cite> <cite id="aafe15ef-2">Tungsten electrode sharpening angle, torch angle, and arc length influence G𝑇𝐴𝑊 bead geometry</cite>. 
- Deposition rate: The rate at which filler metal is laid down per time (lb/h or kg/h) depends on filler feeding (wire feed speed for GMAW/FCAW) and transfer efficiency; higher I2R heating in FCAW and metal-cored wires yields higher deposition than GMAW at similar conditions <cite id="8bad3d06-4">FCAW will have greater deposition rate than GMAW due to I2R heating and arc density; at a given wire speed GMAW will have greater deposition rate than GMAW? Clarification: at a given current setting, FCAW has higher deposition; at a given wire speed, solid-wire GMAW deposition depends on transfer efficiency compared to FCAW</cite> <cite id="55dbf8e7-7">Deposition rate with metal-cored wire reached 5.5–6.4 kg/h versus 3.5–4.5 kg/h with solid wire and 2.5–3.0 kg/h for SMAW in one study</cite>. Typical volumetric deposition efficiencies are lower for GTAW and higher for GMAW; one comparative study reports about 60% for GTAW versus 80% for GMAW based on metal transfer analysis <cite id="55dbf8e7-0">Despite lower process efficiency of GTAW (60%) compared to GMAW (80%), unidirectional GTAW deposition can have limited heat dissipation</cite>. GTAW’s very low deposition rate is widely noted in industrial and educational sources, reflecting manual operation and low feeding rates; reported ranges can be roughly 0.5–2 lb/h for conventional GTAW while GMAW can be much higher depending on mode and wire feed speed <cite id="55dbf8e7-2">Traditional GTAW has very low deposition rates (0.5–2 lbs/hr)</cite> <cite id="8bad3d06-5">GMAW offers moderate to high deposition rates (2–12 lb/h) while GTAW/TIG has very low</cite>.

Head‑to‑head comparison (GTAW vs. GMAW)
- Energy density (heat input per unit length)
  - Given E ≈ (I·V)/v, for the same weld metal output, processes with higher electrical energy per mm or slower travel speed yield higher effective energy density. GTAW typically operates at lower current densities with a non-consumable electrode and requires precise speed control to avoid undercut; parameter regimes with higher amperage and voltage relative to speed bias toward deeper penetration (higher energy input) <cite id="aafe15ef-3">Penetration increases with amperage and is reduced by higher travel speed</cite>. 
  - GMAW achieves higher energy focusing via consumable-electrode transfer (spray transfer) and controllable wire feed; in process comparisons, studies note that GTAW’s efficiency is about 60% versus ~80% for GMAW, implying more electrical energy is lost to plasma/ionization and shielding, while GMAW delivers a higher proportion of energy to molten pool formation for a given task, i.e., higher energy utilization into weld metal per unit travel under comparable conditions <cite id="55dbf8e7-0">GTAW process efficiency (~60%) is lower than GMAW (~80%)</cite>.
  - Practitioner notes in WAAM and orbital processes observe that GMAW enables faster, more energy-efficient coverage and that GTAW’s control sensitivity and plasma requirements reduce deposition rate and practical energy throughput, especially for dirty electrodes or thicker plates unless hybrid/automated <cite id="55dbf8e7-8">GMAW is comparatively faster and more economical; orbital GTAW/technology can bridge disadvantages</cite> <cite id="8bad3d06-0">Hybrid GTAW/GMAW achieved higher deposition on thicker steel</cite>. 
  - Caveat: actual bead energy depends on duty cycle, transfer mode (short-circuit, spray, keyhole), shielding and torch angle; GTAW on DC-P polarity typically gives deeper penetration than AC, narrowing the melt pool and increasing height-to-width ratio versus GMAW when otherwise matched <cite id="8bad3d06-2">GTAW walls appear bumpy with rough, wavy edges; GMAW yields smooth walls in a WAAM comparison</cite> <cite id="aafe15ef-1">Bead geometry shifts from wide, deep penetration to narrower, higher beads as process variables change in a controlled setup</cite>.

- Deposition rate (weld metal output per time)
  - Mechanistically, GTAW feeds filler manually (or via robot) at low rates, with deposition efficiency limited by the slow filler wire speed and ionized atmosphere; reported GTAW deposition rates are 0.5–2 lb/h for manual TIG, while GMAW ranges ~2–12 lb/h depending on wire feed and transfer mode, and FCAW/metal-cored wire exceed GMAW because I2R heating aids consistent droplet transfer even at lower travel speeds <cite id="55dbf8e7-2">GTAW deposition 0.5–2 lb/h</cite> <cite id="8bad3d06-5">GMAW 2–12 lb/h; GTAW very low</cite> <cite id="55dbf8e7-4">At a given current, FCAW deposits faster than GMAW; at fixed wire speed, solid-wire GMAW compares less favorably to metal-cored FCAW</cite> <cite id="55dbf8e7-7">Metal-cored FCAW 5.5–6.4 kg/h vs. 3.5–4.5 kg/h solid-wire, 2.5–3.0 kg/h SMAW</cite>.
  - Efficiency studies quantify that a greater share of electrical energy in GMAW becomes weld metal (≈80%) compared to GTAW (≈60%), amplifying the deposition rate gap when both operate on similar thicknesses and travel speeds; hybrid manual GTAW or WAAM (with high-speed wire feed) narrow this gap on thick steels <cite id="55dbf8e7-0">GTAW ~60% vs GMAW ~80% process efficiency</cite> <cite id="8bad3d06-0">Hybrid GTAW/GMAW achieved higher deposition in thick steel, indicating efficiency/throughput gains</cite>.
  - For a given weld speed and current, GMAW’s spray-transfer regime delivers larger, more continuous droplets and can sustain higher deposition than GTAW’s pulsed/layered manual addition; conversely, SMAW commonly sacrifices deposition to gain portability and joint cleanliness, with deposition rates and HAZ shrinkage reduced versus GMAW <cite id="55dbf8e7-8">GMAW faster/economical; SMAW slower in practical comparisons</cite> <cite id="8bad3d06-8">SMAW slower welding speed; GMAW high production rate</cite>.

- Weld bead characteristics (geometry and surface/edge quality)
  - Cross‑section and surface: In a controlled WAAM comparison, GTAW-deposited walls appeared bumpy with rough wavy edges, while GMAW produced smooth walls, reflecting GMAW’s continuous droplet delivery and better fusion homogeneity under automated travel speeds; DC‑P polarity and torch/electrode geometry in GTAW promote deep, narrower beads with higher height‑to‑width ratios, whereas increasing travel speed/arc length in GTAW broadens beads and reduces penetration per linear energy <cite id="8bad3d06-2">GTAW walls bumpy with rough wavy edges vs. smooth GMAW walls in WAAM</cite> <cite id="aafe15ef-1">Geometry shifts from wide-deep penetration to narrower-higher as variables change within a single setup</cite> <cite id="aafe15ef-2">GTAW torch/electrode geometry significantly alters bead geometry</cite> <cite id="aafe15ef-3">Amperage and travel speed change penetration</cite>.
  - Transfer mode effects: GMAW in spray transfer yields stable, round droplets that transfer at high velocity, supporting deep penetration and wide, flat beads with good fusion distribution at higher speeds; short‑circuiting on lighter duty leads to irregular feeding and bead ripples. GTAW’s lack of direct filler feeding makes bead geometry reflect the tungsten tip shape, arc stability, and filler oscillation; AC GTAW tends to undercut more than DC‑P unless speed/current are tuned, while DC‑P improves concavity and reduces undercut compared to SMAW <cite id="aafe15ef-1">Alterations in current/voltage and polarity shift beads between wide-deep and narrow-high states</cite> <cite id="aafe15ef-2">GTAW sharpening angle and torch angle change bead width and reinforcement</cite> <cite id="aafe15ef-8">Process parameter changes in GMAW alter bead geometry and distortion</cite>.
  - Practical signatures: GMAW often yields minimal reinforcement and controlled penetration when matched to speed, while GTAW can leave more concavity/undercut if shielding or travel speed is off and requires more pass count for fill/cover; bead edges from GMAW show smoother transitions under similar conditions per comparative data, whereas GTAW edges can be scalloped if filler pulses are uneven <cite id="8bad3d06-2">GMAW beads smoother and GMAW edges cleaner in WAAM head‑to‑head</cite> <cite id="55dbf8e7-8">Orbital GMAW improves bead uniformity; manual GTAW sensitivity is mitigated by automation</cite>. 

Process selection and trade‑offs
- Energy efficiency and heat input: If minimizing heat-affected zone and controlling distortion is paramount, GTAW’s controllable, directional heat and DC‑P penetration can be advantageous; however, for a given weld volume, GMAW’s higher energy utilization (~80% vs ~60% for GTAW) and ability to run higher speeds with spray transfer generally deliver lower effective energy density to the same length and higher throughput <cite id="55dbf8e7-0">GTAW ~60% vs GMAW ~80% process efficiency</cite> <cite id="aafe15ef-3">Weld speed and amperage govern penetration; higher amperage per unit speed increases heat input</cite>.
- Productivity (deposition rate): Choose GMAW (or FCAW/metal‑cored) when high productivity is required; measured deposition rates often exceed GTAW markedly, and FCAW can surpass GMAW substantially due to I2R and droplet stability, enabling fewer passes and shorter cycle times <cite id="55dbf8e7-4">FCAW > GMAW deposition at given current; GMAW deposition depends on wire speed and transfer</cite> <cite id="55dbf8e7-7">Metal‑cored FCAW 5.5–6.4 kg/h outpaces solid‑wire (~3.5–4.5 kg/h) and SMAW (2.5–3.0 kg/h)</cite> <cite id="55dbf8e7-2">GTAW 0.5–2 lb/h vs. GMAW 2–12 lb/h ranges</cite>.
- Bead quality and environment: If smooth fusion profiles and minimal post‑processing are desired on thick sections, GMAW with spray transfer and proper torch guidance tends to produce smoother contour transitions; GTAW excels in root passes and precise, low‑distortion joints but may require more passes and careful parameter control to avoid undercut or waviness; use of orbital or robotic assistance narrows performance gaps in GTAW and improves bead uniformity <cite id="55dbf8e7-8">GMAW faster/economical; orbital tech reduces GTAW drawbacks</cite> <cite id="8bad3d06-2">GMAW bead walls smoother vs. GTAW bumpy</cite>.
- Material/thickness effects: For thicker plates, hybrid or WAAM approaches show GTAW/GMAW combinations and parameter optimization (e.g., higher amperage, spray transfer) can raise deposition and maintain bead integrity; deposition efficiency and achievable bead geometry shift with shielding gas, alloy, and torch angles, so “best method” should be validated per material and joint design <cite id="8bad3d06-0">Hybrid GTAW/GMAW improved deposition on thick steel</cite> <cite id="aafe15ef-2">GTAW electrode/torch geometry alters width and reinforcement</cite> <cite id="aafe15ef-8">GMAW parameter optimization improves bead geometry and reduces distortion</cite>.

Summary comparison (Two methods = GTAW vs GMAW)
- Energy density: GTAW can concentrate heat and achieve deep penetration per mm at proper DC‑P settings, but comparable electrical energy use typically yields lower energy into the weld metal per travel length than GMAW due to lower transfer efficiency and consumable losses (~60% GTAW vs ~80% GMAW); parameter drifts (high speed or arc length) trade penetration for bead width <cite id="55dbf8e7-0">GTAW ~60% vs GMAW ~80% efficiency</cite> <cite id="aafe15ef-3">Amperage and travel speed govern penetration</cite>.
- Deposition rate: GMAW (and FCAW/metal-core) significantly outpace GTAW in weld metal output per hour; manual GTAW is often 0.5–2 lb/h while GMAW is 2–12 lb/h or more, depending on wire feed and transfer mode; with metal-cored FCAW, deposition can reach 5–6 kg/h versus ~3 kg/h solid wire and ~2–3 kg/h SMAW under studied conditions <cite id="55dbf8e7-2">GTAW 0.5–2 lb/h</cite> <cite id="55dbf8e7-7">FCAW 5.5–6.4 kg/h vs 3.5–4.5 kg/h solid wire and 2.5–3.0 kg/h SMAW</cite> <cite id="55dbf8e7-4">At fixed current, FCAW deposits faster than GMAW; wire-speed comparisons favor metal-core</cite>.
- Bead characteristics: Under matched parameters and automation, GMAW typically yields beads with smoother contour transitions, broader or narrower profiles dependent on travel speed/current, and higher penetration-to-height ratios when running spray transfer; GTAW can show scalloped/rougher walls and greater sensitivity to torch/electrode geometry and filler pulsing, with DC‑P offering deeper, more stable root and PA beads than AC <cite id="8bad3d06-2">GMAW walls smoother; GTAW rough/wavy</cite> <cite id="aafe15ef-1">Wide-deep-to-narrow-high geometry shift within controlled settings</cite> <cite id="8bad3d06-0">Hybrid approaches can deliver smoother transitions at higher deposition</cite>.

Practical guidance
- To compare two specific methods on your joint: measure or log travel speed, current, voltage, and wire feed (if applicable); compute energy input as (I·V)/v and note the resulting reinforcement/width/penetration per pass; weigh HAZ distortion and undercut tolerance against cycle time. Use a GTAW-focused pass for root conicity and a GMAW pass for fill/cover on thick joints to leverage each process’ strengths, tuning DC‑P for deep root and faster travel for GMAW to balance energy and productivity <cite id="aafe15ef-3">Travel speed and amperage increase penetration; voltage also affects penetration/shape</cite> <cite id="55dbf8e7-0">Efficiency differences mean GMAW tends to deposit more metal per amp-minute</cite>. 
- Expect substantial gaps in deposition and energy utilization favoring GMAW/FCAW for high-throughput welds, while GTAW remains preferred for cleanliness, control, and reduced distortion in critical root work; automation/orbital GTAW narrows these gaps and should be considered if high precision is needed with improved throughput <cite id="55dbf8e7-8">GMAW faster and more economical; orbital GTAW mitigates disadvantages</cite> <cite id="8bad3d06-0">Hybrid GTAW/GMAW improved thick‑plate deposition</cite>.

query.text: How are the main factors influencing steel end milling experiments selected, and what are the typical ranges used for these factors?
query.answer:
Below is a concise, evidence-backed guide to how end milling experiments are set up for steel, including how key factors are chosen and the typical ranges used.

1) How factors are selected for steel end milling experiments
- Focus on dominant responses and mechanisms. Experimental design commonly targets responses such as surface roughness, cutting/thrust forces, vibration/chatter, and tool wear, and selects factors that are theoretically linked to these responses in the chosen material system (steel, tool, fixture, coolant). <cite id="93f9c19d-0">The most frequently studied control factors are cutting speed, feed rate, and depth of cut because they directly affect surface roughness</cite> and cutting mechanics. <cite id="93f9c1cd-5">Process parameters such as cutting speed, feed, depth of cut, and coolant conditions are the principal levers on surface quality and force generation in machining</cite>.

- Use structured experimental designs to estimate main effects and interactions with a small run count. Taguchi-based orthogonal arrays are widely used to select level combinations that efficiently estimate factor effects and minimize variation in the response. <cite id="78a12775-2">The Taguchi method constructs orthogonal arrays with a set of control factors and levels to screen and estimate the impact of design parameters on product quality</cite>. <cite id="78a12775-5">Taguchi designs use orthogonal arrays to estimate how factor changes affect the mean and variation of the response while using far fewer runs than full factorial designs</cite>. <cite id="78a12775-7">The choice of orthogonal array is driven by the number of factors and the number of levels for each, allowing a principled selection of treatment combinations</cite>.

- Mechanism-guided reduction to a “core few factors.” In milling, practitioners often converge on speed, feed per revolution (axial and radial), and depth of cut (or spandrel width) as the primary factors because they set chip thickness and directly govern forces, tool flank contact, chip evacuation, and roughness. <cite id="78a12775-3">Taguchi optimization has been applied to end milling to optimize cutting parameters using orthogonal arrays for these key factors</cite>. <cite id="78a12775-6">End-milling parameter studies of hardened steel commonly use a three-factor, three-level L18 design for cutting speed, feed, and depth of cut, evaluating surface roughness via S/N ratios and ANOVA</cite>. <cite id="93f9c1cd-3">Surface roughness produced by ball-end milling depends on feed rate, cutting speed, depth of cut, and tool geometry</cite>.

2) Typical factor groups and their experimental targets
- Cutting speed (Vc) and feed rate (fz, axially and radially) determine chip thickness and force; depth of cut (ae) or spandrel width (the engaged flake width) controls material removal per tooth and per pass. <cite id="93f9c1cd-7">Feed rate changes directly affect chip thickness, depth of cut, tool life, and material removal rate</cite>. <cite id="2da61f39-3">Chip thinning (entering angle and radial immersion) spreads chip volume over a larger edge arc, lowering effective chip thickness and altering forces</cite>.

- Tool geometry and edge condition modulate chip flow and flank wear, especially at high speed/low speed extremes. <cite id="2da61f39-4">Edge radius and tool runout influence cutting force models and flank wear progression in micro-end milling</cite>. <cite id="2da61f39-2">The chip thickness to edge radius ratio (or “edge prep”) is critical at miniature scales, where small radii raise flank rubbing and wear</cite>. <cite id="78a12775-8">In optimization, factor selection focuses on parameters like cutting speed, feed, and depth of cut for their dominant effect on roughness</cite>.

- Coolant and process damping set the “envelope” of feasible ranges, especially for stainless steels with high work hardening and heat generation. <cite id="93f9c1cd-5">Coolant is a process parameter affecting surface quality via chip evacuation, temperature, and adhesion; it is often included alongside cutting parameters</cite>.

3) How to choose factor levels and ranges
- Start from tool and material constraints to set the outer bounds. Use tool catalog guidance on chip load limits, horsepower/spindle torque limits, and stability (cutter diameter, radial immersion limits). <cite id="d57aeead-4">Select RPM and IPM so the tool removes chips at a rate consistent with chip load capability to achieve a target surface finish</cite>. <cite id="d57aeead-0">For 304 stainless with carbide end mills, practical cutting speeds are 200–250 SFM (≈60–75 m/min) to avoid built-up edge and chatter</cite>. <cite id="93f9c1cd-5">Minimum chip thickness constraints and maximum allowable forces define conservative lower/upper bounds for feed and depth; coolant strategy (flood/mist) also changes feasible ranges</cite>.

- Anchor on chip thickness and edge radius to avoid abusive regimes. <cite id="2da61f39-1">Micro-milling studies show the cutting edge radius is a key determinant of minimum uncut chip thickness and force behavior, with larger radii raising minimum chip thickness and altering wear patterns</cite>. <cite id="2da61f39-2">Chip-thickness-to-edge-radius ratios drive differences in force and surface response, a phenomenon amplified for miniature tools</cite>. <cite id="2da61f39-5">Too small an uncut chip thickness leads to boundary/oxide-layer rubbing with higher tool wear (e.g., stainless), whereas too large a chip thickness elevates cutting force and risks chatter</cite>. <cite id="2da61f39-3">Adjusting radial immersion and entering angle modifies effective chip thickness via chip thinning, which practitioners exploit to fit material/process constraints</cite>.

- Use force, thrust, and power limits to cap the high-temperature flank. <cite id="78a12775-6">In hardened-steel end milling, force profiles vs. speed/feed/depth are tracked, with thrust forces used to judge runability (stability and chatter limits) in arrays and S/N optimization</cite>.

- Use orthogonal arrays to set a screening grid that spans material- and tool-driven bounds, then collapse to significant factors via S/N ratio and ANOVA. <cite id="78a12775-5">Orthogonal arrays quantify main and interaction effects on mean and variance, enabling factor ranking with minimal runs</cite>. <cite id="78a12775-7">Select the array (e.g., L9 for 3 factors, 3 levels; L27 for 3-level 3–4 factors; L18 for more factors) from the number of parameters and levels</cite>.

Practical step-by-step workflow
- Step 1. Fix tool, spindle (power/torque), and coolant baseline; identify target response(s) (e.g., Ra, cutting force, chatter, wear). <cite id="78a12775-5">Start with a fractional factorial/Taguchi array to estimate the primary drivers</cite>. <cite id="2da61f39-1">Confirm tool edge radius and material’s minimum chip thickness to avoid boundary rubbing, especially for stainless</cite>.
- Step 2. Set low-to-high levels for cutting speed, feed (axial/radial per tooth), and depth of cut to cover sub-critical, optimal, and over-chip-thickness regimes. <cite id="93f9c1cd-7">Feed limits interact with tool life and chip evacuation; depth of cut changes radial immersion and chip thinning</cite>.
- Step 3. Run screening experiments; compute S/N for roughness (lower-is-better) or force/stability (lower force for chatter) and use ANOVA to select significant factors. <cite id="78a12775-6">Hard-machining studies evaluate S/N for surface roughness and use ANOVA to confirm significant factor effects across speed, feed, and depth</cite>.
- Step 4. Refine ranges around significant factor interactions, using horsepower/spindle torque to cap speeds at high feed and depth, and using edge radius to set a lower uncut chip thickness threshold. <cite id="2da61f39-5">Adjusting chip thickness via immersion and entering angle allows fitting forces and chip evacuation within tool and machine limits</cite>.

4) Typical parameter ranges used for steel end milling (carbide tools; metric-first)
Notes on mapping: Many practical sources use SFM/IPM; below convert to m/min and mm/min. Typical ranges vary with material group, tool diameter, and finish target. 

- Carbon/mild steel (e.g., S235/S45C, 1045):
  - Cutting speed: about 80–250 m/min with carbide depending on section and finish; higher than mild steel HSS by ~2.5×. <cite id="93f9c1cd-1">Mild steel cutting speed commonly spans 80–150 m/min with feed 200–400 mm/min in CNC milling; higher speeds work for shallow cuts</cite>. <cite id="d57aeead-0">Carbide roughing of 304 stainless uses 60–75 m/min; HSS is lower, illustrating material groups’ typical bands</cite>. 
  - Feed rate (per tooth): for roughing, fz ~0.1–0.3 mm/z for 10 mm tool at mid-speed; finish fz ~0.02–0.08 mm/z for Ra 0.8–3.2 μm. <cite id="93f9c1cd-5">Ball-end milling Ra trends decline with increased feed to a chip-thickness-limited minimum; tool/geometry influence the transition</cite>. <cite id="93f9c1cd-1">Commonly used feed ranges 200–400 mm/min in CNC milling for mild steel, scalable per tooth by tool diameter</cite>.
  - Depth of cut (radial/spandrel width): roughing ae up to D/2 for light stability; finishing ae ~0.5–2 mm for flat-end mills to avoid excessive chip thinning. <cite id="93f9c1cd-3">Depth of cut, feed, and cutting speed jointly determine surface roughness with tool geometry; deeper cuts raise force and roughness if not compensated</cite>.
  Example Taguchi plan: L9 (3^3) with Vc1, Vc2, Vc3 (e.g., 120, 180, 240 m/min) and fz1–3 (e.g., 0.15, 0.25, 0.35 mm/z), ae1–3 (e.g., 1.0, 2.0, 3.0 mm) for 10–20 mm tools, Ra as S/N response.

- Stainless steel (304/301/17-4PH, 12–20 mm tools):
  - Cutting speed: lower than mild carbon steels to control BUE/work hardening; carbide ~60–150 m/min, HSS ~30–70 m/min. <cite id="d57aeead-0">304 stainless: carbide Vc 200–250 SFM (~60–75 m/min); HSS much lower</cite>. <cite id="d57aeead-9">Stainless steels are commonly in the 30–75 m/min practical range</cite>.
  - Feed: conservative fz to keep chip thinning in ductile regime and reduce chatter. fz ~0.08–0.2 mm/z for roughing; ~0.02–0.1 mm/z for finish (smaller for deep cuts). <cite id="2da61f39-1">Edge radius and chip thickness interplay dictates safe chip loads; larger radii tolerate somewhat higher minimum chip thickness</cite>. 
  - Depth of cut: start at ae ≤ D/3 and iterate upward while monitoring thrust (force) and roughness; compensate with SFM and fz limits. <cite id="93f9c1cd-6">Cutting force responses increase strongly with speed and material, guiding the high-end caps on feed/depth</cite>. 
  Example ranges: Vc 80–120 m/min; fz 0.1–0.3 mm/z; ae 1–3 mm; refine via Taguchi L9 or L18 with thrust/Ra S/N.

- Hardened steels (carbide tools; grinding-like finish):
  - Speed/force optimization dominates due to high work hardening; studies use 3-level L18 arrays and S/N/ANOVA to identify significant factors and lower thrust to prevent chatter. <cite id="78a12775-6">A L18 array for hardened steel end milling evaluates speed, feed, depth, and uses S/N for surface roughness with ANOVA to confirm the significant factor</cite>.
  - Ranges tend to be tighter and lower-speed to control heat/tool wear, with fz and ae set to avoid deep narrow-slot “chatter sweetspots.” <cite id="78a12775-0">EN19 steel milling optimization by Taguchi method used three parameters, three levels (L9), reflecting constrained material-tool interaction</cite>.
  Example: Vc 40–100 m/min; fz 0.1–0.2 mm/z; ae 0.5–2 mm; responses: Ra and cutting/thrust force.

5) Additional selection rules and cross-checks
- Clearance and chip evacuation: select axial depth (immersion) so chips clear; too much depth at low SFM causes rubbing/plug. <cite id="2da61f39-5">Minimum chip thickness too low causes rubbing/edge wear in stainless; too high raises cutting force and chatter risk</cite>. Use positive immersion ramps or higher SFM to lower effective chip thinning at depth. <cite id="2da61f39-3">Control of entering angle and chip thickness is used to manage force and chip formation</cite>.
- Edge radius and tool condition: larger radii raise minimum chip thickness and flank contact; compensate by capping feed at depth or lowering speed. <cite id="2da61f39-2">Chip thickness versus edge radius governs whether milling behaves like micro-machining or macro, affecting surface response</cite>.
- Power limit check: torque = power/(rpm) and cutting force estimates bracket the machine’s horsepower; if Fz·Vc > machine torque capacity, reduce speed/depth or use more flutes/larger diameter. <cite id="93f9c1cd-6">Cutting force increases with material and speed, constraining the high-speed end of feasible ranges</cite>.
- Orthogonal array choice and center points: for highly nonlinear responses (e.g., stainless finishes), supplement screening with small center arrays to detect curvature and force minima. <cite id="78a12775-5">Taguchi designs quantify linear effects; follow-up designs can address curvature and noise across material/process regimes</cite>.

6) Concrete examples and how ranges are set in studies
- Mild/low-alloy steel Taguchi studies: three factors (V, fz, ae) with L9 or L27, S/N on Ra, ANOVA ranks effects. They start with broad spindle-speed-friendly bands for mild steel and step fz/ae to meet force limits. <cite id="78a12775-3">An end-milling optimization used Taguchi arrays for cutting parameters with response evaluation against cutting speed, feed, and depth of cut</cite>. <cite id="78a12775-1">Machining of mild steel by CNC milling used Taguchi methods to reduce Ra, organizing factors and levels for efficient mapping</cite>.
- Stainless steel practical bands: carbide end mills target ~60–75 m/min (304), with per-tooth feeds tuned to tool diameter and flute count to maintain a consistent chip load without chatter. <cite id="d57aeead-0">Stainless 304 commonly used 60–75 m/min (200–250 SFM) to avoid built-up and maintain stability</cite>.
- Feed per tooth and chip load per edge: selection often ties to chip load recommendations by tool diameter and to spindle power. <cite id="d57aeead-4">Selecting proper chip load and RPM/IPM per tool and material provides a consistent starting envelope for cutting</cite>.

7) Validation, analysis, and moving to production
After the screening DOE and parameter refinement, confirm final parameters at a few tool-life trials for your specific tool overcut length and coolant condition. Use ANOVA to ensure factors are significant at your setup and examine force-time signatures for chatter. Finally, phase-in tool condition (sharp new tools vs. radius-wear) and coolant fidelity when transferring from lab to shop. <cite id="78a12775-6">Studies hard-machining with Taguchi/ANOVA report S/N-optimized parameters for roughness and then validate that significant factors drive improvements across speed–feed–depth planes</cite>. <cite id="78a12775-5">Orthogonal arrays provide a compact estimate of factor effects and variation on the response, enabling rapid transfer to production with fewer trials</cite>.

Summary
- Main factors: cutting speed, feed rate (axial and radial), depth of cut/spandrel width, tool geometry/edge radius; optionally coolant and process damping. <cite id="93f9c1cd-0">Studies of milling EN19 set speed, feed, and depth of cut as the core factors for roughness control</cite>.
- How to pick levels: anchor on chip-thickness limits (minimum chip thickness to avoid boundary rubbing; edge radius), force and power/torque constraints, chatter stability, and surface transition regimes; then build orthogonal arrays and evaluate with S/N ratios and ANOVA. <cite id="2da61f39-1">Minimum uncut chip thickness depends on the edge radius and material, dictating the lower bound of feasible chip loads</cite>. <cite id="93f9c1cd-6">Force grows with speed and work material, setting the upper envelope</cite>. <cite id="78a12775-5">Taguchi/orthogonal designs efficiently estimate main effects for factor selection and level setting</cite>.
- Typical ranges (carbide, metric, ±20% within material group):
  - Mild carbon steel: Vc 80–200 m/min; fz 0.15–0.4 mm/z (roughing); ae 1–4 mm (flat end). <cite id="93f9c1cd-1">Machining practice lists ~80–150 m/min and 200–400 mm/min feed for mild steel</cite>.
  - Stainless (304): Vc 60–120 m/min; fz 0.08–0.25 mm/z (roughing) and 0.02–0.1 mm/z (finish); ae 0.8–3 mm starting point, tighten to 0.5–2 mm for finishing. <cite id="d57aeead-0">Stainless 304 often 60–75 m/min carbide; HSS much lower</cite>. 
  - Hardened steel: Vc 40–100 m/min; fz 0.1–0.2 mm/z; ae 0.5–2 mm; optimize with Taguchi L18 and S/N on thrust/Ra. <cite id="78a12775-6">Hardened-steel end milling uses three‑factor, three‑level designs (L18) to optimize surface roughness via S/N and ANOVA</cite>.

Notes and caveats
- Spandrel width is the radial width of cut (radial depth of cut); “entering angle” and immersion set effective chip thickness per edge. Adjusting these with rpm/feed per tooth moves you across chip-thickness regimes with different roughness and force scaling. <cite id="2da61f39-3">Entering angle reduces chip thinning at high immersion, allowing higher feed while maintaining chip thickness</cite>. 
- Coolant path and nozzle distance, tool coating, and workpiece heat treatment change feasible bounds; include in factor lists for stainless/high-speed operations or as blocking/noise factors in Taguchi designs. <cite id="93f9c1cd-5">Coolant and chip evacuation affect cutting temperature, adhesion, and surface quality alongside speed, feed, and depth</cite>.
- If your shop uses HSS rather than carbide, drop speed by ~5–8× and scale feed accordingly to maintain similar chip load and surface finish. <cite id="d57aeead-0">HSS cutting speeds for 304 stainless are markedly lower than carbide, reflecting 10–15× SFM differences in practice</cite>.

This selection and range-setting pattern has been repeatedly validated across steel milling studies and practical feeds-and-speeds guides; it emphasizes mechanistic mapping of chip formation, force, and surface generation to factor choice, and then tunes levels through DOE and statistical validation. <cite id="78a12775-6">End-milling in hardened steels exemplifies the process: select V, fz, ae; run L18; optimize S/N for Ra; validate with ANOVA</cite>. <cite id="93f9c1cd-1">Machining practice guides the initial numeric envelope for steel, which is then refined via Taguchi screening and force/roughness checks</cite>.

fully_underspecified.text: How are the main factors influencing experiments selected, and what are the typical ranges used for these factors?
fully_underspecified.answer:
Below is a synthesis of how experiments are scoped by selecting main factors and how typical factor ranges are chosen across methods and domains. Where conventions vary, we highlight when to prefer screening versus optimization and how to align ranges with objectives and noise.

How to select main factors

- Begin with a hypothesis and feasibility check. Candidate factors are drawn from domain knowledge, literature, and preliminary data; screening is used when many inputs are plausible but relevance is uncertain, while optimization (RSM/algorithmic tuning) is used when a small set of factors has been validated as influential by screening or prior analysis. <cite id="d2c6723b-6">Plackett–Burman “screening designs” are used to investigate a large number of factors to identify the most significant few, cutting variables early</cite> <cite id="d2c6723b-3">PB designs are very efficient screening designs when only main effects are of interest, confounding main effects with two‑factor interactions but allowing economical estimation of main effects</cite> <cite id="d44971a5-4">Response-surface designs then follow after screening identifies a few key factors to be optimized</cite>.

- Use resolution/criteria-aligned designs to separate effects when feasible; if interactions might matter, choose higher resolution or augment later. <cite id="d2c6723b-1">Resolution III designs allow estimation of main effects but alias them with two‑factor interactions</cite> <cite id="d2c6723b-4">PB performance depends on the assumption that interaction effects are negligible</cite> <cite id="ce327f6b-0">D‑optimal designs optimize the information matrix |X′X| to shrink parameter covariances by selecting factor levels and runs</cite> <cite id="ce327f6b-8">A- and G‑optimality target average and maximal prediction variance, respectively</cite>.

- Prefer principled selection over ad hoc “one-at-a-time” changes. Algorithmic or model-based procedures evaluate marginal/interaction impacts in silico before running more tests. <cite id="ce327f6b-5">Designs can be chosen using classic factorial/stepped screening or modern algorithmic approaches to estimate and separate effects efficiently</cite> <cite id="27c06974-0">Greedy forward selection iteratively adds the feature that most improves the model, while backward removes the least important for a specified model family</cite> <cite id="27c06974-4">In applied ML, feature selection is commonly performed under cross‑validation to choose subsets that improve predictive performance and manage multiple tradeoffs</cite> <cite id="27c06974-7">Regularization-based methods (e.g., LASSO) select features during training to improve generalization and interpretability</cite>.

- Match model to objective. If linear/main-effects suffices, main‑effects screening and 2‑level designs suffice; if curvature/interactions are expected, move to 3‑level factorials, central composites, or Box–Behnken and fit quadratic models. <cite id="d2c6723b-3">Plackett–Burman designs are efficient when only main effects are of interest</cite> <cite id="ce327f6b-7">Response-surface designs model responses as functions of factors to locate optima</cite> <cite id="ce327f6b-9">Software implementations let you “select optimal design” by D-optimality to minimize covariance of parameter estimates</cite>.

Practical workflows

1) Candidate generation and screening
- Enumerate plausible drivers (materials, process conditions, inputs with known leverage) and randomize effects with PB for cost efficiency; confirm assumptions that interactions are small or negligible over the operating window, and plan follow‑up with higher‑resolution designs where needed. <cite id="d2c6723b-6">Screening with PB reduces runs when many factors are plausible</cite> <cite id="d2c6723b-4">PB screening is robust if two‑factor interactions are negligible</cite>.

2) Transition to optimization
- After screening confirms a short list, construct D-optimal or full/3‑level designs with center points to detect curvature; fit appropriate models (linear, quadratic) and verify model adequacy (lack-of-fit) before tuning. <cite id="ce327f6b-0">D‑optimality maximizes the determinant of X′X to reduce parameter covariance</cite> <cite id="ce327f6b-9">D‑optimal designs iteratively choose points to improve precision</cite> <cite id="ce327f7b-7">Response surface designs support modeling and optimization of factors</cite>.

3) Model/feature-based selection in nonlinear settings
- Use embedded or wrapper selectors with CV to avoid overfitting; prefer L1 regularization for sparse relevance and fast search; use greedy forward/backward for interpretability. <cite id="27c06974-0">Forward stepwise adds the best feature at each step</cite> <cite id="27c06974-7">L1 methods yield sparse feature sets; relaxed LASSO can improve stability</cite> <cite id="27c06974-4">Cross‑validated feature selection prevents overfitting</cite>.

Typical factor ranges: how to choose numerical windows

- Two-level main-effects screening (coded ±1) to estimate signs and relative impacts; practical range selection practices map onto coded scales to economize runs:
  - Choice: 2^k or 2-level PB (k factors, run number ≈k) with low cost and rapid ranking; interactions assumed small. <cite id="d2c6723b-3">PB designs are efficient for main-effect screening</cite> <cite id="d2c6723b-1">Resolution III main-effect estimates are aliased with two‑factor interactions</cite>.
  - Typical coding: map practical low/high to −1/+1 (sometimes 0 at midpoints). Practical engineering practice uses 2-level “center” or mid settings for sign estimation when budgets are tight, or later add center points to probe curvature. <cite id="ce327f6b-9">D‑optimization chooses runs and levels to estimate the model of interest</cite>.

- Three-level full factorials and Box–Behnken/central-composites if curvature is suspected; default step from 2-level ±1 to 3-level −1/0/+1, with “alpha” distance chosen to fold the cube or fit a circumscribed design:
  - Choice: 3^k for few factors when quadratic curvature is plausible; include center points and axial points for RSM (central composite: α = 2^(1/4) ≈ 1.19 for cube edge folding; α ≈ 1–1.5 for Box–Behnken); this is the canonical “typical” layout in response-surface practice.
  - Rationale: 3-levels enable curvature diagnostics and quadratic term estimation; α scales define whether vertices are kept on the “cube” or stretched to create face/facet vertices for rotatability/equivariance. <cite id="ce327f6b-7">Response surface designs model the response over factor ranges to find optima</cite> <cite id="ce327f6b-9">D-optimization can be used to select the exact levels/runs to estimate quadratic models with minimal covariance</cite>.

- Practical engineering robustness windows (manufacturing, controls)
  - Typical perturbation bands: ±5–10% around nominal for robustness screening; ±1–3 sigma for process capability contexts; larger if tolerances are tight and variation dominates.
  - Rationale: small deltas isolate sensitivity and main effects while staying within tolerance/variation-dominated regimes; if factors are controllable, center on target and explore noise windows; if factors are random variation, align ranges with process sigma limits. These are common industrial conventions to balance effect detection and feasibility.

- Biology/bioprocess screening windows (exemplary)
  - Typical order-of-magnitude sweep: 10-fold dilution series for concentration–response (e.g., 10^0–10^2 nM/µM), aiming to bracket EC50/IC50 and verify monotonicity/nonlinearity; start near prior literature means and expand if flat or steep.
  - Rationale: such “titration” ranges are widely used in enzyme/HTS and cell-based assays to map dose–response shapes and identify active windows; once a lead range is found, refine with centered 3–5 points for EC50 precision. <cite id="d2c6723b-3">Screening efficiently narrows variables when many concentrations are candidates</cite>.

- Machine learning hyperparameter ranges (illustrative, task-agnostic)
  - Learning rates: common log-uniform(1e-5, 0.1) with grid or random search; warm restarts/decay reduce sensitivity; regularization: log-uniform(1e-4, 1.0); network depth/mesh size: small integers with coarse-to-fine sweeps; all coupled to dataset scale and layer counts.
  - Rationale: log-spaces cover orders of magnitude typical for step sizes and decay schedules; ranges are “typical” in scikit-learn/optimize guidance and are tuned with CV within broader, coarse-to-fine search strategies. <cite id="27c06974-0">Greedy selection chooses one parameter change at a time, but embedded/CV methods are preferred</cite> <cite id="27c06974-4">Cross-validated search selects hyperparameters likely to improve predictive performance</cite>.

- Clinical/biostatistics context: factor “magnitudes” and MAR-based deltas
  - Clinical trials often define factor changes relative to a typical patient value or “typical” effect size range; “typical” treatment effect windows are explored via simulations to ensure expected outcomes fall within observed ranges; in dose–response, stepwise dose increments (e.g., 25–100% over baseline) are used to bracket toxicity and efficacy.
  - Rationale: ranges are set by biological plausibility, prior efficacy/toxicity data, and minimum clinically important differences (MCID), typically explored with model-informed design (dose grid) and confirmatory runs.

- Control/sensitivity analysis windows
  - Typical sensitivity scan: ±5–20% of nominal component tolerances or set points for each factor, with 100–1,000 Hz perturbation amplitudes; use Latin hypercube or Morris/Random Forest screening to catch dominant variables before concentrated DoE near targets. <cite id="ce327f6b-0">Information‑matrix optimization focuses runs where the model is most uncertain</cite>.

Putting it together: a pragmatic, evidence-aligned recipe

1) Scope the problem and seed candidates. Use domain knowledge and preliminary pilot runs to propose variables; then run an efficient screening matrix. <cite id="d2c6723b-6">PB designs screen many variables quickly</cite> <cite id="d2c6723b-4">Assumptions about negligible interactions govern PB viability</cite>. 2) Map coding and initial ranges. Use −1/1 for 2-level tests; for suspected curvature or quadratic terms, adopt 3-level designs with axial distances per standard response-surface practice (e.g., central composite with α≈1.414 for cube foldover, or Box–Behnken with factorially wrapped equidistant points); include centers to detect curvature. <cite id="ce327f6b-7">Response-surface designs support fitting and optimizing response surfaces</cite> <cite id="ce327f6b-9">Select designs by D/A/G optimality to reduce uncertainty</cite>. 3) Select levels by effect and variance reduction. Prefer D-optimal or alphabetic optimal selection when feasible; add points where prediction variance (G-optimality) is high or Fisher information is low. <cite id="ce327f6b-0">D-optimality maximizes determinant of X′X</cite> <cite id="ce327f6b-8">A- and G-optimal criteria respectively minimize average and maximal prediction variance</cite>. 4) If using model-based selectors, embed selection within CV and regularization. Use LASSO/subset searches in ML tasks and stepwise forward/backward in regression to choose truly influential factors and avoid overfitting. <cite id="27c06974-0">Forward selection iteratively adds the most beneficial feature</cite> <cite id="27c06974-7">Regularization-based feature selection is widely used for relevance and stability</cite> <cite id="27c06974-4">Cross-validation is essential to guard against overfitting during selection</cite>.

Typical factor ranges: cross-cutting conventions and examples

- Encoding conventions:
  - Two-level screening: factor low/med/high coded at −1, 0, +1; practical low/high are often chosen as 10–50% deviations from a target setpoint or nominal material level to test leverage while staying operational. <cite id="d2c6723b-3">Main-effects screening with PB uses economical 2-level mappings</cite>.
  - Three-level factorial or central-composite: −1/0/+1 with axial α to fold cube edges or wrap faces; practitioners often keep the factor factor levels as multiples of the 2-level span (e.g., −1.0, 0, +1.0, +1.414 for CC) so curvature is diagnosable and optima localizable. <cite id="ce327f6b-7">Response-surface designs use 3-level structures to fit quadratic models for optimization</cite>.

- Industrial/controls:
  - Ranges are commonly set at 5–10% perturbations around targets for robustness; tolerances and process capability constraints (1–3 sigma) guide feasible windows; if the factor is a controllable setpoint, center near target and scan left/right; if a noise factor, range the factor by sigma levels to reflect variability. <cite id="ce327f6b-8">D-optimality focuses sampling where parameter uncertainty is highest</cite>.

- Biomedical screens:
  - Concentration–response assays often start with decade spans (e.g., 10 nM to 10 µM), identifying EC50 and then refining the active decade (e.g., 1–10 nM or 10–100 nM) with centered spacing; viability assays may use log2 doses covering −5 to +5 steps relative to a baseline. <cite id="d2c6723b-3">Screening identifies variables with large main effects before deep sweeps</cite>.

- Machine learning tuning:
  - Hyperparameters are swept on log-scales: learning rates 1e-4–0.1 (often 1e-5–0.1), regularization 1e-4–1.0; schedulers/decay/weight decay use analogous ranges; grid/random/LHS search explores coarse grids with CV shrinkage to typical operational ranges where generalization peaks. <cite id="27c06974-4">Feature selection under cross-validation picks parameters that best generalize</cite> <cite id="27c06974-0">Greedy sequential criteria focus on marginal gains per parameter change</cite>.

- Clinical/dose-ranging:
  - Dose levels are spaced as multiples of the prior ED/IC values (e.g., 25–50% increments) or by isoeffect relationships to bracket efficacy and safety, guided by simulations ensuring expected effect sizes and adverse-event probabilities fall in observed ranges. <cite id="ce327f6b-8">Alpha-G optimization focuses runs around regions with high predictive uncertainty</cite>.

Selection pitfalls and remedies

- Forgetting interactions: Screen quickly but verify with a follow-up DOE with resolution V or add “folded” runs if initial PB suggests large curvature. <cite id="d2c6723b-4">PB performance depends on interaction-negligibility assumptions; otherwise, two‑factor effects can bias main‑effect estimates</cite>.
- Overfitting during selection: Prevent overfitting by using embedded CV and penalization; avoid sequential search without CV; predefine a budget of re-runs for confirmation. <cite id="27c06974-4">Cross-validated feature/hyperparameter selection is crucial to avoid overfitting</cite>.
- Mis-scaled ranges: If ranges are too narrow, curvature is missed; if too wide, effects are diluted and variance inflates. Use D-optimality to tighten selection where covariances are largest and add center/axial points if prediction variance (G-optimality) is unacceptably high. <cite id="ce327f6b-0">D-optimization reduces parameter covariance</cite> <cite id="ce327f6b-8">G-optimality targets maximal prediction variance</cite>.

Summary

- If you have many candidate factors and need speed/efficiency, use two‑level main‑effects screening (PB) with −1/1 coding and the assumption that interactions are small; this typically covers 10–90% of influential discovery if the model goal remains linear. <cite id="d2c6723b-3">PB designs are very efficient for main‑effect screening</cite> <cite id="d2c6723b-1">In resolution III designs, main effects are aliased with two‑factor interactions</cite>.
- If you have few factors and need curvature/optimization, choose 3‑level factorial or central-composite with axial distances set per standard response-surface practice and model the fitted surface. <cite id="ce327f6b-7">Response-surface designs model responses across factors to find optima</cite>.
- Across domains, “typical” ranges are set to bracket expected biological or engineering plausibility (e.g., 5–20% perturbations, decade dose–responses) and then compressed around detected effects; selection of factor values is reinforced by D/A/G optimality to reduce parameter variance and improve prediction across the region of interest. <cite id="ce327f6b-8">Alpha-G criteria explicitly target prediction-variance performance across the design space</cite> <cite id="ce327f6b-0">D-optimality directly improves precision of estimated parameters</cite>.

These patterns are general workflows; exact ranges are always anchored to domain knowledge, feasibility, and model adequacy checks (lack‑of‑fit, CV error, residual plots), and may be iteratively refined from screening to optimization designs. <cite id="ce327f6b-4">Minitab’s selection frameworks emphasize D-optimality and distance-based criteria to choose design points that improve the fitted model</cite> <cite id="27c06974-4">Applied workflows incorporate cross-validatory selection to ensure the chosen factors truly improve generalization</cite>.

without_scope.text: How are the main factors influencing experiments selected, and what are the typical ranges used for these factors?
without_scope.answer:
Below is a practical, evidence‑backed guide to how main factor influences are chosen for an experiment and what “typical ranges” look like in common experimental frameworks and domains. It blends design principles, quantitative structure of runs/levels, and domain examples.

Overview: Goals, candidates, and reduction
- Start from experiment goals and factor count: The first choice is always whether you need screening (many candidates, few runs) to identify the dominant drivers, or a full/surrounding‑response surface (RSM) if you expect curvature and interactions and can afford more runs per factor. <cite id="ab0b4074-9">The choice of an experimental design depends on the objectives of the experiment and the number of factors to be investigated</cite>.
- Use screening designs to narrow candidates if factor space is large. <cite id="ab0b4074-0">Plackett–Burman is a two‑level fractional factorial used for screening many factors with minimal combinations focusing on main effects</cite>. <cite id="ab0b4074-4">Plackett–Burman designs analyze a few selected combinations to evaluate main effects with no interaction confounding, feeding into response surface follow‑up</cite>. <cite id="ab0b4074-3">Fractional factorial screening identifies the most important variables but does not capture interactions, so RSM or follow‑up is often needed</cite>.
- When the objective is system comprehension and robustness and factor effects are largely linear over a neighborhood, Taguchi/orthogonal arrays and RSM are complementary. <cite id="de313ee4-0">Taguchi designs use orthogonal arrays to estimate factor effects on the mean and variation; orthogonality ensures clean effect estimation</cite>. <cite id="de313ee4-9">Orthogonal arrays focus on main effects and are selected based on the number of factors, levels, and interactions to be modeled</cite>. <cite id="de313ee4-2">Taguchi orthogonal arrays examine many variables in as few experiments as possible and are more effective than OFAT for factor screening</cite>. <cite id="de313ee4-8">Selecting an orthogonal array depends on the number of factors/interactions and the number of levels for the factors</cite>.

Coding and level structure: how ranges are typically set
- Two‑level (−1, +1) screening: These designs set each factor at two coded levels, often chosen to bracket a hypothesized operating region where the response is linear in the factor. <cite id="ab0b4074-1">Factorial designs enumerate factor level combinations and allow estimation of main and interaction effects under orthogonality</cite>. <cite id="ab0b4074-2">Two‑level full factorials are orthogonal methods; fractional subsets reduce runs while preserving main‑effect resolution</cite>. <cite id="ab0b4074-0">Plackett–Burman two‑level fractional designs evaluate main effects only, making many factor screens tractable</cite>.
- Three‑level (−1, 0, +1) for curvature/RSM: When curvature is suspected or a quadratic model is planned, move to three levels per factor and center points. <cite id="6b4cd463-0">Box–Behnken designs always have three levels per factor, unlike central composite designs which can have up to five</cite>. <cite id="6b4cd463-3">Central composite designs in RSM are built from full factorials plus axial and center points, enabling quadratic modeling</cite>. <cite id="6b4cd463-2">Box–Behnken designs are rotatable or nearly rotatable but can have regions of poor prediction quality</cite>.
- Five‑level central composite designs (CCD): Add two axial “face” points per factor beyond the low, middle, and high, for total five levels, to achieve rotatability/“circumscribed” geometry. <cite id="6b4cd463-6">A central composite design includes only continuous factors, each tested at five levels: two axial, low, middle, and high</cite>. <cite id="6b4cd463-5">CCD often uses a full factorial at the five levels and is common in RSM for response surfaces</cite>. <cite id="6b4cd463-9">For three factors, Box–Behnken uses the three −1/0/+1 levels with a specific number of experiments; a central composite with three factors includes 5 levels per factor for “circumscribed” designs</cite>.
- Axial distance and rotatability: Rotatability requires a specific spacing α between the center and axial points; α is typically 1.682 when factor levels are coded −1 to +1 and you want constant variance of predictions with respect to distance from center. <cite id="6b4cd463-7">For three factors, the axial distance α is usually set around 1.682 to maintain rotatability, which can result in generated values below the minimum or above the maximum practical values</cite>. <cite id="6b4cd463-2">Box–Behnken is rotatable or nearly so, but the canonical Box–Behnken and central composite designs can exhibit prediction quality differences over the design space</cite>.
- Effects and interpretation: In Taguchi and classical orthogonal arrays, columns are assigned to factors/interactions to estimate effects; interactions may be assigned to secondary columns or folded to reduce runs. <cite id="de313ee4-1">Taguchi’s catalog of orthogonal arrays is grounded in factorial design and difference set theory, enabling orthogonal estimation of factor effects</cite>. <cite id="de313ee4-8">Orthogonal arrays are selected based on the number of factors, interactions, and levels so that main effects are estimable with minimal confounding</cite>. <cite id="de313ee4-5">Taguchi uses orthogonal arrays and signal‑to‑noise ratios to study variables and their interactions systematically</cite>.

Practical rules for selecting factor ranges and levels
- Start from engineering or scientific operating points and uncertainty: Pick a central value from process knowledge or benchmarks, then expand low/high by ranges where meaningful changes are expected. In bioprocessing, for example, cultures are typically narrow around physiological baselines; pH near 7.0, temperature near 37°C, DO moderate, and substrate near basal concentrations, with small windows of variability tolerated for reproducibility. <cite id="66590a1c-3">Cells generally prefer narrow ranges in temperature, pH, osmolality, and substrate concentrations for optimal performance, hence large deviations reduce viability</cite>. <cite id="66590a1c-6">In early culture, pH 7.0–7.4 is regulated via bicarbonate equilibrium by CO2 addition</cite>. <cite id="66590a1c-4">A bioprocess DOE used three pH levels (6.5, 7.0, 7.5), three temperatures (35.5, 37.0, 38.5°C), and multiple cultivation times</cite>. <cite id="66590a1c-1">Center points were replicated three times to estimate experimental error in a bioreactor DOE, with factor ranges chosen around such operating windows</cite>. <cite id="66590a1c-8">Noise/Tolérance Operating Range (NOR) examples set temperature target 37°C with NOR ±2°C, i.e., 35–39°C</cite>.
- Use factor‑level coding to plan runs and interpret effects: Two levels (−1, +1) map naturally to low/high relative to a central baseline; three levels include a 0 at the center to probe curvature; five levels for CCD add two outer axial points. <cite id="ab0b4074-1">Factorial designs combine factor levels to estimate effects; orthogonal designs separate factor impacts for clearer interpretation</cite>. <cite id="6b4cd463-6">CCD tests five levels: two axial outer points, the low, middle, and high; axial selection trades off space coverage and rotatability</cite>. <cite id="6b4cd463-7">When α≈1.682 for rotatability, axial points may land beyond your specified practical bounds, requiring careful engineering validation</cite>. <cite id="de313ee4-9">Assignments of columns to main effects and interactions in orthogonal arrays are guided by the number of required levels and factor count</cite>.
- Balance resolution and interactions: If you care about interactions, avoid pure two‑level screens without follow‑up, and choose full factorials or higher resolution designs; otherwise, fractional two‑level designs are efficient. <cite id="ab0b4074-3">Fractional factorials are efficient at screening but do not capture factor interactions; follow‑up is required if interactions are of interest</cite>. <cite id="ab0b4074-2">Full factorials at two levels are orthogonal and capture main and interaction structure exactly, while fractional designs approximate it at lower cost</cite>.
- Add center points and replicates to detect curvature and estimate pure error: When you suspect curvature or want RSM, include multiple center runs to estimate lack‑of‑fit and process noise. <cite id="6b4cd463-3">RSM central composite designs rely on full factorials combined with axial and center points</cite>. <cite id="66590a1c-1">Replicating the center point three times estimates experimental error in bioprocess DOE</cite>.

Typical factor ranges and coding in common domains
- Bioprocess/bioreactor optimization
  - Ranges: <cite id="66590a1c-4">pH commonly explored around 6.5–7.5 in steps of 1 unit; temperature near 35.5–38.5°C with 37°C the physiological center; cultivation time with a few discrete levels</cite>. <cite id="66590a1c-6">pH control bands often target 7.0–7.4 via bicarbonate equilibria</cite>. <cite id="66590a1c-3">Bench‑scale cultures operate in narrow windows and are sensitive to temperature, pH, osmolality, and substrate levels</cite>. <cite id="66590a1c-8">Temperature NORs are often ±2°C around a nominal 37°C</cite>.
  - Levels: <cite id="6b4cd463-6">Three‑level RSM for bioprocess variables (low, center, high) plus axial points and center replicates</cite>. <cite id="6b4cd463-7">If rotatable CCD with α≈1.68 is chosen, outer axial ranges can extend beyond the routine 35–39°C band</cite>. 
  - Screening choice: <cite id="ab0b4074-0">Plackett–Burman two‑level screens are favored to identify most influential variables among many, followed by RSM</cite>. <cite id="ab0b4074-3">Given bioprocess nonlinearity, interactions can arise; follow‑up DOE is recommended</cite>.
- Chemistry/materials and composition space
  - Ranges: Many composition and process factors are encoded on bounded scales where 0–100% by weight or fraction is a natural domain; concentration ranges then select a central concentration (e.g., 50 wt% solvent), low (25 wt%), high (75 wt%), and outer axial ranges (e.g., 12.5 and 100 wt%) if a 5‑level CCD is used; temperature ranges are set near melting/transition windows with small operating bands for solidification/manufacturing steps. <cite id="6b4cd463-0">RSM in composition often uses three levels per factor due to Box–Behnken or three‑level full factorials</cite>. <cite id="6b4cd463-6">Five‑level CCDs are used when broader axial exploration is needed in composition or thermal processing</cite>. <cite id="66590a1c-3">Operating windows for sensitive chemistry are typically narrow to remain near optimal performance</cite>.
  - Levels and coding: <cite id="6b4cd463-9">Three −1/0/+1 levels are typical for factors like composition or temperature to test curvature and center responses</cite>. <cite id="6b4cd463-7">CCD axial steps can push beyond your initial high/low if α>1; plan feasibility checks</cite>.
- Imaging and signal processing
  - Ranges: Pixel intensities often sweep full 8‑bit range 0–255 or normalized [0,1] for gray/RGB channels; binary masks are {0,1}. Time or wavelength axes follow device ranges and known spectral features. <cite id="ab0b4074-1">Factor levels define the design matrix; common practice is to pick level bounds based on measurable ranges (e.g., pixel 0–255)</cite>.
- Machine learning (bounded continuous/discrete hyperparameters)
  - Ranges and logs: Learning rates in SGD‑family are often bounded wide with log scaling—e.g., low 1e-6, center 1e-3, high 0.1; regularization strengths similarly span 1e-8 to 1.0. These ranges bracket under‑/over‑regularization with a central “reasonable” value chosen from prior baselines. <cite id="de313ee4-1">Taguchi/orthogonal principles scale to discrete/continuous bounded ranges with levels chosen to separate effects</cite>. <cite id="de313ee4-5">Systematic screening (grid/orthogonal subsets) and robust design via S/N ratios mirror bioprocess DOE tradeoffs for learning/hyperparameter selection</cite>.
  - Levels and centering: <cite id="ab0b4074-1">Use factorial coding so main effects are additive and easily separable; two or three levels per hyperparameter depending on suspected curvature</cite>. <cite id="6b4cd463-6">Five‑level CCDs can probe “corner” and “face” regions in hyperparameter spaces when large‑step exploration matters</cite>.

Putting it together: a practical workflow
1) Candidate set and goals. <cite id="ab0b4074-9">Enumerate plausible factors and state objectives (effect/significance discovery vs. model fitting/optimization)</cite>.
2) Pre‑screening to find drivers. <cite id="ab0b4074-0">Run a two‑level fractional factorial (Plackett–Burman or orthogonal array) to identify main effects with few experiments</cite>. <cite id="ab0b4074-3">Expect limited detection of interactions; plan follow‑up</cite>.
3) Confirm curvature and optimize locally. <cite id="6b4cd463-0">If curvature matters, move to three‑level Box–Behnken or</cite> <cite id="6b4cd463-6">five‑level central composite designs with axial and center points</cite>. <cite id="6b4cd463-7">Select α to maintain rotatability or sample wider ranges if process limits preclude it</cite>. <cite id="6b4cd463-2">Expect rotatability as a guideline with trade‑offs in prediction quality at the design extremes</cite>.
4) Choose levels using engineering windows and coding. <cite id="66590a1c-6">For bioprocess factors like pH, use operating setpoints 7.0–7.4 as a practical window then widen with symmetric steps (6.5/7.5) if needed</cite>. <cite id="66590a1c-4">Represent main effects with two levels and add center/axials for curvature with 35.5–38.5°C examples</cite>. <cite id="de313ee4-8">Use orthogonal arrays when factor counts and level counts require alias management to preserve main‑effect separability</cite>.
5) Include center points and noise estimation. <cite id="6b4cd463-3">Add center runs to fit quadratic terms and to assess lack‑of‑fit in RSM</cite>. <cite id="66590a1c-1">Replicate center points multiple times to separate experimental error from signal</cite>.
6) Cross‑validate with one‑factor‑at‑a‑time (OFAT) neighborhood checks. Taguchi robust design principles motivate verifying optimal settings outside pure effect screening by checking signal‑to‑noise ratios and noise tolerance. <cite id="de313ee4-5">Signal‑to‑noise selection complements DOE by assessing robustness after finding nominal optimal settings</cite>.
7) Boundary and corner exploration. If multiple factors interact or “synergize,” sample corners and axial “faces” with CCD or Box–Behnken to avoid local optima. <cite id="6b4cd463-6">CCD explicitly includes axial faces to probe mixed synergistic regions with center responses</cite>. <cite id="6b4cd463-7">Be mindful that rotatability can force axial points beyond practical ranges; add constraints or broaden initial ranges</cite>.

Limits and when to adjust the plan
- No design guarantees all interactions are discovered early. <cite id="ab0b4074-3">Two‑level factorials miss interactions; screeners must be followed by full factorials or specialized designs</cite>.
- Rotatability is a convenience, not a magic pill. <cite id="6b4cd463-2">Box–Behnken can still have regions of poor prediction even if rotatable; model diagnostics and validation are required</cite>.
- Engineering feasibility often trumps theoretical optimality. <cite id="6b4cd463-7">Axial steps near α≈1.68 may violate process bounds, so replace with larger ranges or drop rotatability</cite>.

In summary, “main factors” are selected by aligning scientific/engineering knowledge with experimental goals, using screening (two‑level orthogonal or fractional factorial) to separate main effects quickly, then moving to response‑surface designs (three or five levels with centers and, if needed, larger axial ranges) to fit curvature and confirm optima; typical numeric ranges are built around the factor’s operating window (e.g., pH 6.5–7.5, temperature 35.5–38.5°C, pixel 0–255, learning rate 1e-6–0.1 on a log scale), with effect coding and orthogonal/rotatable structure guiding run placement and interpretation. <cite id="ab0b4074-9">Design choice hinges on objectives and factor count</cite> <cite id="ab0b4074-0">Plackett–Burman screens main effects quickly</cite> <cite id="ab0b4074-4">and feed into RSM</cite> <cite id="ab0b4074-3">but require follow‑up for interactions</cite> <cite id="6b4cd463-0">Box–Behnken uses three levels per factor</cite> <cite id="6b4cd463-6">central composite adds five levels including axial and center</cite> <cite id="6b4cd463-7">with axial spacing often 1.682 for rotatability, possibly beyond initial bounds</cite> <cite id="66590a1c-4">Three pH levels 6.5–7.5 and temperatures 35.5–38.5°C are representative bioprocess ranges</cite> <cite id="66590a1c-6">pH often controlled around 7.0–7.4 via bicarbonate</cite> <cite id="66590a1c-8">temperature NOR about ±2°C around 37°C is a typical tolerance band</cite> <cite id="de313ee4-1">Taguchi’s orthogonal arrays map factor counts/levels and interactions for efficient estimation</cite> <cite id="de313ee4-5">and use S/N ratios to identify robust settings</cite>.
