questions.original_query: What are the best practices for pre-processing Sentinel-2 data to enhance the accuracy of land cover classification?

query.text: What are the best practices for pre-processing Sentinel-2 data to enhance the accuracy of land cover classification?
query.answer:
Below is a practical, evidence-backed checklist of preprocessing steps that consistently improve land-cover classification accuracy with Sentinel-2. Each step is followed by rationale and key cautions, with citations to studies and comparative assessments.

1) Start with Level-2A reflectance if available
- Use Sentinel-2 Level-2A products (16‑bit/uint2) when available, as they incorporate many pre-processing steps (dark-object subtraction, adjacency correction, cloud/shadow masking) and deliver improved consistency for mapping from 5‑ to 30‑m land cover classes. <cite id="6d579132-0">Atmospheric correction is one of the key parts of remote sensing preprocessing because it can influence and change the final classification result</cite>. <cite id="0401ece3-2">A model using Level‑2A imagery achieved 90.79% overall accuracy for 5 Copernicus Land Cover classes in an ArcGIS template application</cite>.
- If operating in platforms like GEE, many built‑in Sentinel‑2 collections are Level‑2A already, easing downstream steps. <cite id="ba0b0227-7">A global LULC product derived from ESA Sentinel‑2 Level‑2 imagery demonstrates that standardized Level‑2A processing can directly support large‑scale land‑cover mapping</cite>.

2) Remove clouds and shadows; prefer clear-sky composites
- Mask clouds, cloud shadows, and sun-proximal glint before classification to avoid spectral noise and mislabeling of bright targets (e.g., snow, bare soil under shadows). <cite id="6d579132-0">Atmospheric correction and cloud masking strongly influence downstream classification outcomes for Sentinel‑2</cite>.
- For multi-date mapping, build temporally robust composites (e.g., median-of-clear pixels per tile/season) rather than using single scenes; this reduces speckle-like artifacts and stabilizes spectral signatures across dates. <cite id="ba0b0227-0">Winter tree and terrain shadow detection approaches emphasize that persistent canopy and topographic shading can mimic or mask land cover unless explicitly removed, reinforcing the need for time-aware shadow handling in composites</cite>.

3) Atmospheric correction to surface reflectance
- Apply consistent atmospheric correction across the study period (e.g., Sen2Cor/SEN2COR, MAJA, 6S, or commercial S2SR/COGEMA) and validate against “truth” dates or ground spectra. <cite id="6d579132-1">Comparisons of atmospheric correction approaches across Mediterranean shrubland and grassland show measurable differences in derived Level‑2A reflectance quality that affect downstream mapping</cite>. <cite id="6d579132-3">Inter-comparison of SEN2COR, MAJA, and 6S demonstrates method-dependent impacts on Sentinel‑2 reflectance used for cropland applications</cite>.
- Expect higher gains in turbid/coastal and hazy continental scenes; ensure aerosol and water‑vapor estimates are constrained by surface reflectance behavior and local climatology. <cite id="6d579132-0">A comparative study of five atmospheric correction pipelines found that the choice of correction pathway significantly impacts land-cover classification accuracy with Sentinel‑2</cite>.
- Avoid overfitting to a single correction: cross-validate per scene/season by comparing reflectance plausibility vs. spectral angle or by using a small ground-truth subset to calibrate per-date bias.

4) Radiometric terrain correction (topographic normalization)
- Correct illumination and slope effects (topographic radiometric correction) to reduce “valley darkening” and “ridge brightening” that bias spectral separability. Techniques include histogram matching to a Lambertian “standard” or direct gamma correction using slope/aspect/altitude from a DEM. <cite id="ba0b0227-1">An evaluation in northern Spain quantified improvements from combining atmospheric, topographic, and BRDF corrections, with topographic correction reducing slope-driven spectral bias for land-cover purposes</cite>. <cite id="ba0b0227-4">A practical Sentinel‑2 topographic correction workflow outlines flattening terrain and rescaling radiance to mitigate slope-induced brightness differences</cite>.
- For very mountainous terrain and subtle canopy mosaics, DEM-informed normalization can recover class separability that degrades under topographic masking. <cite id="ba0b0227-0">Topographic shadows complicate winter land-cover detection, and dedicated detection/correction improves discrimination</cite>.

5) BRDF/illumination normalization across dates
- Normalize BRDF using a seasonal “white paper” (e.g., Soave-style cosine and empirical BRDF correction) when building multi-date time series, especially where seasonal illumination (date, sun elevation) changes classes (e.g., snow/freeze/thaw, canopy angle). <cite id="6d579132-0">BRDF/illumination corrections can significantly change reflectance used for classification in Sentinel‑2 analyses</cite>.
- Be cautious: gains are scene- and season-dependent. <cite id="6d579132-6">In summer acquisitions, BRDF corrections in Spain did not significantly improve land‑cover classification accuracy</cite>. <cite id="6d579132-5">A multi‑method assessment also found modest or non‑significant BRDF gains in some regimes</cite>. Use cross-validation to decide whether BRDF steps add value in your domain (arid/shallow vs. temperate/mosaic canopies).
- A practical simplification: align composites to a fixed solar geometry (e.g., summer solstice) per biome or season and rescale to that white, or combine a DEM-based topographic correction with a date-specific cosine term.

6) Time-series design, smoothing, and seasonality
- Aggregate multi-date pixels into coherent stacks (e.g., per pixel chronological series), then smooth with localized filters (LOESS/MAD-based) or seasonal moving windows to reduce noise while preserving phenology. <cite id="6d579132-9">Machine-learning classifiers (e.g., SVM) can be sensitive to atmospheric correction choice; within-classifier consistency across dates is important for accuracy</cite>.
- Exploit seasonality to split training/validation by season or to create annual maps, but pre-process consistently within each window to prevent classifier drift across regimes. <cite id="0401ece3-7">A global review shows Sentinel‑2 improves monitoring of crops, forests, and urban areas, with accuracy driven by consistent preprocessing and phenological signal</cite>. <cite id="0401ece3-0">For heterogeneous landscapes, integrating auxiliary data with Sentinel‑2 and cross-validating across seasons improves overall classification performance</cite>.
- For freeze–thaw or snow masks, flag winter snow/ice explicitly and either exclude or normalize to avoid biasing reflectance of vegetated vs. snow-covered surfaces.

7) Masking and mosaicking across tiles
- Systematically mask borders and artefacts (edge effects, mismatched orthorectification) between tiles, and fill small gaps either by temporally adjacent clear pixels or by date-matched mosaics to preserve spectral integrity. <cite id="ba0b0227-7">Global LULC pipelines emphasize reprojection, masking, and mosaicking of Level‑2A Sentinel‑2 tiles to produce coherent wall-to-wall maps</cite>.
- Harmonize nodata and fill values; prefer majority-of-clear composites or percentile-based mosaics (e.g., 90th percentile of valid pixels per tile/patch) to suppress cloudy “bright” pixels. <cite id="0401ece3-8">Model-based pipelines generate class inferences for all available Sentinel‑2 across tiles and dates, integrating temporal coverage to reduce mosaic-related uncertainty</cite>.
- For very large regions, mosaic Level‑2A first and perform masking/quality filtering in a single CRS and resolution, rather than per‑tile supervised training, to reduce domain shift between neighboring tiles.

8) Reprojection, resampling, and pixel footprint control
- Choose a classification CRS and pixel size that balance geodesy and signal stability (e.g., UTM for regional tiles at 10–30 m). Reproject/resample to a common grid before training to avoid mixing pixels skewed by different projections/ellipsoids.
- Use area-preserving or NN-conservative resampling for spectral consistency (e.g., majority-of-clear pixel composites). <cite id="0401ece3-7">Accurate land-cover protocols recommend reprojection to consistent grids, masking, and harmonization when fusing Sentinel‑2 tiles with auxiliary datasets</cite>.
- Maintain per-pixel time series integrity during resampling and masking; avoid averaging across heterogeneous land patches that confound training pixels.

9) Band selection and feature design for classification
- With Sentinel‑2’s 10-band MSI (B2–B12), construct band-scaled reflectances and common vegetation indices (NDVI, DVI, SAV, EVI) and texture features; select subsets using cross-validation on a small labeled cohort to reduce overfitting in small sample regimes. <cite id="0401ece3-9">A global LULC methodology reports up to ~90% accuracy across seven surface cover classes with 10‑band Sentinel‑2 inputs trained with deep models</cite>.
- For water/shadow/urban scenes, add spectral separability features (e.g., shortwave infrared wetness or “glint” indicators) and ensure appropriate near-infrared thresholds, but cross-validate to prevent contamination by shadows.
- Preprocess consistently (radiometric terrain, BRDF, and atmospheric steps) before feature extraction; classifier choice interacts with preprocessing (e.g., SVMs often tolerate per-pixel normalization; CNNs benefit from standardized BRDF/illumination).

10) Training data and validation strategy
- Extract training pixels with stratified sampling across dates/seasons to reflect real-world spectral-temporal variability; prefer larger, representative windows for heterogeneous classes (e.g., agriculture, urban mosaics). Use time-series signatures where seasonal change matters. <cite id="0401ece3-0">Reviews of Sentinel‑2 for land cover highlight improved monitoring of crops and urban areas when temporal variability and auxiliary data are integrated</cite>.
- Perform per-date or per-season cross-validation, and explicitly compare classification accuracy across alternative preprocessing pipelines to quantify ROI for each step (e.g., adding S2SR vs. Sen2Cor, adding BRDF normalization). <cite id="6d579132-0">A five-method atmospheric correction comparison directly links correction choices to classification accuracy changes in land cover tasks</cite>.

11) Practical sequence to deploy
- Sequence: Raw TOA → Dark-object/Aerosol correction (S2SR or Sen2Cor) → Quality mask (cloud/shadow/snow) → Radiometric terrain correction using DEM slope/aspect/alt → Optional BRDF/illumination normalization if cross-date or seasonal changes are material → Median-of-clear composites per tile/season → Reproject/resample to common grid → Extract time-series training pixels; add NDVI/texture; train SVM/CNN; cross-validate by season; build annual wall-to-wall map. <cite id="6d579132-1">Atmospheric correction quality varies by method and site, as shown in Mediterranean shrub/grassland intercomparisons</cite>. <cite id="ba0b0227-1">Atmospheric, topographic, and BRDF corrections together can yield measurable improvements, though gains are domain-dependent</cite>. <cite id="6d579132-6">BRDF corrections may not materially improve accuracy during certain seasons, warranting empirical checks</cite>.
- Optional: Use Level-2A to skip steps if available; otherwise, document per-scene bias corrections and cross-check with GROUND truth where possible. <cite id="0401ece3-2">An ArcGIS workflow shows robust accuracy at ~91% using Level‑2A and standardized preprocessing</cite>.

Key pitfalls to avoid
- Mixing reflectance from different atmospheric correction pipelines; ensure a single chosen method across the study period. <cite id="6d579132-3">SEN2COR, MAJA, and 6S produced differing Sentinel‑2 reflectance for croplands, underscoring method consistency</cite>.
- Neglecting terrain: mountainous regions without topographic correction lose separability in slope-facing classes. <cite id="ba0b0227-1">Topographic correction reduced slope-induced bias, improving land-cover classification outcomes</cite>.
- One-size BRDF: validate seasonal effects; in many temperate summer scenes, added BRDF steps yield small deltas. <cite id="6d579132-6">Summer BRDF gains were not significant for Spanish landscapes</cite>.
- Over-smoothing phenology: use date-aware windows and classifier-specific regularization to preserve seasonality while removing noise. <cite id="6d579132-9">SVM performance varied with atmospheric correction and aggregation design</cite>.

Summary: The most effective preprocessing stack is consistent atmospheric correction to surface reflectance, rigorous cloud/shadow/snow masking, DEM-informed radiometric terrain correction, conditional BRDF/illumination normalization for cross-date scenes, seasonally coherent compositing and smoothing, and reprojection/resampling to a common grid with careful training pixel extraction. Evaluate each step’s contribution empirically in your domain; in many land-cover tasks, well-calibrated atmospheric correction and terrain normalization plus robust compositing deliver 85–92% accuracy with 10‑band Sentinel‑2, while adding BRDF improves some regimes but not all. <cite id="0401ece3-9">Custom models trained on 10‑band Sentinel‑2 can reach up to ~90% accuracy across key surface cover classes</cite>. <cite id="0401ece3-8">Operational pipelines aggregate per-tile, per-date inference and mosaic over time to build wall‑to‑wall land‑cover maps</cite>. <cite id="ba0b0227-1">Across methods, pairing atmospheric, topographic, and context-aware BRDF steps yields the most robust reflectance for classification</cite>.

fully_underspecified.text: What are the best practices for pre-processing data to improve classification accuracy?
fully_underspecified.answer:
Below are evidence‑backed best practices for preprocessing to improve classification accuracy, organized by pipeline stage. Domain and task specifics drive exact choices; use cross‑validated ablations to tune and justify steps.

1) Define problems, labels, and splits first
- Split before any preprocessing. Decide on a time cutoff; hold out final test to estimate generalization. Fit only train for scalers, encoders, imputers; never use test or CV folds for fit parameters that depend on “all data.” This avoids leakage from scalers, selectors, and model‑aware encoders (e.g., target/ordered encodings, embeddings) <cite id="ee833b75-0">Always split the data into train and test subsets first, particularly before any preprocessing steps</cite> <cite id="ee833b75-9">Avoid leakage in preprocessing by ensuring estimators are fit only on training data and handling unseen values in test via explicit vocabulary/transformers</cite> <cite id="ee833b75-6">Standard scaling causes leakage if fit on full data; use per‑fold means/standard deviations so each fold’s transform depends only on its training data</cite>. 
- Use proper evaluation for imbalanced targets (PR/AUC, Fβ) and resampling methods; do not rely solely on accuracy <cite id="ee833b75-0">Use cross‑validation and splits to fairly assess preprocessing choices, as naive pipelines can overfit</cite>.

2) Clean and handle missingness with domain context
- Prefer domain‑informed imputation (domain features, domain rules, regression trees) over naive mean/mode imputation, especially when missingness is predictive. Arbitrary thresholds and “drop missing” can discard signal; chained/imputation models reduce bias and variance compared with single mean imputation in high‑dimensional supervised problems <cite id="606b9453-0">Comprehensive reviews emphasize that preprocessing choices (e.g., handling missing data) materially affect downstream classification performance</cite> <cite id="c8ccefe0-5">Missing data arise commonly and must be treated explicitly; preprocessing defines how much signal remains for classifiers</cite>. 
- For tables and ML platforms, use iterative/multiple imputation or monotone regression strategies to model relationships; when in doubt, try several strategies and compare cross‑validated AUC/accuracy on holdout <cite id="606b9453-8">Data cleaning and preprocessing are foundational to reliable performance and accuracy</cite>.

3) Encode categorical variables and respect cardinality
- Low/ordinal categories: label/ordinal encoders can help where order matters. One‑hot/label are reasonable when nats are few relative to sample size; be careful with high cardinality and rare labels. <cite id="f5be0520-2">One‑hot creates high‑dimensional sparse spaces that increase overfitting risk and degrade generalization</cite> <cite id="f5be0520-3">One‑hot is common but simplicity can mean it captures only indicators rather than predictive structure</cite>. 
- High cardinality/nats: prefer learned, model‑aware encodings (target/ordered encodings with smoothing) or embeddings trained within the model to summarize label‑contingent information. Recent work shows smoothing target encodings and class center–based methods reduce error from noisy/imbalance and missing categories in categorical predictive pipelines; embeddings can generalize better as dimensionality explodes <cite id="c8ccefe0-0">Categoricals are core inputs; smoothing target encodings and class center‑based schemes mitigate over‑fitting and missing‑value effects while improving predictive performance</cite> <cite id="c8ccefe0-1">Target‑aware smoothing improves stability and accuracy for high‑cardinality categorical variables</cite> <cite id="f5be0520-8">Embedding‑based encodings outperform frequency/label encodings on tabular benchmarks, with better calibration and accuracy</cite> <cite id="f5be0520-9">Models with embedding encoders outperform methods like frequency, binary, and label encodings for high‑cardinality features</cite>. 
- Missing categories: treat “missing” as a genuine category and encode separately; handle with the same smoothing/regularization that addresses noisy leaves. <cite id="863432976">Target/ordered encodings with explicit treatment for missingness outperform naive imputation/omission when missingness encodes information</cite>. 
- Practical rule: start with label binning; add cross‑validation ablations to try target/ordered and embeddings. Prefer embeddings when nat counts exceed sample size raised to ~0.5–0.6 or when sparsity/imbalance is severe; use target encoders with cross‑validation smoothing and shrinkage. <cite id="f5be0520-2">High‑cardinality forces sparsity; use compact representations to control overfitting</cite> <cite id="c8ccefe0-0">Smoothing target encoding is a robust default in supervised categorical preprocessing</cite>.

4) Transform numerical features: scaling, robustness, and compatibility
- Scale features compatible with your model family. Use StandardScaler (per‑feature z‑scores) for linear/models sensitive to scales; MinMax/robust scalers when outliers dominate or when metric compatibility matters. Crucially, refit transforms per CV fold and avoid sample‑wise normalization that leaks class structure. <cite id="ee833b75-0">Preprocessing fit on test or global mean/standard deviation leaks information; split first and refit transformers per fold</cite> <cite id="ee833b75-6">Standard scaling leakage arises when using global mean/standard deviation rather than per‑fold statistics</cite>. 
- Avoid arbitrary cutoffs (“normalize to 0–100” without domain basis). Winsorize extreme tails only if supported by diagnostics. Treat nonlinearities with careful domain features; polynomial features with shrinkage; be wary that polynomial sparsity harms generalization. Empirical benchmarks show that poor preprocessing choices (e.g., distance metric–mismatched scalers, global leakage) degrade accuracy, whereas per‑fold scaling and compatible kernels improve it. <cite id="606b9453-0">Preprocessing design (cleaning, encoding, scaling) is a primary determinant of achievable classification accuracy</cite> <cite id="ee833b75-0">Correct split‑then‑fit flows and per‑fold transforms improve model performance and trustworthiness</cite>.

5) Engineer features and select dimensions with purpose
- Derive features from domain knowledge (interaction terms between key factors, engineered ratios) but regularize and cross‑validate aggressively to avoid overfitting. <cite id="606b9453-0">Feature design and transformation can unlock meaningful signal that raw encodings miss</cite>. 
- For large, noisy feature sets, use model‑agnostic filters (chi‑squared, ANOVA F‑features, mutual information) to reduce dimension, then pursue model‑aware wrappers (Recursive Feature Elimination, L1 wrappers). In high dimension with moderate sample sizes, PCA/TruncatedSVD can help but risk discarding label‑contingent variance; use stability/consistency across CV folds. <cite id="606b9453-7">Empirical comparisons show feature selection and model choice materially change performance; selection reduces noise and improves accuracy</cite> <cite id="f5be0520-2">PCA/one‑hot can inflate dimensionality; compact representations control overfitting</cite>. 
- Be cautious with pure dimensionality reduction when class structure is nonlinear; gradient boosted trees often achieve strong accuracy out of the box with careful preprocessing, while kernel/PF‑based models benefit from feature selection and sparse transforms. <cite id="606b9453-0">Different methods handle high‑dimensionality differently; choosing transform plus model matters for accuracy</cite> <cite id="606b9453-3">High‑dimensional classification performance varies by method and preprocessing</cite>.

6) Text and tokenization pipelines (NLP tasks)
- Lowercase and remove HTML/irrelevant markup/HTML tags early; tokenize consistently; remove rare tokens only after n‑gram exploration. <cite id="606b9453-0">Preprocessing choices (cleaning and tokenization) materially change classification accuracy</cite>. 
- Apply stopword removal with care: remove only those documented to hinder your classifier on your domain and evaluate both ondev and holdout. <cite id="606b9453-0">Cleaning rules should be validated empirically; generic removals can harm or help depending on task</cite>. 
- Use TF–IDF weighting for bag‑of‑words to separate term frequency from document rarity; add n‑grams (unigrams and bigrams often) to capture multi‑token concepts. Control n‑gram vocabulary size via frequency caps to reduce overfitting and memory usage; evaluate uni/bi/tri impact with CV. <cite id="606b9453-0">TF–IDF and n‑gram selection are core to modern text classification accuracy</cite>. 
- Consider lemmatization (morphological normalization) over simple stemming when POS and broader semantic control is beneficial; evaluate both on your data, because domain morphology and error profiles differ. <cite id="606b9453-0">Preprocessing strategies for text carry nontrivial, empirically measurable effects on accuracy</cite>. 
- Keep a small held‑out “dev set” for iterative feature switches (stopwords, bigrams, lemmas) so you can A/B without leaking into final eval. <cite id="ee833b75-0">Use explicit splits/pipelines so validation faithfully reflects preprocessing influence</cite>.

7) Handle class imbalance and cost sensitivity responsibly
- Imbalance can wreck accuracy‑driven choices and ROC metrics; use resampling (SMOTE/Tomek links, ADASYN) or cost‑sensitive learning, and evaluate PR/AUC/average precision and misclassification costs on holdout. Use Tomek links or EasyEnsemble/RandomUnder/SMOTE variants to clean noisy boundaries; cross‑validate resampling to avoid overfitting to synthetic samples. <cite id="ee833b75-0">Choose evaluation metrics and preprocessing that reflect real costs; leakage‑free resampling and AP are recommended under imbalance</cite>. 
- Progressive approaches: try undersampling major classes, oversampling minor classes (SMOTE/ADASYN), class‑weighted loss, and ensemble combinations; pick what yields best AP or cost‑weighted accuracy on CV, then finalize with a small holdout. <cite id="606b9453-3">Different methods exhibit distinct performance behavior under high dimensionality; imbalance compounds this, calling for resampling/metric changes</cite>.

8) Pipeline, CV, and production hygiene
- Wrap each preprocessing step in a Pipeline/ColumnTransformer; refit estimators per fold (StandardScaler refit=False, selectors refit=True); cache complex transforms; use FunctionTransformer to inject cross‑validation‑stable post‑processing. <cite id="ee833b75-0">Avoid leakage by refitting transforms in each fold and by splitting before preprocessing</cite>. 
- Choose CV and scoring by business risk: time‑series use expanding/testing walks; general tabular use stratified K‑fold with PR/AUC or cost‑aware scoring under imbalance; always ensure no data laterally contaminates a fold via data capture pipelines. <cite id="ee833b75-0">Scikit‑learn pitfalls document leakage modes; pipelines and fold‑wise refit are the defenses</cite>. 
- Monitor drift across features you engineered/encoded; retrain on out‑of‑sample forward‑looking windows when distributions shift, and re‑validate full pipelines. <cite id="606b9453-0">Preprocessing and feature transforms that ignore distribution changes can erode accuracy over time</cite>.

9) Practical checklist and trade‑offs
- Missing data: try mode/median, KNN/multiple imputation, and model‑based (GPR, XGBoost imputer); compare CV accuracy on raw vs engineered splits. <cite id="606b9453-8">Cleaning improves reliability and accuracy</cite>. 
- Categoricals: start with label/one‑hot; if high cardinality/imbalance or many nats, adopt target/ordered with smoothing and/or embeddings; treat missing as category. <cite id="c8ccefe0-0">Smoothing target encodings reduce error from noisy leaves and missing categories</cite> <cite id="f5be0520-2">One‑hot adds dimensionality that raises overfit risk</cite>. 
- Scaling: use per‑fold StandardScaler; avoid distance‑mismatch (e.g., tree models may not need scaling, while SVM/LSTM may benefit); avoid global mean/SD. <cite id="ee833b75-0">Split then scale; refit each fold</cite> <cite id="ee833b75-6">Global scaling leaks signal and inflates accuracy; per‑fold scaling fixes it</cite>. 
- Feature engineering/selection: add domain features, use chi2/ANOVA/MutualInfo filters, then L1/RFEC; validate PCA/UMAP only if class structure is preserved and stable across folds; prefer tree models when interactions and nonlinearities dominate. <cite id="606b9453-7">Feature selection and model choice jointly determine performance</cite> <cite id="606b9453-3">Accuracy varies by method and dimensionality</cite>. 
- Text: lowercasing, punctuation removal; TF–IDF; uni/bi‑grams with frequency caps; optional lemmatization; evaluate both with/without stopword removal; use small dev set for exploration. <cite id="606b9453-0">These transformations have measurable effects on text classification accuracy</cite>. 
- Imbalance: check baseline precision/recall; apply SMOTE/Tomek/ADASYN or class weights; report average precision and Fβ; choose final metric matching business loss. <cite id="ee833b75-0">Use proper metrics and avoid misleading accuracy; resampling/cost sensitivity address imbalance</cite>. 
- Anti‑patterns to explicitly avoid: mean/mode imputation when missingness predicts target; arbitrary global scaling or sample‑wise scalers; encoding missingness after train/test split; using the same folds to pick scalers/encoders and to train/evaluate; omitting CV‑aware refit for transformers. <cite id="ee833b75-0">These leakages inflate apparent accuracy and mislead evaluation</cite> <cite id="ee833b75-6">Global scaling averages and spreads leak future information</cite> <cite id="ee833b75-9">Fit transformers only on train; handle out‑of‑vocabulary at inference</cite>.
- Optional but effective: monotone regression imputers, Bayesian splines for monotonic relationships, quantile transformers for nonlinear marginal distributions, and embeddings for multi‑modal categorical data, with cross‑validated A‑UC comparisons to justify choices <cite id="f5be0520-7">Regularized target encoding compared favorably to one‑hot/label in multiple categorical learning scenarios</cite> <cite id="f5be0520-8">Embeddings for high‑cardinality outperform simpler encodings</cite>.

A compact workflow you can iterate:
1) Split and validate plan; define final holdout. 
2) Clean: domain‑aware handling of missingness; remove unusable/irrelevant columns; de‑duplicate tokens; create a dev fold for try‑fast‑fail engineering. 
3) Encode: one‑hot/label for low ordinal; target/ordered with smoothing and/or embeddings for high cardinality; treat missingness explicitly. 
4) Transform: per‑fold scaling only; PCA/selection only in high‑dimensional or noisy regimes and validated across folds; TF–IDF + n‑grams for text. 
5) Engineer: add domain interactions/derived ratios; filter with chi2/ANOVA/MutualInfo; consider embeddings for multi‑modal content. 
6) Imbalance: diagnose; resample/cost‑weight; evaluate AP and misclassification cost. 
7) Pipeline and CV: scikit‑learn‑style ColumnTransformer/Pipeline with refit=False; stratified CV; early stopping by cross‑validated AIC/MAPE. 
8) Ablate: compare baseline vs each major change on dev and CV; confirm no leakage; retrain final model on train set only, then report on holdout. <cite id="ee833b75-0">Use pipelines, per‑fold refit, and proper splitting to maximize accuracy and prevent leakage</cite> <cite id="c8ccefe0-0">Model‑aware encodings increase accuracy over raw indicator-only schemes in categorical-heavy tasks</cite> <cite id="606b9453-3">Selection of transforms and models must be tuned to data properties for best accuracy</cite>.

Summary: The single biggest lever is a leakage‑free, model‑aware preprocessing pipeline that respects your data’s structure. For tabulars, adopt target/ordered or embeddings for high‑cardinality categories and refit all transforms per fold; for text, apply TF–IDF and principled n‑grams; for missingness, favor domain‑informed imputers; and under imbalance, resample/weight and evaluate with PR‑centric metrics. All while cross‑validating and ablation‑testing changes on an untouched holdout set <cite id="ee833b75-0">Correct split‑then‑fit and refit practices are essential for reliable gains</cite> <cite id="c8ccefe0-0">Categorical smoothing and class center encoders improve accuracy and stability</cite> <cite id="606b9453-0">Comprehensive preprocessing reviews highlight that these choices directly improve classification performance</cite> <cite id="f5be0520-2">Sparsity and overfitting are the central risks to watch and mitigate</cite>.

without_scope.text: What are the best practices for pre-processing data to enhance the accuracy of land cover classification?
without_scope.answer:
Below are evidence-backed best practices to improve land cover classification accuracy. We organize them from raw data through modeling, with guidance on when to apply steps and how they affect performance.

1) Core image-level preprocessing: radiometric and geometric alignment
- Radiometric calibration is foundational. Convert digital numbers (DNs) to physical units (radiance/reflectance) to enable comparable spectral signatures across dates and sensors, using sensor-specific calibration parameters and detector-specific gains/offsets; this is a prerequisite for downstream atmospheric, BRDF, and terrain corrections and for model robustness across scenes and epochs <cite id="8bf2561f-0">A typical image preprocessing includes sensor calibration, conversion to radiance/reflectance, and subsequent corrections</cite> <cite id="8bf2561f-8">Radiometric calibration makes it possible to convert recorded DN to physical quantities (radiation or reflectance)</cite> <cite id="8bf2561f-6">Preprocessing commonly includes georegistration, co-registration, conversion to radiance, reflectance or brightness, and BRDF/topographic corrections</cite> <cite id="8bf2561f-7">Landsat data are corrected for geometric, radiometric, and terrain features using accurate measurements and stringent calibration</cite> <cite id="0e330e42-7">Radiometric calibration, speckle reduction, geometric and terrain correction are essential preprocessing steps for SAR data</cite>.
- Co-registration, orthorectification, and geometric correction (including terrain correction for SAR and optical) ensure pixel areas are comparable. Use precise sensor ephemeris and Digital Elevation Model (DEM) data; for SAR, radiometric terrain correction (RTC) corrects backscatter for geometry and terrain to stabilize classification <cite id="0e330e42-1">Radiometric Terrain Correct (RTC) for Sentinel‑1 products accounts for terrain</cite> <cite id="8bf2561f-6">Georeferencing and co-registration are standard preprocessing steps for Landsat</cite> <cite id="0e330e42-6">A data recipe demonstrates radiometric terrain correction of Sentinel‑1 in S1 Toolbox</cite> <cite id="0e330e42-9">Radiometric terrain correction requires orthorectification, with speckle filtering controls available</cite>.
- For multisource mosaics, harmonize the illumination domain to prevent confounding effects from viewing geometry and BRDF. Use cross-sensor BRDF models or products (e.g., MCD43 BRDF/Albedo) and, for multi-date scenes, apply atmospheric correction to align conditions <cite id="8bf2561f-0">Preprocessing typically includes sensor calibration, atmospheric correction, geometric correction, and BRDF/topographic corrections</cite> <cite id="8bf2561f-1">Atmospheric correction reduces atmospheric effects, improving clarity and consistency for applications like land cover</cite> <cite id="8bf2561f-4">Atmospheric correction is a common preprocessing step before change detection or classification; multiple correction families exist</cite>.

2) Atmospheric and SAR-specific corrections, and their accuracy impact
- For optical imagery, perform atmospheric correction (AC) to remove path radiance, aerosol and water-vapor effects, and to retrieve surface reflectance; modern AC methods differ notably in classification accuracy, so test multiple algorithms (e.g., SNIC, MAIAC, Fmask/SEVIRI-based, 6S-driven) for your site/sensor and retain consistent masking for clouds and aerosols <cite id="8bf2561f-3">The impact of five atmospheric correction methods on Sentinel‑2 land cover classification accuracy is examined</cite> <cite id="8bf2561f-1">Applying AC improves imagery clarity and is commonly recommended</cite> <cite id="8bf2561f-4">Atmospheric correction mitigates atmosphere-driven confounders for change detection and classification</cite>.
- SAR preprocessing: apply radiometric calibration to sigma0 or gamma0, then terrain correction (gamma‑naught is often preferred because it normalizes for incidence angle) and speckle filtering tuned to the scene statistic and window sizes; recognize that resampling in terrain correction can alter speckle statistics and texture, so choose filters that preserve scale-invariant details for classification (e.g., large windows for strong speckle suppression and texture preservation) <cite id="0e330e42-0">Speckle filters are designed for SAR’s statistics; terrain correction resampling can alter these, affecting classification</cite> <cite id="0e330e42-5">Good speckle removal often needs larger windows while preserving texture; the choice of speckle filter and window size trades off noise reduction with detail retention for classification</cite> <cite id="0e330e42-2">Speckle filtering choice significantly influences Sentinel‑1 classification accuracy; evaluation over multiple algorithms and terrain conditions is advised</cite>.
- Quantified impact: studies show that atmospheric or terrain corrections can increase land cover accuracy and reduce confounding by illumination/geometry; conversely, omitting corrections degrades homogeneity across scenes/seasons and reduces classifier performance <cite id="8bf2561f-0">Atmospheric and topographic correction effects on classification accuracy are directly examined; sensor calibration and corrections are core preprocessing</cite> <cite id="8bf2561f-6">A Landsat preprocessing “survival guide” shows that calibration and corrections reduce misclassification by improving radiometric consistency</cite> <cite id="8bf2561f-3">Selecting among AC algorithms yields measurable differences in Sentinel‑2 classification</cite> <cite id="8bf2561f-9">For change detection, registration, radiometric corrections, and atmospheric corrections are core preprocessing to improve accuracy</cite>.

3) Quality masking and temporal harmonization
- Mask clouds, cloud shadows, and snow/ice before classification to avoid mislabeling; for multi-date analyses, maintain explicit masks and prefer AC algorithms that separate aerosol/shadow effects from surface reflectance. Time-series workflows should co-register and harmonize scenes to a common date and solar geometry before aggregation to reduce spurious land-cover change or confusion among classes <cite id="8bf2561f-4">Atmospheric correction and masking steps are central to reducing atmospheric influence and improving change detection performance</cite> <cite id="8bf2561f-1">AC practices improve imagery used for land cover analysis by reducing atmospheric effects</cite>.
- When fusing data across sensors and dates for harmonization (e.g., pan-sharpening or time-series smoothing), ensure spectral/illumination consistency and test for bias shifts in derived indices like NDVI; cross-sensor harmonization reduces misclassification in mixed-sensor panchromatic products <cite id="7a65f8ad-8">Comparative analyses of land cover performance across data sources highlight the need to harmonize spectral domains to avoid performance degradation</cite>.

4) Spectral–spatial feature engineering
- Use spectral indices and ratio-based features to separate biophysical land cover types (e.g., vegetation vs. impervious surfaces vs. water), and consider vegetation, water, and urban indices; indices can stabilize classification under illumination variation and improve separability when coupled with texture <cite id="7f189e6b-7">Alphabetical lists and use-cases for spectral indices (NDVI, fire fuel, urban indices) show practical value for land cover discrimination</cite> <cite id="7f189e6b-9">Automatically designed urban spectral indices improved classification accuracy and mapping of urban land covers</cite> <cite id="7f189e6b-2">Seasonality and topography strongly influence spectral signatures; incorporating seasonality and topography improves land cover classification accuracy</cite>.
- Add spatial-context features such as grey-level or multi-scale grey-tone/edge/variability texture to capture patch patterns and reduce “salt-and-pepper” misclassification. Studies show that jointly using spectral and spatial information improves classification accuracy over spectral-only features <cite id="7f189e6b-4">Use of spatial information during classification via textural and spectral images reduces misclassification and improves accuracy</cite> <cite id="7f189e6b-2">Accounting for seasonality and topography improves accuracy in heterogeneous forests</cite>.
- Where available, combine spectral data with height (e.g., LiDAR or SAR backscatter) to build spectral–topographic features. In urban environments, height and spectral indices jointly help separate buildings, impervious surfaces, and vegetation <cite id="7f189e6b-9">Urban classification benefits from new spectral indices and automated classification leveraging spectral–textural features</cite> <cite id="8bf2561f-1">Atmospherically corrected, georegistered multi-sensor data improve classification</cite>.
- For optical–SAR fusion, apply spectral-sharpening of multispectral data with coherent SAR to sharpen spectral detail into SAR-derived structural classes (e.g., vegetation/water/urban), while ensuring both are AC/RTC and harmonized by time and location <cite id="8bf2561f-0">A complete chain from calibration to topographic correction underpins robust classification of fused optical–SAR products</cite> <cite id="0e330e42-1">RTC products allow coherent fusion with multi-temporal optical data after harmonization</cite>.

5) Data-centric preprocessing for machine learning and deep learning
- Curate training samples by stratifying across spatial heterogeneity and seasonality; prefer larger, well-distributed patches and collect labels from multiple clear days to reduce label noise and class confusion. Recent reviews emphasize that dataset composition and labeling strategy dominate model performance in LULC tasks <cite id="7a65f8ad-1">A systematic review of deep-learning LULC classification outlines data preparation, labeling, and model design as key aspects</cite> <cite id="8bf2561f-1">Corrective preprocessing improves data quality for applications like land cover</cite>.
- Manage class imbalance and label uncertainty: oversample rare classes, use focal loss or class weights, or generate synthetic samples; for semi-supervised approaches, confidence-based pseudo-labeling can expand annotations while controlling quality <cite id="7a65f8ad-1">Deep-learning reviews highlight dataset biases and labeling errors as limiting factors; mitigation strategies are recommended</cite>.
- Standardize/whiten input features before modeling; for CNNs, consider data augmentation (rotations, illumination normalization), and for time series, normalize each spectral band to zero mean/unit variance across the training window and apply per-scene mean/median subtraction when using multiple dates <cite id="7a65f8ad-1">Reviews recommend preprocessing and augmentation strategies to stabilize training and improve generalization in LULC classification</cite>.
- Evaluate classifier robustness and AC interplay: object-based ML studies show that AC strategy and spatial segmentation strongly modulate accuracy; test multiple AC pipelines and segment-level normalization strategies to identify the most robust setup for your site and seasons <cite id="7a65f8ad-4">A unified framework finds AC strategies and classifier robustness interact; choosing AC and normalization jointly impacts performance</cite>.
- Transfer learning and domain adaptation are effective when labeled data are scarce or site-specific variations are large; using pre-trained CNNs (e.g., Inception-v3, DenseNet121) and fine-tuning on local LULC datasets yields robust improvements over training from scratch, particularly when transferring from similar biomes/climates <cite id="7a65f8ad-7">Transfer learning with Inception-v3 and DenseNet121 improved land cover classification reliability</cite> <cite id="7a65f8ad-3">Cross-scale frameworks integrating transfer learning with deep learning improve urban land-cover mapping</cite> <cite id="7a65f8ad-5">Inter-region transfer learning is proposed to enhance performance and reduce sample requirements under regional variability</cite>.
- For time series, segment continuous scenes into coherent patches, remove outliers via per-band z-scores, apply moving-window AC or harmonization, and experiment with single-date versus composite windows; evidence shows that scene-level harmonization reduces misclassification relative to uncorrected stacks <cite id="8bf2561f-4">Atmospheric correction is a common and effective preprocessing step before change and classification tasks</cite> <cite id="8bf2561f-6">Standardized preprocessing pipelines for Landsat stabilize per-pixel values before classification</cite>.

6) Practical, end-to-end preprocessing pipeline
- Optical stack:
  1) Download orthorectified surface reflectance products (e.g., Landsat SR, Sentinel-2 SR), or if using raw scenes, perform georegistration/co-registration, radiometric calibration to TOA, atmospheric correction to surface reflectance, and BRDF/illumination normalization; apply terrain/DEM-based corrections where required; mask clouds/shadows/snow before labeling and inference <cite id="8bf2561f-6">A Landsat preprocessing workflow enumerates georegistration, co-registration, conversion to radiance/reflectance, BRDF and topographic corrections</cite> <cite id="8bf2561f-3">Choice of AC method materially affects Sentinel‑2 classification accuracy</cite> <cite id="8bf2561f-4">Atmospheric correction mitigates atmosphere-driven signal to reduce misclassification</cite>.
  2) Engineer indices (NDVI, NDBI, NDMI, urban indices), compute multi-scale texture (GLCM), and optionally combine with LiDAR-derived metrics for spectral–spatial fusion; validate improvements on a held-out panel <cite id="7f189e6b-7">Spectral index families and their land cover applications support index engineering</cite> <cite id="7f189e6b-4">Joint spectral–textural information reduces misclassification</cite>.
  3) Stratify training/validation by land cover and terrain; use spatial cross-validation or leave-one-scene-out when scenes differ strongly; evaluate seasonal vs. annual composites; apply transfer learning if generalizing across regions <cite id="7a65f8ad-1">Deep learning LULC reviews detail cross-validation and dataset design practices as central to robustness</cite> <cite id="7a65f8ad-7">Transfer learning improves performance with limited labeled data and enhances robustness</cite>.
- SAR stack:
  1) Preprocess SLC to RTC: radiometric calibration, speckle filtering tuned to window sizes and statistics, and terrain correction to gamma‑naught; if fusing with optical, co-register and resample consistently; assess multiple filters and window sizes for your land cover and slope regimes <cite id="0e330e42-1">ASF RTC guide details calibration, terrain correction, and outputs</cite> <cite id="0e330e42-5">Larger windows can reduce speckle but smooth details; balance is key for classification</cite> <cite id="0e329e42-2">Speckle filtering choice impacts classification accuracy; empirical evaluations are recommended</cite>.
  2) Generate texture features and coherence-derived metrics where helpful; in urban areas, combine SAR with spectral indices to separate impervious surfaces and vegetation; mask strong backscatter/layover/edge zones known to misclassify <cite id="0e330e42-5">Speckle/texture considerations guide selection of features that stabilize classification</cite> <cite id="7f189e6b-2">Topography affects signatures; topography-aware or terrain-corrected data improve accuracy</cite>.
  3) Use CNNs/FCNs with data augmentation when data are limited; apply per-scene normalization and class-weights for rare classes; or use object-based approaches with AC-aware segmentation and shape/size features <cite id="7a65f8ad-1">Deep-learning LULC reviews outline data augmentation and class imbalance as key preprocessing considerations</cite> <cite id="7a65f8ad-4">Combining AC choices with segment-level statistics yields robust object-based classification</cite>.
- Hybrid and multi-sensor:
  1) Spectral sharpening can convert coarse spectral SAR/LS into fine spectral but robust structural classes using multi-date coherence or texture; harmonize viewing geometry and dates for consistent illumination; quantify gains on a test set before deploying <cite id="8bf2561f-0">Complete calibration and correction chains support robust hybrid product classification</cite> <cite id="0e330e42-1">RTC outputs are designed for consistent, harmonized fusion</cite> <cite id="7a65f8ad-8">Cross-source analyses highlight the importance of harmonization and clear training/validation protocols for accurate LULC mapping</cite>.

7) Pitfalls and how to choose among options
- Do not skip atmospheric correction for land cover; even “clear” scenes suffer from aerosols and path radiance that shift spectral means and reduce separability; test at least two AC methods and keep consistent masks for clouds/aerosols/shadows <cite id="8bf2561f-3">Sentinel‑2 classification accuracy varies with AC choice; testing multiple methods is advised</cite> <cite id="8bf2561f-4">Atmospheric correction reduces confounding for classification and change detection</cite>.
- For SAR, avoid over-smoothing; select speckle filters and window sizes to preserve edges/texture; terrain correction should precede filtering/feature extraction to ensure geometry is correct <cite id="0e330e42-0">Resampling in terrain correction alters speckle statistics; select filters accordingly</cite> <cite id="0e330e42-5">Larger windows reduce speckle but can remove fine details; balance for classification</cite>.
- Normalize per scene/season; use batch normalization in CNNs and class weights for rare classes; be cautious with cross-sensor fusion—harmonize reflectance scales and illumination; document all preprocessing steps for reproducibility and to diagnose misclassification hotspots <cite id="7a65f8ad-1">Reviews emphasize preprocessing, labeling, and model design as primary levers for LULC performance</cite> <cite id="7a65f8ad-4">AC and normalization choices jointly determine robustness; evaluate systematically</cite>.
- Start with well-curated benchmarks (e.g., high-resolution labels) to calibrate pipelines; then scale with harmonized time-series and transfer learning if generalizing across biomes or cities <cite id="7a65f8ad-7">Transfer learning improved urban land cover accuracy using pre-trained deep networks</cite> <cite id="8bf2561f-8">Radiometric and atmospheric correction standards provide a solid basis for benchmarking</cite>.

Summary: The most impactful preprocessing steps that measurably improve land cover accuracy are accurate radiometric/geometric corrections and atmospheric/SAR-specific normalization; coupled with robust quality masking and carefully engineered spectral–spatial features, these stabilize signatures and reduce misclassification. For data-driven models, stratified, high-quality training, augmentation, and imbalance handling are essential; testing AC strategies and leveraging transfer learning further boost robustness, especially across seasons and sensors <cite id="8bf2561f-0">Sensor calibration, atmospheric and topographic corrections substantially affect land cover classification accuracy</cite> <cite id="8bf2561f-3">Selection of atmospheric correction markedly changes classification outcomes for Sentinel‑2</cite> <cite id="8bf2561f-6">Landsat preprocessing guides clarify steps like co-registration and reflectance conversion before classification</cite> <cite id="0e330e42-1">Radiometric terrain correction and speckle control are core for Sentinel‑1 fusion and mapping</cite> <cite id="0e330e42-2">Speckle filtering choices have clear, quantifiable effects on classification accuracy</cite> <cite id="7f189e6b-4">Combining spectral and spatial information reduces misclassification and improves mapping accuracy</cite> <cite id="7a65f8ad-1">Deep-learning LULC reviews: data preparation and labeling quality are central to performance</cite> <cite id="7a65f8ad-8">Comparative analyses across data sources underscore the need to harmonize preprocessing and evaluation for reliable performance</cite>.

without_term.text: What are the best practices for pre-processing satellite data to enhance the accuracy of land cover classification?
without_term.answer:
Summary and key takeaways
- Preprocessing for land cover classification should begin with sensor- and mission-specific calibration, then correct atmospheric effects (optical), geometric terrain (orthorectify), and mask clouds/shadows (optical) or speckle, terrain artifacts (SAR). These steps consistently improve accuracy; otherwise, distortions and noise degrade class separability and introduce bias. <cite id="d5c69a19-0">Core Landsat preprocessing includes georeferencing/co-registration and conversion from raw counts to surface reflectance to remove sensor and atmospheric distortions before classification</cite><cite id="d5c69a19-3">USGS Landsat processing defines L1TP (terrain-flattened surface reflectance) as the highest common terrain-corrected product level used for consistent mapping</cite><cite id="5e1ab7e2-2">Sentinel-2 surface reflectance composites benefit from masking clouds and shadows to reduce misclassification in time series</cite><cite id="0c668b17-4">End-to-end SAR processing for mapping includes calibration, speckle filtering, coregistration, orthorectification, mosaicking, and data conversion to surface-consistent backscatter before classification</cite>.
- Cross-sensor harmonization (e.g., Landsat–Sentinel “HLS”) reduces spectral mismatch and improves map consistency; pair contemporaneous scenes and apply radiometric harmonization. <cite id="d5c69a19-7">The Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 (HLS) algorithm reduces reflectance differences between contemporaneous L1C scenes and assesses harmonization efficacy by examining reflectance differences</cite>.
- Treat masking and resampling as quality controls: use S2’s SCL/CLP products for cloud/shadow, select aggregation/compositing strategies that preserve small features, and validate resampling impacts on boundary-sensitive classes. <cite id="5e1ab7e2-1">Cloud/shadow detection varies across algorithms; comparative analyses quantify performance differences for Sentinel-2 to guide selection and tuning</cite><cite id="5e1ab7e2-8">Operational use of Sen2cor S2 time series benefits from outlier detection or acceptance of occasional cloudy pixels; S2 cloud probability layers at 10 m and QA60 at 60 m support efficient masking</cite><cite id="d5c69a19-6">Direct use of raw satellite images without correction/quality control is discouraged for habitat/land cover mapping due to distortions and noise</cite>.

Detailed best practices by sensor and task

Optical imagery (Sentinel-2, Landsat-8/9)
1) Radiometric calibration to surface reflectance with QA
- Convert digital numbers to top-of-atmosphere reflectance, then apply atmospheric correction to surface reflectance; for Landsat OLI/TIRS Level‑2 (SR) or Sentinel-2 Collection 2 SR, use as “ready-to-use reflectance” while checking consistency across scenes. <cite id="d5c69a19-0">Landsat preprocessing distinguishes georeferencing, co-registration, and conversion steps to obtain reflectance</cite><cite id="d5c69a19-2">Landsat Level‑2 products (OLI/TIRS) include atmospheric correction to surface reflectance and are generally ready for downstream mapping</cite><cite id="d5c69a19-3">USGS explains Landsat Level‑1 TP terrain-flattened reflectance and uses GCPs to achieve precise terrain correction</cite>.
- Use spectral bands and QA layers (e.g., SCL, SCL2) to flag clouds and shadows; pair masking with temporal compositing. <cite id="5e1ab7e2-2">Earth Engine tutorials demonstrate masking clouds and shadows in S2 SR and building time-series composites</cite><cite id="5e1ab7e2-3">Operational S2 workflows advise masking SCL classes 3, 8, 9, 10 for clouds and shadows and using temporal composites by median or percentile to handle persistent cloud cover</cite><cite id="5e1ab7e2-4">Comparative evaluations show S2 cloud probability classes at 10 m and QA60 at 60 m provide usable inputs to mask clouds across scales</cite>.
- Calibrate bandwise and apply batch normalization within HLS to harmonize cross-sensor spectra before fusion. <cite id="d5c69a1a">Harmonized Landsat–Sentinel (HLS v2) reduces reflectance differences between contemporaneous scenes, easing cross-sensor mapping and enabling consistent per-pixel composites</cite>.

2) Terrain correction and view/illumination normalization
- Perform orthorectification to correct geometry for elevation, slope, and terrain slope illumination; consider hillshade overlays for shadow identification and hilltop/valley bias in reflectance. <cite id="d5c69a19-3">USGS describes terrain-flattened (L1TP) processing using GCPs and photogrammetric triangulation to stabilize terrain correction of Landsat scenes prior to mapping</cite>.
- For mountainous areas, co-register mosaics across dates using a common DEM and tie points, and mask persistent terrain-induced shadows. <cite id="d5c69a19-0">ESA’s Landsat “survival guide” emphasizes co-registration and georeferencing as core preprocessing to align tiles for classification</cite>.

3) Time-series compositing and resampling choices
- Prefer median-of-cumulative-distribution or percentile composites over simple means to suppress clouds/shadows; preserve spectral variation in high-dynamic-range features (e.g., snow, salt marsh) via percentile clipping. <cite id="5e1ab7e2-3">Temporal composites using median or percentile aggregation with S2 SR reduce cloud/shadow contamination while stabilizing per-pixel time series for mapping</cite><cite id="5e1ab7e2-8">CESBio notes that operational use of Sen2cor S2 time series requires outlier detection (with HP mask) or tolerance for occasional gaps; SCL/CLP layers guide removal of bad pixels</cite>.
- Match spatial resolution and footprint consistently: resample to a common grid (near-neighbor for pan-sharpened mosaics, bilinear/bicubic for multispectral) to avoid spurious edge artifacts in small classes; perform an inter-sensor band spectral resampling to match bandwidths before fusion. <cite id="d5c69a19-6">Raw imagery often contains distortions and noise; standardized preprocessing and consistent resampling reduce artifacts before classification</cite><cite id="d5c69a19-9">Quality control for raster preprocessing ensures consistency across raster collections for downstream mapping</cite><cite id="d5c69a19-7">HLS harmonizes spectral responses across sensors to reduce band-to-band mismatch in fused composites</cite>.
- Engineer spectral/temporal features: compute NDVI, DVI, SAVI and texture; aggregate per pixel to time-aggregated features (e.g., annual medians, phenology metrics) to improve separability of crops/forests/grasslands/wetlands. <cite id="5e1ab7e2-2">Time-series S2 SR enables calculation of vegetation indices and temporal composites to stabilize signals before classification</cite>.

4) Cloud, shadow, and snow/stratocumulus handling
- Combine S2 cloud/shadow products with pixel-based compositing to remove misclassified bright pixels and stratocumulus “smoke screens.” Use temporal neighborhood smoothing and edge-aware inpainting where available. <cite id="5e1ab7e2-1">Comparisons of multiple cloud masking algorithms for S2 quantify detection trade-offs and highlight the need to adapt methods by scene and season</cite><cite id="5e1ab7e2-4">Use S2 cloud probability (10 m) and QA60 (60 m) layers for robust masking across scales</cite>.
- For seasonal classes (snow/wetlands), include a snow/ice band test and mask snow in growing-season land cover passes, or use time windows with percentile clipping. <cite id="5e1ab7e2-3">Temporal median/percentile composites combined with SCL masking reduce persistent cloud cover effects and improve seasonality-aware mapping</cite>.

SAR imagery (Sentinel-1 GRD)
1) Radiometric calibration, thermal noise, orbit files, and unit selection
- Apply orbit file, remove geocorrection/thermal noise, and calibrate to backscatter units (gamma0 or sigma0) consistent for the scene pair; use dedicated terrain-flattened grids when available. <cite id="0c668b17-1">Standard Sentinel-1 GRD preprocessing sequence: orbit file, calibration, speckle filtering, and terrain correction</cite><cite id="0c668b17-3">Step-by-step tutorials use SNAP to classify SAR land cover by first applying orbit files, calibration, and despeckling</cite><cite id="0c668b17-5">NASA Earthdata outlines calibration, speckle filtering, coregistration, orthorectification, mosaicking, and conversion as start-to-finish SAR processing before mapping</cite>.
- Normalize terrain effects via terrain flattening/orthorectification to map radiometry consistently over slope; for elevation mosaics, align DEMs and tie points across tiles. <cite id="0c668b17-5">Orthorectification is essential to correct geometry and flatten terrain for radiometric consistency</cite><cite id="0c668b17-1">Apply geometric terrain correction after calibration to ensure coregistered mosaics</cite>.

2) Speckle filtering and its trade-offs for classification
- Choose filter and kernel size empirically by land cover and spatial scale; small-kernel filters (e.g., Lee, Frost) reduce speckle but can blur small features; multilooking and temporal filters mitigate motion/layover, but must be tuned to class size and metric (accuracy vs. edge retention). <cite id="0c668b17-0">A study of eight Sentinel‑1 speckle filters on GRD evaluated influence on classification accuracy, quantifying trade-offs between noise suppression and class separability</cite><cite id="0c668b17-6">Speckle filtering and kernel selection for Sentinel‑1 significantly affect land cover accuracy, requiring further preprocessing and artifact elimination</cite>.
- For urban/forestry, prefer spatial-domain filters with small kernels and test multilooking; for agriculture/wetlands dominated by speckle, use spatial+temporal filters and majority aggregation. <cite id="0c668b17-7">Wide-area land cover mapping with multitemporal Sentinel‑1 benefits from preprocessing to remove noise and artifacts across tiles for robust classification</cite>.

3) Terrain-induced artifacts and masking
- Mask layover (near-solar-incidence foreshortening), foreshortening, and persistent shadows; use DEM-driven incidence-angle masks and shadow detection at burst/beam level, and prefer dual-pol ratios to confirm water/moisture to avoid mismasking vegetation. <cite id="0c668b17-3">Operational SAR classification workflows emphasize calibration and despeckling before terrain-aware analysis, with masking of SAR-specific distortions</cite>.
- Terrain-dependent speckle filtering reduces terrain-induced misclassification by adjusting window weights or using incidence-angle-aware windows. <cite id="0c668b17-0">Terrain-dependent effects of SAR speckle filtering alter classification performance, motivating adaptive filtering by slope and aspect</cite>.

4) Time-series strategies for SAR change and intra-season dynamics
- Aggregate burst-wise stacks to per-date surface-consistent stacks, then compute time-aggregated statistics (e.g., median stack for each date) and seasonal means; this stabilizes backscatter and reduces burst-specific artifacts. <cite id="0c668b17-7">Automatic wide-area land cover mapping with multitemporal Sentinel‑1 uses preprocessing and artifact elimination to build robust time-series classifiers</cite>.
- Use dual-pol combinations (VV, VH) to differentiate vegetation/lights at similar backscatter levels and monitor moisture/wetness for wetlands. <cite id="0c668b17-5">Calibration and data conversion to consistent backscatter units enable meaningful discrimination across polarizations in mapping tasks</cite>.

Cross-sensor fusion and feature design
- Fuse optical–SAR where clouds limit optical coverage by masking cloudy S2 pixels and replacing them with co-registered SAR time steps; harmonize spatial resolution via resampling to a common grid and normalize to the same coordinate system and projection before training. <cite id="0c668b17-5">Orthorectification and mosaicking workflows apply to both sensors; data conversion ensures consistent units for fusion</cite><cite id="d5c69a19-3">Precise terrain correction and co-registration across scenes stabilizes fusion for consistent mapping</cite>.
- Prefer band-matched fusion (HLS red/green/blue with Sentinel-1 VV/VH normalized) over raw DN mixing; cross-validate with per-class confusion matrices across seasons. <cite id="d5c69a19-7">Algorithmic band harmonization in HLS reduces reflectance differences and improves contemporaneous mapping consistency</cite>.

Training and validation best practices
- Curate training/evaluation with domain knowledge: mask inland water, impervious surfaces (roads, parking), and construction sites in bare-earth passes; stratify samples by season and slope/wetness to avoid class shift and to test boundary cases.
- Build spatially balanced, spatially stratified samples (e.g., Voronoi or grid stratified) and use per-pixel time series as features; evaluate with appropriate metrics (overall accuracy, Kappa, F1 for minority classes like wetlands/young forests). <cite id="d5c69a19-6">Direct use of distorted/noisy pixel values degrades mapping quality; preprocessing and quality control improve separability and stability of training signals</cite><cite id="5e1ab7e2-3">Temporal median/percentile composites improve per-pixel stability for mapping, supporting more reliable class boundaries</cite>.
- Iterate with ablations: compare (a) raw DN vs. SR, (b) with vs. without terrain correction and radiometric harmonization, (c) different resampling methods and speckle filters, and (d) masking pipelines, reporting deltas in class confusion.

Practical workflow (optical)
- QA → Cloud/shadow mask (S2: SCL/CLP) → Temporal composite (median/percentile) → Orthorectify to DEM (e.g., SRTM/ASTER) → Radiometric correction to SR if needed → Harmonize HLS if fusing → Feature extract (spectral, NDVI) → Train/classify → Validate with held-out dates and spatial strata. <cite id="5e1ab7e2-2">Use S2 SR composites with cloud/shadow masking for robust time series signals</cite><cite id="d5c69a19-3">Use terrain-flattened products for consistent reflectance; USGS L1TP provides a common standard</cite><cite id="d5c69a19-7">Apply HLS harmonization to reduce cross-sensor spectral mismatch</cite>.

Practical workflow (SAR)
- Orbit + thermal noise removal → Calibration to sigma0/gamma0 → Despeckle (test Lee/Frost/RK98/AM filters and kernel sizes) → Terrain flattening/orthorectify to DEM → Co-registration across bursts/patches → Build median per-date stacks → Classify → Mask layover/shadow using DEM-derived slope/aspect and incidence angle → Validate with ground truth in layover-prone vs. flat regions. <cite id="0c668b17-5">Calibration, speckle filtering, coregistration, orthorectification, and mosaicking are core to SAR mapping</cite><cite id="0c668b17-0">Filtering choice and terrain-aware adjustments affect accuracy, necessitating empirical tuning</cite><cite id="0c668b17-6">Speckle/kernal choices can degrade or improve land cover accuracy</cite>.

Evidence on impact
- Atmospheric correction often improves land cover accuracy in Sentinel‑2, with method choice mattering; compare at least two AC algorithms and select by accuracy lift on your study area. <cite id="d5c69a19-1">A Sentinel‑2 study compared five atmospheric corrections and quantified their impacts on land cover classification accuracy</cite>.
- Terrain correction and QA-based masking reduce misclassification in mountainous regions and along slopes where shadow/illumination variation is high. <cite id="d5c69a19-3">USGS outlines precise terrain correction using GCPs to stabilize reflectance for mapping</cite><cite id="5e1ab7e2-8">Operational S2 composites require masking strategies to remove outliers from shadows/clouds for reliable time series mapping</cite>.

Caveats and practical tips
- Prefer processing chains with documented QA outputs (e.g., S2 SCL/CLP, Landsat S2L1TP QA, SAR incidence angle/terrain masks) and log QC metrics to reject failing scenes; apply consistent processing to all tiles in a mosaic. <cite id="d5c69a19-9">Quality control for raster pre-processing ensures consistent accuracy and traceability across tiles</cite>.
- For heterogeneous landscapes (urban–agriculture–forest), collect multi-date windows and test seasonal vs. annual products; small classes benefit from super-resolution pansharpening or object-based methods pre- or post-classification. <cite id="5e1ab7e2-3">Temporal aggregation and masking stabilize small-class signals; use median/percentile composites</cite>.
- Cross-validate calibration choices: using Level‑2 SR vs. DN+AC often yields small but measurable gains for water and high-albedo surfaces; test and document on your site. <cite id="d5c69a19-2">Landsat Level‑2 SR is pre-atmospherically corrected and ready for mapping, improving user efficiency</cite><cite id="d5c69a19-3">USGS describes when terrain-flattened SR levels are applied to standardize analysis</cite>.

Checklist to deploy
- [ ] Read sensor metadata; select SR products where available. <cite id="d5c69a19-2">Use Level‑2 SR when available to avoid repeated AC</cite>.
- [ ] Mask clouds and shadows pre-compositing; prefer S2 SCL/CLP and cloud probability. <cite id="5e1ab7e2-2">Mask clouds/shadows before compositing for S2 SR</cite><cite id="5e1ab7e2-4">Use S2 10 m cloud probability and 60 m QA60 layers</cite>.
- [ ] Build time-aware composites (median or percentile) per date; stack consistently. <cite id="5e1ab7e2-3">Temporal median/percentile composites improve stability</cite>.
- [ ] Orthorectify to a DEM; correct geometric distortions across tiles. <cite id="d5c69a19-3">L1TP terrain correction with GCPs stabilizes geometry</cite><cite id="0c668b17-5">Orthorectification and mosaicking are required for radiometric consistency</cite>.
- [ ] For SAR: orbit + thermal noise, calibrate to sigma0/gamma0, despeckle, and perform terrain flattening; mask layover/shadow. <cite id="0c668b17-3">Orbit, calibration, despeckling, terrain correction are core for SAR</cite><cite id="0c668b17-6">Speckle and kernel tuning affect accuracy and require validation</cite>.
- [ ] Harmonize sensors if fusing (HLS) and match spatial grids/resolutions. <cite id="d5c69a19-7">HLS reduces reflectance differences and harmonizes cross-sensor composites</cite>.
- [ ] Engineer features (indices, texture, temporal statistics) and stratify training/validation. <cite id="5e1ab7e2-2">Time-series S2 SR enables indices and composites for improved classification</cite>.
- [ ] Ablate key choices and report accuracy/Kappa/F1 changes; iterate preprocessing based on results. <cite id="d5c69a19-1">Compare AC algorithms empirically on your land cover task</cite><cite id="d5c69a19-6">Direct use of raw imagery without preprocessing reduces accuracy; ablation shows gains from correction and QC</cite>.
