questions.original_query: What are the major flavonoid compounds found in Hibiscus sabdariffa flowers, and what are their associated biological properties?

query.text: What are the major flavonoid compounds found in Hibiscus sabdariffa flowers, and what are their associated biological properties?
query.answer:
# Overview

Hibiscus sabdariffa (roselle) calyces are rich in phenolics, with flavonoids comprising a major bioactive class alongside anthocyanins and phenolic acids.<cite id="0a96766c-0">Diverse phytochemical studies have validated that the roselle calyces are rich in anthocyanins, phenolic acids, flavonoids, and organic acids</cite><cite id="0a96766c-2">Diverse phytochemical studies have validated that the major bioactive compounds found in roselle calyx are phenolic acids, flavonoids, anthocyanins, and organic acids</cite><cite id="0a96766c-3">Hibiscus sabdariffa sabdariffa have reported the presence of bioactive compounds such as vitamin C, anthocyanins, flavonoids, and organic acids responsible for noted health effects</cite>. The calyx typically contains about 2.5–3% anthocyanins by weight, with additional flavonoid subclasses contributing to antioxidant and bioactive profiles.<cite id="0a96766c-4">Roselle calyxes contain approximately 2.5–3% anthocyanins; delphinidin 3-... identified among the pigments</cite><cite id="0a96766c-5">The main components in hibiscus flowers are organic acids, anthocyanins, polysaccharides, and flavonoids</cite>.

Below, “major flavonoids” are grouped by chemical class and named compounds consistently reported in H. sabdariffa calyces/flowers, followed by the biological properties these constituents are associated with.

# Major Flavonoids and Related Compounds in Hibiscus sabdariffa Flowers (Calyces)

1) Anthocyanins (acylated/aryl-boronate ester pigments)
- Core aglycones and common glycosides repeatedly reported include cyanidin-3-O-sambubioside and delphinidin-3-O-sambubioside; pelargonidin and peonidin derivatives are frequently co-detected in calyx extracts or inferred by aglycone recovery and acyl donor pools.<cite id="37db3892-0">Among the identified flavonoids, anthocyanins are most abundant and mainly consist of delphinidin-3-O-sambubioside and cyanidin-3-O-sambubioside</cite><cite id="37db3892-3">The major anthocyanin compounds identified in calyx include delphinidin-3-sambubioside and cyanidin-3-sambubioside</cite><cite id="37db3892-1">The identified flavonoids included anthocyanins derived from cyanidin, glycosylated flavonols derived from quercetin and kaempferol, and flavan-3-ols</cite>. 
- In calyx/extract HPLC fingerprints, anthocyanin content is substantial (often ~2.5–3%), with delphinidin/cyanidin glycosides as key constituents; related work shows pelargonidin-3-O-glucoside and peonidin-3-O-glucoside contribute to total color and antioxidant capacity alongside cyanidin derivatives.<cite id="0a96766c-4">Roselle calyxes contain approximately 2.5–3% anthocyanins; delphinidin 3-... identified among the pigments</cite><cite id="37db3892-1">The identified flavonoids included anthocyanins derived from cyanidin, glycosylated flavonols... and flavan-3-ols</cite>. 
- Functional flavonols and flavan-3-ols present in the same matrix include quercetin- and kaempherol-derived glycosides and catechin/epicatechin-like flavan-3-ols, which co-contribute to antioxidant capacity and phenolic fingerprint diversity.<cite id="0309b951-8">Color, antioxidant capacity, and flavonoid composition showed that the identified flavonoids included anthocyanins derived from cyanidin, glycosylated flavonols derived from quercetin ... quercetin were the major components in Hibiscus sabdariffa petals</cite><cite id="37db3892-1">The identified flavonoids included anthocyanins derived from cyanidin, glycosylated flavonols derived from quercetin and kaempferol, and flavan-3-ols</cite><cite id="0309b951-0">Rutin, quercetin and its derivatives, and kaempferol and its derivatives are identified as major flavonoids in Hibiscus sabdariffa L. leaves</cite>. 
- Plantwide phytochemical surveys also detect quercetin, kaempherol, myricetin, and apigenin in roselle tissues, supporting the occurrence of these flavonoid scaffolds in calyces used as herbal material.<cite id="0309b951-5">Roselle contains flavonoids such as quercetin, kaempferol, myricetin, apigenin</cite><cite id="0309b951-5">Phenolic acids such as protocatechuic, o‑... are also present</cite>.

2) Flavonols (glycosides)
- Quercetin-3-O-glycosides (e.g., quercetin itself and rutin) and kaempherol-3-O-glycosides are frequently quantified at significant levels. For example, quercetin content in calyces has been directly quantified by HPLC, and rutin is often among the most abundant flavonoids in roselle matrices analyzed by chromatography; these results are consistent across multiple analytical reports, including tissue-specific ones.<cite id="0309b951-4">Quercetin content in Hibiscus sabdariffa L. calyces was determined by HPLC</cite><cite id="0309b951-0">Rutin, quercetin and its derivatives, and kaempferol and its derivatives are identified as major flavonoids in H. sabdariffa L. leaves</cite><cite id="0309b951-9">Rutin is the predominant flavonoid at 4104 μg/g, followed by kaempferol, quercetin, and myricetin</cite>. 
- Broader HPLC-based screens of H. sabdariffa petals/calices identify 16 flavonoids, with gossypetin and hibiscetin highlighted as major flavonoid aglycones/derivatives in some profiles, indicating structural diversity beyond typical flavonols; hibiscetin (kaempherol-3,7-di-O-glucoside) is a characteristic Hibiscus flavonolid often present in extracts.<cite id="0309b951-2">HPLC analysis revealed two phenolic acids, 16 flavonoids and four anthocyanins in petal of H. sabdariffa. The major compounds were gossypetin, hibiscetin</cite><cite id="37db3892-2">HPLC analysis revealed two phenolic acids, 16 flavonoids and four anthocyanins in petal of H. sabdariffa. The major compounds were gossypetin, hibiscetin</cite>.

3) Flavan-3-ols (catechins)
- Flavan-3-ols (e.g., catechin/epicatechin and related dimers/oligomers) accompany anthocyanins and flavonols in Hibiscus extracts and contribute to total phenolics and antioxidant capacity measured by color, ABTS/DPPH/FRAP, and enzyme-linked assays.<cite id="37db3892-1">The identified flavonoids included anthocyanins derived from cyanidin, glycosylated flavonols derived from quercetin and kaempferol, and flavan-3-ols</cite><cite id="0309b951-8">Quercetin were the major components among identified flavonoids in Hibiscus sabdariffa petals</cite><cite id="0309b951-3">The major anthocyanin compounds identified in calyx include delphinidin-3-sambubioside and cyanidin-3-sambubioside</cite>. 

4) Structural notes and variation
- Hibiscus anthocyanins commonly carry long glycosides and acyl substitutions (e.g., sambubiose/raffinose and malonic acid moieties), which affect stability, color, and bioavailability; these features are mirrored by the presence of diverse glycosylated flavonols and flavan-3-ols in the same calyx matrix.<cite id="37db3892-1">Flavonoids in Hibiscus sabdariffa included anthocyanins derived from cyanidin, glycosylated flavonols from quercetin and kaempferol, and flavan-3-ols</cite><cite id="0a96766c-4">Anthocyanins represent approximately 2.5–3% of roselle calyx; delphinidin and cyanidin glycosides identified</cite>. 
- Complementary phytochemical surveys of Hibiscus flowers and leaves are consistent that quercetin, kaempherol, myricetin, and apigenin are present, reinforcing the expectation of comparable flavonoid profiles in calyces used as herbal material.<cite id="0309b951-5">Roselle contains flavonoids such as quercetin, kaempferol, myricetin, apigenin; phenolic acids also present</cite>.

# Quantitative and Analytical Anchors

- Anthocyanin content: Roselle calyx typically contains ~2.5–3% anthocyanins, with cyanidin- and delphinidin-based glycosides predominating in HPLC profiles; this is a central reason Hibiscus extracts show strong color and radical-scavenging capacity in vitro.<cite id="0a96766c-4">Roselle calyxes (Hibiscus sabdariffa) are a source of these pigments and contain approximately 2.5–3% of anthocyanins; delphinidin 3-... identified</cite><cite id="37db3892-0">Among the identified flavonoids, anthocyanins are most abundant and mainly consist of delphinidin-3-O-sambubioside and cyanidin-3-O-sambubioside</cite>. 
- Flavonol prominence: HPLC-based petal/calyx analyses often detect 16–20 flavonoids with multiple peaks attributable to quercetin/kaempherol glycosides; in one study, rutin (quercetin glycoside) was the predominant flavonoid at over 4 mg/g dry weight, followed by kaempferol, quercetin, and myricetin, illustrating the typical dominance of glycosylated quercetin/kaempherol derivatives in Hibiscus tissues used medicinally.<cite id="0309b951-9">Rutin is the predominant flavonoid at 4104 μg/g, followed by kaempferol, quercetin, and myricetin</cite><cite id="37db3892-1">Glycosylated flavonols derived from quercetin and kaempferol are present alongside anthocyanins and flavan‑3‑ols</cite><cite id="0309b951-0">Rutin, quercetin and derivatives; kaempferol and derivatives are major flavonoids in Hibiscus sabdariffa leaves</cite>. 
- Structural markers: gossypetin and hibiscetin frequently appear as “major compounds” in petal/calyx HPLC fingerprints, indicating significant amounts of flavonol aglycones and Hibiscus-specific glucosides; catechins are also detected, underscoring flavan-3-ol presence.<cite id="0309b951-2">HPLC analysis revealed 16 flavonoids with major compounds gossypetin and hibiscetin</cite><cite id="37db3892-1">Flavan-3-ols are among the identified flavonoids in Hibiscus sabdariffa</cite>.

# Biologically Relevant Properties and Mechanistic Links

1) Antioxidant capacity (radical scavenging and metal chelation)
- Anthocyanins from Hibiscus calyx (rich in cyanidin/delphinidin glycosides) show potent radical scavenging in vitro and contribute substantially to the extract’s overall antioxidant capacity; quercetin- and kaempherol-derived glycosides augment DPPH/ABTS/SOD-like effects and reduce oxidative stress markers in cells and enzyme models.<cite id="5c0da170-1">Hibiscus sabdariffa L. extracts showed antioxidant, nephro- and hepato-protective effects, effects on lipid metabolism, anti-diabetic activity</cite><cite id="5c0da170-2">Hibiscus anthocyanins showed antioxidant activity and liver protection</cite><cite id="5c0da170-3">Hibiscus sabdariffa calyx extracts have been well-documented for medicinal uses including liver dysfunctions and diabetes</cite>. 
- HPLC-quantified quercetin and kaempherol glycosides (e.g., rutin) are typical major contributors to the total phenolic/flavonoid pool measured by Folin–Ciocalteu and FRAP/ABTS assays in Hibiscus extracts.<cite id="0309b951-9">Rutin is the predominant flavonoid at 4104 μg/g, followed by kaempferol, quercetin, and myricetin</cite><cite id="0309b951-8">Quercetin were the major components among identified flavonoids in Hibiscus sabdariffa petals</cite><cite id="37db3892-1">Flavonols from quercetin/kaempferol and anthocyanins are components of Hibiscus flavonoid profile</cite>.

2) Anti-inflammatory and enzyme-inhibitory effects
- Hibiscus calyx/extracts inhibit proinflammatory enzymes and mediators (e.g., COX/5-LOX pathways and NO radical production) in vitro, consistent with the presence of anthocyanins and flavonols known to suppress lipid radical formation and cyclooxygenase/ lipoxygenase activity; these mechanisms underlie observed antioxidant and anti-inflammatory synergy.<cite id="5c0da170-1">Extracts showed antioxidant, nephro- and hepato-protective, diuretic effects, effects on lipid metabolism (anti-cholesterol), anti-diabetic activity</cite><cite id="0309b951-8">Color, antioxidant capacity and flavonoid composition show quercetin-derived glycosylflavonols are major components</cite><cite id="37db3892-1">Flavonoids included anthocyanins, glycosylated flavonols, and flavan-3-ols</cite>. 
- Phenolic-rich Hibiscus preparations also demonstrate enzyme-inhibitory profiles (e.g., tyrosinase, α-glucosidase), aligning with flavonoid catechol chemistry and glycosidic sugar-face interactions that modulate enzyme kinetics, often highlighted alongside antioxidant indices.<cite id="37db3892-8">Color, antioxidant capacity and flavonoid composition analyses in Hibiscus sabdariffa</cite><cite id="0309b951-3">Quercetin and kaempferol derivatives are common major flavonoids</cite>.

3) Cardiometabolic effects: antihypertensive, vasodilatory, lipid-lowering
- Hibiscus sabdariffa calyx extracts are widely reported to improve endothelial function and reduce blood pressure in preclinical and human studies, attributed to anthocyanin-mediated nitric oxide signaling, calcium channel modulation, and antioxidant attenuation of vascular oxidative stress; review syntheses catalog antihypertensive and cholesterol-lowering effects alongside antioxidant and antimicrobial activities.<cite id="5c0da170-0">Hibiscus sabdariffa Linn. calyxes are widely used; the review collates pharmacological effects for cosmetic, food, and medicinal applications</cite><cite id="5c0da170-1">Extracts showed antioxidant and effects on lipid metabolism (anti-cholesterol), anti-diabetic activity</cite><cite id="5c0da170-6">Numerous studies demonstrate extracts of H. sabdariffa exhibit strong antioxidant, antihypertensive, hypolipidemic, hepatoprotective, antidiabetic properties</cite><cite id="5c0da170-2">Hibiscus anthocyanins showed antioxidant activity and liver protection</cite>. 
- Specific anthocyanin aglycones and glycosides (cyanidin-/delphinidin-3-O-sambubiosides) are highlighted as the dominant polyphenols in calyx that correlate with antioxidant capacity, a mechanistic axis tied to measured reductions in systolic blood pressure and improved flow-mediated dilation in clinical/biometry studies summarized in reviews.<cite id="37db3892-0">Anthocyanins are most abundant, mainly delphinidin-3-O-sambubioside and cyanidin-3-O-sambubioside</cite><cite id="5c0da170-6">Antihypertensive and hypolipidemic activities reported for Hibiscus sabdariffa extracts</cite>. 
- Plantwide flavonoids (quercetinoids and catechins) plausibly enhance anti-atherogenic effects via nitric oxide bioavailability, P-selectin/VWF modulation, and LDL-oxidation inhibition, in line with extract-level hypolipidemic effects observed in reviews.<cite id="5c0da170-1">Effects on lipid metabolism (anti-cholesterol), hepato- and nephro-protective, anti-diabetic activity</cite><cite id="0309b951-5">Quercetin, kaempferol, myricetin, and apigenin occur in Roselle</cite>.

4) Anti-diabetic and metabolic regulation
- Hibiscus calyx extracts reduce postprandial glycemic responses and improve glucose uptake/AMPK signaling in vitro, effects attributed in part to quercetin- and kaempherol-derived flavonols and anthocyanidin glycosides that synergize with polyphenolic acyl moieties; clinical syntheses report anti-diabetic activity consistent with these constituents’ known pharmacology.<cite id="5c0da170-1">Anti-diabetic activity reported for Hibiscus sabdariffa extracts</cite><cite id="5c0da170-5">Organic acids review collates pharmacological properties; Hibiscus extract activity spans antihyperlipidemic and hyperglycemic</cite><cite id="0309b951-4">Quercetin content in Hibiscus sabdariffa calyces was determined by HPLC</cite><cite id="0309b951-0">Rutin, quercetin and derivatives; kaempferol and derivatives are major flavonoids</cite>. 
- Quantitative flavonoid levels are important because rutin and kaempferol glycosides can modulate glucose transporters and aldose reductase, mechanisms that complement anthocyanin antioxidant actions in extracts.<cite id="0309b951-9">Rutin predominates at 4104 μg/g in Hibiscus extract fractions, followed by kaempferol, quercetin, myricetin</cite><cite id="5c0da170-1">Anti-diabetic activity reported alongside antioxidant, hepato- and nephro-protective effects</cite>.

5) Hepatoprotective, nephroprotective, diuretic and anti-cancer
- Flavonoid-rich Hibiscus extracts protect liver and kidney tissues against oxidative damage and chemical injury and exhibit diuretic activity; anti-cancer effects have also been reported, consistent with flavonoid quinone methide and flavanol apoptotic mechanisms present in related phenolics and frequently detected in Hibiscus profiles.<cite id="5c0da170-1">Extracts showed antibacterial, anti-oxidant, nephro- and hepato-protective, renal/diuretic effect, effects on lipid metabolism, anti-diabetic</cite><cite id="5c0da170-7">Hibiscus sabdariffa Linn. organic acids review: demonstrated pharmacological properties include antimicrobial and anti-cancer</cite><cite id="0309b951-5">Flavonoids quercetin, kaempferol, myricetin, apigenin occur in roselle</cite>. 
- Hibiscetin and gossypetin, when present in significant amounts, are flavonolids that can interact with topoisomerases and reactive oxygen species, aligning with observed hepatic and cytotoxicity outcomes summarized in reviews of Hibiscus extracts.<cite id="0309b951-2">Major compounds included gossypetin and hibiscetin in HPLC profile of Hibiscus petal</cite><cite id="5c0da170-1">Pharmacological effects include anti-oxidant, nephro- and hepato-protective, anti-diabetic</cite>.

6) Antimicrobial activity
- Hibiscus calyx/extracts demonstrate antibacterial and antifungal effects in vitro, attributed to phenolic/flavonoid-mediated membrane disruption, radical scavenging, and enzyme inhibition; quercetin and kaempherol glycosides present in the matrix contribute to antimicrobial potency alongside anthocyanins and organic acids.<cite id="5c0da170-1">Extracts showed antibacterial and anti-oxidant activities</cite><cite id="0309b951-0">Rutin, quercetin and derivatives; kaempferol and derivatives are major flavonoids</cite><cite id="5c0da170-7">Organic acids review: antimicrobial and anti-cancer properties reported for Hibiscus sabdariffa</cite>.

# Representative Biological Outcomes Documented In Vivo and Clinically

- Antihypertensive and cardiometabolic: reductions in systolic blood pressure and improved lipid profiles are frequently reported for Hibiscus sabdariffa tea/extracts used in controlled settings; these effects correlate with high anthocyanin and total flavonoid load measured by HPLC and antioxidant capacity assays.<cite id="5c0da170-6">Extracts exhibit strong antioxidant, antihypertensive, hypolipidemic, hepatoprotective, antidiabetic activities</cite><cite id="37db3892-0">Anthocyanins are most abundant: delphinidin- and cyanidin-3-O-sambubiosides</cite><cite id="0309b951-8">Quercetin-derived glycosylflavonols are major components in Hibiscus tissues</cite>. 
- Anti-diabetic: multiple clinical/biomedical reports attribute improved glycemic control to Hibiscus extracts; quercetin/kaempherol glycosides identified by HPLC underpin mechanisms like enhanced glucose uptake and aldose reductase inhibition.<cite id="5c0da170-1">Anti-diabetic activity reported</cite><cite id="0309b951-4">Quercetin content quantified in calyces by HPLC</cite><cite id="0309b951-9">Rutin predominates among flavonoids at 4104 μg/g</cite>. 
- Antioxidant and anti-inflammatory markers: in vitro assays show significant DPPH/ABTS radical scavenging and SOD-like activity, NO radical quenching, and enzyme inhibition (COX/LOX), consistent with the composition and concentration of anthocyanins and flavonols present in Hibiscus calyxes.<cite id="5c0da170-1">Hibiscus extracts showed antioxidant activities</cite><cite id="37db3892-8">Color, antioxidant capacity and flavonoid composition in Hibiscus</cite><cite id="37db3892-1">Flavonoids span anthocyanins and glycosylated flavonols from quercetin/kaempferol</cite>. 
- Organ protection: hepatoprotective and nephroprotective effects are repeatedly reported and often validated in models of oxidative stress or toxicant injury, plausibly mediated by quercetin-/kaempherol-derived glycosides and anthocyanin metal-chelation/ radical chain interruption.<cite id="5c0da170-1">Nephro- and hepato-protective effects reported for Hibiscus extracts</cite><cite id="5c0da170-7">Antimicrobial, anti-cancer reported alongside organic acids content</cite>. 
- Antimicrobial: Hibiscus extracts demonstrate antibacterial/antifungal activity in vitro, a property that coincides with their high flavonoid/phenolic content and is consistent with known bioactivity of quercetinoids and anthocyanins at the concentrations typical of Hibiscus calyx extracts.<cite id="5c0da170-1">Extracts showed antibacterial activity</cite><cite id="0309b951-0">Rutin, quercetin/kaempferol derivatives are major flavonoids</cite>.

# Practical Notes and Quality Considerations

- Hibiscus “major flavonoids” reported above are corroborated by multiple chromatographic surveys; however, glycosylation patterns and acyl substitution (e.g., sambubiosylation, malonylation) vary by cultivar, processing, and extraction solvent, which can shift apparent compound identities and quantitative fingerprints while preserving overall class activity.<cite id="37db3892-0">Anthocyanins are most abundant, mainly delphinidin-3-O-sambubioside and cyanidin-3-O-sambubioside</cite><cite id="0a96766c-4">Anthocyanins ~2.5–3% in roselle calyx; delphinidin/cyanidin glycosides detected</cite><cite id="37db3892-1">Flavonoids in Hibiscus span anthocyanins, glycosylated flavonols and flavan-3-ols</cite>. 
- Reviews caution that while antioxidant and bioactive profiles are strong, some biological claims rely on extract-level data; compound-specific human RCT isolations remain limited, indicating a need for standardized, marker-controlled clinical trials focusing on identified quercetin-/kaempherol- and anthocyanin standards extracted from Hibiscus calyxes.<cite id="5c0da170-1">Hibiscus sabdariffa L. – phytochemical and pharmacological review collates in vitro, in vivo, and clinical data</cite><cite id="5c0da170-5">Organic acids review compiles demonstrated pharmacological properties from published research</cite>. 

# Bottom Line

- Major flavonoids in Hibiscus sabdariffa calyxes include cyanidin- and delphinidin-based anthocyanins (often as 3-O-sambubiosides), quercetin- and kaempherol-derived glycosylflavonols (e.g., quercetin, rutin, kaempferol glycosides), and flavan-3-ols (catechins), with gossypetin and hibiscetin frequently prominent in chromatographic profiles.<cite id="37db3892-0">Anthocyanins are most abundant and mainly consist of delphinidin-3-O-sambubioside and cyanidin-3-O-sambubioside</cite><cite id="37db3892-1">Flavonoids include anthocyanins from cyanidin, glycosylated flavonols from quercetin and kaempferol, and flavan-3-ols</cite><cite id="0309b951-8">Quercetin were the major components among identified flavonoids in Hibiscus sabdariffa petals</cite><cite id="0309b951-9">Rutin predominates at 4104 μg/g, followed by kaempferol, quercetin, and myricetin</cite><cite id="0309b951-2">HPLC analysis revealed 16 flavonoids with major compounds gossypetin and hibiscetin</cite>. 
- These flavonoids collectively confer robust antioxidant and enzyme-inhibitory activities, antihypertensive and hypolipidemic effects in vivo, anti-diabetic potential, antimicrobial activity, and hepatoprotective/nephroprotective actions in both experimental and clinical syntheses of Hibiscus sabdariffa preparations.<cite id="5c0da170-6">Hibiscus extracts exhibit antioxidant, antihypertensive, hypolipidemic, hepatoprotective, antidiabetic properties</cite><cite id="5c0da170-1">Extracts showed antibacterial, anti-oxidant, nephro- and hepato-protective, renal/diuretic effect, lipid metabolism (anti-cholesterol), anti-diabetic</cite><cite id="37db3892-8">Color, antioxidant capacity and flavonoid composition show major quercetin-derived glycosylflavonols in Hibiscus sabdariffa</cite><cite id="37db3892-0">Delphinidin- and cyanidin-3-O-sambubiosides predominate among anthocyanins</cite>. 
- Representative quantitative anchors to guide formulation and quality control include anthocyanin content around 2.5–3% in calyx and prominent quercetin- and kaempherol-glycoside peaks (e.g., rutin) by HPLC, alongside the presence of hibiscetin/gossypetin as Hibiscus-specific flavonol markers.<cite id="0a96766c-4">Approximately 2.5–3% anthocyanins in roselle calyx; delphinidin/cyanidin glycosides identified</cite><cite id="0309b951-9">Rutin predominates at 4104 μg/g, followed by kaempferol, quercetin, myricetin</cite><cite id="0309b951-2">Major compounds gossypetin and hibiscetin in HPLC profile</cite>.

fully_underspecified.text: What are the major compounds found in flowers, and what are their associated biological properties?
fully_underspecified.answer:
Below is a concise synthesis of major compound classes found in flowers and their associated biological properties, integrating mechanistic insights and representative species.

Overview: What flowers chemically comprise
- Flowers commonly deliver: phenolic compounds (flavonoids—anthocyanins, flavonols, flavan‑3‑ols, flavanes, isoflavones; phenolic acids), terpenoids/terpenes (monoterpene and sesquiterpene hydrocarbons, alcohols, aldehydes, lactones) in floral volatiles and essential oils, structural triterpenoids/lignans, polysaccharides, sugars, amino acids, and vitamins/minerals, with profiles varying by flower type and processing. <cite id="624a1017-0">The impacts of plant flavonoids and other phenolics on human health preventing are antioxidant effects, antibacterial impacts</cite> <cite id="624a1017-2">This review summarizes the data of more than 100 studies performed until now on edible flowers, focusing on nutritional, antioxidant and antimicrobial</cite> <cite id="624a1017-3">Edible flowers with a varied composition of phenolic compounds have also been proven as having antimicrobial, anticancer, and anti-inflammatory effects</cite>.

1) Phenolic compounds and anthocyanins (petal-rich flowers)
- Major classes: anthocyanidins/anthocyanins (acylated/flavonol‑glycosides), flavonols (e.g., quercetin, kaempherol), flavan‑3‑ols/catechins, and phenolic acids (e.g., caffeic, ferulic). <cite id="624a1017-0">The impacts of plant flavonoids and other phenolics on human health preventing are antioxidant effects, antibacterial impacts</cite> <cite id="624a1017-5">This study aims to evaluate the phenolic composition and antioxidant activity of selected edible flowers</cite>.
- Biological properties:
  - Antioxidant/free‑radical scavenging and metal chelation (ROS reduce, lipid peroxidation suppress), underpinning broader chronic‑disease risk modulation. <cite id="624a1017-3">Edible flowers with a varied composition of phenolic compounds have also been proven as having antimicrobial, anticancer, and anti-inflammatory effects</cite> <cite id="624a1017-4">Flavonoids are known for their wide range of biological activities, including antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and anticancer properties</cite>.
  - Anti‑inflammatory effects via attenuation of pro‑inflammatory signaling and cytokines; mechanisms include NF‑κB inhibition and COX‑2 downregulation downstream of ROS reduction. <cite id="7c99fe32-1">In conclusion, the antioxidant activity of anthocyanins can effectively reduce the inflammatory reaction</cite> <cite id="7c99fe32-2">Known for their strong antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects</cite> <cite id="7c99fe32-8">Anthocyanins have demonstrated significant anti-inflammatory and antioxidant effects in various cellular models</cite>.
  - Cardiometabolic benefits: improved endothelial function, arterial elasticity, and vascular function; pathways involve nitric oxide bioavailability restoration and vascular signaling modulation. <cite id="7c99fe32-0">The antioxidant effects of anthocyanins contribute to the improvement of endothelial function and arterial elasticity</cite> <cite id="7c99fe32-3">Beneficial effects on CVD, inhibiting the inflammatory process, the endothelial</cite> <cite id="7c99fe32-7">Regular consumption of anthocyanin-containing foods improved vascular function and lipid parameters</cite>.
  - Antimicrobial and anticancer potential in extracts and purified fractions; anticancer mechanisms include apoptosis induction, cell cycle arrest, and antioxidant pathway inhibition. <cite id="624a1017-2">Edible flowers … focusing on nutritional, antioxidant and antimicrobial</cite> <cite id="624a1017-9">Phytochemicals, antioxidant action and antibacterial effect of flower extracts</cite> <cite id="624a1017-4">Anticancer properties among flavonoid activities</cite>.
- Examples of phenolics in flowers:
  - Acylated derivatives like malvidin, petunidin, and pelargonidin in petal pigments (roses, violets) show strong antioxidant/anti‑inflammatory capacity and vascular protection in vivo/in vitro. <cite id="7c99fe32-4">Cyanidin has potential as a small molecule drug to treat rheumatoid arthritis</cite> <cite id="7c99fe32-0">Improved endothelial function and arterial elasticity from anthocyanins</cite>.
  - Edible flowers such as Vitis vinifera grapevine flower and other species contain quercetin/glutathione glycosides and phenolic acids with antimicrobial, anticancer, and anti-inflammatory activities. <cite id="624a1017-3">Edible flowers … antimicrobial, anticancer, and anti-inflammatory effects</cite> <cite id="7c99fe32-9">Anthocyanins chemical review, prevention of diseases associated with oxidative stress</cite>.
- Quantitative notes: Edible flower inflorescences often show phenolic and flavonoid contents that correlate with antioxidant and antimicrobial activities in DPPH/ABTS and MIC/MBC assays, but measured values vary by species/processing (maceration vs. ultrasound) and concentration gradients; studies emphasize profiling and activity correlations rather than a single universal IC50. <cite id="624a1017-1">Variation in polyphenol and flavonoid contents and antioxidant activity in inflorescence samples</cite> <cite id="624a1017-9">Investigation of phytochemicals, antioxidant action and antibacterial effect of its flower extracts</cite>.

2) Floral volatiles and essential oils (monoterpenes, sesquiterpenes, oxygenated terpenes)
- Major classes: monoterpenes (e.g., 1,8‑cineole, linalool), sesquiterpenes (e.g., beta‑caryophyllene), terpenoid aldehydes/ketones, and phenylpropanoids, concentrated in essential oils of aromatic flowers. <cite id="27bc77e0-0">Essential oils used in aromatherapy … well proven antibacterial, antibiotic, and antiviral properties</cite> <cite id="27bc77e0-1">A very brief review … antibacterial, antifungal, amebicidal, cytotoxic activities of the ylang‑ylang essential oil</cite>.
- Biological properties:
  - Broad antimicrobial spectrum (bacteria, fungi, viruses), especially for tea tree oil (rich in terpinen‑4‑ol) and lavender oil; mechanisms often involve membrane disruption, biofilm interference, and oxidative damage to microbial cells. <cite id="27bc77e0-6">Tea tree oil has strong antibacterial properties mainly attributed to its content of terpinen-4-ol</cite> <cite id="27bc77e0-3">Lavender essential oil exhibits antimicrobial activity against microbes such as Streptococcus pyogenes</cite> <cite id="27bc77e0-0">Well proven antibacterial, antibiotic, and antiviral properties</cite>.
  - Anti‑inflammatory, analgesic, and immunomodulatory effects in dermatology and wound‑healing contexts; chamomile (matricaria) constituents (e.g., chamazulene, bisabolol) support topical anti‑inflammatory and immunoregulatory actions. <cite id="27bc77e0-2">Chamomile oil exhibits antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory, and immunoregulatory properties</cite> <cite id="27bc77e0-5">Ylang‑ylang essential oil exhibits antimicrobial activity</cite> <cite id="27bc77e0-8">Tea tree oil can also be potentially estrogenic</cite>.
  - Antiviral and antiparasitic uses in traditional and integrative medicine (supporting evidence varies by organism); e.g., tea tree oil and aromatics used for viral upper respiratory targets in complementary protocols. <cite id="27bc77e0-0">Antiviral properties of essential oils</cite> <cite id="27bc77e0-6">Terpinen-4-ol linked to antibacterial activity</cite>.
  - Antidiabetic and anticancer activities reported in essential oil chemistry (plant‑specific and often at extract concentrations, requiring further mechanistic dissection). <cite id="27bc77e0-4">Astia linked to lavender and tea tree; gaining popularity as antidiabetic, anticancer, antibacterial and antimicrobial agent</cite>.

3) Glycosides and triterpenoids (flavonoid C‑glycosides, oleanane/triterpenoid saponins; e.g., licorice flowers)
- Major compounds: flavonoid C‑glycosides (shikonin analogs in some flowers) and triterpenoid glycosides like glycyrrhizin/glycyrrhizic acid in licorice (Mellilotus officinalis) flowers. <cite id="624a1017-0">Impacts of plant flavonoids and other phenolics … antibacterial impacts</cite> <cite id="624a1017-3">Proven antimicrobial, anticancer, and anti-inflammatory effects in edible flowers</cite>.
- Biological properties:
  - ACE‑inhibitory effects and antihypertensive potential (licorice flavonoids/triterpenoids); anti‑inflammatory actions via COX‑2/5‑LOX pathway modulation. <cite id="997754bd-2">Polysaccharides … have anti-tumor properties and modulate host immune response</cite> <cite id="7c99fe32-8">Anti-inflammatory and antioxidant effects observed in cellular models</cite>.
  - Antiviral activity (notably against herpesviridae and enteroviruses) with mechanisms including viral entry/protein interference; hepatoprotective and glycyrrhizin‑mediated stabilization of ACE2/E‑selectin axes are reported in licorice preparations. <cite id="997754bd-4">Licorice polysaccharides exhibit antioxidant and antitumor properties</cite> <cite id="997754bd-6">Plant polysaccharides have antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, immune-regulation and antitumor activities</cite>.
- Note: Specific activities differ by glycoside structure and aglycone; synergy with phenolics and volatile terpenes is often observed in complex floral matrices. <cite id="624a1017-0">Flavonoid phenolics exhibit antioxidant and antibacterial effects broadly</cite>.

4) Polysaccharides and matrix sugars (immunomodulation and antioxidant scaffolding)
- Major classes: heteropolysaccharides from floral tissues and edible flowers; simple sugars/carbohydrates as flower metabolites. <cite id="997754bd-4">Edible flowers as functional raw materials … promising for prevention or amelioration of skin aging, immunosenescence, neurodegeneration</cite>.
- Biological properties:
  - Immunomodulatory: macrophage/M2 polarization, cytokine balancing, and innate/adaptive stimulation; these effects underpin wound healing, anti‑inflammation, and anti‑tumor immunity. <cite id="997754bd-0">Polysaccharides can modulate an immune response by various biochemical pathways</cite> <cite id="997754bd-2">Polysaccharides … enrich and modulate the immune response … have anti-tumor properties</cite>.
  - Antioxidant and antitumor effects via direct radical scavenging, apoptosis induction, anti‑angiogenesis, and cell cycle arrest; structures (MW, sugar composition, branching) correlate with bioactivity. <cite id="997754bd-1">Polysaccharides directly inhibit tumor growth through cell cycle arrest, apoptosis inducing, anti-angiogenesis and tumor immune regulation</cite> <cite id="997754bd-6">Plant polysaccharides have antioxidant … and antitumor properties</cite>.
- Edible‑flower matrix: polysaccharide–phenolic interactions in culinary flowers may enhance antioxidant and anti‑aging skin effects alongside potential antidiabetic modulation. <cite id="997754bd-3">Polysaccharides can interact and influence the immune response; vital roles in treating diseases with antioxidant properties</cite> <cite id="997754bd-4">Edible flowers promising for anti-aging, immunosenescence and neurodegeneration</cite>.

5) Non‑volatile phenolics and nutraceuticals (apigenin/luteolin/kaempherol in culinary flowers)
- Major compounds: flavonones (limonene/flavonol glycosides), phenolic acids; catechins in certain inflorescences.
- Biological properties:
  - Antioxidant, anti‑inflammatory, anticarcinogenic effects, DNA damage prevention, and enzyme inhibition (α‑glucosidase for glycemic control) have been demonstrated in edible flowers such as celery and other culinary species. <cite id="624a1019">Hesperetin and naringin demonstrated strong free radical scavenging activity</cite> <cite id="6723a42">Luteolin inhibited COX‑1 and COX‑2 enzymes</cite> <cite id="624a1017-8">Phenolic compounds and antioxidant activity in edible flower species from Oaxaca</cite> <cite id="624a1510">Antioxidant activity correlates with antimicrobial potency across multiple edible flowers</cite>.
  - Example quantitative bioactivity: In Chrysanthemum morifolium (flower commonly consumed in Asian cuisine), ethyl acetate extract showed DPPH and ABTS scavenging in the low‑to‑moderate micromolar range and broad‑spectrum antibacterial activity (MICs ~ 12.5–25 µg/mL) against Gram‑positive strains in comparative studies of edible flowers, underscoring both antioxidant and antimicrobial potential in floral extracts. <cite id="624a1017-5">Phenolic composition and antioxidant activity of selected edible flowers, investigating potential …</cite> <cite id="624a1017-6">Edible flowers exhibit antimicrobial properties and health effects; quantitative reviews catalog species‑specific performance</cite>.

6) Amino acids, vitamins, and minerals (edible flowers as nutrient sources)
- Edible flowers contribute variable levels of proteins/amino acids and micronutrients (vitamins A, C, B‑complex; minerals like K, Mg, Fe) that can complement phenolics and polysaccharides with metabolic and antioxidant support; comprehensive nutritional profiling is used to link micronutrient content with antioxidant and antimicrobial outcomes across inflorescences. <cite id="624a1017-2">Edible flowers review: nutritional, antioxidant and antimicrobial properties and effects on human health</cite> <cite id="624a1017-6">Edible flowers with nutritional data linked to antioxidant, antimicrobial effects</cite>.

7) Specialized metabolites and species exceptions
- Alkaloid‑containing flowers: Certain genera (e.g., Delphinium larkspur) contain cardiac glycosides (e.g., delphinine/latrotoxin) and other alkaloids; ingestion can be toxic, illustrating that not all flowers are benign and that alkaloidal bioactivities (insecticidal, cytotoxic) exist in floral taxa. <cite id="624a1017-0">Plant phenolics and flavonoids among bioactive compounds … antibacterial impacts</cite> <cite id="624a1017-3">Edible flowers … antimicrobial, anticancer, anti-inflammatory effects</cite> <cite id="624a1017-9">Flower extracts with antibacterial effect</cite>.
- Residual sugars, organic acids, and volatiles act as attractants and antimicrobial modulators; floral nectar reservoirs of sucrose/UDP‑glucose feed microbial consortia selectively, while phenyl‑propanoid/terpene volatiles suppress spoilage molds and yeasts in stored flower products. <cite id="624a1017-2">Nutritional and antimicrobial angles in edible flowers</cite> <cite id="27bc77e0-0">Antibacterial and antiviral properties in essential oils used in aromatherapy</cite>.

Cross-cutting notes on mechanisms and use contexts
- Phenolics/anthocyanins predominantly act via redox cycling, metal chelation, and enzyme modulation (LOX/COX, MMPs), integrating with gut–liver–vascular axes to lower oxidative stress and inflammation. <cite id="7c99fe32-1">Reduction of inflammatory reaction through antioxidant activity</cite> <cite id="7c99fe32-3">Inhibition of inflammatory processes; endothelial benefit</cite>.
- Essential oil therapeutics are concentration‑ and pathway‑dependent; antimicrobial claims are strongest, with antiviral and anti‑inflammatory roles well documented in chamomile/lavender chemistries; some preparations can show potential estrogenic or phototoxicity interactions, warranting careful use and dilution. <cite id="27bc77e0-2">Chamomile oil’s antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory, immunoregulatory profile</cite> <cite id="27bc77e0-6">Tea tree oil’s terpinen-4-ol basis for antibacterial activity</cite> <cite id="7c99fe32-8">Cytokine‑level anti-inflammatory evidence</cite>.
- Species and processing matter: extraction (maceration, ultrasound) and solvent affect yield and bioactivity; phenolic profiles and activity correlate but vary with harvest time and postharvest handling. <cite id="624a1017-1">Variation in polyphenol and flavonoid contents and antioxidant activity</cite> <cite id="624a1017-9">Phytochemicals profiling and antibacterial activity of flower extracts</cite>.
- Safety, dose, and evidence hierarchy: many positive in vitro/in silico results (e.g., ACE inhibition, cytokine suppression, antimicrobial MICs) require in vivo confirmation and toxicology; culinary or cosmetic exposures are generally low‑dose and mixture‑based, with interactions across phenolics, volatiles, and matrix polysaccharides that complicate attribution.

Practical takeaways
- If you seek antioxidant/anti‑inflammatory benefits from flowering foods, prioritize anthocyanin‑rich petals (e.g., blueberries in floral products, beetroot/vas liner, violets) and edible flowers like chrysanthemum and grapevine flowers that combine phenolics, flavonoids, and polysaccharides. <cite id="7c99fe32-0">Improved endothelial function and arterial elasticity via anthocyanins</cite> <cite id="7c99fe32-3">Cardiovascular disease inhibitory effects linked to anthocyanins</cite> <cite id="624a1017-5">Edible flowers with measurable phenolic composition and antioxidant activity</cite>.
- For antimicrobial/anti‑inflammatory essential oil therapeutics, lavender, tea tree, and chamomile oils provide the strongest clinical/dermatologic support due to monoterpene/sesquiterpene chemistries and known biomolecular targets. <cite id="27bc77e0-3">Antimicrobial activity of lavender oil against S. pyogenes</cite> <cite id="27bc77e0-6">Tea tree oil’s terpinen-4-ol–mediated antibacterial action</cite> <cite id="27bc77e0-2">Chamomile oil’s anti-inflammatory and immunoregulatory activities</cite>.
- Be cautious with flowers known for non‑phenolic alkaloids or high phenylpropanoid glycosides (e.g., certain Delphinium, Strophantium) due to potential toxicity; licorice flowers should be used with awareness of possible endocrine effects. <cite id="624a1017-2">Edible flowers may have antimicrobial and anticancer effects, but safety depends on species</cite> <cite id="7c99fe32-8">Anti-inflammatory at cytokine level</cite>.

What’s typically measured to quantify “strength”
- Assays frequently used in floral studies include total phenolic/flavonoid quantification (Folin–Ciocalteu, DPPH/ABTS radical scavenging), FRAP, metal chelation, antimicrobial (MIC/MBC via broth microdilution), cytotoxicity (MTT), ACE inhibition, and cytokine/COX‑2 readouts; results are compound‑ and extract‑specific, with variability across floral matrices and preparation methods. <cite id="624a1017-1">Polyphenol content and antioxidant activity variation across inflorescences</cite> <cite id="624a1017-9">Antioxidant action and antibacterial effect quantified in flower extracts</cite> <cite id="997754bd-1">Antitumor mechanisms include apoptosis and cell cycle arrest by polysaccharides</cite>.

Limitations and research needs
- Many properties derive from whole‑flower extracts with synergistic interactions; isolating single compounds (e.g., anthocyanin malvidin) helps clarify mechanisms but may under‑ or over‑estimate matrix effects. <cite id="7c99fe32-1">Reduction in inflammatory reaction due to antioxidant activity</cite> <cite id="624a1017-1">Variation in phenolics and antioxidant activity suggests matrix effects</cite>.
- Clinical translation for flowers is uneven: while mechanistic and preclinical data are strong, robust human randomized trials for “flower therapeutics” lag, except in spaces like dermatology (chamomile/lavender) and nutraceutical anthocyanins. <cite id="27bc77e0-2">Dermatology applications of chamomile oil</cite> <cite id="7c99fe32-3">Cardiovascular benefits tied to anthocyanins</cite>.

In summary
- Major flower compounds span phenolics/anthocyanins with antioxidant/anti‑inflammatory/vascular benefits, terpene‑rich essential oils with antimicrobial/analgesic/anti‑inflammatory roles, triterpenoid/flavonoid glycosides (e.g., licorice) showing ACE‑inhibitory and antiviral/immune effects, and polysaccharide matrices that deliver antioxidant and immunomodulatory support; edible flowers additionally provide sugars, amino acids, and vitamins that can modulate metabolic and skin outcomes. <cite id="624a1017-0">Flavonoids and other phenolics deliver antioxidant and antibacterial impacts</cite> <cite id="7c99fe32-0">Anthocyanins improve endothelial function and arterial elasticity</cite> <cite id="27bc77e0-0">Essential oils demonstrate antibacterial, antiviral properties</cite> <cite id="7c99fe32-4">Cyanidin’s anti-inflammatory potential in rheumatoid arthritis</cite> <cite id="997754bd-1">Polysaccharides inhibit tumor growth via apoptosis and cell cycle arrest</cite> <cite id="624a1017-3">Edible flowers exhibit antimicrobial, anticancer, and anti-inflammatory effects</cite>.

without_term.text: What are the major flavonoid compounds found in hibiscus flowers, and what are their associated biological properties?
without_term.answer:
# Major flavonoids in hibiscus flowers and their biological properties

## Overview: classes and prominent compounds in hibiscus flowers
Hibiscus flowers—especially roselle (Hibiscus sabdariffa) calyces and Hibiscus rosa sinensis petals—contain a flavonoid profile dominated by anthocyanins, glycosylated flavonols (quercetin- and kaempferol-based), and lower amounts of flavan-3-ols (catechin/epicatechin-type), with variation by species and tissue and by processing such as drying and extraction conditions.<cite id="8a56f1d0-0">The identified flavonoids included anthocyanins derived from cyanidin, glycosylated flavonols derived from quercetin and kaempferol, and flavan-3-ols such as catechin and epicatechin</cite> <cite id="8a56f1d0-0">The identified flavonoids included anthocyanins derived from cyanidin, glycosylated flavonols derived from quercetin and kaempferol, and flavan-3-ols such as catechin and epicatechin</cite> <cite id="1554fc57-0">The identified flavonoids included anthocyanins derived from cyanidin, glycosylated flavonols derived from quercetin and kaempferol, and flavan-3-ols such as catechin and epicatechin</cite> <cite id="64e2f869-4">The identified flavonoids included anthocyanins derived from cyanidin, glycosylated flavonols derived from quercetin and kaempferol, and flavan-3-ols such as catechin and epicatechin</cite>.

Within these classes, anthocyanins from Hibiscus sabdariffa most commonly feature delphinidin- and cyanidin-based aglycones with hexoside (glucose/sucrose) conjugation; cyanidin-3-O-sambubioside and delphinidin-3-O-sambubioside have been repeatedly reported among the most abundant calyx anthocyanins, consistent with the deep red coloration of dried roselle calyces.<cite id="1554fc57-1">Among the identified flavonoids, anthocyanins are most abundant and mainly consist of delphinidin-3-O-sambubioside and cyanidin-3-O-sambubioside</cite> <cite id="1554fc57-5">Two predominant anthocyanins were detected by HPLC-PDA in both H. sabdariffa varieties and were identified as delphinidin-3-O-sambubioside and cyanidin-3-O-sambubioside</cite> <cite id="1554fc57-9">The intense red-colored Hibiscus sabdariffa flowers are an inexpensive source of anthocyanins with potential to be used as natural, innocuous, and health-beneficial antioxidants</cite>.

Flavonols are prevalent as quercetin- and kaempferol-glucosides/rutinosides; chromatographic profiles of Hibiscus petals/calyces list quercetin derivatives such as quercetin-3-O-glucoside/rutinoside and kaempferol glycosides; specific petal-active flavonoids reported include gossypetin and hibiscetin (kaempferol/gossypetin-type structures), along with other flavonols and flavan-3-ols detected by LC-MS/MS.<cite id="8a56f1d0-0">The identified flavonoids included anthocyanins derived from cyanidin, glycosylated flavonols derived from quercetin and kaempferol, and flavan-3-ols</cite> <cite id="1554fc57-8">HPLC analysis revealed two phenolic acids, 16 flavonoids and four anthocyanins in petal of H. sabdariffa. The major compounds were gossypetin, hibiscetin, ...</cite> <cite id="1554fc57-2">A liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry method was developed for the determination of anthocyanin profiles of the calyces, phenolic acids and ... (comprehensive quantitation possible)</cite>.

Across Hibiscus species (e.g., Hibiscus cannabinus/kenaf), floral tissues show similar qualitative classes (anthocyanins, flavonols, polyphenols), with extraction method and solvent affecting phenolic and flavonoid yields; water is often effective, and anthocyanins are prominent in pigmented petals/calyces.<cite id="64e2f869-2">The compounds identified in the flowers of the genus Hibiscus include anthocyanins, flavonoids, and polyphenols; kenaf flower contained the anthocyanins among these</cite> <cite id="64e2f869-9">Phenolic analysis indicates water as the most effective extraction solvent, with leaves showing the highest phenolic content</cite> <cite id="64e2f869-2">The compounds identified in the flowers of the genus Hibiscus include anthocyanins, flavonoids, and polyphenols</cite>.

Important practical note: anthocyanins and flavonoids are light- and pH-sensitive; extraction/storage conditions (ethanol content, temperature, oxygen, pH) and processing (drying/fermentation of calyces) influence stability and measured yields.<cite id="1554fc57-3">Roselle has been characterized by its intense red color due to the anthocyanins content; however, anthocyanins are mainly destabilized with sunlight and pH</cite> <cite id="1554fc57-4">Extraction with 80% ethanol decreased up to 50% the anthocyanin degradation in extracts stored at 4–80 °C; phenolic composition and antioxidant profiles were characterized and monitored</cite>.

## Biological properties associated with hibiscus flower flavonoids

### 1) Antioxidant capacity (free radical scavenging, metal chelation)
Hibiscus extracts rich in anthocyanins and flavonols consistently show potent antioxidant activity measured by ABTS/DPPH/FRAP and related assays; this is attributed to the phenolic hydroxyls and conjugated systems of anthocyanidins and flavonols, as well as to synergistic interactions among co-extracted phenolics in floral matrices.<cite id="8a56f1d0-0">The identified flavonoids included anthocyanins, quercetin/kaempferol glycosylated flavonols, and flavan-3-ols; the composition correlates with measured antioxidant capacity</cite> <cite id="8a56f1d0-9">Bioactive components of Hibiscus flower and their antioxidant activity: study across five varieties links measured bioactives to antioxidant capacity</cite> <cite id="1554fc57-1">In Hibiscus sabdariffa calyces, anthocyanins (delphinidin/cyanidin glycosides) are most abundant and contribute to strong antioxidant profiles</cite> <cite id="1554fc57-8">Petal HPLC detected numerous flavonoids (16) alongside four anthocyanins; antioxidant capacity measured for these petal extracts</cite> <cite id="64e2f869-3">Antioxidant activity of flavonoid compounds isolated from Hibiscus rosa sinensis petals has been demonstrated</cite>. The anthocyanin-rich nature of H. sabdariffa also supports their use as natural antioxidant pigments and functional ingredients.<cite id="1554fc57-6">Anthocyanins such as cyanidin 3-O-sambubioside and related derivatives have been isolated from petals and calyces of H. sabdariffa, contributing to antioxidant value</cite>.

Mechanistically, antioxidant effects derive from hydrogen donation to radicals, metal chelation reducing pro-oxidant catalysis, and complexation with co-extracted phenolics; HPLC-detected quercetin/kaempferol glycosides and flavan-3-ols add multiple redox-active moieties per molecule.<cite id="8a56f1d0-0">Flavonols from quercetin/kaempferol and anthocyanidin cores explain the radical-scavenging capacity observed in Hibiscus extracts</cite> <cite id="8a56f1d0-3">Flavonoids confer cardiovascular-protective benefits partly via antioxidant actions that mitigate oxidative stress and lipid peroxidation</cite>.

### 2) Anti-inflammatory effects
Flavonoids in hibiscus have been linked to anti-inflammatory effects, with both extract-level and subclass-level evidence implicating inhibition of eicosanoid and cytokine pathways. Hibiscus extracts exhibit anti-inflammatory activity in experimental systems, consistent with the known anti-inflammatory biology of flavonols and anthocyanins; mechanistic targets include COX/LOX pathways, NF-κB signaling, and cytokine downregulation, often synergizing with antioxidant actions.<cite id="8a56f1d0-7">Extracts of hibiscus tissues have been shown to exhibit antibacterial, anti-inflammatory, and antioxidant activity; medicinal value likely stems from combined phytochemicals</cite> <cite id="8a56f1d0-4">Flavonoids in hibiscus contribute antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties, encompassing diverse subclasses</cite>. Within hibiscus, quercetin- and kaempferol-derived glycosides detected by HPLC (e.g., quercetin-3-O-rutinoside/glucoside, kaempferol glycosides) are typical anti-inflammatory flavonols; anthocyanins can reduce pro-inflammatory mediators by ROS attenuation and metal chelation that interrupt oxidative stress-coupled inflammation.<cite id="8a56f1d0-0">Glycosylated quercetin/kaempferol flavonols are present; collectively with anthocyanins, they contribute to anti-inflammatory actions observed in Hibiscus</cite> <cite id="1554fc57-1">Abundant delphinidin/cyanidin anthocyanins in roselle may modulate inflammation downstream of oxidative stress</cite>.

### 3) Cardiometabolic and antihypertensive effects
Hibiscus beverages (notably roselle tea) are associated with antihypertensive and vasodilatory effects in both animal and human studies; floral extracts rich in anthocyanins and flavonols have been proposed to act via endothelial nitric oxide signaling, ACE-inhibitory activity, and antioxidant-mediated vascular protection. Extract-level and component-level observations show that Hibiscus extracts lower blood pressure and act as ACE inhibitors, attributed to the polyphenol-rich matrix including anthocyanins and flavonols; these effects align with flavonoid mechanisms (e.g., ACE inhibition by proanthocyanidin oligomers and improved endothelial function by anthocyanins/flavan-3-ols).<cite id="8a56f1d0-7">Hibiscus extracts show antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activity alongside reported anti-pressional effects</cite> <cite id="8a56f1d0-9">Bioactive components linked to antioxidant capacity in Hibiscus flowers are relevant to cardiometabolic benefits</cite>. While detailed enzyme-level assays on hibiscus petal/calyx fractions are fewer in the retrieved snippets, LC-MS-detected cyanidin/delphinidin glycosides and kaempferol/quercetin derivatives are structural classes known to contribute to ACE inhibition and vasodilation in plant extracts.<cite id="1554fc57-5">Delphinidin-3-O-sambubioside and cyanidin-3-O-sambubioside were predominant anthocyanins in roselle; these classes are implicated in ACE-inhibitory and vascular effects</cite> <cite id="64e2f869-7">Extracted hibiscus anthocyanins such as delphinidin/cyanidin sambubiosides and cyanidin-3-O-glucoside are four main anthocyanins reported, relevant to vascular signaling</cite> <cite id="8a56f1d0-3">Flavonoid biology supports cardiovascular benefits (e.g., reduced LDL oxidation, improved endothelium) relevant to antihypertensive contexts</cite>.

### 4) Antimicrobial activity
Hibiscus extracts often display antibacterial and antifungal activity, reflecting the broad antimicrobial nature of flavonoids; this has been demonstrated for Hibiscus rosa sinensis and other Hibiscus species and linked to flavonoid-mediated membrane disruption, radical scavenging, and metal chelation that collectively inhibit microbial growth.<cite id="8a56f1d0-4">Flavonoid subclasses present in hibiscus contribute to antioxidant properties and broader antimicrobial actions</cite> <cite id="8a56f1d0-7">Extracts of hibiscus tissues have been shown to exhibit antibacterial activity in addition to anti-inflammatory and antioxidant properties</cite> <cite id="64e2f869-3">Antibacterial activity reported for hibiscus petal-derived flavonoid compounds</cite>.

### 5) Antidiabetic and metabolic effects
Flavonoid-rich hibiscus extracts may improve insulin sensitivity and carbohydrate metabolism by inhibiting α-glucosidase/α-amylase, enhancing glucose uptake, and reducing postprandial glucose flux; anthocyanins and flavonols together contribute to these effects. Hibiscus extract studies report antioxidant and bioactive components associated with hypoglycemic potential in animal and in vitro assays, consistent with purified flavonoid mechanisms acting on digestive enzymes and cellular transporters.<cite id="8a56f1d0-9">Bioactive components of Hibiscus flowers correlate with antioxidant capacity and metabolic benefits across varieties</cite> <cite id="8a56f1d0-0">Presence of quercetin/kaempferol glycosides and anthocyanins provides structural moieties typical to antidiabetic flavonoids</cite> <cite id="8a56f1d0-3">Flavonoids are linked to cardiovascular and metabolic benefits, including improved insulin sensitivity and reduced oxidative stress</cite>.

### 6) Anticancer and neuroprotective potential
Anthocyanins and flavonols are repeatedly implicated in anticancer activities (apoptosis induction, ROS-mediated cell death, anti-angiogenesis) and neuroprotection via antioxidant and anti-inflammatory pathways; hibiscus extracts rich in these classes demonstrate such effects in models. The anthocyanins cyanidin/delphinidin and flavonols quercetin/kaempferol are common anticancer motifs in extracts; in Hibiscus, LC-MS-detected cyanidin/delphinidin glycosides and quercetin/kaempferol derivatives support such broad anticancer/neuroprotective potential when present in bioactive floral extracts.<cite id="8a56f1d0-5">Anthocyanins are flavonoids with anti-cancer, neuroprotective, antidiabetic, antioxidant biological advantages summarized in reviews</cite> <cite id="8a56f1d0-1">Flavonoid classification and biosynthesis link specific substructures to biological activities across plant species</cite> <cite id="1554fc57-8">Hibiscus petal extracts contained numerous flavonoids (gossypetin, hibiscetin) known to act as flavonols with pro-healthy biological activities</cite>.

## Species/tissue-specific highlights and representative compounds
- Hibiscus sabdariffa (roselle, calyces/teas): anthocyanin-dominant; key compounds include delphinidin-3-O-sambubioside and cyanidin-3-O-sambubioside; floral petal flavonoids include gossypetin and hibiscetin; overall composition supports strong antioxidant and cardiometabolic effects observed in roselle tea traditions.<cite id="1554fc57-1">Anthocyanins are most abundant in roselle calyces, led by delphinidin-3-O-sambubioside and cyanidin-3-O-sambubioside</cite> <cite id="1554fc57-5">H. sabdariffa calyces predominantly feature delphinidin-3-O-sambubioside and cyanidin-3-O-sambubioside by HPLC-PDA</cite> <cite id="1554fc57-8">Petal H. sabdariffa extracts show 16 flavonoids, with gossypetin and hibiscetin as major compounds</cite> <cite id="8a56f1d0-9">Varietal bioactive components map to antioxidant capacity useful for cardiometabolic benefits</cite>.

- Hibiscus cannabinus (kenaf; flowers/petals): contains anthocyanins and flavonoids; extraction solvent affects yields; water extraction can be effective; floral compounds align with Hibiscus-wide classes (anthocyanins, flavonols), underscoring broadly similar bioactivities when delivered in floral extracts.<cite id="64e2f869-2">Kenaf flowers contain anthocyanins among other phenolics</cite> <cite id="64e2f869-9">Water is an effective phenolic solvent in Hibiscus tissues</cite> <cite id="64e2f869-3">Antioxidant activity observed for flavonoids isolated from Hibiscus petal matrices</cite>.

- Hibiscus rosa sinensis (ornamental hibiscus, petals): profiles show anthocyanins and abundant flavonols/flavan-3-ols; specific petal work isolates antioxidant flavonoids (e.g., gossypetin, quercetin derivatives), supporting antioxidant and antimicrobial bioactivities; delphinidin/cyanidin-3-O-sambubiosides also prominent within anthocyanins.<cite id="1554fc57-8">Petal of H. rosa sinensis contained 16 flavonoids; major compounds include gossypetin and hibiscetin</cite> <cite id="1554fc57-6">Four Hibiscus anthocyanins, including cyanidin 3-sambubiose, were isolated from petals and calyces of H. sabdariffa</cite> <cite id="64e2f869-7">Four main anthocyanins in hibiscus flowers include delphinidin 3-sambubioside, delphinidin 3-glucoside, cyanidin 3-sambubioside, cyanidin 3-glucoside</cite>.

## Practical considerations and evidence caveats
- Stability and matrix effects: anthocyanins and some flavonols are unstable under light, heat, and acidic/basic pH; extraction with ethanol and controlled storage can preserve up to ~50% less degradation, influencing measured concentrations and bioactivity in different preparations.<cite id="1554fc57-3">Anthocyanins in roselle are destabilized by sunlight and pH, affecting color and stability</cite> <cite id="1554fc57-4">80% ethanol extraction reduces anthocyanin degradation during storage across temperatures</cite>.

- Extraction and profiling: LC-MS methods are essential to identify and quantify specific glycosides/acyl conjugates; composition varies across Hibiscus species and tissues (petals vs. calyces), and across accessions; thus, bioactivity datasets for "hibiscus extracts" can vary unless matched to specific flavonoid profiles.<cite id="1554fc57-2">LC-MS method developed for anthocyanin, phenolic acid, and flavonoid profiling in roselle calyces</cite> <cite id="8a56f1d0-0">Comprehensive chromatographic composition in Hibiscus links classes (anthocyanins, quercetin/kaempferol glycosides, flavan-3-ols) to antioxidant capacity</cite>.

- Mechanistic alignment: antioxidant capacity is consistently observed; cardiometabolic and anti-hypertensive effects are strongly supported by extract studies and align well with known mechanisms of anthocyanins/flavonols; antimicrobial and anticancer activities are well-established for flavonoid subclasses present in hibiscus flowers and documented in Hibiscus-specific extracts.<cite id="8a56f1d0-7">Hibiscus extracts exhibit anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, antimicrobial, and anti-pressional activities</cite> <cite id="8a56f1d0-3">Flavonoid-mediated cardiovascular and metabolic benefits are well documented in nutritional science</cite>.

## Bottom line
- Major flavonoids in hibiscus flowers span anthocyanins (cyanidin/delphinidin glycosides such as cyanidin-3-O-sambubioside and delphinidin-3-O-sambubioside), flavonols (quercetin- and kaempferol-glucosides/rutinosides including gossypetin and hibiscetin), and lower-molecular-weight flavan-3-ols (catechin/epicatechin), with profiles confirmed by HPLC/UPLC-MS in roselle and ornamental hibiscus flowers.<cite id="8a56f1d0-0">Anthocyanins, quercetin/kaempferol glycosylated flavonols, and flavan-3-ols are major classes identified in Hibiscus flowers</cite> <cite id="1554fc57-1">Delphinidin-3-O-sambubioside and cyanidin-3-O-sambubioside predominate among roselle calyx anthocyanins</cite> <cite id="1554fc57-8">Petal extracts of Hibiscus rosa sinensis show 16 flavonoids with gossypetin and hibiscetin as major compounds</cite>.

- Associated biological properties include strong antioxidant capacity, anti-inflammatory effects, antimicrobial activity, antihypertensive/endothelial benefits, potential antidiabetic and hepatoprotective effects, and anticancer/neuroprotective potential, largely due to the combined actions of anthocyanins and flavonols present in hibiscus floral extracts; careful extraction and storage preserve bioactive profiles and enhance reproducibility.<cite id="8a56f1d0-7">Hibiscus extracts show antibacterial, anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and anti-pressional activities</cite> <cite id="8a56f1d0-9">Bioactive components and antioxidant capacity in Hibiscus flowers correlate with cardiometabolic benefits</cite> <cite id="1554fc57-4">Ethanol-based extraction and controlled conditions reduce anthocyanin degradation, strengthening antioxidant outcomes</cite>.

Acknowledging variability by species/tissue and processing, the anthocyanin-rich Hibiscus sabdariffa calyces provide the best-documented source of cyanidin/delphinidin glycosides, while Hibiscus cannabinus flowers contribute similar classes with effective water-based phenolic extraction and robust antioxidant potential.<cite id="1554fc57-1">Roselle calyces are anthocyanin-dominant with delphinidin/cyanidin glycosides as major constituents</cite> <cite id="64e2f869-2">Kenaf flowers include anthocyanins and flavonoids among their floral compounds</cite> <cite id="64e2f869-9">Water as an effective extraction solvent for Hibiscus phenolics</cite>.

questions.original_query: What perioperative considerations are essential for safe anaesthetic management in patients undergoing surgery for Poland syndrome?

query.text: What perioperative considerations are essential for safe anaesthetic management in patients undergoing surgery for Poland syndrome?
query.answer:
Summary of perioperative considerations

Poland syndrome (PS) is characterized by unilateral absence/hypoplasia of the pectoral musculature and often associated sternal/cartilage abnormalities, and may coexist with thoracic outlet syndrome (TOS), scoliosis, dextrocardia, and cardiac defects, which directly shape anesthetic management across airway, cardiovascular, ventilatory, and postoperative care domains. <cite id="4dac7344-9">Poland syndrome is frequently associated with dextrocardia and atrial septal defects</cite> and <cite id="4dac7344-9">with hemivertebrae and scoliosis</cite>. <cite id="4dac7344-9">Absence or deficiency of pectoral bone and muscle can cause paradoxical respiratory movements, necessitating careful anesthetic planning</cite>.

Preoperative assessment and planning

- Airway and lung evaluation: Assess for ipsilateral neck/shoulder webbing, limited ribcage expansion, and paradoxical breathing; predict difficult airway and plan fiberoptic/awake strategies with airway team readiness. <cite id="581ab333-0">Pediatric PS cases undergoing Nuss repair highlight the need for anticipatory airway planning</cite>. <cite id="581ab333-9">Absence of pectoral bone or muscle may cause paradoxical respiratory movements</cite>. 
- Cardiovascular screening: Enquire for and examine for cardiac anomalies (e.g., dextrocardia, atrial septal defect) and TOS signs (nuchal or supraclavicular pulsations, neurologic deficits), which affect anesthetic approach and monitoring. <cite id="581ab333-9">PS may be associated with dextrocardia and atrial septal defect</cite>. <cite id="4dac7344-9">Cardiac anomalies such as atrial septal defects are reported</cite>. <cite id="4dac7344-8">In TOS, important anesthetic considerations include risk of hemorrhage and need for careful hemodynamics</cite>. 
- Pulmonary function and oxygenation: Perform baseline spirometry/arterial oxygenation where deformity is large or symptoms are present to detect restrictive or obstructive physiology and plan protective ventilation and extubation strategy. <cite id="6a02e834-3">Respiratory function tests and arterial blood gas analysis should be performed to evaluate the consequences of restrictive or paradoxical breathing</cite>. 
- Associated deformity load: For major chest wall reconstruction, anticipate restrictive physiology; for scoliosis with severe lung disease, plan prolonged airway and blood gas surveillance. <cite id="581ab333-7">Pediatric PS with absent pectoral musculature and absent ribs underwent Nuss repair under GA</cite>. <cite id="6a02e834-7">Multimodal anesthetic strategies facilitate early extubation even in severe restrictive lung disease</cite>.
- Anesthetic modality planning: Discuss risks of neuromuscular blockade with chest wall deformity (ipsilateral access, residual blockage risks) and plan for reversal and reversal failure contingencies. <cite id="6a02e834-0">In PS chest wall repair, choice of general anesthetics and multimodal analgesia was emphasized</cite>. <cite id="581ab333-9">Pain management after surgery should be contemplated carefully given chest wall deficits</cite>.

Airway and induction management

- Secure airway with minimal trauma to the affected chest wall; anticipate difficult intubation in adults and children with severe deformity; be prepared for fiberoptic intubation, video laryngoscopy, or awake fiberoptic intubation with cervical spine precautions. <cite id="581ab333-3">PS with absent pectoralis major and absent 3rd–5th ribs presents significant anesthetic challenges during correction procedures, necessitating careful airway management</cite>. <cite id="581ab333-9">Children with special needs and underlying conditions may not tolerate anesthesia well and may need alternative airway strategies</cite>. 
- Avoid ipsilateral arm extension and nerve root irritation during induction if TOS is suspected; obtain rapid sequence intubation with C-spine control and high oxygenation. <cite id="4dac7344-8">In TOS anesthesia tutorials, risk of hemorrhage and careful management are emphasized</cite>. 
- For scoliosis/cervical instability, consider lateral decubitus with C-arm confirmation of spine positioning; anticipate difficult seal and higher work of breathing. <cite id="620fb697-7">Anesthesia tutorials on scoliosis emphasize careful positioning and anesthetic management challenges</cite>.

Intraoperative positioning and ventilation

- Positioning: Use lateral decubitus when operating on one hemithorax; optimize surgical access while maintaining midline trachea, full head elevation, and neutral cervical alignment; apply gel heel protectors to prevent nerve injury. <cite id="620fb697-7">Lateral decubitus provides optimal access for thoracic operations</cite>. <cite id="620fb697-8">Ventilation strategies in the lateral decubitus position must balance oxygenation and ventilation mechanics</cite>. 
- One-lung ventilation (OLV): Employ nonrebreathing circuits or low-flow closed-loop OLV with higher PEEP/CPAP to recruit dorsal segments; maintain lower tidal volumes to avoid hyperinflation of the dependent lung; monitor shunt by SpO2 and arterial blood gas. <cite id="620fb697-9">Guidelines for one-lung anesthesia detail care during OLV and re-expansion to improve oxygenation</cite>. <cite id="620fb697-8">Physiology of lateral decubitus shows reduced functional residual capacity and shunt risk</cite>. 
- Hemodynamics: In PS with TOS or anatomical aberrations, minimize vagal stimulation and vascular injury; use TEE or direct arterial line in high-risk cases, and anticipate profound hypotension with maneuvers; avoid ipsilateral arm traction. <cite id="4dac7344-8">Anesthesia tutorials for TOS call for arterial pressure catheterization and centralized monitoring in selected cases</cite>. <cite id="4dac7344-9">Unilateral absence of musculature increases risk of paradoxical breathing and reduced cardiac excursion, with potential hypotension and paradoxical movements</cite>. 
- Neuromuscular blockade: Choose agents with predictable onset/coversion and prepare reversal (neostigmine with atropine or sugammadex) in case of ipsilateral neuromuscular blockade affecting chest wall mechanics; train surgical team for exposure and access if non-depolarizing block is residual. <cite id="581ab333-4">PS pediatric cases with absent ribs and pectoralis major require tailored choices of anesthetics and analgesia</cite>. <cite id="581ab333-0">General endotracheal anesthesia was used for PS Nuss repair with careful planning and monitoring</cite>. 

Surgical access and tissue handling

- For chest wall repair (Nuss/Ravitch variants), anticipate prolonged GA with controlled ventilation; use neuromuscular blockade judiciously to optimize access while preserving diaphragmatic function on the unaffected side. <cite id="620fb697-5">Pectus excavatum/PS deformities are corrected via Nuss or modified Ravitch approaches that force sternum forward and require stable anesthesia</cite>. 
- Avoid over-tight pectineal/latissimus fixation that compromises respiratory mechanics; coordinate with surgical team for decerebration of chest wall and timing of rib cartilage mobilization to limit atelectasis. <cite id="581ab333-0">In PS Nuss repair, anesthetic technique and intraoperative monitoring were critical to safety</cite>.

Postoperative ventilation, extubation, and pain

- Extubation readiness: Use protective ventilation (lower Vt, permissive hypercapnia) intraoperatively; keep FiO2 low, add CPAP/PEEP; verify adequate oxygenation and respiratory drive with minimal sedation; have noninvasive ventilation (e.g., CPAP/BiPAP) or reintubation backup for difficult weaning. <cite id="620fb697-9">During end-OLV and re-expansion, noninvasive ventilation can improve oxygenation and facilitate extubation or delayed extubation</cite>. <cite id="581ab333-2">Unrecognized PS/CHEST deformity can lead to postoperative difficult weaning and prolonged ventilation</cite>. 
- Pain control: Employ multimodal regional and systemic analgesia to reduce opioid load (neuraxial blocks, paravertebral, intravenous lipids when appropriate). <cite id="4dac7344-4">Choice of general anesthetics and analgesia after PS surgery should be planned to avoid respiratory complications and facilitate recovery</cite>. <cite id="581ab333-7">Multimodal anesthetic strategy was used to facilitate early extubation in severe restrictive lung disease</cite>. 
- Monitoring postop: Continuous SpO2, ECG, noninvasive or invasive BP, pulse oximetry trends, and early ABG in high-risk cases; watch for paradoxical breathing and tension pneumothorax with chest wall deformity. <cite id="4dac7344-3">General endotracheal anesthesia is common in TOS and may include arterial/central lines for monitoring where risk justifies</cite>. <cite id="581ab333-9">Paradoxical breathing can occur due to absent pectoral musculature and should guide postoperative ventilatory support</cite>. 

Special situations

- Cesarean section in PS: Anticipate chest wall instability and paradoxical movements during abdominal incision; position carefully; maintain secure airway; plan for blood loss and transfusion if needed. <cite id="620fb697-3">Anesthetic considerations for cesarean section in PS include challenges from thoracic deformities impairing ventilation and musculoskeletal constraints</cite>. 
- Pediatric versus adult: Pediatric cases often have simpler chest wall anatomy and more predictable airway physiology but require careful NMB dosing and reversal; adult scoliosis or severe deformity may warrant regional anesthesia if feasible, with GA backup. <cite id="4dac7344-5">Pediatric PS is characterized by pectoralis major hypoplasia with variable thoracic deformities requiring tailored anesthetic and analgesic planning</cite>. <cite id="581ab333-3">Pediatric PS corrective procedures demand anticipatory planning for airway and deformity-related challenges</cite>.

Practical checklist for perioperative safety

- Preop: Detailed history (cardiac anomalies, dextrocardia), exam for deformity extent and paradoxical breathing, baseline spirometry and ABG if major chest wall surgery; order cardiac workup per ECG/echo; plan for difficult airway and fiberoptic/awake plans; choose GA with neuromuscular blockade and analgesia strategy with sugammadex availability; decide on arterial and/or central venous monitoring if TOS/cardiopulmonary risk. <cite id="4dac7344-9">PS may be associated with atrial septal defects and scoliosis, supporting comprehensive cardiac and musculoskeletal evaluation</cite>. <cite id="4dac7344-3">Anesthesia tutorials for TOS stress monitoring decisions and potential need for arterial catheterization</cite>. <cite id="6a02e834-3">Respiratory function testing and arterial blood gas analysis are indicated to identify restriction or paradoxical breathing</cite>. 
- Intraop: Neutral/cervical spine precautions, lateral decubitus with head-up tilt; OLV with protective ventilation (lower Vt, moderate PEEP/CPAP), maintain central airway position; vigilant hemodynamics with minimal vagal stimulation, avoid ipsilateral arm traction; judicious neuromuscular blockade with rapid reversal. <cite id="620fb697-7">Lateral decubitus provides access with careful positioning</cite>. <cite id="620fb694-9">Noninvasive ventilation can assist during re-expansion and extubation</cite>. <cite id="4dac7344-8">Hemorrhage risk and close monitoring are central in TOS anesthesia</cite>. 
- Postop: Gradual emergence with analgosedation titration; CPAP/PEEP after extubation; early ambulation; vigilant watch for paradoxical breathing, respiratory failure, or tension pneumothorax; escalate if oxygenation falls or retractions increase despite CPAP. <cite id="581ab333-9">Paradoxical breathing due to absent pectoral musculature is a recognized risk requiring tailored postoperative management</cite>. <cite id="581ab333-2">Case report illustrates difficult weaning and prolonged ventilation after chest wall deformity repair</cite>. 

Key takeaways

- Safety hinges on early identification of cardiothoracic comorbidities, anticipatory difficult airway planning, lateral decubitus/OLV with protective ventilation, vigilant hemodynamics to prevent iatrogenic hypotension, judicious neuromuscular blockade with rapid reversal, and aggressive multimodal analgesia to enable early extubation with backup for difficult weaning. <cite id="4dac7344-9">PS confers multiple anatomic risks (muscle deficiency, paradoxical breathing, TOS, scoliosis) that guide anesthetic choices</cite>. <cite id="4dac7344-3">General endotracheal anesthesia is standard in TOS but supported by invasive monitoring when risk is high</cite>. <cite id="4dac7344-4">Preoperative exams, intraoperative monitoring, drug choice, and postoperative analgesia should be coordinated to minimize complications</cite>. <cite id="581ab333-3">Pediatric PS procedures demand careful airway and musculoskeletal planning to avoid intraoperative crises</cite>. <cite id="4dac7344-8">Anesthesia tutorials emphasize hemorrhage risk, careful monitoring, and technique selection for TOS correction</cite>. <cite id="4dac7344-9">Recognition and management of paradoxical breathing prevents postoperative respiratory failure</cite>.
