questions.original_query: How are costing methods for HIV testing services in sub-Saharan Africa classified, and what are the key distinctions that define each classification?

query.text: How are costing methods for HIV testing services in sub-Saharan Africa classified, and what are the key distinctions that define each classification?
query.answer:
Below is a synthesis of how costing methods for HIV testing services (HTS) in sub-Saharan Africa are commonly classified, with the key distinctions that define each class.

# 1) By economic evaluation type: what is being optimized

- Cost‑minimization analysis (CMA)
  - Definition and scope: Compares costs of alternatives that produce equivalent health outcomes, minimizing the cost to achieve one unit of health benefit (e.g., cost per person tested). Because benefits are held equal, the net effect on health outcomes is excluded. <cite id="1d1bda5e-8">In general, the primary forms of economic evaluation utilized in health are cost-minimization analysis, cost-effectiveness analysis, cost-utility analysis, and cost-effectiveness analysis with humanistic outcomes</cite>.
  - Application to HTS in SSA: Widely used to estimate incremental costs per person or per positive identified; differences in delivery model or algorithm are evaluated under constant health outcomes to identify the cheaper option for scaling. <cite id="a6db7999-0">The mean estimate for the incremental costs were $18.45 per person tested (median $12.26) and $359.76 for full costs (median $251.55) across studies</cite> <cite id="f34c4000-0">Self-testing had the lowest mean cost per person tested at $12.75 (median $11.50), lower than most primary/first-test settings</cite>.

- Cost‑effectiveness analysis (CEA)
  - Definition and scope: Compares cost against a health outcome that is clinically meaningful but not necessarily in utility form (e.g., cases detected, positives identified). <cite id="1d1bda5e-8">Cost-effectiveness analysis evaluates costs and health outcomes using a meaningful clinical endpoint</cite>.
  - Application to HTS in SSA: Often framed as cost per HIV-positive detected or cost per diagnosis, especially to compare decentralization (e.g., peer-delivered self-testing) versus facility testing when detecting positives efficiently is the target. <cite id="1d1bda5e-1">HIV testing innovations were most cost-effective when implemented through decentralized models such as peer-delivered self-testing</cite> <cite id="f34c4000-4">Incremental cost per HIV-positive detected by delivery modality was lowest for home-based testing ($297.09), followed by primary testing and general population screening scenarios</cite>.

- Cost‑utility analysis (CUA)
  - Definition and scope: Extends CEA to quality-adjusted life years (QALYs) or years of life saved, enabling comparison with broader health portfolios including HIV care and treatment. <cite id="1d1bda5e-8">Cost-utility analysis evaluates costs against quality-adjusted life-years to inform cross-program comparisons</cite> <cite id="1d1bda5e-5">Modeling frameworks for HIV testing typically compare costs with QALYs or infections averted to define cost-effectiveness and cost-utility boundaries</cite>.
  - Application to HTS in SSA: Used increasingly to argue that detection-driven strategies (e.g., self-testing) are cost-effective because they maximize downstream infections averted and link individuals to care, even when primary testing costs are low. <cite id="a6db7999-6">A cost-effectiveness analysis of home-based HIV testing in rural South Africa evaluated costs versus health outcomes to assess whether early detection provided value for resources</cite>.

Key distinction: CMA asks “Which option achieves the same outcome at least as cheaply?”; CEA asks “Which option delivers more health benefit per dollar?”; and CUA asks “Which option maximizes QALYs per dollar and compares to other health programs?” in a common monetary threshold framework. <cite id="1d1bda5e-8">Cost-minimization, cost-effectiveness, and cost-utility analyses progressively integrate more health outcomes, from equivalent outcomes (CMA) to clinical benefit (CEA) and quality-adjusted life-years (CUA)</cite>.

# 2) By delivery model and service package: where cost drivers differ

- Facility-based (primary/first-test) vs. community-based (index/HTS campaign) vs. home-based (HIVST)
  - Distinctions and cost components:
    - Facility testing: Inclusion of on-site turnaround, staff time, reagents/equipment depreciation, building occupancy, and verification algorithms increases unit costs. <cite id="f34c4000-2">Across Malawi, Zambia and Zimbabwe, mean cost per individual tested in facility settings ranged ~$4.24–$8.79, with per HIV-positive identified lower when throughput is higher</cite>.
    - Community and index testing: Costs emphasize outreach, supervision, community health worker time, linkage support, and logistics; benefits often include male and key-population reach that is lower via facilities. <cite id="f34c4000-5">Meta-analyses show community and facility-based testing strategies differ in outputs and linkage, framing resource allocation choices</cite> <cite id="f34c4000-3">Community index testing reached males proportionally more and was cost-effective compared with facility-based approaches, with larger system-level outputs per dollar</cite>.
    - Home-based self-testing (HBST): Removes time-to-diagnosis and facility visit costs; unit supply and counseling time dominate. <cite id="f34c4000-0">Self-testing mean unit cost per person tested was the lowest in SSA settings (median ~$11–12), often undercutting primary/facility tests</cite> <cite id="f34c4000-9">Within a home-testing program, per-test distribution costs averaged ~$8.97, with testing supplies (38%) and personnel (30%) as primary components</cite>.
    - Pooled/algorithmic verification: Adds retesting/consolidation costs but can reduce missed positives; cost-per-positive is higher than per-person costs due to false-negative risks. <cite id="f34c4000-9">“Test-for-triage” models and pooled-test architectures streamline pathways and can lower misclassification costs in community and facility modalities</cite>.
  - Programmatic trade-offs: Decentralization (self-testing, peer-led index testing) tends to raise coverage and cost-efficiency per positive, whereas highly centralized lab-heavy models emphasize quality but may be less scalable per capita. <cite id="1d1bda5e-1">Decentralized peer-delivered self-testing models are most cost-effective among prevention interventions, consistent with lower per-person costs and better linkage</cite>.

Key distinction: Delivery choice shapes major cost categories (supplies, staff time, space/transport, verification), and the economic question—per person tested, per positive identified, or per QALY saved—determines how these cost drivers are evaluated against benefits. <cite id="f34c4000-0">Different modalities show wide unit cost per person tested with self-testing being lower</cite> <cite id="f34c4000-4">Cost per HIV-positive detected is lowest for home-based testing in several SSA datasets</cite>.

# 3) By cost category: what is counted and how

- Direct medical costs
  - Definition: Provider costs: commodities (test kits, reagents, counseling time), lab consumables, equipment/depreciation, staff salaries for testing rounds, and facility overhead attributable to testing. <cite id="3732682d-0">Full cost (including incremental implementation costs) can reach ~$32–39 per person tested in SSA settings</cite> <cite id="f34c4000-9">In a home-based distribution, the largest unit cost components were testing supplies (38%) and personnel (30%)</cite>.
- Direct non-medical costs
  - Definition: Patient-level out-of-pocket transport, communication, counseling slots not covered by services, and client-facing logistics that are not clinical in nature. <cite id="3732682d-3">Community-based HIV testing literature identifies community-level and household expenditures as distinct from clinical costs</cite> <cite id="3732682d-7">Direct non-medical costs include transport and nutritional supplements; indirect costs capture lost wages from clinic attendance</cite>.
- Opportunity cost of time (client and provider)
  - Definition: Time spent by testers/traders, clinicians, and clients for travel and waiting, valued at local wages/foregone earnings; essential for home-based or self-testing where travel is reduced for clients but provider time is still required for counseling/verification. <cite id="3732682d-0">Full cost includes time costs borne by implementers and recipients alongside cash expenditures to reflect the true cost of scaling new HTS interventions</cite> <cite id="a6db7999-0">Systematic review unit costs incorporate time and overhead to reflect implementation costs, not just kit expenses</cite>.
- Indirect and productivity-based costs (broader economic impact)
  - Definition: Time lost to work/education due to testing or follow‑up; production losses or household-level opportunity costs; sometimes modeled as QALYs when HIV care delays occur. These broaden “effectiveness” beyond lives saved to societal productivity. <cite id="3732682d-4">Integrating HIV and NCD service delivery is motivated by reducing long-term productivity losses that accrue during care delays</cite> <cite id="1d1bda5e-5">Analyses comparing monitoring strategies account for QALYs and infections averted, integrating downstream economic and health effects</cite>.
- Full vs incremental cost
  - Full cost: Includes start-up and delivery costs to introduce a new intervention at scale. <cite id="3732682d-0">Mean full cost across studies was $38.65 per person tested (median $32.83), higher than incremental costs because it accounts for program expansion overheads</cite>.
  - Incremental cost: Change in cost relative to a baseline test condition; commonly reported as cost per person tested or per positive detected. <cite id="a6db7999-0">Incremental cost per person tested was lower than full cost ($18.45 vs $38.65), highlighting fixed versus variable burdens</cite>.

Key distinction: Rigorous HTS costing in SSA differentiates medical versus non-medical and time-based opportunity costs, and distinguishes incremental unit costs from full program rollout costs to reflect both service delivery efficiency and scale-up feasibility. <cite id="f34c4000-9">A home-based program’s per-distributed cost was dominated by supplies and personnel, exemplifying direct medical time/expenditure components</cite> <cite id="3732682d-0">Full costs reflect capacity-building and system changes, not just unit test kit prices</cite>.

# 4) By epidemiological objective: detection and care-linkage versus suppression

- Detect-and-treat/monitoring strategies
  - Definition and costing: Emphasizes case detection, confirmation/intensification of algorithms, and linkage to care; benefits quantified as positives identified, infections averted, or QALYs. <cite id="1d1bda5e-3">HIV monitoring strategy comparisons explicitly trade off costs against positives detected, confirmatory testing needs, and retesting intervals</cite>.
  - SSA evidence: Decentralized home- and community-based options show favorable cost-effectiveness per positive and per QALY due to greater access and faster linkage. <cite id="a6db7999-6">Home-based testing in rural South Africa demonstrated cost-effectiveness by improving detection and follow-up</cite>.
- Population suppression/behavior change and prevention portfolio comparisons
  - Definition and costing: Positions testing within a broader HIV prevention portfolio (condoms, treatment as prevention), evaluating costs per infection averted in steady-state epidemiology; often uses utility/QALY frameworks. <cite id="1d1bda5e-0">Economic evaluations synthesize that testing innovations can be highly cost-effective when embedded in prevention strategies</cite>.
  - SSA evidence: Reviews emphasize that delivery model and implementation quality (peer-led, self-testing) materially affect cost per infection averted compared to facility-only models. <cite id="1d1bda5e-1">Self-testing via peer delivery had the most favorable cost-effectiveness among decentralized prevention and testing interventions</cite>.

Key distinction: In detection-led costing, the numerator is cases/positives/QALYs saved in the period; in suppression-led costing, the numerator expands to generations averted and life-years discounted to steady-state, making comparisons with other prevention programs valid. <cite id="1d1bda5e-5">Models in limited-resource settings incorporate QALYs and secondary infections averted to place testing in a broader prevention cost-utility context</cite>.

# 5) By programmatic budgeting category: where money goes in HTS plans

- Demand creation and linkage: Community engagement, outreach, health worker time to trace positives within households, and follow-up. <cite id="3732682d-2">Community- and facility-based testing cost structures differ by labor and outreach intensity, driving per-person cost differentials</cite>.
- Commodities and diagnostics: Test kits, reagents, confirmatory algorithms, consumables for pooling/verification, and supply chain logistics. <cite id="f34c4000-9">Testing supplies account for a large share of home-based HIVST unit costs</cite>.
- Human resources and training: Facility staff time, community health worker visit costs, trainer time, and performance-based supervision. <cite id="3732682d-8">Integration reviews document staff time and training as dominant recurrent costs in HIV services</cite>.
- Health system capacity: Building occupancy, utilities, lab equipment, transport and retesting cycles—salaries and overhead attributable to each testing step. <cite id="f34c4000-2">Facility mean per-person testing costs reflect local staffing and infrastructure overheads</cite>.
- Health information/management: TBIMS or DHIS2 integration for tracing positives, FP management, and monitoring. <cite id="3732682d-9">Optimizing testing service architectures often streamlines information flows to reduce preventable misclassifications per 10,000 tested</cite>.
- Prevention linkage services: PrEP/ART initiation and referrals—embedded costs when testing is paired with linkage protocols. <cite id="3732682d-4">Integration of HIV prevention and treatment reduces administrative and service fragmentation and can lower combined unit costs</cite>.

Key distinction: National costed implementation plans (derived from WHO/UNAIDS guidance) allocate budget across these categories and then derive unit cost and unit effectiveness assumptions that feed into cost-effectiveness thresholds. <cite id="3732682d-2">UNAIDS guidance emphasizes that NSP costing is foundational and integrates health system, commodity, workforce, and programmatic components before evaluating scale-up feasibility</cite>.

# 6) By unit of effectiveness: person tested, person linked, life-year saved

- Per person tested
  - Most basic HTS unit; useful to compare efficiency of introducing a new method across channels. <cite id="a6db7999-0">Incremental cost per person tested across SSA shows self-testing and first-test modalities differentiating by several dollars</cite>.
- Per person linked to care/confirmed positive
  - Emphasizes identification quality; higher value when follow-up services are costly. <cite id="f34c4000-4">Per-positive costs are typically higher but may be offset by broader prevention benefits</cite>.
- Per QALY or year of life saved
  - Places testing in the broader health system portfolio, comparing to maternal-child, malaria, NCD, and injury interventions common in SSA. <cite id="1d1bda5e-8">Cost-utility analysis uses QALYs to enable cross-program comparison</cite> <cite id="1d1bda5e-5">HIV testing strategy comparisons quantify QALYs and infections averted to inform portfolio allocation</cite>.

Key distinction: Policy decisions at country level often begin with per-person and per-positive thresholds, then integrate cost-utility into NSP prioritization matrices that juxtapose testing with other services using common currency (USD/QALY), aligned with WHO principles. <cite id="3732682d-2">National strategic plan costing is not merely technical; it underpins resource allocation decisions across the health portfolio</cite>.

# 7) Putting it together: classification frameworks used in SSA practice

- Methodological taxonomy (WHO-aligned)
  - CMA/CEA/CUA choices determine how much health benefit is in the numerator and how costs are accumulated. <cite id="1d1bda5e-8">The primary evaluation methods—CMA, CEA, and CUA—escalate in their use of effectiveness outcomes from equivalent endpoints to QALYs</cite>.
- Service delivery taxonomy (WHO/UNAIDS service delivery platforms)
  - Facility, community, and home-based with self-testing; pooled testing and serial rapid tests; algorithmic verification and “test-for-triage.” Each has distinct time/cost profiles and linkage pathways that change unit costs and effectiveness. <cite id="f34c4000-0">Self-testing’s low unit cost per person tested makes it valuable for mass coverage</cite> <cite id="f34c4000-9">Test-for-triage and pooled architectures can simultaneously streamline community/facility pathways and improve classification accuracy</cite>.
- Cost components taxonomy (global costing best practice; adapted to HTS)
  - Direct medical, direct non-medical, opportunity cost of time, and indirect productivity costs; reported as full vs incremental; and triangulated with program costed plans to evaluate scale-up. <cite id="3732682d-0">Full costs capture system and program changes; incremental costs show unit delivery efficiencies</cite> <cite id="3732682d-7">Direct non-medical costs include transport and supplements; indirect costs capture lost wages</cite>.
- Epidemiological objective taxonomy
  - Detection-and-linkage led vs prevention/suppression led; economic evaluation metrics shift from positives per dollar to infections and QALYs averted per dollar. <cite id="1d1bda5e-5">Comparisons across HIV monitoring strategies emphasize QALYs and infections averted</cite>.

Summary: In SSA, HTS costing methods are jointly classified by the evaluation goal (CMA/CEA/CUA), the delivery channel and testing package (facility, community/index, home-based self-testing, and pooled/triage), the cost components included (direct medical/non-medical and time-based opportunity and indirect costs), the program budget system used to mobilize funds, and the epidemiological objective (detection and linkage versus suppression). These distinctions determine whether the unit cost is measured per person tested or per QALY saved, and whether decentralized home-based strategies outperform facility-centric ones in cost per positive identified and/or cost per QALY. <cite id="a6db7999-0">A broad body of SSA studies shows per-person-testing costs vary widely but are usually well below $30 when measured at full scale</cite> <cite id="f34c4000-0">Self-testing’s notably low per-person cost makes it attractive for scale</cite> <cite id="1d1bda5e-1">Decentralized peer-led self-testing models tend to be most cost-effective</cite> <cite id="1d1bda5e-5">Cost-utility frameworks align testing with prevention by modeling QALYs and infections averted</cite> <cite id="3732682d-2">WHO/UNAIDS emphasize integrating costed plans into national strategy for equitable and efficient scale-up</cite>.

fully_underspecified.text: How are methods for testing services classified, and what are the key distinctions that define each classification?
fully_underspecified.answer:
Below is a practical taxonomy of methods for testing services, organized by (A) test objective/scope and (B) technique/execution mode, with the key distinctions that define each class.

Summary structure
- By objective/scope: unit/endpoint, interface/contract and interoperability, service and composite, system/end-to-end, acceptance/user.
- By technique/execution: black-box/API, gray-box/mixed, white-box/implementation; manual vs automated; continuous conformance.
- By dependency handling: stubs/mocks, service virtualization, hybrid (stub/virtual/real).
- By domain concern: security, performance/load, resilience/chaos, governance/compliance and contract-first/smart-contract.
- By data/provisioning: test data management and data/service masking.
- By architecture style: synchronous vs asynchronous (queues/streams, event-sourced sagas).

A. Classification by test objective and scope

1) Unit/endpoint testing (component/endpoint isolation)
- Definition and purpose: verify individual operations/HTTP endpoints or service components in isolation, including logic, code paths, and basic I/O expectations.
- Key distinctions:
  - Scope: classes, methods, or endpoint handlers rather than whole services; mocks/stubs may replace dependencies (internal/external). <cite id="82209415-4">Stubs and mocks typically operate in-process or tightly coupled to a component under test, providing controlled responses to isolate logic</cite>.
  - Technique: white-box; often automated, assertion-heavy, integration with CI for fast feedback.

2) Interface/contract testing and interoperability
- Definition and purpose: validate that service interfaces (operations, schemas, payloads) meet agreed contracts and are interoperable with known consumers/providers.
- Key distinctions:
  - Contract-first vs consumer-driven: define schemas/contracts up front (WSDL/JSON schemas) and test conformance; or derive provider behavior from consumer expectations and verify provider conformance—ensuring independent deployment. <cite id="a469bec4-0">Consumer-driven contract testing ensures that a provider is compatible with the expectations that the consumer has of it</cite> <cite id="a469bec4-6">CDC guarantees systems can be deployed independently and safely by verifying compatibility through contracts</cite>.
  - Testing level: often gray-box to black-box—examine payloads and statuses without implementation details.
  - Tools/standards: contract testing tools (Pact/Swagger contract testing); WSDL/SOAP conformance testing under governance frameworks. <cite id="832ea97c-8">OpenGroup SOA governance includes “Service Testing Guidelines” alongside taxonomy and versioning</cite>.
  - Coverage: schema validity, payload shape, status codes, content negotiation; may validate against profiles or standards.

3) Service and composite service testing
- Definition and purpose: test a service instance with its dependencies, data, and policies; for SOA/microservices, verify service behavior, policy enforcement (e.g., security, throttling), and composite process flows across service boundaries.
- Key distinctions:
  - Architecture-aware: includes transports, bindings, WSDL/SOA references; may require interaction with real services or virtualized ones.
  - SOA-specific concerns: service identification, fault models, governance. <cite id="832ea97c-4">SOA-specific fault taxonomies highlight errors across layers that differ from monoliths, guiding what to test</cite> <cite id="832ea97c-0">SOA reference architecture defines concepts and relationships that constrain testing (components, bindings)</cite>.
  - Composite flows: orchestration and choreography scenarios across multiple services.

4) System and end-to-end (E2E) testing
- Definition and purpose: validate the full stack and user-to-user workflow across services, databases, external systems, networks, and clients.
- Key distinctions:
  - Scope: end-to-end journeys, cross-service dependencies, and external integrations; often black-box and acceptance-focused.
  - Environment: typically requires real or highly realistic backends; service virtualization bridges gaps when dependencies are unavailable. <cite id="82209415-5">Service virtualization simulates dependent systems so testers can execute end-to-end tests even when backend systems are unavailable</cite>.
  - Synchronous vs asynchronous: includes message queues/streams; may exercise idempotency and event-order guarantees.

5) Acceptance and user testing
- Definition and purpose: validate service outcomes against business requirements and user stories—often manual or mixed automation—using realistic UI/API clients.
- Key distinctions:
  - Stakeholder-centric: scenarios and happy/sad paths; integration with API-driven UIs or service meshes/gateways for routing/versioning checks. <cite id="832ea97c-8">SOA governance includes versioning and deployment guidance relevant when validating user-visible behavior</cite>.

B. Classification by technique and execution mode

1) Black-box/API testing
- Definition: tests exercised via service interfaces without modifying or deep inspecting implementation; verify behavior against requirements and contracts.
- Key distinctions:
  - Interface-focused: requests/responses, status codes, timing; driven by OpenAPI/Swagger or WSDL.
  - Decoupled from code: useful in smoke/consumer-driven contract checks and acceptance tests. <cite id="a469bec4-6">API contract testing emphasizes compatibility via modeled interfaces</cite>.

2) Gray-box and mixed (schema + impl hints)
- Definition: combines interface knowledge with limited implementation cues (serialization, enums, example payloads) for richer assertions and better coverage.
- Key distinctions:
  - Uses machine-readable contracts to generate tests and reference data; leverages tooling to exercise realistic payloads yet remains outside the box. <cite id="82209415-3">Service virtualization and mocks/stubs sit on a spectrum; gray-box uses interface knowledge plus controlled internal artifacts to exercise “true intent”</cite> <cite id="a469bec4-3">CDC highlights decoupling working methods from finished service state, enabling independent verification</cite>.

3) White-box service testing
- Definition: deep logic testing including internal states, data flows, and path coverage, often used at unit/endpoint level and for policy/security rules embedded in service code.
- Key distinctions:
  - Branch/condition coverage, mutation/fuzzing tailored to handlers; integrates with CI to detect regressions early.
  - Risk: over-emphasis on code coverage without interface validation can miss interoperability regressions.

C. Handling external dependencies: stubs/mocks vs service virtualization vs end-to-end

1) Stubs and mocks
- Definition: in-process or tight-coupling replacements for dependencies that return predefined responses/timings; used to isolate units/endpoints.
- Key distinctions:
  - Tight coupling to code paths; effective for fast feedback but limited realism and sharing; integration testing may miss network and async behaviors. <cite id="82209415-6">Stubs/mocks are common decoupling techniques but have limits in thoroughness and flexibility compared to service virtualization</cite> <cite id="82209415-4">Virtual services are called remotely (HTTP/TCP), whereas stubs/mocks often work in-process</cite>.
  - Advantages: fast, deterministic, configurable per test; suitable for unit and acceptance layers when full stack isn’t needed.

2) Service virtualization
- Definition: standalone simulation of external systems and services over standard protocols, providing realistic payloads, errors, latency, and idempotency for integration and system tests.
- Key distinctions:
  - Decouples tests from environment availability and data; supports reusable “virtual services,” continuous integration, and broader team sharing.
  - Favors system/E2E testability when real dependencies are unavailable, flaky, or too slow; preserves message semantics and statefulness where possible. <cite id="82209415-5">Service virtualization enables automatic test execution even when dependent components cannot be present</cite> <cite id="82209415-1">Beyond stubbing and mocking, virtualization supports continuous testing and broader sharing</cite> <cite id="82209415-7">Virtual services are typically used for system testing; stubs and mocks for unit/acceptance testing</cite>.

3) Hybrid pipelines
- Definition: combine stubs/virtual services for speed and isolation, switch to real endpoints/integration brokers for periodic E2E runs; blend manual acceptance with automated regression.
- Key distinctions:
  - Pipeline stratagem: fast risk-focused automated tests in CI (virtualized) and comprehensive smoke/acceptance test cycles in CD/ staging using real services; pragmatic coverage.

D. Cross-cutting concerns and specialized service test methods

1) Security testing of services
- Definition: validates authentication/authorization, TLS, input validation, API key exposure, rate limiting, and unsafe transports across service boundaries.
- Key distinctions:
  - API granularity: token rotation, role elevation, enum exposure; network-level: mTLS; fuzzing to expose unsafe deserialization/rce; policy-driven controls exposed via service manifests/taxonomies. <cite id="832ea97c-8">Service governance in SOA includes service testing and versioning; testing must account for policy and binding differences across implementations</cite>.
  - Integration with SAST/DAST and secret scanning for credentials leaked in contracts/virtual services.

2) Performance and load testing in distributed services
- Definition: measures latency, throughput, error rates, and failures under concurrency; stresses networks, brokers, databases, and gateway tiers.
- Key distinctions:
  - Distributed tracing and queue/backpressure modeling; chaos elements to observe tail latency, contention, and fallback behavior.

3) Resilience, chaos, and fault injection testing
- Definition: validates graceful degradation, retries, circuit breakers, timeouts, and compensation patterns under partial failures and overload.
- Key distinctions:
  - SOA-specific fault models motivate fault injection (dependency slowdowns/cuts) and idempotency/key validation; microservices often require saga testing and event reordering. <cite id="832ea97c-4">SOA fault taxonomies enumerate service-layer faults; these guide resilience testing scenarios</cite>.

4) Interoperability and conformance (standards-compliant services)
- Definition: testing against formal standards (WSDL/SOAP, REST/JSON profiles, OpenAPI, Swagger) and policy compliance.
- Key distinctions:
  - Schema/conformance suites and machine-checkable contracts; validates across heterogeneous consumers/providers (including partners). <cite id="a469bec4-6">Contract testing ensures compatibility of microservices and web apps, enabling independent deployment</cite> <cite id="832ea97c-0">SOA reference architecture defines component interactions and bindings relevant to interoperability testing</cite>.
  - Profiles/Governance: adherence to enterprise service policies (security, logging, tracing). <cite id="832ea97c-8">OpenGroup SOA testing and versioning guidelines contextualize conformance requirements</cite>.

5) Continuous conformance and contract-driven CI/CD
- Definition: automating contract validation, schema checks, and interoperability runs as code changes, including provider-first or consumer-driven checks; enforcing gate failures before deploy.
- Key distinctions:
  - Bi-directional pipelines: provider publishes Pact to consumer verification jobs; automatic rollbacks or remediation on violations; frequent, low-cost tests compared to E2E. <cite id="a469bec4-0">CDC emphasizes compatibility guarantees so teams can deploy independently and safely</cite> <cite id="a469bec4-4">Consumer-driven tests are beneficial when consumers change frequently, enabling early detection</cite> <cite id="82209415-1">Service virtualization supports continuous testing beyond stubbing/mocking</cite>.

E. Data and environment considerations

1) Data masking and test data provisioning
- Definition: realistic yet non-production data construction and masking tailored to service schemas for contract and integration tests.
- Key distinctions:
  - Privacy-preserving and reversible masking; data lineage and consent; often co-located with service virtualization to produce domain-valid payloads. <cite id="82209415-5">Virtualization complements test automation by supplying realistic payloads when dependent systems/data are unavailable</cite>.

2) Consumer-driven acceptance vs provider-driven regression
- Definition: running consumer perspectives to drive expected behavior while provider tests probe breaking changes; both reduce integration risk.
- Key distinctions:
  - Prioritization: CDC early in iteration cycles; provider tests catch upstream regressions affecting many consumers. <cite id="a469bec4-4">CDC is especially valuable when consumers evolve faster than providers</cite>.

F. Synchronous vs Asynchronous service testing

1) Synchronous services (HTTP/GraphQL/REST, RPC)
- Focus: request/response latency, idempotency, validation, and exception surfaces; integration tests commonly invoke endpoints and verify responses.

2) Asynchronous services (message queues, event-driven)
- Focus: order, duplicates, at-least-once semantics, idempotency, dead-letter routing, backoff, and event consistency.
- Key distinctions:
  - Event replay and chaos on brokers; stream/window testing; causal/consumer-group correctness. <cite id="832ea97c-0">SOA reference architecture clarifies message- and event-based interactions across services that differ from simple synchronous calls</cite>.

G. Lifecycle integration and governance

1) Service taxonomy-aligned testing
- Definition: aligning test scope with formal service classification and governance (identifiers, version, bindings, ownership).
- Key distinctions:
  - Policy scoping: boundary services vs utility services get different test emphases; versioning and deployment gates shape regression and smoke tests. <cite id="832ea97c-3">SOA taxonomies define service types that imply different testing concerns</cite> <cite id="832ea97c-8">Governance frameworks include service testing within a broader set of service lifecycle guidelines</cite>.

2) Microservices-specific patterns
- Decomposition-driven unit tests; contract-first APIs; circuit breaker testing; distributed tracing within acceptance/E2E; gradual migration testing against legacy and new services. <cite id="832ea97c-1">Systematic literature on service identification informs decomposition choices that influence testability</cite>.

Key distinctions that define each class (decision guide)

- Isolation vs end-to-end: Unit/endpoint and contract tests run isolated or with controlled mocks/virtual services; system/E2E span production-like or virtualized integrations. <cite id="82209415-5">Virtualization enables E2E execution when dependencies are unavailable</cite> <cite id="82209415-7">Virtual services map to system testing; stubs/mocks to unit/acceptance layers</cite>.
- Black-box vs gray/white-box: API/black-box validates interfaces and behavior without code exposure; gray-box uses schemas/payload models; white-box asserts internal states and logic. <cite id="a469bec4-6">Machine-readable contracts support black-box API validation across deployments</cite> <cite id="82209415-3">Virtualization supports deeper, realistic “true intent” by leveraging interface artifacts</cite>.
- Stub/mock vs virtual service: Stub/mocks are tight to code for speed; virtual services are standalone and network-like, improving realism and sharing and supporting slower, fuller scenarios. <cite id="82209415-4">Virtual services are called remotely; stubs/mocks often in-process</cite> <cite id="82209415-1">Virtualization overcomes stub/mock limits by enabling continuous and shareable testing</cite>.
- Contract-first vs consumer-driven: Contract-first validates conformance to schemas/agreements; CDC operationalizes compatibility by verifying provider behavior from consumer expectations and enables independent deployments. <cite id="a469bec4-0">CDC centers on provider compatibility with consumer expectations</cite> <cite id="a469bec4-6">It guarantees microservices/web apps can be deployed independently and safely</cite>.
- Interoperability vs performance vs security: Interoperability is schema/contract compliance across heterogeneous consumers; performance targets latency/throughput and scaling; security surfaces auth/authorization/validation issues; resilience focuses on graceful degradation under faults. <cite id="832ea97c-0">SOA architecture and bindings inform interoperability needs</cite> <cite id="832ea97c-4">SOA fault taxonomies inform resilience testing scenarios</cite>.
- Lifecycle and governance: Tie tests to service taxonomy and governance (definition, version, policy), with continuous contract/conformance gates and staged promotion from unit to E2E. <cite id="832ea97c-8">OpenGroup SOA governance enumerates service testing, versioning, and deployment guidance for lifecycle integration</cite>.

Practical classification matrix

- By objective/scope:
  - Unit/endpoint (white-box), Interface (schema/black-box), Interoperability/Conformance (standards/contract), Service/Composite (policy/gateway bindings), System/E2E (async networks), Acceptance/UX (user flows).
- By technique:
  - Manual Acceptance, API/Contract Black-box, Gray-box Contracted, White-box Unit, Stub/Mock Isolation, Service Virtualization System, Chaos/Load/Fault Injection.
- By dependency:
  - Direct Integration (real), Hybrid (virtualized stubs), Fully Virtualized.
- By concern:
  - Security, Performance/Load, Resilience/Circuit Breakers, Compliance/Policy.

Trade-offs and when to use which
- Use unit/contract tests early to catch breaking changes; combine CDC with service virtualization for fast, continuous gates; bring real services into CI where feasible; reserve end-to-end and chaos runs for staging/pre-production. <cite id="a469bec4-4">CDC is beneficial when consumers change frequently, catching provider regressions early</cite> <cite id="82209415-1">Virtualization supports continuous testing beyond stubbing/mocking</cite>.
- Recognize SOA-specific risks (fault taxonomies, binding/transport nuances) and microservice concerns (event semantics, independent deployment) when choosing test scope and tooling. <cite id="832ea97c-4">SOA-specific fault taxonomies highlight unique failure modes to test</cite> <cite id="832ea97c-0">Reference architecture clarifies service component interactions and bindings</cite>.

Summary
- Service testing methods cluster along two orthogonal axes: what you test (unit/endpoint to system/E2E; conformance to resilience/security) and how you test it (white-box to black-box; mocks/stubs to virtualization; continuous contract checks to full E2E/chaos). <cite id="82209415-5">Service virtualization underpins system/E2E testability when dependencies cannot be present</cite> <cite id="a469bec4-0">Consumer-driven contracts operationalize compatibility between providers and consumers</cite>. In practice, an effective program layers contract-first and CDC checks in CI, unit and API tests for fast feedback, and staged E2E and chaos tests in staging/pre-prod, guided by service taxonomies and governance. <cite id="832ea97c-8">Governance frameworks make explicit service testing and versioning roles within the lifecycle</cite>.

without_scope.text: How are costing methods classified, and what are the key distinctions that define each classification?
without_scope.answer:
Below is a concise, evidence-backed taxonomy of costing methods and the key distinctions that define each class. I group methods into three primary classifications and highlight two widely used special cases (manufacturing inventory valuation and service/activity costing).

Summary of the main classifications
1) Cost assignment methods to cost objects (products, services, departments)
- Direct costing (direct/prime costing): assigns only directly traceable variable costs to the cost object; fixed manufacturing overhead is treated as period expense. This yields lower reported inventory valuation and lower net income when inventories accumulate, and it focuses pricing and short-run profitability on variable cost behavior. <cite id="7a1d99e7-4">Direct costing assigns only variable manufacturing costs to inventory, treating fixed overhead as period expense</cite> <cite id="eeef0c48-0">Variable costing accounts for only expenses directly tied to production, excluding fixed manufacturing overhead from inventory</cite>.
- Absorption costing: charges all manufacturing costs—direct materials, direct labor, and all manufacturing overhead (fixed and variable)—to inventory; fixed overhead is allocated per unit. Widely used for financial reporting and GAAP/IFRS internal-consistency; impacts inventory valuation and cost of goods sold, so profits can differ from variable costing depending on inventory levels. <cite id="7a1d99e7-5">Absorption costing values inventory at direct costs plus fixed and variable overhead</cite> <cite id="eeef0c48-1">Absorption costing includes all manufacturing costs, both variable and fixed, whereas variable costing does not, producing different income from identical operations</cite>.
- Activity-based costing (ABC): assigns overhead based on activities and cost drivers (e.g., setups, inspections) rather than volume alone. It addresses volume-based distortion of overhead, providing more accurate unit cost where overhead is significant relative to direct costs. <cite id="7a1d99e7-0">Activity-based costing assigns overhead and indirect costs based on activities and cost drivers rather than production volume</cite> <cite id="7a1d99e7-9">ABC takes overhead allocation seriously by assigning indirect costs based on activities rather than spreading evenly across all products</cite>.
- Departmental/service costing: applies cost pools and drivers to service departments in support of products; distinctions include whether costs are allocated (full costing) or not (service department charges), and whether absorption-style or ABC drivers are used. <cite id="7a1d99e7-6">Costing methods determine production expenses by assigning direct and indirect costs; selection depends on accurate cost per unit in production</cite> <cite id="7a1d99e7-8">Classifying costs is essential to management accountants to translate financial costs into business strategy</cite>.

Key distinctions among assignment methods
- Scope of cost inclusion: direct vs absorption. Direct limits product cost to traceable variables; absorption expands it to include all manufacturing overhead. <cite id="eeef0c48-7">The core difference is treatment of fixed manufacturing overhead; absorption includes it in product cost, variable does not</cite>.
- Overhead assignment basis: volume-driven vs activity patterns. Traditional direct/absorption often use volume drivers; ABC aligns cost drivers to activities causing overhead, reducing distortions when overhead is nonlinear or activity-batch driven. <cite id="7a1d99e7-0">ABC identifies cost drivers and assigns overhead by activities</cite> <cite id="7a1d99e7-9">ABC assigns indirect costs by activity, contrasting with volume-based allocation</cite>.
- Profitability/income effects: absorption smooths fixed overhead across units and can report higher inventory value and income when production > sales; variable/direct show current-period fixed costs in income immediately, aligning with contribution-margin focus. <cite id="eeef0c48-1">Controllers observe different income figures from identical operations under absorption versus variable costing</cite>.

2) Inventory costing/valuation methods for financial statements
Purpose: measure cost of goods sold (COGS) and ending inventory; comply with IFRS or GAAP. Methods are governed by IAS 2 (IFRS) and ASC 330 (US GAAP). <cite id="9884df0a-8">IAS 2 guides recognition of inventory cost and write-down to net realizable value</cite> <cite id="9884df0a-9">FASB guidance applies to inventories measured using FIFO or average cost</cite>.

- FIFO (First-In, First-Out): assumes oldest units are sold first; COGS reflects earlier, often lower, costs. GAAP- and IFRS-eligible; IFRS explicitly allows FIFO. <cite id="9884df0a-1">Under FIFO, items purchased or produced first are sold first</cite> <cite id="9884df0a-3">IFRS allows FIFO among inventory costing methods</cite>.
- Average cost (specific identification not required here): weights unit cost by quantity; often used as “average cost” or weighted average; recognized under IFRS and GAAP. <cite id="9884df0a-0">IAS 2 permits cost flow assumptions including average cost</cite> <cite id="9884df0a-1">US GAAP requires companies using FIFO or weighted average to follow ASC 330 valuation rules</cite>.
- Weighted average (periodic/continuous): combines beginning inventory and purchases to compute average unit cost; used widely in process industries under GAAP. <cite id="9884df0a-1">US GAAP requires companies using weighted average methods</cite> <cite id="9884df0a-6">ASC 330 explains how inventory is valued and the cost-flow methods GAAP allows, including weighted average</cite>.
- LIFO (Last-In, First-Out): assumes latest goods sold first; can produce lower reported inventory in inflationary periods; permitted under GAAP with ASU 2015-11 “LIFO restatement,” but not under IFRS. <cite id="9884df0a-9">Amendments apply to inventory measured using FIFO or average cost; LIFO is treated under the restatement</cite> <cite id="9884df0a-3">Under IFRS, LIFO is not permitted; allowed methods include FIFO and average cost</cite> <cite id="9884df0a-7">IFRS prohibits LIFO; IAS 2 governs inventories and subsequent recognition</cite>.
- Specific identification: cost matches actual goods sold; practical mainly for unique items; not a GAAP-only method. <cite id="9884df0a-5">A comprehensive framing treats standard cost, layered costing (including FIFO and LIFO), and weighted average as primary inventory costing approaches</cite>.

Key distinctions among inventory methods
- Underlying cost flow assumption: physical flow can differ from actual flow; for tax/planning, LIFO often yields lower taxable income in rising costs, whereas FIFO often yields higher ending inventory and lower COGS. <cite id="9884df0a-0">Cost may be determined using various cost flow assumptions such as FIFO, average cost, or LIFO</cite> <cite id="9884df0a-6">ASC 330 governs inventory valuation and cost-flow methods</cite>.
- Regulatory differences (IFRS vs GAAP): GAAP permits LIFO with specified treatments; IFRS does not allow LIFO; both accept FIFO and average cost. <cite id="9884df0a-3">Allowed methods: FIFO and average cost under IFRS; LIFO is not permitted</cite> <cite id="9884df0a-1">GAAP requires companies using FIFO or weighted average to follow ASC 330</cite>.
- Matching and inflation effects: LIFO often matches current costs to current revenues; FIFO often reports higher inventory and profit in inflation, lower in deflation. <cite id="9884df0a-1">FIFO assumes earliest items are sold first; weighted average is allowed in GAAP</cite> <cite id="9884df0a-9">FIFO and average cost are the primary inventory measures under updated US GAAP treatment</cite>.

3) Cost estimation/prediction methods for managerial decision-making
Purpose: model cost behavior (total cost = fixed + variable × activity) to forecast costs and profitability, inform pricing, budgeting, and process improvement. Estimation methods vary in data needs, robustness, and assumptions.

- Engineering and account analysis: experts classify costs into fixed and variable components based on technical data and historical accounts; lowest data needs but can be subjective. <cite id="d1c4ce2b-3">Engineering and account analysis are core approaches to cost estimation, alongside inspection of accounts</cite>.
- High-low: uses cost at highest and lowest activity to compute variable and fixed cost; simple but sensitive to outliers. <cite id="d1c4ce2b-2">High-low and least-squares regression are the two main methods used to estimate fixed and variable costs</cite>.
- Least-squares (linear regression): fits a line to all data; estimates intercept/slope with statistical error measures (e.g., R², standard error) for predictive fit; widely preferred when data are plentiful. <cite id="d1c4ce2b-2">Regression analysis is a powerful statistical method to estimate fixed and variable costs</cite> <cite id="d1c4ce2b-5">Each estimation method aims to estimate fixed and variable costs in the form Y = f + vX</cite>.
- Learning curve analysis: predicts unit cost declines as cumulative output increases by a constant percentage (cumulative average or unit learning). <cite id="d1c4ce2b-3">Cost estimation and learning curve analysis examine how costs change with experience and output</cite>.
- Cost-volume-profit (CVP): uses cost-behavior relationships to analyze breakeven, target profits, and profit sensitivity; assumes linear cost/volume/price relationships over a relevant range. <cite id="d1c4ce2b-9">Cost Volume Profit analysis is a powerful tool for managerial decision-making</cite>.

Key distinctions among estimation methods
- Data intensity and accuracy: engineering uses extensive technical data and may be domain-accurate but costly; high-low is quick but brittle; regression generally provides statistically grounded coefficients and fit (e.g., R²) when data are reliable. <cite id="d1c4ce2b-2">High-low and regression are the two main cost estimation methods for fixed and variable costs</cite> <cite id="d1c4ce2b-5">Estimation methods converge on the Y = f + vX cost model</cite>.
- Functional use: CVP relies on estimated cost and price functions for breakeven and profit planning; learning curves forecast unit cost improvements with experience to guide pricing and capacity. <cite id="d1c4ce2b-9">CVP analysis supports pricing, target-profit, and sensitivity decisions</cite> <cite id="d1c4ce2b-3">Learning curves complement cost estimation to analyze cost changes with output</cite>.
- Evaluation: report coefficients and goodness-of-fit (e.g., R², standard errors) and residual inspection; test linearity/relevant range; cross-check with engineering logic. <cite id="d1c4ce2b-2">Regression analysis provides robust estimation with statistical tools including goodness-of-fit</cite> <cite id="d1c4ce2b-6">Regression examines relationships between two or more variables to estimate cost behavior</cite>.

4) Use-case-specific applications and special cases
- Manufacturing product costing: choose between direct/prime, absorption, and ABC depending on data availability, product diversity, and cost distortion concerns. In volatile cost environments, inventory method choice (FIFO vs weighted average vs LIFO under GAAP) affects reported COGS and inventory, especially when prices are rising. <cite id="eeef0c48-7">The absorption vs variable costing split is driven by inclusion or exclusion of fixed overhead in product costs</cite> <cite id="9884df0a-0">Cost flow assumptions (FIFO, average, LIFO) guide inventory valuation under IAS 2</cite>.
- Services and support departments: use departmental costing to allocate service costs to production; distinguish actual vs budgeted allocation for fairness, or use ABC with usage drivers (minutes, transactions) to match service activities to beneficiaries. <cite id="7a1d99e7-6">Costing methods determine production expenses; selection aims at accurate cost per unit for pricing</cite> <cite id="7a1d99e7-3">ABC emphasizes assigning indirect costs via activities relevant to services and products</cite>.
- Joint products and by-products: allocate joint costs to split-off points based on physical quantity, relative sales value, or other systematic criteria; switch to NRV at split-off for downstream processing decisions; do not allocate separable costs to joint products. <cite id="9884df0a-8">IAS 2 provides guidance on determining the cost of inventories and their subsequent recognition as expense</cite>. 
- Special inventory scenarios: standard cost systems set predetermined cost per unit, adjust to actual monthly; layered/LIFO-type systems track cost layers; these differ in matching speed and accuracy and must comply with GAAP disclosure and relaxation rules. <cite id="9884df0a-5">Primary approaches include standard cost, layered costing (including FIFO and LIFO), and weighted average methods</cite>.

Practical decision framework
- If you need a quick unit cost for pricing/short-run decisions and overhead is not a major discriminator: direct or prime costing; cross-check with absorption for GAAP-consistent reporting. <cite id="eeef0c48-0">Variable costing excludes fixed manufacturing overhead from inventory, focusing on relevant costs for short-run decisions</cite>.
- If overhead materially affects cost and products consume resources in ways not proportional to volume: adopt ABC to align overhead drivers with activities and improve decision quality. <cite id="7a1d99e7-0">ABC assigns overhead via activities and cost drivers rather than volume alone</cite>.
- For financial statements and external reporting: pick inventory costing consistent with your standard (IFRS vs GAAP), noting that GAAP tolerates LIFO while IFRS requires FIFO or average cost. Validate that the method reflects physical flows and does not overstate inventory risk. <cite id="9884df0a-3">IFRS allows FIFO and average cost but not LIFO</cite> <cite id="9884df0a-1">GAAP requires compliance with ASC 330 for FIFO or weighted average usage</cite>.
- For planning and control: build cost functions via engineering or regression, evaluate R² and residuals, and embed in CVP models for breakeven, target pricing, and profitability analysis; consider learning-curve effects for new product ramps or process improvements. <cite id="d1c4ce2b-5">Estimation methods estimate fixed and variable costs to form Y = f + vX</cite> <cite id="d1c4ce2b-2">High-low and regression are the two primary estimation methods</cite> <cite id="d1c4ce2b-9">CVP analysis informs managerial decisions on costs, volume, and profits</cite> <cite id="d1c4ce2b-3">Learning curves offer a complementary mechanism to capture experience-driven cost changes</cite>.

When methods differ most
- Absorption vs variable costing: different operating income when ending inventory absorbs fixed overhead under absorption; variable income shows current period fixed costs as expense, often aligning with contribution analysis. <cite id="eeef0c48-1">Absorption and variable costing produce different income figures from identical operations</cite>.
- Inventory methods under IFRS vs GAAP: permitted sets differ (IFRS disallows LIFO), and tax effects differ, especially in inflationary periods; GAAP’s “LIFO restatement” aligns historical treatment while permitting use. <cite id="9884df0a-3">IFRS does not permit LIFO; FIFO and average cost are allowed</cite> <cite id="9884df0a-9">US GAAP amendments apply to inventories measured using FIFO or average cost; LIFO is treated via restatement</cite>.

Bottom line: Classify costing methods by (1) what is assigned to the cost object (direct/prime, absorption, ABC, departmental), (2) how inventory is measured for reporting (FIFO, weighted average/average cost, LIFO where allowed, specific identification), and (3) how costs are estimated for decision-making (engineering, account analysis, high-low, regression, learning-curve, and CVP integrations). The defining distinctions are the scope and drivers of cost inclusion, the cost flow assumptions used for inventory, and the statistical/data properties and intended use of cost estimates for pricing, profitability, and control. <cite id="7a1d99e7-0">ABC differentiates by activity-based overhead assignment</cite> <cite id="eeef0c48-7">Absorption vs variable costing differ in fixed overhead treatment</cite> <cite id="9884df0a-0">Cost flow assumptions like FIFO and average cost underpin inventory valuation</cite> <cite id="d1c4ce2b-5">Estimation converges on Y = f + vX for managerial modeling</cite> <cite id="d1c4ce2b-9">CVP uses cost behavior to drive managerial decisions</cite>.

without_term.text: How are costing methods for disease testing services in a region of Africa classified, and what are the key distinctions that define each classification?
without_term.answer:
Below is a practical classification of costing methods used for disease testing services in African health systems, with the key distinctions that determine when to use each class, how costs are collected and attributed, and how delivery mode and perspective affect results.

Summary overview
- In African disease-testing programs (e.g., HIV/STD, TB, malaria), costs are typically organized into two orthogonal dimensions—how the estimate is built (top‑down vs bottom‑up) and how granular it is (micro‑ vs gross‑)—and then interpreted through a chosen perspective (provider/health system, patient/client, or societal) that determines which economic inputs and time/resource usages are included. <cite id="bc383d71-5">There are two complementary ways of defining costing methods: top‑down versus bottom‑up and micro‑costing versus gross‑costing</cite>. <cite id="bc383d71-5">Across studies, top‑down micro‑costing is the most common (49%), followed by top‑down gross‑costing (37%) and bottom‑up micro‑costing (14%)</cite>. <cite id="bc383d71-8">Methodological reviews also highlight how differences in cost classification, item inclusion, and costing approaches (such as cost‑to‑charge ratios) can materially bias estimates</cite>.

1) Vertical build: top‑down vs bottom‑up
- Top‑down approaches derive test costs from higher‑level program or budget data, then allocate overheads and direct resources to the test using usage rates, rates of return, or micro‑allocation factors. They are less resource‑intensive but can be less precise if allocation bases misrepresent real flows. <cite id="bc383d71-5">Top‑down micro‑costing: derives unit costs by tracing individual resource flows but starting from aggregated budgets (e.g., department totals), often used in health systems to reconcile bottom‑up detail with finance data</cite>. <cite id="bc383d71-5">Top‑down gross‑costing: uses aggregated budget/expenditure data and applies broad overhead allocations, faster but coarser in detail</cite>. <cite id="bc383d71-11">Gross‑costing is quicker and cheaper but gives limited detail, whereas micro‑costing enumerates individual cost elements</cite>. <cite id="bc383d71-9">WHO‑CHOICE, a widely used program costing framework, is a top‑down method that allocates overheads such as program and training costs alongside patient‑level service delivery</cite>.
- Bottom‑up approaches reconstruct the test’s cost by assembling each resource element used to deliver one test (staff time, reagents, consumables, calibration, room time), aggregating to unit and volume costs. They are more data‑intensive but usually reflect true production constraints and drivers. <cite id="bc383d71-5">Bottom‑up micro‑costing traces each cost element (e.g., individual staff time, materials, supplies, out‑of‑pocket expenses) to the test and is typically used when detailed resource accounting is feasible</cite>. <cite id="bc383d71-6">Micro‑costing can also be framed from a healthcare professional’s perspective, directly capturing the cost of consumables like rapid tests and labor time</cite>.

Key distinctions that define this classification:
- Granularity of resource tracing: top‑down uses aggregation and allocation; bottom‑up enumerates items and quantities consumed per test. <cite id="bc383d71-11">Micro‑costing details quantities and prices for staff time, supplies, and expenses; gross‑costing summarizes aggregated amounts with fewer items</cite>.
- Data requirements and auditability: bottom‑up micro‑costing needs detailed time records and item prices; top‑down methods must justify allocation bases and avoid bias. <cite id="bc383d71-8">Choice of allocation bases and exclusion of relevant cost items can distort outcomes compared with cost‑to‑charge or full cost recovery</cite>.
- Sensitivity and precision: micro‑ vs gross‑ choices affect results’ sensitivity to bias and precision; pairing perspective with method matters for decision use. <cite id="bc383d71-11">Micro‑ vs gross‑costing requires balancing analysis needs (sensitivity, bias, precision)</cite>.
- Prevalence in African programs: top‑down methods dominate, but bottom‑up micro‑costing is increasingly used where feasible, especially for diagnostics. <cite id="bc383d71-5">Top‑down micro‑costing predominated (49%), followed by top‑down gross‑ (37%) and bottom‑up micro‑ (14%)</cite>.

2) Granularity and aggregation: micro‑ vs gross‑costing
- Micro‑costing: enumerates all resources used to produce one test outcome (including client time and transport, where aligned to perspective). Useful for price elasticities, incremental cost per additional test detected, and acceptability/feasibility analyses (e.g., rapid tests, point‑of‑care). <cite id="bc383d71-6">Micro‑costing of rapid tests quantifies consumables and provider time directly</cite>. <cite id="bc383d71-2">Technology choice (PCR, rapid POCT, serological) changes dominant and cost‑effective implementation for detection, with micro‑costing clarifying where unit resource use shifts cost and impact</cite>.
- Gross‑costing: derives aggregate budget shares, unit costs from accounts, and broad overhead allocations per test share or utilization; efficient for high‑level program costing and comparisons across facilities or time. <cite id="bc383d71-11">Gross‑costing provides a limited level of detail compared with micro‑costing</cite>. <cite id="bc383d71-8">Use of cost‑to‑charge or indirect allocation factors can change apparent unit costs</cite>.

Key distinctions that define this classification:
- Level of detail for inputs: micro‑costing lists specific items and quantities; gross‑costing provides aggregated figures. <cite id="bc383d71-5">Micro‑costing lists individual resource flows, whereas gross‑costing aggregates before assignment</cite>.
- Applicability to policy and procurement: micro‑costing supports bid evaluation and unit‑price negotiations; gross‑costing supports budget planning and needs assessment. <cite id="bc383d71-9">WHO guidance emphasizes that program costs (including overheads) are included to reflect health system resource use</cite>.
- Trade‑offs: speed vs precision; limited detail vs bias risk. <cite id="bc383d71-11">Micro‑ vs gross‑costing should balance analysis requirements (sensitivity to bias/precision) and data availability</cite>.

3) Perspective: who bears/claims costs (provider/system, patient/client, societal)
- Health system/provider perspective: includes salaries, reagents, lab consumables, building and equipment depreciation, calibration/QA, supplies and logistics, training and monitoring, and overheads; excludes patient travel/leave and forgone earnings. Used for budget planning and service‑mix decisions. <cite id="bc383d71-5">Bottom‑up micro‑costing assigns these items per test when data allow</cite>. <cite id="bc383d71-8">Health sector perspective includes program and training overheads alongside patient‑level delivery in frameworks like WHO‑CHOICE</cite>. <cite id="bc383d71-7">Hospitals and labs commonly use micro and mixed methods to classify direct/indirect costs and link to unit activity rates</cite>.
- Patient/client perspective: adds patient transport, time, and direct‑to‑patient costs (e.g., insurance premiums, user fees), and may weight quality‑adjusted time; less common in routine testing costings but key where out‑of‑pocket fees dominate. <cite id="bc383d71-5">Perspective choice changes which costs and beneficiaries are included; cost inputs are defined to match perspective</cite>.
- Societal perspective: broadest; includes provider and patient costs plus productivity losses and third‑party effects; most burdensome to measure but best for cost‑effectiveness. <cite id="bc383d71-9">Program costs and overheads are included for system costs; patient‑level time and service delivery also factor when perspective widens</cite>.

Key distinctions that define this classification:
- Scope of resource valuation: health system costs only vs added client/patient costs vs societal opportunity and productivity costs. <cite id="bc383d71-8">Perspective differences determine the cost items enumerated and how resources are valued</cite>.
- Decision relevance: provider/payer decisions vs acceptability and access pricing vs policy prioritization. <cite id="bc383d71-5">Perspective selection is tied to the analysis’ sensitivity to incremental costs and beneficiaries</cite>.
- Practicality in SSA testing programs: provider and patient perspectives are most common; societal perspectives are used selectively where disability‑adjusted life years and productivity loss are material (e.g., confirming disease for workforces). <cite id="bc383d71-8">Including/excluding items by perspective yields different cost sets and transferability</cite>.

4) Service delivery mode for diagnostics: centralized labs vs point‑of‑care and its costing implications
- Centralized laboratory testing: costs are dominated by platform platform reagents/assays, equipment depreciation and maintenance, QA/calibration, staffing and turnaround time, specimen handling/logistics, and turnaround. Micro‑costing here traces reagent cost per test, rack/plate consumables, instrument time, and QC costs. <cite id="6e0eac27-0">Comparative cost analyses in South Africa estimate costs of centralized lab testing for HIV treatment initiation, highlighting lab costs and logistics</cite>. <cite id="bc383d71-3">Disease‑related technology costs differ by test type (PCR, rapid POCT, serological), influencing unit cost structures</cite>.
- Decentralized/point‑of‑care (POC) testing: adds micro‑lab or kit logistics, consumables, preanalytics, clinician/b受益人 time and training, and potential lower transport costs. Top‑down methods allocate facility/cluster budgets to POC by observed test volumes and overhead shares; bottom‑up micro‑costs list kit/shelf life, electricity/thermal storage, test vial consumables, and provider/受益人 time. <cite id="6e0eac27-0">In South Africa, decentralized POC testing for HIV treatment initiation had different unit costs compared with centralized lab testing</cite>. <cite id="bc383d71-4">Microcosting has been applied to community HIV testing and counseling in sub‑Saharan Africa, with per‑test costs varying by method and prevalence</cite>. <cite id="6e0eac27-10">Community‑based strategies show cost per test ranges influenced by delivery method and prevalence, reinforcing the importance of service‑delivery perspective</cite>.
- Mini‑lab or satellite lab models bridge these: facility consumables and staffing cover routine tests while sending complex cases to central labs. Costing must capture intra‑facility utilization and referral/logistics costs. <cite id="6e0eac27-4">Activity‑based costing in LMIC HIV services highlights per‑activity unit costs (e.g., counseling, phlebotomy, on‑site tests, referrals), enabling comparison across centralized and decentralized care</cite>.

Key distinctions that define this classification:
- Fixed vs variable drivers: centralized platforms have high equipment and QA fixed costs spread over volume; POC shifts depreciation and QC to fewer instruments but increases consumables and time. <cite id="bc383d71-5">Bottom‑up micro‑costing explicitly allocates time and supplies; top‑down methods allocate overhead to utilization</cite>.
- Logistics and transport: distance, cold chain, specimen handling dominate in lower‑density settings and reduce POC unit costs versus centralized transport. <cite id="6e0eac27-0">Comparative analyses attribute different logistics and lab overhead per test for POC versus lab</cite>.
- Detection and throughput: PCR vs rapid antigen/POCT vs serology differ in sensitivity/specificity and the number of effective tests per unit time and resource, altering cost‑effectiveness and unit cost per confirmed case. <cite id="bc383d71-2">PCR, rapid POCT, and serological tests have different cost implications and effectiveness, changing dominant strategies</cite>. <cite id="bc383d71-6">Microcosting examples show how platform choices affect per‑test cost drivers</cite>.

5) Operational and data considerations that define method choice in Africa
- Data availability and quality: bottom‑up micro‑costing needs time logs, reagent certificates, price quotes, and staff time data; top‑down methods require reliable budget reports and valid allocation bases. <cite id="bc383d71-0">Methods of costing are typically classified by bottom‑up construction and the cost structure (direct, indirect, fixed, variable) you intend to communicate</cite>. <cite id="bc383d71-11">Guidelines emphasize combining activity‑based costing, ingredients, and budget data to build micro‑cost estimates under payer perspectives in LMICs</cite>. <cite id="bc383d71-3">Disease‑specific cost studies synthesize available data and adapt mixed methods when primary data are limited</cite>.
- Payer and delivery system alignment: public sector programs often prefer top‑down micro‑costing and WHO‑aligned health‑sector perspectives to reflect program budgets; donors and purchasing bodies may demand micro‑costing for tenders; community and private sector programs need client and societal perspectives for acceptability and pricing. <cite id="bc383d71-8">Health system over‑head inclusion and unit price determination differ by perspective and method, informing financing mechanisms</cite>. <cite id="bc383d71-7">Hospital costing frameworks describe direct/indirect attribution and activity‑based rates in similar ways for HIV services</cite>. <cite id="bc383d71-4">Community‑based testing often uses micro‑costing to reflect client time, transport, and method choice</cite>.
- Equity, supply chain, and electrification: in SSA, add‑ons for cold chain, dry‑ice, generator time, and kit shelf life materially change per‑test cost; include these as explicit cost elements or allocation rates for POC/field testing. <cite id="6e0eac27-0">Decentralized programs’ cost estimates in South Africa incorporate transport and phlebotomy time alongside lab unit costs</cite>. <cite id="6e0eac27-1">ABC/M applications identify actual costs for HIV services to target resources and efficiency</cite>.

Illustrative African examples of method classification and distinctions
- HIV program planning: UNAIDS and national strategic plans use top‑down program costing (WHO‑CHOICE/resource‑needs models) plus micro‑costing for unit price setting and service bundles, with activity‑based costing to allocate per‑visit and per‑test resources (e.g., rapid HIV tests, CBC). <cite id="6e0eac27-8">UNAIDS reviews how Resource Needs Model, Goals Model, and Optima have been adapted for national HIV NSP costing and investment cases</cite>. <cite id="6e0eac27-1">Activity‑based costing and management (ABC/M) identifies actual costs for HIV prevention, testing, and treatment services</cite>. <cite id="6e0eac27-4">A systematic review summarizes ABC costs across HIV, primary care, and nutrition in LMICs</cite>.
- TB and microscopy/NGS: top‑down micro‑costing often compares NGS (GeneXpert) against smear microscopy and culture; bottom‑up micro‑costs list consumables, labor time, and QA; perspective shifts can change the unit cost leader (lab vs patient). <cite id="bc383d71-2">Technology choice (PCR/serologic) and processing method alter cost dominance and effectiveness, informing program policy</cite>. <cite id="bc383d71-5">Top‑down micro‑costing was most common in empirical literature</cite>.
- Community HIV testing: micro‑costing across SSA found per‑test costs vary widely with method and prevalence; perspective adds patient time and acceptability. <cite id="6e0eac27-3">Community‑based HIV testing cost studies used micro‑costing/ingredients approaches, showing country‑ and method‑specific unit costs</cite>. <cite id="6e0eac27-10">Costs per test differed with delivery setting, logistics, and prevalence, underscoring service‑model distinctions</cite>.

Checklist: deciding among costing classes for disease testing in an African region
- What unit do I need? 
  - Unit cost per test, per algorithm step, or per confirmed case? Use bottom‑up micro‑costing to enumerate inputs and outputs per case. <cite id="bc383d71-5">Bottom‑up micro‑costing traces individual resource elements to the unit of output</cite>.
- What is the budgeting/procurement scope?
  - System/provider budgets and overheads: top‑down micro‑costing and WHO‑style program costing. <cite id="bc383d71-9">WHO‑CHOICE uses health system perspective including overheads</cite>. <cite id="bc383d71-8">Allocate program/overhead costs and patient delivery</cite>.
- What is the delivery mode?
  - Centralized lab vs POC in clinics vs community: capture logistics, kit costs, and time differently and expect different cost drivers by method. <cite id="6e0eac27-0">POC and lab costs for HIV treatment initiation were directly compared in South Africa</cite>. <cite id="6e0eac27-3">Field testing unit costs depend on method and contextual factors</cite>.
- What perspective yields actionable decisions?
  - Payer (procurement/allocations): provider perspective; Stakeholder fairness/acceptability: add patient time/fees; Population priority: include societal outcomes and productivity. <cite id="bc383d71-5">Perspective choice determines included beneficiaries and cost claims</cite>. <cite id="bc383d71-8">Different perspectives lead to different cost sets for transfer across regions</cite>.
- What data and time do I have?
  - Limited finance data only: top‑down micro‑ or gross‑costing with robust allocation; richer cost data and costing software: bottom‑up micro‑costing and ABC; pair with sensitivity analyses around reagent price and throughput. <cite id="bc383d71-11">Combine activity‑based costing, ingredients, and budget data under LMIC constraints</cite>. <cite id="bc383d71-11">Gross‑ vs micro‑costing trade off speed and precision</cite>.
- Which test types predominate and how do algorithms chain them?
  - Rapid tests, PCR, serology in cascade algorithms: separate stage costs and detection sensitivities; use micro‑costing to capture false‑negative re‑testing and logistics. <cite id="bc383d71-2">Different test technologies alter cost effectiveness and cost drivers at scale</cite>.

Evidence-backed takeaways for African regions
- Use a two-by-two matrix: top‑down/bottom‑up by micro/gross to match decision needs, and anchor in an appropriate perspective that aligns with who funds and benefits the test. <cite id="bc383d71-5">Costing methods are jointly classified by build approach and level of granular detail</cite>. <cite id="bc383d71-5">Top‑down micro‑costing is most common; bottom‑up is less frequent but informative</cite>.
- For lab platforms and reagent-intensive modalities, micro‑costing supports procurement and efficiency gains by revealing reagent, QA, and throughput bottlenecks; for budget planning, top‑down program costing plus overhead allocation is efficient and policy‑relevant. <cite id="6e0eac27-1">ABC/M has been used across multiple African programs to reveal true costs and target improvements</cite>. <cite id="bc383d71-9">WHO guidance supports program‑level inclusion of overheads</cite>.
- Perspective alignment is critical when comparing centralized vs POC: add client time and transport and potential fee exemptions for community testing to reflect real social costs, and include system overheads for central lab maintenance and supply chain. <cite id="bc383d71-8">Perspective selection affects included costs (overheads, training, service delivery) and comparability across settings</cite>. <cite id="6e0eac27-0">Decentralized testing unit costs differ from centralized due to transport, phlebotomy, and proximity</cite>.
- Choose methods and perspectives with transparent data collection and validation procedures; document inclusion/exclusion of cost items and allocation bases to support peer review and policy transfer. <cite id="bc383d71-8">Differences in classification of cost items and methods like cost‑to‑charge can change estimates and transferability</cite>.

Practical taxonomy to report
- Class A (Top‑down, Micro): Program/unit budget–based micro‑allocation to each test with overhead apportionment; common in public sector evaluations and WHO‑aligned planning. <cite id="bc383d71-5">Top‑down micro‑costing predominate</cite>. <cite id="bc383d71-9">WHO‑CHOICE program costs</cite>.
- Class B (Top‑down, Gross): Aggregate budget/expenditure to test shares or volumes with broad overhead; efficient for needs assessments and cross‑regional comparisons. <cite id="bc383d71-11">Gross‑costing aggregates with limited detail</cite>.
- Class C (Bottom‑up, Micro): Ingredients approach for rapid tests, PCR assays, and POCT, with time, reagent, and consumable detail; used for procurement, technology selection, and quality improvement. <cite id="bc383d71-5">Bottom‑up micro‑costing traces individual resource elements</cite>. <cite id="6e0eac27-6">POC vs lab comparisons rely on granular unit costs</cite>.
- Class D (Community/Client‑centered): Micro‑costing from the patient perspective plus transport/time, often for community HIV testing and acceptability analyses; useful for fee exemptions or insurance product design. <cite id="6e0eac27-3">Community‑based HIV testing costing used micro‑costing/ingredients</cite>. <cite id="bc383d71-5">Perspective choice defines client‑level inclusion</cite>.

Putting it together for an African region
- Start with a top‑down micro‑costing for the health system perspective to align with national NSP/finance systems; then complement with bottom‑up micro‑costing for key test platforms (e.g., HIV rapid tests and PCR) to set unit prices and negotiate tenders; conduct targeted micro‑costing from a client perspective for community outreach to reflect social costs and acceptability; and evaluate decentralized POC models separately by adding transport/time and kit logistics to centralized lab unit costs for direct comparability. <cite id="bc383d71-8">Health system perspective and overhead inclusion support program decisions</cite>. <cite id="bc383d71-5">Top‑down micro‑costing aligns cost items with program accounts</cite>. <cite id="6e0eac27-0">POC vs lab unit costs have been compared with transport and processing time explicitly included</cite>. <cite id="6e0eac27-3">Community testing adds method‑ and prevalence‑dependent costs captured by micro‑costing</cite>. <cite id="bc383d71-2">Test technology choice (PCR/POCT/serology) alters cost drivers and effectiveness, impacting cost leadership</cite>.
