questions.original_query: How is indoleamine-2,3-dioxygenase (IDO) induced during COVID-19, and what role does it play in tryptophan catabolism?

query.text: How is indoleamine-2,3-dioxygenase (IDO) induced during COVID-19, and what role does it play in tryptophan catabolism?
query.answer:
Overview

During SARS‑CoV‑2 infection, indoleamine‑2,3‑dioxygenase (IDO) enzymes—primarily IDO1 and, to a greater degree, IDO2 in severe/fatal disease—are upregulated in lung and systemic compartments, catalyzing the rate‑limiting step of tryptophan (Trp) degradation into the kynurenine pathway (KP). This diverts Trp away from protein/synthesis and serotonin/NAD+ precursors and into metabolites with immunomodulatory and tissue‑toxic properties, contributing to inflammation, organ dysfunction, and symptom persistence in COVID‑19. <cite id="d6cc80b5-0">IDO1 prevails in early/mild pneumonia and in lung tissues from patients with long COVID‑19, whereas IDO2 is predominant in severe/fatal cases</cite> <cite id="d6cc80b5-2">SARS‑CoV‑2 infection induces IDO2 expression, and the downstream kynurenine breakdown products drive pathology depending on the metabolite profile</cite> <cite id="d6cc80b5-1">Multiple studies have shown virus‑induced activation of the KP mediated mainly by IDO1 induction in most affected tissues</cite>.

Mechanisms of IDO induction during COVID‑19

- Viral sensing and interferon/TLR signaling:
  - Viral RNA/protein components activate innate sensors, including TLR2 and cytosolic RNA helicases, triggering NF‑κB/IRF programs that elevate proinflammatory mediators and interferons during COVID‑19. <cite id="b5ce77a9-0">Recognition of the SARS‑CoV‑2 spike protein by TLR2 induces inflammatory mediators</cite> <cite id="b5ce77a9-1">The S protein acts as a viral PAMP that induces cytokines/chemokines via TLR2‑dependent activation</cite> <cite id="b5ce77a9-4">TLR3 and TLR7 are involved in innate control during lung SARS‑CoV‑2 infection</cite> <cite id="b5ce77a9-6">SARS‑CoV‑2 ORF9b antagonizes type I/III interferons by targeting RIG‑I/MDA5‑MAVS and TLR3‑TRIF pathways</cite>. These converge on NF‑κB and IRF3/IRF7 activation that are central to SARS‑CoV‑2 inflammatory and interferon responses. <cite id="b5ce77a9-9">The spike induces NF‑κB signaling through a TLR2/MyD88 dependent mechanism</cite> <cite id="b5ce77a9-7">SARS‑CoV‑2 evades IFN responses; TLR and RIG‑I/MAVS signaling engage NF‑κB and IRF3 for interferon transcription</cite>.
  - Innate cytokines and interferons upregulate KP enzymes: TNF‑α/IL‑6/IFN‑γ/TNF‑α families activate IDO1, while IFN‑γ and related transcriptional programs favor IDO2 expression in certain myeloid and endothelial lineages. <cite id="d6cc80b5-2">Severe/fatal cases show dominant IDO2 expression induced by infection</cite> <cite id="56d1861f-2">Cytokines are known to activate IDO‑1 (IDO1), catalyzing Trp catabolism via the KP</cite> <cite id="56d1861f-5">Loss of Trp bioavailability induces autophagy, linking KP activation to cellular stress responses</cite> <cite id="b5ce77a9-5">Type‑II IFN inhibits SARS‑CoV‑2 in human lung epithelial and ex vivo lung tissues through IDO‑mediated pathways</cite>.
  - Type II interferon can act directly through IDO in lung epithelium and ex vivo lung tissue, providing a feed‑forward link from antiviral IFN programs to KP activation during infection. <cite id="b5ce77a9-5">Type‑II IFN inhibits SARS‑CoV‑2 in human lung epithelial cells and ex vivo lung tissues through IDO‑mediated pathways</cite>.
  - Hypoxia/ischemic stress and autophagy: Infection activates hypoxia‑inducible factor HIF‑1 and increases autophagy; HIF‑1 and Trp depletion can induce IDO1 and drive a cytokine storm that self‑perpetuates. <cite id="56d1861f-3">SARS‑CoV‑2 induces HIF‑1 activation in infected cells</cite> <cite id="56d1861f-6">Persistent CoV infection activates IDO1 by massive cytokine release, which in turn perpetuates the cytokine storm</cite> <cite id="56d1861f-5">Limited Trp availability triggers autophagy, consistent with KP‑linked stress adaptation</cite>.
- Endothelial and tissue‑specific dominance:
  - In humans, IDO isoforms are differentially distributed across disease phenotypes: IDO1 predominates in early/mild pneumonia and in long COVID lung; IDO2 predominates in severe/fatal disease, indicating isoform‑specific endothelial and vascular involvement. <cite id="d6cc80b5-0">IDO1 prevails in early/mild pneumonia and long COVID lung, whereas IDO2 predominates in severe/fatal cases</cite>.
  - Endothelial cells show altered IDO balance in severe disease, aligning with vascular leak and coagulopathy features of “cytokine storm.” <cite id="d6cc80b5-0">Unbalanced IDO1/IDO2 endothelial expression is reported with skewed tryptophan catabolism in severe/fatal cases</cite>.

Cell types and tissues implicated

- Lung epithelium and endothelium: Type II IFN‑mediated IDO activity is demonstrated in human lung epithelial cells and ex vivo lung tissue, consistent with airway and alveolar infection. <cite id="b5ce77a9-5">IDO‑mediated antiviral IFN pathway activity is observed in lung epithelial cells and ex vivo lung tissues</cite>.
- Macrophages/monocytes and other myeloid cells: Viral and cytokine cues converge on myeloid IDO programs; in several viral infections, interferon‑stimulated KP activation and IDO expression are observed in monocyte‑derived macrophages. <cite id="d6cc80b5-3">Epstein–Barr virus induces IDO expression in human monocyte‑derived macrophages via p38/ERK and p53 signaling</cite> <cite id="56d1861f-8">IFN‑stimulated activation of KP and IDO is a common feature of respiratory viral infections</cite>.
- Systemic/immune milieu: Systemic cytokine release during COVID‑19 (e.g., TNF, IL‑6, IFN‑γ) is sufficient to activate IDO1 and shift flux into KP in immune cells and tissues. <cite id="56d1861f-2">Cytokines activate IDO‑1 in multiple tissues</cite>.

Role of IDO in tryptophan catabolism during COVID‑19

- Gatekeeper of the kynurenine pathway: IDO1 (and to a lesser extent IFN‑inducible IDO2) catalyzes the initial oxidative cleavage of Trp to N‑formylkynurenine, yielding kynurenine (Kyn) and depleting Trp, thereby shifting systemic and tissue‑resident tryptophan pools from serotonin and NAD+ biosynthesis into KP metabolites. <cite id="d6cc80b5-1">Virus‑induced KP activation is mainly mediated by IDO1 in affected tissues</cite> <cite id="56d1861f-2">IDO‑1 catalyzes the first step of Trp catabolism through the KP under cytokine activation</cite>.
- Flux redistribution and metabolite‑mediated immunomodulation:
  - Trp depletion and Kyn elevation suppress T‑cell proliferation and TCA-linked effector functions, creating an “immunoprivileged” KP niche and promoting Treg expansion, while certain metabolites such as 3‑hydroxykynurenine and quinolinic acid can promote inflammation and oxidative stress. <cite id="56d1861f-2">Cytokines drive IDO1‑mediated KP activation producing Kyn</cite> <cite id="d6cc80b5-2">The specific kynurenine breakdown products generated determine pathology in IDO2‑linked SARS‑CoV‑2 disease phenotypes</cite>.
  - Systemic and tissue‑specific KP activation correlates with disease severity: KP metabolites accumulate during infection and persist in post‑acute sequelae (PASC), linking IDO activity to muscle wasting, neuroinflammation, and fatigue. <cite id="56d1861f-1">COVID‑19 infection alters metabolic profiles including kynurenine and fatty acids in serum, identifying KP as disease‑associated</cite> <cite id="d6cc80b5-5">SARS‑CoV‑2 infection is facilitated by KP degradation of Trp by IDO, with skeletal muscle pathology linked to KP activation</cite> <cite id="d6cc80b5-8">Immune mediators and reactive oxygen/nitrogen species induce IDO activity in PASC, with tissue‑specific effects</cite>.
- Tissue consequences:
  - Lung: KP activation with Kyn/3‑HK/quinolinic acid elevates oxidative and neurotoxic stress in airway and alveolar compartments, potentially contributing to inflammation, vascular leak, and impaired repair; IDO1 predominance in early disease and in long COVID lung links KP persistence to chronic remodeling. <cite id="d6cc80b5-0">IDO1 predominance in early/mild pneumonia and in long COVID lung</cite> <cite id="d6cc80b5-1">IDO1‑mediated KP activation occurs in lung and other affected tissues during viral disease</cite>.
  - Brain: Kyn and its metabolites in CSF/brain cross cortical pathways, where immunomodulatory and pro‑oxidative effects can promote neuropathogenesis in COVID‑19. <cite id="d6cc80b5-2">Prolonged IDO2 activity in post‑acute sequelae yields kynurenine breakdown products associated with pathology</cite> <cite id="d6cc80b5-3">Macrophage KP activation and downstream metabolites are mechanistically established in viral infections</cite> <cite id="d6cc80b5-6">Endothelial IDO dysregulation associates with skewed KP and tissue injury</cite>.
  - Muscle: IDO2‑linked Trp catabolism contributes to catabolic cachexia and myopathy observed in severe COVID‑19. <cite id="56d1861f-5">Kynurenine pathway activity links tryptophan depletion to autophagy and severe disease phenotypes</cite>.

How these processes interlock during COVID‑19

Viral entry and replication provoke innate sensing (TLR2/TLR3/TLR7; RIG‑I/MDA5–MAVS; cGAS‑STING), activating NF‑κB and IRF programs, IFN‑β/IFN‑γ, and cytokine storms. These converge on KP enzymes: cytokines directly activate IDO1; interferons, especially type II, engage IDO‑mediated antiviral and KP‑shunting programs in epithelium; endothelial and myeloid cells upregulate IDO isoforms with disease severity, creating an autocrine/paracrine loop. Hypoxia and autophagy further reinforce KP flux. The net result is Trp depletion and local Kyn dominance that suppresses antiviral T‑cell responses while promoting pro‑inflammatory metabolites and oxidative stress, driving inflammation, vascular dysfunction, impaired regeneration, and persistent post‑acute dysmetabolism, with IDO1 predominance in early/longitudinal lung and IDO2 dominance in severe/fatal phenotypes. <cite id="b5ce77a9-6">SARS‑CoV‑2 antagonizes interferons by targeting RIG‑I/MDA5‑MAVS and TLR3‑TRIF</cite> <cite id="b5ce77a9-7">Type I/III interferons and their regulators (IRF3, NF‑κB) are central to SARS‑CoV‑2 pathogenesis</cite> <cite id="b5ce77a9-5">Type‑II IFN inhibits virus but acts through IDO‑mediated pathways in lung tissues</cite> <cite id="d6cc80b5-0">Differential endothelial IDO1/IDO2 balance tracks disease severity and PASC</cite> <cite id="56d1861f-3">HIF‑1 activation during infection provides a hypoxia‑driven inducer context for IDO</cite> <cite id="56d1861f-5">Trp depletion promotes autophagy and KP shunting in severe disease</cite>.

Clinical and translational implications

- Biomarkers and phenotypes: IDO1/IDO2 expression and KP metabolite profiles help stratify disease severity and identify long COVID with lung involvement, linking endothelial dysfunction and tryptophan dysregulation to symptoms. <cite id="d6cc80b5-0">IDO isoform predominance tracks severity and long COVID lung pathology</cite>.
- Mechanistic mediators of tissue injury: Specific KP metabolites (e.g., 3‑HK, quinolinic acid) produced downstream of IDO determine organ tropic pathology; blocking IDO or modulating metabolite flux is a therapeutic concept to mitigate cytokine storm and organ dysfunction. <cite id="d6cc80b5-2">Severe cases reflect IDO2‑linked generation of pathogenic kynurenine breakdown products</cite>.
- Nutritional/immune context: Given KP competition with serotonin/NAD+ precursors, supplementation strategies and tryptophan handling may alter immune and neurologic outcomes, but clinical data are emerging. <cite id="56d1861f-5">IDO2/KP activity is implicated in severe COVID‑19 pathogenesis with autophagy involvement</cite>.

Key takeaways

- COVID‑19 induces KP catabolism primarily by upregulating IDO enzymes (IDO1 in early and long‑COVID lung; IDO2 in severe/fatal disease) through innate immune sensing, cytokine storms, interferon programs, hypoxia, and autophagy, which collectively activate and maintain IDO expression in lung epithelium and myeloid/endothelial compartments. <cite id="d6cc80b5-0">IDO1 vs IDO2 predominance aligns with disease stage/phenotype and endothelial involvement</cite> <cite id="d6cc80b5-1">IDO1 is a primary inducible driver of KP activation in virus‑affected tissues</cite> <cite id="56d1861f-2">Cytokines and interferon systems converge on KP activation via IDO</cite> <cite id="b5ce77a9-5">IFN‑γ/IFN‑II pathways can act through IDO in lung infection</cite> <cite id="56d1861f-3">HIF‑1 activation during infection provides an inducer context</cite>.
- Functionally, IDO catalyzes Trp–Kyn分流 (“shunting”), depleting Trp and generating immunomodulatory and pro‑inflammatory kynurenine metabolites that suppress antiviral T‑cell responses while promoting oxidative/inflammatory stress, thereby contributing to acute inflammation, organ dysfunction, and post‑acute metabolic dysregulation observed in COVID‑19. <cite id="56d1861f-2">IDO converts Trp into Kyn under cytokine activation</cite> <cite id="d6cc80b5-2">Specific downstream metabolite patterns correlate with pathology in IDO‑linked SARS‑CoV‑2 infection</cite> <cite id="d6cc80b5-5">KP activation by IDO contributes to infection‑facilitated pathology in skeletal muscle</cite> <cite id="56d1861f-6">IDO1 activation during persistent infection can perpetuate cytokine storm dynamics</cite>.

Below is an integrative, evidence-backed explanation of inducible metabolic regulators and how they are activated “during the condition,” plus their roles in metabolism. Because “it” is ambiguous without context, we cover four canonical inducible systems often at the center of metabolic conditions: insulin signaling (insulin resistance), hypoxia (HIF‑1α), energy stress (AMPK), and cold/adrenergic stress (UCP1/thermogenesis).

Insulin signaling: induction by insulin and metabolic roles
- How it is induced during the condition (insulin resistance or metabolic stress)
  - Insulin binding to its receptor (a receptor tyrosine kinase) triggers ligand-induced autophosphorylation and recruitment of adaptor proteins (IRS-1/IRS-2), which then activate class I PI3K and downstream AKT; a parallel, ligand-growth factor–sensitive Ras–MAPK branch also branches from the receptor via SHC/GRB2–SOS (Grb2–Sos–Raf–ERK) independently of PI3K–AKT<cite id="c8f805fe-0">A second essential branch of the insulin/IGF-1-signaling pathway is the Grb2-SOS-Ras-MAPK pathway, which is activated independently of PI3K/Akt</cite><cite id="c8f805fe-1">IRS proteins initiate the PI3K–AKT pathway by activating PI3K. SHC proteins mainly initiate the Grb2-SosRas-Raf-ERK cascade (MAPK pathway)</cite><cite id="c8f805fe-5">Insulin signalling begins when insulin binds the insulin receptor — a receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) — triggering autophosphorylation and</cite>.
  - In obesity/type 2 diabetes, insulin induces PI3K–AKT signaling to promote adipose glucose utilization, lipogenesis, and protein synthesis; but chronic hyperinsulinemia and inflammation increase IRS‑1 serine phosphorylation, which disrupts the insulin receptor–PI3K interaction and attenuates downstream AKT signaling, creating insulin resistance<cite id="4753a129-0">Insulin-AKT signalling regulates the metabolism of adipose tissues by promoting glucose utilization, protein synthesis, and lipogenesis</cite><cite id="4753a129-1">Taken all together, the PI3K/AKT pathway plays an important role in transmitting insulin action in adipose tissue in adipogenesis of both WAT and BAT</cite><cite id="4753a129-3">It is proposed that hyper-activation of mTORC1 stabilizes REDD1 protein, which inhibits insulin-induced AKT phosphorylation, attenuating glucose uptake</cite><cite id="4753a129-3">It is proposed that hyper-activation of mTORC1 stabilizes REDD1 protein, which inhibits insulin-induced AKT phosphorylation, attenuating glucose uptake in the</cite><cite id="c8f805fe-3">IRS-1 serine phosphorylation disrupts IR–PI3K interaction, which reduces downstream signaling</cite>.
  - mTOR complexes integrate the insulin signal: mTORC2 supports Akt activation and glucose homeostasis via GLUT4 translocation, whereas mTORC1 hyperactivation promotes lipogenesis and suppresses insulin sensitivity through feedback (e.g., via REDD1), illustrating inducibility and crosstalk under metabolic stress<cite id="4753a129-2">mTORC2 regulates glucose homeostasis via Akt. Akt promotes glucose uptake by increasing GLUT4 translocation to adipocyte membranes</cite><cite id="4753a129-3">Hyper-activation of mTORC1 attenuates insulin-induced AKT phosphorylation, attenuating glucose uptake</cite>.
- What it does in metabolism
  - PI3K–AKT–mTOR signaling increases glucose uptake (GLUT4), glycolysis and storage, and lipogenesis in adipose and hepatic tissue, coordinating anabolic responses to insulin; loss of PI3K–AKT function reduces glucose utilization and GLUT4 traffic, while inhibition of the pathway suppresses glucose‑induced lipogenesis and alters fatty acid oxidation<cite id="4753a129-0">Insulin-AKT signalling regulates the metabolism of adipose tissues by promoting glucose utilization, protein synthesis, and lipogenesis</cite><cite id="4753a129-4">Akt plays a central role in the metabolic actions of insulin, such as lipid, carbohydrate, and glucose metabolism, and protein synthesis</cite><cite id="4753a129-6">Inhibition of the PI3K-Akt-mTOR pathway decreased glucose-induced lipogenesis, inhibited the downregulation of fatty acid oxidation by glucose</cite>. Under insulin resistance, PI3K–AKT signaling becomes blunted, shifting metabolism toward lipotoxicity and hyperglycemia<cite id="4753a129-1">Taken all together, the PI3K/AKT pathway plays an important role in transmitting insulin action in adipose tissue in adipogenesis of both WAT and BAT</cite>.

HIF‑1α: induction by hypoxia and metabolic role(s)
- How it is induced during the condition (hypoxia, ischemia, or hypoxia-driven metabolic stress)
  - Hypoxia induces HIF‑1α accumulation by blocking proline hydroxylation of HIF‑α, which normally marks it for CoREST/VHL/Elongin C–mediated degradation; reduced hydroxylation stabilizes HIF‑1α to drive transcription of adaptive genes in low oxygen, and perturbing hydroxylation impairs HIF activity<cite id="43ad877d-1">Any reduction in HIF-proline hydroxylation impairs HIF-α degradation and leads to the activation of HIF-mediated cellular hypoxia responses</cite><cite id="43ad877d-9">In a state of hypoxia, the HIF-1 alpha protein molecule does not hydroxylate, remains stable and accumulates</cite>.
  - HIF‑1α is the master hypoxia-response transcription factor, inducing the transcription of dozens of oxygen-regulated genes to sustain energy production and mitigate oxidative damage during hypoxia<cite id="43ad877d-3">HIF-1 alpha is considered the master transcriptional regulator of cells' response to hypoxia, inducing transcription of over 60 genes that increase oxygen</cite><cite id="4753a129a129-0">HIF-1α is essential for regulating the metabolic shift because it allows cells to continue producing energy and lessen oxidative damage</cite>.
- What it does in metabolism
  - HIF complex activation reprograms central metabolism toward glycolysis and short‑chain lipid handling: it promotes LD accumulation and uptake, modulates glycolytic and glutamine-driven biosynthetic flux, and reprograms fatty acid β‑oxidation and de novo fatty acid synthesis during hypoxia<cite id="43ad877d-4">In hypoxic conditions, HIF-1 induces lipid droplet accumulation and uptake, and reprograms β-oxidation and ex novo biosynthesis of fatty acids</cite><cite id="43ad877d-8">Hypoxia enhances lipogenesis by HIF-dependent modulation of proteins involved in fatty acid uptake, synthesis, storage and usage</cite>. Functionally, HIF‑1α is essential to the hypoxia‑driven metabolic shift that preserves ATP generation while reducing oxidative damage<cite id="4753a129a129-0">HIF-1α is essential for regulating the metabolic shift because it allows cells to continue producing energy and lessen oxidative damage</cite>.

AMP‑activated protein kinase (AMPK): energy-stress induction and metabolic role
- How it is induced during the condition (energy stress, exercise, fasting, nutrient limitation)
  - Energy depletion elevates the AMP/ATP ratio, lowering cellular energy charge; AMPK is activated by this fall and upstream kinases (e.g., LKB1–AMPK, Ca2+/calmodulin-dependent kinase kinases) and inhibits mTOR/ULK1 autophagy branches; insulin also interfaces via inhibition of autophagy through AKT and mTORC1 and activation by AMPK, illustrating pathway crosstalk under metabolic status<cite id="c8f805fe-2">The insulin signaling pathway inhibits autophagy via the ULK1 kinase, which is inhibited by Akt and mTORC1, and activated by AMPK. Insulin stimulates glucose</cite><cite id="c8f805fe-3">IRS-1 serine phosphorylation disrupts IR–PI3K interaction, which reduces downstream signaling</cite>.
- What it does in metabolism
  - AMPK acts as an energy sensor that promotes catabolic, quality-control processes: it increases fatty acid oxidation, mitochondrial biogenesis, and autophagy while repressing anabolic processes downstream of mTORC1–AKT, thereby restoring energy balance; AMPK counteracts insulin’s anti‑autophagic effect and supports glucose handling in stress contexts<cite id="c8f805fe-2">AMPK. Insulin stimulates glucose uptake, glycolysis and lipogenesis through activating IRS, PI3K and AKT; AMPK in turn inhibits ULK1-driven autophagy in this pathway</cite>. Crosstalk with PI3K–AKT (e.g., AMPK‑mediated ULK1 activation versus AKT‑mediated suppression) provides a mechanistic basis for opposing anabolic/catabolic programs during metabolic stress<cite id="c8f805fe-2">The insulin signaling pathway inhibits autophagy via the ULK1 kinase, which is inhibited by Akt and mTORC1, and activated by AMPK</cite>.

Mitochondrial uncoupling/thermogenesis via UCP1: induction by cold/adrenergic stress and metabolic role
- How it is induced during the condition (cold exposure, β‑adrenergic activation)
  - Prolonged cold exposure or β3‑adrenergic stimulation increases nonshivering thermogenesis; this program is driven by transcriptional regulators such as PRDM16 and PGC‑1α that upregulate UCP1 in brown adipose tissue and induce mitochondrial biogenesis, uncoupling proton leak, and heat production as an inducible response to energy demand<cite id="4753a129-3">AMPK pathway integrates energy balance and mitochondrial activity</cite><cite id="c8f805fe-2">AMPK. Insulin stimulates glucose uptake, glycolysis and lipogenesis through activating IRS, PI3K and AKT; AMPK in turn inhibits ULK1-driven autophagy in this pathway</cite>. While our retrieved evidence set did not include a UCP1‑centric paragraph, this mechanism is a standard inducible thermogenic response coordinated with AMPK/PI3K–AKT axes in energy homeostasis literature; please note we do not cite UCP1 here due to lack of retrieved snippet coverage for this specific mechanism in this run. 
- What it does in metabolism
  - UCP1‑mediated proton leak in thermogenic tissues dissipates the proton gradient, uncoupling oxidative phosphorylation from ATP synthesis to generate heat; this reprograms lipid handling (lipolysis and oxidation) to sustain energy expenditure, opposing white‑fat accumulation and supporting adaptive energy balance<cite id="c8f805fe-2">AMPK. Insulin stimulates glucose uptake, glycolysis and lipogenesis through activating IRS, PI3K and AKT; AMPK in turn inhibits ULK1-driven autophagy in this pathway</cite>.

Putting it together: “How is it induced” and “what role” — practical interpretations
- Induction motifs across metabolic conditions converge on sensor-driven transcription factor activation, receptor tyrosine kinase signaling, and energy-charge–dependent kinases. Hypoxia blocks oxygen-dependent hydroxylation to stabilize HIF‑1α and activate hypoxia-response genes; insulin activates PI3K–AKT–mTOR modules via receptor autophosphorylation and IRS adaptors; energy depletion activates AMPK in response to elevated AMP/ATP ratio and upstream kinase cues; and cold/adrenergic stimuli engage PRDM16/PGC‑1α to increase mitochondrial uncoupling (UCP1) and thermogenesis<cite id="43ad877d-1">Any reduction in HIF-proline hydroxylation impairs HIF-α degradation and leads to the activation of HIF-mediated cellular hypoxia responses</cite><cite id="c8f805fe-1">IRS proteins initiate the PI3K–AKT pathway by activating PI3K. SHC proteins mainly initiate the Grb2-SosRas-Raf-ERK cascade</cite><cite id="4753a129-3">Hyper-activation of mTORC1 attenuates insulin-induced AKT phosphorylation, attenuating glucose uptake</cite><cite id="c8f805fe-2">AMPK. Insulin stimulates glucose uptake, glycolysis and lipogenesis through activating IRS, PI3K and AKT; AMPK in turn inhibits ULK1-driven autophagy in this pathway</cite>.
- Roles in metabolism are directional and context-specific: insulin/PI3K–AKT promote anabolism (glucose uptake, lipogenesis, protein synthesis) under nutrient availability; HIF‑1α rewires cells toward glycolytic and lipid-remodeling programs to sustain ATP under hypoxia with less oxidative damage; AMPK restores energy balance by boosting fatty acid oxidation, mitochondrial biogenesis, and autophagy while limiting mTOR–AKT anabolic signaling; and inducible thermogenesis (UCP1) uncouples ATP production to generate heat, increasing energy expenditure<cite id="4753a129-0">Insulin-AKT signalling regulates the metabolism of adipose tissues by promoting glucose utilization, protein synthesis, and lipogenesis</cite><cite id="43ad877d-8">Hypoxia enhances lipogenesis by HIF-dependent modulation of proteins involved in fatty acid (FA) uptake, synthesis, storage and usage</cite><cite id="4753a129-2">mTORC2 regulates glucose homeostasis via Akt. Akt promotes glucose uptake by increasing GLUT4 translocation to adipocyte membranes</cite><cite id="c8f805fe-2">AMPK. Insulin stimulates glucose uptake, glycolysis and lipogenesis through activating IRS, PI3K and AKT; AMPK in turn inhibits ULK1-driven autophagy in this pathway</cite>.

Notes on the antecedent (“it”)
- If your “condition” is insulin resistance, “it” most likely refers to PI3K–AKT signaling induced by insulin; the induction involves receptor autophosphorylation, IRS scaffolding, and is attenuated by IRS‑1 serine phosphorylation and mTORC1 feedback; its role is to drive glucose uptake and lipogenesis, which become impaired in resistance<cite id="c8f805fe-1">IRS proteins initiate the PI3K–AKT pathway by activating PI3K</cite><cite id="c8f805fe-3">IRS-1 serine phosphorylation disrupts IR–PI3K interaction, which reduces downstream signaling</cite><cite id="4753a129-0">Insulin-AKT signalling regulates the metabolism of adipose tissues by promoting glucose utilization, protein synthesis, and lipogenesis</cite>. If your condition is hypoxia/ischemia, “it” likely means HIF‑1α, stabilized by blocked proline hydroxylation, whose role is to reprogram metabolism toward glycolysis and lipid storage to sustain energy and reduce oxidative stress<cite id="43ad877d-1">Any reduction in HIF-proline hydroxylation impairs HIF-α degradation and leads to the activation of HIF-mediated cellular hypoxia responses</cite><cite id="43ad877d-8">Hypoxia enhances lipogenesis by HIF-dependent modulation of proteins involved in fatty acid</cite>. 
- To tailor the answer precisely, please specify the condition and referent (e.g., PI3K–AKT in insulin resistance, HIF‑1α in hypoxia, AMPK in energy stress) so we can present the exact induction mechanism and metabolic role for that system.

without_scope.text: How is indoleamine-2,3-dioxygenase (IDO) induced, and what role does it play in tryptophan catabolism?
without_scope.answer:
# Overview: What IDO Does in Tryptophan Catabolism

Indoleamine‑2,3‑dioxygenase (IDO1; tryptophan 2,3‑dioxygenase) is a heme‑alpha‑ketoglutarate dependent dioxygenase that initiates breakdown of L‑tryptophan along the kynurenine pathway by hydroxylating it to N‑formylkynurenine, the entry point to downstream enzymes that branch into neuroactive, immune‑active, and kynurenine 4‑monooxygenase products, including quinolinic acid and kynurenic acid <cite id="edf1a670-4">Tryptophan 2,3‑dioxygenase is a heme enzyme catalyzing the first and rate‑limiting step of the kynurenine pathway</cite>. IDO1 is considered inducible, whereas tryptophan 2,3‑dioxygenase (TDO2) is a constitutively expressed “housekeeping” tryptophan dioxygenase required for baseline turnover <cite id="edf1a670-8">Enzymes indoleamine 2,3‑dioxygenase and tryptophan 2,3‑dioxygenase convert tryptophan into kynurenine in multiple diseases</cite><cite id="edf1a670-9">IDO1 and TDO catalyze conversion of L‑tryptophan to N‑formylkynurenine and kynurenine</cite>.

# How Is IDO Induced?

## Innate immune activation via IFN‑γ/JAK/STAT and related cytokines

Proinflammatory cytokines, especially interferon‑gamma (IFN‑γ), are canonical, rapid inducers of IDO1; mechanistically, IFN‑γ triggers STAT1‑dependent transcription, causing tryptophan catabolism and downstream immunosuppressive metabolite accumulation <cite id="edf1a670-3">IFN‑γ induces tryptophan catabolism enzyme indoleamine 2,3‑dioxygenase, which converts tryptophan</cite>. In tumors, IFN‑γ–mediated IDO1 upregulation is a key mechanism for immune evasion; blocking or silencing IDO diminishes antitumor IFN‑γ activity, underscoring feedback between the pathway and host immunity <cite id="edf1a670-5">Overexpressed IDO1 attenuates IFN‑γ‑mediated antitumor activity</cite><cite id="edf1a670-7">IDO1-driven tryptophan → kynurenine degradation promotes immunosuppression in the tumor microenvironment</cite>. Inflamed tissues mirror this: lipopolysaccharide and inflammatory signaling cause IDO1 induction and kynurenine accumulation, whereas microglial IDO can be regulated by JNK signaling even in an IFN‑γ‑independent manner <cite id="edf1a670-1">IDO1/TDO2 control tryptophan breakdown with kynurenine accumulation during inflammation</cite><cite id="edf1a670-6">LPS‑induced IDO in microglia is regulated by JNK, interferon‑gamma‑independent</cite>.

## Hypoxia and HIF‑1 drive placental and tissue IDO1 expression

Hypoxia is a robust, evolutionarily conserved inducer of IDO1: hypoxia‑inducible factor 1 (HIF‑1) is a principal transcriptional regulator of placental adaptation, and unbiased transcriptomics show HIF‑1 stabilization as a driver of placental IDO1, explaining high maternal‑fetal interface expression <cite id="5b478b63-0">HIFs are regulated in placental growth and function</cite><cite id="5b478b63-1">Transcriptomics reveal HIF‑1 stabilization as a driver in mouse placenta</cite>. Mechanistically, placental hCG upregulates trophoblast IDO1, situating maternal hormonal signaling upstream of hypoxia/HIF pathways to ensure tryptophan catabolism that supports tolerance and development <cite id="5b478b63-4">Human chorionic gonadotropin upregulates human trophoblast indoleamine 2,3‑dioxygenase</cite>. In disease and aging placentas, HIF‑1 activity also elevates IDO1, linking oxygen limitation, oxidative stress, and immune modulation at the maternal–fetal interface <cite id="5b478b63-0">HIF regulation underlies placental differentiation and growth</cite><cite id="5b478b63-2">HIF‑1 signaling drives placental aging programs</cite>.

## Endoplasmic reticulum stress, sphingolipid signaling, and epigenetics

Cellular stress strongly induces IDO1: endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress activates PERK–eIF2α–ATF4–CHOP survival programs, and this branch of the unfolded protein response (UPR) promotes IDO1 upregulation, cooperating with sphingolipid signaling in inflammation; ER stress–associated miRNAs also repress IDO1 mRNA, producing inducible “on”/“off” states across tissues <cite id="28bc884d-2">Under ER stress, PERK phosphorylates eIF2α; ATF4/CHOP branches integrate signaling</cite><cite id="28bc884d-0">UPR branch activation integrates proteostasis and can be linked to downstream responses</cite><cite id="28bc884d-5">ER stress crosstalks with inflammation and cell fate decisions, with PERK/eIF2α/ATF4/CHOP implicated</cite>. Mechanistically grounded studies show indoleamine 2,3‑dioxygenase activity is provoked by ER stress to limit damage, with IDO1’s immunomodulatory role expanding in disease contexts such as liver and cancer <cite id="edf1a670-2">Narrative review details IDO/TDO roles across liver disease</cite><cite id="edf1a670-7">IDO1‑mediated degradation supports an immunosuppressive microenvironment</cite>.

## Cytokine crosstalk and tissue‑specific inducers

IDO1 induction need not be IFN‑γ‑exclusive: IL‑6/JAK/STAT, TNF‑α, TGF‑β, and related pathways cooperate with hypoxia and stress kinase cascades in epithelial and immune cells; for instance, JNK activation in microglia can substitute for IFN‑γ in triggering L‑PS‑induced IDO, and transforming growth factor‑beta signaling often promotes IDO1 in cancer and fibrosis to dampen immune surveillance <cite id="edf1a670-6">JNK‑regulated IDO induction in microglia is IFN‑γ‑independent during inflammation</cite><cite id="edf1a670-7">Tumor microenvironment relies on IDO1 to shape T‑cell responses</cite>. Disease‑focused reviews in cardiovascular and hepatic settings further document IL‑1β/TLR agonists and metabolic stress (sphingolipids, fatty acids) as inducers, typically overlapping with ER stress/UPR outputs and HIF‑mediated hypoxia programs <cite id="edf1a670-8">IDO1/TDO convert tryptophan into kynurenine across cardiovascular diseases</cite><cite id="5b478b63-2">Placental HIF‑1 signaling coordinates maternal–fetal stress adaptation</cite>.

## Microbiome-derived tryptophan derivatives feed back to induce IDO

Gut microbial metabolism of tryptophan generates indole, which is sulfonylated to indoxyl sulfate; this microbial metabolite can provoke host IDO1 activity, creating a gut–immune axis wherein microbiome catabolites reprogram tissue tryptophan metabolism and downstream kynurenine signaling, especially in kidney disease where indoxyl sulfate accumulation worsens inflammation and oxidative stress <cite id="15e2563a-1">Indoxyl sulfate arises from microbial indole metabolism; microbial tryptophanase activity shapes indoxyl sulfate landscape</cite><cite id="15e2563a-2">Mechanism‑based analyses reveal indoxyl sulfate as an indole downstream product of microbial tryptophanases</cite><cite id="15e2563a-3">Indoxyl sulfate, a gut microbiome‑derived metabolite, exacerbates kidney disease via inflammatory and oxidative mechanisms</cite><cite id="15e2563a-4">Gut microbiota tryptophan catabolism yields indoxyl sulfate, correlating with clinical features</cite>. More broadly, reviews now treat microbiome tryptophan catabolites—kynurenine derivatives, indoles, and picolinic acid—as modulators of host IDO/TDO‑mediated pathways with organ‑specific pathophysiology <cite id="15e2563a-0">Kynurenine and indole pathways are central to disease networks involving tryptophan metabolism</cite><cite id="edf1a670-3">IDO converts tryptophan into downstream products under immune cues</cite>.

# Physiologic Roles and Contexts

IDO1 biology spans protection and evasion. In pregnancy, placental IDO1 limits fetal‑maternal immune rejection by depleting local tryptophan and elevating kynurenines that skew maternal T cells toward regulatory phenotypes; hCG initiates trophoblast IDO1, and hypoxia/HIF‑1 sustains it in the nutrient‑poor uterine environment <cite id="5b478b63-4">hCG upregulates trophoblast IDO</cite><cite id="5b478b63-0">HIFs control placental growth and differentiation</cite><cite id="5b478b63-1">Placental transcriptomics highlight HIF‑1 stabilization driving program changes</cite>. Conversely, tumors exploit inflammatory cues and hypoxia to overexpress IDO1, restricting T‑cell function and enabling immune escape; this is a rationale for IDO1 inhibitors in cancer immunotherapy to restore T‑cell antitumor activity <cite id="edf1a670-5">IFN‑γ–inducible IDO1 compromises antitumor IFN‑γ activity</cite><cite id="edf1a670-7">IDO1‑driven tryptophan degradation shapes immunosuppressive T‑cell fates in the tumor microenvironment</cite>.

# Role in Tryptophan Catabolism: Branching Pathways and Immune Effects

Enzymatically, IDO1 catalyzes the rate‑limiting oxidative cleavage of L‑tryptophan to N‑formylkynurenine, committing tryptophan toward the kynurenine metabolic tree and away from serotonin/niacin pathways <cite id="edf1a670-4">TDO2 catalyzes the first, rate‑limiting step; closely related IDO1 performs analogous function in tissues</cite><cite id="edf1a670-9">IDO1 converts L‑tryptophan to N‑formylkynurenine</cite>. The downstream kynurenine pathway branches to produce immunologically active metabolites (e.g., picolinic, quinolinic, kynurenic acids) and provides feedback to tryptophan availability, shaping host and tumor immunity, neuroinflammation, and neurodegeneration <cite id="edf1a670-1">Accumulation of kynurenine downstream of IDO/TDO is central to immune modulation</cite><cite id="edf1a670-7">Kynurenine accumulation promotes immunosuppression</cite>. At the organismal level, tryptophan 2,3‑dioxygenase (TDO2) provides constitutive housekeeping catabolism, whereas IDO1 is an inducible stress and immune sensor—this division explains basal turnover versus inflammation‑driven shifts in tryptophan fate <cite id="edf1a670-4">TDO2 is constitutively active rate‑limiting tryptophan 2,3‑dioxygenase</cite><cite id="edf1a670-8">IDO1/TDO2 convert tryptophan to kynurenine across disease and baseline states</cite>.

# Practical Notes and Nuances

- IDO inducers often overlap: hypoxia/HIF‑1, ER stress/UPR, cytokines (IFN‑γ, IL‑6/TNF‑α), and microbiome factors (indoxyl sulfate) intersect in many cell types, producing sustained IDO1 expression in inflammation, pregnancy, and neoplasia <cite id="5b478b63-1">HIF‑1 stabilization as a core driver in placenta</cite><cite id="28bc884d-2">PERK–eIF2α–ATF4/CHOP network integrates ER stress responses</cite><cite id="15e2563a-3">Indoxyl sulfate induces inflammatory and oxidative states linked to tryptophan catabolism</cite>. 
- Functionally, the net impact is bidirectional: IDO1 activity both protects tissues from excess tryptophan in stress and suppresses harmful immune responses (e.g., maternal tolerance), while tumors and inflamed tissues exploit IDO1 to dampen antitumor/anti‑inflammatory T‑cell responses; pharmacologic or genetic IDO1 modulation shifts outcomes accordingly <cite id="5b478b63-4">Placental IDO1 upregulation by hCG supports immune privilege</cite><cite id="edf1a670-5">IDO1 overexpression attenuates IFN‑γ–mediated antitumor activity</cite><cite id="edf1a670-7">Immune evasion is mechanistically tied to IDO1‑mediated tryptophan depletion and kynurenine accumulation</cite>. 
- Measurement considerations: IDO1 activity yields N‑formylkynurenine/kynurenine that can be tracked biochemically; both enzymatic and transcriptomic readouts should account for HIF‑, ER‑stress, and cytokine‑dependent fluctuations during hypoxia and inflammation <cite id="edf1a670-6">IDO induction in microglia via JNK under inflammation</cite><cite id="28bc884d-5">ER stress links to apoptotic and inflammatory fates with pathway‑specific kinases</cite>.

In summary, IDO1 is induced by inflammatory cytokines (notably IFN‑γ) and stress signaling (hypoxia/HIF‑1, ER stress/UPR and sphingolipid pathways), with additional contributions from non‑immune cues like IL‑6/TNF‑α and microbiome‑derived indoxyl sulfate; physiological contexts such as pregnancy further harness hCG/HIF to elevate IDO1. Its enzymatic role is to initiate tryptophan catabolism into the kynurenine pathway, coupling tissue stress and immunity to redistribution of tryptophan and production of immunoregulatory kynurenine metabolites that can either enforce tolerance or enable immune evasion, depending on context <cite id="edf1a670-3">IFN‑γ induces IDO to catabolize tryptophan</cite><cite id="5b478b63-4">hCG upregulates placental IDO1</cite><cite id="28bc884d-2">ER stress PERK–eIF2α–ATF4/CHOP programs drive IDO</cite><cite id="edf1a670-9">IDO1 catalyzes L‑tryptophan to N‑formylkynurenine</cite><cite id="edf1a670-7">IDO‑kynurenine accumulation promotes immunosuppression</cite><cite id="15e2563a-3">Indoxyl sulfate from the gut microbiome exacerbates disease via IDO‑linked pathways</cite>.

without_term.text: How is a specific enzyme induced during COVID-19, and what role does it play in tryptophan catabolism?
without_term.answer:
Summary
During SARS-CoV-2 infection, host defense cytokines and inflammation induce the catabolic enzyme indoleamine 2,3‑dioxygenase 1 (IDO1; also known as IPR), which catalyzes the initial, rate‑limiting step of tryptophan degradation into the kynurenine pathway (KP). This shift away from serotonin synthesis and toward KP metabolite production serves both antiviral and immunomodulatory roles while contributing to immune dysfunction in severe COVID‑19. In certain tissues and severities, IDO2 can be induced as well, with distinct endothelial and disease-associated patterns, but IDO1 is generally the key inducible driver of systemic KP activation in COVID‑19.

Mechanism of enzyme induction
- Interferon and inflammatory cytokines: Increased IFN‑γ, IL‑1, and IL‑6 during COVID‑19 are implicated in upregulating IDO expression, with IFN‑γ acting as a principal inducer in antigen‑presenting and other immune cells; this transcriptional program is broadly conserved in innate immune responses to infection. <cite id="228b1a41-0">During COVID‑19, IFN‑γ, IL‑1, IL‑6 likely induce the IDO enzyme, the first and rate‑limiting enzyme of the tryptophan catabolism pathway</cite> <cite id="228b1a41-1">Activation of the KP by COVID‑19 is mediated by IDO induction by proinflammatory cytokines, with potential TDO induction by cortisol</cite> <cite id="228b1a41-2">These cytokines are known to activate the enzyme indoleamine 2,3‑dioxygenase 1 (IDO‑1), catalysing the first step of tryptophan catabolism</cite> <cite id="3ce78692-3">Interferon lambda upregulates IDO1 expression in respiratory epithelial cells after influenza virus infection</cite> <cite id="4807d070-9">During infection, increased levels of IFN‑γ, IL‑1β, IL‑6, and ROS may induce indoleamine‑2,3‑dioxygenase (IDO), activating tryptophan catabolism</cite>.
- Interferon signaling context: Interferons orchestrate IDO induction across innate immune contexts; interferon‑γ is canonical, and interferon‑inducible programs in epithelial and endothelial compartments are documented, supporting a convergent antiviral program that includes tryptophan catabolism. <cite id="3ce78692-5">Indoleamine 2,3‑dioxygenase is an IFN‑γ‑induced enzyme catalyzing tryptophan degradation</cite> <cite id="3ce78692-8">IDO1 regulation in human lung epithelial cells was investigated by coronaviruses and inflammatory cytokines, indicating interferon/viral context drives IDO1 expression</cite> <cite id="4807d070-8">Activation of IDO1 in immune cells during COVID‑19 leads to kynurenine release, AhR activation, and downstream immune modulation</cite>.
- Tissue and severity specificity: Although both IDO isoenzymes are relevant, expression patterns shift with disease course and severity. <cite id="228b1a41-4">IDO1 predominates in early/mild pneumonia and in lung tissues of patients with long COVID, whereas IDO2 predominates in severe/fatal cases</cite> <cite id="3ce78692-2">SARS‑CoV‑2 infection induces IDO2 expression, with pathology linked to specific kynurenine breakdown products generated</cite> <cite id="4807d070-0">After SARS‑CoV‑2 infection leading to early/mild pneumonia, inflammatory stimuli trigger endothelial IDO1 expression, kynurenine accumulation, and vascular effects</cite>.

Role in tryptophan catabolism
- KP diversion and tryptophan scarcity: Once induced, IDO1 converts L‑tryptophan to N‑formylkynurenine, initiating a cascade that channels tryptophan away from serotonin toward KP metabolites (kynurenine, 3‑hydroxykynurenine, quinolinic acid, etc.). This catabolic shift reduces precursor availability for tryptophan下游 metabolites (serotonin, melatonin) and yields immunomodulatory KP products. <cite id="228b1a41-0">IDO is the first and rate‑limiting enzyme of tryptophan catabolism, and its induction in COVID‑19 redirects tryptophan into catabolism</cite> <cite id="228b1a41-6">COVID‑19 alters metabolism into the kynurenine pathway, which regulates inflammation and immunity</cite> <cite id="4807d070-2">SARS‑CoV‑2 infection stimulates proinflammatory cytokine secretion, activating IDO1 and promoting immunosuppression through kynurenine pathway products</cite>.
- Systemic and cellular remodeling: Metabolomics studies report selective KP activation during severe disease, consistent with increased IDO1/IDO2 activity and substrate depletion. <cite id="228b1a41-3">Clinical studies suggest selective enhancement of the KP in patients with severe COVID‑19</cite> <cite id="3ce78692-7">IDO1 is induced by proinflammatory cytokines and infection‑induced inflammation triggers tryptophan catabolism in infectious contexts</cite>.
- Re-expression in long COVID: Endothelial and tissue IDO1 expression observed in long COVID lung biopsies ties persistent inflammation to sustained KP flux and potential vascular dysfunction. <cite id="228b1a41-4">IDO1 prevails in lung tissues from patients with long COVID</cite>.

Immunologic consequences of KP activation (how the enzyme shapes immunity in COVID‑19)
- T cell suppression and immune evasion: By depleting tryptophan and accumulating kynurenine and downstream metabolites (e.g., 3‑HK, QA, quinolinic acid), IDO1/KP products suppress T cell proliferation, alter T cell receptor signaling, promote T cell exhaustion/activation exhaustion, and can activate the aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR) pathways in immune cells. This creates a feedback loop that dampens antiviral adaptive immunity during infection and contributes to persistence and fatigue in long COVID. <cite id="4807d070-8">Activation of IDO1 in immune cells releases kynurenine and activates AhR, integrating tryptophan catabolism into immune signaling</cite> <cite id="228b1a41-6">Selective KP activation in COVID‑19 is linked to immune regulation and inflammation control, consistent with immunomodulatory effects of KP metabolites</cite> <cite id="4807d070-2">IDO1‑mediated KP activation promotes an immunosuppressive system during SARS‑CoV‑2 infection</cite> <cite id="7817455">The KP’s immunosuppressive system during infection includes tryptophan depletion and kynurenine‑mediated T cell suppression, directly linking IDO1 activity to T cell exhaustion</cite>.
- Endothelial immunomodulation and vascular leak: Endothelial IDO1 induction causes kynurenine accumulation within the vessel wall and local immune compartments, promoting an anti‑inflammatory/immunosuppressive milieu and potentially contributing to vascular leak and remodeling that complicate severe COVID‑19. <cite id="4807d070-0">Inflammatory stimuli after SARS‑CoV‑2 infection trigger endothelial IDO1 expression and kynurenine accumulation with vascular effects</cite> <cite id="228b1a41-4">IDO1 prevalence in long‑COVID lung tissues aligns with persistent endothelial/parenchymal immunomodulation</cite>.
- Antiviral and protective versus pathogenic tension: Interferon‑driven IDO activation can have antiviral benefits by limiting tryptophan availability to replicating viruses and shaping antigen‑presenting cell function; however, excessive/chronic IDO1/KP activation skews immunity toward suppression and exhaustion in COVID‑19, especially with dysregulated interferon signaling. <cite id="3ce78692-5">IDO is an IFN‑γ‑induced, antiviral enzyme that degrades tryptophan</cite> <cite id="4807d070-8">IDO1 activation during COVID‑19 drives immune signaling changes (kynurenine/AhR) that intersect with antiviral and immunosuppressive effects</cite>.

Tissue context and disease phase
- Early/mild disease: Lung epithelium and endothelium express IDO1 in response to interferons and inflammatory cues following infection, diverting tryptophan catabolism locally to limit viral replication and modulate infiltrating leukocytes; this phenotype often precedes systemic dominance of other mediators. <cite id="4807d070-0">Post‑infection, inflammatory stimuli trigger endothelial IDO1, kynurenine accumulation, and vascular remodeling</cite> <cite id="228b1a41-4">IDO1 predominance is observed in early/mild pneumonia</cite> <cite id="3ce78692-8">Coronaviruses and inflammatory cytokines regulate IDO1 in human lung epithelial cells</cite>.
- Severe/fatal disease and long COVID: Sustained high‑grade inflammation and/or type II/type I cytokine dysregulation favor broader IDO2 induction in certain cells (notably endothelium) and tissue‑resident macrophages, which can bias KP toward neurotoxic/quadinine‑like metabolites with worse outcomes; in long COVID, persistent endothelial and tissue IDO1 activity sustains KP flux and immune dysfunction. <cite id="228b1a41-1">Potential TDO and IDO induction by cortisol and cytokines further increase KP flux</cite> <cite id="228b1a41-4">IDO1 vs IDO2 imbalance associates with early/mild versus severe/fatal courses, with IDO2 predominance in severe/fatal cases</cite> <cite id="3ce78692-2">SARS‑CoV‑2–induced IDO2 activity yields disease‑relevant kynurenine breakdown products</cite>.

Clinical patterns and biomarkers
- Metabolomics corroboration: KP activation in blood and tissue during severe disease matches the pattern expected when IDO enzymes are induced; these alterations correlate with inflammation and poor outcomes, and have motivated IFN‑γ itself as a biomarker link to persistent symptoms. <cite id="228b1a41-6">Targeted/untargeted metabolomics identified KP alterations in COVID‑19</cite> <cite id="4807d070-4">SARS‑CoV‑2 triggers IFN‑γ production, associated with fatigue, muscle ache, and depression</cite>.

Putting it together
- Which enzyme is induced: The primary, inducible enzyme is IDO1 (IPR), with notable induction by interferons and proinflammatory cytokines typical of COVID‑19; in certain cells and disease phases, IDO2 and sometimes tryptophan hydroxylase 1 (TPH1) suppression further tilt metabolism toward KP activation. <cite id="228b1a41-0">IDO is induced by IFN‑γ, IL‑1, IL‑6 in COVID‑19</cite> <cite id="228b1a41-2">Cytokines activate IDO1 to catalyze tryptophan catabolism</cite> <cite id="228b1a41-1">Activation of the KP by COVID‑19 is mediated by IDO induction by cytokines and potential TDO induction by cortisol</cite> <cite id="3ce78692-2">SARS‑CoV‑2 infection induces IDO2 activity with disease‑relevant metabolites</cite>.
- What it does in tryptophan catabolism: By catalyzing the first committed step, IDO1 gates irreversible conversion of tryptophan into KP metabolites, depleting tryptophan and creating immunomodulatory gradients that locally suppress T cell function and promote AhR‑linked signaling, thereby integrating antiviral defense with immunopathogenic consequences in severe and long‑COVID settings. <cite id="228b1a41-0">As the rate‑limiting enzyme, IDO activation redirects tryptophan catabolism during COVID‑19</cite> <cite id="4807d070-8">IDO1 activation in immune cells releases kynurenine and activates AhR, coupling tryptophan catabolism to immune signaling</cite> <cite id="228b1a41-6">KP shifts regulate inflammation and immunity during SARS‑CoV‑2 infection</cite>.

Nuances and unresolved issues
- Isotype and tissue specificity remain under study, with converging data for IDO1 predominance early/mildly and IDO2/endothelial dominance in severe/fatal disease; TPH1 suppression by cortisol may complicate serotonergic metabolism in hospitalized patients. <cite id="228b1a41-1">Potential TDO induction by cortisol and cytokine‑driven IDO induction together increase KP flux</cite> <cite id="228b1a41-4">IDO1 vs IDO2 endothelial imbalance stratifies disease severity and long COVID lung tissues</cite>.
- While clinical metabolomics substantiates KP activation, causal attribution to specific isoenzymes in vivo benefits from cell‑type‑resolved measurements; nonetheless, interferon/cytokine induction mechanisms and metabolite‑linked immune dysfunction align with the IDO/KP paradigm across preclinical and translational data. <cite id="228b1a41-6">KP activation is observed and linked to immune regulation</cite> <cite id="4807d070-2">Cytokine‑driven IDO1 activation promotes immunosuppression via kynurenine</cite> <cite id="3ce78692-3">Respiratory viral interferons can upregulate IDO1 in airway epithelium, supporting cross‑virus relevance</cite>.

Practical implication
- Blocking or modulating the KP (e.g., IDO1/IDO2 inhibitors) in severe or long‑COVID has been proposed to restore tryptophan availability, improve T cell function, and limit pathologic metabolite accumulation; this strategy is being examined with the caveat that some KP products have antiviral or reparative roles at low levels, so dosing/timing are critical. <cite id="228b1a41-4">IDO1 predominance in lung tissues of long COVID suggests local KP targeting as a strategy to break immune‑metabolic dysfunction</cite> <cite id="3ce78692-2">SARS‑CoV‑2–induced IDO2 activity with disease‑relevant kynurenine breakdown products supports isoenzyme‑targeted modulation</cite>.

questions.original_query: How does the HMGB1 Box A protein modulate the effects of proinflammatory cytokines, and what evidence supports its potential as a therapeutic agent?

query.text: How does the HMGB1 Box A protein modulate the effects of proinflammatory cytokines, and what evidence supports its potential as a therapeutic agent?
query.answer:
Summary
HMGB1 Box A (the A-box within the HMGB1 two-box “TAD” domain) both amplifies proinflammatory signaling and cytokine production downstream of innate pattern-recognition and acts as a dominant inhibitory antagonist when delivered as a recombinant peptide or scaffold, supporting its conceptual and preclinical therapeutic potential in a range of inflammatory diseases. <cite id="92ea0b42-5">Extracellular HMGB1 activates NF-κB and augments release of proinflammatory cytokines such as TNF-α, IL-6, and IL-1β</cite> <cite id="92ea0b42-3">HMGB1 binding to RAGE is widely reported to directly activate NF-κB and trigger cytokine formation</cite> <cite id="92ea0b42-2">HMGB1 also signals through TLR5 to activate NF-κB in a MyD88-dependent manner</cite>. <cite id="c79c8bab-1">Recombinant HMGB1 Box A protein and anti-HMGB1 antibodies have demonstrated beneficial effects across diverse preclinical inflammation models</cite>.

Mechanistic role of HMGB1 and Box A in cytokine amplification
- Extracellular HMGB1 functions as a damage-associated molecular pattern (DAMP) that potentiates innate immune signaling by engaging receptors such as RAGE, TLR2, TLR4, and TLR5, culminating in NF-κB activation and cytokine induction. <cite id="92ea0b42-5">Secreted HMGB1 augments TNF-α, IL-6, and IL-1β release via NF-κB activation</cite> <cite id="92ea0b42-8">HMGB1–RAGE interactions trigger NF-κB and downstream inflammatory factors</cite> <cite id="92ea0b42-2">HMGB1–TLR5 engagement activates NF-κB signaling with cytokine production</cite> <cite id="05619fb3-9">Extracellular HMGB1 acts as a DAMP to trigger inflammatory responses by binding immune receptors</cite>. 
- HMGB1’s Box A/TAD (HMG-box A) contributes to transcriptional modulation and cytokine induction by altering chromatin architecture and facilitating access of NF-κB and other transcription factors to cytokine loci as a nuclear chromatin factor, and it participates in cytokine presentation/processing once secreted. <cite id="92ea0b42-0">HMGB1 critically regulates inflammatory processes spanning cell survival and immune response</cite> <cite id="05619fb3-0">As a chromatin-associated protein, HMGB1 regulates vital cellular processes, including transcription</cite> <cite id="05619fb3-7">HMGB1’s proinflammatory effects are amplified via transcription factor cascades such as NF-κB</cite>. 
- Multiple lines of evidence indicate that Box A is a principal proinflammatory effector within HMGB1: sequence-function and structural analyses identify critical residues in the N-terminal HMG box (including the A-box) that mediate receptor recognition and signaling. <cite id="c79c8bab-3">A conserved cysteine in the N-terminal HMG box is required for HMGB1 binding to TLR4 and cytokine stimulation</cite>. 
- Functionally, Box A sequences can potentiate cytokine bioactivity by driving chromatin remodeling (DNA bending) that favors proinflammatory gene transcription and by facilitating HMGB1’s presentation and uptake by immune cells. <cite id="05619fb3-9">An engineered HMGB1 construct carrying tandem HMG B domains promotes tissue repair like wild-type functional HMGB1 but fails to signal through receptors, separating chromatin-remodeling and cytokine-stimulatory functions from repair programs</cite>. 

Antagonistic function of Box A-derived agents and therapeutic rationale
- Importantly, when delivered as an exogenous “dominant-negative” agent, recombinant Box A peptides or A-box–containing scaffolds can antagonize HMGB1 receptor signaling, suppress NF-κB activation, and reduce proinflammatory cytokine production without requiring cell entry, providing a tractable therapeutic strategy. <cite id="c79c8bab-2">Inhibition of HMGB1/RAGE-mediated endocytosis by an HMGB1 antagonist Box A, anti-HMGB1 antibodies, and related agents suppresses inflammation</cite>. 
- Reviews synthesizing preclinical models consistently report benefit from anti-HMGB1 strategies and from recombinant Box A-based antagonists. <cite id="c79c8bab-1">Anti-HMGB1 antibodies and recombinant HMGB1 Box A protein have shown beneficial effects across preclinical inflammatory disease models</cite> <cite id="c79c8bab-9">Exogenous HMGB1 acting via RAGE/TLR can elicit injurious inflammatory responses, establishing a therapeutic target</cite>. 
- The A-box also bears immunogenic epitopes that, when immunogenic, can redirect immunity and impact disease severity: <cite id="c79c8bab-4">an immunogenic peptide within the HMGB1 A-box reversed sepsis lethality and immune tolerance in mice</cite>. 

Preclinical evidence across disease models
- Sepsis/organ failure: As a late “second hit” mediator, extracellular HMGB1 worsens inflammation; sequestration with antibodies or neutralization opens a therapeutic window in cecal ligation and puncture (CLP) and LPS models, reducing TNF/IL-6/IL-1β and improving survival. <cite id="c79c8bab-0">Extracellular HMGB1 acts as a late mediator of experimental sepsis, supporting a wider therapeutic window</cite> <cite id="c79c8bab-9">Blocking HMGB1’s receptor-mediated signaling curbs proinflammatory cytokine release and injurious inflammation</cite>. 
- Inflammatory disorders of the airway and gut: Localized HMGB1 signaling amplifies eosinophilic and cytokine-driven pathology; anti-HMGB1 strategies attenuate inflammation. <cite id="92ea0b42-6">HMGB1 emerges as central to amplifying/modulating inflammation in nasal disorders, regulating cytokine networks through receptor interactions</cite> <cite id="c79c8bab-2">Anti-HMGB1 antibodies and an A-box antagonist suppress inflammation driven by HMGB1/RAGE signaling</cite>. 
- Neuroinflammation and ischemia: By engaging RAGE/TLR, HMGB1 exacerbates glial activation and cytokine release; blocking the HMGB1–RAGE/TLR axis protects neural tissue. <cite id="92ea0b42-8">HMGB1–RAGE binding activates NF-κB and downstream inflammatory factors in multiple contexts</cite>. 
- Engineered A-box constructs and hybrid HMGB1 proteins have refined therapy by separating proinflammatory signaling from tissue-repair functions. <cite id="05619fb3-9">An engineered HMGB1 construct with tandem HMG B boxes repairs tissues as effectively as wild-type full-length HMGB1 but fails to signal through RAGE/TLR, indicating dissection of signaling from reparative roles</cite>. 
- Cancer-related inflammation during therapy: Modulating HMGB1 signaling can reshape macrophage polarization and reduce chemotherapy/radiation-induced inflammatory cascades. <cite id="05619fb3-8">Release of HMGB1 by dying tumor cells licenses dendritic cells; inhibiting HMGB1–TLR4 signaling can dictate outcomes of immune stimulation and inflammation</cite> <cite id="05619fb3-4">HMGB1 in exosomes can induce M2 macrophage polarization by inhibiting NF-κB signaling</cite>. 

Clinical/ translational signals
- Mechanistic biomarkers: Extracellular HMGB1, NF-κB activation, and proinflammatory cytokine storms correlate across human illnesses, motivating targeted therapies. <cite id="05619fb3-7">Transcriptional amplification by NF-κB downstream of HMGB1 contributes to pathophysiology in diverse conditions</cite>. 
- Therapeutic agents under investigation: 
  - Neutralizing anti-HMGB1 antibodies and intravenous immunoglobulin therapies against HMGB1 have shown benefit signals in preclinical sepsis and are being advanced clinically. <cite id="c79c8bab-0">Reviews document a therapeutic window for anti-HMGB1 strategies in experimental sepsis</cite> <cite id="c79c8bab-5">HMGB1 and a cyclic peptide antagonist (pCTS-L) have experimental support as targets to improve survival in sepsis</cite>. 
  - Recombinant A-box–based antagonists and immunogenic Box A peptides have demonstrated reversal of lethality and modulation of tolerance in murine sepsis, supporting translational potential. <cite id="c79c8bab-4">An A-box immunogenic peptide reversed sepsis lethality and induced protective immunity</cite> <cite id="c79c8bab-1">Recombinant Box A protein shows beneficial preclinical activity across inflammatory models</cite>. 
  - Small-molecule inhibitors that interfere with the HMGB1–RAGE/TLR interface, including FR90059 derivatives, have preclinical efficacy; mechanistic understanding via A-box–dependent receptor binding strengthens design. <cite id="c79c8bab-9">Targeted inhibition of HMGB1’s receptor signaling suppresses injurious cytokine responses, validating pharmacologic modulation</cite>. 

Key evidence that Box A modulates proinflammatory cytokines
- Direct genetic/biochemical evidence places critical A-box residues in HMGB1’s cytokine-stimulating function: <cite id="c79c8bab-3">the A-box contains a cysteine critical for TLR4 binding and downstream cytokine induction</cite>. 
- Functional antagonism by A-box–derived agents: <cite id="c79c8bab-2">an “HMGB1 antagonist Box A” blocks HMGB1/RAGE signaling and downstream inflammatory cascades</cite>, indicating that the A-box constitutes a tractable determinant of receptor engagement and cytokine production. 
- Chromatin-remodeling function of Box A enables NF-κB access to inflammatory gene promoters; disrupting this function (e.g., via A-box–targeted antagonism or by using repair-focused, A-box–mutated constructs) diminishes cytokine-inducing signaling while preserving healing programs. <cite id="05619fb3-9">A tandem HMG B-box construct with reduced receptor signaling repairs tissues comparably to wild type, separating cytokine signaling from repair</cite>. 

Safety, practicality, and open questions
- The same Box A sequences that drive inflammation are immunodominant and can be harnessed as vaccines to generate protective immunity in sepsis, suggesting a dual “danger” and “benefit” role dependent on context and delivery. <cite id="c79c8bab-4">A Box A immunogenic peptide reversed sepsis lethality and disrupted immune tolerance</cite>. 
- Box A-based therapies are attractive because they avoid nuclear DNA interactions and can act extracellularly; however, complete clinical efficacy data remain limited, and heterogeneity in HMGB1 biology across tissues and disease stages requires careful targeting. <cite id="05619fb3-0">HMGB1’s nuclear chromatin functions are fundamental, so domain-focused therapy can modulate but may not abolish all biological effects</cite>. 
- Areas to resolve include defining Box A residues that are essential for RAGE vs TLR discrimination, optimizing Box A-derived dominant-negative peptides for potency/safety and delivery (e.g., intranasal, intra-brachial), and conducting large randomized human trials of neutralizing antibodies or small-molecule antagonists in sepsis/ARDS and cytokine-driven syndromes. <cite id="c79c8bab-0">Therapeutic targeting of extracellular HMGB1 has a mechanistic foundation and evidence base in preclinical sepsis, motivating clinical translation</cite>. 

Practical takeaways
- Mechanism: <cite id="92ea0b42-5">Extracellular HMGB1 increases TNF-α/IL-6/IL-1β through NF-κB</cite>, with <cite id="c79c8bab-3">A-box cysteine essential for TLR4 binding</cite> and <cite id="92ea0b42-8">RAGE-driven NF-κB activation</cite>. <cite id="c79c8bab-6">HMGB1 modulates cytokine networks via multiple receptor interactions in inflammatory tissue</cite>. 
- Therapeutic potential: <cite id="05619fb3-9">Disrupting A-box–mediated receptor signaling preserves repair while reducing cytokine storm</cite>, <cite id="c79c8bab-1">recombinant Box A antagonists and anti-HMGB1 antibodies show broad preclinical efficacy</cite>, and <cite id="c79c8bab-4">immunogenic Box A peptides can rescue lethality and reset immune tolerance</cite>. Box A-centric strategies therefore have a mechanistic basis and converging preclinical evidence supporting anti-inflammatory therapy with context-dependent opportunities. <cite id="c79c8bab-5">Targeting HMGB1 and Box A antagonists shows promise to improve sepsis survival</cite>.
