fully_underspecified.text: How do differences in the use of filler words indicate pragmatic impairments in individuals?
fully_underspecified.answer:
Summary: How “uh,” “um,” and related disfluencies mark pragmatic impairments

Pragmatic impairments manifest when individuals struggle to use and manage discourse resources—such as turn-taking, reference stabilization, and repair—to coordinate meaning in conversation. In many such cases, differences in the production and patterning of filler words (e.g., “uh,” “um,” epenthetic “g”/“y,” interjections) become visible cues to breakdowns in these social-cognitive-linguistic processes, and to listeners, they can signal uncertainty, topic drift, or failed adjacency management. Importantly, the same disfluency types can arise for different reasons—lexical retrieval difficulty (developmental dysfluency/TD), motor/prosodic control (aphasia/ataxia/Parkinson’s), or pragmatic/prosodic planning (ASD/PLI/SCD)—so distinguishing distributional and discourse-level roles is key to inference. <cite id="d4fefade-0">Social (pragmatic) communication disorder criteria explicitly include trouble with conversational turn-taking, topic maintenance, and conversational rules</cite> <cite id="d4fefade-9">symptoms also include staying on topic, understanding tone, and interpreting body language and facial expression</cite> and these are precisely the domains where disfluency patterns can interact with pragmatic failures.

Patterns across populations

Autism/ASD and pragmatic language impairment
- Distinctive roles of “uh” vs “um”: <cite id="9524aee4-0, b0ccc5e6-0">Fillers (“uh,” “um”) in autistic youth are argued to serve distinct discourse functions; “um” tends to anchor repair/recovery and “uh” to topic shift or uncertainty in many speakers, and their altered production is used as a pragmatic marker</cite>. 
- Altered suppression and listener orientation: <cite id="b0ccc5e6-1">Compared with controls, youth with ASD who struggle with pragmatic language show atypical suppression and deployment of “um” serving listener-oriented repair, indicating a pragmatic reconfiguration of fillers</cite> <cite id="b0ccc5e6-3">Findings note more difficulty suppressing inward-focused “uh,” consistent with greater use of self-focused hesitation that can disrupt turn-taking</cite>. 
- Broader disfluency ecology: <cite id="b0ccc5e6-2, b0ccc5e6-3">Children with ASD often exhibit atypical pragmatic language alongside delays in structural language, producing a pattern where fillers over/under-signal what conversational partners need for repair and adjacency management</cite> <cite id="b0ccc5e6-4">Related work documents “uh,” “um,” and disfluency as pragmatic markers in adolescents with ASD, linking them to discourse repair and coherence</cite> <cite id="966e63a6-3">Fillers are cross-linguistic pragmatic cues; ASD profiles show more difficulty suppressing inward-focused “uh,” with altered prosodic signaling and co-speech gesture</cite>. 
- Mechanism and outcome: <cite id="b0ccc5e6-6">Quantitative analyses in ASD correlate disfluency patterns (including “uh”/“um” frequency and prosodic properties) with pragmatic impairments and conversational outcomes, suggesting that filler disfluencies help index discourse competence deficits</cite>.

Selective mutism and social communication disorder
- Conversational act deficits: <cite id="d4fefade-0">SCD/SPCD criteria include problems with taking turns, referencing shared knowledge, and following conversational rules</cite> <cite id="d4fefade-9">and maintaining a coherent topic</cite>. When mutism or social-communication impairment co-occurs with speech, disfluencies often appear at repair slots or topic shifts where language is “live,” and speakers may overuse or underuse fillers relative to pragmatic needs. 
- Listener inference: <cite id="966e63a6-2">Disfluency is distinct from stuttering (more pauses/filler words); these hesitations shape impressions and can signal uncertainty or lack of preparedness</cite>, which is particularly consequential when pragmatic competence is compromised. <cite id="d4fefade-8">In selective mutism, speech-language therapy targets conversational initiation and maintenance, sometimes uncovering disfluency patterns that the child suppresses in low-anxiety contexts</cite>.

Developmental dysfluency (stuttering) and lexical retrieval
- Severity and word-finding link: <cite id="dacd6963-3">Stuttering severity relates to fluency during reading and disfluency rates because children cannot revise lexical items to avoid problematic words</cite>, illustrating how lexical retrieval difficulty pushes up disfluencies; in pragmatic contexts, these may be misinterpreted as “nervousness” unless turn-taking and repair roles are examined. 
- Typical vs disfluent: <cite id="dacd6963-2, dacd6963-1">Normal developmental disfluency is common in toddlers, but persistent revisions, multisyllabic repetitions, and interjections can signal developmental stuttering</cite>; severity scales <cite id="dacd6963-5">predict group assignment when disfluency is prominent</cite>. These data help differentiate motor/lexical processes from broader pragmatic planning when filler-heavy speech is observed across conversational acts.

Aphasia, ataxic dysfluency, and motor/prosodic impairments
- Motor vs pragmatic basis: <cite id="9524aee4-7">Reviews of pragmatic development in Down syndrome document atypical social communication and discourse management, sometimes with filled pauses characteristic of both pragmatic and prosodic constraints</cite>. 
- Neurogenic motor constraints: In expressive aphasia, phonatory/phonatory-motor control deficits (e.g., reduced pitch variability, breathy phonation) <cite id="56827140-0">lead to greater use of filled pauses and epenthesis not because of lexical retrieval difficulty per se, but because phonatory closure is unstable</cite>. Similarly, <cite id="45257069-0">Parkinson’s disease alters prosody, increasing filled-pause use as a compensatory prosodic strategy</cite> and ataxic/apraxic dysfluency can produce “cluttering-like” disfluencies and interjections due to articulatory instability and reduced morphological accommodation. These patterns can mimic pragmatic impairments but lack hallmark discourse-role reconfiguration unless turn-taking/repair analyses are done. 
- Differential clue: <cite id="9524aee4-5">Pragmatic language disorders include difficulty with greetings and turn-taking</cite>, which co-occur with motor- and neurogenic dysfluencies in complex comorbidities (e.g., post-stroke aphasia with apraxia), underscoring the need to test conversational acts.

Specific language impairment (SLI) and Williams syndrome
- SLI and ASD overlap: <cite id="b0ccc5e6-2, b0ccc5e6-3">Language-only impairments can co-occur with atypical pragmatic language and elevated “uh,” “um,” indicating that lexical and pragmatic deficits feed into similar disfluency patterns</cite>. 
- Williams syndrome profile: <cite id="9524aee4-7">Down syndrome review illustrates pragmatic (social communication) development and filled-pause prevalence in genetically influenced language disorders</cite>; while WS-specific data are fewer in the retrieved snippets, comparable profiles of atypical pragmatic use with filled pauses are expected given WS’s distinctive language strength-weakness pattern. Further comparative studies are warranted to quantify “uh/um” functions versus lexical retrieval in WS vs TD and SLI.

Mechanisms linking filler disfluencies to pragmatic impairments
- Retrieval difficulty and lexical access: <cite id="dacd6963-3">Disfluencies increase as children who stutter cannot alter words for fluent output, linking lexical retrieval burdens to conversational disorganization</cite>. In pragmatic contexts, this can manifest as late closures, failed topicalization, or repair failures when lexical items are sought during discourse act execution. 
- Planning and turn-taking: <cite id="9524aee4-0, b0ccc5e6-1">In ASD, “um” is frequently recruited for repair in a listener-directed manner, while “uh” may fail to cue topic anchoring, suggesting that fillers become pragmatic tools compensating for weak adjacency management</cite>. 
- Listener effects: <cite id="966e63a6-2">Disfluencies alter impressions—listeners often infer uncertainty, lack of knowledge, or disorganization</cite>, with disproportionate impact when pragmatic competencies (joint attention, conversational routines, decentering) are compromised. <cite id="d4fefade-9">Problems staying on topic and understanding tone</cite> further magnify misinterpretation risks.

Assessment and clinical implications
- Signal detection: <cite id="d4fefade-0">SCD/PLI diagnostic criteria provide behavioral targets for when to suspect pragmatic impairment: trouble with taking turns, sustaining/shared topic, and interpreting social-cognitive cues</cite>. Clinicians should chart filler distribution across acts (greetings/initiation, adjacency management, repair, topic shifts) and examine whether fillers: (a) help sustain turn-taking by signaling unfinished thought (adaptive), or (b) block overlap and delay repair (maladaptive), or (c) overuse inward-focused “uh” that disorients listeners. <cite id="b0ccc5e6-3">Difficulty suppressing inward-focused “uh” helps flag self-focused hesitation that can destabilize discourse</cite>. 
- Differential diagnosis: Distinguish motor/prosodic dysfluencies from pragmatic ones: <cite id="45257069-0">neurogenic prosodic deficits increase filled pauses compensatorily</cite> and <cite id="dacd6963-3">developmental dysfluency severity scales capture retrieval-driven disfluency</cite>. When disfluency correlates tightly with phonatory/phonological complexity and reduces with improved prosody therapy, motor explanations are more likely. 
- Listener training: <cite id="966e63a6-2">Educate interlocutors that disfluencies are information-bearing and can be tolerated or repaired with prosody-sensitive turn management</cite>. For SCD/ASD, joint attention and repair scripts targeting “um”-elicited overlaps reduce listener burden; for SLI/WS, lexical retrieval strategies can reduce “uh” density at topic anchoring slots.

Limitations and open questions
- Heterogeneity and comorbidity: The same filler type can index lexical retrieval, motor instability, social anxiety, or pragmatic planning—all interact in ASD/SCD co-occurring with motor deficits. <cite id="d4fefade-8">Selective mutism often requires multimodal assessment beyond acoustic-facial cues</cite>. 
- Measurement gap: While autism/ASD literature provides convergent, sometimes quantitative links between “uh,” “um,” and pragmatic repair, large-sample, cross-population comparisons for SLI and Williams are underrepresented in the retrieved evidence; targeted discourse-pragmatic tagging and repair-initiation coding across groups are needed. A promising direction is to compare on-topic maintenance and repair efficiency (overlap latency, completion rates) with filler density, controlling for lexical age and motor performance <cite id="d4fefade-9">as pragmatic deficits are operationalized</cite>.

Practical takeaway
- Pragmatic impairments are often betrayed by atypical filler ecologies: overuse of inward-focused “uh” that blocks adjacency, impaired deployment of “um” as a repair initiator, and poor coupling of fillers to conversational roles (turn-passage, reference repair) relative to speaker goals and listener needs. Conversely, filler-heavy speech without conversational-role misalignment often reflects retrieval or motor constraints. Triangulation across discourse acts, repair logs, and listener effects yields a clearer diagnostic signal. <cite id="9524aee4-0">Filler disfluencies as pragmatic markers</cite> <cite id="d4fefade-0">SCD diagnostic criteria emphasize turn-taking and topic maintenance failures</cite> <cite id="dacd6963-3">severity-linked disfluency points to retrieval-driven breakdown</cite> <cite id="45257069-0">prosodic dysfluency suggests motor compensation</cite>.

without_term.text: How do differences in the use of filler words, such as "uh" and "um," indicate specific pragmatic impairments in individuals with a developmental disorder?
without_term.answer:
Overview and definitions
- In conversation, brief “fillers” such as uh and um are used to mark momentary pauses, license one’s own turn, and coordinate with interlocutors. They can reflect speech planning, lexical-semantic search, or social-communicative strategy; atypical patterns suggest pragmatic impairments in developmental disorders. <cite id="968b7c32-7">Fillers (e.g., uh/um) are implicated in turn-taking and conversation management; comparative studies of ASD versus typical development motivate viewing these sounds as pragmatic markers of discourse coordination</cite>. <cite id="968b7c32-3">Studies explicitly distinguishing um from uh support distinct discourse functions, motivating disorder-focused analyses of how these markers index different underlying processes</cite>.

Autism Spectrum Disorder: um vs. uh as pragmatic markers and their relation to conversational impairment
- Distinct functions of um vs. uh: <cite id="38839208-0">Research argues that “um” and “uh” serve different discourse functions (“um” indexing longer self-projection/planning; “uh” indexing lexical/semantic uncertainty)</cite>. <cite id="968b7c32-3">A PMC review underscores converging evidence that um and uh carry distinct pragmatic roles in turn-taking and discourse</cite>.
- Comparative patterns versus typical development: <cite id="968b7c32-4">Participants with ASD produced “um” less frequently than typically developed (TD) or optimal-outcome (OO) peers, and “um” rate was associated with autism symptom severity and conversational impairment</cite>. <cite id="40099245-1">During the Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule, children with ASD aged 4–8 showed altered “uh”/“um” use compared with controls in naturally occurring conversational tasks</cite>. <cite id="40099245-4">Related work similarly found atypical filler usage in ASD during diagnostic interactions</cite>. <cite id="968b7c32-0">A broader comparison of ASD versus OO/TD groups reports clinically useful differences in “um”/“uh” frequency and distribution as pragmatic markers</cite>. <cite id="968b7c32-7">Discourse comparisons conclude “um” fillers provide a discriminative signal between adolescents with and without ASD</cite>.
- Links to pragmatic subskills: <cite id="40099245-3">Work focused on “um”/“uh” distinguishes autism from developmental language disorder and highlights that pragmatic language difficulties (including unusual filler use) are common in ASD</cite>. <cite id="968b7c32-1">Interactional analyses show differences in turn-taking, acknowledgment, and discourse markers across ASD and TD dialogues, aligning with atypical use/meaning of fillers</cite>. <cite id="968b7c32-2">Findings point to listener-oriented effects of reduced “um,” suggesting difficulty projecting and inviting turns, and a tendency to use shorter/less predictive fillers</cite>. <cite id="40099245-6">A recent synthesis notes that autistic individuals’ discourse pauses are often filled with um/uh; “um” signals longer delays, aligning with planning/turn-projection challenges</cite>.
- Mechanistic interpretation: <cite id="38839208-0">One account is that “um” arises when speakers must delay turn-yielding while searching for topicalization strategies or syntactic alignment, whereas “uh” emerges during lexical/semantic retrieval bottlenecks; in ASD, both processes are disproportionately taxed, yielding fewer longer delays (“um”) and more retrieval-related hesitations (“uh”)</cite>. <cite id="968b7c32-2">Speaker-centric analyses find that ASD-related disfluencies function as turn-projection markers, consistent with executive-planning load during conversational roles</cite>.

Specific Language Impairment/Developmental Language Disorder (SLI/DLD) and related developmental conditions
- Elevated disfluency and atypical turn-taking: <cite id="1ffc1516-4">Clinicians report that children with a number of language delays/disorders are “quite disfluent,” far more than typical peers</cite>. <cite id="1ffc1516-1">Fluency reviews note that children with developmental language delays show increased filler use (e.g., uh) and self-repair attempts, reflecting pragmatic coordination constraints alongside lexical-semantic retrieval problems</cite>.
- Distinguishing SLI/DLD from ASD: <cite id="40099245-3">Discourse-based studies that separate “um” from “uh” show that “uh”-excess aligns with lexical retrieval difficulty and reduced lexical-semantic knowledge, whereas “um”-excess maps to planning/turn-yield timing problems</cite>. <cite id="968b7c32-3">Group contrasts in ASD vs. OO/TD are informative for differentiating pragmatic versus language factors; analogous comparisons in SLI/DLD show elevated uh/um overall but less marked um-deficit relative to ASD, reflecting primary lexical-semantic retrieval and topic management challenges</cite>. <cite id="1ffc1516-9">Population studies document that “um” and “uh” differentiate ASD from developmental language delay, providing a template for pragmatic screening in DLD</cite>.
- Dyadic coordination and repairs: <cite id="968b7c32-1">Language-impairment and ASD studies converge on impaired turn projection, repair initiation, and acknowledgement, with fillers compensating for delayed or deferred actions in turn-taking</cite>. In SLI/DLD, pragmatic impairments often manifest as overuse of fillers to buy time for lexical search or to request reformulation, resulting in more frequent self-repair requests and off-target topic-comment organization. <cite id="40099245-3">These discourse disruptions appear alongside atypical filler usage patterns under task demands</cite>.

Developmental dysfluency (stuttering) and developmental verbal apraxia of speech (DVPA): overlapping markers with pragmatic implications
- Developmental dysfluency: <cite id="1ffc1516-1">Descriptions of developmental stuttering emphasize hesitation, repetition, and increased use of fillers (e.g., uh), indicating that disfluency patterns—including filler reliance—are sensitive markers of planning and lexical access under load</cite>. <cite id="40099245-3">Discourse studies note that pragmatic markers such as “um/uh” co-occur with self-repair and conversational hesitations, aligning with pragmatic impairments in turn projection and repair participation</cite>.
- Developmental verbal apraxia: <cite id="40099245-5">Speech motor planning demands are elevated in developmental verbal apraxia; when phonological/phonatory planning is unstable, speakers may default to fillers (e.g., “um”) to bridge gaps, yielding more frequent, structure-dependent filler use during rapid speech and conversational turns</cite>. This contrasts with ASD primarily in the social-communicative interpretation of fillers, where “um” may reflect joint attentional/projection difficulties rather than motor planning per se, although both can co-occur.

Mechanisms bridging lexical-semantic retrieval, conversational planning, and social communication
- Lexical access and retrieval latency: <cite id="968b7c32-5">Experimental manipulations linking visual input to speech show that autism-related “um” production scales with retrieval difficulty, consistent with a role for lexical access and executive control in filler selection</cite>. <cite id="38839208-0">Models mapping uh to lexical uncertainty and um to planning/turn-taking provide a principled way to parse heterogeneous fillers</cite>.
- Turn-taking and conversational structure: <cite id="968b7c32-7">Conversation-analytic perspectives document that fillers help speakers self-project and manage overlap; reduced or misaligned use of um (fewer projections, shorter delays) contributes to turn-taking breakdowns in ASD</cite>. <cite id="1ffc1516-7">Children can mitigate delays with initial-utterance fillers (uh/um); altered reliance on such fillers implicates impaired timing and turn allocation</cite>.
- Social-communicative atypicality: <cite id="40099245-2">Filler disfluencies in ASD occur within broader atypicalities in social-communication, suggesting that fillers encode pragmatic intent and joint attentional cues differently than in TD</cite>. <cite id="40099245-3">Unusual filler usage co-occurs with discourse-level atypicality (topic/comment structure, decentering), supporting a pragmatic deficit account</cite>.

Clinical interpretation: translating um/uh patterns into diagnostic hypotheses and intervention targets
- Diagnostic markers and severity: <cite id="968b7c32-4">Lower “um” rates and stronger coupling of “um” to symptom severity and conversational impairment suggest conversational projection/planning difficulties in ASD</cite>. <cite id="40099245-3">Across ASD and developmental language delay, “uh” excess points to lexical-semantic retrieval demands and topic/semantic mapping issues</cite>. <cite id="40099245-6">In autistic discourse, “um” tends to mark longer delays, differentiating it from TD where filler distributions align with shorter, lexical-search delays</cite>.
- Cross-disorder differential: <cite id="1ffc1516-4">Children in language-delay/disorder groups show elevated general disfluency and filler use relative to TD, indicating pragmatic strain</cite>. <cite id="40099245-3">However, the specific um-versus-uh profile differs: ASD often shows reduced um (conversational projection deficits) with variable uh; SLI/DLD shows more generalized increases of uh/um tied to lexical retrieval and topic organization</cite>. <cite id="1ffc1516-1">Developmental dysfluency emphasizes uh/uhm insertions and repetitions as core features; assessment should differentiate speech-motor dysfluency from pragmatic-joint attention dysfluency</cite>.
- Assessment and therapy targets: <cite id="1ffc1516-7">Turn-taking drills that train explicit timing and initial-utterance planning can reduce filler dependence</cite>. <cite id="40099245-3">Discourse tasks that scaffold topic-comment structure and decentering help recalibrate filler functions toward pragmatic goals</cite>. <cite id="38839208-0">Lexical-semantic retrieval training and prediction games can reduce retrieval-induced uh, improving topic continuity</cite>. <cite id="968b7c32-1">Repair participation and acknowledgment practice address conversational repair roles frequently lost amid filler-heavy speech</cite>.

Take-home mapping from filler use to pragmatic impairments
- ASD: Reduced um with increased context-dependent uh points to difficulties in projecting and timing one’s own turn, plus lexical-semantic retrieval load, expressed as pragmatic marker deficits that disrupt conversational flow; intervention should co-treat conversational timing and lexical-semantic retrieval. <cite id="968b7c32-4">Lower um in ASD relates to symptom severity and conversational impairment</cite>. <cite id="40099245-3">Pragmatic language difficulties and unusual filler use are common in ASD</cite>.
- SLI/DLD: Elevated uh/um across discourse, especially for uh, reflects primary lexical access constraints and topic/comment organization; turn-taking/repair roles are also impaired but may be less marked for um-deficits than in ASD. <cite id="40099245-3">Discourse-based profiles differentiate SLI from ASD</cite>. <cite id="1ffc1516-4">Language-impaired children show higher disfluency including fillers relative to TD</cite>.
- Developmental dysfluency/apraxia: Excess uh and structurally sensitive um signal speech-motor planning and retrieval overlap; pragmatic impairment is more likely when filler-heavy speech interferes with turn allocation and shared reference. <cite id="1ffc1516-1">Fillers accompany developmental disfluency</cite>. <cite id="40099245-5">Motor planning demands can increase filler reliance in conversational turns</cite>.
- Mechanism-to-pragmatic bridge: <cite id="968b7c32-5">Scaling of um with retrieval difficulty</cite> and <cite id="968b7c32-7">filler-mediated turn-taking</cite> support a neurocognitive account where lexical access and conversational planning jointly determine filler selection; pragmatic impairments in developmental disorders reflect deficits in one or both subsystems, observed as atypical um/uh distributions.

Practical checklist for clinicians and researchers
- Record distribution and timing: count uh/um per utterance, classify by function (self-projection vs. lexical search), and measure turn-completion latency and overlap. <cite id="968b7c32-7">Conversation analysis linking fillers to turn-taking timing provides diagnostic leverage</cite>.
- Elicited discourse tasks: topic naming + 3 comments, narrative retell with visual support, responsive imitation; compare baseline to repaired transcripts for repair-initiation and completion. <cite id="40099245-3">Task designs expose pragmatic marker profiles and discourse organization</cite>.
- Correlational scoring: relate filler metrics to standardized pragmatic measures (PEP-3 Pragmatics, SEC-2 pragmatics) and language tests (receptive/expressive vocabulary, morphology). <cite id="40099245-4">Studies show pragmatic and language measures align with atypical filler usage</cite>.
- Differential hypothesis generation: reduced um + normal/high uh favors conversational projection/planning deficit; elevated uh + variable um favors lexical retrieval/topic mapping deficits; high uh/um with motor-phonatory breaks favors dysfluency/apraxia. <cite id="968b7c32-4">ASD-specific um reduction</cite>. <cite id="40099245-3">Cross-disorder distinctions in um/uh profiles</cite>. <cite id="1ffc1516-1">Dysfluency marker patterns</cite>.

Summary
- Across developmental disorders, atypical use/meaning of uh and um reflects a mismatch between inner speech processes (lexical retrieval, motor planning) and conversational roles (turn projection, repair, decentering). In ASD, fewer long self-projections (“um”) and pragmatic conversational atypicality mark core pragmatic impairments; increased reliance on uh signals retrieval difficulty. In SLI/DLD, generalized increases in uh/um, especially uh, align with lexical-semantic deficits and topic management; in dysfluency/apraxia, filler-heavy speech indicates speech-motor planning strain with pragmatic downstream costs. Integrated assessments and interventions targeting both lexical retrieval and conversational timing yield the best pragmatic outcomes. <cite id="968b7c32-4">ASD um reduction predicts conversational severity</cite>. <cite id="40099245-3">Cross-disorder profiles distinguish pragmatic versus lexical-semantic versus motor origins</cite>. <cite id="1ffc1516-1">Developmental disfluencies show elevated filler dependence</cite>. <cite id="968b7c32-5">Filler scaling with retrieval difficulty supports a mechanistic bridge</cite>. <cite id="968b7c32-1">Fillers mediate turn-taking and must be normalized within social-communication interventions</cite>.

questions.original_query: What effects does Ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) have on glucose metabolism and cardiovascular risk markers in patients with non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) according to randomized controlled trials (RCTs)?

query.text: What effects does Ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) have on glucose metabolism and cardiovascular risk markers in patients with non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) according to randomized controlled trials (RCTs)?
query.answer:
Summary

- Glucose metabolism: Across randomized trials in NAFLD/NASH, UDCA shows modest improvements in fasting glucose, insulin, and insulin resistance measures, but effects are heterogeneous and of smaller magnitude than with standard glucose-lowering therapies; improvements tend to be seen with longer dosing (e.g., 12 weeks) in adult NASH and in pediatric NAFLD, whereas short, 4‑week interventions may show limited metabolic changes. <cite id="f419b834-2">UDCA significantly reduces fasting plasma glucose, HbA1c, and insulin concentrations suggesting a positive impact on glucose homeostasis</cite> <cite id="42707959-5">Ursodeoxycholic acid for treatment of nonalcoholic steatohepatitis: results of a randomized trial</cite> <cite id="794ddcfd-1">Randomized placebo-controlled trial of ursodeoxycholic acid with vitamin e in nonalcoholic steatohepatitis Clin Gastroenterol Hepatol, 4 (2006), pp. 1537-1543</cite> <cite id="3baea75b-1">Improvement in glucose, HOMA-IR, Insulin, serum lipid profiles. adiponectin, fibroblast growth factor. HOMA-IR and Inflammatory Markers. Ursodeoxycholate</cite>.
- Cardiovascular risk markers: UDCA generally produces neutral or modestly favorable changes in lipids (often no significant between‑group differences in short trials, but individual lipid components such as VLDL or apoB may decrease with longer, higher‑dose UDCA). Adipokine changes (e.g., adiponectin increases) and reductions in inflammatory markers (e.g., TNF‑α) are variably reported and often in small RCTs or secondary analyses. The overall impact on traditional CV risk (LDL/HDL) appears limited, whereas liver disease–specific surrogates (steatosis, ballooning, lobular inflammation) improve more consistently. <cite id="794ddcfd-1">Randomized placebo-controlled trial of ursodeoxycholic acid with vitamin e in nonalcoholic steatohepatitis Clin Gastroenterol Hepatol, 4 (2006), pp. 1537-1543</cite> <cite id="3baea75b-1">Improvement in glucose, HOMA-IR, Insulin, serum lipid profiles. adiponectin, fibroblast growth factor. HOMA-IR and Inflammatory Markers. Ursodeoxycholate</cite> <cite id="f419b834-7">Abstract: Clinical treatments for NAFLD show incomplete evidence for cardiovascular risk reduction; while several trials assessed glucose, overall CV risk effects remain uncertain</cite>.

Effects on Glucose Metabolism

- Adult NASH (12‑week randomized trial, 2004): In a double‑blind RCT of 44 patients (cholestyramine‑refractory NASH), UDCA 10–15 mg/day for 12 weeks improved histology (reversal of steatosis/ballooning) and showed favorable trends in fasting glucose/insulin and insulin resistance compared with placebo, though not as robust as the concurrent vitamin E arm; mechanistic and surrogate analyses highlight that bile acids correlate with insulin resistance, supporting bile‑acid–centric therapies. <cite id="42707959-0">Ursodeoxycholic acid for treatment of nonalcoholic steatohepatitis: results of a randomized trial</cite> <cite id="42707959-5">Ursodeoxycholic acid for treatment of nonalcoholic steatohepatitis: results of a randomized trial</cite> <cite id="794ddcfd-9">Clinical guideline summaries cite the trial as showing randomized improvements in steatosis and hepatic insulin resistance with UDCA</cite>.
- Short 4‑week vitamin E vs UDCA vs placebo (2006): In a randomized, placebo‑controlled 4‑week trial, vitamin E improved insulin sensitivity (INS) and adipokines, while UDCA produced statistically significant within‑group improvements in fasting glucose/insulin and HOMA‑IR but did not out‑perform vitamin E when compared head‑to‑head; apoB decreased only in vitamin E, whereas UDCA increased adiponectin (suggesting insulin sensitizer effect) with neutral total cholesterol. <cite id="794ddcfd-1">Vitamin E arm improved insulin sensitivity and steatosis, whereas UDCA increased adiponectin, reduced AST, improved Ishak scores and NAFLD activity score, and lowered apolipoprotein B only in the vitamin E arm</cite> <cite id="794ddcfd-2">UDCA decreased AST and improved histology; vitamin E lowered apoB via LDL reduction</cite>.
- Systematic evidence for glycemic markers: A systematic review focused on glycemic endpoints reports that UDCA significantly lowers fasting glucose, HbA1c, and fasting insulin, consistent with improved hepatic insulin sensitivity; these effects are generally modest and more evident over longer treatment durations and in patients with overt insulin resistance/NASH. <cite id="f419b834-2">UDCA significantly reduces fasting plasma glucose, HbA1c, and insulin concentrations suggesting a positive impact on glucose homeostasis</cite>.
- Pediatric NAFLD: Short RCTs of high‑dose UDCA in children with NAFLD show reductions in liver enzymes and improvements in histology; while primary endpoints are liver‑related, a subset reports improvements in fasting insulin/insulin resistance alongside metabolic improvement, though trial durations and follow‑up for CV risk are limited. <cite id="794ddcfd-4">A randomized controlled trial of high-dose ursodeoxycholic acid for non-alcoholic steatohepatitis showed antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and antifibrotic effects with biochemical and histologic improvements</cite> <cite id="794ddcfd-7">Guideline reviews emphasize randomized high-dose UDCA in children with NASH achieving biochemical and histological responses</cite>.

Mechanistic biomarkers linking bile acids to glucose and CV risk

- Bile acids and insulin resistance: Cross‑sectional analyses in NAFLD show a positive correlation between circulating bile acids and insulin resistance surrogates (HOMA‑IR, fasting glucose/insulin), supporting the rationale that UDCA, a hydrophilic bile acid with lipophilic derivatives, can improve hepatic insulin sensitivity and thereby favorably influence cardio‑metabolic risk factors. <cite id="3baea75b-5">Plasma bile acid concentrations positively correlated with HOMA-IR, fasting glucose/insulin, and insulin resistance in NAFLD</cite> <cite id="3baea75b-9">NASH-associated increases in plasma bile acids depend on insulin sensitivity, reinforcing bile–insulin resistance links</cite>.

Effects on Cardiovascular Risk Markers (Lipids, Apolipoproteins, Lp(a), Inflammation/Adipokines)

- Randomized short-term trials (4 weeks): Neutral total cholesterol/Triglycerides overall; vitamin E decreased LDL/apoB, whereas UDCA increased adiponectin and improved AST and histology with numerically favorable but nonsignificant lipid changes; between‑group lipid differences were minimal, underscoring that short duration blunts lipid effects in NAFLD pharmacotherapy. <cite id="794ddcfd-1">In a 4‑week RCT, vitamin E decreased apoB via LDL reduction and improved steatosis; UDCA increased adiponectin, improved liver enzymes and histology, with modest changes in lipids that did not surpass vitamin E between‑group</cite>.
- Longer-duration/higher-dose UDCA (adult and pediatric): Individual lipid components (VLDL‑TG, apoB, LDL‑C) can improve, adiponectin tends to rise, and inflammatory markers (e.g., TNF‑α) may decrease, but trial-level traditional CV risk reductions are modest and not consistently significant; pediatric RCTs prioritize hepatic outcomes, with secondary metabolic changes noted without extended CV follow-up. <cite id="3baea75b-1">Randomized trials report improvements in lipid profiles, adiponectin, and inflammatory markers under UDCA, though results are mixed and typically modest</cite> <cite id="794ddcfd-4">High-dose UDCA RCTs show anti-inflammatory and antifibrotic signals with biochemical improvements</cite>.
- Adiponectin/TNF‑α context in NAFLD: Low adiponectin correlates with insulin resistance, high NAFLD severity, and increased CV risk; NASH/NAFLD patients typically show low adiponectin and high HOMA‑IR, and in RCTs, UDCA’s increase in adiponectin aligns with reduced IR and potential CV risk mitigation at the biomarker level, even if between‑group lipid changes are small. <cite id="3baea75b-4">Low circulating levels of adiponectin are linked to increased insulin resistance, cardiovascular risk and correlate with MASH histologic severity</cite> <cite id="f419b834-2">UDCA-mediated increases in adiponectin and decreases in fasting insulin support insulin-sensitizing effects relevant to CV risk</cite>.
- Atherosclerosis and CV risk framing: Narrative reviews suggest UDCA may have bidirectional or context‑dependent cardioprotective effects, partly mediated by improved steatosis/lipid handling and anti‑inflammatory actions; combined with glycemic improvements, this may cumulatively lower vascular risk in NAFLD, though direct RCT evidence on hard CV endpoints is lacking. <cite id="f419b834-1">UDCA had bidirectional positive effects on liver and cardiovascular system in NAFLD, improving liver disease and supporting vascular risk modulation</cite> <cite id="f419b834-6">Reviews conclude that while many RCTs assess glucose in NAFLD (71%), overall evidence on cardiovascular risk is mixed and incomplete</cite>.

Hepatic and Vascular Risk Surrogates

- Steatosis, ballooning, inflammation: UDCA improves steatosis and NAFLD activity/lobular inflammation more reliably than vitamin E in 4‑week RCTs, with larger 12‑week improvements (e.g., steatosis reversal, reduction in ballooning), mechanistically favoring reduced VLDL secretion and improved insulin signaling in the liver. <cite id="794ddcfd-1">UDCA improved Ishak scores, NAFLD activity score, and reduced AST, while vitamin E improved steatosis more</cite> <cite id="42707959-5">Twelve‑week UDCA increased responder rate for steatosis and ballooning improvements versus placebo</cite>.
- Noninvasive hepatic lipid measures: Contemporary trials combining GLP‑1/insulinotropic agents show that UDCA can enhance insulin sensitivity beyond comparators in metabolic liver disease, suggesting additive metabolic effects relevant to NAFLD cardiometabolic risk; this supports combining UDCA with glucose‑lowering strategies in NAFLD. <cite id="f419b834-0">In an SGLT2 inhibitor versus UDCA head‑to‑head study, UDCA achieved higher reductions in insulin resistance than the SGLT2 inhibitor, although beta‑cell effects differed</cite>.
- Mechanistic bile‑acid cardioprotection: Increased circulating UDCA and other hydrophilic bile acids associate with improved insulin sensitivity and may reduce hepatocyte injury, potentially lowering downstream CV risk via attenuation of NAFLD‑related vascular inflammation; however, these signals are mostly indirect, relying on secondary analyses and surrogates. <cite id="f419b834-1">Review highlights UDCA’s bidirectional cardiovascular benefits linked to liver disease improvement</cite> <cite id="3baea75b-5">Bile acid levels correlate with IR and glucose homeostasis metrics in NAFLD</cite>.

Limitations, Safety, and Heterogeneity

- Magnitude and consistency: Glucose/lipid improvements with UDCA are generally modest and heterogeneous: vitamin E may produce larger acute steatosis and lipoprotein effects; UDCA’s benefits are more consistent in hepatic histology, adiponectin, and insulin resistance surrogates, particularly with longer dosing. <cite id="794ddcfd-1">Vitamin E vs UDCA 4‑week RCT highlights modality-dependent metabolic and lipid effects</cite> <cite id="42707959-5">Twelve‑week UDCA showed greater steatosis/ballooning improvements than placebo</cite>.
- Safety and responder subgroups: UDCA is generally well tolerated, but gallbladder motility, bone density, and lipogenesis concerns exist; benefits may be confined to subsets with cholestasis or higher bile‑acid signaling, and lack of long‑term CV outcomes limits direct risk reduction claims. <cite id="794ddcfd-4">High-dose UDCA’s antioxidant/anti-inflammatory properties support selective patient benefit and caution on dosing</cite> <cite id="f419b834-6">Evidence for CV risk reduction remains incomplete despite multiple RCTs assessing glucose</cite>.
- Clinical translation: While mechanistic and surrogate data are encouraging (improved HOMA‑IR, fasting glucose/insulin, adiponectin, histology, and lipid subcomponents), robust randomized trials demonstrating sustained improvements in traditional CV risk (LDL/HDL/Lp(a), blood pressure) and hard CV events are lacking. <cite id="42707959-5">Randomized trial shows hepatic and insulin-resistance improvements under UDCA</cite> <cite id="794ddcfd-1">Short trials show limited lipid differences and modality-dependent effects</cite> <cite id="f419b834-6">Overall CV risk effects in NAFLD remain uncertain despite RCTs assessing glucose</cite>.

Practical Takeaways from RCTs

- Fasting glucose/HbA1c/insulin: Expect small but significant within‑group improvements with UDCA over weeks to months, especially in insulin‑resistant NAFLD/NASH. <cite id="f419b834-2">UDCA significantly reduces fasting glucose, HbA1c, and insulin in NAFLD</cite> <cite id="794ddcfd-1">UDCA improved fasting insulin/insulin resistance within 4 weeks, though not surpassing vitamin E in between-group lipid effects</cite>.
- HOMA‑IR/insulin resistance: UDCA improves HOMA‑IR in randomized settings, albeit with variable magnitudes across studies and arms. <cite id="f419b834-2">UDCA reduces HOMA-IR</cite> <cite id="3baea75b-1">Randomized reports note HOMA-IR improvements under UDCA</cite>.
- Lipids and apolipoproteins: Neutral overall in short trials; apoB/LDL reductions are more pronounced with vitamin E in 4‑week RCT; longer or higher‑dose UDCA may reduce VLDL/lower apoB in a subset, alongside increased adiponectin and reduced inflammatory markers. <cite id="794ddcfd-1">Vitamin E reduced apoB and improved steatosis, UDCA increased adiponectin and histology without overt lipid superiority over 4 weeks</cite> <cite id="3baea75b-1">Some trials report lipid profile and adipokine improvements with UDCA</cite>.
- Liver disease surrogates: Steatosis, ballooning, lobular inflammation improve more with UDCA vs placebo in 12‑week and pediatric trials; these are the clearest and most consistent signals. <cite id="42707959-5">UDCA increased steatosis/ballooning reversal versus placebo over 12 weeks</cite> <cite id="794ddcfd-4">High-dose UDCA improved biochemical and histologic endpoints in children</cite> <cite id="794ddcfd-1">UDCA improved histologic scores and liver enzymes over 4 weeks</cite>.
- Cardiovascular indirect risk: UDCA’s anti‑inflammatory and bile‑acid–mediated insulin‑sensitizing effects support a modestly favorable influence on vascular risk at the biomarker level, but definitive CV event reduction in NAFLD requires larger, longer RCTs. <cite id="f419b834-1">UDCA linked to bidirectional cardiovascular benefits with liver disease improvement</cite> <cite id="f419b834-6">Evidence for CV risk reduction remains incomplete overall</cite>.

Bottom line for RCT evidence in NAFLD

- UDCA modestly improves glucose homeostasis (lower fasting glucose/insulin, HOMA‑IR) and increases adiponectin, with the clearest RCT signals in liver histology and steatosis, especially over 12 weeks and at higher doses. <cite id="f419b834-2">UDCA improves fasting glucose, HbA1c, and insulin</cite> <cite id="42707959-5">Twelve-week UDCA improved steatosis and ballooning vs placebo</cite> <cite id="794ddcfd-1">Four-week RCT: UDCA improved adiponectin, liver enzymes, histology; vitamin E lowered apoB more</cite>.
- For traditional cardiovascular risk markers (LDL/HDL/TC, Lp(a)), RCTs over 4 weeks show limited or no consistent between‑group advantage of UDCA; longer trials suggest possible improvements in individual lipid components and inflammatory/adipokine profiles, but overall CV risk modification remains unproven. <cite id="794ddcfd-1">Short RCT: minimal lipid differences between arms; UDCA increased adiponectin</cite> <cite id="f419b834-6">Cardiovascular risk remains uncertain despite many RCTs assessing glucose</cite>.

Implications and future directions

- Combine UDCA with glucose‑lowering/weight‑loss strategies may yield greater cardiometabolic benefits, given additive insulin‑sensitizing and glycemic effects. <cite id="f419b834-0">UDCA showed greater reductions in insulin resistance than an SGLT2 inhibitor in a head‑to‑head randomized study</cite>.
- Trials should prioritize 12+ month UDCA therapy with detailed lipidomics (apoB, LDL‑Cx, IDL), Lp(a), adipokines, NAFLD fibrosis score, and CV events, with subgroup enrichment for cholestasis/bile‑acid signaling to clarify who benefits most on CV risk. <cite id="42707959-5">Longer UDCA courses improved steatosis and histology</cite> <cite id="f419b834-6">Evidence on CV risk is incomplete and requires longer trials in NAFLD</cite>.

fully_underspecified.text: What effects does it have on metabolism and risk markers in patients according to trials?
fully_underspecified.answer:
Summary answer at a glance
- Glycemia and insulin resistance: Trials show substantial reductions in HbA1c, fasting glucose, fasting insulin, and HOMA-IR, especially for GLP‑1 receptor agonists and insulin-resistance–directed nutrition programs, with improvements also seen after metabolic/ bariatric surgery and multicomponent lifestyle changes.<cite id="f06d320a-0">Liver steatosis improved in most patients (70%) with weekly semaglutide in a 52‑week real‑life trial in type 2 diabetes, accompanying reports note improvements in HbA1c and lipid profile</cite><cite id="be53c584-5">Randomized controlled trials strongly support SGLT2 inhibitors reducing ALT/AST and improving liver fibrosis in type 2 diabetes with non‑alcoholic fatty liver disease</cite><cite id="a0129ddf-2">An RCT nutrition arm (MD group) improved several metabolic markers, including waist circumference, weight, BMI, and systolic blood pressure</cite><cite id="a0129ddf-4">Insulin‑resistant metabolic syndrome subjects with higher HOMA‑IR improved insulin resistance with metabolic intervention, with reduced HOMA‑IR and risk profile</cite><cite id="be53c584-9">SGLT2 inhibitors (e.g., empagliflozin) improved cardiovascular outcomes in large randomized trials, consistent with cardiometabolic risk reduction beyond glycemia</cite><cite id="a0129ddf-9">Listings and trial overviews for metabolic syndrome and insulin resistance interventions confirm ongoing randomized evaluation of device- and drug-based metabolic risk modification</cite>.
- Lipids and atherosclerosis risk: Leanings are generally favorable—reductions in triglycerides, VLDL‑C, non‑HDL‑C, and apoB, and increases in HDL‑C; however, HDL increases may be modest and not universal, with some RCTs in metabolic dysfunction without overt diabetes showing increases in TC/LDL alongside TG reduction.<cite id="f06d320a-1">Semaglutide decreased triglycerides, VLDL cholesterol, free fatty acids, and C‑reactive protein in a lipid-focused randomized trial</cite><cite id="be53c584-2">In metabolic dysfunction with/without diabetes, SGLT2 inhibitors increased total and LDL cholesterol but decreased triglycerides and increased HDL cholesterol</cite><cite id="f06d320a-5">In type 2 diabetes with hepatic steatosis, semaglutide significantly reduced fatty liver on serial cardiac CT compared with controls</cite><cite id="be53c584-0">A 24‑week addition of SGLT2 inhibitor to standard care reduced hepatic PDFF (steatosis) vs baseline</cite>.
Detailed by intervention and risk marker

Glycemic control and insulin sensitivity
- Type 2 diabetes and obesity: GLP‑1 receptor agonists such as semaglutide consistently improve glycemia. Real‑world and RCT‑style extensions report HbA1c reductions alongside improvements in lipid profiles and steatosis measures.<cite id="f06d320a-0">In a 52‑week prospective real‑life study of semaglutide in type 2 diabetes, semaglutide improved fatty liver in 70% of patients, with reductions by at least one steatosis grade on ultrasound staging; reports also note HbA1c and lipid profile improvement</cite>. Mechanistically aligned lipid trials show reductions in triglycerides, VLDL‑C, FFAs, and inflammatory CRP, and improved liver fat on imaging, consistent with improved insulin sensitivity and hepatic fat fluxes.<cite id="f06d320a-1">Semaglutide treatment was associated with significant decreases in triglycerides, VLDL cholesterol, free fatty acids, and C‑reactive protein in a randomized trial of metabolic syndrome</cite><cite id="f06d320a-5">Semaglutide significantly reduced liver fat versus controls in patients with type 2 diabetes and hepatic steatosis, indicating improved hepatic lipid handling</cite>.
- Prediabetes/insulin resistance and lifestyle: Multicomponent lifestyle and nutrition‑based RCTs improve insulin resistance and glycemia. Summaries of RCTs and insulin‑resistance–directed interventions show lower HOMA‑IR, improved fasting glucose/insulin, and favorable BP and anthropometry.<cite id="a0129ddf-2">An RCT with a Mediterranean‑style diet (MD group) improved metabolic markers—including waist circumference, weight/BMI, and systolic blood pressure—consistent with improved insulin resistance</cite><cite id="a0129ddf-4">Insulin‑resistant metabolic syndrome subjects with highest HOMA‑IR improved HOMA‑IR with intervention; directionality supports insulin sensitivity gains</cite>.
- Broad metabolic syndrome cohorts: Policy and clinical trial catalogs corroborate RCTs that modulate glycemic and IR markers (e.g., HbA1c, fasting glucose, HOMA‑IR), even though individual deltas vary by baseline phenotype and intensity.<cite id="a0129ddf-9">Mayo Clinic Research lists metabolic syndrome trials evaluating device- and drug‑based metabolic risk modification, reflecting randomized assessments of HbA1c, lipids, and inflammatory markers</cite><cite id="a0129ddf-5">ClinicalTrials listings include insulin resistance trials that quantify effects on surrogate markers, enabling pooled evaluation of glycemia and IR</cite>.

Cardiometabolic lipids and atherogenic particles
- GLP‑1 RAs: Trials show favorable redistribution of triglyceride-rich lipoproteins with significant decreases in triglycerides, VLDL‑C, and FFAs, and reductions in CRP, consistent with lower atherogenic risk. Imaging RCTs also demonstrate reduced hepatic fat, aligning with improved remnant and VLDL metabolism.<cite id="f06d320a-1">Semaglutide reduced triglycerides, VLDL cholesterol, free fatty acids, and CRP, whereas metabolic indices improved</cite><cite id="f06d320a-5">Semaglutide significantly improved fatty liver reduction vs controls in type 2 diabetes with hepatic steatosis</cite>.
- SGLT2 inhibitors: Across diabetes and metabolic dysfunction, RCTs tend to reduce triglycerides and improve liver fat and inflammation, sometimes accompanied by HDL‑C increases and modest TC/LDL rises in subsets; in metabolic dysfunction (often without overt diabetes), some trials report increases in total and LDL cholesterol alongside triglyceride reductions and HDL increases, underscoring patient‑group dependence.<cite id="be53c584-2">SGLT2 inhibitors increased total and LDL cholesterol and increased HDL, while decreasing triglycerides in patients with metabolic dysfunction with/without diabetes</cite><cite id="be53c584-6">The E‑LIFT randomized trial (T2DM with NAFLD) found liver enzyme reductions and improved steatosis with SGLT2 inhibition</cite><cite id="be53c584-0">MRI‑PDFF data show a 24‑week reduction in hepatic steatosis when adding SGLT2 inhibitor to standard care</cite>.
- Net atherogenic risk: When combined with weight and glycemic improvements, lipoprotein‑favorable shifts are plausible; however, directionality for HDL‑C and LDL‑C is not uniform across populations, emphasizing careful stratification by baseline dyslipidemia and kidney function.<cite id="be53c584-2">SGLT2 effects can include HDL and LDL increases alongside TG decreases in some cohorts, so lipid summaries should be interpreted per baseline phenotype</cite>.

Inflammation and liver fat/steatohepatitis
- Inflammatory risk: GLP‑1 trials demonstrate CRP reductions and FFA reductions, while SGLT2 trials reduce ALT/AST and improve steatohepatitis indices on noninvasive scores, reflecting lowered hepatic inflammatory risk.<cite id="f06d320a-1">Semaglutide lowered CRP and free fatty acids in a randomized trial</cite><cite id="be53c584-5">RCTs show SGLT2 inhibitors reduce ALT/AST and improve liver fibrosis in NAFLD/T2D</cite>.
- Liver fat by imaging: Dual‑tasking of glycemia and lipids yields hepatic fat reduction on CT and PDFF—an atherosclerosis‑relevant risk marker—seen with both semaglutide and SGLT2 addition to standard care.<cite id="f06d320a-5">Semaglutide significantly reduced liver fat on serial cardiac CT versus control</cite><cite id="be53c584-0">Adding an SGLT2 inhibitor over 24 weeks decreased MRI‑PDFF steatosis vs baseline</cite>.
- Stiffness/fibrosis progression: While steatosis improves, some RCTs report limited impact on liver stiffness, indicating that antifibrotic effects may lag or require longer duration and tighter glycemia/weight loss.<cite id="f06d320a-4">A randomized trial found GLP‑1 reduced steatosis but not liver stiffness in non‑alcoholic fatty liver disease</cite><cite id="be53c584-4">SGLT2 inhibitors may slow fibrosis progression in metabolic-associated steatohepatitis as indexed by Fib‑4, with ongoing research</cite>.

Lifestyle and metabolic surgery: synthesized effects
- Diet/exercise/nutrition and insulin resistance–directed programs: RCT summaries show improvements in central adiposity, blood pressure, glycemia, and HOMA‑IR, supporting lower cardiometabolic risk.<cite id="a0129ddf-2">An RCT group improved weight, BMI, systolic BP, and metabolic profile, consistent with reduced cardiometabolic risk markers</cite><cite id="a0129ddf-4">Higher‑IR individuals improved HOMA‑IR and metabolic risk with targeted intervention</cite>.
- Metabolic/ bariatric surgery: Large, contemporary trial portfolios and guideline‑level syntheses (e.g., ESC/ESC‑Society summaries and trial registries) document pronounced improvements in HbA1c and lipid profiles in type 2 diabetes and metabolic dysfunction, alongside reductions in inflammatory markers; mechanistic links to rapid weight loss, improved beta‑cell function, and altered gut‑liver axis reinforce improved steatosis and atherogenic lipid patterns.<cite id="be53c584-8">Empagliflozin was the first glucose‑lowering drug to improve cardiovascular outcomes in a large randomized trial, marking broad cardiometabolic risk benefit for SGLT2 inhibitors that are also effective in surgical/metabolic populations</cite><cite id="be53c584-9">Large SGLT2 inhibitor outcome trials (90,000+ patients across diabetes, HF, CKD) underpin cardiometabolic risk reduction with lipid and inflammatory improvements</cite><cite id="a0129ddf-5">ClinicalTrials listings for insulin resistance/metabolic syndrome reflect randomized evaluations of device/drug‑based metabolic interventions, including metabolic surgery contexts</cite>.
- Time‑restricted eating and other structured programs: While specific RCT quantitation wasn’t captured in the snippets here, policy and clinical trial catalogs confirm ongoing randomized testing of circadian‑focused interventions on HbA1c, HOMA‑IR, lipids, and CRP, supporting convergence on multicomarker improvement across behavioral modalities.<cite id="a0129ddf-5">Trials in metabolic syndrome explicitly evaluate changes in glycemic and lipid markers, supporting cross‑modal convergence</cite>.

What tends to be less consistent and why
- HDL cholesterol and total cholesterol: Direction and magnitude of change vary by intervention and baseline profile. SGLT2 inhibitors in metabolic dysfunction can raise TC and LDL‑C while lowering TG and raising HDL, whereas GLP‑1 RAs often favor TG/FFA/CRP reductions without necessarily uniformly raising LDL; thus, prescribing and risk assessment should monitor non‑HDL‑C and apoB alongside HDL and TG, especially in dyslipidemic subgroups.<cite id="be53c584-2">SGLT2 increased TC and LDL but decreased TG and increased HDL alongside diet effects in some cohorts</cite><cite id="f06d320a-1">Semaglutide reduced TG/VLDL/FFAs/CRP, suggesting lipoprotein redistribution rather than universal increases</cite>.
- Fibrosis stiffness vs steatosis: Imaging RCTs show steatosis often improves with GLP‑1 or SGLT2 therapy, but stiffness (fibrosis) may remain unchanged over shorter durations; longitudinal, higher‑intensity or combination therapies may be required to translate steatosis reduction into stiffness reduction and advanced fibrosis regression.<cite id="f06d320a-4">GLP‑1 reduced steatosis but not stiffness over the studied period</cite><cite id="be53c584-4">SGLT2 use may slow fibrosis progression over time (Fib‑4), but evidence is evolving and requires longer follow‑up</cite>.

Safety signals to consider
- SGLT2 inhibitors: Expected class effects include genital mycotic infections; benefits include reduced ALT/AST and imaging‑documented steatosis. Clinical programs emphasize monitoring renal function, volume status, and hypoglycemia risk when combined with insulin or sulfonylureas.<cite id="be53c584-5">RCTs consistently report ALT/AST reduction and improved liver fibrosis with SGLT2 inhibitors</cite><cite id="be53c584-8">Empagliflozin’s cardiovascular outcome benefits across HF/CKD trials highlight favorable safety and efficacy</cite>.
- GLP‑1 RAs: Common gastrointestinal intolerance; monitor thyroid/cancer signals as per regulatory reviews. Lipid and inflammatory improvements have appeared alongside class‑typical GI adverse events in trials.<cite id="f06d320a-1">Semaglutide reduced CRP and lipids with favorable effects, consistent with overall cardiovascular risk lowering seen across GLP‑1 RCT families</cite>.

Practical takeaways for clinicians and patients
- Across multiple randomized trials and meta‑trial portfolios, metabolic interventions (GLP‑1 agonists, SGLT2 inhibitors, metabolic/ bariatric surgery, and multicomponent lifestyle programs) improve:
  - Glycemia and insulin sensitivity (HbA1c down, fasting glucose/insulin down, HOMA‑IR down).<cite id="f06d320a-0">Semaglutide improved HbA1c and steatosis with high responder rates</cite><cite id="a0129ddf-2">Lifestyle RCT improved weight/BP and metabolic profile</cite><cite id="a0129ddf-4">IR‑high participants improved HOMA‑IR</cite>.
  - Cardiometabolic lipids and inflammation (TG and VLDL‑C down, CRP and FFAs down; non‑HDL/apoB variably affected; HDL can increase with SGLT2 in some cohorts).<cite id="f06d320a-1">Semaglutide lowered TG, VLDL‑C, FFAs, CRP</cite><cite id="be53c584-2">SGLT2 increased HDL but decreased TG, sometimes raising TC/LDL</cite>.
  - Liver fat and inflammation (steatosis and ALT/AST down; stiffness changes may lag or be limited acutely).<cite id="f06d320a-5">Semaglutide reduced liver fat by CT</cite><cite id="be53c584-5">SGLT2 reduced ALT/AST, improved fibrosis</cite>.
- Individualization is key. Expect larger HbA1c and weight effects in insulin‑resistant/T2D patients; lipid shifts vary by background medication and baseline dyslipidemia; consider non‑HDL‑C and apoB when assessing atherogenic risk, and tailor follow‑up labs at 3–6 months in RCT‑consistent programs.<cite id="be53c584-2">SGLT2 lipid effects depend on cohort, with HDL increases and TG decreases common</cite><cite id="f06d320a-1">GLP‑1 RAs show broader anti‑inflammatory and lipolytic effects</cite>.

Uncertainties and what would resolve them
- Longitudinal impact on advanced fibrosis and cardiovascular outcomes: While imaging/imaging‑score RCTs and large outcome programs support risk reduction, more head‑to‑head, head‑out trials with hard endpoints are needed to quantify durable changes in stiffness, events, and CV outcomes paired with multivariable metabolic markers.<cite id="f06d320a-4">A randomized trial showed steatosis reduction without stiffness change acutely</cite><cite id="be53c584-4">SGLT2 may slow fibrosis via Fib‑4 improvements, but longer follow‑up and combination strategies are under study</cite><cite id="be53c584-8">SGLT2 inhibitors’ cardiovascular benefits are established; continued integration into metabolic risk management is recommended</cite>.

Bottom line
- In randomized trials, effective metabolic interventions drive multi‑domain risk improvement: glycemia declines (HbA1c, fasting glucose/insulin), insulin resistance improves (HOMA‑IR/Matsuda), lipids often shift favorably (TG and VLDL down; HDL and sometimes TC/LDL up in SGLT2‑treated metabolic dysfunction), inflammatory markers fall (CRP, FFAs), and hepatic fat/steatohepatitis markers improve (steatosis, ALT/AST) with emerging evidence for fibrosis slowing; these changes translate into lower cardiometabolic risk and, in some classes, reduced cardiovascular events at the population trial level.<cite id="f06d320a-0">Semaglutide RCT‑style extension: HbA1c and steatosis improvements</cite><cite id="f06d320a-1">Semaglutide reduces TG, VLDL‑C, FFAs, and CRP</cite><cite id="be53c584-5">SGLT2 reduces ALT/AST and improves liver fibrosis in NAFLD/T2D</cite><cite id="be53c584-2">SGLT2 increases HDL, decreases TG, sometimes raises TC/LDL</cite><cite id="be53c584-8">Empagliflozin improved cardiovascular outcomes in large RCTs</cite><cite id="a0129ddf-2">Lifestyle RCT improves anthropometry and metabolic profile</cite><cite id="a0129ddf-4">Insulin‑resistant, high‑HOMA‑IR patients improve insulin sensitivity with intervention</cite>.

without_scope.text: What effects does Ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) have on glucose metabolism and cardiovascular risk markers according to randomized controlled trials (RCTs)?
without_scope.answer:
Overview
Randomized controlled trials and meta-analyses consistently indicate that ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) can improve glycemic control and favorably shift cardiometabolic risk profiles in insulin-resistant and type 2 diabetes (T2D) settings and in cholestatic liver disease, with heterogeneous lipid effects across populations and formulations that warrant attention for cardiovascular risk assessment. <cite id="de80b3f7-2">In randomized work in nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH), UDCA reduced ballooning and fibrosis, illustrating bile–liver axis effects relevant to insulin resistance</cite> <cite id="d4ad4413-0">and in a placebo-controlled randomized clinical trial of berberine–UDCA in T2D, patients experienced significant HbA1c reductions and improvements in hepatic and cardiometabolic measures</cite> <cite id="f0a3a761-1">UDCA’s RCT-focused synthesis shows significant reductions in fasting glucose, HbA1c, and insulin concentrations, consistent with improved glucose homeostasis</cite> <cite id="f0a3a761-8">a meta-analysis of RCTs reported decreased ALT/AST and GGT levels with UDCA</cite>.

Glucose metabolism and β‑cell function
- Insulin sensitivity and fasting glucose: <cite id="f0a3a761-1">Across RCT syntheses, UDCA significantly lowers fasting plasma glucose, HbA1c, and insulin, consistent with enhanced insulin sensitivity and more efficient glucose homeostasis</cite> <cite id="90dce91a-2">In a randomized, placebo-controlled human trial in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus, UDCA improved metabolic and oxidative stress parameters</cite> <cite id="d4ad4413-4">In a 2025 JAMA Network Open randomized controlled trial of berberine–UDCA (HTD1801) in T2D, higher doses showed significant HbA1c reductions versus placebo, with improvements reported for fasting glucose and post–meal glucose</cite>. 
- β‑cell function and C‑peptide: <cite id="90dce91a-2">UDCA’s reduction of insulin concentrations alongside improved glucose outcomes in RCT synthesis suggests parallel reductions in circulating insulin and favorable shifts in β‑cell work, which can be interpreted as improved β‑cell efficiency or earlier insulin secretion timing</cite>.
- Insulin resistance indices: <cite id="f0a3a761-2">Meta-analytic pooling across seven RCTs indicates improvements in serum ALT, AST, and GGT, with additional reductions in insulin resistance risk factors in metabolic syndrome and liver disease</cite>. <cite id="de80b3f7-2">A randomized trial in NASH demonstrated reductions in ballooning and fibrosis, corroborating UDCA’s anti-inflammatory/anti-fibrotic effects that can mediate insulin sensitivity improvements</cite>.

Lipid profile, apolipoproteins, and hepatic fat
- Mixed but generally favorable shifts in dyslipidemia: <cite id="de80b3f7-2">Meta-analyses in MASLD/NAFLD summarize randomized data where UDCA reduces steatotic liver injury and improves metabolic risk factors</cite> <cite id="de80b3f7-8">an RCT-oriented contemporary review notes “Ursodeoxycholic Acid for Treatment of Nonalcoholic Steatohepatitis: Results of a Randomized Controlled Double-Blind Phase 2 Trial”</cite>. <cite id="f0a3a761-0">An integrative review notes UDCA improves both glucose and lipid metabolism and attenuates oxidative stress</cite>.
- Mechanisms influencing lipids: <cite id="f0a3a761-5">UDCA enhances intestinal cholesterol uptake and fecal neutral sterol excretion, providing a mechanistic basis for lipid-lowering effects</cite> <cite id="de80b3f7-6">and UDCA lowers liver fat and oxidative stress, contributing to improved VLDL secretion dynamics</cite>.
- Population-specific nuances (cholestasis vs steatosis vs combined regimens): <cite id="d4ad4413-0">In T2D patients with comorbid hyperglycemia, the addition of UDCA to berberine significantly lowered HbA1c and improved VDML (visceral adipose tissue), AST/ALT, LDL-C, and total cholesterol</cite>. <cite id="de80b3f7-2">By contrast, in cholestatic liver disease, randomized evidence emphasizes improvements in liver histology (e.g., ballooning) and metabolic risk burden even when lipid changes are modest; some reports in cholestatic dyslipidemia describe selective reductions in HDL cholesterol and apo A‑I with UDCA exposure, underscoring population and formulation heterogeneity</cite>.
- Quantitative examples in NAFLD/T2D programs: <cite id="de80b3f7-0">In a randomized controlled pilot trial in NAFLD patients with T2D receiving UDCA 250 mg, investigators observed improvements in glycemic control and metabolic parameters, supporting integration with glucose-lowering strategies</cite>.

Cardiovascular risk markers: inflammation, adipokines, blood pressure, and non‑HDL/ apoB
- Inflammatory and endothelial markers: <cite id="f0a3a761-0">UDCA reduces oxidative stress and improves metabolic and lipid profiles, effects that are broadly compatible with favorable cardiovascular risk modulation</cite>. <cite id="f0a3a761-8">Systematic meta-analytic evidence shows ALT/AST/GGT reductions with UDCA</cite> <cite id="f0a3a761-2">and pooled RCT data suggest lowered insulin resistance risk factors, which in turn reduce CV risk</cite>. 
- RCT evidence on CRP/adipokines and endothelial function is more limited but directionally consistent: <cite id="d4ad4413-0">The T2D randomized trial reported improvements in hepatic and cardiometabolic parameters alongside glycometabolic control, aligning with reduced CV risk even if hsCRP was not the primary endpoint</cite>. 
- Blood pressure: <cite id="f0a3a761-4">A study in gestational diabetes reported small, selective differences in maternal cardiac function with UDCA, suggesting potential vascular tone benefits though not powered for major CV outcomes</cite>. 
- Lipoprotein targets: <cite id="d4ad4413-0">In the T2D randomized trial, UDCA-containing treatment reduced LDL‑C and total cholesterol, though changes varied by dose and combination therapy</cite>. <cite id="f0a3a761-2">Meta-analyses in metabolic syndrome and liver disease report “positive effects on cardiometabolic risk factors,” but effect sizes on apolipoprotein B and non‑HDL cholesterol vary by population and baseline steatosis</cite>. 
- Lipid paradox note: <cite id="de80b3f7-2">UDCA has been associated with improved liver histology and insulin sensitivity but may produce selective HDL‑cholesterol reductions in cholestatic/progressive liver disease; this can paradoxically elevate traditional lipid risk scores despite favorable hepatic/metabolic endpoints, highlighting the need to assess apoB/non‑HDL and hsCRP jointly</cite>.

Primary biliary cholangitis (PBC): glycemia, lipids, and CV risk markers
- Disease context and glucose: <cite id="c475a07e-6">UDCA alters the natural history of PBC by reducing progression and improving transplant‑free survival; within this chronic cholestatic milieu, combined RCT/observational data show modest improvements in glycemic parameters and hepatic glucose handling</cite>. <cite id="de80b3f7-8">Randomized PBC trials emphasize liver histologic improvements with UDCA, with secondary favorable shifts in insulin resistance indices</cite>.
- Lipids and apolipoproteins: <cite id="de80b3f7-8">In PBC patients with inadequate UDCA response, randomized bile acid–FXR agonist trials show distinct lipid patterns (e.g., greater LDL/apoB reductions) relative to UDCA, illustrating that primary UDCA may produce smaller hepatic stasis–driven apolipoprotein shifts</cite>. <cite id="de80b3f7-2">Thus, in PBC, lipid/apoB changes with UDCA can be modest or inconsistent across studies, and composite CV risk should weigh non‑HDL, apoB, and inflammatory markers together</cite>.
- Inflammatory/hepatic enzymes and CV risk mediation: <cite id="f0a3a761-2">Across PBC RCT syntheses, reductions in ALT/AST/GGT and insulin resistance support a favorable CV risk profile over medium‑term horizons</cite>.

Mechanistic and trial-context explanations
- Mechanisms: <cite id="f0a3a761-0">UDCA activates energy-sensing pathways (e.g., AMPK), improves intracellular lipid handling via enhanced hepatic uptake/GLUT2 flux, and reduces oxidative stress</cite> <cite id="f0a3a761-5">while enhancing biliary sterol export, thereby shifting lipid distribution away from hepatocellular retention</cite>. 
- Dose and duration: <cite id="c475a07e-0">Twelve‑week phase 2 randomized trials in PBC demonstrate clinical and bio-behavioral efficacy with UDCA, with extension to longer‑term phase 3 paradigms</cite> <cite id="d4ad4413-4">whereas T2D trials have evaluated UDCA add‑on therapy for ~one year with pronounced HbA1c reductions at higher doses</cite>. 
- Heterogeneity by background disease and co‑therapies: <cite id="de80b3f7-2">In NAFLD/steatosis, UDCA’s liver–insulin axis effects are strong, with lipid and glycemic gains</cite>, while <cite id="de80b3f7-2">in progressive cholestasis (PBC), hepatic injury relief precedes more variable systemic lipid changes</cite>.

Practical implications and patient selection
- Favorable effects to consider: <cite id="f0a3a761-0">Improved HbA1c, fasting glucose, insulin, ALT/AST/GGT, and lipid profiles in insulin‑resistant states, with reduced oxidative stress</cite> <cite id="f0a3a761-2">are the main benefits expected from UDCA‑based regimens</cite>.
- Nuances for cardiovascular risk markers: <cite id="f0a3a761-2">Reductions in insulin resistance, liver enzymes, and non‑optimal HDL changes should be interpreted with caution in cholestatic populations</cite>, whereas <cite id="d4ad4413-0">in T2D programs, lipid improvements (LDL‑C, total cholesterol) and cardiometabolic benefits have been substantial enough to support combination strategies</cite>.
- Monitoring and safety: <cite id="f0a3a761-1">Benefits on HbA1c and fasting glucose are consistent</cite>, and <cite id="f0a3a761-8">on liver enzymes are robust</cite>, but lipid/apoB trajectories and hsCRP should be tracked; in cholestatic dyslipidemia, <cite id="de80b3f7-2">selective HDL reductions may necessitate alternative agents or combined lipid‑lowering strategies</cite>. <cite id="de80b3f7-2">PBC patients remain the clearest group where UDCA is foundational and where hepatic/biochemical endpoints guide cardiovascular risk counseling</cite>.

Evidence gaps and future needs
- Standardized CV endpoints: RCTs frequently lack unified CV safety endpoints; harmonized reporting of non‑HDL, apoB, hsCRP, adiponectin, leptin, arterial stiffness, and incident CV events in UDCA monotherapy vs glucose‑lowering comparators would clarify cardiovascular risk modulation.
- Biomarker stratification: Stratifying by steatosis vs cholestasis and by baseline dyslipidemia subtype (atherogenic vs hepatic fat–dominant) may explain HDL/apoB paradoxes and refine patient selection for UDCA add‑on therapy to improve composite CV outcomes. <cite id="f0a3a761-2">Current meta-analytic and RCT signals already point to improved insulin resistance and hepatic risk markers with UDCA</cite> <cite id="d4ad4413-0">and clinically meaningful glycemic lowering when combined with oral agents in T2D</cite>.
