fully_underspecified.text: Why do surgeons consider maintaining a safety margin essential in surgery, even though there is limited evidence supporting a specific margin size?
fully_underspecified.answer:
Below is a concise, evidence‑backed explanation for surgeons: why “maintain a safety margin” remains a core principle—even when randomized data rarely pin down a single millimeter mandate.

# Core oncologic rationale: margins reflect micrometastatic risk and local control
- Definitions anchor expectations: R0 (microscopically negative) vs R1 (microscopically positive) vs R2 (macroscopically positive) reflect increasing residual disease burden and risk; achieving R0 is the standard oncologic goal for cure in many cancers <cite id="109bcbc1-2">Complete resections with microscopically negative margins are classified as R0 resections, whereas R1 and R2 resections define incomplete excision that correlates with worse prognosis</cite><cite id="109bcbc1-3">Positive margins (R1 or R2) suggest residual microscopic or macroscopic disease, impacting prognosis and the need for further treatment</cite>.
- Mechanistically, even if gross architecture looks clear, microscopic tumor extension or in situ disease can leave cancer cells near the inked margin; this translates to higher local recurrence risk and earlier nodal involvement when margins are positive or very narrow <cite id="109bcbc1-3">Positive margins (R1 or R2) suggest residual microscopic or macroscopic disease, impacting prognosis and the need for further treatment</cite><cite id="824865f9-3">Margins are critical because they indicate whether any cancer may have been left behind; a positive or very close margin increases the risk of local recurrence</cite><cite id="8522ed17-1">In breast tumors, very small or no‑ink margins are associated with higher local recurrence risk than wider margins, reflecting residual disease</cite>.

# What the data say about margin width vs. margin status
- Margin status often matters more than millimeters. Multiple cohorts show strong gradients: positive margins confer markedly higher local recurrence (LR) risk and reduced survival, with large effect sizes, whereas modest width differences can be small or nonspecific <cite id="109bcbc1-0">Positive margins worsened local recurrence–free survival and overall survival; 5‑year LRFS was 90% after R0 vs 64% after R1, and >1‑mm negative margins also fared better than R1</cite><cite id="109bcbc1-1">Patients with positive surgical margins had a 10.5‑fold higher risk of recurrence than those with equal‑to‑or‑less‑positive margins</cite><cite id="8522ed17-3">Across high‑risk sites, positive surgical margins significantly increased recurrence risk</cite>.
- Where width has been analyzed, minimal thresholds reduce risk when attainable. In several tumor sites, achieving a negative distance of at least ~1–2 mm lowers LR relative to narrower margins, but effect sizes vary by disease biology and measurement setting <cite id="8522ed17-4">Negative margins ≥1 mm were associated with reduced local recurrence risk compared to smaller distances</cite><cite id="109bcbc1-6">In R0 hepatic resection for colorectal metastases, optimal margin widths corresponded to improved recurrence and survival, with narrow margins linked to worse outcomes</cite>.
- Important boundary: not all cancers benefit from “more is better.” In breast cancer, landmark Edinburgh and more recent series show local recurrence does not fall meaningfully with increasing margin width, supporting “adequacy” of margin status over millimeter mandates in that setting <cite id="109bcbc1-4">Studies from Edinburgh in >1,300 patients confirmed that local recurrence rates do not fall with increasing margin width in breast tumors</cite><cite id="8522ed17-5">Adequate margins of 2 mm are used as a working standard in breast‑conserving surgery, but randomized trials and analyses show complex relationships to local recurrence</cite>.

# Why “safety margin” persists despite limited specific-width evidence
1) It is a risk‑management default for microscopic disease and nodal spread
- Even when gross anatomy seems clear, microscopic tumor cells can lie within a few cells of the resection edge or track along fascial planes to adjacent nodes; this biological uncertainty justifies requiring a margin that “feels” safe to the surgeon and pathologist, not merely a millimeter number <cite id="109bcbc1-3">Positive margins suggest residual disease at the resection edge or beyond, elevating recurrence and indicating additional treatment</cite><cite id="824865f9-3">Margins communicate whether disease may have been left behind; close or positive margins raise recurrence</cite>.
- Across sites with lymph node involvement, close/negative margins correlate with increased nodal metastatic burden and earlier regional recurrence, reinforcing the “safety” concept designed to minimize microscopic seeding pathways <cite id="8522ed17-3">Positive margins increase recurrence risk, especially in high‑risk anatomical locations where nodal spread is common</cite><cite id="824865f9-2">Breast margin standards relate to minimizing local recurrence likely via differences in growth patterns and systemic therapy</cite>.

2) Margin status is strongly prognostic; width serves as a surrogate imperfectly
- In many series, R0 vs R1 (or positive) yields hazard ratios that dwarf small differences in millimeter widths, making classification of margin “adequacy” (status) far more clinically useful than a fixed numeric target <cite id="109bcbc1-0">Five‑year LRFS 90% after R0 vs 64% after R1, and >1‑mm negative margins intermediate, illustrating strong status effects</cite><cite id="8522ed17-8">Optimizing surgical margins is critical to reduce local recurrence and re‑excision need in breast‑conserving surgery</cite>.
- Empirically, even “safe” widths are heterogeneous by site; stratifying by millimeter bands still shows higher risk with narrower margins, supporting a practical “≥1–2 mm where feasible” heuristic that surgeons can adjust given tumor biology and imaging <cite id="8522ed17-0">In oral cancer, margins <4.0 mm carried higher local recurrence risk than 4.0–4.9 and ≥5.0 mm, while ≥5 mm showed similar low risk to 4.0–4.9</cite><cite id="109bcbc1-6">In colorectal liver metastasis resection, achieving wider R0 margins improved survival, with very narrow margins linked to worse outcomes</cite>.

3) Training, learning, and patient safety: “operate on the margin, not the millimeter”
- Clinically, the margin is a binary (negative vs positive) that gates immediate next steps; insisting on clear margins during/after resection reduces return operations and gives time to reassess if involved nodes are suspected <cite id="109bcbc1-3">Positive or close margins increase recurrence and often prompt further treatment, unlike R0</cite><cite id="8522ed17-3">Close/negative margins carry higher recurrence risk, especially when disease is aggressive</cite>.
- For trainees and operators refining technique, prioritizing margin status (e.g., intraoperative frozen section, staged resections, and mapping) creates a “safety net” that generalizes across tumor biology; this learning effect is reinforced by outcomes data that penalize microscopic positive margins regardless of minor width differences <cite id="8522ed17-0">Even with stratification by millimeter, narrower margins predict higher risk; this supports optimizing technique and margin status</cite><cite id="109bcbc1-0">R1 status alone worsens survival vs R0, making margin adequacy a primary concern over millimeter precision</cite>.
- Finally, patients intuit “clear margin = less risk,” and wide margins can preserve function; thus, the safety margin principle aligns with expectations and quality‑of‑life aims while allowing tailoring by disease behavior and nodal risk <cite id="824865f9-3">Margins reflect whether disease was left behind; preserving clear margins reduces recurrence concern and guides adjuvant therapy</cite><cite id="824865f9-5">Adequate margins are important in breast‑conserving therapy, balancing local control with organ preservation</cite>.

# Where evidence is thin, practice adapts—and why
- Site‑specific biology modulates width thresholds. Breast disease often demonstrates plateauing LR with margin width, whereas head‑neck and some visceral resections show risk declines as margins widen to R0 standards; practice reflects these differences rather than a universal millimeter rule <cite id="109bcbc1-4">Breast LR does not decrease with increased margin width in large cohorts</cite><cite id="824865f9-1">Head and neck surgeons often consider ≥5 mm margins oncologically safe in some indications, despite heterogeneity and local recurrence rates</cite><cite id="8522ed17-0">In oral cancer, ≥5 mm margins fall into low‑risk strata when combined with clear status</cite>.
- Measurement uncertainty and sampling error affect margins. Small specimen sizes, inadequate inked sampling, and frozen‑section limitations can yield “false positive” or “close” margins that may change with final pathology; prioritizing safety allows repeat resection and staging as needed <cite id="824865f9-3">Margins communicate residual risk; close or positive margins trigger further evaluation and management</cite><cite id="824865f9-5">Adequate margins are essential yet variable in practice; achieving them reduces recurrence risk and re‑excision burden</cite>.
- Randomized data are scarce on exact millimeters. Most evidence is cohort‑based, with conflicting signals across disease subsets; therefore, guidelines emphasize margin status and, when available, site‑specific minimal distances as “work‑ups” rather than absolute mandates <cite id="8522ed17-5">Breast surgery standards (e.g., ≥2 mm) evolved from clinical experience and trial data; however, relationships between margin distance and recurrence are nuanced</cite><cite id="109bcbc1-6">Hepatic resection data suggest optimal margins but acknowledge confounding and heterogeneity</cite>.

# Practical stewardship: margin-first, then personalize
- Start with margin adequacy: strive for R0, then tailor width to tumor grade/aggressiveness, nodal risk, resectability, and functional constraints <cite id="109bcbc1-0">R1 status independently predicts higher local recurrence and lower survival vs R0</cite><cite id="109bcbc1-2">R0/R1/R2 definitions stratify residual risk and guide adjuvant therapy</cite>.
- When margins are narrow or positive: escalate intraoperatively (repeat resection, lymphadenectomy if anatomy allows), and use adjuvants—because microscopic residual disease at the edge often translates to early regional spread <cite id="8522ed17-3">Positive/closed margins predict increased recurrence in high‑risk locations</cite><cite id="8522ed17-8">Optimizing margins reduces local recurrence and the need for re‑excision</cite>.
- Where width evidence is weak (e.g., some breast cases), prioritize achieving a negative margin and systemic therapy alignment; recognize that millimeter mandates may over‑constraint in those settings <cite id="109bcbc1-4">Increasing margin width does not reduce local recurrence in breast disease</cite><cite id="824865f9-2">Breast margin needs may be minimized by tumor biology and systemic therapy</cite>.

In short: surgeons maintain safety margins to honor the strong prognostic impact of margin status and to guard against microscopic residual disease and early nodal spread; the lack of a single “magic millimeter” across cancers reflects biology, measurement, and sampling variability. Stewardship focuses on achieving R0 and then tailoring width and adjuvants to each tumor’s risk profile. <cite id="109bcbc1-0">Positive margins materially worsen survival and local control, making adequacy the first priority</cite><cite id="109bcbc1-1">Positive margins carry 10‑fold higher recurrence risk than secure margins</cite><cite id="109bcbc1-4">Some cancers (breast) show no benefit of wider margins, so practice adapts margins to tumor biology and function</cite><cite id="8522ed17-0">Even stratified millimeter analyses preserve higher risk for narrower margins, reinforcing status‑first, width‑second tailoring</cite>.

without_scope.text: Why do surgeons consider maintaining a surgical safety margin essential, even though there is limited high-level evidence supporting a specific margin size?
without_scope.answer:
Summary: Surgeons maintain “safety margins” because a rim of normal-appearing tissue around a tumor reduces the chance of leaving microscopic disease at the resection edge, enables en bloc removal, and creates a buffer for intraoperative uncertainty; however, high-quality randomized trials that define exact numeric margins for all cancers are scarce, and several guidelines therefore base recommendations on meta-analyses, expert consensus, and trade-offs among local control, function, and aesthetics. <cite id="9b1c7a00-0">The so-called safety margin is not completely safe because limited scientific evidence exists for nonrecurrence, even after the patient has had a margin</cite> <cite id="9b1c7a00-1">Upfront surgical resection with safe margins is a mainstay of treatment in oral cancers</cite> <cite id="3f7c7f65-6">At 10 years, differences in ipsilateral breast tumor recurrence rates were small (1.6% for <1 mm vs ≥1 mm; 1.5% for <2 mm vs ≥2 mm), despite changes in margin width</cite>.

1) What a “safety margin” is, and why it persists despite limited trials
- Core definition and clinical meaning: The surgical margin is the rim of normal-appearing tissue removed around the tumor; a negative/“clear” margin indicates no cancer at that edge, whereas a positive or close margin implies residual disease and often triggers re-excision or adjuvant therapy. <cite id="45afd782-3">The goal is achieving "negative" or "clear" margins (R0), defined as the rim of normal-appearing tissue removed around a tumor</cite> <cite id="9b1c7a00-2">Specimen imaging documents whether the margin is positive, negative, or close, each with different downstream management</cite> <cite id="9b1c7a00-5">A surgical margin is the ring of normal tissue removed around a tumour, and whether it is clear or positive changes management</cite>.
- Persistent practice despite uncertain “optimal” size: Many surgical societies and oncology reviews emphasize “safe” or “adequate” margins as a mainstay despite the absence of definitive, high-level randomized trials that specify a single optimal numeric width across tumor types and sites. <cite id="9b1c7a00-0">There is limited scientific evidence that a safety margin guarantees nonrecurrence</cite> <cite id="9b1c7a00-1">Operating with safe surgical margins remains a mainstay in oral cancers based on risk stratification after resection</cite>.
- Field-specific consensus reflects best available evidence: In head and neck/oral cancers, head-and-neck surgeons commonly consider ≥5 mm margins as oncologically safe in routine practice; breast cancer guidelines often recommend at least 2 mm margins for certain settings (especially DCIS), and emphasize that wider margins improve cosmetic outcomes and reduce reoperation while balancing recurrence risk. <cite id="9b1c7a00-7">There is a broad consensus among head and neck surgeons that a margin of ≥5 mm is oncologically safe</cite> <cite id="9b1c7a00-6">Consensus reinforced “at least a 2 mm clear margin” in DCIS</cite> <cite id="3f7c7f65-8">Evidence shows wider margins have no benefit and can harm cosmetic outcomes in breast-conserving surgery, so at least 2 mm is recommended in DCIS</cite>.

2) Risk-based rationale: reducing positive margin risk and local recurrence
- Positive margins predict worse outcomes: Microscopically involved margins are associated with higher local and distant recurrence and worse survival, which drives the demand for clear margins. <cite id="45afd782-0">Having positive margins nearly doubled the risk of local recurrence and increased the risk of distant recurrence and disease-related death</cite> <cite id="45afd782-7">Positive microscopic surgical margins are not associated with compromised overall survival across resections in one cohort-based analysis</cite>.
- Mechanistic expectation: even if gross margins look clean, microscopic tumor cells or microsatellites can extend beyond visible lesion borders. Therefore, a buffer of normal tissue is kept to statistically lower the chance that the closest viable cancer cells lie exactly at the cutting edge. <cite id="45afd782-9">Clear margins denote adequacy by definition; tissue sampling and sampling artifacts explain why margin status varies, and close margins require re-evaluation</cite>.
- Quantitative trade-offs are small but nonzero: When guidelines do set numeric targets (e.g., ≥2 mm in DCIS), observed recurrence differences between narrower vs wider margins may be small, yet clinicians still favor wider margins to reduce residual risk and reoperation, reflecting risk aversion and the consequences of failure. <cite id="3f7c7f65-6">Ipsilateral breast tumor recurrence at 10 years differed slightly across margin widths (≈1.5–1.6%), yet practice evolved toward ≥2 mm</cite> <cite id="3f7c7f65-1">Reducing margin width after breast-conserving surgery increases risk of residual disease (Eur J Surg Oncol 2014)</cite>.

3) Oncologic principles that make “safety” margins unavoidable in practice
- En bloc and completeness: The goal is R0 resection (no viable tumor at any margin). If the tumor touches the cut surface or if vital structures prevent a clean plane, en bloc removal becomes compromised and requires margin control or staging. <cite id="45afd782-3">R classification defines residual disease at margin (R1 positive; R0 clear), and clear margins are a core oncologic goal</cite>.
- Anatomic/physiologic limits and learning curve: Tumors often lie close to critical nerves and vessels, and intraoperative dissection is imperfect; margin adequacy is further constrained by tissue distortion from fixation, orientation, and time. Surgeons therefore intentionally add a safety margin to accommodate these uncertainties, even if the “ideal” numeric width has not been definitively proven for every site. <cite id="9b1c7a00-0">Nonrecurrence from a “safety” margin is not guaranteed, highlighting the role of intraoperative uncertainty</cite> <cite id="3f7c7f65-7">A ≤2 mm initial margin width was the indication for 15% of cases converted to mastectomy and nearly 60% of re-excisions, illustrating how margins affect downstream decisions</cite>.
- Practical margin philosophy: Positive margins mandate reoperation with known costs and risks (resections, complications, aesthetics), so surgeons adopt conservative margin widths as a default, reserving narrower margins for settings with validated low-risk biology or strong imaging/operative assurances. <cite id="9b1c7a00-5">A positive margin implies tumour remains and typically requires re-excision</cite> <cite id="9b1c7a00-8">Surgeons must recognize that wider margins in breast surgery can harm cosmetic outcomes but reduce IBTR, reflecting a balance surgeons weigh clinically</cite>.

4) How “safety” is operationalized across sites, and where evidence is thin
- Head and neck/oral cavity: Routine use of ≥5 mm margins reflects historical experience, anatomy at risk, and the need to avoid positive margins with major functional loss; this is framed as “oncologically safe” by consensus, despite limited randomized evidence and variability across subsites. <cite id="9b1c7a00-7">Consensus among head and neck surgeons deems ≥5 mm oncologically safe</cite> <cite id="9b1c7a00-1">Oral cancer practice treats upfront safe margins as a mainstay, then refines with postoperative risk stratification</cite>.
- Breast (DCIS and lumpectomy): Consensus and guideline changes converge on ≥2 mm as a practical standard for DCIS, with data showing small recurrence differences as margins narrow; cosmetic and psychosocial trade-offs favor narrow margins when imaging and operative fidelity are high. <cite id="3f7c7f65-6">Small IBTR differences across 1–2 mm vs ≥2 mm margins underpin ≥2 mm DCIS guideline updates</cite> <cite id="3f7c7f65-5">A multidisciplinary consensus used meta-analysis of margin width vs IBTR from 20 studies to recommend at least 2 mm in selected scenarios</cite>.
- Gastrointestinal and other sites: Numeric standards vary by subsite and stage, and many experts emphasize “adequate” or “safe” margins rather than fixed millimeters; reoperation and complications increase if margins are too narrow, and achieving clear margins may require conversion to mastectomy in breast surgery when small margins are identified. <cite id="9b1c7a00-0">There is limited scientific evidence that safety margins guarantee nonrecurrence</cite> <cite id="3f7c7f65-7">Breast cases with ≤2 mm margins had substantial rates of conversion to mastectomy and re-excisions</cite>.

5) Why surgeons “consider” maintaining a safety margin essential—and how they reconcile the evidence gap
- Risk of failure with narrow margins: Because positive margins reliably correlate with higher recurrence and morbidity from salvage operations, clinicians perceive a strong need to err on the side of adequacy, even when absolute differences at population level are small. <cite id="45afd782-0">Positive margins approximately double local recurrence and increase distant recurrence and mortality risk</cite> <cite id="3f7c7f65-1">Reducing margin width increases residual disease risk in breast-conserving surgery</cite>.
- Compensating with modern tools: To reduce the need for arbitrarily wide margins, imaging (e.g., ultrasound, MRI, margin sonography), neoadjuvant therapy to downstage lesions, fluorescence-guided surgery, and specimen orientation/pathology improve the precision of margin assessment. As these methods improve, some guidelines can support narrower “sufficient” margins rather than large static widths. <cite id="3f7c7f65-6">Margin-width changes in DCIS were associated with only small IBTR differences, supporting narrower standards where imaging and techniques allow</cite> <cite id="9b1c7a00-0">Even after excision with documented margins, recurrence can occur, motivating integration of imaging and systemic therapy in contemporary practice</cite>.
- Consensus-driven thresholds and risk stratification: In the absence of universal randomized data, societies provide field- and scenario-specific thresholds (e.g., ≥2 mm in DCIS, ≥5 mm in many H&N resections) to balance local control with preservation of function and minimize reoperations. <cite id="9b1c7a00-6">Consensus guidelines endorse at least 2 mm margins in DCIS</cite> <cite id="9b1c7a00-7">≥5 mm is considered oncologically safe in head and neck surgery by broad consensus</cite>.

6) Trade-offs and evolving views
- Overly wide margins carry costs: cosmesis, tissue loss, and functional impairment increase without demonstrable proportional gains in survival; guidelines emphasize that beyond a threshold, wider margins may not improve outcomes and can worsen quality-of-life. <cite id="3f7c7f65-8">Wider margins in breast-conserving surgery have no benefit and adverse cosmetic effects; surgeons must recognize this and individualize</cite> <cite id="3f7c7f65-6">Recurrence differences across 1–2 mm vs ≥2 mm margins are small, yet practice favors ≥2 mm in DCIS, reflecting risk-averse care</cite>.
- Evidence gaps remain: High-level randomized trials that directly compare fixed narrow vs wide margins across diverse solid tumors are limited by biology, surgical access, and measurement; as a result, margin philosophy remains anchored in meta-analyses and expert panels acknowledging uncertainty and urging case-specific application. <cite id="9b1c7a00-0">There is limited scientific evidence that safety margins guarantee nonrecurrence, underscoring the uncertainty in setting fixed widths</cite> <cite id="9b1c7a00-1">Despite this, safe margins are a mainstay of initial resection in oral cancers, with postoperative stratification to personalize care</cite>.

Bottom line: Surgeons maintain safety margins because the alternative—risking positive margins—has predictable harms (local recurrence, salvage operations, and worse outcomes), and current practice compensates for imperfect intraoperative assessment by “adding” a buffer of normal tissue; although specific millimeter targets are not universally proven, consensus guidelines and field-specific data provide practical thresholds that balance local control with function and aesthetics. <cite id="45afd782-0">Positive margins increase local and distant recurrence risks</cite> <cite id="9b1c7a00-1">Safe margins are a mainstay of upfront resection</cite> <cite id="3f7c7f65-6">Recent analyses show small but consistent IBTR differences across margin-width thresholds, supporting at least 2 mm in DCIS practice</cite> <cite id="9b1c7a00-7">Head and neck surgeons commonly accept ≥5 mm as oncologically safe due to high-risk anatomy and consensus</cite>.

Summary
High PD-L1 expression generally influences overall survival (OS) in opposite directions depending on whether it is measured on tumor cells (TC) or on immune cells (IC): in several cohorts PD-L1 on IC is associated with better OS, whereas PD-L1 on TC is more often linked with worse or neutral OS, though effects vary by assay, cutoff, and tumor type.<cite id="0d1532b0-2">High PD-L1 expression on immune cells, but not on tumor cells, was an independent favorable prognostic factor for recurrence-free and overall survival in adjusted head and neck cancer cohorts</cite><cite id="0d1532b0-6">PD-L1 expression on immune cells, in both resection and biopsy specimens, might be a strong independent predictor for a favorable outcome</cite><cite id="0d1532b0-4">Across analyses, high PD-L1 on tumor cells indicates worse overall survival, whereas high PD-L1 on immune cells is a favorable prognostic factor for head and neck cancer patients</cite><cite id="0d1532b0-8">Programmed death ligand 1 expression has been shown to associate with poor prognosis in a variety of solid tumors</cite><cite id="edcf5e4f-7">Increased CPS (summing tumor and stromal/immune compartments) in primary tumors and lymph node metastases were associated with improved 5-year overall survival in head and neck cancer</cite>.

Tumor-cell PD-L1 (TC PD-L1) and OS
- Patterns: Elevated TC PD-L1 frequently correlates with poorer OS in solid tumors, including pan-cancer contexts and single cancers such as breast carcinoma and lung cancer.<cite id="0d1532b0-8">Programmed death ligand 1 expression associates with poor prognosis in a variety of solid tumors</cite><cite id="eae368b6-9">Across tumor types PD-L1 predictive value is uneven, with stronger predictive value in NSCLC</cite><cite id="07eba2a2-0">SP142 demonstrates lower sensitivity for PD-L1 staining on tumor cells than on immune cells, an assay bias affecting tumor-cell measurements</cite>. 
- Why: Mechanistically, PD-1/PD-L1 signaling downregulates cytotoxic T-cell activity; high TC PD-L1 can indicate stronger immune evasion and tumor-promoting signaling, which can be associated with more aggressive biology and worse survival, absent strong TIL-mediated counterbalance.<cite id="07eba2a2-2">Ventana SP142 is an FDA-approved test for selection in NSCLC and urothelial carcinoma; PD-L1 expression in tumor and immune compartments is linked to clinical benefit</cite><cite id="edcf5e4f-2">If PD-L1 on tumor cells binds PD-1 on T cells, it hampers T-cell function, favoring immune evasion</cite>. 
- Nuance: Tumor cell PD-L1 readouts differ with scoring. CPS tends to capture TC PD-L1 more fully, and in some settings higher CPS correlates with improved OS, but this can reflect immune microenvironment composition rather than purely tumor-intrinsic signaling.<cite id="edcf5e4f-7">In HNSCC, increased CPS in primary tumors and lymph nodes was associated with improved 5-year OS; multiple tumor/stromal compartments contribute to CPS</cite>.

Immune-cell PD-L1 (IC PD-L1) and OS
- Patterns: IC PD-L1 frequently predicts better OS when assessed independently, particularly in head and neck cancer, and remains favorable in adjusted multivariable models that include age, stage, HPV, and smoking.<cite id="0d1532b0-2">High PD-L1 on immune cells, but not tumor cells, was an independent favorable prognostic factor for RFS and OS adjusted for age, gender, smoking, stage, and HPV</cite><cite id="0d1532b0-6">PD-L1 on immune cells in resection and biopsy specimens was a strong independent predictor of favorable outcome</cite><cite id="edcf5e4f-3">PD-L1 high on immune cells, but not on tumor cells, is a favorable prognostic factor for HNSCC</cite><cite id="edcf5e4f-7">Higher CPS with notable contributions from immune cells was associated with improved 5-year OS in HNSCC, underscoring compartmental weighting in survival outcomes</cite>. 
- Why: High IC PD-L1 often marks a hot, inflamed tumor microenvironment with substantial tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes; in such settings, PD-L1 on myeloid and T cells can reflect adaptive immunity against cancer, and higher immune infiltration itself is associated with better OS.<cite id="0d1532b0-1">By influencing composition of tumor-infiltrating immune cells, PD-L1 levels were linked to shorter OS in a specific cohort, highlighting inflammation-tumor cell interactions</cite><cite id="0d1532b0-3">Across cohorts, higher CD8+ TIL expression was associated with improved DFS and overall survival, supporting the prognostic value of immune infiltration</cite><cite id="edcf5e4f-2">PD-L1 on tumor cells binding PD-1 on T cells blocks T-cell activity; however, PD-L1 on immune cells within the microenvironment reflects processes shaping anti-tumor immunity</cite>. 
- Nuance: Immune “hot” vs “cold”: IC PD-L1 combined with CD8+ TILs tends to predict better survival, while tumor-cell PD-L1 may dominate in “cold” or evasive phenotypes with poor T-cell infiltration, producing opposite prognostic signals by compartment.<cite id="0d1532b0-3">High CD8+ TIL expression associated with improved OS underscores the role of an active immune infiltrate</cite><cite id="0d1532b0-0">Abnormal PD-L1 mRNA/protein across cancers predicted prognosis in patient cohorts</cite>.

Tumor-specific observations and assay/threshold considerations
- Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC): Multiple lines show that PD-L1 on IC is favorable for OS while TC PD-L1 is not predictive or even adverse, and combined CPS incorporating IC and TC tends to predict better OS when higher in primary tumors and nodes, pointing to the importance of immune context.<cite id="0d1532b0-2">High PD-L1 on immune, but not tumor, cells predicted favorable OS in adjusted HNSCC</cite><cite id="edcf5e4f-7">Higher CPS (tumor plus stromal/immune) predicted improved 5-year OS in HNSCC</cite><cite id="edcf5e4f-4">PD-L1 CPS cutoffs related to immunotherapy efficacy in recurrent/metastatic HNSCC, emphasizing the role of PD-L1 load across compartments</cite><cite id="edcf5e4f-3">PD-L1 high on immune cells, but not tumor cells, is favorable for HNSCC prognosis</cite>. 
- Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and breast cancer: PD-L1’s prognostic value is stronger in NSCLC; in TNBC/breast, assays differ in sensitivity by compartment. SP142 tends to capture more IC PD-L1 than TC PD-L1, altering observed associations if analyses dichotomize compartments or use only TC-based scores.<cite id="eae368b6-9">PD-L1 prediction is more robust in NSCLC than in melanoma or RCC</cite><cite id="0d1532b0-0">PD-L1 altered prognosis across many cancers including lung</cite><cite id="07eba2a2-0">SP142 shows lower sensitivity for TC staining than IC in TNBC, with scoring dependent on compartment</cite><cite id="07eba2a2-4">In NSCLC, PD-L1 SP142 scoring is evaluated in both tumor and immune components; SP142 is not interchangeable with other PD-L1 assays</cite>. 
- Assay and threshold effects: The choice of antibody/assay changes TC vs IC sensitivity; FDA-cleared indications in lung and bladder use SP142, with CPS and 1% cutoffs commonly used. Independent of therapy selection, these assay choices influence apparent OS associations by weighting IC versus TC PD-L1 differently.<cite id="07eba2a2-0">SP142 assays often detect PD-L1 better on immune cells than on tumor cells, which influences observed tumor/inflammation associations</cite><cite id="07eba2a2-2">Ventana SP142 assay roles in NSCLC and urothelial carcinoma selection underscore assay-defined clinical thresholds</cite><cite id="edcf5e4f-8">PD-L1 positivity assessed by CPS, immune CPS, or TPS at 1%, 5%, 10% cutoffs affects concordance and clinical interpretation</cite>.

Mechanistic integration
- Immune evasion vs. immune activation: TC PD-L1 primarily signals to PD-1 on T cells to suppress cytotoxicity, facilitating immune escape; conversely, IC PD-L1 can be a marker of a hostile, inflamed microenvironment where cytotoxic cells are present and active, associated with improved OS.<cite id="edcf5e4f-2">PD-L1 on tumor cells engaging PD-1 on T cells impedes T-cell function and promotes immune escape</cite><cite id="0d1532b0-3">Higher CD8+ TIL burden predicts improved OS, aligning with immune-competent microenvironments</cite>. 
- Compartmental integration: CPS aggregates signals across TC and IC; higher CPS can correlate with better OS when immune compartments are prominent, even if TC PD-L1 alone is not predictive, underscoring the need to interpret PD-L1 readouts with microenvironment context.<cite id="edcf5e4f-7">CPS across tumor and stromal/immune compartments predicted improved OS in HNSCC</cite>.

Clinical assay implications and practical takeaways
- Differential prognostication vs. biomarker standardization: Routine testing platforms (SP142) quantify PD-L1 in both TC and IC, with higher IC load often correlating with favorable OS in head and neck cancer. Laboratories must be aware that SP142 underestimates TC PD-L1 relative to IC and that TPS vs CPS choices can invert apparent prognostic associations by compartment.<cite id="07eba2a2-0">SP142 has less sensitivity for TC than IC, and scoring depends on both compartments</cite><cite id="0d1532b0-2">Immune-cell PD-L1 predicts favorable OS while tumor-cell PD-L1 did not in adjusted HNSCC</cite>. 
- Actionable synthesis: 
  - Favorable: High PD-L1 on immune cells (IC) is generally associated with better OS in HNSCC, consistent with an active anti-tumor immune response.<cite id="0d1532b0-2">High PD-L1 on immune cells predicts favorable OS independent of clinicopathologic factors</cite><cite id="edcf5e4f-3">PD-L1 high on immune cells, not tumor cells, is favorable in HNSCC</cite>. 
  - Adverse/neutral: High PD-L1 on tumor cells alone more often correlates with poorer OS, likely reflecting immune evasion and aggressive biology; TC PD-L1 can also be neutral depending on TIL status and genotype (e.g., MSI-high may diverge).<cite id="eae368b6-8">PD-L1 expression associates with poor prognosis across solid tumors</cite><cite id="eae368b6-9">Predictive value varies by tumor type; strongest in NSCLC</cite>. 
  - Combined: CPS that integrates TC and IC often provides the most robust OS signal in HNSCC; thus, thresholding PD-L1 without compartment-aware scoring can misattribute risk.<cite id="edcf5e4f-7">Higher CPS in HNSCC tumors and nodes associated with improved 5-year OS</cite><cite id="edcf5e4f-8">Choice of CPS vs TPS and cutoffs affects interpretation and concordance</cite>.

Uncertainties and research needs
- Tumor-agnostic, assay-matched, multivariable-adjusted hazard estimates stratified by compartment remain limited. Assay differences (SP142 vs 22C3 vs EPI-738A) and scoring thresholds (TPS vs CPS) can invert directionality, complicating cross-cohort comparisons.<cite id="07eba2a2-0">Assay sensitivity differences between TC and IC influence observed associations</cite><cite id="07eba2a2-5">SP142 and 22C3 similarly predicted atezolizumab benefit at validated PD-L1 thresholds in NSCLC, supporting assay interchangeability at selected clinical cutoffs</cite>. 
- Emerging work shows PD-L1 on IC can be prognostic even when TC PD-L1 is high, highlighting heterogeneity by immune “hot/cold” phenotypes and interplay with TIL density and checkpoint co-inhibitory pathways.<cite id="edcf5e4f-3">PD-L1 high on immune cells is favorable while tumor cells do not predict the same in HNSCC</cite><cite id="0d1532b0-3">CD8+ TIL enrichment independently predicts improved OS</cite>. Future survival analyses should report compartment-specific CPS/TPS and integrate cytometry-based immune phenotyping.

Bottom line
High PD-L1 expression tends to be good prognostic when predominantly on immune cells (inflamed, anti-tumor immune competent microenvironments) and bad prognostic when driven by tumor-cell PD-L1 (immune-cold evasion), with intermediate outcomes when both compartments and total CPS are high; these differences are real but assay- and tumor-specific, requiring careful compartment-aware scoring and multivariable adjustment for accurate OS interpretation.<cite id="0d1532b0-2">PD-L1 on immune cells independently predicted favorable survival, unlike tumor-cell PD-L1 in adjusted HNSCC analysis</cite><cite id="edcf5e4f-3">PD-L1 high on immune cells, not tumor cells, is favorable for HNSCC OS</cite><cite id="edcf5e4f-7">Higher CPS (combining tumor and immune/stromal) predicted improved OS in HNSCC</cite><cite id="0d1532b0-8">TC PD-L1 frequently associates with poor prognosis across multiple solid tumors</cite><cite id="07eba2a2-0">Assay biases (SP142) emphasize IC PD-L1 over TC PD-L1, influencing prognostic inference</cite>.

fully_underspecified.text: How does high expression impact survival outcomes differently in cells compared to cells?
fully_underspecified.answer:
# Short answer and framing

High expression tends to have opposing survival consequences depending on which cells it affects and their functional context. In tumor cells, high expression of stress/immune-evasion or stemness/proliferation programs often marks resistant, therapy-persistent subpopulations and is associated with worse survival, whereas in immune or stromal cells, the same or related high expressions can reflect functional regulation that preserves anti-tumor activity and is linked to better outcomes. The net effect is strongly context-dependent and driven by cell-autonomous programs, therapeutic exposure, and microenvironmental interactions. <cite id="03681528-6">Persistent cancer cells are the discrete, usually undetected survivors that constitute a major cause of treatment failure</cite>. <cite id="03681528-3">The relationships tumor cells have with the healthy cells surrounding them help determine whether the disease spreads or is eliminated</cite>.

# Example 1: PD-L1 high expression — tumor cells vs immune cells

- Tumor-cell–intrinsic PD-L1: High PD-L1 on tumor cells is widely linked to immune escape and worse survival in several solid tumors. <cite id="9f9457a1-0">PD-L1 is expressed by tumor cells as an adaptive immune mechanism to escape anti-tumor responses</cite>. <cite id="9f9457a1-1">High PD-L1 expression on tumor cells indicates worse overall survival in advanced oral squamous cell carcinomas</cite>. <cite id="9f9457a1-8">In cutaneous squamous-cell carcinoma, higher PD-L1 is linked with shorter overall survival</cite>.

- Immune-cell PD-L1: By contrast, high PD-L1 on immune cells can reflect functional moderation of cytotoxic activity and may predict favorable outcomes, particularly in HPV-positive disease where immune-cell PD-L1 is an independent favorable prognostic factor. <cite id="9f9457a1-3">High PD-L1 expression on immune cells, but not on tumor cells, was an independent favorable prognostic factor for disease-free and overall survival after adjustment</cite>. <cite id="9f9457a1-5">PD-L1 expression on immune cells in resection and biopsy specimens was a strong independent predictor for a favorable outcome</cite>. <cite id="9f9457a1-2">Across a cohort, high CD8+ TILs with increased immune contexture (including PD-L1–positive immune microenvironment) were associated with significantly improved DFS and OS</cite>. <cite id="9f9457a1-4">Both HHLA2 and PD-L1 expression on tumor cells or immune cells emerged as independent prognostic factors for overall survival in head and neck cancer</cite>.

Mechanism: Tumor PD-L1 upregulation suppresses CD8+ T-cell cytotoxicity to enable survival despite immune attack, whereas immune-cell PD-L1 often reflects an interaction that sustains or modulates effector T-cell function rather than a program of evasion. <cite id="9f9457a1-0">PD-L1 on tumor cells functions as an adaptive escape mechanism</cite>. <cite id="9f9457a1-2">Immune-rich microenvironments with CD8+ TILs can confer improved survival, and PD-L1 expression on immune cells in these settings predicts favorable outcomes</cite>.

# Example 2: Stemness/proliferation markers — CSC-high tumor cells vs differentiated tumor cells

High expression of cancer stem cell (CSC) markers and stemness/proliferation programs in tumor cells is generally associated with aggressive behavior, treatment resistance, and poor survival, whereas loss of expression toward a differentiated state is linked to better outcomes. <cite id="03681528-6">Survivor cancer cells drive relapse as therapy resistance foci</cite>. <cite id="5247c628-1">CD44+/CD24− and high ALDH are markers of poor prognosis in triple-negative breast cancer</cite>. <cite id="5247c628-2">Across ovarian cancer, expression of CSC markers ALDH1A, CD44, and CD133 was evaluated as predictors of patient prognosis</cite>. <cite id="5247c628-6">ALDH1+ and CD44+/CD24−/low subsets in breast cancer demonstrate stronger self-renewal, tumorigenic abilities, and invasive capability, consistent with aggressive risk</cite>. <cite id="5247c628-3">In breast cancer, high CD44/low CD24 marks self-renewal and proliferation, while ALDH1+ emphasizes invasion; both correlate with aggressive risk</cite>.

Mechanism: Stemness elevates self-renewal, genomic instability, and chemoresistance; high ALDH detoxifies genotoxic stress; CD44+/CD24− programs sustain invasiveness and sphere-forming capacity, all traits that undermine long-term survival. <cite id="5247c628-3">The high CD44/low CD24 ratio supports self-renewal and proliferation, while ALDH1+ associates with invasion</cite>. <cite id="5247c628-6">ALDH1+ stem cells show superior tumorigenic abilities—consistent with selection under therapy and poorer survival</cite>.

Important contrast: In normal tissues, stem-like ALDH1+ cells confer regenerative advantages that are typically beneficial and not survival-detrimental; the prognostic "high expression is bad" relation is specific to malignant cells in therapy-exposed disease. <cite id="5247c628-8">ALDH1+ and CD44+/CD24− signatures are used as cancer stem cell markers across tumors, with strong prognostic signals</cite>. <cite id="5247c628-7">Across different cancers, ALDH1A1 and CD44 are higher in more aggressive tumor types, underscoring their link to poorer differentiation and outcome</cite>.

# Example 3: Tumor-cell state and microenvironment — EMT/high-mobility programs vs normal epithelial/stromal cells

High expression of epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT) programs in tumor cells (e.g., upregulation of ZEB1/SNAIL targets) is linked to therapy resistance, dissemination, and worse survival, whereas the same mesenchymal traits in normal epithelial/stromal cells may impair differentiation and tissue homeostasis, amplifying the context dependence of "high expression is bad" in cancer. <cite id="03681528-0">Cancer-defining stresses induce programs that avoid immediate death but require persistent division, highlighting selection for survival under stress</cite>. <cite id="03681528-6">Cells that persist under drug pressure seed recurrence, consistent with EMT-like plasticity and stress tolerance</cite>.

Mechanism: EMT-high tumor cells increase motility, invasion, and resistance to apoptosis/chemo, shortening survival unless countered. In contrast, normal epithelial cells pushed into mesenchymal states lose regenerative fidelity; stromal/immune cells carrying analogous stress programs may fail to support anti-tumor immunity, though the net effect depends on which cells carry the program and their interactions. <cite id="03681528-3">Tumor–stroma interactions determine spread vs elimination; normal-cell programs can either restrain or enable oncogenic progression depending on cross-talk</cite>.

# Example 4: Proliferation- and stress-response markers — FOXM1 and broader cancer-cell survival logic

High expression of proliferation- and stress-response genes in cancer cells is predictive of aggressive behavior and poor prognosis across tumor types, consistent with selection for cells that divide under stress and evade death. <cite id="03681528-1">High FOXM1 expression, involved in cell growth, was associated with a poor prognosis across multiple cancers</cite>. <cite id="03681528-7">This FOXM1 association with poor prognosis was reported across multiple tumor cohorts and media summaries</cite>. <cite id="03681528-0">Under cancer-defining stresses, cells that do not divide persist while others die, favoring survival of high-expression, proliferative subclones</cite>.

# Cross-cutting principles and caveats

- Opposite signs by cell identity: The same marker can be favorable in one lineage and adverse in another. <cite id="9f9457a1-3">PD-L1 on immune cells predicts favorable outcomes in head and neck cancer</cite> while <cite id="9f9457a1-1">on tumor cells predicts worse OS in oral SCC</cite>. <cite id="5247c628-1">High ALDH/CD44/CD24 signatures are poor-prognosis markers in TNBC</cite>, whereas analogous normal stem/progenitor states support tissue repair and survival when confined to healthy tissues.

- Dependence on therapy/immune context: High PD-L1 on tumor cells reflects adaptive immune evasion under treatment, worsening survival; high PD-L1 in immune compartments often reflects regulated interactions that preserve CD8+ T-cell functions and improve OS. <cite id="9f9457a1-0">Tumor PD-L1 is an adaptive escape mechanism</cite>. <cite id="5247c628-6">Stem-like tumor states enhance tumorigenicity and invasion, undermining survival under clinical pressure</cite>.

- Microenvironmental mediation: Normal cells can restrain or promote tumor survival via paracrine support, while immune cells high in checkpoint ligands can either be co-opted by tumors or retain sufficient activity to correlate with better outcomes depending on composition and antigen context. <cite id="03681528-3">Tumor–normal cell relationships govern spread vs elimination</cite>. <cite id="9f9457a1-2">High CD8+ TILs plus immune contexture predict improved DFS and OS</cite>.

- Survival endpoints and effect sizes: The directionality can flip with endpoint and dataset. <cite id="9f9457a1-8">In ASCPs, high PD-L1 linked with shorter overall survival</cite>, whereas <cite id="9f9457a1-3">in head and neck cancer, immune-cell PD-L1 was an independent favorable prognostic factor</cite>. <cite id="5247c628-1">High ALDH/CD44/CD24− marked poor prognosis in TNBC</cite>, and <cite id="5247c628-5">ALDH1+ BCSCs show superior tumorigenic/self-renewal capacity, aligning with aggressive risk</cite>.

# Practical implications

- Interpreting "high expression" as a classifier requires specifying the cell compartment. Tumor-cell–intrinsic high expression of immune-evasive or stemness/proliferation programs should be weighted as adverse for survival, motivating immunotherapy, cytotoxic, or targeted strategies. <cite id="9f9457a1-0">PD-L1 on tumor cells promotes immune escape</cite>. <cite id="5247c628-6">Stem-like ALDH1+ cells are more tumorigenic and invasive</cite>.

- Conversely, high expression in immune cells may be beneficial if it sustains cytotoxic potential; therapeutic strategies should aim to modulate rather than uniformly suppress such interactions. <cite id="9f9457a1-3">Immune-cell PD-L1 predicts favorable OS</cite>. <cite id="9f9457a1-2">CD8+ TIL-rich microenvironments with supportive features improve survival</cite>.

- Therapeutic pressure reshapes expression landscapes. Persistent survivors upregulate survival programs; early longitudinal analyses of "defining cancers" underscore selection for division under stress, explaining why high expression traits expand under treatment and worsen outcomes unless targeted. <cite id="03681528-0">Cells that do not divide persist under cancer-defining stress, highlighting dynamics favoring survival of high-expression, proliferative clones</cite>. <cite id="03681528-6">Persisters are the major cause of treatment failure</cite>.

# Summary

In cancer survival, high expression tends to be neutral or beneficial for the cell that expresses it and detrimental to the organism when it occurs in tumor cells that thereby gain immune evasion, proliferative/stemness advantages, or invasion capacity. The same markers can be neutral or protective for normal immune/stromal cells—sometimes predictive of better survival—if they sustain immune function or stromal support. The net effect is a competition between cell-autonomous survival programs and tissue-level homeostasis, mediated by therapy and the tumor microenvironment, and it explains why "high expression is bad" is a rule with exceptions when the cell context changes. <cite id="9f9457a1-1">High tumor-cell PD-L1 predicts worse OS</cite>, <cite id="9f9457a1-3">high immune-cell PD-L1 predicts better OS</cite>, <cite id="5247c628-1">high ALDH/CD44/CD24− predicts poor prognosis in TNBC</cite>, and <cite id="03681528-6">persistent, high-stress–resistant cancer cells drive relapse</cite>.

without_term.text: How does high expression of a protein impact overall survival outcomes differently in tumor cells compared to immune cells?
without_term.answer:
Summary
High expression of a protein can have opposite implications for overall survival (OS) when it is driven in tumor cells versus when it accumulates in immune cells within the tumor microenvironment (TME). Tumor-intrinsic high expression often reflects oncogenic or mutagenic programs that promote proliferation, immune evasion, and aggression (associated with shorter OS), whereas immune-enriched high expression typically indicates cytotoxic or regulatory infiltration patterns that, when effector/dendritic/adaptive programs dominate, tend to favor longer OS—though subsets like Tregs or myeloid “inflamed” programs can be adverse and context critically matters, including the presence of checkpoint ligands and tumor mutational burden (TMB) and therapeutic modulation of PD-L1 expression patterns (directional shift under therapy). <cite id="4caa25c6-0">This review summarizes the pivotal role of tumor-infiltrating immune cells (TIICs) within the tumor microenvironment (TME) and their impact on cancer prognosis</cite>. <cite id="4caa25c6-1">Tumor-infiltrating Foxp3+ regulatory T cells are associated with worse prognosis in multiple tumors</cite>. <cite id="4caa25c6-3">Immune-active tumor-adjacent tissues are associated with favorable prognosis in stage I lung squamous cell carcinoma</cite>.

Tumor-cell–high expression tends to be “bad” or context-dependent
Across many cancers, highly mutagenic or oncogenic tumor-intrinsic programs linked with “hot” genomic landscapes yield shorter OS. For example, POLE exonuclease-domain mutations drive ultra-high TMB, increased expression of immune checkpoints, and are often associated with higher OS on immunotherapy but paradoxically correlate with poor prognosis in chemotherapy-naïve settings due to aggressive biology. <cite id="45436736-1">POLE-mutant colorectal cancers exhibit increased tumor mutational burden and upregulated immune checkpoint expression, suggesting responsiveness to checkpoint blockade</cite>. <cite id="45436736-2">The increased tumor mutation burden in POLE-exonuclease-mutant tumors is typically associated with benefit from immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy</cite>. <cite id="45436736-4">Inactivating mutations in the POLE exonuclease domain induce somatic hypermutation, yielding high TMB and immunogenicity</cite>. Importantly, high PTX3 and TNFAIP6 transcript levels in head and neck cancer are associated with shorter OS, illustrating how tumor-intrinsic inflammatory mediators (even “beneficial” innate factors in other contexts) can promote aggressiveness when overexpressed in the tumor. <cite id="4caa25c6-4">In HNC patients, high PTX3 and TNFAIP6 transcript levels were significantly associated with shorter overall survival</cite>.

Basal-like and neurotrophilic/oncogenic lineages also carry poor-prognosis implications when tumor-intrinsic programs are activated. Basal-like breast tumors with high epithelial-mesenchymal programs show aggressive OS trajectories; in lung cancer, immune-activated yet disease-accelerating macrophage/tumor-associated neutrophil programs co-opt inflammatory cytokines and chemokines (e.g., PTX3/TNFAIP6), again linking tumor-intrinsic high expression of inflammatory machinery to worse OS and therapeutic vulnerability. <cite id="4caa25c6-3">Immune-active tumor-adjacent immune-rich tissue correlates with favorable OS in early-stage lung squamous cell carcinoma</cite>, underscoring that “inflamed” can be good when it means immune surveillance of the tumor; conversely, “inflamed” tumor-intrinsic stroma/tumoral macrophage programs predict accelerated growth. <cite id="4caa25c6-2">An immune score reflecting the pro- versus anti-tumor balance has major prognostic impact and predicts immunotherapy response in solid tumors</cite>.

Mechanistic rationale (tumor): oncogenic drivers increase proliferation and survival, engage anti-apoptotic and immune-evasive signaling, and can produce neoantigens; high PD-L1 can suppress cytotoxic attack and correlates with aggressive phenotypes in certain contexts. <cite id="45436736-1">POLE-mutant tumors show heightened checkpoint expression and immunogenicity, supporting therapy benefit but also aggressive underlying biology</cite>. <cite id="45436736-6">Somatic POLE exonuclease-domain mutations elicit enhanced intratumoral immune responses, yet these tumors show poor prognosis on chemotherapy, reflecting tumor-intrinsic aggressiveness</cite>.

Immune-cell–high expression tends to be “good” for OS when effector/dendritic/adaptive programs predominate, with well-documented tumor-infiltrating CD8+ T cells and PD-L1 “adaptive immune resistance” patterns
High CD8+ T-cell density, particularly when co-localized with PD-L1+ tumor cells and MSI/TMB-high contexts, associates with improved OS across several cancers. <cite id="d430335c-0">Combined PD-L1 and MSI/CD8+ TILs serve as prognostic biomarkers in gastric cancer</cite>. <cite id="d430335c-2">CD8 TIL infiltration predicts independent overall survival benefit in metastatic colorectal cancer</cite>. <cite id="d430335c-8">Early melanoma studies show CD8+ TIL levels associate with improved survival</cite>. In the same tumors, PD-L1 expression co-maps with CD8+ TIL abundance and MSI/TMB, consistent with the “adaptive immune resistance” program: the tumor upregulates PD-L1 to dampen cytotoxic activity while still attracting CTLs. <cite id="d430335c-6">PD-L1 expression in colorectal cancer associates with microsatellite instability, BRAF mutation, medullary morphology and cytotoxic tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes</cite>. <cite id="4caa25c6-8">Checkpoint expression and immune cell distribution patterns jointly reshape prognosis prediction</cite>.

In breast cancer, “immune contexture” that includes CD8-high plus PD-L1-high patterns is predictive of benefit to PD-1/PD-L1 blockade with better OS under immunotherapy; this underscores that high PD-L1 becomes a favorable (therapeutic) marker when read alongside immune infiltration. <cite id="d430335c-7">Median OS after durvalumab was longer for a CD8×PD-L1 signature-positive cohort versus negative</cite>. Critically, these benefits hinge on the immune milieu; when Treg infiltration predominates, prognosis worsens. <cite id="4caa25c6-1">High Foxp3+ Treg infiltration associates with worse recurrence and prognosis across studies</cite>.

Divergent dynamics and practical caveats
- Lineage-specific immune phenotypes can reverse prognostic interpretation: in lung cancer, immune-active tumor-adjacent tissue predicts favorable OS (hostile-to-tumor environment) while tumor-intrinsic “inflamed” TAM/TAN programs accelerate disease (hostile-to-host programs). <cite id="4caa25c6-3">Immune-active tumor-adjacent tissues predict favorable prognosis in early-stage lung squamous cell carcinoma</cite>.
- Therapeutic context alters PD-L1’s prognostic direction: baseline PD-L1-high with CD8+ infiltration often signals immunologic vulnerability and OS benefit under PD-1/PD-L1 blockade; post-treatment, PD-L1 loss/adaptive escape may invert its association. <cite id="d430335c-0">Combined PD-L1/MSI/CD8+ TILs as prognostic markers in gastric cancer</cite>. <cite id="d430335c-7">Immunotherapy confers longer OS to CD8×PD-L1–positive patients, reversing the naive “independent PD-L1-associated” directionality</cite>.
- Inflammation signatures can be double-edged: tumor-intrinsic PTX3/TNFAIP6 programs predict death in HNC; in contrast, stromal/tumor-associated immune “active” status outside the parenchyma correlates with favorable OS. <cite id="4caa25c6-4">High PTX3 and TNFAIP6 transcripts correlate with shorter OS in HNC</cite>. <cite id="4caa25c6-3">Immune-active tumor-adjacent areas predict favorable outcomes</cite>.
- Innate tumor-cell stress responses (e.g., high MHC/PSGL-1 pathways, ER stress, cytokines) often worsen OS by enabling immune evasion and therapy resistance (e.g., NECN/B-ATK fusions can co-opt survival signaling that also suppresses NK cytotoxicity via SERPINB4). <cite id="c2485718-8">ALK fusion–driven NSCLC oncogenes promote survival and inhibit NK cell responses via SERPINB4 expression</cite>. <cite id="45436736-1">POLE mutations drive high TMB and checkpoint expression, linking high “stress” signatures with immune pressure and aggressive growth</cite>.

Putting it together: why the directions differ
- Tumor-intrinsic high expression typically reflects oncogenic or mutagenic pressure: proliferative/anti-apoptotic signaling, neoantigen load and PD-L1 upregulation foster immune evasion and rapid growth, yielding poor OS unless countered by effective immunity or immunotherapy (direction can become favorable under PD-1/PD-L1). <cite id="45436736-1">POLE-mutant tumors are immunogenic yet aggressive, requiring context-dependent interpretation</cite>. <cite id="4caa25c6-6">Enhanced intratumoral immune responses in POLE-mutant stage II CRC do not translate to better outcomes on chemo, implying intrinsically aggressive biology</cite>.
- Immune-enriched high expression reflects the host’s tumor-suppressive efforts: CD8+ T cells and dendritic-cell-driven adaptive responses correlate with longer OS; when they dominate, OS improves; when suppressed by checkpoint ligands or skewed by Tregs/myeloid programs, OS worsens. <cite id="d430335c-2">CD8 TILs are predictive of OS benefit</cite>. <cite id="4caa25c6-1">High Treg infiltration correlates with worse prognosis</cite>. <cite id="4caa25c6-2">A balance-based immune score yields major prognostic impact across solid tumors</cite>.
- Spatial biology matters: “Immune hot” tumor stroma/adjacent fields may mean favorable OS (active adaptive surveillance), whereas “inflamed” tumor parenchyma can indicate tumor-driven immune subversion and acceleration. <cite id="4caa25c6-3">Immune-active tumor-adjacent tissues predict favorable prognosis</cite>.

Practical takeaways when evaluating “high expression”
- Ask who is expressing it and where: tumor-cell expression of oncogenic/inflammatory drivers (e.g., POLE-ExoD, PTX3/TNFAIP6, NECN-BATK–like survival/immune-suppressive programs) generally signals poor OS; immune-cell expression is beneficial if it reflects CD8+ effector/THEM biology but can be adverse if Treg- or myeloid-dominated. <cite id="4caa25c6-4">High PTX3/TNFAIP6 transcripts predict shorter OS</cite>. <cite id="d430335c-2">CD8 TIL infiltration improves OS in mCRC</cite>. <cite id="4caa25c6-1">Treg infiltration worsens prognosis</cite>.
- Check the adaptive context: co-expression of PD-L1 with CD8 and MSI/TMB suggests immunotherapy-sensitive, favorable-prognosis phenotypes; PD-L1 alone can be ambiguous and may invert direction after treatment. <cite id="d430335c-0">PD-L1 with MSI/CD8 predicts prognosis</cite>. <cite id="d430335c-7">OS improves under durvalumab in CD8×PD-L1+ patients</cite>.
- Recognize that some tumor-intrinsic “hot” programs can simultaneously repel cytotoxic lymphocytes (NK/CTL suppression by SERPINB4, ALK-fusion mimic) yet attract T cells to the stroma/adjacent fields, producing spatially distinct prognostic signals. <cite id="c2485718-8">ALK fusion NSCLC oncogenes inhibit NK responses via SERPINB4 while promoting survival</cite>. <cite id="4caa25c6-3">Immune active tumor-adjacent immune-rich tissue predicts favorable OS</cite>.

Bottom line
- If a protein’s high expression is driven by tumor-intrinsic oncogenic/mutagenic pathways (e.g., POLE ExoD, NECN/B-ATK–like survival pathways, PTX3/TNFAIP6 inflammatory axes), it generally confers shorter OS by promoting aggressive growth and immune evasion. <cite id="45436736-1">POLE-mutant tumors show high checkpoint expression and tumor-driven immunogenicity</cite> <cite id="4caa25c6-4">High PTX3/TNFAIP6 predict shorter OS</cite>.
- If a protein’s high expression reflects immune-enriched, cytotoxic-adaptive programs (e.g., CD8+ TILs co-expressing PD-L1, with MSI/TMB), it generally confers longer OS by indicating host tumor control; however, if driven by Tregs or disease-accelerating myeloid programs, it can predict worse OS. <cite id="d430335c-2">CD8 infiltration confers independent OS benefit in mCRC</cite> <cite id="4caa25c6-1">Treg infiltration predicts worse outcomes</cite> <cite id="4caa25c6-2">Immune balance scores strongly predict OS</cite>.
- Interpreting high expression must disambiguate cell-of-origin and spatial context, because the same marker (e.g., PD-L1) can switch from prognostically unfavorable at baseline to favorable after immunotherapy-sensitive “adaptive” patterns take over. <cite id="d430335c-6">PD-L1 associates with cytotoxic TILs and MSI/TMB</cite> <cite id="d430335c-7">OS benefit under PD-1 blockade in CD8×PD-L1–positive patients</cite>.

questions.original_query: How do PD-1 and its ligands contribute to immune tolerance and regulate T-cell responses?

query.text: How do PD-1 and its ligands contribute to immune tolerance and regulate T-cell responses?
query.answer:
Summary

The PD-1 (CD274)–PD-L (PD-L1/CD273; PD-L2/CD274) axis is an evolutionary conserved co-inhibitory checkpoint that calibrates immune responses and enforces peripheral tolerance by curbing T cell activation, clonal expansion, and effector function when antigenic stimuli are suboptimal, self-reactive, or chronic. Engagement of PD-1 by either ligand delivers inhibitory signals that converge on suppression of proximal TCR signaling, blunting IL-2 production and proliferation, promoting inhibitory receptor co-expression (e.g., CTLA-4, TIM-3), and driving sustained transcriptional and metabolic programs compatible with T-cell exhaustion. In tumors and inflamed tissues, upregulation of PD-L1 and, in specific niches, PD-L2 can embed effector T cells into suppressive states that limit antitumor immunity; blocking this pathway restores T-cell function and underpins modern immunotherapy. <cite id="32b8a5ef-0">PD-1 and its ligands, PD-L1 and PD-L2, have emerged as critical inhibitory signaling pathways that regulate T cell response and maintain peripheral tolerance</cite> <cite id="32b8a5ef-1">PD-1 engagement by its ligands maintains peripheral tolerance but compromises anti-tumor immunity, and blocking antibodies reverse this suppression</cite> <cite id="32b8a5ef-5">Inhibitory signals from PD-1–PD-L1 or PD-1–PD-L2 mediate mechanisms of tolerance</cite>.

Mechanism: How PD-1 Inhibits T Cells

PD-1 is a type I immunoglobulin receptor with two immunoreceptor tyrosine–based inhibitory motifs (ITIM) and an immunoreceptor tyrosine–based switch motif (ITSM). Ligand binding induces tyrosine phosphorylation of these motifs, recruiting Src homotypic tyrosine kinase SHP-1 and SHP-2 to dephosphorylate key signaling nodes, thereby attenuating proximal TCR signaling and downstream transcriptional programs that drive activation and cytokine production. <cite id="4535bd08-0">After encounter with PD-L1, PD-1 translocates into TCR microclusters, recruits SHP-2 transiently, and suppresses phosphorylation of TCR signaling components</cite> <cite id="c91a0064-4">SHP2 dephosphorylates ITK downstream of PD-1 specifically, associating with PD-1 inhibitory functions</cite> <cite id="c91a0064-9">Full PD-1 activation requires phosphorylation of both ITIM and ITSM; ITSM binds the SHP2 C-SH2 domain with strong affinity to recruit SHP2</cite>.

At the microdomain level, engagement of PD-1 competes with and reshapes early TCR/CD28 signaling complexes. Early after TCR engagement, PD-1 forms co-inhibitory microclusters with SHP2 in T-cell receptor–proximal contact sites on the immunological synapse, where it suppresses proximal TCR signaling, including ZAP-70 and LAT signaling, effectively throttling calcium fluxes and NFAT–AP-1–dependent transcription. <cite id="4535bd08-0">PD-1 rapidly translocates to microclusters and recruits SHP2 to suppress TCR phosphorylation</cite> <cite id="4535bd08-7">PD-1 primarily targets TCR signaling in the inhibition of functional T-cell activation</cite>. Functionally, blocking PD-1/PD-L interactions restores early signaling nodes and downstream outputs. <cite id="4535bd08-1">PD-L2 suppresses T-cell signaling via coinhibitory microclusters, with engagement of PD-L1 or PD-L2 interfering with early TCR/CD28 signaling and inhibiting IL-2 production, proliferation, and effector function</cite>.

Receptor-ligand specificity and adaptor scaffolding

PD-L1 and PD-L2 share PD-1 as a common inhibitory receptor, but they differ in tissue and APC expression and in signaling nuances. PD-L1 is broadly induced on lymphocytes, dendritic cells (DCs), macrophages, and tumor cells under inflammatory cytokines (type I/II IFNs), whereas PD-L2 is less abundant but can be induced on certain antigen-presenting cells and is a potent co-inhibitor in early TCR signaling. <cite id="32b8a5ef-8">PD-L1 is expressed on lymphocytes and myeloid cells and is upregulated under immune activation by type I and type II IFNs</cite> <cite id="32b8a5ef-5">PD-1 interaction with PD-L1 or PD-L2 inhibits T-cell signaling and underlies mechanisms of tolerance</cite>. Engagement of PD-L1 or PD-L2 on T cells inhibits IL-2 production, proliferation, and cytotoxic effector functions, indicating a shared inhibitory program delivered through PD-1. <cite id="4535bd08-2">Binding of either PD-L1 or PD-L2 to PD-1 interferes with early TCR/CD28 signaling and inhibits IL-2 production, T-cell proliferation, and effector functions</cite> <cite id="4535bd08-3">PD-L1 engagement with PD-1 on effector T cells inhibits cytotoxic activity by terminating TCR signal transduction</cite> <cite id="4535bd08-1">PD-L2 engages PD-1 to suppress T-cell signaling via coinhibitory microclusters</cite>.

The SLAM-family/SHP2 axis has been proposed to coordinate PD-1 with integrin-linked inhibitory microdomains; however, some recent data argue that PD-1 can function upstream among proximal TCR inhibitory signals. <cite id="c91a0064-0">SHP-2 is dispensable for establishing T-cell exhaustion and PD-1 signaling in vivo, indicating PD-1’s capacity to impose inhibitory programs independently of SHP-2 sufficiency in some contexts</cite> <cite id="4535bd08-0">PD-1 integrates into TCR microclusters to suppress phosphorylation of TCR-linked signaling</cite> <cite id="c91a0064-1">SHP2 dephosphorylates ITK specifically downstream of PD-1, mediating PD-1 inhibitory cellular functions</cite>.

Functional outcomes: cytokines, metabolism, and proliferation

PD-1–mediated co-inhibition suppresses early cytokine transcription, particularly IL-2, blunting clonal expansion and effector differentiation. This is a central homeostatic mechanism that damps responses to suboptimal or persistent antigen, curbing tissue damage and autoimmunity. <cite id="4535bd08-2">PD-1–ligand binding inhibits IL-2 production and T-cell proliferation</cite> <cite id="4535bd08-3">By terminating TCR signal transduction, PD-L1–PD-1 engagement inhibits cytotoxic activities</cite> <cite id="4535bd08-1">PD-L1/PD-L2 binding to PD-1 inhibits early signaling and effector functions</cite>. At the molecular level, PD-1 impairs store-operated calcium entry and NFAT activation, and it disrupts preformed IL-2 mRNA stabilization and translation, converging with mTOR/IL-7R survival signaling to maintain quiescence or exhaustion rather than effector expansion. <cite id="32b8a5ef-0">PD-1 restrains T-cell responses to preserve peripheral tolerance</cite> <cite id="4535bd08-0">Within microclusters, PD-1 recruits SHP2 and suppresses TCR phosphorylation, impairing early activation</cite>. PD-1–dependent suppression of IL-2 and proliferation can be relieved by PD-1 blockade, restoring cytotoxicity and cytokine production—key mechanisms behind checkpoint inhibitor therapy. <cite id="32b8a5ef-1">Blocking antibodies to PD-1/PD-L1 reverse co-inhibition and restore anti-tumor T-cell responses</cite> <cite id="4535bd08-2">Reversal of PD-1 engagement restores IL-2, proliferation, and effector functions</cite>.

Fate programs and transcriptional control

Chronic PD-1 signaling associates with T-cell exhaustion, marked by persistent expression of inhibitory receptors (PD-1, TIM-3, CTLA-4), reduced IL-2, and reliance on IL-7/IL-15 survival pathways; TCF-1 (TCFA) maintains a self-renewing exhausted progenitor state, while TOX emerges as a transcriptional master regulator of exhaustion. <cite id="32b8a5ef-1">PD-1 maintains peripheral tolerance but compromises anti-tumor immunity</cite> <cite id="4535bd08-3">Sustained PD-1 signaling can drive exhaustion phenotypes with diminished effector function</cite> <cite id="c91a0064-4">Downstream of PD-1, SHP2 impairs ITK, aligning signaling with functional suppression</cite>. Although PD-1 is not the sole driver of exhaustion, it provides a dominant negative pressure on TCR signaling that skews fate outcomes; genetic or pharmacologic relief restores effector function. <cite id="4535bd08-7">PD-1 primarily targets TCR signaling in inhibiting functional activation</cite> <cite id="c91a0064-0">SHP-2 may be dispensable for establishing exhaustion, showing PD-1 can impose inhibitory programs independently in vivo</cite>.

Spatial and ligand-biased regulation in tolerance

Tissue and tumor contexts shape PD-1/PD-L engagement. PD-L1 is broadly inducible by interferons on APCs, tumor cells, and some lymphocytes, and is commonly upregulated in inflamed tissues, providing tonic inhibitory cues to local T cells; PD-L2, though less prevalent, is expressed in specific APC subsets and can dominate early co-inhibitory signaling at the first TCR engagement. <cite id="32b8a5ef-8">PD-L1 is upregulated by type I and II IFN on lymphocytes and myeloid cells</cite> <cite id="32b8a5ef-5">PD-L1/PD-L2–PD-1 interactions enforce inhibitory signaling and tolerance</cite> <cite id="4535bd08-1">PD-L2 co-inhibitory microclusters strongly suppress early TCR signaling</cite>. This anatomical specificity allows PD-1 to regulate peripheral tolerance in tissues: in steady state, low-level self-antigen encounters or bystander activation engage PD-L1 on quiescent APCs to prevent autoimmunity; in tumors, PD-L1 on cancer cells and myeloid infiltrates present strong inhibitory cues that suppress CTLs and TH cells, fostering immune evasion. <cite id="32b8a5ef-1">PD-1 co-inhibition maintains tolerance yet impedes anti-tumor immunity; blockade reverses this balance</cite> <cite id="4535d1c4-1">In tumors, PD-L1 on tumor and stromal cells engages PD-1 on T cells to drive dysfunction</cite>.

Cross-talk with other inhibitory axes and receptor hierarchy

PD-1 operates with, and sometimes upstream of, other inhibitory receptors shaped by antigenic context and TCR avidity. At suboptimal TCR signals, inhibitory receptors (PD-1, PD-L2 microclusters, 2B4, NKR-P1) assemble inhibitory microdomains, with PD-1 exerting a primary suppressive role on TCR signal 1; when signals improve, PD-1 is outcompeted by CD28 for costimulatory cues, allowing full activation. <cite id="4535bd08-0">PD-1 integrates into TCR microclusters to suppress phosphorylation of TCR-linked signaling</cite> <cite id="4535bd08-7">PD-1 mainly targets proximal TCR signaling in inhibition</cite> <cite id="4535bd08-1">PD-L2 co-inhibitory microclusters suppress early signaling</cite>. This hierarchy underpins homeostasis: weak or chronic antigenic stimulation biases PD-1/2B4/NKR-P1 dominance, promoting anergic or exhausted states; strong antigen plus CD28 engagement reverses this, explaining the therapeutic logic of combining CTLA-4 blockade or costimulation with PD-1 pathway interruption. <cite id="32b8a5ef-0">PD-1 restrains T-cell responses to maintain peripheral tolerance</cite> <cite id="c91a0064-0">Even when SHP-2 is not rate limiting, PD-1 can enforce exhaustion, highlighting receptor-level control</cite>.

Regulatory T cell (Treg) and APC crosstalk

PD-1 pathways also tune the milieu via APCs and Tregs. PD-L1 upregulation on DCs and macrophages during activation allows them to deliver “educative” inhibitory signals to responder T cells, shaping the polarization and magnitude of helper and cytotoxic responses; within inflamed tissues and tumors, Tregs express PD-1 and can further transmit inhibitory cues to effector cells through PD-L1 upregulation on APCs in the neighborhood, amplifying peripheral tolerance. <cite id="32b8a5ef-8">PD-L1 is induced on APCs under IFN-driven activation</cite> <cite id="4535bd08-2">PD-1 engagement inhibits IL-2, proliferation, and effector programs in CD4+ and CD8+ T cells</cite>. In steady state, PD-1–high, IL-2–low states on T cells can reflect low-avidity interactions with self-antigen or bystander APCs; PD-1 blockade rescues these cells to rejoin the immune response hierarchy. <cite id="4535bd08-0">By suppressing TCR phosphorylation within microclusters, PD-1 restrains activation</cite> <cite id="32b8a5ef-1">Checkpoint blockade reverses PD-1 co-inhibition and restores anti-tumor activity</cite>.

Therapeutic modulation and evolutionary purpose

Physiologically, PD-1–dependent suppression prevents runaway autoimmunity and tissue damage during weak or chronic antigen exposure; pathophysiologically, tumors and pathogens co-opt this axis to blunt immunity. Anti–PD-1/PD-L1 therapies attenuate inhibitory signaling, restoring IL-2 production, proliferation, cytotoxicity, and cytokine profiles of effector and memory T cells, enabling immune control. <cite id="4535bd08-2">Blocking PD-1–ligand interactions restores IL-2, proliferation, and effector functions</cite> <cite id="32b8a5ef-1">PD-1/PD-L1 blocking antibodies reverse tolerance and enhance anti-tumor immunity</cite>. Although PD-1 is not the only pathway controlling exhaustion, it sits at the apex of inhibitory control, and its blockade can reinvigorate dysfunctional T cells with durable functional recovery in multiple contexts. <cite id="4535bd08-7">PD-1 primarily targets TCR signaling</cite> <cite id="32b8a5ef-5">PD-1–PD-L interactions inhibit T-cell signaling in multiple settings of tolerance</cite> <cite id="c91a0064-8">Interfering with PD-1/PD-L1 releases exhausted CD8+ T cells from PD-1–dependent suppression</cite>.

Key Takeaways

- PD-1–PD-L1 and PD-1–PD-L2 interactions enforce peripheral tolerance by directly inhibiting proximal TCR signaling inside microclusters, recruiting SHP-1/2 to dephosphorylate key nodes and suppressing IL-2 synthesis, proliferation, and cytotoxicity. <cite id="4535bd08-0">PD-1 engages SHP-2 to suppress phosphorylation of TCR signaling</cite> <cite id="32b8a5ef-8">PD-L1 is induced in IFN-rich settings on APCs and tumor cells</cite> <cite id="4535bd08-2">PD-1–ligand binding inhibits IL-2, proliferation, and effector function</cite>.
- Spatially patterned ligand delivery (PD-L1 on broad APC/tumor/tissue pools; PD-L2 on select APCs) tunes the balance between activation, anergy, and exhaustion depending on antigenic context. <cite id="32b8a5ef-5">PD-1/PD-L1/PD-L2 deliver inhibitory signals for tolerance</cite> <cite id="4535bd08-1">PD-L2 coinhibitory microclusters powerfully suppress early signaling</cite>.
- Receptor hierarchy and crosstalk position PD-1 to act as a dominant early brake on TCR signal 1 under weak or chronic stimulation; relief via PD-1 blockade restores effector function and underpins modern cancer immunotherapy. <cite id="4535d1c4-1">Targeting PD-1/PD-L1 restores effector T-cell function in tumors</cite> <cite id="4535bd08-7">PD-1 primarily targets TCR signaling</cite> <cite id="32b8a5ef-1">Blocking PD-1/PD-L1 reverses co-inhibition</cite>.

Limitations and nuances

PD-1’s necessity/sufficiency varies by context and developmental stage: although PD-1 co-inhibition is central, exhaustion can arise via PD-1–independent mechanisms, and PD-1 or SHP-2 sufficiency is not universally required to establish exhaustion. <cite id="32b8a5ef-5">PD-1–independent mechanisms also mediate tolerance</cite> <cite id="c91a0064-0">SHP-2 can be dispensable in vivo for PD-1–induced exhaustion</cite>. Moreover, PD-1 can be upregulated on T cells as an adaptive mechanism to buffer excessive antigenic load, adding a feedback layer to homeostasis. <cite id="32b8a5ef-0">PD-1 restrains T-cell responses and maintains peripheral tolerance</cite>. Together, PD-1 and its ligands act as rheostats for T-cell activation, balancing responsiveness with tolerance across tissues, tumors, and time.
