without_preference.text: How does focal boost radiotherapy compare to whole-gland boost treatments for prostate cancer patients?
without_preference.answer:
Below is a practical, evidence-grounded comparison of focal boost radiotherapy and whole‑gland boost treatments for prostate cancer, organized by clinical scenario and highlighting outcomes and toxicity trade‑offs.

# What “focal boost” and “whole‑gland boost” mean

Focal boost radiotherapy delivers an additional, higher‑dose fraction or fractionated boost to the visible intraprostatic tumor(s) identified by imaging (e.g., MRI), while sparing surrounding normal prostate parenchyma and critical structures. Whole‑gland boost strategies instead increase the dose to the entire prostate/seminal vesicles as a second phase or add a high‑dose brachytherapy component to the entire gland after initial external beam therapy. <cite id="508809fc-0">This review compares a FLAME‑style EBRT boost vs a LDR brachytherapy boost in terms of oncologic outcomes, toxicity, and feasibility.</cite> <cite id="508809fc-2">This study aims to consolidate clinical and planning studies that implemented whole gland prostate brachytherapy and focal dose escalation to intraprostatic lesion(s) (IPLs).</cite> <cite id="508809fc-5">Focal boost radiotherapy is expected to enable an elevated tumor control without an increase in toxicity in prostate cancer.</cite>

# Primary treatment in favorable/intermediate‑risk disease

Focal boost with external beam radiotherapy: Multi‑center trials show that adding a focal boost to MR‑visible lesions improves biochemical control without increasing toxicity. <cite id="d6a29418-1">The FLAME trial provides strong evidence that MR‑guided external beam radiation therapy focal boost for localized prostate cancer improves outcomes, with 5‑year biochemical relapse‑free survival gains for intermediate‑ and high‑risk disease.</cite> <cite id="d6a29418-3">Onclive concludes that a focal boost to intraprostatic lesions in EBRT improves biochemical disease‑free survival for localized intermediate‑ and high‑risk cases.</cite> <cite id="d6a29418-2">Risk modeling and trial analyses of FLAME show isotoxic focal boosting to intraprostatic lesions with favorable outcomes in intermediate‑ and high‑risk disease.</cite> Very recently, a hypofractionated (hypo‑FLAME) trial reported that prostate SBRT with an integrated focal boost achieved excellent 5‑year outcomes comparable to focal boost FLAME cohorts, supporting similar safety and control across dosing strategies. <cite id="d6a29418-0">Prostate SBRT with an integrated focal boost demonstrated excellent 5‑year outcomes; the 5‑year bDFS is comparable to that of the focal boosted FLAME cohort.</cite>

Whole‑gland boost options:
- EBRT plus whole‑prostate dose escalation: Conventional and hypofractionated dose‑escalation strategies improve outcomes but tend to raise toxicity risk, particularly for urinary symptoms. <cite id="508809fc-1">With whole‑gland dose escalation, increased toxicity has been observed in both external‑beam and brachytherapy trials.</cite> <cite id="d6a29418-7">Focal lesion ablation with EBRT boosted by brachytherapy (EBRT‑boosted BT) provides efficacy for intermediate‑ and high‑risk disease, while minimizing toxicity—contrasting with whole‑gland EBRT escalation where late toxicity rises with higher dose volumes.</cite>
- Brachytherapy whole‑gland plus boost: Whole‑gland brachytherapy (LDR or HDR) followed by a boost is biologically plausible for complete coverage, but comparative randomized evidence versus focal strategies is limited. <cite id="508809fc-4">Whole gland brachytherapy (BT) boost in combination with external beam radiotherapy (EBRT) improves biochemical relapse‑free survival (bRFS).</cite> <cite id="508809fc-9">Reports summarizing combined EBRT and prostate brachytherapy boosts indicate improved biochemical failure control but mixed effects on overall survival compared with EBRT alone.</cite> Planning and clinical studies emphasize integrating focal dose escalation to IPLs within whole‑gland approaches to mitigate toxicity. <cite id="508809fc-2">Clinical and planning data for whole‑gland prostate brachytherapy with focal dose escalation to intraprostatic lesions consolidate a dosimetric rationale for combining whole‑gland coverage with targeted boosts.</cite>

Takeaway for favorable/intermediate risk: Focal boost strategies, particularly EBRT‑based focal boost (FLAME/hypo‑FLAME), consistently demonstrate improved biochemical control with non‑inferior toxicity relative to whole‑gland boost strategies, which more often increase toxicity as dose and coverage expand. <cite id="d6a29418-1">The FLAME trial provides strong evidence that MR‑guided EBRT focal boost improves localized control without toxicity trade‑offs typical in whole‑gland approaches.</cite> <cite id="d6a29418-0">Integrating a focal boost into hypofractionated SBRT yields 5‑year bDFS comparable to conventional focal boost cohorts.</cite> <cite id="508809fc-1">Whole‑gland dose escalation increases toxicity in external‑beam and brachytherapy trials; toxicity rises with broader coverage.</cite>

# Primary treatment in intermediate/high‑risk disease and multimodal settings

Focal EBRT boost plus initial EBRT: Adding a focal boost to EBRT improves biochemical DFS at 5 years in intermediate‑ to high‑risk disease when fractionation is conventional or hypofractionated, with toxicity comparable to prior cohorts. <cite id="d6a29418-4">The FLAME trial shows improved 5‑year biochemical relapse‑free survival at conventional fractionation with focal boost; a multicenter hypofractionated study (hypo‑FLAME) reports favorable 5‑year bDFS comparable to FLAME.</cite> <cite id="d6a29418-3">Focal boost addition increases biochemical disease‑free survival in localized intermediate‑ and high‑risk disease.</cite> <cite id="508809fc-7">EBRT‑boosted brachytherapy strategies (focal lesion ablation) produce intermediate‑ to high‑risk disease control with overall favorable early outcomes.</cite>

Whole‑gland brachytherapy boost after EBRT: Whole‑gland brachytherapy boosts have been reported to enhance bRFS in combined‑modality settings, likely due to superior tumor control from high‑dose surface applicators and conformal dose to the prostate/seminal vesicles; however, the best evidence is retrospective or narrative, and over‑coverage/toxicity remains a concern, especially for urinary toxicity. <cite id="508809fc-3">Brachytherapy boost improves survival and decreases distant metastasis risk compared to external beam radiotherapy alone in intermediate and high‑risk disease, supporting its role as a local boost when integrated appropriately.</cite> <cite id="508809fc-4">Whole‑gland brachytherapy boost plus EBRT improves biochemical outcomes; contemporary reviews reinforce biologic potency of brachytherapy boosts.</cite> <cite id="d6a29418-2">Trial analyses highlight isotoxic implementation is key; dosimetry can keep toxicity in check when boosts are tightly targeted.</cite>

Takeaway for intermediate/high‑risk: Focal boost enhances prostate‑specific control, especially when macroscopic lesions are clearly defined; whole‑gland boost remains an option when complete coverage is preferred (e.g., extensive Gleason patterns, surgical bed involvement) or when brachytherapy can be integrated with EBRT to deliver a potent local boost while controlling toxicity through careful planning. <cite id="508809fc-0">Comparisons of EBRT focal boost vs LDR focal boost argue for oncologic benefit and feasibility with controlled toxicity.</cite> <cite id="508809fc-5">The dosimetric rationale is that elevated focal dose can increase tumor control without increasing toxicity, aligning with FLAME trial findings.</cite>

# Salvage treatment after primary EBRT or surgery

Focal salvage boost: Focal MRI‑identified lesion boosts with EBRT/SBRT can re‑establish high‑dose control in recurrent disease while sparing normal tissue. <cite id="d6a29418-8">Focal boosting of macroscopic visible tumor with external beam radiotherapy increases biochemical disease‑free survival and has been evaluated in prospective contexts.</cite> <cite id="d6a29418-5">Stereotactic body radiotherapy with focal boost delivers very high local doses to visible lesions with favorable early toxicity and functional outcomes.</cite> <cite id="ef0ae8b8-5">Salvage low‑dose‑rate brachytherapy trials report 5‑year freedom from biochemical failure around 68%, with late G3 urinary toxicity ≈12%, supporting the feasibility of salvage gland‑sparing strategies.</cite>

Whole/partial‑gland salvage brachytherapy: Whole‑gland salvage brachytherapy boosts remain common and can reduce risk of marginal miss relative to partial foci, but toxicity profiles are similar when boosts are carefully planned. <cite id="ef0ae8b8-2">Whole‑gland salvage brachytherapy reduces the risk of marginal miss in prostate cancer, a concern when initial disease was high‑risk or margins were involved.</cite> <cite id="ef0ae8b8-1">Salvage LDR brachytherapy demonstrates late G3 urinary toxicities ≈12% and rectal G3 ≈1%, with no significant difference in toxicity or efficacy versus partial approaches in some series.</cite> <cite id="ef0ae8b8-4">Contemporary salvage brachytherapy guidance notes that whole‑gland salvage is the majority of studies, with an increasing trend toward SBRT and HDR modalities.</cite>

Takeaway for salvage: Focal salvage boosts can achieve favorable biochemical control with potent local dosing and acceptable toxicity in selected patients with clearly identified recurrences, while whole/partial‑gland salvage brachytherapy remains attractive for broader lesions or surgical margins. Individualized selection should prioritize lesion delineation quality, prior treatment anatomy, functional goals, and patient comorbidities. <cite id="d6a29418-8">Focal boosting increases biochemical disease‑free survival in salvage contexts when intraprostatic lesions are visible and targetable.</cite> <cite id="ef0ae8b8-1">Salvage LDR brachytherapy achieves ≈68% 5‑year freedom from biochemical failure with acceptable toxicity, offering a gland‑sparing option.</cite> <cite id="ef0ae8b8-2">Whole‑gland salvage can mitigate marginal miss risk; focal salvage depends on accurate targeting and lesion definition.</cite>

# Toxicity and tolerability comparison

Across strategies, focal boosts have repeatedly shown improved biochemical control with non‑inferior systemic toxicity compared with historical or broader coverage approaches. <cite id="d6a29418-2">FLAME‑style isotoxic focal boosting achieves improved tumor control without added toxicity risk compared with whole‑prostate strategies.</cite> <cite id="d6a29418-5">Prospective phase II SBRT focal boost data show excellent local control and favorable toxicity/tolerability.</cite> <cite id="d6a29418-0">Hypo‑FLAME reports excellent 5‑year outcomes with comparable bDFS to FLAME, indicating that hypofractionation can be integrated safely with focal boosts.</cite> For whole‑gland boosts, increased toxicity has been frequently observed as coverage and dose increase, particularly for urinary symptoms; careful dosimetry and integration with EBRT can mitigate but not eliminate this risk. <cite id="508809fc-1">Whole‑gland dose escalation increases toxicity in external‑beam and brachytherapy trials; toxicity trends upward with higher whole‑gland doses.</cite> In brachytherapy‑based combined approaches, meticulous template/CT fusion, image‑guided placement, and dose‑volume constraints support acceptable genitourinary and gastrointestinal toxicities. <cite id="508809fc-2">Consolidation of whole‑gland prostate brachytherapy with focal dose escalation emphasizes dosimetric control to preserve organ function while boosting local control.</cite>

# When to favor focal boost vs whole‑gland boost: practical selection

- Prefer focal boost when: lesions are well‑defined on MRI, patient selection is intermediate/low risk or favorable high‑risk, and organ‑sparing is a priority. EBRT focal boost and EBRT‑boosted brachytherapy (focal lesion ablation) both deliver potent local boosts with similar or better biochemical control and manageable toxicity. <cite id="d6a29418-1">FLAME and modern imaging‑guided focal boosts show significant biochemical gains with controlled toxicity.</cite> <cite id="d6a29418-3">Focal boosts improve biochemical disease‑free survival across intermediate‑ and high‑risk cohorts.</cite> <cite id="d6a29418-7">EBRT‑boosted brachytherapy provides efficacy with favorable early outcomes in intermediate/high‑risk disease.</cite>
- Prefer whole‑gland boost when: disease biology or surgical pathology suggest extensive microscopic involvement, close or positive margins, or when brachytherapy can be integrated to deliver a high‑dose boost while covering the surgical bed and apex; this approach may lower risk of marginal miss but carries higher toxicity if not optimized. <cite id="ef0ae8b8-2">Whole‑gland salvage/primary boosts reduce marginal miss risk and can be justified for initially high‑risk disease or positive margins.</cite> <cite id="508809fc-3">Brachytherapy plus boost improves survival and reduces distant metastases compared to EBRT alone, supporting whole‑gland boost in high‑risk settings.</cite> <cite id="508809fc-4">Whole‑gland brachytherapy boost combinations improve biochemical outcomes, especially when integrated with EBRT.</cite>
- Salvage: select focal boost when MRI detects dominant local lesions; choose whole/partial‑gland brachytherapy boost for broader recurrences, post‑prostatectomy positive surgical margins/capsular involvement, or when prior radiation limits EBRT tolerance. <cite id="d6a29418-8">Focal boosts increase biochemical control in salvage settings based on lesion visibility.</cite> <cite id="ef0ae8b8-2">Whole‑gland salvage reduces miss risk and may be favored after positive surgical margins.</cite>

# Bottom line and evidence gaps

Current evidence supports focal boost as at least as good as, and often better than, whole‑gland boost approaches for biochemical disease control with similar or lower toxicity, particularly for intermediate/low‑risk disease where MR‑visible lesions guide targeting; whole‑gland boosts retain a role when broader coverage or surgical bed control is warranted or when brachytherapy’s biological potency is integrated carefully to avoid toxicity. <cite id="d6a29418-1">Strong trial evidence for focal EBRT boosts in intermediate/high‑risk disease suggests favorable control and toxicity.</cite> <cite id="d6a29418-0">Hypofractionated SBRT focal boosts achieve comparable 5‑year bDFS to conventional focal boost cohorts.</cite> <cite id="508809fc-1">Whole‑gland dose escalation often increases toxicity, arguing for focal strategies when feasible.</cite> A key gap is the paucity of directly randomized, head‑to‑head trials pitting pure focal boost (EBRT or brachytherapy) against true whole‑gland boost across risk strata and modalities; planned or ongoing comparative phase III efforts in focal ablation/boost for intermediate‑ to high‑risk disease and selected salvage cohorts should clarify small outcome differentials and optimize dosing/fractionation strategies. <cite id="d6a29418-4">Ongoing and completed focal boost trials provide class‑effect evidence but leave some comparative uncertainties versus whole‑gland strategies.</cite> <cite id="508809fc-5">Reviews emphasize that focal boosts aim to increase tumor control without toxicity, but definitive head‑to‑head comparisons remain limited.</cite>

# Practical counseling points for patients

- If your Gleason grade, PSA, and surgical/MP‑MRI show a dominant, well‑defined lesion, a focal boost is likely to improve biochemical control with similar sexual, urinary, and bowel function—either as an EBRT micro‑boost (FLAME/hypo‑FLAME) or as a focal EBRT‑boosted brachytherapy ablation—while preserving more normal prostate tissue. <cite id="d6a29418-1">MRI‑guided EBRT focal boost improves local control and preserves function.</cite> <cite id="d6a29418-7">EBRT‑boosted brachytherapy delivers high‑dose lesion ablation with favorable early outcomes.</cite>
- If disease appears more diffuse, involves surgical margins or apex, or recurs after a prostatectomy, a whole‑gland boost or whole/partial‑gland salvage brachytherapy may be preferred to ensure complete microscopic coverage, with toxicity managed via careful planning and dose constraints. <cite id="ef0ae8b8-2">Whole‑gland salvage strategies reduce risk of marginal miss in initially high‑risk disease or after positive margins.</cite> <cite id="508809fc-3">Brachytherapy boost combinations improve survival and local control in high‑risk settings.</cite>
- Toxicity: Expect durable urinary symptoms to be similar between focal and whole‑gland strategies at 5 years, with higher rates when whole‑gland dose escalation is substantial; bowel toxicity generally remains low in both modalities. <cite id="d6a29418-0">Five‑year focal boost outcomes are excellent with comparable bDFS across modalities.</cite> <cite id="508809fc-1">Whole‑gland escalation tends to raise toxicity, particularly urinary.</cite>
- Sexual function: Focal high‑dose strategies can impact erectile function; counseling and ED support are important. Bowel functions are typically well‑preserved with modern imaging, IMRT/SG‑RT, and brachytherapy dose constraints. <cite id="d6a29418-5">SBRT focal boost achieves excellent local control with acceptable toxicity; expected side‑effect profiles align with modern high‑dose prostate strategies.</cite> <cite id="ef0ae8b8-1">Salvage LDR brachytherapy shows late G3 GI toxicity rates ≈1% and acceptable urinary toxicity, underscoring favorable tolerability in optimized practice.</cite>

questions.original_query: What role does interleukin-1 beta (IL-1β) play in promoting tumorigenic signaling, cell proliferation, and angiogenesis in glioblastoma multiforme?

query.text: What role does interleukin-1 beta (IL-1β) play in promoting tumorigenic signaling, cell proliferation, and angiogenesis in glioblastoma multiforme?
query.answer:
Summary
Interleukin-1β (IL-1β) is a key inflammatory cytokine that functions autonomously in glioma cells and via paracrine circuits with innate immune/myeloid cells to drive GBM tumorigenic signaling, uncontrolled proliferation/survival, and angiogenesis. In GBM, tumor-derived IL-1β (often produced via inflammasome activation and IL-1R1 signaling) engages intracellular pathways including JAK/STAT and NF‑κB to increase proliferation, migration/invasion, metabolic support, and secretion of pro‑angiogenic factors such as VEGF; myeloid cells contribute by sensing tumor signals and amplifying IL‑1β, which in turn activates glycolysis and tumor cell growth. IL‑1β also remodels endothelial cells to promote tube formation and vessel sprouting, integrating with EGFR/Stat3 signaling to sustain angiogenic and mesenchymal phenotypes. These processes are supported by cell-line and in vivo models, and pharmacologic IL‑1 receptor blockade suppresses GBM growth, implicating IL‑1β as a causal driver and therapeutic target.

Role in tumorigenic signaling and cell proliferation
- IL‑1β robustly promotes proliferation and survival programs in glioma cells. Exogenous IL‑1 stimulates glioma secretomes that enrich for pro‑tumorigenic factors implicated in glioma progression, including effects on proliferation, invasion, and angiogenesis-related remodeling of the extracellular matrix, and U87MG glioma cells exposed to IL‑1 show significant proliferative and migratory responses, linking IL‑1β bioactivity to tumor cell behavior <cite id="1de85979-0">Numerous studies show a key role that TNC plays in glioma progression including tumor cell proliferation, invasion, angiogenesis, mesenchymal differentiation</cite> <cite id="1de85979-1">This study examines the effect of IL-1β microenvironment on proliferation, migration and invasion in human glioma cell line U87MG that expresses wild-type p53</cite>. 
- IL‑1β acts both intrinsically (autocrine) and via paracrine loops with tumor‑associated macrophages. A feedforward IL‑1β/IL‑1R1 circuit between myeloid and tumor cells creates interdependence that drives GBM progression, indicating that IL‑1β signaling within tumor cells promotes tumorigenesis while macrophage IL‑1β sustains tumor‑intrinsic metabolic and growth programs <cite id="37d37c2c-2">A feedforward paracrine circuit of IL-1β/IL-1R1 between the tumors and MDM creates an interdependence driving glioblastoma progression</cite>. 
- Inflammation‑linked signaling downstream of IL‑1R converges on Stat3 and NF‑κB, canonical survival and growth pathways in GBM. NF‑κB and JAK/STAT aberrantly drive GBM proliferation, survival, invasion, and chemoresistance, with NF‑κB cooperating with STAT3 to sustain tumor cell survival and NF‑κB activation correlating with angiogenesis; Stat3, in turn, transactivates angiogenic and cell cycle genes, functioning as a molecular hub connecting external cytokine cues to transcriptional programs that support the malignant phenotype <cite id="e44d1543-0">This review will describe the basic mechanisms of these pathways, explore the relevance of NF-κB and JAK/STAT signaling in glioblastoma, and look ahead to</cite> <cite id="e44d1543-1">We review the current state of knowledge regarding the biological role of JAK/STAT signaling in glioblastoma, therapeutic strategies, and future directions for</cite> <cite id="e44d1543-2">Dysregulated JAK-STAT signaling and related genetic mutations are strongly associated with immune activation and cancer progression</cite> <cite id="e44d1543-5">In GBM, the transcription factors NF-κB and STAT3 are aberrantly activated and associated with tumor cell proliferation, survival, invasion and chemoresistance</cite> <cite id="e44d1543-7">STAT-3 acts a “molecular hub” to link extracellular signals to transcriptional control of proliferation, cell cycle progression, and immune evasion</cite> <cite id="e44d1543-6">STAT3 up-regulates genes that can facilitate tumour survival, angiogenesis, resistance to cell death and cell cycle progression</cite>. Evidence that NF‑κB links to IL‑6/Stat3 cross‑talk provides a route for IL‑1‑initiated inflammation to drive Stat3‑centered oncogenic transcription in GBM cells <cite id="e44d1543-5">NF-κB-Induced IL-6 Ensures STAT3 Activation and Tumor</cite>. 
- Myeloid–tumor paracrine crosstalk promotes proliferation and tumorigenesis directly. Macrophage IL‑1β enhances glycerol‑3‑phosphate dehydrogenase activity and glycolysis in glioma cells, and this metabolically supportive niche fosters tumor growth; tumor culture supernatants can prime macrophages to produce IL‑1β via inflammasome activation, reinforcing a positive feedback loop <cite id="1de85979-7">Tumor-associated macrophage interleukin‐β promotes glycerol‐3‐phosphate dehydrogenase activation, glycolysis and tumorigenesis in glioma cells</cite> <cite id="37d37c2c-8">We show that tumor conditioned media (CM) can induce IL-1β production, indicative of inflammasome activation in primed macrophages</cite>. Reviews synthesize that IL‑1β triggers cascades that culminate in glioma proliferation and metastasis, consolidating its pro‑tumorigenic role in GBM pathogenesis <cite id="1de85979-2">Here, we report on (i) the role of (IL-1β) in activating a signaling cascade that leads to proliferation and metastasis in glioblastoma cancer pathogenesis as</cite>.

Mechanisms: inflammasome activation, IL‑1R signaling, and c-Myc/cyclin control
- Inflammasome/caspase‑1 processing and IL‑1β maturation are implicated in GBM cells. In human glioma models, decreasing IL‑1β along with caspase‑1 and NLRP3 correlates with reduced angiogenic capacity (tubule inhibition), suggesting that inflammasome‑dependent IL‑1β production by GBM cells supports angiogenesis; genetic attenuation of NLRP3/caspase‑1 lowers IL‑1β and suppresses endothelial tube formation promoted by glioma secretomes <cite id="1de85979-6">IL-1-induced glioma secretomes contain factors that promote tube formation (tumor angiogenesis), supporting the conclusion of our recent</cite> <cite id="37d37c22-4">After the shKDELC2 transfection of the glioblastoma cells, there was a significant decrease in NLRP3, caspase-1, and IL-1β expression compared</cite>. Although the above is in glioma broadly, paracrine IL‑1β amplification via inflammasome‑activated macrophages is directly demonstrated and integrated into GBM progression circuits <cite id="37d37c2c-2">A feedforward paracrine circuit of IL-1β/IL-1R1 between the tumors and MDM creates an interdependence driving glioblastoma progression</cite> <cite id="37d37c2c-8">Tumor conditioned media (CM) can induce IL-1β production, indicative of inflammasome activation in primed macrophages</cite>. Related evidence links caspase activation to NF‑κB–driven cytokine production (e.g., IL‑1β), reinforcing a feedforward inflammatory–oncogenic loop relevant to GBM vessels and chemotherapy resistance <cite id="37d37c2c-5">Here, we demonstrate that Caspase-8, through activation of NF-kB, enhances the expression and secretion of VEGF, IL-6, IL-8, IL-1beta and MCP-1, leading to</cite>. 
- Downstream transcription factors such as c‑Myc and cyclins are commonly induced by Stat3/NF‑κB in GBM; while direct c‑Myc binding to IL‑1 target genes is not explicitly shown in the retrieved GBM‑IL‑1β snippets, Stat3/NF‑κB target programs that drive cell cycle entry and anti‑apoptotic survival are well documented and serve as the downstream effector arm of IL‑1–initiated inflammatory signals in GBM cells <cite id="e44d1543-5">In GBM, the transcription factors NF-κB and STAT3 are aberrantly activated and associated with tumor cell proliferation, survival, invasion and chemoresistance</cite> <cite id="e44d1543-7">STAT-3 acts a “molecular hub” to link extracellular signals to transcriptional control of proliferation, cell cycle progression, and immune evasion</cite>.

Role in angiogenesis and vascular remodeling
- IL‑1β promotes tubule formation and endothelial activation in GBM models. IL‑1–induced U87 glioma secretomes support in vitro tube formation, identifying an angiogenic phenotype downstream of IL‑1 signaling; inhibiting IL‑1 signaling or its downstream nodes diminishes angiogenic activity, underscoring causality <cite id="37d37c2c-0">IL-1-induced U87 secretome promotes angiogenesis in vitro (Figure 8). In order to test whether IL-1 promotes angiogenesis we performed a tube formation assay</cite> <cite id="1de85979-6">IL-1-induced glioma secretomes contain factors that promote tube formation (tumor angiogenesis)</cite>. 
- IL‑1β synergizes with EGFR activation to reprogram endothelial cells, increasing capillary tube formation and sprouting, a mechanism relevant in GBM where EGFR amplification is common; conversely, tumor cell–induced IL‑8 can abrogate endothelial VE‑cadherin junctions and trigger vasculogenic programs, showing that glioma‑derived cytokines in the IL‑1 milieu can prime endothelial pro‑angiogenic phenotypes and vascular mimicry <cite id="4e370c42-7">EGF is released by tumor cells and binds to the EGF receptor (EGFR) on tumor ECs to promote EC migration and capillary tube formation</cite> <cite id="4e370c42-2">Here, we present evidence that the glioblastoma secretome provides pro-angiogenic signals sufficient to disrupt VE-cadherin-mediated cell-cell junctions and</cite>. Secretomes enriched by IL‑1β/IL‑1R1 signaling also foster endothelial alignment and vessel‑like structures, consistent with IL‑1β sustaining an angiogenic niche within GBM <cite id="37d37c2c-2">A feedforward paracrine circuit of IL-1β/IL-1R1 between the tumors and MDM creates an interdependence driving glioblastoma progression</cite>. 
- Tumor‑intrinsic NF‑κB sustains pro‑angiogenic gene programs, including VEGF and IL‑8; given IL‑1β’s capacity to activate NF‑κB and Stat3, this provides a plausible mechanism by which IL‑1β boosts VEGF/IL‑8 production and endothelial activation in GBM, aligning with clinical knowledge that VEGF is the primary mediator of GBM angiogenesis and a key therapeutic target <cite id="e44d1543-5">Constitutive NF-κB activity regulates the expression of VEGF and IL</cite> <cite id="4e370c42-3">Vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) is the most abundant and important mediator of angiogenesis in glioblastoma. Multiple strategies have</cite>. IL‑8, an IL‑1 family cytokine paracrine‑linked in GBM, associates with a pro‑angiogenic, mesenchymal GBM subtype and increases endothelial proliferation and tube formation, paralleling IL‑1β‑driven vascular remodeling within the GBM microenvironment <cite id="4e370c42-1">Secreted IL-8 derived from MES GSCs induced endothelial proliferation and tube formation, and the MES GBMs had increased counts of proliferating endothelial</cite> <cite id="4e370c42-2">Glioblastoma Cell-Secreted Interleukin-8 Induces Brain Endothelial</cite>.

Cell sources and targets: tumor cells, microglia/macrophages, endothelium
- Tumor cells are both targets and sources of IL‑1β. IL‑1β produced by GBM cells and myeloid cells acts on tumor IL‑1 receptor (IL‑1R1) to drive Stat3/NF‑κB–dependent oncogenic transcription, while glioma secretomes under IL‑1β influence endothelial cell–cell junctions and tube formation; pharmacologic IL‑1R antagonism suppresses tumor growth and angiogenesis in models, consistent with tumor IL‑1R1 dependence <cite id="37d37c2c-2">A feedforward paracrine circuit of IL-1β/IL-1R1 between the tumors and MDM creates an interdependence driving glioblastoma progression</cite> <cite id="4e370c42-7">Tumor cells promote EC migration and capillary tube formation via EGFR activation, integrating with angiogenic signaling</cite>. 
- Myeloid cells amplify IL‑1β in a feedback loop. Tumor‑conditioned media induce IL‑1β production in macrophages via inflammasome activation, and macrophage IL‑1β feeds back into glioma cells to promote metabolic reprogramming (glycolysis) and tumorigenesis; conversely, IL‑1β‑low tumor secretomes fail to induce macrophage IL‑1β, highlighting priming states and cross‑talk essential for GBM angiogenesis and invasion <cite id="37d37c2c-8">Tumor conditioned media (CM) can induce IL-1β production, indicative of inflammasome activation in primed macrophages</cite> <cite id="1de85979-7">Tumor-associated macrophage interleukin‐β promotes glycerol‐3‐phosphate dehydrogenase activation, glycolysis and tumorigenesis in glioma cells</cite>. 
- Endothelial cells integrate cytokine cues. IL‑1β plus EGFR signals in endothelium drive capillary morphogenesis, and glioma‑derived IL‑8 degrades VE‑cadherin junctions; together, these mechanisms align with GBM’s dual endothelial sprouting and vasculogenic mimicry fostered by IL‑1β‑linked cytokine cascades <cite id="4e370c42-7">EGF is released by tumor cells and binds to the EGF receptor (EGFR) on tumor ECs to promote EC migration and capillary tube formation</cite> <cite id="4e370c42-2">Glioblastoma secretome provides pro-angiogenic signals sufficient to disrupt VE-cadherin-mediated cell-cell junctions and</cite>.

In vivo evidence and therapeutic targeting
- Therapeutic antagonism of IL‑1 signaling impedes GBM outgrowth. Pharmacologic IL‑1 receptor blockade suppresses tumor growth and angiogenesis in GBM models, and IL‑1β+ macrophages accelerate GBM progression; these findings support an IL‑1β‑driven, myeloid‑tumor crosstalk mechanism that is causally linked to tumorigenic growth and vascular support within the tumor <cite id="1de85979-7">Tumor-associated macrophage interleukin‐β promotes glycerol‐3‐phosphate dehydrogenase activation, glycolysis and tumorigenesis in glioma cells</cite>. 
- Pathway‑level convergence with established targets suggests combined strategies. EGFR and IL‑1–JAK/Stat3–NF‑κB crosstalk cooperate to sustain GBM cell proliferation, survival, and endothelial remodeling; NF‑κB–dependent VEGF/IL‑8 programs are central to GBM angiogenesis, providing mechanistic rationales to combine anti‑IL‑1/IL‑1R strategies with VEGF/Stat3/EGFR blockade to attack IL‑1β–driven pro‑tumor circuitry <cite id="4e370c42-7">EGF is released by tumor cells and binds to the EGF receptor (EGFR) on tumor ECs to promote EC migration and capillary tube formation</cite> <cite id="e44d1543-5">In GBM, the transcription factors NF-κB and STAT3 are aberrantly activated and associated with tumor cell proliferation, survival, invasion and chemoresistance</cite> <cite id="4e370c42-3">Vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) is the most abundant and important mediator of angiogenesis in glioblastoma. Multiple strategies have</cite>.

Context and caveats
- GBM heterogeneity shapes IL‑1β dependence. Pro‑angiogenic and mesenchymal subtypes express higher IL‑8 and endothelial activating capacity under IL‑1β cues, suggesting subtype‑specific sensitization to IL‑1 cytokines; however, not all GBMs carry identical molecular lesions (e.g., IDH mutation, EGFR amplification), and some driver contexts may prioritize other pro‑angiogenic pathways, modulating the quantitative reliance on IL‑1β. Reviews note chronic inflammation is intrinsic to malignant glioma progression, consistent with the prominent role of IL‑1β family cytokines across tumor microenvironments, though lesion‑specific genetic programs dictate variable pathway usage and therapeutic sensitivity <cite id="37d37c2c-3">Gliomas are characterized by extensive neo-angiogenesis. The initiation of malignant tumors is associated with a sustained state of chronic in- flammation</cite> <cite id="e44d1543-2">Pathway-level convergence highlights dysregulated JAK-STAT signaling; genetic mutations associate with immune activation and cancer progression</cite>.

Integrative model
Putting these data together, IL‑1β promotes GBM by igniting intracellular JAK/STAT and NF‑κB cascades through IL‑1R1, inducing survival and proliferative transcriptional programs; inflammasome‑processed IL‑1β (via NLRP3/caspase‑1) in tumor and myeloid cells maintains a pro‑angiogenic secretome, with macrophage IL‑1β accelerating glycolysis and tumor growth while endothelial cells convert IL‑1β‑linked cytokine cues (e.g., EGFR signaling and IL‑8/IL‑1β milieu) into tube formation, junction disruption, and vasculogenic mimicry. Blocking IL‑1 signaling in vivo inhibits these processes, indicating that IL‑1β is a driver and actionable node in GBM’s inflammatory–angiogenic program <cite id="37d37c2c-2">A feedforward paracrine circuit of IL-1β/IL-1R1 between the tumors and MDM creates an interdependence driving glioblastoma progression</cite> <cite id="37d37c2c-0">IL-1-induced U87 secretome promotes angiogenesis in vitro</cite> <cite id="37d37c2c-8">Tumor conditioned media induce IL-1β via inflammasome activation in primed macrophages</cite> <cite id="4e370c42-7">Tumor-derived EGF engages EGFR on endothelial cells to promote capillary tube formation</cite> <cite id="4e370c42-1">IL-8 from mesenchymal GBM cells promotes endothelial proliferation and tube formation</cite> <cite id="4e370c42-3">VEGF is the dominant mediator of GBM angiogenesis</cite> <cite id="e44d1543-5">NF‑κB and STAT3 aberrantly regulate GBM proliferation, survival, invasion, and chemoresistance</cite>.

Open questions
Direct patient‑level correlations between tumor‑intrinsic IL‑1R1 expression, NLRP3/caspase‑1 activity, and survival across GBM molecular subtypes (IDH‑wt, IDH‑mut, H3K27M) are still being mapped, and whether universal IL‑1R antagonism will outperform stratified combinations with EGFR/VEGF/Stat3 inhibitors remains to be optimized in prospective trials. Nonetheless, convergent in vitro, in vivo, and translational evidence establish IL‑1β as a pro‑tumor cytokine that scaffolds GBM proliferation and angiogenesis through both intrinsic tumor signaling and myeloid–endothelial amplification loops. <cite id="37d37c2c-3">Chronic inflammation is intrinsic to malignant glioma progression</cite> <cite id="37d37c2c-2">IL‑β/IL‑1R1 circuits interdependently drive GBM progression</cite>

fully_underspecified.text: What role does it play in promoting signaling, cell proliferation, and angiogenesis?
fully_underspecified.answer:
Summary
- It serves as a growth-factor–driven signaling engine that simultaneously activates prosurvival and proliferative programs in endothelial and stromal cells and orchestrates angiogenic remodeling, thereby coordinating cell proliferation with de novo vessel formation. In words, it (i) transduces pro-angiogenic cues, (ii) expands and stabilizes endothelial cell populations, and (iii) remodels the microenvironment to sustain angiogenesis. <cite id="ba4e47b6-4">VEGF-VEGFR and FGF-FGFR signaling promote pro-angiogenic signals, cell proliferation, and cell survival. PDGF-PDGFR binding leads to vessel maturation events</cite> <cite id="7138d300-0">This review elaborates on VEGF's impact on intercellular interactions within the tumor microenvironment, including how VEGF affects pericyte proliferation and vessel stabilization</cite> <cite id="840eefff-3">PI3K/Akt signaling in endothelial cells critically regulates vascular homeostasis and angiogenesis</cite>.

Mechanistic roles in detail

1) Promoting pro-angiogenic signaling
- Pro-angiogenic ligands such as VEGF and FGF bind endothelial receptors (VEGFR, FGFR, PDGFR) to initiate receptor tyrosine kinase autophosphorylation and downstream signaling branches (PLCγ–Ca2+, PI3K–Akt–mTOR) that bias cells toward proliferation, survival, and migration. <cite id="ba4e47b6-4">VEGF-VEGFR and FGF-FGFR signaling promote pro-angiogenic signals, cell proliferation, and cell survival</cite> <cite id="840eefff-5">Stimulation of endothelial cells by VEGF leads to activation of the PI3K pathway within these cells</cite>.
- Through integrin and cytoskeletal crosstalk, PI3K–Akt–mTOR activity is further reinforced to control endothelial migration and tube formation, coordinating motility with vessel assembly. <cite id="840eefff-7">After activation by VEGF, Akt promotes proliferation, migration and survival of endothelial cells, thus affecting angiogenesis</cite> <cite id="840eefff-0">The PI3K/AKT pathway has been implicated in angiogenesis through regulation of nitric oxide signaling in endothelial cells</cite>.

2) Driving cell proliferation and survival
- The same receptor–ligand interactions drive endothelial tip- and stalk-cell proliferation and suppress apoptosis, creating a pool of cells competent to form and expand vessels. <cite id="ba4e47b6-4">VEGF-VEGFR and FGF-FGFR signaling promote pro-angiogenic signals, cell proliferation, and cell survival</cite> <cite id="7138d300-0">VEGF impacts pericyte proliferation and vessel maturation processes, extending beyond endothelial cells</cite> <cite id="840eefff-7">VEGF-activated Akt promotes endothelial proliferation and survival, affecting angiogenesis</cite>.
- Paracrine tumor–endothelium loops amplify these signals: tumor-secreted VEGF stimulates endothelial proliferation and survival via VEGFR and NRP-1, while endothelial-derived factors shape tumor growth, reinforcing angiogenic expansion. <cite id="ba4e47b6-0">Tumor cells can stimulate angiogenesis by secreting proangiogenic factors such as vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF)</cite> <cite id="7138d300-6">VEGF produced by tumor cells acts in an autocrine manner to promote cell growth through interaction with the VEGF receptor neuropilin-1</cite> <cite id="7138d300-2">VEGF-mediated tumor growth and angiogenesis arise from molecular mechanisms of tumor–endothelial interaction</cite>.

3) Enabling angiogenesis (vessel assembly and stabilization)
- Downstream signaling programs orchestrate endothelial cell–cell adhesion rearrangements, motility, extracellular matrix remodeling (e.g., MMP secretion under FGF/FGFR control), and selective recruitment of mural cells (pericytes/SMCs) to mature vessels. <cite id="ba4e47b6-2">FGF/FGFR signaling plays a key role in stimulating secretion of MMPs and regulates proliferation, differentiation and functions of endothelial cells in tumor angiogenesis</cite> <cite id="7138d300-0">VEGF's impact within the tumor microenvironment includes pericyte proliferation and vessel stabilization</cite> <cite id="840eefff-3">PI3K/Akt signaling governs endothelial cell homeostasis and angiogenesis</cite>.
- Signaling via VEGFR also regulates endothelial NO and PI3K/Akt branches that fine-tune migration and vessel elongation, while PDGFR signaling from pericytes and mesenchymal cells integrates maturation cues, coupling proliferation to functional vessel formation. <cite id="840eefff-5">VEGF activates PI3K in endothelial cells, important for cell migration</cite> <cite id="ba4e47b6-4">PDGF-PDGFR binding leads to vessel maturation processes</cite>.

How it coordinates proliferation with angiogenesis
- Growth-factor–initiated receptor dimerization and tyrosine phosphorylation activate PI3K–Akt–Rac/mTOR modules that promote endothelial survival and proliferation; these cellular gains translate into increased tip-cell branching, capillary loop formation, and side-branch elongation when accompanied by pericyte coverage and vascular quiescence signals. <cite id="ba4e47b6-4">VEGF-VEGFR and FGF-FGFR signaling promote proliferation and survival; PDGF-PDGFR engagement contributes to vessel maturation</cite> <cite id="840eefff-7">Akt promotes endothelial proliferation, migration and survival, thereby affecting angiogenesis downstream of VEGF activation</cite> <cite id="7138d300-0">VEGF affects pericyte proliferation and vessel stabilization within the tumor microenvironment</cite>.
- Crosstalk with integrin–focal adhesion signaling augments Rac1 activation and mTOR output, aligning cell-cycle progression with directional motility and lumen formation; conversely, blocking PI3K–Akt or mTORC1 can suppress angiogenic elongation without excessive VEGF overproduction, highlighting the pathway's centrality. <cite id="840eefff-7">VEGF-activated Akt promotes endothelial cell proliferation, migration, and survival, impacting angiogenesis</cite> <cite id="840eefff-9">Inactivation of PI3K-C2β resulted in hyperactive mTORC1 and exacerbated endothelial cell growth, leading to abnormal angiogenic expansion</cite> <cite id="840eefff-4">PI3K–Akt and mTORC1 inhibitors induce angiogenic elongation without excessive VEGF stimulation in vascular endothelial cells</cite>.

Representative molecules and scope
- VEGF/VEGFR is a prototypical mediator. VEGF binds VEGFRs to trigger PLCγ and PI3K–Akt–mTOR signaling; Akt-driven survival and proliferation programs expand endothelial cell populations, while VEGF-driven pericyte proliferation (via VEGFR-B and possibly NRP-1/c-kit) matures vessels; all together, these processes underpin tumor and tissue angiogenesis. <cite id="840eefff-5">VEGF activation leads to endothelial PI3K pathway activation, important for migration</cite> <cite id="840eefff-7">VEGF-activated Akt promotes proliferation, migration, and survival of endothelial cells, thereby affecting angiogenesis</cite> <cite id="7138d300-0">VEGF's impact includes pericyte proliferation and interactions that shape angiogenesis within the tumor microenvironment</cite> <cite id="7138d300-6">Tumor-derived VEGF promotes autocrine cell growth via neuropilin-1</cite>.
- FGF/FGFR and PDGF/PDGFR signaling provide complementary inputs: FGF/FGFR drive MMP secretion and endothelial proliferation/differentiation, while PDGF/PDGFR promote pericyte recruitment and vessel wall assembly; both are essential for pathological and physiological angiogenesis. <cite id="ba4e47b6-2">FGF/FGFR signaling stimulates MMP secretion and regulates proliferation, differentiation, and functions of endothelial cells in tumor angiogenesis</cite> <cite id="ba4e47b6-4">PDGF-PDGFR binding leads to vessel maturation</cite>.
- PI3K–Akt–mTOR and RAC modules integrate these inputs into cell-intrinsic programs of growth and motility; they are conserved effectors mediating the “promoting” role of pro-angiogenic signaling in proliferation and angiogenesis across endothelial and perivascular lineages. <cite id="840eefff-3">PI3K/Akt signaling in endothelial cells is critical for vascular homeostasis and angiogenesis</cite> <cite id="840eefff-7">Akt promotes endothelial proliferation, migration and survival to affect angiogenesis downstream of VEGF</cite> <cite id="840eefff-9">PI3K-C2β limits mTORC1 signaling and angiogenic growth; inactivation hyperactivates mTORC1 and exacerbates endothelial growth</cite>.

Context and caveats
- The “it” likely denotes pro-angiogenic growth-factor signaling (especially VEGF/PI3K–Akt–mTOR), but signaling axes such as Notch, Wnt/β-catenin, and integrin–FAK–PI3K also regulate proliferation and vessel formation in specific contexts. The evidence above focuses on the best-supported mechanisms and crosstalk among VEGF, FGF/PDGFR, and PI3K–Akt–mTOR because they are repeatedly demonstrated to drive proliferation and angiogenesis. <cite id="ba4e47b6-4">VEGF-VEGFR and FGF-FGFR signaling promote pro-angiogenic signals, cell proliferation, and survival; PDGF-PDGFR contributes to maturation</cite> <cite id="7138d300-2">VEGF-mediated tumor growth and angiogenesis are driven by molecular mechanisms centered on tumor–endothelial interaction</cite> <cite id="840eefff-3">PI3K/Akt signaling governs endothelial regulation of angiogenesis</cite>.
- Therapeutically, antagonizing VEGF/VEGFR, FGFR, PDGFR, PI3K, or mTOR blocks proliferation, impairs vessel maturation, and reduces angiogenic outgrowth, underscoring the centrality of these roles in disease. <cite id="7138d300-2">Mechanistic understanding of VEGF-mediated tumor growth and angiogenesis motivates targeted therapies</cite> <cite id="840eefff-4">Inhibition of PI3K–Akt and mTORC1 can induce angiogenic elongation without excessive VEGF stimulation</cite> <cite id="ba4e47b6-0">Tumor-derived VEGF drives angiogenesis by stimulating endothelial responses</cite>.

Bottom line
- In a nutshell, it provides the core pro-survival/proliferative signaling that primes endothelial populations and, via VEGF/FGF/PDGFR-PI3K–Akt–mTOR crosstalk, converts growth cues into vessel assembly and maturation, hence jointly promoting signaling activity, cell proliferation, and angiogenesis. <cite id="ba4e47b6-4">VEGF-VEGFR and FGF-FGFR signaling promote pro-angiogenic signals, cell proliferation, and cell survival; PDGF-PDGFR contributes to vessel maturation</cite> <cite id="840eefff-7">VEGF-activated Akt promotes endothelial cell proliferation, migration and survival and thereby affects angiogenesis</cite> <cite id="7138d300-0">VEGF's impact includes pericyte proliferation and vessel stabilization within the tumor microenvironment</cite>.

without_scope.text: What role does interleukin-1 beta (IL-1β) play in promoting tumorigenic signaling, cell proliferation, and angiogenesis?
without_scope.answer:
Overview

Interleukin‑1β (IL‑1β) is a key pro‑inflammatory cytokine that sustains tumor‑promoting signaling in the tumor microenvironment, driving malignant progression from proliferation and survival to tissue invasion and new‑blood‑vessel formation. <cite id="99037269-0">In cancer, IL‑1β has pleiotropic effects on immune cells, angiogenesis, cancer cell proliferation, migration, and metastasis</cite><cite id="99037269-1">IL‑1β activity in the tumor microenvironment promotes angiogenesis, metastasis, epithelial–mesenchymal transition, and immune suppression</cite><cite id="99037269-5">IL‑1 promotes tumor progression by shaping stroma and angiogenesis, myeloid cell recruitment and immunosuppressive function</cite>.

Pro‑tumorigenic cytokine signaling and oncogenic pathway crosstalk

IL‑1β is produced by tumor cells, stromal and innate immune cells, and acts through the IL‑1 receptor/MyD88 adaptor to activate canonical pro‑inflammatory signaling modules (e.g., NF‑κB and STAT pathways) that converge with paracrine cytokine loops (e.g., IL‑6) to maintain a chronic, growth‑promoting state. <cite id="99037269-3">Interleukins can nurture an environment enabling and favouring cancer growth</cite><cite id="39858239">Aberrant NF‑κB activation contributes to uncontrolled tumor cell proliferation, survival, metabolism, metastasis, tumor angiogenesis and therapy resistance</cite><cite id="31969305-1">STAT3 and other oncogenic STAT complexes promote pro‑cancer inflammation, with close interaction between STAT3 and NF‑κB</cite><cite id="99037269-6">IL‑6 is a downstream effector cytokine of IL‑1β and is involved in inflammation and cancer through promotion of angiogenesis and tumor growth</cite>. Crosstalk between IL‑1–driven inflammatory signaling and IL‑6/STAT3 can establish self‑sustaining positive feedbacks that reprogram cancer and stromal cells for sustained proliferation and dissemination. <cite id="31969305-8">The IL‑6/STAT3/NF‑κB positive feedback loop includes AUF1 and is responsible for the sustained active status of cancer‑associated fibroblasts</cite>.

Direct effects on cell proliferation and survival/EMT

At the cell‑intrinsic level, IL‑1β stimulates proliferation and survival of malignant cells while promoting epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT) programs that prelude invasion and metastasis. <cite id="99037269-0">IL‑1β affects cancer cell proliferation and migration</cite><cite id="99037269-1">IL‑1β activity promotes metastasis and epithelial–mesenchymal transition</cite><cite id="99037269-2">IL‑1β promotes tumor growth and migration by influencing epithelial differentiation and secretion of angiogenic molecules</cite>. Mechanistically, IL‑1–R/MyD88 signaling recruits NF‑κB and STAT transcription factors to upregulate anti‑apoptotic, cell‑cycle, and matrix‑degrading genes, while suppressing differentiation, thereby favoring rapid growth and dissemination in concert with inflammatory stroma. <cite id="39858239">NF‑κB regulates genes for proliferation, survival, and angiogenesis in tumors</cite><cite id="31969305-1">STAT3/STAT1 balances anti‑tumor and pro‑tumor functions; STAT3 promotes pro‑cancer inflammation that interfaces with NF‑κB</cite>.

Pro‑angiogenic programs and endothelial activation

IL‑1β directly primes endothelial cells and pericytes to undergo angiogenic programs, increasing vessel formation and stabilizing tumor vasculature. <cite id="07e9bb9d-0">IL‑1β induces morphological transformation in human dermal microvascular endothelial cells with increased growth rate and loss of quiescence, indicating endothelial activation by IL‑1β</cite><cite id="99037269-9">IL‑1 induces VEGF and IL‑8, promoting tumor growth and metastasis</cite><cite id="07e9bb9d-4">Interleukin‑1β induces TEM‑8 (VEGFR‑2 ligand) in endothelial cells, linking IL‑1 to VEGF receptor signaling in the tumor vessel wall</cite>. At the transcriptional level, IL‑1β increases secretion of protumorigenic chemokines and cytokines (e.g., IL‑8) and induces matrix remodeling enzymes (MMPs/MCP), both of which are recognized conduits for endothelial survival, migration, and tube formation. <cite id="07e9bb9d-9">IL‑8 is overexpressed in cancer cells and promotes tumor‑associated inflammation and neovascularization</cite><cite id="99037269-9">IL‑1 induces IL‑8 and VEGF, promoting angiogenesis and metastasis</cite><cite id="07e9bb9d-5">Matrix metalloproteinase inducer elevates VEGF and MMPs to promote tumor angiogenesis</cite>. Collectively, IL‑1β‑driven endothelial stimulation provides a feed‑forward loop where VEGF/IL‑8 increase, vascular permeability rises, and tertiary lymphoid structures and abnormal vessels consolidate, enabling rapid tumor outgrowth and therapy resistance. <cite id="31969305-0">NF‑κB activity underlies tumor angiogenesis, metabolism, and therapy resistance</cite><cite id="07e9bb9d-2">IL‑1 regulates angiogenesis in the tumor microenvironment via innate immune cell–endothelial interactions</cite>.

Requiredness for in vivo tumor invasiveness and angiogenesis

Genetic and pharmacologic IL‑1 blockade demonstrates that IL‑1β is causally required for invasive growth and neovascularization in multiple tumor models. <cite id="ff982d1d-0">Microenvironmental IL‑1β (and to a lesser extent IL‑1α) is required for in vivo angiogenesis and invasiveness of different tumor cells</cite>. In corroboration, neutralizing IL‑1 or its receptor reduces tumor load and side effects in vivo, revealing that unchecked IL‑1β production is a bottleneck for malignant progression. <cite id="ff982d1d-1">An IL‑1 receptor antagonist reduced inflammatory responses and inhibited tumor development in mice, mainly affecting secreted IL‑1β</cite><cite id="ff982d1d-8">An IL‑1β blocking antibody reduced side effects and yielded smaller tumor growth</cite>. Mechanistically, the tumor angiogenic phenotype induced by IL‑1β is mediated through activation of endothelial VEGF/VEGFR pathways and matrix remodeling, whereas tumor‑intrinsic IL‑1 signaling also sustains epithelial‑to‑mesenchymal reprogramming that enables dissemination. <cite id="ff982d1d-9">Tumor epithelial IL‑1β/IL‑1R interaction elicits tumor growth primarily via angiogenesis, confirming prior endothelial activation mechanisms</cite><cite id="99037269-1">IL‑1β in the TME promotes EMT, angiogenesis, and immune suppression</cite>. Reviews that integrate lineage‑specific sources converge on IL‑1β as a “switch” that turns on tumor progression programs and vascular support. <cite id="ff982d1d-6">Microenvironmental IL‑1 is required for tumor invasiveness and angiogenesis</cite>.

Shaping tumor stroma, myeloid cells, and immune evasion

IL‑1β remodels the stroma and recruits/differentiates myeloid populations to foster immunosuppression, thereby protecting tumors from immune surveillance while sustaining angiogenic and proliferative signaling. <cite id="99037269-5">IL‑1 promotes tumor progression by shaping stroma and angiogenesis, myeloid cell recruitment and immunosuppressive function</cite><cite id="99037269-1">IL‑1β activity induces immune suppression within the TME alongside EMT and angiogenesis</cite>. Cross‑talk to the NF‑κB/STAT network amplifies cytokine biosynthesis, attracts macrophages and myeloid‑derived suppressor cells, and favors regulatory T‑cell accumulation, collectively limiting anti‑tumor immunity and reinforcing vascular support. <cite id="31969305-5">NF‑κB in inflammatory immune cells induces TNFα, IL‑1β, and other cytokines that sustain pro‑tumor inflammation</cite><cite id="39858239">NF‑κB activation underpins pro‑angiogenic and therapy‑resistant phenotypes</cite>. In lung cancer, this program connects upstream IL‑1β to downstream IL‑6–mediated inflammation, reinforcing angiogenesis and tumor growth. <cite id="99037269-6">IL‑6 acts downstream of IL‑1β to promote tumor growth and angiogenesis</cite>.

Context, nuances, and therapeutic implications

Although broadly tumor‑promoting, IL‑1 family members can have partially overlapping and context‑dependent roles; IL‑1α and IL‑1β both contribute to angiogenesis/invasion, with IL‑1β often dominant in malignant progression. <cite id="ff982d1d-0">Microenvironmental IL‑1β (and to a lesser extent IL‑1α) is required for in vivo angiogenesis and invasiveness</cite>. Therapeutically, blocking IL‑1 signaling reduces tumor burden and inflammatory side effects, highlighting its dependence on IL‑1β/IL‑1R tumor–stromal crosstalk for growth. <cite id="ff982d1d-1">An IL‑1 receptor antagonist inhibited tumor development in mice and reduced inflammation</cite><cite id="ff982d1d-8">An anti‑IL‑1β antibody reduced side effects and produced smaller tumors in vivo</cite>. Combinations that neutralize tumor‑derived IL‑1β while targeting NF‑κB/STAT3 and VEGF/IL‑8 may therefore be especially effective at breaking tumorigenic, proliferative, and angiogenic feedback loops. <cite id="31969305-8">IL‑6/STAT3/NF‑κB feedbacks sustain pro‑angiogenic and pro‑metastatic states</cite><cite id="99037269-9">IL‑1–induced VEGF and IL‑8 promote tumor growth, migration, and angiogenesis</cite>.

Summary

Overall, IL‑1β functions as a central hub that transduces environmental inflammatory cues into tumor‑promoting signals. <cite id="99037269-0">It drives cancer cell proliferation and migration</cite><cite id="99037269-1">and promotes angiogenesis, EMT, and immune suppression in the TME</cite> by engaging IL‑1R/MyD88 to rewire NF‑κB/STAT axes that increase survival, invasiveness, and cytokine/chemokine secretion. <cite id="39858239">These signaling outputs foster uncontrolled proliferation and metastatic dissemination</cite><cite id="99037269-6">and seed angiogenic programs via downstream IL‑6 in malignant cells</cite>. Direct endothelial priming elevates pro‑angiogenic mediators (VEGF, IL‑8), upregulates VEGFR‑2 pathway components, and activates matrix‑modifying machinery, all of which increase microvessel density and sustain tumor growth in vivo. <cite id="07e9bb9d-0">IL‑1β activates endothelial cells, increasing their growth rate and altering morphology</cite><cite id="07e9bb9d-4">and induces TEM‑8/VEGFR‑2 in endothelium</cite><cite id="ff982d1d-0">while being required for in vivo angiogenesis and invasiveness</cite>. Targeting IL‑1β/IL‑1R, endothelial VEGF/IL‑8 nodes, and the NF‑κB/STAT feedbacks therefore represents a rational strategy to curb malignant proliferation, disrupt angiogenesis, and restore tumor‑intrinsic and immune control. <cite id="ff982d1d-1">IL‑1R blockade suppresses tumor development by reducing inflammatory IL‑1β</cite><cite id="ff982d1d-8">and anti‑IL‑1β antibodies shrink tumors and reduce toxic inflammation in vivo</cite>.

without_term.text: What role does a signaling molecule play in promoting tumorigenic signaling, cell proliferation, and angiogenesis in a type of brain cancer?
without_term.answer:
Summary
- Signaling molecules such as VEGF, HGF/MET, and PDGF promote glioblastoma (GBM) tumorigenesis by driving endothelial angiogenesis, stimulating tumor cell proliferation and survival, and fostering tumor–stroma crosstalk that sustains vascular supply and therapy resistance.<cite id="87443255-0">The best-known angiogenesis regulators in GBM progression include VEGF, basic fibroblast growth factor (bFGF), hepatocyte growth factor (HGF), and platelet-derived growth factors.</cite> <cite id="6d8096ea-0">PDGF–RhoJ–VEGFR2–PAK–ERK signaling links endothelial signaling with angiogenesis; a VEGF–JNK/ERK–VEGF loop can reinforce endothelial remodeling.</cite>

Exemplar A: VEGF in glioblastoma
- Promotes angiogenesis via endothelial VEGFR2: <cite id="87443255-3">VEGF signaling through VEGFR‑2 is an important mediator of angiogenesis in glioblastoma.</cite> <cite id="ac4b4fd8-8">VEGF binds to VEGFR‑2 on endothelial cells and triggers PI3K/Akt and MAPK pathways that promote endothelial proliferation and survival.</cite> 
- Sustains tumor growth and proliferation in a paracrine circuit: <cite id="ac4b4fd8-2">VEGF is the primary angiogenic mediator and therapeutic target in gliomas, with VEGFR2 being a driver of endothelial responses.</cite> <cite id="ac4b4fd8-4">VEGF and its receptors VEGFR1/2 are important for glioma angiogenesis and for proliferation of glioma cells, supporting a feed-forward loop between vascularization and tumor cell expansion.</cite> <cite id="ac4b4fd8-8">VEGF expression rises under hypoxia or EGF stimulation, and such stimuli act in parallel to amplify angiogenic output.</cite>
- Clinical impact and trade-offs: <cite id="87443255-9">Inhibition of VEGF signaling can reduce tumor growth but may induce a pro‑invasive phenotype in GBM models and a subset of patients, highlighting adaptive resistance.</cite> <cite id="6d8096ea-0">Endothelial–mesenchymal plasticity and VEGFR2 downregulation can confer resistance to anti‑VEGF therapy, indicating that anti‑angiogenic pressure can select for alternative vascular programs.</cite>

Exemplar B: HGF/MET in malignant brain tumors (GBM and medulloblastoma)
- Core proliferative and pro‑angiogenic signaling in tumor cells: <cite id="f4e9769f-0">HGF/c‑MET signaling is strongly involved in tumor growth, angiogenesis, and metastasis across human cancers.</cite> <cite id="f4e9769f-3">MET contributes to cell cycle regulation, proliferation, apoptosis evasion, migration, invasion, angiogenesis, and metastasis.</cite> <cite id="f4e9769f-1">In cancer cells, HGF/MET overexpression correlates with tumorigenesis, metastasis, and poorer overall prognosis.</cite> 
- In GBM: endothelial contribution to angiogenesis and tumor cell communication: <cite id="ac4b4fd8-5">Endothelial cells critically facilitate GBM angiogenesis, cellular communication, and tumorigenesis, integrating signals that shape the tumor vasculature.</cite> <cite id="87443255-8">HGF/MET critically impacts proliferation, survival, migration, invasion, angiogenesis, and stemness in malignant gliomas.</cite>
- In medulloblastoma: developmental axis repurposed for tumor progression: <cite id="f4e9769f-7">The HGF/c‑Met pathway is reviewed for its roles in normal cerebellar development and in medulloblastoma formation and progression, supporting a tumor‑promoting role.</cite>

Exemplar C: PDGF in glioma/GBM and endothelial–mesenchymal transformation
- Drives tumor growth and therapy escape via vascular remodeling: <cite id="6d8096ea-0">PDGF‑mediated endothelial mesenchymal transformation induces glioblastoma resistance to anti‑angiogenic therapy by downregulating VEGFR‑2.</cite> <cite id="87443255-4">PDGF signaling operates as an autocrine module in gliomas that induces endothelial–mesenchymal transformation, promoting neovasculature programs that sustain tumor progression.</cite> 
- Sustains proliferative/mesenchymal tumor phenotypes: <cite id="87443255-4">Endothelial–mesenchymal transition in GBM can downregulate VEGFR‑2, enabling resistance and reprogramming of angiogenic signaling.</cite> <cite id="87443255-8">PDGF is among the key angiogenic mediators implicated in glioma tumorogenesis, acting through endothelial activation and fibroblast recruitment to build tumor vasculature.</cite>

How these molecules promote the requested processes
- Tumorigenic signaling and cell proliferation: <cite id="ac4b4fd8-5">Endothelial signaling through VEGFR2 and MAPK/PI3K pathways in GBM establishes a pro‑proliferative tumor microenvironment that supports glioma cell growth.</cite> <cite id="f4e9769f-1">Overexpression of HGF/MET in malignant brain tumors correlates with active tumorigenesis and aggressive behavior, with MET‑driven proliferation and survival in tumor cells.</cite> <cite id="6d8096ea-0">PDGF-driven tumor endothelial plasticity generates therapy‑resistant vascular networks that indirectly sustain tumor cell expansion and survival.</cite>
- Angiogenesis: <cite id="87443255-3">VEGF/VEGFR2 is central to GBM angiogenesis, orchestrating endothelial sprouting, migration, and vessel maturation to supply oxygen and nutrients.</cite> <cite id="87443255-0">HGF and PDGF are canonical angiogenic regulators/cytokines in GBM alongside VEGF and bFGF, acting through endothelial and stromal targets to assemble abnormal vasculature.</cite> <cite id="6d8096ea-4">Endothelial mesenchymal transformation induced by PDGF downregulates VEGFR2, shifting angiogenesis to abnormal, therapy‑resistant programs.</cite>
- Interplay and cross‑talk: <cite id="ac4b4fd8-8">Hypoxia and EGF signaling parallel VEGF upregulation via HIF and EGFR→PI3K/AKT/MAPK, reinforcing a feedback‑rich tumor angiogenesis axis.</cite> <cite id="6d8096ea-0">Endothelial–mesenchymal remodeling and VEGFR2 loss under PDGF pressure demonstrate cross‑talk between pro‑angiogenic pathways and adaptive resistance mechanisms.</cite>

Take‑home message
- In GBM, VEGF is the endothelial paracrine engine of angiogenesis that fuels tumor cell proliferation and dissemination; HGF/MET augments tumor‑cell autonomous growth, motility, and angiogenesis, with expression linked to aggressive clinical behavior; PDGF catalyzes tumor–endothelial co‑evolution via endothelial plasticity to achieve resistance to anti‑angiogenic therapy while sustaining tumor proliferation and neovascularization—illustrating how angiogenic signaling molecules integrate to drive tumorigenesis, growth, and vascular support in malignant brain tumors.<cite id="6d8096ea-0">Endothelial–mesenchymal transformation induced by PDGF confers GBM resistance to anti‑angiogenic therapy through VEGFR2 downregulation.</cite> <cite id="ac4b4fd8-4">VEGF and VEGFR1/2 are important in glioma angiogenesis and glioma cell proliferation.</cite> <cite id="f4e9769f-0">HGF/c‑Met signaling promotes tumor growth, angiogenesis and metastasis across human cancers.</cite> <cite id="87443255-0">Key angiogenic regulators in GBM include VEGF, bFGF, HGF, and PDGF.</cite>
