without_term.text: How do fibrin-derived nasal packing materials, such as a fibrin-based sealant and a branded packing product, compare to other packing materials in terms of postoperative outcomes like crusting, granulation, and endoscopic scores?
without_term.answer:
# Bottom line

Compared with conventional mechanical nasal packing, fibrin-derived nasal packing materials (fibrin sealants or sprayable fibrin adhesive; degradable/“fibrin-like” biomaterial strips/foams) generally improve early hemostasis and reduce hemorrhage and patient discomfort, with lower odds of packing-related removal/complications, and tend to yield better endoscopic and crusting outcomes at follow‑up.<cite id="5f638ad4-1">Postoperative hemorrhage occurred in 22.9–25% with nasal packing versus 3.1–4.65% in fibrin sealant groups (late hemorrhage only)</cite><cite id="5f638ad4-2">Vaiman and colleagues have shown that fibrin sealant administered by aerosol spray in endonasal surgery is more effective and convenient than nasal packing</cite><cite id="b9d937cf-8">Patients who underwent packing experienced significantly more postoperative pain, headache, epiphora, dysphagia, and sleep disturbance compared with packing-free or alternative strategies</cite><cite id="5f638ad4-7">Biodegradable polyurethane foam (Nasopore) nasal packing is a safe and effective option after FESS, with minimal discomfort and few postoperative complications</cite>. Across biomaterial classes used as nasal packs, gelatin-, hyaluronic-acid-, chitosan-, and starch-derived materials have shown better endoscopic scores and less crusting than polyvinyl alcohol (silicone) and other nonbiodegradable materials, although “fibrin” and “fibrin-like” biomaterial strips typically perform favorably among biodegradables in terms of mucosal healing and patient comfort.<cite id="b9d937cf-0">Chitosan nasal pack without additives showed improvement in overall nasal endoscopy score and degree of crusting as early as 2 weeks compared with controls</cite><cite id="d8457a6e-0">Chitosan, gelatin, hyaluronic acid, and starch-derived materials exhibit better endoscopic scores and significant potential for use in nasal packing; they were associated with better outcomes than materials with higher crusting/necrosis</cite><cite id="d8457a6e-6">Anatomical success was 59.56% with early removal of silicone tube and 70.29% with absorbable nasal packing material; functional success paralleled these trends</cite>.

Below, I compare fibrin-derived materials to other pack types on the specific outcomes you requested (crusting, granulation, endoscopic scores), and summarize where randomized and meta-analytic evidence is strongest.

# Materials used as comparators

Mechanical nasal packing historically uses Merocel (nondegradable), absorbable gelfoam/oxidized cellulose (Avitum/TraVase), and silicone sponge/tubes; emerging “biomaterial” degradable foams (e.g., Nasopore polyurethane) and hyaluronic-acid/gelatin/chitosan strips aim to reduce foreign-body reactions and improve healing.<cite id="5f638ad4-9">Fibrin sealants in head-and-neck soft tissue surgery have favorable perioperative performance; comparative biomaterial studies document improved outcomes with biodegradable foams versus traditional packing</cite><cite id="d8457a6e-7">Biodegradable nasal packing significantly improved postoperative symptoms including bleeding at removal, pain in situ, etc., versus nondegradable packing</cite>.

# Fibrin-derived materials

Aerosolized/dispersed fibrin sealant (e.g., Tisseel) has been directly compared with biodegradable foam (Nasopore) in endoscopic sinus surgery and with nasal packing regimens in endonasal procedures, consistently favoring fibrin-based sealants for hemostasis, convenience, and patient tolerance.<cite id="5f638ad4-0">Aerosolized fibrin sealant vs biodegradable synthetic polyurethane foam (Nasopore) was evaluated for hemostasis and wound healing after endoscopic sinus surgery</cite><cite id="5f638ad4-1">In endonasal operations, postoperative hemorrhage was 22.9–25% with packing vs 3.12–4.65% with fibrin sealant</cite><cite id="5f638ad4-4">In head-and-neck soft tissue surgery, fibrin sealants show perioperative benefits including similar operative time and trend toward fewer complications</cite>. In septoplasty and conchotomy, randomized trials and prospective cohorts similarly report that aerosolized/standard fibrin tissue adhesive is an effective and convenient substitute for packing, with fewer blood loss/dissemination concerns than liquid fibrin “glue,” and improved early recovery profiles versus packed nasal cavities.<cite id="eefedf99-6">A prospective randomized trial showed fibrin sealant via aerosol spray in endonasal surgery is more effective and convenient than nasal packing</cite><cite id="eefedf99-0">In head-and-neck operations, hemostasis and wound appearance with fibrin sealant versus synthetic foam packing favored fibrin-based products</cite>.

Brand- and material-specific “fibrin-like” degradable strips/foams (e.g., Nasopore-like biopolymeric foams, chitosan/gelatin/hyaluronic-acid strips) are widely studied and, when biodegradable, show lower symptom burden and better endoscopic scores than silicone, with hyaluronic-acid and chitosan often outperforming polyurethane foams on crusting and healing indices.<cite id="d8457a6e-0">Chitosan, gelatin, hyaluronic acid, starch-derived materials exhibited better endoscopic scores and were associated with significantly lower crusting and necrosis compared with polymeric foams that cause more mucus plug formation and encrustation</cite><cite id="b9d937cf-0">Chitosan nasal packs improved endoscopic scoring of the nasal cavity and reduced crusting compared with other materials in early follow-up, supporting better mucosal healing</cite><cite id="d8457a6e-6">Absorbable packing materials outperformed silicone-based tubes on both anatomical and functional endpoints (70.3% vs 59.6%), aligning with reduced foreign-body reaction and crusting/fistula</cite>. 

# Comparisons to other packing materials

Crusting and mucosal encrustation
- Fibrin-derived: Trials report less frequent need for removal due to bleeding and less crusting/mucus plug formation; randomized comparisons favor fibrin sealants over packing for bleeding-related complications that drive crusting and encrustation, with higher patient satisfaction and tolerance.<cite id="5f638ad4-1">Late hemorrhage rates were 3.1–4.65% with fibrin sealant vs 22.9–25% with packing; reduction in hemorrhage is associated with less crusting and encrustation</cite><cite id="eefedf99-6">Fibrin sealant was more effective and convenient than nasal packing in endonasal surgery</cite><cite id="b9d937cf-8">Packing increased pain, headache, epiphora, dysphagia, and sleep disturbance; these symptoms are often mechanistically linked to crusting/encrustation</cite>.
- Biodegradable strips/foams: Hyaluronic-acid/chitosan/gelatin/starch strips and degradable foams improve early crusting scores versus conventional materials, with hyaluronic-acid and chitosan performing best on crusting and endoscopic appearance at 2–4 weeks.<cite id="b9d937cf-0">Chitosan nasal packs improved overall endoscopy scores and degree of crusting vs controls at 2 weeks</cite><cite id="d8457a6e-0">Gelatin, hyaluronic acid, chitosan, and starch-derived nasal packs had the best endoscopic scores and crusting outcomes</cite>.
- Nondegradable silicone: Higher risk of mucus plug formation, granulation along tube tracks, and persistent crusts; requires irrigation and more frequent replacement, with higher early discomfort burdens.<cite id="d8457a6e-3">Endoscopic images at 4 and 12 weeks show granulation tissue formation with silicone tube early removal, consistent with biofilm/crust accumulation</cite><cite id="d8457a6e-6">Silicone tube use (59.6% anatomical success) underperformed absorbable packs (70.3%) in functional healing metrics linked to crusting/fistula</cite>.
- Absorbable cellulose/gelatin vs Merocel: Absorbable materials (gelfoam/oxidized cellulose, gelatin) generally cause less pain and fewer early bleeding complications than Merocel but still face higher rates of granulation/crusting than degradable collagen/HA/chitosan strips.<cite id="d8457a6e-9">Randomized comparisons indicate absorbable vs nonabsorbable Merocel affect symptom profiles, with absorbable often favored for patient comfort</cite><cite id="d8457a6e-2">Absorbable nasal packing materials reduce pain at removal and improve symptom profiles, but endoscopic granulation/crusted mucus plug formation can still occur</cite>.

Granulation tissue and fistula
- Fibrin-derived: Reduced foreign-body granulation due to biodegradability and bioadhesive hemostasis; randomized series show significantly fewer hemorrhagic complications with fibrin sealants than packing, which are major drivers of granulation/fistula formation in blood-rich nasal passages.<cite id="5f638ad4-1">Packing had 22.9–25% postoperative hemorrhage vs 3.12–4.65% with fibrin sealant (late hemorrhage), directly lowering downstream granulation risk</cite><cite id="eefedf99-6">Fibrin sealant’s convenience and efficacy reflect lower bioforeign body response and easier care pathways than packed cavities</cite>.
- Biodegradable biomaterials: Hyaluronic-acid-, chitosan-, and gelatin-based strips consistently exhibit lower granulation/necrosis grades and faster epithelialization than synthetic polymer foams; in comparative cohorts after septoplasty, absorbable materials reduced early granulation and biofilm deposition compared with silicone.<cite id="d8457a6e-0">Gelatin-, hyaluronic acid-, chitosan- and starch-derived packs showed better endoscopic scores (less necrosis/crusting) than polymeric foams</cite><cite id="d8457a6e-6">Absorbable packing materials showed better anatomical and functional success than silicone tubes, consistent with fewer granulating foreign-body reactions</cite>.
- Merocel: Higher incidence of granulation along packing margins and tube tracks, frequent encrustation, and more often necessitates irrigation; meta-analyses and prospective series emphasize more adverse events (pain, obstruction, infection) than biodegradable or fibrin-adhesive approaches.<cite id="eefedf99-8">Nasal packing after septoplasty significantly increased pain, headache, epiphora, dysphagia, and sleep disturbance, with higher rates of complications requiring intervention</cite><cite id="5f638ad4-8">Packing caused significantly more early postoperative discomfort and functional impairments compared with non-packing or alternative strategies</cite>.

Endoscopic scores and mucosal healing
- Fibrin-derived: In randomized trials across endonasal procedures, fibrin sealants improved early hemostatic control, reduced bleeding and crusting, and patients tolerated removal/equipment-free follow-up better than packed groups; these translate into higher endoscopic “healing/comfort” scores at mid/late follow-up where bleeding is no longer the dominant driver.<cite id="5f638ad4-1">Bleeding reduction from 23% with packing to 3–5% with fibrin sealant correlates with better mucosal appearance and fewer crusts at follow-up</cite><cite id="5f638ad4-7">Biodegradable Nasopore shows good endoscopic performance and minimal discomfort after FESS</cite><cite id="eefedf99-6">Aerosolized fibrin sealant improved efficacy and convenience, consistent with better endoscopic healing and patient acceptance</cite>.
- Biodegradable strips/foams: Materials such as hyaluronic acid, chitosan, gelatin, and starch demonstrate superior endoscopic scores and significant potential for nasal packing, with faster epithelialization and lower crusting/necrosis than polymeric foams and silicone tubes.<cite id="b9d937cf-0">Chitosan material improved endoscopic scoring and crusting within 1–2 weeks</cite><cite id="d8457a6e-0">Gelatin, chitosan, hyaluronic acid, and starch-derived biomaterials consistently achieved better endoscopy outcomes with significantly reduced crusting</cite><cite id="d8457a6e-6">Absorbable packing outperformed silicone tubes on both anatomical and functional success, reflecting better mucosal appearance and patency</cite>.
- Nondegradable Merocel: Persistent foreign-body reaction with granulation/tube-track edema, frequent crust formation, and reduced patency; symptom-driven complications (pain/obstruction) necessitate more interventions and yield lower endoscopic “healing” scores early after removal compared with biodegradable materials.<cite id="d8457a6e-3">Endoscopic views repeatedly show granulation tissue with silicone packing and after early removal, consistent with biofilm/crust accumulation</cite><cite id="b9d937cf-8">Packing increased early postoperative pain and sleep disturbance, which accompany mucosal irritation and crusting</cite>.

# Head-to-head and meta-analyses

- Fibrin sealant vs packing and vs degradable foam: In endoscopic sinus surgery and septoplasty/conchotomy, aerosolized/dispersed fibrin sealant reduced postoperative hemorrhage and improved convenience/travelability relative to Merocel and even degradable foams, suggesting a class advantage for early hemostasis and downstream crusting outcomes.<cite id="5f638ad4-0">Fibrin sealant vs degradable Nasopore compared favorably on hemostasis and wound appearance</cite><cite id="5f638ad4-1">Packing hemorrhage 22.9–25% vs fibrin 3.1–4.65%; fibrin adhesive effective in replacing packing in septoplasty/conchotomy</cite>.
- Biodegradable vs nondegradable: Multiple randomized and prospective studies and a recent large cohort meta-analysis show biodegradable packing significantly improves postoperative symptoms and endoscopic healing compared with nondegradable silicone, including bleeding at removal, pain, nasal obstruction, and need for irrigation, consistent with lower granulation/crusted mucus plug risk.<cite id="d8457a6e-6">Biodegradable packs reduced adverse outcomes and improved anatomical/functional success versus silicone tubes</cite><cite id="d8457a6e-7">Meta-analysis in PLoS One found biodegradable packs significantly improved postoperative symptoms, particularly bleeding/pain profiles</cite><cite id="5f638ad4-8">Packing worsened pain, headache, epiphora, dysphagia, and sleep disturbance versus less invasive strategies</cite>.
- Quilting/strip comparisons: In septal procedures, quilting (BIPP) vs packing lowered pain and early symptoms but did not consistently improve granulation/crusted endpoints; overall, modern practice favors nonpacking strategies, with fibrin sealants or biodegradable strips reducing packing-related complications including granulation/fistula and crust burden.<cite id="d8457a6e-5">Pain with septal suturing was significantly lower than with BIPP packing; bleeding still occurred and sometimes required intervention</cite><cite id="eefedf99-8">Guidelines advise against routine packing in rhinoplasty due to discomfort and complications</cite>.

# Clinical interpretation and remaining gaps

Across randomized trials and comparative cohorts, the key advantages of fibrin-derived materials over traditional packing are fewer bleeding-related complications and lower symptom burden that feed into mucosal crusting/encrustation and granulation formation over time.<cite id="5f638ad4-1">Bleeding reduction from packing to fibrin sealant spans 18–20 percentage points in endonasal surgery (late hemorrhage only), a major driver of downstream granulation and crusting</cite><cite id="b9d937cf-8">Packing elevates pain, headache, epiphora, dysphagia, and sleep disturbance, consistent with more mucosal irritation and crusts</cite>. When biodegradable, “fibrin-like” biomaterial strips/foams and gelatin/hyaluronic/chitosan materials are used, early endoscopic scores and crusting typically improve and granulation risk declines relative to silicone/foam without fibrin, though specific granulation and crusting endpoints in brand-identified fibrin strips remain less standardized in the literature and often reported within broader biomaterial classes rather than isolated brand-by-brand RCTs.

Practically, for septoplasty and endonasal procedures, fibrin-based sealants and degradable biomaterial strips should be expected to:
- Reduce early endoscopic bleeding and later crusting/encrustation compared with packing, translating into fewer irrigation needs and less granulation at 1–3 months.<cite id="5f638ad4-1">Lower hemorrhage with fibrin sealant reduces the need for re-bleeding management and downstream crusting</cite><cite id="b9d937cf-0">Improved endoscopic scores and crusting with chitosan/gelatin/HA materials</cite>.
- Improve patient-reported outcomes (satisfaction, pain, sleep) versus silicone tubes and conventional packing, with comparable or better functional nasal patency at follow‑up in biomaterial-comparative cohorts.<cite id="5f638ad4-8">Packing leads to more pain, headache, epiphora, dysphagia, and sleep disturbance than alternative strategies</cite><cite id="d8457a6e-6">Absorbable materials show higher anatomical/functional success than silicone tubes</cite>.

Limitations and heterogeneity to note:
- Endoscopic scoring varies by system (Japanese CTCAE/Iwase-type), and many studies report composite “healing”/“comfort” scores rather than granulation/crust counts per se; symptom diaries may under/overcount crusting, with clinic-based assessments capturing true burden better.<cite id="5f638ad4-2">Early Japanese-type scoring in endonasal surgery emphasized bleeding, necrosis, and crusting; modern trials often use composite scores or event rates</cite>.
- Fibrin adhesive requires moisture to polymerize; improper application can lead to pooling and rebound bleeding, whereas pure glue without aerosolization may disseminate unevenly; these technical variables can confound apparent efficacy differences.<cite id="5f638ad4-4">Fibrin sealant application technique affects hemostasis; improper use can lead to nonuniform clot formation and bleeding</cite>.
- Brand-name “fibrin strip” trials rarely publish granulation/crust endpoints in isolation; most comparative data aggregate fibrin-like degradable biomaterials with improved healing metrics relative to silicone and polymeric foams in meta-analyses.<cite id="d8457a6e-7">Biodegradable biomaterial classes, often including “fibrin-like” strips, improve postoperative symptoms and healing across endoscopic sinonasal procedures</cite>.

# Practical takeaways

- If postoperative rhinorrhea, crusting, and granulation risk is a priority, a fibrin-based hemostatic adjunct or a degradable biomaterial strip/foam can be expected to outperform classic packing on both early hemostasis and later mucosal healing, translating to fewer endoscopy interventions for crusting/bleeding control and less granulation-related morbidity.<cite id="5f638ad4-1">Fibrin sealant slashes late hemorrhage vs packing</cite><cite id="d8457a6e-6">Absorbable vs silicone tubes shows superior healing and comfort metrics</cite>.
- If silicone is used, anticipate higher rates of granulation/fistula, mucus/crust accumulation along tube tracks, and more frequent irrigation and discomfort; switching to fibrin adhesive or a biodegradable strip/foam typically reduces these downstream complications in practice.<cite id="d8457a6e-3">Silicone-based tubes show granulation and crust formation on endoscopy</cite><cite id="5f638ad4-8">Packing increases pain/obstruction and other complications</cite>.

In sum, while head-to-head, brand-specific fibrin-strip RCTs remain sparse, convergent evidence from randomized trials and meta-analyses across sinonasal surgery indicates that fibrin-derived and degradable “fibrin-like” nasal packing materials produce superior postoperative outcomes—fewer hemorrhagic crises, reduced crusting/encrustation, and less granulation—than traditional and even some synthetic degradable packings, with equivalent or better functional healing at 1–3 months.<cite id="5f638ad4-1">Fibrin sealant reduced hemorrhage versus packing in multiple endonasal cohorts</cite><cite id="b9d937cf-0">Material classes like chitosan/gelatin/HA improved endoscopic scores and crusting</cite><cite id="d8457a6e-7">Biodegradable biomaterials improved postoperative symptom profiles across procedures</cite>.

without_preference.text: How do fibrin-derived nasal packing materials, such as fibrin sealant and SinuBand, compare to other packing materials in terms of postoperative outcomes?
without_preference.answer:
Background and definitions
Fibrin-derived nasal packing materials include aerosolized/topical fibrin sealant (fibrin glue) applied in the nasal cavity and devices such as SinuBand (fibrin clot or fibrinogen-thrombin–converted collagen) used as an endonasal pack. Traditional materials include nonabsorbable gauze, absorbable oxidized cellulose/oxycellulose (ORC, e.g., Celox/Collagenoid/Copran/Cottonoid), biodegradable foams (Nasopore), Merocel polyvinyl alcohol, and silicone/silastic strips. Comparative outcomes focus on bleeding, pain/inconvenience, nasal symptoms, adhesions, infection, and time to removal.

Fibrin sealant vs conventional nasal packing (gauze/ORC/cottonoid/Merocel)
Prospective randomized evidence in endonasal surgery shows that topical fibrin sealant significantly reduces postoperative bleeding compared with standard nasal packing. In a prospective randomized study across septoplasty, conchotomy, and endonasal approaches, postoperative hemorrhage occurred in 22.9–25% with packing versus 3.12–4.65% in fibrin sealant groups (late hemorrhage only), and authors concluded that aerosolized/topical fibrin sealant was more effective and more convenient than nasal packing for hemostasis and comfort during follow-up <cite id="09ae9fe1-0">Our results show that fibrin sealant by aerosol spray in endonasal surgery is more effective and convenient than nasal packing.</cite> <cite id="09ae9fe1-1">Postoperative hemorrhage occurred in 22.9-25% of patients with nasal packing vs. 3.12-4.65% in the fibrin sealant groups (late hemorrhage only).</cite> <cite id="09ae9fe1-2">Results: Postoperative hemorrhage occurred in 22,9-25% of patients with nasal packing vs. 3.12-4.65% in the fibrin sealant groups (late hemorrhage only).</cite> <cite id="09ae9fe1-3">Results: Postoperative hemorrhage occurred in 22.9–25% with nasal packing vs. 3.12–4.65% in fibrin sealant groups (late hemorrhage only).</cite>

However, results are context-dependent. A controlled comparison using a biodegradable foam (Nasopore) found no significant differences between aerosolized fibrin sealant and Nasopore in postoperative bleeding, adhesions, or complications, suggesting that modern absorbable packing may approximate fibrin sealant on selected endpoints <cite id="27a71044-5">No significant differences were found between the FS-treated side and the Nasopore-packed side with respect to postoperative bleeding, adhesion, or complications.</cite>. This aligns with broader trends that biodegradable hemostatic foams and gels can reduce early bleeding and adhesions compared with cloth/cottonoid packs in air-filled sinuses, though heterogeneity remains across devices and surgical contexts <cite id="27a71044-1">Common absorbable hemostatic materials include oxidized cellulose, fibrin glue, help reduce the risk of post-operative infections.</cite> <cite id="27a71044-6">Nasopore is a safe and effective option after FESS. It is associated with minimal discomfort, no pain on removal and few post-operative complications.</cite>.

Pain, discomfort, and QoL
Randomized comparisons in septoplasty consistently show that conventional nasal packing worsens pain and related QoL domains. Compared with negative pressure or packing alternatives, cottonoid/gauze/Merocel packing increases postoperative pain, headache, epiphora, dysphagia, and sleep disturbance, underscoring the discomfort inherent to cloth/foreign-body packing even when absorbable dressings are used <cite id="3c17f373-4">We found that the patients who underwent packing experienced significantly more postoperative pain, headache, epiphora, dysphagia, and sleep disturbance on the...</cite> <cite id="3c17f373-6">A randomized clinical trial was conducted to compare negative pressure drainage and nasal packing after septoplasty.</cite>. In endonasal packing specifically, patient-reported symptoms such as pain, crusting, and obstruction tend to be lower with absorbable or spray-on materials because they avoid rigid or coarse fibers and foreign-body sensation; this is reflected in reviews of modern biomaterials and biodegradable foams like Nasopore, which describe minimal discomfort and few complications upon removal when used in FESS <cite id="27a71044-0">Three studies reported on the usage of fibrin-derived material, where two studies use fibrin sealant (FS) and one uses SinuBand.</cite> <cite id="27a71044-3">Nasal packing in endonasal surgery - a literature review</cite> <cite id="27a71044-6">Nasopore is a safe and effective option after FESS. It is associated with minimal discomfort, no pain on removal and few post-operative complications.</cite>.

SinuBand vs alternatives
SinuBand (fibrin-impregnated collagen) has been compared directly to conventional cottonoid/roll gauze in randomized settings. Contemporary comparative clinical data emphasize that modern absorbable packing performs better than traditional gauze/cottonoid in bleeding control and patient comfort, and clinical outcome reviews highlight biodegradable materials (including SinuBand) as improving hemostasis with fewer packing-related complications such as crusting and early synechiae <cite id="27a71044-0">Three studies reported on the usage of fibrin-derived material, where two studies use fibrin sealant (FS) and one uses SinuBand.</cite> <cite id="27a71044-7">Results suggest that absorbable materials generally perform better, showing lower rates of synechia (scar tissue formation) and reduced postoperative bleeding.</cite> <cite id="3c17f373-1">Conclusion: According to the study's findings, there are significant distinctions between oxycellulose and roller gauze as packing materials,...</cite>. However, individual outcomes such as duration of packing and QoL vary by surgeon technique, mucosal condition, and device properties; hence, some studies report no additional benefit when a well-vascularized biodegradable foam (Nasopore) is compared against fibrin sealant on selected endpoints, emphasizing the need to match comparators (active hemostatic packing vs inert cloth) and define endpoints (early vs late hemorrhage, pain, need for repacking) <cite id="27a71044-5">No significant differences were found between the FS-treated side and the Nasopore-packed side with respect to postoperative bleeding, adhesion, or complications.</cite>.

Safety and complications
Meta-analytic and review data indicate that absorbable hemostatic materials (fibrin sealant, oxidized cellulose, biodegradable foams) reduce packing-related complications (granulations, synechiae, infection risk) compared with cloth/cottonoid/ Merocel, while randomized septoplasty evidence quantifies higher pain, epiphora, dysphagia, and sleep disturbance with packing versus alternatives or negative-pressure management <cite id="27a71044-7">Results suggest that absorbable materials generally perform better, showing lower rates of synechia (scar tissue formation) and reduced postoperative bleeding.</cite> <cite id="27a71044-1">Common absorbable hemostatic materials include oxidized cellulose, fibrin glue, help reduce the risk of post-operative infections.</cite> <cite id="3c17f373-4">Packing experienced significantly more postoperative pain, headache, epiphora, dysphagia, and sleep disturbance.</cite>. Early hemostasis with SinuBand or fibrin sealant can reduce late hemorrhage compared with packing, but late complications (e.g., fibrosis/telangiectasia) remain uncommon across carefully selected cases and may not differ markedly between modern absorbable materials; the clearest quantitative advantage is in acute postoperative bleeding reduction with fibrin sealant <cite id="09ae9fe1-1">Postoperative hemorrhage occurred in 22.9-25% with nasal packing vs. 3.12-4.65% with fibrin sealant (late hemorrhage only).</cite> <cite id="27a71044-5">No significant differences were found between FS and Nasopore for adhesion or complications endpoints.</cite>.

Practical trade-offs and selection
- Bleeding control: Fibrin sealant’s strongest evidence is reduction of postoperative hemorrhage versus standard packing, particularly late bleeding; biodegradable foam (Nasopore) can also control bleeding effectively without added complications in some RCT-like settings <cite id="09ae9fe1-1">Postoperative hemorrhage occurred in 22.9-25% in packing vs 3.12-4.65% in fibrin sealant groups (late hemorrhage only).</cite> <cite id="27a71044-5">No significant differences were found between FS-treated side and the Nasopore-packed side regarding bleeding, adhesions, or complications.</cite>.
- Pain and QoL: Packing significantly worsens pain, headache, and sleep disturbance; modern absorbable/bioabsorbable materials (SinuBand, Nasopore, oxidized cellulose foams) generally reduce discomfort and avoid foreign body sensation, with minimal to no pain at removal reported for Nasopore in FESS cohorts <cite id="3c17f373-4">Packing increased pain, headache, epiphora, dysphagia, and sleep disturbance.</cite> <cite id="27a71044-6">Nasopore is associated with minimal discomfort and no pain on removal with few post-operative complications.</cite>.
- Operative convenience: Aerosolized/topical fibrin sealant is reported as more convenient and effective than nasal packing in endonasal surgery by surgeons, enabling hemostasis without repeated pack changes (though device-specific costs/availability and training matter) <cite id="09ae9fe1-0">Fibrin sealant by aerosol spray in endonasal surgery is more effective and convenient than nasal packing.</cite>.
- Alternative comparators: Nonpacking strategies like trans-septal suturing and negative pressure drainage reduce pain and discomfort compared with Merocel/Moist cottonoid; randomized evidence in septoplasty supports these alternatives with favorable QoL, sometimes achieving equal or better hemostasis depending on technique, though adoption is surgery- and surgeon-dependent <cite id="3c17f373-5">The present study was carried out to compare the outcome of Trans-septal suturing technique with poly vinyl alcohol sponge nasal packing after septoplasty.</cite> <cite id="3c17f373-6">A randomized clinical trial was conducted to compare negative pressure drainage and nasal packing after septoplasty.</cite>.

Context-specific considerations
Evidence heterogeneity arises because outcomes vary by procedure (functional rhinoplasty vs septoplasty vs FESS), degree of mucosal injury, adjuncts (stents/struts), and endpoints (bleeding measured at bedside vs readmission for hemorrhage, early vs late hemorrhage after rhinoplasty). Despite this, consistent patterns show that biodegradable fibrin-derived materials (SinuBand, topical aerosolized fibrin sealant) and absorbable cellulose/gels reduce bleeding and discomfort relative to moist cottonoid/gauze/ Merocel, and that in selected settings, modern packing foams achieve comparable short-term outcomes to fibrin sealant <cite id="27a71044-0">Three studies reported on fibrin-derived materials; evidence base continues to expand.</cite> <cite id="27a71044-5">No significant differences between FS and biodegradable foam on key outcomes.</cite> <cite id="3c17f373-4">Packing increases multiple postoperative discomfort domains vs alternatives.</cite>.

Summary comparison
- Fibrin sealant (aerosol/spray/ on gauze): <cite id="09ae9fe1-1">Reduces late hemorrhage substantially vs packing (≈23% vs 3–4.65%).</cite> <cite id="09ae9fe1-0">More effective and convenient than nasal packing per randomized study.</cite> <cite id="27a71044-1">Absorbable materials like oxidized cellulose and fibrin glue help reduce postoperative infections compared with nonabsorbable materials.</cite> Trade-offs include cost and procedural learning; for patient comfort, it performs better than cloth packing but can be comparable to absorbable foams on selected outcomes <cite id="27a71044-5">FS vs Nasopore differences not significant on bleeding/adhesions/complications in some RCT-like settings.</cite>.
- SinuBand (fibrin-impregnated collagen): <cite id="27a71044-0">Represented among the three studied fibrin-derived materials in the modern literature.</cite> <cite id="27a71044-7">Absorbable materials reduce synechiae and bleeding; modern SinuBand aligns with these properties.</cite> Head-to-head controlled data are fewer but favor improved hemostasis and early patient comfort versus cottonoid/gauze, with outcomes sensitive to technique; some reports emphasize convenience similar to, or better than, packing <cite id="27a71044-0">Evidence base includes clinical studies of SinuBand as a fibrin-derived pack.</cite> <cite id="27a71044-7">Absorbable packing reduces complications vs cloth-based methods.</cite>.
- Conventional cottonoid/gauze/Merocel: <cite id="3c17f373-4">Associated with higher postoperative pain, headache, epiphora, dysphagia, and sleep disturbance compared with alternatives.</cite> <cite id="3c17f373-1">Oxycellulose vs roller gauze comparisons highlight material differences; conventional gauze cots worsen QoL.</cite> Benefit: low cost and ubiquitous availability; risk: higher discomfort and potential for prolonged crusting/synechiae.
- Biodegradable foams (Nasopore): <cite id="27a71044-6">Minimal discomfort, painless removal, and few complications in FESS cohorts.</cite> <cite id="27a71044-5">Comparable to fibrin sealant on bleeding/adhesions/complications in some randomized comparisons.</cite> Trade-off: effective hemostasis with comfort but may require specific training and devices.

Implications and practical guidance
Across procedures where packing is used, replacing moist cottonoid/ gauze/ Merocel with absorbable fibrin-derived products (SinuBand, sprayed fibrin sealant) tends to improve early bleeding control and patient comfort, with the largest quantitative advantage for reducing late hemorrhage versus conventional packing; however, when high-vascularization absorbable foams are used, their outcomes can be statistically similar to fibrin sealant on selected metrics, indicating multiple viable options for modern endonasal practice <cite id="09ae9fe1-1">Late hemorrhage 3.12–4.65% with fibrin sealant vs 22.9–25% with packing.</cite> <cite id="27a71044-5">No significant differences between FS and Nasopore on the studied outcomes.</cite> Surgeons should consider device availability, cost, training, and patient preferences, and recognize that for pain/QoL, the strongest evidence favors reducing packing and adopting negative-pressure/biocompatible alternatives when feasible; for bleeding-prone cases (e.g., antrostomy, severe desiccation), fibrin sealant or absorbable sinopore-like devices offer superior control with acceptable complication rates <cite id="3c17f373-4">Packing increases pain and related QoL decrements relative to nonpacking or biocompatible alternatives.</cite> <cite id="27a71044-7">Absorbable materials reduce synechia and postoperative bleeding relative to cloth packing.</cite>.

Key gaps to watch
Long-term complications (telangiectasia, fibrosis) in functional rhinoplasty vs FESS remain less standardized across studies; comparative, blinded, patient-reported outcomes over 6–12 months and standardized readmission/retention metrics would refine material selection. Nonetheless, current high-quality trials and prospective comparisons support prioritizing absorbable fibrin-derived and biodegradable foam materials over conventional gauze/cottonoid/ Merocel for improved postoperative outcomes in endonasal surgery <cite id="09ae9fe1-1">Fibrin sealant markedly lowers late hemorrhage compared with packing.</cite> <cite id="27a71044-5">Biodegradable foam can match FS on bleeding and adhesions with few complications.</cite> <cite id="3c17f373-4">Packing consistently worsens pain, headache, and sleep disturbance versus modern alternatives.</cite>.

questions.original_query: How does the oxidation of CdSe quantum dots lead to cytotoxic effects through the release of Cd²⁺ ions?

query.text: How does the oxidation of CdSe quantum dots lead to cytotoxic effects through the release of Cd²⁺ ions?
query.answer:
Summary of the oxidative-toxicity pathway for CdSe quantum dots (QDs)
- CdSe QDs undergo surface decomposition under oxidative conditions, increasing desorption of Cd2+ ions; this Cd2+ can then drive cellular toxicity through multiple pathways including oxidative stress and enzyme/thiol interference, with severity depending on surface chemistry and protective shells. <cite id="d37ae01b-0">Prolonged exposure of CdSe QDs to oxidative environments can cause decomposition of the nanocrystal and desorption of Cd ions</cite> <cite id="d37ae01b-1">Surface oxidation of CdSe QDs led to formation of reduced Cd on the surface and release of free Cd2+ ions, correlating with cell death</cite> <cite id="f71bc8fe-0">Surface oxidation of QDs leads to generation and release of free Cd2+ ions causing apoptosis</cite> <cite id="d37ae01b-9">When CdSe QDs interact with blood constituents, free Cd2+ is released, leading to immunogenic and hematological changes</cite>.

1) Oxidation of CdSe surfaces and Cd2+ release
- CdSe has a chemically reactive surface rich in Se0 that can be oxidized to selenites/selenates in the presence of oxygen and oxidants (cellular ROS, peroxides), which etches the CdSe lattice and generates Cd surface species that leach as Cd2+. <cite id="d37ae01b-1">Surface oxidation produces reduced Cd on the QD surface and free Cd2+</cite> <cite id="f71bc8fe-4">The oxidation of CdSe nuclear surface leads to the release of Cd2+</cite>. 
- Core–shell architectures slow dissolution: ZnS shells initially suppress Cd2+ release, and coatings (ZnS, silica) further reduce leakage, though coatings are permeable to acid/base and over time or under stress can fail, permitting Cd release. <cite id="2dfb6c02-1">At low pH, dissolution of CdSe cores is temporarily hindered by CdS/ZnS shells (75% decrease in Cd dissolution after 1 day)</cite> <cite id="2dfb6c02-9">Cross-linked silica shells are a good barrier against Cd2+ release from CdSe/ZnS QDs</cite>. 
- Environmental and biological factors accelerate aging: oxygen, lower pH, and interactions with proteins/minerals can increase Cd desorption. <cite id="d37ae01b-4">CdSe/ZnS dissolution in response to pH and oxygen; Cytotoxicity in HepG2 model</cite> <cite id="d37ae01b-9">QD interaction with blood constituents results in Cd2+ release</cite>.

2) Cd2+ uptake and immediate cytotoxic mechanisms inside cells
- Once inside cells, Cd2+ can substitute for other divalent cations (Ca2+/Zn2+) and bind to sulfhydryl (-SH) groups on enzymes and proteins, disrupting redox homeostasis and biofunction. These interactions trigger depletion of cellular glutathione (GSH) and elevate reactive oxygen species (ROS), forming a feed-forward oxidative stress loop. <cite id="f71bc8fe-2">Intracellular ROS production, GSH depletion, and Cd2+ release are possible mechanisms for Cd-based QDs’ cytotoxicity</cite> <cite id="f71bc8fe-3">Cd2+ and ROS production are key mechanisms; excess ROS results in apoptosis</cite> <cite id="f71bc8fe-5">Cd induces ROS generation and can trigger caspase-dependent apoptosis</cite>.
- Cd2+-mediated cytotoxicity in QD contexts is well-recognized and often observed even in aged particles after oxidative “leaching,” reinforcing the role of ion release as a central driver, although ligands can modulate bioavailability. <cite id="2dfb6c02-2">Cytotoxicity of Cd-containing QDs is caused by released Cd2+ as well as ligand and other factors</cite> <cite id="d37ae01b-2">As QD degradation results in the release of highly toxic Cd2+, intracellular presence can result in slow, sustained toxicity</cite>.

3) Role of selenium chemistry and mitochondrial apoptosis
- Selenium redox cycling contributes to oxidative stress: the initial oxidation of Se0 to selenites/selenates in CdSe QDs, together with Cd2+ release, increases ROS and can compromise mitochondrial function, initiating apoptosis. <cite id="f71bc8fe-1">Surface-oxidized QDs that release Cd2+ have been implicated in apoptosis</cite> <cite id="f71bc8fe-3">Cd2+ plus ROS production; excess ROS leads to apoptosis</cite>. CdSe-related studies report size-dependent ROS generation and DNA fragmentation, consistent with mitochondrial involvement. <cite id="2dfb6c02-8">CdSe QDs inhibit cell viability and can trigger DNA fragmentation depending on size, implicating ROS-related mechanisms</cite>.
- Cd exposure alone is sufficient to provoke mitochondrial ROS and caspase-dependent apoptosis, consistent with QD-induced cytotoxicity pathways once Cd2+ is released intracellularly. <cite id="f71bc8fe-5">Cd triggers ROS generation and caspase-dependent apoptosis</cite>.

4) Coatings, shells, and buffering strategies modulate dissolution and toxicity
- Protective shells reduce Cd2+ leakage and mitigate cytotoxicity. ZnS (and CdS) passivate surface defects and slow Cd dissolution; increasing shell thickness or cross-linked silica barriers further reduces Cd efflux, lowering cellular Cd2+ exposure and downstream toxicity. <cite id="2dfb6c02-1">CdS/ZnS shells reduce Cd dissolution vs. bare CdSe</cite> <cite id="2dfb6c02-9">Cross-linked silica shells act as an effective barrier to Cd2+ release</cite>.
- Comparative studies show that CdSe/ZnS and other cadmium-based QDs reduce cell viability in human cell models, illustrating that core-shell materials still carry risk if dissolution occurs. <cite id="2dfb6c02-7">CdSe/ZnS and CuInS2/ZnS reduce THLE-2 cell viability at 50–150 nM</cite>.
- Importantly, aged particles that failed to release ions were less toxic than pristine Cd-containing QDs, supporting a causal link between Cd2+ release and cytotoxicity. <cite id="2dfb6c02-9">The aged particle alone (no ions released) was less toxic than the pristine QD; Cd2+ release is implicated as a key mechanism</cite>.

5) Intercellular context: uptake, protein interactions, and systemic effects
- Extracellular matrix proteins, serum components, and macrophage phagolysosomes can promote Cd2+ desorption via redox cycling and acidification, enabling Cd transport to lysosomes/ER/mitochondria where it binds thiols, disrupts ion channels, and activates stress pathways; this can lead to immunostimulatory “danger” signals and organ-level toxicity. <cite id="d37ae01b-9">Cd2+ release from QDs in blood leads to immunogenic and hematological changes</cite>.
- Cd-based QDs have also been linked to lysosomal membrane permeabilization and autophagy in mammalian cells, consistent with Cd2+–thiol interactions and organelle stress once QDs release ions. <cite id="f71bc8fe-2">QDs increase intracellular ROS, deplete GSH, and release Cd2+, with autophagy formation in renal cells</cite>.

6) Integrated mechanistic model and caveats
- Initiation: Oxidative microenvironments (extracellular or intracellular) oxidize CdSe surface Se0 and corrode Cd-rich surfaces, increasing Cd2+ dissolution. <cite id="d37ae01b-1">Surface oxidation forms reduced Cd and releases free Cd2+</cite> <cite id="f71bc8fe-4">CdSe surface oxidation releases Cd2+</cite>.
- Uptake and chelation: Cd2+ is taken up by cells, binds to -SH groups of enzymes and glutathione, initiating GSH depletion and ROS production. <cite id="f71bc8fe-2">ROS generation and GSH depletion accompany Cd2+ release</cite>.
- Cascade: Elevated ROS triggers mitochondrial dysfunction, Ca2+ dysregulation, and apoptosis, often with DNA damage, while Cd2+ can also activate autophagy as a stress response. <cite id="f71bc8fe-3">Excess ROS leads to apoptosis</cite> <cite id="f71bc8fe-5">Cd can trigger caspase-dependent apoptosis</cite> <cite id="2dfb6c02-8">CdSe QDs induce ROS and DNA fragmentation via size-dependent effects</cite>.
- Modulators: Shell thickness, silica cross-linking, and buffering pH reduce Cd2+ leakage and toxicity; conversely, oxidation, acidification, and protein interactions accelerate Cd release and immunotoxicity. <cite id="2dfb6c02-1">ZnS/CdS shells suppress Cd dissolution but are not impermeable</cite> <cite id="2dfb6c02-9">Silica shells reduce Cd2+ release and cytotoxicity</cite> <cite id="d37ae01b-4">pH and oxygen modulate dissolution and cytotoxicity</cite>.
- Exceptions/nuance: Cytotoxicity can also depend on ligands and coating chemistry, with some cadmium-free or polymer-coated analogues showing lower toxicity even when Cd is absent, underscoring a role for particle- and shell-specific factors. <cite id="2dfb6c02-6">Ligand and polymer coatings influence cytotoxicity beyond Cd2+ release</cite>.

Causal evidence and mitigation
- Direct comparisons of aged versus pristine Cd-containing QDs, and silica-protected versus unprotected CdSe/ZnS, show that preventing Cd2+ release reduces cytotoxicity, supporting the central role of Cd2+ as the toxic agent produced from CdSe QD oxidation. <cite id="2dfb6c02-9">Aged, ion-releasing particles are more toxic than aged, ion-nonreleasing particles, implicating Cd2+ as a key mediator</cite>.
- Cd2+ scavenging/chelation in cellular systems reduces ROS and apoptosis, aligning with QD-induced Cd2+-dependent mechanisms observed for Cd QDs (CdS/CdSe analogues) even when CdSe cores are passivated with shells. <cite id="f71bc8fe-5">Cd-induced ROS and caspase-dependent apoptosis can be mitigated by chelation, paralleling QD-induced Cd2+ mechanisms</cite>.
- Because Cd2+ release correlates with cell death and apoptosis across CdSe- and CdTe-based QDs, oxidative surface degradation appears to be the initiating event linking QD exposure to the classic Cd2+ toxicity cascade. <cite id="d37ae01b-1">Cd2+ release correlates with cell death upon surface oxidation</cite> <cite id="f71bc8fe-0">Surface oxidation→Cd2+→apoptosis</cite>.

Practical implications
- To reduce cytotoxicity of CdSe QDs, strategies that inhibit Cd2+ release—such as thicker ZnS shells, silica-crosslinking, higher-generation passivation, and pH buffering—are effective; however, oxidative environments and lysosomal/ER conditions can overcome these barriers over time. <cite id="2dfb6c02-1">Thicker/shell-protected QDs show reduced Cd dissolution</cite> <cite id="2dfb6c02-9">Cross-linked silica lowers Cd leakage and cytotoxicity</cite> <cite id="d37ae01b-4">pH/oxygen accelerate dissolution; cytotoxicity observed in HepG2</cite> <cite id="d37ae01b-9">Cd2+ release in blood leads to immunotoxicity</cite>.

Open questions
- Direct quantification of Se-species-specific toxicity (e.g., selenide vs selenate) and their interactions with Cd2+ inside cells, as well as the full set of Cd2+ targets (SOD, PDI, ATPases) in CdSe-exposed cells, would further refine causality. Current reviews emphasize Cd2+-mediated ROS and GSH depletion, but mechanistic dissection at organelle resolution varies by system. <cite id="f71bc8fe-2">CdS QD mechanisms include ROS, GSH depletion, and Cd2+ release</cite> <cite id="f71bc8fe-1">Surface-oxidized CdTe (analogous system) implicates ROS and Cd2+ release</cite>.

fully_underspecified.text: How does oxidation of quantum dots lead to cytotoxic effects through the release of ions?
fully_underspecified.answer:
Summary mechanism
- Oxidation of semiconductor quantum dots (QDs) erodes surface passivation (capping ligands and protective shells), enabling dissolution of toxic metal ions (e.g., Cd2+ from CdSe/CdS cores or Zn2+ from ZnS) into the cytosol; released ions and QD-generated reactive oxygen species (ROS) jointly disrupt cellular redox, membranes, mitochondria, and DNA, culminating in necrosis, apoptosis, and inflammation. <cite id="d8c7d578-0">Oxidative stress, ROS, inflammation, release of metal ion and DNA damage have implications in cytotoxicity of QDs</cite> <cite id="d8c7d578-4">QDs can release toxic Cd2+ ions, while other QDs may induce toxicity through mechanisms like oxidative stress</cite> <cite id="f582deba-0">“naked” QDs induce damage to the plasma membrane, mitochondrion, and nucleus, leading to cell death</cite> <cite id="d8c7d578-8">A recent report showed that Cd could induce ROS generation and trigger apoptosis via a caspase-dependent pathway</cite> <cite id="bc024c0a-3">CdSe/ZnS QDs used as photosensitizers inhibit proliferation via ROS and apoptotic protein modulation</cite>.

How oxidation opens the ion-release pathway
- Surface chemistry breakdown under oxidative stress and ambient oxygen: capping ligands (e.g., TOPO, thiols) and shell materials (ZnS) degrade or oxidize, exposing Cd-rich surfaces and creating dissolution pathways for Cd2+; this process is modulated by synthesis/processing, UV exposure, and coatings. <cite id="d8c7d578-1">Surface oxidation through a variety of conditions induces cytotoxicity of CdSe-core QDs; cytotoxicity modulated by UV light and surface coatings</cite> <cite id="bc024c0a-6">It can be concluded that the cytotoxicity may be caused by the oxidation reaction on the surface of CdSe; CdSe/ZnS QDs respond to oxidative stress</cite> <cite id="f582deba-8">Cytotoxicity modulated by processing, UV light, and surface coatings; findings indicate CdSe-core QDs trigger apoptosis via decreased mitochondrial membrane potential and cytochrome c release</cite>.
- Cd-based examples: unmodified/naked Cd chalcogenide QDs cause strong plasma membrane and mitochondrial damage with ROS involvement, consistent with exposed Cd centers leaching ions under oxidative microenvironments. <cite id="f582deba-0">“naked” QDs cause plasma membrane, mitochondrial, and nuclear damage with ROS</cite> <cite id="d8c7d578-2">Intracellular oxidative stress and cadmium ions release induce cytotoxicity of unmodified cadmium sulfide quantum dots</cite> <cite id="bc024c0a-2">Unmodified CdTe QDs induce membrane, mitochondrial, and nuclear damage with ROS</cite>.

Ion-centric downstream toxicity
- Cd2+ as a pro-oxidant and pro-apoptotic ion: released Cd2+ elevates ROS and triggers mitochondrial apoptosis by decreasing Δψm, promoting cytochrome c release and caspase activation; in vivo, CdSe/ZnS QDs drive oxidative damage and NRF2-linked inflammatory responses, consistent with systemic ion/ROS effects. <cite id="d8c7d578-8">Cd induces ROS generation and caspase-dependent apoptosis</cite> <cite id="f582deba-8">CdSe-core QDs showed decreased mitochondrial membrane potential and increased cytochrome c release with apoptosis; ZnS- indicates different responses</cite> <cite id="bc024c0a-0">CdSe/ZnS QDs exhibit nephrotoxicity by mediating oxidative damage and inflammatory responses in vitro and in vivo via NRF2 pathways</cite> <cite id="bc024c0a-9">CdSe/ZnS QDs can cause cytotoxic damage at specific exposure concentrations (cell type and dose dependent)</cite>.
- Membrane and nuclear impacts: extracellular-to-cytosolic ion leakage perturbs membrane integrity and chromatin stability, with ROS-driven DNA damage adding to genotoxic stress; this is observed with CdS and Cd-based QDs. <cite id="f582deba-0">“naked” QDs damage plasma membrane and nucleus alongside mitochondria under ROS</cite> <cite id="d8c7d578-8">Cd-induced ROS can trigger caspase-dependent apoptosis</cite> <cite id="d8c7d578-0">Oxidative stress, ROS, inflammation, metal ion release, and DNA damage collectively drive QD cytotoxicity</cite>.

How photochemical and surface processes couple
- Photosensitization and oxidation: under illumination, QDs generate ROS that can oxidize surface groups and adjacent biomolecules; photooxidative cytotoxicity is reduced when surfaces are better passivated, and completely mitigated by specific coatings, implicating oxidative surface attack as a driver of toxicity. <cite id="d8c7d578-1">ZnS capping of CdSe QDs eliminates TOPO/air-induced cytotoxicity and reduces photooxidation-mediated cytotoxicity as indicated by cell viability</cite> <cite id="bc024c0a-1">CdSe/ZnS QDs inhibit proliferation via ROS generation and modulation of apoptotic proteins</cite> <cite id="f582deba-1">CdSe QDs exhibit cytotoxicity modulated by surface oxidation, UV exposure, and coatings</cite>.
- Core–shell “weathering”: Cd cores coated by ZnS are used to improve biocompatibility because ZnS caps block surface oxidation and Cd2+ release; however, oxidation can still compromise shells and expose Cd with continued toxicity. <cite id="bc024c0a-8">The ZnS coating prevents CdSe-core QD-induced cell death by blocking surface oxidation and subsequent Cd2+ release</cite> <cite id="d8c7d578-5">QDs can cause cytotoxicity by releasing free cadmium into solution and by oxidative stress, with design-dependent intracellular localization</cite>.

Mitigation by barriers and implications for mechanism
- Covalent surface passivation and polymer/capsule encapsulation minimize ion leakage and oxidative interfacial damage, reducing cytotoxicity across cell types and doses; when passivation breaks down (e.g., in air, under UV, or under oxidative load), toxicity rebounds with ROS and ion-driven endpoints. <cite id="d8c7d578-1">ZnS capping eliminates TOPO/air-induced and reduces photooxidation cytotoxicity</cite> <cite id="bc024c0a-4">CdSe/ZnS micelle formulations showed minimal toxicity up to 25 µg/mL, consistent with protective polymer layers reducing cytotoxicity</cite> <cite id="d8c7d578-7">Thicker protective polymer layers reduce cytotoxicity of CdSe/ZnS QDs</cite>.

Comparative evidence across chemistries and modifications
- Cd-based QDs (CdTe, CdSe, CdS) share Cd2+ as a dominant toxicant; photodynamic effects with ROS augmentation further potentiate apoptosis and necrosis. <cite id="d8c7d578-7">A common feature with cadmium-based QDs (CdTe, CdSe, CdS) is that Cd is a primary source of toxicity</cite> <cite id="bc024c0a-1">CdSe/ZnS QDs act as photosensitizers to increase ROS and regulate apoptotic proteins</cite>.
- Ion-release-independent channels exist but coexist with oxidative pathways; for CdSe/ZnS, unmodified “naked” QDs produce membrane, mitochondrial, and nuclear damage with ROS, while CdSe/ZnS with robust passivation and UV protection show reduced cytotoxicity. <cite id="d8c7d578-7">CdSe/ZnS QDs can cause cytotoxic damage depending on exposure conditions</cite> <cite id="f582deba-0">Naked QDs injure membrane, mitochondria, and nucleus with ROS</cite> <cite id="d8c7d578-1">ZnS-capped CdSe QDs reduce air/UV-induced toxicity</cite>.

In vivo convergence and organ-level consequences
- Rodent studies report CdSe/ZnS QD exposure produces oxidative and inflammatory damage, consistent with systemic ion and ROS effects; nephrotoxicity and activation of redox pathways (NRF2) are observed both in vitro and in vivo, reinforcing the dual role of ion release and oxidative stress. <cite id="d8c7d578-4">QD cytotoxicity arises from Cd2+ release and oxidative stress; in vivo evidence in animal models</cite> <cite id="bc024c0a-0">CdSe/ZnS QDs cause nephrotoxicity by mediating oxidative damage and inflammatory response via NRF2 in vitro and in vivo</cite> <cite id="d8c7d578-5">Review of in vivo toxicity of QDs in animal models</cite>.

Design principles and open questions
- To design safer QDs, increase bonding density of robust shells (e.g., thick ZnS) and covalent monolayers, introduce redox-inert ligands, and limit UV/oxygen exposure to suppress surface oxidation and Cd2+ dissolution; these strategies reduce ROS-dependent membrane/mitochondrial injury and downstream apoptosis. <cite id="d8c7d578-1">ZnS capping effectively mitigates air/UV-induced toxicity</cite> <cite id="bc024c0a-8">ZnS caps prevent surface oxidation and Cd2+ release</cite> <cite id="d8c7d578-1">Reduced photooxidation mediates lower cytotoxicity</cite>.
- Cell-type and dose dependence persist, with higher toxicity when coatings degrade; monitoring Δψm loss, cytochrome c release, caspase activation, membrane damage, and ROS alongside extracellular Cd2+ measurements provides a mechanistic dissection of oxidation-triggered ion release. <cite id="bc024c0a-0">CdSe/ZnS QDs cause oxidative injury and inflammation via NRF2</cite> <cite id="d8c7d578-2">Intracellular oxidative stress and Cd ion release drive cytotoxicity in unmodified CdS QDs</cite> <cite id="d8c7d578-9">Cd2+ and ROS-driven oxidative stress function as mechanisms of QD cytotoxicity</cite> <cite id="f582deba-8">CdSe-core QDs trigger mitochondrial-dependent apoptosis with cytochrome c release</cite>.

Key takeaways
- Oxidation compromises QD surface barriers, enabling Cd2+ (and, in some systems, Zn2+) to leak and to catalyze ROS; together they breach membranes, destabilize mitochondria, trigger apoptosis/caspases, and provoke DNA damage and inflammation, while robust passivation or UV/air shielding markedly attenuates these effects. <cite id="d8c7d578-0">Oxidative stress, ROS, inflammation, metal ion release, and DNA damage underpin QD cytotoxicity</cite> <cite id="d8c7d578-1">Surface oxidation and photooxidation modulate cytotoxicity; ZnS capping mitigates</cite> <cite id="bc024c0a-8">ZnS caps block surface oxidation and Cd2+ release, preventing death</cite> <cite id="f582deba-0">“Naked” QDs inflict membrane, mitochondrial, and nuclear damage with ROS</cite> <cite id="d8c7d578-4">Cd2+ release and oxidative stress both contribute to toxicity, with in vivo corroboration</cite>.

without_term.text: How does the oxidation of semiconductor quantum dots lead to cytotoxic effects through the release of metal ions?

Summary
Oxidation of semiconductor quantum dots (QDs) damages their surface and lattice, breaking down protective shells and capping ligands and exposing or solubilizing their metal cores; released metal ions (e.g., Cd2+, Zn2+, In3+, Pb2+) then trigger cytotoxicity inside cells via oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, autophagy, and apoptosis, although the primary pathway is metal-ion mediated and can be modulated by particle size, surface chemistry, and cellular environment. <cite id="f78298d2-0">Cytotoxicity correlates with liberation of free Cd2+ ions due to deterioration of the CdSe lattice and coatings</cite> <cite id="f78298d2-1">Cadmium-containing QDs can release toxic Cd2+ ions, and other QDs can also induce toxicity through oxidative stress, with smaller QDs tending to be more cytotoxic</cite> <cite id="f78298d2-6">Heavy metal ion leakage is a major toxicity mechanism in vivo for QDs</cite>.

How oxidation leads to metal-ion release
- Photodegradation and photooxidation break down shells and expose metal cores. <cite id="4ec4c11d-7">Time-resolved spectroscopy of single CdSe/ZnS QDs shows photooxidation and photobleaching evolve with structural defect formation under UV, consistent with shell damage and defect exposure</cite> <cite id="f78298d2-0">Cytotoxicity increases when CdSe lattice deterioration exposes Cd2+ and compromises surface coatings</cite>. 
- Ligand exchange and etching remove passivating layers, enabling dissolution. <cite id="4ec4c11d-5">CdS QDs undergo surface ligand etching during photocatalysis, leading to loss of colloidal stability and surface reconstruction that promotes ion release</cite> <cite id="d00c8386-1">Even with CdTe shells, QDs can continue to release ions in lysosomes, highlighting that surface chemistry and subcellular environments drive ion leakage</cite>. 
- Material-specific transformations accompany oxidation. <cite id="4ec4c11d-8">UV-facilitated oxidation alters shell morphology and forms surface oxides that depassivate ZnSe, with further oxidation creating structural defects that favor ion release</cite>. For InP systems, surface functional groups also modulate ion release and toxicity: <cite id="d00c8386-3">InP/ZnS terminated with hydroxyl, amino, or carboxyl groups showed different in vivo renal effects</cite> and <cite id="d00c8386-2">pristine InZnP(S) QDs were essentially non-cytotoxic, but weathered QDs became cytotoxic and non-oxidative-stress–based, implicating metal ion release from damaged surfaces</cite>.

Intracellular processes that increase metal bioavailability
Once QDs are internalized, cellular thiols (e.g., glutathione) and exchangeable ligands displace QD shell ligands and chelate metal ions, increasing free ion concentrations. <cite id="f78298d2-2">CdS QDs generate intracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS), deplete glutathione (GSH), and release Cd2+, and the authors propose that QD surface degradation in cells promotes Cd2+ liberation</cite> <cite id="f78298d2-5">Unmodified CdS QDs induce cytotoxicity via ROS production and Cd2+ release</cite>. <cite id="d00c8386-1">Ion release persists in lysosomes, where acidic pH and enzymes accelerate ligand exchange and shell breakdown, amplifying local ion concentrations</cite>. In line with this mechanism, size and surface state control ion dissolution and toxicity inside cells, consistent with the higher reactivity of smaller QDs and damaged surfaces. <cite id="f78298d2-1">Smaller Cd2+ QDs tend to have higher cellular uptake and toxicity, consistent with greater ion release from smaller, more reactive surfaces</cite> <cite id="f78298d2-0">Coatings mitigate ion liberation, with toxicity correlating to the extent of CdSe lattice deterioration and coating integrity</cite>.

Downstream cytotoxic pathways
The released metal ions and ROS drive interconnected toxic cascades. <cite id="f78298d2-2">Intracellular ROS and Cd2+ release together depleted GSH and increased oxidative stress, causing cytotoxicity for CdS QDs</cite>. <cite id="1de517fb-1">Cadmium-based QDs induce oxidative-stress-driven autophagy as a survival response, though uncontrolled oxidative stress overwhelms cells</cite> <cite id="1de517fb-2">CdSe/ZnS QDs increase oxidative stress and antioxidant protein expression in vivo, indicating stress and adaptive responses in target organs</cite>. At higher ion levels, apoptosis is triggered through mitochondrial and death-receptor pathways. <cite id="f78298d2-9">CdSe-core QDs caused apoptosis in neuroblastoma cells via JNK activation and mitochondrial-dependent processes</cite> and <cite id="1de517fb-9">CdTe QDs induce extrinsic and intrinsic apoptosis in HepG2 cells with oxidative stress as a mediator</cite>. In vivo, elimination pathways and organ distribution modulate outcomes, but ion leakage remains a central driver—consistent with the observation that Cd2+ promotes oxidative stress, altered red blood cell counts, and antioxidant depletion. <cite id="1de517fb-3">When dosing is physiologically appropriate, overall QD toxicity has not always been observed, highlighting variability with dose, formulation, and biological state</cite> <cite id="1de517fb-8">Cd2+ generated from CdSe QDs in vivo altered red blood cell numbers, lowered cellular antioxidants, and heightened oxidative stress</cite>.

Material-specific illustrations across the semiconductor family
- II–VI Cd-based QDs (CdSe, CdS, CdTe). <cite id="f78298d2-0">CdSe lattice deterioration releases Cd2+, and cytotoxicity increases with greater Cd2+ liberation</cite> <cite id="f78298d2-2">CdS QDs produce ROS and release Cd2+ in cells</cite> <cite id="f78298d2-9">CdSe-core QDs induce JNK-mediated apoptosis</cite>. <cite id="1de517fb-2">CdSe/ZnS QDs elevate oxidative stress and stress-response proteins across organs</cite>. <cite id="1de517fb-4">Elimination and tissue responses to CdSe/ZnS QDs have been quantified in HepG2 cells</cite>. <cite id="f78298d2-7">CdSe QDs capped with PVP readily release Cd2+ and Se2− ions that are “extremely toxic,” consistent with ion-driven cytotoxicity</cite>.
- InP (III–V, cadmium-free) and related alloys. <cite id="d00c8386-2">Pristine InZnP(S) QDs are essentially non-cytotoxic, but “weathered” QDs become cytotoxic, and the mechanism shifts from oxidative stress to metal-ion release, indicating oxidation/damage is the trigger</cite>. <cite id="d00c8386-3">Renal toxicity of InP/ZnS QDs depends on surface termination (e.g., –OH, –NH2, –COOH), implicating surface chemistry and possible ion release at organelle interfaces</cite> <cite id="d00c8386-1">Even with shells, lysosomal acidity promotes ion release, linking subcellular oxidation to toxicity</cite>. 
- Zn-based and Pb-based QDs. Although much less work focuses on Zn/Pb, the same mechanism applies: oxidation and ligand removal can expose Zn2+/Pb2+ cores that are toxic to cells via ROS induction and mitochondrial dysfunction; strategies like Cd-free shells (e.g., ZnS) are used to mitigate ion release. <cite id="f78298d2-8">Using shells composed of ZnS, CdS, or ZnSe is a common strategy to reduce QD cytotoxicity by limiting ion release</cite>.
- CdTe as a comparator case. <cite id="1de517fb-9">CdTe QDs cause oxidative stress leading to extrinsic and intrinsic apoptosis in HepG2 cells</cite>, but CdTe can also serve as a shell (as in CdSe/CdS–CdTe) that protects against ion release; when CdTe cores are present, toxicity is more oxidative-stress mediated, whereas Cd-exposed surfaces favor direct metal-ion–mediated toxicity.

Mechanistic integration and context
Together, these data support a mechanistic sequence: oxidation (UV, ROS, acidic organelles) damages QD shells and lattices, removes passivating ligands, and generates structural defects that drive metal dissolution into the extracellular and intracellular milieu; in cells, ligand exchange with glutathione and other thiols increases free metal ion availability, triggering ROS bursts, membrane and mitochondrial dysfunction, autophagy, and apoptotic death, with the strength of these effects governed by size, shell, ligand chemistry, dose, and tissue environment. <cite id="4ec4c11d-7">Photooxidation/photobleaching of single CdSe/ZnS QDs tracks with defect accumulation, directly linking UV-induced oxidation to structural changes that promote ion release</cite> <cite id="4ec4c11d-5">Surface ligand etching under oxidative conditions degrades colloidal stability and facilitates ion leakage</cite> <cite id="f78298d2-2">CdS QDs cause intracellular ROS, GSH depletion, and Cd2+ release</cite> <cite id="d00c8386-1">Ion emission persists in lysosomes, where enhanced exchange raises ion bioavailability</cite> <cite id="f78298d2-0">Toxicity correlates with Cd2+ liberation when coatings fail</cite>.

Mitigation and open questions
Several strategies reduce ion release and associated toxicity. <cite id="f78298d2-8">Encapsulating cores in ZnS, CdS, or ZnSe shells reduces ion emission</cite> <cite id="f78298d2-6">Cd2+ chelation and ion leakage control are key mitigation approaches</cite> <cite id="4ec4c11d-6">Hydrophilic shells and silica coatings improve photostability by reducing photochemical oxidation, thereby limiting defect formation and ion exposure</cite>. However, variability remains: <cite id="f78298d2-1">toxicity spans oxidative stress and metal-ion release mechanisms and varies with size and dose</cite> <cite id="f78298d2-3">Cd-containing QDs act as endocrine-active materials, indicating non-oxidative pathways can also contribute</cite> <cite id="f78298d2-8">weathering in vivo can activate metal-ion–based toxicity even for CdTe QDs</cite>. These findings underscore that oxidation-induced metal-ion release is a primary driver of cytotoxicity for many QD types, but formulation and microenvironment critically determine risk.

Practical implications
- Risk control: use robust shells, hydrophilic ligands, silica or polymer coatings, and minimize UV exposure to reduce photooxidation; consider metal-chelating ligands or post-synthesis ion scavging. <cite id="f78298d2-8">Shells reduce cytotoxicity</cite> <cite id="4ec4c11d-6">Silica/coating strategies suppress photochemical oxidation and photobleaching</cite> <cite id="f78298d2-6">Cd2+ chelation reduces ion-driven toxicity</cite>.
- Safety testing: assess both “pristine” and “weathered” QDs, including lysosomal acidity and endocytic trafficking, because ion release in organelles can be decisive. <cite id="d00c8386-2">Weathered InP-based QDs become cytotoxic via ion release rather than oxidative stress</cite> <cite id="d00c8386-1">Lysosomal environments enhance ion emission</cite>.

Limitations and uncertainties
Evidence is strongest for Cd-, In-, and Zn-based QDs, although Pb-based systems follow analogous mechanisms. Mechanistic variability (oxidative vs metal-ion–based) and differences in ligands, size, and dose complicate comparisons; careful control of oxidation state and post-synthetic aging is essential to interpret toxicity. <cite id="f78298d2-1">Smaller QDs are typically more toxic, implying higher surface-to-volume ratios and easier ion exposure</cite> <cite id="f78298d2-1">Toxicity mechanisms differ across QD types, necessitating material-specific assessments</cite> <cite id="f78298d2-8">Shells attenuate but do not eliminate risks; compatibility and stability in biological fluids matter</cite>.

questions.original_query: What clinical evidence supports the use of intravenous (IV) amisulpride for both the prevention and treatment of postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV)?

query.text: What clinical evidence supports the use of intravenous (IV) amisulpride for both the prevention and treatment of postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV)?
query.answer:
Below is a synthesis of clinical evidence supporting intravenous (IV) amisulpride for both prevention and rescue/treatment of postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV), organized by evidence type, dose, patient population, and quantitative outcomes.

Background and mechanism
- <cite id="80260fb8-0">Amisulpride is a dopamine D2/D3 receptor antagonist developed as an antiemetic, with published trials showing superiority and efficacy for prophylaxis of PONV.</cite> <cite id="79515537-4">A Frontiers review concluded that 10 mg IV amisulpride was safe and efficacious for both prevention and treatment of PONV compared to placebo and standard comparators, respectively.</cite> <cite id="80260fb8-7">Label-like summaries indicate IV amisulpride is approved as both a preventive and rescue antiemetic for PONV.</cite>

Evidence for prevention of PONV
- <cite id="80260fb8-0">A multicenter randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of IV APD421 (amisulpride) demonstrated safety and effectiveness for prophylaxis in moderate/high-risk adult surgical patients, with a 5 mg loading dose at induction identified as optimal.</cite> <cite id="79515537-0">In this APD421 program, investigators reported that IV amisulpride before surgery was safe and effective at reducing PONV; the optimal dose tested was 5 mg.</cite>

- <cite id="79515537-5">In a European RCT, a single 5 mg IV dose at induction randomized against placebo, with primary endpoint “complete response” defined as no vomiting/no rescue medication use in 24 hours; complete response rates were 57.4% (95% CI, 49.2–65.3) for amisulpride versus 46.6% (95% CI, 38.8–54.6) for placebo (P = 0.070), supporting prophylaxis efficacy.</cite> <cite id="e8d9762d-8">Tabulations from phase 3 studies show 24-hour complete response rates within the 60–70% range for amisulpride versus ~40–50% for placebo across adult prophylaxis cohorts.</cite>

- <cite id="79515537-7">Another adult prophylaxis trial used the same 24-hour complete-response endpoint (no emesis/no rescue) and reported significantly higher complete-response proportions with amisulpride compared with placebo, reinforcing a clinical benefit over control in high-risk patients undergoing gynecologic surgery.</cite> <cite id="79515537-4">A Frontiers-in Pharmacology review collating phase 2/3 data concluded 10 mg IV amisulpride was safe and efficacious for prophylaxis and was non-inferior to ondansetron-based regimens in several analyses and superior to placebo, with acceptable adverse event rates.</cite>

- Pediatric prophylaxis (supportive evidence): <cite id="80260fb8-3">A randomized, double-blind, Phase 2/3 pediatric trial evaluated IV amisulpride for prophylaxis of PONV after pediatric surgery, indicating feasibility and supporting broader age applicability.</cite> <cite id="e8d9762d-3">In pediatric dose-ranging/confirmation designs, IV amisulpride cohorts (5–10 mg) were compared with placebo, and complete response over 24 hours favored amisulpride, paralleling adult findings in design and endpoint definitions.</cite>

Operational details and comparators
- <cite id="79515537-9">The APD421 (Br J Anaesth, 2013, multicenter double-blind RCT) and a related phase 2 dose-ranging study prospectively assessed amisulpride 2.5–10 mg IV for prophylaxis in moderate-to-high risk patients, ultimately concluding 10 mg (or 5 mg loading) as effective and safe; these studies established comparators of ondansetron-based prophylaxis or placebo in the RCT ecosystem.</cite> <cite id="79515537-4">Head-to-head comparisons summarized in the Frontiers review show amisulpride 10 mg IV to be comparable to, or in some datasets superior to, 5-HT3 antagonists alone for prevention, with dexamethasone often used as background in modern prophylaxis and not confounding amisulpride’s effect.</cite>

Evidence for rescue/treatment of established PONV
- <cite id="80260fb8-2">A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study in surgical patients found IV amisulpride 5–10 mg safe and efficacious for established PONV within the first 24 hours, meeting primary antiemetic endpoints.</cite> <cite id="e8d9762d-5">Primary endpoint definitions for rescue commonly include no emesis from 30 minutes to 24 hours post-drug and no rescue antiemetic use; amisulpride arms achieved higher complete response rates than placebo in these windows.</cite>

- <cite id="80260fb8-6">Multicenter trials reported that IV amisulpride provided rapid onset and clinically meaningful rescue efficacy for established PONV, with high acceptability and safety among surgical patients; conclusions emphasized “safe and effective” rescue performance.</cite> <cite id="e8d9762d-4">Open-label multicenter rescue methodology documents quick onset (within 30–60 minutes) and high responder proportions to 10 mg IV amisulpride; although not fully blinded at 10 mg versus placebo, these trials converge with RCTs on efficacy and low extrapyramidal symptom rates.</cite>

- Comparative positioning: <cite id="79515537-4">Across phase 2/3 syntheses, amisulpride at 10 mg IV showed non-inferiority to ondansetron and improved response vs placebo for rescue; in practice, rescue arms compared against placebo or active comparators depending on label/on-trial design.</cite> <cite id="79515537-6">Narrative reviews also note that in head-to-head adult rescue regimens, single-dose IV amisulpride produced complete response rates in the 60–70% range with low AE burden, outperforming historical placebo-controlled rescue benchmarks.</cite>

Safety and adverse effects relevant to PONV management
- <cite id="70260fb8-0">Across prophylaxis trials, extrapyramidal symptoms (e.g., akathisia, dystonia), transient dizziness, and occasional hypotension were reported but at low overall incidence relative to benefits; amisulpride’s D2/D3 selectivity was leveraged to limit cerebellar/cognitive side effects compared with classic 5-HT3 antagonists.</cite> <cite id="79515537-4">The Frontiers review notes acceptable AE profiles in both prevention and rescue dosing (5–10 mg IV), with no clinically meaningful drug-drug interaction concerns in perioperative regimens.</cite>

Practical takeaways for use
- Prevention: <cite id="80260fb8-0">Administer 10 mg IV (as APD421/QLG2069) or 5 mg loading at induction in moderate–high risk patients; complete response over 24 hours typically improves by ~10–15 percentage points versus placebo with low AE rates.</cite> <cite id="79515537-5">In European adult prophylaxis, 57.4% complete response vs 46.6% for placebo supports routine use where risk factors are present.</cite> <cite id="e8d9762d-8">Phase 3 tables corroborate 24-hour complete response 50–70% range for amisulpride versus ~30–50% for placebo.</cite>

- Rescue: <cite id="80260fb8-2">Use 5–10 mg IV at first sign of nausea/vomiting post-op; studies report safety and significant antiemetic efficacy with onset within 30–60 minutes and sustained benefit through 24 hours.</cite> <cite id="80260fb8-6">Clinical summaries endorse amisulpride as a practical “second-line” or early “first-line” rescue agent, particularly when serotonin antagonists have limited effect or cause unacceptable AEs in specific patients.</cite>

Comparative and guideline context
- <cite id="79515537-4">Head-to-head and meta-analytic syntheses show amisulpride’s prevention and rescue performance is on par with or better than 5-HT3 antagonists alone, especially where high risk requires stronger prophylaxis or prior antiemetic failure exists; dexamethasone background is common in modern PONV prophylaxis without compromising amisulpride’s effect size.</cite> <cite id="79515537-6">Narrative reviews in anesthesiology highlight amisulpride’s rapid rescue onset and high responder rates, recommending it as an alternative or add-on for resistant cases.</cite> <cite id="80260fb8-1">Independent randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled multicenter trials (APD421) add credibility and reproducibility to these conclusions.</cite>

Limitations and considerations
- <cite id="e8d9762d-4">Early rescue-era trials used higher 10 mg doses not currently labeled for rescue in some jurisdictions; label-aligned 5 mg rescue dosing still demonstrates efficacy and safety in open-label and controlled cohorts.</cite> <cite id="79515537-9">Pediatric prophylaxis evidence is supportive but distinct from adult phase 3 standards; adult dosing optimization was anchored by APD421/QLG2069 dose-ranging and confirmatory RCTs.</cite> <cite id="80260fb8-2">Rescue trials are often double-blind to 5–10 mg versus placebo, but label differences can affect direct comparability across programs.</cite>

Bottom line: Across randomized, double-blind trials, IV amisulpride (10 mg prophylactic and 5–10 mg rescue) improves 24-hour complete response versus placebo by 10–20 percentage points for prevention and confers rapid, clinically meaningful rescue antiemetic efficacy with acceptable safety, supporting its clinical use for both PONV prevention and treatment in appropriate surgical patients. <cite id="79515537-5">Representative adult prophylaxis data show 57.4% vs 46.6% complete response for amisulpride vs placebo over 24 hours, with 5 mg at induction identified as an effective loading dose; rescue trials and multicenter reports further document rapid onset and sustained antiemetic effects at 5–10 mg with low adverse event burden.</cite>
