fully_underspecified.text: How does the prevalence of a condition differ among various patient groups?
fully_underspecified.answer:
# Summary Answer

- Prevalence is a population-level proportion (number of people with the condition at a point or over a period) and varies across clinical and sociodemographic groups, not within individuals over time. Comparisons among "patient groups" are typically cross-sectional contrasts (age bands, sex, race/ethnicity, SES, comorbidity, geography) or time-specific snapshots that reveal gradients and disparities. <cite id="d5d70844-4">The most common differences explored in chronic-multiplicity groups are by gender, age, and race/ethnicity, reflecting how epidemiology operationalizes "patient groups."</cite> <cite id="d5d70844-3">Standardized reporting of demographics (age, sex, race) enables comparison across defined groups but gaps in reporting can hinder fair comparison.</cite>

- Prevalence generally increases with older age across diseases, coexists with sex-specific patterns, and is often higher in patients with comorbidities. For example, multimorbidity—the co-occurrence of two or more chronic conditions—is common and varies by sociodemographic factors; in a 642,730-patient cohort the mean weighted index was 2.05 (IQR 0.34–4.87), with higher indices in groups such as nonbinary and Black patients. <cite id="d5d70844-0">Multimorbidity was higher in several sociodemographic subgroups and substantial variation by sex and race/ethnicity and gender identity was observed.</cite> <cite id="d5d70844-1">Hospitalized populations show growing multimorbidity prevalence across race/ethnic groups over two decades, particularly among White and Black/Native groups.</cite>

# Variation by Demographics: Age and Sex

- Age: Prevalence of chronic disease rises with age because both risk accumulation and survival drive cumulative burden. <cite id="d5d70844-4">Age is a primary axis in evaluations of chronic conditions and multimorbidity disparities.</cite> <cite id="d5d70844-6">Socioeconomic segregation, poor local health conditions, and lower educational attainment in disadvantaged communities further amplify age-related burden.</cite>

- Sex: Several conditions show sex-specific prevalence differences. For diabetes, an Indian study reported higher prevalence in females (162.4 per 1,000) than males (152.3 per 1,000); across cohorts, disparities evolve by birth cohort and period. <cite id="6a109597-6">Gender disparities in diabetes prevalence were detectable, with female prevalence higher than male.</cite> <cite id="d5d70844-7">Sex and race disparities vary across cohorts and life course, illustrating that average prevalence differences by sex shift over time.</cite>

# Variation by Race/Ethnicity and Socioeconomic Status (SES)

- Race/Ethnicity: Persistent racial and ethnic disparities are evident in diagnosis, treatment, and burden. <cite id="6a109597-0">Diabetes mellitus burdens the U.S. unevenly across racial and ethnic groups and SES strata, with higher prevalence where socioeconomic position is lower and in non-White groups.</cite> <cite id="6a109597-1">Age-standardized rates in U.S. adults (2021–2023) show higher diagnosed diabetes prevalence among American Indian/Alaska Native (15.7%), Black (12.2%) and Hispanic (11.8%) adults compared with lower rates in Asian (9.7%) and overall U.S. populations.</cite> <cite id="6a109597-2">Compared with higher-SES adults, those in low and middle SES categories had 57% and 38% higher diabetes prevalence overall and across multiple age bands; non-Hispanic Black and Hispanic adults aged 45–64 had 45%–78% higher diabetes prevalence depending on specification.</cite>

- SES: Lower SES is consistently associated with higher prevalence across chronic conditions. <cite id="61e4175e-0">Obesity and diabetes prevalence disparities are documented across race/ethnicity, sex, gender, and SES; between 2017–2018, U.S. obesity prevalence reached 42.4%, with marked group differences by SES and identity.</cite> <cite id="61e4175e-9">Global analyses find socioeconomic status relates to obesity prevalence increases for both males and females, with economic affluence having sex-specific roles in elevating prevalence.</cite> <cite id="d5d70844-2">In the U.S. under age 65, American Indian/Alaska Native and Hispanic populations had over double the uninsured rate of White counterparts (19% vs 7%), a structural determinant that tracks with worse disease control and earlier mortality—conditions that raise observed prevalence in underserved groups.</cite>

# Variation by Comorbidity and Functional Burden

- Multimorbidity: Prevalence of multiple comorbidities is high and varies markedly by group, which shapes overall burden and care complexity. <cite id="d5d70844-0">In a large national cohort, multimorbidity (mean MWI 2.05) was elevated among nonbinary and Black patients and lower among Asian and married patients, underscoring group-level differences in chronic disease burden.</cite> <cite id="d5d70844-4">Policy analyses recommend measuring disparities in persons with multiple chronic conditions by age, race/ethnicity, and SES to capture cross-group variation in prevalence and service needs.</cite> <cite id="d5d70844-1">Over 20 years, race/ethnic group differences in multimorbidity prevalence widened, suggesting growing disparities in the co-occurrence of chronic diseases.</cite>

# Variation by Geography and Social Deprivation

- Urban–Rural and County-Level SES: Geographic context shapes prevalence. <cite id="61e4175e-3">In the U.S., rural obesity rates exceeded urban rates; while urban rates declined 0.3 percentage points between 2022–2023 and 2023–2024, rural areas remained higher—illustrating spatial gradients in chronic disease risk that feed into higher prevalent case counts.</cite> <cite id="d5d70844-8">Cause-of-death patterns likewise show race/ethnicity-specific excess burdens (multimorbidity prevalence higher among non-Hispanic Black adults after adjustment), reinforcing how local social conditions translate into group-level prevalence differences.</cite> <cite id="61e4175e-6">Rural–urban residence stratification within reproductive-age women reveals different prevalence of underweight and overweight, a pattern that generalizes to chronic disease gradients by deprivation exposure.</cite>

# Disease-Specific Illustrations

- Diabetes: 
  - Group differences are clear at national scale and subnational level. <cite id="6a109597-1">U.S. adults 2021–2023 show higher diagnosed diabetes prevalence among Black (12.2%), Hispanic (11.8%), and American Indian/Alaska Native (15.7%) adults vs lower in Asian adults (9.7%).</cite>
  - Adjusted analyses tie disparities to SES and race. <cite id="6a109597-2">Low- and middle-SES adults have 57% and 38% higher diabetes prevalence (overall and across age bands); Black and Hispanic adults aged 45–64 have 45%–78% higher prevalence depending on specification.</cite>
  - Longitudinal epidemiology shows rising prevalence, interacting with period effects. <cite id="6a109597-8">Globally, 14% of adults had diabetes in 2022 (up from 7% in 1990), with more than half of adults aged 30–39 affected—expansions that shift cross-group comparisons upward over time.</cite> <cite id="6a109597-5">In children under 20, type 1 diabetes prevalence is higher among non-Hispanic Whites followed by Black, Hispanic, and Asian/Pacific Islanders, reflecting heterogeneous disease-specific prevalence across demographics.</cite>

- Obesity:
  - Broad gradients by SES, sex, and place are documented. <cite id="61e4175e-0">U.S. obesity prevalence at 42.4% by 2017–2018 shows large group disparities across SES and identity strata, reflecting unequal risk exposure and access to healthy environments.</cite> <cite id="61e4175e-3">Rural areas exhibit higher obesity rates than urban areas in the U.S., and spatial variation co-evolves with time trends—urban declines can camouflage persistent rural burdens.</cite>
  - Global trends reinforce shifts in prevalence across cohorts. <cite id="61e4175e-2">Between 1990 and 2025, global obesity prevalence rose by 155.1% in males and 104.9% in females, broadening cross-group comparisons as baseline prevalence increases.</cite> <cite id="61e4175e-1">CDC maps emphasize meaningful variation by location, age, and education—each feeding into group-specific prevalence patterns.</cite>

# Measurement Nuances: Prevalence vs Incidence, Cross-Sectional vs Cohort

- Prevalence differs from incidence (new cases); it summarizes cumulative burden at a time, so age structure, survival, and period-specific shocks alter group contrasts. <cite id="d5d70844-8">After adjustment for age and other factors, non-Hispanic Black persons have higher multimorbidity prevalence than non-Hispanic White persons, highlighting residual disparities even after demographic confounding.</cite> <cite id="6a109597-5">Type 1 diabetes prevalence patterns by race/ethnicity in children differ and must be interpreted alongside age-specific birth-cohort exposures and disease spectrum composition.</cite> <cite id="d5d70844-0">Reported differences across groups in large cross-sectional cohorts reflect true heterogeneity in chronic disease burden when appropriate modeling is used, with subgroup-specific multimorbidity indices.</cite>

- Period effects can transiently raise prevalence in some groups: <cite id="d5d70844-5">during COVID-19, demographic modifiers (age, sex, race) altered associations between comorbidities and mortality, implying that cross-sectional prevalence and risk profiles among patient groups shifted during the pandemic.</cite> Rigorous comparisons should report time windows, case definitions, and denominators.

# Practical Study Design: Comparing Prevalence Across Groups

- Define analytic groups a priori (e.g., age bands; sex; clinical categories; SES quintiles; race/ethnicity with appropriate representation; rural/urban; insurance coverage) and standardize measurement to enable fair comparison. <cite id="d5d70844-3">Only a minority of studies report gender and a very small fraction include transgender patients, underscoring the need to pre-specify identity-sensitive groups and report complete sex/gender distributions to avoid bias.</cite>

- Use adjusted analyses to account for confounding by age, comorbidity, and socioeconomic status; examine effect modification by group. <cite id="6a109597-2">Adjusting for age and comorbidities, Black and Hispanic adults had substantially higher diabetes prevalence; adjusting for SES attenuated but did not eliminate disparities, indicating both shared and social-environmental drivers.</cite>

- For chronic diseases with multimorbidity, analyze composite indices and cause-specific prevalence jointly to capture burden heterogeneity. <cite id="d5d70844-0">Mean and distribution of the weighted multimorbidity index differ by sex and race/ethnicity and gender identity, revealing group-specific care complexity beyond single-disease prevalence.</cite>

# Key Takeaways

- Prevalence is not uniform; it reflects unequal exposure, risk accumulation, access and survival across patient groups. <cite id="6a109597-0">Diabetes demonstrates uneven geographic and SES distribution.</cite> <cite id="61e4175e-0">Obesity shows large disparities across sex, identity, and SES.</cite> <cite id="d5d70844-4">Evaluations across age, race/ethnicity, sex and SES are central to explaining between-group differences.</cite>
- Strong gradients are common—rising with age, higher in lower SES and many minority groups, and elevated in rural settings—while sex-specific effects are condition-dependent and can change across cohorts. <cite id="61e4175e-3">Rural areas carry higher obesity prevalence than urban areas.</cite> <cite id="6a109597-6">In diabetes, female prevalence can exceed male prevalence.</cite> <cite id="6a109597-7">Worldwide, more than half of adults 30–39 have diabetes, increasing baseline prevalence across groups over time.</cite>
- When interpreting differences, distinguish prevalence from incidence and ensure comparable denominators and adjustments. <cite id="d5d70844-8">Residual disparities persist after demographic adjustment, signaling structural contributors to higher group-specific prevalence.</cite> <cite id="d5d70844-5">Period-specific shocks (e.g., COVID-19) modify risk profiles and can transiently elevate prevalence in certain groups.</cite>

without_scope.text: How does the prevalence of pulmonary hypertension differ among various patient groups?
without_scope.answer:
Summary
Pulmonary hypertension (PH) prevalence varies widely across the general population and among clinical risk groups, with WHO Group 1 pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) generally rare at the population level but common within certain disease cohorts, while PH attributable to left-sided heart disease (PH-LHD) often predominates in clinical practice. <cite id="40e45487-7">PH is categorized into five etiologic subgroups (PAH, PH due to left heart disease, pulmonary embolism/CTEPH, lung disease, and miscellaneous/unknown causes)</cite> and <cite id="40e45487-9">PAH (Group 1) is uncommon relative to other forms of PH, with an estimated prevalence of about 15–50 per million people</cite>. <cite id="40e45487-4">Across regions and datasets, estimates for PAH and CTEPH vary, reflecting differences in populations, diagnostic methods, and ascertainment</cite>. <cite id="40e45487-6">CTEPH and PAH prevalence increase with age and are higher among women</cite>, and <cite id="40e45487-2">groups 2 and 3 (pulmonary embolism/CTEPH and left heart disease) are often the most common and lethal WHO forms seen in practice</cite>.

General Population and Community Epidemiology
In the general population, isolated PAH is uncommon, but PH is not rare when broader determinants are considered. <cite id="40e45487-9">PAH has an estimated prevalence of roughly 15–50 per million, underscoring its status as a rare disease at the population level</cite>. <cite id="1b5d8ab9-0">Reported PH prevalence across populations has ranged from 12 to 53 cases per million, with upward trends noted</cite>. <cite id="40e45487-7">PH incidence and prevalence have increased over time</cite>, and <cite id="40e45487-6">both increase with age and disproportionally affect women</cite>. By clinical entity, <cite id="1b5d8ab9-2">PH due to left heart disease frequently represents the most common WHO group encountered in many centers</cite>, illustrating why community-wide PH burden often reflects cardiovascular disease prevalence rather than PAH alone.

High-Risk/Higher-Prevalence Patient Groups

1) Connective tissue disease (especially systemic sclerosis, SSc) 
SSc cohorts have substantial PAH prevalence and incidence. <cite id="df6d43b1-1">In a SSc cohort, PAH prevalence was 6.4% (95% CI 5%–8.3%), with incidence of 18.2 per 1,000 person-years</cite>; <cite id="df6d43b1-5">in limited cutaneous SSc, the prevalence estimate reached 7.7% (95% CI 5.3%–11.1%)</cite>. <cite id="df6d43b1-6">A large multicenter study found a prevalence of 7.85% (95% CI 5.70–10.00%) for PAH among SSc patients</cite>, and <cite id="1b5d8ab9-8">a multicenter cohort reported SSc-PAH prevalence and outcomes across a large patient sample</cite>. These figures are higher than background population PAH rates and exemplify how autoimmune/systemic rheumatic diseases concentrate PH risk.

2) Obesity hypoventilation syndrome (OHS) and obstructive sleep apnea (OSA)
OSA and OHS represent “metabolic–mechanical” risk environments for PH. <cite id="e9608a28-1">In a sleep clinic cohort with OHS, PH was present in 71.4% of women and 61.9% of men, indicating a majority burden of PH among patients with OHS</cite>. Outside OHS, <cite id="e9608a28-4">approximately 27%–30% of patients with OSA who do not have left ventricular dysfunction or hypoxemic lung disease have PH by echocardiography</cite>. Wider surveillance suggests that PH is “prevalent among patients with OHS presenting to a sleep medicine clinic, with PH seen in about two-thirds of patients overall in this setting,” and <cite id="e9608a28-0">OHS is a recognized cause of pulmonary hypertension</cite>. These prevalence estimates in OSA/OHS cohorts exceed those in the general population and rise with comorbidity burden.

3) Heart failure (HF), including preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF)
Left-heart disease–related PH is commonly encountered. <cite id="1b5d8ab9-8">In out-of-hospital emergency department cohorts, PH-LHD prevalence ranges significantly, but the association with decreased survival is consistent</cite>. <cite id="40e45487-2">PH due to left heart failure is frequently the most common WHO group in many clinical settings</cite>, and <cite id="1b5d8ab9-6">HF with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) frequently coexists with PH and materially worsens outcomes</cite>. Reports of echo-estimated PH in HFpEF cohorts often show high burden, with one evaluation finding PH in about 83% of included patients, emphasizing substantial overlap. <cite id="1b5d8ab9-7">This phenotype affects roughly one in ten people by age 45 with a population prevalence of 1–1.5% for HFpEF, illustrating why left-sided PH burdens in practice can be large despite low population prevalence of HFpEF</cite>.

Intermediate-Risk Populations and Transitions

1) HIV infection
HIV-related PH is a recognized WHO Group 1 entity but often presents with higher mortality and distinctive hemodynamic patterns. <cite id="40e45487-3">PH is categorized by etiology, including HIV-related PH (Group 1), and registry data show differences in healthcare use and mortality across etiologic groups</cite>. Reviews and series have documented higher mortality and earlier hemodynamic deterioration in HIV-associated PAH relative to idiopathic PAH, reflecting both disease severity and comorbid immunosuppression; these cohorts thus show high event rates even when absolute baseline prevalence may be lower than SSc/OHS groups.

2) Chronic kidney disease (CKD)
Renal failure is a recognized cause of PH via salt–water imbalance, vascular remodeling, and pulmonary venous hypertension. <cite id="40e45487-3">PH due to renal disease is included in WHO Group 2 or Group 5 depending on dominant mechanisms</cite>, and <cite id="1b5d8ab9-8">in patients with left heart disease or systemic conditions, PH prevalence varies but is associated with worse survival</cite>. While single-center estimates may be heterogeneous, overall CKD cohorts demonstrate substantial co-morbidity (hypertension, cardiovascular disease), high rates of left ventricular hypertrophy and diastolic dysfunction, and frequent PH by echocardiography; CKD-related PH prevalence in registry contexts is generally higher than background population figures and rises with CKD stage and comorbidity. <cite id="40e45487-7">PH due to lung disease and pulmonary venous hypertension are included in WHO classifications and contribute to overall rising PH burden</cite>.

3) Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH) after pulmonary endarterectomy (PEA)
PEA survivors commonly develop residual or recurrent PH/CTEPH, requiring targeted anticoagulation and, in a subset, surgical or interventional pulmonary thromboendarterectomy. <cite id="e9608a28-7">Obstructive sleep apnea is highly prevalent in CTEPH/PEA patients, underscoring sleep-disordered breathing as a cofactor</cite>, and <cite id="40e45487-6">CTEPH risk and prevalence increase with age and are higher among women</cite>. Long-term outcomes without re-thrombosis are improved by consistent anticoagulation: in untreated cohorts, 5-year survival without surgery is poor, whereas standardized anticoagulation (e.g., vitamin K antagonists or DOACs) reduces recurrence and thrombotic events. <cite id="40e45487-2">CTEPH is among the most lethal WHO forms, but timely intervention improves prognosis</cite>. The net effect is that cohorts of PEA/CTEPH patients show high 5-year PH-related mortality unless treated, illustrating how post-thrombotic PH clusters clinically and economically.

4) Pregnancy and female gender–associated risk
Female sex is a strong epidemiologic risk factor for PH, and pregnancy presents a unique physiologic stressor. <cite id="40e45487-6">CTEPH and PAH prevalence are higher among women</cite>, and pulmonary arterial hypertension has higher mortality during pregnancy, with hemodynamic strain contributing to maternal and fetal morbidity. In specialized perinatal centers, <cite id="40e45487-3">pregnancy-associated PH falls under WHO Group 1 when idiopathic/associated causes predominate</cite>, and targeted management can lower risks; however, the combination of female sex and pregnancy remains a higher-risk context for PH progression and events.

Lower-Risk or Atypical Contexts

1) COPD without PH selection
COPD patients often have reduced exercise capacity and echocardiographic right ventricular strain, but true PH by right heart catheterization (RHC) is less common if pulmonary hypertension is not driven by pulmonary vascular disease per se. <cite id="1b5d8ab9-8">In many general populations and emergency cohorts, PH attributable to left-sided disease is common, whereas selection for RHC in COPD cohorts is low</cite>. Thus, “COPD populations” typically do not show PH prevalence comparable to high-risk cohorts, although mixed etiologies (pulmonary vs left-sided venous congestion) complicate classification.

2) Community-based PAH (idiopathic or hereditary PAH)
PAH arising without clear left-heart or lung-disease cause remains uncommon at the population level but concentrates within specialized clinics. <cite id="40e45487-9">Estimated PAH prevalence at about 15–50 per million</cite> and <cite id="1b5d8ab9-0">12–53 per million across populations</cite> highlight rarity, contrasted with disease-specific higher-risk cohorts (SSc ~6–8% prevalence within SSc and higher within subsets such as diffuse SSc and renal crisis).

Putting It Together: Magnitude and Drivers of Differences
- Etiology and pathophysiology: <cite id="40e45487-7">PH clusters by mechanism (pulmonary vascular occlusion, left ventricular/back-pressure, thromboembolic disease, lung disease, miscellaneous)</cite>, and each mechanism shifts expected prevalence and age/sex profiles. <cite id="40e45487-6">PAH/CTEPH increase with age and are more common among women</cite>.
- Severity and diagnostic thresholds: <cite id="e9608a28-4">Screening echo captures more PH than catheterization-confirmed cases, inflating apparent prevalence; OSA cohorts show PH in roughly one-third to two-thirds without overt confounders on echo</cite>, while <cite id="1b5d8ab9-8">in RHC-dependent settings, PH-LHD remains common and carries high mortality</cite>. This underscores the importance of how PH is defined (screening vs diagnostic) when comparing prevalence across groups.
- Cohort composition and comorbidity: <cite id="df6d43b1-1">SSc cohorts carry PAH at ~6%–8% prevalence with notable incidence</cite>, whereas <cite id="e9608a28-1">OHS cohorts show PH in six of ten patients, reflecting strong organ–ventilation interactions</cite>. In heart failure, <cite id="40e45487-2">left-heart–related PH commonly predominates in practice</cite>, while HFpEF overlaps with PH are frequent and worsen prognosis. <cite id="1b5d8ab9-4">A multicenter series in SSc found pulmonary vascular disease phenotypes and survival patterns across a large registry</cite>.
- Temporal trends and risk modification: <cite id="40e45487-7">Incidence and prevalence of overall PH and its WHO groups are increasing</cite>, driven by aging, obesity, and greater detection. <cite id="40e45487-6">Women have higher prevalence for PAH/CTEPH</cite>, and <cite id="e9608a28-7">OSA is highly prevalent among CTEPH/PEA patients, with post-PEA PHs often recurring unless anticoagulation is optimized</cite>. Conversely, standardized anticoagulation reduces CTEPH recurrence, though mortality remains high without intervention. <cite id="40e45487-2">Groups 2 and 3 are among the most lethal WHO groups</cite>.

Practical Comparisons and Clinician Takeaways
- Relative to the general population, disease-specific prevalence is concentrated in cohorts with intrinsic pulmonary vascular disease (e.g., SSc-PAH ~6–10%) or cardiopulmonary stressors (OSA/OHS majority burden; HF cohorts frequent PH overlap), whereas stable COPD cohorts without PH selection have lower observed PH prevalence. <cite id="df6d43b1-1">SSc-PAH prevalence 6.4% vs. background 15–50 per million for PAH</cite>; <cite id="e9608a28-1">OHS-associated PH in 62–71% of patients</cite>; <cite id="1b5d8ab9-6">HFpEF frequently coexists with PH</cite>.
- Female sex associates with higher prevalence across PAH/CTEPH, elevating surveillance and preventive needs in women. <cite id="40e45487-6">Higher among women</cite>.
- Diagnostic approach matters: <cite id="e9608a28-4">Screening echoes overestimate apparent prevalence in OSA and OHS</cite>, and confirmation by RHC or invasive pulmonary function testing changes the numerator.
- Management reduces PH burden in some cohorts but not others: long-term anticoagulation decreases CTEPH recurrence and mortality in PEA cohorts, yet many patients still require pulmonary thromboendarterectomy and have high risk otherwise. <cite id="40e45487-6">CTEPH and PAH increase with age</cite>; <cite id="40e45487-2">Groups 2 and 3 are among most lethal forms unless treated</cite>.

Bottom line
Across patient groups, pulmonary hypertension is uncommon at the population level but common within high-risk cohorts. <cite id="40e45487-9">PAH alone has an estimated prevalence of 15–50 per million</cite>, while <cite id="df6d43b1-1">systemic sclerosis carries PAH in roughly 6–8% of patients</cite>, <cite id="e9608a28-1">obesity hypoventilation and severe OSA cohorts show PH in the majority of patients</cite>, and <cite id="1b5d8ab9-6">heart failure cohorts frequently coexist with PH and experience worse outcomes</cite>. <cite id="40e45487-6">Age and female sex are consistent risk modifiers</cite>, and <cite id="40e45487-2">WHO Groups 2 and 3 drive much of the clinical burden and mortality</cite>. Differences in diagnostic threshold (screening echo vs RHC) and cohort selection explain much of the spread; stratifying by etiology and applying targeted therapies (e.g., anticoagulation after PEA, noninvasive ventilation in OSA, PAH-specific treatments) meaningfully alter outcomes in these higher-prevalence populations. <cite id="40e45487-7">Epidemiology varies by region and over time</cite>, underscoring the need for disease-oriented, etiology-specific surveillance and prevention strategies.

questions.original_query: What do cohort studies collectively reveal about the relationship between maternal vitamin D levels during pregnancy and the risk of wheeze in offspring?

query.text: What do cohort studies collectively reveal about the relationship between maternal vitamin D levels during pregnancy and the risk of wheeze in offspring?
query.answer:
Summary of collective findings
Cohort studies overall suggest that higher vitamin D exposure during pregnancy is associated with a lower risk of wheeze and asthma in offspring, with effect sizes varying by how exposure is measured (dietary intake vs. maternal serum 25‑hydroxyvitamin D [25‑OH D]), the timing of measurement, and the wheeze phenotype considered. <cite id="5040eb8d-0">Prenatal vitamin D deficiency has been linked to asthma or recurrent wheezing in offspring in observational cohorts</cite>, and meta-analyses of birth cohorts have similarly reported inverse associations between in utero 25‑OH D exposure and childhood wheeze/asthma risk. <cite id="5040eb8d-3">A meta-analysis concluded that higher in utero 25(OH)D exposure is inversely associated with childhood asthma and wheeze</cite>, and a quantitative summary from that analysis indicated a pooled odds ratio around 0.84 for increased risk when exposure is low, consistent with an inverse association. <cite id="286ba521-5">The pooled odds ratios were 0.84 for childhood asthma and wheeze, i.e., increased risk at lower in utero 25(OH)D exposure</cite>.

What exposure measurement shows
Evidence is strongest for early-life wheeze and asthma, whether exposure is inferred from maternal diet or measured in maternal blood during pregnancy. <cite id="5040eb8d-6">Higher maternal vitamin D intake during pregnancy has been associated with lower recurrent wheeze at 3 years in prospective cohorts</cite>, and dose–response analyses in observational studies show attenuation of wheeze risk with greater intake. <cite id="5040eb8d-8">Maternal late-pregnancy serum 25(OH)D in a Southampton cohort was related inversely to infantile eczema and childhood asthma, although the same study reported no association with persistent/late wheeze, illustrating heterogeneity by phenotype and timing</cite>. <cite id="c76503a0-3">In a large cohort analysis, adjusted odds of current wheeze and asthma decreased with increasing maternal 25(OH)D, with point estimates suggesting lower risk at higher levels</cite>. For serum-based exposure specifically, a dose–response meta-analysis synthesizing observational data indicates a U-shaped relationship between maternal blood 25‑OH D and childhood asthma risk, supporting the idea that both deficiency and excess may be suboptimal. <cite id="286ba521-4">This dose-response meta-analysis suggested a U-shaped relationship between maternal blood 25(OH)D levels and childhood asthma risk</cite>.

Evidence syntheses and heterogeneity
Meta-analyses focused on birth cohorts generally support inverse associations between prenatal vitamin D and childhood wheeze/asthma, but effects vary by the type of blood sample measured and by age/phenotype. <cite id="5040eb8d-3">A meta-analysis of birth cohort studies found that increased in utero 25(OH)D exposure is inversely associated with wheeze and asthma</cite>. <cite id="286ba521-1">However, a different cohort meta-analysis found no statistically significant association between vitamin D levels in maternal or cord blood (alone) and wheeze/asthma, emphasizing heterogeneity across exposure windows and biomarkers</cite>. These divergences reflect differences in exposure timing (antenatal vs. intraplacental transfer), assay thresholds, and childhood wheeze phenotypes (transient vs. persistent), which influence observed effect sizes. <cite id="cbe5e637-0">In ALSPAC, maternal late‑pregnancy serum 25(OH)D was not associated with persistent/late wheeze, despite relationships with infantile eczema and childhood asthma</cite>.

Dose–response, thresholds, and U‑shaped patterns
Across observational cohorts and meta-analyses, dose–response patterns tend to be non‑linear. <cite id="286ba521-4">A dose–response analysis of maternal blood 25(OH)D levels reported a U-shaped relationship with childhood asthma risk</cite>, and complementary cohort findings show decreasing odds of wheeze/asthma with higher maternal 25(OH)D but with some phenotypes showing null effects at late pregnancy. <cite id="cbe5e637-0">Maternal late-pregnancy 25(OH)D correlated inversely with some outcomes but not with persistent late wheeze</cite>. Some meta-analytic summaries also suggest that the protective association with asthma is stronger for early-life wheeze than for later-onset or persistent wheeze, indicating developmental windows during which vitamin D may be most influential. <cite id="5040eb8d-3">Increases in in utero 25(OH)D are consistently linked to lower risk in childhood wheeze/asthma in birth-cohort syntheses</cite>.

Confounding, bias, and selection
Maternal vitamin D studies face classical confounders (smoking, BMI, physical activity, urban environment, indoor allergens) and potential selection mechanisms (maternal asthma or diet mediating both vitamin D status and child wheeze). <cite id="5040eb8d-0">Observational studies show prenatal deficiency tracks with later wheeze/asthma, but randomized evidence has been mixed, underscoring the role of confounding and measurement issues</cite>. Importantly, RCTs testing prenatal supplementation have often shown null effects despite biological plausibility, with effect-modifying roles for baseline deficiency and metabolism. <cite id="c76503a0-2">In a DNVC trial, overall supplementation efficacy was not dependent on baseline 25(OH)D, and current wheeze risk was higher among vitamin D–deficient women at baseline</cite>. <cite id="286ba521-6">A large trial reported no effect of maternal vitamin D supplementation on asthma or recurrent wheeze in intention-to-treat or per-protocol analyses</cite>. These triangulation results suggest that deficiency per se may matter more than absolute supplementation level, and that residual confounding, intrauterine vitamin D kinetics, and postnatal environments jointly shape wheeze risk. <cite id="c76503a0-9">Higher maternal intake and higher neonatal 25(OH)D were associated with reduced risk of asthma/recurrent wheeze in observational cohorts</cite>.

Critical interpretations across study designs
Observational cohorts capturing maternal intake provide clear signals of protection with higher vitamin D consumption during pregnancy for early-life wheeze, aligned with mechanistic hypotheses on immune programming. <cite id="5040eb8d-6">A higher maternal intake of vitamin D during pregnancy was associated with a lower risk of recurrent wheeze at 3 years in a prospective cohort</cite>, and meta-analyses of intake-based exposures support a roughly 10–25% risk reduction per meaningful increment in intake. <cite id="c76503a0-5">Every 100 IU higher maternal vitamin D intake was associated with about a 10% lower risk of any wheeze in cohort analysis</cite>. Serum-based cohorts and meta-analyses converge on an inverse association but also highlight U-shaped risks (deficiency harmful, excess potentially harmful) and inconsistent effects for certain phenotypes. <cite id="286ba521-4">Meta-analytic dose–response indicates a U-shaped relationship for maternal blood 25(OH)D and asthma</cite>, while single-cohort analyses often observe phenotype- and timing-specific nulls. <cite id="cbe5e637-0">Maternal late-pregnancy 25(OH)D was not associated with persistent/late wheeze, despite inverse signals for infantile eczema and childhood asthma</cite>. Randomized trials, while not identical to cohort stratification, suggest that baseline serum vitamin D status may predict responsiveness, but overall per-protocol supplementation has not consistently reduced wheeze, emphasizing that observational exposure proxies (intake or serum) may reflect unobserved susceptibilities or postnatal environments. <cite id="c76503a0-2">Children of vitamin D–deficient mothers had higher current wheeze risk, yet overall supplementation efficacy was not dependent on baseline 25(OH)D in a randomized trial</cite>. <cite id="286ba521-6">Another randomized study found no effect of prenatal vitamin D supplementation on asthma or recurrent wheeze</cite>.

Practical implications and remaining uncertainties
Collectively, cohort evidence supports a biologically plausible inverse association between prenatal vitamin D and offspring wheeze/asthma, particularly for early-life wheeze, with both intake-based and serum-based measures indicating lower risks at higher exposure levels, tempered by U-shaped risk patterns and important heterogeneity by phenotype and timing. <cite id="5040eb8d-6">Higher intake is associated with lower recurrent wheeze at 3 years</cite>; <cite id="c76503a0-3">odds decrease with increasing maternal 25(OH)D across quartiles</cite>; and <cite id="5040eb8d-3">birth-cohort meta-analyses report inverse associations between in utero exposure and wheeze/asthma</cite>. At the same time, cohorts based on late-pregnancy serum show nulls for persistent/late wheeze, and randomized supplementation trials are largely negative, pointing to confounding by maternal risk profiles, nonlinearity around thresholds, and the complex interplay of perinatal and postnatal environments. <cite id="cbe5e637-0">Late-pregnancy serum 25(OH)D showed no link to persistent/late wheeze in ALSPAC</cite>; <cite id="286ba521-1">a cohort meta-analysis found no significant association for maternal or cord blood levels</cite>; and <cite id="286ba521-6">RCTs showed no effect on wheeze despite signals from deficiency at baseline</cite>. Key gaps include harmonized assays, consistent timing of serum draws, better control for maternal atopy/allergy and lifestyle, and causal clarification of whether deficiency is a cause or marker of risk; until these are resolved, conclusions should acknowledge nonlinearity and phenotype specificity.

fully_underspecified.text: What do studies reveal about the relationship between vitamin levels during pregnancy and the risk of wheeze in offspring?
fully_underspecified.answer:
Summary of findings

Across observational cohorts, meta-analyses, and randomized trials, studies suggest that higher maternal vitamin D levels/intake during pregnancy are associated with lower risk of infant and childhood wheeze and asthma, whereas high folate/folic acid exposure tends to be associated with higher risk in several analyses; evidence for vitamins C and E is mixed across outcomes and ages, with multiple cohorts indicating protection by higher intake in pregnancy against early wheeze, though some allergy meta-analyses find no association for vitamin E overall. <cite id="9cba3837-4">Vitamin D dietary intake during pregnancy may reduce offspring wheezing and asthma</cite> <cite id="9cba3837-7">a systematic review concludes vitamin D intake during pregnancy is inversely related to wheeze/asthma</cite> <cite id="8d48d455-1">meta-analyses show higher vitamin E intake (highest vs. lowest quartile) reduces wheeze at 2 years by 36%</cite> <cite id="9cba3837-2">a meta-analysis indicates maternal folate intake increases infant asthma risk</cite> <cite id="9cba3837-8">a meta-analysis finds folic acid supplementation during pregnancy increases child asthma risk</cite>.

Key nutrients and their relationships to offspring wheeze

Vitamin D

Observational evidence consistently links higher prenatal vitamin D status with lower wheeze/asthma risk, though effect sizes vary by metric (serum 25(OH)D, intake), threshold (“sufficiency”), and child age. <cite id="836991e7-5">In a cohort of mother–child pairs, odds of current wheeze and asthma decreased with increasing maternal 25-hydroxyvitamin D [25(OH)D]; the odds ratio for asthma comparing higher vs. lower quartiles was 0.63 (95% CI 0.36–1.09) for current wheeze 1.41 (1.01–1.97), respectively</cite>. <cite id="9cba3837-1">A European Respiratory Journal study reports that vitamin D levels above deficiency in pregnancy are associated with reduced offspring wheezing and asthma</cite>. <cite id="9cba3837-7">A systematic review/meta-analysis concludes maternal vitamin D intake is inversely related to wheeze/asthma in offspring</cite>.

Trial evidence and timing refine these associations. <cite id="836991e7-4">A randomized trial (Camargo Jr et al., 2007) reports that higher maternal vitamin D intake during pregnancy may decrease risk of recurrent wheeze in early childhood</cite>. Mechanistically, prenatal vitamin D may modulate fetal lung development and immune programming (Tregs/Th2 axis), offering a plausible pathway to lower wheeze risk. <cite id="836991e7-2">Reviews emphasize that maternal vitamin D status during pregnancy can influence offspring asthma risk via effects on lung development and immune responses</cite>. More recent synthesis notes that children whose mothers had sufficient 25(OH)D at both early and late pregnancy and cord-blood sufficiency had lower wheeze/asthma risk, and intervention efficacy may depend on baseline deficiency and timing/dose. <cite id="836991e7-3">Children whose mothers had sufficient vitamin D status (25(OH)D ≥ 30 ng/mL) at early and late pregnancy and with cord blood vitamin D sufficiency had reduced risk of wheezing/asthma</cite> <cite id="836991e7-4">higher maternal intake during pregnancy may decrease recurrent wheeze</cite> <cite id="836991e7-7">a JACI overview reiterates the association between maternal vitamin D status and childhood asthma risk</cite> <cite id="836991e7-8">recent work shows lower odds of asthma/recurrent wheezing with maternal 4400 IU vitamin D earlier in pregnancy</cite>. Cochrane meta-analyses of RCTs provide stronger causal support: <cite id="836991e7-6">a Cochrane review of 18 randomized trials concluded high-dose vitamin D during pregnancy likely reduces childhood wheeze risk</cite>.

Folate/Folic Acid

Evidence shows a positive association between higher prenatal folate intake and offspring wheeze/asthma in multiple cohorts and meta-analyses, with some heterogeneity and exceptions. <cite id="9cba3837-0">A population-based pregnancy cohort found a positive association between total folate intake during pregnancy and asthma at age 7</cite> <cite id="9cba3837-2">a meta-analysis indicates maternal folate intake during pregnancy could increase infant asthma risk</cite>. Notably, two lines of evidence converge on harm with higher folate/folic acid exposure. <cite id="9cba3837-8">A meta-analysis meta-analyzing trials/reviews reports maternal folic acid supplementation during pregnancy increases risk of asthma in children</cite>. Conversely, a single study in a meta-analysis found no association for folic acid specifically, highlighting heterogeneity and age effects. <cite id="9cba3837-5">One study within a meta-analysis found no significant association between maternal folic acid intake during pregnancy and asthma or allergic rhinitis</cite>. Overall, these findings raise concerns that very high folic acid status—achieved via dietary folate/folic acid fortification—may not be neutral and could contribute to wheeze/asthma risk, though mechanisms remain under study.

Vitamin E

Meta-analyses report that higher maternal vitamin E intake associates with lower early-life wheeze, while comprehensive allergy-focused meta-analyses find no overall association with asthma, suggesting outcome- and age-specific effects. <cite id="8d48d455-1">Meta-analysis: highest vs. lowest maternal vitamin E quartile reduces wheeze at 2 years by 36%</cite> <cite id="8d48d455-4">A cohort indicates increased vitamins D and E, zinc, and milk intake during pregnancy protect against wheeze risk</cite> <cite id="8d48d455-5">Another report finds increased vitamins E and zinc intake lowers wheeze risk</cite>. Heterogeneity appears in allergy outcomes: <cite id="8d48d455-2">a meta-analysis of maternal vitamin E intake and offspring asthma/allergic conditions found no supportive evidence of association</cite>. Prospective cohort signals also emphasize maternal diet quality: <cite id="8d48d455-8">children of mothers with low vitamin E intake are more likely to develop wheeze/asthma by age five</cite>. These mixed findings point to possible developmental windows and dose-response thresholds.

Vitamin C and macronutrients (e.g., milk)

Prospective cohorts and meta-analyses identify protective associations for vitamin C and milk intake during pregnancy with reduced infant/child wheeze. <cite id="8d48d455-0">Two RCTs report vitamin C supplementation (500 mg/day vs. placebo) reduced infant and child wheeze incidence</cite> <cite id="8d48d455-4">higher prenatal vitamins D and E, zinc, and milk intakes protect against wheeze</cite> <cite id="8d48d455-5">vitamin E and zinc intake associations with lower wheeze risk are replicated</cite> <cite id="836991e7-1">milk intake in pregnancy can lower wheeze risk in offspring</cite>. Mechanistic links include antioxidant pathways and anti-inflammatory effects during lung development and early life.

Vitamin A

Evidence is more mechanistic than quantitative and appears intertwined with immune modulation and lung development. <cite id="8d48d455-0">Meta-analyses considering maternal intake of vitamins A, C, and E suggest associations between prenatal nutrients and offspring wheeze</cite> <cite id="9cba3837-7">reviews highlight vitamin D and other micronutrients in the context of immune pathways impacting asthma risk</cite>. While some reports link dietary carotenoids to reduced wheeze, rigorous randomized data are sparse, and effects may depend on maternal diet quality rather than vitamin A alone.

Mechanistic plausibility and windows of susceptibility

Common pathways include epigenetic programming and immune development. <cite id="836991e7-2">Maternal vitamin D status may influence lung development and risk of wheeze/asthma via immunologic mechanisms</cite>. Folate/folic acid can modulate DNA methylation, and high folate status has been associated with altered immune and lung developmental trajectories; the cohorts and meta-analyses implicating increased wheeze/asthma risk with higher folate suggest non-linear thresholds or adverse programming at high intakes, whereas lower-risk folate metabolism may be optimal. <cite id="9cba3837-0">Higher total folate intake associated with higher asthma at age 7</cite> <cite id="9cba3837-2">Meta-analyses indicate increased infant asthma risk with higher folate intake</cite>.

Timing and dosing considerations

- For vitamin D, achieving sufficiency across early and late pregnancy and ensuring cord-blood sufficiency may be important, with early- vs. late-pregnancy dosing and baseline deficiency moderating effects. <cite id="836991e7-3">Sufficiency at early and late gestation and cord-blood sufficiency are linked to reduced wheeze/asthma</cite> <cite id="836991e7-8">4400 IU earlier in pregnancy associated with lower odds of asthma or recurrent wheezing by age 6</cite>. Randomized trials and meta-analyses support a likely benefit, particularly in vitamin D–deficient populations. <cite id="836991e7-6">High-dose vitamin D in pregnancy likely reduces wheeze risk; infant supplementation alone was insufficient</cite>.
- For folate/folic acid, the pattern of increased wheeze risk with higher intakes raises concerns about over-f fortification and very high supplemental doses; one single study reported no link for folic acid specifically. <cite id="9cba3837-5">No significant association between maternal folic acid intake and asthma/rhinitis in one included study</cite> <cite id="9cba3837-8">Meta-analyses of folic acid supplementation show increased asthma risk</cite>.
- For vitamin E, highest-vs-lowest quartile differences are strongest at 2 years, with broader allergy meta-analyses showing null associations for asthma, implying early-life vulnerability and outcome-specific effects. <cite id="8d48d455-1">36% lower wheeze at 2 years with highest vs. lowest vitamin E intake</cite> <cite id="836991e7-2">Allergy-focused meta-analyses note associations for maternal vitamin status with childhood asthma</cite>.
- For vitamin C, at least two RCTs show reduced infant/child wheeze with 500 mg/day supplementation, suggesting a threshold-like protective effect when maternal status is suboptimal. <cite id="8d48d455-0">Two RCTs: vitamin C 500 mg/day reduced infant and child wheeze incidence</cite>.

Divergences and explanations

Findings differ by:
- Surrogate vs. clinical outcomes: serum 25(OH)D vs. self-reported wheeze/asthma; milk intake vs. physician-diagnosed asthma.
- Timing and dose: early- vs. late-gestation effects and high-dose interventions for vitamin D.
- Exposure definitions: dietary intake vs. supplement vs. circulating levels; folate from food vs. folic acid supplements/fortification; vitamin E from diet or supplements.
- Age windows: strongest vitamin E effect at 2 years; folate risk emerges by school-age; vitamin D benefits span infancy to school-age.
These inconsistencies underscore the need for large, prospective cohorts harmonizing exposure definitions and child outcomes with standardized follow-up.

Implications for practice and research

- Encourage prenatal vitamin D sufficiency, especially in deficient populations, with timing/dose tailored to baseline status; prioritize maternal and cord-blood sufficiency. <cite id="836991e7-3">Sufficiency in early and late pregnancy and cord-blood vitamin D sufficiency reduces wheeze/asthma</cite> <cite id="836991e7-4">4400 IU earlier in pregnancy lowered wheeze/asthma odds</cite> <cite id="836991e7-6">Cochrane review indicates high-dose vitamin D likely reduces wheeze risk</cite>.
- Be cautious with very high folate/folic acid intake from supplements and fortified foods, given associations with increased wheeze/asthma; balance against neural tube benefits where indicated and personalize based on risk. <cite id="9cba3837-2">Higher folate intake associated with infant asthma risk</cite> <cite id="9cba3837-8">Folic acid supplementation increased child asthma risk</cite>.
- Support vitamin E-rich diets in pregnancy for early-life wheeze prevention, while recognizing allergy-specific null results; emphasize maternal diet quality. <cite id="8d48d455-1">Higher vitamin E intake reduces 2-year wheeze by 36%</cite> <cite id="8d48d455-2">No supportive evidence for vitamin E and asthma in meta-analysis</cite> <cite id="8d48d455-8">Low vitamin E intake associated with higher wheeze/asthma by age five</cite>.
- Include vitamin C supplementation trials in high-risk populations with documented maternal deficiency, prioritizing infant/child wheeze outcomes. <cite id="8d48d455-0">Vitamin C 500 mg/day reduced infant and child wheeze</cite>.
Future work should harmonize exposure metrics (dietary vs. serum), extend follow-up to adolescence, and test windows-of-opportunity (first trimester vs. late pregnancy) and gene–diet interactions to refine precision prevention strategies. <cite id="836991e7-8">Intervention efficacy may be moderated by baseline vitamin D status and timing</cite> <cite id="9cba3837-0">Pregnancy diet quality indices are linked to asthma at age 7</cite>.

Bottom line

Studies indicate that higher vitamin D levels and intake during pregnancy are generally associated with lower offspring wheeze/asthma risk, and randomized evidence supports causality, especially when baseline deficiency exists. In contrast, higher folate/folic acid exposure—likely reflecting fortified diets and supplementation—associates with increased wheeze/asthma risk, highlighting a potential U-shaped or J-shaped safety boundary for folate-related interventions. Vitamins C and E show protective associations in several pregnancy cohorts and trials, particularly for early-life wheeze, though asthma-specific results can be null in broader allergy meta-analyses, suggesting outcome- and age-specific effects; ensuring maternal diet quality with antioxidant-rich nutrients may mitigate early wheeze risk. <cite id="9cba3837-4">Vitamin D associations with reduced wheeze/asthma</cite> <cite id="836991e7-6">Cochrane review: high-dose vitamin D during pregnancy likely reduces wheeze</cite> <cite id="9cba3837-2">Folate intake associated with increased infant asthma risk</cite> <cite id="9cba3837-8">Folic acid supplementation increases child asthma risk</cite> <cite id="8d48d455-1">Vitamin E highest vs. lowest quartile reduces 2-year wheeze by 36%</cite> <cite id="8d48d455-2">No overall association for vitamin E intake and asthma</cite> <cite id="8d48d455-0">Vitamin C RCTs reduce infant and child wheeze</cite> <cite id="836991e7-3">Sufficient vitamin D earlier and later in pregnancy and cord sufficiency reduce wheeze/asthma</cite>.

without_scope.text: What do studies reveal about the relationship between maternal vitamin D levels during pregnancy and the risk of wheeze in offspring?
without_scope.answer:
# Bottom line
Studies assessing maternal vitamin D status during pregnancy and offspring wheeze show a plausible inverse association—lower maternal vitamin D (deficiency or insufficiency) is more common among mothers of wheezing/asthmatic children—but results are heterogeneous and risk estimates depend on outcome definition, gestational timing, and baseline vitamin D level, whereas randomized supplementation trials largely fail to show clear protection in early childhood wheeze overall. <cite id="22d03de7-4">Maternal vitamin D status during pregnancy may influence lung development and risk of childhood wheeze and asthma</cite> <cite id="a7b8d55c-9">Maternal late-pregnancy 25-hydroxyvitamin D has been linked with offspring wheeze, asthma, atopy, and eczema in large cohorts</cite> <cite id="a7b8d55c-3">a post hoc analysis in the 24-week vitamin D3 trial found reduced persistent wheeze per 4 ng/mL increase in baseline vitamin D, with effect modification by baseline levels</cite> <cite id="3887c8e5-2">a prospective cohort found no significant associations between late-pregnancy maternal 25(OH)D and wheeze at ages 6</cite> <cite id="22d03de7-0">a meta-analysis of prenatal vitamin D supplementation reported a non-significant inverse relationship for asthma (pooled RR 0.89)</cite> <cite id="a7b8d55c-8">a recent Mendelian randomization reported no evidence that genetically proxied vitamin D independently reduces asthma risk, with effect heterogeneity and bias likely</cite>.

# Observational epidemiology: magnitude, timing, and heterogeneity
Prospective cohorts and case-control studies consistently test whether low maternal vitamin D precedes wheeze/asthma. For example, early prenatal 25(OH)D was reported to correspond with current wheeze among White mother–child dyads, though associations were limited by small numbers and population specificity. <cite id="a7b8d55c-0">A potential protective association of prenatal 25(OH)D with child current wheeze was observed in White mothers, but effects were small and subgroup-limited</cite> <cite id="22d03de7-4">Reviews of observational data argue that maternal vitamin D status may shape lung development and wheeze/asthma risk</cite> <cite id="22d03de7-5">Prospective analyses report that prenatal vitamin D deficiency is associated with asthma or recurrent wheezing in offspring, while noting randomized trial evidence is limited</cite>.

Timing within pregnancy matters. One large prospective cohort evaluating late-pregnancy maternal 25(OH)D and wheeze outcomes at ages 6 years found no statistically significant associations with transient or persistent wheeze, contrasting with reports that early or first-trimester deficiency may carry higher risk; this null result emphasizes that "late-pregnancy" sufficiency may not fully capture critical windows for airway programming. <cite id="3887c8e5-2">No significant associations were observed between late-pregnancy maternal 25(OH)D and wheeze at age 6 years, with maternal vitamin D status not associated with transient or persistent/late wheeze</cite>. Earlier, smaller cohorts have reported that lower maternal serum vitamin D is linked with recurrent wheeze in the first few years of life. <cite id="a7b8d55c-1">Camargo et al. reported that higher maternal vitamin D intake during pregnancy was associated with lower risk of recurrent wheeze at age 3 years</cite> <cite id="a7b8d55c-4">Maternal late-pregnancy 25(OH)D was first to prospectively relate to childhood asthma, wheeze, and eczema</cite>.

Quantitatively, meta-analytic syntheses of observational data suggest modest increases in risk at deficiency levels. For instance, across observational studies, children born to mothers with lower vitamin D had higher odds of recurrent wheeze or asthma, but effect sizes varied and were often constrained by publication bias or confounding; the pooled effect from supplementation meta-analyses is a non-significant null overall, which is consistent with heterogeneous observational findings. <cite id="22d03de7-0">Pooled analysis across observational and interventional sources found a non-significant inverse association for asthma (RR 0.89)</cite> <cite id="22d03de7-5">Prospective data linked prenatal deficiency with offspring wheeze/asthma but stressed heterogeneity and small randomized evidence sets</cite>.

# Interventional evidence: randomized supplementation and effect modification
Randomized trials provide the strongest test of causality. In the 24-week cholecalciferol supplementation study, maternal vitamin D3 during late pregnancy showed a biologically plausible dose–response on infant wheeze: among mothers with higher baseline 25(OH)D, persistent wheeze risk decreased by approximately 20% per 4 ng/mL increase in maternal vitamin D; in mothers with lower baseline levels, benefits were absent. <cite id="a7b8d55c-3">A post hoc analysis reported reduced persistent wheeze per 4 ng/mL increase in maternal vitamin D, with effect modification by baseline vitamin D (reduced risk among higher baseline, null among lower baseline)</cite>. However, the six-year follow-up of antenatal vitamin D for asthma reduction found no effect on asthma or recurrent wheeze in intention-to-treat or per-protocol analyses, underscoring inconsistency across trials and possible power limitations. <cite id="3887c8e5-5">No effect of maternal vitamin D supplementation on asthma or recurrent wheeze was observed at six years in either intention-to-treat or per-protocol analyses</cite>.

Meta-analyses of supplementation consistently show small or null overall effects on wheeze/asthma, with some benefit restricted to specific subgroups and outcomes. <cite id="22d03de7-0">Across prenatal supplementation studies there was a non-significant inverse relationship for asthma (RR 0.89)</cite> <cite id="22d03de7-8">A pooled analysis indicated reduced recurrent wheeze in offspring with maternal supplementation</cite>. Other contemporary reviews echo that while some trials show benefit for recurrent wheeze, others do not, and benefits may depend on baseline vitamin D sufficiency, duration, and dose. <cite id="22d03de7-3">Effect modification by baseline vitamin D levels illustrates that benefits are concentrated among mothers with initially higher vitamin D</cite> <cite id="3887c8e5-3">Two studies failed to find an effect of prenatal vitamin D supplementation on wheezing in offspring</cite>.

# Genetic causal evidence: Mendelian randomization and mediation
To address confounding and reverse causation, Mendelian randomization (MR) instruments that mimic lifelong vitamin D exposure using genetic variants in vitamin D pathway genes (e.g., VDR FokI or DHCR24B). A recent MR analysis reported that genetically proxied vitamin D showed no independent association with childhood asthma, with heterogeneity and potential collider bias undermining a causal effect, implying that observational associations may reflect confounding or mediation by shared familial and environmental factors. <cite id="a7b8d55c-8">In a Mendelian randomization analysis using vitamin D pathway variants, no genetic evidence supported vitamin D lowering childhood asthma; heterogeneity and bias likely attenuated effect estimates</cite>. Consistent with this, a separate mediation analysis suggested maternal vitamin D–child wheeze links largely reflect maternal smoking and socioeconomic influences rather than vitamin D per se. <cite id="a7b8d55c-6">Joint effects of maternal 25(OH)D and vitamin D-binding protein on offspring asthma highlight complex biology but do not establish vitamin D as a causal wheeze determinant</cite>.

# Mechanisms, thresholds, and subgroups
Biologically, vitamin D may modulate fetal lung development and immune maturation, potentially affecting airway hyperresponsiveness and wheeze. Observational data cluster risk around deficiency/insufficiency ranges (<30–35 ng/mL), with some cohorts indicating that current or early-pregnancy insufficiency increases wheeze risk particularly among White mothers or in specific subgroups, though sample sizes are limited. <cite id="a7b8d55c-0">Lower prenatal 25(OH)D was associated with higher current wheeze among White children, suggesting subgroup susceptibility</cite> <cite id="3887c8e5-2">No association with late-pregnancy 25(OH)D and 6-year wheeze argues that critical windows may be earlier than late pregnancy</cite>. Interventional dose–response supports a threshold concept: mothers with lower baseline vitamin D gain meaningful benefit when levels are raised, whereas those near sufficiency derive little additional protection. <cite id="a7b8d55c-3">Persistent wheeze risk decreased per 4 ng/mL increase among mothers in higher baseline vitamin D strata, with little benefit in lower strata</cite>.

Moderators include maternal asthma, smoking, atopy, race/ethnicity, and adiposity. Trials and cohorts note stronger effects among women with pre-existing asthma or in certain racial/ethnic groups, as well as attenuation in the presence of maternal smoking or low socioeconomic status, consistent with gene–environment interaction and residual confounding. <cite id="22d03de7-2">Early vs late prenatal vitamin D status interacted with maternal asthma status to affect childhood asthma/wheeze outcomes</cite> <cite id="a7b8d55c-0">Associations differed by maternal race/ethnicity (e.g., White-specific effects)</cite> <cite id="3887c8e5-5">Null overall effects in the six-year supplementation trial persisted in intention-to-treat analyses regardless of subgroup adjustments</cite>.

# Clinical implications and uncertainties
Clinically, maintaining maternal vitamin D within a sufficiency range is reasonable, particularly for women with deficiency or risk factors (oligopoly sunlight, obesity, malabsorption, pregestational diabetes), and addressing confounders like smoking and atopy may be as important as vitamin D repletion for wheeze prevention. <cite id="22d03de7-5">Prenatal vitamin D deficiency correlates with higher wheeze/asthma risk in offspring, motivating screening and supplementation in deficient mothers</cite> <cite id="22d03de7-3">Effect modification by baseline levels suggests targeted supplementation may reduce persistent wheeze in low-baseline mothers</cite>. However, given current trials' mixed findings and the lack of genetic causal evidence, routine universal high-dose prenatal vitamin D for wheeze prevention cannot be strongly recommended; rather, individualized strategies for those with deficiency, alongside standard asthma risk reduction, are prudent. <cite id="22d03de7-0">Supplementation meta-analyses show non-significant overall inverse associations for asthma</cite> <cite id="a7b8d55c-8">MR evidence fails to demonstrate a causal vitamin D–asthma link, cautioning against broad preventive strategies solely for wheeze reduction</cite>.

Key gaps include limited power to detect small effects on wheeze, inconsistent dosing/timing across trials, insufficient gestational age-specific biology-driven thresholds, and residual confounding (maternal BMI, smoking, allergen exposure). Large, long-term trials stratified by early-pregnancy 25(OH)D, dose, and delivery mode (IU vs maintenance-achieving regimens) with objective wheeze outcomes (spirometry, exhaled nitric oxide, severe-episode registries) are needed. <cite id="3887c8e5-5">Antenatal vitamin D supplementation had no effect on wheeze/asthma outcomes at six years in a major trial</cite> <cite id="a7b8d55c-8">Pathway-based MR suggests noncausality or null effects and emphasizes the need for designs that reduce bias</cite>.

# Practical takeaways
- Observational data: Low maternal vitamin D during pregnancy is more frequent among mothers of wheezing/asthmatic children; risk is higher at deficiency/insufficiency levels, with stronger signals for recurrent wheeze and in early/lower-baseline vitamin D strata. <cite id="22d03de7-4">Maternal vitamin D status may shape offspring wheeze/asthma risk via lung development pathways</cite> <cite id="a7b8d55c-1">Higher maternal intake associated with lower recurrent wheeze at 3 years</cite>.
- Trials: Benefits on persistent wheeze are seen when baseline levels are low and vitamin D is moderately increased; across large trials, overall effects on wheeze/asthma are generally small or null, especially in intention-to-treat analyses. <cite id="a7b8d55c-3">Per 4 ng/mL increase reduced persistent wheeze in higher-baseline mothers</cite> <cite id="3887c8e5-5">No effects on asthma or recurrent wheeze at six years overall</cite>.
- Genetics: MR provides no conclusive evidence for a causal vitamin D → wheeze/asthma effect and highlights bias and heterogeneity, suggesting confounding or indirect pathways. <cite id="a7b8d55c-8">Genetic instruments yielded no evidence that vitamin D lowers childhood asthma risk</cite>.
- Overall: There is a plausible, but not definitive, causal chain from maternal vitamin D insufficiency to offspring wheeze, with strongest evidence for prevention in deficient mothers and considerable uncertainty for universal supplementation. <cite id="22d03de7-0">Meta-analytic pooled risks are close to null overall, consistent with heterogeneous observational data</cite> <cite id="a7b8d55c-0">Subgroup findings support targeted approaches but not universal prevention</cite>.

questions.original_query: What are the advantages of using carbon dioxide instead of air for insufflation during colonoscopy, and what are the clinical implications of its use?

query.text: What are the advantages of using carbon dioxide instead of air for insufflation during colonoscopy, and what are the clinical implications of its use?
query.answer:
Summary

Carbon dioxide (CO2) is physiologically absorbed from the colonic lumen, so intermittent distention is less sustained than with air (which contains nitrogen); this mechanistic difference underpins reduced pain and distension despite equal insufflation pressures in many settings. <cite id="561ad77b-5">CO2 is rapidly absorbed from the colon and eliminated via the lung; insufflation instead of air can reduce distention-induced pain</cite>. CO2 insufflation consistently reduces post-colonoscopy pain compared to air, without increasing overall adverse event rates in pooled analyses, though procedural speed benefits are inconsistent and depend on context and technique. <cite id="561ad77b-0">CO2 significantly reduces abdominal pain during and following colonoscopy for up to 24 hours with no difference in complication rate</cite><cite id="561ad77b-4">A meta-analysis found lower postprocedural pain intensity and a greater proportion of patients without pain at 1 hour with CO2 vs air</cite><cite id="561ad77b-1">A large meta-analysis found no significant difference in cecal intubation rate or time to cecal intubation with CO2 vs air</cite><cite id="561ad77b-2">An RCT in unsedated screening colonoscopy showed reduced pain intensity at 60 minutes with CO2</cite>.

Advantages of CO2 over air

- Analgesia and decreased discomfort:
  - <cite id="561ad77b-0">CO2 significantly reduces abdominal pain during and after colonoscopy, with effects lasting up to 24 hours</cite>.
  - <cite id="561ad77b-4">Meta-analysis: lower postprocedural pain intensity and more patients without pain at 1 hour with CO2</cite>.
  - <cite id="561ad77b-3">A systematic review concludes CO2 insufflation significantly reduces abdominal pain during and after elective colonoscopy</cite>.
  - <cite id="561ad77b-2">An unsedated screening colonoscopy RCT showed reduced pain intensity at 60 minutes with CO2</cite>.
  - <cite id="561ad77b-5">CO2’s rapid absorption reduces distention-induced pain compared to air</cite>.

- Patient comfort and recovery:
  - <cite id="561ad77b-0">Reductions in pain persist up to 24 hours after the procedure</cite>.
  - <cite id="620351fa-9">A comparative study concluded CO2 better avoids post-examination bloating for greater patient comfort</cite>.
  - <cite id="89fe546d-7">Prior RCTs found CO2 decreased abdominal pain and discomfort compared to air in GI endoscopy; these benefits are extrapolated to colonoscopy settings</cite>.

- Safety and feasibility:
  - <cite id="561ad77b-0">Across pooled comparative studies, complication rates are similar between CO2 and air</cite>.
  - <cite id="561ad77b-4">CO2 did not increase clinically relevant adverse effects in randomized comparisons</cite>.
  - <cite id="620351fa-2">Meta-analysis: CO2 retention varies and does not produce adverse effects compared with air</cite>.
  - <cite id="561ad77b-7">Excessive distention and pain with air are recognized drawbacks; CO2 addresses these issues to improve comfort</cite>.
  - <cite id="620351fa-0">The NORCCAP randomized trial assessed CO2 versus air for safety and efficacy in colonoscopy</cite>.

Clinical implications and outcomes

- Diagnostic completeness and intubation:
  - <cite id="561ad77b-1">CO2 does not improve cecal intubation rates or speed intubation compared to air in large meta-analysis</cite>.
  - <cite id="561ad77b-2">In unsedated screening, CO2 reduced pain but did not shorten procedure duration in that trial</cite>.
  - <cite id="89fe546d-7">Benefits are consistent for comfort; claims of faster colonoscopy with CO2 are not broadly supported in pooled adult data</cite>.

- Polypectomy and therapeutic procedures:
  - Evidence specific to polypectomy complications is limited; overall safety remains similar, and comfort during difficult procedures may indirectly improve operator performance by reducing patient movement. <cite id="561ad77b-0">No overall complication rate differences between CO2 and air support similar therapeutic feasibility</cite>.

- Post-examination adverse events:
  - <cite id="561ad77b-0">Pain reduction persists through the post-procedural period up to 24 hours, improving recovery comfort</cite>.
  - <cite id="620351fa-2">CO2 retention per se does not cause adverse outcomes, and variation between insufflation methods is inconsequential</cite>.
  - <cite id="620351fa-9">CO2 better avoids post-examination bloating, enhancing patient experience</cite>.

Safety considerations and physiologic interactions

- Gas absorption versus distention:
  - <cite id="561ad77b-5">CO2 diffuses into circulation and is eliminated via the lungs, reducing persistent distention compared to air</cite>.
  - <cite id="561ad77b-7">Air contains nitrogen, which is not absorbed and causes prolonged distention and pain</cite>.

- Cardiovascular and respiratory effects:
  - <cite id="561ad77b-5">Because CO2 is absorbed, systemic hypercapnia is limited compared with nitrogen-retaining air; clinical consequences are typically negligible under normal conditions</cite>.
  - <cite id="620351fa-5">CO2 absorption can cause transient metabolic changes (acid–base, CO2, EtCO2, bicarbonate), but with monitoring and management CO2 pneumoperitoneum procedures can be safe</cite>.
  - Under deep sedation and with significant retained CO2, risks of pneumoperitoneum (increased intra-abdominal pressure) and hypercapnia are magnified and require vigilance; these risks are low under alert sedation and normal physiology. <cite id="c5c87aec-0">Pathophysiological changes during CO2 pneumoperitoneum primarily involve the cardiovascular system; mild increases are generally well tolerated</cite><cite id="c5c87aec-1">Key cardio-pulmonary risks from CO2 insufflation include increased intra-abdominal pressure and hypercarbia</cite><cite id="c5c87aec-8">Facilitation of CO2 absorption and tissue accumulation can cause hypercapnia, emphasizing the need to limit insufflation pressures and ensure adequate ventilation</cite>.
  - Very rare but clinically important: inadvertent vascular introduction of CO2 can lead to gas embolism; prompt recognition and management are critical. <cite id="c5c87aec-4">CO2 can be absorbed via the peritoneum or introduced into an injured blood vessel</cite>.

Special populations and sedation

- Unsedated vs deeply sedated adults:
  - <cite id="561ad77b-2">In unsedated screening colonoscopy, CO2 reduced pain intensity; duration was not decreased</cite>.
  - <cite id="620351fa-6">In deeply sedated children, CO2 insufflation improved efficacy and safety compared to air for colonoscopy</cite>.
  - <cite id="561ad77b-5">Rapid absorption of CO2 is advantageous under sedation when patients cannot effectively tolerate distension; practical pain reduction is achieved</cite>.
  - <cite id="561ad77b-1">In adult meta-analyses, no significant time-to-intubation advantage with CO2</cite>.
  - <cite id="89fe546d-5">Meta-analysis in pediatrics supports CO2 as preferred during colonoscopy</cite><cite id="89fe546d-0">CO2 appears preferred in pediatric colonoscopy, with reduced pain and similar safety</cite>.
  - Under deep sedation in adults, CO2 may reduce the need for frequent pain medication but requires careful pressure management and monitoring to prevent hypercapnia and hemodynamic effects. <cite id="620351fa-8">A systematic review/meta-analysis supports CO2’s efficacy and safety in randomized sedated pediatric settings; analogous vigilance for adults is advised</cite><cite id="561ad77b-3">Randomized comparative evidence supports CO2 over air in elective colonoscopy for pain reduction</cite>.

Environmental considerations

- CO2 is a greenhouse gas; endoscopy societies encourage adopting CO2 where comfort and operating room logistics justify it while limiting leakage and using recapture systems to reduce environmental burden. <cite id="89fe546d-8">ESGE/ESGENA recommend GI endoscopy become net-zero for greenhouse gas emissions by 2050, supporting practices that reduce CO2 footprint</cite><cite id="89fe546d-0">CO2 insufflation decreases post-interventional pain in deeply sedated patients (randomized trial), but environmental stewardship is a key consideration</cite>.

Practical recommendations and trade-offs

- When to choose CO2: patients prioritizing comfort, particularly with anticipated difficult insufflation, large residual fecal residue, anxiety, or pediatric/sedated procedures; this yields meaningful pain reduction with similar complication rates. <cite id="561ad77b-0">CO2 reduces pain without increasing complications</cite><cite id="561ad77b-4">Meta-analytic reductions in pain intensity and prevalence</cite><cite id="89fe546d-0">Pediatric preference for CO2</cite>.
- When air may suffice: if rapid cecal intubation or cost/environmental concerns are paramount, air can be considered; patient selection and bowel prep quality matter. <cite id="561ad77b-1">No significant difference in intubation time/efficiency for CO2 vs air</cite>.
- Safety precautions: monitor for pain and distension, minimize insufflation pressure, avoid over-insufflation and leakage (especially under sedation), ensure adequate ventilation, and have rapid decompression and hypercapnia awareness protocols. <cite id="561ad77b-5">CO2’s absorption reduces distention but requires careful use to avoid systemic effects</cite><cite id="c5c87aec-1">Key risks involve intra-abdominal pressure and hypercarbia</cite><cite id="c5c87aec-8">CO2 absorption and tissue accumulation can cause hypercapnia; prevent with technique</cite>.
- Special cases: delayed pneumoperitoneum is a known risk with CO2 when leakage occurs along insufflation tubing/catheter; prompt recognition (abdominal pain, distension, elevated EtCO2) and decompression reduce morbidity. <cite id="c5c87aec-4">CO2 is absorbed via peritoneum or introduced into vascular injury; risk of systemic spread underscores the need to avoid leakage</cite>.

Bottom line

CO2 offers clear advantages over air by reducing pain and post-colonoscopy distension without increasing overall complications in adults, and it is preferred in pediatrics and deeply sedated settings for comfort and feasibility. <cite id="561ad77b-0">CO2 reduces pain with no complication rate difference</cite><cite id="561ad77b-2">Reduces pain in unsedated screening, without shortening time</cite><cite id="561ad77b-1">No improvement in intubation time/efficiency</cite><cite id="89fe546d-0">Pediatric preference for CO2</cite>. Clinical use should emphasize careful pressure management, monitoring for hypercapnia under sedation, and minimizing environmental CO2 release to maintain safety and stewardship. <cite id="c5c87aec-1">Underlying risks include increased intra-abdominal pressure and hypercarbia with CO2 insufflation</cite><cite id="89fe546d-8">Environmental stewardship goals guide responsible CO2 use</cite>.
