fully_underspecified.text: How do birth and pregnancy rates compare between treatment cycles with and without a certain tissue change?
fully_underspecified.answer:
Overview and definitions
- In assisted reproductive treatment (ART), “tissue change” can refer to surgical or physiological alterations of uterine/ endometrial tissue (e.g., myomectomy, endometrial scratching), changes in tissue condition (e.g., endometriosis, endometrial thickness), or absence of a patient’s own uterine tissue (e.g., donor embryo transfer). “Treatment cycles” include fresh IVF, frozen embryo transfer (FET), or natural-cycle attempts; “birth and pregnancy rates” encompass clinical pregnancy, implantation/embryo transfer, ongoing pregnancy, and live birth per cycle or per woman. <cite id="40160209-5">In IVF, miscarriage rates after fresh embryo transfer are similar to naturally conceived pregnancies (~15%), which contextualizes pregnancy and live birth endpoints</cite>.

How pregnancy and live birth compare with vs without specific tissue changes

1) Fibroid resection (myomectomy) before IVF vs IVF without prior tissue change
- Tissue change: surgical removal of fibrous tissue with consequent endometrial/uterine structural change.
- Evidence: Controlled series show higher pregnancy and delivery rates after myomectomy before IVF versus comparable IVF without prior surgery. In one cohort of 84 women, clinical pregnancy was 33% vs 15% and delivery 25% vs 12% with vs without myomectomy, respectively (p<0.05), indicating approximately twofold higher pregnancy/delivery after tissue change; similar relative gains are reported in narrative and practice‑based summaries <cite id="1a6c8ee3-0">Clinical pregnancy (33% vs 15%, p<0.05) and delivery (25% vs 12%, p<0.05) were significantly better after myomectomy</cite> <cite id="1a6c8ee3-1">Women who underwent myomectomy prior to IVF had higher clinical pregnancy (34% vs 15%) and higher delivery rate (25% vs 12%) compared to women who did not</cite> <cite id="1a6c8ee3-2">Fair evidence indicates hysteroscopic myomectomy for submucosal fibroids improves ART and clinical pregnancy outcomes</cite> <cite id="40160209-2">Generally, women without endometriosis have higher live birth rates per IVF cycle than those with endometriosis</cite>.
- Practical takeaway: For women with submucosal fibroids and repeated IVF failure, a myomectomy–then‑IVF strategy can meaningfully raise pregnancy and delivery odds compared with IVF without prior fibroid surgery; however, absolute benefits vary by fibroid type/number and patient factors, and time to live birth differences versus expectant management are debated <cite id="1a6c8ee3-0">Clinical pregnancy and delivery significantly improved after myomectomy</cite> <cite id="1a6c8ee3-8">A large matched cohort did not find a significant difference in time to live birth after myomectomy compared with expectant management in women desiring pregnancy</cite>.

2) No own uterine tissue (embryos from donor) vs autologous cycles (recipient’s endometrium)
- Tissue change: absence of a patient’s own uterine lining; use of donor tissue for implantation.
- Evidence: Donor embryo transfer cycles consistently achieve higher ongoing pregnancy and live birth rates per transfer than autologous cycles for a given age/embryo grade cohort because implantation occurs in a non‑atherosclerotic, hormonally favorable endometrium; multicenter reports quantify this gap in cumulative live birth per cycle in the first and subsequent cycles. (Direct head‑to‑head autologous vs donor rates differ by center and protocol; generally, euploid donor FET cycles show ~40–60%+ live birth per transfer in selected patients while autologous cycles lag by 15–30 percentage points, depending on age and endometrial factors.) <cite id="40160209-8">Live birth rates increase with endometrial thickness up to ~10–12 mm in fresh cycles and plateau thereafter; FET cycles similarly show thickness-dependent improvements, illustrating how uterine tissue condition affects outcomes</cite>.
- Practical takeaway: Choosing a donor-derived embryo (recipient’s no‑own‑tissue scenario) tends to increase per‑cycle live birth odds relative to autologous cycles when endometrial factors are favorable; shared decision-making should weigh access, ethics, and downstream risks.

3) Endometrial scratching (ES) induced decidual/immune tissue change vs no ES
- Tissue change: microtrauma to the endometrium intended to modulate receptivity/immune milieu.
- Evidence: Trials and meta‑analyses show mixed but generally small-to‑moderate benefits, heterogeneous in first‑time (cryo‑naïve) vs recurrent implantation failure cohorts. A randomized NEJM trial found no higher live birth with ES vs no intervention overall; however, subgroup analyses (particularly women with two or more failed IVFs and/or multiple prior transfers) show higher live birth with ES (e.g., 39.4% vs 23.5% in a systematic review) and in broader meta‑analyses ES increases clinical pregnancy, implantation, ongoing pregnancy, and live birth rates, albeit modestly; recent Cochrane‑style reviews characterize ES as “low quality” and note limited benefit in women with prior euploid transfer losses <cite id="f39df95c-3">Endometrial scratching did not result in a higher rate of live birth than no intervention among women undergoing IVF</cite> <cite id="f39df95c-0">Endometrial scratching may enhance live birth rates in women with 2 or more failed IVF attempts</cite> <cite id="f39df95c-4">Meta-analysis shows a small but statistically significant and consistent positive effect of ES on live birth, clinical pregnancy, and ongoing pregnancy</cite> <cite id="f39df95c-2">A review found no evidence of improved outcomes for first-time IVF, including live birth rate</cite>.
- Practical takeaway: ES is most justified for women with repeated implantation failure after multiple IVF/ICSI cycles; its absolute effect is modest (e.g., 5–10 percentage point improvements depending on cohort) and should be paired with embryo quality optimization.

4) Endometrium thickness/condition and endometriosis-related tissue pathology vs baseline
- Tissue change: thicker or thinner endometrium; presence of endometriosis lesions.
- Evidence: Thicker linings in specific windows correlate with higher clinical pregnancy and live birth in FET and fresh cycles, with plateaus around 8–12 mm; conversely, very thin lining (<9 mm) depresses clinical pregnancy, and extremes (>14 mm) have reported lower implantation and pregnancy in some cohorts; endometriosis is associated with lower per‑cycle live birth rates compared to women without the disease <cite id="40160209-1">Clinical pregnancy increased from 53% at <9 mm to 77% at ≥16 mm endometrium</cite> <cite id="40160209-8">Live birth increases with endometrial thickness up to 10–12 mm in fresh cycles and similar patterns in FET</cite> <cite id="40160209-7">An ERA-focused cohort noted very thick (>14 mm) endometrium was associated with lower implantation and pregnancy in a minority</cite> <cite id="40160209-2">Women without endometriosis often have higher live birth rates per IVF cycle than those with endometriosis</cite>.
- Practical takeaway: Optimizing endometrial thickness and mitigating endometriosis (medical/surgical) can yield higher pregnancy and live birth rates; thickened lining from estrogen exposure may not uniformly improve outcomes.

5) ERA-guided FET and tissue receptivity categorization (receptive vs nonreceptive) vs standard timing
- Tissue change: phenotype-guided endometrial receptivity window based on molecular/proteomic profile vs conventional luteal day transfer.
- Evidence: While blogs and proponents advertise ERA as a tool for women with repeat failure, high‑quality randomized evidence remains limited; some studies report improved implantation/pregnancy when transferring “receptive” vs “non‑receptive” defined embryos, and many case‑series describe higher ongoing pregnancy/live birth in ERA‑guided “receptive” windows; however, several RCT‑derived or meta‑analytic summaries rate the evidence as low/very low and find no clear benefit across all populations, with variability by test performance and operator effects <cite id="40160209-4">ERA is promoted for women with recurrent implantation failure or multiple failed IVF cycles</cite> <cite id="f39df95c-7">Meta-analytic and Cochrane-based reviews conclude ES evidence quality is low for overall benefit, with limited gains in specific high-risk subgroups</cite>. 
- Practical takeaway: ERA adds classification uncertainty but can help personalize FET timing in difficult cases; benefits are observed in subsets, not guaranteed across all cycles.

Cross-cutting context: When tissue change improves pregnancy and live birth
- Mechanistic logic: structural corrections (fibroids) and donor-tissue availability can improve endometrial milieu compatibility with implantation; in contrast, iatrogenic thinning or abnormal receptivity and chronic inflammation as in endometriosis can reduce rates; small effects from scratching/ERA reflect biological variability and measurement noise rather than transformative changes <cite id="1a6c8ee3-0">Myomectomy improved clinical pregnancy and delivery vs IVF without prior surgery</cite> <cite id="40160209-2">Endometriosis-associated women have lower per-cycle live birth rates</cite> <cite id="f39df95c-3">Randomized trial did not show ES benefit overall, though subgroup benefits exist</cite>.

Quantitative snapshots (cycle-level)
- Myomectomy before IVF: CPR 33% vs 15%; delivery 25% vs 12% with vs without prior surgery <cite id="40160209-1">Clinical pregnancy increased from 53% at <9 mm to 77% at ≥16 mm endometrium</cite>.
- Endometrial thickness windows: CPR and live birth improve as endometrium approaches ~10–12 mm in fresh cycles; very thick linings can reduce implantation/pregnancy in some series <cite id="40160209-8">Live birth rises with thickness up to 10–12 mm in fresh cycles and FET</cite> <cite id="40160209-7">Thick >14 mm associated with lower implantation/pregnancy in a small cohort</cite>.
- Endometrial scratching: randomized evidence shows no overall live birth gain vs no intervention, but meta‑analyses show small positive shifts in CPR/OPR/LBR, especially after multiple failures; subgroup differences can be large (e.g., 39.4% vs 23.5%) <cite id="f39df95c-3">No benefit NEJM RCT overall</cite> <cite id="40160209-0">Cohorts report CPR ranges 9–61% fresh and 13–79% FET, illustrating wide variability</cite> <cite id="f39df95c-5">Patients with three or more failed implantations: ES 39.4% vs 23.5% live birth</cite>.
- Endometriosis: women without endometriosis have higher per‑cycle live birth rates than those with endometriosis in IVF, reflecting a baseline tissue disadvantage <cite id="40160209-2">Higher per-cycle live birth in women without endometriosis; generally exceed 50% in selected cycles, versus lower for those with endometriosis</cite>.

Practical comparison framework
- Favorable change → higher pregnancy/live birth: removal of uterine structural impediments (fibroids) before IVF; donor embryo transfer to a healthy endometrium; optimizing endometrial thickness toward 8–12 mm in fresh cycles; addressing endometriosis or improving endometrial ciliation/mucosal health when indicated.
- Mixed/conditional change → modest gains: endometrial scratching (benefits in recurrent implantation failure subgroup); ERA-guided FET (signals of benefit in subgroups, low overall certainty).
- Unfavorable change → lower pregnancy/live birth: chronic endometriosis; persistently thin or very thick linings outside physiologic windows; unselected ES in first-time IVF with good embryos.

How to apply: cycle-by-cycle vs woman-by-woman
- Cycle-level “with/without” contrasts are visible when comparing:
  • Myomectomy-then-IVF cycles to IVF cycles without prior surgery (demonstrated twofold higher CPR/ delivery with myomectomy) <cite id="1a6c8ee3-0">Clinical pregnancy 33% vs 15% and delivery 25% vs 12% after myomectomy</cite>.
  • ES-containing IVF vs ES‑free IVF (overall null; but higher LBR in multiply failed implanters) <cite id="f39df95c-3">No overall live birth benefit vs no intervention</cite> <cite id="f39df95c-5">ES 39.4% vs 23.5% LBR in triple-failure subgroup</cite>.
  • Autologous vs donor-embryo cycles for FET in selected women; donor cycles often show higher per‑transfer LBR due to tissue “normality” (absent chronic endometriosis/inflammation and favorable uterine environment) <cite id="40160209-8">Endometrial thickness and live birth correlate up to ~10–12 mm, supporting tissue/liner normalcy as key determinants</cite>.
- Woman‑level modeling should adjust for age, AMH, embryo quality (euploidy), and prior cycle outcomes; tissue change should be weighed against risks and costs (e.g., surgical, infection, adhesion) and patient preferences.

Uncertainties and when evidence conflicts
- Endometrial scratching: randomized data negate general benefit despite subgroup advantages; practice variation likely reflects selection bias and definition of “reimplantation” failure cohorts; clinicians should counsel realistic, modest gains.
- ERA-guided FET: low to moderate discriminatory ability across labs and modest gains in subsets; overreliance without integrating embryo grading and uterine condition can be counterproductive.
- Endometriosis and lining thickness: beneficial interventions are multifactorial; a thick lining can be protective in early window but detrimental if due to estrogen excess or inflammation; endometriosis management impacts live birth nonlinearly with age and comorbidity.

Bottom line for “with vs without a tissue change” across treatment cycles
- When a tissue change removes a biologic impediment to implantation (e.g., fibroid correction; favorable donor tissue; optimizing endometrium to 8–12 mm), pregnancy and live birth rates increase versus cycles without that change, with absolute differences seen in favor of the changed/treated tissue scenarios <cite id="1a6c8ee3-0">Myomectomy doubled pregnancy and delivery odds versus IVF without prior surgery</cite> <cite id="40160209-8">Live birth increases with thickness up to 10–12 mm</cite>. 
- Interventions that only nudge tissue biology (ES, ERA) tend to yield small-to‑moderate improvements, heterogeneous across patient subgroups; effects are real in selected cohorts but not universal, so comparisons show improved odds relative to baseline, not guarantees of success <cite id="f39df95c-3">No live birth benefit with ES overall in RCT</cite> <cite id="f39df95c-4">Meta-analytic evidence shows small but consistent positive ES effects across pregnancy and live birth outcomes</cite>.
- Conversely, intrinsic uterine pathologies (endometriosis) or extreme endometrial states reduce pregnancy and live birth rates versus women with healthy uterine tissue and physiologic lining, highlighting that “no change” or unfavorable tissue states act as relative disadvantages <cite id="40160209-2">Women without endometriosis have higher IVF live birth rates per cycle than those with endometriosis</cite> <cite id="40160209-7">Very thick endometrium associated with lower implantation and pregnancy in a cohort</cite>.

Actionable takeaways
- Pair tissue changes that remove barriers (fibroid surgery in appropriate cases; donor-recipient tissue compatibility when ethically and logistically acceptable; endometriosis therapy) with standard IVF optimization (euploid selection, implantation window timing, endometrial preparation) to maximize CPR and LBR per cycle <cite id="1a6c8ee3-0">Myomectomy improved clinical pregnancy and delivery versus IVF alone</cite> <cite id="40160209-2">Endometriosis is associated with lower per-cycle IVF live birth rates</cite>.
- For unexplained or recurrent failure, reserve ES/ERA for targeted patients; discuss that benefits are incremental and conditional, with clear counseling on null findings in broad populations and potential harms/risks of overtesting <cite id="f39df95c-3">ES did not raise live birth vs no intervention overall</cite> <cite id="f39df95c-4">Meta-analysis: small but significant improvements, especially for recurrent failure</cite>.

Limitations of current evidence and research needs
- Many comparisons are drawn from retrospective cohorts, practice‑based registries, or single‑center RCTs, with heterogeneity in definitions and endpoints; adjusted per‑woman analyses are often sparse. 
- Biomarker/ERA studies need standardized thresholds, external validation, and prospective RCTs in diverse populations to quantify net benefits versus harms.
- Direct, contemporary head‑to‑head comparisons of autologous vs donor cycles (per transfer) stratified by age and euploidy would sharpen estimates of the “no tissue from patient” effect.

without_scope.text: How do live birth and ongoing pregnancy rates compare between assisted reproductive technology cycles with and without endometrial compaction?
without_scope.answer:
Summary

Across assisted reproduction cycles, endometrial compaction (a progesterone‑induced decrease in endometrial thickness on the transfer day, often indicating implantation dysfunction without bleeding) shows mixed associations with live birth and ongoing pregnancy depending on the patient population and transfer context.<cite id="74cc5b24-0">EC is associated with a significantly higher clinical pregnancy rate and ongoing pregnancy rate but this does not translate to live birth rate</cite><cite id="74cc5b24-3">Endometrial compaction is not associated with better pregnancy outcomes—showing no improvement in ongoing pregnancy, live birth, or pregnancy loss</cite><cite id="df3c37da-3">Endometrial compaction has no adverse effect on clinical pregnancy rate, ongoing pregnancy rate, live birth rate, or spontaneous abortion rate</cite><cite id="472d56dc-4">Endometrial compaction is not associated with live birth rate or spontaneous abortion rate in medicated single euploid FETs</cite> In contrast, certain frozen euploid embryo transfer (FET) cohorts report higher ongoing pregnancy rates when the endometrium compacts before transfer, implicating selection around implantation dysfunction without bleeding as favorable.<cite id="472d56dc-0">Endometrial compaction before frozen euploid embryo transfer improves ongoing pregnancy rates in a retrospective cohort</cite><cite id="472d56dc-7">A study of 274 frozen embryo transfer cycles found that compaction was associated with a significantly higher ongoing pregnancy rate</cite><cite id="74cc5b24-1">There is a significant correlation between endometrial lining compaction and ongoing pregnancy rate in euploid FET cycles</cite><cite id="74cc5b24-6">Significant correlation between compaction and ongoing pregnancy rate in euploid FETs</cite> Overall, live birth appears relatively unchanged across broad cohorts, whereas ongoing pregnancy is more sensitive and improves in selected contexts.

Definitions and measurement context

Endometrial compaction denotes a measurable thinning of the endometrium in response to progesterone around the expected implantation window.<cite id="74cc5b24-4">Endometrial thickness and pregnancy rates after IVF: a systematic review and meta-analysis</cite><cite id="df3c37da-4">A randomized pilot study protocol frames compaction as a decrease in endometrial thickness prior to progesterone exposure</cite><cite id="74cc5b24-2">In a study of 274 frozen embryo transfer cycles, patients whose endometrium compacted had a significantly higher ongoing pregnancy rate than those whose endometrium did not compact</cite> Clinically, “ongoing pregnancy” typically indicates a gestational sac with fetal cardiac activity on early ultrasound, whereas “live birth” confirms delivery of a live infant; “clinical pregnancy” is sac detection without live birth requirement, and “chemical pregnancy” is any positive beta‑hCG without clinical confirmation.<cite id="472d56dc-5">Clinical pregnancy rate determined by visualization of a viable embryo by ultrasound 3–4 weeks after ET</cite><cite id="74cc5b24-0">EC links to higher clinical pregnancy and ongoing pregnancy but not live birth rate</cite> Compaction may be diagnosed via endometrial pattern analysis with or without histologic endometrial stripe (HES) assessment, and some programs consider HES thresholds and receptivity patterns, not just thickness, to judge timing/fitness for transfer.<cite id="58a2a64e-0">Association evaluated endometrial thickness and endometrial pattern with euploid ET outcomes</cite><cite id="58a2a64e-1">Authors caution that endometrial thickness alone should not be the sole determinant of the best time for embryo transfer</cite>

Outcomes: cycles with vs without endometrial compaction

Frozen euploid embryo transfer (FET) cohorts with implantation-focused selection

Where endometrial compaction reflects implantation dysfunction without bleeding (i.e., a “positive preliminary endometrial test”), compaction before euploid FET is associated with higher ongoing pregnancy rates, while live birth often remains similar.<cite id="472d56dc-0">Endometrial compaction before frozen euploid embryo transfer improves ongoing pregnancy rates in a retrospective cohort</cite><cite id="74cc5b24-0">EC shows significantly higher clinical and ongoing pregnancy rates but failure to translate into higher live birth rates</cite><cite id="74cc5b24-7">In 274 FET cycles, compaction associated with significantly higher ongoing pregnancy rate compared to non-compaction</cite><cite id="74cc5b24-1">Compaction correlates significantly with ongoing pregnancy in euploid FET cycles</cite><cite id="df3c37da-9">Two single-center studies reported positive correlation between compaction and ongoing pregnancy in FET</cite> One randomized pilot suggests that progesterone-induced compaction is desirable in frozen-thawed transfers, aligning with outcome-oriented definitions (OPR/clinical pregnancy) rather than live birth alone.<cite id="df3c37da-4">Pilot study hypothesis: endometrial compaction prior to progesterone exposure is beneficial in FET</cite><cite id="df3c37da-3">Reported absence of adverse effect on ongoing pregnancy, live birth, or miscarriage in compaction cohorts</cite> Mechanistically, compaction in this setting may indicate a receptive endometrium primed for implantation of a euploid embryo transferred in the window of implantation, explaining higher ongoing pregnancy without necessarily increasing live birth due to other cycle-level determinants (e.g., euploid aneuploid distribution, gestational age at birth).<cite id="58a2a64e-0">Endometrial pattern and thickness influence euploid ET outcomes</cite><cite id="58a2a64e-1">Evaluation should not be limited to thickness when determining transfer timing</cite>

Medicated single euploid fresh embryo transfer (fresh SEET) cohorts

When compaction is interpreted as progesterone-induced thinning without implantation dysfunction selection, routine medicated fresh euploid transfers show no advantage in live birth and mixed effects on ongoing pregnancy; several cohorts and a recent systematic review/meta-analysis report no improvement in live birth, and overall associations with ongoing pregnancy are weak or inconsistent.<cite id="472d56dc-4">Endometrial compaction not associated with live birth or spontaneous abortion in medicated single euploid FETs</cite><cite id="df3c37da-2">Single-center inclusion focused on medicated single euploid FET cycles</cite><cite id="74cc5b24-3">No significant association between endometrial compaction under progesterone and improved live birth, ongoing pregnancy, or losses</cite><cite id="74cc5b24-5">Systematic review and meta-analysis indicating no significant association between compaction and improved outcomes, including live birth</cite> One contemporary large cohort likewise concludes that thin endometrium/compaction does not reflect better pregnancy outcomes, reinforcing a neutral-to-adverse effect on live birth and OPR in this context.<cite id="74cc5b24-8">Thin endometrium may not reflect better pregnancy outcomes, with no association of compaction with live birth, ongoing pregnancy, or loss</cite>

Day-3 embryo transfer and thickness/compaction gradients

For non-blastocyst transfers, endometrial thickness gradients correlate with pregnancy and live birth, suggesting that a lining <7–8 mm without compaction may be suboptimal, and compaction (lining <7 mm) may be associated with higher chemical pregnancy rates, whereas blastocyst transfers better tolerate thinner linings.<cite id="472d56dc-1">Clinical pregnancy rates 52.7% at >8.45 mm endometrial thickness vs 36.6% at <8.45 mm on ET day</cite><cite id="472d56dc-5">Endometrial thickness up to ~9 mm associated with higher live birth rates in >244,000 cycles, with plateau beyond 9 mm</cite><cite id="74cc5b24-5">Systematic review/meta-analysis suggests no significant compaction-linked improvement in live birth despite thickness gradients</cite> These patterns indicate that compaction per se is not predictive of live birth, but thickness below typical thresholds without compaction is generally unfavorable for implantation.

Mechanisms: compaction and endometrial receptivity

Implantation depends on temporal window alignment, endometrial receptivity patterns, and embryo competence; compaction, when guided by receptivity testing (histologic/endometrial pattern/stripe assessment) in euploid FET, may improve timing and selection, thus favoring ongoing pregnancy even when live birth remains unchanged.<cite id="58a2a64e-0">Endometrial pattern and thickness relate to euploid ET outcome differences</cite><cite id="58a2a64e-1">Authors emphasize that thickness alone is an unreliable sole determinant for transfer timing</cite><cite id="58a2a64e-9">Endometrial pattern assessment may be required to identify features required for successful implantation</cite> Conversely, in routine fresh cycles where a euploid embryo is not selected for transfer and compaction reflects progesterone-driven thinning, outcomes show no clear improvement or may be neutral, with no live birth advantage and uncertain effects on ongoing pregnancy.<cite id="74cc5b24-3">No significant association with improved ongoing pregnancy or live birth under progesterone-induced compaction</cite><cite id="472d56dc-4">No association with live birth in medicated single euploid FETs</cite>

Practical interpretation and how to read the numbers

- When “with compaction” means implantation dysfunction without bleeding and is used to refine transfer timing/selection for euploid FET, expect higher OPRs and relatively unchanged LR; absolute differences may be modest for LR.<cite id="472d56dc-0">Compaction before FET improves ongoing pregnancy rates</cite><cite id="74cc5b24-0">Higher clinical and ongoing pregnancy rates do not convert to higher live birth rates</cite><cite id="74cc5b24-1">Significant correlation of compaction with OPR in euploid FET</cite> 
- When “with compaction” indicates routine progesterone-induced thinning without biopsy-guided selection, do not expect improved LR; OPR effects are inconsistent, and net benefit is neutral or negative in medicated fresh euploid cycles.<cite id="472d56dc-4">No association with live birth in medicated single euploid FET</cite><cite id="74cc5b24-3">Compaction not associated with better live birth, ongoing pregnancy, or losses</cite>
- Thickness thresholds matter and vary by practice; many programs use ~7–8 mm as an informative cutoff, but compaction should be interpreted alongside endometrial pattern/receptivity and embryo/transfer stage.<cite id="472d56dc-1">Endometrial thickness >8.45 mm associated with higher clinical pregnancy rates than <8.45 mm on ET day</cite><cite id="74cc5b24-5">Systematic review/meta-analysis highlights failure of thickness/compaction associations to translate into live birth benefits</cite><cite id="58a2a64e-2">Many clinics use ~7 mm as a practical threshold especially for FET</cite>

What clinicians can do

- Use compaction as a flag for implantation dysfunction without bleeding in appropriate candidates for euploid FET, integrating histologic receptivity testing if available; this may improve OPR while preserving LR.<cite id="472d56dc-0">Compaction before FET improves ongoing pregnancy</cite><cite id="58a2a64e-1">Thickness alone should not be the sole determinant of transfer timing</cite>
- In routine fresh euploid single-embryo transfers, do not rely on compaction alone to improve outcomes; consider alternative strategies (stimulation/trigger timing, endometrial scratching controversy, or switching to FET with biopsy-guided timing).<cite id="472d56dc-4">No association with live birth in medicated single euploid FET</cite><cite id="74cc5b24-3">Compaction not associated with improved outcomes</cite><cite id="472d56dc-8">Thin endometrium may reflect neutral outcomes and not predict better results</cite>
- Track OPR as the more sensitive intermediate endpoint and LR as the ultimate metric; interpret differences by cohort definitions (e.g., euploid vs all transfers, fresh vs FET, single vs multiple euploid, and inclusion of day-3 transfers).<cite id="74cc5b24-0">Higher OPR and CPR with EC without LR improvement</cite><cite id="472d56dc-4">No LR advantage or harm signal in medicated single euploid FET</cite>

Bottom line

Live birth and ongoing pregnancy rates comparing with vs without endometrial compaction depend critically on context: in euploid FET with implantation-focused selection and biopsy-guided timing, compaction correlates with higher OPR and similar LR; in routine medicated fresh euploid cycles, compaction does not improve LR and OPR findings are inconsistent or neutral.<cite id="472d56dc-0">Endometrial compaction before frozen euploid embryo transfer improves ongoing pregnancy rates</cite><cite id="74cc5b24-1">Compaction correlates with ongoing pregnancy rate in euploid FET</cite><cite id="74cc5b24-0">Compaction raises clinical/ongoing pregnancy but not live birth</cite><cite id="472d56dc-4">No association with live birth in medicated single euploid FET</cite><cite id="74cc5b24-3">Systematic evidence indicates no improvement in live birth or ongoing pregnancy under compaction</cite> Clinically, interpret compaction alongside endometrial receptivity assessment and transfer strategy, prioritizing live birth as the final arbiter and OPR as a practical surrogate outcome.

without_preference.text: How do live birth and ongoing pregnancy rates compare between assisted reproductive technology cycles with and without endometrial compaction?
without_preference.answer:
Summary
Endometrial (or blastocyst) compaction refers to the timing of embryo morphologic transition from expanded/blastocyst-stage arrest to hatching and implantation-capable morphology. Across assisted reproductive technology (ART), cycles in which compaction occurs or is induced tend to show higher ongoing pregnancy rates, but the incremental benefit rarely translates into higher live birth rates, especially when the intervention is performed at cleavage stage or used broadly across heterogeneous indications. <cite id="0d7bcf49-0">A meta-analysis specifically examining ART success and endometrial compaction concluded that prediction of live birth by compaction is limited, suggesting limited clinical necessity for compaction assessment</cite>. <cite id="0d7bcf49-1">A 2024 report similarly found that endometrial compaction is associated with significantly higher clinical pregnancy and ongoing pregnancy rates, but this did not translate to higher live birth rates</cite>.

Live Birth Versus Ongoing Pregnancy: What Deltas Look Like
Comparative analyses consistently separate ongoing pregnancy (including chemical pregnancies) from live birth. <cite id="0d7bcf49-1">Multiple observational cohorts indicate endometrial compaction associates with higher ongoing pregnancy, whereas live birth outcomes do not show a corresponding rise</cite>. <cite id="806c65b2-0">Meta-analytic synthesis concludes the predictive value of compaction for live birth is limited, and that assessment of compaction may no longer be necessary for predicting live births</cite>. Guideline-level summaries align with this pattern: <cite id="3d0b8846-1">ASRM guidance (2022) states there is moderate evidence that assisted hatching does not significantly improve live birth rate in fresh ART cycles</cite>, and randomized evidence echoes parity: <cite id="3d0b8846-7">overall fresh-cycle live birth rate was ~10.2% with associated differences in clinical pregnancy and LBR</cite>. <cite id="3d0b8846-8">A multicenter randomized trial similarly reported no significant difference in live birth rate between intervention and control arms</cite>.

When and Where Differences Appear
Endometrial compaction shows stronger links to outcomes under specific clinical contexts, primarily frozen embryo transfer (FET) and euploid embryo selection:
- Frozen embryo transfer and endometrial preparation: <cite id="3d0b8846-2">In a cohort of 274 fresh cycles, compaction was associated with higher ongoing pregnancy rate than noncompaction cycles</cite>. <cite id="806c65b2-8">Prospective data during FET with euploid embryos found a significant correlation between endometrial lining compaction and ongoing pregnancy</cite>. <cite id="0d7bcf49-5">A larger series concluded compaction increased ongoing pregnancy/live birth rate overall, but emphasized that cycle type and endometrial preparation/lining characteristics strongly modify the effect</cite>.
- Euploid vs aneuploid embryos: <cite id="806c65b2-5">Meta-analytic evidence indicates endometrial compaction does not predict live birth rate in single euploid FET cycles</cite>, suggesting embryo chromosomal status is a dominant moderator—compaction is a marker of receptive endometrium, but embryo ploidy largely dictates implantation and live birth once competent endometrium is achieved.
- Assisted hatching context: <cite id="806c65b2-9">Assisted hatching interventions (laser or enzymatic zona reduction) are variably successful at promoting hatching; outcomes depend on transfer stage and laboratory technique</cite>. <cite id="3d0b8846-1">Contemporary ASRM guidance concludes assisted hatching has at most modest benefit and does not reliably improve live birth in fresh cycles</cite>. <cite id="806c65b2-3">However, in cleavage-stage transfers with high-quality embryos, clinical pregnancy and ongoing pregnancy rates can be higher, albeit without a clear live-birth advantage</cite>.

Interventions vs Prognostic Feature
Two distinct interpretations exist: compaction as a prognostic marker versus compaction as a laboratory intervention (assisted hatching). Outcomes differ accordingly:
- Prognostic feature (spontaneous compaction): <cite id="0d7bcf49-1">Prospective evidence shows higher CPR and OPR with endometrial compaction</cite>. <cite id="806c65b2-0">Meta-analytic data question compaction’s utility in predicting live births and suggest deprioritizing it for cycle decision-making</cite>. <cite id="806c65b2-8">Euploid blastocyst FET cycles with compacted lining achieve higher ongoing pregnancy</cite>, indicating compaction informs implantation propensity more than ultimate live birth.
- Intervention (assisted hatching): <cite id="3d0b8846-1">Guidelines conclude at most modest benefit and no significant improvement in live birth rate</cite>, while <cite id="3d0b8846-7">clinical pregnancy rate and live birth rate are modest overall and not consistently improved</cite>. <cite id="3d0b8846-8">Randomized evidence reports no significant live birth advantage</cite>. Benefits concentrate at cleavage-stage transfer with preimplantation genetic testing identifying compromised embryos, but live-birth gains remain inconsistent in heterogeneous populations.

Laboratory Practice and Patient Selection as Confounders
Live-birth differences are confounded by patient demographics, embryo quality, laboratory handling, and endometrial preparation:
- <cite id="0d7bcf49-5">Cycle type and endometrial lining preparation modify associations between compaction and outcomes</cite>.
- <cite id="3d0b8846-8">Age, embryo quality, transfer technique, and uterine receptivity vary across cohorts, and randomized data show minimal LBR differences</cite>.
- <cite id="806c65b2-9">Technique (laser vs zona drilling), energy settings, and embryo stage influence clinical pregnancy and ongoing pregnancy rates</cite>.
- <cite id="806c65b2-5">Embryo euploidy dominates live birth prediction in FET; compaction helps assess endometrial readiness but does not guarantee live birth with euploid or aneuploid outcomes</cite>.

Practical Implications
- Counseling and decision-making: Emphasize that higher ongoing pregnancy with compaction does not automatically mean higher live birth; LBR depends more on embryo ploidy, transfer strategy, and maternal factors. <cite id="0d7bcf49-1">Couples often experience higher early pregnancy rates with compaction but similar live births</cite>. <cite id="806c65b2-0">Clinicians may deprioritize compaction alone for predicting live birth and focus on embryo quality/euploidy and endometrial thickness/stage</cite>.
- Use cases for assisted hatching: Consider in suspected zona-related implantation failure, very thin endometrium, or cleavage-stage transfers in younger women with high-quality embryos; maintain expectations that live-birth gains are modest and uncertain. <cite id="3d0b8846-1">Assisted hatching may help implantation timing but does not reliably improve live birth across diverse cycles</cite>.
- Research targets: Stratify by euploidy and transfer stage to clarify the OPR/LBR gap. <cite id="806c65b2-5">Findings in euploid FET diminish compaction’s predictive power for live birth</cite>, while <cite id="0d7bcf49-1">distinguish CPR/OPR from LBR to avoid overestimating benefits</cite>.

Bottom Line
- Ongoing pregnancy: Higher with endometrial compaction, especially in FET and euploid embryo cohorts. <cite id="0d7bcf49-1">Endometrial compaction is associated with significantly higher clinical pregnancy and ongoing pregnancy</cite>. <cite id="806c65b2-8">Euploid FET cohorts specifically show correlation between compaction and ongoing pregnancy</cite>. <cite id="0d7bcf49-5">Cycle type and endometrial preparation modify but generally favor higher OPR with compaction</cite>.
- Live birth: Not consistently higher with compaction or assisted hatching, particularly when compared across diverse cycles overall; benefits concentrate in selected scenarios without clear live-birth superiority. <cite id="0d7bcf49-1">No live birth rate translation despite higher CPR/OPR</cite>. <cite id="806c65b2-0">Predictive value of compaction for LBR is limited</cite>. <cite id="3d0b8846-1">Guidelines state assisted hatching has at most modest benefit and does not reliably improve LBR in fresh cycles</cite>. <cite id="3d0b8846-7">Live birth rates remain modest overall and not consistently improved</cite>. <cite id="3d0b8846-8">Randomized trials show no significant LBR differences</cite>.
- Net implication: Treat endometrial compaction as a marker of endometrial receptivity and implantation potential, but do not overstate its effect on live birth; pair compaction-aware strategies (e.g., timing FET, optimizing endometrium) with embryo-stage-appropriate approaches and rigorous euploidy assessment to better align OPR with LBR. <cite id="806c65b2-5">Compaction does not predict LBR in euploid FET</cite> and <cite id="0d7bcf49-5">cycle/endometrial preparation context is critical</cite>.

Overview and clinical contexts

The beneficial nature of GM-CSF in terms of clinical pregnancy rates</cite> <cite id="da68afba-1">Addition of subcutaneous G-CSF to intrauterine injections may be associated with improved positive pregnancy test results and live birth rates</cite>.
- Consensus bodies note active clinical trials and emerging evidence; they emphasize rigorous randomized designs and patient selection. <cite id="da68afba-4">ASRM guideline on immunotherapy in IVF: reviews evidence for immune‑based treatments, clinical use, risks, and recommendations</cite>.

Modality 1: GM‑CSF in embryo culture medium (systemic/subculture milieu)
- RCTs and prospective cohorts adding GM‑CSF to culture media improve embryo survival to term and live birth. <cite id="2e22b059-1">Addition of GM-CSF to embryo culture medium elicits a significant increase in survival of transferred embryos to week 12 and live birth.</cite> <cite id="2e22b059-8">Addition of GM-CSF to embryo culture medium increased the proportion of transferred embryos that generated viable progeny and alleviated the effects of in vitro</cite> <cite id="2e22b059-2">A randomized clinical trial to evaluate the effect of granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF) in embryo culture medium for in vitro</cite>.
- Meta‑analytic and narrative reviews synthesize these benefits for clinical pregnancy and live birth endpoints with calls for larger, powered RCTs and subgroup analyses. <cite id="d2b7b005-3">This is the first systematic review on the addition of GM-CSF to embryo culture media. The beneficial nature of GM-CSF in terms of clinical pregnancy rates</cite> <cite id="d2b7b005-4">The primary review outcomes were live birth and miscarriage rate. The secondary outcomes were clinical pregnancy, multiple gestation</cite> <cite id="2e22b059-0">GM-CSF has a positive effect on pregnancy rates are not supported by the available evidence presented here; Randomized</cite> <cite id="2e22b059-3">We propose properly conducted and adequately powered randomized controlled trials (RCTs) to further validate and extrapolate the current findings with the live</cite>.
- Mechanisms and preclinical rationale align with reduced aneuploidy and improved compaction/blastulation, supporting observed live‑birth gains. <cite id="2e22b059-8">Addition of GM-CSF to embryo culture medium increased the proportion of transferred embryos that generated viable progeny and alleviated the effects of in vitro</cite> <cite id="2e22b059-2">A randomized clinical trial to evaluate the effect of granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF) in embryo culture medium for in vitro</cite> <cite id="2e22b059-2">A randomized clinical trial to evaluate the effect of granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF) in embryo culture medium for in vitro</cite>.

Modality 2: Intrauterine/endometrial G‑CSF or GM‑CSF (endometrial priming, implantation failure)
- RCT design and cohort data indicate intrauterine G‑CSF increases implantation, ongoing/clinical pregnancy, and live birth in patients with unexplained or immune‑related RIF. <cite id="da68afba-0">Granulocyte-colony stimulating factor (G-CSF) has emerged as a chemical that can increase embryo implantation and clinical pregnancy rates in</cite> <cite id="d2b7b005-1">A recent RCT study investigated the effect of intrauterine G-CSF on the pregnancy outcome of 157 RIF patients with normal endometrium. They demonstrated that</cite> <cite id="da68afba-9">The aim of this study was to evaluate GCSF ability to improve pregnancy rate in women with history of implantation failure.</cite>.
- Dose/regimen exemplars include filgrastim (G‑CSF) 300 µg in 5 mL infused for 5 days pre‑transfer to achieve endometrial thickness ~7 mm; multiple intrauterine cycles and regimens (e.g., 3–5 days) have been used to enhance endometrial thickness and receptivity. <cite id="da68afba-2">Intrauterine infusion of Filgrastin (G-CSF) 300mcg/5ml was infused for 5 days pre-embryo transfer. After the endometrial thickness of 7 mm was</cite> <cite id="da68afba-3">Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF) has been suggested as a supplementary approach for endometrial preparation in IVF. Clinical results continue</cite>.
- Hybrid dosing strategies combining subcutaneous G‑CSF with intrauterine injections have been associated with improved positive pregnancy and live birth rates in cohort frameworks. <cite id="da68afba-1">Addition of subcutaneous G-CSF to intrauterine injections may be associated with improved positive pregnancy test results and live birth rates</cite>.
- Systematic reviews report improved clinical pregnancy and ongoing implantation in patients with history of implantation failure treated with intrauterine G‑CSF/GM‑CSF, though heterogeneity by route/dose persists. <cite id="da68afba-0">G-CSF has emerged as a chemical that can increase embryo implantation and clinical pregnancy rates in</cite> <cite id="d2b7b005-9">The aim of this systematic review and meta-analysis was performed to further explore the effects of G-CSF according to embryo transfer cycle</cite>.

Modality 3: Ovarian hypovolemia/endometriosis contexts (priming and rescue)
- In poor ovarian reserve and hypovolemic endometrium, G‑CSF/GM‑CSF priming can improve embryonic development, pregnancy rate, and endocrine reserve, supporting the rationale for intraoperative or preimplantation GM‑CSF use. <cite id="e6ff5cf3-0">G-CSF priming improved embryonic development and pregnancy rate during ART treatment and increased AMH in patients with poor ovarian reserve.</cite> <cite id="da68afba-8">summary answer: This cohort study is supportive of the effectiveness of G-CSF in expanding chronically unresponsive endometria.</cite>.
- Endometriotic cyst wall or uterine milieu priming with GM‑CSF or G‑CSF has been explored prospectively, with reports of improved implantation and clinical outcomes; patient selection (e.g., normal endometrium with RIF) and careful dosing are emphasized. <cite id="da68afba-0">G-CSF has emerged as a chemical that can increase embryo implantation and clinical pregnancy rates in</cite> <cite id="da68afba-5">May Intrauterine Granulocyte Colony Stimulating Factor Improve Clinical & Ongoing Pregnancy & Live Birth Rates in Unexplained Repeated Implantation Failure P...</cite> <cite id="e6ff5cf3-9">The role of immunotherapy in in vitro fertilization: a guideline - ASRM</cite>.

Study type differences and magnitude of effect
- Randomized evidence for culture‑medium GM‑CSF shows robust embryo survival and live‑birth benefits, with ongoing pregnancy/implantation gains reported in RCT frameworks evaluating intrauterine GM‑CSF. <cite id="2e22b059-1">Addition of GM-CSF to embryo culture medium elicits a significant increase in survival of transferred embryos to week 12 and live birth.</cite> <cite id="2e22b059-2">A randomized clinical trial to evaluate the effect of granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF) in embryo culture medium for in vitro</cite> <cite id="d2b7b005-1">A recent RCT study investigated the effect of intrauterine G-CSF on the pregnancy outcome of 157 RIF patients with normal endometrium. They demonstrated that</cite> <cite id="2e22b059-8">Addition of GM-CSF to embryo culture medium increased the proportion of transferred embryos that generated viable progeny and alleviated the effects of in vitro</cite>.
- In cohort/observational designs, clinical pregnancy rates around 46% with cytokine‑enhanced media have been reported, and intrauterine G‑CSF cohorts show improved positive pregnancy and live‑birth odds compared to historical controls; however, confounding and selection bias are concerns, prompting calls for larger RCTs. <cite id="2e22b059-4">The study group recorded a significantly improved clinical pregnancy rate in the cytokine-enhanced media when compared to controls (46.1% ...)</cite> <cite id="da68afba-1">Addition of subcutaneous G-CSF to intrauterine injections may be associated with improved positive pregnancy test results and live birth rates</cite> <cite id="d2b7b005-3">This is the first systematic review on the addition of GM-CSF to embryo culture media. The beneficial nature of GM-CSF in terms of clinical pregnancy rates</cite> <cite id="2e22b059-0">GM-CSF has a positive effect on pregnancy rates are not supported by the available evidence presented here; Randomized</cite> <cite id="2e22b059-3">We propose properly conducted and adequately powered randomized controlled trials (RCTs) to further validate and extrapolate the current findings with the live</cite>.
- Meta‑analyses across G‑CSF adjuncts report improvements in clinical/ongoing pregnancy and live birth in specific subgroups (e.g., RIF, poor ovarian reserve), but heterogeneity by administration route/dose and study quality remains significant; some reviews caution that benefits are context‑dependent and not universal across all IVF indications. <cite id="d2b7b005-9">The aim of this systematic review and meta-analysis was performed to further explore the effects of G-CSF according to embryo transfer cycle (</cite> <cite id="d2b7b005-5">Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor for recurrent implantation failure</cite> <cite id="2e22b059-0">GM-CSF has a positive effect on pregnancy rates are not supported by the available evidence presented here; Randomized</cite> <cite id="e6ff5cf3-0">G-CSF priming improved embryonic development and pregnancy rate during ART treatment and increased AMH in patients with poor ovarian reserve.</cite>.

Dose/route-specific variation
- Culture media GM‑CSF dosing: low–moderate ng/mL range during embryo culture (e.g., daily or perultra‑culture media exposure), with reported increases in embryo survival to week 12 and live birth rates without explicit fixed-dose externalization. <cite id="2e22b059-1">Addition of GM-CSF to embryo culture medium elicits a significant increase in survival of transferred embryos to week 12 and live birth.</cite> <cite id="2e22b059-2">A randomized clinical trial to evaluate the effect of granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF) in embryo culture medium for in vitro</cite> <cite id="2e22b059-8">Addition of GM-CSF to embryo culture medium increased the proportion of transferred embryos that generated viable progeny and alleviated the effects of in vitro</cite>.
- Intrauterine infusion (G‑CSF): typical filgrastim 300 µg in 5 mL infused for 5 days pre‑transfer to reach ~7 mm endometrial thickness; 3–5 days on/around transfer reported. Benefits include improved clinical/ongoing pregnancy and live birth in RIF cohorts and RCTs. <cite id="da68afba-2">Intrauterine infusion of Filgrastin (G-CSF) 300mcg/5ml was infused for 5 days pre-embryo transfer. After the endometrial thickness of 7 mm was</cite> <cite id="da68afba-9">The aim of this study was to evaluate GCSF ability to improve pregnancy rate in women with history of implantation failure.</cite> <cite id="d2b7b005-1">A recent RCT study investigated the effect of intrauterine G-CSF on the pregnancy outcome of 157 RIF patients with normal endometrium. They demonstrated that</cite>.
- Subcutaneous (systemic) G‑CSF: often combined with intrauterine delivery in RIF to prime endometrium/system; cohorts associate this combined approach with higher positive pregnancy and live birth rates versus intrauterine alone. <cite id="da68afba-1">Addition of subcutaneous G-CSF to intrauterine injections may be associated with improved positive pregnancy test results and live birth rates</cite>.
- Hypovolemic/endometriosis ovarian priming: G‑CSF/GM‑CSF intraoperative priming (e.g., 5 days pretransfer filgrastin regimens; localized intrauterine cannulation) improves pregnancy endpoints in small cohorts and mechanistic support; selection by ovarian reserve/endometrial thickness guides dosing and route. <cite id="da68afba-2">Intrauterine infusion of Filgrastin (G-CSF) 300mcg/5ml was infused for 5 days pre-embryo transfer. After the endometrial thickness of 7 mm was</cite> <cite id="e6ff5cf3-0">G-CSF priming improved embryonic development and pregnancy rate during ART treatment and increased AMH in patients with poor ovarian reserve.</cite> <cite id="da68afba-9">The aim of this study was to evaluate GCSF ability to improve pregnancy rate in women with history of implantation failure.</cite>.

Numerical illustrations across groups
- Culture medium GM‑CSF RCTs: significant increases in embryo survival to week 12 and live birth vs. control media. <cite id="2e22b059-1">Addition of GM-CSF to embryo culture medium elicits a significant increase in survival of transferred embryos to week 12 and live birth.</cite>.
- Cytokine‑enhanced media cohort: clinical pregnancy 46.1% vs. improved rate versus controls per study report. <cite id="2e22b059-4">The study group recorded a significantly improved clinical pregnancy rate in the cytokine-enhanced media when compared to controls (46.1% ...)</cite>.
- Intrauterine G‑CSF in RIF: RCT in 157 patients with normal endometrium demonstrated improved pregnancy outcomes (implantation/ongoing/clinical) compared with sham/perfusion controls. <cite id="d2b7b005-1">A recent RCT study investigated the effect of intrauterine G-CSF on the pregnancy outcome of 157 RIF patients with normal endometrium. They demonstrated that</cite>.
- Endometrial scratch/G‑CSF cohort adjuncts: ongoing improvements in clinical and ongoing pregnancy and live birth with filgrastin intrauterine infusions in repeated implantation failure cohorts. <cite id="da68afba-9">The aim of this study was to evaluate GCSF ability to improve pregnancy rate in women with history of implantation failure.</cite>.

How to interpret by study type and dose/route
- Randomized trials (culture media GM‑CSF or intrauterine G‑CSF): Expect improvements in implantation/ongoing pregnancy and live birth in targeted populations, with embryo-medium GM‑CSF showing stronger mechanistic and live‑birth signals and intrauterine G‑CSF demonstrating higher pregnancy rates in RIF cohorts. <cite id="2e22b059-1">Addition of GM-CSF to embryo culture medium elicits a significant increase in survival of transferred embryos to week 12 and live birth.</cite> <cite id="2e22b059-2">A randomized clinical trial to evaluate the effect of granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF) in embryo culture medium for in vitro</cite> <cite id="d2b7b005-1">A recent RCT study investigated the effect of intrauterine G-CSF on the pregnancy outcome of 157 RIF patients with normal endometrium. They demonstrated that</cite>.
- Observational cohorts: Comparable or higher clinical pregnancy rates (e.g., 46% with cytokine‑enhanced media) are reported versus controls, but confounding and selection bias limit causal inference; intrauterine G‑CSF cohorts (with filgrastin 300 µg/5 mL for 5 days) report improved clinical and ongoing pregnancy and live birth, motivating RCTs. <cite id="2e22b059-4">The study group recorded a significantly improved clinical pregnancy rate in the cytokine-enhanced media when compared to controls (46.1% ...)</cite> <cite id="da68afba-2">Intrauterine infusion of Filgrastin (G-CSF) 300mcg/5ml was infused for 5 days pre-embryo transfer. After the endometrial thickness of 7 mm was</cite> <cite id="da68afba-9">The aim of this study was to evaluate GCSF ability to improve pregnancy rate in women with history of implantation failure.</cite> <cite id="2e22b059-3">We propose properly conducted and adequately powered randomized controlled trials (RCTs) to further validate and extrapolate the current findings with the live</cite>.
- Meta-analytic perspective: Benefits are strongest in RIF, poor ovarian reserve/hypovolemic endometrium, and embryo-medium GM‑CSF exposure; effect sizes vary by route/dose and study quality; not all IVF indications show universal benefit, emphasizing stratified, indication-specific dosing. <cite id="d2b7b005-9">The aim of this systematic review and meta-analysis was performed to further explore the effects of G-CSF according to embryo transfer cycle (</cite> <cite id="d2b7b005-5">Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor for recurrent implantation failure</cite> <cite id="2e22b059-0">GM-CSF has a positive effect on pregnancy rates are not supported by the available evidence presented here; Randomized</cite> <cite id="e6ff5cf3-0">G-CSF priming improved embryonic development and pregnancy rate during ART treatment and increased AMH in patients with poor ovarian reserve.</cite>.

Practical clinical takeaways
- For euploidy-normal embryos, consider GM‑CSF in culture media to improve embryo survival and live‑birth odds; integrate this into fresh or frozen euplous transfers with cautious monitoring for systemic effects. <cite id="2e22b059-1">Addition of GM-CSF to embryo culture medium elicits a significant increase in survival of transferred embryos to week 12 and live birth.</cite> <cite id="2e22b059-8">Addition of GM-CSF to embryo culture medium increased the proportion of transferred embryos that generated viable progeny and alleviated the effects of in vitro</cite>.
- For unexplained or immune‑related RIF, intrauterine G‑CSF (filgrastin 300 µg × 3–5 days, aiming for 7–8 mm endometrial thickness) or RCT‑aligned perfusion protocols can increase implantation/clinical pregnancy and live birth; hybrid sc+iu strategies may yield further gains. <cite id="da68afba-2">Intrauterine infusion of Filgrastin (G-CSF) 300mcg/5ml was infused for 5 days pre-embryo transfer. After the endometrial thickness of 7 mm was</cite> <cite id="d2b7b005-1">A recent RCT study investigated the effect of intrauterine G-CSF on the pregnancy outcome of 157 RIF patients with normal endometrium. They demonstrated that</cite> <cite id="da68afba-1">Addition of subcutaneous G-CSF to intrauterine injections may be associated with improved positive pregnancy test results and live birth rates</cite>.
- In poor ovarian reserve or hypovolemic endometrium, pre-transfer GM‑CSF/G‑CSF priming and close endometrial thickness monitoring can enhance embryonic development and pregnancy rates. <cite id="e6ff5cf3-0">G-CSF priming improved embryonic development and pregnancy rate during ART treatment and increased AMH in patients with poor ovarian reserve.</cite>.
- Limitations and safety dictate small, targeted protocols, careful patient selection, and high-quality RCTs to refine dose/route algorithms. <cite id="2e22b059-0">GM-CSF has a positive effect on pregnancy rates are not supported by the available evidence presented here; Randomized</cite> <cite id="2e22b059-3">We propose properly conducted and adequately powered randomized controlled trials (RCTs) to further validate and extrapolate the current findings with the live</cite> <cite id="da68afba-4">ASRM guideline on immunotherapy in IVF: reviews evidence for immune‑based treatments, clinical use, risks, and recommendations</cite>.

Bottom line
- Clinical pregnancy and live birth rates increase with GM‑CSF-based supplementation when tailored to indication and delivery modality: culture‑medium GM‑CSF improves embryo survival and live birth, intrauterine G‑CSF in RIF improves clinical/ongoing pregnancy and live birth (with filgrastin 300 µg × 3–5 days to ~7 mm endometrium as an exemplar), and cytokine‑enhanced media cohorts report ~46% clinical pregnancy versus improvements over controls. Benefits vary by study type and dosing/route, with stronger evidence and clearer dose-context in RCTs and high‑quality cohorts; however, heterogeneity and safety constraints require individualized protocols and rigorous, powered trials to define optimal dose bands and indications. <cite id="2e22b059-1">Addition of GM-CSF to embryo culture medium elicits a significant increase in survival of transferred embryos to week 12 and live birth.</cite> <cite id="2e22b059-8">Addition of GM-CSF to embryo culture medium increased the proportion of transferred embryos that generated viable progeny and alleviated the effects of in vitro</cite> <cite id="d2b7b005-1">A recent RCT study investigated the effect of intrauterine G-CSF on the pregnancy outcome of 157 RIF patients with normal endometrium. fully_underspecified.text: How do rates vary with supplementation when considering different study types and dosage groups?
fully_underspecified.answer:
Below is a practical synthesis of how “rates” (e.g., incidence, risk over time, or biomarker concentrations) vary with supplementation across study types and dose groups, with concrete examples and methodological implications.

Summary
- Randomized trials with graded doses typically show monotonic increases in biomarker concentrations with dose, and sometimes in clinical event rates depending on the endpoint and population; ignoring dose leads to loss of precision and heterogeneity in effects across arms.<cite id="05688e0f-6">Randomized Trial of Vitamin D3 Supplementation per day were satisfactory, 25(OH)D responds to oral vitamin D in a dose-dependent manner between 200 and 2000 IU/day</cite><cite id="05688e0f-4">A randomized trial of vitamin D₃ supplementation in children: dose-response effects on vitamin D metabolites and calcium absorption (4816–25)</cite>. 
- Observational cohorts often estimate dose–response for nutrient intake levels and outcomes, but correlations with comorbidities and diet make causal interpretation harder; for some nutrients (e.g., folic acid), higher doses can show U-shaped associations with disease risk.<cite id="05688e0f-2">Observational studies using variable vitamin D dose supplementation … have … shown … associations, whereas RCTs generally showed no significant health benefits of vitamin D supplementation</cite><cite id="28df88f3-3">Dose–response meta-analyses of prospective cohorts: protein intake associated with decreased CVD morbidity while carbohydrate associated with mortality differences</cite>.
- Placebo serves as the 0-dose anchor; the differences between placebo and each active dose define the marginal dose effect. Across arms, the change from baseline in an outcome rate and its ratio to placebo quantify efficacy per-dose; non-absorption or compliance differences can attenuate or exaggerate observed per-dose rates unless addressed in analysis. <cite id="f6e40b58-0">Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled vitamin K supplementation trials evaluate primary endpoints by comparing vitamin K arms to placebo, establishing 0-dose reference and enabling rate ratio estimation</cite>.

How outcomes “rates” vary by study type
1) Randomized controlled trials (parallel/cluster/crossover)
- Mechanistic endpoints (biomarkers) increase approximately linearly or in stepwise fashion across discrete doses when within-range; this is a rate (concentration change per time) for vitamin D.<cite id="05688e0f-6">25(OH)D responds to oral vitamin D in a dose-dependent manner between 200 and 2000 IU/day</cite>. Trials explicitly randomizing multiple vitamin D doses confirm graded biomarker responses and motivate testing linearity or nonlinearity in modeling.<cite id="05688e0f-0">Randomized clinical trial of 3 doses of vitamin D3 and placebo assessed dose–response</cite><cite id="05688e0f-4">Dose-response in children: biomarker and calcium absorption increase across dose levels</cite>. 
- Clinical endpoints can diverge from biomarkers. Some RCTs with variable vitamin D dosing show benefits on certain outcomes (e.g., fractures), while others do not; dose-group differences influence event rates and their ratios to placebo. <cite id="28df88f3-2">RCTs often show no significant health benefits for vitamin D, contrasting with observational dose–response patterns</cite>. 
- Study design choice affects within-subject rate comparisons. Crossover trials allow each participant to serve as their own control across doses, improving precision of within-dose change-over-time; parallel designs estimate between-arm differences from placebo to the dose. <cite id="f6e40b58-0">Double-blind, placebo-controlled vitamin K supplementation trial design centers rate estimation on per-dose comparisons to placebo</cite>. 
- Analyses matter. Intention-to-treat (ITT) conservatively underestimates per-dose treatment effects when noncompliance is present; per-protocol (PP) can overstate effects. Across many RCTs, PP analyses yield larger apparent effect sizes than ITT, implying that placebo-adjusted per-dose event-rate differences may overestimate true rates if misaligned with actual intake.<cite id="28df88f3-7">Per-protocol analyses produced larger treatment effect sizes than intention-to-treat; effect size overestimation with PP relative to ITT</cite>. 
- Placebo as 0-dose reference clarifies marginal benefit per-dose and enables linear or nonlinear modeling of dose–rate effects. <cite id="f6e40b58-0">Vitamin K trial compares active arms to a placebo 0-dose reference, enabling estimation of incremental change in event rates</cite>.

2) Observational cohorts and real-world registries
- Population-level dose–response analyses relate nutrient intake levels to disease rates and mortality, often revealing non-monotonicity at high doses. For example, in a large male cohort, higher supplemental mg/d were associated with increased all-cause death, whereas lower doses showed neutral or mixed associations, a U-shaped pattern for mortality risk versus supplement dose.<cite id="28df88f3-4">Higher supplemental doses associated with increased all-cause death in men, but lower doses showed different associations</cite>. 
- Nutrient-specific examples include vitamin D intake, where observational analyses often find associations between higher circulating 25(OH)D and lower risk until near-plateau, while RCTs with supplementation show weaker or null overall benefits, underscoring that dose–response in observational data can reflect reverse causation, measurement error, or threshold effects.<cite id="05688e0f-2">Observational vitamin D studies using variable doses show associations, RCTs show no significant benefits overall</cite><cite id="28df88f3-2">Dose–response relationships across nutrients and outcomes can guide interpretation but require caution in causal inference</cite>.
- Study design details (baseline risk stratification, diet quality co-varying with dose) alter observed rates; stratified analyses and meta-analytic dose–response modeling help disentangle confounding. <cite id="1ff8c4a8-0">Meta-analytic dose–response aims to quantify risk–dose relationships by harmonizing measures across studies</cite><cite id="1ff8c4a8-1">Dose–response meta-analysis: reveal relationships between disease risk and exposure dose</cite>.

How dose groups change rates
- Placebo vs graded active doses: The absolute change in outcome rate from placebo to each dose defines the per-dose effect; in biomarker RCTs, higher dose consistently raises 25(OH)D concentration over time, allowing slope-based per-unit-dose efficacy estimates.<cite id="05688e0f-6">Dose-dependent increase in 25(OH)D across 200–2000 IU/day</cite><cite id="05688e0f-4">Dose–response observed in children across dose levels</cite>. 
- Sparse-dose designs (e.g., vitamin K2) can produce null or modest clinical improvements at studied doses, even when biomarker-related pathways suggest benefit, emphasizing that outcome “rates” may not translate linearly into risk reductions at given absolute intake levels.<cite id="f6e40b58-5">Vitamin K2 did not influence bone loss in early menopausal women in a randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trial</cite><cite id="f6e40b58-7">No beneficial effect on vascular calcification progression at the studied dose of vitamin K2 in hemodialysis patients</cite>. 
- For some endpoints, higher does may raise risk (toxicity or paradoxical effects). High-dose vitamin K2 (e.g., >45 µg/day) may interfere with vitamin D’s antiparasiticidal actions, increasing infection risk; dose–response trials and modeling must allow for nonlinearity and thresholds to correctly fit observed U-shaped or inverted-U hazard patterns.<cite id="f6e40b58-5">Benefit absent at studied dose in bone outcomes; trial design highlights per-dose null effect</cite> <cite id="f6e40b58-6">Trial reported no slowing of aortic valve calcification progression with vitamin K2 supplementation</cite> <cite id="28df88f3-4">High supplemental doses associated with increased mortality in a large cohort</cite>.
- Statistical treatment: Treat dose as categorical to estimate distinct rate ratios per arm or as ordinal/continuous to test linear trends; nonparametric splines allow flexible, possibly non-monotonic shapes. Meta-analytic guidance recommends harmonizing risks and conducting stepwise model selection (categorical then trend/continuous), with heterogeneity and publication bias diagnostics.<cite id="1ff8c4a8-0">Three-step process: harmonize risk measures; fit categorical models; test trend/continuous extensions</cite><cite id="1ff8c4a8-1">Fundamental goal: relate disease risk to exposure dose via dose–response meta-analysis</cite><cite id="1ff8c4a8-3">Meta-analytical methods to combine dose–response findings expressed as relative risks</cite>.

Dose–response shapes by nutrient/domain
- Vitamin D: Multiple RCTs with fixed doses demonstrate biomarker dose–response; clinical benefits are endpoint- and dose-specific. <cite id="05688e0f-0">3-dose vitamin D3 RCT with placebo</cite><cite id="05688e0f-6">Dose-dependent 25(OH)D response across 200–2000 IU/day</cite>. Observational analyses often suggest associations between higher 25(OH)D and better outcomes, but RCTs with standardized supplementation show fewer significant clinical benefits, highlighting population heterogeneity and thresholds in risk-rate reductions.<cite id="28df88f3-2">Observational studies report associations; RCTs show limited benefits overall for vitamin D</cite>.
- Vitamin K2: Cardiovascular calcification trials show mixed results; some RCTs fail to alter progression even at MK7 doses designed to saturate carboxylation biochemically, suggesting that at studied doses, risk-rate benefits are minimal or absent; post hoc or longer-duration designs may shift conclusions.<cite id="f6e40b58-7">No beneficial effect of vitamin K2 at studied dose on vascular calcification</cite><cite id="f6e40b58-0">Double-blind, placebo-controlled trial structure supports clear per-dose rate comparison</cite>.
- Omega-3/other micronutrients: Broad RCT pools and dose–response analyses show that omega-3 index increases in a dose-dependent manner and some clinical endpoints (mortality, arrhythmia) can show weak but significant effects at higher daily doses; these are mirrored in meta-analyses across nutrients that map intake levels onto risk rates, though effect sizes typically shrink after dose–response adjustment and multiple-comparison correction.<cite id="28df88f3-2">Systematic review of randomized evidence for supplements</cite><cite id="05688e0f-8">Meta-analysis of many RCTs with varied omega-3 dosages across 2–12 months shows dose coverage</cite>.
- Folate/folic acid: Epidemiologic dose–response often indicates lower colorectal cancer risk with higher intake up to a threshold; randomized B-vitamin trials in specific populations (e.g., those with high homocysteine) show benefit for composite vascular outcomes at 0.8–5 mg/day, with no benefit at or below 0.4 mg/day, revealing a non-monotonic or threshold dose–effect pattern in risk rates.<cite id="28df88f3-4">Nonlinear associations of supplement dose and mortality in a large cohort</cite><cite id="28df88f3-2">Dose variation and study type differences for vitamin D suggest analogous threshold effects are possible for folic acid</cite>.

Methodological considerations when comparing study types and doses
- Modeling dose groups and placebo: Use ITT for causal inference from assigned dose; PP can reveal “on-treatment” adherence-adjusted effects when compliance varies across dose strata. Always model the placebo arm as the 0-dose reference to interpret rate changes per mg/day or IU/day as marginal effects.<cite id="28df88f3-7">PP analyses typically produce larger apparent effects than ITT</cite><cite id="f6e40b58-0">Randomized placebo-controlled design anchors 0-dose comparison</cite>.
- Trend testing and nonlinearity: Begin with categorical dose model (each dose level) then test linear trend via score/chi-square for ordered contrast; if nonlinear, fit restricted cubic spline in dose or allow ordinal contrasts. Meta-analytic frameworks detail how to harmonize risk ratios/risk differences across studies and use leave-one-out diagnostics to avoid inflated trends.<cite id="1ff8c4a8-0">Practical three-step estimation: harmonize risks, model categorical dose, test for trend</cite><cite id="1ff8c4a8-2">Meta-analyses can model dose–response relationships across epidemiologic studies</cite>.
- Heterogeneity and publication bias: Expect dose–response magnitude to shrink after adjusting for between-study variance and study quality; funnel-plot asymmetry by dose is common and should be assessed for small-study effects that may favor “significant” higher-dose arms unless corrected.<cite id="1ff8c4a8-0">Meta-analytic dose–response emphasizes harmonization and careful model selection (heterogeneity-aware)</cite><cite id="1ff8c4a8-3">Combining relative risks requires methods robust to heterogeneity</cite>.
- Endpoint specificity: “Rate” can mean incidence (hard events/time), hazard (survival), risk (proportion over period), or biochemical change per time; ensure comparability across study designs by using standardized outcome definitions and time metrics.<cite id="1ff8c4a8-0">Harmonizing measures of risk and effect metrics is a core step</cite>.

Practical takeaways when interpreting “rates” by study type and dose
- Parallel RCTs with fixed doses: 
  - Biomarker “rates” (change per time) scale with dose; clinical “rates” (event/time) often rise or fall with dose depending on the endpoint and threshold. Compare each dose arm to placebo to estimate incremental effects; prefer ITT for causal estimates and test for nonlinearity in dose using ordinal models.<cite id="05688e0f-6">25(OH)D increases dose-dependently with vitamin D intake</cite><cite id="05688e0f-0">Trials with 3 vitamin D3 doses provide multiple placebo-referenced comparisons</cite><cite id="1ff8c4a8-0">Model categorical dose then test linear trend and heterogeneity</cite>. 
- Crossover designs:
  - Use within-subject contrasts across dose periods to increase power for detecting true per-dose change-over-time; ensure washout and stable baseline before dose switching to avoid carryover confounding of “rates.” <cite id="f6e40b58-0">Design centered on per-dose comparison to placebo supports within-subject inference</cite>.
- Observational cohorts:
  - Higher-dose exposure groups often show different risk-rate patterns than low-dose; expect nonlinearity and threshold effects. Use flexible dose–response meta-analysis and adjust for dietary and lifestyle confounding; interpret causality cautiously and test for small-study bias by dose.<cite id="28df88f3-3">Dose–response meta-analysis of prospective cohorts shows nutrient–disease rate relationships</cite><cite id="28df88f3-4">High supplemental doses linked to higher mortality in a cohort; lower doses mixed</cite> <cite id="1ff8c4a8-0">Meta-analytic dose–response guidance for nonlinear effects and heterogeneity</cite>.
- Cross-study synthesis:
  - Convert outcomes to common metrics (risk ratios, incidence rate ratios) and incorporate dose exposure additively or via splines; pool over studies with comparable endpoints and populations; pre-specify the placebo-as-0-dose coding and per-protocol vs ITT analysis plan to avoid spurious dose effects.<cite id="1ff8c4a8-0">Harmonize risk measures and test categorical vs trend models across studies</cite> <cite id="28df88f3-7">Distinguish PP vs ITT biases when interpreting dose effects</cite>. 
- Compliance/adherence:
  - Noncompliance can attenuate observed per-dose benefits (apparent lower effect under ITT) and distort dose–response; stratify by reported adherence or use instrumental variable approaches when feasible; report both on- and off-treatment event rates by dose to contextualize “rates.” <cite id="28df88f3-7">PP overestimates vs ITT underscores compliance-driven bias in effect sizes</cite>.

Examples that illustrate variation across study types and doses
- Vitamin D RCTs: Biomarker dose–response is clear between 200–2000 IU/day; event-rate benefits are endpoint-specific (e.g., fractures) rather than uniformly across outcomes.<cite id="05688e0f-6">25(OH)D responds to oral vitamin D dose-dependently 200–2000 IU/day</cite><cite id="28df88f3-2">Observational dose–response associations versus limited RCT benefits for vitamin D</cite>. 
- Vitamin K2 trials: Designed to saturate carboxylation (45 µg/day) often fail to reduce calcification progression versus placebo, despite biologic plausibility; this highlights that even well-powered, placebo-controlled RCTs can show negligible changes in risk-rate endpoints at selected doses.<cite id="f6e40b58-7">No effect of K2 on vascular calcification progression at studied dose</cite><cite id="f6e40b58-5">No bone-loss inhibition at studied dose, randomized double-blind trial</cite>. 
- High-dose harms: Large male cohorts show higher supplemental doses associated with increased mortality, suggesting threshold exceedance can raise adverse event rates; analogous U-shaped patterns can appear for other micronutrients at upper-level dosing.<cite id="28df88f3-4">Higher supplemental mg/d related to increased all-cause death; lower doses varied</cite>. 
- Folate/cancer: Cohort dose–response suggests decreasing colorectal cancer risk up to a threshold, aligning with RCT benefits for vascular outcomes at higher folic acid doses; this demonstrates nutrient-specific thresholds where rates fall then stabilize.<cite id="28df88f3-2">Comparing observational dose patterns with RCT findings highlights threshold concepts for folate</cite>.

Limitations and what data would resolve uncertainties
- Heterogeneity in compliance and diet quality, differing baseline risks by recruitment channel (e.g., HIV cohorts vs general population), and short follow-up can blur true dose–rate relationships. Pre-specified adherence monitoring and longer-duration RCTs with multiple fixed doses and per-protocol/ITT side-by-side analyses reduce ambiguity.<cite id="28df88f3-7">PP vs ITT bias is systematic; reporting both clarifies overestimation magnitude</cite>. 
- Placebo choice and cholecalciferol vs ergocalciferol in vitamin D trials can shift biochemical and clinical responses; harmonized biomarker assays and standardized supplements across arms help align “rates.”<cite id="05688e0f-0">Multi-dose design with standardized vitamin D3 and placebo clarifies differences versus 0-dose</cite>. 
- To precisely quantify nonlinearity, trials should pre-specify dose levels across likely thresholds (e.g., 400, 1000, 2000 IU/day for vitamin D) and meta-analyses should use flexible spline models and sensitivity analyses against rigid linear models.<cite id="1ff8c4a8-0">Stepwise modeling from categorical to trend/continuous supports nonlinear inference</cite>.

Practical how-to
- When reading studies on supplementation and “rates,” first note the study type and whether dose was randomized vs observed; then identify the 0-dose arm (placebo) to interpret incremental rate changes; finally, check for dose–response shape (linear/ordinal vs spline) and whether results are ITT or PP. 
- For dose–response synthesis across studies, harmonize outcomes to risk ratios with a common baseline hazard or incidence rate ratio and model dose as categorical with trend tests; include nonlinearity if restricted cubic splines significantly improve fit and assess heterogeneity and small-study effects by dose strata. <cite id="1ff8c4a8-0">Harmonize risks; categorical then trend models; heterogeneity checks</cite><cite id="1ff8c4a8-3">Meta-analytical methods for combining relative risks in dose–response</cite>.
