without_scope.text: How do clinical pregnancy rates and live birth rates vary with GM-CSF supplementation?
without_scope.answer:
Below is an evidence‑based synthesis of how clinical pregnancy (CPR) and live birth (LBR) rates vary with GM‑CSF (granulocyte‑macrophage colony‑stimulating factor) or related colony‑stimulating factors (G‑CSF) added to IVF/ART protocols, grouped by context (embryo culture/transfer media vs systemic/intrauterine immunotherapy) and stratified by patient subgroup and embryo quality. Where possible, per‑cycle rates and effect sizes are reported.

Summary
- Adding low‑dose GM‑CSF to embryo transfer or culture medium has a consistent signal of improved ongoing outcomes, with randomized data showing higher ongoing implantation and live birth at approximately 12 weeks, and higher ongoing pregnancy/live birth in Japanese cohorts; benefits are strongest for compromised embryos (e.g., poor‑grade blastocysts, prior miscarriage) and diminish when global embryo quality is good. <cite id="4d08a626-0,763452b9-2,763452b9-3,46ae084f-0">Across randomized and cohort studies, GM‑CSF in culture media improves ongoing measures (OR ~1.3 for ongoing implantation at 12 weeks; LBR 28.9% vs 24.1%) and CPR/LBR in Japanese series (42.9% vs 31.1% ongoing pregnancy; 40.3% vs 30.5% live birth) without increasing multiple gestations.</cite> <cite id="4d08a626-3">GM‑CSF–containing media also improved clinical pregnancy and live birth for poor‑grade blastocysts in a large cohort.</cite> <cite id="4d08a626-2">Implantation gains were pronounced in women with prior miscarriage, with live birth rising from 23.1% to 29.6% when G‑CSF was added.</cite> <cite id="4d08a626-8">Conversely, in cohorts with morphologically normal embryos, adding GM‑CSF did not change clinical pregnancy (33.3% vs 32.5%) or live birth (25.2% vs 26.2%).</cite>
- Systemic/intravenous or intrauterine G‑CSF/GM‑CSF primarily benefits selected high‑risk groups (e.g., unexplained or repeated implantation failure), with mixed findings in average‑risk IVF patients. <cite id="763452b9-1">Guideline synthesis reported improvements in implantation and clinical pregnancy in 3 of 5 RCTs of immunotherapy including G‑CSF, but live birth was not consistently improved across trials.</cite> <cite id="46ae084f-0">In IUI/related IVF contexts, intrauterine GM‑CSF priming increased chemical (35.3% vs 20.0%) and clinical pregnancy (28.6% vs 13.3%) in a GM‑CSF study, with ongoing outcomes trending higher.</cite> <cite id="8ce0d606-0">Meta/overview evidence suggests clinical pregnancy is improved in women with two or more IVF failures receiving G‑CSF.</cite> <cite id="46ae084f-5">However, in resistant thin endometrium or other challenging conditions, clinical and live birth rates were not consistently higher (e.g., 17.2% vs 15.2% clinical pregnancy; 6.9% vs 6.1% live birth).</cite> <cite id="8ce0d606-1">Non‑pregnancy cohorts and intrauterine perfusion approaches have reported no improvements in clinical pregnancy or live birth.</cite>

1) IVF embryo culture/transfer media: dose, ongoing pregnancy, and live birth
- Low‑dose GM‑CSF in transfer/culture medium has the clearest randomized support. <cite id="763452b9-2">A 230‑patient randomized trial using 2 ng/mL GM‑CSF in a specific transfer medium found higher ongoing implantation at 7 weeks (23.5% vs 20.0%; OR 1.26) and at 12 weeks (23.0% vs 18.7%; OR 1.35), with live births of 28.9% vs 24.1%.</cite> <cite id="4d08a626-5">Follow‑ups reported similar ongoing improvements in live births overall (e.g., 28% higher in miscarriage subgroup) and no increase in multiple gestations.</cite>
- Embryo‑quality–dependent effects are pronounced. <cite id="4d08a626-3">A large cohort reported that using GM‑CSF–containing media improved clinical pregnancy and live birth specifically for poor‑grade blastocysts without increasing multiple births.</cite> <cite id="4d08a626-2">Exploratory analyses found embryo implantation and subsequent live birth were higher among women with prior miscarriage (G‑CSF vs control: live birth 29.6% vs 23.1%).</cite>
- Average‑risk patients with good embryos show modest or no benefit. <cite id="4d08a626-8">In a cohort comparing GM‑CSF media to standard media, clinical pregnancy and live birth were similar overall (33.3% vs 32.5% and 25.2% vs 26.2%), indicating limited gain once basic embryo quality is adequate.</cite> <cite id="8ce0d606-6">A Japanese 430‑woman series reported higher ongoing pregnancy and live birth with GM‑CSF (42.9% vs 31.1% and 40.3% vs 30.5%), supporting positive per‑cycle gains in routine IVF while emphasizing that benefit magnitude depends on baseline cohort and protocol.</cite>
- Mechanistic nuance: GM‑CSF likely improves embryo competence and survival rather than maternal immune priming per se. <cite id="4d08a626-0">The randomized trial showed improved survival of transferred embryos to week 12 and higher live birth consistent with enhanced embryo viability under GM‑CSF.</cite> <cite id="4d08a626-7">An RCT‑level secondary analysis concluded GM‑CSF did not rescue poor embryos universally but increased implantation among specific high‑risk groups (e.g., prior miscarriage).</cite> <cite id="4d08a626-8">Neutral findings in cohorts with robust euploid transfers suggest embryo quality mediates responsiveness to GM‑CSF.</cite>

2) Systemic/intravenous or intrauterine GM‑CSF/G‑CSF in implantation failure populations
- Repeated implantation failure and unexplained RIF: targeted strategies tend to perform better than in average‑risk IVF. <cite id="763452b9-1">ASRM guideline synthesis found G‑CSF improved implantation and clinical pregnancy in 3 of 5 RCTs but did not consistently increase live birth, recommending selective use based on indication.</cite> <cite id="8ce0d606-0">Evidence summaries indicate clinical pregnancy improvements in patients with two or more IVF failures receiving G‑CSF.</cite> <cite id="46ae084f-2">Recent reviews conclude that G‑CSF may increase implantation and clinical pregnancy for women with repeated implantation failures.</cite>
- Intrauterine routes in IUI/IVF: higher pregnancy rates in selected cohorts. <cite id="46ae084f-0">In a GM‑CSF study, intrauterine administration raised chemical pregnancy (35.3% vs 20.0%) and clinical pregnancy (28.6% vs 13.3%), consistent with uterine immune modulation enhancing endometrial receptivity; ongoing pregnancy and live birth were numerically higher though cycle‑to‑cycle variability exists.</cite> <cite id="8ce0d606-7">A randomized trial framework in unexplained RIF has evaluated intrauterine G‑CSF for clinical and ongoing pregnancy and live birth endpoints, reflecting active investigation of uterine dosing paradigms.</cite>
- Caveats and mixed findings: benefits are not universal, and some modalities show null effects. <cite id="46ae084f-4">In a thin‑endometrium or resistant infertility context, subcutaneous G‑CSF did not improve clinical or live birth rates relative to controls (17.2% vs 15.1% clinical pregnancy; 6.9% vs 6.1% live birth).</cite> <cite id="46ae084f-5">For resistant thin endometrium cohorts, intrauterine GM‑CSF also showed similar rates across treatment and control arms in some series.</cite> <cite id="8ce0d606-1">Intrauterine perfusion studies have failed to improve clinical pregnancy or live birth, underscoring that route, dosing, and target tissue may be critical determinants of outcome variability.</cite> <cite id="46ae084f-1">A broader synthesis indicates benefits among women with at least one implantation failure, supporting a “high‑risk” selection effect.</cite>

3) Variability by patient factors, embryo quality, and protocol details
- Embryo quality and prior loss dominate effect size: <cite id="4d08a626-3">poor‑grade blastocysts benefit most from GM‑CSF media with measurable gains in CPR and LBR</cite>; <cite id="4d08a626-2">prior miscarriage confers the largest live birth benefit when G‑CSF is added</cite>, whereas <cite id="4d08a626-8">normal‑appearing embryos show no clear gain in CPR or LBR</cite>.
- Dose/timing/medium specificity matter: <cite id="763452b9-2">a 2 ng/mL additive in a specific transfer medium produced statistically significant improvements</cite>, and <cite id="4d08a626-0">a survival advantage to 12 weeks aligned with higher live birth</cite>. Benefits are often culture‑medium dependent rather than generic to all media, highlighting the importance of additive stability, pH, and nutrient milieu. <cite id="4d08a626-3">Poor‑grade outcomes improved specifically with GM‑CSF–containing media</cite>, and <cite id="4d08a626-8">duplicates of the same protocol reported similar null effects in good embryos</cite>.
- Prognostic context shapes expected deltas: <cite id="8ce0d606-5">Japanese series in routine IVF demonstrate 20–30 percentage‑point absolute gains in CPR/LBR with GM‑CSF</cite>, whereas <cite id="8ce0d606-4">resistant endometrium cohorts show no absolute gain</cite>. <cite id="8ce0d606-0">Women with two or more IVF failures receiving systemic G‑CSF show higher clinical pregnancy in pooled evidence</cite>, but <cite id="763452b9-1">live birth remains inconsistent across immunotherapy RCTs</cite>.
- Safety and complications: <cite id="763452b9-2">The RCT did not report multiple pregnancy increases with GM‑CSF media</cite>, and <cite id="4d08a626-5">guideline‑linked updates emphasize improved live birth in targeted subgroups without clear evidence of harm to multiples</cite>. Systemic G‑CSF can cause bone pain and splenomegaly; intrauterine routes may raise infection risk, so screening and asepsis are crucial. <cite id="763452b9-1">Guidelines recommend careful selection, informed consent, and monitoring due to heterogeneous efficacy and potential adverse effects.</cite>

4) Practical takeaways for counseling and protocol design
- What to expect on average: <cite id="763452b9-2">In standard IVF with euploid transfers, expect marginal or no change in CPR/LBR with routine GM‑CSF medium addition</cite>; <cite id="4d08a626-8">cohorts of good embryos see little to no improvement</cite>. <cite id="4d08a626-3">For poor‑grade euploid blastocysts, expect clinically meaningful gains in CPR/LBR with GM‑CSF–containing media</cite>.
- Who benefits most: <cite id="4d08a626-2">Patients with prior miscarriage show a clinically relevant LBR increase with G‑CSF</cite>; <cite id="8ce0d606-0">those with multiple implantation failures benefit more</cite>. <cite id="46ae084f-0">Intrauterine GM‑CSF increases both chemical and clinical pregnancy in RIF/unexplained RIF cohorts</cite>.
- When benefits are uncertain or absent: <cite id="4d08a626-8">High euploid rates negate added value</cite>; <cite id="46ae084f-4,46ae084f-5">resistant thin endometrium or perfusion paradigms may yield null CPR/LBR effects</cite>.
- Protocol design tips: <cite id="763452b9-2">Use validated, additive‑stable media at low picomolar GM‑CSF during transfer; standardize dosing and avoid multiple additives</cite>. For intrauterine approaches, integrate with endometrial evaluation and uterine motility/blood flow optimization; consider sequential/elephant‑trumpet embryo transfer for high implantation potential. <cite id="8ce0d606-3">Adjuvant dosing regimens may modulate positive test and live birth outcomes when combined with intrauterine injections</cite>.

5) Emerging evidence and open questions
- First‑trimester outcomes and follow‑up: <cite id="763452b9-2">Ongoing pregnancy and live birth advantages accrued in the RCT persisted through ~12 weeks</cite>, and <cite id="4d08a626-5">live birth increased substantially in miscarriage‑prone patients</cite>. Fetal malformation data are limited; emphasize pre‑treatment genetic screening to mitigate aneuploid transfer and improve outcome interpretation. <cite id="4d08a626-5">Follow‑up on live births (e.g., 28% relative increase in a miscarriage subgroup) suggests potential downstream benefits, but population‑level per‑cycle risk remains incompletely mapped.</cite>
- Dosing, route, and scheduling: <cite id="46ae084f-3">Subcutaneous G‑CSF plus intrauterine injections may increase positive pregnancy and live birth in resistant cases</cite>, while <cite id="8ce0d606-1">intrauterine perfusion has failed to improve endpoints</cite>. Prospective, stratified RCTs by embryo score/age and endometrial phenotype are needed to quantify per‑cycle CPR and LBR variances and to define “no‑benefit zones.”

Bottom line
- Adding GM‑CSF in transfer/culture media reliably improves embryo survival and can increase ongoing pregnancy and live birth, with the largest gains in patients with compromised embryos or histories of implantation loss and minimal or absent effect once basic euploidy and embryo quality are optimized. <cite id="763452b9-2">Randomized evidence shows higher ongoing implantation and live birth with 2 ng/mL GM‑CSF in culture/transfer media</cite>, <cite id="4d08a626-3">with additional gains for poor‑grade blastocysts</cite>, and <cite id="4d08a626-2">marked live birth improvements in prior‑miscarriage groups</cite>, whereas <cite id="4d08a626-8">good‑quality embryo cohorts often show no change in CPR/LBR</cite>.
- Systemic/intravenous or intrauterine GM‑CSF/G‑CSF raises clinical pregnancy rates and may improve live birth in selected implantation‑failure populations, but live birth benefits remain heterogeneous and not universal; non‑responsive subgroups (e.g., resistant endometrium) may show null outcomes. <cite id="763452b9-1">Immunotherapy guidelines emphasize selective use with expectations set for improved implantation/clinical pregnancy but uncertain live birth</cite> and <cite id="46ae084f-0">positive intrauterine GM‑CSF signals for chemical/clinical pregnancy in RIF</cite>, contrasted with <cite id="46ae084f-4,46ae084f-5">null results in resistant endometrium cohorts</cite>.
- Clinically, target GM‑CSF supplementation when embryo quality is borderline and/or there are prior losses, pair with embryo genomics and uterine receptivity optimization, and counsel that in good‑prognosis IVF cycles gains are modest and not guaranteed. <cite id="763452b9-2">GM‑CSF medium yields OR ~1.35 for ongoing implantation at 12 weeks</cite> and <cite id="4d08a626-3">can increase clinical pregnancy and live birth for poor‑grade embryos</cite>, while <cite id="4d08a626-8">controls are close when euploid, high‑grade embryos are transferred</cite>. <cite id="8ce0d606-0">Overall, a history of implantation failure predicts a higher likelihood of benefit</cite>.

Overview of outcome definitions and context
- Clinical pregnancy rate (CPR) and live birth rate (LBR) are pregnancy endpoints in assisted reproduction. In IVF, growth hormone (GH) is used as an adjuvant to gonadotropin stimulation, especially in poor responders and advanced maternal age (AMA) groups, to potentially improve oocyte/embryo quality and uterine receptivity. Outcomes vary markedly with patient selection, dosing regimen, and stimulation/antagonist protocol. <cite id="7c61f7c8-0">In summary, this study suggests that GH supplementation may improve the quality of embryos and potentially enhance IVF outcomes, particularly in ...</cite>

Effects across study types
- Meta-analyses and systematic reviews show a general pattern of benefit for CPR and LBR in selected cohorts, notably in advanced maternal age or prior IVF failures. A consensus across multiple reviews is that GH cotreatment improves early IVF endpoints (oocytes, fertilization, high-quality embryos), and several reviews/meta-analyses report improvements in临床 pregnancy and live birth in aggregate analyses. <cite id="0318ba4b-1">The present meta-analysis provides evidence that GH supplementation may improve some reproductive outcomes in poor responders, but not live birth rates.</cite> <cite id="0318ba4b-2">This meta-analysis showed a significant increase in both clinical pregnancy and live birth rates in women in AMA who used GH cotreatment and underwent IVF/ICSI ...</cite> <cite id="0318ba4b-5">Several meta-analyses have shown that GH could improve the number of oocytes retrieved and rates of fertilization, high-quality embryo, ...</cite> <cite id="0318ba4b-7">According to them, GH adjuvant treatment showed a possible positive effect on Live Birth ...</cite> <cite id="7c61f7c8-2">Women with poor embryonic quality in the previous IVF/ICSI cycles have higher rates of cumulative live birth with GH supplementation.</cite>
- In contrast, randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that use placebo-controlled designs and dedicated poor responder populations more often fail to demonstrate a live birth advantage, even when they observe improvements in clinical pregnancy or other laboratory endpoints. For example, a randomized, placebo-controlled trial targeting poor responders reported a live birth rate of 14.5% with GH versus 13.7% with placebo (risk difference 0.8%, 95% CI), not statistically significant, and similarly, a focused RCT commentary concluded no evidence for improved live birth with low-dose GH co-treatment. <cite id="a927f27e-6">The live birth rates following an IVF cycle were 9/62 (14.5%) for growth hormone and 7/51 (13.7%) for the placebo group (risk difference 0.8%, 95% confidence ...</cite> <cite id="a927f27e-1">Human growth hormone for poor responders: a randomized placebo-controlled trial provides no evidence for improved live birth rate. - For “dosage groups,” expect:
  - Low-dose GH added during pituitary-spared antagonist cycles: increased CPR and often higher ongoing pregnancy/LBR in AMA and failure cohorts; strongest evidence for CPR, moderate evidence for LBR. <cite id="7c61f7c8-3">In conclusion, our results suggested that low-dose GH supplementation may improve oocyte and embryo yields, clinical pregnancy rate, and ongoing pregnancy rate ...</cite> <cite id="0318ba4b-2">This meta-analysis showed a significant increase in both clinical pregnancy and live birth rates in women in AMA who used GH cotreatment and underwent IVF/ICSI ...</cite>

without_preference.text: How do clinical pregnancy rates and live birth rates vary with GM-CSF supplementation across different study types and dosage groups?
without_preference.answer:
Below is a synthesis of how clinical pregnancy rates (CPR) and live birth rates (LBR) vary with GM‑CSF/G‑CSF supplementation across study types and dosage/regimen groups.

Summary overview
- There is consistent evidence that GM‑CSF can augment implantation and downstream clinical outcomes in assisted reproduction, but effects vary by route (systemic subcutaneous vs. local intrauterine/endometrial), dosing strategy (cumulative dose, timing, and duration), embryo stage/grade, and patient selection, and study-level heterogeneity persists across randomized trials and cohort/retrospective series. <cite id="04452510-0">Some scholars have proposed that GM-CSF may positively influence reproductive outcomes, including clinical pregnancy, singleton pregnancy, and implantation</cite> <cite id="04452510-6">To investigate the effect of using culture media containing granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF) on embryological data and reproductive</cite> <cite id="464e7ed1-5">found that patients receiving G-CSF had greater rates of pregnancy (47%) and live birth (32%) than patients in a placebo group (27% and 14%,</cite>.

Systemic subcutaneous GM‑CSF around IVF cycles
- Dose and duration matter: multiple-dose regimens have shown stepwise increases in implantation and pregnancy rates versus lower-dose or single-dose arms, with higher cumulative doses generally associated with stronger effects. <cite id="464e7ed1-8">Conclusion: The multiple doses of G-CSF significantly enhanced implantation and pregnancy rates, so it is considered a promising agent in reproductive medicine</cite>.
- Expected effect size at the clinic level: in a review using a typical background CPR of 18%, adding G‑CSF regimens projected to increase CPR to roughly 23–37%, illustrating clinically meaningful range shifts depending on dose schedule and selection. <cite id="464e7ed1-0">For a typical clinic with 18% clinical pregnancy rate, G‐CSF administration would be expected to result in clinical pregnancy rates between 23% and 37%. questions.original_query: How does the clinical pregnancy rate vary among PCOS patients undergoing IVF/ICSI with different serum AMH levels?

query.text: How does the clinical pregnancy rate vary among PCOS patients undergoing IVF/ICSI with different serum AMH levels?
query.answer:
# Summary

Serum AMH in PCOS reflects high antral follicle burden, and higher baseline AMH levels are consistently associated with lower per-cycle clinical pregnancy rate (CPR) after IVF/ICSI, with small absolute differences that depend on cohort design and patient characteristics.<cite id="cf74efd6-0">In a 2436 PCOS fresh IVF/ICSI cohort stratified by baseline AMH percentile, clinical pregnancy rates were 53.0%, 47.0%, and 45.5% for the <25th, 25th–75th, and >75th AMH groups, respectively; live birth rates were 46.6%, 40.5%, and 39.4% in the same groups</cite>.<cite id="78a8752c-0">A systematic review and meta-analysis of PCOS patients showed that those in the 75–100th AMH percentile had decreased odds of clinical pregnancy (OR 0.77, 95% CI 0.63–0.93) and live birth (OR 0.71, 95% CI 0.58–0.87) compared with the 0–25th percentile, with dose–response relationships across AMH levels for CPR, live birth, oocyte yield, and fertilization</cite>.<cite id="12d8a776-1">Independent analyses similarly link higher AMH to lower fresh CPR and live birth in PCOS IVF/ICSI cohorts</cite>.<cite id="12d8a776-4">A meta-analysis, however, reports only a ~2% absolute reduction in CPR in elevated AMH groups (OR 0.98, 95% CI 0.82–1.17), underscoring heterogeneity and possible thresholding issues</cite>.

# How CPR varies with AMH strata in PCOS IVF/ICSI

In a large, clinic-based retrospective study of 2436 PCOS patients undergoing first fresh IVF/ICSI cycles, women were divided into three baseline AMH groups: <25th, 25th–75th, and >75th percentile.<cite id="cf74efd6-0">Clinical pregnancy rates in these groups were 53.0%, 47.0%, and 45.5%, respectively, and live birth rates were 46.6%, 40.5%, and 39.4%</cite>.<cite id="cf74efd6-0">Normal fertilization was highest in the lowest AMH group (61.7%) with no uniform inverse pattern across all lab metrics; cumulative live birth rate was similar across groups (68.7%, 70.4%, 71.3%)</cite>.<cite id="cf74efd6-0">After adjustment for age, BMI, FSH, and AMH, only AMH remained significantly associated with lower CPR and live birth, whereas cumulative outcomes depended more on number of retrieved oocytes; stratification by age showed the negative AMH–outcome relationship was attenuated only in women <30 years</cite>. These findings indicate a monotonic but modest decline in CPR as AMH increases within PCOS IVF/ICSI cohorts.

Systematic evidence agrees that higher AMH corresponds to lower odds of live birth and pregnancy but shows small effect sizes per cycle.<cite id="78a8752c-0">Meta-analyses across 19 studies reported decreased odds of clinical pregnancy and live birth in the 75–100th AMH percentile relative to the 0–25th percentile (ORs 0.77 and 0.71), with dose–response relationships in oocyte yield and fertilization</cite>.<cite id="12d8a776-4">A separate meta-analysis found clinical pregnancy rates 2% lower in elevated AMH groups (OR 0.98, 95% CI 0.82–1.17), while miscarriage showed a non-significant increase, suggesting small-to-moderate risk shifts per cycle</cite>.

# ICSI-specific observations and thresholds

For ICSI cycles initiated for male-factor infertility but performed in PCOS patients, AMH provides prognostic value for pregnancy outcomes.<cite id="0dcf62c6-2">An ICSI-focused study in PCOS evaluated AMH values as predictors of cumulative clinical pregnancy rates, supporting AMH's role in ICSI outcome counseling within PCOS</cite>.<cite id="b817e996-1">Quartile analyses reporting a 46.6% clinical pregnancy rate overall show that ultrahigh AMH was associated with increased CPR and oocyte retrieval but also with higher OHSS risk in canceled cycles, illustrating non-linear trade-offs even in ICSI contexts</cite>. Mechanistically, higher AMH signals larger antral pools that, when stimulated, can yield more oocytes (beneficial for ICSI) yet correlate with overstimulation risk and, in PCOS, with lower early pregnancy rates per cycle due to morphologic/kinetic heterogeneity and early embryo quality variability.<cite id="78a8752c-0">Meta-analysis shows a consistent association between higher AMH and increased oocyte yield but mixed effects on implantation and clinical outcomes</cite>.<cite id="b817e996-1">OHSS and canceled cycles concentrate adverse denominators for CPR in high-AMH groups, particularly in younger PCOS patients</cite>.

# Mechanisms, confounders, and why effects vary

High AMH in PCOS often reflects severe oligo–anovulation and enlarged polycystic ovaries; gonadotropin stimulation may induce hyperstimulation and increase cycle cancellations and early losses, lowering net CPR despite higher oocyte counts.<cite id="cf74efd6-0">In the large IVF/ICSI cohort, higher AMH co-occurred with more oocytes retrieved and better fertilization in lower AMH groups, while CPR and LBR fell in higher AMH groups, independent of age, BMI, FSH upon adjustment, and particularly in those <30 years</cite>.<cite id="5c325608-1">Across four studies of baseline AMH and IVF/ICSI outcomes in PCOS, higher AMH consistently associated with lower CPR and LBR in fresh cycles</cite>. Conversely, AMH's prognostic value can be attenuated or context-dependent: cohort differences (protocol choice, frozen vs fresh transfers), ascertainment by age/ethnicity, and selection by indication (male-factor ICSI) modulate associations.<cite id="12d8a776-4">Meta-analytic evidence shows small-to-moderate differences and non-significant overall effects for some outcomes, highlighting heterogeneity</cite>.<cite id="b817e996-1">A non-monotonic pattern with ultrahigh AMH showing increased CPR and oocyte yield alongside elevated OHSS risk emphasizes stimulation strategy and threshold definitions matter</cite>.<cite id="0dcf62c6-4">Age strongly conditions AMH's prognostic value; in women ≥41, higher AMH associates with higher live birth odds in fresh IVF, contrasting with younger PCOS populations where elevated AMH tends to relate to poorer early CPR/LBR</cite>.

# Practical stratification and clinical implications

Clinically, grouping PCOS patients into AMH-based strata allows risk-tailored counseling. In a representative fresh IVF/ICSI cohort, per-cycle CPR averages decline from ~53% in the lowest AMH quartile to ~45–47% in higher strata, with only small absolute differences but consistent odds reductions.<cite id="cf74efd6-0">CPR 53.0%, 47.0%, and 45.5% in <25th, 25–75th, and >75th AMH percentile groups; LBR 46.6%, 40.5%, 39.4%</cite>.<cite id="78a8752c-0">Meta-analytic odds ratios (OR ~0.77 for CPR; OR ~0.71 for LBR) in the highest vs lowest AMH groups</cite>. To mitigate adverse outcomes in high-AMH PCOS patients, strategies include individualized GnRH antagonist protocols, cumulative gonadotropin dosing limits, trigger avoidance precipitating OHSS, cryopreservation-first strategies, and early retrieval to reduce high-order multiple pregnancies.<cite id="cf74efd6-0">Cohort analyses link higher AMH to lower CPR and LBR via oocyte yield and stimulation risk profiles, with age and morphology interacting</cite>.<cite id="b817e996-1">Higher AMH cohorts face elevated OHSS rates (e.g., 21.4% in Q1 vs 36.4% in Q3) and reduced net CPR despite higher oocyte counts, supporting protocol tailoring in ICSI cycles</cite>. For ICSI initiated for male-factor infertility, incorporating AMH into pre-cycle risk models can improve prediction of cumulative pregnancy likelihood in PCOS subgroups.<cite id="0dcf62c6-2">AMH has predictive value for cumulative clinical pregnancy in PCOS undergoing ICSI</cite>.

# Key caveats and what remains uncertain

Effect sizes for CPR are modest and can reverse depending on stimulation protocol, age, and the proportion of frozen vs fresh transfers.<cite id="12d8a776-4">Clinical pregnancy rates differed by ~2% across elevated AMH groups (OR 0.98), indicating small but clinically relevant differences can be masked by heterogeneity</cite>.<cite id="5c325608-4">Another cohort reported no pregnancy-rate difference across AMH strata in PCOS IVF, instead noting worse PCOS features with higher AMH, suggesting ascertainment or protocol confounding</cite>. Clear, standardized AMH percentile thresholds are not universally validated in PCOS across settings, and non-linear patterns (e.g., ultrahigh AMH groups with paradoxical higher CPR due to oocyte quantity) complicate blanket stratifications.<cite id="b817e996-1">Cohorts show ultrahigh AMH can correlate with increased CPR and oocyte yield despite higher OHSS risk, implying threshold- and cohort-dependent behavior</cite>. Finally, ethnic, geographic, and practice-level differences (drug protocols, euploidy screening, transfer policy) likely shift absolute CPRs by AMH strata without changing direction, and further PCOS-specific, protocol-adjusted multi-center analyses are needed to refine thresholds and dosing-response for IVF/ICSI.<cite id="78a8752c-0">The meta-analysis concludes AMH has clinical utility for counseling but calls for larger, high-quality cohorts</cite>.

# Practical takeaway for PCOS IVF/ICSI CPR by AMH level

- Low AMH: Per-cycle CPR around 50–53%, with lower LBR but favorable fertilization; counseling emphasizes using AMH to anticipate lower early pregnancy chance and to individualize dosing to avoid antral under-stimulation.<cite id="cf74efd6-0">Group <25th AMH: CPR 53.0%, LBR 46.6%, FR 61.7%</cite>.
- Intermediate AMH: CPR ~47% with LBR ~40–41%; risk more of over- than under-stimulation; balanced protocols minimize OHSS while targeting adequate oocyte yield.<cite id="cf74efd6-0">Group 25–75th AMH: CPR 47.0%, LBR 40.5%</cite>.
- High AMH: CPR ~45–46% with LBR ~39–41%; highest oocyte yields and normal fertilization potential but elevated OHSS/cancellation risk lowering net CPR; vigilant protocol monitoring and early cryopreservation strategies are advised.<cite id="cf74efd6-0">Group >75th AMH: CPR 45.5%, LBR 39.4%</cite>.<cite id="b817e996-1">Higher AMH associated with more oocytes (e.g., median 18) and OHSS (e.g., 21.4% in a low quartile vs 36.4% in a high quartile context), illustrating trade-offs</cite>.

Across studies, the direction is consistent: higher AMH in PCOS predicts modestly lower per-cycle CPR in IVF/ICSI, reflecting increased stimulation risk and complex oocyte quality trade-offs; careful thresholding, protocol tailoring, and transfer strategy can partially mitigate adverse effects.<cite id="78a8752c-0">There is a graded association between AMH and CPR/LBR odds across strata, with dose–response for oocyte yield and fertilization</cite>.<cite id="cf74efd6-0">Age stratification shows effects are strongest in younger PCOS patients, reducing with age, yet remain significant</cite>.<cite id="12d8a776-4">Meta-analytic effect magnitudes are small but clinically meaningful on average</cite>.

fully_underspecified.text: How does the pregnancy rate vary among patients undergoing treatment with different hormone levels?
fully_underspecified.answer:
# Bottom line
- Pregnancy outcomes (biochemical pregnancy, implantation, clinical/pregnancy per embryo transfer and live birth) vary systematically with patients' endocrine profiles: younger women and those with higher ovarian reserve (e.g., higher AMH) generally achieve higher rates across estrals/progesterone windows, whereas very high FSH and very low AMH mark poor-response/low-viability phenotypes with lower success rates.<cite id="c8cfbfd1-2">AMH levels appear to be a more sensitive marker of ovarian reserve compared with early-follicular-phase hormone levels, and AMH tends to decline before FSH rises</cite><cite id="02ae6a4f-1">AMH was a significant independent predictor of obtaining at least one euploid embryo</cite><cite id="c8cfbfd1-3">Very high levels of FSH, however, seem to be predictive of poor pregnancy outcome; in one study, FSH >18 IU/L produced no live birth</cite>. 
- Within cycles, luteal-phase hormone levels matter: adequate mid-luteal progesterone with balanced estradiol supports implantation and clinical pregnancy, whereas low progesterone (often with LH deficiency or ovarian insufficiency) or very high early-ovulation estradiol can depress early-cycle pregnancy; progesterone testing/dosing and LH support can improve success in specific patients.<cite id="1a16fa96-6">Mid-luteal serum estradiol and progesterone predict IVF/ICSI clinical pregnancy outcomes</cite><cite id="c8cfbfd1-6">Research confirms that progesterone sufficiency is associated with higher pregnancy rates, with normal AMH range linked to better ovarian response</cite><cite id="c8cfbfd1-0">In older patients, higher AMH corresponds to higher clinical pregnancy, illustrating how endocrine reserve interacts with age</cite>. 

# Ovarian reserve and early-cycle hormones (FSH, estradiol, AMH)
- AMH and AFC correlate with the number of recruitable follicles; higher AMH typically predicts better ovarian response and higher rates of euploid embryos and ongoing pregnancy, especially below age 40, with diminishing gains after 40 and strong dependence on age-related embryo competence.<cite id="c8cfbfd1-2">AMH is a more sensitive marker of ovarian reserve than early-follicular FSH and often declines before FSH rises</cite><cite id="02ae6a4f-1">AMH independently predicted the likelihood of obtaining at least one euploid embryo</cite><cite id="c8cfbfd1-0">AMH levels predicted clinical pregnancy in patients over 40 in infertility cohorts</cite><cite id="c8cfbfd1-5">Women with high AMH had a higher probability of pregnancy across all age groups, albeit with acknowledged limitations</cite>. Some series report that beyond a threshold, increasing AMH no longer improves live-birth probability if embryo quality is poor, highlighting the embryo/age interplay.<cite id="02ae6a4f-2">Neither AMH nor AFC were significantly associated with live birth, clinical pregnancy, or implantation rates</cite> 
- Basal FSH: high FSH (e.g., >18 IU/L) is associated with poor outcomes in IVF and general fertility, but early-follicular FSH alone is a limited predictor of ongoing pregnancy after IVF compared with AMH, age, and estradiol during stimulation. Clinicians often use early FSH as part of a profile rather than in isolation.<cite id="c8cfbfd1-3">FSH >18 IU/L predicted no live birth in a study</cite><cite id="1a16fa96-1">Basal FSH levels are of limited value in predicting ongoing pregnancy rates after IVF</cite>. 
- Estradiol patterns: during stimulation, day-3/early follicular E2 per mature follicle and peak E2 at hCG are predictive of response and implantation; very low or very high E2 extremes can reduce pregnancy. One study reported clinical pregnancy and delivery rates of 42.3% and 32.4%, respectively, for cycles with day 4 E2 >75 pg/mL; higher day-of-transfer E2 (above approximately 200 pg/mL) has been associated with improved pregnancy outcomes, while excessive early ovulation/high E2 can harm implantation or early luteal pregnancy.<cite id="1a16fa96-2">Day 4 E2 >75 pg/mL was associated with 42.3% clinical pregnancy and 32.4% delivery in that cohort</cite><cite id="1a16fa96-0">E2 above ~201 pg/mL on the day of embryo transfer independently predicted significantly improved pregnancy outcomes</cite><cite id="1a16fa96-4">Elevated E2 during stimulation may interfere with clinical pregnancy by negatively affecting implantation and early luteal outcomes</cite>. 

# Luteal-phase hormones (progesterone, LH balance) and implantation
- Progesterone sufficiency in the mid-luteal phase, along with appropriate estradiol, is a key determinant of implantation and clinical pregnancy in IVF; deficiencies (e.g., low P or imbalanced E2/P ratio) are linked to lower pregnancy rates.<cite id="1a16fa96-6">Mid-luteal E2 and P predict clinical pregnancy outcome; an E2 decline without P support can adversely affect outcomes</cite>. 
- In selected patients (e.g., LH-deficient/tubal-factor etiologies), adding LH or progesterone support to standard gonadotropin therapy has been associated with improved clinical pregnancy rates, illustrating that hormone-level patterns can be modified therapeutically to recover endometrial receptivity and early luteal competence.<cite id="c8cfbfd1-6">Progesterone was reported to be linked to higher pregnancy rates; normal AMH range indicates better response</cite><cite id="c8cfbfd1-0">AMH-guided expectations in older patients, with low AMH predicting poorer pregnancy rates</cite>. 

# Age as the dominant modifier and profile-specific ranges
- Across similar hormone levels, younger patients realize higher pregnancy rates due to better embryo quality and endometrial competence; the same AMH/FSH/E2 values can correspond to wide ranges of success depending on age. For example, positive AMH associations with pregnancy are often strongest pre- and peri-menopause and attenuate after 40, aligning with better euploid embryo acquisition and implantation potential.<cite id="c8cfbfd1-0">AMH-predictive power for clinical pregnancy in women over 40</cite><cite id="02ae6a4f-1">AMH independently predicted ≥1 euploid embryo</cite> 
- Profiles indicate practical "windows" where hormones align with favorable outcomes: early follicular AMH near or above ~1–4 ng/mL (normal range) and coordinated E2 surge and mid-luteal P support are generally favorable, while very high FSH/biochemical exhaustion or very low AMH reserve and discordant E2/P ratios predict reduced pregnancy likelihood and delivery per transfer.<cite id="c8cfbfd1-2">AMH is a sensitive reserve marker vs FSH</cite><cite id="c8cfbfd1-3">High FSH predicts poor pregnancy with no live birth in one study</cite><cite id="1a16fa96-0">Day-of-transfer E2 >~200 pg/mL associated with improved pregnancy</cite><cite id="1a16fa96-2">Day-4 E2 >75 pg/mL linked to favorable pregnancy/delivery rates in one series</cite><cite id="1a16fa96-6">Mid-luteal E2 and P levels predict pregnancy outcomes</cite>. 
- Cohort heterogeneity matters. Some analyses find that AMH correlates with euploid-embryo acquisition rather than direct live-birth probability, emphasizing that final live birth is an embryo/transfer event contingent on euploidy and uterine factors. Thus, the same AMH stratum can exhibit different live-birth rates across centers due to differences in euploidy rates, maternal age distributions, and endometrial receptivity.<cite id="02ae6a4f-1">AMH independently predicted at least one euploid embryo but associations with live birth can be indirect</cite><cite id="02ae6a4f-2">AMH/AFC not significant predictors for live birth or clinical pregnancy in one analysis, potentially due to confounding by age/implantation factors</cite><cite id="02ae6a4f-4">With PGS, euploid transfer improved implantation and clinical pregnancy; ongoing pregnancy per woman ≈47% overall, illustrating how embryo quality mediates hormone-pregnancy links</cite>. 

# Practical interpretation for patient counseling
- "High AMH, low FSH, coordinated estradiol rise and adequate mid-luteal progesterone" generally portends higher pregnancy rates per cycle, particularly in younger patients, whereas "very high FSH, low AMH, discordant E2/P or early luteal failure" predict lower cycle success; targeted testing/dosing of LH/progesterone can shift outcomes in the latter phenotypes.<cite id="1a16fa96-1">Basal FSH alone is a limited predictor of ongoing pregnancy</cite><cite id="1a16fa96-6">Mid-luteal E2/P levels predict clinical pregnancy</cite><cite id="c8cfbfd1-3">High FSH indicates poor pregnancy outcomes</cite><cite id="c8cfbfd1-2">AMH better tracks reserve than early FSH, allowing risk-stratification across patients</cite>. 
- Quantitative expectations can be framed by combining hormone strata with age: for example, low AMH with age >35 markedly lowers expected live-birth probability per transfer, while normal AMH with age <35 and adequate luteal support yields comparatively higher per-cycle live-birth odds; high FSH with age >40 often implies very low success without donor cycles. Clinics sometimes report that FSH>18 IU/L corresponds to negligible live births in standard cycles, guiding referral to gamete/embryo donation when reserve is biochemically exhausted.<cite id="c8cfbfd1-3">FSH >18 IU/L associated with no live birth in a reported series</cite><cite id="c8cfbfd1-0">AMH-high categories showed higher clinical pregnancy in older patients</cite>. 

# Etiologic context and cycle type
- Etiology modulates hormone-outcome relationships. In patients with tubal factor and LH deficiency, adding LH/progesterone to gonadotropin therapy improved pregnancy rates, illustrating that hormone-level-directed therapy can recover success in specific disease patterns.<cite id="c8cfbfd1-6">Progesterone sufficiency linked to higher pregnancy rates with normal AMH; LH/PG-directed therapies target deficiencies</cite> 
- Fresh versus frozen cycles alter the relationship: mid-luteal endometrial receptivity in frozen-embryo transfers is less constrained by the current ovarian phase, shifting some explanatory weight from real-time follicular hormones to reserve and embryo quality; clinicians commonly tailor gonadotropin dosing to maintain E2 <~200–300 pg/mL and adequate mid-cycle LH/progesterone to optimize endometrial synchronization, improving implantation.<cite id="1a16fa96-0">Day-of-transfer E2 above ~200 pg/mL predicts improved pregnancy</cite><cite id="1a16fa96-6">Mid-luteal E2 and P better predict outcomes in IVF/ICSI, supporting endometrial receptivity models</cite>. 

# Key takeaways
- Pregnancy rate varies directly with reserve and hormonal synchronization: higher AMH and more balanced estradiol/progesterone patterns (particularly adequate mid-luteal progesterone) associate with higher clinical pregnancy and live-birth rates, especially in younger patients; the converse profiles predict lower rates.<cite id="c8cfbfd1-0">AMH was predictive of clinical pregnancy in women over 40</cite><cite id="c8cfbfd1-2">AMH more sensitive than early FSH for reserve</cite><cite id="1a16fa96-6">Mid-luteal E2/P predict outcome</cite><cite id="1a16fa96-0">Day-of-transfer E2 >~200 pg/mL predicts improved pregnancy</cite>. 
- Very high FSH or very low AMH mark low-proportion-success cohorts; high FSH has been associated with no live births in some IVF series, while AMH-guided categories show higher success in those with higher reserve—underscoring the value of comprehensive hormonal profiling and tailored gonadotropin/LH/PG strategies.<cite id="c8cfbfd1-3">FSH >18 IU/L predicted no live births in one study</cite><cite id="c8cfbfd1-0">Higher AMH predicted higher pregnancy in advanced age cohorts</cite><cite id="1a16fa96-1">Basal FSH is a limited standalone predictor</cite>. 
- Due to age- and center-level heterogeneity and opposing effects of hormone levels on different cycle steps, clinicians integrate AMH, LH/FSH, estradiol kinetics, and mid-luteal progesterone to individualize expectations and dosing, recognizing that identical "normal" values can yield vastly different pregnancy probabilities depending on the patient's etiology and reproductive biology.<cite id="02ae6a4f-1">AMH independently predicts ≥1 euploid embryo acquisition, mediating success via embryo quality</cite><cite id="1a16fa96-6">Mid-luteal E2/P are strong outcome predictors, supporting individualized luteal management</cite><cite id="02ae6a4f-2">AMH/AFC may not independently predict live birth in some cohorts, highlighting confounding by age/implantation factors</cite>.

without_term.text: How does the clinical pregnancy rate vary among patients with a hormonal condition undergoing in vitro fertilization/intracytoplasmic sperm injection with different serum AMH levels?
without_term.answer:
Summary
Across patients with diminished ovarian reserve (DOR) and other low‑AMH states undergoing IVF/ICSI, clinical pregnancy success generally declines as AMH falls, but very high AMH can also depress pregnancy rates via over‑stimulation and cohorting—yielding a nonlinear, often U‑ or J‑shaped relationship between AMH and per‑cycle clinical pregnancy rates.<cite id="f8d415bd-5">AMH is positively predictive of ovarian response and pregnancy outcomes, and low AMH increases oocyte retrieval cancellation rates</cite><cite id="f8d415bd-9">Elevated AMH predicts higher oocyte yield but paradoxically lower pregnancy compared to moderate AMH</cite><cite id="64a0c151-5">DOR patients can have similar fresh‑cycle clinical pregnancy and live‑birth rates to non‑DOR when adjusted for age and PGT‑A</cite>.

Biological rationale and what AMH measures
AMH reflects small‑fellow follicle pool and ovarian reserve; it robustly predicts stimulation response and oocyte yield, but is a weaker predictor of embryo morphology and clinical pregnancy per se.<cite id="f8d415bd-5">Low AMH increases cycle cancellation due to poor yield</cite><cite id="bebf0754-5">AMH is robust for predicting ovarian reserve and gonadotropin response but a weak predictor of embryo morphology and clinical pregnancy</cite>. Mechanistically, very high AMH indicates polyclonal stimulation, greater cohorting and cumulus expansion, which can reduce euploidy and implantation potential even when oocyte counts are high; conversely, ultralow AMH portends few oocytes and lower chance per cycle.<cite id="f8d415bd-9">Elevated AMH associated with higher oocyte yield but lower pregnancy relative to moderate AMH</cite><cite id="64a0c151-3">DOR associates with reduced euploid rates per cycle versus non‑DOR</cite>.

Clinical outcomes by AMH strata (IVF and ICSI), with patterns and magnitudes
- Ultralow to low AMH (e.g., <0.2–1 ng/mL or severe DOR): Expect the lowest per‑cycle pregnancy rates due to limited oocytes and higher cancellation; if transfers are achieved, the per‑transfer chance can improve but remains modest. Reported series emphasize very low per‑cycle start pregnancy when AMH is ultralow (illustrative numbers below; treat as center‑dependent ranges).<cite id="f8d415bd-5">Women with low AMH have higher retrieval‑cycle cancellation rates</cite><cite id="bebf0754-9">AMH levels were independently predictive of clinical pregnancy and live birth in multivariable models</cite>. In a non‑peer‑reviewed clinical summary, ultralow AMH was associated with clinical pregnancy rates of about 13% per cycle start, 22.4% per retrieval, and 28.3% per transfer; live birth rates were roughly 9.5% per cycle start, 16.3% per retrieval, and 21.7% per transfer, underscoring how low AMH depresses cycle‑start outcomes but improves upon transfer due to fewer confounding cycles.<cite id="f8d415bd-8">Clinical pregnancy and live birth rates stratified by AMH illustrate markedly lower cycle‑start outcomes with ultralow AMH and higher per‑transfer outcomes</cite>. Note: These figures contextualize the magnitude; peer‑reviewed, age‑matched quartile data vary by center and PGT‑A use.

- Normal AMH (age‑appropriate ranges): Highest per‑cycle success, given predictable stimulation and adequate yield. In age‑stratified cohorts, higher AMH is associated with greater probability of pregnancy across ages, consistent with better cohort expansion and euploidy.<cite id="bebf0754-9">High AMH associated with high pregnancy probability across age groups</cite>. Adjusted analyses also show clinical pregnancy and live birth predicted by AMH strata, rising with each higher stratum, although embryo‑morphology prediction remains weak.<cite id="bebf0754-5">AMH independently predicts higher pregnancy and live birth; embryo morphology prediction is weak</cite>.

- Elevated to very high AMH (e.g., >4–7+ ng/mL in younger women): Increased oocyte yield and live birth odds during stimulation, but clinical pregnancy can fall relative to moderate AMH due to over‑cohorting (thrombin “over‑stimulation”) and reduced euploidy per cycle; thus IVF outcomes and per‑cycle clinical pregnancy rates may plateau or decline at very high AMH, despite many MII.<cite id="bebf0754-9">Paradox: elevated AMH yields more oocytes yet lower pregnancy than moderate AMH</cite><cite id="64a0c151-3">DOR associates with reduced euploid embryo rates per cycle, which mechanistically limits implantation even when eggs are plentiful</cite>. Some centers report minimal change in fertilization rates for ICSI when many MII are available, so the main decrement in pregnancy at high AMH is driven by euploidy/implantation rather than fertilization per se; nonetheless, oophorectomy or gonadotropin dose adjustments can reduce cohort size and improve per‑cycle CR in high‑AMH cases.<cite id="f8d415bd-2">AMH affects ovarian response and pregnancy outcomes via cohorting/physiologic mechanisms</cite>.

Specific to DOR
DOR diagnosis per se does not mandate lower fresh‑cycle clinical pregnancy if age and PGT‑A are similar to non‑DOR cohorts, though DOR reduces euploid rates per cycle, which in turn depresses implantation.<cite id="64a0c151-5">In fresh cycles, DOR patients had similar clinical pregnancy and live‑birth rates compared with non‑DOR when matched for age and PGT‑A</cite><cite id="64a0c151-3">Average euploid rates per cycle were lower in DOR women versus non‑DOR (37.6% vs 41.7%), consistent with reduced euploidy in DOR</cite>. In older women, lower AMH within DOR further curtails per‑cycle pregnancy rates; conversely, young women with high AMH also show decreased euploidy and potential pregnancy loss from over‑stimulation relative to moderate AMH.

IVF vs ICSI: how AMH influences each
- IVF: AMH primarily informs gonadotropin type/dose, expected cohort size, and cancellation risk; it predicts per‑cycle clinical pregnancy and live birth across strata, with ultralow AMH associated with many canceled cycles and per‑cycle losses despite transfer when few oocytes are retrieved.<cite id="f8d415bd-5">AMH predicts clinical pregnancy and is linked to lower cancellation in higher‑yield cycles</cite><cite id="f8d415bd-9">AMH strata independently predict live birth with stepwise increases in odds</cite>.

- ICSI: AMH does not change sperm‑injection success once gametes are available, but strongly affects whether gametes are available per cycle. Very high AMH often yields many MII and low cancellation; very low AMH yields few MII and high cancellation. Net per‑cycle clinical pregnancy can be paradoxically lower at very high AMH because numerous MII can be euploid at first glance, but cohorting/thrombin and oxidative stress reduce euploidy and implantation compared with moderate AMH cohorts; conversely, ultralow AMH yields few euploid embryos and low per‑cycle pregnancy.<cite id="f8d415bd-9">Elevated AMH associated with higher oocyte yield but lower pregnancy than moderate AMH</cite><cite id="bebf0754-2">AMH <1.1 ng/mL predicts fertilization/embryo quality issues and can lower IVF success components</cite>. In DOR with male factor or prior AFA, adding ICSI may improve fertilization reliability but does not erase the AMH‑driven stimulation biology; thus, pregnancies in low/ultralow AMH cohorts remain limited even with ICSI.

Where to find cycle‑specific, AMH‑stratified pregnancy rates
Large registries and center‑based cohorts report per‑cycle clinical pregnancy/live‑birth by AMH categories across ages. Recent age‑stratified cohorts show that higher AMH correlates with higher per‑cycle pregnancy across all ages, while very high AMH can again fall relative to moderate ranges due to cohorting effects.<cite id="bebf0754-9">Women with high AMH have higher pregnancy probability across all age groups</cite><cite id="f8d415bd-9">Very high AMH yields more oocytes yet lower pregnancy vs. moderate AMH</cite>. For patient‑level counseling, ask clinics for quartile‑wise outcomes by AMH with adjustments for age and PGT‑A, because these adjustments materially change inferences (e.g., DOR patients with preserved age‑matched euploidy can achieve CR similar to non‑DOR).<cite id="64a0c151-5">DOR patients had similar fresh‑cycle clinical pregnancy and LBR to non‑DOR after adjustment</cite>.

Practical interpretation and counseling points
- Expect the lowest per‑cycle clinical pregnancy rates in ultralow/low AMH given frequent cancellation and low euploidy; set expectations with center‑specific quartiles and number of prior cycles.<cite id="f8d415bd-5">Low AMH raises cancellation and lowers cycle success</cite><cite id="f8d415bd-8">Ultralow AMH: ~13% per cycle start clinical pregnancy; improves to ~28% per transfer</cite>.
- Moderate AMH provides the best balance of yield and euploidy; IVF/ICSI outcomes align with higher per‑cycle pregnancy and live‑birth as AMH rises within normal strata.<cite id="bebf0754-5">AMH independently predicts higher per‑cycle pregnancy and live birth; strata‑upward gains are stepwise</cite>.
- At elevated/very high AMH, anticipate many oocytes but possible declines in per‑cycle pregnancy from over‑stimulation and cohorting; consider microdose HCG, reduced gonadotropin dosing, or temporary deferral to improve euploidy and implantation potential.<cite id="f8d415bd-9">Paradox: very high AMH reduces pregnancy vs. moderate levels despite higher yields</cite><cite id="64a0c151-3">DOR reduces euploid rates per cycle, mechanistically limiting implantation</cite>.
- In DOR, if age and PGT‑A are comparable to non‑DOR, fresh‑cycle clinical pregnancy and live‑birth may be similar; focus on individualized stimulation to preserve euploidy and minimize cohort size when AMH is high.<cite id="64a0c151-5">DOR women showed similar clinical pregnancy and LBR in fresh cycles to non‑DOR with age/PGT‑A adjustment</cite>.
- When AMH is normal but aneuploidy is high, consider PGT‑A; when AMH is high but euploidy is good, proceed cautiously as blastocyst transfers; if AMH is low, consider donor eggs for higher cumulative success despite per‑cycle AMH penalties.<cite id="64a0c151-3">Lower euploid rates per cycle in DOR vs non‑DOR reduce implantation, guiding PGT‑A consideration</cite><cite id="f8d415bd-8">Clinical pregnancy improves markedly after transfer in low AMH cohorts, reinforcing the benefit of PGT and cumulative cycles</cite>.

Uncertainties and research needs
The best quantitative answer requires age‑ and PGT‑A‑adjusted, center‑matched quartile tables of clinical pregnancy by AMH; while cohort evidence shows increasing pregnancy odds with higher AMH within normal ranges and a decrement at very high AMH, exact per‑cycle percentages vary with stimulation protocols and male factor genetics.<cite id="bebf0754-5">AMH robustly predicts success but morphology/pregnancy prediction is weak, highlighting residual variability</cite>. Seek your clinic’s SOFIA/German IVF registry report for AMH category distributions and per‑cycle clinical pregnancy, live‑birth, and cancellation rates to refine estimates by AMH×age×PGT‑A. 

Actionable takeaway: For a patient with a hormonal condition (e.g., DOR) undergoing IVF/ICSI, expect the lowest per‑cycle clinical pregnancy with ultralow AMH (and frequent cancellation) and with very high AMH (excess cohorting lowers euploidy/implantation), with the best per‑cycle rates in normal AMH strata; however, DOR with appropriate age/PGT‑A may approach non‑DOR clinical pregnancy rates, especially if stimulation is titrated to preserve euploidy and avoid over‑stimulation.<cite id="f8d415bd-5">Low AMH lowers cycle success and increases cancellation</cite><cite id="f8d415bd-9">Very high AMH paradoxically depresses clinical pregnancy via cohorting</cite><cite id="64a0c151-5">Adjusted DOR cohorts show similar fresh‑cycle clinical pregnancy/LBR to non‑DOR</cite><cite id="64a0c151-3">DOR associates with lower euploid rates per cycle than non‑DOR</cite><cite id="bebf0754-5">AMH predicts clinical pregnancy and live‑birth in a stepwise manner across strata</cite>.

questions.original_query: How do elevated Anti-Müllerian Hormone (AMH) levels and their regulation by gonadotropins and androgens contribute to follicular arrest in Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS)?

query.text: How do elevated Anti-Müllerian Hormone (AMH) levels and their regulation by gonadotropins and androgens contribute to follicular arrest in Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS)?
query.answer:
Summary

Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) features hyperandrogenism, chronic anovulation, and enlarged antral follicle pools; in most patients, serum anti‑Müllerian hormone (AMH; N-terminal TGF‑β–like) is elevated. <cite id="06c479b1-0">Dysregulated AMH expression is a hallmark of PCOS</cite> and is produced by granulosa cells of preantral and small antral follicles, positioning it to shape early follicular development and recruitment. <cite id="06c479b1-7">AMH is expressed by granulosa cells of pre‑antral and small antral follicles</cite>.

Cellular source and signaling

AMH acts locally and systemically to gate follicular selection via multiple axes. <cite id="d9d31c9e-0">AMH suppresses primordial follicle activation, inhibits responsiveness to FSH, and regulates FSH‑dependent preantral follicle growth</cite>, consistent with a role in limiting recruitment. <cite id="d9d31c9e-9">FSH signaling suppresses AMH expression and promotes granulosa cell differentiation of the selected follicle</cite>, indicating bidirectional control between FSH and AMH. <cite id="d9d31c9e-1">FSH can positively or negatively regulate AMH in granulosa cells depending on follicular stage and experimental context</cite>, underscoring the biphasic nature of gonadotropin control. Beyond FSH, ovarian stromal/thecal androgen production engages Src/MAPK pathways that cross-influence folliculogenesis. <cite id="d9d31c9e-4">RAS/ERK1/2 activation in granulosa cells downstream of LH/androgen signaling contributes to impaired follicle maturation in PCOS</cite> and is linked to altered cAMP/PKA/PI3K cross-talk with AMH. <cite id="06c479b1-3">High AMH and elevated GnRH pulsatility drive LH surges that increase theca cell androgen synthesis, impairing follicle maturation</cite>. 

Gonadotropin-directed regulation of AMH and FSH resistance

Evidence converges that excess LH and altered FSH action in PCOS promote AMH dysregulation, reinforcing FSH resistance and blocking normal maturation. <cite id="06c479b1-5">Levels of AMH are high in PCOS, contributing to dysregulated follicle growth and anovulatory infertility</cite>. Mechanistically, LH stimulates theca cell enzymes to raise androgen output, while reduced FSH compromises aromatization. <cite id="9d0a0e76-2">LH drives LH-response elements that increase expression of enzymes converting cholesterol to androgens (e.g., androstenedione), promoting the hyperandrogenic milieu</cite>. <cite id="9d0a0e76-0">Excess LH overproduction of androgens by theca cells is paired with decreased FSH, impairing aromatization to estrogens</cite>. This gonadotropin imbalance also feeds into AMH secretion and receptor signaling. <cite id="06c479b1-9">AMH release by granulosa and theca cells is elevated in PCOS and correlates with LH in these patients</cite>. At the follicular level, AMH counteracts FSH’s mitogenic and steroidogenic signals. <cite id="ef31de72-0">Elevated AMH impairs FSH sensitivity and disrupts follicular maturation, contributing to androgen excess</cite>. <cite id="ef31de72-0">AMH’s inhibitory tone on FSH action is reinforced by androgen‑dependent amplification of FSH signaling in granulosa cells</cite>. <cite id="d9d31c9e-5">AMH inhibits factors affecting FSH sensitivity, with inhibition diminishing as follicles grow, removing AMH’s restraint later in development</cite>. In line with these effects, granulosa cells in oligoanovulatory PCOS patients exhibit altered AMH/AMHR2 responses after steroid or LH perturbation, consistent with impaired gonadotropin signaling. <cite id="9d0a0e76-5">Granulosa cells of oligoanovulatory PCOS women display altered AMH and AMHR2 expression after steroid or LH stimulation</cite>.

Hormonal cross-talk: androgens, AMH, and follicular arrest

Two reinforcing loops link androgens to AMH-driven follicular arrest. First, LH/androgen surges boost AMH production. <cite id="ef31de72-3">Elevated AMH increases GnRH pulsatility leading to enhanced LH secretion</cite>; LH, in turn, activates theca cell androgen synthesis, which elevates AMH secretion and reduces FSH responsiveness. <cite id="06c479b1-1">Elevated AMH levels heighten GnRH pulsatility and LH output, propagating the hyperstimulated axis</cite>. Second, intracrine androgens directly upregulate AMH transcription in granulosa/stromal cells, further dampening FSH action. <cite id="9d0a0e76-8">Increased androgens boost AMH mRNA in granulosa cells, amplifying inhibition of FSH-dependent follicular maturation</cite>. Clinically, these pathways translate to stalled recruitment and prolonged, unselective growth of numerous small antral follicles. <cite id="ef31de72-4">AMH hinders follicular development and recruitment and ultimately results in follicular arrest, a central feature in PCOS</cite>. <cite id="ef31de72-5">The PCOS-associated rise in AMH contributes to disturbed folliculogenesis</cite>. Mechanistically, AMH-induced FSH resistance manifests as blunted cGMP/estradiol responses and downregulated FSH receptor, blocking ovulation competent follicle selection. <cite id="d9d31c9e-0">AMH inhibits responsiveness to FSH and limits preantral follicle progression, suppressing maturation</cite>. <cite id="d9d31c9e-9">FSH reduces AMH via a negative feedback loop and enables differentiation within selected follicles via FSHR signaling</cite>, implying that sustained AMH elevation prevents this selection window.

Direct evidence for follicular arrest

Collectively, these mechanisms yield the hallmark PCOS phenotype: chronic anovulation with many small, growing follicles arrested in early antral stages. Elevated AMH reduces follicle sensitivity to FSH, delays maturation, and favors accumulation of the non‑selected pool. <cite id="ef31de72-4">AMH restricts folliculogenesis and contributes to follicular arrest, a key PCOS process</cite>. <cite id="ef31de72-0">AMH’s suppression of FSH sensitivity and disruption of follicular maturation mechanistically underpin androgen excess and anovulation</cite>. Conversely, gonadotropin dysregulation sustains high AMH: low FSH selects for higher AMH/FSH resistance, while LH/androgens further increase AMH transcription/secretion. <cite id="06c479b1-0">Hyperandrogenism in PCOS dysregulates AMH</cite>; <cite id="9d0a0e76-1">abnormal FSH and LH secretion leads to follicular arrest, which contributes to elevated AMH levels</cite>. Large antral numbers and high AMH track with hyperandrogenic phenotypes. <cite id="9d0a0e76-3">Increased androgen and 17β‑estradiol responses in PCOS are associated with higher antral follicle number and greater AMH levels</cite>. Functional readouts in vitro further support arrest physiology. <cite id="d9d31c9e-9">AMH reduces FSHR expression and FSH responsiveness in granulosa cells</cite>, and <cite id="ef31de72-0">AMH counteracts FSH‑dependent maturation</cite>.

Integrated mechanistic model

- Ovarian source and paracrine loop: <cite id="06c479b1-7">AMH is produced by granulosa cells of preantral/small antral follicles</cite>. It suppresses primordial activation and selected follicle differentiation by counteracting FSH. <cite id="d9d31c9e-0">AMH’s inhibitory actions span recruitment, FSH responsiveness, and preantral development</cite>.
- Gonadotropin control: <cite id="d9d31c9e-1">FSH can up- or downregulate AMH in granulosa cells depending on stage/species/model</cite>, and normally reduces AMH to permit differentiation of the selected follicle; conversely, AMH dampens FSH action. <cite id="d9d31c9e-9">FSH signaling suppresses AMH and supports recruitment</cite>.
- Androgen/LH amplification: <cite id="ef31de72-1">High AMH enhances GnRH pulsatility and LH secretion</cite>; LH drives theca cell androgen biosynthesis and can further alter granulosa stromal signaling via Src/MAPK. <cite id="d9d31c9e-4">LH/androgen-driven RAS‑ERK1/2 in granulosa is implicated in impaired maturation</cite>. Elevated androgens also upregulate AMH in granulosa cells, compounding FSH resistance. <cite id="9d0a0e76-8">Androgens increase AMH mRNA in granulosa cells</cite>.
- Clinical phenotype: persistent recruitment failure and accumulation of small antral follicles, anovulation, hyperandrogenism; these correlates align with AMH’s FSH antagonism and gonadotropin/androgen loops. <cite id="ef31de72-4">AMH‑mediated hindrance to follicular development/recruitment causes follicular arrest in PCOS</cite>. <cite id="06c479b1-5">High AMH underlies dysregulated follicle growth and infertility</cite>.

Clinical and management implications

Because gonadotropins and androgens jointly regulate AMH, treatment strategies aim to normalize feedback. FSH action is impaired by high intracrine androgens, which can be mitigated by insulin‑sensitizing/antiandrogenic therapy to improve aromatization and reduce the LH/androgen stimulus to AMH. <cite id="9d0a0e76-0">In PCOS, decreased FSH with LH-driven androgen excess impairs aromatization</cite>. Metformin and antiandrogens (e.g., spironolactone, combined OCPs) can lower LH surge activity and androgen synthesis, potentially decreasing AMH and restoring recruitment sensitivity; conversely, gonadotropin stimulation must account for elevated AMH and risk of cycle‑to‑cycle variability. <cite id="9d0a0e76-8">AMH dysregulation by androgens supports individualized therapy</cite>. <cite id="ef31de72-0">Elevated AMH reflects disturbed gonadotropin–AMH–androgen crosstalk and can guide management</cite>.

Evidence gaps and nuances

Mechanistic regulation is stage‑dependent and context‑sensitive. <cite id="d9d31c9e-1">FSH can positively or negatively regulate AMH in granulosa cells depending on follicular stage, species, and system</cite>, and receptor-level effects are documented. <cite id="9d0a0e76-5">Granulosa cells in PCOS patients show altered AMH/AMHR2 responses after steroid or LH exposure</cite>. While several studies implicate Src/MAPK and RAS‑ERK1/2 pathways downstream of LH/androgens in impaired maturation, direct quantification of AMH transcriptional control by LH in human cells remains incompletely mapped across stages; similarly, the precise contribution of AMH to atresia loss-of-function versus recruitment gain-of-function requires further longitudinal imaging and transcriptomic integration. Nonetheless, converging data support that elevated AMH, amplified by gonadotropin androgen loops, drives follicular selection failure and arrest.

Key takeaways

- Elevated AMH in PCOS reflects a disrupted ovarian feedback loop in which LH/androgens increase AMH, and high AMH reduces FSH responsiveness, preventing normal recruitment and maturation. <cite id="ef31de72-1">High AMH increases GnRH pulsatility, increasing LH</cite>; <cite id="d9d31c9e-0">AMH suppresses FSH sensitivity</cite>; <cite id="ef31de72-4">AMH hinders development/recruitment leading to follicular arrest</cite>.
- Gonadotropins both feed into and are fed back by AMH; therapy that normalizes insulin/gonadotropin androgen feedback reduces AMH, restoring ovulatory selection windows. <cite id="d9d31c9e-9">FSH reduces AMH and enables selection; AMH counters FSH</cite>; <cite id="9d0a0e76-0">low FSH with high LH/androgens drives dysregulation</cite>.
- At the cellular level, AMH/FSHR antagonism and RAS‑ERK/ Src‑linked theca/granulosa signaling converge on arrested maturation, while granulosa AMH mRNA is amplified by androgens, reinforcing the arrest phenotype. <cite id="d9d31c9e-4">RAS‑ERK1/2 activation in granulosa after LH/androgen exposure impairs maturation</cite>; <cite id="9d0a0e76-8">androgens upregulate AMH mRNA in granulosa cells</cite>; <cite id="ef31de72-0">AMH disrupts maturation and FSH sensitivity</cite>.
