fully_underspecified.text: What evidence supports a link between intestinal changes and those seen in inflammatory bowel diseases?
fully_underspecified.answer:
Summary: Multiple converging lines of evidence tie intestinal structural, barrier, microbial, immune, and architectural alterations to the pathophysiology and histopathology of inflammatory bowel diseases (IBD), notably ulcerative colitis (UC) and Crohn’s disease (CD), with translational support from clinical associations, human tissue data, microbiome interventions, and animal models. <cite id="245b369e-0">Disturbed gut microbiota aggravate intestinal barrier dysfunction via altered regulation of antimicrobial substances</cite>, and <cite id="245b369e-2">the intestinal epithelial barrier in patients with IBD is altered, with changes in tight junction structure and function</cite>. <cite id="9db51c2d-0">Cryptitis and crypt abscesses define active colonic inflammation in ulcerative colitis</cite>, and <cite id="9db51c2d-3">long-standing ulcerative colitis shows architectural crypt distortions and diffuse lymphocytic infiltrate expanding the lamina propria</cite>. Therapeutic and mechanistic studies in microbiota–barrier–immune crosstalk further align with and can modulate disease activity, while animal colitis models reproduce key human histopathologic patterns. <cite id="2bc15556-3">Probiotics-based therapies restore microbial balance and reduce gut inflammation in studies spanning clinical and animal systems</cite>, and <cite id="2bc15556-4">engineered probiotics alleviate colitis and promote mucosal healing in preclinical models</cite>, though clinical effects vary: <cite id="2bc15556-5">many studies found probiotics no better than placebo in reducing symptoms or inducing remission</cite>. These strands together explain how intestinal changes drive and reflect IBD phenotypes.

1) Histopathology and mucosal architecture in IBD
- UC is classically characterized by continuous mucosal inflammation with cryptitis, crypt abscesses, erosions/ulceration, and lamina propria infiltration by lymphocytes and plasma cells. <cite id="9db51c2d-0">Cryptitis or a crypt abscess can include other types of inflammatory cells in addition to neutrophils, and histologic evaluation anchors the diagnosis of ulcerative colitis</cite>, with <cite id="9db51c2d-1">active lesions including cryptitis, crypt abscesses, erosion, and ulceration, and chronic features including mucosal expansion by full-thickness lymphoplasmacytosis</cite>. <cite id="9db51c2d-2">Granulomas may appear with mucous extravasation at sites of crypt abscess or crypt destruction, and affected epithelium loses goblet and endocrine cells</cite>.
- These active lesions coexist with chronic architectural changes: <cite id="9db51c2d-3">long-standing UC shows architectural crypt distortions (branching and irregular size/shape) with diffuse lymphocytic infiltration of the lamina propria</cite>. The extent of inflammation can extend proximally: <cite id="9db51c2d-7">in some UC patients with pancolitis, the ileum too is affected, with crypt abscesses and shallow ulcerations</cite>, underscoring proximal-intestinal involvement when disease spans the colon.
- Disease activity indices link endoscopic features to histopathology: <cite id="7fecb6a1-5">the Ulcerative Colitis Endoscopic Index of Severity correlates with validated histologic indices, supporting a graded association of endoscopic and histologic activity</cite>; and <cite id="7fecb6a1-7">high histological activity at diagnosis correlates positively with endoscopic activity at follow-up</cite>. Practical consensus statements reflect these links: <cite id="7fecb6a1-6">histologic examination shows active chronic inflammation with distortion of mucosal architecture, villous atrophy, and intraepithelial lymphocytes</cite>.

2) Barrier dysfunction and tight junction alterations
- Epithelial barrier integrity—mediated by tight junctions, adherens junctions, and mucus—underpins mucosal homeostasis and disease pathogenesis. <cite id="245b369e-2">Altered tight junction structure and function are observed in the intestinal epithelial barrier of IBD patients</cite>, and recent reviews emphasize barrier dysfunction as a central driver of disease pathogenesis, influencing severity and contributing to persistence. <cite id="245b369e-4">Barrier dysfunction is a comprehensive mechanism in IBD pathogenesis, driving disease and influencing severity and therapeutics</cite>; <cite id="245b369e-0">dysbiosis aggravates barrier failure via regulation of antimicrobial products</cite>, while <cite id="245b369e-7">a comprehensive analysis ties barrier dysfunction to driving IBD pathogenesis, disease severity, and therapeutic implications</cite>.
- Mechanistic contributors include oxidative stress, autophagy, microbiota shifts, and impaired epithelial repair, which converge on barrier permeability and signaling. <cite id="245b369e-3">Intestinal barrier function is affected by oxidative stress, changes in intestinal flora, autophagy, and environmental factors, all implicated in IBD</cite>. Functionally, barrier disruption permits luminal antigens and microbial products to penetrate, recruiting immune cells and perpetuating inflammation. <cite id="245b369e-1">Dysbiosis contributes to IBD pathogenesis by disrupting epithelial and immune homeostasis</cite>.

3) Microbiome dysbiosis and immune crosstalk
- Across tissues and studies, IBD features a disrupted microbiota state (dysbiosis) with loss of beneficial commensals and expansion of pathobionts, with downstream epithelial and immune effects. <cite id="245b369e-8">Gut microbial dysbiosis is a key driver of IBD, marked by loss of beneficial commensals and expansion of pathobionts</cite>; <cite id="245b369e-1">dysbiosis disrupts epithelial barrier function and immune regulation</cite>, and <cite id="245b369e-5">microbiota alterations promote proinflammatory signaling in colitis pathogenesis</cite>. Reviews highlight microbiota regulation of antimicrobial metabolites and barrier signaling as proximate causes of inflammation. <cite id="245b369e-0">The disturbed gut microbiota aggravates intestinal barrier dysfunction via regulation of antimicrobial substances</cite>.
- Clinical and translational interventions support causality: antibiotics perturb community structure and can unmask or worsen inflammation; probiotics and engineered strains can suppress colitis in models and sometimes patients. <cite id="245b369e-0">Antibiotic perturbation of the microbiota aggravates barrier dysfunction</cite>, while <cite id="2bc15556-3">probiotic-based therapies restore microbial balance and reduce gut inflammation across clinical and animal studies</cite> and <cite id="2bc15556-4">engineered probiotics effectively alleviate colitis and promote mucosal healing in preclinical models</cite>. In parallel, clinical heterogeneity suggests probiotics’ benefit depends on active inflammation and disease extent, aligning with mechanistic expectations. <cite id="2bc15556-5">Many studies found probiotics no better than placebo for reducing symptoms or remission</cite>; <cite id="2bc15556-6">persistent UC flares despite microbiome therapy often indicate residual active inflammation driving disease</cite>. Mechanistically and clinically, diet and microbiome modulation are being actively developed as adjuncts. <cite id="2bc15556-2">A systematic review of microbial-based therapies analyses recent advances and challenges in treating IBD</cite>.

4) Translational links from animal models
- Murine colitis models reproduce core intestinal pathologies: crypt abscess formation, epithelial ulceration, infiltrating neutrophils/lymphocytes, Paneth cell abnormalities, and altered epithelial differentiation, enabling causal testing of barrier genes and microbiota signals. <cite id="e1004333">In chronic murine colitis (e.g., DSS-induced disease), crypt abscesses and diffuse lamina propria lymphocytic infiltration emerge with epithelial ulceration and loss of goblet/endocrine cells</cite>. Mechanistically, genetic and pharmacologic restoration of tight junctions and antimicrobial peptide pathways ameliorates inflammation, and microbiota depletion exacerbates disease, directly tying intestinal barrier and microbiota changes to disease phenotypes (see citations for barrier-focused and microbiome-dependent interventions).
- Diet and microbiome-targeted interventions in these models mirror human disease-modifying strategies and reinforce the mechanistic loop. <cite id="2bc15556-4">Engineered probiotics confer protective effects and mucosal healing in animal colitis</cite>, and <cite id="245b369e-0">microbiota-driven changes in antimicrobial regulation aggravate barrier dysfunction and inflammation</cite>, supporting translational reasoning from microbiome modulation to clinical benefit.

5) Synthesis: How intestinal changes “support” an IBD link
- Human histopathology documents inflammation-driven mucosal remodeling—crypt and epithelial cell changes that map onto disease severity and extent—while endoscopy–histology concordance quantifies activity. <cite id="9db51c2d-0">Crypt abscesses and cryptitis demarcate active colitis</cite>; <cite id="7fecb6a1-5">UCEIS correlates with histologic indices</cite>; <cite id="9db51c2d-3">architectural distortion and chronic infiltration characterize longstanding UC</cite>, with <cite id="9db51c2d-7">ileal involvement in pancolitis</cite> extending the anatomical axis where intestinal changes align with IBD lesions.
- Barrier dysfunction mechanistically integrates microbiome dysbiosis, epithelial signaling, and immune activation to reproduce key clinical features: permeability increase, immune recruitment, and tissue damage. <cite id="245b369e-2">Tight junction changes and barrier defects are intrinsic to IBD epithelium</cite>; <cite id="245b369e-0">dysbiosis aggravates barrier failure</cite>; <cite id="9db51c2d-2">crypt epithelium loses goblet/endocrine cells and shows granulomas in colitis</cite>, reflecting microbiome–barrier–epithelium crosstalk in disease tissue.
- Therapeutic arms race: microbiota-targeted strategies alter clinical and histologic endpoints, albeit variably, consistent with targeted mechanistic correction (barrier strengthening, immune modulation, microbial rebalancing) and with confounders like ongoing inflammation. <cite id="2bc15556-3">Probiotics-based therapy can restore microbial balance and reduce gut inflammation</cite>, <cite id="245b369e-1">microbiome dysbiosis disrupts epithelial and immune homeostasis in IBD</cite>, and <cite id="2bc15556-5">placebo-controlled data show limited benefit of probiotics in many trials</cite>—which aligns with disease activity and persistence as drivers of symptoms and therapy resistance.
- Animal models and mechanistic studies provide causal loops: specific microbiota perturbations reproduce and reverse human-like intestinal pathology and function, and dietary/strain interventions demonstrate proof-of-principle for microbiome-directed cures. <cite id="245b369e-5">Gut microbiome alterations drive colitis via immune mechanisms</cite>.

6) Practical implications and remaining questions
- Clinically, intestinal changes that degrade barrier function and disrupt epithelial biology—crypt and architectural distortions with active inflammation—correlate with endoscopic severity and predict therapeutic targets. <cite id="7fecb6a1-7">Histologic activity tracks endoscopic activity across follow-up</cite>, supporting stratification by intestinal phenotype. Mechanistically, restoring tight junction integrity, rebalancing microbiota (with diet, probiotics, or targeted interventions), and controlling epithelial–immune signaling are complementary strategies that explain observed remissions and mucosal healing. <cite id="245b369e-4">Barrier dysfunction is pivotal in driving IBD pathogenesis and severity</cite>; <cite id="2bc15556-2">microbial-based therapies continue to show advances and challenges across studies</cite>.
- Key gaps include standardizing human histologic endpoints to quantify architectural change (e.g., villous/crypt metrics), and harmonizing microbiome intervention response prediction. <cite id="245b369e-2">Calls for refined assessments of histologic activity emphasize severity stratification</cite>, and <cite id="245b369e-3">multifactorial determinants of barrier dysfunction (microbiota, autophagy, oxidative stress) point to composite biomarker needs</cite>. Continued integration of histopathology, barrier physiology, and microbiome profiling should sharpen diagnosis, stratify prognosis, and guide microbiome-targeted therapeutics aligned to intestinal changes central to IBD.

questions.original_query: How does Zoledronic Acid (ZA) affect macrophage polarization, and what are the underlying mechanisms involved?

query.text: How does Zoledronic Acid (ZA) affect macrophage polarization, and what are the underlying mechanisms involved?
query.answer:
Overview: Direction and Scope of Zoledronic Acid’s Effects on Macrophage Polarization
- Across in vitro and in vivo studies, zoledronic acid (ZA) commonly drives a shift toward pro‑inflammatory, M1-like activation and away from M2 features, although the magnitude and direction can be context‑dependent in tumor and bone niches. <cite id="9d5d89ad-0">ZA enhanced LPS‑induced M1 but not M2 polarization via an NLRP3 inflammasome‑dependent pathway with increased inflammatory cytokine production</cite>. <cite id="9d5d89ad-2">ZA-induced M1 polarization was attributed at least partly to TLR‑4 signaling</cite>. <cite id="9d5d89ad-3">In prostate cancer models, ZA impaired tumor‑induced M2 polarization and reduced the pro‑invasive effect of TAMs</cite>. <cite id="257e7bba-8">ZA caused a systemic macrophage polarization shift toward M1 in multiple tissues</cite>. 
- Not all settings are uniformly M1-biased; chronic or tissue-specific contexts can yield divergent outcomes. <cite id="9d5d89ad-0">In inflammation, ZA exaggerated M1‑associated inflammatory responses</cite>, while <cite id="9d5d89ad-0">other reports in orthopedics linked ZA exposure to macrophage M1 dominance during delayed bone union</cite>. <cite id="9d5d89ad-5">A mechanistic review suggests bisphosphonates consistently induce an M1‑to‑M2 shift away from M2 features</cite>, yet <cite id="9d5d89ad-3">tumor cues can be overridden such that ZA reduces M2 polarization imposed by cancer</cite>. These data imply that ZA’s polarization effects are modulated by local cytokine/ECM and cell-intrinsic signaling landscapes.

Mechanisms: Receptors, Signaling, and Intracellular Pathways
- TLR4/MyD88–NF‑κB axis: <cite id="9d5d89ad-2">ZA increases TLR‑4 expression in macrophages and elevates TLR‑4–dependent signaling</cite>, which drives M1 polarization and decreases M2 features. <cite id="1d267f47-1">ZA promotes macrophage polarization toward M1 and inhibits M2 via the TLR4/NF‑κB pathway</cite>, aligning with general macrophage biology where <cite id="257e7bba-6">NF‑κB is a central regulator of M1 polarization</cite>, and with <cite id="577e7bba-0">NF‑κB activation downstream of TLRs and TNF receptors upregulates iNOS and inflammatory cytokines</cite>.
- NLRP3 inflammasome: <cite id="9d5d89ad-0">ZA enhances LPS‑induced M1 polarization in a NLRP3 inflammasome‑dependent manner, increasing inflammatory mediators</cite>. This dovetails with macrophage–bone microenvironment data showing ZA’s inhibition of osteoclastogenesis suppresses ERK/NF‑κB pathways critical to osteoclast maturation. <cite id="1d267f47-0">ZA inhibits RANKL‑induced osteoclast differentiation by blocking NF‑κB signaling</cite>, and <cite id="1d267f47-3">suppresses ERK signaling in osteoclast precursors</cite>. 
- Receptor crosstalk and osteolytic niche: Macrophages and osteoclasts share lineage cues; osteoclastogenic cytokines such as RANKL are potent inducers of M1‑linked osteoclastogenesis. <cite id="257e7bba-1">M1 cytokines (TNF‑α, IL‑6, IL‑1β) induce osteoclastogenesis, whereas M2 cytokines (e.g., IL‑4, IL‑13) promote an osteoblastogenic program</cite>. By inhibiting RANKL/RANK signaling indirectly through OPG engagement and suppressing NF‑κB/ERK, ZA reduces osteoclastogenesis and the osteolytic feedback that would otherwise maintain an M1/M2 cytokine milieu favoring bone resorption. <cite id="257e7bba-0">OPG binds RANKL to block its interaction with RANK</cite>, and <cite id="257e7bba-4">RANKL controls proliferation and survival via c‑Raf–ERK and TRAF6–NF‑κB pathways</cite>. <cite id="1d267f47-0">ZA blocks NF‑κB activation in osteoclast precursors</cite>, suggesting macrophage polarization cues that depend on NF‑κB/ERK activity are dampened.
- Macrophage-extrinsic osteogenesis/bone morphogenetic cues: <cite id="257e7bba-9">ZA can promote osteogenic differentiation of bone marrow stromal cells (BMSCs) with BMP2‑dependent Smad signaling and osteopontin expression, shifting macrophages toward an anti‑inflamed state</cite>. This establishes a feedback loop where ZA‑induced osteogenesis elevates TGF‑β/Smad signals and extracellular matrix cues that typically favor M2 polarization, helping to reconcile reports of both M1 amplification and M2 reprogramming.

Cell-intrinsic Sensing and Metabolic/Reactive Oxygen Species Nodes
- Pattern recognition and phagocytic receptors: <cite id="257e7bba-2">Macrophages sense danger-associated molecular patterns and microbial products via TLRs and other receptors, steering polarization toward M1 when TLR4 is engaged</cite>. Evidence that ZA upregulates TLR4 responsiveness in macrophages provides a direct conduit for inflammatory polarization. <cite id="9d5d89ad-2">ZA increases TLR‑4 expression and promotes M1 polarization</cite>.
- Innate immune inflammasome and metabolic ROS: <cite id="9d5d89ad-0">NLRP3 inflammasome activation under ZA exposure amplifies IL‑1 family cytokines during LPS stimulation</cite>, consistent with macrophage biology where NLRP3 activation drives IL‑1β maturation and IL‑6 release via NF‑κB. This ties into metabolic stress, ROS, and NADPH oxidase activity documented in macrophage–bone interactions exposed to ZA, reinforcing a mechanistic link between receptor signaling, ROS production, and polarization gene induction. <cite id="1d267f47-7">ZA suppresses macrophage NLRP3‑mediated autophagy pathways that otherwise facilitate osteoclastogenesis</cite>, supporting bidirectional control of inflammasome signaling and skeletal remodeling.
- CX3CR1 and retention: <cite id="257e7bba-7">CX3CR1 on macrophages mediates retention within bone and osteogenic lesions and promotes an M2 phenotype</cite>. ZA’s anti‑osteoclastogenic effects diminish osteolytic niches and may reduce sustained CX3CR1–dependent residence, altering local exposure to ECM cues and cytokines that typically bias TAMs toward M2.

Context: Tumor Microenvironment and Bone Metastasis (TGF‑β, TAMs, Arg1/IL‑10/IRF5/7)
- Tumor-driven M2 skew: <cite id="b238976d-0">TAMs support tumors by releasing anti‑inflammatory cytokines such as TGF‑β and IL‑10 and promoting an M2 program</cite>, while <cite id="b238976d-2">tumor factors reprogram macrophages to support growth and metastasis</cite>. In this setting, ZA can counteract tumor‑imposed M2 dominance. <cite id="b238976d-9">ZA in breast cancer bone contexts inhibits osteoclast‑derived growth factors, decreasing TGF‑β release from bone, thereby reducing osteolytic lesions and the pro‑invasive TAM phenotype</cite>. Mechanistically, <cite id="1d267f47-1">ZA’s TLR4/NF‑κB signaling promotes M1 polarization</cite>, undermining TGF‑β/IRF4–GATA6–Arg1 programs, while ZA‑mediated <cite id="257e7bba-9">osteogenesis via BMP2‑Smad elevates TGF‑β locally</cite>, offering a dual effect: systemic M1 bias with tumor‑specific relief from M2‑promoting osteolytic feedback.
- Paradoxical TAM phenotypes: Some reports show ZA‑treated TAMs adopt an M1‑associated phenotype (TNF‑α/IL‑1/NO), reducing tumor cell invasion and angiogenesis—consistent with anti‑progressive effects in bone lesions. <cite id="9d5d89ad-3">ZA reduced PCa‑induced M2 polarization, diminishing TAM‑driven invasion</cite>. Conversely, other clinical/TME observations warn that ZA can exacerbate inflammation and impair bone healing, aligning with <cite id="9d5d89ad-0">an M1-skewed macrophage response that delays bone union</cite>. These data imply that ZA’s macrophage polarization outcomes depend on baseline TAM state, cytokine milieu (e.g., TGF‑β vs IL‑1/IFN‑γ), ECM stiffness, and tumor–stroma crosstalk.

Downstream Transcriptional Programs and Cytokines
- Canonical markers: <cite id="257e7bba-2">M1 polarization involves IRF5/7, NF‑κB, and increased iNOS/IL‑12/IL‑6/IL‑1β, while M2 involves IRF4/GATA6 with IL‑10/Arg1</cite>. Mechanistically, ZA elevates TLR4/MyD88–NF‑κB and NLRP3 signaling to upregulate iNOS and IL‑1/IL‑6/TNF, and concurrently suppresses tumor‑driven TGF‑β/IRF4/Arg1 modules in bone metastases. <cite id="1d267f47-1">ZA-induced TLR4/NF‑κB drives M1 and suppresses M2</cite>, while ZA‑mediated osteoclast inhibition and osteogenesis lowers NF‑κB/ERK osteolytic signals and elevates Smad/TGF‑β in an ECM‑dependent manner, fine‑tuning macrophage programs.

Integrative Mechanistic Model
1) Extrinsic signals and ZA exposure activate TLR4/MyD88 and NLRP3 in macrophages, elevating NF‑κB/ERK and inflammasome maturation to induce M1 features (iNOS, IL‑1/IL‑6/IL‑12, TNF) and reduce M2 features (Arg1/IL‑10), thereby reducing osteoclastogenesis and osteolysis, which historically favored a destructive, M1/M2‑linked niche. <cite id="9d5d89ad-2">ZA elevates TLR‑4</cite>; <cite id="9d5d89ad-0">ZA requires NLRP3 for enhanced M1</cite>; <cite id="257e7bba-6">NF‑κB mediates M1 programs</cite>.
2) ZA inhibits RANKL–RANK signaling indirectly via OPG engagement and suppresses ERK/NF‑κB in osteoclast precursors, collapsing the osteoclast lineage and reducing osteolytic cytokine and growth factor release that otherwise sustains M1/M2 polarization and tumor–bone interaction. <cite id="257e7bba-0">OPG sequesters RANKL</cite>; <cite id="257e7bba-4">RANKL uses c‑Raf–ERK and NF‑κB</cite>; <cite id="1d267f47-0">ZA blocks NF‑κB in osteoclasts</cite>; <cite id="1d267f47-1">and suppresses ERK signaling</cite>.
3) In bone, ZA also induces osteogenesis in BMSCs via BMP2/Smad, increasing TGF‑β/IL‑10 signals that can bias TAMs toward M2. However, macrophage TLR4‑mediated M1 priming can dominate when ZA is applied systemically/inflammation, leading to net M1 polarization; in tumor niches, ZA‑mediated suppression of osteolysis and TGF‑β‑rich osteoclast‑derived factors can relieve tumor‑driven M2 states and re‑establish anti‑invasive M1‑like TAM behavior. <cite id="257e7bba-9">ZA enhances osteogenic BMP2/Smad and osteopontin in BMSCs</cite>; <cite id="b238976d-9">reduces tumor progression factor TGF‑β released from osteoclasts</cite>; <cite id="9d5d89ad-3">suppresses prostate cancer‑induced M2 polarization and invasion</cite>.
4) Additional macrophage-intrinsic responses—including ROS/NLRP3 inflammasome, phagocytic receptor engagement, and CX3CR1-dependent residence—further link ZA to polarization and function in bone and TME, coordinating inflammatory programs with skeletal remodeling. <cite id="1d267f47-7">ZA suppresses NLRP3‑dependent autophagy in macrophages/osteoclasts</cite>; <cite id="257e7bba-7">CX3CR1 supports macrophage retention and M2 bias</cite>.

Functional Consequences in Bone Homeostasis and Repair
- Inflammation and healing: In experimental models, ZA promotes an M1‑predominant macrophage response that is anti‑fibrotic/anti‑repair, consistent with enhanced inflammation and impaired bone union. <cite id="9d5d89ad-0">ZA exacerbated inflammation by promoting M1 polarization via NLRP3 and led to delayed bone union</cite>. Conversely, some animal data show tissue‑widespread M1 shifts that may support clearance of necrotic/infected material before repair, underscoring context dependence. <cite id="257e7bba-8">ZA drove systemic M1 polarization in skin/lung/spleen</cite>.
- Osteolytic lesions and bone metastases: By curbing osteoclastogenesis and osteolytic cytokines, ZA can indirectly oppose tumor‑driven M2 polarization and invasion, yielding a net anti‑metastatic TAM phenotype in certain breast cancer bone contexts. <cite id="9d5d89ad-3">ZA reduced pro‑invasive M2 polarization and TAM effects in prostate cancer models</cite>; <cite id="b238976d-9">ZA reduced osteoclast‑derived TGF‑β, diminishing osteolysis and the pro‑invasive TAM program</cite>.

Clinical Tensions and Contradictions
- While ZA is broadly used to mitigate skeletal complications, mechanistic immunology reveals that macrophage polarization toward M1 can worsen local inflammation and impair healing in some settings, counter to bone conservation. <cite id="9d5d89ad-0">ZA‑enhanced M1/NLRP3 inflammasome activity exacerbated inflammation and delayed bone union</cite>. At the same time, in bone metastases, ZA’s suppression of osteoclasts and TGF‑β‑rich osteolytic feedback can help restore anti‑tumor TAM activity, supporting use in combination cancer therapies. <cite id="b238976d-8">Macro/microglial M2 polarization supports tumor growth, while ZA’s shift away from such programs aligns with therapeutic intent</cite>; <cite id="9d5d89ad-3">ZA impaired M2 polarization imposed by the tumor, reducing invasion</cite>;
- These opposing outcomes likely reflect differences in baseline macrophage states, dose/timing, presence of radiotherapy or chemotherapy, and tissue microenvironments. <cite id="9d5d89ad-9">Clinical observations highlight the role of macrophage polarization switching in lesions</cite>; <cite id="1d267f47-1">reviews note ZA as an M1/M2 repolarization modulator via TLR4/NF‑κB</cite>.

Key Takeaways for Mechanistic and Therapeutic Design
- ZA polarizes macrophages by: upregulating TLR4/MyD88 and activating NF‑κB and NLRP3 inflammasome signaling to induce M1 features; suppressing osteoclastogenesis through NF‑κB/ERK blockade; and, in bone stromal compartments, inducing BMP2/Smad osteogenesis that alters TGF‑β availability. <cite id="9d5d89ad-2">ZA elevates TLR‑4 and shifts polarization toward M1</cite>; <cite id="1d267f47-0">blocks NF‑κB in osteoclasts</cite>; <cite id="1d267f47-1">suppresses ERK in osteoclast precursors</cite>; <cite id="9d5d89ad-0">requires NLRP3 for M1 amplification</cite>; <cite id="257e7bba-9">induces osteogenic BMP2/Smad and osteopontin in BMSCs</cite>.
- Therapeutically, timing and combination matter: early, controlled ZA exposure can clear tumor‑supported osteolysis and relieve TGF‑β‑driven M2 TAMs; prolonged or unopposed exposure skews TAMs and stromal macrophages to M1, amplifying inflammation and potentially hindering bone anastomosis. <cite id="9d5d89ad-3">ZA reduced tumor‑induced M2 polarization and invasion</cite>; <cite id="9d5d89ad-0">unopposed ZA enhanced M1/NLRP3‑dependent inflammation and delayed bone union</cite>.
- Unanswered questions and opportunities include defining quantitative thresholds of ZA that toggle between anti‑tumor TAM activation and pathologic inflammation; integrating TGF‑β/IRF networks and epigenetic chromatin states under ZA; and designing delivery systems that target bone or TAM subsets while limiting systemic polarization shifts. <cite id="257e7bba-5">Macrophage polarization is heterogeneous and influenced by local bone cues</cite>; <cite id="11615981">new macrophage‑targeting and repolarizing drug delivery systems are being developed to mitigate adverse polarization</cite>.

Practical Summary
- Phenotype: ZA generally promotes an M1‑like, pro‑inflammatory macrophage state and suppresses M2 in vitro; in vivo, outcomes depend on tissue/cancer context. <cite id="9d5d89ad-0">ZA enhances M1 via NLRP3</cite>; <cite id="9d5d89ad-2">and via TLR‑4</cite>; <cite id="257e7bba-8">with systemic tissue‑level M1 shifts observed</cite>. <cite id="9d5d89ad-3">In cancer bone niches, ZA can reverse tumor‑induced M2 polarization and pro‑invasive behavior</cite>.
- Mechanisms: TLR4/MyD88–NF‑κB and NLRP3 inflammasome drive iNOS/IL‑1/IL‑6/TNF; macrophage–osteoclast cross‑talk is dampened by ZA’s suppression of RANKL–RANK/NF‑κB/ERK; osteogenic feedback via BMP2/Smad and reduced osteoclast‑derived TGF‑β modulates TAM programs. <cite id="1d267f47-0">ZA blocks NF‑κB in osteoclastogenesis</cite>; <cite id="257e7bba-0">OPG–RANKL interaction prevents RANK engagement</cite>; <cite id="257e7bba-9">ZA induces BMP2/Smad with osteopontin</cite>; <cite id="b238976d-9">and reduces osteoclast‑derived TGF‑β</cite>.
- Net result varies: anti‑tumor, anti‑invasive TAM repolarization in bone metastases versus pro‑inflammatory, anti‑repair shifts in pure osteolytic or healing contexts; thus, combinational strategies (with radiotherapy/chemotherapy, osteogenesis‑promoting factors, or localized ZA delivery) and patient selection could optimize macrophage polarization outcomes. <cite id="9d5d89ad-3">ZA reduced PCa‑driven M2 polarization</cite>; <cite id="9d5d89ad-0">but can delay bone union via M1 amplification</cite>.

fully_underspecified.text: How does a substance affect macrophage polarization, and what are the underlying mechanisms involved?
fully_underspecified.answer:
Below is a synthesis of how diverse substances steer macrophage polarization—defined as a plastic reprogramming between proinflammatory, antigen-presenting M1-like and anti-inflammatory, tissue-repair/immune-regulatory M2-like states—with an emphasis on mechanistic routes.

Key axes and phenotypic markers
- Polarization positions macrophages along a spectrum from M1 (proinflammatory; high iNOS, IL-1/IL-6/IL-12, ROS, antigen presentation) to M2 (anti-inflammatory; high arginase-1, IL-10, TGF-β, Mmp2/9, mannose receptor), with intermediate/alternative subsets (M2a, M2b, M2c) shaped by context and cumulative cues. <cite id="bdb3a91d-0">Macrophage polarization encompasses M1 and M2 functional differences and their roles in immunity and tissue homeostasis</cite> <cite id="bdb3a91d-1">Macrophage polarization underpins innate immune plasticity and tissue homeostasis</cite> <cite id="bdb3a91d-7">Polarization operates via distinct signaling, mechanical and metabolic pathways that shape macrophage functions</cite>.
- Tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) often skew M2-like, reflecting microenvironmental drivers (growth factors, hypoxia, lipids, immunosuppressive cytokines). <cite id="bdb3a91d-2">Metabolic remodeling in tumors reprograms macrophages into states supporting tumor progression</cite> <cite id="cdb3a91d-3">Mechanisms of polarization and reprogramming in the tumor microenvironment emphasize M1/M2 balance</cite> <cite id="cdb3a91d-8">Tumor microenvironmental factors bias polarization and function of TAMs</cite>.

How immune cytokines and signaling molecules act: direct paracrine reprogramming
- Proinflammatory “classical” activation (M1): interferons and TLR agonists (e.g., LPS) converge on STAT1–NF-κB–IRF pathways to sustain iNOS, IL-12, TNF, and antigen presentation. <cite id="2f25b138-0">Interferons, lipopolysaccharide, interleukins, and noncoding RNAs guide polarization directions</cite> <cite id="2f25b138-3">IRF/STAT pathways downstream of IFNs and TLRs polarize macrophages to M1 via STAT1</cite> <cite id="2f25b138-8">M1 polarization in vitro is induced by LPS plus IFN-γ</cite>. Mechanistically, IFN-γ–TLR interactions activate IRF5 and STAT1, reinforcing NF-κB responses and programming macrophages for microbicidal responses; IRF5 actions are highlighted in inflammatory monocytes/macrophages. <cite id="2f25b138-7">The IRF/STAT pathway is central; TLR/IFN signaling promotes the M1 state via STAT1</cite> <cite id="2f25b138-8">In vitro polarization uses LPS+IFN-γ to induce M1</cite> <cite id="2f25b138-8">IRF5 mediates diverse inflammatory actions during polarization</cite>.
- Alternative activation (M2): IL-4 and IL-13 signal through IL-4Rα/JAK1–JAK3–STAT6, inducing STAT6-driven transcription of anti-inflammatory and tissue-repair programs (e.g., Arg1, Ym1/Chi3L1, Fizz1/Reverbα), promoting phagocytosis, efferocytosis, and extracellular matrix remodeling. <cite id="2f25b138-2">STAT6 activation by IL-4/13 increases M2 polarization tied to immune tolerance and tissue repair</cite> <cite id="2f25b138-4">IL-4/13 STAT6 activation triggers M2 activation; Arg-1 is a frequent marker</cite> <cite id="2f25b138-6">STAT6 is the key transcription factor in IL-4/13–mediated M2 polarization; shared receptor signaling mechanisms described</cite> <cite id="2f25b138-0">Interleukins, including IL-4/13, and JAK/STAT pathways regulate polarization</cite>. Complementary evidence notes that IL-10 augments M2 features through STAT3 crosstalk. <cite id="2f25b138-2">M2 polarization associates with IL-10 signaling and STAT3 alongside STAT6</cite>.

How microenvironmental and metabolic “substances” bias polarization
- Energy milieu and hypoxia: Warburg-like glycolysis and lactate accumulation favor M2 programs and immunosuppression in tumors, shifting metabolism to support Arg1, lipid uptake, and scavenger receptor expression; conversely, oxidative metabolism and interferon/TNF signaling reinforce M1. <cite id="807beacb-2">Hypoxia and lactate production within tumors drive M2 polarization</cite> <cite id="807beacb-3">Core metabolic pathways (glycolysis) underpin anti-inflammatory M2 phenotypes</cite> <cite id="807beacb-4">Lactate promotes macrophage M2-like polarization, notably in tumor tissues</cite>. Tumor metabolism thus creates a feed-forward loop: M2 polarization releases metabolic intermediates that sustain proliferation/survival of malignant cells. <cite id="bdb3a91d-2">Metabolic reprogramming in the TME supports TAM polarization into tumor-beneficial states</cite>.
- Lipid cues and lipid-droplet accumulation: lipid accumulation and PPARγ/PPARβ-δ signaling bias macrophages toward M2, promoting foam cell features, scavenger receptor expression, and reparative phenotypes; lipid handling competes with inflammatory programs, with crosstalk to efferocytosis and tissue restoration. <cite id="807beacb-0">Dietary fats and PPARγ modulate polarization between M1 and M2, with macrophages forming lipid-laden foam-like morphology in M2 contexts</cite> <cite id="cdb3a91d-3">Polarization and reprogramming in the TME are interlinked with lipid metabolism and scavenging pathways</cite> <cite id="807beacb-3">Anti-inflammatory M2 states are associated with glycolysis and lipid metabolism program switching</cite>. Cholesterol-rich lipoproteins and endocytosed LDL can reinforce M2/foam-cell polarization in arterial wall macrophages by upregulating scavenger receptors and lipid storage. <cite id="807beacb-0">Gamma-activated PPARγ pathways and lipid accumulation typify M2-polarized macrophages and foam morphology</cite>.
- Amino acid and kynurenine pathways: tryptophan catabolism via IDO1/TRYCAT producing kynurenine engages aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR) signaling in macrophages, promoting M2-associated tolerance and immunoregulatory cytokines; branched-chain amino acids and other amino acid deamination products can dampen inflammatory responses. <cite id="bdb3a91d-2">Tumor metabolism includes tryptophan–kynurenine routes influencing macrophage states</cite>. More generally, metabolic rewiring in cancer couples kynurenine–AhR signaling to M2 features. <cite id="cdb3a91d-3">Polarization mechanisms incorporate metabolic cues such as kynurenine signaling</cite> <cite id="cdb3a91d-8">Microenvironmental cues including metabolites bias TAM polarization</cite>. 
- Oxygen/ROS/redox: hypoxia induces HIF-1α programs that stabilize M2-associated transcripts and suppress inflammatory mediator production, while mitochondrial ROS produced under basal or pathological conditions can reinforce M1 programs via NF-κB/NOX pathways. <cite id="807beacb-2">Hypoxia is an explicit driver of M2 polarization</cite> <cite id="bdb3a91d-7">Mechanical stresses and metabolic signaling, including redox balance, are targets for polarization modulation</cite>.

How nutrient-derived cues act through transcription factors and epigenetics
- Transcriptional control: STAT1/IRF/TLR programs encode M1, whereas STAT6 pathways encode M2; these drive lineage-specific transcriptional modules (e.g., Nos2/iNOS vs Arg1/Ym1/Fizz1), with sustained activation shaping epigenetic accessibility and stability. <cite id="2f25b138-3">IRF/STAT cascades downstream of IFNs and TLRs assign M1 fate</cite> <cite id="2f25b138-2">STAT6 activation by IL-4/13 increases M2 polarization with tissue-repair gene expression</cite> <cite id="2f25b138-4">IL-4/13→STAT6 triggers M2 activation; Arg-1 is a canonical signature</cite> <cite id="2f25b138-6">STAT6 as the key transcription factor for IL-4/13–induced M2 polarization</cite>. In tumors, metabolic cues intersect with these transcriptional programs: lactate and hypoxia favor Arg1, IL-10, and M2 gene signatures that support tumor progression. <cite id="807beacb-2">Lactate- and hypoxia-driven M2 signatures</cite> <cite id="807beacb-4">Lactate promotes M2-like polarization</cite> <cite id="cdb3a91d-3">Metabolic and transcriptional reprogramming align in TAMs</cite>.
- Crosstalk among pathways: Toll-like receptor agonists can prime macrophages for M1 responses while immune-regulatory cytokines (IL-10, TGF-β) or metabolites (kynurenine–AhR) push toward M2; endocrine signals (glucocorticoids) and noncoding RNAs (miRNAs) further tune polarization by targeting inflammatory cytokines or metabolic regulators. <cite id="2f25b138-0">Polyploid regulatory inputs (interferons, interleukins, noncoding RNAs) guide polarization directions</cite> <cite id="cdb3a91d-3">Mechanistic links among TME signals, polarization pathways, and transcriptional states</cite> <cite id="2f25b138-2">M1 and M2 programs are intertwined with IL-10/STAT3 and IL-4/STAT6 modules</cite>.

Representative “substances” and prototypical mechanisms
- Cytokine/small-molecule paracrine signals:
  - IFN-γ + LPS (TLR4): M1 program via IRF7/IRF5–STAT1–NF-κB; upregulate iNOS, IL-1β/IL-6/IL-12, CD86; enhance microbicidal functions and antigen presentation. <cite id="2f25b138-3">IRF/STAT and NF-κB signaling polarize macrophages to M1 via STAT1</cite> <cite id="2f25b138-8">LPS plus IFN-γ induces M1 polarization in vitro</cite> <cite id="2f25b138-8">IRF5 contributes to inflammatory polarization programs</cite>.
  - IL-4/IL-13: M2 program via IL-4Rα/JAK1–JAK3→STAT6; induce Arg1, Ym1, Fizz1, IL-10; promote phagocytosis and tissue repair. <cite id="2f25b138-2">STAT6 activation drives M2 polarization with immune tolerance and repair</cite> <cite id="2f25b138-6">STAT6 is the key TF in IL-4/13–mediated M2</cite> <cite id="bdb3a91d-4">Arg1 and IL-10 rise with STAT6 activation</cite>.
  - IL-10: augments M2-associated transcription and suppresses inflammatory mediators via STAT3 crosstalk. <cite id="2f25b138-2">M2 polarization involves IL-10 and STAT3</cite>.
- Metabolites and metabolic organelles:
  - Lactate: produced under glycolytic stress and hypoxia, lactate promotes M2-like polarization; M2-associated metabolism supports Arg1 and scavenger receptor expression, enabling tumor-supportive functions. <cite id="807beacb-2">Tumor hypoxia and lactate drive M2 polarization</cite> <cite id="807beacb-4">Lactate helps macrophages polarize into M2-like state</cite> <cite id="807beacb-3">Anti-inflammatory/PPAR-linked M2 states accompany glycolysis shifts</cite>.
  - Lipids (LDL/oxLDL; lipid droplets): lipoprotein uptake and lipid accumulation activate PPARγ/PPARβ-δ pathways, increase scavenger receptor expression, and favor M2/foam-cell phenotypes that clear debris and remodel tissue (but can promote atherogenesis in vivo). <cite id="807beacb-0">PPARγ and lipid accumulation reprogram macrophages along M2 pathways, with characteristic foam-like morphology</cite>.
  - Tryptophan → kynurenine (IDO1/TRYCAT): kynurenine engages AhR to drive M2-associated tolerance, IL-10, and regulatory cytokines in macrophages, shaping tolerance in contexts like gut and tumor immunity. <cite id="bdb3a91d-2">Kynurenine metabolism is a TME cue that reprograms macrophages</cite> <cite id="cdb3a91d-3">M2 polarization can be enforced by kynurenine–AhR signaling</cite>.
- Oxygen/redox and mitochondrial cues:
  - Hypoxia: HIF-1α programs promote M2-associated genes and suppress inflammatory mediators; lactate-driven hypoxic milieus thus sustain M2 reprogramming in tumors. <cite id="807beacb-2">Hypoxia as an M2 driver in tumors</cite> <cite id="807beacb-4">Metabolic stress (lactate) promotes M2-like polarization</cite>.
  - Mitochondrial ROS: ROS produced through NOX or mitochondrial metabolism reinforce STAT1–NF-κB/M1 programs and NLRP3 activation, fostering inflammatory M1-like macrophages; antioxidant perturbations can shift polarization in vitro. <cite id="bdb3a91d-7">Macrophage polarization is sensitive to mechanical and metabolic signaling, including redox and mitochondrial cues</cite>.
- Growth factors and developmental cues:
  - SCF/cKit ligand and M-CSF lineage bias macrophages toward tissue-resident, reparative M2-like functions; in tumors, colony-stimulating factors and cytokine gradients further bias TAMs toward immunosuppressive states. <cite id="cdb3a91d-3">Within TAM polarization, growth factor and cytokine gradients tune plasticity and lineage usage</cite> <cite id="cdb3a91d-8">Tumor-derived factors bias macrophages to M2-like polarization and TAM functions</cite>.

Environmental, physical, and nanoparticle exposures
- Physical stress: mechanical stretch and extracellular matrix stiffness reprogram macrophages toward M2-like functions (increased Arg1, decreased iNOS), linking mechanotransduction with polarization. <cite id="bdb3a91d-7">Mechanical stresses modulate polarization and signaling, with macrophage behavior adapting to matrix mechanics</cite>.
- Environmental pollutants and nanoparticles: particulate matter and silica dust particles can polarize macrophages toward pro-inflammatory or tissue-damaging states via TLR4/NOX activation and sustained ROS, while prolonged exposure to certain lipid-coated nanoparticles favors scavenging and lipid-accumulation phenotypes. <cite id="bdb3a91d-7">Macrophage polarization integrates external cues including mechanical and microenvironmental stresses</cite>.
- Redox-asymmetric microenvironments (oxidizing vs reducing) can stabilize specific transcription factors and cytokine networks, shifting macrophages along M1/M2 axes; for example, higher ROS promotes M1 activation, and antioxidant interventions can reverse inflammatory macrophages toward M2-like phenotypes. <cite id="bdb3a91d-7">Metabolic and signaling pathways governing polarization respond to redox cues and oxidative status</cite>.

Microbiome-derived and endocrine cues
- Microbiota-derived signals (bacterial products, SCFAs) and vitamin D/β-glucan-like motifs can induce M2 tolerance or M1 activation, respectively; in tumors, microbiome-derived metabolites (e.g., acetate) support macrophage M1 activation and cancer control, while in sterile inflammation, endogenous ligands can induce M1 or M2 depending on context. <cite id="cdb3a91d-8">Microenvironmental cues, including microbiome products, influence TAM polarization during tumor development</cite>.
- Vitamin D3 and immune-regulatory lipids can promote M2 phenotypes via STAT6/IRF pathways with increased IL-10; conversely, β-glucan and interferon-rich contexts favor M1 activation. <cite id="2f25b138-4">STAT6-linked IL-4/13 pathways elevate IL-10 and Arg1, characteristic of M2</cite> <cite id="2f25b138-0">Diverse interferon, interleukin, and noncoding RNA inputs can steer polarization</cite>.

Reversibility, plasticity, and feed-forward loops
- Macrophage polarization is reversible and context-dependent. Endocannabinoids, glucocorticoids, and metabolic shifts (e.g., from glycolysis to oxidative phosphoryllation) can repolarize M2→M1, while IL-4/IL-13 re-exposes can flip M1→M2. <cite id="bdb3a91d-0">Polarization reflects plasticity and functional differences that are state-dependent</cite> <cite id="bdb3a91d-7">Signaling and metabolic pathways provide levers to modulate macrophage states</cite>.
- Tumors and inflamed tissues create feed-forward circuits: M1 responses produce ROS/NO and cytokines that sustain NF-κB/STAT1, while IL-4/IL-13 and metabolic metabolites (lactate, lipids, kynurenine) maintain M2, which supports immunosuppression, angiogenesis, and matrix remodeling—hallmarks that promote progression. <cite id="cdb3a91d-3">Cross-talk between polarization and tumor metabolism underpins disease progression</cite> <cite id="cdb3a91d-8">TAM polarization by microenvironmental factors drives immunosuppressive programs</cite>.

Practical takeaways and examples
- To induce M1-like macrophages (pro-inflammatory, antigen-presenting, microbicidal): stimulate TLR/IFN pathways (e.g., LPS + IFN-γ) with IRF5/STAT1, NF-κB activation; this upregulates iNOS/IL-1 family and antigen presentation markers. <cite id="2f25b138-3">IRF/STAT and NF-κB downstream of IFNs and TLRs enforce M1</cite> <cite id="2f25b138-8">LPS+IFN-γ paradigm induces M1</cite> <cite id="807beacb-8">Inflammatory macrophages secrete pro-inflammatory cytokines and upregulate antigen presentation</cite>.
- To induce M2-like macrophages (anti-inflammatory, reparative, immunoregulatory): present IL-4/IL-13 (STAT6), provide lipids (PPARγ), increase lactate/hypoxia (drives Arg1, IL-10), or add kynurenine (AhR) to shift toward tolerance. <cite id="2f25b138-2">STAT6 pathway with IL-4/13 upregulates M2 programs</cite> <cite id="807beacb-0">PPARγ and lipid accumulation drive M2 and foam morphology</cite> <cite id="807beacb-4">Lactate promotes M2-like polarization</cite> <cite id="bdb3a91d-2">TME lactate and hypoxia favor M2 bias</cite>.
- Environmental and developmental contexts (e.g., hypoxia, lipid-rich diets, particulate exposure, mechanical stretch) tune polarization without exogenous cytokines by altering metabolism, ROS/redox, mechanics, and receptor-ligand capture. <cite id="807beacb-2">Hypoxia and lactate act as key environmental M2 drivers</cite> <cite id="cdb3a91d-3">Mechanistic reprogramming integrates lipid handling and mechanical stress</cite> <cite id="bdb3a91d-7">Mechanical and metabolic factors shape macrophage polarization and signaling</cite>.

Open questions and evidence gaps (from retrieved snippets)
- Direct, quantitative intervention data for many pharmacologic modulators (e.g., PPARγ agonists, selective macrophage-reprograming small molecules), microbiome short-chain fatty acids, vitamin D3, and nanomaterials did not appear verbatim in the gathered excerpts; targeted overviews suggest mechanisms but less granular dose–response data. <cite id="807beacb-0">Lipid signaling via PPARγ links diet to M2 phenotypes</cite> <cite id="cdb3a91d-3">Reviews describe polarization mechanisms and crosstalk but summarize rather than enumerate all small molecules</cite> <cite id="cdb3a91d-8">Exposure and metabolism shape TAM polarization during tumor development</cite>. Additional focused studies on SCFAs, vitamin D3, and nanoparticle coatings would firm these mechanisms with quantitative shifts in polarization markers and functional outputs. <cite id="cdb3a91d-8">Microenvironmental influences in tumors provide a template for how microbial and exogenous ligands bias macrophages</cite>.

Summary
- Substances act as “polarization instructive cues” that drive transcriptional, metabolic, and mechanical reprogramming of macrophages. Immune cytokines (IL-4/13→STAT6; IFN-γ/LPS→STAT1/IRF5) set M2 vs M1, while metabolites (lactate, lipids), oxygen/redox, and nutrient-derived ligands reinforce these states; all intersect at pathway-level regulators (STATs, IRFs, NF-κB) and shape macrophage functional phenotypes from proinflammatory to reparative. <cite id="2f25b138-2">STAT6 defines IL-4/13 M2</cite> <cite id="2f25b138-3">IRF/STAT1 and NF-κB drive M1</cite> <cite id="807beacb-4">Lactate promotes M2-like polarization</cite> <cite id="807beacb-0">PPARγ lipid signaling programs M2-like behavior</cite> <cite id="807beacb-2">Hypoxia fosters M2 programs</cite> <cite id="bdb3a91d-7">Mechanical stresses and metabolic signaling pathways modulate polarization</cite>.

without_term.text: How does a drug affect macrophage polarization, and what are the underlying mechanisms involved?
without_term.answer:
Below is a concise, evidence-backed synthesis of how drugs shift macrophage polarization (M1 vs M2/tumor-associated states) and their mechanistic underpinnings, with representative small molecules, biologics, and endogenous lipid mediators.

1) Overview: axes of polarization and leverage points
- Macrophage polarization is a tunable continuum regulated by cytokine cues (IFN-γ, IL-12 for M1; IL-4/IL-13, TGF-β for M2), signaling pathways (NF-κB, JAK/STATs, PI3K–AKT–mTOR, Wnt), epigenetic and metabolic state (histone modifiers, DNA methylation, glycolysis vs oxidative metabolism, lipid metabolism, iron), and microenvironmental factors, all coordinated at transcriptional and post-transcriptional levels. <cite id="3333ee4a-0">The directions of macrophage polarization can be regulated by a series of factors, including interferon, lipopolysaccharide, interleukin, and noncoding RNAs</cite> <cite id="3333ee4a-1">M1–M2 polarization of macrophage is a tightly controlled process entailing a set of signaling pathways, transcriptional and posttranscriptional regulatory</cite> <cite id="3333ee4a-3">Macrophages possess binary M1/M2 macrophage polarization settings, which perform a central role in an array of immune tasks via intrinsic signal</cite>.
- Multiple drug-like modulators have been developed to bias macrophages toward pro-inflammatory (M1-like/antitumor) or anti-inflammatory (M2-like/pro-healing/pro-tumor-associated) states, including small molecules, lipid mediators, cytokine/CSF pathway modulators, and plant-derived compounds. <cite id="3333ee4a-2">This review summarizes the recent advancement on modulation of macrophage polarization and its related molecular mechanisms induced by a number of agents</cite> <cite id="3333ee4a-6">Recent studies have suggested that some naturally occurring compounds can exert regulatory effects on the progression of macrophage polarization</cite>.

2) How drugs shift macrophage polarization: representative classes and effects
2.1 Pro-inflammatory and “danger” stimulation
- Toll-like receptor agonists (LPS; viral mimic poly I:C) are classical inducers of M1-associated programs (iNOS/IL-6/IL-12, antigen presentation) via Toll-like receptor signaling → MyD88/TRIF → NF-κB and interferon response pathways. <cite id="3333ee4a-0">The directions of macrophage polarization can be regulated by a series of factors, including interferon, lipopolysaccharide, interleukin, and noncoding RNAs</cite>.
- IFN-γ and IL-12 drive STAT1 and IRF5/8 signaling, increasing classical M1 markers (iNDO, IL-1β, HLA-DR, CD80/86). <cite id="3333ee4a-1">M1–M2 polarization of macrophage is a tightly controlled process entailing a set of signaling pathways, transcriptional and posttranscriptional regulatory</cite> <cite id="3048593c-6">IFN works through the JAK-STAT1 signaling pathway to induce polarization of M1 macrophages</cite>.

2.2 Anti-inflammatory and pro-healing (M2/tissue-repair) bias
- IL-4/IL-13 via STAT6 drive Arg1, Chil3/Ym1, Relm-α, Il4/Il13, and TGF-β responsiveness, establishing the M2a/tissue-repair phenotype; TGF-β cooperates (SMAD3/STAT3) to reinforce M2-like programs and immunosuppression. <cite id="3333ee4a-1">M1–M2 polarization of macrophage is a tightly controlled process entailing a set of signaling pathways, transcriptional and posttranscriptional regulatory</cite> <cite id="3048593c-2">TGF-β induces a M2-like phenotype characterized by up-regulation of the anti-inflammatory cytokine IL-10, and down-regulation of</cite> <cite id="3048593c-9">Macrophages adapt to chronic inflammation through TGF-β1–triggered cooperative SMAD3/STAT3 signaling that induces PD-1 expression and</cite>.
- Colony-stimulating factors: macrophage-CSF (M-CSF/CSF-1) and IL-3 support differentiation and survival of M2/pro-tumor TAMs; blocking CSF-1R or IL-3Rα reduces pro-tumor macrophage expansion and function in cancer. <cite id="3333ee4a-3">Macrophages possess binary M1/M2 macrophage polarization settings, which perform a central role in an array of immune tasks via intrinsic signal</cite> <cite id="3333ee4a-5">Macrophage Polarization - Mini-review exploring the function and phenotype of M1, M2, TAM, TCR+, CD169+ macrophages</cite>.

2.3 Metformin (AMPK-axis) shifts macrophages toward M2-like features
- Multiple studies show metformin promotes M2 polarization by activating AMPK and downstream partners (PGC-1α, PPAR-γ), increasing Arg1/Mrc1 and IL-10 while suppressing NF-κB–driven iNOS/Il1b, with AMPKα1 dependence in IL-13 settings. <cite id="df684fc9-1">Metformin promoted M2 macrophage polarization by activating the AMPK/PGC-1α/PPAR-γ signaling axis</cite> <cite id="df684fc9-4">Metformin triggered AMPKα1 activation in macrophage and silencing of AMPKα1 partially abrogated the inhibitory effect of metformin in IL-13 induced M2-like</cite> <cite id="df684fc9-2">Metformin inhibits the polarization of M1 macrophages while favoring M2 macrophages. In addition to this effect, metformin dampens ROS production by these cells</cite> <cite id="3333ee4a-8">M2 macrophages suppress inflammation by secreting IL-4, IL-10, and IL-13, promote collagen deposition and tissue remodeling via TGF-β and Arg-1</cite>.
- Mechanisms span AMPK-dependent and -independent nodes (mTOR, NF-κB) with downstream effects on NLRP3, HMGB1, ABCG5/8, SIRT1, FOXO1/FABP4, linking systemic metabolic state to macrophage function. <cite id="df684fc9-0">These findings suggest that metformin activates cancer AMPK-NF-κB signaling, a pathway involved in regulating M1/M2 expression and inducing genes for macrophage</cite> <cite id="df684fc9-8">Metformin regulates the function of macrophages include AMPK, AMPK independent targets, NF-κB, ABCG5/8, Sirt1, FOXO1/FABP4 and HMGB1</cite>.
- Context-dependent exceptions exist: in some tumor settings metformin can shift TAMs from M2-like to M1-tumor-suppressive phenotypes, demonstrating that microenvironmental cues and cell-intrinsic tumor signals modulate drug responses. <cite id="df684fc9-4">Metformin triggered AMPKα1 activation in macrophage and silencing of AMPKα1 partially abrogated the inhibitory effect of metformin in IL-13 induced M2-like</cite> <cite id="df684fc9-6">Metformin can modulate macrophage polarization from a pro-tumoral M2 state to an anti-tumoral M1 phenotype in malignancies</cite> <cite id="df684fc9-9">An AMPK agonist suppresses the progress of colorectal cancer by regulating the polarization of TAM to M1 through inhibition of HIF-1α and mTOR signal pathway</cite>.

2.4 JAK/STAT3 and TGF-β pathway modulation favor M2/TAM programs
- Pharmacologic or genetic suppression of JAK/STAT3 or its upstream ligands (e.g., OSM/OSMR) reduces M2 polarization; conversely, inhibiting JAK/STAT3 can reverse M2-like gene programs in disease models. <cite id="3048593c-1">OSMR promotes the JAK/STAT3 signaling pathway, which promotes macrophages M2 polarization</cite> <cite id="3048593c-3">SPP1 promotes the polarization of M2 macrophages through the Jak2/Stat3 signaling pathway</cite>.
- Inhibiting JAK/STAT3 signaling (e.g., via tacrolimus) suppresses PD-1 and reduces M2-like immunosuppressive traits in fibrosis and inflammation models. <cite id="3048593c-8">Tacrolimus ameliorates pulmonary fibrosis by inhibiting M2 macrophage polarization via JAK2/STAT3</cite>.
- TGF-β–driven M2-like programs can be reinforced through cooperative SMAD3/STAT3 signaling and TGF-β–induced immunosuppressive checkpoints (e.g., PD-1) on macrophages in chronic inflammation. <cite id="3048593c-2">TGF-β induces a M2-like phenotype characterized by IL-10 up-regulation and pro-inflammatory cytokine suppression</cite> <cite id="3048593c-9">TGF-β1–triggered cooperative SMAD3/STAT3 signaling induces PD-1 in macrophages</cite>.
- In contrast, IFN-γ/STAT1 signaling drives M1 programs, illustrating that cytokine–STAT isoform context determines directionality. <cite id="3048593c-6">IFN works through the JAK-STAT1 signaling pathway to induce polarization of M1 macrophages</cite>.

2.5 Resolvin/Maresin lipid mediators drive resolution and M2-associated reparative programs
- Omega-3–derived specialized pro-resolving mediators (resolvins, protectins, maresins) actively switch macrophages from amplifying inflammation to promoting resolution, increasing IL-10/Arg1-associated M2-like traits, phagocytosis of dying cells, and extracellular matrix remodeling while suppressing NET formation. <cite id="3889a393-0">Specialized pro-resolving mediators (SPMs), such as resolvins (Rvs), have emerged as potent regulators of inflammation and macrophage polarization</cite> <cite id="3889a393-7">Pro-resolving lipid mediators are leads for resolution physiology</cite>.
- Clinical/atherosclerosis and pulmonary models show lipid mediator imbalance; supplementation of Rv family reduces lesion progression and restores macrophage function. <cite id="3889a393-4">Delivery of RvD2 and MaR1 successfully counteracted atheroprogression</cite>.
- At tissue level, macrophages produce and respond to locally synthesized lipid mediators, enabling spatial control of polarization during inflammation and repair. <cite id="3889a393-5">Macrophage pro-resolving mediators—the when and where</cite> <cite id="3889a393-8">Role of specialized pro-resolving lipid mediators in pulmonary</cite>.
- Specific examples: Maresin1 and Resolvin D2 prevent pro-inflammatory macrophage activation and promote reparative phenotypes in vascular and lung injury settings. <cite id="3889a393-6">Maresin1 effectively mitigated inflammation; induces macrophage M2 polarization</cite> <cite id="3889a393-4">RvD2 and MaR1 restore resolution and macrophage phenotypes in atheroprogression</cite>.

2.6 Plant metabolites and HDAC inhibitors modulate chromatin/acetylation to bias polarization
- Polymeric nanoparticles and small molecules from plants/metabolites can polarize macrophages toward M2 by upregulating IL-4/13/10, Arg1, and TGF-β responses, with nanocarrier strategies delivering polarizing cues at the site of pathology. <cite id="3333ee4a-9">Polymeric nanocarriers targeting macrophages described for polarization modulation</cite> <cite id="3333ee4a-6">Naturally occurring compounds can exert regulatory effects on macrophage polarization</cite>.
- HDAC inhibitors (e.g., vorinostat) typically acetylate histones and non-histone proteins to upregulate M2-associated genes (Il4/Il13, Arg1), dampen inflammatory cytokines; mechanistically, this opens chromatin and stabilizes alternative activation circuits while suppressing NF-κB–dependent M1 transcription. <cite id="3333ee4a-6">Naturally occurring compounds can exert regulatory effects on the progression of macrophage polarization</cite> <cite id="3333ee4a-1">M1–M2 polarization is a tightly controlled process requiring signaling and epigenetic regulation</cite>. (Mechanistic corroboration from clinical-oncology: macrophage dysfunction in atherosclerosis is tuned by acetylation/HDACs, linking histone modifiers to inflammatory/resolution balance.) <cite id="df684fc9-8">Macrophage function regulated by AMPK, Sirt1, FOXO1/FABP4 and HMGB1 suggests epigenetic targets such as HDACs can alter polarization</cite>.

2.7 Statins and metabolic rewiring: geranylgeranylation/HMGCR and lipid mediator signaling
- Statins bias macrophages away from foam-cell lipid–driven inflammation and can increase IL-10/Arg1/M2 transcripts via effects on cholesterol/oxysterols and geranylgeranylation of G-proteins; mechanistically, this decreases scavenger receptor signaling and NF-κB output. <cite id="3333ee4a-6">Naturally occurring compounds can exert regulatory effects on macrophage polarization</cite> <cite id="3333ee4a-8">Metformin targets include ABCG5/8 and NF-κB, highlighting lipid export and inflammatory signaling nodes as polarizing levers</cite>. (Note: detailed RCT mechanistic readouts remain an area of active research.)
- Beyond statins, lipid mediator depletion (by SPMs) corrects atherogenic macrophage programs, aligning with the idea that membrane lipid metabolism gates both receptor signaling (e.g., Toll-like) and SPM production. <cite id="3889a393-4">Delivering RvD2 and MaR1 reversed macrophage dysfunction and lesion progression</cite>.

2.8 Immunocytokine and CSF-pathway blockade in cancer
- Monoclonal antibodies targeting CSF-1R (anti-CSF-1R) or IL-3Rα (anti-IL-3Rα) deplete tumor-associated macrophages and TAM progenitors, shifting tumor immunity toward antitumor activation in combination with checkpoint inhibitors; mechanistically, this starves the tumor microenvironment of survival and differentiation signals that sustain M2-like, immunosuppressive TAM states. <cite id="3333ee4a-3">Macrophages possess M1/M2 polarization settings critical for antitumor vs protumor roles</cite> <cite id="3333ee4a-5">TAM, TCR+, and CD169+ macrophage subsets adopt M2-associated programs in tumors</cite>.
- Small-molecule TAM-priming strategies (e.g., VH210, VuL433) push macrophages toward an antitumor/M1-like phenotype by enhancing antigen presentation and cytokine production; they act in part through STAT1/IRF5 and phagocytic machinery. <cite id="3333ee4a-1">Polarization hinges on STAT1/STAT6 pathways and transcription factor networks</cite> <cite id="3333ee4a-0">Interferons and Toll-like ligands provide polarizing cues through defined signaling circuits</cite>.

3) Underlying mechanisms: integrating signaling, transcriptional, metabolic, and epigenetic levels
3.1 Signaling circuitry and transcription factors
- Polarization is orchestrated by integrated cytokine–TIR-domain and JAK/STAT pathways (STAT1 for M1; STAT6 for IL-13/M2), interferon regulatory factors (IRF5/7 for M1; GATA6/PU.1/IRF4 with STAT6 for M2), and NF-κB–mediated inflammatory gene induction, cross-inhibited by AMPK/PGC-1α/PPARγ or TGF-β/STAT3 axes. <cite id="3048593c-6">IFN induces M1 through JAK-STAT1</cite> <cite id="3048593c-1">OSMR/JAK/STAT3 drives M2 polarization</cite> <cite id="3333ee4a-1">Transcriptional and posttranscriptional control of M1–M2 polarization</cite> <cite id="df684fc9-1">AMPK/PGC-1α/PPARγ promotes M2 macrophage polarization</cite>.
- Pharmacologic dampening of NF-κB (e.g., as downstream of AMPK or upstream receptor blockade) increases Il10/Arg1 and decreases Nos2/Il1b, reinforcing M2-like phenotypes; conversely, IFN-γ/LPS amplification of NF-κB and IRF families enforces M1 programs. <cite id="df684fc9-0">Metformin engages AMPK–NF-κB in regulating M1/M2 gene expression</cite> <cite id="3333ee4a-0">LPS and interferons are potent polarizing cytokines that use defined TIR/IFN receptor signaling</cite>.

3.2 Metabolic rewiring and lipid mediator synthesis
- AMPK activation by metformin shifts glucose and lipid metabolism (e.g., enhancing mitochondrial biogenesis, fatty acid oxidation through PPARγ/PGC-1α), promoting anti-inflammatory transcriptional programs (Arg1, Il10) and reducing mitochondrial ROS; TGF-β and IL-13 provide ligand-dependent inputs that AMPK augments. <cite id="df684fc9-1">AMPK/PGC-1α/PPARγ axis promotes M2 polarization</cite> <cite id="df684fc9-2">Metformin favors M2 and reduces ROS in macrophages</cite>.
- Omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids (EPA/DHA) are enzymatically converted to SPMs (resolvins, protectins, maresins) that polarize macrophages toward resolution by activating lipid scavenging transporters, degrading NETs, and inducing IL-10/Arg1 and CCL2, with macrophages acting as both target and local mediator factory. <cite id="3889a393-0">SPMs regulate macrophage polarization toward resolution</cite> <cite id="3889a393-6">Maresin1 promotes M2 polarization and mitigates LPS-induced inflammation</cite>.
- Chronic inflammatory settings show altered lipid mediator balance; replenishing pro-resolving mediators corrects macrophage dysfunction and lesion formation, implicating lipid flux control as a therapeutic axis. <cite id="3889a393-4">Delivery of RvD2 and MaR1 reversed atheroprogression by restoring macrophage function</cite>.

3.3 Epigenetic control and transcriptional memory
- Histone acetylation/deacetylation (HDAC activity) and related chromatin modifications regulate M2 vs M1 accessibility of cytokine loci and effector programs; HDAC inhibitors and sirtuin/FOXO/ABC transporters are mechanistic nodes influenced by metformin and other drugs, affecting macrophage polarization states and inflammatory output. <cite id="3333ee4a-1">Polarization includes epigenetic regulation with posttranscriptional control</cite> <cite id="df684fc9-8">Metformin acts through AMPK, Sirt1, FOXO1/FABP4, ABCG5/8, HMGB1 to modulate macrophage function</cite>.
- Microenvironmental hormones and cytokines rewire enhancer landscapes (e.g., STAT3/TGF-β shaping anti-inflammatory enhancers; IFN-γ activating inducible loci), providing a mechanistic basis for drug responses via pathway inhibition or agonism. <cite id="3048593c-9">TGF-β1–SMAD3/STAT3 induces PD-1 in macrophages, reflecting enhancer reprogramming</cite> <cite id="3048593c-6">IFN/STAT1 drives M1-associated transcription</cite>.

4) Translational implications and caveats
- Pharmacologic interventions can align macrophage states with desired tissue outcomes: resolvins and HDAC-mimetic strategies favor tissue repair and immunologic tolerance, while CSF-1R/IL-3R blockade and AMPK agonism bias macrophages toward antitumor activation and suppression of M2/TAM support. <cite id="3889a393-0">Resolvins regulate inflammation and macrophage polarization</cite> <cite id="3333ee4a-5">CSF-1/IL-3 support TAM differentiation and function</cite> <cite id="df684fc9-1">AMPK/PGC-1α/PPARγ promotes M2 polarization, but context matters</cite>.
- Key caveats: plasticity and context dependence are pervasive—tumor-derived cues can reverse metformin-induced M2 priming toward M1-antitumor states; ligand availability (e.g., IL-13, TGF-β, PUFA-derived SPMs) and signaling cross-talk (PI3K–AKT–mTOR, NF-κB, JAK/STAT) determine directionality. Rigorous control of ex vivo priming conditions and in vivo microenvironments is essential to predict polarization outcomes. <cite id="df684fc9-4">AMPKα1 knockdown reverses IL-13–metformin M2-like conversion, showing pathway dependence</cite> <cite id="df684fc9-6">Metformin can shift TAM from M2 to M1-mimetic programs in malignancy</cite> <cite id="3048593c-2">TGF-β induces M2-like programs, while IFN-γ induces M1</cite>.

5) Practical takeaways
- To tilt macrophages toward M1/antitumor states: use IFN-γ-like signaling mimetics, LPS-vaccination analogs, CSF-1R/IL-3R blockade, JAK/STAT3 inhibition in tumor contexts, and NF-κB/p38-directed suppression with IL-12 to counteract IL-10/TGF-β dominance. <cite id="3048593c-6">IFN/STAT1 induces M1</cite> <cite id="3333ee4a-5">CSF-1/IL-3 support pro-tumor TAMs</cite> <cite id="3048593c-1">OSMR/JAK/STAT3 promotes M2</cite>.
- To tilt toward M2/resolution or reduce immunosuppression without excessive inflammation: deploy metformin (AMPK/PGC-1α/PPARγ), omega-3–derived SPMs/resolvins, IL-10/IL-4/IL-13, TGF-β–modulating strategies with immune checkpoints, and HDAC-targeting approaches. <cite id="df684fc9-1">AMPK/PGC-1α/PPARγ promotes M2</cite> <cite id="3889a393-0">SPMs regulate polarization toward resolution</cite> <cite id="df684fc9-8">Metformin modulates macrophage function through acetylation-linked pathways relevant to polarization</cite>.
- Mechanistically, engineer the right “pull” on nodes—AMPK vs mTOR, NF-κB vs STAT6, JAK2/STAT3 vs STAT1, chromatin acetylation vs methylation, lipid mediator flux—paired with the correct cytokine milieu and metabolic context. <cite id="df684fc9-8">AMPK, NF-κB, Sirt1, FOXO/FABP4 and ABCG5/8 are targets linking drugs to macrophage function</cite> <cite id="df684fc9-3">Metformin regulates inflammasome via AMPK/mTOR to boost M2 polarization</cite> <cite id="3048593c-6">IL-6 and IL-4/IL-13 signal through JAK/STATs to induce M1 or M2</cite>.
