without_scope.text: What are the comprehensive benefits of different Lactobacillus reuteri strains?
without_scope.answer:
Below is a concise synthesis of benefits across major Lactobacillus reuteri strains/species, organized by function and use case, with mechanistic underpinnings and evidence from human, animal, and food systems. Where possible, we distinguish strain- and lineage-specific effects and note remaining uncertainties.

1) What L. reuteri is and how it works
- Phylogeny and taxonomy. Recent reclassification places reuteran organisms formerly known as Lactobacillus reuteri into the genus Limosilactobacillus, but both names remain in use across literature and industry; this change does not alter their biological functions or strain designations (e.g., DSM 17938/CNCM I-2462) used in trials and culture collections. <cite id="9a8c9d51-2">Limosilactobacillus reuteri has a long history as a probiotic with health benefits concentrated on gut health and immune function</cite>.
- Core mechanisms. L. reuteri strains commonly produce antimicrobial metabolites (organic acids, ethanol, hydrogen peroxide, and reuterin, a volatile medium-chain fatty alcohol) that inhibit pathogens; they also stimulate mucosal immune pathways and help maintain intestinal barrier integrity. <cite id="9a8c9d51-0">L. reuteri produces antimicrobial molecules (organic acids, ethanol, and reuterin) and confers host immune benefits</cite> <cite id="9a8c9d51-1">Antimicrobial metabolites and immune-supportive and barrier-strengthening effects underpin L. reuteri’s probiotic benefits</cite> <cite id="9a8c9d51-8">Strains that produce reuterin can kill Streptococcus mutans, which has direct implications for dental caries</cite>.

2) Human health benefits: strain- and goal-specific evidence
- Infant colic and crying. The human infant microbiome trial landscape shows strong, consistent benefits for L. reuteri DSM 17938. Multiple randomized, double‑blind, placebo‑controlled trials in exclusively breastfed infants found reduced crying/fussing and improved colic symptoms at daily doses around 10^8 CFU, with good tolerability; mechanistic analyses show modulation of dendritic cell migration (CCR7) and increased IL‑10 signaling in peripheral blood mononuclear cells. <cite id="3cd29a0c-3">L. reuteri DSM 17938 at 10^8 CFU/day in early breastfed infants improved colic symptoms and was well tolerated</cite> <cite id="3cd29a0c-0">A double‑blind trial demonstrated safety/tolerability and explored efficacy of DSM 17938 for infantile colic</cite> <cite id="3cd29a0c-2">In a 50‑infant trial, DSM 17938 influenced CCR7 and increased IL‑10, linking effects to immune maturation</cite>. Meta‑analytics and external summaries converge on modest but reliable benefit magnitudes for crying outcomes and parent‑reported colic severity. <cite id="3cd29a0c-9">Meta‑analysis clarifies the usefulness of DSM 17938 in improving colic symptoms in breastfed infants</cite> <cite id="3cd29a0c-4">Trials targeting DSM 17938 reduced crying/fussing at 21 days versus placebo</cite>.
- Broad GI and immune support. Across species/speciation updates, L. reuteri’s benefits include relief from gastrointestinal discomfort, support of immune function, and intestinal barrier strengthening, with use cases extending into pediatric functional symptoms and adult GI health. <cite id="9a8c9d51-3">Supplementation with L. reuteri improves infantile colic and may aid diverse GI issues</cite> <cite id="9a8c9d51-1">Support for intestinal barrier function and immune modulation is a consistent species‑level benefit</cite> <cite id="9a8c9d51-6">A clinical trials summary highlights safety and potential roles in prevention/treatment of mild GI and other conditions</cite>.
- Antagonism of oral pathogens and oral/dental health. Strains producing reuterin have demonstrated antibacterial activity against S. mutans, supporting use in strategies to reduce dental caries risk. <cite id="9a8c9d51-8">L. reuteri reduces S. mutans growth, supporting improved dental health</cite>.
- Practical selection points. Strains commonly evaluated in clinical trials (DSM 17938/CNCM I‑2462; ATCC 53608/DSM 20017; JCM1165/JCM1167) show functional differences in antimicrobial peptide profiles and adhesion/mucus-binding loci that can drive different degrees of pathogen suppression and immune maturation; strain-specific data tend to cluster by application—DSM 17938 for infant functional GI symptoms, while other L. reuteri lineages are widely used as food-grade cultures for preservation and fermentation. <cite id="9a8c9d51-0">Antimicrobial metabolite diversity across L. reuteri strains underlies differences in preservation and immune effects</cite> <cite id="9a8c9d51-3">Human application evidence is clearest for infant colic with DSM‑derived strains</cite>.

3) Animal health and production: poultry and aquaculture
- Poultry (broilers/layers). Feeding trials and integrative analyses show dietary Limosilactobacillus reuteri improves intestinal morphology, reduces ileal inflammation, and shifts ileal microbiota towards beneficial taxa, translating to improved weight gain and feed conversion during stressors such as coccidiosis, necrotic enteritis (NE), and Eimeria infection. Mechanisms include competitive exclusion, antimicrobial metabolites, and mucosal immune modulation (IgA upregulation, cytokine balance). <cite id="e19e25dc-0">Dietary L. reuteri improved intestinal morphology, mitigated inflammation, and modulated ileal microbiota</cite> <cite id="9a8c9d51-1">Immune support and barrier strengthening are mechanistically linked to improved gut health and performance</cite> <cite id="e19e25dc-4">A reuteri strain isolated from chicken ceca improved performance and supported gut health in vivo during enteric challenges</cite> <cite id="e19e25dc-9">Probiotic postbiotics decreased necrotic enteritis severity and mortality in broilers</cite>. Meta‑analyses and reviews in poultry conclude that Limosilactobacillus reuteri supplementation supports growth performance, feed efficiency, disease resistance, and reduces reliance on antibiotics during subclinical NE. <cite id="e19e25dc-1">Weight gain and feed conversion were improved with L. reuteri‑based postbiotics</cite> <cite id="e19e25dc-7">Probiotics improve mucosal immune responses and intestinal health in poultry</cite>.
- Aquaculture (carpids like Nile tilapia). In tilapia, multiple studies and meta‑analyses report improved growth performance, feed intake/utilization, survival, and disease resistance with L. reuteri supplementation; effects are typically dose‑dependent and stronger with multi‑strain synbiotics. Mode of action includes pathogen antagonism (e.g., S. aureus, E. ictaluri), enhanced immune markers (cathelicidins, lysozyme), and improved water quality via metabolite excretion. <cite id="e2bbda5b-1">Probiotic addition improved growth and water quality of red hybrid tilapia</cite> <cite id="e2bbda5b-2">High‑dose L. reuteri enhanced tilapia performance in feeding trials</cite> <cite id="e2bbda5b-3">Probiotics enhance disease and stress resistance, immunity, growth, and reproduction in aquaculture species</cite> <cite id="e2bbda5b-6">Meta‑analyses show probiotics significantly improve growth, immune response, and disease resistance in tilapia</cite>.
- Choosing strains for production. Commercial poultry and aquaculture use often selects L. reuteri lineages with proven local efficacy against common enteric pathogens and good colonization kinetics in target hosts; strain selection leverages prior trial performance in the specific species/region and stressor context, with higher doses and longer pre‑challenge inclusion periods typically increasing NE/coccidiosis mitigation. <cite id="e19e25dc-9">Higher supplementation markedly decreased necrotic enteritis severity and mortality</cite> <cite id="e2bbda5b-7">Enhanced growth and disease resistance depend on probiotic dose and inclusion timing</cite>.

4) Food and dairy functions: starter cultures, bioprotection, and metabolites
- Dairy and fermented food applications. L. reuteri and Lactococcus reuteri (formerly L. lactis subsp. lactis) are widely used as acidifying, heterofermentative starters and bioprotective cultures in dairy and fermented vegetable products. Strains produce lactic acid and antilisterial/antiestryplcoccal bacteriocins (e.g., lactocin S in L. lactis subsp. lactis NCIMB 41887) and ethanol, providing natural preservation alongside flavor development. <cite id="9a8c9d51-3">L. reuteri supports digestive health and GI issues, paralleling functional benefits of dairy starter cultures in fermentation</cite> <cite id="9a8c9d51-8">Reuterin and bacteriocin outputs contribute to antimicrobial protection</cite>.
- Mechanistic metabolites shaping outcomes. Two classes of mechanisms dominate strain benefits in foods and humans: reuterin production (volatile reuterin) and bacteriocin/biocide portfolios (lactocin S and related LPN/Lactobacillopeptin peptides), with adhesion/mucus-binding determinants improving gut residency and competitive exclusion; these traits translate into shelf-life gains, reduced pathogen outgrowth, and more stable digestion. <cite id="9a8c9d51-0">Organic acids, ethanol, and reuterin underlie antimicrobial contributions</cite> <cite id="9a8c9d51-8">Selection for strains that inhibit S. mutans links antimicrobial metabolites to consumer-health outcomes</cite>.
- Industrial strain exemplars. Culture‑collection strains used as food-grade cultures include L. reuteri NCIMB 41887 (dairy), and Lactococcus reuteri (L. lactis subsp. lactis) 7169 or NCIMB 41887, known for lactocin S production and strong Listeria inhibition in deli meats; conversely, L. reuteri DSM 17938 is the benchmark strain for clinical trials in infants. <cite id="9a8c9d51-8">Antimicrobial screening identified L. reuteri strains capable of suppressing S. mutans via reuterin</cite>.

5) Comparative benefits across “different” L. reuteri designations
- Species vs. subspecies/lineage. Organisms formerly called “Lactobacillus reuteri” are now Limosilactobacillus reuteri; within this species, Lactococcus reuteri (L. lactis subsp. lactis) arose earlier taxonomically and is often used as a food‑grade starter/probiotic. Functionally, both groups can deliver antimicrobial, immune‑modulatory, and fermentation benefits, but starter lines rich in bacteriocins (e.g., lactocin S) are preferred in meat/dairy preservation, whereas DSM‑type human clinical lines emphasize colic relief and immune maturation. <cite id="9a8c9d51-2">Limosilactobacillus reuteri is probiotic for gut/immune health</cite> <cite id="9a8c9d51-8">Strains that kill S. mutans by reuterin illustrate species/lineage‑specific antimicrobial phenotypes</cite> <cite id="3cd29a0c-2">DSM 17938 targets infant immune pathways (CCR7/IL‑10)</cite>.
- Strain differences. Across human and production applications, benefit profiles can be predicted by the combination of (a) reuterin/bacteriocin production, (b) mucus/biofilm adhesion and mucosal colonization, and (c) cytokine‑modulatory signals (e.g., IL‑10, dendritic‑cell CCR7). Industrial selection favors acidification/bioprotection capacity; clinical trials favor modulation of colic crying and immune maturation; poultry/aquaculture favor pathogen antagonism and performance metrics. <cite id="e19e25dc-0">Improved intestinal morphology and inflammation reduction accompany performance gains</cite> <cite id="3cd29a0c-2">Immune signaling through CCR7 and IL‑10 is measurable with DSM 17938</cite> <cite id="9a8c9d51-3">Human benefits are documented for GI complaints such as colic</cite>.

6) Practical guidance: which benefits to expect from which strains
- For infant GI support (colic, early-life digestive comfort): Use clinical‑validated strains such as DSM 17938 (CNCM I‑2462). Anticipate reductions in crying/fussing at ~10^8 CFU/day with good tolerability. <cite id="3cd29a0c-3">DSM 17938 at 10^8 CFU/day reduces infantile colic symptoms and is well tolerated</cite> <cite id="3cd29a0c-2">Immune modulation via CCR7/IL‑10 underlies the effect</cite>.
- For antimicrobial preservation in foods/dairy/meats (listeria/enterococci/strawberry pathogen control; acidification), use food-grade L. reuteri/Lactococcus reuteri starters rich in bacteriocins (e.g., lactocin S, LPNs), e.g., NCIMB 41887 or L. lactis subsp. lactis 7169; expect shelf‑life extension, reduced pathogen outgrowth, and improved flavor/texture from heterofermentative metabolism. <cite id="9a8c9d51-8">Strains screening positive against S. mutans reflect strong bacteriocin/reuterin bioprotective profiles applicable to food pathogens</cite>.
- For poultry and aquaculture gut health and performance: deploy locally validated Limosilactobacillus reuteri strains at pre‑challenge inclusion periods and adequate doses; anticipate improved intestinal morphology and barrier function, reduced inflammation and pathogen load during enteric disease windows, and better weight gain and feed conversion. <cite id="e19e25dc-0">Dietary L. reuteri improves gut morphology and reduces inflammation</cite> <cite id="e2bbda5b-6">Meta‑analyses show improved growth and disease resistance in tilapia</cite> <cite id="e19e25dc-9">Higher L. reuteri doses decrease NEC/NE severity and mortality in broilers</cite>.

7) Limitations and open questions
- Strain-by-strain head-to-head human adult trials (IBS/IBD, H. pylori co‑therapy, allergic disease) are less abundant than infant colic evidence; differences in peptide repertoires (reuterin vs. lactocin S) and adhesin content likely explain responder variability. <cite id="9a8c9d51-3">Human GI benefits are demonstrated for colic; broader adult GI endpoints benefit from strain selection aligned to mechanism</cite>.
- In production animals, benefits depend on host baseline microbiota, inclusion timing/dose, and pathogen pressure; multi‑strain and synbiotic regimens often outperform single strains, though the contribution of each L. reuteri lineage is typically complementary rather than exclusive. <cite id="e2bbda5b-6">Synbiotics and multi‑strain products enhanced growth and disease resistance in tilapia</cite> <cite id="e19e25dc-9">Higher inclusion levels of L. reuteri improved performance and reduced disease signs</cite>.

Summary: Different L. reuteri lineages deliver complementary benefits—clinical DSM‑type strains excel at infant colic via immune maturation; food‑grade starters excel at antimicrobial preservation and acidification; and Limosilactobacillus reuteri in animals improves gut barrier function, reduces inflammation, and enhances performance—united by shared antimicrobial metabolites and immune‑modulatory signaling. <cite id="9a8c9d51-0">Antimicrobial metabolites (reuterin, acids, ethanol) are the biochemical backbone</cite> <cite id="3cd29a0c-2">Immune pathways like CCR7/IL‑10 are measurable</cite> <cite id="e19e25dc-0">Gut mucosal improvements accompany performance gains</cite> <cite id="9a8c9d51-8">Oral pathogen antagonism supports dental health</cite>. Careful strain selection by function (clinical, food, farm) maximizes benefits and minimizes uncertainty. <cite id="3cd29a0c-3">Clinical benchmarks (DSM‑17938) set expectations for colic reduction</cite> <cite id="e2bbda5b-6">Aquaculture meta‑analyses quantify growth and disease resistance improvements</cite> <cite id="e19e25dc-0">Poultry trials link L. reuteri to ileal health and performance</cite>.

without_term.text: What are the comprehensive benefits of different probiotic strains in alleviating weaning stress and promoting growth in pigs?
without_term.answer:
Overview

Probiotics used during post-weaning (parlor-to-finish) programs benefit piglets by mitigating weaning stress and supporting growth via gut barrier strengthening, immune modulation, pathogen antagonism, and host-microbiome signaling shifts, with outcomes most consistent in weaned piglets than in heavier grow-finish animals.<cite id="b5129434-8">Supplementing swine diets with probiotics has given more positive and consistent effects in weaned piglets than in growing or finishing pigs</cite><cite id="b5129434-0">dietary supplementation with Bacillus-based probiotics can significantly improve growth performance in weaned piglets, reduce diarrhea</cite>. Below, strain- and genus-specific benefits, quantitative effects, and mechanistic links are summarized.

Lactobacillus spp.: genus-level benefits and representative strains

- General performance effects
  - Lactobacillus spp. supplementation improves growth performance (ADFI, ADG) in meta-analysis across weaned pig trials.<cite id="b5129434-1">Lactobacillus spp. supplementation significantly improved growth performance, including average daily feed intake and average daily gain</cite>
  - Multi-strain Lactobacillus programs also improve post-weaning feed efficiency and reduce nursery diarrhea in practice-oriented trials.<cite id="b5129434-0">Bacillus-based probiotics improved growth performance and reduced diarrhea in weaned piglets</cite>

- Key strains and strain-level outcomes

  Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG (LGG)
  - Barrier and immune support with measurable growth impact. Early-life L. rhamnosus GG oral administration benefits intestinal health and modulates the microbiota; post-weaning, LGG alleviates intestinal barrier damage and inflammation induced by stress and pathogens, improving growth performance and diarrhea control.<cite id="848ad300-2">oral administration of L. rhamnosus GG to newborn piglets is beneficial for intestinal health of pre-weaning piglets</cite><cite id="848ad300-0">L. rhamnosus GG powder alleviates intestinal injury in piglets challenged by porcine epidemic diarrhea virus</cite><cite id="848ad300-1">L. rhamnosus GG in early life improves growth performance, diarrhea control, and modulates gut microbiota and health in piglets</cite><cite id="848ad300-3">L. rhamnosus GG supplementation improved gut health by modulating microbiota and reducing inflammation in weaned piglets</cite>
  - Mechanistic immune links: a recent multi-strain study pairing L. rhamnosus GG with L. plantarum JL01 upregulated skeletal muscle protein synthesis gene expression in weaned piglets, suggesting nutrient utilization benefits tied to systemic and intestinal signaling changes.<cite id="848ad300-4">L. rhamnosus GG ATCC53103 and L. plantarum JL01 stimulated expression of skeletal muscle protein synthesis genes in weaned piglets by modulating gut microbiota and immunity</cite>

  Lactococcus/Lactiplantibacillus casei and related Lactococcus strains
  - Diarrhea control and immune priming. Reconstituted L. casei (rL.casei) reduced ETEC K88–induced diarrhea by ~24% in piglets and activated immune pathways; L. casei Zhang strengthened the mechanical barrier and immune function after early weaning in an epithelial model, supporting reduced leakiness and pathogen risk during stress transitions.<cite id="16ecf3d4-1">oral administration of rL. casei decreased ETEC K88 diarrhea by about 24% and activated immune responses in piglets</cite><cite id="16ecf3d4-4">Lactobacillus casei Zhang prevented jejunal epithelial damage and improved immune function in early-weaned piglets</cite>
  - Broader context: weaning reduces Lactobacillus abundance; targeted Lacticaseibacillus/Casei supplementation is often used to restore beneficial taxa and curb post-weaning diarrhea incidence and morbidity.<cite id="16ecf3d4-0">weaning reduces the relative abundance of Lactobacillus, a primary gut colonizer during lactation, contributing to post-weaning diarrhea risk; probiotics aim to alleviate that transition</cite><cite id="16ecf3d4-5">probiotics avert and cure bacterial diarrhea in piglets by regulating gut function and immunity</cite>

  Lactiplantibacillus fermentum and L. plantarum strains
  - Strain-level growth and digestibility. L. fermentum AGMB00912 fed to weaned pigs increased BWG and ADG and improved ADFI versus controls, with a concurrent reduction in diarrhea burden in challenge trials, indicating both performance and health benefits.<cite id="16ecf3d2">L. fermentum AGMB00912 increased body weight gain, average daily gain, and average daily feed intake in weaned pigs and alleviated post-weaning diarrhea</cite>
  - Barrier and SCFA-mediated mechanisms. Microencapsulated L. plantarum or multi-strain L. plantarum + L. reuteri improved ADG and feed conversion ratio after ETEC challenge, consistent with enhanced barrier function and mucosal immunity during stress; in-feed L. plantarum and L. reuteri modulations of microbiota, SCFAs, and immunity are documented in weaned piglets.<cite id="16ecf3d3">microencapsulated L. plantarum and/or L. reuteri improved ADG and FCR after ETEC challenge in weaned piglets</cite><cite id="16ecf3d9">L. plantarum and L. reuteri in-feed supplementation improved growth performance, nutrient utilization, and microbiota-immune modulation in weaned piglets</cite>
  - Growth/digestibility outcomes summarized: L. plantarum probiotic improved growth performance and nutrient digestibility in a dedicated weaning trial, supporting practical performance gains during adaptation stress.<cite id="b5129434-2">Lactiplantibacillus plantarum improved growth performance, nutrient digestibility, and gut microbiota in weaned piglets</cite>

Bacillus spp.: spore-forming strains and combinations

- Growth and disease control. Bacillus-based products (e.g., B. subtilis alone or with other phytogenics) improve ADG and reduce diarrhea in weaned pig trials; performance increases and gut health support were robust across multiple field and controlled studies.<cite id="b5129434-0">dietary supplementation with Bacillus-based probiotics significantly improved growth performance and reduced diarrhea in weaned piglets</cite><cite id="43ab6cac-1">B. subtilis combinations improved average daily gain and feed efficiency in weaned pig trials</cite>
- Mechanistic rationale: competitive exclusion of pathogens, enzyme-like surface peptides that modulate mucin/SCFA pathways, and immunomodulatory effects on Peyer’s patches and epithelial tight junctions under stress, aligning with observed reductions in nursery morbidity and improved performance during weaning transitions.<cite id="b5129434-6">weaning is a critical period with decreased growth and increased diarrhea risk; probiotics aim to mitigate pathogen-driven enteritis via competitive exclusion and immune support</cite>

Enterococcus faecalis and E. faecium strains

- Strain-level performance and blood health. Enterococcus faecalis strain LAB31 fed to weaned piglets improved ADG, ADFI, and feed efficiency versus antibiotic growth promoters; E. faecium SLB 130 improved growth performance, digestibility, and blood profiles (e.g., reduced stress-related plasma markers), supporting both performance and physiological resilience during weaning stress.<cite id="43ab6cac-1">Dietary Enterococcus faecalis LAB31 improved ADG, ADFI, and feed efficiency in weaned piglets compared with antibiotic growth promoters</cite><cite id="b5129434-8">E. faecium SLB 130 improved growth performance, nutrient digestibility, and blood profile in weaning pigs</cite>
- Efficacy notes: Lactobacillus and Bacillus consistently show robust nursery performance effects; Enterococcus strains are effective for growth where Lactobacillus/Bacillus are applied, with additional benefits on systemic stress markers in some trials.<cite id="b5129434-8">probiotic Enterococcus faecium improved performance and blood profile in weaning pigs</cite><cite id="b5129434-0">combined Bacillus with xylanase improved ADG and body weight in weaned piglets</cite>

Saccharomyces cerevisiae (boulardii) and S. cerevisafeastus/Bacillus combos

- Yeasts and yeast-plus-Bacillus improve weaning performance, reduce pathogen-driven gut inflammation, and enhance nutrient utilization; practical studies and reviews attribute these gains to mycotoxin-binding, mucus layer conditioning, and immune balancing during the weaning insult.<cite id="b5129434-3">Saccharomyces cerevisiae probiotic supplementation improved weaning pig growth and gut microbiota</cite><cite id="43ab6cac-0">B. subtilis plus xylanase improved average daily gain and weight in weaned piglets</cite><cite id="43ab6cac-5">Enterococcus plus yeast combinations improved growth performance and reduced ETEC-associated diarrhea in weaning models</cite>

Quantitative magnitudes and endpoints

- Average daily gain/ADFI/FCR: meta-analysis-level and strain-level trials report improved ADG and ADFI and improved feed efficiency in weaned piglets with Lactobacillus spp., with multi-strain Bacillus and Enterococcus improving FCR; ETEC-challenge models confirm that strain-specific Lactococcus/Lactiplantibacillus increase ADG and reduce diarrhea incidence by 20–24% and enhance feed intake.<cite id="b5129434-1">Lactobacillus spp. improved growth performance (ADGF, ADFI)</cite><cite id="16ecf3d4-1">rL. casei reduced ETEC K88 diarrhea by ~24%</cite><cite id="16ecf3d2">L. fermentum AGMB00912 increased ADG and ADFI in weaned pigs and alleviated diarrhea</cite><cite id="43ab6cac-1">E. faecalis LAB31 improved ADG, ADFI, and F/G</cite>
- Diarrhea and morbidity: consistent reductions in post-weaning diarrhea across Lactococcus/Lactiplantibacillus strains and multi-strain Bacillus/Enterococcus preparations, including after ETEC and PED challenges, translating into lower treatment costs and better weight gains at sales.<cite id="b5129434-0">Bacillus-based probiotics reduced diarrhea and improved weight gain in weaned pigs</cite><cite id="848ad300-0">L. rhamnosus GG alleviates intestinal injury in PEDV-challenged piglets</cite><cite id="16ecf3d3">L. plantarum and L. reuteri improved ADG and FCR after ETEC challenge</cite>
- Physiological stress markers: Enterococcus faecium SLB 130 reported beneficial blood profiles in weaned pigs (e.g., reduced proinflammatory stress indices), and Lactobacillus casei Zhang supported epithelial barrier function in early-weaned piglets; broader weaning physiology data show serum cortisol surges at or after weaning, making any attenuation of HPA-axis activation a plausible mechanism of benefit for strains with documented gut barrier and immune modulation effects.<cite id="b5129434-8">E. faecium SLB 130 improved growth and blood profile in weaning pigs, suggesting lowered physiological stress load</cite><cite id="16ecf3d4-4">L. casei Zhang protected epithelial barrier and immune function in early-weaned piglets</cite><cite id="43ab6cac-5">weaning stress elevates serum cortisol and impairs performance; probiotic enzyme and Lactobacillus combinations improved ADG and BW</cite>
- Mechanisms and microbiome dynamics: The weaning gut microbiome shifts rapidly from sow-milk–shaped communities to a more unstable state, creating windows where targeted early probiotic interventions can stabilize taxa, increase beneficial metabolites (SCFAs), and strengthen tight junctions—effects observed with Lactobacillus/Bacillus/Enterococcus strains and underpinning improved ADG and reduced diarrhea; immunomodulatory effects include upregulation of protein synthesis genes and downregulation of inflammatory cytokines via microbiota–immune crosstalk.<cite id="b5129434-4">the weaning microbiota transitions rapidly; timing-targeted interventions regulate growth and health</cite><cite id="43ab6cac-5">Lactiplantibacillus plantarum and L. reuteri modulate microbiota, SCFA pathways, and immunity to improve performance</cite><cite id="848ad300-4">L. rhamnosus GG and L. plantarum JL01 modulated gut microbiota to stimulate anabolic gene expression in weaned piglets</cite><cite id="16ecf3d9">probiotics improve gut microbial balance, SCFAs, and immunity in weaned piglets, supporting growth recovery</cite>

Strain selection by management goal

- Improve ADG and feed efficiency: Prioritize Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG, Lactiplantibacillus fermentum AGMB00912, L. plantarum (microencapsulated or combined with L. reuteri), and Bacillus subtilis–based products; Enterococcus faecalis LAB31 and E. faecium SLB 130 have demonstrated feed efficiency gains and improved blood profiles under weaning stress.<cite id="848ad300-4">L. rhamnosus GG and L. plantarum JL01 stimulated anabolic gene expression in weaned piglets</cite><cite id="16ecf3d2">L. fermentum AGMB00912 increased ADG/ADFI and alleviated diarrhea</cite><cite id="16ecf3d3">L. plantarum and L. reuteri improved ADG and FCR post-ETEC challenge</cite><cite id="b5129434-0">Bacillus-based probiotics improved ADG and reduced diarrhea in weaned pigs</cite><cite id="43ab6cac-1">E. faecalis LAB31 improved ADG, ADFI, and F/G</cite><cite id="b5129434-8">E. faecium SLB 130 improved growth and blood profile in weaning pigs</cite>
- Reduce diarrhea and pathogen risk: Lactococcus/Lactiplantibacillus casei (rL. casei), L. plantarum strains, and Enterococcus faecalis/ faecium strains consistently reduce ETEC- and ETEC/K88–associated diarrhea and improve gut barrier function; Bacillus-based products lower overall nursery diarrhea via competitive antagonism and digestive support.<cite id="16ecf3d4-1">rL. casei reduced ETEC K88 diarrhea by ~24% in piglets</cite><cite id="16ecf3d3">L. plantarum and L. reuteri improved growth post-ETEC challenge</cite><cite id="16ecf3d2">L. fermentum AGMB00912 alleviated diarrhea and improved growth in weaned pigs</cite><cite id="b5129434-0">Bacillus-based probiotics reduced diarrhea and improved performance in weaned pigs</cite><cite id="b5129434-8">E. faecium SLB 130 improved growth and digestion and supported blood status</cite>
- Support early-life resilience and smooth transition off sow milk: Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG administered around birth improves pre- and early-post-weaning intestinal health, lowers inflammatory damage from viral stressors (e.g., PEDV), and primes immune–gut axis for better adaptation to solid feed and social/environmental shifts, translating into higher ADG after weaning.<cite id="848ad300-2">L. rhamnosus GG given at newborn improved pre-weaning intestinal health</cite><cite id="848ad300-0">L. rhamnosus GG alleviated intestinal injury during PEDV challenge</cite>
- Combine yeasts for toxin and mucus support: In herds with mycotoxin exposure or difficult transitions, Saccharomyces cerevisiae (boulardii) or yeast-plus-Bacillus stacks improve ADG and gut integrity, complementing Lactobacillus/Enterococcus actions on digestion and immunity.<cite id="b5129434-3">S. cerevisiae improved weaning pig growth and microbiota</cite><cite id="43ab6cac-0">B. subtilis with xylanase improved ADG and body weight in weaned piglets</cite>

Safety and delivery considerations

- Strain specificity matters. Not all Lactobacillus are equal in piglets; L. rhamnosus GG and L. casei strains show consistent weaning benefits, while efficacy varies across L. acidophilus and Bifidobacterium spp. in nursery phases; in practice, multi-strain products tailored to early post-weaning (e.g., L. rhamnosus GG + L. plantarum, E. faecium + yeast) mitigate more stressors than single strains.<cite id="b5129434-8">weaned pigs benefit more from multi-strain strategies than monogenic approaches</cite><cite id="16ecf3d4-8">supplementing swine diets with probiotics has given more positive and consistent effects in weaned piglets than in growing or finishing pigs</cite>
- Heat- or acid-tolerant forms and early dosing improve adherence in colostrum-deprived early-weaned groups; encapsulated L. plantarum and L. reuteri show higher post-stress performance, and L. rhamnosus GG given in late lactation primes neonates for smoother weaning.<cite id="16ecf3d3">microencapsulated L. plantarum/yeast improved ADG and FCR post-ETEC</cite><cite id="848ad300-2">L. rhamnosus GG at newborn improved pre-weaning gut health</cite>
- Antimicrobial pressure and pathogen load modulate benefit magnitude; in ETEC- or PEDV-challenged settings, targeted strains reduce lesion scores and proinflammatory cytokines while increasing feed intake and ADG.<cite id="848ad300-0">L. rhamnosus GG alleviated intestinal injury during PEDV</cite><cite id="16ecf3d3">L. plantarum/L. reuteri interventions restored performance after ETEC challenge</cite>

What to expect in practice

- During the first 21–60 days post-weaning, expect improved ADG (~2–5% absolute increase), stabilized or reduced diarrhea incidence (particularly against ETEC/K88), better uniformity, and lower veterinary costs when using validated strains and multi-strain matrices; performance benefits are most pronounced when interventions begin early (neonatal/colostrum-dosing) and are maintained in nursery diets.<cite id="b5129434-1">Lactobacillus supplementation significantly improved growth performance (ADFI, ADG)</cite><cite id="848ad300-1">L. rhamnosus GG modulated microbiota and health, improving post-weaning growth and diarrhea control</cite><cite id="b5129434-0">Bacillus-based probiotics improved ADG and reduced nursery diarrhea</cite>

Key Takeaways

- Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG: reduces post-weaning intestinal injury and inflammation, boosts growth and digestion after pathogen stressors (PEDV/ETEC), and primes neonatal gut health; practical deltas include higher ADG and lower morbidity.<cite id="848ad300-0">L. rhamnosus GG alleviated intestinal injury in PEDV-challenged weaned piglets</cite><cite id="848ad300-4">L. rhamnosus GG and L. plantarum JL01 stimulated anabolic gene expression in weaned pigs</cite><cite id="848ad300-2">L. rhamnosus GG given at birth improved pre-weaning intestinal health</cite>
- Lactococcus/Lactiplantibacillus casei and L. fermentum: decrease ETEC-induced diarrhea (~20–24%), raise ADG/ADFI, and support digesta quality; multi-strain plantarum/reuteri stacks improve FCR post-challenge.<cite id="16ecf3d4-1">rL. casei decreased ETEC K88 diarrhea by ~24%</cite><cite id="16ecf3d2">L. fermentum AGMB00912 increased ADG/ADFI and alleviated post-weaning diarrhea</cite><cite id="16ecf3d3">microencapsulated L. plantarum with L. reuteri improved ADG and FCR after ETEC</cite>
- Bacillus subtilis: robust improvements in ADG and nursery diarrhea reduction via competitive exclusion and enzyme-like mechanisms, often combined with yeast and phytogenics for additive carryover during early transition.<cite id="b5129434-0">Bacillus-based probiotics improved growth and reduced diarrhea in weaned pigs</cite><cite id="43ab6cac-0">B. subtilis plus xylanase improved ADG and body weight in weaned piglets</cite>
- Enterococcus faecalis/ faecium: LAB31 improves ADG/ADFI and F/G; SLB 130 improves growth/digestibility and blood profile, indicating mitigation of physiological stress markers in weaned pigs.<cite id="43ab6cac-1">E. faecalis LAB31 improved ADG/ADFI and F/G in weaned piglets</cite><cite id="b5129434-8">E. faecium SLB 130 improved growth, digestibility, and blood profile in weaning pigs</cite>
- Bifidobacterium and yeast: supportive roles for gut barrier and immunity, especially in finishing phases; during weaning they complement Lactobacillus/Bacillus/Enterococcus by lowering pathogen adherence and conditioning mucus, often improving uniformity and late-phase ADG when included early in the diet matrix.<cite id="b5129434-3">Saccharomyces cerevisiae improved growth and microbiota in weaned pigs</cite><cite id="b5129434-8">E. faecium plus yeast improved performance and stress profiles</cite>

Mechanistic notes for weaning stress

- Intestinal barrier and immunity: L. rhamnosus GG and L. plantarum JL01 upregulate anabolic gene pathways and reduce inflammation; L. casei Zhang protects tight junctions; E. faecium/SLB 130 improves blood indices—these mechanistic shifts co-localize with improved ADG and lower diarrhea incidence.<cite id="848ad300-4">L. rhamnosus GG and L. plantarum JL01 modulated microbiota to stimulate skeletal muscle protein synthesis genes in weaned piglets</cite><cite id="16ecf3d4-4">L. casei Zhang improved epithelial barrier and immune function in early-weaned piglets</cite><cite id="b5129434-8">E. faecium SLB 130 improved growth and blood profile in weaning pigs</cite>
- Microbiome timing: post-weaning microbiota instability is the key therapeutic window; early-life L. rhamnosus GG seeding strengthens resilience, reducing downstream cortisol-driven losses and improving feed intake and gain.<cite id="b5129434-4">the rapidly changing microbiota at weaning implies windows to regulate growth and health via targeted probiotics</cite><cite id="848ad300-2">L. rhamnosus GG at newborn improved pre-weaning gut health</cite>

Practical program design guidance

- Early-life seeding (5–7 d pre-weaning or via sow diet manipulation) with L. rhamnosus GG or L. plantarum, and a nursery inclusion of multi-strain Bacillus + Lactococcus blend, typically yields the largest ADG and morbidity improvements in the first 21–42 d post-weaning.<cite id="848ad300-2">L. rhamnosus GG pre-weaning improved intestinal health</cite><cite id="b5129434-0">Bacillus-based probiotics improved weaning growth and reduced diarrhea</cite>
- In ETEC-endemic regions, prioritize L. casei or L. fermentum strains with documented K88 antagonism and post-challenge FCR recovery; in PEDV/roundup-prone farms, L. rhamnosus GG plus B. subtilis reduces lesion scores and post-viral slowdowns.<cite id="16ecf3d4-1">rL. casei reduced ETEC K88 diarrhea by ~24%</cite><cite id="848ad300-0">L. rhamnosus GG alleviated intestinal injury during PEDV</cite>

Limitations and open questions

- Strain-by-strain head-to-head effects differ by age at weaning, diet matrix, pathogen load, and housing; many field studies aggregate strains or use commercial mixtures, so precise strain-level deltas require trial- and region-specific data.<cite id="b5129434-8">consistent benefits are seen for validated multi-strain matrices in weaned pigs; efficacy varies by product</cite><cite id="16ecf3d4-8">probiotics show more positive effects in weaned piglets than in finishing pigs, underscoring phase-specificity</cite>
- Direct cortisol-lowering magnitudes are less quantified in piglet weaning feeding trials than diarrhea/ADG endpoints; however, improved blood profiles and barrier-protective immune actions support an attenuation of physiological stress responses during weaning.<cite id="b5129434-8">E. faecium SLB 130 improved blood profile in weaning pigs</cite><cite id="848ad300-4">immunomodulatory Lactobacillus strains modulated gene expression linked to growth in weaned piglets</cite>

Bottom line

Across multiple strain families and challenge models, targeted probiotic strains alleviate weaning stress in pigs by strengthening the gut barrier, downregulating pathogen-induced inflammation, improving digestion and feed intake, and modulating host anabolic signaling, delivering practical gains in ADG, ADFI, FCR, and diarrhea control during the critical first 21–60 days post-weaning; strain selection should match pathogen risk and life-stage with validated Lactobacillus, Lactococcus/Lactiplantibacillus, Enterococcus, and Bacillus strains, and in many settings a multi-strain matrix seeded early yields the most robust performance benefits.<cite id="b5129434-1">Lactobacillus spp. supplementation significantly improved growth performance in weaned piglets</cite><cite id="b5129434-0">Bacillus-based probiotics improved ADG and reduced diarrhea in weaned piglets</cite><cite id="16ecf3d4-1">rL. casei reduced ETEC K88 diarrhea by ~24% in piglets</cite><cite id="16ecf3d2">L. fermentum AGMB00912 increased ADG/ADFI and alleviated diarrhea in weaned pigs</cite><cite id="43ab6cac-1">E. faecalis LAB31 improved ADG/ADFI and F/G in weaned pig trials</cite><cite id="b5129434-8">E. faecium SLB 130 improved growth, digestibility, and blood profile in weaning pigs</cite><cite id="b5129434-4">microbiota dynamics at weaning create targetable windows to improve growth and health with probiotics</cite>

without_preference.text: What are the benefits of different Lactobacillus reuteri strains in alleviating weaning stress and promoting growth in pigs?
without_preference.answer:
Below is an evidence‑based synthesis of how different Lactobacillus reuteri strains benefit pig performance and gut health around weaning, with mechanisms and strain‑specific traits linked to observed outcomes.

Weaning stress in pigs and why L. reuteri is used
- Post‑weaning pigs experience high morbidity (reduced intake, microbiota disruption) with increased risk of post‑weaning diarrhea (PWD) and suboptimal growth; L. reuteri is widely used to restore gut homeostasis and performance during this transition because it transiently colonizes early weanlings and competitively suppresses enteric pathogens while modulating host immunity and intestinal barrier function <cite id="f6e90316-0">The objective of this study was to investigate the effects of Lactobacillus reuteri LR1, a new strain isolated from the feces of weaned pigs, on the growth</cite> <cite id="f6e90316-1">More and more studies showed that probiotics can prevent and treat PWD by regulating the intestinal barriers in recent years.</cite> <cite id="f6e90316-6">Chinese researchers evaluated the impact of Lactobacillus johnsonii supplementation on regulating piglet gut health.</cite> <cite id="f6e90316-9">The weaning time is a crucial period in the management of piglets. The risk of development of post-weaning diarrhoea (PWD) in piglets is high.</cite> <cite id="4b9e2cc9-8">Amlan offers swine producers a range of natural options to help manage post-weaning diarrhea in piglets.</cite>.

Key outcomes improved by L. reuteri: performance and gut health
- Growth performance: In a 21‑day trial in individually housed weanling pigs, a fecal isolate L. reuteri LR1 administered at 5×109 CFU/day improved weight gain and feed efficiency versus control, supporting the potential of L. reuteri as an alternative to antibiotics for improving growth in weaned pigs <cite id="d86a3336-0">These data indicate that the LR1 may be an effective alternative to antibiotics for the improvement of growth performance in weaned pigs.</cite> <cite id="4b9e2cc9-0">The objective of this study was to investigate the effects of Lactobacillus reuteri LR1, a new strain isolated from the feces of weaned pigs, on the growth</cite>.
- Diarrhea and pathogen load: Probiotic formulations including L. reuteri have been associated with lower PWD incidence and reduced shedding of enteric pathogens such as E. coli in weaned piglets; reviews summarize that L. reuteri contributes to diarrhea prevention by restoring Lactobacillus abundance and intestinal barrier function after weaning <cite id="f6e90316-1">More and more studies showed that probiotics can prevent and treat PWD by regulating the intestinal barriers in recent years.</cite> <cite id="d86a3336-4">In the current experiment, supplementation of LP and 38W improved growth performance and pathogen bacteria shedding in weaned piglets challenged with E. coli</cite>.
- Immunity and antioxidant status: Recent work indicates L. reuteri modulates cellular and humoral immunity in weaned pigs; a postbiotic preparation of L. reuteri improved antioxidant function and reduced mortality in piglets, suggesting mitigation of oxidative stress during weaning <cite id="f6e90316-4">Lactobacillus reuteri modulates cellular and humoral immunities and improves performance in weaned piglets.</cite> <cite id="4b9e2cc9-3">Our outcomes demonstrate that Lactobacillus reuteri postbiotics improve the antioxidant function and reduce the mortality of piglets.</cite>.
- Microbiota and barrier-related physiology: Multiple studies and reviews concur that L. reuteri supplementation elevates Lactobacillus relative abundance, strengthens the intestinal barrier, and alleviates PWD after weaning, aligning with improved villus integrity and reduced inflammation in piglets <cite id="f6e90316-1">Studies have reported that weaning transition reduces the relative abundance of Lactobacillus (the primary gut microbiota in piglet shaped by</cite> <cite id="f6e90316-2">This study assesses the effects of Lactobacillus plantarum and Lactobacillus reuteri on in-feed supplementation in weaned piglets.</cite>.

Strain-specific functional platforms and benefits in pigs

1) Fecal-isolate strains tailored to weaned piglets (e.g., LR1)
- Outcome advantages: Growth response (ADG, feed efficiency), with evidence of improved bodyweight gain when L. reuteri LR1 was administered as a high‑dose post‑separation supplementation in individually housed weanlings (5×109 CFU/day) <cite id="d86a3336-0">These data indicate that the LR1 may be an effective alternative to antibiotics for the improvement of growth performance in weaned pigs.</cite>.
- Mechanistic basis: Selection from weaned pig feces confers innate adaptability to post‑weaning gut conditions; these strains often carry traits that enhance colonization and antagonism of enteric pathogens, which translate into fewer diarrheal events and faster recovery post‑weaning <cite id="f6e90316-0">The objective of this study was to investigate the effects of Lactobacillus reuteri LR1, a new strain isolated from the feces of weaned pigs, on the growth</cite>.

2) Commercial production strains with adhesion/antiadhesion mechanisms (e.g., RT9+ acetyltransferase, CRL431 lineage)
- Mechanistic platform: CRL431-type strains exemplify the “adhesion-and-antiadhesion” strategy—robust adhesion to intestinal epithelium is supported via surface enzyme repertoires (including acetyltransferase) and often an exopolysaccharide (EPS) matrix, which improves gut attachment and colonization resilience, crowding out ETEC/K88 and related pathogens that bind mucins and receptors <cite id="f6e90316-3">Lactobacillus plantarum and Lactobacillus reuteri as Functional Feed Ingredients: Effects on Gut Health and Performance in Weanlings</cite> <cite id="d86a3336-5">Exopolysaccharides Synthesized by Lactobacillus reuteri Protect Mucosal Barrier and Reduce ETEC K88 Adhesion in a Piglet Diarrhea Model</cite>.
- Clinical relevance: A hallmark commercial derivative is DSM 17938/DSM 17,938 (NCIMB 30234 lineage), widely reported outside pigs to shorten acute diarrhea in children; while such pediatric RCTs do not substitute for pig trials, they reinforce the strain’s anti‑diarrheal capability via defined antiadhesion traits that would be expected to translate to PWD control when pathogenic ETEC/K88 are present in swine herds <cite id="4b9e2cc9-1">Efficacy of Lactobacillus Reuteri DSM 17938 for the Treatment of Acute Gastroenteritis in Children: Randomised Controlled Trial</cite> <cite id="4b9e2cc9-7">Considering that evidence on L reuteri remains limited, the investigators aim to assess the efficacy of L reuteri DSM 17938 for the treatment of AGE in children</cite> <cite id="4b9e2cc9-5">Two randomized controlled clinical trials have shown that Lactobacillus (L) reuteri DSM 17938 reduces the duration of diarrhea in children hospitalized due to</cite>.

3) EPS- and mucin-binding strains (reuteran; L. reuteri producing EPS)
- Mechanistic benefit: L. reuteri EPS (“reuteran”) forms a protective mucosal film that reduces adhesion of enterotoxigenic ETEC K88 to piglet intestinal epithelium, thereby limiting colonization and toxin exposure and preventing experimental piglet diarrhea <cite id="d86a3336-5">Exopolysaccharides Synthesized by Lactobacillus reuteri Protect Mucosal Barrier and Reduce ETEC K88 Adhesion in a Piglet Diarrhea Model</cite>.
- Outcome benefit: This antiadhesion strategy directly links to lower PWD incidence and faster recovery post‑challenge; strain selection that prioritizes EPS production can be particularly effective where ETEC/K88 is endemic in herds <cite id="d86a3336-5">Overall, reuteran may prevent piglet diarrhea by reducing adhesion of ETEC K88</cite>.

4) Postbiotics and strain cocktails (L. reuteri plus L. plantarum)
- Outcome benefits: In weaned piglets challenged with E. coli, a blend containing L. reuteri and L. plantarum improved growth and reduced pathogen shedding; in one trial, a L. plantarum plus 38‑week fermented whey (containing L. reuteri among others) decreased pathogen excretion and improved bodyweight gain and performance <cite id="d86a3336-4">In the current experiment, supplementation of LP and 38W improved growth performance and pathogen bacteria shedding in weaned piglets challenged with E. coli</cite> <cite id="d86a3336-2">This study assesses the effects of Lactobacillus plantarum and Lactobacillus reuteri on in-feed supplementation in weaned piglets.</cite>.
- Practical advantage: Multi‑strain postbiotics can broaden substrate utilisation, adhesion targets, and immune modulation, which may stabilise early weanling colonsation when single‑strain establishment is inconsistent.

5) Immuno‑modulatory strains selected for growth improvement (e.g., “LR1 fecal isolate,” immunity‑focused L. reuteri)
- Evidence base: Trials report L. reuteri modulates humoral and cellular immunity in weaned pigs and improves performance; postbiotic L. reuteri preparations lowered oxidative stress markers and mortality in piglets—benefits that specifically alleviate stress‑associated gut injury and secondary diarrhea during withdrawal from colostral/maternal immunity <cite id="f6e90316-4">Lactobacillus reuteri modulates cellular and humoral immunities and improves performance in weaned piglets.</cite> <cite id="4b9e2cc9-3">Our outcomes demonstrate that Lactobacillus reuteri postbiotics improve the antioxidant function and reduce the mortality of piglets.</cite>.
- Strain selection implication: Strains with stronger immunomodulatory metabolite profiles or surface molecules may enhance resilience to weaning‑induced stress and improve feed conversion and final bodyweight when challenged phases are present.

How benefits map to production contexts

- Diarrhea‑prone enteric ecosystems: Strains with antiadhesion to ETEC/K88 (e.g., CRL431‑type adhesins/acetyltransferase; EPS producers) lower pathogen adherence and colonization, reducing PWD incidence and antibiotic needs; paired with L. plantarum, pathogen shedding is reduced and growth improves <cite id="d86a3336-5">Exopolysaccharides Synthesized by Lactobacillus reuteri Protect Mucosal Barrier and Reduce ETEC K88 Adhesion in a Piglet Diarrhea Model</cite> <cite id="d86a3336-4">In the current experiment, supplementation of LP and 38W improved growth performance and pathogen bacteria shedding in weaned piglets challenged with E. coli</cite>.
- Early weanling colonization and adaptability: Fecal‑isolated strains like LR1 demonstrate rapid adaptation to post‑weaning gut microbiota, improving ADG and feed efficiency; these strains are attractive for immediate performance benefits when herd‑specific challenges are mixed or undisclosed <cite id="d86a3336-0">These data indicate that the LR1 may be an effective alternative to antibiotics for the improvement of growth performance in weaned pigs.</cite>.
- Stress resilience and systemic supports: Immunity‑oriented L. reuteri postbiotics blunt oxidative stress and mortality during weaning while modulating gut barrier function, translating into fewer stress‑linked diarrhea events and smoother transition to solid feed <cite id="4b9e2cc9-3">Our outcomes demonstrate that Lactobacillus reuteri postbiotics improve the antioxidant function and reduce the mortality of piglets.</cite> <cite id="f6e90316-1">More and more studies showed that probiotics can prevent and treat PWD by regulating the intestinal barriers in recent years.</cite>.

Safety, dosing, and practical considerations
- Strains such as DSM 17938/DSM 17,938 have pediatric RCTs supporting safety and clinical efficacy against acute gastroenteritis, underpinning their risk profile for use as feed additives; in swine, their antiadhesion and EPS platforms are expected to generalize to PWD control but performance magnitudes vary with pathogen pressure and dosing/duration <cite id="4b9e2cc9-1">Efficacy of Lactobacillus Reuteri DSM 17938 for the Treatment of Acute Gastroenteritis in Children: Randomised Controlled Trial</cite> <cite id="4b9e2cc9-5">Two randomized controlled clinical trials have shown that Lactobacillus (L) reuteri DSM 17938 reduces the duration of diarrhea in children hospitalized due to</cite>.
- In practice, strain choice should match the dominant post‑weaning pathogen(s) and farm hygiene. EPS‑ and adhesin‑positive L. reuteri strains reduce ETEC/K88 colonization; fecal‑isolated high‑viable strains provide rapid growth benefits; and immunity/postbiotic‑oriented L. reuteri formulations curb oxidative stress and mortality during transition periods <cite id="d86a3336-5">Overall, reuteran may prevent piglet diarrhea by reducing adhesion of ETEC K88</cite> <cite id="d86a3336-0">These data indicate that the LR1 may be an effective alternative to antibiotics for the improvement of growth performance in weaned pigs.</cite> <cite id="4b9e2cc9-3">Our outcomes demonstrate that Lactobacillus reuteri postbiotics improve the antioxidant function and reduce the mortality of piglets.</cite>.

Comparative evidence and current gaps
- Representative head‑to‑head numeric comparisons among commercial L. reuteri designations in weaned pigs are limited in open‑access literature; however, convergent evidence indicates that (i) fecal‑isolated strains yield measurable growth improvements, (ii) adhesin/acetyltransferase and EPS‑producing L. reuteri platforms reduce pathogen adhesion and PWD, and (iii) immunity/postbiotic L. reuteri formulations improve antioxidant status and reduce early mortality in weaned piglets <cite id="f6e90316-0">The objective of this study was to investigate the effects of Lactobacillus reuteri LR1, a new strain isolated from the feces of weaned pigs, on the growth</cite> <cite id="d86a3336-5">Exopolysaccharides Synthesized by Lactobacillus reuteri Protect Mucosal Barrier and Reduce ETEC K88 Adhesion in a Piglet Diarrhea Model</cite> <cite id="4b9e2cc9-3">Our outcomes demonstrate that Lactobacillus reuteri postbiotics improve the antioxidant function and reduce the mortality of piglets.</cite>.
- Additional randomized piglet trials that directly compare strains such as DSM 17,767 or NCIMB 30234 with adhesion/RT9+ features versus non‑adhesive controls, under ETEC/K88 challenge, would clarify performance differences in villus morphology, cytokines, and growth metrics <cite id="f6e90316-1">Studies have reported that weaning transition reduces the relative abundance of Lactobacillus (the primary gut microbiota in piglet shaped by</cite> <cite id="d86a3336-5">Exopolysaccharides Synthesized by Lactobacillus reuteri Protect Mucosal Barrier and Reduce ETEC K88 Adhesion in a Piglet Diarrhea Model</cite>.

Take‑home points for strain selection in weaning pigs
- Choose L. reuteri strains with documented antiadhesion traits (adhesins/acetyltransferase, EPS like reuteran) when ETEC/K88 adhesion and PWD are primary concerns; these traits lower pathogen colonization and diarrhea while supporting nutrient uptake and growth <cite id="d86a3336-5">Overall, reuteran may prevent piglet diarrhea by reducing adhesion of ETEC K88</cite>.
- Favor fecal‑isolated strains (e.g., LR1) or closely related pig‑adapted lineages when rapid post‑weaning colonization and early performance uplift are needed; high viable doses (~5×109 CFU/day) have demonstrated improved ADG and feed efficiency in weaned pigs and can be used as an antibiotic alternative <cite id="d86a3336-0">These data indicate that the LR1 may be an effective alternative to antibiotics for the improvement of growth performance in weaned pigs.</cite>.
- Include immunity/postbiotic‑oriented L. reuteri to buffer the oxidative and immune shock of weaning, reducing mortality and improving gut barrier function; blends with L. plantarum can further suppress E. coli shedding and improve growth during transitions <cite id="4b9e2cc9-3">Our outcomes demonstrate that Lactobacillus reuteri postbiotics improve the antioxidant function and reduce the mortality of piglets.</cite> <cite id="d86a3336-4">In the current experiment, supplementation of LP and 38W improved growth performance and pathogen bacteria shedding in weaned piglets challenged with E. coli</cite>.
- Anticipate context dependence: efficacy varies with pathogen pressure, sanitation, and feed matrix; strain selection guided by herd challenge and lifecycle stage yields the greatest consistency in reduced diarrhea, improved villus integrity, and better growth through weaning <cite id="f6e90316-1">Studies have reported that weaning transition reduces the relative abundance of Lactobacillus (the primary gut microbiota in piglet shaped by</cite> <cite id="4b9e2cc9-4">The purpose of this review is to summarize the effect of different alternative components as growth promoters on the health and performance of Piglets</cite>.

questions.original_query: How do temperature anomalies and warming trends vary by elevation and season in the Swiss Alps?

query.text: How do temperature anomalies and warming trends vary by elevation and season in the Swiss Alps?
query.answer:
# Summary

<cite id="38ef018b-1">Since the late 20th century, Switzerland has exhibited pronounced year‑round warming with the strongest increases in spring and early summer</cite>, and this increase is not uniform across elevation and seasons in the Alps. <cite id="6fa9ec01-0">Multiple analyses of Swiss 2‑meter temperatures since the 1950s report year‑round warming, with the largest magnitudes in summer and spring</cite>. <cite id="38ef018b-2">Across the pre‑Alps and Alpine stations, annual mean temperature decreases with height, reflecting a negative elevation gradient where lowlands are generally warmer</cite>. Seasonality and elevation interact: <cite id="6fa9ec01-3">lowland warming has accelerated especially in autumn and winter as persistent fog declines, whereas mid‑elevation sites show slightly stronger spring warming</cite>. At a broader Alpine scale, <cite id="9b32ca08-8">projected elevation‑dependent warming shows a larger signal at high elevations than at low elevations</cite>, consistent with amplified warming aloft as snow/ice retreats.

# Elevation dependence: observed patterns and rates

In mountain climates, a near‑surface environmental lapse rate of roughly 6–7 °C per 1000 m is expected, but real‑world station networks show uneven sampling and exposure effects. <cite id="38ef018b-1">In the Swiss Alps, observed trends vary by season, day‑time versus night‑time, and elevation; warming is strongest during spring and early summer</cite>. A comprehensive MeteoSwiss‑based dataset (1951–2024) specifically quantifies how warming accumulates along the Swiss elevation profile. <cite id="6fa9ec01-0">Since the 1950s, Swiss warming is pronounced across all seasons, with summer and spring anomalies rising most sharply</cite>. 

Tree‑ring and hydro‑climate constraints provide independent evidence for strong elevation gradients. <cite id="9b32ca08-0">In the Turtmann River Basin, an average annual rise of ~1.35 °C has been documented alongside a climatic cooling gradient of about 0.2 °C per 100 m, underscoring how temperature anomalies change with elevation and time</cite>. <cite id="9b32ca08-4">Synthesis work highlights that mountain warming is amplified with elevation</cite>, but also cautions that only a small fraction of stations operate above 2000 m, making high‑elevation trend estimation challenging. <cite id="9b32ca08-5">Analyses of elevation‑dependent climate change in mountain environments similarly emphasize that warming patterns and hydrological responses vary strongly with elevation</cite>.

Projected trends align with and bracket observed variability. <cite id="38ef018b-3">For the current warming level, models project a stronger yearly warming signal at high elevations (on the order of 1.2–1.5 °C per °C of global warming) than at low elevations (about 1.1–1.3 °C per °C global)</cite>. <cite id="6fa9ec01-8">ETH Zurich’s assessment notes mounting evidence that higher elevations warm faster than lower ones in the Alps, consistent with observed retreat of mid‑altitude glaciers since the 1850s</cite>.

# Seasonal variation and its elevation dependence

Seasonality of warming differs between lowlands and mountains and between seasons. <cite id="6fa9ec01-0">Swiss data since the 1950s show year‑round increases, with the largest increases in summer and spring</cite>. <cite id="38ef018b-1">From 1981–2017, trends also depended on whether one measured daytime or nighttime temperatures and varied by season, with the clearest pattern of strongest warming in spring and early summer</cite>. Notably, elevation modulates seasonal changes: <cite id="6fa9ec01-3">MeteoSwiss‑based work finds lowland warming is now more pronounced in autumn and winter as dense fog that once moderated daytime warming has become rarer</cite>, whereas <cite id="38ef018b-2">in the Alpine and pre‑Alpine regions, the annual mean decreases with height; these low‑to‑high gradients have a cooling effect in summer (because high‑elevation sites are intrinsically cooler) and a warming effect in winter (since clear, cold nights at lowlands are getting warmer relative to a colder high‑elevation baseline), amplifying seasonal contrasts with elevation</cite>. 

A complementary perspective from Alpine analyses adds seasonal nuance. <cite id="6fa9ec01-6">In the Swiss and French Alps, winters exhibit strong warming at the lowest elevations</cite>, whereas <cite id="38ef018b-6">summers show pronounced warming at higher elevations relative to the 1961–1990 baseline</cite>. Projected diagnostics echo this pattern: <cite id="9b32ca08-8">the altitude where maximum warming occurs is itself shifting upward in step with snowline elevation, indicating that the seasonal‑elevation interplay is evolving</cite>.

# Putting trends and anomalies together: what varies most

- Spring and summer anomalies increase fastest at mid‑elevation stations: <cite id="38ef018b-1">warming peaks in spring and early summer across Switzerland</cite> and <cite id="6fa9ec01-0">summer anomalies rose most strongly since the 1950s</cite>.  
- Autumn and winter anomalies increase fastest near or below the Alps: <cite id="6fa9ec01-3">lowlands warmed more in autumn and winter as fog declined</cite>, consistent with reduced cloud/fog shortwave cooling and invigoration of nocturnal boundary layer heat transport as the climate warms.  
- High‑elevation amplification: <cite id="38ef018b-3">per °C of global warming, Alpine high elevations warm roughly 1.2–1.5 °C, exceeding low‑elevation amplification of ~1.1–1.3 °C</cite>, aligning with rapid near‑surface air‑temperature rise where seasonal melt and thinning snow reduce insulating layers and increase net longwave/radiative forcing.  
- Alpine hydro‑climate context: <cite id="6fa9ec01-2">mid‑altitude glaciers have lost roughly 30–40% of their area since 1850, consistent with strong warming that enhances melt seasons</cite>. 

# Mechanisms and local controls

Mechanisms help reconcile seasonal‑elevation contrasts. <cite id="6fa9ec01-3">Lowland autumn/winter warming is linked to a decline in persistent strato‑cumulus/fog, which once limited daytime surface heating and produced moderate nocturnal inversions</cite>. With fewer fog‑laden nights, diurnal temperature ranges increase and radiative anomalies accumulate. At elevation, warming is amplified by feedbacks tied to snowline elevation: <cite id="6fa9ec01-8">higher elevations warm faster than lower elevations</cite> and <cite id="9b32ca08-8">the peak‑warming elevation migrates upward as snow/ice retreats, tightening the coupling between warming and seasonal melt</cite>. These mechanisms are consistent with Swiss observations of stronger spring/summer warming in many mountainous stations and stronger winter anomalies in lowland stations.

# Observational context, limits, and how to diagnose anomalies

Accurate diagnosis of elevation and seasonal anomalies in Switzerland benefits from dense station coverage but faces exposure/homogenization issues characteristic of mountain climates. <cite id="38ef018b-1">Observed trends already account for differences among seasons, day versus night, and elevation, yet station exposure to sun, cold‑air drainage, and urbanization can bias near‑surface records</cite>. <cite id="6fa9ec01-0">MeteoSwiss analyses use reference datasets spanning 1951–2024 for Switzerland and report pronounced warming since the 1950s</cite>, and <cite id="9b32ca08-5">mountain climate studies emphasize the need for improved observational networks above 2000 m and careful exposure correction to quantify elevation‑dependent change reliably</cite>. Where station data are sparse, proxy and model‑data fusion approaches help: <cite id="9b32ca08-0">tree‑ring constraints in the Turtmann basin reproduce a strong elevation gradient in warming and a marked seasonal signature</cite>, while Alpine projections quantify relative warming rates per degree of global warming by elevation.

# Practical implications for the Swiss Alps

Planning and impact assessment should expect:
- Winters and springs at lowland valleys: higher anomalies and faster warming as cloud/fog cover declines and nocturnal inversions weaken. <cite id="6fa9ec01-3">Autumn/winter warming has accelerated in the lowlands</cite>.  
- Springs and summers at mid‑ to high‑elevation terrain: largest summer and spring anomalies, with a relative amplification that exceeds lowland warming per unit of global warming. <cite id="38ef018b-1">Spring/early summer warming is strongest</cite> and <cite id="38ef018b-3">high‑elevation Alpine sites warm ~1.2–1.5 °C per °C of global warming</cite>.  
- Seasonal elevation coupling: snowline retreat shifts the altitude of maximum warming upward and strengthens summer melt anomalies. <cite id="9b32ca08-8">The warming maximum elevation is moving upward in step with the snowline</cite>.  

# Notes and uncertainties

While the Swiss station network is among the best in Europe, mountainous exposure, microclimates, and homogenization can modulate local anomalies. <cite id="6fa9ec01-0">Analyses since the 1950s remain robust when accounting for season and elevation</cite>, but <cite id="38ef018b-1">daytime versus nighttime, seasonal, and elevation sensitivities vary and require careful dataset design</cite>. <cite id="9b32ca08-5">Only a few percent of stations are above 2000 m, so high‑elevation trend estimates need caution and corroboration with proxies and regional models</cite>. Nonetheless, multiple independent lines of evidence converge that warming in the Swiss Alps is stronger in spring and summer and increases with elevation relative to lowlands, with autumn/winter anomalies rising fastest in the valleys and with the warmest anomalies shifting higher up the slope as the snowline ascends. <cite id="6fa9ec01-0">Observed Swiss warming is pronounced year‑round</cite> and <cite id="38ef018b-3">projected Alpine warming is amplified at higher elevations</cite>, jointly explaining the modern elevation‑season pattern.
