questions.original_query: How do relative humidity and desorption time affect the desorption capacity of cigarette smoke chemicals from various indoor materials?

query.text: How do relative humidity and desorption time affect the desorption capacity of cigarette smoke chemicals from various indoor materials?
query.answer:
Overview and mechanisms
- Cigarette smoke chemicals (semivolatile organic compounds such as nicotine, nitrosamines, and oxidation products) partition between gas phase and indoor surfaces, creating “third-hand smoke” layers that both attenuate pollutant peaks and prolong indoor exposure via desorption over days to weeks. <cite id="c2a74396-0">Relative humidity and desorption time have notable impacts on the desorption capacity of cigarette smoke chemicals from indoor materials</cite>. <cite id="71281f0d-2">Carpet acts as a strong sink for nonpolar VOCs, while virgin gypsum board is a significant sink for highly polar VOCs</cite>, highlighting that both sorbent type and chemical polarity determine deposition burdens and later release.

Relative humidity (RH): sorption vs. desorption effects
- <cite id="c2a74396-4">Relative humidity significantly affects nicotine adsorption, but its direct influence on desorption is much smaller</cite>. <cite id="d1a46445-6">Measurements on curtains and carpets show that ambient RH and ammonia modulate nicotine sorption to common indoor surfaces</cite>, consistent with the general humidity dependence of SVOC–surface partitioning. <cite id="d1a46445-2">Building parameters including RH control nicotine dynamics by altering partitioning, reaction, and emission rates</cite>. <cite id="71281f0d-0">In controlled room simulations, gypsum wallboard near sources accumulated nicotine in the low μg/m3 range over multiple weeks at moderate RH</cite>.
- Mechanistically, water modulates both physicochemical partitioning and surface reactions. <cite id="d1a46445-3">Quantified nicotine sorption on polypropylene carpet at 0%, 50%, and 90% RH shows stronger retention at higher RH due to increased water activity and polarity interactions</cite>. <cite id="c2a74396-4">While RH enhances adsorption, the resulting equilibrium surface load often depresses the gas-phase peak and shifts the time-profile of desorption to longer durations</cite>. <cite id="d1a46445-2">Material polarity and RH co-determine adsorption strength and the fraction retained</cite>. <cite id="c2a74396-4">Adsorption on paper and gypsum wallboard under different RH histories shows that increased RH raises the burden that later must desorb, i.e., RH “pumps” chemicals onto surfaces where they re-emit more slowly</cite>.
- Oxidation on surfaces can make desorption less likely even at high RH. <cite id="d1a46445-3">Surface oxidative fate of nicotine occurs concurrently with sorption/desorption and depends on RH and ammonia</cite>. <cite id="1b11f1c7-1">Experiments show surface oxidation is competitive with desorption, substantially reducing long-term re-emissions of nicotine from oxidized residues</cite>. <cite id="c2a74396-4">Reviews of third-hand smoke report that oxidation products formed on surfaces can lower desorption capacity relative to parent SVOCs</cite>.

Desorption time and capacity across materials
- Sorbed nicotine and related alkaloids exhibit slow, time-dependent release. <cite id="d1a46445-0">Carpet and wallboard show much stronger sorption than air, with nicotine equilibrium partitioning 2–3 orders of magnitude higher, and desorption rates substantially slower than sorption, prolonging indoor persistence</cite>. <cite id="c2a74396-8">Within 10 hours after one cigarette, ~22% of sidestream particles by mass deposit on interior surfaces in low-ventilation rooms, providing a substrate for subsequent slow desorption</cite>. <cite id="c2a74396-3">Nicotine evaporates and deposits in denuders with time-dependent behavior set by its volatility and particle growth kinetics, illustrating the kinetic separation between gas-phase loss and surface accumulation processes</cite>.
- Duration matters: days to weeks typically govern measurable desorption from porous, polar surfaces. <cite id="71281f0d-0">Gypsum wallboard exposed to cigarette emissions accumulated nicotine over time and remained measurable over six weeks, demonstrating slow release back into air</cite>. <cite id="71281f0d-9">Experiments that incubated carpets and drywall at elevated relative humidities (50–95%) for four weeks tracked microbial and VOC changes, illustrating that extended exposure at high RH sustains both retention and potential emissions</cite>.
- Material class and surface polarity govern desorption capacity at fixed RH. <cite id="71281f0d-2">Highly polar surfaces (e.g., virgin gypsum board) retain more nicotine, while nonpolar surfaces like carpet accumulate substantial residues and desorb over longer time frames</cite>. <cite id="d1a46445-0">Carpet and wallboard together account for a large fraction of the sorbent capacity, explaining why desorption capacity from room/office surfaces can remain significant for weeks</cite>. <cite id="c2a74396-6">Deposited nicotine on indoor surfaces can re-enter the gas phase, where it may be captured downstream (e.g., by denuders or air-cleaning devices)</cite>.
- RH–time interplay and hysteresis. <cite id="c2a74396-7">Dynamic vapor sorption (DVS) of tobacco under RH cycling shows strong hysteresis: materials gain moisture with each humidity cycle and shift sorption/desorption thresholds, indicating that prior moisture history changes the amount and rate of later desorption</cite>. <cite id="d1a46445-1">Hysteresis in sorption–desorption curves is observed for semivolatile organics on textiles and building materials, with higher equilibrated moisture at increased RH leading to greater surface binding and slower release</cite>. <cite id="71281f0d-9">Experiments with RH stepping (50–95%) over four weeks on carpets and drywall show sustained retention and potential for moisture-driven desorption bursts as materials equilibrate at different RH plateaus</cite>.

Chemical-specific notes (nicotine, oxidation products, alkaloids)
- Parent nicotine. <cite id="d1a46445-2">Nicotine uptake on fabrics, wood, and gypsum is strongly modulated by RH and ammonia, which can influence cationicity and binding to polar surfaces</cite>. <cite id="2a74396-4">On cotton and similar fabrics, adsorption increases with moderate RH (65–70%) compared with dry air; during desorption the fraction released is slower and can be reduced by oxidation products</cite>. <cite id="1b11f1c7-5">Nicotine preferably sorbs to high-polarity materials, and sorption is facilitated at higher RH</cite>.
- Oxidized metabolites and alkaloids (e.g., cotinine, trans-3‑oxohexenoyl–nicotine). <cite id="c2a74396-4">Reviews emphasize that oxidation on surfaces lowers the desorption capacity of third-hand smoke alkaloids, so the most volatile fraction of nicotine-related chemicals can escape early, leaving less-volatile oxidation products to persist</cite>. <cite id="1b11f1c7-1">Ozone exposure accelerates surface oxidation and reduces long-term re-emission, illustrating that chemical aging decreases cumulative desorption capacity over time</cite>. <cite id="c2a74396-9">Cigarette smoke deposition on surfaces yields oxidation of some components, forming surface films whose composition reduces subsequent volatility and release</cite>.

Forensic and artifact materials: paper, textiles, wood, vinyl
- Paper and high-polarity substrates. <cite id="c2a74396-4">Paper exposed to cigarette smoke deposits nicotine and related alkaloids; increased RH during sorption raises surface burden, and the desorption profile is slow and time-extended</cite>. <cite id="c2a74396-6">Nicotine deposited on paper can re-volatilize and be recaptured, suggesting potential for measurable desorption during artifact handling or environmental fluctuations</cite>.
- Textiles and upholstery. <cite id="d1a46445-0">Polypropylene carpet shows strong sorption (orders of magnitude greater than air) and slow desorption kinetics, so desorption capacity from upholstery and draperies remains appreciable over weeks</cite>. <cite id="71281f0d-2">Carpet is a dominant sink for nonpolar SVOCs, so desorption capacity from textiles can exceed that of low-sorbency materials at equal RH and time</cite>. <cite id="1b11f1c7-6">On fabrics, some alkaloids (nicotine, myosmine) turnover during aging via desorption and chemical transformation, with relative humidity and aging duration governing the balance</cite>.
- Wood, gypsum, and paints. <cite id="71281f0d-0">Painted gypsum wallboard acts as a nicotine sink, with μg/m3 concentrations sustained over multiple weeks, indicating that porosity and sorbate polarity drive both adsorption and subsequent slow release</cite>. <cite id="d1a46445-0">Wallboard and carpet together dominate indoor nicotine sorption, implying a high ceiling for desorption capacity when these materials are present</cite>. <cite id="c2a74396-3">Adsorption onto painted surfaces like wood and gypsum depends on smoke composition and RH; over days, desorption can recapture a fraction of emitted nicotine</cite>.
- Vinyls and plastics. <cite id="c2a74396-7">Thermodynamic sorption analysis of polymers relevant to plastics and tobacco shows pronounced RH-dependent hysteresis; polymer swelling at higher RH increases binding sites and slows desorption, whereas drying accelerates release</cite>. <cite id="d1a46445-0">Moderate RH increases adsorption to porous plastics by one to two orders of magnitude, which in turn extends desorption time constants</cite>.

Practical implications for desorption capacity control
- RH management modifies initial uptake and long-term emissions. <cite id="d1a46445-3">Lower RH reduces nicotine sorption to surfaces, thereby leaving a larger fraction in the air stream to be filtered or exhausted; higher RH does the opposite, raising initial deposition and shifting release to later times</cite>. <cite id="c2a74396-4">Because oxidation concurrently reduces desorption, ventilation and air cleaning strategies that lower RH quickly after smoking events can reduce the surface reservoir formed at high RH and accelerate decay of desorption capacity</cite>. <cite id="1b11f1c7-1">Chemical aging (ozone) can be leveraged to remove accumulated nicotine by increasing the fraction lost irreversibly or irreparably via reaction, or to catalyze desorption by generating more volatile intermediates</cite>.
- Time scales. <cite id="d1a46445-0">On common materials, nicotine’s desorption follows slow, diffusion-limited kinetics—weeks are often required to reduce surface loads substantially</cite>. <cite id="71281f0d-0">Experiments show μg/m3 nicotine levels persisting on gypsum wallboard over six weeks, implying that practical “cleaning” times must exceed days to materially reduce desorption capacity</cite>.
- Surface type and polarity. <cite id="71281f0d-2">Highly polar surfaces (gypsum, paper) adsorb more nicotine and desorb less, so they constitute major sources for long-term emissions</cite>. <cite id="d1a46445-0">Nonpolar surfaces like carpet adsorb massively but release slowly; aggressive drying or mechanical removal is needed to lower desorption capacity</cite>.

Key takeaways
- Increasing RH during exposure increases sorption and builds a larger surface reservoir; this typically raises short-term air-burden but transfers a chemically persistent fraction to long-term surface storage, whose desorption capacity decays slowly and is strongly time-limited, especially on porous/polar materials. <cite id="c2a74396-4">Relative humidity significantly enhances adsorption while only minimally altering immediate desorption</cite>. <cite id="d1a46445-0">Carpet and wallboard exhibit orders-of-magnitude higher sorption and slow desorption, prolonging indoor persistence</cite>. <cite id="71281f0d-0">Measured desorption can be detectable over six weeks on gypsum wallboard</cite>.
- Desorption capacity rises with longer desorption times due to diffusion-limited release and can be further lowered by surface oxidation, which preferentially eliminates the more volatile fraction. <cite id="d1a46445-1">Hysteresis and moisture conditioning shift sorption/desorption thresholds with RH cycling</cite>. <cite id="1b11f1c7-1">Oxidation competes with desorption and reduces long-term re-emissions</cite>.
- Material selection and cleaning strategies matter: low-sorbency coverings (e.g., vinyl) can be periodically dried to flush trapped nicotine; porous polars (carpet, paper, painted wallboard) require mechanical removal plus time/drying to diminish their substantial desorption capacity. <cite id="71281f0d-2">Carpet concentrates nonpolar SVOCs; gypsum board retains polar SVOCs</cite>. <cite id="c2a74396-4">Adsorption on paper and wallboard builds a long-lived reservoir that slowly replenishes air concentrations</cite>.

Notes on uncertainties and research needs
- Many studies isolate parent nicotine or a limited set of metabolites and focus on sorption; fewer provide full chemical-specific desorption profiles across weeks for oxidized species at controlled RH histories. <cite id="c2a74396-0">Reviews report minor RH effects on desorption for some materials and chemicals, underscoring that effects are chemical- and material-specific</cite>. <cite id="d1a46445-1">Hysteresis complicates interpretation: prior RH exposure modifies current desorption capacity</cite>.
- Forensic artifacts (ancient/long-aged residues) may show lower desorption capacity due to extensive oxidation and crosslinking, suggesting chemical aging can lock away up to an order of magnitude of originally deposited nicotine-related mass. <cite id="c2a74396-9">Surface films formed by deposition and oxidation reduce volatility and release</cite>. <cite id="1b11f1c7-6">Turnover via desorption/chemical transformation during aging means older residues desorb less readily</cite>.

Practical summary for indoor environments and cleaning
- Immediately after smoking, keep RH low to limit deposition; use ventilation and HEPA+carbon systems to remove airborne nicotine before it becomes surface-trapped. <cite id="d1a46445-3">Lower RH reduces sorption to surfaces</cite>. <cite id="c2a74396-6">Air capture devices can intercept re-volatilized nicotine</cite>.
- After the event, expect residual desorption capacity to decay slowly; plan for days-to-weeks of natural decay on porous/polar materials. <cite id="71281f0d-0">Nicotine measurable on wallboard for six weeks</cite>. <cite id="d1a46445-0">Slow desorption kinetics on carpet and wallboard</cite>.
- Combine mechanical removal (vacuuming, washing) with drying cycles to collapse surface reservoirs, especially on textiles and high-sorbency substrates; periodic elevated-temperature/desiccant cleaning aids rapid desorption for weeks. <cite id="c2a74396-4">Adsorption on paper and wallboard creates long-lived reservoirs needing drying to reduce desorption capacity</cite>. <cite id="d1a46445-0">High sorption on carpet and wallboard necessitates aggressive mitigation to reduce reservoirs</cite>.

fully_underspecified.text: How do environmental conditions affect the removal of chemicals from materials?
fully_underspecified.answer:
# Summary

Environmental conditions modulate the removal of chemicals from materials primarily through four levers: thermodynamics (pH and complexation), kinetics (temperature and reaction media), transport (water activity, contact area/time, porosity), and interfacial chemistry (ionic strength, oxygen/redox, biofilms). Together, these factors determine whether a contaminant partitions into, reacts within, or diffuses out of a solid matrix at detectable rates under given exposure conditions. <cite id="67f2c64f-3">The rate of metals leaching depends on the chemical and physical properties of the solid and the prevailing environmental conditions</cite> <cite id="67f2c64f-0">Increasing temperature typically accelerates reactions and adjusting pH can enhance solubility of specific metal compounds</cite>.

# Temperature, Contact Time, and Moisture

Raising temperature generally increases leaching rates by boosting diffusion and reaction kinetics. In food-contact systems, heat enhances monomer and plasticizer migration from plastics into water; for polycarbonate (PC), high temperatures or boiling (acid–base shift upon CO2 degassing) markedly increase bisphenol A (BPA) release, with temperature identified as the dominant factor elevating BPA migration from PC bottles into water. <cite id="12db585d-0">High temperature and pH can increase BPA release from PC containers into foodstuff</cite> <cite id="12db585d-3">High temperature and high pH (from degassing CO2 when boiling) degrade PC and raise BPA levels in water</cite> <cite id="12db585d-1">Temperature was the dominant significant factor enhancing BPA migration from PC bottles into water</cite>. 

Temperature also promotes PFAS leaching from materials; in a food-packaging system, ∑9PFAS concentrations rose from 46 to 70 to 102 ng/L as temperature increased from 35 to 45 to 55 °C, evidencing Arrhenius-like acceleration. <cite id="4c368da6-0">Increasing temperature promoted PFAS leaching, reaching 46.3, 70.4, and 102 ng/L at 35, 45, and 55 °C</cite>. Moisture and vapor-phase exchange couple similarly: high RH and use history increase PFAS release from contaminated concrete, and thermal removal protocols target temperature thresholds to accelerate desorption from impacted media. <cite id="4c368da6-5">PFAS thermal desorption research aims to confirm temperature thresholds and quantify removal rates</cite> <cite id="4c368da6-3">Long-chain PFAS leaching from concrete increased at high pH, while short-chain PFAS were less sensitive</cite>.

# pH, Ionic Strength, and Chemical Speciation

pH governs both dissolution and sorption, often by protonating or deprotonating functional groups, altering solubility, or triggering mineral dissolution. Red mud leaching profiles show near-complete pH windows where most elements mobilize, highlighting how acidity liberates major and toxic trace metals; pH 2–13 scans demonstrate strong leaching dependence on solution pH. <cite id="67f2c64f-2">Leaching characteristics of major and toxic elements from red mud were systematically analyzed across pH 2–13</cite> <cite id="67f2c64f-5">Leaching behavior of elements from coal depended on pH, time, and element identity, with many elements leached at pH 2.0</cite>. For soils and sediments, Ca2+ in the percolate can suppress or promote cationic leaching via competitive adsorption or precipitation, while fly ash studies show pH and Ca2+ concentration shift metal release pathways. <cite id="67f2c64f-6">pH significantly affects leaching, and high Ca2+ in fly ash mixtures alters release behavior</cite> <cite id="67f2c64f-8">High concentrations of Ca2+ both in fly ash and mixtures with high concentrations of fly ash affect leaching outcomes</cite>.

PFAS show pH-dependent release patterns by chain length and speciation; long-chain PFAS leach more at higher pH, whereas short-chain PFAS are less pH-sensitive. <cite id="4c368da6-3">Leaching of long-chain PFAS increased at high pH, while short-chain PFAS were less sensitive</cite>. In polymer leaching, polar solvents such as ethanol extract more BPA than water, and temperature drives diffusion-controlled flux; pH effects appear for alkaline/acid washes that hydrolyze ester or carbonate linkages. <cite id="12db585d-2">BPA migrates more readily into ethanol than water; temperature is an important factor influencing BPA diffusion</cite> <cite id="12db585d-8">Alkaline detergents and hot-water dishwashing increase leaching of BPA from polycarbonate baby bottles</cite>.

# Redox and Microbial Activity (Bioleaching)

Oxygen and microbial consortia can remove metals by oxidative dissolution, desorption from sulfide ores, and extracellular enzymatic processes. Ore oxidation begins with redox potential rise and pH drop, with copper from chalcopyrite leaching slowly as protective oxide films form; conversely, chelators and alkaline media accelerate extraction. <cite id="9f768003-1">Onset of leaching was associated with increased redox potential and decreased pH; copper from chalcopyrite leached slowly under oxidative attack</cite>. Bioleaching performance depends on environmental factors including pH, agitation, aeration, and solid/water ratios; microbes sustain high pH (often 10–12) to favor alkaline dissolution while suppressing undesired side reactions. <cite id="9f768003-4">Bioleaching performance is influenced by pH, solid concentration, agitation, irrigation, aeration, and energy source</cite> <cite id="9f768003-2">Alkaline chemical leaching sustains pH 10–12 to inhibit hydrolysis of primary metals while promoting dissolution</cite>.

For environmentally occurring minerals such as jarosite, dissolution rates are pH-dependent but composition-sensitive; arsenic dissolves faster and faster at acidic conditions, whereas neutral-to-alkaline pH can stabilize or reprecipitate metals. <cite id="9f768003-3">Jarosite dissolution increased from pH 4.0 to 8.0; arsenic dissolved more and faster at pH 4.0–5.0 than at pH 6.5–8</cite> <cite id="9f768003-5">Dissolution rate curves of K-jarosite vary with pH at room temperature, illustrating strong pH dependence</cite>.

# Material-Specific Examples

- Polyfluorinated materials (PFAS): Higher temperature and pH can increase leaching for long-chain PFAS; ionic strength and competing cations (e.g., Ca2+) in percolating water alter transport/speciation and net flux; thermal remediation leverages temperature thresholds to remove PFAS from solids. <cite id="4c368da6-0">PFAS leached more rapidly at 35–55 °C in packaging contact tests</cite> <cite id="4c368da6-3">Long-chain PFAS leaching increased at high pH, short-chain less sensitive</cite> <cite id="4c368da6-6">All-acid leaching at pH 1 for 3 h, followed by pH 4 neutralization, was used to quantify PFAS removal from lithium-ion battery residue</cite>.

- Metals/minerals/alloys (lab/process context): Alkaline leaching with complexants (e.g., EDTA) at pH 9–10 can achieve >80% nickel extraction, highlighting how ligand–metal complexes and pH control removal efficiency; carbonates/bicarbonates and hydroxides can raise extraction yields when optimized (e.g., K2CO3 at pH 12 for gold yields up to ~92%). <cite id="9f768003-0">Nickel extraction efficiency reached 82.4–88.9% using NaOH/KOH/NH4OH at pH 9–10 with 0.1 M EDTA–Na2S</cite> <cite id="9f768003-6">At 0.75 mol/L K2CO3 and initial pH 12, gold leaching rate increased to 91.69%</cite>. For environmental matrices, leaching tests that vary temperature and extractant chemistry (pH control, ionic strength) are needed to predict risk; industry and academic guidance emphasize these parameters’ strong influence on measured “leachability.” <cite id="67f2c64f-8">PFAS leachability assessments compare batch and column percolation approaches to reflect environmental exposure conditions</cite>.

- Polymers and plasticizers: Temperature and water activity increase phthalate and related plasticizer migration from plastics; pH swings during boiling/degassing can both mobilize chemicals and trigger polymer hydrolysis. BPA specifically migrates faster in polar solvents (ethanol) and increases with exposure time and temperature; alkaline detergents and hot cycles in dishwashers elevate migration from baby bottles. <cite id="12db585d-2">BPA diffusion into ethanol exceeds water, and temperature is a controlling factor</cite> <cite id="12db585d-1">Longer exposure times and higher temperatures yield more BPA migration from PC</cite> <cite id="12db585d-8">Hot water and alkaline detergents increase BPA leaching from polycarbonate baby bottles</cite> <cite id="12db585d-9">Heating plastics can increase leaching of phthalates into water and food</cite>.

- Electronics and etchant residues: Acidic/alkaline etchants leave reactive residues on circuit boards and packaging; removal efficiency depends on pH, temperature, ionic strength, and contact time—conditions that govern both dissolution and emulsion-cutting of organics. Standard practice controls extractant composition and temperature to maximize residue removal while avoiding damage. <cite id="4c368da6-6">Leaching parameters included acid at pH 1 for 3 h and subsequent pH 4 neutralization to remove PFAS from metals processing residues</cite> <cite id="67f2c64f-8">High concentrations of cations in fly ash analogs to etchant streams affect leachate chemistry and metal removal</cite>.

# Standards and Test Method Implications

Extraction protocols (e.g., batch/percolation) encode environmental controls to make results comparable and predictive. Studies show equivalence of batch and column (percolation) tests for PFAS leachability, while reviews stress that pH, time, and extractant composition must be standardized to capture real-world removal rates, including effects of ionic strength and solution flow. <cite id="4c368da6-2">Batch and column leaching tests for PFAS can be compared to evaluate leachability under controlled environmental conditions</cite> <cite id="67f2c64f-3">Leaching protocols vary environmental parameters (pH, ionic strength, contact time) to reflect risk-relevant conditions</cite>.

# Practical Takeaways

- Control temperature: Raising temperature usually increases removal rates for diffusion- and reaction-limited migrants, including PFAS, metals, and plastics; however, excessive heat can also trigger polymer degradation and acid–base shifts that promote release. <cite id="4c368da6-0">PFAS release increased from 46 to 102 ng/L as temperature rose 35–55 °C</cite> <cite id="12db585d-3">Boiling/degassing raised pH and degraded PC, increasing BPA in water</cite>.

- Tune pH and buffer capacity: Acidify to dissolve cations/oxides and mobilize metals; increase pH to weaken polymer ester linkages and mobilize certain alkali-salt residues, but manage for precipitation/adsorption at neutral pH. <cite id="9f768003-0">pH 9–10 with EDTA achieved 82–89% Ni leaching</cite> <cite id="12db585d-8">Alkaline washes increase BPA leaching from polycarbonate</cite> <cite id="67f2c64f-2">Red mud element leaching showed pronounced pH dependencies across 2–13</cite>.

- Design solvent/matrix and ionic environment: Use polar solvents for polar migrants (e.g., ethanol for BPA) and leverage complexing agents (EDTA, carbonate) to chelate metals; high Ca2+ or bicarbonate can suppress or enhance metal mobility via precipitation or ion-exchange pathways. <cite id="12db585d-2">BPA migrates more readily into ethanol than water</cite> <cite id="9f768003-0">EDTA at pH 9–10 enhances Ni dissolution</cite> <cite id="67f2c64f-6">Ca2+ in fly ash mixtures and solutions strongly influences leaching behavior</cite>.

- Provide sufficient mass transfer: Increase surface area, agitation, and residence time; for porous solids, percolation/flowing leachates outperform static baths to flush away precipitated species and maintain driving force. <cite id="9f768003-4">Agitation, aeration, and irrigation rate impact bioleaching performance</cite> <cite id="4c368da6-2">Column percolation tests emulate flow-driven environmental leaching to quantify PFAS release</cite>.

- Anticipate biological enhancement: Microbial communities can accelerate metal removal via oxidative and acidogenic processes; in remediation, bioleaching with controlled pH/air supply can outperform abiotic methods over time. <cite id="9f768003-1">Oxidation raised redox potential and lowered pH, initiating copper leaching from chalcopyrite</cite> <cite id="9f768003-4">Bioleaching depends on microbial access to pH, oxygen, and nutrients</cite>.

# Risk and Mitigation

In practice, environmental conditions often co-vary: hot beverages or dishwasher cycles simultaneously increase water activity and pH, amplifying monomer/plasticizer release from plastics. For PFAS-contaminated media, choosing appropriate pH and temperature strategies—acid leaching to mobilize fluorinated species, or thermal desorption to raise desorption rates—can sharply change measured removal efficiencies but must be balanced with matrix stability and secondary pollution. <cite id="12db585d-8">Hot-water dishwashing increased BPA leaching from polycarbonate bottles</cite> <cite id="4c368da6-5">PFAS field demonstrations target temperature thresholds to quantify removal rates</cite> <cite id="12db585d-8">Alkaline detergents and hot cycles elevate PFAS/plasticizer migration</cite>. Across systems, the most predictive removal estimates come from tests that explicitly encode solution chemistry, temperature, humidity/flow, and contact time, matching intended use conditions. <cite id="67f2c64f-3">Leaching depends on solid properties and prevailing environmental conditions, motivating controlled test design</cite> <cite id="4c368da6-2">Equivalence of batch vs. column leaching tests underscores the importance of including percolation/humidity effects in PFAS assessments</cite>.

questions.original_query: What qualitative and quantitative methods have been used to assess thermal comfort among users of misting stations?

query.text: What qualitative and quantitative methods have been used to assess thermal comfort among users of misting stations?
query.answer:
Below is a synthesis of qualitative and quantitative methods used to assess thermal comfort among users of misting stations, drawing on field studies of misting stations, mist-spraying environments, cooling centers, and allied public-spatial mist cooling interventions.

Overview and scope
- Reviews and practice syntheses indicate that evaluations of misting stations combine both qualitative and quantitative data to capture perceived comfort and the physical mechanisms by which misting alters the thermal microclimate.<cite id="a64ce8f2-1">The thermal comfort of people using misting stations was evaluated with qualitative and quantitative data.</cite> <cite id="a64ce8f2-2">Misting station use was evaluated with temperature and related microclimate metrics in syntheses of urban cooling interventions including misting stations.</cite> <cite id="a64ce8f2-0">Misting systems can reduce ambient air temperature by roughly 2–5 °C while elevating relative humidity substantially, altering the thermal environment that comfort assessments measure.</cite>

Quantitative methods

Microclimate and environmental measurements
- Instrumented monitoring of air temperature, humidity, air speed, and mean radiant temperature before, during, and after misting to quantify changes in the local thermal environment and relate them to comfort outcomes.<cite id="a64ce8f2-0">Misting reduced ambient air temperature by 2.4–4.9 °C and increased relative humidity by ~17–20% in field assessments of misting systems.</cite> <cite id="a64ce8f2-6">Standard thermal comfort measurements include dry-bulb temperature, relative humidity, air speed, and radiant temperature, which are core microclimate variables for quantitative assessment.</cite>
- Airflow characterization near nozzles and user zones using particle image velocimetry (PIV) or anemometry to capture spatiotemporal air motion affecting evaporation, contact wetting, and convective heat transfer.<cite id="a64ce8f2-7">Air-assisted “dry mist” systems have been studied with ultrafine droplets and PIV to measure and optimize airflow-mist interactions for comfort.</cite>
- Wind chill/evaporative enhancement metrics and field indices: quantitative studies compute heat and wind-related indices to capture combined effects of cooling and discomfort from excessive wind, e.g., via mean radiant temperature, operative temperature, or wind speed at user face/exposed skin levels in mist zones.<cite id="a64ce8f2-3">Case studies of water mist cooling show strong thermal sensation shifts and emphasize wettedness and wind effects on perceived comfort.</cite> <cite id="a64ce8f2-1">Protocols explicitly integrate quantitative microclimate and user-reported measures for misting station evaluation.</cite>
- Thermal environment before/after interventions: comparative measurements quantify temperature, humidity, and air speed inside misting zones versus adjacent reference areas and correlate changes with comfort votes and behavior (standing/sitting, pausing, re-entry).<cite id="a64ce8f2-2">Syntheses report temperature reductions across multiple metrics and evaluate use with temperature and related measures in misting stations and cool pavements.</cite>

Physiological sensing
- Wearable and contactless sensors capture core and skin temperature, heart rate/heart rate variability, and sweat-related measures to index thermal strain and local discomfort under mist exposure.<cite id="a64ce8f2-5">Field surveys and physiological sensing quantify perceived and physiological responses during activities under mist-spraying environments.</cite> <cite id="2a904d40-3">Physiological indicators used in thermal comfort assessment include brainwave activity, heart rate and HRV, and blood flow proxies, linking physiological responses to comfort states.</cite>
- Physiological monitoring provides objective, model-informed validation against subjective reports; groups identify key metrics for high heat exposure (e.g., core and skin temperatures, heart rate, sweat rate) and use them to monitor risk tolerance during misting.<cite id="2a904d40-5">Physiological monitoring (body core and skin temperatures, heart rate, sweat rate) is useful for heat stress monitoring in hot conditions relevant to misting environments.</cite> <cite id="2a904d40-8">Heart rate, skin and core body temperature, and sweat rate are standard physiologic measures used to determine heat stress.</cite>
- Cross-referencing physiology with microclimate improves predictive power, e.g., relating operative temperature and air velocity to skin/wettedness and heart-rate responses in misting zones.<cite id="2a904d40-4">Crowdsourced microclimate-personal comfort-heat exposure studies aim to link microclimate parameters with physiological responses to assess personal thermal comfort.</cite> <cite id="a64ce8f2-9">Instruments to assess outdoor thermal comfort include those measuring microclimate and personal physiological responses.</cite>

Model-based indices and predictive models
- Use of physiological or comfort models that predict local or overall comfort under misting: models consider clothing, activity level, wettedness, and local microclimate to produce local thermal comfort predictions and compare against user reports; some applications adapt standard indices (e.g., PMV/SET/ENF) to evaporative regimes and mist-on skin conditions.<cite id="a64ce8f2-7">Dry-mist systems with ultrafine droplets are analyzed via flow measurements and modeled for comfort improvements under evaporative cooling.</cite> <cite id="a64ce8f2-1">Protocols synthesize model usage with field data for misting stations.</cite>
- Field and lab adaptations: quantitative changes in thermal sensation after misting are reported, providing numeric deltas that calibrate indices (e.g., SET/PMV) for misting scenarios and reveal when standard indoor indices under-predict evaporative benefits.<cite id="a64ce8f2-3">Thermal sensation dropped from +2.7 to −1.4 on a 0–30 scale in water-mist case studies, illustrating substantial perceived cooling.</cite> <cite id="a64ce8f2-5">Studies quantify physiological perception and evaluation of misting systems by users to refine predictive models for such settings.</cite>

User behavior and performance indicators
- Behavioral telemetry: counts and dwell times at misting stations, frequency of use, re-entry/queueing, and movement patterns to quantify perceived benefit and trade-offs in practice; paired with microclimate measurement, these reveal when environmental conditions drive usage or discomfort.
- Crowdsourcing and mobile sensing: smartphone sensors and surveys capture microclimate and comfort votes from the public in real time, enabling large-sample assessments and correlation of environmental parameters with personal comfort at misting nodes.<cite id="2a904d40-4">Mobile-sensed microclimates, personal comfort, and heat exposure were linked to assess the feasibility of crowdsourcing-based comfort evaluation.</cite>
- Microclimate-performance balance: quantify cooling (air temperature drop) versus humidity increase and wind exposure and relate them to user activity tolerance and comfort thresholds.<cite id="a64ce8f2-0">Temperature reductions of 2–5 °C and RH increases of ~17–20% characterize the cooling–humidification trade-off at misting stations.</cite> <cite id="a64ce8f2-2">Interventions are evaluated with multiple temperature and humidity-related metrics to capture net effects on comfort and heat exposure.</cite>

Qualitative methods

Surveys and questionnaires
- Direct subjective ratings: Likert or ordinal scales for thermal sensation/thermal comfort, preference for mist intensity and duration, and overall satisfaction; often paired with microclimate measurements to triangulate perceived vs. measured conditions.<cite id="0ff186cc-0">Evaluations synthesize both qualitative and quantitative data to characterize user comfort at misting stations.</cite> <cite id="0ff186cc-3">Questionnaires commonly include thermal sensation votes (TSV) and demographic data in public-space thermal studies used for misting interventions.</cite> <cite id="2a904d40-2">Field protocols compare questionnaires across locations (e.g., Rome and Ancona) to assess comfort and the effectiveness of misting station interventions.</cite>
- Restaurant/leisure settings: surveys that combine microclimate measurements and subjective perception to quantify how misting guests rate perceived comfort, satisfaction, and willingness to stay or return, including demographic/behavioral covariates.<cite id="0ff186cc-4">Surveys combine microclimatic measurements with perceptions of misting systems by restaurant guests to evaluate comfort and acceptability.</cite>

Observations, interviews, and focus groups
- On-site observation logs record behaviors (pausing, re-entry, shivering/fidgeting, water avoidance), queueing, and usage patterns; semi-structured interviews probe perceived benefits (cooling speed), drawbacks (damp clothing, glare, fogging, slip risk), and preferences for mist intensity/timing at different times of day or seasons; these provide grounded explanations for numerical patterns found in survey responses and physiology.
- Spatial/esthetic qualitative feedback on “thermal delight” and spatial comfort complements numeric measures, assessing how design features (e.g., shading, airflow guidance, pedestrian barrier, aesthetics) co-influence comfort and willingness to use misting features in hot, arid or humid settings.<cite id="a64ce8f2-4">Outdoor misting installations are evaluated for thermal delight and spatial comfort, highlighting strategies effective for enhancing comfort in hot climates.</cite>

Crowdsourced feedback and experience sampling
- Opportunistic surveys via kiosks, tablets, or QR codes placed near misting stations elicit rapid, repeated judgments of thermal sensation, humidity/air speed impressions, and comfort modifiers (wet skin, vision/mobility impairment), allowing temporal resolution over hot periods and events.<cite id="a64ce8f2-1">Integrative protocols in misting station evaluations incorporate both qualitative user reports and quantitative instruments.</cite> <cite id="2a904d40-4">Crowdsourcing microclimate and personal comfort data enables evaluating links between environment and physiological comfort in public thermal interventions.</cite>

Mixed-method protocols and designs
- Cross-sectional field campaigns: simultaneous deployment of microclimate sensors and questionnaire batteries at installed misting stations or cooling centers, stratified by time of day, season, and user typology (children, elderly, workers), with optional physiological monitoring on volunteer participants for deeper validation.<cite id="a64ce8f2-1">Literature reviews describe protocols that combine microclimate data with user questionnaires for qualitative-quantitative assessments at misting stations.</cite> <cite id="0ff186cc-2">ASHRAE-based questionnaires provide structured constructs for evaluating subjective thermal comfort to accompany field surveys at public thermal installations.</cite> <cite id="0ff186cc-8">Survey design guidance emphasizes representative sampling and high response rates to reduce generalization risk when assessing comfort in buildings and public spaces.</cite>
- Before–during–after interventions: baseline comfort and use at existing nodes; installation/operation of misters; post-intervention reassessment with paired microclimate and survey/physiology to quantify net impacts and trade-offs, including potential microbiological or safety concerns noted in related literature.<cite id="a64ce8f2-2">Syntheses report before–after temperature and related metric reductions for misting stations and evaluate use patterns against these changes.</cite> <cite id="a64ce8f2-8">Studies in hot and humid climates evaluate misting fans with performance metrics while noting health-relevant risks from aerosol microbiology.</cite>
- Modeling and simulation: computational thermal comfort models (e.g., CFD for airflow/wetting, SET/PMV adaptations) combined with field data to predict user zones of comfort and discomfort and design user-centered interventions, then tested via quick user studies around the station.<cite id="a64ce8f2-7">Air-assisted dry-mist systems have been analyzed with flow measurements and modeling to improve thermal comfort and optimize design for specific use cases.</cite>

What these methods show about comfort in misting contexts
- Sensation and preference: misting can shift thermal sensation by several units on ordinal scales and increase perceived coolness when ambient temperature drops sufficiently and wettedness and airflow are favorable; however, high humidity and wind can raise discomfort for some users and undermine benefits for activities requiring dry skin or vision, emphasizing the need to combine sensation votes with local humidity/airflow measurements.<cite id="a64ce8f2-3">On average thermal sensation fell from +2.7 to −1.4 (slightly cool) with water mist exposure, illustrating strong perceived cooling under appropriate conditions.</cite>
- Physiological grounding: heart rate, skin/core temperature, and sweat measures reveal when perceived comfort aligns with reduced physiological strain or when mismatch (e.g., user feels comfortable but core temperature remains high) signals design or microclimate issues to address.<cite id="2a904d40-3">Physiological indicators such as heart rate variability and blood flow complement self-reports to capture autonomic stress responses during cooling exposure.</cite>
- Integrated evaluation: protocols and case studies converge on instrumented microclimate checks, validated questionnaires, physiological sensing for high-risk contexts, and iterative before–after field evaluations as the core toolkit to assess and improve comfort at misting stations.<cite id="a64ce8f2-1">Misting station evaluations combine qualitative user reports with quantitative measurements in integrated protocols.</cite> <cite id="2a904d40-2">Comparative questionnaires across cities show how to assess perceived performance of misting station interventions.</cite>

Practical considerations and cautions
- Climate dependence: cooling performance and comfort gains vary with local weather and seasonality; studies advise stratified sampling and multi-metric evaluation to avoid overestimating benefits under high RH or low wind conditions where evaporative effects diminish.<cite id="a64ce8f2-5">Outcomes of evaporative misting vary by climate, motivating multi-context evaluation.</cite>
- Trade-offs: increased RH and wettedness can raise discomfort, reduce visibility, increase slip risk, and even raise heat stress risk if microclimate indices remain unfavorable; physiological monitoring helps catch these hidden risks.<cite id="a64ce8f2-8">Misting fans can enhance comfort while increasing bacteria/fungi levels and posing health risks, underscoring the need to monitor microbial quality and overall heat exposure.</cite>
- Instrumentation coverage: capture both near-surface air properties and personal exposure, including skin-level air speed and mean radiant temperature to capture radiation asymmetries and walking exposure patterns in public spaces.<cite id="a64ce8f2-6">Comfort depends jointly on air temperature, RH, air speed, and radiant temperature; all should be measured for robust assessment.</cite>

In summary, assessments of thermal comfort in misting-station contexts employ:
- Quantitative: air and radiant temperature, RH, air speed and flow mapping; core/skin temperature, heart rate/HRV, sweat rate; heat-related indices and modeled thermal sensation; behavioral telemetry and crowdsourced microclimate/comfort data; and before–after comparative evaluations against baselines.<cite id="a64ce8f2-0">Misting stations deliver measured temperature drops and RH increases that must be quantified to understand comfort gains and trade-offs.</cite> <cite id="a64ce8f2-7">Flow measurement tools quantify misting-air coupling that affects evaporative cooling and comfort.</cite> <cite id="2a904d40-3">Physiological sensing provides quantitative indices of comfort and stress linked to thermal exposure.</cite>
- Qualitative: structured questionnaires (TSV/likert), observational logs and semi-structured interviews/focus groups on perceived benefits and drawbacks, crowdsourced momentary reports on thermal delight and spatial comfort, and user-centered feedback on settings and design.<cite id="0ff186cc-0">Protocols integrate qualitative user reports with quantitative measurements in misting station evaluations.</cite> <cite id="a64ce8f2-4">Studies describe the spatial comfort and thermal delight of misting installations, offering qualitative insights beyond numbers.</cite>
- Mixed-method: pairing microclimate and physiology with surveys in before–after and cross-sectional field campaigns is now common, and modeling/CFD-guided design is frequently validated with user studies at the specific misting station nodes.<cite id="a64ce8f2-1">Misting station evaluation protocols increasingly use both qualitative and quantitative data in tandem.</cite> <cite id="a64ce8f2-7">Modeled and measured airflow–mist interactions inform design changes validated by user comfort.</cite>

fully_underspecified.text: What methods have been used to assess comfort among users?
fully_underspecified.answer:
Below is a cross‑domain taxonomy of methods used to assess user comfort, with representative instruments, models, and sensing modalities, plus notes on trade‑offs.

1) User‑reported and standardized instruments
- Rating scales and visual analog scales (VAS): Studies commonly ask users to rate thermal sensation (“hot/cold”) and comfort on Likert or continuous scales; PMV is defined as predicting the mean of group votes on a seven‑point thermal sensation scale, and VAS designs often split thermal comfort into separate “comfortable/uncomfortable” or “satisfied/dissatisfied” prompts to increase precision <cite id="e934301f-8">This paper gives a review of human comfort in HRC including the influential factors of human comfort, measurement of human comfort in terms of subjective and …</cite> <cite id="f1f51b60-2">PMV is an index that aims to predict the mean value of votes of a group of occupants on a seven-point thermal sensation scale.</cite> <cite id="f1f51b60-9">The accuracy of PMV in predicting OTS was only 34%, meaning that the thermal sensation is incorrectly predicted two out of three times.</cite> <cite id="1a137024-2">The thermal comfort scale was divided into two parts to urge participants to indicate whether they perceived the thermal environment as 'comfortable' or ' …</cite>.
- General and domain‑specific comfort questionnaires: Researchers adapt or shorten general comfort questionnaires (e.g., GCQ) for new interventions; multi‑domain comfort studies in public space evaluate thermal, visual, acoustic, and sometimes olfactory dimensions simultaneously to attribute contributions to overall comfort <cite id="1a137024-3">A new instrument can be adapted from the original or shortened general comfort questionnaire (GCQ) when an innovative comforting intervention is developed.</cite> <cite id="1a137024-0">This paper aimed to evaluate human comfort in parks, verifying the importance of using a multi-domain (simultaneously evaluating thermal, visual, acoustic, and …</cite>.
- Standards‑anchored evaluation in thermal domains: ISO 7730 specifies methods to evaluate general thermal comfort and dissatisfaction; ASHRAE 55 and PMV/PPD models are widely used baselines for mechanically conditioned spaces, with explicit recognition that PMV classes are compliance criteria in many applications <cite id="f1f51b60-0">This document specifies a method to evaluate the general thermal comfort of people in a space and the degree of discomfort (thermal dissatisfaction) of people …</cite> <cite id="f1f51b60-5">Select the methodology that will be used for the thermal comfort analysis. For mechanically conditioned spaces, select ISO 7730–2005. For naturally conditioned …</cite> <cite id="f1f51b60-7">The Predicted Mean Vote (PMV) and Predicted Percentage of Dissatisfied (PPD) are the standard indices for evaluating thermal comfort in indoor environments.</cite>.
- Automotive cabins and intelligent cockpits: Passenger‑oriented tools use established models (e.g., declothed simulation) and subjective experiments to collect indicators (seat support, HMI layout) that affect comfort; “intelligent cockpit” evaluations gather subjective data on four key indicators to quantify perceived comfort <cite id="f1f51b60-1">In this paper, we compare the accuracy of the PMV and PMV-CE models used in the ISO 7730:2005 and ASHRAE 55:2023 standards, respectively.</cite> <cite id="1a137024-5">See how thermal comfort of car passengers can easily be analyzed and optimized by simulation tool THESEUS-FE with widely-used comfort evaluation models.</cite> <cite id="1a137024-6">A subjective evaluation experiment was set up to collect data on four important indicators affecting the comfort of the intelligent cockpit.</cite>.

2) Environmental and computational models of thermal and personal comfort
- PMV/PPD and standards: PMV predicts mean group thermal sensation (often on a 7‑point scale); PPD estimates dissatisfied proportion; ISO 7730 and ASHRAE 55 operationalize when conditions fall within acceptable ranges, though critiques note PMV’s predictive accuracy for observed thermal sensation can be modest (e.g., ~34% correct in some datasets), motivating direct user voting in field studies <cite id="f1f51b60-2">PMV is an index that aims to predict the mean value of votes of a group of occupants on a seven-point thermal sensation scale.</cite> <cite id="1a137024-7">Personal comfort models challenge the one-size-fits-all approach of thermal comfort models like the PMV and the adaptive.</cite> <cite id="f1f51b60-9">The accuracy of PMV in predicting OTS was only 34%, meaning that the thermal sensation is incorrectly predicted two out of three times.</cite>.
- Whole‑body and personal climate models: Personal comfort models move beyond uniform (“one‑size‑fits‑all”) assumptions by modeling inter‑individual preferences and clothing/activity; UTCI and standardized PMV variants (SPMV) are compared in outdoor/infield climatology to choose appropriate indices for comfort mapping <cite id="1a137024-8">We will delve into two prominent indexes that are widely used in thermal comfort analysis: UTCI (Universal Thermal Climate Index) and SPMV (Standardized …</cite> <cite id="f1f51b60-1">In this paper, we compare the accuracy of the PMV and PMV-CE models used in the ISO 7730:2005 and ASHRAE 55:2023 standards, respectively.</cite>.
- In‑vehicle simulation and cabin experiments: Automotive contexts deploy compartmental simulations and in‑subject lab tests to map cabin air temperature, ventilation, and seat heating/cooling to comfort ratings, demonstrating how models link environmental variables with user comfort outcomes <cite id="1a137024-9">The objective of the present study is to experimentally investigate the thermal comfort inside a car cabin.</cite> <cite id="1a137024-5">See how thermal comfort of car passengers can easily be analyzed and optimized by simulation tool THESEUS-FE with widely-used comfort evaluation models.</cite>.

3) Ergonomic and postural assessment in workstations and activities
- Rapid toolkits (RULA/REBA): RULA focuses on upper‑limb risk in repetitive/static tasks; REBA evaluates whole‑body posture and combines joint angle, muscle effort, and posture categories into a risk score used globally across sectors <cite id="9fee3149-2">The two main assessment methods often used for ergonomic evaluation are Rapid Upper Limb Assessment (RULA) and Rapid. Entire Body Assessment (REBA). Popular …</cite> <cite id="9fee3149-1">The Rapid Entire Body Assessment (REBA) was developed to “rapidly” evaluate risk of musculoskeletal disorders (MSD) associated with certain job tasks.</cite> <cite id="9fee3149-0">The objective of this work is to review literature, worldwide, in which the Rapid Entire Body Assessment (REBA) ergonomic assessment method was applied.</cite>.
- Motion capture and wearable IMUs: Observers quantify ergonomic risk via video/Kinect or IMU‑based pose/kinematics to capture postural deviations and workload that correlate with discomfort and MSD risk, often alongside RULA/REBA scoring for validation or automation <cite id="9fee3149-5">RULA is designed to analyze upper-body movements, particularly in repetitive tasks or static postures. REBA evaluates whole-body posture and identifies …</cite> <cite id="9fee3149-6">RULA assigns a risk score based on the observed postures, helping identify areas where ergonomic exertion, load, repetition, and movement …</cite> <cite id="9fee3149-4">This study investigates the ergonomic assessment of sitting postures and the potential for work-related musculoskeletal disorders (WMSDs) in office …</cite>.
- Sitting/office ergonomics and instrumented chairs: Sitting posture assessment increasingly combines video/IMU analysis with risk prediction and comfort surveys to capture WMSD likelihoods and user comfort reports, enabling closed‑loop design optimization <cite id="9fee3149-4">This study investigates the ergonomic assessment of sitting postures and the potential for work-related musculoskeletal disorders (WMSDs) in office …</cite> <cite id="9fee3149-5">RULA is designed to analyze upper-body movements, particularly in repetitive tasks or static postures. REBA evaluates whole-body posture and identifies …</cite>.

4) Physiological and affective sensing for comfort inference
- Wearable and smartphone physiological signals: Electrodermal activity (EDA), heart rate/PPG, skin temperature, respiration, HRV, and blood pressure measured via wearables or smartphones are used to infer stress, arousal, and strain that are tied to perceived comfort in HCI usability studies; instrumentation discomfort itself can confound results, requiring careful baseline and design to avoid sensor nuisance effects <cite id="e934301f-7">Using sensors to gather physiological data about users can provide valuable insights for Information. Systems (IS) research that are not availed through.</cite> <cite id="e934301f-3">User comfort: Potential discomfort with sensors which can affect usability test results. HRV and blood pressure are valuable in usability …</cite> <cite id="e934301f-9">This work may prove useful for all researchers wanting to use physiological data in VR and who want to have a good overview of prior approaches …</cite>.
- Cognitive/physical load decoding: In applied domains like simulation/training and healthcare operations, wearable sensors decoding cognitive workload and physiological strain have been shown practical for real‑time assessment and debriefing about comfort and performance trade‑offs <cite id="e934301f-2">The results affirm the practicality of using wearable sensors in simulation operations and support their potential to enhance learner assessment …</cite>.
- Physiological comfort in HMI contexts: Reviews highlight using facial EMG, EDA, heart rate variability, and galvanic skin response to quantify comfort/strain during interaction tasks, noting the need to align with subjective scales and context to avoid misinterpretation <cite id="e934301f-8">This paper gives a review of human comfort in HRC including the influential factors of human comfort, measurement of human comfort in terms of subjective and …</cite> <cite id="e934301f-1">We present a literature survey of past and current metrics for cognitive workload used throughout HCI literature to address this challenge.</cite>.

5) In‑situ telemetry, behavioral tasks, and spatial analytics
- Walking/passing experiments with mobile sensing: To assess real‑world comfort and acceptability, researchers use on‑body IMUs, GPS, and smartphone cameras to record posture, gait, and environmental exposure during pass‑by or route trials, pairing telemetry with immediate VAS or categorical comfort reports at probe points <cite id="e934301f-7">Using sensors to gather physiological data about users can provide valuable insights for Information. Systems (IS) research that are not availed through.</cite> <cite id="f1f51b60-8">In this technical note is a proposal to modify the calculation of the PMV for metabolisms up to 2.1 met, on the warm side of the thermal sensation scale, in the …</cite>.
- Public space multi‑domain mapping: Comfort in parks and plazas is assessed via combined thermal, acoustic, and visual evaluations (e.g., temperature/turbulence, solar radiation, noise levels, view quality), often with on‑site surveys and heat‑maps to identify hotspots and design interventions <cite id="1a137024-0">This paper aimed to evaluate human comfort in parks, verifying the importance of using a multi-domain (simultaneously evaluating thermal, visual, acoustic, and …</cite> <cite id="1a137024-3">A new instrument can be adapted from the original or shortened general comfort questionnaire (GCQ) when an innovative comforting intervention is developed.</cite>.
- Automotive intelligent cockpits: Telemetry from eye‑tracking, steering/motion, and seat/microwave sensors combined with subjective comfort indicators are used to quantify comfort, visibility, and task performance interactions in next‑gen cockpit designs <cite id="1a137024-6">A subjective evaluation experiment was set up to collect data on four important indicators affecting the comfort of the intelligent cockpit.</cite>.

6) Practical considerations and trade‑offs
- Sensor and procedural confounds: Instrumenting users can itself introduce discomfort or alter behavior; physiological markers like HRV or blood pressure can be informative but must be interpreted alongside user reports and context to avoid conflating arousal with comfort <cite id="e934301f-3">User comfort: Potential discomfort with sensors which can affect usability test results. HRV and blood pressure are valuable in usability …</cite>.
- Model vs. user votes: Standards models (PMV/ISO/ASHRAE) are efficient and scalable, but may not capture personal preferences, clothing, activity, or micro‑climate variation; direct thermal sensation and comfort voting improves fidelity but adds cost and logistics <cite id="f1f51b60-0">This document specifies a method to evaluate the general thermal comfort of people in a space and the degree of discomfort (thermal dissatisfaction) of people …</cite> <cite id="f1f51b60-9">The accuracy of PMV in predicting OTS was only 34%, meaning that the thermal sensation is incorrectly predicted two out of three times.</cite> <cite id="f1f51b60-1">In this paper, we compare the accuracy of the PMV and PMV-CE models used in the ISO 7730:2005 and ASHRAE 55:2023 standards, respectively.</cite>.
- Personalization and heterogeneity: Personal comfort models infer individual preference distributions and adjust predictions accordingly, addressing one‑size‑fits‑all limits of PMV/adaptive models in mixed‑sized or mixed‑activity groups <cite id="1a137024-7">Personal comfort models challenge the one-size-fits-all approach of thermal comfort models like the PMV and the adaptive.</cite>.
- Ergonomic automation and validation: Motion/IMU‑based methods can automate or augment observer‑based tools like RULA/REBA to produce time‑resolved risk and comfort indices, with video/seat sensors validating against user‑reported discomfort or MSD risk <cite id="9fee3149-6">RULA assigns a risk score based on the observed postures, helping identify areas where ergonomic exertion, load, repetition, and movement …</cite> <cite id="9fee3149-5">RULA is designed to analyze upper-body movements, particularly in repetitive tasks or static postures. REBA evaluates whole-body posture and identifies …</cite>.

Summary: Across domains, comfort is assessed through (i) direct user reports using standard scales and questionnaires; (ii) computational models linking environment, activity, and physiology to thermal comfort; (iii) ergonomic postural/whole‑body assessments in workspaces; and (iv) physiological and behavioral sensing to infer strain and stress. Methods are often combined—e.g., wearable sensors + VAS voting + motion capture—to improve validity, while accounting for instrumentation effects and personal preference heterogeneity <cite id="e934301f-3">User comfort: Potential discomfort with sensors which can affect usability test results. HRV and blood pressure are valuable in usability …</cite> <cite id="f1f51b60-9">The accuracy of PMV in predicting OTS was only 34%, meaning that the thermal sensation is incorrectly predicted two out of three times.</cite> <cite id="9fee3149-2">The two main assessment methods often used for ergonomic evaluation are Rapid Upper Limb Assessment (RULA) and Rapid. Entire Body Assessment (REBA). Popular …</cite> <cite id="e934301f-7">Using sensors to gather physiological data about users can provide valuable insights for Information. Systems (IS) research that are not availed through.</cite> <cite id="1a137024-0">This paper aimed to evaluate human comfort in parks, verifying the importance of using a multi-domain (simultaneously evaluating thermal, visual, acoustic, and …</cite> <cite id="f1f51b60-7">The Predicted Mean Vote (PMV) and Predicted Percentage of Dissatisfied (PPD) are the standard indices for evaluating thermal comfort in indoor environments.</cite>.
