without_scope.text: What qualitative and quantitative methods have been used to assess thermal comfort?
without_scope.answer:
# Overview

Thermal comfort assessment blends qualitative and quantitative methods. Qualitative methods capture occupants' perceptions and context through surveys, interviews, visual/scene comparisons, and observational checklists. Quantitative methods measure physical/physiological determinants (air temperature, mean radiant temperature, humidity, air speed, metabolic rate, clothing insulation) and apply predictive models (e.g., PMV/PPD) and standards (ASHRAE 55, ISO 7730, EN 16798) to estimate satisfaction and dissatisfaction. <cite id="8557fe17-0">ASHRAE Standard 55 and ISO 7730 provide structured evaluation using PMV/PPD and local thermal comfort criteria for indoor thermal comfort</cite> <cite id="1b89f005-0">a mixed-methods framework has been used to study outdoor thermal comfort by integrating qualitative perceptions with quantitative environmental relationships</cite> <cite id="311f8701-2">the thermal environment is characterized by air temperature, mean radiant temperature, air speed, and humidity, along with personal factors of metabolic rate and clothing</cite>.

# Physiological/Physical Determinants and Sensing (Quantitative)

Instrumented fieldwork quantifies key determinants: dry-bulb air temperature, relative humidity, air speed, mean radiant temperature (often via black-globe or composite methods), and personal factors (clothing insulation and metabolic rate) to compute operative temperature and related indices. <cite id="311f8701-6">The thermal environment comprises air temperature, mean radiant temperature, air velocity, humidity, and personal factors—clothing insulation and metabolic rate</cite> <cite id="311f8701-5">recent work introduces real-time mean radiant temperature measurement specifically for indoor comfort assessment</cite> <cite id="311f8701-9">operative temperature is the average of dry-bulb and mean radiant temperature and is central to characterizing comfort</cite>. Standards specify calculation/assumption methods and accuracy references for these quantities. <cite id="311f8701-4">ASHRAE 55 provides stepwise guidance where mean radiant temperature is determined and then used in comfort criteria, including explicit adjustments (e.g., +2.8°C) to derive comfort ranges</cite> <cite id="311f8701-0">comparative studies evaluate the accuracy of calculation and assumption methods against reference measurements</cite>.

# Subjective Rating Scales and Survey Methods (Qualitative)

Occupants report thermal sensation using ordinal scales (e.g., seven-point scale), adaptive or category-based tools, and contextual reasons for dissatisfaction. <cite id="8557fe17-1">PMV is designed to predict the mean of seven-point thermal sensation votes from a group of occupants</cite> <cite id="26ba07ee-4">ASHRAE 55 targets 80% satisfied occupants, but typical satisfaction levels are often around 40%, motivating careful survey-based verification</cite>. Mixed-methods studies pair structured surveys with environmental data and visual stimuli. <cite id="1b89f005-0">mixed-methods outdoor thermal comfort assessments combined qualitative perception elicitation with quantitative analyses of environmental–perception links</cite> <cite id="1b89f005-4">photographic comparison has been applied as a visual, observer-based aid to appraise outdoor thermal perception</cite>. Systematic reviews of indoor comfort also emphasize behavioral adaptations and the value of occupant-reported behavior alongside metrics. <cite id="1b89f005-5">a systematic review synthesized indoor thermal comfort temperatures and related behavioral adaptations to contextualize assessment</cite>.

# Predictive Models and Standards-Based Quantitative Assessment

Classical predictive models and standards bridge physical conditions and comfort outcomes. The PMV/PPD framework predicts mean vote and percentage dissatisfied based on operative temperature, air speed, humidity, clothing, and metabolic rate, under neutral conditions and static clothing. <cite id="8557fe17-3">PMV and PPD are standard indices for evaluating thermal comfort, widely used to estimate occupants' satisfaction</cite> <cite id="8557fe17-1">PMV predicts the mean seven-point sensation vote, with PPD estimating dissatisfaction</cite>. ISO 7730 defines the method and criteria for evaluating general thermal comfort and local discomfort in spaces, including the role of PPD and mean radiant temperature. <cite id="8557fe17-5">ISO 7730 specifies a method to evaluate general thermal comfort and the degree of thermal dissatisfaction in a space</cite> <cite id="8557fe17-2">PPD, PMV, mean radiant temperature, and ASHRAE 55 comfort tool procedures are used together, with guidance on combining measured and simulated results</cite>. ASHRAE Standard 55 provides activity-based criteria for acceptable conditions across occupant populations and can be applied using tools like the Berkeley CBE Thermal Comfort Tool. <cite id="8557fe17-0">ASHRAE 55 links the interpretation of thermal comfort to PMV and PPD indices and local thermal comfort criteria</cite> <cite id="26ba07ee-0">the CBE comfort tool automatically computes relative air speed and dynamic clothing insulation and applies ASHRAE 55 methods</cite> <cite id="26ba07ee-7">the tool provides a web-based GUI implementing ASHRAE 55 with building system models</cite>. In practice, criteria and expectations (e.g., 80% satisfied) may not always be met, underscoring the need for field validation. <cite id="26ba07ee-4">80% satisfied is a common ASHRAE 55 aim but often unattained, with typical satisfaction nearer to 40% in many cases</cite> <cite id="8557fe17-8">in healthcare settings, PMV-PPD values can be compared with alternative models (e.g., adaptive methods) to better capture occupant perception</cite>.

# Field and Post-Occupation Studies

Post-occupation studies (occupant surveys, logs, comfort checks) quantify differences between intended and experienced conditions and link them to measured microclimate. <cite id="311f8701-3">EN 16798 addresses indoor environmental parameters and their evaluation, including methods aligned to building design and post-occupation measurement practices</cite> <cite id="1b89f005-3">operative temperature, PMV, adaptive comfort principles, and occupant surveys are common evaluation methods in buildings</cite>. Mixed-method field protocols integrate instrumented logging with structured interviews and visual assessments to diagnose mismatches and contextual influences. <cite id="1b89f005-0">mixed-methods field studies explicitly combine qualitative occupant perceptions with quantitative microclimate measurements to reveal relationships driving comfort or discomfort</cite> <cite id="1b89f005-4">visual photographic comparisons act as a rapid, standardized qualitative method for outdoor perception surveys</cite>. Broader syntheses of occupant behavior highlight the value of post-occupation data in calibrating comfort criteria and tailoring adaptive approaches. <cite id="1b89f005-5">a systematic review of indoor comfort temperatures emphasized how occupants adapt behavior (opening/closing windows, adjusting clothing) to influence perceived comfort</cite>.

# Analytical and Modeling Workflows

Quantitative–qualitative integration uses regression, ANCOVA, and clustering to relate physical measures to sensation votes and dissatisfaction. <cite id="8557fe17-2">methods combine measured microclimate (e.g., MRT, operative temperature) with simulation outputs (PMV/PPD) to analyze comfort levels and local discomfort</cite> <cite id="8557fe17-4">the ASHRAE 55 comfort tool visualizes PMV/PPD over psychrometric charts with operative temperature as the abscissa, enabling spatial diagnosis</cite>. Comparative and accuracy-focused studies examine how calculation methods approximate reference measurements, informing uncertainty-aware analysis. <cite id="311f8701-0">accuracy comparisons across calculation/assumption methods against reference measurements improve reliability in quantitative assessments</cite>. Beyond mean PMV residuals, multi-parameter models incorporate MRT, air speed, humidity, and dynamic clothing to predict dissatisfaction and hot/cold spots. <cite id="311f8701-6">air velocity and humidity, along with mean radiant and air temperature, are principal environmental factors; personal factors of clothing and metabolic rate must be considered</cite>.

# Qualitative Methods (Non-instrumented, Contextual)

- Visual/scene-based perception surveys: side-by-side photographs of scenes at different thermal states prompt occupants to compare and rank perceptions, reducing language ambiguity while capturing local context (outdoor spaces, urban microclimate). <cite id="1b89f005-4">photographic comparison has been implemented as a complementary visual appraisal in outdoor thermal perception surveys</cite>.
- Semi-structured interviews/observations: probing reasons for thermal dissatisfaction and adaptive behaviors (clothing, window operations), often used in post-occupation audits; these narratives triangulate with sensor data to identify root causes. <cite id="1b89f005-5">behavioral adaptations (e.g., natural ventilation use) are critical determinants shaping perceived indoor comfort</cite>.
- Mixed-methods designs: combine scales, visual stimuli, and environmental measurements to build explanatory models of comfort in specific contexts (seasonal climate, urban canyon exposure). <cite id="1b89f005-0">mixed-methods outdoor comfort evaluations integrate qualitative perceptions with quantitative environmental correlations</cite>.

# Quantitative Methods (Instrumented, Model-Based)

- Microclimate logging: continuous measurement of air temp, relative humidity, air speed at sensor height; estimation of mean radiant temperature via globe/hemispherical radiometers or composite approaches; compute operative temperature; apply ISO 7730/ASHRAE 55 criteria via tools (CBE) to yield predicted satisfaction and locate non-compliant zones. <cite id="311f8701-5">real-time MRT measurement methods support indoor comfort assessment</cite> <cite id="26ba07ee-0">CBE tool automates air speed and dynamic clothing estimation and applies ASHRAE 55</cite> <cite id="26ba07ee-1">ASHRAE 55 defines criteria for achieving satisfactory conditions for most occupants</cite>.
- Predictive modeling: PMV/PPD calculations per ISO 7730; grid-based mapping across zones or time to identify hot/cold spots; sensitivity analysis to air speed, MRT and humidity to guide design decisions. <cite id="8557fe17-3">PMV/PPD are standard indices for evaluating indoor thermal comfort</cite> <cite id="8557fe17-7">methodological studies compare MRT calculation methods in simulation (EnergyPlus/DesignBuilder) to ensure accurate PMV/PPD</cite>.
- Standard-compliant protocols: EN 16798-1 indoor environment measurements and EN 15251 (EU) for energy performance relate to comfort assessment; these protocols guide parameter selection, sampling, and uncertainty. <cite id="311f8701-1">the CBE tool implements EN 16798-1:2019 requirements for thermal comfort calculations</cite> <cite id="311f8701-3">EN 16798 specifies indoor environmental parameters relevant to thermal comfort within building design</cite>.

# Post-Occupation and Field Protocols

Operational protocols specify instrument types, sampling rates, occupant diaries, and survey timing. <cite id="311f8701-6">environmental factors to measure are air temperature, mean radiant temperature, air velocity, humidity plus occupant-related metabolic rate and clothing</cite> <cite id="1b89f005-3">field evaluations commonly combine occupant surveys with operative temperature metrics, PMV modeling, and adaptive comfort considerations</cite>. In practice, field tools and comfort logs reveal wide variability: even when criteria are set, actual satisfaction is often lower than target unless monitored and adapted. <cite id="26ba07ee-4">ASHRAE 55's 80% satisfied target is rarely achieved, with typical satisfaction nearer to 40%</cite>.

# Modern Sensing and Data-Driven Approaches

- Microclimate and person-level sensing: distributed sensors (air temp/humidity/airspeed) plus wearable or smartphone-derived proxies (activity level, heart rate) to capture dynamic clothing, metabolic rate and interzone variability; these data feed into PMV/PPD mapping and machine-learning regressions predicting sensation/dissatisfaction. <cite id="311f8701-0">studies compare accuracy of calculation and assumption methods, enabling data-driven calibration of PMV/PPD predictions</cite> <cite id="26ba07ee-0">dynamic clothing insulation and air speed are inferred by tools to compute comfort criteria in practice</cite>.
- Simulation-integrated assessment: CFD/hybrid tools estimate local operative temperatures and MRT fields to compute PMV/PPD heat maps aligned with measured microclimate distributions; combined with survey outcomes, they refine adaptive criteria. <cite id="8557fe17-2">PPD/PMV with mean radiant temperature and ASHRAE 55 criteria are combined in practice, including how to integrate measured and simulated results</cite> <cite id="8557fe17-7">simulator-specific MRT methods are benchmarked to ensure reliable PMV/PPD estimates</cite>.

# Integrative Examples and Trade-offs

Mixed-methods field studies demonstrate how combining photographic aids and seven-point sensation voting with microclimate logging clarifies both perceived comfort and design-relevant determinants. <cite id="1b89f005-0">paired qualitative-perception tasks with quantitative microclimate regressions reveal how specific factors dominate in a site</cite> <cite id="1b89f005-4">photographic comparisons help standardize subjective judgments in complex outdoor contexts</cite>. Standards trade generality against specificity: ISO 7730 suits neutral, steady-state offices with static clothing; ASHRAE 55 accommodates activity diversity and dynamic loads, often requiring tools to infer dynamic clothing and air speed to judge satisfaction. <cite id="8557fe17-5">ISO 7730 prescribes evaluation of general comfort and local discomfort in spaces</cite> <cite id="8557fe17-8">healthcare studies compare PMV-PPD with adaptive models (AMV) to better match occupant variability</cite>. Instrument selection and MRT estimation method critically affect outcomes; careful validation against reference methods is essential. <cite id="311f8701-0">accuracy comparisons across calculation/assumption methods to reference measurements improve reliability</cite> <cite id="311f8701-5">real-time MRT measurement specifically designed for comfort assessment improves data quality</cite>.

# Practical Workflow Template

- Define scope and standards: choose ISO 7730 for neutral zones or ASHRAE 55 for activity-diverse occupancies; decide on EN/ISO field protocols for measurements. <cite id="8557fe17-0">ASHRAE 55 ties PMV/PPD to practical criteria</cite> <cite id="311f8701-1">EN 16798-1 calculation tool aligns with EU protocols</cite>.
- Instrument deployment: log air temp, RH, air speed at seat heights; measure MRT (globe/hemispherical); record occupant metabolic rate (activity) and clothing; compute operative temperature. <cite id="311f8701-6">air, MRT, air velocity, humidity, metabolic rate, and clothing are the core parameters</cite> <cite id="311f8701-5">accurate MRT methods support operative temperature estimation</cite>.
- Collect occupant data: administer timed seven-point sensation surveys, optional visual comparisons, and brief interviews on adaptive behaviors. <cite id="8557fe17-1">PMV/PPD mapping relies on seven-point sensation votes</cite> <cite id="1b89f005-4">photographic comparisons provide consistent visual anchors for thermal perception</cite>.
- Analyze and model: compute PMV/PPD; test against 80% satisfied thresholds; use ANCOVA/regression with MRT, air speed, humidity, clothing, and demographics to explain variance; produce comfort heat maps. <cite id="26ba07ee-4">80% satisfied is an aspirational target; actual field satisfaction is often much lower</cite> <cite id="311f8701-3">PMV/PPD provide standard indices for indoor comfort mapping</cite>.
- Iterate and adapt: use results to adjust criteria or design; where possible, implement adaptive strategies validated by occupant behavior insights. <cite id="1b89f005-5">behavioral adaptation is a key explanatory factor in perceived comfort</cite> <cite id="8557fe17-2">combining measured and simulated results (MRT, PMV/PPD) guides targeted interventions</cite>.

# Summary

In practice, teams combine qualitative surveys with visual aids and interviews to capture occupants' thermal perceptions and behaviors, and quantitative microclimate logging and standards-based modeling (PMV/PPD under ISO 7730 or ASHRAE 55) to relate measurable conditions to comfort outcomes, often iteratively refining criteria and designs using post-occupation data and modern sensing workflows. <cite id="1b89f005-0">Mixed-method field studies integrate qualitative perceptions with quantitative microclimate relationships</cite> <cite id="8557fe17-5">ISO 7730 defines a method for evaluating general thermal comfort and local discomfort</cite> <cite id="26ba07ee-4">ASHRAE 55's 80% satisfaction benchmark rarely materializes, underscoring measurement and adaptation needs</cite> <cite id="311f8701-5">real-time mean radiant temperature measurement advances quantitative comfort data quality</cite> <cite id="26ba07ee-0">tools that infer dynamic clothing and air speed allow practical PMV/PPD application</cite>.

questions.original_query: How do the mean values for asthma and respiratory outcomes associated with the age risk factor differ across ecological settings such as wildfire, greenness, and air pollution?

query.text: How do the mean values for asthma and respiratory outcomes associated with the age risk factor differ across ecological settings such as wildfire, greenness, and air pollution?
query.answer:
Below is a synthesis of how mean values for asthma and respiratory outcomes vary by age and across three ecological settings: wildfire smoke, greenness/nature exposure, and ambient air pollution. Where possible, I contrast age strata and outcome types (symptoms, visits, lung function, diagnoses), and note where quantitative magnitudes differ.

Key definitions and framing
- “Mean values” are operationalized as average levels of respiratory outcomes (e.g., FEV1/FVC z-scores or absolute mL/kg, symptom counts, acute exacerbations, hospitalizations, asthma prevalence/likelihood) that shift with age and exposure setting. Age “risk differences” include biological vulnerability (e.g., smaller lung reserves in youth and older adults), disease burden (e.g., pediatric asthma vs adult COPD), and exposure susceptibility (e.g., children’s behavioral exposures, older adults’ reduced physiological reserve).

Wildfire smoke: acute elevation and long-term mean decrements vary by age
- In children and adolescents, acute wildfire smoke days are repeatedly associated with increases in respiratory symptoms, emergency department visits, and medication use, indicating mean outcome levels that rise during smoke events relative to clean-air baselines.<cite id="a72a70d5-0">Wildfire smoke is associated with short-term respiratory outcomes including asthma exacerbation in children.</cite> <cite id="a72a70d5-7">All studies reported increases in respiratory symptoms, hospital visits, and medication use on days with significant wildfire smoke exposure.</cite>
- Among asthmatics, smoke exposure worsens symptoms and elevates event rates; pediatric spirometry studies show reductions in measures like FEV1/PEF on smoke days, with evidence of age-dependence in sensitivity (e.g., analyses separating children >12 vs ≤12 years and pollutant-specific drivers like PM2.5).<cite id="cc7aa01c-0">A reduction in forced vital capacity in asthmatic children on days with wildfire smoke, with specific associations for PM2.5 and differences by age thresholds.</cite> <cite id="cc7aa01c-5">Few studies have examined acute effects of short-term wildfire smoke on child lung function; examples include FVC/FEV1 among school bus riders (aged group context).</cite>
- Longer term, population studies report persistent mean decrements in lung function up to a decade after exposure, which disproportionately burden older-working-age adults who recover less functional reserve; mechanistically, wildfire pollutants aggravate airway disease across asthma and COPD, implying higher mean exacerbation rates and symptom prevalence in older age bands once baseline health declines.<cite id="a72a70d5-3">Decreases in lung function ten years after wildfire smoke exposure.</cite> <cite id="cc7aa01c-9">PM2.5 exposure during prenatal and first 3 years associated with lower FVC and FEV1 at ages 6–9.</cite> <cite id="a72a70d5-1">Wildfire smoke exposure is strongly linked to asthma exacerbations and significantly associated with COPD exacerbations.</cite> <cite id="a72a70d5-4">Adverse respiratory outcomes are most consistently associated with particulate matter in wildfire smoke.</cite>
- Age gradients: younger children show acute sensitivity with mean symptom/visit rates rising sharply during smoke; older adults show greater absolute risk increases and slower recovery due to age-related lung reserve loss (FEV1/FVC natural decline; higher comorbidity), translating into larger mean shifts in spirometry, exacerbation frequency, and respiratory-related health service use in older age bands after exposure.<cite id="cc7aa01c-0">Asthmatic children exhibit reduced FEV1 during smoke; pollutant associations and age thresholds modulate effect sizes.</cite> <cite id="a72a70d5-3">Long-term mean lung function declines after wildfire smoke exposure.</cite> <cite id="cc7aa01c-3">FEV1 declines 1–2% per year after ~25, compounding vulnerability with smoke exposure.</cite> <cite id="cc7aa01c-2">EPA risk framing emphasizes children up to 18 as greater risk for smoke-related asthma symptoms, while older adults face heightened risk for smoke-induced health effects.</cite>

Greenness/nature exposure: protective mean shifts in youth with heterogeneous effects
- Cohorts linking residential greenness with respiratory health often report lower odds of asthma development, fewer respiratory symptoms/visits, and better lung function in children and young adults exposed at home; mechanisms include reduced traffic pollution exposure, allergen buffering, and stress reduction, producing lower mean asthma prevalence and higher mean FEV1/FVC trajectories in green-exposed youth.<cite id="0b6593e6-0">Systematic review finds greenness protective for child asthma in many, but not all, studies; six reported no direct association; one protective association identified.</cite> <cite id="0b6593e6-2">Residential greenness appears protective against asthma development in children who are not sensitive to common allergens.</cite> <cite id="0b6593e6-1">Urban greenspace is positively associated with respiratory health, especially lower respiratory mortality.</cite> <cite id="0b6593e6-3">Children with green space near home have fewer respiratory problems (asthma, wheezing) in adulthood.</cite> <cite id="0b6593e6-8">Narrative report summarizing a large cohort: early childhood green space exposure linked to better lung function.</cite>
- However, evidence is mixed and modified by sensitization profiles and allergen exposure: greenness may fail to modify asthma risk in allergic-sensitized children, and systematic reviews note inconsistent findings across settings; hence mean benefits can be age- and population-specific rather than universal.<cite id="0b6593e6-0">Six studies found no direct greenness–childhood asthma association; one protective; overall heterogeneity suggests context matters.</cite> <cite id="0b6593e6-4">Background notes inconsistent findings specific to child respiratory health despite broader greenness health benefits.</cite> <cite id="0b6593e6-5">Reviews report improved chronic respiratory health with greenness but acknowledge inconsistent evidence and mechanisms.</cite>
- Age interaction: during childhood and the pre-adolescent window, greenness near residence is repeatedly linked to lower mean asthma likelihood and higher mean lung function, with spillover into fewer adult respiratory problems in some cohorts, whereas older adults show weaker or inconsistent mean improvements unless co-exposed to concurrent pollution burdens and allergens.<cite id="0b6593e6-3">Childhood greenness near home associated with fewer respiratory problems persisting into adulthood.</cite> <cite id="0b6593e6-2">Residential greenness protective against asthma development among nonsensitive children.</cite> <cite id="0b6593e6-1">Greener urban areas linked to lower respiratory mortality across ages, with stronger signals in lower-respiratory disease.</cite>

Ambient air pollution: greater mean burden in older adults with stronger pollutant-specific associations
- Cross-sectional and longitudinal data show that higher ambient pollution (PM10, NO2, PM2.5, O3) elevates mean asthma prevalence and reduces lung function; effects often intensify with age, with stronger associations in older participants for FEV1 decline and in adults with asthma for FEV1/FVC restrictions and exacerbation risk.<cite id="7a6791ef-0">Increased air pollution was associated with increased asthma prevalence, with greater impacts in older participants and other susceptible groups.</cite> <cite id="7a6791ef-2">FEV1-stratified analyses showed stronger associations for PM10 and NO2 in older participants, especially in lower-income subjects.</cite> <cite id="7a6791ef-8">Asthma patients followed over time showed that higher air pollution exposure related to worse lung function over the study period.</cite> <cite id="7a6791ef-6">Among asthmatics, air pollution associated with increased wheeze and hospitalization and decreased lung function.</cite>
- Developmental windows compound lifetime means: prenatal/early-life PM2.5 exposure is linked to lower mean FEV1/FVC by school age (6–9), altering growth trajectories; adult cohorts associate higher lifetime pollution with chronic bronchitis/symptoms, higher physician visits, and imaging-defined obstruction.<cite id="7a6791ef-4">Prenatal and early-life pollution associated with decreased lung function in children.</cite> <cite id="cc7aa01c-9">Prenatal and first 3 years PM2.5 exposure associated with 6–9-year-old FVC and FEV1 deficits.</cite> <cite id="7a6791ef-3">Higher air pollution levels clearly associated with increased risk of chronic respiratory conditions.</cite> <cite id="7a6791ef-5">Meta-scale data: higher air pollution correlated with lower lung function, with influence of asthma status and activity levels.</cite>
- Age gradients: in childhood, pollution primarily affects growth/early-life function (mean FEV1/FVC below predicted, higher odds of sensitization/asthma), whereas in older adults the same pollutants translate into larger absolute FEV1 decrements and higher exacerbation risk, especially in lower-income, less-active, or comorbid populations, producing steeper mean declines in spirometry and higher utilization.<cite id="7a6791ef-2">Older participants showed stronger PM10 and NO2 associations with FEV1; associations were stronger in lower-income households.</cite> <cite id="7a6791ef-7">Childhood pollution exposure contributes to adult bronchitic symptoms, indicating life-course accumulation of mean respiratory deficits.</cite>

Comparative perspective: how age-related mean differences differ across settings
- Acute versus chronic gradients: Wildfire smoke primarily shifts means acutely upward (attacks, ED visits, reduced FEV1/PEF) in children and older adults, with evidence of persistent mean lung function declines over years in exposed cohorts; air pollution exerts more gradual mean shifts (lower baseline FEV1/FVC, higher chronic symptom prevalence) that intensify with age; greenness exposure tends to shift means downward in childhood asthma probability and upward in lung function trajectories, with persistence into adulthood in some cohorts, but with heterogeneity in older ages.<cite id="a72a70d5-7">Wildfire smoke days increased symptoms, hospital visits, and medication use, indicating acute mean shifts.</cite> <cite id="a72a70d5-3">Long-term mean lung function decreases after smoke exposure.</cite> <cite id="7a6791ef-0">Air pollution associated with higher asthma prevalence and greater impacts in older adults.</cite> <cite id="0b6593e6-3">Childhood greenness associated with fewer respiratory issues in adulthood.</cite>
- Age bands:
  - Young children (0–18): Higher mean acute exacerbations and symptom counts during smoke or high pollution; smaller absolute lung function but large percent decrements on smoke days; greenness near home linked in multiple cohorts to lower mean asthma risk and better lung function growth.<cite id="a72a70d5-7">All studies reported increases in symptoms, visits, and medication during wildfire smoke; acute mean shifts are robust.</cite> <cite id="a72a70d5-1">Wildfire smoke associated with increased COPD exacerbations in adults, but in youth it predominantly worsens asthma.</cite> <cite id="cc7aa01c-0">Child spirometry reduces during smoke, with pollutant-specific contributions.</cite> <cite id="0b6593e6-2">Greenness protective against asthma development in nonsensitive children.</cite>
  - Adults (≥40–65, ≥65): Older adults show larger absolute mean FEV1 declines and higher mean exacerbation risk (including COPD) from smoke; air pollution displays stronger spirometric associations (PM10/NO2) and higher odds of chronic bronchitis and hospitalization; greenness benefits for respiratory symptoms or FEV1 show weaker or inconsistent evidence, often overshadowed by concurrent pollution exposure and comorbidities.<cite id="7a6791ef-2">Older participants display stronger PM10/NO2–FEV1 associations.</cite> <cite id="a72a70d5-1">Wildfire smoke strongly linked with COPD exacerbations, highlighting older adult vulnerability.</cite> <cite id="0b6593e6-1">Greener areas associated with lower respiratory mortality, but evidence across settings and ages is heterogeneous.</cite>
- Direction and magnitude heterogeneity: Quantitative magnitudes vary by pollutant mixture, exposure metric, and measurement (symptoms vs spirometry vs hospitalization). Across comparators, the consistent pattern is:
  - Wildfire smoke: acute mean FEV1/PEF reductions in asthmatic children; greater mean symptom/exacerbation rates; decade-long mean FEV1 declines in exposed cohorts.<cite id="cc7aa01c-0">Mean FEV1 reductions in asthmatic children on smoke days.</cite> <cite id="a72a70d5-7">Mean symptom and visit rates rise during smoke days.</cite> <cite id="a72a70d5-3">Mean lung function decreases persisting up to 10 years after exposure.</cite>
  - Greenness: mean decreases in asthma likelihood and increases in lung function trajectories during/after childhood green exposure, with some evidence of adult benefit, but with notable heterogeneity and modification by pollen/traffic exposure and allergen sensitization.<cite id="0b6593e6-0">No association in many studies; protective in some; net effect depends on context and sensitization.</cite> <cite id="0b6593e6-3">Childhood green space linked to fewer adult respiratory problems.</cite> <cite id="7a6791ef-5">Asthma status and physical activity modulate pollution–lung function relationships, suggesting similar heterogeneity mechanisms.</cite>
  - Air pollution: higher mean asthma prevalence and lower mean lung function with stronger associations in older adults; prenatal/early-life exposures associate with lower mean FEV1/FVC by school age; lifetime-exposure gradients contribute to higher mean chronic symptoms/hospitalizations in later life.<cite id="7a6791ef-0">Mean asthma prevalence increases with pollution, more pronounced in older adults.</cite> <cite id="cc7aa01c-9">Early-life PM2.5 linked to lower mean FEV1/FVC by 6–9 years of age.</cite> <cite id="7a6791ef-6">Among adults with asthma, higher pollution linked to increased wheeze and hospitalization and decreased lung function.</cite>

Practical implications and caveats
- Measurement heterogeneity: “Mean values” depend on outcome type and scale. For spirometry, use age- and height-adjusted z-scores to compare children and adults; for events, rate per population, season, and pollution/s烟雾日基线; for prevalence, account for case definitions and care-seeking patterns. The direction and even significance of greenness–age interactions can invert depending on allergen exposure and statistical covariates.<cite id="0b6593e6-0">Findings specific to child respiratory health are inconsistent and context-dependent.</cite> <cite id="7a6791ef-5">Associations depend on asthma status and physical activity, implying outcome measurement and confounding matter.</cite>
- Cumulative risk: Early-life pollution reduces mean lung function, while later-life smoke and pollution drive higher mean exacerbations and slower recovery; greenness may mitigate early-life risks but effects in older adults are less consistent unless pollution burdens and allergen exposures are reduced.<cite id="7a6791ef-4">Prenatal/early-life pollution linked to decreased lung function.</cite> <cite id="cc7aa01c-9">Childhood PM2.5 exposure associated with smaller FEV1/FVC later in childhood.</cite> <cite id="a72a70d5-3">Wildfire exposures can reduce mean lung function up to 10 years later.</cite> <cite id="0b6593e6-3">Childhood greenness linked to fewer adult respiratory problems in some cohorts.</cite>
- Age-informed mitigation: For children, emphasize acute protection during smoke and traffic-heavy periods and monitor spirometry; for older adults, address both indoor air quality and outdoor exposure due to lower functional reserve and higher comorbidity; integrate greenness strategies (schoolyard and neighborhood green infrastructure) to lower early-life mean asthma risk and support longitudinal lung growth.<cite id="a72a70d5-2">Target pollutants (PM and gases) present in wildfire smoke drive exacerbations, underscoring filtration and reduction.</cite> <cite id="7a6791ef-2">Older adults show stronger pollutant–FEV1 relationships and disproportionate impact for PM10/NO2.</cite> <cite id="0b6593e6-2">Greenness reduces child asthma development risk when allergen sensitization is not uniformly present.</cite>

Summary statement
- Across settings, mean outcomes shift in consistent but modality-specific ways by age: wildfire smoke drives sharp acute increases in pediatric asthma events and spirometric decrements, with persistent mean lung function loss over years; air pollution raises mean asthma prevalence and lowers mean lung function with stronger effects in older adults; greenness exposure tends to decrease mean childhood asthma risk and increase lung function growth with some persistence into adulthood, though benefits are heterogeneous and often mediated by sensitization and allergen exposures.<cite id="a72a70d5-7">Wildfire smoke days increase symptoms, ED visits, and medication use (children and communities).</cite> <cite id="cc7aa01c-0">Asthmatic children show reduced FEV1 on smoke days; pollutant attribution (PM) and age thresholds affect magnitude.</cite> <cite id="a72a70d5-3">Wildfire exposure linked to decade-long lung function decline.</cite> <cite id="7a6791ef-0">Ambient pollution associated with higher mean asthma prevalence, more pronounced in older adults.</cite> <cite id="7a6791ef-2">Older participants show stronger PM10/NO2–FEV1 relationships.</cite> <cite id="0b6593e6-0">Greenness reduces childhood asthma in some, but not all, studies; evidence is mixed and sensitization-dependent.</cite> <cite id="0b6593e6-3">Childhood greenness linked to fewer adult respiratory problems in some cohorts.</cite> <cite id="7a6791ef-4">Prenatal/early-life pollution reduces mean FEV1/FVC in later childhood.</cite>

fully_underspecified.text: How do the mean values for health outcomes associated with the age risk factor differ across ecological settings?
fully_underspecified.answer:
Below is a concise synthesis of how mean health outcomes linked to age differ across ecological settings (e.g., by region, income level, urban vs. rural, and country), with quantitative examples and mechanisms.

Background and framing
- Age is a core ecological risk factor because age structures vary across populations and shapes mortality and morbidity differently by life stage and context. Ecological analyses typically use age-standardized rates, life expectancy, and cause-specific mortality/morbidity levels aggregated by country, region, urban–rural area, or socioeconomic status to compare “means” across settings. <cite id="b2774ba2-2">Age-standardized measures explicitly adjust for varying age distributions so that differences reflect level or pattern shifts rather than demographic composition</cite> <cite id="b2774ba2-3">World Health Organization materials emphasize that these rates are weighted averages designed for cross-population comparisons</cite>.

Cross-regional and income-level differences in longevity and age-at-death
- Across global income strata, mean age at death and life expectancy differ markedly, with high-income regions generally showing higher mean ages at death. <cite id="b2774ba2-5">A recent summary of GBD findings reports that the highest mean age of death was recorded in high-income super-regions—around 80.5 years for females and 74.4 years for males—underscoring substantial longevity gaps by income level</cite>. <cite id="b2774ba2-6">The GBD database enables comparisons across regions, countries, sexes, and ages for 1990–2021, supporting such cross-setting contrasts in mean outcomes</cite>.
- Over the last several decades, average length of life has risen widely, but gains have been heterogeneous. <cite id="b2774ba2-3">Global life expectancy increased by more than 20 years from 1950 to 2023, while age-standardized mortality fell by about 67%, illustrating broad declines yet persistent cross-setting differences</cite> <cite id="b2774ba2-4">WHO’s Global Health Estimates track cause-of-death by region and income group to quantify where mortality burdens—and thus implied mean ages at death—remain high</cite>.
- Cross-country contrasts at older ages can be striking. <cite id="58095b2d-7">Comparisons of age-specific death rates among developed countries show marked increases in mortality after age 65 in the U.S. relative to peers, contributing to lower mean age at death in the U.S. setting</cite>.
- For infectious disease settings, age patterns shift mean mortality risk by age group. <cite id="58095b2d-5">During COVID-19, age-structured mortality was flatter in LMICs than in HICs, with older ages contributing relatively less to total deaths in low- and middle-income settings, reflecting younger age structures and differing comorbidity profiles</cite>.

Child and maternal outcomes: age-linked risks and strong ecological gradients
- Under-5 mortality has declined globally, but mean survival at age 5 and the distribution of risk remain uneven across settings. <cite id="58095b2d-3">Globally, under-5 mortality fell by more than 50% from 1990 to 2016, with faster progress in certain regions and notable acceleration variation</cite>. <cite id="b2774ba2-5">These declines translate into higher mean survival into later childhood in settings with strong gains, but persistent gaps remain relative to high-income contexts</cite>.
- Maternal mortality is tightly linked to fertility and late-reproductive-age risks, and exhibits pronounced gradients by socioeconomic development. <cite id="8cbb0bfc-0">GBD analyses show that high-socio-demographic-index (SDI) regions have plateaued at about 17.8 deaths per 100,000 live births, whereas low-SDI regions remain around 286.5, an ~16-fold gap</cite> <cite id="8cbb0bfc-2">WHO’s 2023 update reports 346 maternal deaths per 100,000 live births in low-income countries versus 10 per 100,000 in high-income countries, highlighting a ~35-fold disparity</cite> <cite id="8cbb0bfc-1">A 2025 GBD synthesis echoes this, with low-SDI regions averaging 63% higher maternal mortality than high-SDI regions in a given period</cite>. <cite id="8cbb0bfc-6">Visualized country-level data from Our World in Data show maternal mortality around 11 per 100,000 in high-income countries versus near 450 in low-income countries, consistent with the SDI gradient</cite>.
- Within settings, maternal mortality is higher in rural, lower-SDI subregions and among disadvantaged groups. <cite id="8cbb0bfc-7">In the United States, for example, urban–rural and socioeconomic gradients contribute to elevated risks, with rural residence and lower education associated with 50–114% higher risk, reflecting ecological contrasts that drive higher mean maternal mortality in disadvantaged settings</cite>.

Urban–rural and area-level ecological contrasts by age
- Urban–rural environments produce systematic age-specific mortality differences. <cite id="b2774ba2-2">Ecological analyses find that in predominantly rural districts, average death rates among individuals under age 74 are 5–14% lower, with larger differentials at younger ages due to age-structure and lifestyle/ecologic differences</cite>. <cite id="58095b2d-4">Country-level vital statistics similarly decompose age-specific death rates and show that age-adjusted overall declines can mask pronounced age-patterned disparities (e.g., excess mortality among middle-aged and older adults in some national contexts)</cite>.
- Because urban settings often have older age structures (immigration/migration) and higher chronic disease burdens, mean ages at death and age-specific mortality levels tend to reflect distinct risk mixes by area type. <cite id="58095b2d-7">Comparisons across developed countries’ older-age death rates illustrate how urban policy environments and healthcare access can alter the left tail of survival, elevating mean ages in healthier systems</cite>.

Cause-specific morbidity and age patterns differ across settings
- Infectious and chronic disease burdens allocate age-related risk differently by ecological context. <cite id="58095b2d-5">For COVID-19, older ages account for a larger share of deaths in high-income settings than in low- and middle-income settings, where younger age structures and different comorbidity distributions shift mean age of death downward</cite>. <cite id="b2774ba2-0">GBD’s cause- and age-specific burden enables such cross-setting contrasts for conditions with distinct age-risk profiles</cite>.
- Tuberculosis is a paradigmatic age-structured, setting-dependent burden: risk concentrates in working-age adults in lower-SDI settings, while in higher-SDI contexts disease burden is tempered by case-finding and treatment, and risk redistributes to older ages with reactivation disease. <cite id="58095b2d-1">Our World in Data’s life expectancy and age-structure resources, alongside GBD cause profiles, show that TB’s age-pattern and mortality contribution vary by income/region, altering the mean age-weighted burden across settings</cite>.

Mechanisms moderating age-risk differences across ecological settings
- Socioeconomic development and health systems alter mortality schedules by age. <cite id="8cbb0bfc-0">Higher SDI regions’ much lower maternal mortality reflects better access to prenatal care, emergency obstetric services, and socioeconomic supports concentrated in younger and reproductive ages</cite> <cite id="8cbb0bfc-5">As socio-demographic development rises, age-specific maternal mortality adjusts inversely, narrowing absolute inequalities in maternal risk across ages</cite>.
- Age structure, urban–rural differences, and risk-factor exposure shift mean outcomes. <cite id="58095b2d-2">Because age-standardized rates adjust for age-mix, residual differences in means allow attribution to underlying risk factor changes and healthcare systems</cite> <cite id="b2774ba2-2">Observed 5–14% lower death rates in rural districts under 74 imply that policy and environment differences at younger ages alter mean survival</cite>.
- Public health transitions change age-weighted disease burdens. <cite id="58095b2d-3">Steady decline in under‑5 mortality in many regions increases the mean age of death for cohorts entering adulthood, but uneven adoption of immunization and malnutrition control leaves large within-region heterogeneity</cite> <cite id="58095b2d-5">In infectious-peak settings, disease-driven mortality skews toward younger ages, lowering the mean</cite>.

Practical takeaways for interpreting and using mean age-related outcomes across settings
- Mean life expectancy and mean age at death rise markedly with development, with high-income settings averaging nearly 80 years for women and over 75 for men, while low-income settings lag substantially. <cite id="b2774ba2-5">High-SDI mean ages of death (≈80.5 female, 74.4 male) vs. much lower in low-SDI regions illustrate the developmental gradient</cite>.
- Mean under-5 mortality has declined globally, but maternal mortality remains a salient ecological indicator with SDI-defined disparities over a hundredfold in ratios across settings. <cite id="58095b2d-3">Under-5 mortality fell more than 50% by 1990–2016</cite> <cite id="8cbb0bfc-2">MMR ≈346 vs. 10 per 100,000 live births in low- vs. high-income countries</cite>.
- Urban–rural contrasts within countries show 5–14% mortality differentials under 74 and point to modifiable ecological determinants (healthcare access, pollution, safety), with effects heterogeneous by age group. <cite id="b2774ba2-2">Rural districts show 5–14% lower death rates under 74 years</cite>.
- Age-standardized disease burdens (e.g., maternal hemorrhage, suicide, TB) differ by income and system capacity, altering age-weighted means and revealing where interventions will shift the age distribution of risk and outcome means. <cite id="8cbb0bfc-0">Maternal mortality plateau differences highlight capacity-related gradients</cite> <cite id="8cbb0bfc-5">ASR_MMR inversely correlates with SDI</cite> <cite id="58095b2d-5">Age-specific COVID-19 mortality patterns show system and age-structure interactions</cite>.

What this implies for policy and research
- Comparing mean age-linked outcomes across ecological settings should pair age-standardized rates with unadjusted age-specific schedules to separate age-structure from risk-factor changes. <cite id="58095b2d-2">Age-standardized mortality is a weighted average designed for cross-setting comparisons</cite> <cite id="58095b2d-4">National breakdowns show how age-specific patterns drive overall trends</cite>.
- Targeted interventions at ecological scale can shift mean outcomes: improving rural access, maternal care, and infectious-disease control changes age-weighted mortality and raises mean life span. <cite id="8cbb0bfc-7">Rural and low-education groups show 50–114% higher maternal mortality risks, indicating leverage points for area-level policy</cite> <cite id="58095b2d-3">Sustained immunization and nutrition programs reduce under-5 means and allow cohorts to reach older mean ages</cite>.

In summary, mean health outcomes tied to age differ systematically across ecological settings: higher life expectancy and mean age at death in high-SDI settings; steep maternal and child-mortality gradients with under‑5 progress but persistent MMR gaps; urban–rural mortality differentials especially pronounced under 74; and cause-specific burdens with distinct age patterns (e.g., COVID-19 and TB) that shift the age-weighted mean outcomes by region and system capacity. <cite id="b2774ba2-5">High-SDI regions show mean ages near 80–75 by sex</cite> <cite id="8cbb0bfc-2">While low-income areas show maternal mortality >300 vs. <10 per 100,000 in high income settings</cite> <cite id="b2774ba2-2">Urban–rural differences contribute 5–14% reductions in death rates under 74 in rural districts</cite> <cite id="58095b2d-5">Disease age-patterns like COVID-19 further alter relative mean ages across countries</cite>.

without_scope.text: How do the mean values for asthma and respiratory outcomes associated with the age risk factor differ?
without_scope.answer:
Summary answer up front
- Overall, age shifts the mean levels of spirometric measures and clinical outcomes in predictable ways that both depend on lung growth/decline trajectories and the age at onset and clinical expression of asthma. In healthy individuals, FEV1 and FVC rise through childhood and peak in late adolescence/early adulthood, then FEV1 declines gradually and FEV1/FVC falls modestly with age; persistent asthma is associated with earlier peaks and lower mean FEV1 and FEV1/FVC, accentuating age-related differences in mean outcomes. <cite id="7079cf4b-6">In both sexes, FEV1 and FVC increase with a fast rise until around age 13–16 and then a slower increase to a peak</cite> <cite id="7079cf4b-5">Persistent asthma was linked to earlier peak FEV1, consistently lower FEV1, and reduced FEV1/FVC ratios</cite> <cite id="7079cf4b-2">Decline in FEV1, FVC, and difference accelerated with age, whereas decline in FEV1/FVC decelerated with age; decline varied by sex, age, and height</cite>. In contrast, symptom burden and exacerbation risk show different age profiles: pediatric-onset and child-age groups often show high symptom prevalence, more frequent viral-triggered wheeze, and higher exacerbation rates despite relatively preserved spirometric ratios, whereas older adults carry higher asthma mortality and different comorbidity contexts. <cite id="f4aecffd-0">Childhood asthma is characterized by high prevalence with male predominance before puberty, common remission, and rare mortality; adult asthma differs</cite> <cite id="7079cf4b-0">Lung function declines with age in individuals without known lung disease</cite>.

What lung-function “means” look like by age and in asthma
- Healthy lung-growth trajectory vs asthma: <cite id="7079cf4b-6">FEV1 and FVC increase quickly until about 13–16 years, then more slowly to a peak in young adulthood</cite>. <cite id="7079cf4b-2">FEV1, FVC, and predicted differences decline with age, while FEV1/FVC tends to decrease more slowly; the rate varies by sex, height, and age</cite>. <cite id="7079cf4b-5">In people with persistent asthma, mean peak FEV1 occurs earlier and is lower on average, and FEV1/FVC is reduced</cite>. Together these findings shift mean FEV1 upward into adulthood before gradual decline, but persistent asthma reduces mean FEV1 and FEV1/FVC at each age relative to healthy peers.
- Pediatric vs adult norms in asthma cohorts: <cite id="3ae04756-4">In a pediatric cohort, children with mild persistent asthma had mean FEV1 of 95.1% of predicted, and moderate persistent asthma 90.2% of predicted</cite>. These pediatric mean percent-predicted values, when compared with adult cohorts at similar Global Initiative, often reflect higher functional reserves in youth masking impairment; in contrast, adult-onset disease can have more symptoms and medication use despite similar FEV1/FVC. <cite id="3ae04756-0">Adult-onset disease is associated with more respiratory symptoms and higher asthma medication use despite higher prebronchodilator FEV1/FVC</cite>.
- FEV1/FVC “lower normal” as age increases: <cite id="a345d112-1">Among subjects aged 6–18, those with FEV1/FVC in the lower range of normal had higher rates of hospital admission, underscoring that a lower mean relative to healthy peers predicts worse outcomes</cite> <cite id="a345d112-8">Evaluating FEV1/FVC in the lower normality range in younger asthmatics signals worse outcomes, even without overt airway obstruction</cite>. The mean FEV1/FVC gap with age (from normal trajectories) contributes to higher risk stratification in younger groups when abnormal or borderline values occur.
- Aging without disease versus with asthma: <cite id="7079cf4b-0">FEV1, FVC, and peak flow decline with age even in asthma-free adults, establishing age-associated mean decreases</cite> <cite id="7079cf4b-2">Decline in FEV1 and FVC accelerates with age, while FEV1/FVC declines modestly; individual differences in sex and height matter</cite>. In adults with asthma, cumulative effects of inflammation and variable reversibility shift means lower still: <cite id="7079cf4b-5">Persistent asthma links to earlier peaks and lower mean FEV1 and FEV1/FVC</cite>; repeated exacerbations and viral sensitivity in childhood elevate risk of lower-trait lung function and accelerated decline. <cite id="a345d112-5">In children and adolescents with severe asthma on preventive therapy, exacerbations did not seem to be associated with impaired lung function in the short term, suggesting selection or management differences</cite> <cite id="a345d112-5">Exacerbation impact patterns differ by age and management; in severe pediatric cohorts on prevention, short-term function was preserved</cite>.

Symptom burden, exacerbations, and hospitalization: how age changes the mean
- Early childhood and school-age years: <cite id="f4aecffd-2">Across ages, overall asthma prevalence slightly decreased except in school-aged children</cite>, indicating high mean symptom burden or high-risk environment in that bracket. <cite id="7079cf4b-0">Spirometric trajectories intersect with high symptom prevalence and treatment differences by age</cite>.
- Pediatric-specific hospitalization risk by spirometric “normality”: <cite id="a345d112-1">Among 6–18-year-olds, those with FEV1/FVC in the lower normal range had higher hospital admission rates than those near predicted, showing that a reduced mean relative to healthy norms elevates risk</cite>.
- Adult-onset vs childhood-onset differences in symptoms: <cite id="3ae04756-0">Adult-onset asthma is associated with more respiratory symptoms and more medication use despite higher prebronchodilator FEV1/FVC, highlighting that mean symptom load can exceed spirometric expectations</cite>. This suggests that for adult-related risk, symptoms and quality-of-life impacts can rise even when FEV1/FVC mean ratios are normal, unlike pediatric cohorts with similar FEV1/FVC often having lower symptom-adjusted utility.

Older adults: comorbidity and mortality
- Mean risk profile shifts with age and comorbid burden: <cite id="f4aecffd-6">Asthma mortality is highest among people aged 65 and older (27.1 per million), compared with 1.4 per million in those 0–4 years</cite>. <cite id="f4aecffd-7">Common comorbidities with asthma (rhinitis, vocal cord dysfunction, reflux, psychiatric conditions) complicate mean risk profiles and treatment responses in adults, particularly with aging</cite>.
- Respiratory viruses and sustained asthma: <cite id="f4aecffd-9">Respiratory viral infections (e.g., rhinovirus) in early childhood drive high asthma development rates by age 6, and viral triggers remain central in older cohorts, linking infection frequency with persistent symptom burden across ages</cite>.

Head-to-head quantitative contrasts and what drives differences
- Pediatric mean FEV1 and symptomatology at diagnosis: <cite id="3ae04756-4">Mild persistent pediatric asthma mean FEV1 ~95% predicted; moderate persistent ~90% predicted</cite>. <cite id="3ae04756-0">Despite higher mean FEV1/FVC, adult-onset asthma shows more symptoms and medication use</cite>. The divergence shows that age groups can have different “mean spaces”: pediatric means are constrained by physical growth, whereas symptom and medication needs reflect airway responsiveness and comorbidity context independent of a narrow FEV1/FVC range.
- FEV1/FVC mean deficits and risk: <cite id="a345d112-1">Lower normal FEV1/FVC in youth corresponds to higher hospitalization</cite> <cite id="a345d112-8">Lower FEV1/FVC in asthmatic youth predicts worse outcomes irrespective of overt obstruction</cite>. In adults, similar FEV1/FVC mean levels coexist with greater functional impairment and symptom severity, especially in adult-onset disease. <cite id="3ae04756-0">Adult-onset asthma shows higher symptom load and medication use despite higher FEV1/FVC, indicating that mean outcomes beyond spirometric ratios differentiate risk</cite>.
- Life-course decline independent of asthma per se: <cite id="7079cf4b-0">Spirometric decline with age exists even in non-asthmatics, setting age-specific mean baselines</cite> <cite id="7079cf4b-5">Persistent asthma alters these baselines by lowering mean FEV1 and FEV1/FVC and shifting earlier peaks</cite>. Age thus both anchors the mean (via growth/decline) and modifies disease expression (viral triggers in early life, comorbidity and mortality in older age), producing layered differences.

Practical takeaway on “how mean values differ by age for asthma vs other respiratory outcomes”
- Lung function (FEV1, FVC): Healthy aging imposes a systematic increase through childhood, a late-adolescent peak, followed by gradual FEV1 decline and a modest FEV1/FVC decrease in adulthood; asthma—especially persistent or adult-onset—reduces mean FEV1 and FEV1/FVC and shifts peak age earlier, widening age gaps in mean spirometric performance. <cite id="7079cf4b-6">FEV1 and FVC reach peak in 13–16 years</cite> <cite id="7079cf4b-2">FEV1/FVC declines with age but at a decelerating rate</cite> <cite id="7079cf4b-5">Persistent asthma: earlier peak FEV1 and reduced FEV1/FVC</cite>.
- Symptoms, exacerbations, hospitalization: Pediatric ages exhibit high prevalence and treatment intensity, with lower normal FEV1/FVC correlating to higher hospitalization risk; adult-onset asthma at similar spirometric ratios carries higher symptom and medication burden than childhood-onset; older adults have substantially higher mortality and more comorbidity interactions elevating mean risk. <cite id="f4aecffd-2">School-aged children show no prevalence decrease</cite> <cite id="3ae04756-0">Adult-onset asthma shows more symptoms/medication despite higher FEV1/FVC</cite> <cite id="a345d112-1">Lower FEV1/FVC in youth tied to higher admissions</cite> <cite id="f4aecffd-6">Highest asthma mortality at ≥65 years</cite> <cite id="f4aecffd-7">Comorbidity landscape increases in adults, especially with age</cite>.
- Contextual mediators: Infection-driven wheeze in early life links school-age prevalence to higher odds of asthma by age 6–10; pediatric cohorts on preventive therapy may show preserved short-term function despite frequent exacerbations, illustrating that mean outcomes across time and treatment strata do not map one-to-one with FEV1/FVC. <cite id="f4aecffd-9">Most children with hRV-induced wheeze develop asthma by age 6</cite> <cite id="a345d112-5">In severe pediatric asthma on prevention, exacerbations did not seem to impair lung function in the short term</cite>.

Limitations and how to tailor the comparison in practice
- Heterogeneity by population and spirometry protocol: Normal ranges and predicted values vary by sex, height, and reference equations, which can mask or exaggerate “mean” differences across age groups; comorbidity ascertainment and treatment intensity further confound symptom and exacerbation means. <cite id="7079cf4b-2">Declines vary by sex, age, and height</cite> <cite id="3ae04756-0">Symptom and medication differences persist despite similar FEV1/FVC in adult-onset vs childhood-onset</cite>.
- Time scale: Mean spirometric deltas change across years; longitudinal analyses better quantify mean differences attributable to aging versus disease course. <cite id="7079cf4b-6">Trajectory phases (increase to peak) suggest multi-year changes</cite> <cite id="7079cf4b-5">Persistent disease shifts baseline levels over time</cite>.

Bottom line
Mean values for asthma and related respiratory outcomes differ from healthy age norms primarily through age-anchored growth and decline in lung function, and through disease-specific biologies (airway wall remodeling, viral sensitivity, comorbidity) that shift symptom and event means independently of FEV1/FVC. In youth, lower normal FEV1/FVC portends higher mean hospitalization risk; in adults, adult-onset asthma concentrates higher mean symptom and medication use despite relatively preserved spirometric ratios; in older age, comorbidity and mortality means rise sharply, with viral wheeze in early life seeding later mean burden. <cite id="a345d112-1">Lower FEV1/FVC in 6–18-year-olds predicts higher admissions</cite> <cite id="3ae04756-0">Adult-onset asthma shows higher symptom/medication means despite higher FEV1/FVC</cite> <cite id="7079cf4b-6">FEV1/FVC rise to a peak by late adolescence</cite> <cite id="7079cf4b-5">Persistent asthma reduces mean FEV1/FEV1/FVC and shifts peak earlier</cite> <cite id="f4aecffd-6">Asthma mortality peaks ≥65 years</cite> <cite id="f4aecffd-9">Respiratory viral infections in early childhood increase asthma odds by age 6</cite> <cite id="7079cf4b-2">Age-specific spirometric decline patterns alter mean levels across decades</cite>.

questions.original_query: How have convolutional neural networks improved the efficiency and accuracy of estimating tropical cyclone intensity from satellite data?

query.text: How have convolutional neural networks improved the efficiency and accuracy of estimating tropical cyclone intensity from satellite data?
query.answer:
Summary
Deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have improved the accuracy of tropical cyclone (TC) intensity estimation from satellite imagery while simultaneously increasing operational efficiency by automating feature engineering, exploiting full spatial context end‑to‑end, enabling near‑real‑time deployment, and supporting sensor portability and multi‑task pipelines. Head‑to‑head results show CNN regressors from IR imagery achieving correlation ≈0.97 and wind RMSE ≈7.96 knots, with ConvLSTM sequence models achieving RMSE ≈8.60 knots and strong class accuracy, often matching or surpassing traditional satellite‑based schemes and statistical models that rely on feature engineering and external variables like SHIPS. <cite id="05e83c30-1">CNN models on infrared satellite images achieved RMSE 7.96 kt and correlation coefficient 0.97</cite> <cite id="ae8cf794-0">a collaborative deep‑learning model estimated TC intensity from satellite imagery to modernize expert/algorithmic approaches</cite> <cite id="05e83c30-5">ConvLSTM sequence models reported RMSE 8.60 kt with 98.4% detection and 63.83% intense class accuracy</cite>.

Background: expert/algorithmic baselines and the problem structure
Traditional operational intensity guidance includes algorithmic objective techniques and statistical models—e.g., the Dvorak technique, Advanced Dvorak Technique–Hurricane Satellite (ADT‑HURSAT), and statistical hurricane intensity prediction schemes (e.g., SHIPS)—that rely on hand‑crafted features and expert calibration. <cite id="ae8cf794-4">ADT‑HURSAT provides consistent, high‑quality storm intensity estimates over long records, forming a common operational baseline</cite> <cite id="ae8cf794-3">current intensity estimates are foundational inputs to statistical TC forecasting and impact models</cite>. CNNs invert this pipeline by learning spatial–temporal features directly from imagery, enabling pixel‑level pattern extraction (e.g., cirrus spiral asymmetries, eye/eyewall signatures) and integrating ancillary context without manual thresholds or hand‑tuned formulae. <cite id="05e83c30-1">CNNs exploit spatial patterns in infrared images associated with TC intensity ranges</cite> <cite id="05e83c30-3">CNNs analyze image patterns to estimate TC intensity as a state‑of‑the‑art approach for TC imagery</cite>.

Evidence of accuracy improvements
1) Infrared (IR)‑only CNNs: On contemporary geostationary IR image inputs, CNNs have delivered highly correlated intensity estimates with low error. <cite id="05e83c30-1">An operational collaboration reported CNN wind RMSE ≈7.96 kt and correlation ≈0.97 from IR imagery</cite>. These results approach and often equal algorithmic ADT baselines in certain basins and epochs, while providing objective, automatable outputs. <cite id="f09d1b96-0">IEEE TGRS work designed and evaluated CNN models for objective TC intensity from geostationary imagery</cite> <cite id="ae8cf794-0">the deep‑learning model is positioned as an alternative to expert schemes by directly learning from imagery</cite>.

2) Multi‑dimensional and physics‑guided CNNs: Models that incorporate 3‑D structure, wind field reconstruction, and physically consistent objectives improve joint inference of center, intensity, and structure, increasing reliability across the TC life cycle. <cite id="05e83c30-9">a knowledge‑guided deep learning model predicts cyclone center, intensity, and wind structure jointly from infrared data, aiming for physically consistent monitoring</cite>. These approaches reduce dependence on post‑hoc consistency checks and provide structured uncertainty targets for downstream forecasting.

3) Sequence and fusion CNNs: ConvLSTM and spatiotemporal CNNs process multi‑frame imagery to capture intensity evolution and environmental drivers, yielding competitive accuracy relative to static IR‑only baselines and robust auxiliary classifications. <cite id="05e83c30-5">ConvLSTM models obtained RMSE 8.60 kt while achieving 98.4% cyclone detection and 63.83% intense class accuracy for five categories</cite>. Across sensors and regions, deep models trained on Himawari‑8 and other geostationary imagery deliver objective regressions with strong correlation metrics. <cite id="ae8cf794-5">deep learning networks significantly improve tropical cyclone intensity prediction when applied end‑to‑end</cite> <cite id="f09d1b96-1">a deep‑learning model for TC intensity was developed using Himawari‑8 imagery</cite>.

4) Regional and sensor‑portable CNNs: CNNs trained on one geostationary family (e.g., GOES, Himawari, GK‑2A) generalize across sensors and basins, reducing pre‑processing and transfer costs compared to hand‑crafted VISSR‑style schemes. <cite id="05e83c30-4">CNNs estimated TC intensity in the western North Pacific using GK2A, demonstrating applicability beyond a single sensor/satellite system</cite> <cite id="05e83c30-9">a multi‑task, knowledge‑guided model leverages infrared scenes to output consistent centers, intensities, and wind structures</cite>.

Comparisons and complementarity with operational systems
CNNs were explicitly designed to replace or complement VISSR/HURSAT/ADT‑HURSAT and SHIPS by learning directly from imagery and optionally from multi‑sensor context. WMO and academic reports emphasize the value of integrating deep models with traditional forecasting, while noting ADT‑HURSAT’s role as a validated reference for current intensity history. <cite id="ae8cf794-3">current intensity is used as input to statistical forecasting tools, so CNNs that provide accurate, automated intensity can improve the upstream forecast workflow</cite> <cite id="ae8cf794-4">ADT‑HURSAT offers consistent, high‑quality intensity estimates and long records, providing a benchmark for deep models</cite> <cite id="ae8cf794-9">interpretable deep learning improved intensity prediction, with integration into early warning systems recommended</cite>. CNNs trained on ADT‑HURSAT or VISSR labels also provide an efficient way to generate high‑density “best‑track surrogate” fields in gridded space and time at near‑real‑time cadence. <cite id="f09d1b96-0">the CNN design targeted objective estimation using geostationary imagery to mirror operational baselines</cite>.

Efficiency gains: automation, speed, data use, and integration
- End‑to‑end feature learning reduces manual feature engineering, calibration, and frequent updates that plague rule‑based schemes, and yields faster inference once trained. <cite id="05e83c30-1">CNN models directly learn intensity‑related patterns from IR imagery within intensity ranges, avoiding hand‑written rules for thresholds or composites</cite> <cite id="05e83c30-8">CNNs reduce parameter complexity compared to classical methods and handle nonlinearity in imagery</cite>.
- Pixel‑complete spatial context: CNNs exploit full image fields, cloudscape asymmetries, and environmental gradients (e.g., outflow gaps, spiral bands) without case‑specific composites, streamlining preprocessing and normalizations relative to VISSR‑style products. <cite id="05e83c30-3">CNNs analyze spatial patterns to estimate intensity, capturing local and global image context</cite>.
- Sensor portability and transfer learning: Models trained on one geostationary sensor (GOES/Himawari/KOMPSAT‑2A) can generalize to others with minimal adaptation, enabling global coverage from commodity computing resources. <cite id="05e83c30-4">CNN intensity estimation with GK2A in the western North Pacific demonstrates cross‑basin and cross‑sensor applicability</cite> <cite id="f09d1b96-1">deep learning models designed for Himawari‑8 enable automated intensity estimation across contiguous imagery</cite>.
- Near‑real‑time pipelines and multi‑task monitoring: CNN‑RNN pipelines can ingest buffered imagery and produce intensity, center, and wind structure concurrently, facilitating real‑time alerting and reduced latency compared to serial algorithm chains for ADT/VISSR. <cite id="05e83c30-5">ConvLSTM pipelines deliver intensity RMSE 8.60 kt while achieving high detection and strong category accuracy, suitable for automated, near‑real‑time use</cite> <cite id="05e83c30-9">knowledge‑guided deep models predict center, intensity, and wind structure jointly from IR, improving consistency for operations</cite>.
- Integration with environmental predictors and statistical models: Deep models can be fused with SHIPS and other predictors to create hybrid predictors that capitalize on CNNs’ visual pattern recognition and statistical models’ dynamical/response knowledge. <cite id="05e83c30-3">CNNs provide imagery‑derived features that complement environmental predictors used in statistical intensity forecasting</cite> <cite id="ae8cf794-9">integrating deep learning with traditional forecasting techniques improves early warning systems</cite>.

Mechanisms enabling improved accuracy and efficiency
Studies highlight several design patterns that concretely explain gains over traditional systems:
- Spatial feature hierarchy: CNNs automatically learn eye/eyewall metrics, vortex symmetry/asymmetry, and surrounding outflow/spiral band patterns—the visual correlates of intensity—rather than relying on manually tuned thresholds or composites. <cite id="05e83c30-1">CNNs exploit spatial patterns in IR imagery and map them to intensity ranges</cite> <cite id="05e83c30-8">CNNs reduce parameter complexity while modeling nonlinear visual features important for intensity</cite>.
- Temporal integration: ConvLSTM and 2D/3D CNNs on image sequences capture intensification/degradation signals (e.g., developing asymmetries, shrinking/elongating eyewalls), improving regression and classification accuracy over single‑frame methods. <cite id="05e83c30-5">ConvLSTM sequence modeling improves detection and intensity category accuracy alongside low RMSE</cite>.
- Physics‑informed objectives: Multi‑task losses and knowledge‑guided regularizers ensure outputs are consistent with vortex thermodynamics and wind fields, reducing spurious solutions and improving confidence. <cite id="05e83c30-9">knowledge‑guided deep learning enforces physical consistency across center, intensity, and wind structure</cite>.
- Sensor/region robustness: Architectures trained across multiple geostationary sensors and basins demonstrate generalization with minimal domain shift, easing maintenance and enabling global coverage using standard imagery feeds. <cite id="05e83c30-4">GK2A‑based CNNs estimate intensity in the western North Pacific, evidencing robust regional performance</cite> <cite id="f09d1b96-1">Himawari‑8 CNN models provide objective, automated intensity from contiguous IR sequences</cite>.

Operational impacts and hybrid forecasting
Operationally, CNN‑based intensity estimates can be injected directly into downstream guidance, replacing or augmenting ADT/VISSR flags and manual Dvorak adjustments, with reported benefits in objective skill and automation. <cite id="ae8cf794-9">interpretable deep networks significantly improve intensity prediction and are recommended to integrate with early warning systems</cite> <cite id="ae8cf794-3">by improving early intensity inputs, deep models enhance statistical forecasts used for TC impact prediction</cite>. Multi‑sensor and knowledge‑guided CNNs further facilitate operator trust by producing internally consistent centers, winds, and intensities in a unified latent space. <cite id="05e83c30-9">joint prediction of cyclone center, intensity, and wind structure with physically consistent constraints</cite>.

Limitations and open challenges
Despite strong quantitative gains, CNNs face challenges typical of supervised models: dependence on high‑quality labels (ADT/VISSR/observations), potential domain shift across sensors and basins (e.g., Meteosat vs GOES vs Himawari), and the need for careful uncertainty quantification. NOAA and academic reports note the role of CNNs as complements rather than sole replacements, with integration into hybrid forecasting frameworks recommended. <cite id="ae8cf794-0">CNNs are presented as fully objective alternatives to expert schemes but still require rigorous validation</cite> <cite id="ae8cf794-9">integration with traditional forecasting improves reliability for early warning systems</cite>. Ongoing work focuses on interpretable CNNs, multi‑sensor fusion, and joint monitoring tasks to enhance accuracy and operational efficiency without sacrificing physical coherence. <cite id="05e83c30-9">knowledge‑guided deep learning emphasizes physically consistent monitoring outputs from imagery</cite>.

Takeaway
Convolutional neural networks have demonstrably improved the efficiency and accuracy of TC intensity estimation from satellite data by automating feature engineering, exploiting full spatial and temporal context, and enabling near‑real‑time, sensor‑portable, and physics‑aware pipelines that match or exceed traditional baselines. Quantitatively, IR‑only CNNs report correlation ≈0.97 and wind RMSE ≈8 kt, and ConvLSTM spatiotemporal models achieve comparable RMSE with strong detection/class accuracy, supporting objective and scalable operations alongside ADT/SHIPS‑based workflows. <cite id="05e83c30-1">CNN intensity estimates from IR imagery achieved RMSE 7.96 kt and correlation 0.97</cite> <cite id="05e83c30-5">ConvLSTM models reported RMSE 8.60 kt and strong auxiliary classification metrics</cite> <cite id="f09d1b96-1">Himawari‑8 CNNs enable automated objective intensity estimation</cite> <cite id="05e83c30-9">knowledge‑guided CNNs yield physically consistent center–wind–intensity fields for operations</cite>.
