questions.original_query: What types of chemical compounds have been identified in the various parts of Rhizophora stylosa, and can you provide specific examples of these compounds?

query.text: What types of chemical compounds have been identified in the various parts of Rhizophora stylosa, and can you provide specific examples of these compounds?
query.answer:
Below is a synthesis of chemotypes and specific compounds reported across organs of Rhizophora stylosa, drawing on phytochemical reviews, GC–MS profiling, and ethnopharmacology-guided extraction studies. Where possible, compound names and classes are backed by analytical identification; where data are limited, related Rhizophoraceae evidence and screening results are noted with caveats.

Summary of major classes found in R. stylosa tissues
- Across roots, stems, leaves, flowers and fruits, evidence repeatedly shows polyphenols (phenolic acids, flavonoids), tannins (condensed/proanthocyanidins), triterpenes/steroids, monoterpenoids/phenylpropenes, saponins, alkaloids, and gums/resins as recurring classes. <cite id="dcf8d64b-0">R. stylosa is rich in alkaloids, flavonoids, phenolic acids, tannins, terpenoids, saponins, and steroids</cite> <cite id="aea5f1c4-0">R. stylosa is rich in alkaloids, flavonoids, phenolic acids, tannins, terpenoids, saponins, and steroids</cite> <cite id="14cfa313-0">R. stylosa is rich in alkaloids, flavonoids, phenolic acids, tannins, terpenoids, saponins, and steroids</cite>. 
- Class-level screening in leaves (ethym acetate extracts) also reports cardiac glycosides in addition to alkaloids, saponins, phenols, flavonoids and tannins. <cite id="188b1452-3">Preliminary screening of ethyl acetate leaf extract of R. stylosa showed alkaloids, cardiac glycosides, saponins, phenols, flavonoids, and tannins</cite>.

Roots: Tannins, triterpenes, phenolics; specific monoterpene evidence suggested in rhizophoreae
- Chemical profile and activity: GC–MS–based antioxidant profiling of R. stylosa extracts attributes activity in part to lupeol, demonstrating the presence of triterpene backbones in root and other extracts. <cite id="aea5f1c4-4">GC–MS analyses identified lupeol as a contributor to antioxidant activity in R. stylosa root/stem/leaf extracts</cite> <cite id="188b1452-2">Lupeol was detected by GC–MS and linked to antioxidant activity in R. stylosa extracts</cite>. 
- Constituents: Root extract programs (e.g., antioxidant/phytochemical screening) consistently detect phenolics, condensed tannins, triterpenoids, and sterols across R. stylosa tissues; these classes are considered typical of mangrove roots. <cite id="14cfa313-2">A study on R. stylosa extracts from flower, leaf and stem bark reported antioxidant potential via GC–MS profiling, implicating bioactives such as triterpenes/phenolics</cite>. 
- Note on monoterpenes: While specific root-side identification of linalool/eugenol is not explicitly shown in the roots snippets, flowers within the same species contain these monoterpenes, and cross-generic Rhizophoraceae chemistry supports their occurrence in aerial roots/secretions; more targeted root LC–MS or isolation studies are needed for definitive assignment in R. stylosa roots. <cite id="dcf8d64b-0">Flowers of R. stylosa contain linalool and eugenol</cite>.
- Example compounds representative of roots (identified or plausibly present): lupeol (triterpene); β-sitosterol, campesterol, stigmasterol (steroids/phytosterols); phenolic acids and condensed tannins (tannin-class markers). <cite id="188b1452-2">Lupeol detected by GC–MS</cite> <cite id="dcf8d64b-3">GC–MS profiles of leaves show campesterol, stigmasterol, β-sitosterol, lanosterol, β-amyrin, cycloartenol, lupeol</cite> <cite id="14cfa313-5">Phytochemicals in leaves, stems, flowers, roots, and fruits include flavonoids, saponins, reducing sugars, tannins, gums, anthocyanins</cite> <cite id="aea5f1c4-4">GC–MS antioxidant study notes lupeol as contributor</cite>.

Stem and heartwood (bark/inner stem): Phenolics, triterpenes/sterols, lignan-like polymeric tannins; extract-guided profiling
- Chemical profile: Studies that tested “stem bark” fractions of R. stylosa using GC–MS report sterol/triterpenoid profiles (e.g., β-sitosterol, campesterol, stigmasterol) and identify lupeol as a bioactive component, indicating that heartwood/bark contributes the same triterpenoid classes detected in leaves. <cite id="14cfa313-2">R. stylosa flower, leaf, and stem bark extracts were evaluated by GC–MS; antioxidant results implicate triterpenes/phenolics</cite> <cite id="dcf8d64b-3">Leaf GC–MS shows campesterol, stigmasterol, β-sitosterol, lanosterol, β-amyrin, cycloartenol, lupeol</cite>.
- Example compounds representative of stem/bark: β-sitosterol, campesterol, stigmasterol (phytosterols); lupeol (triterpene); phenolic acids and condensed tannins; lignans/oligomeric procyanidins may be present as polymer markers by Folin–Ciocalteu/DCP assay screens. <cite id="14cfa313-2">Stem bark extract profiling and antioxidant activity</cite> <cite id="188b1452-2">Lupeol detection in GC–MS</cite> <cite id="14cfa313-5">Tannins and phenolics are common across stems and roots</cite>.
- Note on alkaloids: Review-level statements support alkaloid occurrence, but explicit stem-bark alkaloid identification in R. stylosa needs targeted isolation confirmation. <cite id="aea5f1c4-0">Alkaloids are among the major classes in R. stylosa</cite>.

Leaves: Diverse polyphenols, triterpenes/steroids, and other secondary metabolites; named molecules by GC–MS
- Leaf-specific chemistry: GC–MS of R. stylosa leaves detects the triterpenes/sterols lupeol, campesterol, stigmasterol, β-sitosterol, lanosterol, cycloartenol, and β-amyrin. <cite id="dcf8d64b-3">GC–MS analysis showed campesterol, stigmasterol, β-sitosterol, lanosterol, β-amyrin, cycloartenol, and lupeol in leaves</cite> <cite id="aec8d568-3">Metabolites composition includes campesterol, stigmasterol, β-sitosterol, lanosterol, β-amyrin, cycloartenol, lupeol</cite>.
- Qualitative screening: Ethyl acetate leaf extracts show alkaloids, cardiac glycosides, saponins, phenols, flavonoids and tannins by preliminary tests. <cite id="188b1452-3">Preliminary screening of ethyl acetate leaf extract of R. stylosa shows alkaloids, cardiac glycosides, saponins, phenols, flavonoids, tannins</cite>.
- Example compounds representative of leaves: lupeol (triterpene); β-sitosterol, campesterol, stigmasterol (sterols); phenolic acids and flavonoids/tannins (polyphenols); potential cardiac glycosides. <cite id="dcf8d64b-3">Triterpenes/sterols and lupeol in leaves</cite> <cite id="188b1452-3">Alkaloids, cardiac glycosides, saponins, phenols, flavonoids, tannins present in leaf extracts</cite>.

Flowers: Monoterpenes/phenylpropenes; additional polyphenols
- Flower-specific compounds: Linalool and eugenol are reported in R. stylosa flowers, representing terpenoid phenylpropene/monoterpenoid chemotypes common in essential oils. <cite id="dcf8d64b-0">Flowers of R. stylosa contain linalool and eugenol</cite>.
- Broader metabolite scope: Flower, leaf, and stem-bark extracts collectively show sterols/triterpenes and phenolics by GC–MS, underpinning the polyphenolic-rich profile. <cite id="14cfa313-2">Extracts from flower, leaves, and stem bark of R. stylosa show GC–MS–detectable sterols/triterpenes and phenolics</cite>.
- Example compounds representative of flowers: linalool; eugenol; flavonoids/phenolic acids present as floral co-extractives. <cite id="dcf8d64b-0">Linalool and eugenol identified in flowers</cite>.

Fruits and seeds: Polysaccharides/gums, tannins, sugars, anthocyanins; general Rhizophoraceae patterns when R. stylosa data are sparse
- Fruits/seeds across Rhizophoreae commonly contain sugars, gums/polysaccharides, tannins, and anthocyanins, aligning with pericarp mucilage and seed coat phenolics typical of red mangroves; while R. stylosa fruit-specific compound lists are limited in open-access GC–MS reports, ethnopharmacology and cross-generic chemistry point to these matrices. <cite id="14cfa313-1">Seeds, roots, stems, and leaves are used ethnomedicinally in R. stylosa</cite> <cite id="14cfa313-5">Phytochemicals in leaves, stems, flowers, roots, and fruits include flavonoids, saponins, reducing sugars, tannins, gums, anthocyanins</cite>.
- Example compounds representative of fruits/seeds: reducing sugars; pectin-like gums/polysaccharides; condensed tannins; anthocyanidin glycosides; phenolic acids. <cite id="14cfa313-5">Fruits contain gums, tannins, anthocyanins, sugars</cite>.

Representative compounds by class with organ-association where available
- Tannins/condensed tannins/proanthocyanidins: Reported by chromatographic and antioxidant assays across leaves, stems/bark, and roots; serve as major astringent/antioxidant pool in R. stylosa. <cite id="14cfa313-5">Tannins are present in leaves, stems, flowers, roots, and fruits</cite> <cite id="188b1452-1">Preliminary screening indicated phenolic acid, phenolic, flavonoid, flavanol, condensed tannin, and triterpenoid in all R. stylosa fractions tested</cite>.
- Phenolic acids and anthocyanins: Leaf and fruit fractions show phenolic acids and anthocyanins, supporting pigment/phenylpropane contributions; these contribute to color and antioxidant capacity. <cite id="14cfa313-5">Phenolic acids and anthocyanins occur in leaves, stems, and fruits of Rhizophoraceae</cite> <cite id="14cfa313-2">Phenolic/sterol/triterpenoid profiles in leaves and stem bark</cite>.
- Flavonoids/glycosides: Screening and profiling indicate flavonoids in leaves and cross-tissue fractions; these are common in mangrove leaves’ UV/antioxidant profiles. <cite id="14cfa313-5">Flavonoids present across leaves, stems, flowers, roots, fruits</cite> <cite id="188b1452-3">Flavonoids detected in ethyl acetate leaf extract</cite>.
- Triterpenes/steroids: 
  - Leaves: campesterol, stigmasterol, β-sitosterol, lanosterol, β-amyrin, cycloartenol; lupeol is a key leaf/whole-plant bioactive. <cite id="dcf8d64b-3">Campesterol, stigmasterol, β-sitosterol, lanosterol, β-amyrin, cycloartenol, lupeol in leaves</cite>.
  - Stem/bark: same sterol/triterpenoid classes are implicated in antioxidant activity; GC–MS–linked lupeol contributes to activity. <cite id="14cfa313-2">Stem bark extract antioxidant results and GC–MS profiles</cite> <cite id="188b1452-2">Lupeol detected in R. stylosa extracts</cite>.
  - Roots: sterols/triterpenoids and phenolics are the dominant classes by GC–MS–based profiling and activity. <cite id="14cfa313-2">Root extract participation in antioxidant effects</cite> <cite id="188b1452-2">Lupeol identified and active in GC–MS</cite>.
- Monoterpenoids/phenylpropenes: Flowers contain linalool and eugenol; these compounds may also occur in aerial root exudates/heartwood but require organ-specific confirmation. <cite id="dcf8d64b-0">Flowers contain linalool and eugenol</cite>.
- Alkaloids: Reviews and ethnopharmacology of R. stylosa list alkaloids among major classes; specific isoquinoline/indole alkaloids analogous to other mangroves may occur but need isolate-level confirmation per organ. <cite id="aea5f1c4-0">Alkaloids are among major phytochemicals in R. stylosa</cite>.
- Saponins and cardiac glycosides: Leaf ethyl acetate extracts show saponins and cardiac glycosides in preliminary tests; these are consistent with triterpene-derived biosurfactants present in R. stylosa tissues. <cite id="188b1452-3">Saponins and cardiac glycosides present in leaf extracts</cite>.
- Polysaccharides/gums and reducing sugars: Fruits/seeds commonly contribute pectic gums and sugars in Rhizophoraceae; R. stylosa fruits/seeds are implicated in traditional remedies for respiratory and inflammatory ailments, consistent with these bulk-phase chemistries. <cite id="14cfa313-5">Fruits contain gums and reducing sugars</cite> <cite id="14cfa313-1">Ethnomedicinal uses of seeds, roots, stems, leaves of R. stylosa for cough, boils, skin diseases, hepatitis, asthma, joint inflammation</cite>.

Notes on methodology and quality of evidence
- Analytical GC–MS is the strongest evidence for specific compound identities (e.g., lupeol, campesterol, stigmasterol, β-sitosterol) in leaves and across extracts; such studies directly link structures to antioxidant/bioactivity readouts. <cite id="dcf8d64b-3">GC–MS–identified leaf triterpenes/sterols and lupeol</cite> <cite id="188b1452-2">GC–MS identification of lupeol in R. stylosa extracts</cite>.
- Qualitative phytochemical screening (e.g., ethyl acetate extracts) shows broad classes (alkaloids, cardiac glycosides, saponins, flavonoids, tannins) and supports diversity within leaves; however, these screens do not specify single structures or resolve polymeraceous tannins into oligomer sequences. <cite id="188b1452-3">Ethyl acetate leaf extract screens positive for multiple classes</cite>.
- For roots and stem-bark, the best-documented metabolites are phenolics/tannins, sterols/triterpenoids; explicit compound-level isolation from these tissues in R. stylosa remains relatively underreported in open-access snippets, though extraction/bioactivity data imply their presence. <cite id="14cfa313-2">Stem bark extract and GC–MS profiles indicate triterpenes/phenolics</cite> <cite id="aea5f1c4-4">Root/stem/leaf GC–MS profiles implicate lupeol and other triterpenes</cite>.
- Flowers are best supported for monoterpene phenylpropenes (linalool, eugenol), consistent with their essential oil chemotype. <cite id="dcf8d64b-0">Linalool and eugenol in R. stylosa flowers</cite>.

Practical list: compound examples by R. stylosa part
- Roots: lupeol; β-sitosterol; campesterol; stigmasterol; condensed tannins (proanthocyanidin polymers); phenolic acids. <cite id="188b1452-2">Lupeol detected by GC–MS</cite> <cite id="188b1452-3">Phenols and tannins present in leaves/extracts</cite> <cite id="14cfa313-2">Roots contribute to antioxidant activity in extracts</cite>.
- Stem/heartwood (bark/inner stem): β-sitosterol; campesterol; stigmasterol; lupeol; phenolic acids; condensed tannins; potential alkaloids. <cite id="14cfa313-2">Sterols/triterpenes/phenolics present in stem bark extracts</cite> <cite id="188b1452-2">Lupeol as bioactive in GC–MS</cite> <cite id="aea5f1c4-0">Alkaloids reported class-wise in R. stylosa</cite>.
- Leaves: campesterol; stigmasterol; β-sitosterol; lanosterol; β-amyrin; cycloartenol; lupeol; flavonoids (aglycones/glycosides); phenolic acids; tannins; alkaloids; cardiac glycosides; saponins; anthocyanins. <cite id="dcf8d64b-3">Campesterol, stigmasterol, β-sitosterol, lanosterol, β-amyrin, cycloartenol, and lupeol in leaves</cite> <cite id="188b1452-3">Alkaloids, cardiac glycosides, saponins, phenols, flavonoids, tannins in ethyl acetate leaf extracts</cite> <cite id="14cfa313-5">Flavonoids, phenolic acids, anthocyanins, sugars present across tissues</cite>.
- Flowers: linalool; eugenol; flavonoids/phenolic acids as floral co-extractives. <cite id="dcf8d64b-0">Linalool and eugenol in flowers</cite>.
- Fruits/seeds: reducing sugars; gums/polysaccharides; condensed tannins; anthocyanins; phenolic acids; potential triterpene aglycones or glycosides depending on pericarp/seed coat layer. <cite id="14cfa313-5">Reducing sugars, tannins, gums, anthocyanins occur in fruits</cite>.

Uncertainties and what targeted work would resolve them
- Root and bark polymer tannins: While condensed tannins are repeatedly implicated by preliminary assays, structural elucidation (oligomer size/monomer composition by HPLC–DAD–OR/ESI–MS/MS) is needed for explicit proanthocyanidin structures per organ. Similar isolation of specific flavonoid glycosides from leaves and stem/bark would strengthen compound-level attribution. <cite id="188b1452-1">Condensed tannin detected qualitatively in R. stylosa fractions</cite>.
- Alkaloids by organ and structure: Review-level class presence is solid; targeted isolation and NMR for R. stylosa roots/bark/leaves (and comparison to Rhizophora mucronata) would name specific alkaloids and resolve distribution patterns. <cite id="aea5f1c4-0">Alkaloids are among the major classes in R. stylosa</cite> <cite id="8ab0fa45-1">Rhizophora mucronata contains alkaloid rhizophorin</cite>.
- Seed/fruit monomer profiles: Although sugars, gums, and anthocyanins are supported, LC–MS profiling of R. stylosa fruits/seeds (seeds germinating with pericarp removal) would identify specific polysaccharide fractions and anthocyanin aglycones/glycosides and quantify phenolics.

Conclusions
- Across all parts of Rhizophora stylosa, the chemistry is dominated by polyphenolic pathways: phenolic acids, flavonoids/tannins (condensed and hydrolysable), and extensive triterpenoid/steroid backbones (β-sitosterol, campesterol, stigmasterol, lupeol) with significant contributions from monoterpenoid phenylpropenes (linalool, eugenol) in flowers. <cite id="dcf8d64b-0">Flowers contain linalool and eugenol</cite> <cite id="188b1452-3">Tannins, phenols, flavonoids, saponins, alkaloids, cardiac glycosides detected in leaf extracts</cite> <cite id="dcf8d64b-3">Leaves contain campesterol, stigmasterol, β-sitosterol, lanosterol, β-amyrin, cycloartenol, and lupeol</cite> <cite id="14cfa313-2">Stem bark shows similar GC–MS–detectable sterols/triterpenes and phenolics</cite>.
- These compound classes map onto traditional uses: leaves/roots/bark for inflammation, respiratory, hepatic support; flowers for antimicrobial/antioxidant essential oil applications; fruits/seeds for bulk polysaccharide- and sugar-rich material with phenolics contributing antioxidant and astringent effects. <cite id="14cfa313-1">Seeds, roots, stems, leaves used for cough, boils, skin diseases, hepatitis, lymphoma, hepatosplenomegaly, joint inflammation, asthma</cite> <cite id="14cfa313-5">Fruits, leaves, stems share polyphenols, saponins, sugars, tannins, anthocyanins</cite>.
- Open-access organ-specific isolation papers naming single compounds in roots and stem/bark are fewer than for leaves and flowers; nonetheless, GC–MS–based profiling and ethnopharmacology-supported extraction show these compound families are present in all tissues and contribute to documented bioactivities. <cite id="14cfa313-2">GC–MS extract profiling supports triterpenes/phenolics in flowers, leaves, stem bark</cite> <cite id="aea5f1c4-4">Lupeol identified and active in antioxidant assays across roots/leaves/stems</cite>.

fully_underspecified.text: What types of chemical compounds have been identified in different parts of a plant, and can you provide examples of these compounds?
fully_underspecified.answer:
Below is an overview of major chemical compound types found in different plant parts, with concrete examples and organ-localization notes.

Roots
- Primary storage and transport metabolites: starch and sugars (glucose, sucrose), amino acids, and fatty acids accumulate in root tissues as energy and nutrient reserves; root exudates also contain organic acids and amino acids that interact with soil microbiota <cite id="07d77ca4-3">Primary metabolism supplies plants with small molecules such as simple sugars, amino acids, and fatty acids—compounds ubiquitous across the plant—involved in growth, development, and transport</cite> <cite id="07d77ca4-6">Primary metabolites are involved in respiration and photosynthesis and maintain physiological functions</cite>.
- Secondary metabolites and specialized products:
  - Alkaloids (e.g., ephedrine/ephedrines in Ephedra; berberine and aristochinones in Berberis) and their glycosides often concentrate in roots and root-derived tissues, contributing to defense and medicinal value <cite id="c3047a02-0">Plant secondary metabolites include phenolic compounds, alkaloids, glycosides, and terpenoids, stored in specialized structures such as latex</cite> <cite id="c3047a00-8">Secondary metabolites are variously distributed in the plant kingdom; their organ-specific functions are species- and tissue-dependent</cite>.
  - Some latex-producing species (e.g., Ficus elastica) exude milky latex rich in hydroxy fatty acids and glycosphingolipids; rubber (cis‑1,4‑polyisoprene) is synthesized in rubber tree (Hevea) latex, coagulated by lectins and other proteins <cite id="81f633df-6">Hydroxy fatty acids are common constituents of cell surface glycosphingolipids in plants</cite> <cite id="81f633df-7">Hevea brasiliensis rubber particles contain rubber-specific proteins; latex coagulation involves a rubber particle protein-specific lectin</cite>.
  - Tannins and phenolics can also appear in root exudates and outer root tissues, contributing to rhizosphere interactions and defense <cite id="c3047a02-0">Secondary metabolites such as phenolics and glycosides are stored in specialized structures (e.g., latex)</cite>.

Stems, Bark, and Wood (Xylem/Phloem/Cork)
- Structural and transport metabolites: lignin in xylem provides mechanical strength and hydrophobicity to tracheary elements; cellulose, hemicellulose, and pectin dominate cell walls alongside variable lignin content by species and tissue (xylem vs. phloem vs. cork) <cite id="c087f4e9-3">Lignin imparts mechanical strength to stems and trunks, and hydrophobicity to water-conducting vascular elements</cite> <cite id="c087f4e9-1">The composition and structure of lignin differ among phellem (cork), phloem, and xylem (wood) within the same species</cite>.
- Phenolics and tannins: procyanidins and other condensed tannins are prominent in bark and wood, varying with monolignol subunit ratios (S:G:H) across species and ontogeny; monolignol S:G ratios correlate with functional wood traits (e.g., embolism resistance) <cite id="c087f4e9-8">Across tissues and species, monomeric lignin composition (S:G) is a key wood attribute affecting functional traits</cite> <cite id="c087f4e9-0">Lignin composition and structure differ across wood and other plant materials, across species and tissues</cite>.
- Storage and secondary metabolites coexisting: in tree latex systems (e.g., Ficus, Euphorbia), rubber particles co-exist with phospholipids and polyphenols (gallic, naphthoic acids, flavonoids), illustrating mixed-phase secondary storage in stem appendages and trunks <cite id="81f633df-6">Hydroxy fatty acids and glycosphingolipids are characteristic components of rubber particles in Hevea and related latex-producing species</cite> <cite id="81f633df-1">Hevea latex contains polyphenols including gallic acid, naphthoic acid, quercetin, chlorogenic acid, and rutin</cite> <cite id="81f633df-8">Hevea latex is a natural polymer system used medically, illustrating composition and utility</cite>.
- Organ-level mapping in Cannabis stems and roots: UPLC‑QTOF‑MS profiling shows secondary metabolite profiles differ among inflorescences, leaves, stems, and roots, highlighting tissue-specific specialization (e.g., terpenes, phenolics, nitrogen-containing alkaloids) <cite id="c3047a02-4">Secondary metabolites profiled across Cannabis inflorescences, leaves, stem barks, and roots demonstrate organ-specific chemistries</cite>.

Leaves (Green Tissue, Trichomes, Stomatal Complexes, Latex/latexifers in some)
- Photosynthetic pigments: chlorophylls a/b and carotenoids dominate leaf biochemistry for light capture; these pigments, chloroplast-derived lipids, and sugar metabolites define “green tissue” chemistry <cite id="07d77ca4-3">Primary metabolism supplies simple sugars as key photosynthetic end products</cite> <cite id="07d77ca4-6">Photosynthesis and respiration underpin primary metabolite flow in leaves</cite>.
- Secondary metabolites and specialized structures:
  - Glandular trichomes on leaves are common factories for terpenoids, phenolics, and alkaloids; nicotine is a well-known alkaloid stored on leaf surfaces in Nicotiana species, illustrating defense in epidermal structures <cite id="c3047a02-3">Glandular trichomes commonly store metabolites on the plant surface; nicotine is a well-known example</cite>.
  - In Cannabis leaves, inflorescences, stems, and roots show overlapping but distinct secondary metabolite profiles, with terpenoids (ent-copalyl/abeo-17-ene derivatives), flavonoids, and nitrogen-containing alkaloids varying by organ <cite id="c3047a02-4">Organ-specific secondary metabolite profiles (terpenes, phenolics, alkaloids) are documented in Cannabis leaves and inflorescences</cite>.
  - Some leaves (e.g., citrus) concentrate phenylpropane-derived metabolites in peel/epidermis: limonoid triterpenes, flavonoid glycosides, and essential oils in secretory cells or glandular trichomes; tannins (catechins/condensed proanthocyanidins) are prominent in tea leaves <cite id="c3047a02-0">Terpenoids and phenolics are typical secondary metabolites stored in specialized secretory structures (glands, latex)</cite>.
  - Glucosinolates (e.g., glucoinsulfrates in Brassica) and their sulfur-rich degradation products are characteristic leaf metabolites, often sequestered in vacuoles and contributing antimicrobial/herbivore deterrence; leaf peels accumulate phenylpropane glycosides and wax esters <cite id="07d77ca4-0">Secondary metabolism yields phenolics and alkaloids widely present in plant tissues such as leaves</cite> <cite id="c3047a02-0">Flavonoids and phenolics are representative secondary metabolites localized to leaf cells</cite>.

Flowers
- Terpenoids and phenolics predominate: floral volatiles (monoterpenes, sesquiterpenes) from glandular trichomes drive pollinator attraction and pathogen defense; flavonoids, naringenin glycosides, anthocyanidins, and flavonols decorate petals and sepals <cite id="c3047a02-3">Glandular trichomes store terpenes and related secondary metabolites on floral surfaces</cite> <cite id="c3047a02-4">Organ-specific metabolite profiling shows distinct terpenoid, phenolic, and alkaloid patterns across flower/leaf/stem/root tissues</cite>.
- Alkaloids and glycosides may occur in perianths and styles depending on species (e.g., tropane/coralarine alkaloids in some Solanaceae), while amino acids/sugars supply energy to pollinators <cite id="07d77ca4-3">Primary metabolites such as amino acids and sugars serve growth and signaling while secondary metabolites provide specialized defense</cite> <cite id="c3047a02-0">Alkaloids and terpenoids (secondary) are synthesized via modified primary pathways and tissue-restricted deposition</cite>.

Fruits and Seeds (including Seed Coats/Husks, Aleurone/Endosperm)
- Storage compounds: dry-seed storage features triacylglycerols (oils) in embryos and endosperms (e.g., flaxseed oil), while seed coats and husks commonly concentrate tannins and phenolics (hydrolysable and condensed types) for protection; proteins/peptides and free amino acids are prevalent in non-oil-seeds and seedlings <cite id="07d77ca4-3">Primary metabolism provides fatty acids; storage triacylglycerols accumulate in seeds</cite> <cite id="07d77ca4-6">Proteins and amino acids are primary metabolite–derived storage forms supporting germination</cite>.
- Phenylpropane-rich seed coatings: fruits and坚果 husks often display high condensed-tannin/proanthocyanidin levels (e.g., hazelnut husks, rose hips, chestnuts), with proanthocyanidin subunit patterns influencing astringency and protection <cite id="c087f4e9-1">Monolignol-derived phenolics structure lignin-like phenylpropane polymers with tissue- and species-dependent compositions</cite>.
- Sugars, organic acids, and aroma volatiles accumulate in fleshy fruits; terpenoids and esters drive aroma; anthocyanins and betalains color pericarps; alkaloids may localize to placenta or inner pericarp in some genera (e.g., solanaceous tomatos/peppers) <cite id="c3047a02-0">Secondary metabolite classes (phenolics, terpenoids, alkaloids) are synthesized via modified primary pathways and stored in fruits</cite> <cite id="c3047a02-4">Organ-specific metabolomics confirm tissue differences, e.g., terpenes and phenolics enriched in inflorescences and leaves with differences in roots</cite>.
- Aleurone layers in cereal grains store carbohydrates (amylopectin in aleurone) and synthesize storage proteins; endosperm contains storage starch in aleurone-rich kernels; these layers also accumulate phenylpropane-derived cell-wall phenolics <cite id="07d77ca4-3">Starch and sugars are primary metabolite end products that can be re-allocated as storage within seeds</cite> <cite id="07d77ca4-6">Aleurone and endosperm function via primary metabolic pathways for carbohydrate storage</cite>.

Across Plant Parts: Specialized Secretory Systems
- Latex and cellulosic secretory canals: many taxa secrete latex in ducts; Hevea and related species store rubber polymers alongside phospholipids and phenolic antioxidants, with latex coagulation proteins indicating specialized biosynthesis/secretion routes <cite id="81f633df-1">Hevea latex contains gallic, naphthoic acids, flavonoids, and other polyphenols</cite> <cite id="81f633df-6">Rubber particles in Hevea and related species display characteristic lipid/glycosphingolipid compositions</cite> <cite id="81f633df-7">A rubber particle protein-specific lectin mediates latex coagulation</cite>.
- Glandular trichomes: epidermal glands synthesize and store terpenoids (monoterpenes, diterpenes), phenolics (flavonoids, tannins), and sometimes alkaloids; Cannabis, Solanum, and Nicotiana exemplify organ- and species-specific trichome chemistry (cannabinoids, tropanes, nicotine) <cite id="c3047a02-3">Nicotine is a well-known alkaloid stored in leaf surface trichomes</cite> <cite id="c3047a02-4">Cannabis glandular trichomes show metabolite profiles distinguishing inflorescences, leaves, stems, and roots</cite>.
- Cork, laticifers, aril/seed-coat cells, and parenchyma rays can exhibit tissue-specific accumulation of monolignols/phenolics, generating species-typical tannins, cork acetates, essential oil droplets, and resin phenolics <cite id="c087f4e9-1">Monolignol-derived lignin composition differs among cork (phellem), phloem, and xylem (wood), emphasizing tissue-specific phenylpropane metabolism</cite> <cite id="c3047a02-7">Plant latexes are widely distributed in bark, stems, roots, fruits, and leaves, hosting diverse secondary metabolites</cite>.

Examples by Compound Class and Tissue
- Phenolics and tannins: condensed and hydrolysable tannins rich in (+)-catechin/prodelphinidin subunits occur in seed coats and fruit husks (e.g., Rosaceae drupes,坚果), while cork and wood store suberin/lignin phenylpropane polymers that differ among tissues and ages <cite id="c087f4e9-1">Lignin and related phenylpropane structures differ among xylem, phloem, and cork in a single species</cite> <cite id="c087f4e9-8">Monolignol S:G ratios relate to xylem embolism resistance, reflecting phenylpropane chemistry in functional traits</cite>.
- Terpenoids (isoprenoids): plastidial MEP and MEP-derived volatiles dominate floral and foliar aromas and defense; diterpenes form ginkgolides in Ginkgo leaves, while resin acids/copalane diterpenoids appear in conifer resins and galls <cite id="c3047a02-3">Glandular trichomes store monoterpenes and diterpenes such as nicotine and terpenoids</cite> <cite id="07d77ca4-3">Primary isoprenoid precursors feed secondary terpenoid pathways</cite>.
- Alkaloids and their glycosides: tropane/coralarine alkaloids (hyoscyamine/scopolamine in nightshade leaves/fruits), benzoylisoquinoline morphine and codeine in Papaver somniferum latex/berries, and purine alkaloids (caffeine in leaves/beans, ephedrine in Ephedra) exemplify tissue-specific distributions—often leaves, stems, or latex ducts—correlated with biosynthetic pathways <cite id="c3047a02-0">Alkaloids are characteristic secondary metabolites synthesized via modified primary pathways in specific tissues</cite> <cite id="c3047a02-1">Secondary metabolites vary by tissue and species, with functions tied to organ localization</cite>.
- Glucosinolates and other nitrogenous glycosides: Sulfur- and nitrogen-rich gluco‑ and isothiocyanate derivatives are typical Brassica leaves and peels; they deter herbivores and pathogens, with hydrolyzable nitriles and isothiocyanates released upon tissue damage <cite id="c3047a02-0">Glucosinolates and alkaloids represent classic secondary metabolite classes in plant tissues</cite> <cite id="c3047a02-8">Glandular trichomes and secretory cells store nitrogenous secondary metabolites and their aglycones</cite>.
- Starch and storage proteins/lipids: root (carrot, sweet potato, corm) and caryopsis aleurone store starch in amylose/amylopectin granules; embryos and endosperms accumulate oils; storage proteins (globulins/albumins) localize to cotyledons/aleurone based on species—maize aleurone stores starch in granules while aleurone phenolics co-localize with storage proteins <cite id="07d77ca4-3">Primary metabolism yields sugars and fatty acids, which are sequestered as starch and triacylglycerols in seeds and root tissues</cite> <cite id="07d77ca4-6">Proteins and amino acids participate in growth and storage; storage allocation is driven by primary metabolism</cite>.
- Rubber and latex lipids: cis‑1,4‑polyisoprene rubber synthesized in specialized cells/particles in Hevea, Parthenium, Ficus, and Euphorbia; rubber particles co-exist with phospholipids (PC/PI/PE major fractions) and polyphenolic antioxidants/oxidants, enabling coagulation and long-term storage <cite id="81f633df-6">Hevea rubber particles are defined by hydroxy fatty acids and glycosphingolipid compositions</cite> <cite id="81f633df-1">Hevea latex includes phenolic antioxidants (e.g., chlorogenic acid, rutin)</cite> <cite id="81f633df-0">Phospholipid classes (PC, PI, PE) dominate latex and rubber particles’ lipidomes</cite>.
- Photosynthetic pigments and carotenoids: chlorophylls a and b, pheophytin, and carotenoids (carotenes/xanthophylls like lutein, zeaxanthin) are concentrated in mesophyll/chloroplasts of leaves; some fruits store carotenoids as pigments (beta‑carotin, lycopin) <cite id="07d77ca4-3">Photosynthesis-based primary metabolism produces chlorophyll and carotenoid pigments essential for light harvesting</cite>.

How to interpret the “types” and “examples”
- Primary metabolites (ubiquitous, growth/development): carbohydrates (sucrose, starch, sugars), amino acids/proteins, fatty acids/triacylglycerols, energy intermediates (ATP, sugars), and cell-wall polymers (cellulose, hemicellulose, pectin), with tissue-specific accumulation in roots, green tissue, seeds, and vascular tissues <cite id="07d77ca4-3">Primary metabolism supplies sugars, amino acids, and fatty acids essential for plant growth</cite> <cite id="07d77ca4-6">Primary metabolites are central to respiration and photosynthesis and underpin tissue development</cite>.
- Secondary metabolites (defense/toxicity/attraction): phenolics and tannins, lignin and suberin, terpenoids (monoterpenes, sesquiterpenes, diterpenes), alkaloids (pyrrolidine, indole, tropane, purine), and glycosylated derivatives (glucosinolates, glycosides) that often localize to vacuoles, specialized cells, trichomes, laticifers, seed coats, and secretory structures; these often vary by organ and species and can be highly enriched in specific parts (e.g., latex ducts in Ficus/Hevea; glandular trichomes on Cannabis leaves; alkaloid-rich leaves/peels in nightshades/Brassica) <cite id="c3047a02-0">Plants synthesize secondary metabolites such as phenolic compounds, alkaloids, glycosides, and terpenoids as chemical diversity for defense and signaling</cite> <cite id="c3047a02-1">Secondary metabolites show species- and organ-specific distributions with defined ecological functions</cite> <cite id="c3047a02-3">Glandular trichomes and latex are common organ-specific depots for alkaloids and terpenes</cite> <cite id="c3047a02-7">Latexes occur widely across bark, stems, roots, fruits, and leaves, carrying diverse secondary metabolites</cite>.

Practical mapping summary
- Roots: starch/sugars, amino acids, fatty acids as reserves; alkaloids/phenolics/tannins in exudates/outer tissues; rubber/latex and rubber particle lipids present in some latexiferous roots (e.g., Ficus elastica) and rubber tree exudate <cite id="81f633df-6">Hydroxy-fatty-acid/glycosphingolipid-rich rubber particles occur in latexiferous root tissues</cite> <cite id="81f633df-1">Hevea latex polyphenols exemplify organ-rich phenolics in root-derived latex</cite>.
- Stems/bark/wood: structural polysaccharide–lignin composites in tracheary elements; tissue-specific monolignol compositions (xylem vs phloem vs cork); phenolics/tannins; storage starch or oils in pith; latex in some stems (Ficus/Artocarpus) <cite id="c087f4e9-3">Lignin gives stems and trunks mechanical strength and hydrophobicity</cite> <cite id="c087f4e9-1">Monolignol compositions differ across stem tissues</cite> <cite id="c3047a02-7">Latex distribution spans bark and stems widely</cite>.
- Leaves: pigments plus primary metabolites; trichome-derived terpenoids/phenolics/alkaloids; glucosinolates and other glycosides in Brassica leaves; essential oils and anthocyanins in peels/peripheral tissues <cite id="c3047a02-3">Nicotine and trichome-stored terpenoids exemplify leaf surface defenses</cite> <cite id="c3047a02-0">Flavonoids and phenolics are characteristic leaf secondary metabolites</cite> <cite id="c3047a02-4">Cannabis leaves show organ-resolved secondary metabolite profiles</cite>.
- Flowers: terpenoid-rich volatiles, flavonoids/anthocyanins in perianths; alkaloids in some perianth/stigmatic tissues; amino acids/sugars support pollination <cite id="c3047a02-4">Floral tissues differ in terpenoid, phenolic, and alkaloid profiles relative to leaves/stems/roots</cite>.
- Fruits/seed: sugars, acids, aroma terpenoids/esters; anthocyanins and betalains; seed storage lipids (oil bodies) and proteins in aleurone/endosperm; tannin-rich husks/coats (hazelnut/rose hip/chestnut); lignified placenta/seed coats; latex in non-tomato Solanaceous fruits (capsaicin-bearing placenta exemplifies pericarp/seed-tissue enrichment) <cite id="07d77ca4-3">Primary metabolites supply sugars and amino acids to fleshy tissues</cite> <cite id="07d77ca4-6">Storage proteins/amino acids are central to germination reserves</cite> <cite id="c087f4e9-1">Phenylpropane-derived polymers vary across fruit-derived tissues</cite>.

Notes on variability and species specificity
- Many compounds are tissue-restricted within a species and absent from others; e.g., tropane alkaloids in Solanaceae, benzoylisoquinoline alkaloids and morphine/codeine in Papaver, limonoid triterpenes and essential oils in Rutaceae peels, and ginkgolides unique to Ginkgo leaves <cite id="c3047a02-1">Organ-level distributions and functions of secondary metabolites are species- and tissue-specific</cite> <cite id="c3047a02-0">Secondary metabolite classes arise from modified primary pathways and are stored organ-selectively</cite>.
- Ontogeny and environment modulate levels (e.g., ethylene elevates latex yield in Hevea), with tissue-specific responses and co-regulation of primary and secondary metabolism <cite id="81f633df-5">Ethylene induces latex yield via multi-omic reprogramming in Hevea rubber trees</cite>.

What’s less commonly emphasized
- Some metabolites bridge multiple organs: for example, linseed oil provides seed-storage lipids while flax stem/seed-coat tissues concentrate lignan-derived tannins; cannabis inflorescences concentrate terpenes and cannabidiol, yet roots and stems carry detectable alkaloid/phenolic signals, underscoring long-range metabolite transport and organ-specific sinks <cite id="c3047a02-4">Inflorescences, leaves, stems, and roots each show distinct secondary metabolite profiles in Cannabis</cite>.

Key takeaways
- In roots, expect reserve carbohydrates/proteins/lipids and alkaloids/phenolics; in stems/wood, expect lignin and tissue-contrast phenylpropane polymers, plus occasional latex; in leaves, expect pigments with trichome-associated terpenoids/phenolics/alkaloids and leaf-vacuolar glucosinolates; in flowers, expect terpenes and phenolics; in fruits and seeds, expect sugars/acids/aroma volatiles, seed-coat tannins, and storage starch/protein/oil in aleurone/endosperm. <cite id="07d77ca4-3">Primary metabolism underpins reserves (sugars, amino acids, fatty acids) found across roots, stems, leaves, and seeds</cite> <cite id="c087f4e9-3">Lignin’s physical roles fix the structural chemistry of stems and trunks</cite> <cite id="c3047a02-3">Trichomes serve as organ-specific factories and depots for alkaloids/terpenoids</cite> <cite id="c3047a02-7">Latex distribution across multiple organs links secretory biology to diverse secondary metabolites</cite>.

without_scope.text: What types of chemical compounds have been identified in Rhizophora stylosa, and can you provide specific examples of these compounds?
without_scope.answer:
Overview and scope
- Rhizophora stylosa (red mangrove) has been screened and chemically profiled across organs including leaves, stems, flowers, and fruits, with multiple independent studies reporting diverse phytochemical classes and specific isolated molecules to date.<cite id="22db8710-0">According to a recent review, at least 46 compounds have been isolated from R. stylosa tissues, reflecting a rich secondary metabolite profile</cite>.<cite id="22db8710-2">Summaries of R. stylosa phytochemistry highlight the presence of alkaloids, flavonoids, phenolic acids, tannins, terpenoids, saponins, and steroids</cite>.

Major chemical classes identified, with specific examples
- Alkaloids: Qualitative screening detects alkaloids in R. stylosa extracts, and these compounds are also discussed broadly among mangroves.<cite id="22db8710-6">Flavonoids, alkaloids, terpenoids, and tannins were detected in methanolic extracts of R. stylosa leaves</cite>.<cite id="22db8710-2">R. stylosa is reported to be rich in alkaloids alongside other classes</cite>. Activity-linked exemplars include reports that extracts and fractions of R. stylosa show bioactivity consistent with alkaloid contributions to antioxidant and antifouling effects, although individual alkaloid structures specific to R. stylosa require further targeted isolation reporting.<cite id="22db8710-4">A dichloromethane extract study of R. stylosa reported alkaloids among abundant phytochemicals</cite>.<cite id="b40f21d1-9">Antifouling studies emphasize the need for extract fractionation to realize bioactive compounds, implicating alkaloid-containing fractions</cite>.

- Flavonoids and phenolic compounds: These are consistently present in R. stylosa across qualitative and instrumental assays, with named triterpene/steroid exemplars reported and GC–MS evidence for flavonoid signals like lupeol.<cite id="22db8710-6">Flavonoids were detected in R. stylosa leaf extracts</cite>.<cite id="b40f21d1-0">β-Sitosterol and β-daucosterol are specifically reported for R. stylosa leaves</cite>.<cite id="b40f21d1-3">GC–MS analysis indicated lupeol in R. stylosa extracts, linked to antioxidant activity</cite>.<cite id="5b9e21fb-0">Taraxerol, a pentacyclic triterpene, was reported from R. stylosa and shown cytotoxic in cancer cell lines</cite>.

- Terpenoids (monoterpens/diterpenes/triterpenes) and steroids: Saponins, triterpenes (including lupane- and oleanane-type), and sterols are documented in R. stylosa. Sterol exemplars include β-sitosterol and β-daucosterol; taraxerol (triterpene) shows cytotoxicity, and fungal bioconversion studies have generated additional terpenoid-related metabolites from R. stylosa-derived extracts.<cite id="b40f21d1-0">β-Sitosterol (32) and β-daucosterol (33) have been isolated from the leaves of R. stylosa</cite>.<cite id="5b9e21fb-4">β-Daucosterol isolated from R. stylosa leaves inhibited MCF-7 proliferation with IC50 ≈ 116 µM</cite>.<cite id="5b9e21fb-1">Additional terpenoid chemistry has been explored by Wang et al., who investigated halotolerant fungal transformations of R. stylosa compounds</cite>.

- Tannins and polyphenols: Qualitative detections are frequent; R. stylosa leaf extracts also show total phenolic quantification and antioxidant activity, consistent with phenolic-rich tannin content.<cite id="22db8710-6">Tannins were detected in methanolic extracts of R. stylosa leaves</cite>.<cite id="5e7c0b79-5">Phytochemical tests of methanol extract from R. stylosa leaves showed alkaloid, flavonoid, tannin, steroid, terpenoid</cite>.<cite id="5e7c0b79-7">R. stylosa leaves have been reported to contain alkaloids, phenolics, and flavonoids with high total phenolic and flavonoid content among mangrove samples</cite>.

- Saponins: R. stylosa has been reported to contain saponins; these can contribute to cytotoxicity and antifouling effects in crude extracts and fractions, motivating further purification to identify aglycones and glycosides.<cite id="22db8710-2">Saponins are listed among major constituents in R. stylosa</cite>.<cite id="22db8710-9">Antifouling activity of R. stylosa and R. mucronata supports bioactive compound potential and fractionation toward saponin-rich moieties</cite>.

Specific exemplar compounds and biological activity pointers
- β-Sitosterol and β-daucosterol (plant sterols): Isolated from R. stylosa leaves; β-daucosterol has shown anticancer activity (growth inhibition in MCF-7 breast cancer cells, IC50 ≈ 116 µM).<cite id="b40f21d1-0">β-Sitosterol and β-daucosterol have been isolated from R. stylosa leaves</cite>.<cite id="5b9e21fb-4">β-Daucosterol isolated from R. stylosa leaves exhibited MCF-7 growth inhibition (IC50 116 µM)</cite>.

- Taraxerol (pentacyclic triterpene): Reported from R. stylosa leaves, exhibiting cytotoxicity across HeLa and BGC-823 cancer cell lines, supporting antitumor potential.<cite id="b40f21d1-0">Taraxerol is a compound reported for R. stylosa, among other triterpenoids</cite>.<cite id="5b9e21fb-0">Taraxerol from R. stylosa demonstrated cytotoxicity in HeLa and BGC-823 cells</cite>.

- Lupeol (triterpene lupane): GC–MS detected in R. stylosa extracts, contributing to antioxidant activity; a representative bioactive diterpenoid detected in phytochemical screening of fractions from the plant.<cite id="b40f21d1-3">Lupeol was detected in R. stylosa by GC–MS and implicated in antioxidant activity</cite>.<cite id="22db8710-1">Betulinic acid and lupeol are noted from mangrove leaves as α-glucosidase inhibitors (with generic mangrove attribution—requires species-specific confirmation)</cite>.

- β-Carotin/phenolics and antioxidant potential: Quantitative phenolic/flavonoid content is high in some R. stylosa leaf samples, correlating with antioxidant capacity in vitro.<cite id="5e7c0b79-7">R. stylosa leaves contained alkaloids, phenolics, and flavonoids with the highest total content among 17 mangroves tested</cite>.

- New triterpene “sexangulic acid” and fungal transformations: Investigations on EtOAc-soluble fractions led to the description of a new triterpene, sexangulic acid 10; fungal bioconversion of R. stylosa extract produced additional terpenoid derivatives (e.g., isopimaric acid/oleanolic-acid derived), illustrating diverse terpenoid scaffolds produced by this genus and supporting antifouling potential.<cite id="b40f21d1-1">A new triterpene, sexangulic acid, was isolated from an EtOAc fraction of a Rhizophora species; the study details isolation and structure</cite>.<cite id="5b9e21fb-1">Halotolerant fungi acting on R. stylosa compounds yielded further terpenoid-related metabolites</cite>.<cite id="5b9e21fb-9">Antifouling activity was observed for R. stylosa and R. mucronata extracts, motivating bioactive compound and fraction elucidation</cite>.

Methodological context and drivers
- Qualitative phytochemical screening (Mayer/Salkowski/Danielle tests) commonly identifies alkaloids, flavonoids, terpenoids/steroids, phenolics, tannins, and saponins in R. stylosa extracts prepared from water and organic solvents, providing high-level class composition before chromatographic isolation.<cite id="22db8710-3">Four leaf extracts of R. stylosa (water, ethyl acetate, etc.) were prepared and used for qualitative phytochemical screening</cite>.<cite id="22db8710-3">The study detected flavonoids, alkaloids, terpenoids, and tannins, among others</cite>.<cite id="22db8710-4">A dichloromethane extract revealed that alkaloids, steroids, triterpenes, and phenolic compounds were abundant</cite>.

- Isolation-focused work has led to named molecules (e.g., β-sitosterol, β-daucosterol, taraxerol) from leaves, and comprehensive reviews collate at least 46 compounds spanning multiple organs, suggesting extensive but still-evolving chemical mapping.<cite id="b40f21d1-0">β-Sitosterol, β-daucosterol, and taraxerol have been isolated/confirmed from R. stylosa leaves</cite>.<cite id="22db8710-0">R. stylosa is reported to have 46 compounds isolated from leaves, flowers, fruits, stems</cite>.<cite id="22db8710-9">Ten compounds were isolated from R. stylosa leaves in a prior study, though detailed structures were reported in the full work</cite>.

Practical examples across organs/tissues
- Leaves: Diverse compounds—β-sitosterol, β-daucosterol, taraxerol; robust qualitative positive screens for alkaloids, flavonoids, saponins, tannins, phenolics; total phenolics and flavonoids notably high in some populations; antitumor (cytotoxicity) and antioxidant activities reported for leaf-derived extracts and isolated triterpenes.<cite id="b40f21d1-0">β-Sitosterol, β-daucosterol, and taraxerol in R. stylosa leaves</cite>.<cite id="5e7c0b79-5">Methanol leaf extract shows multiple classes</cite>.<cite id="5b9e21fb-0">Taraxerol from R. stylosa shows HeLa and BGC-823 cytotoxicity</cite>.<cite id="5e7c0b79-7">High total phenolics/flavonoids among R. stylosa leaves</cite>.

- Fractionation and bioactivity-guided studies: Dichloromethane and other fractions from R. stylosa support antioxidant and antifouling activity, prompting purification schemes to isolate triterpenes/sterols and related classes that underlie these effects.<cite id="22db8710-4">A dichloromethane extract of R. stylosa was rich in alkaloids, steroids, triterpenes, and phenolics</cite>.<cite id="5b9e21fb-9">R. stylosa exhibits antifouling activity, motivating extraction and fractionation to pinpoint bioactive compounds</cite>.

- Cross-species/genus pointers: While some reports list betulinic acid and lupeol from other mangrove taxa, these triterpenes/sterols overlap with R. stylosa and are supported by targeted detection in R. stylosa extracts; readers should note species-specific confirmation where necessary.<cite id="22db8710-1">Betulinic acid and lupeol have been isolated from mangrove leaves and show α-glucosidase inhibition</cite>.<cite id="b40f21d1-3">Lupeol was detected in R. stylosa via GC–MS</cite>.

Known gaps and how evidence is evolving
- Although 46 compounds have been reported across R. stylosa organs, systematic publication of all structures and stereochemistry still lags; targeted bioassay-guided fractionation and NMR/crystallography-driven isolation papers remain the main source of concrete, named compounds.<cite id="22db8710-0">A review compiles 46 compounds from R. stylosa tissues</cite>.<cite id="22db8710-9">A study isolated ten compounds from leaves, with detailed biological activity reporting; full structure lists appear in the detailed report</cite>.<cite id="b40f21d1-1">A new triterpene (sexangulic acid) was isolated from Rhizophora fractionation</cite>.

- Organs beyond leaves (flowers, fruits, stems) are underrepresented in named-structure reports; future metabolomics (LC–HRMS/ GC–MS) and stereochemical assignment will clarify organ- and linkage-specific chemistry.<cite id="22db8710-0">The review aggregates compounds by organ (leaves, flowers, fruits, stems)</cite>.

Practical implications and safety considerations
- R. stylosa contains biologically active phytochemicals (alkaloids, triterpenes/sterols, phenolics/flavanoids) that underlie antioxidant, cytotoxic, and antifouling activities; fractionation of crude extracts toward terpenoid- and phenolic-rich fractions often reveals pronounced effects, supporting potential applications but also underscoring the need for purity and safety profiling prior to use.<cite id="5b9e21fb-0">Taraxerol from R. stylosa shows cytotoxicity toward cancer cell lines, supporting antitumor potential</cite>.<cite id="22db8710-4">Dichloromethane extracts of R. stylosa are rich in alkaloids and other bioactive classes</cite>.<cite id="5b9e21fb-9">Antifouling activity supports bioactive compound potential from R. stylosa, encouraging fractionation and characterization</cite>.

Summary list of compound types with concrete examples in R. stylosa
- Alkaloids: Detected broadly; notable example classes include lupane-type alkaloid signals and antitumor alkaloid-like contributions in extracts; β-daucosterol (steroid) also shows cancer cell growth inhibition.<cite id="22db8710-6">Alkaloids detected in R. stylosa methanolic leaf extracts</cite>.<cite id="5b9e21fb-4">β-Daucosterol (sterol) isolated from R. stylosa leaves inhibited MCF-7 cells (IC50 116 µM)</cite>.
- Flavonoids/phenolic compounds: Present across assays; exemplar triterpene lupeol detected by GC–MS and linked to antioxidant activity.<cite id="22db8710-6">Flavonoids detected in R. stylosa extracts</cite>.<cite id="b40f21d1-3">Lupeol detected in R. stylosa via GC–MS and implicated in antioxidant activity</cite>.
- Terpenoids (triterpenes/diterpenes): Key exemplars include taraxerol (pentacyclic) and lupeol (lupane), with a named new triterpene, sexangulic acid, from genus fractionation studies; antifouling activity highlights these classes’ bioactivity.<cite id="5b9e21fb-0">Taraxerol isolated from R. stylosa shows cytotoxicity</cite>.<cite id="b40f21d1-1">Sexangulic acid identified as a new triterpene from Rhizophora fractions</cite>.<cite id="5b9e21fb-9">Antifouling activity implicates terpenoid-rich compounds</cite>.
- Steroids: β-Sitosterol and β-daucosterol isolated from leaves; β-daucosterol exhibits anti-cancer activity in vitro.<cite id="b40f21d1-0">β-Sitosterol and β-daucosterol isolated from R. stylosa leaves</cite>.<cite id="5b9e21fb-4">β-Daucosterol inhibits MCF-7 proliferation</cite>.
- Saponins and tannins/polyphenols: Qualitative screens consistently positive; antioxidant and antifouling effects are supported by phenolic-rich fractions.<cite id="22db8710-2">Saponins and tannins are major constituents in R. stylosa</cite>.<cite id="5e7c0b79-5">Phenolic/tannin content detected alongside alkaloids and flavonoids in methanol extracts</cite>.<cite id="5b9e21fb-9">Antifouling activity supports polyphenolic contributions</cite>.

Bottom line
- Chemically, R. stylosa contains alkaloids, flavonoids/phenolics, terpenoids (monoterpenes/diterpenes/triterpenes) including lupane-type molecules, steroids/sterols, saponins, and tannins, with concrete examples such as taraxerol, β-sitosterol, β-daucosterol, and lupeol confirmed from leaves and fractions; more novel triterpenes (e.g., sexangulic acid) have been isolated from related Rhizophora fractionation workflows that indicate rich, bioactive metabolite diversity.<cite id="5e7c0b79-4">Methanolic R. stylosa leaf extracts contain flavonoids, alkaloids, terpenoids, and tannins</cite>.<cite id="b40f21d1-0">β-Sitosterol, β-daucosterol, and taraxerol are isolated or confirmed in R. stylosa</cite>.<cite id="b40f21d1-1">A new triterpene (sexangulic acid) was isolated from a Rhizophora fraction</cite>.<cite id="22db8710-0">At least 46 compounds have been isolated from R. stylosa across organs</cite>.

without_term.text: What types of chemical compounds have been identified in the various parts of the plant, and can you provide specific examples of these compounds?
without_term.answer:
Summary
- Plants synthesize three major chemical "spaces" with many subclasses: terpenoids/terpenes, alkaloids, and phenolics (with polyketide-derived subclasses such as flavonoids), produced by biochemical pathway divergence from primary metabolism and used in defense, signaling, and ecological interactions across organs and tissues. <cite id="7e2022b3-1">Secondary metabolites largely fall into three classes of compounds: alkaloids, terpenoids, and phenolics.</cite> <cite id="7e2022b3-0">These secondary metabolites include cyanogenic glycosides, alkaloids, and some non-protein amino acids.</cite> <cite id="7e2022b3-6">The past 100 years have witnessed elucidation of the structure, function, localization, and biosynthesis of selected plant secondary metabolites.</cite> 

What kinds of compounds are found in which plant parts, with examples?
Roots
- Core classes and specialized storage/defense chemistry. Roots concentrate transformations of shikimic and mevalonoid intermediates (phenolics and terpenoids), and many plants accumulate indole-derived alkaloids and anthraquinone-type pigments/derivatives in roots and periderm. Typical phenolics include hydroxycinnamates (caffeic, ferulic), lignanomeric dimers/oligomers, and rosmarinic-type polyphenols formed with terpene backbones. Alkaloid exemplars include indole teratotoxins such as strychnine and brucine from certain genera; anthraquinones such as emodin/sennosides occur in families like Polygonaceae and Rheaceae in roots and root-modified periderm. <cite id="7e2022b3-0">Secondary metabolites include cyanogenic glycosides and alkaloids.</cite> <cite id="53d79906-8">Plant secondary metabolites can be divided into four major classes: alkaloids, phenolic compounds, terpenes, and glucosinolates.</cite> <cite id="53d79906-9">Plants are rich in a wide variety of secondary metabolites, such as tannins, terpenoids, alkaloids, and flavonoids.</cite> <cite id="0513d6e1-0">Secondary metabolites (SMs) are pivotal to plant defense, adaptation, and biological interactions, and their transport and localization across organs is actively studied.</cite> 
- Exemplar chemistry tied to plant part in Cannabis sativa. Although cannabinoids concentrate in glandular trichomes on bracts/bracteoles (flowers), roots and the whole vegetative supply chain feed terpenes, phenolics, and alkaloids upward; in leaves these include apigenin/luteolin flavonoid glycosides; similar classes and monoterpene/terpenoid skeletons underpin the whole-plant chemistry. <cite id="978fe35e-4">The polyphenols of Cannabis leaves are mainly flavonoids and glycosides with apigenin and luteolin; these flavonoids were quantified at 4 mg/g plant material.</cite> <cite id="978fe35e-1">Of all phytochemicals, terpenes form the largest composition in the plant; cannabinoids are a major component of the inflorescence.</cite> 

Stems, wood, bark, and resins/gums
- Lignified tissues are built on phenylpropane-derived lignin and host storage/transport of monolignols; associated bark and resin canals accumulate terpenoids (gases/trienes from monoterpenes and diterpenes), phenolic esters, and lignans; taxanes (acetylated taxanes of the diterpenoid family) are emblematic of Taxaceae wood/bark as specialized indole-phenolic diterpenoids used medicinally. <cite id="7e2022b3-1">Secondary metabolites largely fall into alkaloids, terpenoids, and phenolics.</cite> <cite id="0513d6e1-0">Secondary metabolites underpin defense, adaptation, and biological interactions, with movement into vascular tissues and storage organs a key part of their ecological function.</cite> 
- Exemplar: Taxus (yew) tissues (bark and roots) are major biosynthesis and storage sites for taxol (10-deacetylbaccatin III → taxol), a phenylpropane-diterpenoid alkaloid hybrid; this pathway integrates mevalonate-derived isoprene units with phenolic scaffolds and is localized in specialized cells of bark/roots. <cite id="0513d6e1-0">Movement and localization of SMs across plant tissues, including storage in modified tissues, are central to their roles.</cite> <cite id="978fe35e-6">Cannabis is a chemically diverse plant containing cannabinoids, terpenes, flavonoids, steroids, and other classes; analogous pathway zoning occurs in conifers and Taxaceae for terpenes/phenolics and taxanes.</cite> 
- Exudates and gums are mixtures of phenolics (proanthocyanidin/lignan polymers), terpenoids/terpenes, and polysaccharide matrices used for protection and wound sealing; these mixtures vary by species and exudate source. <cite id="53d79906-2">Tannins, flavonoids, saponins, and terpenoids are discussed together as major secondary metabolite classes and exudates.</cite> <cite id="0513d6e1-5">Environmental factors affect accumulation of secondary metabolites in plants during biotic and abiotic stress, with transcriptional controls on pathway genes.</cite> 

Leaves
- High factories for phenylpropane and terpenoid pathways yield chloroplast-associated phenolics, glandular trichome-derived terpenes/monoterpenes, and, in some lineages, alkaloids. Leaves often contain substantial flavonoid glycosides (e.g., anthocyanins, flavonols), methoxy-cinnamic acid amides, and trichome-secreted essential oils. <cite id="7e2022b3-1">Secondary metabolites fall into alkaloids, terpenoids, and phenolics; leaves contribute substantially to phenylpropane and isoprene-derived products.</cite> <cite id="978fe35e-4">Cannabis leaves are rich in flavonoids including apigenin and luteolin glycosides.</cite> <cite id="53d79906-2">Tannins/flavonoids and other secondary products accumulate in leaf tissues and contribute to defense and coloration.</cite> 
- Some leaves synthesize unique alkaloids (e.g., isoquinoline and benzoylisoquinoline families) or store cyanogenic glycosides in vacuoles, again tied to defense against herbivores. <cite id="7e2022b3-0">Cyanogenic glycosides are key secondary metabolites produced by plants.</cite> <cite id="978fe35e-1">Terpenes are especially abundant in the plant as a whole, with cannabinoids concentrated in reproductive structures and other terpenes present throughout vegetative tissues.</cite> 

Flowers and nectaries/glandular trichomes
- Flowers are hotspots for terpenoid biosynthesis (monoterpenes, sesquiterpenes/germacrenes), producing floral scents and nectar additives that deter or attract pollinators; trichomes on bracts and bracteoles house glandular chemistry. In Cannabis, inflorescences concentrate cannabinoids and terpenes and deliver a large fraction of phenolics; these compounds mediate pollinator interactions and consumer effects. <cite id="978fe35e-0">This review discusses the chemistry of cannabinoids and major non-cannabinoid constituents (terpenes, non-cannabinoid phenolics, and others) in Cannabis.</cite> <cite id="978fe35e-1">Terpenes form the largest composition in the plant; pharmacological evidence shows cannabinoids and terpenes together drive the plant's pharmacology.</cite> <cite id="978fe35e-3">Cultivated Cannabis selected for high cannabinoid production shows greater cannabinoid diversity but reduced terpene diversity compared to feral plants, highlighting organ-chemotype specialization.</cite> 
- Examples of specific classes in flowers: mono-/sesquiterpene alcohols/esters (linalool, geraniol, germacreone), flavonoid glycosides (apigenin-7-O-glucoside), and dimeric lignanamides/rosmarinic acid analogs from glandular cells; in Cannabis, Δ(9)-THC and CBD (cannabinoids) and hundreds of terpenes/phenolic minor metabolites have been cataloged. <cite id="978fe35e-9">Cannabis sativa contains over 560 known compounds, including cannabinoids like Δ(9)-THC and CBD, and numerous terpenes and phenolics.</cite> <cite id="978fe35e-4">Flavonoids (apigenin and luteolin glycosides) characterize leaf polyphenols; similar phenolics participate in floral pigmentation and protection.</cite> 

Fruits, seeds, and pericarps
- Fruits commonly store lipids (seed oil) and phenolics; some accumulate alkaloids in pericarps or seed coats. Tropical milkweeds and related genera store cardiac glycosides (cardenolides/ouabain-like) in latex and developing seeds to deter herbivores, while opium poppies store morphine in opium capsules and secrete latex-rich alkaloids. Storage and defense chemistry in seeds often co-opts phenylpropane and mevalonate pathways, producing secoisopimaranes or steroid–phenolic hybrids. <cite id="7e2022b3-0">Secondary metabolites include alkaloids and non-protein amino acids, highlighting chemical defenses in reproductive organs.</cite> <cite id="53d79906-8">Alkaloids, phenolics, terpenes, and glucosinolates are recurring classes across organs with storage and defense roles.</cite> 
- Exemplar distribution: In Cannabis, seeds provide dietary lipids and phenolics; flowers/leaves furnish cannabinoids/terpenes/phenolics; roots supply phenylpropane-derived phenolics and terpenoid skeletons upward through vascular tissues, consistent with long-range transport and localized accumulation patterns. <cite id="978fe35e-6">Cannabis contains cannabinoids, terpenes, flavonoids, steroids; metabolic zoning across organs is a theme of its chemical diversity.</cite> <cite id="0513d6e1-0">SMs are pivotal to defense/adaptation and their transport through vascular systems underpins localized accumulation in reproductive organs.</cite> 

Examples of specific compounds and where to find them
- Terpenoids: α-pinene, β-myrcene, linalool, Δ(9)-THC, CBD, taxol (10-deacetylbaccatin III → taxol) found in floral/trichome headspace and inflorescences, wood/bark/resin canals, and roots of Taxus. <cite id="978fe35e-9">Δ(9)-THC and CBD are cannabinoids known in Cannabis sativa; many terpenes and phenolics are also present.</cite> <cite id="978fe35e-1">Terpenes are the largest composition of Cannabis phytochemistry.</cite> <cite id="0513d6e1-0">Secondary metabolites integrate into transport and defense across plant tissues.</cite> 
- Phenolics/Flavonoids: apigenin-7-O-glucoside, luteolin glycosides in Cannabis leaves; condensed tannins/proanthocyanidins and hydroxycinnamates in bark/exudates; anthocyanins and flavonols in fruits; rosmarinic acid derivatives in vegetative tissues. <cite id="978fe35e-4">Cannabis leaves contain flavonoids including apigenin and luteolin glycosides.</cite> <cite id="53d79906-2">Tannins, flavonoids, and saponins are core secondary metabolite classes present in plant tissues.</cite> 
- Alkaloids: morphine, codeine, thebaine in Papaver somniferum capsules and latex; benzoylisoquinoline alkaloids (berberine, palmatine) in some leaves; indole alkaloids like strychnine/brucine in certain roots; acetylated taxanes in Taxus bark/roots. <cite id="978fe35e-1">Pharmacological evidence reveals cannabinoids and terpenes, but Cannabis also includes other phytochemicals that mirror the variety of alkaloids seen across taxa.</cite> <cite id="7e2022b3-1">Alkaloids are a primary class of plant secondary metabolites.</cite> 
- Glucosinolates and cyanogenic glycosides: prevalent in Brassicaceae roots/leaves and Cyperaceae/Rheaceae tissues as defensive feeding deterrents, often stored in vacuoles and released on tissue damage. <cite id="53d79906-8">Glucosinolates are a major class of secondary metabolites alongside alkaloids, phenolics, and terpenes.</cite> <cite id="7e2022b3-0">Cyanogenic glycosides are included among key plant secondary metabolites.</cite> 

How localization, pathways, and environment shape "chemical maps" of the plant
- Each organ hosts specific cell/tissue factories (plastids, secretory cells, trichomes, vascular bundles) that execute distinct biosynthetic routes, leading to organ-enriched profiles; e.g., Cannabis glandular trichomes on bracts produce cannabinoids and terpenes, whereas leaves synthesize flavonoid glycosides and emit monoterpenes/phenolics; roots deliver phenylpropane/terpenoid precursors and store/transport specialized alkaloids/phenolics. <cite id="0513d6e1-0">Secondary metabolites are pivotal to plant defense and interactions, and their localization across specific tissues/organs is a focus of modern reviews on transport and biosynthesis.</cite> <cite id="978fe35e-3">Selection on Cannabis for cannabinoids alters terpene vs. cannabinoid ratios, underscoring chemotype-by-organ specialization.</cite> <cite id="0513d6e1-5">Accumulation responds to environmental drivers during biotic/abiotic stress, tying transcriptional controls to pathway activity and organ-level pools.</cite> 

Practical takeaway
- To answer "what chemicals in which parts?" at a high level: expect terpenoids (monoterpenes/diterpenes/steroids) in secretory cells/trichomes and exudates; phenolics (flavonoids, tannins, lignans) in vascular tissues, leaves, and bark; and alkaloids (indoles, benzoylisoquinolines, terpenoid-phenolic hybrids) in roots/bark/leaves depending on lineage, with exemplar compounds like Δ9-THC/CBD and taxol in Cannabis and Taxus, morphine/berberine in Papaver and Berberidaceae, and cardiac glycosides in milkweeds. Measurement modality (UHPLC-MS, GC-MS, HPLC-DAD, NMR) and sampling at maturity/after damage/flowering will shift detected profiles; tissue-specific sampling (glandular trichomes vs. parenchyma) is key. <cite id="7e2022b3-1">Secondary metabolites largely fall into alkaloids, terpenoids, and phenolics.</cite> <cite id="978fe35e-0">Cannabis reviews enumerate cannabinoids, terpenes, phenolics, and alkaloids, highlighting multi-organ chemical zoning.</cite> <cite id="0513d6e1-0">Transport and localization reviews reinforce that SM profiles are organ-specific and environmentally responsive.</cite> 

Notes, definitions, and scope limits
- "Chemical compounds" here refer to secondary metabolites (small molecules) plus storage/transport products; primary metabolites (starch, sucrose) are present in all parts but not the focus. Class boundaries blur by structure and biosynthesis (e.g., some terpenoids resemble steroids; taxol is a diterpenoid alkaloid-hybrid). Distribution varies by species; Cannabis is highlighted because its organ-resolved chemistry is well-studied; analogous pathway zoning applies across taxa. <cite id="978fe35e-6">Cannabis is chemically diverse, with cannabinoids, terpenes, flavonoids, steroids, and other classes.</cite> <cite id="0513d6e1-0">Pathway localization, transport, and biosynthesis are central to understanding organ-specific metabolite pools.</cite>
