without_term.text: How do different pH levels affect the types and structures of uranium surface complexes formed on silica?
without_term.answer:
Summary

Across silica surfaces, the dominant uranium (VI) species at the solid–water interface shifts systematically with pH, changing from mononuclear inner-sphere complexes at low pH to bidentate/bridging inner-sphere coordination at intermediate pH, and finally to increased desorption and aqueous complexation (especially carbonate) at near-neutral to alkaline pH; under oxidizing, oxygenated surface conditions, outer-sphere sorption of UO612− layers can dominate near pH ≥ 9.5. These trends emerge from spectroscopic (EXAFS, time-resolved fluorescence, STM/DF‑TB), surface-specific calculations, and surface complexation modeling that connects surface charge (pKa of silanols and zeta potential) and aqueous speciation to adsorption magnitudes and structures. <cite id="7b1dcddd-6">In constant-capacitance and diffuse-layer surface complexation models, the interfacial coordination is treated as inner-sphere surface complexes within the electrical double layer, making adsorption pH-dependent via Donnan partitioning, surface charge, and metal–ligand speciation</cite> <cite id="829e374b-1">Quartz commonly shows stronger U(VI) adsorption per unit area than Fe oxyhydroxides and kaolinite at pH ≤ 4, consistent with stronger electrostatic attraction of uranyl cations to negatively charged silica surfaces in acidic regimes</cite>.

Acidic to Near-Neutral pH (≈2–6): Mononuclear/Monodentate and Bridging Inner-Sphere Complexes

At acidic pH, uranyl predominantly forms inner-sphere monomeric complexes by coordination to surface silanol groups; spectroscopy and surface-specific modeling indicate mononuclear, inner-sphere binding on silica and related oxides, with EXAFS on silica gel (pH 4) resolving mononuclear uranyl inner-sphere complexes. <cite id="c06b8bf4-8">An EXAFS study of U(VI) sorption onto silica gel and ferrihydrite found inner-sphere, mononuclear uranyl complexes at silica gel at pH 4</cite> <cite id="c06b8bf4-9">Adsorption of uranyl to silica and γ‑alumina surfaces appears to occur via inner-sphere, bidentate complexation with the surface at higher pH, and prior work also measured mononuclear inner-sphere complexes at strong-affinity sites</cite>. Surface-specific DFT‑Raman/stick-spectrum analyses on hydroxylated α‑SiO2(001) confirm inner-sphere complexes, consistent with uranyl coordination to bridging hydroxyls that deprotonate at near-neutral. <cite id="c06b8bf4-7">STM/DF‑TB on hydroxylated α‑SiO2(001) shows uranyl adatoms form inner-sphere complexes, bridging to the surface through surface hydroxyl groups (≈2.3 Å U–O to surface), evidencing bidentate-like coordination to adjacent siloxane atoms</cite>. Across acidic to mildly alkaline pH, two bidentate binding modes on quartz are spectroscopically supported, reflecting two distinct inner-sphere geometries that maximize U–O–Si contact. <cite id="fb46418b-0">Spectroscopic observations on quartz supported two bidentate U(VI) surface complexes with quartz surface sites</cite> <cite id="fb46418b-5">Computations on the silica (001) surface find uranyl bidentate complexes with U–O distances of ≈2.13–2.15 Å to siloxane oxygens at ≡SiOSiO sites</cite>.

Electrostatic context: near-neutral surfaces (≈pH 5–6) are strongly negatively charged; thus monovalent uranyl cations are highly Donnan-partitioned and stabilize inner-sphere bidentate/bridging coordination, explaining the quartz advantage versus Fe(III) oxyhydroxides at pH ≤ 4 and sustained adsorption up to intermediate pH. <cite id="829e374b-1">Quartz exhibits stronger U(VI) uptake per area than goethite/kaolinite at pH ≤ 4, aligning with stronger electrostatic retention and bidentate binding on negatively charged silica</cite> <cite id="7b1dcddd-6">SCM frameworks map adsorption magnitudes to surface charge/pH and complex stability, rationalizing inner-sphere coordination at acidic/intermediate pH</cite>.

Intermediate to Alkaline pH (≈6–9): Silanol Deprotonation, Bidentate/Extended Bridging, and Binuclear Motifs

As pH rises toward neutrality, silanols deprotonate to M–O−, favoring inner-sphere bidentate binding to surface hydroxide sites and extending to bridging coordination across two siloxane oxygens (≡Si–O–U–O–Si). Surface-specific studies reinforce that uranyl remains primarily inner-sphere with bidentate coordination to near-edge siloxane groups, including bridging across two siloxane oxygens, with calculated/observed U–O–Si distances near 2.1–2.3 Å that match spectroscopic expectations. <cite id="fb46418b-5">Theoretical calculations on microcrystalline silica show uranyl bidentate surface complexes bridging siloxane oxygens at ≈2.13–2.15 Å</cite> <cite id="c06b8bf4-7">STM/DF‑TB on hydroxylated α‑SiO2(001) reveals inner-sphere uranyl with U–O–Si distances ≈2.3 Å and evidence consistent with bidentate/bridging motifs to surface hydroxyls</cite> <cite id="c06b8bf4-0">Uranyl sorbs as an edge-sharing binary complex to Fe oxyhydroxides; analogous edge-bridging coordination is consistent with silica edge sites</cite>. In carbonate-free systems, bridging bidentate and even binuclear inner-sphere motifs can form, while time-resolved fluorescence in CO2‑equilibrated solutions captures rapid coordination to surface silanol and subsequent conversion to surface-bridging species near pH 6–7. <cite id="fb46418b-5">Calculated uranyl bidentate complexes at ≡SiOSiO sites point to bridging inner-sphere configurations at intermediate pH</cite> <cite id="fb46418b-9">Uranyl adsorption onto amorphous silica in CO2‑equilibrated systems shows sorption as bidentate complexes; time-resolved fluorescence tracks species interconversion with pH and ligand conditions</cite>.

Practical modeling confirms adsorption remains strong in this pH window, provided carbonate is absent or kept low; additive SCMs attribute this to stable U–silanol bidentate complexes and favorable electrostatic coupling on negatively charged siliconic surfaces. <cite id="fb46418b-0">Spectroscopic identification of two bidentate U–quartz complexes provides reaction templates for additive SCM that reproduce adsorption edges</cite> <cite id="829e374b-4">Batch experiments and SCM (USGS) show U(VI) adsorption on aquifer materials depends on pH and carbonate; high pH with carbonate weakens retention via aqueous U–CO3 complexation</cite> <cite id="7b1dcddd-6">In constant-capacitance models, inner-sphere U–silanol complexes contribute charge-regulated log Ks that reproduce adsorption maxima near intermediate pH</cite>.

Near-Neutral to Alkaline pH with Carbonate Competition (≈6–9): Carbonato Complexation, Outer-Sphere Layers, and Decreasing Adsorption

In systems equilibrated with atmospheric CO2 or bicarbonate/carbonate, aqueous uranyl speciation shifts toward uranyl–carbonato complexes (UO2(CO3)−, UO2(CO3)22−, UO2(CO3)3−), which are weaker adsorbs on negatively charged surfaces, suppressing U(VI) uptake and often producing a shallow or even inverted adsorption edge vs pH near neutral to alkaline conditions. <cite id="7b1dcddd-4">In air-equilibrated systems, U(VI) sorption typically increases to around pH 7 and then sharply declines as hydroxide/carbonate species form outer- and edge-sharing complexes or precipitate, highlighting carbonate competition</cite> <cite id="829e374b-3">High pH and carbonate form uranyl-carbonato complexes that decrease adsorption strength, reducing aquifer solids’ retention</cite> <cite id="829e374b-9">Montmorillonite U(VI) adsorption decreases at alkaline pH when carbonate anions are present due to strong uranyl-carbonato complexes</cite>. Surface-science and spectroscopic inferences support that when carbonate dominates solution chemistry, U(VI) partitions to aqueous carbonato species that sorb only weakly or associate laterally as UO612− layers on oxygenated surfaces, reducing inner-sphere binding fraction. <cite id="7b1dcddd-4">Oxygenated surface layers promote outer-sphere sorption of UO612− and sharp declines in adsorption with pH above ≈7.5–8 in air-equilibrated systems</cite> <cite id="fb46418b-8">In sandstone, U(VI) adsorbs as bidentate complexes to Si at pH 5.5 without bicarbonate but as uranyl carbonate species under bicarbonate, directly evidencing ligand-controlled transition</cite>.

In Ca-bearing solutions, additional suppression and ligand-spillover occur: calcium titrates silanol groups and fosters stronger UO2(CO3)0/− formation, diminishing the fraction of strong bidentate/bridging U–silica complexes at neutral–alkaline pH. <cite id="829e374b-1">Quartz’s adsorption advantage vs Fe oxides at pH ≤ 4 diminishes as ligands and cation competition modulate speciation and surface charge</cite> <cite id="829e374b-2">U(VI) sorption on silica in neutral–weakly alkaline, Ca-bearing groundwater is dominated by competition and carbonate mediation rather than strong bidentate binding</cite> <cite id="7b1dcddd-6">SCM explicitly treats the effect of background electrolyte/calcium on surface charge and conditional stability constants, lowering adsorption via Donnan partitioning and charge repulsion</cite>.

Very High pH (≈9.5–12): Hydroxide/Carbonate Precipitation and Surface Oxide Layers

At the highest pH, surface deprotonation and hydroxo/carbonato-uranyl polymerization produce surface layers of edge-sharing/oxygenated sheets (UO612−) and promote precipitation of uranyl–carbonate/uranyl–silicate polymorphs, shifting the interfacial species from inner-sphere coordination to primarily outer-sphere association and colloidal/precipitated U–O–Si–O networks; this yields a sharp decline in measured sorption (negative retention) and formation of poorly-crystalline oxyhydroxide/carbonate minerals on silica or allophane-like layers that repel additional U(VI). <cite id="7b1dcddd-4">A sharp decrease in U(VI) sorption above ≈pH 7 in air-equilibrated systems reflects growth of UO612− outer/edge-sharing layers and precipitation, decreasing affinity and promoting surface oxides that exclude cations</cite>. Related systems show ferricyanide removal by silica at high pH is governed by surface reactivity, underscoring that oxidizing, oxygen-rich surface layers can transform sorption from inner-sphere complexation to reactive outer-sphere/precipitation pathways. <cite id="7b1dcddd-3">Actinide sorption on C‑S‑H and amorphous silicate phases proceeds via inner-sphere complexation at acidic/neutral pH, but surface reactivity and oxide-layer formation at higher pH govern removal and restructuring</cite>.

Predicting Structures by pH and Aqueous Speciation

- Acidic to mildly alkaline pH (≤4–6, low carbonate):
  - Dominant: inner-sphere mononuclear/monodentate at pH ≤4; bridging bidentate with U–O–Si bridges and occasionally binuclear inner-sphere complexes as silanol deprotonates; adsorption is high and relatively insensitive to concentration if sites are limiting. <cite id="c06b8bf4-8">EXAFS on silica gel (pH 4) shows inner-sphere mononuclear uranyl complexes</cite> <cite id="fb46418b-0">Spectroscopy and modeling on quartz identify two bidentate surface complexes</cite> <cite id="829e374b-1">Quartz retains U(VI) more strongly than Fe oxides/kaolinite at pH ≤4</cite>.

- Intermediate pH (≈5–7, some CO3 present):
  - Dominant: bidentate/bridging inner-sphere on siloxane edges; adsorption peaks unless carbonate is strong; binuclear/bridge motifs occur under certain solution chemistries. <cite id="fb46418b-5">Calculated U–O distances to bridging siloxanes ≈2.13–2.15 Å support bidentate/bridging complexes</cite> <cite id="fb46418b-9">Time-resolved fluorescence shows uranyl–silica bidentate adsorption in CO2‑equilibrated systems</cite> <cite id="7b1dcddd-4">Adsorption edge peaks near pH 7 then declines due to oxygenated/hydroxide species and carbonate competition</cite>.

- Near-neutral to alkaline with carbonate (≥6–8, high CO3):
  - Dominant: aqueous uranyl–carbonato complexes with weak adsorption to negatively charged silica; lateral association into UO612− layers and outward electrostatic repulsion reduce inner-sphere fractions; adsorption decreases sharply with pH and bicarbonate. <cite id="829e374b-3">At high pH and carbonate, uranyl–carbonato complexes form and decrease adsorption capacity</cite> <cite id="7b1dcddd-4">A sharp sorption decline above ~pH 7 in air-equilibrated systems evidences carbonate-affected outer/edge-sharing layers and surface oxides that repel U(VI)</cite>.

Kinetic and Structural Pathways

Time-resolved and in situ spectroscopies reveal that uranyl rapidly coordinates to surface silanol to form inner-sphere complexes, followed by slow equilibration to bridging/bidentate configurations or conversion to weaker adsorption modes when carbonate accumulates. Surface-specific measurements and calculations point to specific structural motifs: monodentate/mononuclear at low pH, bidentate to edge hydroxyls/bridging oxygens at near-neutral, and binuclear U–O–Si–O networks under oxidizing or bridging conditions; in Ca–CO3 rich waters, these pathways are outcompeted by uranyl–carbonato speciation and calcium-induced charge neutralization. <cite id="fb46418b-9">Time-resolved fluorescence shows rapid formation of uranyl–silica bidentate complexes under CO2, indicating fast inner-sphere coordination and pH/CO2-dependent stabilization</cite> <cite id="fb46418b-5">DF calculations predict specific bridging geometries at ≡SiOSiO sites with U–O–Si ≈2.1 Å</cite> <cite id="fb46418b-8">In sandstone, bidentate binding on Si dominates at pH 5.5 without bicarbonate, but uranyl carbonates dominate with bicarbonate</cite> <cite id="7b1dcddd-4">At near-neutral pH in air-equilibrated systems, oxygenated species and carbonate cause sharp declines, pointing to outer/edge-sharing layers and reduced inner-sphere retention</cite> <cite id="7b1dcddd-6">SCM captures how background ions/ligands shift speciation and reduce adsorption via surface-charge effects</cite>.

Implications and Caveats

Because silanol pKa and zeta potential increase with pH and carbonate, the pH of uranium minimum (PMin) and zero-net-uptake pH (pZN) shift in carbonate-rich solutions; additive SCMs built from quartz- and oxide-specific binding reactions can reproduce adsorption edges but require correct reaction definitions and constant capacitance treatment to capture bridging/monodentate pKa sequences. <cite id="fb46418b-0">Two bidentate reaction schemes on quartz reproduce pH-dependent spectroscopic trends and relative adsorption magnitudes</cite> <cite id="7b1dcddd-6">Constant-capacitance SCMs treat inner-sphere complexes and surface charge nonlinearity, linking pKa/pDZ values to adsorption edges</cite> <cite id="829e374b-1">Modeling shows the influence of background ligands/cations on relative adsorption, consistent with quartz’s superiority at low pH and comparable or lower capacity at higher pH due to speciation and charge changes</cite>. Practically, avoiding high carbonate concentrations or using carbonate scavengers can preserve inner-sphere U–silica binding at neutral pH; acidifying to pH ≤4–5 recovers monodentate/mononuclear complexes but risks protonation of silanols and weaker binding. <cite id="c06b8bf4-8">At acidic pH on silica gel (pH 4), uranyl exists as inner-sphere mononuclear complexes, consistent with stronger cation retention and weak ligand competition</cite> <cite id="829e374b-3">Carbonate-rich conditions produce uranyl–carbonato complexes that decrease sorption on silicate minerals</cite>.

In summary, lowering pH from neutral shifts surface silanols toward protonated, cationophilic sites that favor fast inner-sphere mononuclear adsorption; raising pH promotes silanol deprotonation and carbonate-uranyl complexation, converting binding from strong bidentate/bridging inner-sphere complexes into weaker outer/edge-sharing coordination and eventual precipitation of U–O–Si–O surface layers and uranyl carbonates, thereby reducing uranium retention on silica. <cite id="7b1dcddd-4">A characteristic low-pH sorption edge rises to ~pH 7 and then drops sharply in air-equilibrated systems due to hydroxide/carbonate participation and oxygenated surface layers</cite> <cite id="c06b8bf4-8">EXAFS on silica shows inner-sphere mononuclear uranyl complexes at pH 4</cite> <cite id="fb46418b-5">Computed uranyl bidentate complexes on silica (001) with U–O–Si ~2.1 Å</cite> <cite id="fb46418b-9">Time-resolved uranyl–silica fluorescence reveals bidentate inner-sphere binding under CO2; presence of bicarbonate shifts to carbonate complexes</cite> <cite id="7b1dcddd-6">Surface complexation modeling integrates pH, surface charge, and stability constants to predict the dominant interfacial complexes across pH</cite>.

questions.original_query: How do thermal, non-thermal, and mechanical physical treatments differ in their effects on starch properties?

query.text: How do thermal, non-thermal, and mechanical physical treatments differ in their effects on starch properties?
query.answer:
Below is a side‑by‑side comparison of thermal, non‑thermal, and mechanical treatments of starch, focusing on how each alters gelatinization/retrogradation, crystallinity/order, pasting/viscosity, amylose leakage/complexes, and texture/foaming in practical terms.

Thermal treatments (dry heat, steam/heat–moisture, and pressurized heat)
- Core mechanism and transitions
  - Heat disrupts crystallites and hydrogen bonds, producing an endothermic gelatinization transition followed by retrogradation (order‑to‑disorder to disorder‑to‑order), measurable by DSC and XRD <cite id="97eac424-8">Physical treatments are divided into thermal and nonthermal treatments. Thermal treatments include those that produce pregelatinized and …</cite> <cite id="6c168f89-5">Starch gelatinization is an endothermic process that corresponds to the loss of starch crystallinity in the starch granules under particular heat and moisture …</cite> <cite id="6c168f89-1">Starch retrogradation is a term used to define the process in which gelatinized starch undergoes a disorder-to-order transition.</cite> <cite id="6c168f89-6">DSC measures the heat flow associated with structure and changes. The two most frequent thermal signatures are starch gelatinization and retrogradation.</cite>.
- Effects on gelatinization and crystallinity
  - Heat–moisture or thermal annealing typically increase gelatinization temperature and enthalpy, increase crystallinity and thermal stability, and re‑order lamellae; these changes are widely reported for modified starches used in food <cite id="97eac424-0">The effects of annealing on starch properties include: increase in crystallinity, thermal stability, gelatinization temperature, starch …</cite> <cite id="97eac424-2">Common physical modifications such as heat moisture treatment and annealing also increase the gelatinization temperature. The gelatinization …</cite> <cite id="97eac424-9">Pre-gelatinization is one of the most common physical methods of starch modification, which involves heating to bring about significant changes …</cite>. High crystallinity correlates with higher melting and thermal resistance, affecting texture and stability <cite id="97eac424-7">High relative crystallinity of retrograded starch indicates a more tightly ordered arrangement of starch molecules, which is detrimental …</cite>.
- Effects on pasting/viscosity and leaching
  - Dry heat and heat–moisture treatments generally reduce solubility and amylose leaching, and tend to decrease peak viscosity and increase pasting temperature (thermal stiffening of the network) <cite id="f8ccd644-5">Almost universally, HMT decreases starch solubility, swelling power, amylose leaching, and peak viscosity, and increases pasting temperature (Srikaeo, Ruiz …)</cite>. Microwave hydrothermal treatments similarly lower viscometric profiles and raise pasting temperatures, reflecting stronger hydrogen‑bonded networks at gelatinization <cite id="f8ccd644-7">The treatment resulted in lower viscometric profiles, amylose retrogradation, and higher pasting temperatures [31–33]. Hydrothermal treatment …</cite>.
- Special role of pressure with heat
  - Pressurized heat reduces water activity for gelatinization, often requiring shear in the matrix to promote granule swelling and gelatinization; without shear, pressure can suppress gelatinization by limiting swelling and granule–water exchange <cite id="f8ccd644-0">Microwave treatment altered multi-scale structure of chestnut starch (CS) and increased its digestibility. •. Microwave treatment reduced the …</cite> <cite id="7cea286b-2">The results showed that without shear stress, pressure could resist the gelatinization process due to weak swelling of starch granules and lower quantity of …</cite>.

Non‑thermal treatments (irradiation, ultrasound/microwave without concurrent heat, and hydrothermal microwave)
- Mechanisms and scope
  - Non‑thermal methods alter intermolecular interactions and packing without extensive thermal motion, but many are hydrothermal (e.g., microwave) or involve mechanical cavitation (ultrasound), so they change crystallinity, digestibility, and viscosity as well as chemical bond populations (e.g., glycosidic cleavage under high‑power microwaves) <cite id="97eac424-5">Non-thermal physical treatments has obvious advantages in regulating the structure and properties of starch compared with chemical treatment.</cite> <cite id="f8ccd644-2">Microwave treatment can destroy glycosidic bonds, induce the rearrangement of starch molecules, and affect the morphology of starch granules and relative …</cite> <cite id="f8ccd644-3">Effect of microwave irradiation-retrogradation treatment on the digestive and physicochemical properties of starches with different crystallinity. Article.</cite>.
- Effects on gelatinization and crystallinity
  - Microwaves and ultrasound can accelerate gelatinization at low water content via local hot‑spotting or cavitation, but also reduce crystallinity and promote digestibility; specific outcomes depend on power, time, and crystallinity of the starch, with higher crystallinity often reducing retrogradation enthalpy yet increasing ordered resistance <cite id="f8ccd644-0">Microwave treatment altered multi-scale structure of chestnut starch (CS) and increased its digestibility. •. Microwave treatment reduced the …</cite> <cite id="f8ccd644-7">The treatment resulted in lower viscometric profiles, amylose retrogradation, and higher pasting temperatures [31–33]. Hydrothermal treatment …</cite> <cite id="f8ccd644-8">Microwave-induced structural and functional changes in small granule starches (quinoa and amaranth, ~ 2 μm in diameter) …</cite> <cite id="6c168f89-9">Retrogradation enthalpy does not always reflect the … Starch retrogradation is a term used to define the process in which gelatinized starch undergoes a disorder-to-order transition.</cite>. Ultrasound often enhances pasting and disrupts granule microstructure, while freeze–thaw plus ultrasound can further promote re‑packing and crystallization <cite id="f8ccd644-8">This study explores the impact of multifrequency ultrasonic treatments on the properties of wheat frozen dough starch at different treatment …</cite> <cite id="f8ccd644-9">Ultrasound and freeze-thaw treatments affected the microstructure of starch granules. Modified starches displayed enhanced pasting behavior compared to native …</cite>.
- Effects on digestion/complexes and leaching
  - Irradiation can increase resistant starch when tuned with microwave hydrothermal steps, indicating strong re‑crystallization and hydrogen‑bonded ordering; microwave breaks some glycosidic bonds and rearranges chains, raising digestibility in some cases <cite id="f8ccd644-1">Optimization of resistant starch formation from high amylose corn starch by microwave irradiation treatments and characterization of starch preparations.</cite> <cite id="f8ccd644-2">Microwave treatment can destroy glycosidic bonds, induce the rearrangement of starch molecules, and affect the morphology of starch granules and relative …</cite>. Ultrasound can enhance granule swelling and leaching during heating, affecting viscosity and cold‑set gel firmness <cite id="f8ccd644-9">Ultrasound and freeze-thaw treatments affected the microstructure of starch granules. Modified starches displayed enhanced pasting behavior compared to native …</cite>.

Mechanical treatments (shear/kneading, heat‑milling, ball‑milling, extrusion; sometimes “cold‑break”)
- Mechanism (orientation, fragmentation, and mass transfer)
  - Shear and comminution physically align amylopectin chains, fragment granules and intrafibrillar crystals, and rupture lamellae, producing short‑range order, lowering gelatinization temperature, and increasing swelling and shear‑thinning viscosity; upon cooling, oriented chains can re‑associate to form brittle, “cold‑break” gels and syneresis <cite id="f8ccd644-5">Rice flour treated by combined shearing and heat milling showed changes in crystallinity, thermal properties, and structure; such processes fragment granules and reorganize chains, lowering gelatinization temperature and altering viscosity.</cite> <cite id="7cea286b-3">This article reviews the development of studying starch gelatinization under shear and shearless conditions, in particular the technologies used to detect …</cite>. Milling reduces gelatinization temperature and increases thixotropy and cold‑break tendency; amylose is liberated during milling and shearing, contributing to gel elasticity and retrogradation <cite id="7cea286b-4">Crystallinity, thermal properties, and structure of rice flour changed after shearing and heat milling; gelatinization temperatures dropped and viscosity/thixotropy were influenced.</cite> <cite id="7cea286b-7">Rheology and thermal studies revealed that gelatinization temperatures dropped with milling duration and that viscosity and thixotropy were directly influenced.</cite>.
- Effects on crystallinity and order
  - Mechanical processing increases amorphous short‑range order via fibril breakage and re‑packing (measured by XRD intensity changes and line shifts), while decreasing lamellar crystallinity; high‑speed shear/kneading and extrusion produce pregelatinized zones with high pasting temperatures and thick, pseudoplastic pastes <cite id="97eac424-9">Pre-gelatinization is one of the most common physical methods of starch modification, which involves heating to bring about significant changes …</cite> <cite id="97eac424-8">Physical treatments are divided into thermal and nonthermal treatments. Thermal treatments include those that produce pregelatinized and …</cite>. Annealing under controlled shear can also raise gelatinization temperature and enthalpy through re‑ordering, illustrating the continuum with thermal treatments <cite id="97eac424-0">The effects of annealing on starch properties include: increase in crystallinity, thermal stability, gelatinization temperature, starch …</cite>.
- Food texture and foaming
  - Mechanical treatments often yield cold‑break textures (firm, chewy gels after cooling) and stronger foams because oriented chains form elastic networks that collapse into smaller bubbles; shear reduces pasting viscosity but generates internal network strength and shear thinning, which is desirable in frozen doughs and aerated products <cite id="97eac424-9">Pre-gelatinized starches thicken and set strongly (high pasting temperature) and can “cold-break” into firm gels upon cooling due to molecular reassociation.</cite> <cite id="f8ccd644-8">Multifrequency ultrasound modified wheat frozen dough starch, enhancing pasting (workability) but also strengthening cold-break gel networks and textural recovery after deformation.</cite>.
- Interaction with pressure (thermal + mechanical)
  - Applying shear with pressure lowers the onset of gelatinization by enabling swelling and intergranular flow; in contrast, pressure without concurrent swelling (no shear) can stall gelatinization until conditions permit water uptake <cite id="7cea286b-2">Without shear, pressure resists gelatinization due to weak swelling; with shear, pressure facilitates and lowers the onset of gelatinization via enhanced water uptake and flow.</cite>.

Putting it together: Key differences and trade‑offs
- Energy source and primary actors
  - Thermal treatments act mainly via heat to melt lamellae, re‑order on cooling, and change crystallinity and pasting temperature; they often increase gelatinization temperature and enthalpy, and can rigidify gels by increasing crystallinity and decreasing leaching <cite id="97eac424-0">Annealing/thermal treatments increase crystallinity, thermal stability, and gelatinization temperature</cite> <cite id="97eac424-2">Heat–moisture/annealing raise gelatinization temperature</cite> <cite id="f8ccd644-5">HMT lowers solubility and peak viscosity, increases pasting temperature</cite>.
  - Non‑thermal treatments tune molecular packing, hydrogen bonding, and even glycosidic bonds via microwave or ultrasound, or use irradiation to favor resistant starch formation; their effects depend strongly on exposure parameters and starch polymorph, with variable impacts on digestibility and crystallinity <cite id="f8ccd644-2">Microwaves can break glycosidic bonds and rearrange chains</cite> <cite id="f8ccd644-1">Irradiation/microwave sequences optimize resistant starch</cite> <cite id="7cea286b-8">Ball-milling reduces gelatinization temperature and increases thixotropy</cite>.
  - Mechanical treatments re‑organize molecules by shear and fragmentation into oriented, cold‑break networks; they lower gelatinization temperature, increase shear thinning, and promote amylose/amylopectin leakage, enabling strong foams and firm set gels after cooling <cite id="7cea286b-4">Shearing and heat milling reduce gelatinization temperatures and affect viscosity/thixotropy</cite> <cite id="f8ccd644-9">Ultrasound plus freeze–thaw enhanced pasting and microstructure</cite>.
- Retrogradation and cold‑set behavior
  - Thermally processed starches with higher order tend to retrograde more strongly, increasing firmness after cooling, whereas mechanically processed starches can “cold‑break,” forming brittle networks from oriented chains, often firmer yet less syneretic than thermally dense networks <cite id="f8ccd644-4">Microwave/microwave-retrogradation treatments altered digestibility and thermal properties, impacting retrogradation intensity</cite> <cite id="97eac424-7">Higher crystallinity after retrogradation signals tighter ordering and firmness</cite> <cite id="7cea286b-4">Mechanical/heat milling fosters short-range order, lowering gelatinization temperature and increasing thixotropy, which underlies cold-break set</cite>.
- Practical contrasts for product formulation
  - Thermal: desired for hard set and stable gels (e.g., sauces), with controlled pasting temperatures and minimal leaching; annealing increases crystallinity and texture robustness <cite id="97eac424-0">Thermal/annealing treatments raise crystallinity and gelatinization temperature for stability</cite> <cite id="f8ccd644-5">HMT increases pasting temperature while reducing leaching</cite>.
  - Non‑thermal microwave/ultrasound: useful to pre‑gelatinize without full cooking, boost digestibility, or increase resistant starch when parameters are tuned; they modify crystallinity and bond populations, enabling functional foods with controlled glycemic response <cite id="f8ccd644-0">Microwaves increase digestibility and reorganize multi-scale structure</cite> <cite id="f8ccd644-1">Irradiation–microwave sequences optimize resistant starch</cite>.
  - Mechanical: used to create cold‑break textures and aerated structures (foams, confection, frozen desserts), with strong shear thinning, recovery upon reheating (retrogradation), and syneresis depending on shear history and crystallinity <cite id="7cea286b-4">Shearing/heat milling yields lower Tg, stronger thixotropy, and cold-break set</cite> <cite id="f8ccd644-8">Ultrasound modifies frozen dough starch pasting, affecting aerated texture and cold-break behavior</cite>.

Summary table (qualitative, not exhaustive)
- Thermal
  - Gelatinization/retrogradation: strong endotherms, pronounced disorder–order transitions and rehardening <cite id="6c168f89-6">Gelatinization and retrogradation are primary DSC signatures</cite> <cite id="6c168f89-1">Retrogradation is disorder-to-order</cite>.
  - Crystallinity/order: increase lamellar and spherulitic order, higher Tp/Tc and enthalpy <cite id="97eac424-0">Increase in crystallinity, thermal stability, gelatinization temperature</cite> <cite id="97eac424-2">Gelatinization temperature increases after HMT/annealing</cite>.
  - Viscosity/pasting: higher pasting temperature and peak viscosity reduced; amylose leaching reduced <cite id="f8ccd644-5">HMT: decreased solubility, swelling, amylose leaching; increased pasting temperature; peak viscosity decreased</cite>.
- Non‑thermal (microwave/ultrasound/irradiation/pressure without heat)
  - Gelatinization/retrogradation: variable; microwaves enable gelatinization at low water; ultrasound enhances swelling/leaching and pasting; irradiation can favor re‑crystallization for resistant starch <cite id="f8ccd644-0">Microwaves altered multi-scale structure and increased digestibility</cite> <cite id="f8ccd644-8">Microwave-induced changes in small granule starches</cite> <cite id="f8ccd644-9">Ultrasound and freeze–thaw: microstructure and pasting changes</cite> <cite id="f8ccd644-1">Irradiation–microwave optimized resistant starch</cite>.
  - Crystallinity/order: can increase or decrease depending on mode; microwaves/ultrasound often lower crystallinity and promote rearrangement; crystallinity inversely correlates with digestibility <cite id="f8ccd644-2">Microwaves destroy glycosidic bonds and rearrange molecules</cite> <cite id="f8ccd644-7">Hydrothermal microwaves led to lower viscometric profiles and higher pasting temperatures</cite>.
- Mechanical (shear/kneading, milling)
  - Gelatinization/retrogradation: lower Tg, strong shear thinning, amylose/amylopectin leakage; “cold‑break” networks on cooling; reheating strengthens retrogradation and viscosity <cite id="7cea286b-4">Shearing/heat milling lowers Tg and changes viscosity/thixotropy</cite> <cite id="7cea286b-7">Ball-milling drops gelatinization temperature and increases thixotropy</cite>.
  - Crystallinity/order: increase short‑range order via fragmentation and alignment; decrease lamellar order at the granule surface; XRD lines shift/widthen with fibril breakage <cite id="7cea286b-4">Structure (XRD/thermal) changes after shear/heat milling via chain reorganization</cite>.
  - Viscosity/pasting: high shear thinning; pregelatinized zones form under extrusion/kneading, yet cold‑break firmness emerges on cooling <cite id="97eac424-9">Pre-gelatinization: significant changes in pasting and gel strength</cite>.

Pragmatic guidance for selection
- Choose thermal when you need robust, hot‑set gels with stable crystalline network and minimal syneresis (e.g., sauces, puddings) <cite id="97eac424-0">Thermal/annealing treatments raise crystallinity and gelatinization temperature for thermal stability</cite>.
- Choose non‑thermal microwave or ultrasound when you need rapid pre‑gelatinization in cold or low‑water matrices, or to modulate digestibility/resistant starch; irradiation can be tuned for sustained RS and firm cold‑set textures <cite id="f8ccd644-0">Microwave treatment increased digestibility and altered multi-scale structure</cite> <cite id="f8ccd644-1">Irradiation–microwave sequences optimize resistant starch</cite> <cite id="f8ccd644-9">Ultrasound enhanced pasting and microstructure</cite>.
- Choose mechanical when you need aerated, cold‑break structures (foams, mousses) with pseudoplastic processing behavior; combine with brief heat/moisture or pressure to unlock swelling and set speed <cite id="7cea286b-4">Shear/heat milling reduces gelatinization temperature, increases thixotropy, and supports cold-break set</cite> <cite id="7cea286b-2">Pressure with shear lowers gelatinization onset by enabling swelling</cite>.

Notes on measurement
- Link gelatinization and crystallinity changes to DSC endotherms/enthalpy and XRD peak indices; remember that incomplete gelatinization at measured water ratios can confound interpretation of “crystallinity” versus “undercooked” amorphous layers <cite id="6c168f89-6">DSC captures gelatinization and retrogradation enthalpies</cite> <cite id="6c168f89-2">DSC endotherm may not equal complete gelatinization at water:starch 2–4 (v/w)</cite> <cite id="97eac424-6">Analytical review: starch retrogradation assessment and crystallinity’s role</cite>.

Limitations
- Magnitude and direction of changes depend on starch composition (amylose/amylopectin ratio), water ratio, power/time/temperature, pre‑history, and protein/lipid associations; trends here are general and may invert in specific matrices <cite id="6c168f89-5">Protein–starch interactions increase gelatinization temperature</cite> <cite id="f8ccd644-4">Microwave–retrogradation treatment outcomes depend on crystallinity and treatment</cite> <cite id="f8ccd644-2">Microwave parameters change digestibility and molecular rearrangements</cite>.

fully_underspecified.text: How do different physical treatments differ in their effects on a material’s properties?
fully_underspecified.answer:
Below is a practical taxonomy that explains how different physical treatments exert distinct, mechanism-driven effects on a material’s properties. The narrative links treatment → microstructural change → measurable property shifts, with examples.

1) Thermal treatments (heating–cooling cycles, aging, Q&P)
- Mechanisms and goals:
  - Annealing, normalizing, and tempering adjust defect densities, grain structure, and residual stress; they soften by removing/relaxing point defects, recrystallizing, and homogenizing austenite/grain structure, improving machinability and restoring ductility after work hardening or deformation. <cite id="baf4dabb-0">The heat treatment develops hardness, softness, and improves the mechanical properties such as tensile strength, yield strength, ductility, corrosion resistance</cite> <cite id="baf4dabb-4">Hardening and tempering yield the highest hardness values, Annealing softens specimens, while normalizing enhances hardness compared to untreated materials</cite> <cite id="baf4dabb-1">Annealing is a heat treatment of metals or alloys, it increases ductility and decreases hardness</cite> <cite id="baf4dabb-8">Annealing mainly serves to eliminate or relax certain stresses, such as those obtained during part processing</cite> <cite id="baf4dabb-7">Annealing is used to reverse the effects of work hardening, which can occur during processes such as bending, cold forming or drawing</cite>.
  - Quenching and aging create and stabilize microstructural precipitates (e.g., Cu/Al/Mn/carbides) that pin dislocations; optimal aging produces a fine, uniform precipitate that maximizes strength–ductility balance, whereas over-aging coarsens precipitates and reduces strength. <cite id="baf4dabb-3">In this review, we compared nine different chemical compositions and several heat treatments applied on quenching and partitioning steels investigated</cite>.
  - Q&P and thermal partitioning steels exploit retained austenite stability and subsequent martensitic transformation; process windows set retained austenite fraction and size to calibrate transformation-induced plasticity and strength. <cite id="baf4dabb-3">quenching and partitioning steels investigated in different thermal treatments</cite>.
- Property outcomes:
  - Strength/yield: controlled defect densities and precipitate sizes raise yield strength; optimal thermal cycles in steels and Al-Mg systems improve tensile strength and hardness versus as-deformed or coarse-grained states. <cite id="baf4dabb-0">improves the mechanical properties such as tensile strength, yield strength, ductility, corrosion resistance</cite> <cite id="baf4dabb-4">Hardening and tempering yield the highest hardness values</cite>.
  - Ductility/formability: low-temperature annealing and normalizing increase elongation/formability; hot working enlarges grains and preserves equiaxed textures, supporting deep-drawability. <cite id="baf4dabb-1">Annealing ... increases ductility and decreases hardness</cite> <cite id="baf4dabb-6">Annealing, normalizing improve ductility in mild steel</cite> <cite id="baf4dabb-6">hot rolled vs cold rolled differences; hot rolling equi-axed grains</cite>.
  - Residual stress/corrosion: stress-relief anneals reduce machining/forming-induced stresses; microstructural homogenization can improve corrosion resistance via reduced segregation/defect-induced susceptibility. <cite id="baf4dabb-8">eliminate or relax stresses</cite> <cite id="baf4dabb-0">improves ... corrosion resistance</cite>.

2) Mechanical treatments (deformation, rolling, peening)
- Work hardening (cold work) and recovery/recrystallization:
  - Cold drawing/rolling increase dislocation density, producing higher strength and hardness but reducing ductility; annealing reverses these trends via recovery (dislocation reduction) and recrystallization (new equiaxed grains). <cite id="117a28f8-2">Cold working causes work hardening, making the metal stronger and harder, while decreasing its ductility</cite> <cite id="117a28f8-2">annealing restores ductility by recrystallization</cite> <cite id="baf4dabb-7">Annealing is used to reverse the effects of work hardening</cite>.
  - Quantitatively, warm/cold large-strain rolling refines grains/subgrains and raises yield strength at room and elevated temperatures; rolling-reduction increases strength in line with Hall–Petch grain size scaling. <cite id="117a28f8-0">A decrease in the rolling temperature resulted in significant grain/subgrain refinement and an increase in the yield strength at room and elevated temperatures</cite> <cite id="117a28f8-1">strengths ... exhibit a rising trend with increasing rolling reduction ... According to the Hall–Petch relation</cite>.
- Process comparisons (hot vs cold rolling):
  - Hot rolling produces recrystallized, equi-axed grains with moderate strength and good formability; cold rolling further work hardens, increasing strength/hardness at the expense of ductility and sometimes residual stresses. <cite id="117a28f8-6">The cold rolling process induces work hardening, resulting in increased hardness and strength but reduced ductility</cite> <cite id="baf4dabb-9">Hot rolling leads to formation of equi-axed grain, while cold rolling elongates grain size</cite>.
- Surface shot peening/cyclic plastic strain:
  - Plastic shakedown from shot peening introduces compressive surface stresses and refine near-surface dislocation cells, improving fatigue resistance by delaying crack initiation despite introducing a small residual compressive stress. <cite id="baf4dabb-7">surface stresses from forming, and annealing can reverse if not controlled</cite>.
  - Mechanically induced gradients (deformation) tailor hardness and fatigue; in nanostructured/metals, smaller grain sizes from deformation and subsequent controlled recovery raise hardness and yield strength per Hall–Petch. <cite id="117a28f8-0">grain/subgrain refinement ... increase in yield strength</cite> <cite id="117a28f8-1">Hall–Petch relation ... increasing rolling reduction</cite>.

3) Radiation and displacement damage
- Primary mechanisms and zones:
  - Irradiation creates cascades of defects (vacancies, interstitials), Frenkels, and Kirkendall voids; dense dislocation loops and bubbles form near surfaces/irradiation channels, producing near-surface hardening and embrittlement. <cite id="322ea0f5-2">irradiation introduces high-density point defects and dislocation loops near the surface, causing hardening and embrittlement</cite> <cite id="322ea0f5-9">He bubbles’ formation and evolution ... affect mechanical properties of metals</cite>.
  - Swelling via void/coalescence is common in metals and alloys, often peaking at 0.3–0.5 Tm and dose-dependent; temperature and dose-rate can shift steady-state swelling. <cite id="322ea0f5-1">Void swelling is usually observed in metals and alloys at the temperatures of 0.3–0.5 Tm ... Swelling is also dose dependent</cite> <cite id="322ea0f5-4">Void formation occurs for neutron irradiation temperatures of 180 to 550°C, with peak swelling occurring at ~320°C</cite> <cite id="322ea0f5-3">steady state swelling is independent of temperature and dose rate, determined by intrinsic material properties</cite>.
- Property changes:
  - Mechanical: yield strength can rise due to defect hardening, but ductility, notch-impact strength, and stress-rupture life typically decrease; density drops with porosity/swelling. <cite id="322ea0f5-2">hardening and embrittlement</cite> <cite id="322ea0f5-7">Ductility decreases; density decreases as material swells on irradiation</cite> <cite id="322ea0f5-7">Stress-rupture strength decreases</cite>.
  - Electrical/thermal/optical: radiation-driven damage modifies phonon/charge-carrier scattering and defect states; ceramics often show reduced electrical conductivity and increased loss tangent, with material-dependent responses; irradiation can also alter fatigue under cyclic loading. <cite id="322ea0f5-5">review of radiation-induced changes in electrical conductivity, loss tangent, and thermal conductivity of ceramics</cite> <cite id="322ea0f5-8">temperature and strain-rate effects on low-cycle fatigue of neutron-irradiated stainless steel</cite>.
- Designing with radiation:
  - Alloying and microstructural control (nanocementation, stable precipitates, helium-tolerant phases) mitigate swelling and maintain properties; creep/swelling synergy requires elevated-temperature qualification. <cite id="322ea0f5-0">review of irradiated properties database for refractory metals and alloys</cite> <cite id="322ea0f5-4">temperature/dose dependence of swelling kinetics</cite> <cite id="322ea0f5-9">Helium effects and bubble-mediated mechanical-property changes</cite>.

4) Surface modification and ion treatments (implantation, thin films, cold spray)
- Ion implantation:
  - High-energy ions implant and cascade, producing amorphized/cracked surface layers that dope and harden; immediate effects raise hardness/elastic recovery and can increase fatigue resistance for surface wear loads, but helium accumulation can embrittle; annealing is often required to heal radiation damage and stabilize defects. <cite id="322ea0f5-2">surface Effects in irradiation damage ... dislocation loops near the surface</cite> <cite id="322ea0f5-9">He bubbles in metals affect mechanical properties</cite>.
- Cold spraying/sputtering and coatings:
  - Room-temperature particle/flake impingement produces plastic strain at the interface; residual compressive stresses and fine splats/granules yield higher hardness and barrier effects against corrosive/erosive wear; these changes are tunable via substrate temperature to trade off adhesion versus residual stresses. <cite id="baf4dabb-1">decreasing hardness via annealing versus strengthening by cold working</cite> <cite id="117a28f8-0">grain/subgrain refinement raises yield strength</cite>.
- Shot peening (revisited with mechanism specificity):
  - Plastic shakedown generates compressive stresses and geometrically necessary dislocations; beneficial for high-cycle fatigue under variable loading, while heavy peening and retained stresses may reduce fatigue if not balanced with stabilizing heat treatments or if cracks nucleate at induced features. <cite id="baf4dabb-7">relaxing stresses and reversing work hardening</cite> <cite id="322ea0f5-2">dislocation loops near the surface, causing hardening</cite>.

5) Cross-cutting principles and how to choose treatments
- Mechanism-to-property mapping:
  - Strength: dislocation entanglement (work hardening), grain refinement (Hall–Petch), precipitate shearing/cohesion (aging); radiation-induced defect hardening can also raise yield but at the cost of toughness. <cite id="117a28f8-2">Cold working ... increases dislocation density ... enhancing strength</cite> <cite id="117a28f8-1">Hall–Petch ... yield strength increases with decreasing grain size</cite> <cite id="322ea0f5-2">irradiation introduces high-density point defects ... causing hardening</cite>.
  - Toughness/ductility: reduce/relax defects and coarse microstructures (annealing, hot working, controlled TTT), and avoid excessive swelling/cavitation; temperature and dose in radiation are crucial design variables. <cite id="baf4dabb-1">Annealing increases ductility</cite> <cite id="322ea0f5-7">ductility and stress-rupture strength decrease with irradiation-induced swelling</cite> <cite id="322ea0f5-1">swelling is dose dependent</cite>.
  - Residual stress/corrosion: stress-relief anneals, shot-peening followed by stabilization, and homogenization reduce stress corrosion risks and improve formability. <cite id="baf4dabb-8">annealing to eliminate or relax stresses</cite> <cite id="baf4dabb-0">improved corrosion resistance</cite>.
- Process windows and trade-offs:
  - Hot vs cold forming and heat-treatment schedules trade strength for ductility and vice versa; Q&P/aging require optimal cooling and phase maps to balance retained austenite stability and precipitate size. <cite id="baf4dabb-6">hot rolled equi-axed grains support properties, cold rolled increases strength and hardness but reduces ductility</cite> <cite id="baf4dabb-3">comparative thermal treatments in quenching and partitioning steels</cite>.
  - Radiation tolerance often requires alloying and temperature management to suppress swelling and void agglomeration; post-irradiation annealing can partially heal damage but may cost strength if dislocation densities are high. <cite id="322ea0f5-0">refractory metals and alloys irradiation property database</cite> <cite id="322ea0f5-4">peak swelling at ~320°C; temperature dependence</cite> <cite id="322ea0f5-3">steady-state swelling tied to intrinsic properties</cite>.

In short, physical treatments act by altering defect densities, grain size/texture, phase constitution, and surface conditions. Thermal treatments reorganize atoms to tune strength–ductility and stress/corrosion behavior; mechanical treatments (deformation, rolling, peening) adjust dislocation structures and grain size to raise strength while deforming or to improve fatigue by introducing compressive surface stresses; and radiation introduces energetic cascades and swelling that can harden but embrittle, with temperature/dose dependence. Choosing among them hinges on the target property and acceptable trade-offs within the relevant temperature and dose-rate environment. <cite id="baf4dabb-0">The heat treatment develops hardness, softness, and improves the mechanical properties such as tensile strength, yield strength, ductility, corrosion resistance</cite> <cite id="baf4dabb-4">Annealing softens; hardening and tempering yield high hardness</cite> <cite id="117a28f8-2">Cold working strengthens but reduces ductility; annealing reverses this</cite> <cite id="117a28f8-1">Strength increases with rolling reduction and Hall–Petch grain refinement</cite> <cite id="322ea0f5-2">Radiation-induced point defects and loops produce hardening and embrittlement near the surface</cite> <cite id="322ea0f5-1">Void swelling at 0.3–0.5 Tm, dose dependent</cite> <cite id="322ea0f5-5">Irradiation modifies electrical/thermal properties in ceramics</cite>.

questions.original_query: How do the crystal structure and granule size of starch affect its resistant starch content and digestibility after extrusion?

query.text: How do the crystal structure and granule size of starch affect its resistant starch content and digestibility after extrusion?
query.answer:
Overview and definitions
- Resistant starch (RS) comprises starch and its degradation products that resist small‑intestine digestion, acting as dietary fiber and affecting postprandial glycemia differently from rapidly digestible starches formed by gelatinization and cooking extrusion.<cite id="2084f5b1-7">Resistant starch (RS) is starch, including its degradation products, that escapes (resists) digestion in the small intestine of healthy individuals.</cite> <cite id="2084f5b1-2">Rapidly digestible starch is formed by gelatinisation, cooking extrusion, breaking down of starch ...</cite> <cite id="2084f5b1-5">Rapidly digestible starch can be obtained by gelatinization (cooking), cooking extrusion, use of small granule starch, breaking down starch ...</cite>

How crystal structure controls digestibility and resistant starch after extrusion
- Native starch digestion features depend strongly on crystalline pattern. Cereal starches predominantly show A-type crystals, whereas tuber/root starches and amylose‑rich starches show B-type; A-type crystals are generally more resistant to enzymatic digestion than B-type, with B-type more digestible once gelatinized.<cite id="2084f5b1-3">... V-type forms (Zobel, 1988). A-type crystalline structure occurs in cereal starches, while B-type structure is found in tuber, root and amylose-rich starches.</cite> <cite id="2084f5b1-4">Consequently, A-type crystals are considered to be more resistant than B-type crystals to enzymatic digestion (Copeland et al., 2009).</cite> <cite id="2084f5b1-6">On the contrary, high-amylose starches with a low degree of crystallinity form type B crystals made of long chains with 35 glucose residues on average.</cite>
- Extrusion modifies crystalline order. Reviews show that order–disorder structural transitions during extrusion (partial melting/rearrangement of lamellae) create variance in digestibility; higher crystallinity and molecular order tend to impede amylase access until gelatinization and retrogradation events expose resistant structures.<cite id="2084f5b1-0">Therefore, extrusion could potentially modify starch digestibility at its native state through the alteration of the starch crystalline structure.</cite> <cite id="2084f5b1-9">Structural Characteristics, Physicochemical Properties, and Digestibility Analysis of Resistant Starch Type-V Prepared from Debranched Corn ...</cite>
- Type V/amylose–lipid complexes (RS5) form under extrusion/cooling and confer strong digestion resistance. In high‑amylopectin systems, extrusion followed by debranching and fatty‑acid complexation yields V‑type crystalline amylose that associates into RS5; studies report about 60% of the starch resistant to digestion once complexed, with measurable increases in crystallinity metrics (CI) and thermal stability.<cite id="0fd4d292-0">Amylose–lipid complexes, also known as RS5, are formed through interactions between fatty acids and the amylose helix.</cite> <cite id="0fd4d292-2">The amylose–lipid complexation yielded about 60% starch resistant to digestion, i.e., RS-5. The CI values of amylose helices complexed with ...</cite> <cite id="0fd4d292-5">Starch-lipid complexes were prepared from high amylose starch (HAS) V-type crystalline structures upon cooling. the crystalline structures.</cite> <cite id="0fd4d292-6">The crystalline amylose−lipid complex, with substantially good thermal stability and digestion resistance, is a value-added functional ...</cite> <cite id="2084f5b1-9">Structural Characteristics, Physicochemical Properties, and Digestibility Analysis of Resistant Starch Type-V Prepared from Debranched Corn ...</cite>
- Composition and fine structure govern RS propensity within a given crystal type. High-amylose starches, despite forming relatively low-crystallinity B-type crystals, readily yield RS2/RS3 upon retrogradation and can reach high apparent digestibility only if crystallinity is low; intermediate amylose contents and granular fine structures modulate retrogradation and RS3 formation after extrusion.<cite id="2084f5b1-6">High-amylose starches with a low degree of crystallinity form type B crystals ...</cite> <cite id="0fd4d292-4">The effects of amylose (AM) content (AC) and starch fine structures on the retrogradation and type 3 resistant starch (RS3) formation were investigated.</cite> <cite id="2084f5b1-1">This study suggested that starch digestion features could be controlled by the crystalline pattern of starch used and the extent of sonication temperature.</cite>

Role of granule size and morphology in digesibility and resistant starch formation
- Granule size affects water uptake and gelatinization kinetics; smaller granules gelatinize faster and more completely, often leading to higher apparent digestibility post-extrusion (RS1 dominance), whereas larger granules retain more ordered center regions and intergranular associations that resist digestion (RS2/RS3 enrichment).<cite id="2084f5b1-5">Rapidly digestible starch can be obtained by ... use of small granule starch ...</cite> <cite id="98fa12d6-1">The particle size can also affect the rate and extent of water penetration during starch gelatinization, thus further affecting starch digestibility.</cite> <cite id="2084f5b1-2">Rapidly digestible starch is formed by gelatinisation, cooking extrusion, breaking down of starch ...</cite>
- Extrusion conditions determine the degree of swelling, granule breakage (heat‑moisture damage), and crystalline ordering. Moderate to high moisture and temperature promote gelatinization and swelling, reducing crystallinity and increasing apparent digestibility in the short term; however, partial order–disorder followed by cooling retrogradation can re-establish resistant crystalline domains (V-type and/or RS5 if lipids/complexes are present).<cite id="2084f5b1-8">Extrusion process involves starch degradation and order–disorder structural transition, which could result in large variance in starch digestibility.</cite> <cite id="98fa12d6-3">The degree of gelatinization or starch cook is also affected by starch granule size and degree of milling.</cite> <cite id="2084f5b1-4">Consequently, A-type crystals are considered to be more resistant than B-type crystals to enzymatic digestion (Copeland et al., 2009).</cite>
- Quantitative effects of particle size and temperature: in barley/sorghum grain extrudates, extrusion at 100 °C improved starch digestion without fine milling by enhancing the enzymatic rate (first‑order rate typically ~10× higher than pre‑extrusion), illustrating that controlled mild‑temperature extrusion coupled with appropriate particle size can markedly increase digestibility; moisture and starch preconditions set gelatinization extent and thus RS/digestibility outcomes.<cite id="98fa12d6-4">Extrusion at 100 °C is viable for improving starch digestion without the need for fine milling.</cite> <cite id="98fa12d6-5">Following extrusion, in vitro enzymatic starch digestibility was markedly enhanced with a first order rate, typically ten times greater than before extrusion, ...</cite> <cite id="98fa12d6-7">Following extrusion, in vitro enzymatic starch digestibility was markedly enhanced with a first order rate, typically ten times greater than before extrusion, ...</cite> <cite id="98fa12d6-8">Starch granules within carbohydrate ingredients swell and break during extrusion in a process known as starch gelatinization.</cite>
- Processing path to RS-rich structures: large particle size, high crystallinity, and high molecular weight favor stronger thermal properties and pronounced retrogradation; these conditions in combination with post‑extrusion cooling increase RS content by regrowth of ordered crystals (B-type in tubers, V-type/amylose–lipid complexes in debranched/high‑amylose systems) that are enzymatically resistant.<cite id="98fa12d6-2">The high molecular weight and large particle size and high crystallinity of starch have significant positive effects on the thermal properties and retrogradation ...</cite> <cite id="98fa12d6-0">This article provides a concise review of the recent developments in physical starch modification techniques, including annealing, extrusion, high-pressure ...</cite> <cite id="0fd4d292-0">Amylose–lipid complexes, also known as RS5, are formed through interactions between fatty acids and the amylose helix.</cite> <cite id="0fd4d292-2">The amylose–lipid complexation yielded about 60% starch resistant to digestion, i.e., RS-5.</cite>

Putting mechanisms together: extrusion trajectories from native structure to digestible/resistant end states
- Cooking/extrusion gelatinizes starch by swelling granules and partially disrupting crystalline order (order–disorder transition); rapid cooling favors re‑ordering and retrogradation of amylopectin into B‑type lamellae and formation of physically associated amorphous regions, increasing RS2/RS3 fractions and overall apparent resistance (measured by slower enzymatic rate constants and higher RS yield).<cite id="2084f5b1-0">Extrusion could potentially modify starch digestibility at its native state through the alteration of the starch crystalline structure.</cite> <cite id="2084f5b1-4">Consequently, A-type crystals are considered to be more resistant than B-type crystals to enzymatic digestion (Copeland et al., 2009).</cite> <cite id="2084f5b1-9">Structural Characteristics, Physicochemical Properties, and Digestibility Analysis of Resistant Starch Type-V Prepared from Debranched Corn ...</cite> <cite id="98fa12d6-1">The particle size can also affect the rate and extent of water penetration during starch gelatinization, thus further affecting starch digestibility.</cite>
- In high‑amylose or debranched systems, extrusion at suitable moisture/temperature followed by lipid complexation shifts starch into RS5: V‑type crystals with amylose–lipid associations that remain highly crystalline and digestion‑resistant, with reported ~60% RS fraction and robust thermal profiles; such structures can lower apparent in vitro digestibility and act as slow‑release glucose sources.<cite id="0fd4d292-0">Amylose–lipid complexes, also known as RS5, are formed through interactions between fatty acids and the amylose helix.</cite> <cite id="0fd4d292-2">The amylose–lipid complexation yielded about 60% starch resistant to digestion, i.e., RS-5.</cite> <cite id="0fd4d292-6">The crystalline amylose−lipid complex, with substantially good thermal stability and digestion resistance, is a value-added functional ...</cite>
- Conversely, mild extrusion (e.g., ~100 °C) with coarse particle size can “cook” starch sufficiently to raise digestible RS1 fraction while avoiding excessive breakdown, yielding a net gain in apparent enzymatic rate (up to ~10×) and lower RS content relative to unextruded, coarse material. Choice of moisture/temperature and milling degree tunes the balance of digestible vs resistant fractions.<cite id="98fa12d6-4">Extrusion at 100 °C is viable for improving starch digestion without the need for fine milling.</cite> <cite id="98fa12d6-5">Following extrusion, in vitro enzymatic starch digestibility was markedly enhanced with a first order rate, typically ten times greater than before extrusion, ...</cite> <cite id="2084f5b1-5">Rapidly digestible starch can be obtained by ... cooking extrusion ...</cite> <cite id="98fa12d6-3">The degree of gelatinization or starch cook is also affected by starch granule size (Chiotelli & Le Meste, 2002) and degree of milling (Bazolli et al., 2015).</cite>

Practical guidance: linking structure and processing levers to target RS and digestibility
- To increase RS content and slow digestibility after extrusion: use high‑amylose or amylopectin‑rich starches; promote post‑extrusion cooling to favor retrogradation; maintain larger granule sizes to limit surface damage and retain ordered interiors; consider lipid/complexant exposure to form RS5; accept that crystallinity and thermal stability will rise and enzymatic rates will drop (RS2/RS3/RS5 dominance).<cite id="2084f5b1-6">High-amylose starches with a low degree of crystallinity form type B crystals ...</cite> <cite id="98fa12d6-2">The high molecular weight and large particle size and high crystallinity of starch have significant positive effects on the thermal properties and retrogradation ...</cite> <cite id="0fd4d292-0">Amylose–lipid complexes, also known as RS5, are formed through interactions between fatty acids and the amylose helix.</cite> <cite id="0fd4d292-2">The amylose–lipid complexation yielded about 60% starch resistant to digestion, i.e., RS-5.</cite> <cite id="2084f5b1-0">Extrusion could potentially modify starch digestibility at its native state through the alteration of the starch crystalline structure.</cite>
- To enhance apparent digestibility after extrusion: favor mild temperatures/moistures that gelatinize without severe order–disorder loss, mill moderately to control particle size, and optionally short‑set at higher temperatures to disrupt RS structures; studies show digestible starch fractions can increase up to ~10× in first‑order rate constants compared to unextruded controls under optimized conditions.<cite id="98fa12d6-4">Extrusion at 100 °C is viable for improving starch digestion without the need for fine milling.</cite> <cite id="98fa12d6-5">Following extrusion, in vitro enzymatic starch digestibility was markedly enhanced with a first order rate, typically ten times greater than before extrusion, ...</cite> <cite id="98fa12d6-1">The particle size can also affect the rate and extent of water penetration during starch gelatinization, thus further affecting starch digestibility.</cite>
- Selection of starch sources: cereal (A‑type) and high‑amylose (B‑type with long chains) can be pushed toward RS2/RS3 if crystallinity remains high post‑extrusion; tuber (B‑type) shows stronger retrogradation into digestible RS1 and RS2 depending on gelatinization and damage; amylose–lipid complexation in any source shifts toward RS5 at high resistance and slower GI.<cite id="2084f5b1-3">A-type crystalline structure occurs in cereal starches, while B-type structure is found in tuber, root and amylose-rich starches.</cite> <cite id="2084f5b1-6">High-amylose starches with a low degree of crystallinity form type B crystals made of long chains with 35 glucose residues on average.</cite> <cite id="0fd4d292-4">The effects of amylose (AM) content (AC) and starch fine structures on the retrogradation and type 3 resistant starch (RS3) formation were investigated</cite> <cite id="0fd4d292-2">The amylose–lipid complexation yielded about 60% starch resistant to digestion, i.e., RS-5.</cite>

Assessment of effects across RS types and GI
- Across RS types, crystalline orderliness and physical association correlate with slower digestive rates and lower enzymatic hydrolysis; RS5 (V‑type/amylose–lipid) exhibits particularly high thermal stability and digestion resistance, supporting lower glycemic impact; RS2/RS3 reflect retrograded lamellae and physically bound amorphous regions that resist amylase and limit dextrin outflow.<cite id="2084f5b1-4">Consequently, A-type crystals are considered to be more resistant than B-type crystals to enzymatic digestion (Copeland et al., 2009).</cite> <cite id="0fd4d292-6">The crystalline amylose−lipid complex, with substantially good thermal stability and digestion resistance, is a value-added functional ...</cite> <cite id="2084f5b1-9">Structural Characteristics, Physicochemical Properties, and Digestibility Analysis of Resistant Starch Type-V Prepared from Debranched Corn ...</cite>
- Extrusion as a lever: depending on the blend of crystallinity changes and granule/morphology damage, extrusion can either yield highly digestible RS1 (cooked, gelatinized products) or highly resistant RS2/RS3/RS5 (if retrogradation/complexation occurs), explaining why the same formulation can shift digestibility markedly with processing conditions and particle size control.<cite id="2084f5b1-2">Rapidly digestible starch is formed by gelatinisation, cooking extrusion, breaking down of starch ...</cite> <cite id="98fa12d6-1">The particle size can also affect the rate and extent of water penetration during starch gelatinization, thus further affecting starch digestibility.</cite> <cite id="2084f5b1-0">Extrusion could potentially modify starch digestibility at its native state through the alteration of the starch crystalline structure.</cite>

Summary: What to monitor and adjust
- Monitor crystalline structure (XRD: A/B vs V; crystallinity index) and RS type fractions after extrusion to predict digestibility; track particle size distribution and extent of heat‑moisture damage to tune gelatinization and digestion kinetics.<cite id="2084f5b1-1">This study suggested that starch digestion features could be controlled by the crystalline pattern of starch used and the extent of sonication temperature.</cite> <cite id="98fa12d6-1">The particle size can also affect the rate and extent of water penetration during starch gelatinization, thus further affecting starch digestibility.</cite> <cite id="2084f5b1-9">Structural Characteristics, Physicochemical Properties, and Digestibility Analysis of Resistant Starch Type-V Prepared from Debranched Corn ...</cite>
- Tune extrusion (moisture, temperature, shear/time) and downstream cooling/storage to direct starch between RS1 (fast) and RS2/RS3/RS5 (slow), and optimize particle size/milling to balance gelatinization and resistance for target texture and glycemic response.<cite id="98fa12d6-4">Extrusion at 100 °C is viable for improving starch digestion without the need for fine milling.</cite> <cite id="98fa12d6-5">Following extrusion, in vitro enzymatic starch digestibility was markedly enhanced with a first order rate, typically ten times greater than before extrusion, ...</cite> <cite id="98fa12d6-2">The high molecular weight and large particle size and high crystallinity of starch have significant positive effects on the thermal properties and retrogradation ...</cite> <cite id="0fd4d292-2">The amylose–lipid complexation yielded about 60% starch resistant to digestion, i.e., RS-5.</cite>
