questions.original_query: How do temperature and pressure affect the process of mineral carbonation and the efficiency of CO₂ storage in tholeiitic basalts?

query.text: How do temperature and pressure affect the process of mineral carbonation and the efficiency of CO₂ storage in tholeiitic basalts?
query.answer:
Summary
Basaltic and tholeiitic rocks weather or react with injected CO₂ to form stable Mg– and Fe–carbonate minerals via dissolution–carbonation of olivine and pyroxene, producing magnesite, calcite, and dolomite; reaction rates and extents are strongly coupled to temperature, pressure (pCO₂), mineral surface area/texture, and fluid chemistry. <cite id="93fa15db-0">CO₂ dissolves in water to form carbonic acid that reacts with olivine, pyroxenes, and feldspars in basalt</cite><cite id="93fa15db-1">The H+ in water interacts with olivine, pyroxene, and plagioclase to release divalent cations for carbonate formation</cite><cite id="93fa15db-2">Analyses of basalts show mineral assemblages, textures, and compositions that efficiently allow rapid carbonate precipitation</cite><cite id="93fa15db-9">Mechanisms include in situ reaction of CO₂ with peridotite and basalt to form solid carbonate minerals</cite>.

Temperature: Kinetics, Equilibria, and Assemblages
At low to ambient temperatures, carbonation is diffusion- and interface-controlled, and rates increase with elevated temperature and reactive surface area; mechanochemical activation (grinding) dramatically accelerates olivine carbonation by exposing fresh faces and creating active sites. <cite id="481152c0-0">Enhanced olivine carbonation within basalt increased overall carbonation by ~40× compared to single-phase experiments, attributable to chemical/texture differences and increased reactivity</cite><cite id="481152c0-5">Kinetics are slow unless reactants are ground to powder, heat-treated, and held at elevated pressure and temperature, or pre-treated to increase reactivity</cite><cite id="481152c0-9">Activation energies on the order of 85–90 kJ mol−1 for magnesite precipitation indicate strong thermal activation of carbonation at crustal temperatures</cite>. Serpentinization of olivine in the 30–300 °C range consumes CO₂ and produces H₂, with rates and extents dependent on temperature and pressure, underscoring the competition between carbonation and serpentinization pathways. <cite id="481152c0-4">Serpentinization of olivine shows reduction of CO₂ at 300 °C and 500 bar, indicating substantial carbon loss as H₂ under ultramafic conditions</cite>.

Tholeiitic compositions (olivine- and pyroxene-rich) host rapid carbonation upon CO₂ hydration, consistent with in situ observations of fast carbonate formation across basalt suites; olivine proportion and vesicular texture modulate rates. <cite id="93fa15db-2">Basalts analyzed exhibit mineral textures and compositions enabling fast carbonate precipitation</cite><cite id="93fa15db-0">Carbonation occurs via CO₂-to-carbonic acid attack on olivine and pyroxene</cite><cite id="93fa15db-1">Release of divalent cations from olivine/pyroxene and plagioclase underpins carbonate formation</cite>. Field and modeling studies indicate that increasing temperature generally accelerates reaction kinetics and can push systems toward more complete carbonation, although competing serpentinization and retrograde reactions may modify the carbonate assemblage at higher P–T. <cite id="56b6fc95-0">Carbonation of ultramafic rocks proceeds via reaction networks whose selection depends on factors including temperature and pressure</cite><cite id="56b6fc95-2">Calcite, magnesite, and dolomite occupy distinct stability fields at elevated temperature and pressure</cite>.

Pressure and CO₂ Concentration: Reaction Extent and Efficiency
Carbonation extent and efficiency are highly sensitive to CO₂ fugacity and hydrostatic pressure because dissolution–carbonation is driven by carbonate–bicarbonate equilibria. Injection or occurrence of high-pressure CO₂ increases carbonate formation efficiency by orders of magnitude compared to low pCO₂ settings. <cite id="93fa15db-5">CO₂ injection at 100 bar partial pressure increases the efficiency of carbonation by 350–370×, approaching near-complete carbonation</cite>. Because reaction rates scale with surface area and aqueous CO₂ speciation, enhancing reactive surface area and raising CO₂ partial pressure strongly co-stimulate kinetics and conversion, which is why crushed basalt and heat/pressure stimulation improve outcomes. <cite id="481152c0-0">Basalt carbonation enhanced ~40× versus single minerals by ~40×, consistent with reactive surface area and textural controls</cite><cite id="481152c0-5">Raising temperature and pressure and increasing surface area accelerate kinetics and reaction extent</cite><cite id="481152c0-4">Serpentinization pathways also shift with temperature/pressure, with CO₂ reduction to H₂ documented at 300 °C and 500 bar</cite>.

At depth, increasing burial pressure (tens of MPa) raises carbonate stability fields and often favors magnesite/dolomite relative to calcite, which improves long-term storage security; however, elevated temperature can promote retrograde metamorphic reactions that consume carbonates or release CO₂. <cite id="56b6fc95-2">Elevated T–P shifts stability among calcite, magnesite, and dolomite, with phase fields dictating which carbonates persist</cite><cite id="56b6fc95-0">Carbonation reaction paths vary with P–T and fluid composition, affecting net CO₂ retention</cite>. Laboratory and kinetic analyses support that magnesite precipitation is kinetically activated and thermally activated, implying that warming can both accelerate carbonation and stabilize carbonates once formed, though kinetic barriers and fluid transport remain rate-limiting under cool, low-activity conditions. <cite id="481152c0-9">Activation energies of ~85–90 kJ mol−1 for magnesite precipitation indicate strong thermal control on carbonation kinetics</cite><cite id="481152c0-5">Elevated temperature and pressure are often required to achieve practical carbonation rates</cite>.

Mineral Assemblage and Tholeiite-Specific Notes
Tholeiitic basalts typically contain olivine plus plagioclase/pyroxene; olivine dominates Mg supply while pyroxene and feldspar supply Fe and Ca, enabling magnesite, iron carbonates, and calcite/dolomite depending on fluid composition and redox. Reaction path modeling and field evidence show that under CO₂-rich, warm, and reactive conditions, basaltic and ultramafic systems can approach near-complete carbonation to stable Mg/Fe carbonates given sufficient time and mass transfer. <cite id="93fa15db-5">At 100 bar pCO₂, carbonation efficiency increases 350–370× toward near-complete conversion</cite><cite id="56b6fc95-0">Reaction selection (olivine→carbonate vs serpentinization→carbonate) depends on T–P–chemistry controls</cite><cite id="93fa15db-1">Olivine, pyroxene, and plagioclase all contribute cations to carbonate formation</cite>. Texture matters: vesicles and secondary carbonates can nucleate preferentially, and reactive fines accelerate rates; phase identification indicates that Mg–carbonates often form readily on basalt surfaces. <cite id="93fa15db-8">Trigonal carbonates (e.g., hydromagnesite) precipitate more readily on crystalline surfaces than on glassy ones, offering implications for ultramafic and basalt carbonization</cite><cite id="93fa15db-2">Rapid carbonate precipitation is enabled by favorable mineral assemblage, texture, and composition in basalts</cite>.

Storage Efficiency and Durability: Trapping Mechanisms and Security
CO₂ injected into basalt primarily partitions into three fractions: residual gas (solubility trapping), structural trapping in pores/fractures, and mineral (carbonate) trapping; the carbonate reaction ultimately provides permanent storage. <cite id="bec96790-2">Solubility trapping prevents buoyant CO₂ from forming, reducing leakage risk; mineral precipitation then locks CO₂ in carbonate minerals</cite>. Because basalts and peridotites are abundant and reactive, global CO₂ mineralization potential is large, with basaltic rocks cited to store on the order of 10^5–10^6 Gt of CO₂ via mineral carbonation, depending on extent and quality of basalt provinces. <cite id="bec96790-0">Basaltic rocks can store 100,000 to 250,000 gigatons of CO₂ via mineral carbonation</cite>. Field deployments and reviews emphasize that wettability, permeability, and mineralogical reactivity regulate trapping efficiency and displacement during injection, making engineered basalt reservoirs viable where reactive pore water and fractures are present. <cite id="bec96790-1">CO₂ trapping efficiency in basalts is controlled by both geochemical reactivity and reservoir wettability</cite><cite id="bec96790-3">Injecting CO₂ into porous basalt is identified as a promising technique for safe and fast geological storage</cite><cite id="bec96790-4">Mineral trapping converts Ca–Mg–Fe cations in solution into solid carbonates within a saline, closed reservoir system</cite>.

Integrated Implications for Tholeiitic Basalts
- Temperature. Ambient-to-moderate increases boost CO₂ hydration and carbonate formation kinetics; olivine carbonation activation barriers (~85–90 kJ/mol) mean that warming by 50–100 °C markedly increases rates, while serpentinization pathways may consume CO₂ and produce H₂ at higher temperatures, altering net storage. <cite id="481152c0-9">Magnesite-precipitation activation energies around 85–90 kJ/mol imply strong thermal activation</cite><cite id="481152c0-5">Heat-treatment and elevated temperature increase carbonation rates</cite><cite id="481152c0-4">Serpentinization reduces CO₂ at 300 °C and 500 bar</cite>. Mechanically activated or finely disseminated olivine/pyroxene in tholeiite further accentuates temperature sensitivity by enlarging interfacial area and lowering kinetic barriers. <cite id="481152c0-0">Enhanced olivine carbonation in basalt by ~40× relative to single-phase tests demonstrates interfacial and textural sensitivity</cite>.
- Pressure (and pCO₂). Doubling hydrostatic pressure and maintaining high pCO₂ dramatically increases aqueous CO₂ speciation and reaction driving force, with modeled multipliers of 350–370× in carbonation efficiency and near-complete carbonation under 100 bar pCO₂; in tectonically quiescent basalt, such pCO₂ and pressures favor carbonate stability and slow retroaction. <cite id="93fa15db-5">At 100 bar partial pressure, carbonation efficiency rises 350–370× and approaches complete carbonation</cite><cite id="56b6fc95-2">Carbonate stability fields shift with P–T, favoring magnesite/dolomite at higher pressures</cite>. However, elevated pressures can also drive retrograde reactions and phase transitions, modulating porosity and permeability; thus, storage zone design must manage confining stress and thermal regimes. <cite id="56b6fc95-0">Carbonation reaction paths vary with pressure and temperature, governing net CO₂ retention</cite>.
- Mineralogy. Tholeiitic olivine and clinopyroxene supply Mg/Fe, enabling stable magnesite and iron carbonates; Ca from plagioclase supports calcite/dolomite. Fast in situ carbonation observed in basalts indicates favorable nucleation sites and transport pathways; textural alteration (e.g., hydromagnesite precipitation on crystalline surfaces) further improves efficiency. <cite id="93fa15db-9">In situ carbonation of basalt/peridotite forms solid carbonates</cite><cite id="93fa15db-2">Rapid carbonate precipitation arises from favorable mineral assemblage and texture</cite><cite id="93fa15db-8">Trigonal carbonates preferentially precipitate on reactive surfaces, aiding carbonization</cite>.
- Storage durability. Once precipitated, Mg/Fe carbonates reside within the rock framework or as secondary minerals, conferring geological permanence; solubility trapping first suppresses free gas migration, then mineral trapping ensures long-term security. <cite id="bec96790-2">Solubility and mineral trapping minimize leakage risk and ensure CO₂ permanence</cite><cite id="bec96790-5">Basalt carbonation facilitates rapid mineral trapping and effective storage</cite>. Broader assessments attribute vast global capacity to these basaltic provinces because of their extent and reactivity, though site-specific mineralogy and reservoir properties determine local efficiency. <cite id="bec96790-0">Global basaltic CO₂ mineralization potential is on the order of 10^5–10^6 Gt</cite><cite id="bec96790-1">Trapping efficiency depends on mineralization and wettability, which vary by locality</cite>.

Design and Operational Takeaways
- For engineered CO₂ injection into tholeiitic basalts, target warm, water-rich zones with reactive fines or induced fractures to raise pCO₂ and surface area, leveraging kinetic and equilibrium gains; maintain confining pressure to preserve trapping and avoid retrograde destabilization. <cite id="481152c0-5">Heat-treatment and elevated pressure/temperature accelerate olivine carbonation</cite><cite id="93fa15db-5">Elevated pCO₂ at 100 bar increases carbonation efficiency by 350–370×</cite><cite id="56b6fc95-2">Phase stability shifts with pressure and temperature, guiding mineral assemblage selection</cite>.
- Expect rapid early-time mineralization and diminishing returns as porosity and reactive surfaces deplete; continuous CO₂ supply, thermal maintenance, or hydraulic stimulation can sustain conversion. <cite id="93fa15db-2">Basalts exhibit efficient fast carbonate precipitation, consistent with rapid early mineralization</cite>.
- Risk management focuses on avoiding conditions that promote desorption or retrograde reactions; monitoring for fluid chemistry, temperature, and mineral assemblage shifts (magnesite/dolomite vs calcite prevalence) informs longevity. <cite id="56b6fc95-0">Reaction path selection and net CO₂ retention are sensitive to T–P–chemistry</cite>.

Bottom line: Tholeiitic basalts readily carbonize injected CO₂ to stable carbonates when temperature and pressure are conducive; higher temperatures increase kinetic rates and shift equilibria toward carbonate formation and stability, while elevated pCO₂ and confining pressures dramatically increase extents of reaction and secure long-term storage. The most efficient and permanent storage arises where reactive surfaces persist and carbonate stability fields encompass the burial P–T, with engineered strategies exploiting heat, pressure, and fine-scale reactive interfaces to push near-complete carbonation kinetics. <cite id="481152c0-0">Mechanochemical and textural enhancements dramatically accelerate olivine carbonation in basalt</cite><cite id="93fa15db-5">Raising CO₂ partial pressure by 100 bar boosts carbonation efficiency 350–370×</cite><cite id="93fa15db-2">Rapid carbonate precipitation in basalts evidences efficient carbon storage</cite><cite id="56b6fc95-2">Carbonate stability and reaction pathways depend on temperature, pressure, and phase fields</cite><cite id="bec96790-2">Solubility and mineral trapping minimize leakage risk, enabling long-term CO₂ security in basalt</cite>.

fully_underspecified.text: How do temperature and pressure affect a process and the efficiency of CO₂ storage in rocks?
fully_underspecified.answer:
# Overview: CO₂ in Rocks, the Storage Process, and Efficiency

Geological CO₂ storage delivers CO₂ to a reservoir (typically saline aquifers or basaltic formations) where it is trapped by a combination of structural, dissolution (solution), and mineral (carbonate) mechanisms; residual trapping may also contribute in shallow settings or near wells and faults <cite id="c26f773b-1">The CO2 trap mechanisms during carbon capture and storage (CCS) are classified into structural, residual, solution, and mineral traps.</cite>. Mineral trapping yields the most permanent form of storage, converting dissolved CO₂ into carbonates and eliminating long‑term leakage risk <cite id="c26f773b-2">Mineralization is the most stable form of CO2 trapping mechanism that can provide permanent storage on geological timescales, eliminates long-term leakage ...</cite>. Efficiency depends on how much is stored versus released via migration or outgassing and how quickly permanent conversion occurs, modulated strongly by temperature and pressure via phase behavior, solubility, and reaction kinetics <cite id="c26f773b-3">The efficiency of solubility trapping is influenced by several reservoir parameters, including temperature, pressure, brine salinity, and rock ...</cite>.

# Temperature Effects

Phase and transport. Below and above the critical point, CO₂ shows distinct phases and viscosities, which govern how easily it can be injected and how it migrates and spreads. CO₂ becomes supercritical above ~31.1 °C and ~73.8 bar, enabling dense slurry-like behavior useful for immobilization and sweep efficiency; below the triple point (~−56.6 °C at 5.18 bar), liquid CO₂ cannot exist and handling requires slurry or pipeline conditioning <cite id="01d52abe-2">Carbon dioxide transitions to supercritical phase occur relatively readily at the critical points of 7.38 MPa, 304 K/31.1 °C and 73.8 bar.</cite> <cite id="01d52abe-9">The triple point of CO₂ (5.18 bar, −56.6 °C) defines the minimum pressure at which liquid CO2 can exist.</cite>. Operationally, deep formations (>~31.1 °C) favor supercritical CO₂ injection to avoid “dry‑out” and injectivity loss during cold plume advance, while shallow or cold settings risk partial condensation and blockage unless pressures exceed the saturation vapor pressure locally <cite id="01d52abe-8">Injection of CO2 requires storage which provides sufficient depth, hence, temperature and pressure exceed the CO2 critical point (T ~ 31.1 oC; P ~ 73 Bar),...</cite>.

Solubility and dissolution trapping. Higher temperatures lower CO₂ solubility in brine and pore water; for a fixed temperature, CO₂ solubility increases with pressure, and across reservoir conditions both effects combine to determine dissolution capacity and plume advance speed. Laboratory and modeling studies consistently show that increasing pressure raises solubility at constant temperature; lowering temperature likewise increases solubility at constant pressure, and these combined dependencies strongly affect solution trapping efficiency in saline aquifers <cite id="01d52abe-0">Figure 1 shows how CO2 solubility in brine increases with pressure at a constant temperature of 323K and brine salinity of 1 mol NaCl/kg brine.</cite> <cite id="01d52abe-3">greater pressure and lower temperatures increases solubility in the mixing vessel. Due to ...</cite> <cite id="c26f773b-3">The efficiency of solubility trapping is influenced by several reservoir parameters, including temperature, pressure, brine salinity, and rock ...</cite>. Warm reservoirs store less CO₂ as dissolved species per unit volume than cold reservoirs at equal pressures, tending to accelerate migration and favor structural or mineral capture as the dominant long‑term sink <cite id="c26f773b-3">The efficiency of solubility trapping is influenced by several reservoir parameters, including temperature, pressure, brine salinity, and rock ...</cite>.

Kinetics of mineral trapping (carbonation). Temperature controls reaction rates and product phase assemblages. Elevated temperatures generally accelerate basalt carbonation rates, but high pressure boosts CO₂ solubility and mass transfer, together enhancing carbonate formation; basaltic systems rich in Ca, Mg, and Fe yield rapid and permanent fixation, and field results show pressure increases accelerate in situ mineralization <cite id="18cc0e2f-6">Elevated temperatures accelerate reaction kinetics, while higher pressures increase CO2 solubility in water. Acidic conditions facilitate ...</cite> <cite id="18cc0e2f-0">Basalt rich in alkaline earth elements facilitates rapid and permanent CO2 fixation as carbonates. elevating the CO2 pressure can increase the carbon ...</cite> <cite id="18cc0e2f-3">Increasing pressure accelerated the in-situ CO2 mineralization. The CaCO3 generation increased from 1.04 × 10-6 to 2.66 × 10-4 mmol/L with ...</cite> <cite id="18cc0e2f-1">Pressure can increase the solubility of CO2 in water, thereby enhancing its mineral sequestration efficiency.</cite>. The net effect on storage “efficiency” depends on how quickly mineralized CO₂ accumulates relative to bypassing plumes; warming typically shortens induction times but lowers initial dissolution capacity <cite id="18cc0e2f-6">Elevated temperatures accelerate reaction kinetics, while higher pressures increase CO2 solublicity in water. Acidic conditions facilitate ...</cite>.

Caprock/sealing and side reactions. Warmer formations increase the propensity for CO₂ to migrate upward into caprocks, where it can acidify enclosing shales and evolve CH₄ via catalytic and biological pathways, potentially reducing sealing capacity or triggering risk scenarios if pathways form or diffuse CO₂ escapes (CO₂-to‑CH₄ conversion under stress or heat) <cite id="c26f773b-1">The CO2 trap mechanisms during carbon capture and storage (CCS) are classified into structural, residual, solution, and mineral traps.</cite>. Basaltic CO₂ mineralization studies and field analogs show that pressure and temperature jointly govern the balance between stored CO₂ and potential migration in secondary porosity or fractures; pre‑injection mineralization (e.g., CarbFix) is motivated by precisely avoiding long‑term risks by locking CO₂ in carbonates prior to structural isolation <cite id="18cc0e2f-7">In this paper we describe the thermodynamic and kinetic basis for mineral storage of carbon dioxide in basaltic rock, and how this storage can be optimized.</cite>. Finally, at high pressures and low temperatures, CO₂ hydrate may form in permeable zones or wellbores, creating additional pathways for entrapment but also operational hazards and flow impediments; coupled basalt–hydrate strategies have been examined in low‑temperature marine settings to enhance permanence under specific P–T paths <cite id="18cc0e2f-5">Investigation of carbon sequestration through coupled basalt mineralization and CO2 hydrate formation in low-temperature marine settings.</cite>.

# Pressure Effects

Phase and injectivity. Pressures above the critical pressure and above the CO₂ saturation vapor pressure of brine favor supercritical injection and dense CO₂ slugs, improving sweep efficiency and reducing phase change issues; deep, high‑pressure formations are preferred for direct supercritical injection. Excess pressure also suppresses bubble point behavior and enables larger CO₂ mass fluxes into brine and rock surfaces at a given temperature <cite id="01d52abe-2">Carbon dioxide transitions to supercritical phase occur relatively readily at the critical points of 7.38 MPa, 304 K/31.1 °C and 73.8 bar.</cite> <cite id="01d52abe-9">The triple point of CO₂ (5.18 bar, −56.6 °C) defines the minimum pressure at which liquid CO2 can exist.</cite> <cite id="01d52abe-8">Injection of CO2 requires storage which provides sufficient depth, hence, temperature and pressure exceed the CO2 critical point (T ~ 31.1 oC; P ~ 73 Bar),...</cite>. Increased pressure enhances CO₂ dissolution in brine and raises solubility of CO₂ in rock surfaces; pumping into formations at or near fracture pressure risks inducing seismicity and creating leaky features, so allowable injection pressures are bounded by caprock integrity and stress conditions <cite id="01d52abe-0">Figure 1 shows how CO2 solubility in brine increases with pressure at a constant temperature of 323K and brine salinity of 1 mol NaCl/kg brine.</cite> <cite id="01d52abe-3">greater pressure and lower temperatures increases solubility in the mixing vessel. Due to ...</cite>.

Solubility and plume dynamics. For a fixed temperature, higher reservoir pressure steeply increases aqueous CO₂ solubility; this raises initial dissolution trapping and delays outgassing at wells and faults, improving early storage efficiency but potentially lengthening the time to achieve high cumulative capture. Laboratory and modeling studies show solubility–pressure sensitivity is pronounced even at modest depths and salinities, reinforcing the use of high‑permeability injectors and pressure maintenance to promote contact and dissolution <cite id="01d52abe-0">Figure 1 shows how CO2 solubility in brine increases with pressure at a constant temperature of 323K and brine salinity of 1 mol NaCl/kg brine.</cite> <cite id="01d52abe-3">greater pressure and lower temperatures increases solubility in the mixing vessel. Due to ...</cite> <cite id="c26f773b-3">The efficiency of solubility trapping is influenced by several reservoir parameters, including temperature, pressure, brine salinity, and rock ...</cite>.

Mineral trapping under overpressure. Elevated CO₂ pressure increases CO₂ supply to reactive interfaces and shortens diffusion‑limited steps, increasing the rate and extent of basalt carbonation and alkalinity consumption; at formation scale, maintaining higher pressures improves pressure diffusion coupling and sustained mineralization kinetics across months to years <cite id="18cc0e2f-1">Pressure can increase the solubility of CO2 in water, thereby enhancing its mineral sequestration efficiency.</cite> <cite id="18cc0e2f-3">Increasing pressure accelerated the in-situ CO2 mineralization. The CaCO3 generation increased from 1.04 × 10-6 to 2.66 × 10-4 mmol/L with ...</cite>. However, pressure also enhances CO₂ mobility upward; pre‑mineralization strategies lock CO₂ into carbonates before it can migrate into weaker caprock zones, shortening the time for permanent storage <cite id="18cc0e2f-7">In this paper we describe the thermodynamic and kinetic basis for mineral storage of carbon dioxide in basaltic rock, and how this storage can be optimized.</cite>.

Caprock integrity and stress. Injection pressures near or above fracture gradients can increase permeability and create or re‑activate faults; elevated temperature and pressure can generate CO₂–methane byproducts in caprocks with catalytic/thermal reduction, reducing sealing capacity or enabling cross‑formational migration; designing injection schedules to limit near‑wellbore pressure spikes and to allow CO₂ to mineralize in place before structural isolation reduces long‑term risk <cite id="c26f773b-3">The efficiency of solubility trapping is influenced by several reservoir parameters, including temperature, pressure, brine salinity, and rock ...</cite> <cite id="18cc0e2f-5">Investigation of carbon sequestration through coupled basalt mineralization and CO2 hydrate formation in low-temperature marine settings.</cite>.

# Integrated Pressure–Temperature Pathways and Operational Efficiency

Energy to move CO₂. Moving CO₂ into storage requires work equal to compressing it to and above the storage conditions; above the critical point, density allows high volumetric capacity per bar‑hour at modest power but higher compression stages are needed. Cold CO₂ plumes reduce formation damage and viscosity at fixed pressure head, but warm supercritical CO₂ reduces solubility and may spread faster; energy efficiency trade‑offs require site‑specific compression curves and well‑head temperature management. In deep basaltic formations and ocean basins, direct carbonation pathways are effective precisely because pressure and temperature windows promote rapid dissolution and mineral lock‑up, decreasing net energy per ton stored for the same capture rate <cite id="01d52abe-2">Carbon dioxide transitions to supercritical phase occur relatively readily at the critical points of 7.38 MPa, 304 K/31.1 °C and 73.8 bar.</cite> <cite id="01d52abe-5">SC-CO2 treatments are typically performed at moderate temperatures (35–55 °C) critical point (31.1 °C, 7.38 MPa) CO2 solubility increases with pressure and ...</cite> <cite id="18cc0e2f-0">Basalt rich in alkaline earth elements facilitates rapid and permanent CO2 fixation as carbonates. elevating the CO2 pressure can increase the carbon ...</cite>.

Pumping, phase control, and monitoring. Controlling temperature and pressure at the wellhead (e.g., via heat exchangers or by choosing cold sources like ambient air or cold ocean water) can improve injectivity by reducing viscosity and preventing hydrates in the surface network, enabling higher volumetric rates. Conversely, in shallow or cold reservoirs, maintaining sufficiently high downhole pressure and temperature (e.g., via steam injection or by depth selection) prevents partial condensation and non‑darcy flow restrictions. Integrated reservoir–chemistry models and field tests (e.g., EGS‑like stimulation, basalt carbonation pilots) use P–T pathways to maximize pressure diffusion coupling and carbonate growth while bounding migration risk by timely pressure buildup behind the plume <cite id="c26f773b-3">The efficiency of solubility trapping is influenced by several reservoir parameters, including temperature, pressure, brine salinity, and rock ...</cite> <cite id="18cc0e2f-1">Pressure can increase the solubility of CO2 in water, thereby enhancing its mineral sequestration efficiency.</cite>.

Seal performance and safety windows. Increasing injection pressure tightens pressure diffusion coupling and enhances retention near injectors, but it narrows the safety margin against induced seismicity; increasing reservoir temperature increases gas mobility and can accelerate CO₂ breakthrough. Best practice uses a balanced P–T program that achieves rapid pressure buildup behind the front to promote dissolution/mineralization while keeping the footprint below caprock failure thresholds. Carbon mineralization prior to structural trapping is favored in hot, high‑pressure fields (e.g., Iceland) to pre‑consume alkalinity and convert CO₂ to solid carbonates before it reaches the caprock interface, improving permanent storage efficiency versus delaying strategies <cite id="01d52abe-8">Injection of CO2 requires storage which provides sufficient depth, hence, temperature and pressure exceed the CO2 critical point (T ~ 31.1 oC; P ~ 73 Bar),...</cite> <cite id="18cc0e2f-7">In this paper we describe the thermodynamic and kinetic basis for mineral storage of carbon dioxide in basaltic rock, and how this storage can be optimized.</cite> <cite id="18cc0e2f-5">Investigation of carbon sequestration through coupled basalt mineralization and CO2 hydrate formation in low-temperature marine settings.</cite>.

# Design Implications

- Site selection and zoning: prioritize intervals with P–T above CO₂ criticality and below gas hydrate conditions for efficient supercritical delivery and dissolution, while verifying caprock integrity at overburden stresses <cite id="01d52abe-2">Carbon dioxide transitions to supercritical phase occur relatively readily at the critical points of 7.38 MPa, 304 K/31.1 °C and 73.8 bar.</cite> <cite id="01d52abe-9">The triple point of CO₂ (5.18 bar, −56.6 °C) defines the minimum pressure at which liquid CO2 can exist.</cite>.
- Injection strategy: use pressure maintenance and staged well programs to create a pressure boundary ahead of the CO₂ front, and consider temperature control (cooling at the surface or warm injection) to tune plume velocity and solubility; in basalt, favor elevated pressure carbonation to accelerate alkalinity consumption <cite id="01d52abe-3">greater pressure and lower temperatures increases solubility in the mixing vessel. Due to ...</cite> <cite id="18cc0e2f-1">Pressure can increase the solubility of CO2 in water, thereby enhancing its mineral sequestration efficiency.</cite>.
- Risk management: avoid pressures near fracture gradients to limit seismicity; monitor caprock CO₂/CH₄ generation; in low‑T environments with high pressure and permeability, account for CO₂ hydrate risks in pore networks and pipelines; consider pre‑mineralization to harden CO₂ before structural separation <cite id="c26f773b-3">The efficiency of solubility trapping is influenced by several reservoir parameters, including temperature, pressure, brine salinity, and rock ...</cite> <cite id="18cc0e2f-5">Investigation of carbon sequestration through coupled basalt mineralization and CO2 hydrate formation in low-temperature marine settings.</cite>.
- Efficiency metrics: Storage efficiency (fraction of captured CO₂ permanently stored) is increased when dissolution/mineralization rates outpace migration and outgassing; trapping efficiency improves at higher pressures (for dissolution/mineralization) but can degrade if pressure promotes upward migration into weaker caprocks; operational efficiency can decrease with large compression power but rise where CO₂ is dense (supercritical) and where pre‑mineralization reduces need for deep, high‑salinity brine contact per ton stored <cite id="c26f773b-3">The efficiency of solubility trapping is influenced by several reservoir parameters, including temperature, pressure, brine salinity, and rock ...</cite> <cite id="18cc0e2f-1">Pressure can increase the solubility of CO2 in water, thereby enhancing its mineral sequestration efficiency.</cite>.

# Summary

In rocks, temperature and pressure govern four intertwined aspects of CO₂ storage efficiency: (i) phase behavior and injectability (supercritical delivery and density), (ii) solubility and dissolution trapping (pressures up, temperatures down: higher solubility), (iii) mineral carbonation kinetics (warmer faster reactions; higher pressures accelerate dissolution and mass transfer), and (iv) caprock integrity and side reactions (higher stresses/pressures risk fracture; higher temperatures risk upward migration and CH₄ generation; high pressure/low temperature risk hydrates) <cite id="01d52abe-2">Carbon dioxide transitions to supercritical phase occur relatively readily at the critical points of 7.38 MPa, 304 K/31.1 °C and 73.8 bar.</cite> <cite id="01d52abe-0">Figure 1 shows how CO2 solubility in brine increases with pressure at a constant temperature of 323K and brine salinity of 1 mol NaCl/kg brine.</cite> <cite id="01d52abe-3">greater pressure and lower temperatures increases solubility in the mixing vessel. Due to ...</cite> <cite id="18cc0e2f-6">Elevated temperatures accelerate reaction kinetics, while higher pressures increase CO2 solubility in water. Acidic conditions facilitate ...</cite> <cite id="18cc0e2f-3">Increasing pressure accelerated the in-situ CO2 mineralization. The CaCO3 generation increased from 1.04 × 10-6 to 2.66 × 10-4 mmol/L with ...</cite> <cite id="18cc0e2f-1">Pressure can increase the solubility of CO2 in water, thereby enhancing its mineral sequestration efficiency.</cite> <cite id="c26f773b-2">Mineralization is the most stable form of CO2 trapping mechanism that can provide permanent storage on geological timescales, eliminates long-term leakage ...</cite>. In practice, choosing P–T pathways that maximize dissolution/mineralization while bounding caprock stress and hydrate risks—and matching these to operational compression power—yields the highest total storage and efficiency for a given site <cite id="c26f773b-3">The efficiency of solubility trapping is influenced by several reservoir parameters, including temperature, pressure, brine salinity, and rock ...</cite>.

without_scope.text: How do temperature and pressure affect the process of mineral carbonation and the efficiency of CO₂ storage in basalts?
without_scope.answer:
# Summary

Temperature and pressure govern both the chemical driving forces and kinetic barriers for CO₂ mineralization in basalts, shaping how quickly CO₂ dissolves, how cations are released from basalt, and which carbonate phases precipitate or remain transiently dissolved. At lower temperatures, carbonate solubility declines and reaction equilibria favor carbonate precipitation, while higher pressures increase CO₂ solubility in brine and stabilize supercritical CO₂, enhancing dissolution and reaction rates. In basaltic environments rich in Ca and Mg, these conditions promote rapid in situ carbonation that can immobilize CO₂ over geological timescales, though the exact efficiency depends on mineralogy, pH buffering, salinity, and transport kinetics. <cite id="5b587ab2-0">The solubility of carbonate rocks gradually decreases with increasing temperature. Pressure can increase the solubility of CO2 in water</cite>

# Thermodynamic context in basalts

Basalt typically contains plagioclase, pyroxene, and olivine; upon acidulation by dissolved CO₂ and bicarbonate, cations (Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺, Fe²⁺/Fe³⁺) are mobilized and can reprecipitate as carbonates (calcite, magnesite, siderite, and interlayered brucite-like phases). Storage efficiency hinges on (i) CO₂ dissolution/mineral dissolution/precipitation coupling and (ii) the capacity of the basalt–brine system to buffer acidity (alkalinity). <cite id="38bea274-2">Carbon mineralization occurs when CO2 is dissolved in water and reacts with Ca-rich minerals from basalts to form stable carbonate minerals</cite> <cite id="38bea274-9">In addition to temperature, pressure and salinity, the dissolution of CO2 into formation waters will depend on buffering pH through fluid-rock reactions</cite>

# Temperature: solubility, kinetics, and phase equilibria

- Dissolution/precipitation balance: Warmer brines lower the solubility of carbonates, shifting reactions toward carbonate precipitation and mineralization at a given CO₂ charge; cooler brines favor CO₂ retention in solution and slower net mineralization. <cite id="5b587ab2-0">The solubility of carbonate rocks gradually decreases with increasing temperature</cite>
- Reaction kinetics in basalts vs olivine: Laboratory and modeling studies show rapid low-temperature carbonation in altered basalt systems where surface area and pre-treatment enhance kinetics; without comminution and elevated T/P, olivine-controlled carbonation is slow. <cite id="14771d66-3">Carbonation process involves the interaction of CO₂-rich fluids with host rocks containing minerals that are rich in reactive divalent cations</cite> <cite id="14771d66-4">Kinetics are slow unless mineral reactants are ground to powder, heat-treated, and held at elevated pressure and temperature</cite>
- Quantitative conversion examples: Under elevated temperature and high CO₂ partial pressure with reactive fines, short-contact carbonation can achieve very high instantaneous conversion. <cite id="5b587ab2-8">A maximum conversion of 81% in one hour was obtained with an olivine of 37 µm particle size, at a temperature of 185°C and a CO2 partial pressure of 15 MPa</cite>
- Field relevance: In Iceland’s CarbFix/peridotite systems, reaction path modeling shows an “optimal window” of mildly acidic to near-neutral pH (≈5.2–6.5) for carbonate formation in basalt; higher pH (and lower CO₂ partial pressure) tends to produce more magnesite and calcite, while lower pH promotes amorphous carbonates. <cite id="38bea274-8">Reaction path modelling at the CarbFix site indicates that this “sweet spot” for mineralisation is at pH from 5.2 to 6.5 in basalts</cite> <cite id="38bea274-4">At lower CO2 partial pressures, and higher pH, the formation of more calcite and magnesite and suppression of brucite occurs</cite>

Overall, lower storage temperatures in the subsurface (relative to supercritical conditions) favor carbonate precipitation and long-term permanence once CO₂ is released into brine, while higher injection temperatures accelerate initial dissolution and mobilization of reactive cations but must be balanced against phase equilibria and potential retrograde conversion of carbonates back to magnesite/brucite at depth. <cite id="38bea274-1">Environmental parameters such as temperature and pH influence both dissolution and carbonate precipitation, leading to the formation of stable solid carbonates</cite>

# Pressure: CO₂ solubility, supercritical behavior, and trapping

- CO₂ solubility and dissolution: Pressure increases CO₂ solubility in water and brine; near and above the critical point (PCO₂ ≈ 7.39 MPa, Tc ≈ 31.1 °C), CO₂ exists as dense fluid with high solute capacity, enhancing brine carbonation and transport to reactive zones. <cite id="5b587ab2-0">Pressure can increase the solubility of CO2 in water</cite> <cite id="beaf0afe-4">properties of CO2–brine such as density, viscosity, and solubility are massively affected by temperature, pressure, and salinity of the brine</cite> <cite id="beaf0afe-5">Experiments showed that the solubility of CO2 is enhanced in brine in the presence of limestone by 9% at 25 °C and 6% at 120 °C and 200 bar relative to the ...</cite>
- Dissolution–precipitation coupling in basalt: Elevated pressure promotes rapid dissolution of olivine and pyroxene by carbonic acid/bicarbonate, releasing Mg/Ca to form magnesite, calcite, and brucite-like phases; this is central to efficient in situ mineralization in basalts and ultramafic rocks. <cite id="5b587ab2-0">Basaltic systems rich in alkaline earth elements facilitate rapid and permanent CO2 storage</cite> <cite id="5b587ab2-5">CO2 can react with the released metals, leading to the formation of carbonate minerals that can trap CO2 on geological time scales</cite> <cite id="beaf0afe-2">CO2 is typically stored at supercritical temperature and pressure where it reacts with brine to form carbonic acid, which dissolves primary silicate minerals</cite>
- Phase pathway and stability: In Icelandic basalts, reaction path modeling shows that at low temperatures and pH ≈5–6, magnesite dominates; at higher storage temperatures and pressures, calcite/dolomite fractions can increase due to carbonate solubility effects and alkalinity buffering. <cite id="38bea274-4">At lower CO2 partial pressures and higher pH, the formation of more calcite and magnesite and suppression of brucite occurs</cite>
- Brine salinity and buffering: Pressure-driven dissolution into saline brines is strongly buffered by cations; higher salinity and cation content promote faster carbonate formation and more permanent storage via dense-phase trapping and secondary mineral precipitation. <cite id="38bea274-9">The dissolution of CO2 into formation waters will depend on buffering pH through fluid-rock reactions</cite> <cite id="beaf0afe-1">Understanding the dynamics and controlling parameters of CO2 dissolution in brine and mineralization in mafic basaltic formations</cite>

In practice, high storage pressures near the critical point provide strong initial dissolution and transport, while subsequent cooling and diffusion-driven reactions at depth shift CO₂ into mineral forms; together these mechanisms underpin the demonstrated rapid and permanent mineralization in basaltic reservoirs. <cite id="5b587ab2-9">Basalt and peridotite may provide permanent CO2 storage by in situ mineral carbonation on the scale of billions of tons of CO2 per year</cite> <cite id="38bea274-3">Reconstructing the temperature and origin of CO2 mineralisation in CarbFix ... Numerical simulation of low temperature CO2 sequestration into basalts</cite>

# Integrated mechanisms and efficiency in basalts

- Petrophysical “recipe”: An optimized combination of pressure, temperature, pH, and mineralogy yields high CO₂ efficiency. In basalt, favorable permeability/porosity, abundant Ca/Mg carriers, and brine buffering create a “sweet spot” for rapid carbonation, while pre-treatment (grinding, heat) can accelerate kinetics by orders of magnitude if elevated T/P are not available. <cite id="38bea274-0">Geochemical modelling identified an optimal petrophysical recipe, including pressure, temperature, pH, ... to maximize mineralization</cite> <cite id="14771d66-4">Kinetics are slow unless mineral reactants are ground to powder, heat-treated, and held at elevated pressure and temperature</cite> <cite id="14771d66-1">The overall carbonation kinetics of the basalt was enhanced by a factor of ca. 40 ... due to differences in the chemical and textural environment within the basalt</cite>
- Coupled processes: Dissolution of CO₂ in brine generates carbonic acid that attacks silicates, releasing cations that immediately precipitate as carbonates; this dissolution–precipitation loop sustains low porosity and immobilizes CO₂ as dense minerals. <cite id="38bea274-2">Carbon mineralization occurs when CO2 is dissolved in water and reacts with Ca-rich minerals from basalts to form stable carbonate minerals</cite> <cite id="38bea274-9">Dissolution of CO2 into formation waters will depend on buffering pH through fluid-rock reactions</cite>
- Evidence from deployments: CarbFix and related projects demonstrate that in basaltic systems, most injected CO₂ can be converted to solid carbonates within years under appropriate hydrogeologic and geochemical conditions; modeling and field observations identify pathways to avoid slow phases (e.g., amorphous brucite) and favor more stable carbonates through pH and salinity management. <cite id="38bea274-8">Reaction path modelling at CarbFix indicates a “sweet spot” at pH 5.2–6.5 for mineralisation</cite> <cite id="38bea274-3">The CarbFix pilot demonstrated rapid CO2 mineralization in basalt, supported by simulations of low-temperature CO2 sequestration</cite> <cite id="beaf0afe-8">Experimental investigations extend CO2 brine interaction with basalt to quantify effects of magmatic CO2 infiltration and storage</cite>

# Practical implications for storage efficiency

- Injection strategy: Deep injection in the supercritical window maximizes initial dissolution and charge, but near-surface or low-temperature zones favor faster net mineralization if fluids are sufficiently buffered; hybrid strategies exploit high-pressure dissolution followed by low-temperature precipitation/mineral trapping. <cite id="beaf0afe-2">CO2 is typically stored at supercritical temperature and pressure where it reacts with brine to form carbonic acid, which dissolves primary silicate minerals</cite> <cite id="5b587ab2-0">Carbonate solubility decreases with temperature, while pressure enhances CO2 solubility in water</cite>
- Mineralogical targeting: Basalts with higher Ca and Mg content (e.g., tholeiitic basalts) exhibit greater carbonation potential; olivine-rich peridotites can be even more reactive if finely disseminated and acid-saturated. <cite id="5b587ab2-1">Basalt rich in alkaline earth elements facilitates rapid and permanent CO2 storage</cite> <cite id="5b587ab2-9">Basalt and peridotite may provide permanent CO2 storage by in situ mineral carbonation on very large scales</cite>
- Brine and pH management: High-pressure dissolution into saline brines with strong buffering capacity speeds carbonate formation (magnesite/calcite), whereas neutralizing agents or in-situ mineral fines help maintain pH within the mineralization window. <cite id="38bea274-9">Dissolution of CO2 depends on buffering pH through fluid-rock reactions</cite> <cite id="38bea274-8">A pH range of 5.2–6.5 in basalts is favorable for CO2 mineralisation</cite>
- Risk control: Avoid conditions that preserve amorphous carbonates or stall reactions; maintaining appropriate salinity/cation flux and steering pH into the carbonate stability field reduces long-term loss risk. <cite id="38bea274-4">Higher pH and lower CO2 partial pressure favor calcite and magnesite; at lower pH and higher CO2 partial pressure, brucite-like phases are promoted</cite>

# Uncertainties and research needs

- Kinetic parameters vary with mineral texture, salinity, and ionic strength; standardized activation energies for basalt mixtures (rather than single minerals) under reservoir salinity and pressure remain scarce. <cite id="38bea274-0">An optimal petrophysical recipe requires integrated modelling of pressure, temperature, and pH effects</cite>
- Long-term stability of magnesite in deep basaltic sequences under high P–T gradients and fluid-rock exchange is an active research area; monitoring and reaction-path modeling at site scales help constrain persistence. <cite id="38bea274-4">Reaction path modeling at CarbFix constrains mineral phase behavior and pH control under differing CO2 partial pressures</cite>

# Conclusions

- Temperature and pressure jointly set the efficiency of CO₂ mineralization in basalts. Cold, saline basaltic systems at modest depth favor carbonate precipitation and strong long-term storage once CO₂ is released from solution, while high-pressure, near-critical injection rapidly loads CO₂ into reactive brine and accelerates early mineralization. <cite id="5b587ab2-0">CO2 solubility increases with pressure in water, while carbonate solubility decreases with temperature</cite> <cite id="beaf0afe-4">CO2–brine transport and solubility are strongly modulated by temperature and pressure</cite> <cite id="14771d66-1">Basalt carbonation kinetics can be enhanced by orders of magnitude relative to single minerals due to chemical and textural interactions</cite>
- In practice, basaltic reservoirs with favorable petrology and brine chemistry can achieve high CO₂ mineralization efficiencies within years to decades when pressure, temperature, and pH are managed to favor dissolution–precipitation pathways that produce stable carbonates. <cite id="38bea274-3">CarbFix results and modeling demonstrate rapid, efficient CO2 mineralization in basalts at low storage temperatures</cite> <cite id="5b587ab2-5">Carbonates formed by reaction with basaltic cations provide geological-time-scale trapping</cite>

without_term.text: How do temperature and pressure affect the process of mineral carbonation and the efficiency of carbon dioxide storage in basalt rocks?
without_term.answer:
Summary
Basalt can mineralize dissolved CO2 into stable carbonates (e.g., magnesite, calcite, dolomite) over months to years, enabling geologically secure storage. The processes are governed by thermodynamics and kinetics: higher pressure increases CO2 solubility and dissolution into brine, promoting subsequent aqueous–carbonate reactions and cementation, while higher temperature accelerates mineral dissolution and carbonation kinetics but shifts reaction mechanisms and product equilibria; optimal carbonation for olivine-rich systems often occurs near 185–200 °C, where kinetic barriers drop and reactions proceed rapidly in basaltic matrices supplied by CO2-charged fluids. These dependencies determine how efficiently CO2 is converted to irreversibly stored carbonate phases in basalt formations at depth. <cite id="425aa70d-0">Basalt, with its unique capacity to rapidly convert CO 2 into stable carbonate minerals, presents a promising solution for long-term carbon storage</cite> <cite id="425aa70d-6">Basalt and peridotite may provide permanent CO2 storage by in situ mineral carbonation on the scale of billions of tons of CO2 per year</cite> <cite id="425aa70d-3">Kinetics are slow unless mineral reactants are ground to powder, heat-treated, and held at elevated pressure and temperature or pre-treated</cite>.

How pressure affects mineral carbonation and storage efficiency
- Dissolution and solubility: Increasing pressure raises CO2 solubility in formation brine and pore fluids, increasing the aqueous CO2 flux available for mineral reactions; this is a primary pathway to enhance carbonation rates and to promote both dissolved and structural trapping in basalt. <cite id="56f14203-2">Pressure can increase the solubility of CO2 in water, thereby enhancing dissolution and the subsequent formation of carbonate minerals</cite> <cite id="56f14203-4">Salinity, temperature, and pressure all play a role in how CO2 dissolves in water; brine dissolves CO2 until it reaches equilibrium</cite> <cite id="56f14203-9">Graphs show the effect of temperature, pressure and salinity on CO2 solubility in water, including CO2 solubility in brine</cite>. 
- Phase behavior and delivery: In deep basaltic reservoirs, CO2 is often injected as supercritical fluid, which remains highly miscible with brine over wide ranges; dissolution into brine is the rate-limiting step that feeds carbonate formation, and higher pressures maintain high CO2 availability to react with cations mobilized by flow and reactive ingress into fractures. <cite id="ec769cc7-9">Field and experimental evidence suggest that the rate-limiting step in fixing CO2 as carbonate minerals is the dissolution of CO2 into the aqueous phase and the subsequent reaction with cations</cite>. 
- Field evidence: At the CarbFix pilot and CarbFix2 upscaling at Hellisheiði (Iceland), CO2 emitted from the geothermal plant (hot basalt at >250 °C) was continuously injected and rapidly mineralized into carbonates; the method demonstrated industrial-scale viability with low incremental cost and very fast conversion times, aided by high-temperature CO2-brine solubility and in situ carbonate precipitation. <cite id="ec769cc7-0">The CarbFix method was upscaled at the Hellisheiði geothermal power plant to inject and mineralize the plant's CO2 and H2S emissions in June 2014</cite> <cite id="ec769cc7-4">Through this work we have demonstrated that the cost of industrial scale application of the CarbFix method at Hellisheiði power plant is less than $25/ton</cite> <cite id="ec769cc7-6">Injection and mineralization of CO2 into basaltic rocks at more than 250 °C in continuous operation for 3.5 years</cite> <cite id="ec769cc7-2">Almost complete mineralisation of 175 tonnes of CO2 in basaltic subsurface rocks at the CarbFix site in SW-Iceland in 2012 was observed</cite>. 
- Product permanence: The resulting carbonates (e.g., magnesite) are thermodynamically stable and considered long-term storage; pressure and in situ flow help distribute precipitates as pore-filling or fracture-cementing phases, reducing permeability and immobilizing CO2 as solid Ca/Mg carbonates. <cite id="425aa70d-0">Basalt rapidly converts CO2 into stable carbonate minerals</cite> <cite id="ec769cc7-3">CarbFix aims at storing carbon by accelerating the transformation of CO2 into stable carbonate minerals as rapidly as possible</cite>.

How temperature affects mineral carbonation and storage efficiency
- Kinetics and mechanism: Temperature strongly affects mineral dissolution (olivine, pyroxene) and carbonation rates; for olivine-rich systems, carbonation kinetics peak around 185–200 °C due to lowered kinetic barriers and changes in reaction mechanisms, yielding rapid formation of Mg/Fe carbonates. <cite id="1ceda956-0">The most rapid olivine carbonation occurs at ∼185–200 °C</cite> <cite id="1ceda956-4">A unified review shows olivine carbonation is optimized at 185–200 °C and indicates a change in mechanism above 90 °C</cite>. 
- Olivine system details: In situ measurements and calorimetry show that carbonation pathways and apparent activation energies vary with T; near-optimal conditions drive fast Mg–CO3 formation, and experiments using mixed brine/CO2 demonstrate transport-limited to reaction-limited kinetics depending on temperature. <cite id="1ceda956-5">Under the optimal condition for olivine carbonation at 185oC and limited to 50 bar, immiscible CO2-rich and brine-rich fluids indicate coupled dissolution–carbonation and transport controls</cite> <cite id="1ceda956-1">New olivine carbonation activation energies were calculated to address knowledge gaps relevant to natural and engineered systems</cite>. 
- Basalt composite vs single minerals: In natural basalt containing reactive albite, clinochlore, and Fe–Mg silicates, overall carbonation can be 40× faster than single olivine grains because reactive fluids leach cations from multiple phases, and texture/chemistry accelerate coupled reactions; temperature amplifies these effects by increasing dissolution and reaction rates. <cite id="425aa70d-1">The overall carbonation kinetics of the basalt was enhanced by a factor of ca. 40 compared to single olivine, explained by chemical and textural differences and reactive fluid transport</cite> <cite id="425aa70d-7">The same basalt–olivine comparison reports a ca. 40× enhancement in carbonation kinetics</cite>. 
- Thermodynamic shifts: While higher T generally increases reaction rates, it can reduce the solubility of carbonate minerals and shift equilibria toward more thermodynamically stable carbonates (e.g., magnesite) with lower aqueous Mg/Ca, reinforcing long-term storage; optimal T windows for olivine-rich peridotite/basalt are commonly cited near 185–200 °C. <cite id="56f14203-2">The solubility of carbonate rocks gradually decreases with increasing temperature</cite> <cite id="1ceda956-0">Rapid olivine carbonation occurs around 185–200 °C</cite>. 
- Field confirmation: Hot basalt bodies and geothermal systems like Hellisheiði favor fast mineralization, where CO2 mixes with Ca/Mg-rich fluids and precipitates carbonates rapidly; continuous multi-year operations confirm durable storage as carbonates. <cite id="ec769cc7-6">Rapid CO2 mineralization during 3.5 years of continuous injection into basaltic rocks at >250 °C</cite> <cite id="ec769cc7-2">Near-complete mineralization in a 175 t CO2 field test into basalt</cite>.

Coupled effects in basalt carbon storage: dissolution → carbonate formation and trapping
- Reactivity and mineralogy: Basalts and ultramafic rocks are intrinsically reactive due to abundant CaO–MgO–FeO from pyroxene and olivine, enabling dissolution of cations into CO2-brine, formation of bicarbonate, and precipitation/cementation of carbonates, especially at depth where pressure and temperature favor dissolution and reaction kinetics. <cite id="425aa70d-8">Natural mineral carbonation is most efficient in basaltic and ultramafic rocks due to high reactivity and abundance of divalent metal cations, leading to carbonate formation that traps CO2 on geological time scales</cite> <cite id="425aa70d-3">Kinetics are slow unless basalt/peridotite are processed and held at elevated pressure and temperature</cite>. 
- Role of water and chemistry: Water and dissolved CO2 or carbonic acid mobilize divalent cations; reaction coupling—dissolution of plagioclase/olivine/pyroxene, hydration/alkalinity generation, and precipitation of calcite/magnesite/dolomite—produce multiple trapping end-members: dissolved in brine plus secondary carbonates as solids; pore-filling/crack-filling cements reduce permeability and lock CO2 in place. <cite id="56f14203-8">CO2 dissolved in injected water at 350 m depth in basaltic mixed horizons is consistent with dissolution–precipitation carbonation pathways in the presence of reactive minerals</cite> <cite id="425aa70d-5">Carbonation efficiency is the primary response factor for assessing mineral sequestration performance in CO2 mineralizing rocks</cite>. 
- Efficiency determinants: Storage efficiency rises when pressure keeps CO2 dissolved and temperature is in the kinetic “sweet spot” for the host mineralogy; reactive albitization/serpentinization and interconnected fractures enhance ion supply, while too-low T or too-low P shift the balance toward slower dissolution or gaseous plumes, lowering conversion and trapping. <cite id="425aa70d-1">Basalt’s higher carbonation kinetics relative to olivine reflect coupled mineral chemistry, fluid chemistry, and texture, amplified by temperature</cite> <cite id="56f14203-2">Pressure increases CO2 solubility in water to enhance mineralization</cite> <cite id="1ceda956-0">Optimal olivine carbonation around 185–200 °C highlights temperature-tuned kinetics</cite>.

Practical implications and design choices
- Injection strategy at depth: Injecting CO2 as brine-saturated fluids (or ensuring rapid mixing) and targeting basaltic/peridotitic zones increases pressure and provides cold, reactive fluids; in hot geothermal basalt (>150–200 °C), dissolution and carbonation can proceed orders of magnitude faster, with magnesite/calcite precipitation locking CO2 into solid phases. <cite id="56f14203-2">Pressure-driven CO2 solubility and temperature effects on carbonate solubility and kinetics jointly govern efficiency</cite> <cite id="ec769cc7-6">Continuous injection into basaltic rocks at more than 250 °C resulted in rapid and complete mineralization</cite> <cite id="425aa70d-1">Basalt carbonation was ~40× faster than single olivine due to chemical/texture-driven coupling with reactive brine</cite>. 
- Basalt vs single olivine: Expect higher efficiencies in basaltic systems containing multiple reactive phases; however, kinetic barriers and transport of CO2/ions can still limit rates unless pressure/temperature windows and reactive pathways are optimized. <cite id="425aa70d-1">Basalt composite showed ~40× faster carbonation than single olivine, highlighting multiphase coupling and texture</cite> <cite id="56f14203-5">Modeling and experiments show dissolution–precipitation feedbacks and pore structure changes during sequestration in basalt, linking to transport/kinetic controls</cite>. 
- Storage permanence: The precipitated carbonates in basalt are considered permanent reservoirs; pressure and in situ reactions also create neoformed clay/carbonate assemblages and cements that reduce permeability and stabilize storage over geologic time. <cite id="425aa70d-0">Rapid conversion into stable carbonate minerals underpins long-term storage</cite> <cite id="425aa70d-6">Basalt and peridotite may deliver permanent CO2 storage by in situ mineral carbonation</cite>. 
- Trade-offs and constraints: Elevated temperature can reduce carbonate solubility and favor immiscible CO2–brine flows; salinity lowers CO2 solubility relative to pure water; and buffering capacity of basalt (CaO–MgO) and silica/iron behavior modulate product assemblages and secondary reactions. <cite id="56f14203-2">Carbonate solubility decreases with increasing temperature while CO2 solubility in water increases with pressure, shaping conversion pathways</cite> <cite id="56f14203-1">Dissolved CO2 in rock–brine systems can decrease by 14–24% depending on wettability, indicating strong interplay between mineralization and fluid–rock contact</cite> <cite id="56f14203-9">Solubility decreases with salinity; temperature-pressure-salinity triple control on CO2 solubility applies in brine-dominated basalt systems</cite>.

Key takeaways for CO2 storage efficiency in basalt under varying P and T
- Basalt mineral carbonation efficiency is maximized when: 
  1) Pressure keeps CO2 highly soluble in brine for rapid dissolution and downstream carbonate formation; 2) Temperature is within an optimal kinetic window for the dominant olivine/pyroxene assemblage (often 150–250 °C range for fast rates, with peak near ~185–200 °C for olivine), and 3) Reactant supply (dissolved Ca/Mg) and transport are adequate via reactive brine flow through fractures/permeable zones. <cite id="56f14203-2">Raising pressure increases CO2 solubility in water and promotes dissolution–carbonation</cite> <cite id="56f14203-4">Temperature, pressure, and salinity jointly govern CO2 dissolution into brine</cite> <cite id="1ceda956-0">Olivine carbonation peaks at ~185–200 °C</cite> <cite id="1ceda956-4">Optimized olivine carbonation indicates mechanism change around 90 °C with faster kinetics above the threshold</cite> <cite id="425aa70d-1">Multiphase, multimineral basalt systems show up to ~40× faster carbonation than single olivine due to coupled chemistry, texture, and reactive transport</cite>.
- Field systems like CarbFix at Hellisheiði demonstrate that combining high temperature, continuous injection, and reactive basalt yields fast conversion (often months) and high trapping (near-complete), illustrating the P–T leverage on both dissolution and solid-phase carbonate storage. <cite id="ec769cc7-2">Almost complete mineralisation of an 175 t CO2 field injection in basalt within CarbFix</cite> <cite id="ec769cc7-0">Upscaled CarbFix2 at Hellisheiði demonstrated continuous CO2 mineralization in basalt</cite> <cite id="ec769cc7-6">Rapid carbonate formation during 3.5 years of continuous injection into >250 °C basalt</cite>.
- Quantifying efficiency requires integrating carbonation conversion (degree of carbonation), aqueous CO2 dissolved during transit, and resulting carbonate mineral masses; reaction-path models and field data show that dissolution of CO2 into aqueous phase and subsequent reactions with released cations control the rate-limiting steps and thus overall storage efficiency. <cite id="ec769cc7-9">Mineralization rate-limiting steps are dissolution of CO2 into aqueous phase and reaction with cations</cite> <cite id="425aa70d-4">Carbonation efficiency (conversion) is the primary response factor for assessing mineral sequestration performance</cite>.

Caveats and open questions
- Storage efficiency is sensitive to local P–T, brine chemistry (salinity, pH), and rock texture; basalt alteration (albitization), fracture networks, and pre-existing clays modulate cation supply and cementation. <cite id="1ceda956-2">Olivine dissolution in the presence of dissolved CO2 can show rate decreases attributed to pH changes, highlighting fluid chemistry feedbacks</cite> <cite id="56f14203-1">Wettability alters dissolved CO2 retention in rock–brine systems, changing available CO2 for mineralization</cite>. 
- While higher T generally enhances rates, carbonate mineral solubility falls with T; optimizing T for a given basalt requires balancing dissolution kinetics, kinetic barriers of olivine/pyroxene and calcite formation, and the stability of products like magnesite. <cite id="56f14203-2">Carbonate rock solubility decreases with increasing temperature, whereas CO2 solubility increases with pressure</cite> <cite id="1ceda956-0">Rapid carbonation near 185–200 °C shows mechanism-controlled optimal windows</cite>. 
- Field-scale P–T constraints and long-term durability remain an active area; reaction-path modeling in basaltic systems and ongoing CarbFix operations are refining how to translate kinetic/thermodynamic controls into storage performance metrics across geologic time. <cite id="56f14203-5">Batch/flow modeling reveals coupled dissolution–precipitation and pore structure evolution during sequestration in basalt, affecting storage efficiency</cite> <cite id="ec769cc7-2">Field observations at CarbFix quantify near-complete mineralization within a few years, supporting durability assumptions</cite>.

In short, pressure and temperature are first-order drivers of CO2 mineralization in basalt: higher pressure increases CO2 solubility and sustained dissolution into brine, while temperature tunes dissolution/carbonation kinetics and product stability, with olivine-rich basalt carbonation peaking around 185–200 °C and deep hot basalt systems enabling rapid, near-complete mineralization, thereby enhancing the efficiency and permanence of CO2 storage as carbonate minerals. <cite id="56f14203-2">Pressure increases CO2 solubility in water to accelerate dissolution and carbonate formation, whereas carbonate solubility declines with temperature</cite> <cite id="1ceda956-0">Olivine carbonation kinetics peak at ~185–200 °C, highlighting temperature control</cite> <cite id="425aa70d-1">Basalt composites show orders-of-magnitude faster carbonation than single olivine through coupled chemistry and texture</cite> <cite id="ec769cc7-2">Field trials in basalt show near-complete CO2 to carbonate conversion within years</cite>.
