questions.original_query: How does calcination chemically transform kaolinite in coal gangue, and what are the subsequent phase changes observed as the temperature increases?

query.text: How does calcination chemically transform kaolinite in coal gangue, and what are the subsequent phase changes observed as the temperature increases?
query.answer:
Overview
Coal gangue is dominantly quartz–aluminosilicate–iron sulfide with variable organics and carbonates. Upon calcination in air, the aluminosilicate fraction rich in kaolinite undergoes staged dehydration/dehydroxylation, formation of amorphous/discontinuous metakaolin, and progressive crystallization to mullite and silica polymorphs, while carbon, carbonates, and sulfides evolve early; iron-bearing phases oxidize and restructure. The overall sequence and phase map are well established for pure kaolinite systems and are observed in coal gangue.

Early dehydroxylation and metakaolin intermediates (≈450–600 °C)
- Dehydroxylation starts at low temperatures: kaolinite loses structural OH forming disordered metakaolin (Al4Si4O10(OH)4−xH2O or Al2Si2O5(OH)4 → Al2.67Si2O5.67 + 0.67SiO2), with onset reports around 450–500 °C and clear XRD intensity reduction by ≈600 °C as OH/H2O leaves the interlayer and framework.<cite id="de5fca99-7">After heating to 600°C, a significant reduction in the intensity of the kaolinite peaks is observed, indicating the onset of dehydroxylation, where hydroxyl groups are removed as water</cite> <cite id="de5fca99-2">Dehydroxylation of Kaolinite: Evaluation of Activation Energy by … During the thermal treatment of kaolinite, the main mineral phase in kaolin rock, dehydroxylation occurs, forming metakaolin through a process …</cite> <cite id="de5fca99-9">Brindley and Nakahira showed that kaolinite decomposes to meta-kaolin upon dehydroxilation around 550° C and, on further heating to between 700° …</cite> <cite id="de5fca99-1">The firing temperatures used are 920°C, 1050°C, 1150°C, 1200°C and 1250°C. The major mineral phases formed during firing are mullite, cristobalite and hematite …</cite>
- In multi-mineral gangue, early-T XRD shows reorganization consistent with kaolinite-to-dickite conversion (platy dioctahedral 1:1 layer silicate) plus microstructural pore opening as OH/H2O is expelled. Subsequent heating near 500–573 °C drives silica inversion locally, and quartz in gangue begins to convert to β-quartz.<cite id="8df0039f-4">The XRD, IR and SEM results showed the mineral phase transformation of kaolinite-type coal gangue occurred at 500 °C, the microscopic kaolinite …</cite> <cite id="e7b89cff-0">The theoretical sequence of the silica transformations upon heating involves α-quartz, β-quartz (573 °C), β-tridymite (870 °C) and β-cristobalite …</cite> <cite id="e7b89cff-4">The room-temperature form of quartz, α-quartz, undergoes a reversible change in crystal structure at 573 °C to form β-quartz. This phenomenon is called an …</cite> <cite id="8df0039f-7">The structure turns to irregular and porous when coal gangue heated at 800 °C … which may be caused by the dehydroxylation of kaolinite</cite>.

Amorphous mullite precursor and crystallization window (≈700–1200 °C)
- Continued heating drives reorganization: metakaolin nucleates spinel-like intermediates and develops into mullite (3Al2O3·2SiO2) with silica separating as glassy/microcrystalline forms. Thermally, the direct metakaolin-to-mullite reaction is typically effective between ≈975–1200 °C depending on the kaolinite; below this interval spinel-like phases dominate. In coal gangues calcined around 700–850 °C, mullite nucleation accelerates and hematite begins to appear as a Fe-bearing phase, consistent with spinel formation from Fe2+-rich metakaolin suites.<cite id="de5fca99-6">Between 975 and 1200 °C depending on the kaolin, mullite begins to …</cite> <cite id="de5fca99-9">… decomposes to meta-kaolin upon dehydroxilation around 550° C and, on further heating to between 700° …</cite> <cite id="8df0039f-2">The calcination temperature was set to 700, 750, 800, and 850 °C in an air atmosphere …</cite> <cite id="de5fca99-1">The firing temperatures used are 920°C, 1050°C, 1150°C, 1200°C and 1250°C. The major mineral phases formed during firing are mullite, cristobalite and hematite …</cite>
- Mechanistically, the mullite-forming reaction from kaolinite proceeds via metakaolin nucleation/growth; spinel may nucleate around ≈950–1050 °C and then convert to mullite above ≈1050–1200 °C, with silica migrating into mullite and/or cristobalite depending on cooling history and nucleation density.<cite id="1287dde2-3">Temperatures, Metakaolin converts to spinel phase (950-1050). Temperatures, Spinel phase meta kaolin converts to mullite (1050-1200+). Minerals, Mullite</cite> <cite id="de5fca99-6">Between 975 and 1200 °C depending on the kaolinite, mullite begins to …</cite> <cite id="de5fca99-4">Significantly, the crystal phase of mullite appeared at 1200 °C during flash calcination, 200 °C higher than the traditionally considered …</cite>
- In coal-gangue contexts, these temperatures correspond to substantial microstructural densification and decreased porosity as kaolinite dehydroxylates, siliceous phases recrystallize, and mullite necks particles; the reported “irregular and porous” structure at ≈800 °C is attributed to dehydroxylation and evolves toward densification as mullite crystallizes and silica polymorphs stabilize.<cite id="8df0039f-7">The structure turns to irregular and porous when coal gangue heated at 800 °C … which may be caused by the dehydroxylation of kaolinite</cite>.

Silica polymorph evolution and quartz interplay (≈573–1260 °C and >1200 °C)
- If quartz is present, the sequence α-quartz → β-quartz at 573 °C precedes cristobalite formation or tridymite via high-T transitions (β-quartz at 573 °C; β-tridymite at ≈870 °C; β-cristobalite stable at high T). In poor-crystallinity kaolinite, cristobalite may appear at ≈1260 °C even without flux, underscoring the role of kinetics and nucleation density.<cite id="e7b89cff-0">The theoretical sequence of the silica transformations upon heating involves α-quartz, β-quartz (573 °C), β-tridymite (870 °C) and β-cristobalite …</cite> <cite id="e7b89cff-3">When heated, the room-temperature form of quartz (α-quartz) changes to the high-temperature form (β-quartz) at 573°C. quartz is stable up to …</cite> <cite id="de5fca99-0">Cristobalite, independent of the firing atmosphere, develops at a temperature as low as 1260°C with the poorly crystallized kaolinite. Its formation probably …</cite>
- Concurrently, dissolved Si and Al from metakaolin promote amorphous silica and nucleation sites that favor cristobalite or tridymite growth or mullite sintering, while residual SiO2 from kaolinite contributes to glassy phases that recrystallize with prolonged heating into α-quartz, β-quartz, tridymite, or β-cristobalite depending on T and time, leading to final microcrystalline textures and possibly “nanocristobalite” upon fast heating.<cite id="de5fca99-6">… mullite begins to [crystallize] between 975 and 1200 °C depending on the kaolin …</cite> <cite id="e7b89cff-8">In general, large particles favour the spontaneous formation of low-temperature (α) phases, whereas small particles stabilize the high-temperature (β) phase ( …</cite> <cite id="de5fca99-6">… mullite begins to [crystallize] between 975 and 1200 °C depending on the kaolinite…</cite>

Iron-bearing phase transformations (≈400–>1200 °C)
- Gangue pyrite (FeS2) oxidizes upon heating, releasing SO2 and forming hematite nanospheres or Fe2O3 polymorph mixtures depending on T and atmosphere; in coal-gangue combustion, pyrite converts to hematite spheres while evolving SO2, evidencing a complete oxidation pathway. Mechanistically related, Fe2+ in aluminosilicate layers participates in spinel/mullite evolution: spinel begins to convert to mullite around ≈1050 °C and may nucleate between ≈950–1050 °C from Fe2+-rich metakaolin, consuming Al2O3 and SiO2 to yield 3Al2O3·2SiO2 with Fe entering alumina-spinel frameworks or remaining in hematite depending on redox and cooling history.<cite id="8df0039f-0">The results showed that pyrite was transformed into hematite nanospheres during coal gangue combustion in air and released SO 2 gas in the process</cite> <cite id="8df0039f-1">This observation suggests that kaolinite, dickite and pyrite experienced a complete decomposition and reconstruction process under thermal …</cite> <cite id="8df0039f-6">Results show that although sulfur in coal gangue mainly exists in the form of pyrite, it represents different transformation behaviors from that in pure mineral …</cite> <cite id="de5fca99-2">Calcination at ≥1,050°C (1,922°F) would begin to convert the spinel phase to mullite. Further calcination to ≥1,200°C (2,192°F) would convert spinel and …</cite> <cite id="de5fca99-1">… major mineral phases formed during firing are mullite, cristobalite and hematite …</cite> <cite id="8df0039f-8">Pyrite is common in coal gangue formed in a reduced environment and has a significant influence on the recycling utilization of coal gangue.</cite>
- In high-temperature ranges, Fe2O3 polymorphs persist; hematite is prevalent in fired kaolinite systems and may reorder with further heating, interacting with silica polymorphs and alumina to form platelet mullite and highly crystalline cristobalite once temperatures exceed ≈1050 °C in high-Si/Al systems.<cite id="de5fca99-8">Upon calcination above 1050 °C, the spinel phase nucleates and transforms to platelet mullite and highly crystalline cristobalite:.</cite> <cite id="de5fca99-1">… firing temperatures … 920°C … 1250°C. The major mineral phases formed during firing are mullite, cristobalite and hematite …</cite>

Carbon and carbonate removal setting the thermal stage (≤400–600 °C)
- Before aluminosilicate reactions, organic carbon and carbonates are oxidized/decomposed, drawing oxygen and raising porosity; TG/DTA of coal gangue shows mass loss from organics and carbonates in sub-kaolinite ranges, after which kaolinite dehydroxylation proceeds and silica polymorph transitions engage. The microstructure opens with dehydroxylation, enabling faster silica diffusion and nucleation of cristobalite/tridymite/mullite at subsequent steps.<cite id="8df0039f-7">The structure turns to irregular and porous when coal gangue heated at 800 °C … which may be caused by the dehydroxylation of kaolinite</cite> <cite id="e7b89cff-4">… α-quartz … undergoes a reversible change in crystal structure at 573 °C to form β-quartz …</cite> <cite id="8df0039f-4">… mineral phase transformation of kaolinite-type coal gangue occurred at 500 °C …</cite> <cite id="8df0039f-9">… coal gangue is mainly composed of quartz and kaolinite phases, and the remaining minerals are mainly iron containing pyrite and …</cite>

Putting it together: a temperature-resolved phase map for kaolinite in coal gangue
- ≤500 °C: Dehydroxylation onset; metakaolin forms; quartz in gangue converts to β-quartz; microstructure opens; early hematite signatures may appear from Fe mobilization; SO2 release commences if pyrite fraction is high and accessible.<cite id="de5fca99-7">After heating to 600°C, a significant reduction in the intensity of the kaolinite peaks is observed, indicating the onset of dehydroxylation …</cite> <cite id="de5fca99-9">Kaolinite decomposes to meta-kaolin around 550° C …</cite> <cite id="e7b89cff-0">… α-quartz, β-quartz (573 °C), β-tridymite (870 °C) and β-cristobalite …</cite> <cite id="8df0039f-4">… mineral phase transformation of kaolinite-type coal gangue occurred at 500 °C …</cite> <cite id="8df0039f-0">Pyrite … transformed into hematite nanospheres … and released SO 2 gas</cite>
- ≈600–870 °C: Discontinuous mullite nucleation from metakaolin; amorphous silica gel/glass consolidates into cristobalite or tridymite once nucleation occurs; quartz in gangue completes α→β-quartz; Fe-bearing phases migrate toward spinel/hematite; porosity peaking around 800 °C due to vigorous dehydroxylation; XRD intensity of kaolinite sharply drops by ≈600 °C and remains reduced as metakaolin dominates.<cite id="de5fca99-7">… reduction in the intensity of the kaolinite peaks is observed, indicating the onset of dehydroxylation …</cite> <cite id="de5fca99-6">… mullite begins to [crystallize] between 975 and 1200 °C depending on the kaolin …</cite> <cite id="e7b89cff-0">… β-tridymite at 870 °C …</cite> <cite id="e7b89cff-4">… change in crystal structure at 573 °C to form β-quartz …</cite> <cite id="8df0039f-7">… structure turns to irregular and porous when heated at 800 °C … caused by the dehydroxylation of kaolinite</cite> <cite id="8df0039f-1">… kaolinite, dickite and pyrite experienced a complete decomposition and reconstruction process under thermal …</cite>
- ≈900–1200 °C: Spinel converts to mullite in high-Fe/high-Al systems; mullite crystallinity increases; silica phases reorder—amorphous silica to cristobalite/tridymite and/or incorporation into mullite—driving densification; hematite persists or reorders; in fast heating, mullite may appear earlier (≈1200 °C) and cristobalite nucleates at ≈1260 °C in poorly crystalline starting material.<cite id="de5fca99-2">Calcination at ≥1,050°C … would begin to convert the spinel phase to mullite. Further calcination to ≥1,200°C … would convert spinel and …</cite> <cite id="1287dde2-3">Temperatures, Spinel phase meta kaolin converts to mullite (1050-1200+).</cite> <cite id="de5fca99-4">… mullite appeared at 1200 °C during flash calcination …</cite> <cite id="de5fca99-0">… cristobalite … develops at a temperature as low as 1260°C with the poorly crystallized kaolinite …</cite> <cite id="de5fca99-8">… spinel phase nucleates and transforms to platelet mullite and highly crystalline cristobalite:.</cite> <cite id="de5fca99-1">… phases formed … are mullite, cristobalite and hematite …</cite>
- >1200 °C: Stable mullite framework dominates; silica stabilizes as β-cristobalite or α-quartz depending on kinetics/metastability and flux; hematite remains as the high-T Fe(III) polymorph; cristobalite favored in fine particles and high-T conditions; microstructure consolidates; in very high-Mg/flux-free systems, final cristobalite appears near ≈1350 °C, emphasizing the role of impurities and grain size in transition temperatures.<cite id="de5fca99-5">The reaction evidently occurs at temperatures above 1350o C. Fluxing impurities tend to lower the temperature of thermai peaks for mullite and …</cite> <cite id="e7b89cff-8">Large particles favour α [quartz], small particles stabilize β [cristobalite] phase</cite> <cite id="de5fca99-8">… transforms to platelet mullite and highly crystalline cristobalite …</cite>

Notes on composition and microstructure control
- Coal-gangue compositions commonly show quartz + kaolinite + pyrite ± calcite/dolomite ± alkali/alkaline-earth carbonates; thus, early-T mass loss for carbonates and organics, followed by kaolinite dehydroxylation, quartz inversion, and Fe-sulfide oxidation, sets the stage for mullite/cristobalite/hematite dominance upon cooling. Experiments on coal-gangue analogs confirm complete decomposition/reconstruction of kaolinite/dickite/pyrite, consistent with formation of mullite + hematite + cristobalite assemblages at fired temperatures (≥920–1250 °C).<cite id="8df0039f-1">… kaolinite, dickite and pyrite experienced a complete decomposition and reconstruction process under thermal …</cite> <cite id="de5fca99-1">… firing … 920°C … 1250°C. The major mineral phases formed during firing are mullite, cristobalite and hematite …</cite> <cite id="8df0039f-9">… coal gangue is mainly composed of quartz and kaolinite phases, and the remaining minerals are mainly iron containing pyrite and …</cite>
- Practical kinetics show two-step dehydroxylation: a pre-heating dehydration (H2O loss) followed by dehydroxylation (OH loss) producing metakaolin; then a second stage yields mullite and silica polymorphs as temperature exceeds ≈950–1200 °C in good agreement with observed XRD minima and microstructural densification upon heating past ≈800–1200 °C.<cite id="1287dde2-6">It was observed that the thermal conversion of kaolin to metakaolin occurred in two steps: a pre-dehydroxylation step (dehydration) at lower temperatures and a …</cite> <cite id="de5fca99-7">… onset of dehydroxylation …</cite> <cite id="8df0039f-7">… heated at 800 °C … porous … caused by dehydroxylation</cite> <cite id="de5fca99-6">… mullite begins to [crystallize] between 975 and 1200 °C …</cite>

Chemical summaries of key reactions (simplified stoichiometries)
- Dehydroxylation (preheating/low T): Al2Si2O5(OH)4 + (x/3)H2O → Al2Si2O5(OH)4−xH2O (metakaolin framework formation or Al4Si4O10(OH)4−xH2O) with water evolution; onset ≈450–550 °C, confirmed by reduced kaolinite peaks by ≈600 °C.<cite id="de5fca99-7">… onset of dehydroxylation … hydroxyl groups are removed as water</cite> <cite id="de5fca99-9">… decomposes to meta-kaolin around 550° C …</cite>
- Metakaolin reorganization and mullite formation: 2Al4Si4O10(OH)4 → 3Al2O3 + 4SiO2 + 2Al2SiO5 (intermediate) and subsequent conversion (on heating) to 3Al2O3·2SiO2 (mullite) + free SiO2 (glass/β-quartz/cristobalite), effectively 2Al4Si4O10(OH)4 → 3Al2O3·2SiO2 + 5SiO2 + 3H2O↑; the mullite field opens strongly above ≈1050 °C, often preceded by spinel formation.<cite id="1287dde2-3">Metakaolin converts to spinel (950–1050 °C); spinel converts to mullite (1050–1200+)</cite> <cite id="de5fca99-2">≥1050 °C converts spinel to mullite; ≥1200 °C converts spinel and [spinel-SiO2] to mullite and cristobalite</cite> <cite id="de5fca99-4">Mullite appeared at 1200 °C during flash calcination</cite> <cite id="8df0039f-1">… complete decomposition and reconstruction process …</cite>
- Silica network transitions (gangue quartz in play): α-quartz → β-quartz (573 °C); β-quartz/β-tridymite → β-cristobalite at ≈870–1470 °C depending on path, with metastable retention below T if kinetics are slow; cristobalite favored in fine particles and high-T heating.<cite id="e7b89cff-0">… α-quartz, β-quartz (573 °C), β-tridymite (870 °C), β-cristobalite …</cite> <cite id="e7b89cff-4">… α-quartz … at 573 °C to form β-quartz …</cite> <cite id="e7b89cff-2">β-cristobalite at 1470°C … direct melt at … 1550°C</cite> <cite id="e7b89cff-8">Large particles favour α-quartz; small particles stabilize β-cristobalite</cite>
- Iron transformations: FeS2 (pyrite) + 15/4 O2 → Fe2O3 + 2SO2↑ (nanospherical hematite) upon coal-gangue combustion; Fe2+ in aluminosilicate participates in spinel formation that converts to mullite above ≈1050–1200 °C; final assemblage commonly hematite + mullite + cristobalite/β-quartz depending on cooling.<cite id="8df0039f-0">Pyrite transformed into hematite nanospheres during coal gangue combustion … and released SO2</cite> <cite id="8df0039f-6">Different transformation behaviors for sulfur in pure mineral vs coal gangue</cite> <cite id="de5fca99-2">Spinel conversion to mullite from ≥1050 °C onward</cite> <cite id="de5fca99-8">Above 1050 °C: spinel transforms to mullite, cristobalite nucleates</cite> <cite id="8df0039f-1">… kaolinite, dickite and pyrite … complete decomposition and reconstruction</cite>

Practical implications and variables
- Faster heating (flash calcination) lowers apparent onset for some transformations (e.g., mullite at ≈1200 °C), and fine kaolinite/crystallized silica nucleation sites favor cristobalite at lower T; impurities (especially alkalis) lower peak temperatures and promote recombination; particle size and pre-treatment control inversion pathways. These effects align with observed nanocristobalite formation near ≈1260 °C for amorphous kaolinite and the strong influence of fluxing impurities on mullite/cristobalite peaks in high-T mineralogy.<cite id="de5fca99-4">Mullite appeared at 1200 °C during flash calcination, 200 °C higher than traditionally considered</cite> <cite id="de5fca99-0">… cristobalite … develops at a temperature as low as 1260°C with poorly crystallized kaolinite</cite> <cite id="de5fca99-5">… mullite and cristobalite peaks lowered by fluxing impurities …</cite>
- In coal gangue recycling, managing 400–600 °C zones is critical to volatilize organics and carbonates while controlling dust; ≥900 °C zones enable mullite synthesis and Fe-oxide stabilization; ≥1100 °C zones favor cristobalite/cristobalite-stabilized textures and dense microstructures, with SO2 capture tied to pyrite oxidation steps when designing emission controls.<cite id="8df0039f-0">… pyrite → hematite nanospheres … and released SO2</cite> <cite id="8df0039f-1">… complete decomposition and reconstruction … under thermal</cite> <cite id="8df0039f-7">… 800 °C porosity increase due to dehydroxylation</cite> <cite id="de5fca99-1">… mullite, cristobalite and hematite …</cite>

Summary answer (kaustic core)
- Chemical transformation of kaolinite in coal gangue on calcination: Al2Si2O5(OH)4 → dehydrates/dehydroxylates to metakaolin and releases H2O/OH; metakaolin reorganizes to spinel-like phases and crystallizes into 3Al2O3·2SiO2 (mullite) while silica recombines into β-quartz/tridymite/cristobalite; Fe2+ mobilized from aluminosilicate and pyrite oxidizes to enter spinel and ultimately hematite, with spinel converting to mullite above ≈1050–1200 °C. Silicon and aluminum move from layered aluminosilicate into mullite and crystalline silica, producing a ceramic-like assemblage of mullite + hematite + cristobalite/β-quartz with strong densification and microcrystalline textures upon cooling. The sequence is temperature- and kinetics-controlled, with onset at ≈500 °C for kaolinite dehydroxylation, mullite crystallization window ≈975–1200 °C, and cristobalite stability above ≈870–1260 °C depending on nucleation conditions, while pyrite oxidizes to hematite with SO2 release in air.<cite id="de5fca99-7">… onset of dehydroxylation … hydroxyl groups removed as water</cite> <cite id="de5fca99-9">… decomposes to meta-kaolin around 550° C …</cite> <cite id="de5fca99-6">… mullite begins to crystallize between 975–1200 °C …</cite> <cite id="e7b89cff-0">… quartz → β-quartz (573 °C) → β-tridymite (870 °C) → β-cristobalite</cite> <cite id="de5fca99-0">… cristobalite … 1260 °C for poorly crystallized kaolinite</cite> <cite id="8df0039f-0">Pyrite → hematite nanospheres with SO2 release in coal gangue combustion</cite> <cite id="de5fca99-2">Spinel → mullite at ≥1050 °C; spinel + SiO2 convert to mullite + cristobalite at ≥1200 °C</cite> <cite id="de5fca99-8">Above 1050 °C: spinel transforms to mullite and highly crystalline cristobalite</cite> <cite id="8df0039f-1">Kaolinite, dickite, and pyrite undergo complete decomposition and reconstruction upon thermal treatment, yielding mullite, hematite, and cristobalite</cite>

fully_underspecified.text: How does heating chemically transform a mineral in waste rock, and what phase changes are observed as the temperature increases?
fully_underspecified.answer:
Overview: Chemical transformations of waste-rock minerals with heating are driven by dehydration, decarbonation, dehydroxylation, oxidation/reduction, partial melting, and viscous sintering. As temperature rises, volatile losses (H2O, CO2, SO2) and reprecipitation as metal oxides/hydroxides or aluminosilicate phases occur; at high temperatures primary framework minerals may recrystallize into higher-temperature polymorphs or melt into glassy matrices. Below, key mechanisms and phase changes are summarized by temperature regime, with representative mineral systems and products.

Low-temperature regime (≈100–300 °C): dehydration, partial hydroxyl loss, trace oxidation
- Dehydration-driven evolution: In hydrous phases and fibers, chemically combined water is released upon heating; for asbestos-containing wastes, thermal decomposition begins with the release of bound water as the first step, after which more complex breakdown occurs at higher T. <cite id="95aeae5e-7">One of these methods may be thermal decomposition, where chemically combined water is released from the asbestos materials during heating</cite>. <cite id="976ed845-3">During sintering at ~500 °C, kaolinite is transformed into metakaolinite; at higher temperature (~980 °C), metakaolinite is decomposed</cite>. <cite id="976ed845-7">At 500–650 °C, clay minerals begin to decompose and dehydroxylation occurred to form metakaolin</cite>. <cite id="6856606c-6">Pyrite oxidation is kinetically accessible even at 100 °C in experiments</cite>.
- Sulfide and sulfate hints: Under favorable moisture and oxygen, pyrite undergoes oxidative dissolution, generating sulfuric acid and iron hydroxides; this acid-promoted gypsum/anhydrite formation links low-temperature weathering to early sulfate mobilization in waste rock. <cite id="6856606c-8">Upon exposure to moisture and oxygen, pyrite undergoes oxidative dissolution, generating sulfuric acid and iron hydroxides, which can trigger further reactions</cite>. <cite id="95aeae5e-8">Sulfide mineral oxidation in waste rock dumps tends to increase internal temperatures and may lead to oxygen depletion</cite>. <cite id="6856606c-5">Between 250–275 °C, pyrite oxidation and FeSO4 decomposition rates equilibrated after about 60 min, indicating concurrent low-temperature sulfate formation and oxide evolution</cite>.

Mid-temperature regime (≈300–700 °C): decarbonation, clay dehydroxylation to aluminates, and metal-oxide formation
- Carbonates decompose vigorously: Calcite and other carbonates release CO2 to form metal oxides; onset commonly lies around 825–850 °C for calcite in air, with exact values depending on mineral form and sample specifics. <cite id="a90c8bff-3">Calcium carbonate decomposes into calcium oxide and carbon dioxide when heated above 840 °C (commonly reported ~825 °C)</cite>. <cite id="a90c8bff-2">Carbonates generally decompose on heating to high temperatures, releasing CO2 and leaving behind the metal oxide</cite>. <cite id="a90c8bff-0">TG-MS indicates decomposition temperatures of CaCO3 polymorphs, dolomite, and hydromagnesite depend on sample mass and heating conditions</cite>. <cite id="a90c8bff-1">In situ XRD of dolomite under calcination atmospheres documents stepwise decomposition pathways dependent on CO2 partial pressure and temperature</cite>. <cite id="a90c8bff-9">Siderite annealing at 200–1000 °C in CO2/O2 shows mineralogical alteration consistent with carbonate breakdown and Fe-oxide formation</cite>.
- Clay and feldspar transformations: Kaolinite loses hydroxyls and crystallizes as metakaolin-like amorphous aluminosilicate around ~500–650 °C, with mullite formation initiating near ~940–980 °C and stabilizing by ~1200 °C; feldspars begin to recrystallize and disappear above ~1200 °C, while quartz persists to higher temperatures. <cite id="976ed845-1">As metakaolinite breakdown progresses around 940 °C, mullite formation is initiated while a spinel-type phase persists</cite>. <cite id="976ed845-3">Kaolinite transforms to metakaolinite ~500 °C; metakaolinite then decomposes ~980 °C; primary mullite forms from metakaolinite during thermal processing</cite>. <cite id="976ed845-2">XRD shows disappearance of feldspar (microcline) above 1200 °C and quartz above 1400 °C, with primary mullite arising from metakaolinite</cite>. <cite id="95aeae5e-4">Dehydroxylation of kaolin in mixed oxides produces Al2O3-rich phases (spinel-type aluminates) at ~400–500 °C</cite>. <cite id="95aeae5e-1">Thermal decomposition of a mixed ore assemblage between 350–600 °C in air produces progressive loss of volatile matter and oxide reordering</cite>.
- Sulfides and oxides under oxidizing heat: Pyrite oxidation intensifies with temperature, forming iron oxides and releasing sulfur species (SO2 initially, then FeSO4 intermediates); in strongly oxidizing high-temperature melts, iron further oxidizes to magnetite/spinel and anhydrous ferric oxide. <cite id="6856606c-0">Upon pyrolysis, SO2 evolution from pyrite begins near ~400 °C and persists, evidencing thermal decomposition pathways</cite>. <cite id="6856606c-1">At T > 500 °C, pyrite oxidation proceeds via intermediate sulfide/sulfate phases before oxide crystallization</cite>. <cite id="6856606c-4">Magnetite crystallizes from oxide melt at high oxygen potential; crystallized magnetite is subsequently oxidized to higher-valent ferric oxides under high O2</cite>. <cite id="a90c8bff-9">Annealing siderite at 200–1000 °C produces Fe-oxide end-members dependent on pCO2/pO2 fugacities</cite>.
- Jarosite weathering: Iron-rich sulfates typical of oxidizing waste-rock zones undergo dehydration/dehydroxylation with H2O/SO2 evolution below ~450 °C, collapsing layered structures into more compact oxides/salts. <cite id="95aeae5e-4">Jarosite decomposes in two steps: dehydration and dehydroxylation between ~250–450 °C via loss of hydroxyl/sulfate groups</cite>.
- Asbestos fibers: At ~500–600 °C in air, chrysotile loses coordinated hydroxyls and dehydrates; complete decomposition typically requires ~≥900 °C with extensive mass and phase loss. <cite id="976ed845-5">Thermal breakdown of chrysotile proceeds via progressive dehydration; at ~1200 °C, structural reorganization yields olivine and enstatite in one reported pathway</cite>. <cite id="95aeae5e-0">Heat treatment at ≥900 °C may be necessary for complete thermal decomposition of chrysotile</cite>. <cite id="95aeae5e-6">Thermal decomposition of asbestos materials releases bound chemically combined water upon heating</cite>.

High-temperature regime (≥700 °C; culminating ≥900–1400 °C): oxide/sulfate melting, spinel/mullite growth, glass and ultra-stable minerals at very high T/P
- Carbonate-oxide reactivity and fluxing: With continued heating in oxidizing conditions, oxide products from carbonates can sinter and form dense spinels/perovskites; dolomite’s decomposition pathways under CO2/air show interplay of carbonation/decarbonation and phase collapse, enabling fluxing behavior that lowers fusion temperatures in mixed wastes. <cite id="a90c8bff-1">In-situ XRD of dolomite in CO2/calcination environments shows concurrent carbonate and oxide phase readjustment with temperature</cite>. <cite id="95aeae5e-5">Ore calcination produces particles’ structural changes due to mineral decomposition at high temperatures</cite>. <cite id="976ed845-5">At high enough temperature, framework cations re-equilibrate into perovskite-like pyroxenes/olivine on complete dehydration</cite>.
- Feldspar-quartz system and glassy zones: Primary rock-forming feldspars and quartz begin to recrystallize and dissolve into silica-rich liquids between ~1000–1400 °C, nucleating mullite and aluminates; above ~1200–1400 °C, quartz commonly disappears by ordering/disordering pathways and feldspar is absent, with mullite and glass dominating. <cite id="976ed845-2">Above 1200 °C, microcline vanishes and mullite grows; quartz remains until ≥1400 °C in XRD analyses of feldspar-bearing rocks</cite>. <cite id="976ed845-9">Mullite can be detected as forming from metakaolinite decomposition by ~1000–1100 °C</cite>. <cite id="976ed845-4">As temperature increases toward ~1250 °C, amorphous phase and mullite content rise; quartz volume reduces with increasing temperature</cite>.
- Anhydrite/gypsum behavior: Under oxidizing high T, sulfate-bearing phases lose water to anhydrous salts, and at sufficiently high temperatures (and often under confining/pressurized conditions characteristic of deep zones) can further decompose to basic ferric sulfates or evolve SO3; in low-pressure settings, dehydration to anhydrite (CaSO4) precedes potential decomposition to CaO and SO3 above ~1000–1200 °C. <cite id="95aeae5e-4">Jarosite dehydration/dehydroxylation (250–450 °C) illustrates high-temperature instability of sulfate/hydroxyl layers in iron systems</cite>. <cite id="6856606c-8">Oxidation-generated sulfuric acid promotes gypsum/anhydrite formation from sulfate ions in near-surface alteration zones</cite>.
- Asbestos and other fibrous silicates: Complete decomposition of serpentine/asbestos requires ≥900 °C, after which refractory silicate products like enstatite/mullite-like phases, spinel, and/or skeletal oxide frameworks can persist; prolonged heating (>1200 °C) favors complete structural collapse and higher oxide/orthosilicate end-members. <cite id="95aeae5e-0">Heat treatment at temperatures of at least 900 °C may be necessary for the complete thermal decomposition of chrysotile</cite>. <cite id="976ed845-5">At ~1200 °C, chrysotile-derived materials can reorganize into olivine and enstatite upon full dehydration</cite>.
- Waste-rock oxidation front: Elevated temperatures in dumps accelerate pyrite oxidation, raising sulfate mobility and lowering pH, which feeds back on dissolution of Fe/Al minerals and clay dehydroxylation and can create oxygen-deficient zones at depth; this oxidative mobilization underpins many acid mine drainage precursors and controls phase changes at mid-to-high temperatures. <cite id="95aeae5e-3">Oxidation of sulfide minerals such as pyrite present in waste rock results in elevated sulfate, enhanced metal loadings and often low pH</cite>. <cite id="95aeae5e-8">Sulfide mineral oxidation in waste rock dumps tends to increase internal temperatures and may lead to oxygen depletion</cite>.

Additional notes on atmosphere and pressure dependence
- Oxidizing vs reducing conditions: In air, sulfides oxidize to ferric/ferrous oxides with SO2/SO3 evolution; in reducing conditions, partial melting and magnetite stabilization can occur at high T, whereas decarbonation produces metal oxides in all cases; clay transformations depend on Al/Si ratio and oxygen fugacity (spinel-type aluminates vs mullite ranges). <cite id="6856606c-1">Pyrite oxidation above ~500 °C proceeds via intermediate sulfates before forming oxide phases</cite>. <cite id="6856606c-4">Magnetite crystallizes from oxide melt at high oxygen levels and further oxidizes to ferric oxides; in reducing zones, oxide melts can persist as FeO- and Fe3C-bearing liquids</cite>. <cite id="95aeae5e-4">Dehydroxylation pathways of jarosite illustrate strong dependence on T and oxygen potential via dehydration/dehydrogenation steps</cite>.
- Carbonate chemistry and buffering: Dolomite and other carbonates show strong CO2 fugacity effects; calcination under CO2 or air shifts decomposition temperatures and growth of carbonate-oxide intermediates. <cite id="a90c8bff-6">The decomposition temperature of dolomite decreases with increasing CO2 partial pressure, with minima between 10–20% CO2</cite>. <cite id="a90c8bff-8">Non-isothermal kinetic studies of dolomite in CO2-enriched conditions reveal altered thermal behavior approaching in-situ geologic settings</cite>.

Putting it together: sequential phase changes with increasing temperature in typical waste-rock minerals
- 100–250 °C: Dehydration and boundary reactions dominate. Kaolinite clays start to dehydroxylate; organic matter in wastes pyrolyzes, releasing volatiles; trace pyrite oxidizes (FeS2 → FeSO4, with SO2), and jarosite begins to lose hydroxyls/sulfates. <cite id="976ed845-7">Clay minerals begin to decompose and dehydroxylation occurs to form metakaolin at 500–650 °C</cite>. <cite id="6856606c-5">At 250–275 °C, FeSO4 formation proceeds in tandem with pyrite oxidation</cite>. <cite id="95aeae5e-7">Thermal decomposition releases chemically combined water from asbestos materials upon heating</cite>. <cite id="95aeae5e-4">Jarosite dehydration/dehydroxylation initiates between ~250–450 °C</cite>.
- 250–500 °C: Decarbonation and sulfate/oxide intermediates become prominent. Carbonates decompose to oxides with CO2 release (calcite ~825–850 °C, dolomite within ~600–850 °C depending on atmosphere), metakaolin forms from kaolinite, and pyrite converts to FeSO4 then Fe3O4/Fe2O3. <cite id="a90c8bff-3">Calcite decomposes to CaO + CO2 around ~825–840 °C</cite>. <cite id="a90c8bff-2">General carbonate-to-oxide decomposition on heating</cite>. <cite id="a90c8bff-1">Dolomite decomposition observed via in situ XRD is controlled by CO2 partial pressure and temperature</cite>. <cite id="976ed845-1">Mullite nucleation commences near ~940 °C from metakaolinite breakdown, indicating clay transformation peak</cite>. <cite id="95aeae5e-0">Chrysotile requires ≥900 °C for complete decomposition, suggesting persistent intermediate phases below that threshold</cite>.
- 500–800 °C: Oxide reordering, glass formation, and deeper oxidation. Feldspars recrystallize and can vanish above ~1200 °C in high-temperature sequences; quartz persists to ≥1400 °C; jarosite collapses; and sulfates evolve anhydrous products (gypsum → anhydrite → CaO + SO3 at high T). <cite id="976ed845-2">Feldspar disappears above 1200 °C and quartz above 1400 °C in XRD; mullite arises from metakaolinite</cite>. <cite id="95aeae5e-4">Jarosite shows two-step dehydration/dehydroxylation between ~250–450 °C</cite>. <cite id="6856606c-1">At T > 500 °C, pyrite oxidation proceeds via intermediates before forming ferric oxides</cite>. <cite id="6856606c-4">At high oxygen, magnetite crystallizes from oxide melt and oxidizes; under reducing melt conditions, FeO can coexist with Fe3C</cite>. <cite id="976ed845-5">By ~1200 °C, complete dehydration can reorganize chrysotile-derived materials into olivine/enstatite frameworks</cite>.
- ≥900 °C: Structural collapse and fusion. Asbestos fibers require ≥900 °C for complete breakdown; mullite stabilizes above ~1000–1200 °C; feldspar and quartz are consumed; carbonates are fully decomposed; pyrite oxidation products order into dense spinels/perovskites or melt into oxide-rich liquids, potentially forming glass-ceramic matrices with enstatite, olivine, spinel, and Fe-oxides. <cite id="95aeae5e-0">Complete chrysotile decomposition generally needs ≥900 °C</cite>. <cite id="976ed845-9">Mullite is detectable from ~1000–1100 °C as metakaolinite decomposes</cite>. <cite id="976ed845-4">At ~1250 °C, mullite and amorphous fraction increase; quartz volume diminishes</cite>. <cite id="976ed845-2">Feldspar disappearance above 1200 °C and quartz above 1400 °C indicate complete silicate fusion in many waste-rock sequences</cite>. <cite id="a90c8bff-2">Carbonates continue to release CO2 and leave behind the metal oxides across increasing temperatures</cite>. <cite id="6856606c-4">Magnetite/spinel and Fe3C crystallize from oxidizing/reducing oxide melts at high temperatures</cite>.

Practical implications for waste rock
- Chemistry: Dehydration and decarbonation drive CO2 and H2O evolution; pyrite oxidation generates sulfate acids and Fe-oxides, mobilizing metals; jarosite dehydration elevates sulfate fractions; overall, pH swings and metal complexation are pronounced. <cite id="95aeae5e-3">Pyrite oxidation elevates sulfate and often yields low pH with enhanced metal loadings</cite>. <cite id="6856606c-8">Pyrite oxidative dissolution creates sulfuric acid and iron hydroxides that can trigger further reactions</cite>. <cite id="95aeae5e-4">Jarosite two-step decomposition removes hydroxyls and sulfates between ~250–450 °C</cite>. <cite id="95aeae5e-9">Sulfide oxidation in dumps increases internal temperatures and can deplete oxygen</cite>.
- Phase changes: Transition from hydrous clays and carbonates to metakaolin/mullite, spinels/perovskites, and silica-bearing melts; formation of enstatite/olivine frameworks; anhydrite/gypsum dehydration; chrysotile to refractory silicates or to olivine/enstatite above ~1200 °C; feldspar and quartz largely consumed by ~1200–1400 °C. <cite id="976ed845-1">Metakaolinite breakdown at ~940 °C initiates mullite</cite>. <cite id="976ed845-2">Feldspar (1200 °C) and quartz (1400 °C) disappearance with mullite growth from metakaolinite</cite>. <cite id="976ed845-3">Kaolinite → metakaolinite at ~500 °C, metakaolinite → mullite around ~980 °C</cite>. <cite id="6856606c-4">Magnetite/spinel crystallization from oxide melts at high oxygen potentials; Fe3C under reducing melt conditions</cite>. <cite id="95aeae5e-0">Chrysotile needs ≥900 °C for full decomposition</cite>.
- Melting/glass formation: In oxidizing mixtures of silicate minerals and carbonates, high-temperature sintering can produce glassy matrices with crystallized mullite, spinel, and orthosilicates; in reducing or carbonaceous wastes, FeO- and Fe3C-bearing liquids facilitate devitrification to lower-temperature ferric/ferrous silicates. <cite id="95aeae5e-5">Calcination of ore causes structural changes via decomposition of minerals at high T</cite>. <cite id="976ed845-4">Rising temperature increases amorphous and mullite content toward ~1250 °C, reducing quartz volume</cite>. <cite id="95aeae5e-1">Thermal decomposition of mixed oxides shows mass loss and phase changes between 350–600 °C in air, consistent with viscous sintering and partial melting</cite>. <cite id="6856606c-4">Under oxidizing high T, magnetite/spinel crystallize from oxide melts; under reducing T, magnetite oxidizes further while Fe3C persists</cite>.

Sensitivity and controls
- Gas-phase chemistry: CO2 and H2O contents in the gas phase shift decarbonation and hydration–dehydration equilibria of carbonates, clays, and sulfates, altering temperatures at which phase changes occur. <cite id="a90c8bff-6">Dolomite decomposition temperature decreases as CO2 partial pressure increases, reaching a minimum at ~10–20% CO2</cite>. <cite id="a90c8bff-0">TG-MS shows decomposition temperatures of CaCO3 polymorphs and dolomite depend on sample mass and heating conditions</cite>. <cite id="95aeae5e-4">Jarosite dehydration/dehydroxylation occurs between ~250–450 °C with T and oxygen potential dependence</cite>.
- Confinement and pressure: In deeper or compacted waste zones, higher effective pressure favors silica polymorph transformations (e.g., quartz to coesite/stishovite) and stabilizes denser aluminosilicate phases at lower temperatures than in free-cooling conditions; in contrast, open-system heating near surfaces promotes dehydration and gas evolution to maintain equilibrium. <cite id="976ed845-4">Quartz volume reduces and mullite stabilizes with increasing temperature, evidencing pressure- and T-driven phase ordering in ceramics analogs</cite>. <cite id="95aeae5e-2">Thermally active minerals show phase transitions or reactions in response to heating in rocks</cite>.
- Organic content: Carbonaceous materials in waste rock pyrolyze in the 250–600 °C range, yielding volatiles and char that can reduce oxygen locally, influence gas compositions, and interact with sulfide oxidation fronts. <cite id="95aeae5e-9">Oxygen depletion can occur in zones where sulfide oxidation heats and consumes O2, affecting phase evolution</cite>. <cite id="95aeae5e-7">Thermal decomposition of asbestos-bearing wastes releases bound water as an initial step</cite>.

In summary, as waste-rock temperature increases, the dominant transformations progress from dehydration of hydrous phases at low T, through decarbonation, clay dehydroxylation and ferric sulfide oxidation in mid T, to oxide reordering, partial melting, and formation of mullite, spinels, orthosilicates, and glassy matrices at high T; complete breakdown of thermally unstable phases like chrysotile often requires ≥900 °C, while feldspar and quartz are consumed by ~1200–1400 °C under oxidizing conditions, with phase stabilities and kinetics strongly modulated by gas composition, oxygen fugacity, and confining pressure. <cite id="95aeae5e-7">Thermal decomposition starts with loss of chemically combined water in asbestos-bearing wastes</cite> <cite id="a90c8bff-2">Carbonates decompose on heating to release CO2 and form metal oxides</cite> <cite id="976ed845-1">Mullite formation begins near ~940 °C from metakaolinite breakdown</cite> <cite id="6856606c-1">Pyrite oxidation above ~500 °C proceeds via sulfate intermediates to ferric oxides</cite> <cite id="976ed845-2">Feldspar disappears above ~1200 °C and quartz above ~1400 °C, with mullite derived from metakaolinite</cite> <cite id="95aeae5e-0">Chrysotile typically requires ~≥900 °C for complete decomposition</cite> <cite id="6856606c-4">Magnetite/spinel and Fe3C crystallize from oxide melts depending on oxygen potential</cite>.

without_scope.text: How does calcination chemically transform kaolinite, and what are the subsequent phase changes observed as the temperature increases?
without_scope.answer:
# Chemical Transformation and Early Stages (Dehydroxylation)

Upon heating, kaolinite (Al2Si2O5(OH)4) undergoes dehydroxylation, i.e., elimination of hydroxyl groups, which collapses the 1:1 dioctahedral clay layer framework and introduces direct Si–O–Al bridging, forming amorphous metakaolin polymorphs as primary reaction products in the 400–650 °C range. <cite id="f191cb1a-5">In the temperature range 450–650 °C, dehydroxylation of kaolinite and formation of metakaolinite takes place</cite> <cite id="f191cb1a-7">This produces a product known as metakaolin and typically happens between 400° – 600°C</cite>. <cite id="8cc4eef8-1">During the thermal treatment of kaolinite, the main mineral phase in kaolin rock, dehydroxylation occurs, forming metakaolin through a ... mechanism</cite>. <cite id="8cc4eef8-3">DTA analysis of preheated kaolinite shows a weak second exothermic peak near ~1250 °C due to mullitization, indicating a distinct, lower-temperature dehydroxylation stage that culminates in metakaolin before mullite formation</cite>. <cite id="8cc4eef8-7">Infrared spectra of kaolinite preheated to 450–460 °C show OH-stretching features characteristic of kaolinite, evidencing the early stage prior to metakaolinization</cite>. At the molecular level, step-wise dehydroxylation and condensation between octahedral Al(OH)6 and tetrahedral Si(OH)4 units yield dehydroxylated “monobasic” intermediates and incipient polymer chains of –Si–O–Al–, prior to the 400–650 °C consolidation to metakaolin. <cite id="8cc4eef8-4">Molecular-dynamics simulations reproduce the thermally induced transformation of kaolinite to metakaolin via step-wise dehydroxylation and condensation, clarifying the sequence of Al–OH/Si–OH removal and framework polymerization</cite>.

Mechanistically, dehydroxylation can proceed by elimination of water (and possibly hydroxides) from interlayer and edge sites, yielding disordered metakaolin with residual OH that progressively decreases with temperature, consistent with IR/TGA trends. <cite id="f191cb1a-9">Endothermic dehydration of kaolinite begins at 550–600 °C producing disordered metakaolin, but continuous hydroxyl loss is observed up to 900 °C</cite>. Kinetic analyses show a single-step (overall) dehydroxylation mechanism for kaolinite with measurable activation energy, consistent with non-isothermal TG/DTA interpretations. <cite id="8cc4eef8-6">A reaction order mechanism is established for dehydroxylation of kaolinite</cite>.

# Metakaolin Stage: Optimal Calcination Ranges

Between roughly 400–650 °C, fully dehydroxylated metakaolin predominates. Its pozzolanic activity peaks when about 30–40% of kaolinite has transformed (i.e., calcination in the 600–800 °C interval), where metakaolin retains reactivity toward cementitious systems without excessive quartz retentation. <cite id="f191cb1a-2">The optimum temperature for heating a kaolin in order to obtain MK with a high pozzolanic index is 600–800°C, where the degree of kaolinite ...
</cite> <cite id="f191cb1a-4">Kaolinite is highly reactive, and the optimal activation temperature of kaolinite is from 600–800 °C</cite> <cite id="f191cb1a-5">In the temperature range 450–650 °C, dehydroxylation of kaolinite and formation of metakaolinite takes place, while at about 1000 °C, mullite was formed</cite>. Industrial practice commonly targets 400–600 °C to “stop” at the metakaolin stage when that product is the goal. <cite id="f191cb1a-7">Typically happens between 400° – 600°C; at this point, the reaction may be stopped if metakaolin is the intended product</cite>. <cite id="f191cb1a-0">Optimal calcination conditions at 800°C for 180 minutes achieved the highest pozzolanic reactivity and mechanical properties in low-grade calcined kaolinite</cite>.

Compositional and mineralogical starting variability shifts the MK optimum; for example, alkali-bearing clays can nucleate feldspars/alkali aluminosilicates at lower temperatures, moving the sweet spot upward or broadening the window. <cite id="f191cb1a-1">Structural changes occur in the feldspars between 600–1000 °C, with higher temperatures forming the liquid phase that bonds the quartz, indicating that alkali-bearing systems crystallize earlier and alter the apparent optimal MK window</cite>.

# Mullite and Silicate Polymorph Evolution (≈850–1200 °C)

As temperature exceeds ~850 °C, metakaolin begins to convert to mullite (Al2SiO5) via solid-state reactions, while silica and alumina components react and/or dissolve into a glassy phase that facilitates diffusion. Mullite formation is typically discernible by XRD/DTA around 950–1100 °C, growing with further heating; a weak exotherm near ~1250 °C is commonly observed during mullitization of preheated kaolin. <cite id="5deb3c2d-0">Kaolinite usually exhibits a weak second exothermic peak at ∼1250°C during DTA due to mullitization</cite> <cite id="5deb3c2d-6">Mullite phase begins to form around 980°C and its amount increases with temperature as 1:1 mullite (sillimanite Al2SiO5) at ~1100°C</cite>. In secondary mullite pathways, silica and alumina derived from kaolinite react at high temperature to produce (1:1) mullite and free quartz, reflecting reaction-sintering of the kaolin-derived aluminosilicate melt/glass. <cite id="5deb3c2d-4">Secondary mullite can be created by reacting silica and alumina at high temperatures; after firing, mullite forms by reaction between the silica- and alumina-containing components</cite>. <cite id="5deb3c2d-5">Mullite is thus formed after firing kaolinite at elevated temperature; since the SiO2 content in kaolinite is higher than in mullite, reaction consumes SiO2 and Al2O3 to form 1:1 mullite and leaves excess SiO2 as quartz</cite>.

Crystallization pathways depend on alumina-to-silica ratio and cooling history. When alumina content is sufficiently high (≈2:1 mullite field), 2:1 mullite (spodumene) and/or alumina spinel may form, whereas 1:1 mullite (sillimanite) plus quartz dominates near the stoichiometric ratio. <cite id="5deb3c2d-2">The sintering temperature is influenced by the alumina content in the mullite system; as Al2O3 reduces from 77 wt.% in a 3/2 mullite field, transformations to 2/1 mullite and higher quartz contents occur</cite>. Structural studies align with these trends: mullite is the principal aluminosilicate product in the 1:1 field (sillimanite) near 1100 °C, with quartz retained in excess. <cite id="5deb3c2d-6">Mullite forms from ~980 °C and increases with temperature as 1:1 mullite at ~1100 °C; crystallization yields a mullite–quartz system</cite>.

# High-Temperature Melting, Liquidus Sintering, and Late Crystallization (≈1200–1400 °C+)

Raising temperature further drives viscous flow and glass formation: alumina and silica react to form low- and then high-viscosity liquids that transport mass and accelerate mullite growth, while cristobalite crystallizes from the melt above ~1400 °C. <cite id="f191cb1a-1">At 600–1000 °C, structural changes in feldspar occur and, at higher temperatures, a liquid phase bonds the quartz, indicating the onset of aluminosilicate melting and cementation</cite>. <cite id="5deb3c2d-3">Cristobalite transforms into an amorphous phase at temperatures above 1400 °C, with implications for high-temperature densification and property development</cite>. Reaction-sintered fused mullites prepared from Al2O3+SiO2 above the liquidus then develop mullite upon cooling, recapitulating the high-temperature evolution from melts. <cite id="5deb3c2d-1">Fused-mullites are prepared by heating alumina and silica mixtures to temperatures above the melting point, followed by cooling, during which mullite recrystallizes from the melt</cite>. Depending on composition and cooling, additional phases (feldspars, spinel) may appear in alkali-rich or highly Al2O3-deficient melts, shifting crystallization temperatures accordingly. <cite id="5deb3c2d-2">As alumina content decreases relative to silica, sintering behavior and phase assemblages shift from 3/2 mullite toward 2/1 mullite, with increased quartz and reduced mechanical response at lower Al2O3 contents</cite>.

# Integrated Temperature-Programmed Sequence and Notes on Mechanism

- 550–600 °C: Dehydroxylation/dehydration of kaolinite proceeds; endothermic steps remove OH, forming disordered metakaolin polymorphs with residual hydroxyl groups that diminish to ~900 °C. <cite id="f191cb1a-9">Endothermic dehydration of kaolinite begins at 550–600 °C producing disordered metakaolin, with hydroxyl loss continuing to 900 °C</cite>.
- 400–650 °C: Metakaolin predominates via step-wise dehydroxylation and Si–O–Al polymerization; stopping here yields pozzolanic MK with peak reactivity around 600–800 °C calcination. <cite id="f191cb1a-5">450–650 °C dehydroxylation to metakaolinite; about 1000 °C for mullite</cite> <cite id="f191cb1a-7">400–600 °C produces metakaolin; reaction may be stopped at this point</cite> <cite id="f191cb1a-2">600–800 °C optimal for MK pozzolanic index</cite>.
- 850–1100 °C: MK → mullite reaction accelerates; mullite crystallizes (1:1 from ~980–1100 °C), consuming SiO2 and Al2O3 while leaving excess quartz; a weak DTA exotherm near ~1250 °C marks near-complete mullitization depending on history. <cite id="5deb3c2d-0">Weak DTA exotherm at ∼1250 °C due to mullitization</cite> <cite id="8cc4eef8-3">Mullitization exotherm near ~1250 °C indicates completion after earlier dehydroxylation</cite> <cite id="5deb3c2d-6">Mullite begins at ~980 °C and becomes prominent ~1100 °C</cite>.
- >1200 °C: Aluminosilicate melt forms and cements quartz; cristobalite may transform to amorphous phases above ~1400 °C during liquidus cooling; mullite grows by reaction at the liquid–solidus boundary. <cite id="f191cb1a-1">At higher temperatures, a liquid phase forms and bonds the quartz, indicating the onset of aluminosilicate melting</cite> <cite id="5deb3c2d-3">Cristobalite transforms into amorphous phase above 1400 °C</cite> <cite id="5deb3c2d-1">Mullite recrystallizes upon cooling from a fused melt</cite>.
- Composition dependence: Higher Al2O3 favors 2:1 mullite/spodumene and alumina spinel; lower Al2O3 yields 1:1 mullite/sillimanite with more quartz and different sintering mechanics. <cite id="8cc4eef8-0">Mullite is built from Al–O–Si–O–Al units; mechanism and phase assemblage are composition-sensitive</cite> <cite id="5deb3c2d-2">Sintering temperature and phase ratio depend strongly on alumina content, moving from 3/2 to 2/1 mullite as Al2O3 decreases</cite>.

# Practical Implications

For materials processing, “calcination” typically refers to stopping at the metakaolin stage around 400–650 °C to preserve high reactivity; “firing” to higher temperatures develops mullite and glassy phases that densify and stabilize refractories and cements. <cite id="f191cb1a-7">Metakaolin production commonly targets 400–600 °C; further heating to >800 °C drives conversion to mullite and structural changes</cite> <cite id="f191cb1a-2">MK with high pozzolanic index forms at 600–800 °C</cite>. Choosing the endpoint controls whether the material acts as a reactive SCM (MK) or as a load-bearing aluminosilicate refractory (mullite/quartz/liquidus products). <cite id="5deb3c2d-5">Mullite forms after firing kaolinite; since SiO2 content is higher than in mullite, crystallization yields 1:1 mullite plus quartz, characteristic of refractory mullite-cement systems</cite>.

without_term.text: How does heating chemically transform a clay mineral in coal waste, and what phase changes are observed as the temperature increases?
without_term.answer:
Overview
Heating clay-bearing coal waste drives a sequence of dehydration (dehydroxylation), interlayer condensation/rearrangement, aluminosilicate polymerization, and, at higher temperatures, crystallization and/or vitrification. The dominant clay minerals in coal fines/ash—kaolinite/halloysite (1:1), illite/muscovite and interlayered illite–smectite (2:1), and chlorite—undergo temperature‑dependent transformations that change porosity, leaching behavior, and mechanical stability of the waste. In the presence of organics, CO2, and mobile cations (Na, K, Ca), these reactions proceed faster, shift slightly in temperature, and produce stabilized secondary minerals (mullite, quartz/cristobalite, glass, leucite, and carbonates/oxides), often with densification and reduced permeability. <cite id="e7cc21f4-1">Kaolinite transforms into meta‑kaolinite around 540 °C while chlorite dehydrogenates at 610 °C and 820 °C with pore changes</cite> <cite id="e7cc21f4-2">Clay dehydroxylation commonly occurs between 450–750 °C, with illite/montmorillonite crystallinity persisting to ~800 °C</cite> <cite id="e7cc21f4-9">Kaolinite dehydroxylation begins at 450–700 °C</cite> <cite id="e7cc21f4-5">Mixed‑layer clays can alter to chlorite/illite near 150 °C and illite can become muscovite above ~200 °C</cite>.

Stage 1: Dehydration/“Meta‑clay” formation, ~300–700 °C
- Mechanism and chemistry
  - Loss of lattice bound hydroxyls (dehydroxylation) converts phyllosilicate hydroxides to aluminosilicate meta‑phases and releases water. In kaolinite, the reaction is often described as forming “meta‑kaolinite” (a dehydroxylated aluminosilicate) with an endothermic peak near ~540–570 °C, associated with interlayer condensation and framework polymerization. Illite, montmorillonite, and other 2:1 clays show dehydroxylation starting around 450–650 °C, with variable onset depending on order/disorder and cation exchange. <cite id="e7cc21f4-1">Kaolinite transforms into meta‑kaolinite near ~540 °C</cite> <cite id="e7cc21f4-2">Dehydroxylation of clays occurs between 450–750 °C, with illite/montmorillonite maintaining crystallinity up to ~800 °C</cite> <cite id="e7cc21f4-9">Initial dehydroxylation of kaolinite spans 450–700 °C</cite>.
  - Chlorite commonly undergoes two-stage dehydroxylation/decomposition: first steps expel structural hydroxyls/magnesium hydroxide around ~610 °C with layer condensation, and a more complete dehydroxylation/layer collapse near ~820 °C. <cite id="e7cc21f4-1">Chlorite dehydrogenates at 610 °C and 820 °C, associated with pore enlargement and structural change</cite>.
  - At low to modest temperatures (~150–200 °C), mixed-layer clays can re‑order into chlorite and illite layers; illite may further order to muscovite above ~200 °C under hydrothermal/pressure conditions, reducing interlayer water and enhancing framework connectivity. <cite id="e7cc21f4-5">Mixed‑layer clays alter to chlorite/illite around 150 °C and illite to muscovite over 200 °C</cite>.
- Effect in coal waste
  - Coal fines are porous and often contain intergrowths of clays with macerals and carbonates. Early stage dehydroxylation removes hydroxyls and weak interlayers, increasing pore connectivity in the early steps (e.g., chlorite dehydrogenation at ~610 °C producing pore enlargement), then transitioning into more compact meta‑phases as dehydration proceeds. The presence of CO2 and moisture can accelerate dehydroxylation and promote carbonation of Ca/Fe‑bearing phases, altering mineralogical progression and alkalinity. <cite id="e7cc21f4-1">Chlorite dehydrogenation around 610 °C produces pore enlargement</cite> <cite id="91955044-3">Hydration/carbonation/oxidation convert metastable ash minerals into stable secondary phases over time</cite>.
- Representative phases
  - Meta‑kaolinite (Al2Si2O5(OH)4 → dehydroxylated Al2Si2O5(OH)2 or analogous), interstratified illite/smectite transitioning to illite, muscovite, and chlorite after reordering. <cite id="e7cc21f4-1">Meta‑kaolinite formation at ~540 °C</cite> <cite id="e7cc21f4-2">Illite/montmorillonite retain crystallinity up to ~800 °C</cite> <cite id="e7cc21f4-5">Illite order/disorder changes near 150–200 °C</cite>.

Stage 2: Aluminosilicate polymerization and liquidus onset, ~700–1200 °C
- Mechanism and chemistry
  - Dehydroxylated aluminosilicate frameworks (from kaolinite/halloysite and illite/muscovite interlayers) begin to polymerize into high‑melting network polymorphs—particularly mullite (3Al2O3·2SiO2) and quartz‑favored crystallization. In pure clays, mullite formation is typically detectable by XRD near ~1250 °C; before full conversion, silica can exist as amorphous/aluminosilicate glass or transform to cristobalite at higher temperatures. <cite id="e7cc21f4-8">Mullite peak around 1250 °C in pure clays; cristobalite absent up to 1350 °C</cite>.
  - Illite and smectite dehydroxylation over 450–800 °C supply Al and Si for mullite growth; intergranular glass forms as network‑forming oxides (Al2O3, SiO2) and alkalis (K, Na) are partially volatilized/exchanged, while CaO acts as a flux, lowering sintering temperatures and promoting glass‑ceramization. <cite id="e7cc21f4-2">Illite/montmorillonite dehydroxylation persists to ~800 °C</cite> <cite id="91955044-7">CaO lowers sintering temperature and yields predominant mullite + cristobalite crystallization when derived from coal fly ash</cite>.
- Coal waste–specific drivers
  - Volatile organics and K/Na loss during heating promote interparticle sintering and glass formation. As organics pyrolyze and release CO/CO2, they also react with alkalies to form gaseous carbon oxides and mobile species, facilitating rearrangement into dense, microporous glass‑ceramic networks. Simultaneously, carbonates in gangue (CaCO3, MgCO3) decompose at ~600–900 °C to CO2 and CaO/MgO, supplying fluxes that hasten vitrification and alter phase equilibria. <cite id="91955044-3">Coal fly ash solids are metastable and alter via hydration/carbonation/oxidation to secondary phases</cite> <cite id="e7cc21f4-2">Dehydroxylation windows overlap carbonate/alkali mobility, enabling polymerization and glass formation</cite>.
- Representative phases
  - Mullite (3Al2O3·2SiO2) appears sharply by XRD around ~1250 °C in pure clays; cristobalite may appear at higher temperatures and in fluxed systems. In coal‑derived systems, CaO/SiO2/Al2O3 can crystallize into mullite + cristobalite, or produce leucite (KAlSi2O6) depending on alkali balance, often coexisting with residual glass to yield durable low‑Porosity bodies. <cite id="e7cc21f4-8">Mullite near 1250 °C; cristobalite absent up to 1350 °C in pure clay</cite> <cite id="91955044-7">Mullite and cristobalite as predominant phases in sintered coal fly ash with CaO</cite>.
  - Quartz and microquartz, formed from supercooled glass, appear as the matrix fills pore spaces; chlorite and illite residues may collapse into muscovite or persist as ordered layers depending on temperature/chemistry. <cite id="e7cc21f4-1">Illite to muscovite ordering above 200 °C; chlorite dehydroxylation progression</cite>.

Stage 3: High‑temperature recalescence and vitrification, ~1100–1500 °C and beyond
- Mechanism and chemistry
  - As quartz/mullite begin to nucleate, the remaining amorphous aluminosilicate plus fluxes (CaO, K2O, Na2O) approach incipient melting; mass transport accelerates via diffusion/melt facilitated sintering, the intergranular phase becomes continuous glass, and density collapses to ~1–3% porosity. In coal‑analog experiments on clay‑bearing siltstone heated to 1400 °C, permeability decreases and mineralogy evolves into stable high‑melting phases, consistent with vitrification into alkali‑aluminosilicate glass with dispersed mullite/quartz. <cite id="e7cc21f4-3">Thermal simulation to 1400 °C of clay‑bearing siltstone shows permeability and mineral changes indicative of progressive sintering and phase transformation</cite>.
  - In highly Ca‑rich gangue, wollastonite (Ca2SiO4) and gehlenite‑type phases can form; leucite may crystallize in K‑rich mixtures, while Al2O3‑rich liquids can yield spinel or re‑precipitate as mullite/clinoplag-silicate near the liquidus. <cite id="91955044-7">CaO‑bearing coal ash sintering favors mullite + cristobalite with glassy matrix</cite>.
- Representative phases and textures
  - Dense microquartz + mullite matrix with minor leucite or wollastonite, or a fully devolatilized glass‑ceramic. XRD often shows strong mullite peaks and quartz reflections; DSC can show weight loss plateaus tied to organic volatilization, then endothermic crystal‑field transitions and glass transition before final recalescence at incipient melting. <cite id="e7cc21f4-8">Mullite at 1250 °C with cristobalite forming at higher temperatures and fluxing</cite> <cite id="e7cc21f4-3">Progressive phase change and permeability decline up to 1400 °C</cite>.

Coal‑waste context: cumulative effects, activation windows, and stabilization
- Activation of coal gangue for geotechnical use commonly targets clay removal and densification near ~600–700 °C; this matches the dehydroxylation and interlayer collapse regime where porosity drops and sintering begins, improving strength and reducing leachability. Optimal “activation” temperatures in the literature cluster around 600–650 °C for gangue improvement, consistent with completion of clay dehydration and early glass formation. <cite id="c3b974b4-8">Reported optimal activation temperatures of coal gangue are ~650 °C and ~600 °C, aligning with completed clay transformations and early vitrification</cite>.
- Weathering and stabilization in situ introduce environmental drivers to the high‑temperature sequence: carbonation converts Ca(OH)2/CaO to CaCO3; oxidation of Fe/Mn alters hematite/goethite; and hydration of aluminosilicate glass produces montmorillonite/illite locally, yielding more stable, lower‑permeability profiles over time. <cite id="91955044-3">Hydration/carbonation/oxidation transform metastable ash minerals to stable secondary phases</cite>.
- Practical implications
  - After heating, clay fractions in coal waste convert endothermically (≤700 °C) to dehydroxylated meta‑phases, then reorganize/sinter (700–1200 °C) into mullite/quartz/cristobalite or leucite‑bearing glass‑ceramics, and above ~1100 °C the system vitrifies into a dense, low‑porosity mass, with CO2 released from carbonates and organics aiding densification and phase conversion. <cite id="e7cc21f4-1">Kaolinite meta‑formation near ~540 °C and chlorite two‑stage dehydroxylation</cite> <cite id="e7cc21f4-2">Clay dehydroxylation windows (450–750 °C)</cite> <cite id="e7cc21f4-8">Mullite at ~1250 °C; cristobalite appearance above</cite> <cite id="91955044-7">CaO lowers sintering temperature; mullite + cristobalite dominance</cite> <cite id="e7cc21f4-3">Up to 1400 °C, mineral changes and densification are observed</cite>.

Key phase‑change map with temperature
- ≤300 °C: minor ordering of mixed‑layers; hydroxyls remain; CO2/humidity initiates slight carbonation/hydration; K/Na exchange. <cite id="e7cc21f4-5">Reordering to chlorite/illite around 150 °C</cite>.
- ~300–450 °C: onset of dehydroxylation and cation release; interlayer water escapes; pore structure modifies. <cite id="e7cc21f4-9">Kaolinite dehydroxylation beginning at 450–700 °C</cite>.
- ~450–650 °C: dehydroxylation of kaolinite/halloysite (meta‑kaolinite) and illite/smectite; chlorite first dehydroxylation (610 °C); porosity may increase then compact as dehydration proceeds. <cite id="e7cc21f4-1">Kaolinite to meta‑kaolinite ~540 °C; chlorite 610 °C</cite> <cite id="e7cc21f4-2">450–750 °C dehydroxylation window for clays</cite>.
- ~650–900 °C: accelerated sintering driven by organics/CaCO3 decomposition; CaO fluxes lower vitrification; mullite begins to crystallize; CO2 promotes carbonation and densification; reported gangue activation peaks in this window. <cite id="91955044-3">Carbonation/oxidation in fly ash stabilization</cite> <cite id="91955044-7">CaO reduces sintering temperature; mullite and cristobalite form</cite> <cite id="c3b974b4-8">Activation temperatures around 600–650 °C</cite>.
- ~900–1200 °C: liquidus approaches; intergranular glass forms; cristobalite emerges; mullite peak intensifies; K/Si promotes leucite; permeability drops; interparticle bonding increases. <cite id="e7cc21f4-8">Mullite near 1250 °C; cristobalite absent up to 1350 °C in pure clays</cite> <cite id="91955044-7">Coal ash sintering yields mullite + cristobalite with glassy matrix</cite>.
- ≥1200 °C: vitrification dominates; quartz/mullite dominate; CO2 release completes; residual carbonate decarbonates; dense glass‑ceramic or partially devitrified rock forms; in siltstone analogs, permeability collapses markedly. <cite id="e7cc21f4-3">Heating to 1400 °C induces mineral transformations and substantial permeability decrease</cite>.

Mechanistic notes distinguishing coal waste from “pure clay”
- Organic carbon lowers the effective onset of clay reactions by supplying heat and gases: volatilization of macerals and CO/CO2 interact with silica and alkalies to form mobile species that rearrange aluminosilicate frameworks and catalyze sintering. <cite id="91955044-3">Weathering of ash proceeds via hydration/carbonation/oxidation that convert metastable solids</cite>.
- Gangue carbonates decompose to CO2 and alkali earth oxides, acting as fluxes that lower sintering temperatures and can crystallize as wollastonite/CA‑S or dissolve into the glass to delay crystallization, shifting phase equilibria. <cite id="91955044-7">CaO significantly lowers sintering temperature and yields mullite + cristobalite</cite>.
- Clay mineralogy matters: kaolinite/halloysite dominate low‑temperature dehydration to meta‑phases and later to mullite; chlorite requires two dehydroxylation steps and collapses at higher T; interlayered illite–smectite tends to order into stable 2:1 phases then dehydroxylate to muscovite, altering expansion/contraction behavior and densification rates. <cite id="e7cc21f4-1">Kaolinite to meta‑kaolinite ~540 °C; chlorite at ~610 and ~820 °C</cite> <cite id="e7cc21f4-5">Illite to muscovite above ~200 °C</cite> <cite id="e7cc21f4-2">Dehydroxylation windows for illite/montmorillonite</cite>.

Summary of observed transformations in heated clay-bearing coal waste
- Initial: Dehydration/interlayer condensation of kaolinite/halloysite and illite/smectite, with chlorite partial dehydroxylation; porosity increases transiently, then collapses as meta‑phases form. <cite id="e7cc21f4-1">Meta‑kaolinite at ~540 °C; chlorite at ~610 °C with pore changes</cite> <cite id="e7cc21f4-2">450–750 °C dehydroxylation window</cite>.
- Intermediate: Fluxing by CO2/CaO lowers temperatures for vitrification; mullite and quartz/cristobalite crystallize; XRD shows mullite peaks near ~1250 °C; permeability and reactivity decline. <cite id="91955044-7">Mullite and cristobalite as predominant crystalline phases from CaO‑rich coal ash</cite> <cite id="e7cc21f4-8">Mullite around 1250 °C; cristobalite appears at higher T</cite> <cite id="e7cc21f4-3">Mineral changes with permeability reduction to 1400 °C</cite>.
- High temperature: Dense glass‑ceramic with microporous quartz/mullite matrix (possibly leucite/wollastonite) forms; CO2/humidity complete carbonation and stabilization; long‑term weathering produces additional clay secondaries (hydration/carbonation). <cite id="91955044-3">Secondary minerals via hydration/carbonation/oxidation stabilize ash</cite>.
These transformations convert reactive, porous clay‑rich coal waste into a more stable, mechanically coherent material suitable for engineering and environmental applications. <cite id="c3b974b4-1">Heating alters physical/chemical properties and leaching behavior of coal gangue</cite> <cite id="c3b974b4-2">Activation characteristics show pronounced changes with temperature</cite>.
