without_preference.text: How do current cervical cancer screening guidelines vary based on a woman's age and HIV status?
without_preference.answer:
Below is a concise, evidence-based overview of how modern cervical cancer screening recommendations change by a woman’s age and HIV status, drawing from U.S., U.K., and World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines and HIV-specialized guidance.

Key principles that link age and HIV
- Most societies now use HPV testing as the primary screen, adding cytology as needed, with screening starting before symptomatic disease and tailored to age, prior test results, and immunocompromise. <cite id="9fb40c1e-4">The updated WHO guidelines recommended a shorter screening interval of every 3 to 5 years with a primary HPV DNA test for women living with HIV</cite>. <cite id="9fb40c1e-6">CDC guidance states that screening should start at age 21 and continue through 65 using HPV or cytology or their combinations, and that annual screening is not recommended at average risk</cite>. <cite id="9fb40c1e-1">NIH’s HIV clinical guidelines advise cytology at the time of HIV diagnosis for women ages 21–29 and then follow HIV-specific algorithms</cite>.

- For average-risk women, age bands control frequency: frequent false positives drive more annual testing if cytology is positive or HPV intermediate/positive. <cite id="9fb40c1e-0">USPSTF directs every 3 years cytology alone for 21–29 and allows in 30–65 co-test HPV/Pap every 5 years or Pap alone every 3 years</cite>. <cite id="f53d07d3-5">Women 30–65 should be co-tested HPV+Pap every 5 years or Pap alone every 3 years</cite>. <cite id="9fb40c1e-6">CDC specifies continuing screening to 65 and supports test-adjacent intervals</cite>. Long-term surveillance beyond 65/70 is based on prior tests remaining negative for many years. <cite id="9fb40c1e-5">Surveillance with HPV-based testing every 3 years for a minimum of 25 years even beyond age 65 is often described, contingent on prior negative history</cite>. <cite id="f53d07d3-8">ACS highlights starting at 25 and HPV-based intervals, with extended surveillance for those who remain Pap-/HPV– for many years</cite>.

How HIV status changes screening across ages
- Immediately after HIV diagnosis and early disease: <cite id="9fb40c1e-1">People ages 21–29 living with HIV should have cervical cytology at the time of initial HIV diagnosis (AII), followed by an HIV-specific 6-month cytology in patients younger than 30 years with immunosuppression; if negative, annual cytology for up to two years and then return to routine schedules</cite>. <cite id="9fb40c1e-2">ASCCP’s patient guidance advises that patients younger than 30 with immunosuppression be screened three times annually with Pap smears before increasing the interval, acknowledging the baseline higher risk and impact of immunosuppression</cite>.

- Ages 30–65 (risk is elevated but manageable with HPV primary): <cite id="9fb40c1e-4">WHO recommends primary HPV DNA testing with 3–5 year intervals, shorter than general-population recommendations, acknowledging higher HIV-attributable disease risk and immune dysfunction</cite>. <cite id="9fb40c1e-1">NIH guidance allows cytology/HPV co-testing to allow longer intervals in older HIV+ women with normal prior results, but stresses intensified surveillance if CD4 is low or cytology abnormal</cite>. <cite id="f53d07d3-0">In women with HIV, cytology/HPV co-testing can permit longer intervals when older than 29 with normal results, but intensity must increase if cytology is abnormal or CD4 is suppressed</cite>. <cite id="f53d07d3-3">HIV guidelines emphasize that older age, high-risk HPV types, and persistent infection increase risk in HIV-positive women</cite>.

- ≥65–70 (stopping/monitoring based on prior negative results; risk remains higher with HIV): <cite id="9fb40c1e-6">CDC recommends screening continues through age 65 based on accumulated risk, prior negative tests, and test modality, and then individualized surveillance</cite>. <cite id="f53d07d3-5">Many guidelines still allow HPV–based stop rules at 65–70; those who remain HPV– for many years and without risk factors can stop</cite>. <cite id="9fb40c1e-5">Surveillance with HPV testing every 3 years beyond 65 can be used for those who meet tail conditions to reduce interval-3 CIN3 risk</cite>. Because HIV elevates lifetime risk, even women who have been HPV/ cytology– may benefit from continued or earlier-in-cycle surveillance and closer partner screening.

- Special immunology considerations: <cite id="9fb40c1e-3">Guidelines for immunosuppressed women (non-HIV) recommend starting earlier (e.g., 25) and more frequent cytology or HPV testing, then tailoring by CD4 count and prior results</cite>. <cite id="9fb40c1e-8">Immunocompromised women are often screened starting at 25 or 21 years, more frequently than general recommendations, and surveillance intensity depends on immune status</cite>. <cite id="f53d07d3-1">Cumulative incidence of CIN2+ over 15 years among HIV-infected women is elevated with CD4<350/µL, underscoring the role of immune suppression and the need for more intensive screening</cite>.

Partner screening and sexual history integration
- For women living with HIV and/or partners with HIV: <cite id="9fb40c1e-1">Screening should begin promptly at HIV diagnosis in women 21–29, and include annual cytology during early immune suppression</cite>. <cite id="9fb40c1e-7">HIV-specific screening standards advise offering cervical and anogenital screening for all adult patients living with HIV and integrating sexual partner screening and treatment</cite>. Partner-directed screening/treatment and safe-sex measures (condom use, pre-exposure prophylaxis) complement cervical testing in HIV-positive women and couples. <cite id="9fb40c1e-8">Partner screening and management are emphasized for women 21–30 with HIV or risk factors to limit onward transmission and early detection</cite>.

Age-specific guidance (average risk) contrasted with HIV-tailored adjustments
- Ages 21–29:
  - Average risk: <cite id="9fb40c1e-0">Cytology-only every 3 years</cite>.
  - HIV+: <cite id="9fb40c1e-1">Cytology at diagnosis; women younger than 30 with immunosuppression should have cytology at 6 months; if negative, then annual cytology up to two years before returning to their risk/treatment-based schedule</cite>. <cite id="9fb40c1e-2">If immunosuppressed, consider 3 normal annual Pap screens before extending to 3-yearly</cite>. <cite id="9fb40c1e-7">HIV-specific algorithms include HPV testing and cytology depending on CD4 and prior results to intensify surveillance in early decades</cite>.
- Ages 30–65:
  - Average risk (combined): <cite id="9fb40c1e-0">HPV/ Pap co-test every 5 years or Pap alone every 3 years</cite>, <cite id="f53d07d3-5">HPV+Pap 5-yearly or Pap 3-yearly</cite>.
  - HIV+: <cite id="9fb40c1e-4">Primary HPV DNA test with shorter intervals (3–5 years)</cite>. <cite id="9d6dd7b8-1">NHS uses 5-year screening but offers HIV clinics with shorter, intensified intervals; HPV-based testing is used for primary screening in high-risk cohorts</cite>. If cytology co-tested is negative at 30–34 and immune reconstitution occurs, intervals can lengthen toward average-risk schedules; if positive or CD4 is low or viral load not suppressed, maintain or intensify screening (e.g., annual cytology), and consider primary HPV more often. <cite id="f53d07d3-0">Cytology/HPV co-testing can allow longer intervals in HIV-positive women older than 29 with normal tests, but intervals shorten if cytology is positive or CD4 is suppressed</cite>. <cite id="f5d3d07d3-3">Risk factors such as older age within the 30s and persistent high-risk HPV increase likelihood of CIN3; screening must be tailored</cite>.
- ≥65–70:
  - Average risk: <cite id="9fb40c1e-6">Screening can stop at 65–70 if long negative histories apply; otherwise, surveillance</cite>. <cite id="f53d07d3-5">HPV–based negative history supports stopping; Pap–based negative history supports every 3 years for some jurisdictions</cite>.
  - HIV+: <cite id="9fb40c1e-6">Continue through 65 based on risk and test results, then surveillance</cite>. <cite id="9fb40c1e-5">HPV-based follow-up every 3 years beyond 65 can reduce CIN3 risk in those who were long HPV–, and is often recommended as long-term surveillance</cite>. In HIV, lifetime risk is high enough that even women who become HPV– may warrant earlier-in-cycle repeat screening and/or partner-directed screening strategies.

Regional/organizational differences in thresholds and intervals
- WHO: <cite id="9fb40c1e-4">Primary HPV DNA testing every 3–5 years; start screening at 25 to optimize detection in women living with HIV</cite>. <cite id="9fb40c1e-9">WHO advises starting at age 25 rather than 30 and recommends 3–5 year HPV intervals specifically for HIV-positive women</cite>.
- UK NHS England: <cite id="9d6dd7b8-1">Invites women 25–64 for cervical screening every 5 years, using primary HPV testing; those with HIV or severe immunosuppression are managed in specialist clinics with risk-appropriate shortening of intervals and use of HPV-based triage</cite>. <cite id="9d6dd7b8-6">First invitation is mailed at 24.5 years; routine invitations align to age bands with 5-year frequency</cite>. <cite id="9d6dd7b8-5">NHS is rolling out personalized screening so that people who meet higher-risk criteria can have a 5-year test interval aligned to risk, including HIV-positive women</cite>. <cite id="9d6dd7b8-3">Evidence supports no interval less than 3 or more than 5 years nationally, with local flexibility; personalized models adjust for HIV and immunosuppression</cite>.
- US (USPSTF/ACS/CDC): <cite id="9fb40c1e-0">Start at 21, 3-year cytology alone to 29; HPV–Pap co-test every 5 years or Pap every 3 in 30–65</cite>, <cite id="f53d07d3-5">HPV–Pap co-test every 5 years or Pap every 3 years ages 30–65</cite>, <cite id="f53d07d3-8">ACS: initiate screening at 25 years with HPV-based co-test every 5 years and Pap alone every 3 years</cite>, <cite id="9fb40c1e-6">CDC: start 21 and continue through 65 using HPV/Pap co-test or Pap alone; annual screening not recommended at average risk, with tailoring for HIV/immunosuppression</cite>. For HIV+, immediate baseline screening (including cytology/Pap) and more frequent follow-up is advised, with primary HPV testing preferred in many programs.

Risk context that drives the guidelines for HIV-positive women
- HIV infection, particularly with CD4 suppression and poor viral suppression, is associated with markedly higher rates of high-grade cervical intraepithelial neoplasia over time. <cite id="f53d07d3-1">The 15-year cumulative incidence of CIN2/3 or worse among HIV-infected women is elevated in those with CD4+ <350/µL</cite>. <cite id="f53d07d3-3">Older age and persistent high-risk HPV typing also increase probability of disease in HIV-positive women</cite>. <cite id="9fb40c1e-2">ASCCP guidance explicitly notes that women under 30 with immunosuppression should have 3 normal annual screens in succession, reflecting higher per-test risk and immune-driven persistence</cite>. WHO and US agencies therefore converge on more frequent initial screening, earlier start, and shorter intervals for HPV primary screening in HIV+ women.

Putting it together: Practical application by age and HIV status
- If you are HIV-negative/average risk:
  - 21–29: cytology-only every 3 years; consider HPV testing per program if offered, but expect the same interval if Pap alone. <cite id="9fb40c1e-0">Every 3 years with cytology alone</cite>.
  - 30–65: HPV/Pap co-test every 5 years or Pap alone every 3 years; maintain as long as tests remain negative and no high-risk factors. <cite id="9fb40c1e-0">HPV/Pap co-test 5-yearly or Pap 3-yearly</cite> <cite id="f53d07d3-5">HPV–Pap co-test 5-yearly or Pap 3-yearly</cite>.
  - ≥65–70: stop in most jurisdictions if long negative history; otherwise continue surveillance (e.g., HPV test to 70 or Pap-based to 65). <cite id="9fb40c1e-6">Screen through 65 with tailoring and then surveillance</cite> <cite id="f53d07d3-5">Stop at 65 if HPV– with many prior negative tests or Pap– based programs</cite>.

- If you are living with HIV (regardless of CD4/ART unless known):
  - Immediately at infection, if reproductive-aged and with a cervix, start screening promptly:
    - Ages 21–29: cytology at diagnosis; if immunosuppressed, 6-month cytology; if negative, then annual cytology up to two years, then align to HIV-risk schedule. <cite id="9fb40c1e-1">Screening at HIV diagnosis for 21–29; 6-month cytology for those younger than 30 with immunosuppression; then annual up to two years</cite> <cite id="9fb40c1e-2">Three normal annual Pap screens if immunosuppressed before increasing intervals</cite>.
    - Consider primary HPV testing 3–5 year intervals, and HPV/Pap co-test if prior cytology negative but CD4 low or viral load not suppressed. <cite id="9fb40c1e-4">Primary HPV test every 3–5 years in HIV</cite> <cite id="f53d07d3-0">In HIV-positive women older than 29 with normal results, co-testing may allow longer intervals; shorten if cytology positive or CD4 low</cite>.
  - Ages 30–65: Prefer HPV-based testing with shorter intervals (often every 3 years; programs may use 3–5 year HPV primary); if Pap/HPV co-test and negative, many women can align to 5-year intervals if immune suppression resolves and viral load is suppressed. <cite id="9fb40c1e-4">3–5 year HPV primary in HIV</cite> <cite id="f53d07d3-0">Co-test to extend interval in HIV if normal, but intensify if positive or CD4 low</cite> <cite id="9fb40c1e-6">Continue to 65 with tailoring</cite>.
  - ≥65–70: Continue surveillance with HPV testing if risk persists (e.g., prior HPV–/low CD4, recent HIV diagnosis, persistent risk factors); otherwise, consider transition to long-term surveillance with HPV-based repeats every 3 years for as long as clinically indicated. <cite id="9fb40c1e-6">Continue through 65 based on history and risk, with personalized surveillance</cite> <cite id="9fb40c1e-5">HPV-based surveillance every 3 years for 25+ years, even beyond 65, is used in tail scenarios to minimize CIN3+ risk</cite>.

- Women with HIV and immunosuppression (including transplant, steroid-treated disease, or CD4<350):
  - Expect more frequent initial screens and lower thresholds for escalation; follow the algorithm elements above and add CD4-viral load–based escalation and partner screening. <cite id="9fb40c1e-2">Three normal annual Pap screens if under 30 and immunosuppressed before extending</cite> <cite id="f53d07d3-1">CD4<350 associated with higher CIN2+ cumulative incidence over 15 years</cite> <cite id="f53d07d3-3">Risk rises with persistent high-risk HPV, older age, and abnormal cytology in HIV-positive women</cite> <cite id="9fb40c1e-7">HIV-specific standards integrate partner screening and HPV-based triage</cite>.

- Special situations:
  - Recent HIV-positive partner diagnosed; recent high-risk sexual behavior: consider baseline HPV colposcopy, expedited cytology/HPV co-test, and partner management. <cite id="9fb40c1e-7">Screening and partner screening/treatment are core in HIV-positive women and couples</cite>.
  - Immunocompromised women without HIV: start earlier and monitor more often; many organizations start at 21–25 and then tailor by immune status. <cite id="9fb40c1e-3">Guidelines for immunosuppressed women recommend starting at 25 or 21 and more frequent testing</cite>.
  - Post-cancer treatment or hysterectomy/surgical history: counsel per individual risk; many programs still recommend surveillance HPV-based testing into older age for those with risk factors. <cite id="9fb40c1e-5">Long-term HPV-based surveillance beyond 65 is recommended in many high-risk cases</cite>.

Summary: Age and HIV interact to shift screening earlier and closer together on the cervix, centered on more sensitive HPV testing and lower escalation thresholds in HIV-positive women. <cite id="9fb40c1e-4">WHO recommends primary HPV testing every 3–5 years beginning at age 25 for women living with HIV</cite> to counteract higher-grade lesion risk; <cite id="9fb40c1e-0">USPSTF uses age-banded plans of 3-year cytology in the 20s and HPV/Pap 5-year or Pap-only 3-year co-tests in their 30s–60s</cite>, and <cite id="9fb40c1e-6">CDC recommends screening continue through 65 with tailoring by HIV status and immune suppression</cite>. <cite id="9fb40c1e-1">US HIV guidelines begin at diagnosis with annual cytology in many early-decade scenarios and then individualize</cite>, while <cite id="9d6dd7b8-1">the UK NHS frames routine 5-year screening for 25–64 with 25-year, HPV-based protocols applied in high-risk cohorts including HIV</cite>.

Caveats and evolving practice
- Some jurisdictions still rely on Pap-smear-only programs; primary HPV offers higher sensitivity and allows less frequent screening, including shorter intervals for HIV+ women. <cite id="f53d07d3-8">HPV-based co-test every 5 years for 30–65 with options for Pap-only 3-yearly</cite> <cite id="9fb40c1e-4">Primary HPV with 3–5 year intervals in HIV</cite>. Shared decision-making should weigh false-positive burden, colposcopy harms, and patient risk (including HPV exposure, recent HIV diagnosis, and partner risk). <cite id="9fb40c1e-5">Surveillance protocols beyond 65 reduce but do not eliminate interval CIN3 risk in high-risk women</cite>.

Practical decision checklist (how to apply)
- At or after HIV diagnosis with a cervix and age ≥21: start screening; if under 30 and immunosuppressed, cytology at 3–6 month intervals for at least two years after initial screening, escalating if any abnormal result or low CD4; consider primary HPV more often. <cite id="9fb40c1e-1">Cytology at diagnosis; 6-month cytology for those under 30 with immunosuppression; annual up to two years</cite> <cite id="9fb40c1e-2">Three annual Pap screens if immunosuppressed under 30</cite>.
- Ages 30–65 and HIV+ with sustained immune recovery and no abnormalities: HPV co-test every 3 years or Pap alone every 3 years (some programs prefer HPV–Pap 5-yearly); tailor shorter if HPV16/other high-risk types or cytology atypical. <cite id="9fb40c1e-4">Primary HPV 3–5 years</cite> <cite id="f53d07d3-0">Co-testing allows extension for normal results; shorten if positive or CD4 low</cite>.
- ≥65 and HIV+: consider surveillance HPV testing every 3–5 years; many programs recommend through 70 with annual Pap if Pap test-only and at least four normal Pap tests in prior decade (adapt for HIV-specific risk). <cite id="9fb40c1e-6">Continue through 65 based on history; then surveillance</cite> <cite id="9fb40c1e-5">HPV-based surveillance every 3 years beyond 65 can reduce CIN3+ risk</cite>.
- Average-risk women and HIV-negative: use your society’s schedule (USPSTF 3-yearly Pap to 29; 3–5 year HPV/Pap co-test 30–65; stop at 65 with appropriate negative histories). <cite id="9fb40c1e-0">USPSTF age-based schedules</cite> <cite id="f53d07d3-5">HPV–Pap options 30–65</cite> <cite id="9fb40c1e-6">CDC through 65</cite> <cite id="9d6dd7b8-1">UK 25–64 every 5 years nationally</cite>.

Bottom line: Cervical screening starts earlier and is more frequent in women living with HIV across all decades compared with average-risk peers, with WHO and U.S. agencies converging on primary HPV testing at shortened intervals (often 3–5 years) beginning in the late 20s and tailored to immune status and prior results, while U.K. programs often deliver routine 5-year HPV-based screening nationally with personalized shortening for high-risk patients such as those with HIV. <cite id="9fb40c1e-4">WHO: 3–5-year primary HPV starting at 25 for HIV</cite> <cite id="9fb40c1e-0">USPSTF: 3-year Pap alone 21–29; HPV/Pap 5-year or Pap 3-year 30–65</cite> <cite id="9fb40c1e-6">CDC: start 21 and continue through 65 with tailored HPV/Pap strategies; annual not recommended at average risk</cite> <cite id="9d6dd7b8-1">NHS: every 5 years 25–64 with HPV based programs and personalized shortening for HIV/immunosuppression</cite> <cite id="9fb40c1e-1">NIH HIV guidelines: immediate cytology at diagnosis, 6-month cytology for under 30 with immunosuppression, then annual for up to two years</cite>.

questions.original_query: How do the risks of adverse events compare between the Pfizer-BioNTech and AstraZeneca COVID-19 vaccines across various symptoms?

query.text: How do the risks of adverse events compare between the Pfizer-BioNTech and AstraZeneca COVID-19 vaccines across various symptoms?
query.answer:
Below is an evidence-backed comparison of adverse event (AE) risks between the Pfizer–BioNTech (BNT162b2, mRNA) and AstraZeneca/Oxford (ChAdOx1, adenoviral vector) COVID‑19 vaccines, organized by symptom category and event type. Unless otherwise noted, effects are typically observed within days after dosing and are stronger in younger adults and males for myocardial events and more prominent after first-dose exposure with the viral-vector vaccine for thrombotic events. Where absolute risks are available, we include per-100,000 or case-per-100,000 ranges and relative comparisons to pre‑COVID background or to each other.

Key overarching comparisons
- Overall/local reactogenicity: Cohort data from general practices and large cohorts report that local reactions (e.g., redness, swelling, hard lump) are more common after Pfizer–BioNTech than after AstraZeneca, whereas overall systemic AEs are broadly similar across platforms in large nationwide comparisons of solicited/unsolicited AEs, with timing differences in onset rather than absolute risk differences after the second dose.<cite id="ad94cad7-4">Local adverse events were more frequent with Pfizer–BioNTech than with AstraZeneca recipients</cite> <cite id="ad94cad7-1">Comparisons of timing of solicited AE onset and prevalence of unsolicited AEs across Pfizer, Moderna, and AstraZeneca showed platform-specific reactogenicity patterns with differences in time-to-onset</cite>.
- Serious cardiocutaneous AEs: In adolescent and young adult males, both mRNA and adenovector vaccines increased risks of myocarditis/pericarditis compared with pre‑vaccine background, with adenovector ChAdOx1 showing larger short‑term excess risks after the first dose; mRNA vaccines also show elevated but generally modest absolute risks concentrated primarily after the second dose in males 18–39 and younger.<cite id="a10dd0b9-3">Self-controlled cohort comparisons found increased risk of myocarditis after first ChAdOx1, BNT162b2, and mRNA‑1273</cite> <cite id="37d18936-0">Among 18–39-year-olds, both mRNA vaccines were associated with increased myocarditis/pericarditis risk; risk estimates were modestly higher after mRNA‑1273 in some settings</cite> <cite id="37d18936-3">Nature study found increased risks of myocarditis after first dose of ChAdOx1 and BNT162b2 and after first and second doses of mRNA‑1273</cite> <cite id="37d18936-4">Meta-analysis estimated five‑fold higher risk of myocarditis or pericarditis with BNT162b2 vs pre‑COVID background</cite> <cite id="37d18936-5">In males 12–17 after the second mRNA dose, myocarditis/pericarditis occurs about 1 in 10,000</cite>.
- Cardiovascular outcomes in the general cohort: In UK-based analyses of acute coronary events and ischemic strokes, event incidence after the second dose was numerically lower with AstraZeneca than with Pfizer; adjusted analyses concluded lower absolute risks post‑vaccination overall and confirmed overall benefit–risk balance.<cite id="3d57d78c-1">Cambridge/UK analyses reported up to 27% lower incidence of heart attacks and strokes after second AstraZeneca dose and up to 20% lower after Pfizer/BioNTech</cite> <cite id="3d57d78c-5">UK regulator reaffirmed vaccines, including AstraZeneca, are effective and generally well tolerated with benefits outweighing risks</cite>.
- Thrombotic and thrombocytopenic events: Large pharmacovigilance (EudraVigilance) comparisons show thrombotic events (e.g., cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, hemorrhagic stroke) are rare but more commonly reported for AstraZeneca than for mRNA vaccines from Moderna and Pfizer, with similar extremely low absolute rates; mechanistic concerns are reduced risk heterogeneity and a theoretical procoagulant contribution for adenovector vaccines.<cite id="3d57d78c-0">Thrombotic adverse events linked to Moderna, Pfizer, and Oxford–AstraZeneca were extremely rare; more events were observed with AstraZeneca than mRNA vaccines</cite> <cite id="3d57d78c-3">EudraVigilance database comparison described occurrence and outcomes of thrombotic events across Moderna, Pfizer, and Oxford–AstraZeneca</cite> <cite id="3d57d78c-6">Thrombotic adverse events were extremely rare for Moderna, Pfizer, and AZ; AZ numerically higher</cite> <cite id="3d57d78c-9">Expert UK inquiry materials summarize reports of thromboembolic events and hemorrhagic stroke after mRNA and AZ vaccines</cite>.
- Neurologic outcomes (GBS and related): Comparative ecological case-series across multiple vaccines suggest AstraZeneca/Oxford has nonzero Guillain–Barré syndrome signals, with mRNA vaccines (Pfizer/Moderna) generally showing lower rates; autoimmune encephalitis/meningitis signals were more strongly associated with AstraZeneca in pooled analyses, though causal attribution is limited by signal detection and confounding.<cite id="ad94cad7-2">Oxford–AstraZeneca had GBS cases across brands (GBS signal with AZ/Oxford and smaller with Pfizer/Moderna/Johnson & Johnson), with age/gender modifiers</cite> <cite id="ad94cad7-8">Nature article highlights cross-vaccine differences in immune response and safety signals</cite>.

Comparative risk by symptom/event category

Local injection-site reactions and immediate systemic AEs
- Injection site and early reactogenicity: Large primary-care cohorts found higher proportions of local AEs (e.g., inflamed, swollen, hard lump, tenderness) after Pfizer–BioNTech compared with AstraZeneca, consistent with reactogenicity literature; unsolicited events by type show platform-specific onset windows rather than a systematic shift in overall burden after the second dose across all ages, with men sometimes showing higher systemic rates in meta-analyses of allergic reactions.<cite id="ad94cad7-4">Pfizer–BioNTech recipients had a higher percentage of local adverse events than AstraZeneca recipients</cite> <cite id="ad94cad7-1">Dose 1 vs 2 differences in timing for solicited AEs and similar prevalence of unsolicited AEs across vaccines compared head-to-head</cite> <cite id="ad94cad7-7">In allergic reactions analyses, allergic AE risk was elevated overall and increased with male sex and age for some brands, with male gender associated with higher risk</cite>.
- Practical implication: Expect higher immediate local reactogenicity (redness, swelling, hard lump) and early systemic reactions with mRNA/Pfizer than adenovector/AstraZeneca, but the absolute risks remain low and temporally limited; provide patient information and reassurance of generally favorable benefit–risk.<cite id="3d57d78c-1">Adjusted analyses found lower heart attack/stroke incidence after second Pfizer and AstraZeneca doses</cite> <cite id="ad94cad7-1">Across national cohorts, platforms differ in reactogenicity onset but overall unsolicited AE prevalence is similar</cite>.

Myocarditis and pericarditis (late young-adult male signal with mRNA; early male signal with AZ)
- Direction and magnitude: Both vaccines increase myocarditis/pericarditis risk relative to pre‑vaccine background; adenovector ChAdOx1 showed pronounced increases after the first dose, whereas mRNA (including Pfizer) showed smaller absolute increases concentrated after the second dose in young males 18–39 and younger, translating to approximately 1/10,000 risk in adolescent males after the second mRNA dose.<cite id="a10dd0b9-3">SCCS evidence of increased risk after first ChAdOx1, BNT162b2, and mRNA‑1273</cite> <cite id="37d18936-0">Age‑stratified cohort (18–39) shows increased risk for both mRNA vaccines; modestly higher after mRNA‑1273 in some analyses</cite> <cite id="37d18936-3">Increased risks after first dose for ChAdOx1 and BNT162b2; after first and second for mRNA‑1273</cite> <cite id="37d18936-5">Males 12–17 after second mRNA dose: about 1 in 10,000</cite> <cite id="37d18936-4">Five‑fold higher risk of myocarditis/pericarditis with BNT162b2 versus pre‑COVID background</cite>.
- Net comparison: AZ tends to produce higher relative increases in short‑term (weeks after first dose) risk in males, while mRNA/Pfizer produces higher absolute background-adjusted small risks mainly after the second dose in males 18–39; overall expected lifetime risks from infection can exceed vaccine risks in many age groups, supporting vaccination despite rare cardiac AEs.<cite id="a10dd0b9-0">Age‑adjusted analysis in 18–39-year-olds shows substantial increased risk of myocarditis/pericarditis with both mRNA and vector vaccines</cite> <cite id="37d18936-8">Comparative counts show 20+ million AZ exposures vs ~17 million Pfizer; overall risk context provided by regulators</cite> <cite id="3d57d78c-2">Pfizer materials emphasize myocarditis risk after COVID‑19 infection is far higher than after vaccination</cite>.
- Timing for counseling: Counsel patients that AZ carries a more pronounced risk immediately after the first dose (in males), with mRNA/Pfizer risks concentrated after dose 2 in young males with persistent relief of symptoms if post‑vaccine pericarditis typically improves with rest/NSAIDs; consider deferral or risk–benefit discussion for high‑risk cardiology comorbidities in male adolescents/young adults.<cite id="37d18936-3">Increased short-term risk after first ChAdOx1 and BNT162b2</cite> <cite id="37d18936-5">Young male adolescents show 1/10,000 risk after second mRNA dose</cite> <cite id="37d18936-4">Meta‑analysis shows low absolute frequency with increased relative risk</cite>.

Thrombotic and thrombocytopenic adverse events (TTS-like, cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, hemorrhagic stroke)
- Direction and magnitude: In EudraVigilance (EU/UK), thrombotic events are extremely rare for mRNA vaccines from Pfizer/Moderna and more frequently reported with AstraZeneca, with similar case counts per million in older age bands but an elevated relative signal for AZ; clinical phenotypes (e.g., CVST with severe headache, visual changes) typically occur in the early post‑vaccination period and prompt urgent review; overall incidence remains low and not clearly dose‑dose beyond rare events.<cite id="3d57d78c-0">Reported thrombotic events—more with Oxford–AstraZeneca than with Moderna/Pfizer; extremely rare absolute rates</cite> <cite id="3d57d78c-3">Database comparison quantified occurrence and outcomes across vaccines with relative concentration for AZ</cite> <cite id="3d57d78c-6">Extremely rare thrombotic adverse events with similar pattern across brands; more events numerically with AstraZeneca</cite> <cite id="3d57d78c-9">Regulators acknowledge rare thromboembolic and hemorrhagic stroke reports after mRNA and AZ; mRNA risks very low</cite>.
- Practical implication: Counsel older adults and those with thrombotic risk factors to be alert for severe headache, sudden vision changes, persistent chest pain, or leg swelling 2–28 days after AZ; for mRNA/Pfizer, risks of thrombotic events are much lower than benefits but not zero; overall population analyses show lower incident events than infection-associated risks.<cite id="3d57d78c-1">Overall cardiovascular events fell after second doses with both AZ and Pfizer</cite> <cite id="3d57d78c-3">Clinical outcome data emphasize low absolute rates with few severe neurovascular events</cite>.

Neurologic/autoimmune syndromes
- Guillain–Barré syndrome (GBS), encephalitis/meningitis: Multi-vaccine cohort analyses identified GBS signals for AZ/Oxford which were lower for mRNA brands, with age and sex modifiers; autoimmune encephalitis/meningitis signals were higher with AZ. While mechanistic links are unproven, temporal clustering and age effects justify careful evaluation and reporting in both platforms.<cite id="ad94cad7-2">GBS events across vaccines showed stronger association with Oxford–AstraZeneca compared with mRNA brands in pooled data; symptoms and age/gender modifiers were described</cite> <cite id="ad94cad7-8">Cross-vaccine safety comparisons highlight differences in rare neurologic syndromes</cite>.

Systemic symptoms and all-cause burden
- General systemic signals (fever, headache, fatigue): Large self-controlled case series comparing ChAdOx1 to mRNA show increased risk of short-term systemic reactions like myalgia and headache following AZ/ChAdOx1 at 6.5–12 days post-dose, whereas Pfizer mRNA cohorts demonstrate higher local AE proportions but broadly similar systemic AE prevalence overall; fever and fatigue patterns align with reactogenicity and are generally milder and self-limited.<cite id="a10dd0b9-3">First-dose SCCS found increased risk of myalgia/myocarditis after ChAdOx1</cite> <cite id="ad94cad7-1">Across national cohorts, timing and prevalence of systemic AEs differ by platform (Pfizer mRNA shows higher local, similar overall systemic)</cite> <cite id="ad94cad7-4">Higher proportion of local AEs with Pfizer vs AstraZeneca</cite>.
- Overlap with infection: Importantly, cardiovascular events, strokes, and other serious outcomes occur much less frequently after vaccination than after natural SARS‑CoV‑2 infection; comparative UK cohort analyses reflect this offset, reinforcing that vaccine risks are small relative to infection risks in most individuals.<cite id="3d57d78c-1">After second vaccination, heart attack/stroke incidence was up to 27% lower with AstraZeneca and up to 20% lower with Pfizer compared with non-vaccination background, indicating benefits outweigh risks; overall event burden remains low</cite> <cite id="3d57d78c-2">Pfizer materials: infection-associated myocarditis risk is far higher than post‑vaccine</cite>.

Age and sex modifiers across platforms
- Young males (16–24 and 18–39): Highest relative risks of myocarditis/pericarditis occur in young males, with SCCS and cohort analyses showing increases after both first and second doses for mRNA and marked increases after the first dose for adenovector; overall absolute risks remain low (around 1/10,000 in adolescent males after second mRNA dose), but providers should recognize a higher risk window and counsel accordingly.<cite id="a10dd0b9-3">Younger males show increased risk of myocarditis after both ChAdOx1 and BNT162b2; SCCS design supports temporality</cite> <cite id="37d18936-3">Risk elevations after first/second doses vary by vaccine platform and age</cite> <cite id="37d18936-5">Young male adolescents: ~1 in 10,000 after second mRNA dose</cite> <cite id="37d18936-0">Age-stratified analysis (18–39): increased risk for both mRNA and vector vaccines</cite>.
- Females and older adults: Signals for myocarditis/pericarditis are present but lower; thrombotic events concentrate with AZ and are rare, with background risk of cardiovascular disease and age increasing overall event risk independent of vaccine.<cite id="a10dd0b9-3">Sex-specific analyses indicate male predominance for myocarditis/pericarditis</cite> <cite id="3d57d78c-1">UK analyses show protection from heart attacks and strokes after both vaccines</cite>.

Practical counseling and decision-making
- If a patient is strongly contraindicated for both myocardial and thrombotic events, discuss deferral or alternative vaccines with shared decision-making; for most ages/sexes the risk of myocarditis/pericarditis is small and vaccine prevents far more serious outcomes. Counsel on symptoms requiring urgent care by symptom category and time window.
- Consider switching a first dose from AZ to mRNA in males 16–29 if available, based on stronger myocarditis temporal signal after AZ; this is consistent with observational data where risks are higher with adenovector platforms in young males, and acceptable to patients with known reactogenicity concerns.<cite id="a10dd0b9-3">Young male excess myocarditis risk after ChAdOx1 and BNT162b2; platform choice can alter short-term risk</cite> <cite id="37d18936-3">Temporal risk elevations after first-dose adenovector</cite> <cite id="37d18936-4">Low absolute but increased relative risk of myocarditis/pericarditis with BNT162b2</cite> <cite id="3d57d78c-1">Net benefit remains substantial; event rates are very low</cite>.

Key limitations and caveats
- Observational designs (SCCS, cohorts, surveillance) rely on temporality and population denominators; causal attribution is stronger for near‑dose temporality but not absolute proof. Differences in dosing regimens, coadministration, and product batches complicate cross‑brand comparisons.
- Background infection risk drives much higher absolute risks of cardiovascular disease and myocarditis than vaccination, so absolute numbers from post‑vaccine cohorts remain low relative to infection; the net public health benefit remains large despite rare AEs.<cite id="37d18936-4">BNT162b2: rare but increased myocarditis/pericarditis vs pre‑COVID background</cite> <cite id="3d57d78c-2">Infection risk greatly exceeds post‑vaccine myocarditis risk</cite>.

Summary
- Pfizer–BioNTech: More local reactogenicity (inflamed/swollen/hard lump, tenderness) and similar overall systemic AE prevalence; absolute myocarditis/pericarditis risk is small, higher in young males post‑dose 2; thrombotic events are very rare and not elevated relative to AZ in population surveillance.<cite id="ad94cad7-4">Higher local AEs with Pfizer vs AstraZeneca</cite> <cite id="37d18936-5">About 1 in 10,000 myocarditis/pericarditis in male adolescents after second mRNA dose</cite> <cite id="3d57d78c-0">Thrombotic events extremely rare overall; numerically more with AstraZeneca</cite>.
- AstraZeneca/Oxford: Stronger short‑term myocarditis/pericarditis signal in males after first dose, and more frequent signals for thrombotic events (e.g., CVST, hemorrhagic stroke) than mRNA, though absolute rates remain extremely low; overall cardiovascular event incidence decreased post‑vaccination in age‑adjusted UK analyses, underscoring benefit–risk balance.<cite id="a10dd0b9-3">Increased risk of myocarditis after first ChAdOx1 and BNT162b2</cite> <cite id="37d18936-3">Young male increased risk after first-dose AZ</cite> <cite id="3d57d78c-1">Heart attacks and strokes were lower after second vaccine doses in UK cohort</cite> <cite id="3d57d78c-0">Thrombotic events are extremely rare but more frequent with AZ</cite>.

Overall, across symptom categories, the platforms’ adverse event profiles diverge by mechanism: mRNA/Pfizer tends to elicit more immediate, local reactogenicity with small absolute risks of rare myocardial events mainly in young males after dose 2, while adenovector/AstraZeneca carries a stronger early myocardial signal in males and more frequent thrombotic event reports than mRNA in pharmacovigilance, with all absolute risks remaining very low compared with those from COVID‑19 infection.<cite id="ad94cad7-4">Pfizer higher local AEs than AstraZeneca</cite> <cite id="37d18936-0">Both mRNA vaccines increase myocarditis/pericarditis risk in 18–39-year-olds</cite> <cite id="3d57d78c-0">Thrombotic adverse events are extremely rare but more often reported with AstraZeneca</cite> <cite id="3d57d78c-1">Cardiovascular events fall after both vaccines in UK analyses</cite> <cite id="3d57d78c-2">Infection-related myocarditis risk far exceeds post-vaccine risk</cite>.

fully_underspecified.text: How do the risks of adverse events compare between two COVID-19 vaccines across various symptoms?
fully_underspecified.answer:
# Summary

Across COVID-19 vaccines, reactogenic and systemic symptoms cluster in the first 1–2 days after dose, with fever, fatigue, headache, chills, muscle pain, and injection-site pain being most frequent, while rare thrombotic and cardiocerebral syndromes (e.g., TTS, CVST, myocarditis/pericarditis) occur at low absolute rates and differ by product and timing relative to the second dose. <cite id="d13917b6-0">The most common systemic reactions were fever, fatigue, and headache; local reactions were pain, erythema, and swelling</cite>. <cite id="d13917b6-6">Across combined Pfizer, Moderna, and Janssen datasets, the ten most frequently reported AEs were headache, fatigue, and injection-site reactions, with fever, chills, and muscle pain also top-tier</cite>.

# Reactogenicity and Common Symptoms

Across platforms, early reactogenicity is dominated by fatigue, headache, chills, fever, myalgia, and injection-site pain; symptom distributions are broadly similar within mRNA vaccines and distinct from vector-based J&J. <cite id="d13917b6-0">Fever, fatigue, and headache were the most common systemic reactions reported</cite>. <cite id="d13917b6-6">Injection-site reactions, fatigue, headache, muscle pain, and chills were among the most frequent across combined mRNA and J&J data</cite>. <cite id="d13917b6-2">Large series corroborate that fatigue, muscle pain, headache, and chills are the most frequent side effects following COVID‑19 vaccination</cite>. 

Within mRNA vaccines, product-specific differences are modest; both elicit comparable reactogenic profiles, with higher local reaction rates for Moderna and distinctive systemic symptom burdens that peak after the second dose. <cite id="d13917b6-1">Pfizer/BioNTech commonly caused fatigue, headache, chills, and muscle pain, especially after dose 2, whereas Moderna more often produced fever, muscle aches, and joint pain</cite>. <cite id="d13917b6-2">Symptom overlap indicates shared reactogenic mechanisms across mRNA products</cite>. In aggregate national reporting spanning over half a million AEs, Moderna-labeled reports slightly exceed Pfizer for overall AE frequency, consistent with higher reactogenicity proportions reported for that product in combined registries. <cite id="9f85eaaa-5">In a meta-analysis of 604,157 reported AEs, proportions by vaccine brand were 43.51% for Pfizer-BioNTech and 47.13% for Moderna</cite>.

# Rare Serious Events by Symptom Domain

Serious adverse events (SAEs) following COVID-19 vaccination remain uncommon, with most platforms showing no higher SAE incidence than placebo in trials, though specific rare events differ by product. <cite id="9f85eaaa-4">Across 25 randomized trials (22 vaccines), none had higher SAE incidence than placebo</cite>. <cite id="9f85eaaa-1">In the Moderna trial, vaccinated participants had a 6% higher SAE risk than placebo (136 vs 129 per 10,000 after dose 1), corresponding to ~1% absolute risk</cite>. 

Thrombotic and thrombocytopenic events (TTS/CVST) and vaccine‐associated immune thrombocytopenia (VIT) are most notably associated with the viral vector Janssen vaccine, with extremely low absolute risk when scaled nationally. <cite id="62afb957-5">TTS after J&J/Janssen vaccination has been rare, approximately 4 cases per one million doses</cite>. <cite id="62afb957-4">Venous thrombotic events were lower than arterial events for mRNA vaccines, whereas the opposite was observed for ChAdOx1 (AstraZeneca); similar platform differences appear when comparing J&J vector products with mRNA</cite>. <cite id="62afb957-9">FDA’s EUA memorandum noted increased risks of thrombotic/adverse event signals in Janssen reports, prompting targeted labeling/safety updates</cite>. 

Myocarditis and pericarditis occur mostly 1–3 days after the second mRNA dose and are rare across platforms; overall vaccine deployment data show largely null associations with a broad set of serious outcomes, though product-specific small excesses are seen. <cite id="62afb957-7">Symptoms of vaccine‑related myocarditis (chest pain, dyspnea, palpitations) usually appear within 1–3 days after the second dose</cite>. <cite id="62afb957-6">A CIDRAP synthesis concluded mRNA vaccines were not associated with significantly higher rates of 23 serious adverse events 1–21 days post‑vaccination</cite>. <cite id="9f85eaaa-3">Systematic reviews indicate higher incidence of myocarditis/pericarditis after vaccination overall, with platform/vaccine‑specific risk signals detectable in meta‑analyses</cite>.

Across vaccines, local reactions and systemic feverish illness within 48 hours are expected after both first and second doses; distribution differences are product‑specific and usually small when rates are standardized by age/exposure. <cite id="9f85eaaa-8">Allergic reaction/anaphylaxis occurred in roughly 0.2–0.3% across partial/fully vaccinated cohorts in a large JAMA cohort</cite>. <cite id="62afb957-2">Platform‑agnostic adverse‑event summaries list anaphylaxis, myocarditis, pericarditis, and thrombosis as rare post‑vaccinal complications alongside common reactogenicity</cite>.

# Head‑to‑Head and Product‑Specific Comparisons

- mRNA (Pfizer vs Moderna): For overall AEs per dose and first‑dose reactogenic clusters, the differences are modest; Moderna shows higher reporting proportions for systemic AEs overall and after dose 2 across pooled registries, whereas Pfizer exhibits pronounced fatigue, headache, chills, and muscle pain post‑second dose. <cite id="9f85eaaa-5">Proportions of reported AEs were 43.51% for Pfizer and 47.13% for Moderna</cite> <cite id="d13917b6-1">Pfizer/BioNTech commonly caused fatigue, headache, chills, and muscle pain after dose 2, while Moderna more often produced fever, myalgias, and arthralgias</cite>.

- J&J vector vs mRNA: J&J has a distinct reactogenic profile (largely minimal local reactogenicity with more systemic malaise days 4–7) and higher signal for thrombotic/adverse‑event clusters per regulator review; risk remains extremely low per dose and is managed with informed consent and pause protocols. <cite id="d13917b6-6">Top reported AEs for J&J include headache, fatigue, chills, and swelling, with much lower incidence of erythema/induration than mRNA</cite> <cite id="62afb957-5">TTS after J&J is ~4 per 1 million doses</cite> <cite id="62afb957-9">Regulatory review indicated increased risks of thrombotic/adverse‑event reports with J&J and prompted risk communication and monitoring</cite>.

- Rare symptom comparisons: Myocarditis/pericarditis and CNS vascular events differ by platform and timing. Venous thrombosis risk appears lower with mRNA than ChAdOx1; myocarditis/pericarditis peaks 1–3 days after the second mRNA dose and is not observed as a known J&J signal to the same extent (J&J’s rare thrombotic events are venous/thrombocytopenic). <cite id="62afb957-4">Venous events were lower than arterial for mRNA, opposite for ChAdOx1</cite> <cite id="62afb957-7">Myocarditis typically manifests 1–3 days after second mRNA dose</cite>.

# Practical Interpretation by Symptom Category

- Local reactions: Injection‑site pain/pain with erythema/swelling dominate; mRNA products show higher local reactogenicity for Moderna than Pfizer, whereas J&J is comparatively lower in local inflammation. <cite id="d13917b6-0">Local reactions: pain, erythema, swelling; systemic: fever, fatigue, headache</cite> <cite id="d13917b6-6">Across platforms, injection‑site reactions are among top reported AEs; proportions vary by product</cite>.

- Early systemic “feverish” illness: Fever, fatigue, headache, chills, myalgia—higher within days of vaccination, much of it expected; Moderna more often associates fever; Pfizer more often associates headache/chills/muscle pain; both mRNA show similar baseline background. <cite id="d13917b6-0">Fever, fatigue, headache are common systemic reactions</cite> <cite id="d13917b6-1">Pfizer common: fatigue/headache/chills/muscle pain; Moderna more often fever/myalgia</cite>.

- Cardiovascular/cerebrovascular rare events:
  - Myocarditis/pericarditis: rare; peaks 1–3 days post‑second mRNA dose; no clear evidence of association with J&J; still report extremely low absolute rates with mRNA. <cite id="62afb957-7">Symptoms usually appear within 1–3 days after second mRNA dose</cite> <cite id="62afb957-6">No significant association with 23 serious outcomes including myocardial infarction/stroke during 1–21 days</cite> <cite id="62afb957-2">J&J vector had myocarditis reports but with a pattern dominated by thrombotic risk signals</cite>.
  - Thrombosis/thrombocytopenia: J&J more prominently associated with TTS/CVST at ~4 per 1 million doses; mRNA generally lower venous thrombotic risk than ChAdOx1 and no consistent thrombocytopenia signal in early reports. <cite id="62afb957-5">TTS after J&J ~4 per 1M doses</cite> <cite id="62afb957-4">Venous events lower for mRNA vs higher for ChAdOx1; arterial events comparatively higher for mRNA</cite>.

- Allergy/anaphylaxis: Overall rare; absolute rates similar across mRNA mRNA cohorts; part of regulators’ risk assessments. <cite id="9f85eaaa-8">Allergic reaction or anaphylaxis were reported in 0.3% after partial vaccination and 0.2% after full vaccination</cite>.

# Synthesis and Safety Implications

Within‑platform, symptom distributions are largely similar across mRNA vaccines, with product‑specific peaks (fever/arthralgia for Moderna; chills/muscle pain for Pfizer) and higher overall AE reporting proportions for Moderna in pooled registries. <cite id="9f85eaaa-5">AE proportions 43.51% (Pfizer) vs 47.13% (Moderna) across 604,157 reports</cite> <cite id="d13917b6-1">Product‑specific symptom profiles differ slightly but are largely within expected reactogenic patterns</cite>. Between platforms, J&J’s overall reactogenicity is lower (fewer local reactions) but carries distinct rare thrombotic risk signals at very low per‑dose incidence, whereas mRNA vaccines present higher reactogenic burden after dose 2 but minimal TTS risk and no clear evidence of higher rates of 23 serious outcomes in early post‑vaccination windows. <cite id="62afb957-5">J&J: TTS ~4 per 1M doses</cite> <cite id="62afb957-6">mRNA not associated with higher rates of 23 serious outcomes 1–21 days post‑vaccination</cite> <cite id="62afb957-9">Regulatory review flagged increased thrombotic risk signals for J&J</cite>.

Clinically and programatically, this means:
- Expect feverish illness and local reactogenicity for both mRNA dosing schedules; prepare symptomatic treatment and counsel patients on symptom triage.
- Counsel patients post‑second mRNA dose for rare myocarditis/pericarditis and immediate evaluation for chest pain/dyspnea.
- For J&J recipients (especially women 30–49 at higher TTS CVST age range), emphasize recognition of thrombotic‑thrombocytopenic symptoms and thrombosis risks within 3 weeks, and follow local pause/consent protocols.
- In risk‑benefit decisions for immunocompromised or thrombotic risk individuals, discuss per‑dose absolute risks and product‑specific trade‑offs, noting that no vaccine shows higher SAE rates than placebo in trials overall. <cite id="9f85eaaa-4">No vaccine had higher SAEs than placebo across trials</cite> <cite id="9f85eaaa-1">Moderna trial: SAEs 136/10,000 vs 129/10,000 for placebo after dose 1</cite> <cite id="9f85eaaa-8">Allergic/anaphylaxis absolute risks: 0.2–0.3% after complete vaccination</cite>.

# Limitations and How to Improve Comparisons

Existing comparisons rely on post‑marketing reporting, trial AE listings, and large observational cohorts; true head‑to‑head symptom incidence requires standardized denominators, schedules, and covariates to avoid confounding by age, comorbidities, and exposure. Future work should harmonize: (1) per‑dose per‑million AE rates by platform stratified to 1–7 vs 8–30 days, (2) symptom clusters with symptom counts rather than diagnoses, and (3) matched placebo/symptom baselines and exposure windows. <cite id="9f85eaaa-0">Placebo recipients alone showed substantial systemic AE burden after dose 1 in JAMA (e.g., headache 19.3%)</cite> <cite id="9f85eaaa-8">Anaphylaxis risk estimates in JAMA cohorts inform background risk</cite> <cite id="d13917b6-6">Symptom‑level profiles across platforms show overlapping reactogenic domains</cite>.

without_scope.text: How do the risks of adverse events compare between the Pfizer-BioNTech and AstraZeneca COVID-19 vaccines?
without_scope.answer:
# Bottom line
<cite id="07f2e076-0">Across clinical and post‑authorization settings, mRNA (Pfizer–BioNTech) vaccines have generally shown lower overall adverse event burden than adenoviral‑vector AstraZeneca vaccines, with a trade‑off: Pfizer–BioNTech is associated with more frequent but mostly mild systemic reactions like myo/peri‑carditis in late teens/20s, while AstraZeneca carries a lower reactogenicity profile but rare injection‑site adverse events including thrombotic and bleeding complications occur at elevated absolute rates in specific age/sex groups and after certain doses. <cite id="a7855b5c-0">Myocarditis risk is statistically significantly associated with mRNA vaccination, particularly in younger adults, and is considered preventable benefit given the vaccine's strong protection against severe COVID‑19.</cite> <cite id="84be52b9-0">In randomized and real‑world health‑worker cohorts, ChAdOx1 produced more AEs overall than BNT162b2 (for example, 91% vs 53% reported any AE after first dose in a health‑worker study), whereas systemic symptom burden with mRNA vaccines is also common (fever, fatigue, headache).</cite> <cite id="e403495c-5">Importantly, mRNA vaccines are not associated with vaccine‑induced thrombotic thrombocytopenia (VITT), unlike AstraZeneca, even as overall thrombotic/bleeding risks with adenoviral vectors rise in younger women.</cite>

# Comparative reactogenicity from trials and early real world
- Overall and local/systemic reactogenicity (ChAdOx1 vs BNT162b2): <cite id="84be52b9-0">A study of UK health care workers found reported adverse events after the first dose were more common with ChAdOx1 nCoV‑19 than with BNT162b2 (90.9% vs 52.5% overall reporting), with higher proportions experiencing grade ≥3 reactions and more days lost to AEs.</cite> <cite id="a7855b5c-1">ChAdOx1 recipients consistently report injection‑site reactions at ~92% and frequent systemic symptoms (fatigue ~81%, headache ~73%, chills ~62%) in prime‑dose series, exceeding BNT162b2 rates.</cite> <cite id="84be52b9-6">In concomitant vaccination studies and heterologous prime‑boost work, reactogenicity summaries show ChAdOx1 has prominent local reactogenicity and higher systemic symptom rates than BNT162b2 at similar immunogenicity and effectiveness.</cite>
- Trial‑based comparative safety framing: <cite id="84be52b9-9">Initial randomized platform trials reported acceptable safety and effectiveness for both vaccines, but descriptive adverse‑event summaries show ChAdOx1's reactogenicity generally outpaces BNT162b2 in local and systemic rates when evaluated head‑to‑head.</cite> <cite id="07f2e076-2">Meta‑descriptions from phase 3 data and early follow‑up emphasize excellent efficacy with mainly mild, transient adverse reactions across platforms; comparative reviews in 2021 underscored that more recipients experienced systemic symptoms with ChAdOx1 than with BNT162b2.</cite>

Implication: When choosing first doses in adults aiming to minimize reactogenicity burdens while avoiding rare but serious vector‑related thrombotic risks, mRNA may have better overall tolerability metrics in routine schedules, especially outside the 18–49 female age band where VITT risk is elevated with vector vaccines. <cite id="a7855b5c-0">For mRNA, myo/peri‑carditis is rare but detectably increased and largely confined to late teens/20s males; this risk is deemed small relative to protection against COVID‑19.</cite>

# Common adverse events and effectiveness context
<cite id="07f2e076-0">Population‑level surveillance and comparative analyses report that ChAdOx1 is associated with a higher overall adverse‑event burden than BNT162b2, aligning with higher frequencies of systemic symptoms like fever, fatigue, and headache reported in platform datasets and early boost‑era summaries.</cite> <cite id="a7855b5c-8">National datasets and cohort reviews attribute most systemic events to the first booster campaign, with vaccine‑preferred recovery predominating; the pattern is that reactogenic symptoms are typically mild and self‑limiting and resolve quickly.</cite> <cite id="a7855b5c-2">CDC/ACIP summaries for BNT162b2 report ~11% versus 2% on placebo with grade ≥3 reactions in youth, underscoring that while reactogenicity is substantial (fever/viral‑like illness), serious downstream sequelae are uncommon.</cite> <cite id="a7855b5c-9">Large mRNA safety summaries also quantify myo/peri‑carditis incidence around 68 per 100,000 recipients in one dataset, with hospitalization/death increased relative to placebo but at low absolute rates.</cite>

# Serious adverse events: thrombotic and bleeding risks, VITT, myocarditis
- AstraZeneca (vector) rare but serious events:
  - VITT and arterial events: <cite id="e403495c-4">Post‑authorization safety analyses from Denmark and Norway reported arterial events, venous thromboembolism, thrombocytopenia, and bleeding after ChAdOx1 that raised safety concerns, with pooled relative risks higher than background and age/sex interactions documented.</cite> <cite id="e403495c-1">A narrative review of thrombotic events after COVID‑19 vaccination highlights epidemiology and mechanisms implicating vector platforms, distinguishing these signals from COVID‑19 disease‑related thrombosis and from mRNA‑related events.</cite> <cite id="e403495c-5">Reviews emphasize that mRNA vaccines have not presented VITT risk in hundreds of millions of doses; despite persistent concerns, no causal VITT signal has been found with BNT162b2.</cite>
  - Myocarditis and broader cardiovascular safety: <cite id="e403495c-9">Reviews of cardiovascular adverse events synthesize pooled incidence of myocarditis and thromboembolic events across vaccine types; ChAdOx1 cohorts show elevated relative risks of arterial events and thromboembolism in younger adults, consistent with VITT patterns.</cite>
- Pfizer–BioNTech (mRNA) rare but serious events:
  - Myocarditis: <cite id="a7855b5c-0">Statistically significant associations with myo/peri‑carditis are observed after BNT162b2, confirmed internationally, with highest absolute risks in males aged 12–15 and 16–19 in early studies and in late‑teens/20s in adult cohorts.</cite> <cite id="e403495c-2">England analyses of over 42 million vaccinations report hospital admission or death from myocarditis greater after COVID‑19 vaccination; Pfizer's available analyses emphasize that benefits outweigh these rare risks, with careful counseling and monitoring recommended—especially after the second dose in males ages 12–17 and 18–24, and after boosters in young males.</cite> <cite id="a7855b5c-9">Across national cohorts (e.g., ACIP summarizing US data), myo/peri‑carditis incidence is low per 100,000 and predominantly affects adolescent/young adult recipients.</cite>
  - Thrombotic/embolic risk: <cite id="e403495c-5">Large cohort reviews conclude no VITT signal with mRNA vaccines, in contrast to vector platforms; COVID‑19 vaccination overall is associated with reduced risks of heart failure, venous thromboembolism, and related complications compared with never‑vaccinated individuals, indicating vaccine‑preferred benefit on cardiovascular risk.</cite>

- Regulatory and national overviews:
  - UK Yellow Card/REACT: <cite id="07f2e076-1">GOV.UK's Yellow Card summary underscores that most reported reactions across vaccines are mild and self‑limiting (fever, fatigue, headache, local reactions), while monitoring identified rare serious adverse events prompting risk management.</cite> <cite id="a7855b5c-4">Similar national aggregation across products shows adverse event reporting patterns and emphasizes rigorous VAERS‑based signal detection for rare events.</cite>

# Disease‑benefit trade‑offs
<cite id="84be52b9-3">Booster‑era analyses show that heterologous schedules (ChAdOx1 then BNT162b2) are safe and boost antibody responses, with no safety concerns from concurrent influenza vaccination; this underscores that reactogenicity differences do not negate overall benefit from complete schedules.</cite> <cite id="84be52b9-9">Trials and early follow‑up showed both vaccines prevent disease with high efficacy; comparative real‑world reviews found no strong evidence of increased risk for pre‑specified adverse outcomes when pooling products, reinforcing that benefits exceed harms for eligible recipients.</cite> <cite id="84be52b9-8">Effectiveness studies in the BMJ reported early real‑world protection that has persisted, with adverse events generally mild; booster data show high effectiveness against symptomatic disease across product types.</cite> <cite id="07f2e076-1">Regulatory summaries emphasize that vaccines prevent serious disease and death; the most commonly reported adverse reactions also occur with natural infection and are typically milder than COVID‑19 illness.</cite>

# How to interpret the risk comparison in practice (adults)
- General adult schedule: <cite id="84be52b9-0">If minimizing immediate reactogenic burden is a priority, mRNA (Pfizer–BioNTech) may have fewer overall adverse events than AstraZeneca, with most AEs being mild systemic symptoms such as fever and fatigue; however, young men can experience more frequent myo/peri‑carditis after mRNA, albeit rarely and preventable by counseling and dose timing.</cite> <cite id="e403495c-4">AstraZeneca carries a lower reactogenicity burden but an elevated risk of rare vector‑related thrombotic and bleeding complications, particularly in younger women aged 18–49 who face higher VITT risk after the first or second doses, reinforcing age‑ and sex‑informed dosing strategies (e.g., extend intervals, consider mRNA in the 18–49 female group where clinically feasible).</cite>
- Females 18–49: <cite id="e403495c-4">Arterial events, venous thromboembolism, and thrombocytopenia were elevated after ChAdOx1 in Scandinavian cohorts, highlighting increased vigilance for facial swelling, headache, visual changes, abdominal pain, leg swelling/pain, and unusual bruising/areas of blue‑purple skin up to 4 weeks post‑vaccination; risk mitigation includes careful consent, interval extension, and switching to mRNA when available or suitable for the 18–49 age group.</cite>
- Males 12+ and boosters: <cite id="a7855b5c-0">Myocarditis risk after mRNA is real but rare and peaks in late teens/20s; clinicians should counsel on chest pain/pressing palpitations, advise rest and deferral of high‑risk activities if symptoms occur, and consider male‑specific booster strategies in this age band.</cite> <cite id="e403495c-2">Large national analyses from England indicate a higher risk of hospital admission or death from myocarditis after vaccination compared with baseline; Pfizer's safety communications recommend these rare events as preventable benefits and warrant careful monitoring—especially after the second primary dose and first boosters in adolescents and young adults.</cite>
- Overall comparative outlook: <cite id="07f2e076-0">Across pooled analyses, ChAdOx1 produced significantly more overall adverse effects than BNT162b2, reflecting higher reactogenicity rates, yet AstraZeneca's serious but rare thrombotic/bleeding risks with vector technology remain salient in select age/sex subgroups.</cite> <cite id="a7855b5c-0">For mRNA vaccines, the dominant serious signal is myocarditis—prevalent enough to track but rare enough that most recipients experience only mild systemic illness, and overall protection against COVID‑19 far exceeds the harms.</cite>

# Key data points illustrating magnitude
- Common reactions: <cite id="a7855b5c-1">ChAdOx1: local pain ~92%, fatigue ~81%, headache ~73%, chills ~62% after the prime dose; mRNA reactogenicity is lower overall but still substantial for systemic symptoms like fever and fatigue.</cite> <cite id="84be52b9-0">In health care workers, 90.9% vs 52.5% experienced adverse events after ChAdOx1 vs BNT162b2 following first dose; more days lost to AEs and grade ≥3 reactions favored ChAdOx1.</cite>
- Myocarditis: <cite id="a7855b5c-0">Across analyses, BNT162b2 shows a statistically significant association with myo/peri‑carditis, with higher adjusted odds in males 18–25 and 26–49 in early U.S. analyses and in males 12–15/16–19 in pediatric/adult datasets; absolute rates are low per 100,000 and are considered preventable benefits.</cite> <cite id="e403495c-2">England analyses with 42M vaccinations show greater risk of myocarditis hospitalization/death after vaccination; Pfizer's available analyses recommend these rare events as preventable benefits, informing risk‑tiered consent and deferral guidance.</cite>
- Thrombotic risks (AstraZeneca): <cite id="e403495c-4">Arterial events, venous thromboembolism, thrombocytopenia, and bleeding were elevated after ChAdOx1 in Scandinavian cohorts (e.g., cases per million and higher relative risks), with age/sex patterns indicating higher risk in women 18–49; these signals informed JCVI and MHRA interval and subgroup dosing recommendations during the first waves.</cite>
- Overall adverse event burden by product (aggregated): <cite id="07f2e076-0">Pooled analyses across jurisdictions conclude BNT162b2 causes significantly fewer adverse effects than ChAdOx1 (p<0.001), supporting the observed pattern of lower overall AE rates for mRNA.</cite> <cite id="a7855b5c-5">Reporting summaries show administered BNT162b2 had 6304 adverse event reports (68.14 per 100,000), contextualizing absolute frequency relative to vector platforms; no product shows an overall excess of serious adverse events versus benefits when matched by age, comorbidity, and exposure.</cite>
- Safety monitoring and effectiveness: <cite id="84be52b9-8">Early real‑world effectiveness for both vaccines was high against symptomatic disease; adverse events were largely mild and consistent with reactogenicity.</cite> <cite id="07f2e076-1">National adverse‑reaction summaries across the UK (GOV.UK Yellow Card) emphasize that while signals for rare serious events are monitored, most reactions are mild and self‑limiting and preventable benefit dominates.</cite>

# Practical guidance and caveats
- For most adults: <cite id="84be52b9-0">Choose the vaccine that balances your tolerability profile and access; mRNA generally yields fewer overall adverse events and lower reactogenic burden in routine first doses but carries a small absolute risk of myocarditis in late teens/20s males—counsel on local/fever symptoms and red‑flag chest pain/pressing palpitations.</cite> <cite id="e403495c-4">For women 18–49, consider adenovector‑based risks of VITT/arterial events when planning primary series and boosters; extending the prime–boost interval or switching to mRNA can lower these rare risks in this demographic.</cite>
- For special populations: <cite id="a7855b5c-0">Young men receiving boosters should be counseled on myo/peri‑carditis warning signs following BNT162b2 and consider deferral or monitoring strategies if personal risk factors (cardiac disease, prior myocarditis) are present.</cite> <cite id="e403495c-5">No evidence links mRNA to VITT; for patients with personal or family thrombotic risk, interval extension and careful selection of vaccine product remain prudent.</cite>
- Across schedules and boosters: <cite id="84be52b9-3">Concomitant influenza vaccination with BNT162b2 is safe and immunogenic; heterologous prime‑boost strategies deliver robust boosting without added safety risks.</cite> <cite id="84be52b9-8">Real‑world data confirm high effectiveness against symptomatic COVID‑19 despite adverse‑event burdens; adverse events are predominantly mild and largely preventable benefit.</cite>
- Remaining uncertainties: <cite id="a7855b5c-8">AE risk is schedule‑, product‑, and boost‑era‑dependent; regional immunogenicity/demographic differences and evolving circulating variants can modify risk–benefit profiles over time.</cite> <cite id="84be52b9-9">Trials and observational studies do not show strong overall excesses of pre‑specified serious adverse outcomes for any vaccine; continued surveillance remains central to detecting rare signals and refining guidance.</cite>

In short, if you want to minimize immediate, overall adverse reactions and avoid rare vector‑related thrombotic risks, an mRNA (Pfizer–BioNTech) primary series often is the safer choice; if you receive AstraZeneca, be vigilant for VITT‑like symptoms (especially in women 18–49 and after second doses) and counsel on early specialist evaluation. For both vaccines, myocarditis after mRNA and thrombotic/bleeding events after AstraZeneca are rare but serious; with careful consent, monitoring, and dose timing, these represent preventable benefits in the context of strong protection against COVID‑19. <cite id="07f2e076-0">Across available pooled analyses, Pfizer–BioNTech is associated with fewer overall adverse events than AstraZeneca on average, aligning with higher reactogenicity for ChAdOx1 and higher rare-event risks with vector technology that are vaccine-preferred preventable benefits for mRNA.</cite>
