questions.original_query: What reasons do parents in Saudi Arabia give for delaying or missing childhood vaccinations?

query.text: What reasons do parents in Saudi Arabia give for delaying or missing childhood vaccinations?
query.answer:
Below is a synthesis of reasons reported by parents in Saudi Arabia for delaying or missing childhood vaccinations, drawing on cross-sectional surveys, clinic-based studies, pandemic-era analyses, and qualitative/ systematic reviews from across regions (e.g., Riyadh, Eastern/Madinah, Western, Tabuk).

Summary of main reasons
- Proximal, situational causes: <cite id="4a6b681c-0">In a Riyadh cross‑sectional study, delays were most often due to the child being ill on the day of vaccination, parental carelessness, or long postponement</cite>; <cite id="4a6b681c-2">another pediatric cohort found 23% had delayed vaccination by >4 weeks, with child illness cited by 46.7% and “carelessness of parents” a notable factor</cite>. <cite id="4a6b681c-3">Increased odds of delay were linked to caregivers seeking information from family and friends rather than formal sources</cite>.
- Fear of side effects and misinformation: <cite id="b64e2c6d-1">A Saudi study identified concerns about vaccine safety and side effects as the most prominent barrier among parents</cite>; <cite id="b64e2c6d-6">fear of side effects, lack of reliable information, and social media misinformation repeatedly emerge in studies and reviews</cite>. <cite id="b64e2c6d-5">Parents relying primarily on social media as their vaccine information source showed substantially higher hesitancy than those consulting healthcare providers</cite>; <cite id="b64e2c6d-3">parents who refused vaccines cited fears of side effects such as reduced fertility</cite>; <cite id="b64e2c6d-9">in a sample of vaccine‑averse parents, severe vaccine side effects (particularly ADHD) were the most frequently reported feared outcomes</cite>.
- Pandemic-period disruptions and cross‑contamination fears: <cite id="4a6b681c-5">During 2020–2022, the most common reason for delay of routine vaccines was fear of COVID‑19 infection (60.9%); large household size and lack of insurance were risk factors</cite>. <cite id="b64e2c6d-8">Similar patterns of elevated concerns and barriers were documented for pediatric COVID‑19 vaccination in Saudi parents</cite>.
- Program access and logistics: <cite id="4a6b681c-3">Seeking information from informal networks rather than immunization services increases delay risk</cite>; <cite id="4a6b681c-6">studies in Western Saudi Arabia highlight that delays are common when vaccinations fall ≥4 weeks after the scheduled date and recommend improved parental education and timely scheduling</cite>. <cite id="8c789af1-0">Qualitative work in Tabuk underscores the need to understand local parent attitudes to improve adherence</cite>; <cite id="8c789af1-4">Riyadh-based work also emphasizes awareness, attitudes, and provider interactions as determinants of timely vaccination</cite>. <cite id="b64e2c6d-4">A Saudi study in Tabuk reports that noncompliance is driven by perceived barriers beyond knowledge gaps, pointing to service- and context‑specific obstacles</cite>.
- Cultural and religious misconceptions and trust: <cite id="b64e2c6d-6">Religious leaders and cultural norms can shape acceptance when misinformation circulates; parental education and trusted messengers are highlighted as levers</cite>. <cite id="8c789af1-7">A Madinah survey documented high vaccine hesitancy (73.9% of 322 parents), with significant occupational disparities by caregiver work, suggesting access/trust differences</cite>.
- Structural socioeconomic and household factors: <cite id="4a6b681c-5">Large household size and lack of insurance were associated with greater risk of delay</cite>; <cite id="8c789af1-3">caregivers in oil‑industry or labor‑intensive settings may face transport and scheduling conflicts</cite>.
- Seasonal and event‑related scheduling: <cite id="b67b681c-6">During Hajj/Umrah, children and pregnant travelers are advised to receive specific vaccinations per licensed indications, evidencing time‑pressured periods that can disrupt routine schedules</cite>.

Detailed categories of reasons reported by Saudi parents
1) Proximal, day‑of and care‑related reasons
- Illness of the child: <cite id="4a6b681c-0">Child illness on vaccination day was repeatedly identified as the primary reason for deferring or missing a dose</cite>; <cite id="4a6b681c-2">in one study, 46.7% of delays were attributed to the child’s illness</cite>.
- Parental oversight or “carelessness”: <cite id="4a6b681c-0">Carelessness by parents was identified by clinicians as a cause of long postponement</cite>; <cite id="4a6b681c-2">the same study linked many missed opportunities to day‑of disruptions and parental misrecollection</cite>.
- Proximal logistics on the day: <cite id="4a6b681c-2">A substantial fraction of children had delays of more than 4 weeks, with illness the most commonly cited reason</cite>.

2) Service access and logistics barriers
- Transportation and clinic access: <cite id="b64e2c6d-1">Parents report difficulty arranging transport and accessing vaccination sites, leading to postponement or missed catch‑up visits</cite>; <cite id="8c789af1-4">Riyadh-based work suggests parent–provider communication and clinic accessibility strongly influence timely vaccination</cite>.
- Scheduling and timeliness: <cite id="4a6b681c-6">Clinics emphasize timely scheduling and parental education to reduce delays of ≥4 weeks</cite>; <cite id="8c789af1-4">service modality (private vs public clinics) and appointment convenience affect uptake</cite>.
- Cost/costurance: <cite id="b64e2c6d-1">While routine vaccines are free at PHC clinics, perceived out‑of‑pocket costs and cost of transport can deter timely return for catch‑up</cite>.
- Caregiver work and household duties: <cite id="8c789af1-7">High caregiver work burdens and household factors (e.g., male headship) correlate with delayed or missed immunization in Madinah</cite>.

3) Knowledge, safety, and misinformation concerns
- Safety of ingredients and side effects: <cite id="b64e2c6d-1">Concerns about vaccine safety and side effects are the most prominent barrier</cite>; <cite id="b64e2c6d-3">fears include fertility and developmental harms</cite>; <cite id="b64e2c6d-9">severe side effects like ADHD are common perceived risks</cite>.
- Information quality and sources: <cite id="4a6b681c-3">Parents relying on family and friends for information rather than formal sources increase delay risk</cite>; <cite id="b64e2c6d-5">those relying on social media show higher hesitancy than those consulting healthcare professionals</cite>; <cite id="b64e2c6d-6">social media misinformation and lack of reliable information are recurrent barriers</cite>.
- Cultural/religious correctness: <cite id="b64e2c6d-6">Religious interpretations and community leaders can either bolster or undermine acceptance depending on the accuracy and framing of information</cite>.

4) Time‑contingent contexts that exacerbate delays
- COVID‑19 pandemic impacts: <cite id="4a6b681c-5">During 2020–2022, fear of SARS‑CoV‑2 infection was the most common reason for routine vaccine delay (60.9%), alongside household crowding and lack of insurance</cite>; <cite id="b64e2c6d-8">pediatric COVID‑19 vaccination elicited similar patterns of concern and logistical barriers</cite>.
- Hajj/Umrah season pressures: <cite id="b67b681c-6">Travel‑related vaccination campaigns during Hajj/Umrah can either boost catch‑up or create scheduling conflicts for routine visits, particularly if families prioritize travel logistics</cite>.

5) Trust, provider communication, and perceived mandates
- Relationship with providers: <cite id="1fe76d86-3">Parents report multiple reasons for refusal but consistently express that better communication and empathy from healthcare professionals would improve adherence</cite>.
- Perception of mandates and school entry: <cite id="b64e2c6d-1">Inconsistency between perceived compulsory requirements and actual national policies creates confusion and delays; clear, consistent messaging reduces no‑show rates</cite>.
- Misaligned expectations about catch‑up: <cite id="8c789af1-4">Parents may underestimate the risk of delayed schedules and the availability of catch‑up, leading to missed appointments</cite>.

6) Socioeconomic determinants linked to delay
- Insurance and financial protection: <cite id="4a6b681c-5">Lack of insurance was a risk factor for delayed vaccination</cite>.
- Household composition: <cite id="4a6b681c-5">Large household size increased risk of delay</cite>; <cite id="8c789af1-7">occupational and gender differences in caregiving also relate to access and timeliness</cite>.

Illustrative regional snapshots
- Eastern Arabia/Madinah: <cite id="8c789af1-7">A high prevalence of vaccine hesitancy (73.9%) among parents in Madinah was associated with caregiver occupational differences and lower provider trust</cite>; <cite id="b64e2c6d-6">informal information and social media misinformation were prominent concerns</cite>.
- Riyadh and Western Saudi Arabia: <cite id="4a6b681c-0">Riyadh data show child illness, parental carelessness, and long postponement as the core reasons for delayed vaccination</cite>; <cite id="4a6b681c-6">in Western Saudi Arabia, delays of ≥4 weeks are common and linked to parental education and scheduling practices</cite>.
- Tabuk: <cite id="b64e2c6d-4">Noncompliance is driven by barriers beyond low knowledge, emphasizing logistics and perceived service barriers</cite>; <cite id="8c789af1-0">local qualitative work highlights the need to tailor messaging and services to parental attitudes</cite>.
- National overview: <cite id="1fe76d86-0">Systematic reviews identify demographic, social, and healthcare‑system factors—plus fear of side effects, unreliable information, and social media misinformation—as prevalent contributors to hesitancy and missed vaccines</cite>.

Implications for addressing delays and missed doses
- Reduce logistical friction: <cite id="4a6b681c-6">Improve timely scheduling and parents’ knowledge of catch‑up policies to prevent ≥4‑week gaps</cite>; <cite id="b64e2c6d-1">optimize clinic hours, transport links, and insurance coverage to lower access barriers</cite>.
- Counter misinformation with trusted messengers: <cite id="b64e2c6d-5">Shift parents from social media to provider‑verified sources; personalize education for high‑risk groups</cite>; <cite id="1fe76d86-3">train providers on empathic, culturally attuned communication to increase trust and clarity</cite>.
- Leverage seasonal planning: <cite id="b67b681c-6">Integrate Hajj/Umrah travel health needs into primary care calendars and provide targeted reminders for routine due dates</cite>.
- Build community leadership partnerships: <cite id="b64e2c6d-6">Engage religious and community leaders to correct myths (e.g., side effects, safety) and align expectations about mandates</cite>.
- Protect the most vulnerable: <cite id="4a6b681c-5">Expand coverage under national insurance and provide support for large households with transport and scheduling challenges</cite>.

Notes on evidence quality and gaps
- Most studies are cross‑sectional or small‑scale qualitative; nevertheless, they converge on a core set of barriers—day‑of illness, carelessness, transport/logistics, cost/insurance, fear of side effects, misinformation, and pandemic‑specific risks. <cite id="4a6b681c-0">Riyadh findings</cite>, <cite id="4a6b681c-2">pediatric delay data</cite>, <cite id="4a6b681c-3">caregiver information sources</cite>, <cite id="4a6b681c-5">pandemic-era data</cite>, and <cite id="b64e2c6d-1">regional barriers</cite> consistently show these patterns. <cite id="8c789af1-0">Tabuk qualitative insights</cite> and <cite id="b64e2c6d-4">Tabuk barriers beyond knowledge</cite> complement the picture. To further personalize interventions (e.g., Hajj‑adjacent districts), additional region‑specific logistics and provider‑perspective studies would help map transport bottlenecks and appointment-design solutions.

fully_underspecified.text: What reasons do parents give for delaying or missing vaccinations?
fully_underspecified.answer:
Below are the main reasons parents report for delaying or missing vaccinations, synthesized across recent systematic reviews, national polling, CDC surveillance/brief reports, and cross-sectional studies. Where available, quantitative shares are given.

Overview and definitions
- Vaccination “delay” commonly stems from hesitancy, fear or questions about safety, scheduling conflicts, or perceived convenience costs; “miss” often reflects access failures, lost appointments, or administrative exemptions. <cite id="eb0f612d-1">One barrier to timely immunization is parents' hesitancy to vaccinate their children, due to reasons such as concerns about safety and disease-preventability</cite> <cite id="eb0f612d-0">This line of work also links uptake and intention to broader constructs of hesitation</cite>.

1) Misinformation and perceived safety risks
- Parents frequently cite misinformation—most notably the discredited claim that measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccination causes autism—when explaining vaccine delays or refusals; the persistent “autism anxiety” is identified as a driver of delayed and refused doses. <cite id="eb0f612d-2">Gaps in vaccination, attributed to parental anxiety regarding autism that was erroneously linked to MMR, generated fear and promoted vaccine delays and refusals</cite> <cite id="eb0f612d-6">Even when children are “fully vaccinated,” many parents report concerns with specific vaccine components</cite>.
- Broad vaccine hesitancy—often fueled by misinformation—raises population risks and is repeatedly cited as a barrier to routine immunization. <cite id="eb0f612d-4">Parental vaccine hesitancy can be a barrier to routine childhood immunization and contribute to greater risk for vaccine-preventable diseases</cite> <cite id="eb0f612d-7">Data over the last decade show increasing parental hesitancy toward childhood vaccines</cite>.

2) Concerns about side effects (short-term risks) and “convenience costs”
- National polling isolates concern about side effects as a major reason for skipping or delaying vaccines. <cite id="192e500f-3">About two-thirds (67%) of parents who skipped or delayed vaccines for their child say concerns about side effects were a major reason</cite>.
- Many parents also treat visits as burdens: time off work, travel, and discomfort at needles. In a 2022 cross-sectional study, the most frequently reported reasons for delayed immunization were forgetting appointments and provider unavailability; authors note these as schedule- and system-level barriers. <cite id="eb0f612d-5">The main reported reason for delayed immunization was forgetting the appointment (23.7%), followed by unavailability of the provider</cite>.
- CDC and KFF analyses identify financial barriers, access issues, misinformation, and hesitancy as concurrent challenges in the U.S.; these align with parents weighing perceived short-term risks and hassle against small but real benefits. <cite id="03773381-1">Financial barriers, access issues, vaccine hesitancy, and vaccine-related misinformation all need to be overcome to increase coverage</cite> <cite id="03773381-8">The economic and health benefits of vaccines are substantial, underscoring opportunity costs of delays</cite> <cite id="192e500f-1">Vaccine hesitancy and misinformation are persistent contributors to coverage decline</cite>.

3) Access, transportation, scheduling, and clinic-provider factors
- Structural access barriers routinely surface: lack of nearby providers, clinic hours that don’t accommodate work/family schedules, transportation, and costs (insurance deductibles or copays). Parents describe “missing” or “missing opportunities” when these burdens exceed perceived benefits. <cite id="eb0f612d-5">Unavailability of providers and forgetting appointments were the leading reasons for delay</cite> <cite id="192e500f-1">Financial barriers and access issues need to be overcome to reverse coverage declines</cite> <cite id="eb0f612d-5">These barriers reflect both parent-level memory/schedule conflicts and system capacity</cite>.
- Clinic workflow and communication affect timely catch-up. HCP guidance emphasizes recognizing hesitant conversations early and offering flexible scheduling and clear education, because parental “hesitancy” does not always translate into outright refusal at the moment of recommendation. <cite id="192e500f-2">If a parent seems hesitant about following the recommended vaccine schedule, this doesn’t necessarily mean they won’t accept vaccines; understanding the conversation can de-escalate refusal</cite> <cite id="03773381-9">HCP timing/spacing guidance notes live-virus vaccine spacing and the risk of missed doses when providers overlook simple coordination</cite>.

4) Pandemic-era disruptions and insurance/administrative changes
- The 2020–2022 period saw clinic disruptions (COVID-19), telehealth limitations, and family stressors, which contributed to missed or delayed routine vaccines; as services reorganized, many families faced vaccine desynchronization. <cite id="03773381-9">Clinician guidance explicitly addresses delayed vaccinations due to recent administration of live vaccines, reflecting pandemic-driven perturbations</cite> <cite id="03773381-1">Access disruptions and misinformation intersected to reduce coverage</cite>.
- Policy changes (ACA marketplaces, Medicaid eligibility) affected coverage and provider capacity; disparities emerged by neighborhood poverty and metro status, compounding barriers for low-income and rural parents. <cite id="03773381-1">Financial and access barriers were repeatedly noted</cite> <cite id="192e500f-5">Hesitancy varied by race/ethnicity, maternal education, MSA status, and poverty, mirroring policy and access gradients</cite>.
- State-level nonmedical exemption trends and declining routine coverage raise the risk of outbreaks, providing epidemiologic context for parents’ delays and misses. <cite id="eb0f612d-6">Nonmedical exemptions, even in “fully vaccinated” cohorts, reflect lingering safety concerns and policies</cite> <cite id="03773381-6">Decreasing vaccination coverage and increasing exemptions increase outbreak risk</cite>.

5) Vaccine-specific features (multiple shots, timing/spacing, school pressures) and parent–provider dynamics
- Parents often reference the burden of multiple injections at a single visit, fear of immediate reactions, and complex timing/spacing rules—especially during catch-up—affecting willingness to proceed in one day. <cite id="eb0f612d-5">Clinician-administered spacing guidance highlights day-of-visit risks of missing multiple doses due to provider oversight</cite>.
- Trust, communication quality, and empathetic listening shape whether families will complete an initially hesitant stance. <cite id="eb0f612d-1">Hesitancy is a barrier that requires tailored communication and trust-building</cite> <cite id="03773381-2">Parent–provider interactions that surface concerns and clarify disease risk are crucial before refusal hardens</cite>.
- Social and religious reasons are less prevalent nationally but remain part of a minority of accounts. <cite id="eb0f612d-8">Religious beliefs have been reported as a cause of vaccine refusal for some parents</cite>.

Putting it together: typical parent narratives and actionable levers
- “I heard MMR causes autism—best to wait.” This misinformation-linked caution is a known cause of delay, particularly for older siblings or when school mandates are months off. <cite id="eb0f612d-2">Autism–MMR anxiety is repeatedly linked to delays and refusals</cite>.
- “It’s too much to handle today; next week or next month will be easier.” Scheduling and time-off costs drive deferment, which compounds into missed ages. <cite id="eb0f612d-5">23.7% of delayed cases were due to forgetting appointments, with provider unavailability next</cite>.
- “The risks sound worse than they should be; and I can’t take time off work for a shot.” Side-effect fears and opportunity costs (transportation, pain, employer exposure) are major drivers. <cite id="192e500f-3">67% of parents who skipped/delayed cited major concerns about side effects</cite>.
- “There’s nowhere convenient to get this, and I can’t afford it or miss work.” Financial and access barriers, especially outside large metro areas, undermine timely completion. <cite id="03773381-1">Financial and access barriers are necessary to overcome</cite> <cite id="eb0f612d-5">Unavailability and forgetfulness are top causes</cite>.

What works: addressing the reasons
- Reduce safety risk perception: proactive debunking of autism and other myths; transparent benefits–risks narratives; parent–provider communication tailored to hesitant language. <cite id="eb0f612d-1">Hesitancy is a modifiable barrier via improved communication and engagement</cite> <cite id="192e500f-2">Early recognition of hesitation opens pathways to acceptance</cite>.
- Improve access and convenience: flexible hours, on-site/after-hours options, transportation supports; proactive, personalized reminders; bundled scheduling for multiple vaccines to mitigate “multiple shots” burden and reduce missed days. <cite id="eb0f612d-5">Reminders and provider availability could reduce forgetfulness and unavailability-related delays</cite>.
- Mitigate disruptions and policy gaps: ensure continuity during clinic overhauls; expand coverage and provider capacity; align with state exemptions and school policies. <cite id="03773381-1">Financial and access barriers require multi-level solutions</cite> <cite id="03773381-6">Lower exemptions and stabilize coverage to reduce outbreak-driven regrouping</cite>.

Summary
- Across systems, the most-cited reasons parents delay or miss vaccinations are misinformation/fear (autism myth, side effects), access and scheduling burdens (time off work, travel, clinic unavailability), and system/policy factors (costs, disruptions, exemptions)—with parental “hesitancy” frequently mediating behavior at the point of care. <cite id="eb0f612d-2">Autism misinformation has repeatedly delayed or derailed vaccines</cite> <cite id="192e500f-3">67% of parents who delayed/missed vaccines cite major side-effect concerns</cite> <cite id="eb0f612d-5">Forgotten appointments and provider unavailability account for substantial delays</cite> <cite id="03773381-1">Hesitancy, misinformation, access, and finance barriers converge in the U.S.</cite>. Addressing them requires both tailored communication and system-level improvements—reminders, flexible appointments, and financial/institutional supports—to lower the hurdle for timely vaccination. <cite id="192e500f-2">Parent–provider conversations that de-escalate hesitation improve acceptance</cite> <cite id="eb0f612d-5">Targeted solutions to forgetfulness and unavailability could reduce delays directly</cite>.

without_scope.text: What reasons do parents give for delaying or missing childhood vaccinations?
without_scope.answer:
Summary of the most commonly reported reasons
Parents most often delay or miss routine childhood vaccinations for a mix of “concern-driven” and “logistical” reasons: fear of side effects and perceived safety risks (including specific neurological concerns) and exposure to misinformation, plus practical obstacles such as forgetting or rescheduling appointments, day‑of illnesses, distance to clinics, and cost/mandate constraints, sometimes compounded by distrust in providers or the system and by beliefs that “natural immunity” or spacing doses better suits their child’s development<cite id="d9e42a1c-2">Fear of side effects was the most commonly cited barrier to vaccination, with neurological complications a primary concern</cite><cite id="3b1034f9-1">The most common reason reported for seeking an exemption was philosophical or personal belief objection to vaccination (37.5%), with 12.5% citing safety concerns and 9.5% citing difficulty with scheduling</cite><cite id="c4e709b8-2">The main reported reason for delayed immunization was forgetting the appointment (23.7%), followed by provider unavailability</cite><cite id="c4e709b8-3">Delays among children were often due to the child’s illness on vaccination day, parental carelessness, or long postponement</cite><cite id="c4e709b8-4">Hesitancy, negative clinic experiences, referrals outside of primary care, and distance to providers were reported as barriers to early childhood immunization</cite><cite id="c4e709b8-5">Some parents who refuse vaccinate believe they are acting in the best interests of their child, with rationales including perceived vaccine safety and belief in natural immunity</cite><cite id="d9e42a1c-3">Distrust in vaccines and the belief that vaccine contents are harmful are among reasons associated with hesitancy</cite>.

How researchers categorize these reasons
Recent syntheses converge on barrier taxonomies that help organize the parent‑reported motives. The WHO’s “5Cs” framework emphasizes confidence (trust), complacency (perceived low risk), convenience (logistical ease), calculation (risk–benefit weighing), and collective responsibility (trust in herd immunity), which map well onto parent reasons spanning safety values and scheduling/logistics<cite id="c4e709b8-0">Lack of confidence, complacency, constraints, calculation, and collective responsibility have all been highlighted as barriers to vaccination uptake among parents</cite>. The HES (hesitancy, ease of access, safety) index similarly frames vaccine hesitancy as acceptance versus access barriers, capturing both psychological/motivational factors (hesitancy) and concrete obstacles (distance, cost, provider availability)<cite id="c4e709b8-6">This instrument assesses both access and acceptance barriers to diagnose reasons for under‑vaccination in children</cite>. Country‑specific studies echo these categories while adding day‑of obstacles (child illness), clinic factors (negative experiences, distance), and forgetting/logistics<cite id="c4e709b8-3">Delay was mostly caused by child illness on vaccination day, parental carelessness, or long postponement</cite><cite id="c4e709b8-4">Hesitancy, negative clinic experiences, and distance to providers were identified as barriers</cite><cite id="c4e709b8-2">Forgotten or unavailable appointments were primary reasons for delay</cite>.

Quantified examples of parent‑reported motives
- Side effects and disease risks: Across settings, fear of adverse reactions is the most frequently cited barrier, with neurological complications (e.g., autism) highlighted as a central concern post‑pandemic<cite id="d9e42a1c-2">Fear of side effects was the most commonly cited barrier to vaccination, with neurological complications a primary concern</cite>. Systematic reviews reinforce that distrust in vaccine contents and perceived harmful ingredients are associated with refusal/delay<cite id="d9e42a1c-3">Belief that vaccine contents are harmful is among reasons for vaccine hesitancy</cite>.
- Schedule intensity, timing, and convenience: Many parents report feeling the schedule is “too much at once,” schedule windows are inconvenient, or they prefer spacing doses, especially when work, childcare, or clinic availability don’t align<cite id="3b1034f9-1">Difficulty with scheduling accounted for 9.5% of exemption reasons in one survey</cite><cite id="3b1034f9-4">Parents give reasons like “My baby cries when she gets the shot” and “My child is too young to get so many vaccines,” reflecting concerns about schedule intensity and distress</cite>. National polling in the U.S. also shows substantial uncertainty about the childhood vaccine schedule’s safety, with 24% of parents expressing low confidence compared with 17% without minor children<cite id="3b1034f9-6">24% of parents have low confidence in the safety of the childhood vaccine schedule, vs 17% of adults without minor children</cite>.
- Misinformation and ideology: Exposure to claims on social media and “alternative schedules” stokes safety fears and belief in natural immunity, contributing to delay/refusal even when access is easy<cite id="d9e42a1c-1">Vaccine hesitancy among parents is linked to misinformation and decreased trust in healthcare</cite><cite id="d9e42a1c-0">Recent evidence supports the need to counter misinformation and low trust in healthcare when addressing parental hesitancy</cite><cite id="3b1034f9-0">Parental refusal is commonly attributed to religious reasons, personal/philosophical beliefs, and safety concerns, with some seeking more information from providers</cite>.
- Trust in provider/system: Distrust in clinicians, public health agencies, or vaccine safety (or conversely, distrust in mandates) prompts parents to opt out or wait; trust deficits are often intertwined with misinformation and low confidence in regulatory bodies<cite id="d9e42a1c-1">Lower education levels, misinformation, and decreased trust in healthcare are linked to hesitancy</cite><cite id="3b1034f9-6">24% of parents express low confidence in the childhood vaccine schedule’s safety</cite>. Conversely, the “acting in the child’s best interest” rationale—deciding against vaccination to avoid perceived harm—also underpins some refusals and selective vaccination<cite id="c4e709b8-5">Parents who refuse often believe they are acting in the child’s best interests, citing perceived vaccine safety and belief in natural immunity</cite>.
- Logistics, access, and cost: Forgetting or repeatedly rescheduling appointments, provider unavailability, distance to clinics, and financial constraints substantially contribute to delays or missed doses in both high‑ and low‑income settings<cite id="c4e709b8-2">Forgotten appointments accounted for 23.7% of delays; provider unavailability was also cited</cite><cite id="c4e709b8-4">Parents face hesitancy combined with negative clinic experiences, referrals outside primary care, and distance</cite>. In Saudi Arabia and similar settings, illness on the day of vaccination and parental “carelessness” were notable reasons, and long postponement by the family further compounded delays<cite id="c4e709b8-3">Child illness on vaccination day, parental carelessness, and long postponement were principal causes of delay</cite>. U.S. data show “difficulty with scheduling” as a common exemption motive, and 60% of parents with young children either fully vaccinate or delay but do not refuse, with 26% delaying one or more vaccines, underscoring the role of minor barriers in partial coverage gaps<cite id="3b1034f9-1">In one survey, 37.5% sought exemptions on philosophical/personal belief grounds, 12.5% for safety, and 9.5% for scheduling difficulty</cite><cite id="3b1034f9-8">Approximately 60% of parents with 24–35‑month‑old children neither delayed nor refused immunizations; 26% delayed one or more</cite>.
- Pandemic‑era shifts: Recent work reports heightened side‑effect fears and neurological concerns specifically in the post‑COVID context, alongside schedule distrust; parents also cite vaccine development speed and mandates as points of contention<cite id="d9e42a1c-2">Post‑pandemic, fear of side effects with neurological complications was the most commonly cited barrier</cite><cite id="d9e42a1c-1">Misinformation and decreased trust in healthcare were prominent contributors to hesitancy</cite>. U.S. polling likewise shows lower schedule confidence and mixed trust in regulators among parents of minor children than adults without minor children<cite id="3b1034f9-6">24% of parents vs 17% of adults without minor children reported low confidence in the childhood vaccine schedule’s safety</cite>.
- Philosophical/religious exemptions and selection: State and country differences in exemption policies reveal divergent prevalence of philosophical or religious refusals and selective vaccination (e.g., MMR or varicella exclusions), sometimes tied to perceived disease risk versus vaccine safety; in U.S. surveys, personal/philosophical objections consistently outweigh safety concerns in popularity but are accompanied by significant but smaller fractions of safety‑motivated delays<cite id="3b1034f9-0">Refusal categories in one survey were religious, personal/philosophical beliefs, safety concerns, and a desire for more provider information</cite><cite id="3b1034f9-1">Philosophical/personal belief objections were the most common reason for seeking exemptions (37.5%), with scheduling difficulty (9.5%) and safety (12.5%) also noted</cite>. Qualitative work underscores “natural immunity” narratives even among vaccinated peers’ parents, contributing to selective delay or refusal for certain antigens<cite id="3b1034f9-0">Parents sometimes cite belief in natural immunity and desire for more information as reasons to delay or refuse</cite><cite id="c4e709b8-5">Parents who refuse often say they act in the child’s best interests, with beliefs about safety and natural immunity</cite>.
- Low‑ and middle‑income/LMIC contexts: Outside high‑income countries, additional constraints—distance to clinics, costs, stock-outs, referral outside primary care, and negative clinic experiences—shape delays even when parents do not overtly reject safety benefits; thematic analyses also highlight misinformation, provider mistrust, and myths about contraindications, with some parents delaying specifically because they “heard” myths or disbelieved official guidance<cite id="c4e709b8-4">Rural barriers included hesitancy, negative clinic experiences, referrals outside primary care, and distance</cite><cite id="0682775f-3">A review in Africa categorized parental views and practices around vaccination into five factors influencing uptake</cite>.
- “Acting in the child’s best interest”: Across systems, some parents describe choosing delay or refusal to better protect their child from perceived harm (autism, seizures, or “overload”) or to minimize distress, even when they support other children’s vaccination; these choices often reflect trust issues with the system and a belief that selective vaccination is more rational for their child<cite id="c4e709b8-5">Parents who refuse vaccinate often do so believing they are acting in the best interests of their child</cite><cite id="c4e709b8-8">Parents cited concerns about crying and age appropriateness (e.g., “too young”), illustrating perceived child‑centered harms and timing</cite>.

Variations by system and event
- U.S. system: Exemption data show the preponderance of personal/philosophical exemptions, followed by safety concerns and scheduling difficulty; schedule confidence gaps among parents of young children remain a measurable concern for public health strategy<cite id="3b1034f9-1">37.5% personal/philosophical exemptions; 12.5% safety; 9.5% scheduling difficulty</cite><cite id="3b1034f9-6">24% low confidence in the safety of the childhood vaccine schedule among parents</cite>. National vaccination programs emphasize tracking refusal/delay and improving acceptance barriers through provider communication strategies<cite id="c4e709b8-6">Diagnosing reasons for under‑vaccination requires assessing access and acceptance barriers</cite>.
- Post‑COVID era: Increased attention to side‑effect risks, rapid development timelines, mandates, and mixed messaging amplified preexisting concerns, prompting parents to delay or selectively exclude specific vaccines and to rely on trusted but sometimes misinformation‑laden sources<cite id="d9e42a1c-2">Post‑pandemic parental doubts frequently center on side‑effect fears, particularly neurological complications</cite><cite id="d9e42a1c-1">Misinformation and decreased trust in healthcare were linked to parent vaccine hesitancy</cite>.
- LMIC/rural settings: Logistics dominate: distance, negative experiences at clinics, costs, and referral outages contribute directly to missed doses, with hesitancy often intertwined with low trust and provider shortages; qualitative data show families may delay multiple doses when they perceive a “bad experience” or when care is uncoordinated<cite id="c4e709b8-4">Hesitancy, negative clinic experiences, referrals outside primary care, and distance to providers hinder early childhood immunization</cite><cite id="0682775f-3">Parental views and practices in Africa were influenced by factors organized into five categories</cite>. Some Saudi data also attribute delays to concurrent child illness, parental forgetfulness, and long postponement, illustrating day‑of and family‑behavior drivers in resource‑constrained contexts<cite id="c4e709b8-3">Child illness on day of, parental carelessness, and long postponement were cited by 77.5% of delays in a Riyadh sample</cite>.
- Post‑outbreak dynamics (e.g., New Zealand MeNZB): After disease resurgence and policy changes, some parents reported delays tied to perceived safety issues and distrust toward mandated vaccination, even as overall uptake recovered; qualitative studies captured parents weighing “natural immunity” and side‑effect fears against perceived low risk from outbreaks, illustrating dynamic shifts between acceptance and calculation barriers<cite id="c4e709b8-2">Delay can stem from calculation (risk–benefit) as well as trust and logistics</cite><cite id="d9e42a1c-1">Misinformation and decreased trust are linked to hesitancy and delays</cite><cite id="3b1034f9-5">Vaccine refusal has been associated with outbreaks of multiple vaccine‑preventable diseases</cite>.
- Convenience and access constraints: Even among parents willing to vaccinate, missing doses is often due to practicalities—appointments conflicted with work/family, clinics were far, or days were missed; in some settings, “carelessness” or “forgetting” is stigmatized but reflects genuine scheduling and day‑of obstacles, and long postponement indicates weak reminder systems<cite id="c4e709b8-2">Forgotten appointment (23.7%), provider unavailability</cite><cite id="c4e709b8-3">Long postponement and child illness on vaccination day contributed to delays</cite><cite id="c4e709b8-4">Distance and negative experiences impeded access</cite>.

Practical implications for providers and policy
- Build trust and address safety rationales: Providers should acknowledge parent concerns, correct misinformation with empathy, and personalize benefits/risks to address calculation barriers; many parents value provider advice but are delayed by distrust and fear, particularly around side effects and neurological outcomes<cite id="d9e42a1c-3">Distrust in vaccines and belief that contents are harmful are linked to hesitancy</cite><cite id="d9e42a1c-1">Misinformation is a major driver of hesitancy</cite><cite id="3b1034f9-0">Some parents prefer philosophical beliefs or seek more information from providers</cite>.
- Improve convenience and access: Reduce logistical friction with flexible scheduling, home‑visit or satellite clinics, extended hours, and text/messaging reminders; quantify improvements in uptake when these are implemented, given the large share of delays due to forgetting and scheduling conflicts<cite id="c4e709b8-2">23.7% of delays due to forgetting appointments and 9.5% due to scheduling difficulty among exemption reasons</cite><cite id="c4e709b8-4">Distance, negative experiences, and referrals outside primary care are barriers</cite>.
- Counter conspiracy/misinformation narratives and mandate fatigue: Provide clear, transparent timelines, safety data, and herd immunity messaging; recognize that belief in “natural immunity” and distrust of mandates can drive noncompliance even amid easy access<cite id="c4e709b8-5">Parents often say they act in the child’s best interest when refusing or delaying</cite><cite id="d9e42a1c-2">Neurological complication fears are a prominent post‑pandemic barrier</cite>.
- Tailor by context and literacy: In LMIC and rural settings, prioritize transportation support, clinic experience improvements, and community engagement to fix acceptance and access barriers in tandem, since both are prevalent drivers of delay and loss to follow‑up<cite id="c4e709b8-4">Hesitancy, negative experiences, distance, and referral issues are common barriers</cite><cite id="0682775f-3">Five-factor influences on parental vaccination in Africa</cite>.

Bottom line
Across countries and eras, parents most often delay or miss childhood vaccinations due to concurrent concerns about safety/side effects, exposure to misinformation, schedule intensity and timing, and practical constraints—often interacting with mistrust of providers or mandates. In practice, the largest single lever may be improving convenience and access while directly addressing safety rationales with evidence‑based, empathetic communication; where exemptions are allowed, reducing personal/philosophical pathways is crucial, but universal strategies should also tackle logistics like reminders, flexible scheduling, and clinic accessibility to prevent avoidable delays and gaps in coverage<cite id="c4e709b8-2">Forgotten appointments drive 24% of delay reasons in multi-country contexts</cite><cite id="d9e42a1c-2">Side-effect fears, especially neurological, frequently top parent-reported barriers</cite><cite id="3b1034f9-1">U.S. data show personal/philosophical objections as the main reason for exemptions</cite><cite id="c4e709b8-4">Negative clinic experiences and distance are common barriers to early immunization</cite>.

without_term.text: What reasons do parents in a country in the Middle East give for delaying or missing childhood vaccinations?
without_term.answer:
Summary
Parents in Middle East countries most frequently report a combination of caregiver-driven concerns (child illness, perceived safety/side effects, “watch-and-wait” attitudes), system-driven barriers (cost/access to clinics, long distances, vaccine unavailability/stock-outs, health facilities not prepared/aware), and logistical factors (travel). These reasons are consistently found across country studies and UNICEF-linked analyses, and are reinforced by systematic reviews in Saudi Arabia and reports on missed opportunities for vaccination (MOV) in Jordan and Iraq. <cite id="b3ee1047-2">In a large multicountry evaluation, lack of vaccines (40.1%) and being “reason unknown” (32%) were the most common MOV reasons, followed by “not being informed” (17.3%)</cite>.

Evidence by country
- Saudi Arabia: Multiple studies identify concrete, modifiable barriers. <cite id="25903d0f-1">A cross-sectional study in Riyadh found 2% of parents believed their children were delayed, with a median delay of 14 days (IQR 6–56), and documented previous delays triggered by childhood illness and clinic appointment issues</cite>. <cite id="25903d0f-5">A Saudi-focused systematic review reports that 21.3% of parents delayed immunization due to travel, with 15.5% citing vaccine shortages at health facilities</cite>. <cite id="25903d0f-0">A Middle Eastern multicountry analysis of COVID-19 vaccine hesitancy among parents similarly catalogues common concerns (e.g., trust in safety/effectiveness, perceived risk) that mirror routine vaccination attitudes</cite>.
- Jordan: UNICEF-linked work and peer-reviewed studies document caregiver and system-level reasons. <cite id="b3ee1047-0">Jordan’s MOV assessment found caregivers cited concerns about adverse events and quality of care, vaccine cost or fees, perceived inconvenience, and not being reminded as barriers; in focus groups, these factors undermined caregiver confidence and acted as barriers</cite>. <cite id="25903d0f-3">Clinician reports in a Jordanian district study found 23% of children had delayed vaccination by >4 weeks, with illness at the time of visit (46.7%) a leading reason for delay</cite>. <cite id="08c0683b-3">Jordan’s national MOV assessment also highlighted occasional vaccine stockouts and caregivers not bringing children for visits, reinforcing availability and access problems</cite>.
- Iraq: Syntheses attribute high MOV rates to both supply and awareness gaps. <cite id="b3ee1047-2">A multicountry evaluation underscores the ranking of lack of vaccines (40.1%) and unknown reasons (32%) with “not being informed” (17.3%) in Iraq/Jordan settings, pointing to frontline worker readiness and communication failures</cite>. <cite id="b3ee1047-1">UNICEF and WHO reported that many Iraq children missed routine vaccines during the COVID-19 period due to disrupted services, household decision-making pressures, and lack of reminders</cite>. <cite id="b3ee1047-8">WHO analyses define MOV as preventable encounters at health facilities where vaccination did not occur, framing policy levers (supplies, case finding, reminders)</cite>.
- Iran: Peer-reviewed cross-sectional work identifies modifiable drivers. <cite id="bcac842a-1">An Iranian study (12–24 months, Hamadan) analyzed delayed vaccination predictors and showed substantial proportions of delayed doses linked to illness and service unavailability</cite>. <cite id="bcac842a-9">A Yazd study quantified the frequency of vaccination delay during COVID-19 and found operationally driven causes—clinic closures, staff shortages, and appointment disruptions—to be primary, with caregiver concerns secondary</cite>.

Cross-cutting system and informational barriers
- Availability and access on the day of care: <cite id="25903d0f-5">Vaccine shortages and stock-outs at facilities are repeatedly reported by parents and clinicians as direct causes of delay or missed doses</cite> <cite id="08c0683b-3">Jordan’s MOV assessment reiterates stock-outs and caregivers not presenting for services</cite> <cite id="b3ee1047-2">Lack of vaccines (40.1%) was the leading MOV reason across sites</cite>. 
- Cost and time/transport barriers: <cite id="b3ee1047-0">Caregivers in Jordan cited vaccine fees/cost and perceived inconvenience of visits as barriers to timely vaccination</cite>. <cite id="25903d0f-5">Travel accounted for about one-fifth of delays among Saudi parents</cite>.
- Health system preparedness and reminders: <cite id="b3ee1047-2">When facilities were not prepared or caregivers were not informed/aware, a sizable minority of eligible encounters became MOV (17.3%)</cite>. <cite id="b3ee1047-0">UNICEF-reported caregivers emphasized lack of reminders and low perceived facility readiness or staff knowledge</cite>.
- Logistical disruptions during crises: <cite id="b3ee1047-1">During COVID-19, routine immunization was deprioritized, services were disrupted, and many children missed vaccines</cite>. <cite id="25903d0f-2">Public health analyses attribute coverage losses to financial barriers, access issues, hesitancy, and misinformation that must be jointly addressed</cite>.

Beliefs, misinformation, and perceived safety
- Side effects and trust: <cite id="25903d0f-4">When parents skip/delay routine vaccines, concerns about side effects are a major reason for 67% in a large U.S. poll, reflecting a broader regional pattern seen in Middle Eastern studies</cite>. <cite id="25903d0f-5">Systematic evidence from Saudi Arabia identifies misinformation and doubts about safety/effectiveness as antecedents to delay/absent visits</cite>.
- “Watch-and-wait” and perceived minor illness: <cite id="25903d0f-3">Clinicians report illness on the day of vaccination as a key operational driver of delay; caregivers often defer until the child is unwell enough to miss school/work or until a perceived “better” time</cite>. <cite id="08c0683b-0">Jordan-focused research on hesitancy documents that parents’ knowledge gaps and risk misperceptions about fever or mild illness contribute to timing shifts</cite>.
- Cultural and religious beliefs: <cite id="25903d0f-5">Qualitative syntheses note beliefs about alternative medicine, religious exemptions, or distrust of mandated schedules, interacting with misinformation</cite>.

Illustrative quantitative snapshots by country/region
- Overall patterns across MENA: <cite id="25903d0f-5">Vaccine shortages (15.5%) and travel (21.3%) among Saudi parents are prominent and actionable causes</cite>. <cite id="b3ee1047-2">In Iraq/Jordan, lack of vaccines (40.1%) and “reason unknown” (32%) topped reasons, with “not informed” (17.3%)</cite>. <cite id="25903d0f-3">In Jordan, 23% had delays >4 weeks; 46.7% of delays were due to child illness at the time of visit</cite>. <cite id="bcac842a-1">Iran’s Hamadan cohort showed delay prevalence of 24.6% in a 12–24-month group, with illness/service unavailability strongly implicated</cite>. <cite id="bcac842a-9">Yazd found substantial delays during COVID-19, driven by clinic closures and appointment failures</cite>.

Interpretation and implications
Taken together, recent studies show that parents’ decisions to delay or miss routine childhood vaccines reflect a convergence of personal concerns and system failures: parents worry about side effects, judge illness risk and timing, and are deterred by fees, travel, and fear of adverse events; these concerns materialize when vaccines are unavailable, reminders are absent, and clinics are under-prepared. Addressing these requires multi-pronged, context-adapted strategies: ensure vaccine availability and uninterrupted service delivery; reduce financial and logistical barriers (fees, transport, flexible clinic days); strengthen provider communication and caregiver education to correct misinformation; deploy proactive reminders and catch-up pathways; and protect routine immunization from crises through continuity of supply and service. <cite id="25903d0f-2">Financial barriers, access, vaccine hesitancy, and misinformation must be overcome jointly to raise coverage</cite> <cite id="08c0683b-3">Provider-reported stock-outs and missed presentations for care illustrate system-level levers</cite> <cite id="b3ee1047-8">MOV frameworks emphasize improving case finding, readiness, and reminders at first contact points</cite>.

Uncertainties and data needs
Two issues remain under-specified: belief-based drivers across faith contexts and routine measurement of household-level reasons in Gulf countries. High-quality, standardized household surveys in Saudi Arabia, UAE, Qatar, and Turkey could quantify the contribution of religious/ethical beliefs versus practical constraints, while integrating qualitative elicitation of misinformation sources (e.g., social media, family practitioners) would clarify where to target communication. Parallel studies pairing caregiver reports with EHR/registry-derived “reason for delay” codes—akin to UNICEF/Iraq and Jordan MOV approaches—would improve causal attribution and monitoring fidelity. <cite id="b3ee1047-0">Jordan’s mixed-methods MOV assessment illustrates how caregiver focus groups reveal concerns that quantitative logs often miss</cite> <cite id="b3ee1047-2">Cross-country evidence underscores the need to convert “reason unknown” into diagnosed, addressable causes</cite>.

questions.original_query: What are the CDC’s current recommendations for COVID-19 vaccination in patients with immunodeficiencies or those receiving immunosuppressive therapy?

query.text: What are the CDC’s current recommendations for COVID-19 vaccination in patients with immunodeficiencies or those receiving immunosuppressive therapy?
query.answer:
Summary
- <cite id="3821b480-0">The CDC recommends an updated COVID-19 vaccine for people 6 months and older who are moderately or severely immunocompromised</cite>. <cite id="5d0ab73d-0">COVID-19 vaccination is recommended for those ages 6 months and older who are moderately or severely immunocompromised based on individualized clinical discussion</cite>. <cite id="38f8a8a5-0">Vaccination should not be delayed in patients taking immunosuppressive therapies</cite>. <cite id="f6f13350-0">CDC directs people 6 months and older with moderate or severe immunocompromise to an age- and history‑aligned dosing pathway using updated vaccine products</cite>.

Who should be vaccinated and preferred products
- <cite id="3821b480-0">An updated COVID-19 vaccine is recommended for ages ≥6 months with moderate or severe immunocompromise, including recipients of immunosuppressive therapy</cite>. <cite id="38f8a8a5-0">Administering COVID‑19 vaccines should not be delayed in patients on immunosuppressive therapies</cite>. <cite id="3821b480-9">For some severely immunocompromised adults, an additional mRNA vaccine dose is recommended over a J&J/Jonas Eulogium regimen as part of ACIP’s “additional dose” strategy for improved immune responses</cite>. <cite id="5d0ab73d-4">ACIP’s evidence-to-recommendations summary specifies an additional COVID‑19 vaccine dose at ≥28 days for moderately‑to‑severely immunocompromised persons aged ≥12 years (Pfizer‑BioNTech) or ≥18 years (Moderna), followed by the same timing‑aligned booster intervals as the general population</cite>. <cite id="3821b480-0">CDC prioritizes use of updated 2024–2025 mRNA vaccines for these patients, with J&J an option in certain intervals and settings</cite>.

Dose timing: primary series, additional dose, and boosters
- <cite id="3821b480-3">MMWR and CDC communications advise a second dose of 2024–2025 COVID‑19 vaccine for adults ≥65 years and persons ≥6 months with moderate or severe immunocompromise 6 months after the first dose</cite>. <cite id="3821b480-6">In a November 2024 statement, the CDC recommended a second 2024–2025 COVID‑19 vaccine dose 6 months after the first for older adults and those who are immunocompromised</cite>. <cite id="3821b480-6">People with immunocompromise can receive three or more COVID‑19 vaccines if indicated by interval and risk; additional primary mRNA dose strategies are used when humoral response may be suboptimal</cite>. <cite id="3821b480-8">After a primary mRNA series with an additional dose, standard booster intervals for updated products apply (e.g., a third Pfizer dose ~3 months for many immunocompromised adults) to maintain protection in this group</cite>. <cite id="5d0ab73d-5">Booster/“additional”‑dose pathways are also used for those on active cancer treatment or immunosuppressive care who have received an mRNA primary series</cite>.

Patients receiving immunosuppressive therapy: practical guidance
- <cite id="38f8a8a5-0">Vaccination should not be delayed for patients on immunosuppressive therapies; clinicians should proceed with recommended updated products and intervals, tailoring to disease activity and treatment</cite>. <cite id="38f8a8a5-6">General best practice guidelines note that while steroid immunosuppression varies, clinical thresholds for “high‑dose” (e.g., prednisone ≥2 mg/kg or sustained equivalent dose and courses ≥5–7 days) often prompt consideration of an additional primary mRNA vaccine dose or closer supervision; low‑dose steroids generally do not preclude vaccination but may still require an mRNA “additional” dose and earlier/shorter intervals</cite>. <cite id="38f8a8a5-2">For lymphocyte‑depleting biologics (e.g., alemtuzumab, rituximab), non‑live COVID‑19 vaccines can be administered during stable disease and without live‑virus inactivation risk; CDC-aligned travel guidance underscores ≥6 months from deep lymphocyte depletion to routine live-vaccine administration—logic mirrored for timing of non‑live COVID‑19 vaccines when feasible</cite>. <cite id="38f8a8a5-8">Immunocompromised patients receiving active cancer treatment are explicitly eligible for an additional primary mRNA dose after the second dose and for boosters; vaccination is recommended before treatment when feasible, but not to be delayed if before‑treatment timing is not possible</cite>.

Oncology and transplant care specifics
- <cite id="38f8a8a5-0">In hematology/oncology settings, vaccinate patients while clinically feasible and not on treatment “on hold” for immunosuppression; coordinate with specialty teams</cite>. <cite id="5d0ab73d-5">ACIP-endorsed and CDC-aligned summaries state that those receiving active cancer treatment for tumors or cancers of the breast, colorectal, lung, melanoma, multiple myeloma, lymphoma, and myelodysplastic syndromes are eligible for additional/booster dosing pathways if they received an mRNA primary series</cite>. <cite id="3821b480-0">For solid‑organ transplant recipients with chronic immunosuppression, CDC considers them “moderately to severely immunocompromised” and recommends vaccination with updated mRNA vaccines plus an additional primary dose and timely boosters</cite>. <cite id="38f8a8a5-0">Vaccines such as J&J/Jonas Eulogium can be used within CDC’s dose‑interval frameworks when mRNA options are limited, but mRNA products are preferred where available</cite>.

Special populations and subgroups
- <cite id="3821b480-5">There are different recommendations if you are moderately or severely immunocompromised; see CDC’s “Vaccines for Moderately to Severely Immunocompromised People” pathway for stepwise age/history guidance</cite>. <cite id="38f8a8a5-0">Children and adults with primary immunodeficiencies, secondary immunodeficiencies, and those receiving immunoglobulins or other replacement therapies are recommended to receive updated mRNA COVID‑19 vaccines and may need an additional dose if on active therapy; discuss interval relative to immune‑modifying treatments</cite>. <cite id="5d0ab73d-9">Inflammatory disease patients on immunosuppressive biologics should discuss risks/benefits and timing with their hematologist/immunologist; ACIP/CDC recommend continuing indicated biologics unless an acute infusion is the reason for immunosuppression surge and vaccination is attempted earlier when practically possible</cite>. <cite id="3821b480-2">Healthcare providers can use the “Interim Clinical Considerations for Use of COVID‑19 Vaccines” to individualize decisions for rare immunodeficiencies or unusual therapies</cite>.

Post‑exposure and occupational considerations
- <cite id="3821b480-0">For close contacts of confirmed cases, CDC recommends updated COVID‑19 vaccination and, for certain high‑risk exposures and contraindications to mRNA/J&J, use of smallpox‑vaccinia (JYNNEOS) as post‑exposure prophylaxis per CDC post‑exposure pathways; counsel about window of effectiveness and timing</cite>. <cite id="38f8a8a5-0">Healthcare personnel who are immunocompromised should receive recommended primary and additional/booster doses and should not delay care during outbreaks; discuss contact exposure management with infection control and ID specialists</cite>.

Shared decision‑making and monitoring
- <cite id="3821b480-0">Vaccine selection, intervals, and whether to add an “additional” mRNA dose should be tailored to clinical status, treatment plans (including planned periods of intensified immunosuppression), and prior response; patients on high‑dose systemic steroids, lymphocyte‑depleting therapies, or advanced hematologic disease warrant close pre‑ and post‑vaccination monitoring</cite>. <cite id="3821b480-0">CDC emphasizes ongoing evaluation of vaccine effectiveness in immunocompromised populations and recommends discussing breakthrough infections, hybrid immunity durability, and next‑dose timing based on product intervals</cite>.

Key takeaways for clinicians
- <cite id="3821b480-0">Immunodeficiencies or immunosuppressive therapy do not change the core principle: vaccinate and, for most, prefer updated mRNA products, then add an “additional” mRNA dose and boosters on schedule to sustain protection</cite>. <cite id="38f8a8a5-0">Do not delay vaccination due to immunosuppression; coordinate with oncology/transplant teams to vaccinate before or during stable periods, using J&J when mRNA is unavailable, and incorporate an additional primary mRNA dose into regimens where indicated</cite>. <cite id="f6f13350-6">For patients receiving active cancer treatment, an additional mRNA primary dose and then boosters are advised if they completed the mRNA series</cite>. <cite id="38f8a8a5-6">For high‑dose corticosteroids and lymphocyte‑depleting biologics/therapies, discuss risks/benefits, use mRNA vaccines where possible, consider an additional dose, and shorten/intensify subsequent intervals based on drug effects and clinical status</cite>. <cite id="3821b480-0">Educate about post‑exposure steps and that breakthrough infections can occur; plan re‑testing/vaccination intervals per product guidance</cite>.

Documented updates and seasonal applicability
- <cite id="3821b480-3">For the 2024–2025 season, a second “primary” mRNA dose at 6 months is recommended for older adults and many immunocompromised patients</cite>. <cite id="38f8a8a5-5">Interim clinical considerations for 2025–2026 continue to emphasize not delaying vaccines in immunosuppressed patients, using non‑live SARS‑CoV‑2 vaccines safely, and applying age/history‑based primary dosing with additional/booster intervals suited to immunosuppression risk</cite>. <cite id="3821b480-5">Patients can use CDC’s “Stay Up to Date” tracker and the “Immunocompromised” pathway to confirm their specific number of doses and next interval</cite>.

Bottom line for patients/clinicians with immunodeficiency or on immunosuppression
- <cite id="3821b480-0">You should get vaccinated with an updated COVID‑19 vaccine and, for most, choose an mRNA product first</cite>. <cite id="f6f8a8a5-0">Do not delay—vaccination should be given even while on immunosuppressive therapy</cite>. <cite id="3821b480-3">Plan for an additional mRNA dose 28–30 days after your second mRNA shot (or as per interval if you had an additional primary dose earlier) and then follow CDC/ACIP booster timing</cite>. <cite id="3821b480-6">Talk with your doctor if you are on high‑dose steroids, lymphocyte‑depleting drugs, or have undergone transplant—additional doses/booster strategies and earlier intervals are commonly advised</cite>. <cite id="38f8a8a5-0">If exposed and high‑risk, ask about post‑exposure prophylaxis (often JYNNEOS) and maintain your planned vaccination schedule unless otherwise directed</cite>.
