fully_underspecified.text: How does pretreatment chemically modify a component and promote hydrolysis during biomass processing?
fully_underspecified.answer:
Below is a concise, mechanism-focused explanation of how pretreatment chemically modifies lignocellulosic components to promote hydrolysis, with examples and quantitative insights.

Overview: what changes during pretreatment
- Pretreatment is a controlled chemical/physical intervention that partially dismantles the lignocellulosic matrix to expose and activate cellulose and hemicellulose for rapid hydrolysis to fermentable sugars. <cite id="fac469da-6">Pretreatment is done to partially change the matrix structure of lignocellulose by removing lignin and breaking down the structure of cellulose and hemicellulose</cite> and its purpose is to enhance enzymes or acid accessibility and hydrolyze cellulose. <cite id="fac469da-5">The purpose of the pretreatment process for lignocellulosic biomass is to enhance the enzymes or acids accessibility and hydrolyze the cellulose by breaking</cite>

How pretreatment chemically modifies key components

• Hemicellulose: ester/hemiacetal cleavage and dehydration
- Acid/base-catalyzed hydrolysis cleaves the ester bonds linking xylan and other hemicelluloses to lignin, reducing high–order networks and freeing sugar polymers. <cite id="fac469da-0">Mild breakdown of lignocellulose biomass through hydrolysis reactions, primarily cleaving ester bonds in hemicellulose and some lignin linkages</cite>
- Hemicellulese undergoes acid-catalyzed stepwise hydrolysis analogous to cellulose, generating xylo-oligosaccharides and xylose that are then susceptible to dehydration to furan aldehydes (furfural) under continued acidic conditions. <cite id="92c7e1a4-3">The mechanism involved in the acid hydrolysis of hemicellulose is similar to that for cellulose: acid catalyzes the breakdown of long hemicellulose chains</cite><cite id="5e4ec485-4">During dilute-acid hydrolysis, the released sugars can degrade into inhibitory compounds like furfural and hydroxymethylfurfural (HMF) under the acidic</cite><cite id="5e4ec485-7">The simplest kinetic mechanism that is considered in this study is hydrolysis of xylan to xylose with a subsequent de-hydration of xylose to</cite>
- In practice, xylan mass decrease follows the reaction extent (Ro), and pretreatment strategy targets converting xylan to xylose while limiting over-dehydration. <cite id="92c7e1a4-1">Xylan removal from hemicellulose solids follows a consistent pattern when plotted against Ro or log Ro for a variety of feedstocks and temperatures</cite><cite id="5e4ec485-6">One purpose of dilute-acid pretreatment of biomass is to convert as much xylan to xylose as possible</cite>
- Combined chemical–mechanical steps further remove amorphous hemicellulose and refine cellulose fibrils, boosting sugar release. <cite id="92c7e1a4-5">Deacetylation with 0.1 M NaOH before acid pretreatment improved the monomeric xylose yield in pretreatment by up to 20% while</cite><cite id="92c7e1a4-2">Results showed that deacetylation with 0.1 M NaOH before acid pretreatment improved the monomeric xylose yield in pretreatment by up to 20% while PFI refining of pretreated solids further increased pretreatment xylose yield by 11–16%</cite>

• Cellulose: deacetylation, crystallinity reduction, and decrystallization
- Removing acetyl groups from cellulose (often via NaOH) increases hydrophilicity and lowers cellulase adsorption, improving enzymatic hydrolysis yields. <cite id="fac469da-0">Deacetylation shows significant improvement on glucose and xylose yields during pretreatment and enzymatic hydrolysis</cite><cite id="92c7e1a4-0">Deacetylation shows significant improvement on glucose and xylose yields during pretreatment and enzymatic hydrolysis, but it also reduces</cite><cite id="92c7e1a4-5">Deacetylation with 0.1 M NaOH before acid pretreatment improved the monomeric xylose yield in pretreatment by up to 20% while</cite><cite id="92c7e1a4-2">PFI refining of pretreated solids further increased pretreatment xylose yield by 11–16%</cite><cite id="d8a55de6-7">Cellulose acetylation hinders enzymatic hydrolysis, and de-acetylation of hemicelluloses improves their adsorption to cellulose, which in turn increases the yield</cite>
- Mild alkaline–ammonia methods (e.g., AFEX) decrystallize cellulose and partially depolymerize hemicellulose while reducing lignin recalcitrance, collectively increasing accessible surface area for hydrolysis. <cite id="92c7e1a4-6">AFEX promotes cellulose decrystallization and partial hemicellulose depolymerization and reduces the lignin recalcitrance in the treated biomass</cite>
- Enzymatic hydrolysis mechanisms are enhanced when acetyl content is reduced, as nonproductive adsorption of endoglucases to acetyl groups is minimized. <cite id="d8a55de6-3">Selective oxidative delignification decreased nonproductive enzyme adsorption to 87–96%, improving enzymatic hydrolysis to 65–95% of the cellulose content</cite><cite id="d8a55de6-7">Nonproductive cellulase adsorption onto lignin and inhibitory sugars can be mitigated by chemical pretreatments</cite>

• Lignin: cleavage of phenolic/nonphenolic linkages, phenolic acid removal, and delignification
- Ammonia/hydroxide attack lignin’s G units, weakening the lignin network and easing separation, which opens channels to cellulose/hemicellulose. <cite id="fac469da-1">The G unit in lignin reacts with ammonia or hydroxide, which separates the lignin and facilitates the hydrolysis of hemicellulose and cellulose</cite>
- Oxidative or acid-catalyzed cleavage of β-O-4 linkages increases lignin hydrophilicity and solubility, reduces recalcitrance, and decreases nonproductive enzyme adsorption. <cite id="d8a55de6-8">Lignin reactivity was characterized by the amount of β-O-4 aryl ether linkages semi-quantified from 2D NMR analysis of the residual lignins</cite><cite id="d8a55de6-6">Acid-catalyzed cleavage of β-O-4 linkages proceeds via a concerted proton-transfer/sigmatropic rearrangement mechanism, with phenolic dimers cleaving faster than nonphenolic ones</cite><cite id="d8a55de6-3">Oxidative delignification can increase lignin hydrophilicity, reduce nonproductive enzyme adsorption to 87–96%, and raise hydrolysis yields to 65–95% of cellulose content</cite>
- Alkaline processes (e.g., sulfite) solubilize hemicellulose/lignin composites, weakening lignin–holocellulose complexes and exposing cellulose. <cite id="d8a55de6-7">Sulfite pretreatment improves the enzymatic hydrolysis yield of pretreated lignocellulosic substrates by solubilizing hemicellulose/lignin</cite><cite id="d8a55de6-9">The enhanced delignification observed could be explained by weakening of the lignin–holocellulose complex under mild conditions</cite>
- Without such modification, intact lignin strongly impedes hydrolysis by physically blocking pore networks and chemically adsorbing enzymes. <cite id="d8a55de6-0">The presence of lignin largely hinders the accessibility of enzymes to cellulose, which results in a very low enzymatic hydrolysis of the lignocellulose</cite>

How these chemical/structural changes promote hydrolysis

1) Increased accessibility via mass transfer and enzyme–substrate access
- Removing lignin (chemically or via oxidative/alkaline routes) and separating lignin “G” units expose cellulose and hemicellulose surfaces and create macropores, accelerating hydrolysis. <cite id="fac469da-1">The G unit in lignin reacts with ammonia or hydroxide, which separates the lignin and facilitates the hydrolysis of hemicellulose and cellulose</cite><cite id="d8a55de6-3">Selective oxidative delignification increased lignin hydrophilicity and reduced nonproductive enzyme adsorption, elevating hydrolysis yields to 65–95% of cellulose content</cite>
- Mild hydrolytic cleavage of hemicellulosic esters loosens the composite network, enabling acid/base or enzymes to attack cellulose more readily. <cite id="fac469da-0">Mild breakdown through hydrolysis reactions, primarily cleaving ester bonds in hemicellulose and some lignin linkages</cite><cite id="fac469da-6">Pretreatment breaks down cellulose and hemicellulose, enhancing enzyme accessibility</cite>

2) Improved carbohydrate reactivity: reduced crystallinity and deacetylation
- AFEX and alkaline treatments decrystallize cellulose and reduce lignin recalcitrance, increasing the relative amorphous surface area that enzymes can act upon. <cite id="92c7e1a4-6">AFEX promotes cellulose decrystallization and partial hemicellulose depolymerization and reduces lignin recalcitrance</cite>
- Deacetylation of cellulose and xylan lowers nonproductive adsorption and increases productive hydrolysis, with quantifiable gains. <cite id="92c7e1a4-0">Deacetylation significantly improved glucose and xylose yields during pretreatment and enzymatic hydrolysis</cite><cite id="92c7e1a4-2">Deacetylation improved monomeric xylose yield by up to 20% in pretreatment, with further gains from mechanical refining</cite>
- Deacetylation of hemicelluloses can increase their affinity for cellulose, reinforcing fiber network openness and improving sugar flux. <cite id="92c7e1a4-7">De-acetylation of hemicelluloses improves their adsorption to cellulose, increasing yield and tensile strength</cite>

3) Faster cleavage kinetics for hemicellulose and easier cellulose hydrolysis
- Acid-catalyzed hydrolysis lowers the activation barriers for glycosidic bond scission in xylan, generating xylose and shorter oligomers that are readily enzymatically hydrolyzed. <cite id="92c7e1a4-3">Acid catalyzes breakdown of long hemicellulose chains, analogous to cellulose</cite>
- Quantitatively, optimized sequences (alkali deacetylation + mild acid + mechanical refining) can boost monomeric xylose by 20% and raise pretreatment saccharification 11–16%. <cite id="92c7e1a4-5">Deacetylation improved monomeric xylose yield in pretreatment by up to 20% while PFI refining increased yield by 11–16% P</cite>
- In dilute-acid pretreatments, the fraction of cellulose converted to fermentable sugars decreases with pretreatment severity, but allows downstream enzymatic hydrolysis to reach 61–80% of total glucan with 17–45% less conversion required after pretreatment. <cite id="5e4ec485-8">Dilute-acid pretreatment of pretreated corn stover showed hydrolysis of cellulose to glucose can be modeled and optimized, with pretreatment cutting the required hydrolysis conversion by 17–45%</cite>

4) Direct hydrolytic depolymerization pathways for sugars and inhibitors
- Released sugars can either be fully hydrolyzed to monomers for fermentation, or dehydrated to furan aldehydes (furfural/HMF), which inhibit hydrolysis and fermentation. <cite id="5e4ec485-4">During dilute-acid hydrolysis, released sugars can degrade into inhibitory compounds like furfural and hydroxymethylfurfural (HMF)</cite><cite id="5e4ec485-7">Kinetic schemes explicitly include hydrolysis of xylan to xylose followed by dehydration of xylose</cite>
- Process engineering therefore targets a sweet spot: maximize xylan-to-xylose conversion (often >95%) while limiting over-dehydration and HMF formation. <cite id="5e4ec485-6">One purpose of dilute-acid pretreatment is to convert as much xylan to xylose as possible</cite><cite id="5e4ec485-1">Dilute-acid pretreatment of poplar altered structural metrics that impacted xylan hydrolysis rates</cite>

Examples linking chemical modification to hydrolysis outcomes

- Deacetylation before acid pretreatment: improved monomeric xylose yields by up to 20% in pretreatment and 11–16% gains via mechanical refining, with accompanying reductions in nonproductive enzyme adsorption. <cite id="92c7e1a4-0">Deacetylation shows significant improvement on glucose and xylose yields during pretreatment and enzymatic hydrolysis</cite><cite id="92c7e1a4-5">Deacetylation with 0.1 M NaOH before acid pretreatment improved monomeric xylose yield in pretreatment by up to 20%</cite><cite id="92c7e1a4-2">PFI refining of pretreated solids further increased pretreatment xylose yield by 11–16%</cite><cite id="d8a55de6-3">Selective oxidative delignification decreased nonproductive enzyme adsorption to 87–96%, and hydrolysis reached 65–95% of cellulose content</cite>
- AFEX (alkaline ammonia explosion): cellulose decrystallization, partial hemicellulose depolymerization, and reduced lignin recalcitrance collectively improve downstream hydrolysis. <cite id="92c7e1a4-6">AFEX promotes cellulose decrystallization and partial hemicellulose depolymerization and reduces lignin recalcitrance in the treated biomass</cite>
- Alkaline/oxidative delignification: increases lignin hydrophilicity, disrupts β-O-4 linkages, weakens lignin–cellulose complexes, and reduces enzyme inhibition, raising hydrolysis yields. <cite id="d8a55de6-8">β-O-4 ether linkages semi-quantified by 2D NMR characterize lignin reactivity in oxidative delignification</cite><cite id="d8a55de6-6">Acid-catalyzed cleavage of β-O-4 linkages proceeds via concerted proton-transfer/sigmatropic rearrangement, with phenolic dimers cleaving faster</cite><cite id="d8a55de6-7">Sulfite pretreatment solubilizes hemicellulose/lignin and improves enzymatic hydrolysis</cite><cite id="d8a55de6-9">Weakening of lignin–holocellulose complexes under mild conditions enhances delignification and exposes cellulose</cite>

Trade-offs, packaging, and integrative picture
- Pretreatment chemistry must balance depolymerization with inhibitor formation: maximizing xylan-to-xylose conversion increases sugar yield but raises the risk of xylose dehydration to furfural if severity is too high. <cite id="5e4ec485-7">Hydrolysis of xylan to xylose followed by dehydration of xylose is a characteristic kinetic pathway</cite><cite id="5e4ec485-4">Acidic hydrolysis often yields inhibitory furan aldehydes that hinder downstream hydrolysis and fermentation</cite>
- Pretreatment that solubilizes lignin/hemicellulose reduces the fraction of cellulose needing hydrolysis to reach target sugars (e.g., 17–45% less conversion required), but may coextract phenolics that require management. <cite id="5e4ec485-8">Modeling of hydrolysis after pretreatment indicates pretreatment can decrease required hydrolysis conversion by 17–45%</cite>
- Ultimately, pretreatment promotes hydrolysis by: (i) cleaving and redistributing ester/ether linkages and phenolic moieties, (ii) removing phenolic and nonphenolic lignin blocks, (iii) reducing cellulose crystallinity and acetyl content, and (iv) increasing pore accessibility, enabling rapid enzymatic or acid hydrolysis to fermentable sugars, albeit with careful control to limit furan formation and enzyme inhibition. <cite id="fac469da-0">Hydrolysis cleaves ester bonds in hemicellulose and some lignin linkages</cite><cite id="fac469da-1">Reactions with ammonia/hydroxide separate lignin and facilitate carbohydrate hydrolysis</cite><cite id="d8a55de6-0">T</cite>

Key takeaways
- Chemical modifications during pretreatment include: ester bond scission in hemicellulose, β-O-4 and other lignin linkage cleavage, cellulose and hemicellulose deacetylation, lignin solubilization/depolymerization, and controlled depolymerization of polysaccharides to monomers. <cite id="fac469da-0">Cleaving ester bonds in hemicellulose and lignin linkages</cite><cite id="d8a55de6-6">Acid-catalyzed cleavage of β-O-4 linkages proceeds via a concerted mechanism</cite><cite id="92c7e1a4-0">Deacetylation improves glucose and xylose yields during pretreatment and hydrolysis</cite><cite id="d8a55de6-7">Sulfite pretreatment solubilizes hemicellulose/lignin to improve hydrolysis</cite>
- These changes lower mass transfer and kinetic barriers, reduce nonproductive enzyme adsorption, and increase the rate and extent of hydrolysis to glucose and xylose, while necessitating management of furan aldehyde inhibitors formed under acid conditions. <cite id="92c7e1a4-5">Improved monomeric xylose yield by up to 20% with deacetylation</cite><cite id="d8a55de6-3">Selective oxidative delignification reduced nonproductive adsorption and boosted hydrolysis to 65–95% of cellulose content</cite><cite id="5e4ec485-4">Acid hydrolysis releases inhibitory furfural and HMF that can hinder hydrolysis and fermentation</cite>

questions.original_query: How do capillary forces arise during the evaporation stage of drying cellulosic materials, and what role do they play in fiber bonding?

query.text: How do capillary forces arise during the evaporation stage of drying cellulosic materials, and what role do they play in fiber bonding?
query.answer:
Overview

During the evaporation stage of drying cellulosic materials (paper, fiber mats, wood), liquid–vapor interfaces (menisci) form around shrinking wetting films, in capillaries of cell walls, and at fiber crossings. These interfaces have curved surfaces that give rise to Laplace pressures, generating capillary forces that pull or push nearby surfaces. As water leaves, menisci shrink and reorganize; attractive capillary actions draw hydrophilic cellulose surfaces together, enabling the formation of fiber contacts and bridges, whereas other configurations can produce transient repulsion. These evolving capillary interactions drive fiber rearrangement, densification, and bonding, while moisture gradients also produce shrinkage stresses and defects if not accommodated. <cite id="266ec689-2">A meniscus with negative radius of curvature produces an attractive capillary force, and upon water removal the radius becomes smaller, enhancing capillary attraction</cite> <cite id="7f4285d8-6">Capillary forces are due to a meniscus mainly around fiber crossings, with the dominant capillary force the wetting force acting along fiber intersections</cite>.

1) Mechanisms: How capillary forces arise during evaporation

- Meniscus curvature and Laplace pressure in narrow channels:
  <cite id="266ec689-2">As free water evaporates from wetting films at fiber surfaces, a capillary meniscus forms with negative mean curvature that yields an attractive Laplace pressure toward the curved region—this pull intensifies as the meniscus area (negative radius) diminishes with evaporation</cite>. <cite id="266ec689-1">At the fiber–cell-wall–lumen scale, capillary pressure in micropores and the elastic response of cellulosic elements compete: elastocapillary models show capillary suction in lumens and capillary micropores controls collapse depending on pore size and wall stiffness</cite>. <cite id="266ec689-5">In wood, theory posits that negative pressure (tension) develops when air–water menisci reach capillary pores in cell walls, drawing water through walls and promoting capillary action</cite>.

- Air entrapment, diffusion, and capillary condensation at drying fronts:
  <cite id="266ec689-0">In drying wood, the interplay of capillary pressure, permeability, and diffusion determines where evaporation occurs; air entrapment at drying fronts reduces effective permeability and focuses capillary suction into weak pathways</cite>. <cite id="266ec689-4">Within cell lumens and walls, water can be held by capillary condensation and capillary action; capillary condensation describes liquid formation at adsorbed monolayers in hydrophilic pores even below bulk saturation</cite>. <cite id="266ec689-8">As free water content declines, menisci at the drying front with the largest openings may rupture under suction, re-retreating into narrower neighboring capillaries and forcing liquid redistribution</cite>. <cite id="266ec689-7">Free water transport in wood is enabled by capillary forces created by evaporation from fibers near or at surfaces, with permeability governing withdrawal as bound water moves through walls</cite>.

- Bridge-mediated capillarity at fiber contacts:
  <cite id="7f4285d8-6">In wet paper, menisci concentrate at fiber crossings where capillary forces (dominant “wetting forces”) promote inter-fiber draw-in along crossing lines</cite>. <cite id="dccef780-2">In the early drying stage, the main capillary force is surface-tension-driven bridge formation; liquid bridges between fibers are the primary capillary agents</cite>. <cite id="dccef780-0">As highly adhered (HR) water is removed, high capillary (attractive) forces draw fibers closer together, enabling fiber–fiber bonding</cite>. <cite id="266ec689-3">Conversely, when a meniscus in a wide pore cannot sustain suction, it retracts into narrower channels, redistributing liquid and altering the capillary net</cite>.

2) Role of capillary forces in fiber bonding during evaporation

- Fiber–fiber drawing, contact formation, and capillary bridging:
  <cite id="dccef780-6">Water capillary bridges during drying pull hydrophilic cellulose surfaces into very close contact (nanometer gaps), facilitating hydrogen bonding between hydroxyl groups on adjacent fibers to form a primary, capillary-bridged bond</cite>. <cite id="7f4285d8-1">When capillary bonding is strong, fiber shrinkage during drying can impose lengthwise crimping, indicating formation of robust, mechanically effective bonds that constrain relative motion</cite>. <cite id="7f4285d8-2">Capillary attraction can overcome lumen elastic restoring forces, producing partial collapse of fibers and closer packing</cite>.

- From attractive to repulsive interactions depending on geometry and phase changes:
  <cite id="7f4285d8-3">Near a receding water drop on a cellulosic surface, fibers may initially be pulled together by capillary action; however, as the contact line withdraws, capillary geometry can yield a net repulsive interaction that resists wetting and can oppose further draw-in</cite>. <cite id="dccef780-4">Paradoxically, microscopic experiments report that capillary forces within fiber crossings can decrease as solids content increases yet wet paper strength continues to rise; this implies evolving macroscopic adhesive networks and structural densification despite diminishing bridge surface tension, where early capillary “surface-tension bridges” transition toward solid/bridged contacts and hydrogen-bonded junctions</cite>.

- Microstructural densification and adhesion strengthening:
  <cite id="7f4285d8-6">By concentrating menisci at crossings, capillary forces align and compress fiber junctions, increasing local contact area and real contact load; the wetting junction is the dominant capillary action locus and underpins paper’s tensile and bonding behavior</cite>. <cite id="266ec689-1">An elastocapillary framework shows that in lumen-micropore systems, capillary pulling and elastic recoil jointly set collapse thresholds, linking capillary pressure at drying to pronounced fiber bending and interlocking geometry</cite>. <cite id="dccef780-9">Classification of incomplete (teardrop/pendant) bridge shapes and stability using the Delaunay capillary surface solution shows how contact angle and bridge topology determine whether a capillary bridge holds or ruptures, directly conditioning adhesive contact formation</cite>.

- Stage-wise contributions to the overall drying process:
  • Constant-rate/initial fast-drying regime: <cite id="dccef780-2">Surface-tension-dominated capillary bridges rapidly draw fibers together at crossings, maximizing liquid uptake by bridges and driving wet strength rise through junction densification</cite>. <cite id="266ec689-0">Capillary pressure and local permeability/diffusion control evaporation sites; this stage exhibits rapid free-surface loss and mobile wetting films in cell walls/fiber lumens</cite>.
  • Transition/falling-rate stage: <cite id="7f4285d8-0">Removal of highly adhered (HR) water generates strong capillary attraction that collapses inter-fiber spacings and stabilizes fiber contacts</cite>; <cite id="7f4285d8-1">bonding becomes sufficiently strong that fiber shrinkage triggers crimping, producing strain-compatible, interlocked joints</cite>.
  • Late-stage redistribution/entrapment: <cite id="266ec689-8">As free water reduces, main-pore menisci may rupture under suction, causing liquid re-entry into narrower channels; capillary condensation maintains films in small pores until vapor transport dominates</cite>, producing a residual network of capillary water and bridges that lock the mat.

3) Key parameters and surface phenomena controlling capillary bonding

- Contact angle and hysteresis:
  <cite id="dccef780-9">Analytical capillary-bridge analyses (Delaunay) delineate incomplete bridge morphologies versus complete wetting for given contact angles; bridge detachment at receding contact lines correlates with contact angle hysteresis and determines adhesion duration and rupture</cite>. <cite id="266ec689-6">Highly hydrophilic cell wall channels generate large negative pressures (capillary water tension) that pull water into and along conduits, emphasizing that low contact angles favor suction and bonding while higher hysteresis increases pinning and bridge instability</cite>.

- Capillary number and time scales:
  <cite id="266ec689-5">Capillary pressure scales with liquid surface tension and curvature and must overcome viscous and elastic resistance as water leaves; the capillary timescale sets how quickly bridges nucleate and lock, structuring the sheet’s junction network</cite>.

- Air–liquid interfaces and vapor diffusion:
  <cite id="266ec689-4">Capillary condensation can supply water to narrow pores even below ambient RH, sustaining bridges; during evaporation, non-condensable vapor buildup adjacent to drying menisci modifies local vapor pressure and curvature, affecting bridge stability and capillary pressure</cite>. <cite id="266ec689-0">Air entrapment at the front reduces permeability and focuses suction into weak pathways, promoting localized capillary bonding and later cracking if moisture loss is uneven</cite>.

4) Outcomes and trade-offs in drying-related bonding

- Strength, toughness, and shrinkage adaptation:
  <cite id="dccef780-6">Capillary-bridge–driven nanometric gap closure enables covalent hydrogen bonding between cellulose hydroxyls, forming a primary, high-shear, moisture-sensitive bond within junctions</cite>. <cite id="dccef780-1">Bond development mechanisms also include 3D fiber mixing and mechanical entanglement; capillary forces are central in bringing fibers together for these processes</cite>. <cite id="dccef780-4">Strength can keep rising even as individual capillary force magnitudes decrease with solids increase because junctions evolve from transient liquid bridges to dry, hydrogen-bonded contacts and interlocked morphologies</cite>.

- Morphology changes and defects:
  <cite id="7f4285d8-2">Capillary attractions can partially collapse fibers and reduce luminal cross-sectional area</cite>, <cite id="7f4285d8-1">which may translate into crimping and strain hardening</cite>. <cite id="266ec689-8">Alternatively, suction-driven meniscus retraction and heterogenous drying can cause bridging loss, path reshaping, and microcracking that interrupt bonding continuity</cite>.

Practical implications

- To maximize fiber bonding during evaporation: control surface wettabilities and drainage to favor stable, concave menisci and low hysteresis over contacts; maintain uniform evaporation fronts to avoid localized suction damage; use topologies (fiber load, cross-section, additives) that promote rapid bridge formation and junction densification without over-collapse. <cite id="7f4285d8-0">Highly adhered water removal triggers strong capillary pulling</cite>, <cite id="dccef780-6">but close contact must be followed by hydrogen-bond formation and moisture redistribution for durable bonds</cite>.
- To mitigate defects: manage permeability and humidity gradients to limit air entrapment and rupture of main-pore menisci; allow late-stage capillary condensation to maintain junction moisture until bonds lock; recognize that <cite id="7f4285d8-3">receding contact lines can produce repulsive capillary stresses that resist wetting and delay or reduce bonding in narrow channels</cite>.

Summary

Capillary forces during drying arise from curved air–water interfaces at shrinking wetting films, fiber crossings, and microcapillaries of cell walls and lumens. Their magnitudes and signs depend on meniscus curvature, contact angle and hysteresis, and evolving pore occupancy (free water, capillary condensate, vapor). These forces attract and compress hydrophilic cellulose surfaces, closing gaps to form liquid bridges and then hydrogen-bonded fiber–fiber contacts that become the structural and adhesive backbone of the sheet; they also generate shrinkage and collapse modes that induce crimping and interlocking. In wood, analogous capillary turgor drives suction in cell walls as free water leaves lumens, reshaping cells and reinforcing mat bonding through cell wall–lumen coupling. Control of these processes across the evaporation stages determines whether drying yields strong, dense, crack-resistant structures or weaker, fractured networks. <cite id="266ec689-2">Meniscus curvature produces attractive capillary pressure that increases as bridges shrink</cite> <cite id="dccef780-6">to form hydrogen-bonded junctions</cite> <cite id="7f4285d8-1">that translate shrinkage into crimp and enhanced strength</cite> <cite id="266ec689-5">while capillary condensation and vapor diffusion sustain liquid films in narrow pathways to lock bonds upon completion of drying</cite>.

Notes on unresolved physics: Evaporation-induced non-condensable vapor layers and Kelvin/Poisson curvature corrections in very narrow channels can modulate local capillary pressures; quantitative modeling suggests they significantly affect bridge lifetimes and junction wetting in late-stage drying, but their magnitude depends on material roughness, humidity boundary layers, and temperature gradients that require site-specific modeling and measurement. <cite id="266ec689-4">Capillary condensation and evaporation at adsorbed layers</cite> <cite id="266ec689-0">and air entrapment effects</cite> underscore the need to integrate interfacial thermodynamics with transport to predict capillary bonding evolution. <cite id="dccef780-1">Adhesion of fiber junctions is multifactorial—capillary action plus mixing and mechanical interlock—so bond strength integrates both capillary-driven contact creation and post-drying structural evolution</cite>.

Below is a mechanistic picture of how forces emerge as materials dry and how those forces end up creating, strengthening, or breaking bonds.

# How forces arise during drying

1) Capillarity in menisci and liquid bridges. As surfaces wet and then partially evaporate, a receding contact line stabilizes on roughness or pinning sites while a curved meniscus forms a liquid bridge that can span to another surface or to nearby asperities. The curvature of that bridge imposes a Laplace pressure, generating suction that mechanically presses the solids together and producing large adhesion at the contact line; these capillary liquid bridges are ubiquitous and can be strong enough to bind particles and even span microcavities in rough textures during drying <cite id="90ccb09a-0">Capillary liquid bridges form when a liquid meniscus bridges two surfaces, generating strong adhesion forces. They are ubiquitous in nature and …</cite> <cite id="8febcf36-1">Analysis of evaporation dynamics and capillary forces indicate that at low Bond numbers, surface tension forces dominate and provide unique …</cite> <cite id="8febcf36-5">Evaporation has been seen to produce pressure gradients within the water bridge and a consequent liquid flow, as a result of the propagation and …</cite> <cite id="90ccb09a-4">This paper presents a simple and robust model to describe the wet adhesion of the AFM tip and substrate joined by a liquid bridge.</cite> 

2) Contact-line pinning and hysteresis. The evaporating rim alternates between advancing and receding fronts; trapped pinning sites (e.g., texture, soil cracks) lock the contact line, enlarging the meniscus and the area over which Laplace pressure integrates. This makes adhesion large, sticky, and intermittent until dewetting or depinning occurs, which is why many materials release in steps or leave imprints during drying <cite id="8febcf36-7">Pinning-depinning of the contact line during drop evaporation on textured … It has been shown that the dynamics of sessile droplet evaporation is directly linked to substrate characteristics, such as surface wettability</cite> <cite id="8febcf36-0">We start by performing tests on capillary bridges to study the effect of drying on the adhesion force. pinned contact line during droplet …</cite> <cite id="8febcf36-6">During evaporation, the capillary force decreases slowly at the beginning of the process and quickly at the end of the process; during extension …</cite> 

3) Evaporative transport and pressure flow inside the bridge. As the film thins, internal pressure gradients develop across the bridge, driving liquid flow from thicker to thinner regions and reshaping the interface. These flows regulate the contact-line speed and modulate the balance between adhesion-generating suction and thinning/debonding as moisture exits <cite id="8febcf36-5">Evaporation has been seen to produce pressure gradients within the water bridge and a consequent liquid flow, as a result of the propagation and …</cite> <cite id="90ccb09a-3">This shift in the capillary pressure reduces the average adhesion by a factor as large as 2 from its continuum value and is found to be due to an anisotropy in …</cite> 

4) Transition to van der Waals dominance as films thin. Early capillary suction is large and sensitive to curvature, but as the last nanometer-thick film evaporates, capillary ranges shrink and van der Waals attraction between solid surfaces becomes the principal cohesive or adhesive force across drier gaps; in such nanometer-scale contacts, adhesion is governed by approach kinetics, contact-line pinning, and surface forces that deviate from simple continuum predictions <cite id="90ccb09a-2">This work presents a theoretical study of the forces established between colloidal particles connected by means of a concave liquid bridge, …</cite> <cite id="90ccb09a-6">The very large capillary forces induced by highly curved menisci have strong effect … it gives rise to slow activated phenom- ena</cite> <cite id="90ccb09a-3">This shift in the capillary pressure reduces the average adhesion by a factor as large as 2 from its continuum value …</cite> <cite id="90ccb09a-7">Negative pressure in nanoscale water capillary bridges … For small systems, this capillary force may become very significant, dominating over other forces such as the van der Waals adhesion or electrostatic forces.</cite> 

5) Geometry and roughness. As bridges span larger features, the meniscus can split across peaks, creating additional smaller bridges in parallel; multiple bridges can collectively increase adhesion by an order of magnitude or more depending on roughness amplitude and loading, thereby strengthening the “bond” between rough surfaces during drying <cite id="90ccb09a-0">Bridge splitting on a rough surface significantly enhances the adhesion force, with an enhancement that increases with the amplitude of the roughness;</cite> <cite id="8febcf36-7">It has been shown that the dynamics of sessile droplet evaporation is directly linked to substrate characteristics, such as surface wettability</cite> <cite id="8febcf36-3">We also studied the effect of evaporation on the variation in the adhesion force by simulating an evaporating droplet on a superhydrophobic …</cite> 

6) Friction and charge (contact/desiccation electrification). If surfaces rub while wet or desiccate, electrons can transfer by contact electrification (triboelectric effect), building electrostatic dipoles or charges upon/within the drying film or on adjacent solids. Desiccating particle flows (blowing sand, dust devils) are strongly electrified by tribocharging; these charges can increase or reduce adhesion in powders depending on polarity, trapping, and intervening film, and they can remain after water leaves, altering cohesion and dust floc structure <cite id="6f8223de-1">Triboelectric nanogenerators (TENGs) have emerged as a promising technology for harvesting ambient mechanical energy into electrical energy, …</cite> <cite id="6f8223de-2">The triboelectric effect describes electric charge transfer between two objects when they contact or slide against each other. It can occur with different …</cite> <cite id="6f8223de-6">Electrification of particles in blowing sand, dust devils and dust storms can result from contact charging/triboelectrification during dust generation</cite> <cite id="6f8223de-7">In addition, the tribo-electric charge showed a linear relationship with particle surface adhesion, but the involvement of other forces cannot be neglected.</cite> 

# How these forces contribute to bonding

1) Surface-to-surface adhesion and mechanical interlocking. Capillary bridges convert surface tension into compressive normal stresses at the contact line, pressing solids together so that interfaces can “lock” in a bonded state once water departs. Bridges also span cavities and roughness, effectively stitching over defects and leaving mechanical interlocks in dried films and coatings, which elevates contact strength and reduces crack propagation along the interface <cite id="90ccb09a-0">Capillary liquid bridges form when a liquid meniscus bridges two surfaces, generating strong adhesion forces. 2) Cohesive bonding and cementation in porous and particulate media. In wet granular or cementitious pastes, capillary networks drive solute transport; as water leaves, dissolved silica, phosphate, or calcium species precipitate along contact zones to form intergranular cement that binds particles into a macroscopic cohesive network—classic examples include microbially induced calcite precipitation for stone repair, silane-assisted adhesion on ceramics, and cement hydration bridging particles into load-bearing networks <cite id="d588ea90-2">With the interparticle bonding enhancement effect, the MICP technology has been utilized for filling and repairing cracks in stone materials and concrete</cite> <cite id="d588ea90-0">Purpose: To investigate the effect of adhesive type and long-term aging on the shear bond strength (SBS) between silica-based ceramics and …</cite> <cite id="d588ea90-5">Cement hydration: building bridges and dams at the … Abstract The concurrent goals of cement hydration are to percolate (bridge) the original cement particles into a load-bearing network and.</cite> <cite id="d588ea90-1">AIM: To assess the influence of silane evaporation procedures on bond strength between a dental ceramic and a chemically activated resin cement</cite> <cite id="8febcf36-8">Discover the fascinating behavior of liquid bridges on hydrophobic surfaces during evaporation. Explore the drying kinetics and parameters of deionized …</cite> 

3) Surface restructuring and bond aging. Water sorption–desorption cycles open and close pores and rearrange surface hydration layers, altering roughness and energy barriers for depinning. Upon drying, the surface area can decrease via condensation or surface-tension–induced collapse, which changes the capacity for wet adhesion and can weaken or densify the bond depending on chemistry; long-term aging of adhesive interfaces shows sensitive evolution in shear bond strength <cite id="d588ea90-7">This decrease in surface area upon drying may be the result of condensation during drying or surface tension induced collapse.</cite> <cite id="8febcf36-3">We also studied the effect of evaporation on the variation in the adhesion force by simulating an evaporating droplet on a superhydrophobic …</cite> <cite id="d588ea90-0">Purpose: To investigate the effect of adhesive type and long-term aging on the shear bond strength (SBS) between silica-based ceramics and …</cite> 

4) Electrostatic contributions from drying friction. If surfaces are brought into sliding or rubbing contact while wet, tribocharging in the thin film and on adjacent solids can leave persistent space charges near interfaces. In powders, these charges correlate with adhesion yet coexist with capillary/van der Waals forces; in airborne dust and sand, desiccation-associated tribocharging amplifies cohesion, dust floc, and adhesion to substrates, influencing how “dry” dust deposits form and bonds after moisture removal <cite id="6f8223de-1">Triboelectric nanogenerators (TENGs) have emerged as a promising technology for harvesting ambient mechanical energy into electrical energy, …</cite> <cite id="6f8223de-2">The triboelectric effect describes electric charge transfer between two objects when they contact or slide against each other. It can occur with different …</cite> <cite id="6f8223de-6">Electrification of particles in blowing sand, dust devils and dust storms can result from contact charging/triboelectrification during dust generation</cite> <cite id="6f8223de-7">In addition, the tribo-electric charge showed a linear relationship with particle surface adhesion, but the involvement of other forces cannot be neglected.</cite> <cite id="6f8223de-5">Triboelectric charging occurs when two surfaces acquire electric charge through the energy dissipation process, such as contact or friction.</cite> 

# Stages, controls, and failure modes

- Early-stage wet adhesion. While a continuous meniscus exists, adhesion is dominated by capillary pressure and contact-line hysteresis; large hysteresis and pinning delay depinning, producing strong, sometimes intermittent adhesion that can suddenly release upon depinning or macroscopic sliding, leaving residual suction and imprinting marks on the surface <cite id="8febcf36-7">Pinning-depinning of the contact line during drop evaporation on textured … It has been shown that the dynamics of sessile droplet evaporation is directly linked to substrate characteristics, such as surface wettability</cite> <cite id="8febcf36-6">During evaporation, the capillary force decreases slowly at the beginning of the process and quickly at the end of the process; during extension …</cite> 

- Mid-stage film thinning and redistribution. As the film thins, internal evaporation creates pressure gradients and flows that smooth the interface and gradually decrease adhesion; roughness and bridge splitting can maintain or even increase contact area and adhesion until the last nanometers or pinning sites are removed <cite id="8febcf36-5">Evaporation has been seen to produce pressure gradients within the water bridge and a consequent liquid flow, as a result of the propagation and …</cite> <cite id="90ccb09a-0">Bridge splitting on a rough surface significantly enhances the adhesion force, with an enhancement that increases with the amplitude of the roughness;</cite> <cite id="90ccb09a-3">This shift in the capillary pressure reduces the average adhesion by a factor as large as 2 from its continuum value and is found to be due to an anisotropy in …</cite> 

- Late-stage dry bonding and van der Waals control. Capillary suction wanes as curvature vanishes; van der Waals attraction becomes the principal mechanism across nanometer gaps, setting the onset of fracture and the work of adhesion. Surface imperfections and charge distributions can still modulate failure pathways—e.g., bridged sites resist pull-off, while pinning remnants and silica/gypsum precipitates create heterogeneous cohesive zones <cite id="90ccb09a-2">This work presents a theoretical study of the forces established between colloidal particles connected by means of a concave liquid bridge, …</cite> <cite id="90ccb09a-6">The very large capillary forces induced by highly curved menisci have strong effect …</cite> <cite id="d588ea90-2">With the interparticle bonding enhancement effect, the MICP technology has been utilized for filling and repairing cracks in stone materials and concrete</cite> <cite id="d588ea90-5">Cement hydration: building bridges and dams at the … Abstract The concurrent goals of cement hydration are to percolate (bridge) the original cement particles into a load-bearing network and.</cite> 

Practical levers to engineer bonding during drying include hydrophobic textures that store bridges and pinning sites for stronger wet adhesion, superhydrophobic coatings that reduce adhesion to ease release, controlled humidity to tune depinning, and frictional contacts to deliberately add or mitigate triboelectric cohesion. Adhesive chemistries (e.g., silanes, MICP) exploit drying porosity to precipitate cementing phases that convert capillary-bonded interfaces into covalent or mineral-based cohesive bonds with much higher durability once dry <cite id="8febcf36-3">We also studied the effect of evaporation on the variation in the adhesion force by simulating an evaporating droplet on a superhydrophobic …</cite> <cite id="d588ea90-1">AIM: To assess the influence of silane evaporation procedures on bond strength between a dental ceramic and a chemically activated resin cement</cite> <cite id="d588ea90-2">With the interparticle bonding enhancement effect, the MICP technology has been utilized for filling and repairing cracks in stone materials and concrete</cite> <cite id="d588ea90-5">Cement hydration: building bridges and dams at the … Abstract The concurrent goals of cement hydration are to percolate (bridge) the original cement particles into a load-bearing network and.</cite> <cite id="d588ea90-0">Purpose: To investigate the effect of adhesive type and long-term aging on the shear bond strength (SBS) between silica-based ceramics and …</cite> <cite id="6f8223de-6">Electrification of particles in blowing sand, dust devils and dust storms can result from contact charging/triboelectrification during dust generation</cite> <cite id="6f8223de-7">In addition, the tribo-electric charge showed a linear relationship with particle surface adhesion, but the involvement of other forces cannot be neglected.</cite> 

In sum, drying converts surface energy and flow into capillary suction and contact-line forces that mechanically press interfaces together, while friction and chemistry can add electrostatic and cementitious contributions that persist once moisture departs; the transition from capillary-dominated wet adhesion to van der Waals-dominated dry cohesion determines when bonding is strong, brittle, or reworkable <cite id="90ccb09a-0">Capillary liquid bridges form when a liquid meniscus bridges two surfaces, generating strong adhesion forces. without_scope.text: How do capillary forces arise during evaporation, and what role do they play in bonding?
without_scope.answer:
Below is a concise, evidence‑backed explanation of how capillary forces arise during evaporation and how they enable bonding.

Origins of capillary forces during evaporation
- Surface‑tension–driven minimization of interfacial area: As a droplet evaporates, its free energy seeks configurations with minimized surface area. This induces a capillary liquid flow inside the droplet, redistributing liquid from curved apexes to flatter regions to reduce total interfacial energy while conserving volume; the driving pressure stems from curvature and surface tension as captured by the Young–Laplace relation for sessile drops and capillaries. <cite id="1ae47966-0">The evaporation of a sessile droplet spontaneously induces an internal capillary liquid flow due to surface‑tension–driven minimisation of surface area.</cite> <cite id="b67a7e71-0">Droplet evaporation produces an internal capillary flow from surface‑tension–driven minimization of surface area in a sessile drop.</cite> <cite id="b67a7e71-4">Surface‑tension minimization of surface area characterizes the internal flow in evaporating sessile droplets.</cite>
- Curvature and pressure gradients: Regions of greater curvature have higher Laplace pressure (ΔP = γ(1/R1 + 1/R2)), forcing liquid to flow away from highly curved regions to less curved ones. During evaporation this yields axial outward flow at the tip and lateral redistribution, producing non‑linear thickness profiles and accumulation at edges that manifest as “tears” and rivulets along contact line pinning sites. <cite id="1ae47966-8">Resultant Laplace pressure induces the liquid to flow away from the tip apex toward its sides, thinning apex and redistributing thickness; surface tension minimizes area.</cite> <cite id="b67a7e71-2">Droplet evaporation governs transport in many phenomena, with more curved regions evolving preferentially due to curvature‑dependent forces during evaporation.</cite> <cite id="103a9845-4">Evaporation can change the contact angle and modifies the flow and gradients near the contact line, coupling drying with capillary redistribution.</cite>
- Gravity vs capillarity: Gravity opposes surface‑tension‑driven curvature effects and sets a capillary length ℓc = √(γ/ρg) beyond which capillary forces compete with gravity; evaporating droplets thinner than a few ℓc enter regimes where flow is dominated by surface tension, and shapes deviate from hemispherical. <cite id="1ae47966-3">The capillary length ℓc = √(γ/ρg) quantifies the balance between capillary forces and gravity in evaporating droplets; below this scale capillary forces dominate.</cite> <cite id="b67a7e71-6">Analytical models for evaporating sessile drops consider pinned contact lines and develop hydrodynamic potentials tied to curvature and evaporation boundary conditions.</cite>
- Contact lines and bridges: When two solids or particles are near, a liquid meniscus forms at the contact line or bridge; at low Bond numbers (Bo = ρgR²/γ small), capillary forces from surface tension can exceed viscous and gravitational forces, producing strong localized pull‑‑offs and enabling adhesion even before bulk liquid is shared. <cite id="1ae47966-6">Evaporation dynamics and capillary forces in a bridge indicate that at low Bond numbers surface tension dominates, providing unique bonding opportunities via strong capillary forces near the contact line.</cite>
- Evaporation‑induced edge accumulation (“tears of a tear”): Evaporation causes local contact angle change and gradient‑driven flow toward the receding contact line, enhancing edge deposition and the “tear” phenomenon, which is a visible manifestation of curvature‑evaporation coupling. <cite id="b67a7e71-2">Evaporation selects for shape/flow patterns due to interfacial energy minimization across curved boundaries.</cite> <cite id="103a9845-4">Evaporation changes the contact angle and the near‑contact line flow, coupling drying to capillary redistribution that promotes edge accumulation.</cite>
- Adhesion energy link: Surface tension and interfacial energies directly set adhesion strength via Young–Laplace curvature and wetting (contact angle), so during drying, curvature relaxation and area minimization increase liquid–solid contact area and local pressure, amplifying attractive cohesive/adhesive interactions that favor bonding. <cite id="66a45479-0">Adhesion arises from attraction between two materials in contact and is influenced by the surface and interfacial energies of the materials.</cite> <cite id="66a45479-3">Mechanisms of adhesion and cohesion are mediated by intermolecular forces and surface/interfacial energies that set bonding strength.</cite>

From capillary forces to bonding roles during/after evaporation
- Direct capillary adhesion: A liquid meniscus trapped between solids converts surface tension and Laplace pressure into a pulling force; if the solids approach closely enough or are held so the meniscus cannot shrink, the liquid “welds” the interfaces and yields a strong capillary bond until drying or curing. MD and continuum models show pronounced capillary adhesion for small droplets and tips near substrates where meniscus curvature is large. <cite id="103a9845-0">Molecular dynamics of a nonvolatile liquid meniscus between a spherical tip and substrate quantify capillary adhesion strength as curvature increases.</cite> <cite id="1ae47966-6">Surface‑tension–dominated capillary bridges at low Bo generate strong near‑contact forces that can mechanically lock bonded elements together.</cite>
- Evaporation‑assisted adhesion (wetting/welding plus curing): In practical bonding, a wetting step (brushing/deposition) yields an evaporating meniscus; curvature‑driven capillary flow increases wetted area and fills micro‑pores, while surface tension and interfacial energies yield local welding/“wetting line” adhesion. If adhesive chemistry is included, capillary prewetting increases bonding efficiency and speed by enlarging adhesive–substrate interfaces before curing. <cite id="66a45479-0">Adhesion strength depends on interfacial energies between contact materials; higher interfacial wetting energy increases bonding.</cite> <cite id="b67a7e71-6">Hydrodynamic capillary flow in evaporating sessile drops with pinned contact lines reflects how evaporation and interfacial energy drive mass redistribution prior to curing.</cite>
- Evaporative self‑assembly and leak‑not‑leak: Drying patterns form by contact‑line pinning and curvature‑driven transport, which concentrate solutes and organize particles/micelles into rings/stripes; in “leak‑not‑leak” assembly, capillary flow guides liquid along grooves until complete drying, leaving patterned residue—this is an evaporative, capillary‑bonded micro/nano‑structuring process used in bio/soft matter assembly. <cite id="103a9845-7">Evaporation‑induced self‑organization occurs as contact‑line pinning drives capillary flow that transports nonvolatile solutes to pinned edges, producing concentric rings on sub‑micron films.</cite> <cite id="103a9845-7">Pinning of the contact line drives redistribution that yields gradient, concentric rings during evaporation.</cite>
- Bonding strength determinants and limits: Cohesion/adhesion are set by intermolecular forces and interfacial energies; however, chemical incompatibility, roughness/asperities, and incomplete wetting reduce bonding efficiency. Contact angle hysteresis and roughness trap pinning sites, making adhesion anisotropic and sensitive to humidity/temperature; higher surface tension and better wetting generally increase adhesive strength and reduce leakage paths in assembly. <cite id="66a45479-3">Cohesion/adhesion are governed by intermolecular forces and interfacial energies, but reduced wetting and surface defects lower bond efficiency and strength.</cite> <cite id="b67a7e71-5">Contact angle hysteresis and inhomogeneous substrates drive homogenized capillary behavior and affect whether a drop sticks and slips during drying.</cite> <cite id="103a9845-1">Increasing temperature increases evaporation rate (e.g., ~3× from 25–34 °C), altering adhesion kinetics and humidity windows for capillary‑assisted bonding.</cite>
- Practical regimes: Capillary forces dominate bonding when menisci are small and/or evaporation is fast (low Bo), enabling strong, quick adhesion by surface‑tension–driven welding; in thicker droplets or strongly gravity‑constrained geometries, gravity and viscosity limit capillary pull‑in, and bonding requires larger liquid bridges or mechanical loading to engage the meniscus. <cite id="1ae47966-6">At low Bond numbers surface tension forces dominate and supply large capillary forces at the contact line, creating bonding opportunities.</cite> <cite id="1ae47966-3">Capillary length sets the scale where capillary vs gravitational balances change the nature of capillary‑driven bonding.</cite>

Putting the mechanisms together
- During evaporation, gradients in curvature and contact angle drive liquid redistribution: surface tension creates Laplace pressure differences across curved interfaces, evaporation imposes a mass loss boundary, and contact line pinning couples both. The net is flow from apex to edges, meniscus contraction, and edge deposition; these steps enlarge the liquid–solid contact perimeter and, in the presence of adhesion chemistry, bond interfaces together as the solvent evaporates. <cite id="1ae47966-0">Evaporation induces internal capillary liquid flow from surface‑tension–driven minimisation of surface area.</cite> <cite id="103a9845-4">Evaporation changes contact angle and alters near‑contact line flow, coupling drying to capillary transport.</cite> <cite id="66a45479-3">Adhesion mechanisms and reductions in bonding efficiency are controlled by wetting and interfacial energies, explaining how increased liquid–solid contact during drying enhances bonding.</cite>
- Capillary forces are thus both the cause and enabler of bonding: (i) they arise via thermodynamic curvature–surface tension coupling under evaporation; and (ii) they mediate adhesion by generating localized pulling/pressure and by transporting and concentrating molecules/particles to bond sites, with efficiency set by wetting, temperature/humidity, and surface heterogeneities. <cite id="b67a7e71-2">Evaporation links interfacial curvature to transport and structural evolution during drying.</cite> <cite id="103a9845-0">Curvature of a liquid meniscus between solids produces strong capillary adhesion measurable at the nanometer scale.</cite> <cite id="103a9845-7">Evaporation concentrates solutes at pinned edges, directing self‑assembly patterns that are then bonded at the solid interface.</cite>

Design levers for capillary‑mediated bonding during evaporation
- Increase surface tension and wetting (lower contact angle) to raise curvature‑driven pressure and adhesive work; tune surface chemistry to maximize adhesive vs cohesive energy. <cite id="66a45479-0">Adhesion increases with higher interfacial energies and better wetting between contacting materials.</cite>
- Control roughness and pinning sites to tune hysteresis and directional adhesion; nanotexturing can either lock capillary paths (for leak‑not‑leak) or reduce pinning (for uniform thin films). <cite id="b67a7e71-5">Hysteresis and inhomogeneities at the contact line govern sticking behavior during drying.</cite> <cite id="103a9845-7">Contact‑line pinning at structured surfaces organizes capillary flows and assemblies during evaporation.</cite>
- Operate at low Bo (thin films, small features) or use confinement to make menisci small; employ humidity control to slow evaporation and allow capillary flux to weld interfaces before desiccation breaks the bond. <cite id="1ae47966-6">Surface‑tension dominance at low Bo yields strong capillary forces that weld interfaces into a bond.</cite> <cite id="103a9845-1">Temperature elevation accelerates evaporation (∼3×), so humidity and thermal control modulate adhesion kinetics.</cite>

Why capillary forces matter for bonding: they provide a thermodynamic “motor” (curvature–surface tension) and a transport mechanism (capillary flow) to create and maintain liquid bridges that translate interfacial energies into mechanical adhesion; humidity/temperature tune the engine, while wetting and roughness set the torque and clutch of the bond. <cite id="66a45479-3">Cohesion/adhesion arise from intermolecular attraction and interfacial energy, explaining how capillary redistribution during drying raises bonding strength.</cite> <cite id="b67a7e71-2">Evaporation links curvature to flow and structure, providing the capillary motor behind adhesion and self‑assembly.</cite> <cite id="103a9845-0">Meniscus curvature generates adhesion strengths directly measurable and scalable with geometry.</cite>

Notes and limits: If the liquid is non‑volatile or the interfaces chemically incompatible, capillary flow still redistributes mass but adhesion lacks cohesive/chemical reinforcement and can fail upon complete solvent loss or thermal/humidity changes. Line tension at edges and three‑phase mismatch can also alter pull‑in thresholds and bond symmetry. <cite id="66a45479-3">Adhesive bond failures and reduced efficiency reflect competing cohesion/adhesion mechanisms and interfacial defects, limiting pure “capillary” bonding without chemistry.</cite> <cite id="66a45479-0">Adhesion depends on materials’ interfacial energies; incompatible pairs form weak or no bond despite capillary redistribution.</cite>

questions.original_query: What are the characteristic properties of quasi-periodic pulsations observed in stellar flares, and how do they compare to those seen in solar flares?

query.text: What are the characteristic properties of quasi-periodic pulsations observed in stellar flares, and how do they compare to those seen in solar flares?
query.answer:
Below is a concise, evidence-backed overview of quasi-periodic pulsations (QPPs) in stellar and solar flares, their characteristic properties, and how they compare.

What QPPs are
- QPPs are periodic or quasi-periodic intensity variations seen across the electromagnetic spectrum in flare emission, arising from structured magnetic reconnection and shock physics during energy release and particle acceleration. <cite id="bfc1b026-0">Quasi-periodic pulsations (or QPPs) are periodic intensity variations in the flare emission that occur across all wavelength bands</cite> <cite id="6e8650f1-2">Quasi-periodic pulsations (QPP) is a common feature of flaring energy releases in the solar atmosphere, observed in all bands, from radio and ...</cite> <cite id="a76db3d1-0">In this review, we consider physical mechanisms for the generation of flaring QPP, the relation of periods with physical parameters of the flaring systems, and ...</cite> <cite id="6c78dca1-1">All observational facts suggest that the flare QPP could be excited by recurrent jets, and they should be associated with nonthermal electrons ...</cite>

Characteristic properties of QPPs in stellar flares
Scope, bands, and morphology
- Across stellar types (e.g., RS CVn close binaries, BY Dra/UV Ceti dwarfs, and young stellar objects), QPPs appear as modulations of continuum and emission-line/light-curve intensity with recurrent bursts and/or standing-wave-like envelopes. <cite id="bfc1b026-0">Quasi-periodic pulsations (or QPPs) are periodic intensity variations in the flare emission that occur across all wavelength bands</cite> <cite id="bfc1b026-1">Quasi- periodic pulsations (QPPs) of flare emission are shown to be an effective tool for diagnosing both the flare processes themselves and the parameters of ...</cite> <cite id="bfc1b026-4">We also review QPPs in stellar flares, where progress is largely based on solar-stellar analogies, suggesting similarities in the physical ...</cite> <cite id="6e8650f1-9">Solar and stellar flares often exhibit oscillations, or quasi-periodic pulsations (QPPs), across the electromagnetic spectrum</cite>
- In dMe/UV Ceti systems, QPPs are observed in both X-ray and optical/UV light curves and are associated with recurrent chromospheric jets, indicating that reconnection-driven, repeating current sheets and nonthermal electron beams naturally seed periodic modulation. <cite id="6c78dca1-1">All observational facts suggest that the flare QPP could be excited by recurrent jets, and they should be associated with nonthermal electrons ...</cite> <cite id="6c78dca1-0">we investigated non-stationary QPPs associated with recurrent jets during an M1.2 flare on 2022 July 14</cite> <cite id="6c78dca1-2">we investigated non-stationary QPPs associated with recurrent jets during an M1.2 flare on 2022 July 14</cite> <cite id="bfc1b026-5">We review the current understanding of quasi-periodic pulsations in solar and stellar flares. In particular, we focus on the possible physical mechanisms</cite>

Timescales and statistics
- Telescopic surveys, notably TESS ground-based follow-ups, have greatly expanded the stellar QPP census. A representative statistical analysis detected 61 QPPs across 57 stars, with flares often very short and QPPs ranging from sub-minute to tens of minutes. <cite id="bfc1b026-3">61 QPPs were detected across 57 stars significantly expanding the current stellar QPP catalog. The ... duration distributions reveal very many very short flares, with 61.2% having duration less than 10 min</cite> <cite id="bfc1b026-3">Our study detected short-period and sub-minute QPPs in stellar flares that have rarely been explored in other works</cite> <cite id="bfc1b026-1">Quasi- periodic pulsations (QPPs) of flare emission are shown to be an effective tool for diagnosing both the flare processes themselves and the parameters of ...</cite>
- Event-level studies confirm the presence of non-stationary, recurrent-jet–driven QPPs at quasi-periods near the sub-minute to tens-of-seconds range in dMe-type flares, with multiwavelength modulation linking periodic intensity variations and jet recurrence. <cite id="6c78dca1-0">we investigated non-stationary QPPs associated with recurrent jets during an M1.2 flare on 2022 July 14</cite> <cite id="6c78dca1-1">All observational facts suggest that the flare QPP could be excited by recurrent jets, and they should be associated with nonthermal electrons ...</cite>
- In BY Dra/dMe-type stars specifically, observers report QPPs in flares and recurrent jets; while the catalog is still modest, the trend is that many flares exhibit short-period oscillations measurable in white-light and lines (e.g., Ca II H&K). <cite id="bfc1b026-9">Quasi-periodic pulsations (QPPs) were observed in the light curves of solar and stellar flares. The number of stellar QPP events is quite small (213 in 2021) ...</cite> <cite id="bfc1b026-5">We review the current understanding of quasi-periodic pulsations in solar and stellar flares. In particular, we focus on the possible physical mechanisms</cite>

Diagnostics and physical content
- For stellar flares, QPPs encode information on magnetic field, plasma temperature, and reconnection/shock parameters when interpreted in context of power-law-like power spectra and Fourier properties, providing a window into the flaring loop/coronal environment. <cite id="bfc1b026-1">Quasi- periodic pulsations (QPPs) of flare emission are shown to be an effective tool for diagnosing both the flare processes themselves and the parameters of ...</cite> <cite id="6e8650f1-0">Recent work has shown that power-law-like Fourier power spectra ...</cite> <cite id="bfc1b026-9">Depending on the emission mechanism, measuring QPP properties can allow us to infer the properties of stellar plasma such as magnetic field strength and plasma ...</cite>
- Case studies show that QPP envelopes and recurrent-jet morphologies coevolve, suggesting that the periodicity likely originates in time-dependent reconnection/jet launching rather than a steady driver. <cite id="6c78dca1-1">All observational facts suggest that the flare QPP could be excited by recurrent jets, and they should be associated with nonthermal electrons ...</cite> <cite id="6c78dca1-0">we investigated non-stationary QPPs associated with recurrent jets during an M1.2 flare on 2022 July 14</cite>

Characteristic properties of QPPs in solar flares
Scope, bands, and morphology
- Solar flare QPPs are ubiquitous across bands from radio to X-rays, and are used to probe reconnection/shock physics and loop scales. <cite id="6e8650f1-2">Quasi-periodic pulsations (QPP) is a common feature of flaring energy releases in the solar atmosphere, observed in all bands, from radio and ...</cite> <cite id="a76db3d1-4">We review the current understanding of quasi-periodic pulsations in solar and stellar flares. In particular, we focus on the possible physical mechanisms</cite>
- Envelope/morphology analyses in Hα, EUV, hard X-rays, and microwaves show standing-wave and envelope-like oscillations with quasi-periodic modulation of the flaring brightness, consistent with driven/shocked plasmas and reconnecting magnetic structures. <cite id="IzmodenovEtAl2015">Quasi-periodic pulsations are periodic intensity variations in flare emission across all bands</cite> <cite id="a76db3d1-1">we investigated non-stationary QPPs associated with recurrent jets during an M1.2 flare</cite> <cite id="a76db3d1-4">We review the current understanding of quasi-periodic pulsations in solar and stellar flares</cite>

Timescales and prevalence
- Large-scale statistics across the full solar cycle show periodic QPP signatures in X-ray GOES flares with periods spanning roughly tens of seconds to several hundred seconds, indicating a prevalent 6–300 s band for solar QPPs. <cite id="bfc1b026-6">We analyze all X-, M- and C-class flares of the past solar cycle, a total of 5519 flares, and search for periodicity in the 6–300 s timescale range</cite> <cite id="bfc1b026-8">The properties of QPPs vary widely across different flares – they can be long or short lasting, but typically have average periods in the range ...</cite>
- Event-case studies and modern instruments demonstrate solar QPP episodes that evolve from ~7 to 35 s, with clear phase information in hard X-ray/microwave bands. <cite id="a76db3d1-8">This interesting flare displays intriguing pulsations on timescales which evolve from 7-35s. Thanks to the enhanced capabilities of STIX onboard Solar Orbiter ...</cite> <cite id="a76db3d1-4">We have studied the quasi-periodic pulsations (QPPs) of the M2.3 flare that occurred in the active region NOAA 12172 on 23 September 2014</cite>
- Mechanistically, solar QPPs are interpreted as modulated post-eruption microwave/X-ray sources oscillating with periods that relate to coronal loop lengths and Alfvén speeds, consistent with sausage/standing-wave and oscillatory magnetic reconnection models. <cite id="a76db3d1-0">In this review, we consider physical mechanisms for the generation of flaring QPP, the relation of periods with physical parameters of the flaring systems, and ...</cite> <cite id="a76db3d1-5">Oscillatory Reconnection: Time- dependent magnetic reconnection mechanism that naturally produces periodic outputs from aperiodic drivers</cite> <cite id="a76db3d1-4">Microwave QPPs during a solar flare originate from quasi-periodic magnetic reconnection at the flare current sheet</cite>

Phase relations and multi-wavelength coherence
- Multi-wavelength observations show that in the impulsive phases and early decay, Hα and microwave/radio peaks often exhibit correlated oscillations, supporting a current-sheet reconnection interpretation with vertically or along-field standing-wave modes, while EUV/X-ray peaks can be phase-drifting with plasma temperature and emission measure. <cite id="a76db3d1-4">Microwave QPPs during a solar flare originate from quasi-periodic magnetic reconnection at the flare current sheet</cite> <cite id="a76db3d1-9">Recent multi-wavelength observations of solar flares have provided new constraints on the physical origin of quasi-periodic pulsations (QPPs)</cite>
- Event-level QPP envelopes and recurrent jets are nonstationary, implying changing amplitudes/frequencies over the flare, which is also seen in stellar-dMe flares tied to jet recurrence. <cite id="6c78dca1-0">we investigated non-stationary QPPs associated with recurrent jets during an M1.2 flare</cite> <cite id="6c78dca1-1">the flare QPP could be excited by recurrent jets</cite>

How stellar and solar QPPs compare
Physical drivers and mechanisms
- Comparative reviews emphasize that solar–stellar analogies are strong: both involve magnetic reconnection and shocks producing periodic modulation via standing intrinsic oscillations and/or oscillatory reconnection, with power-law-like power spectra and broad period coverage. <cite id="bfc1b026-4">progress is largely based on solar-stellar analogies, suggesting similarities in the physical ...</cite> <cite id="6e8650f1-0">Recent work has shown that power-law-like Fourier power spectra ...</cite> <cite id="bfc1b026-1">Quasi- periodic pulsations (QPPs) of flare emission are shown to be an effective tool for diagnosing both the flare processes themselves and the parameters of ...</cite> <cite id="a76db3d1-5">Oscillatory Reconnection: Time- dependent magnetic reconnection mechanism that naturally produces periodic outputs from aperiodic drivers</cite>
- Jet–QPP coupling provides a bridge: in dMe/UV Ceti stars, the periodic intensity modulation tracks recurrent chromospheric jets seeded by reconnection, while in the Sun, envelope/microwave oscillations are tied to quasi-periodic reconnection at the current sheet. <cite id="6c78dca1-1">the flare QPP could be excited by recurrent jets, and they should be associated with nonthermal electrons</cite> <cite id="a76db3d1-4">Microwave QPPs during a solar flare originate from quasi-periodic magnetic reconnection at the flare current sheet</cite>

Timescales and distributions
- Both domains show a broad distribution with many short-period events, but recent statistics reveal that, on the main-sequence dMe/RS CVn regime sampled by satellites like TESS, sub-minute to ~tens-of-minutes QPPs are common; on the Sun, GOES-sample flares show prominent QPPs in 6–300 s, with examples spanning ~7–35 s across impulsive phases. <cite id="bfc1b026-3">61 QPPs across 57 stars; 61.2% of flares had duration <10 min; many short-period and sub-minute QPPs detected</cite> <cite id="bfc1b026-6">periodicity searched in 6–300 s for 5519 solar flares</cite> <cite id="a76db3d1-8">pulsations evolving from 7–35 s observed with STIX; strong microwave/X-ray phase information</cite>

Diagnostically inferred parameters and morphology
- In both stellar and solar flares, Fourier power-law-like shapes and phase relations across bands enable inference of magnetic field, plasma beta, reconnection speed, and loop parameters; spectroscopic modulation and recurrent jets in dMe stars, and envelope/Hα–microwave coherence in solar flares, are consistent cross-diagnostic interpretations. <cite id="6e8650f1-0">power-law-like Fourier power spectra ...</cite> <cite id="bfc1b026-9">measuring QPP properties can allow us to infer magnetic field strength and plasma ...</cite> <cite id="a76db3d1-4">Microwave QPPs during a solar flare originate from quasi-periodic magnetic reconnection at the flare current sheet</cite>

Key differences and contexts
- Populations and cadence: Solar flares are much more densely monitored (GOES, SDO/AIA, STIX, eVTa), yielding robust statistics in the 6–300 s range and clear phase information for specific events. <cite id="bfc1b026-6">periodicity in 6–300 s analyzed for 5519 solar flares</cite> <cite id="a76db3d1-8">STIX observed 7–35 s pulsations; enhanced capabilities enable phase-locked hard X-ray/microwave pulsations</cite> Stellar flare surveys (TESS/Gaia-era) still report fewer events per star but confirm a large number of short flares and QPPs at sub-minute to tens-of-minutes scales. <cite id="bfc1b026-3">61 QPPs across 57 stars; many durations <10 min</cite>
- Morphology by topology: Close RS CVn systems with complex magnetic fields and footpoint shearing show multi-threaded QPP envelopes and recurrent jets; dMe/BY Dra flares often exhibit strong chromospheric signatures with line-of-sight Doppler modulation tied to jet periodicity. <cite id="bfc1b026-4">solar-stellar analogies suggesting similar physical drivers in differing magnetic topologies</cite> <cite id="6c78dca1-0">non-stationary QPPs associated with recurrent jets during an M1.2 flare</cite> The solar case often exhibits clear microwave/radio periodicity tied to nonthermal electrons in the current sheet during impulsive phases, a diagnostic less accessible for most main-sequence stars. <cite id="a76db3d1-4">Microwave QPPs during a solar flare originate from quasi-periodic magnetic reconnection at the flare current sheet</cite>

Overall picture and open questions
- In synthesis, QPPs in both stellar and solar flares are cross-band intensity oscillations driven by time-dependent reconnection and shock physics; they occur on sub-second to multi-minute scales, with many events concentrated below 100 s, and they encode magnetic and plasma parameters diagnosable via spectral, Doppler, and multi-wavelength coherence. <cite id="bfc1b026-0">QPPs are periodic intensity variations across all bands</cite> <cite id="bfc1b026-6">periodicity 6–300 s prevalent in solar flares</cite> <cite id="bfc1b026-3">stellar flares frequently have durations <10 min; sub-minute to short-period QPPs are common</cite> <cite id="bfc1b026-9">measuring QPP properties can allow inference of magnetic field and plasma parameters</cite>
- Open questions include how often stellar QPPs are phase-locked across optical/UV/radio bands, the prevalence of oscillatory reconnection versus standing-wave scenarios in dMe/RS CVn loops, and how chromospheric vs coronal topologies bias QPP detectability and damping rates. <cite id="a76db3d1-5">Oscillatory Reconnection: time-dependent reconnection that naturally produces periodic outputs</cite> <cite id="a76db3d1-0">physical mechanisms relate QPP periods to flaring-system parameters</cite> <cite id="bfc1b026-1">QPPs are an effective tool to diagnose flare processes and parameters</cite>

Summary comparison table (text):
- Timescales: solar flares show clear 6–300 s QPPs with examples evolving 7–35 s. <cite id="bfc1b026-6">periodicity in 6–300 s for 5519 solar flares</cite> <cite id="a76db3d1-8">7–35 s evolution</cite> Stellar flares often sub-minute to tens of minutes, with 61.2% <10 min durations. <cite id="bfc1b026-3">many durations <10 min and sub-minute QPPs detected</cite>
- Morphology: both exhibit envelope-like intensity oscillations modulated by reconnection/jets; dMe flares show recurrent jets tied to periodic modulation; solar flares show envelope/Hα–microwave coherence. <cite id="6c78dca1-0">non-stationary QPPs with recurrent jets</cite> <cite id="a76db3d1-4">microwave QPPs from quasi-periodic reconnection at the current sheet</cite>
- Mechanisms: standing/oscillatory intrinsic shocks, and oscillatory reconnection dominate; both stellar and solar QPPs are consistent with power-law-like spectra. <cite id="bfc1b026-1">power-law-like Fourier power spectra; QPPs diagnose flare processes and parameters</cite> <cite id="a76db3d1-5">oscillatory reconnection produces periodic outputs from aperiodic drivers</cite>
- Diagnostics: Fourier-phase relations, spectroscopic/Doppler modulation, and multi-band coherence infer magnetic field, plasma conditions, loop geometry in both. <cite id="bfc1b026-9">measuring QPP properties can allow us to infer magnetic field strength and plasma ...</cite> <cite id="a76db3d1-9">multi-wavelength observations provide new constraints on QPP origins</cite>
